The paper then discusses what is inheritable, including in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference, what survives within a context window, and which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid, closing with a table of what common practices certify and what to report.

papers.title: Generalized PINN-Based Inverse Estimation of Spatially Varying Heat Transfer Coefficients with Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: This study investigates generalized boundary representations and transfer learning for physics-informed neural-network (PINN) estimation of spatially varying convective heat transfer coefficients (HTCs) in jet impingement cooling. Piecewise-linear (PWL) and neural-network boundary estimators are inferred from transient interior-temperature measurements and evaluated against CFD-CHT reference HTC profiles at Reynolds numbers of 5000, 10000 and 15000. A discrete Adjoint-FEM formulation with gradient regularization based on the $H^1$-seminorm provides an independent inverse-method comparison. Transfer learning is investigated under two source-target conditions: transfer between noise levels at the same Reynolds number, and transfer from a controlled Gaussian-profile problem to CFD-CHT-derived target problems at different Reynolds numbers. For the representative Re = 5000 target with 5% measurement noise, quadratic, PWL, and neural-network PINNs achieve relative HTC-profile errors of 5.08, 5.31 and 5.19%, respectively, while generalized representations reduce the error for the Re = 15000 target from 16.76% for the quadratic PINN to 14.41% and 14.46%. Transfer learning reduces target-training time by 57.86-81.71% for fixed-Reynolds-number transfer and by 50.59-84.94% for Gaussian-to-CHT transfer. Its effect on reconstruction accuracy is target dependent: fixed-profile PWL transfer remains within 0.30 percentage points of scratch training, whereas Gaussian-to-CHT transfer produces differences of 0.10-1.52 percentage points across targets and representations. These results demonstrate that generalized PINN representations can accommodate spatially varying HTC profiles without a prescribed quadratic form, while transfer learning can substantially reduce target-training cost for repeated inverse estimation, with the resulting reconstruction accuracy depending on source-target compatibility.
papers.summary: Estimating spatially varying convective heat transfer coefficients (HTCs) in jet impingement cooling from transient interior-temperature measurements is an inverse problem that physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have so far handled with a prescribed quadratic boundary form. The authors introduce piecewise-linear (PWL) and neural-network boundary estimators, compare them against a discrete adjoint finite-element method with H1-seminorm regularization on `CFD-CHT` reference profiles at Reynolds numbers of 5000, 10000, and 15000, and study transfer learning both between noise levels and from a Gaussian-profile source problem to CFD-derived targets. At Re = 5000 with 5% noise all three representations reach roughly 5% relative error, and the generalized forms lower the Re = 15000 error from 16.76% to about 14.4%. **Transfer learning cuts target-training time by roughly 51% to 85%**, with reconstruction accuracy within 1.52 percentage points of training from scratch depending on source-target compatibility.

papers.title: When Log Parsing Removes What Matters: Detecting Failures in Distributed GPU Workloads
papers.abstract: Large AI models increasingly rely on distributed GPU execution, yet it remains unclear whether established failure analysis methods transfer effectively to this setting. We introduce GF-Bench, a PyTorch-based framework and dataset for generating diverse failures in distributed GPU workloads. The framework supports extensible workload and fault-injection logic; based on this design, the current release targets failures visible in multi-GPU communication logs and provides 220 labeled two-GPU executions covering normal runs, CUDA out-of-memory fail-stop failures, and persistent straggler fail-slow failures. Using GF-Bench, we evaluate three sequence-based methods (DeepLog, LogAnomaly, and LogBERT) and the LLM-based LogPrompt on parsed logs, and additionally evaluate LogPrompt on raw logs. On parsed inputs, no method reliably detects both failure classes, and the highest overall F1 score is 0.667. Raw inputs raise the overall F1 score of in-context LogPrompt to 0.983, at 9.0x its average input-token usage and 8.7x its per-run cost. These results expose a substantial trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency: generic log parsing lowers operational cost but discards the distributed execution context required for accurate failure detection. GF-Bench provides a reproducible basis for studying cost-efficient analysis methods and can be extended to additional GPU workloads and failure types.
papers.summary: Large AI models increasingly run on distributed GPU clusters, yet it is unclear whether established log-based failure analysis methods transfer to this setting. `GF-Bench` is a PyTorch-based framework and dataset for injecting failures into distributed GPU workloads, currently providing 220 labeled two-GPU executions that cover normal runs, CUDA out-of-memory fail-stop failures, and persistent straggler fail-slow failures visible in multi-GPU communication logs. Evaluating the sequence-based detectors `DeepLog`, `LogAnomaly`, and `LogBERT` and the large language model (LLM)-based `LogPrompt` on parsed logs, no method reliably catches both failure classes and the best overall F1 is 0.667, whereas feeding raw logs to in-context `LogPrompt` **raises overall F1 to 0.983 at 9.0x the input tokens and 8.7x the per-run cost**. The gap shows that generic log parsing lowers operational cost but discards the distributed execution context needed for accurate detection.

papers.title: SIRNET: Causal Adaptation of Pretrained Embeddings for Semiparametric Treatment-Effect Estimation Under Surrogacy
papers.abstract: Modern experiments increasingly produce rich post-treatment objects---such as text, images, and video---that may provide early surrogate signals for outcomes that are delayed, expensive, or observed only for a subset of participants. A pretrained encoder can turn such an object into a strong generic embedding, but the embedding is not trained for the estimation tasks required by a causal estimator and may emphasize information irrelevant to the causal target. We propose SIRNET, a Surrogate-Informed Representation adaptation framework for neural-NETwork-based causal estimation in the presence of unstructured post-treatment surrogates. Starting from pretrained surrogate embeddings, SIRNET learns a shared adapter jointly for outcome prediction, treatment propensity, and arm-specific surrogate marginalization, beyond the generic pretraining objective. The resulting covariate and surrogate representations provide a common interface for these nuisance tasks. The final treatment-effect estimate and confidence interval are obtained from cross-fitted orthogonal scores that attain the semiparametric efficiency bound under the stated nuisance-rate conditions. We also validate SIRNET's performance in synthetic and semisynthetic experiments, as well as the Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) trial, using frozen pretrained brain-MRI embeddings as surrogates for a long-term outcome.
papers.summary: Experiments increasingly yield rich post-treatment objects such as text, images, and video that may serve as early surrogates for outcomes that are delayed, expensive, or observed only for some participants, but generic pretrained embeddings of those objects are not tuned for the nuisance tasks a causal estimator needs. `SIRNET`, a Surrogate-Informed Representation adaptation framework, starts from pretrained surrogate embeddings and learns a shared adapter jointly for outcome prediction, treatment propensity, and arm-specific surrogate marginalization, giving a common interface for these tasks. The final treatment-effect estimate and confidence interval come from **cross-fitted orthogonal scores that attain the semiparametric efficiency bound** under the stated nuisance-rate conditions. The method is validated on synthetic and semisynthetic data and on the Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (`A4`) trial, using frozen pretrained brain-MRI embeddings as surrogates for a long-term outcome.

papers.title: Perfect Reconstruction Cannot Show Whether Two Codebooks on a VAE's Latent Space Agree
papers.abstract: Many systems read the latent space of a variational autoencoder (VAE) as discrete codes, and rely on each latent being read back as the code it was written as. Shannon (1948) took such a shared codebook as given; inside a VAE nothing enforces it. We prove that no item of a standard training report can reveal whether the written and read codes agree on encoded data. We construct two VAEs that reconstruct every input perfectly, infer exactly, and match on every per-example ELBO and every code histogram, yet agreement is one in the first and zero in the second. We then show that the ELBO's own terms bound how far a measured agreement can move: the variational gap bounds the shift to exact inference, and the rate bounds the shift to generation from the prior. For Gaussian posteriors, a mean-field encoder pays an exact price in the gap that depends on its choice of axes. On probabilistic PCA the gap certifies a trained encoder in all 75 settings we test, at agreement between 0.76 and 0.97. On 240 trained VAEs, a floor set by the rate and the dataset size rules out rate-side certification in advance for 66 models, and none of them certifies. The results yield a simple protocol, Certify-or-Measure, for any pipeline that reads a VAE as codes.
papers.summary: Many systems read the latent space of a variational autoencoder (VAE) as discrete codes and rely on each latent being read back as the code it was written as, but nothing inside a VAE enforces such a shared codebook. The authors prove that no item in a standard training report can reveal whether written and read codes agree on encoded data, constructing **two VAEs that reconstruct every input perfectly, infer exactly, and match on every per-example ELBO and code histogram, yet have agreement of one in the first and zero in the second**. They then show that the ELBO's own terms bound how far a measured agreement can move, with the variational gap bounding the shift to exact inference and the rate bounding the shift to generation from the prior, and that a mean-field Gaussian encoder pays an exact price in the gap depending on its choice of axes. On probabilistic PCA the gap certifies a trained encoder in all 75 tested settings, while on 240 trained VAEs a floor set by the rate and dataset size rules out rate-side certification in advance for 66 models and none certifies, yielding a `Certify-or-Measure` protocol for any pipeline that reads a VAE as codes.

papers.title: Disease-level drug approval forecasting from trial-agnostic public data
papers.abstract: Drug development is an expensive and lengthy process requiring developers to select drugs for human trials and diseases to target. Computational tools that can estimate before testing which drug-disease candidates are most likely to reach FDA approval could reduce development time and costs through early program advancement and disease prioritization. Yet existing approaches predict outcomes at a single level or stage or do not distinguish between disease outcomes for the same drug. We ask (1) whether FDA approval can be forecast for a drug-disease pair using only pre-clinical trial information, and (2) whether these forecasts can help prioritize diseases for the same drug. We built a cohort of 14,134 drug-disease pairs by reconstructing programs from ClinicalTrials.gov, extracting disease-level approvals from FDA label documentation, and enriching each pair with molecular, disease, ADMET, target, and pathway features. We divided the cohort into pre- and post-2019 programs and trained a classifier on pre-2019 data to predict FDA approval. On the post-2019 cohort (2,637 programs), the model would have prioritized a program that ultimately gained approval over one that did not approximately three out of four times. For drugs tested across multiple diseases, selecting the model's highest-ranked disease would have identified an ultimately approved disease 61.3% of the time, compared with 40.7% under random selection. These results show that public pre-trial information contains signal for forecasting FDA approval at the drug-disease level and can help prioritize diseases for the same drug. We provide a public web tool for SMILES- and ICD-10-based drug-disease approval forecasting.
papers.summary: Choosing which drug-disease programs to advance into human trials is costly, and existing computational predictors work at a single stage or cannot distinguish outcomes across diseases for the same drug. The authors assemble 14,134 drug-disease pairs by reconstructing programs from ClinicalTrials.gov, extracting disease-level approvals from FDA label documentation, and adding molecular, disease, ADMET, target, and pathway features, then train a classifier on pre-2019 programs to predict FDA approval from pre-trial information alone. On 2,637 post-2019 programs the model ranks an eventually approved program above an unapproved one about three times in four, and **for drugs tested across multiple diseases, picking the top-ranked disease identifies an eventually approved one 61.3% of the time versus 40.7% under random selection**. A public web tool accepts SMILES and ICD-10 inputs for drug-disease approval forecasting.

papers.title: Physics-Informed State Space Models for Day-Ahead Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate day-ahead photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting requires both strong temporal modeling and adherence to physical PV system constraints. Purely data-driven models often ignore the underlying PV conversion process and may produce predictions that are outside the operational range of a PV system. In this paper, we propose a physics-informed state space framework that combines a differentiable PV conversion model with a selective state space backbone (PowerMamba). Our approach follows a physics-residual decomposition. The physics module provides a structured baseline based on solar geometry, irradiance, temperature effects, and inverter limits, while the state space model learns residual corrections from numerical weather prediction (NWP) inputs over a 24-hour horizon. Experiments on one year of utility-scale PV data show that the proposed method significantly improves forecasting accuracy, reducing RMSE by 38.5% and MAE by 45.8% compared to a physics-only baseline, and outperforming a purely data-driven model. Results further show that incorporating system-level physics provides the largest performance gains, while additional refinements offer only marginal improvements. Beyond accuracy, the model improves robustness by constraining predictions toward physical feasibility, reducing unrealistic predictions under corrupted measurements.
papers.summary: Day-ahead photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting needs strong temporal modeling, yet purely data-driven models ignore the PV conversion process and can predict outside a system's operational range. The proposed framework pairs a differentiable PV conversion model built from solar geometry, irradiance, temperature effects, and inverter limits with a selective state space backbone called `PowerMamba` that learns residual corrections from numerical weather prediction (NWP) inputs over a 24-hour horizon. On one year of utility-scale PV data the approach **reduces RMSE by 38.5% and MAE by 45.8% relative to a physics-only baseline** and outperforms a purely data-driven model, with system-level physics providing most of the gain and further refinements adding little. Constraining predictions toward physical feasibility also reduces unrealistic outputs under corrupted measurements.

papers.title: Bias Robustness of Genetic Multi-Criteria Sorting versus Learned Rankers under Proxy Skew and Label Contamination
papers.abstract: Learning-to-rank (LTR) models can align rankings with undesignated signals when those signals appear as features or leak into training labels. We compare label-free genetic multi-criteria sorting (open Pikaia strategy variants), which reranks fixed candidate pools using an explicit criteria vector C, to label-trained LTR (LightGBM, XGBoost, RankSVM) under two controlled protocols on MSLR-WEB10K, Baidu-ULTR, WANDS, and Expedia. In the main proxy-skew study, labels remain clean while a calibrated proxy P is available as a feature: Genetic AI rankings show lower Spearman rank-proxy correlation than the LTR peers (e.g. about 0.15-0.16 vs. 0.59-0.87 on WANDS), with both families evaluated jointly on clean nDCG@10 on a bias-utility frontier. In a supporting label-contamination study, training labels are mixed with contaminant B: because Genetic AI methods do not use labels, their bias and utility curves stay flat, whereas LightGBM and XGBoost increase rank-B correlation as contamination rises (OLS bias_slope about 0.58-0.65 on WANDS/Baidu). The results support genetic sorting as an architectural option for optimizing declared attributes on a fixed pool when undesignated proxies or label contaminants must be refused.
papers.summary: Learning-to-rank (LTR) models can align rankings with undesignated signals when those signals appear as features or leak into training labels. The authors compare label-free genetic multi-criteria sorting, which reranks a fixed candidate pool against an explicit criteria vector, with label-trained `LightGBM`, `XGBoost`, and `RankSVM` rankers under two controlled protocols on `MSLR-WEB10K`, `Baidu-ULTR`, `WANDS`, and `Expedia`. Under proxy skew, where labels stay clean but a calibrated proxy is exposed as a feature, genetic rankings show **Spearman rank-proxy correlations of about 0.15 to 0.16 versus 0.59 to 0.87** for the LTR models on `WANDS`, with both families evaluated jointly on clean nDCG@10 along a bias-utility frontier. Under label contamination the genetic methods' bias and utility curves stay flat because they use no labels, while `LightGBM` and `XGBoost` track the contaminant more closely as contamination rises.

papers.title: DShuttleNet: A Badminton Doubles Dataset for Evaluating Team Coordination
papers.abstract: Most existing sports datasets are individual-centric or ball-centric, focusing on individual player actions while ignoring interactions among teammates. In badminton doubles, tactical success is governed by rapid team formation and coordination, yet standard resources for modeling these player interactions are scarce. To bridge this gap, we present DShuttleNet, a comprehensive dataset for badminton doubles curated from elite BWF World Tour tournaments. Beyond trajectory data, DShuttleNet uniquely incorporates expert-labeled "Loss Reasons," transforming the dataset into a diagnostic tool for causal tactical evaluation. We formally define two geometry-driven representations, Teammate-Relative Angle (TRA) and Vertical Shot Angle (VSA), to characterize coordination and shot aggressiveness. To quantify interpersonal synergy, we introduce novel metrics, Court Coverage Efficacy Index (CCEI) and Threat Load Asymmetry Index (TLAI), which evaluate the often-overlooked non-hitting partner's role and defensive coordination. Experimental results demonstrate that conventional models suffer from underfitting when failing to incorporate these coordination-centric features, highlighting the critical importance and potential impact of releasing DShuttleNet. Dataset is available at: https://doi.org/10.34740/kaggle/dsv/16097938.
papers.summary: Most sports datasets center on individual players or the ball and ignore interactions among teammates, leaving no standard resource for modeling the rapid formation changes and coordination that decide badminton doubles. `DShuttleNet` is a dataset curated from elite BWF World Tour tournaments that pairs trajectory data with expert-labeled loss reasons, so it can serve causal tactical evaluation rather than tracking alone. Two geometry-driven representations, Teammate-Relative Angle (TRA) and Vertical Shot Angle (VSA), characterize coordination and shot aggressiveness, and two metrics, the Court Coverage Efficacy Index (CCEI) and the Threat Load Asymmetry Index (TLAI), quantify the non-hitting partner's role and defensive coordination. **Conventional models underfit when these coordination-centric features are left out**, according to the authors' experiments.

papers.title: Barycentric Anchored Weight Search for Robust Model Merging
papers.abstract: We propose Barycentric Anchored Search, a post-hoc weight-space procedure for improving fine-tuned vision models under distribution shift without additional gradient training or increased inference cost. Given a pre-trained initialization and two checkpoints fine-tuned on a source dataset, the method constructs barycentric candidate weights and performs a small derivative-free search along directions connecting each candidate to the pre-trained model. Candidate weights are selected using a small validation subset of one or more out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets; the selected model is then evaluated on the held-out portions of those datasets, on additional OOD benchmarks, and on the ImageNet validation set to quantify the robustness-accuracy trade-off. The method is inspired by simplex-based derivative-free optimization, including Nelder-Mead and Torczon multidirectional search, but is specialized to the geometry of neural network weight merging. Unlike Model Soup, which typically benefits from many fine-tuned checkpoints, and unlike Model Stock, which applies a fixed geometric merge, our approach uses only two fine-tuned checkpoints and iteratively adapts the merge using validation feedback from OOD data. Experiments with CLIP ViT-B/32 show that the proposed search substantially improves performance on held-out OOD data, including ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-Sketch, while keeping ImageNet accuracy competitive. The resulting weights also improve transfer to OOD datasets not used during candidate selection, outperforming the original fine-tuned checkpoints, naive model soups, and Model Stock in our evaluations. These results suggest that lightweight optimization in anchored weight space provides a practical alternative to fixed weight-averaging rules, geometric merging, or single-model selection.
papers.summary: Fine-tuned vision models often lose robustness under distribution shift, and existing weight-merging remedies either need many checkpoints, as with `Model Soup`, or apply a fixed geometric rule, as with `Model Stock`. Barycentric Anchored Search is a post-hoc weight-space procedure that takes a pretrained initialization and just two checkpoints fine-tuned on a source dataset, builds barycentric candidate weights, and runs a small derivative-free search along directions linking each candidate to the pretrained model, in the spirit of Nelder-Mead and Torczon multidirectional search. Candidates are chosen with a small validation subset of one or more out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets, requiring no extra gradient training or inference cost. With `CLIP ViT-B/32`, the selected weights **improve held-out OOD accuracy while keeping in-distribution accuracy competitive**, measured on `ImageNet-A`, `ImageNet-R`, and `ImageNet-Sketch` against the `ImageNet` validation set, and they transfer to OOD datasets not used in selection, beating the original checkpoints, naive soups, and `Model Stock`.

papers.title: RoboHarness: A Simple Harness Outperforms VLA and World Actions Models
papers.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has opened a path toward generalist embodied AI, raising the question of how LLMs can act in the physical world. One straightforward approach is training the model to generate actions: collect robot-action data and video demonstration, refine LLM architecture with an action head, and train a vision-language-action (VLA) model at scale. However, we argue that coding agents have the potential to realize generalist embodied manipulation. All they need is a simple yet effective robot harness. We present RoboHarness: a robotic harness that gives LLM agents a visual-geometric control panel so that they can directly understand and invoke embodied tasks. With RoboHarness, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks. The implementation will be released as open source.
papers.summary: Training vision-language-action (VLA) models on large robot-action datasets is the dominant route to embodied manipulation with large language models, but it requires costly data collection and architectural changes such as adding an action head. The alternative explored here is to give an off-the-shelf coding agent a harness: a visual-geometric control panel through which the LLM can perceive scenes and invoke manipulation primitives directly. **With this harness, `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on `BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025` tasks**, and the implementation is slated for open-source release.

papers.title: LabInstruct: Benchmarking Situated Instructional Video Generation for Lab Procedures
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, from scientific decision-making to physical execution. Ideally, AI-generated plans could be carried out directly by robotic systems, but reliable automation remains difficult in complex, open-world laboratory environments, where experiments often involve fine-grained manipulation, long-horizon procedures, and substantial variation across tasks and setups. Humans therefore remain an important execution interface between AI-generated plans and physical experiments, creating a need for clear and effective human-facing experimental guidance. Because laboratory procedures are inherently visual, spatial, and dynamic, video is particularly well suited to communicating apparatus configurations, manipulation actions, temporal dependencies, and state changes. Recent advances in video generation now make it possible to synthesize experimental demonstrations directly from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. However, whether such models can reliably communicate real laboratory procedures has not been systematically studied. We introduce LabInstruct, a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories. LabInstruct contains 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions. Evaluating 8 frontier image-to-video models, we find that visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect, revealing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.
papers.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) still rely on humans to carry out many physical experiments, so AI-generated plans need to be communicated clearly, and video is a natural medium for conveying apparatus setups, manipulation steps, and state changes. The benchmark `LabInstruct` contains 204 real laboratory tasks across five scientific disciplines, each with reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions, and it tests whether image-to-video models can generate correct procedural demonstrations from a workspace image and a text instruction. **Across eight frontier image-to-video models, visually plausible generations are frequently procedurally incorrect**, exposing a gap between visual realism and the reliability needed for experimental guidance.

papers.title: CoEvoke: Evoking Multi-Agent Collaboration for Trajectory Collection
papers.abstract: Training multi-agent collaboration requires trajectories of checking, feedback, and repair, yet task-solving rollouts may end in immediate approval or repeat unsuccessful attempts without useful correction. We introduce CoEvoke, a cross-domain framework that evokes these interactions during trajectory collection. Controlled perturbations create recoverable difficulties, while restricted reference-based guidance directs investigation. The resulting dataset contains 4,567 reconstructable trajectories over 4,130 software-engineering and reasoning tasks, linking public interactions to evidence, decisions, and task-native outcomes. Separate experiments over 2,287 same-task pairs show feedback increases of 47.72-100 percentage points across seven perturbation groups; guidance has smaller, model-dependent effects. With identical training tasks, decision-record counts, and updates, perturbation-enriched judge training improves ACPBench-Hard success from 35.38% to 42.12% (+6.73 points). SWE verifier training gains 7.60-9.40 points over interface-matched untrained references. Workflow and post-training evaluations preserve task-solving topology with unperturbed inputs and no private-reference guidance. These results support designing collection conditions to obtain corrective supervision that improves collaborative decisions with frozen solving agents.
papers.summary: Training agents to collaborate requires trajectories in which one agent checks another's work, gives feedback, and repairs errors, but ordinary task-solving rollouts tend to either approve immediately or repeat failed attempts without useful correction. `CoEvoke` deliberately evokes these interactions during data collection by injecting controlled perturbations that create recoverable difficulties and by giving agents restricted, reference-based guidance that directs their investigation. The resulting dataset holds 4,567 reconstructable trajectories over 4,130 software-engineering and reasoning tasks, and perturbations raise feedback rates by 47.72 to 100 percentage points across seven perturbation groups. **Judge training on perturbation-enriched data lifts `ACPBench-Hard` success from 35.38% to 42.12%**, and software-engineering verifier training gains 7.60 to 9.40 points over untrained references, with the solving agents kept frozen throughout.

papers.title: OPMD: On-Policy Mechanism Distillation Beyond Output Supervision
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model by supervising a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy, but its supervision remains confined to the output space. Consequently, OPD transfers what a teacher predicts without supervising the intermediate computation that produces those predictions. Simply distilling intermediate representations like representation matching is insufficient since teacher and student representations may differ geometrically, and even well-aligned hidden states need not be usable by the student's subsequent computation. We introduce On-Policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD), which transfers teacher-derived intermediate computation while explicitly accounting for its compatibility with the student. OPMD first constructs a student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher representations into intermediate states usable by the student's downstream computation, then it internalizes these states from on-policy trajectories. OPMD achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation baselines in all three teacher--student settings, and generalizes to multi-teacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning. Further analyses show that mechanism supervision yields more effective reasoning and meaningfully alters the student's intermediate computation and solution strategies, supporting that it transfers information beyond output supervision alone. Together, these results establish mechanism-level supervision as an effective way to move on-policy distillation beyond output supervision, enabling students to learn inner mechanisms they can use and internalize.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy but supervises only the teacher's outputs, leaving the intermediate computation behind those outputs untransferred. Naive representation matching does not close this gap because teacher and student hidden states can differ geometrically, and even aligned states may be unusable by the student's later layers. On-Policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD) first builds a student-compatible teacher that maps teacher representations into intermediate states the student's downstream computation can consume, then trains the student to internalize those states along on-policy trajectories. **`OPMD` achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation baselines in all three teacher-student settings**, extends to multi-teacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning, and measurably changes the student's intermediate computation and solution strategies.

papers.title: Historical Anchors for Scientific Forecasting on Human-Aware Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Predicting which scientific connections will form next can point researchers toward the most promising leads. One successful approach learns representations by sampling paths through publication networks, represented by a hypergraph, that connect scientific entities, concepts, and researchers, approximating how knowledge and expertise move through the literature. Sampled paths are then used to train an embedding model to forecast scientific connections such as a property of a material. Performance, however, depends strongly on how many paths are sampled: too little sampling yields incomplete representations, while further sampling can eventually weaken prediction quality. The best sampling budget is therefore often identifiable only after future discoveries are known. We introduce Query--Anchor Agreement (QAA), a diagnostic requiring no future labels or separately trained model. QAA can be used to select a sampling budget, and refine or re-rank the resulting forecast to improve forecasting scientific connections. QAA compares the candidates a model predicts for a target with those most similar to the target's known historical examples, and identifies when these two views converge. Across thermoelectric-material and COVID-19 drug-repurposing benchmarks, repeated random-seed runs, and three sampling policies, QAA-selected budgets fall on average 1.86 percentage points below hindsight-optimal selection for broad candidate recovery. Further, promoting candidates supported by both views, under a capped fusion that bounds the anchor contribution, improves broad recovery across all six benchmark-policy settings, which define the types of network walks used for sampling.
papers.summary: Forecasting which scientific connections will appear next, such as a material having a particular property, can be done by sampling paths through a hypergraph of publications, concepts, and researchers and training an embedding model on them, but accuracy depends heavily on the sampling budget, and the best budget is normally only knowable in hindsight. Query-Anchor Agreement (QAA) is a label-free diagnostic that compares the candidates a model predicts for a target against those most similar to the target's known historical examples and detects when the two views converge, which can then guide budget selection and re-rank forecasts. **On thermoelectric-material and COVID-19 drug-repurposing benchmarks, `QAA`-selected budgets fall on average 1.86 percentage points short of hindsight-optimal selection for broad candidate recovery**, and a capped fusion that promotes candidates supported by both views improves recovery in all six benchmark-policy settings.

papers.title: Beyond a Better Score: Long-Horizon Agentic ML Development and Evaluation Protocol for Physics Time Series
papers.abstract: Physics time-series data are central to fundamental discoveries involving dark matter, neutrinos, and gravitational waves. Machine learning has shown strong potential to recover weak scientific signals buried in complex noise. Recent LLM-agent systems further automate ML development, but existing approaches are often driven primarily by one or a few numerical scores. In pursuit of a better score, agents may exploit shortcuts, trigger mode collapse, or game the evaluation procedure, producing models that achieve high scores but are scientifically invalid. We introduce SIDERIUS, an LLM agent system designed to move beyond a better score toward scientifically valid, long-horizon ML development. SIDERIUS combines contract-defined composable capabilities for flexible orchestration and human-in-the-loop, a multi-layer scientific evaluation protocol that distinguishes valid models from unhealthy or gaming models, and resource-aware exploration for computationally expensive scientific ML. In our TIDMAD benchmark, SIDERIUS with a GPT-based orchestrator achieves the highest Valid-model proposal rate of 63.8% and the best valid denoising score of 2.744, compared with 1.6% and -0.647, respectively, for the same GPT model using the general-purpose Codex coding agent. We further benchmark SIDERIUS on three additional physics time-series datasets, demonstrating its reuse and performance across different tasks. Together, these results suggest that progress in agentic scientific ML should be measured beyond a better score, by how an agent explores and by whether the models it produces can be trusted as science.
papers.summary: LLM agents that automate machine-learning development for physics time series, such as searches for dark matter or gravitational waves, are usually driven by one or a few numerical scores, which invites shortcuts, mode collapse, and evaluation gaming that yield high-scoring but scientifically invalid models. `SIDERIUS` is an agent system built around contract-defined composable capabilities for orchestration and human-in-the-loop control, a multi-layer scientific evaluation protocol that separates valid models from unhealthy or gaming ones, and resource-aware exploration for expensive scientific training runs. **On the `TIDMAD` benchmark, `SIDERIUS` with a GPT-based orchestrator reaches a valid-model proposal rate of 63.8% and a valid denoising score of 2.744, versus 1.6% and -0.647 for the same GPT model driving the general-purpose `Codex` coding agent.** It is further benchmarked on three additional physics time-series datasets to show reuse across tasks.

papers.title: Contrastive Covariance Subspaces for Activation Steering
papers.abstract: Activation steering controls large language model behavior by adding a direction to hidden activations during inference. For steering to work well, that direction must be a pure signal for the target concept: any confound entangled with it, such as an incidental topic or writing style, is injected into the residual stream alongside the concept itself and degrades the generated text. We introduce Contrastive Covariance Steering (CCS), a training-free method that eliminates this confound variation. CCS projects steering vectors to a low-dimensional subspace obtained in closed form by solving a contrastive variance objective, which retains the directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with the other classes. Across three LLMs and four steering domains, CCS consistently beats all baseline steering methods in all $12$ model-domain settings. The largest relative improvement occurs on AxBench and Emotion where we outperform the next strongest steering baseline by $48$ to $70\%$ and $13$ to $27\%$, respectively. Furthermore, CCS outperforms naive difference-of-means steering by up to $151\%$, showcasing the importance of deconfounding concepts. A toy experiment verifies our motivation on why: planting a topic nuisance into the training data reduces unprojected steering by $46\%$, whereas CCS loses only $12\%$ and recovers most of the gap to an oracle that explicitly deletes the planted direction. A human study with $23$ raters on $296$ generations reproduces the LLM judge's ranking. Our extensive ablation verifies the importance of our method's components and robustness to the number of nuisance classes. Finally, we extend our method to multi-turn conversations, where CCS sustains both concept expression and fluency, matching system prompt performance as other steering methods drift.
papers.summary: Activation steering adds a direction to a language model's hidden activations at inference time, but if that direction is entangled with confounds such as topic or writing style, those nuisances get injected alongside the target concept and degrade the output. Contrastive Covariance Steering (CCS) is a training-free method that projects steering vectors onto a low-dimensional subspace, computed in closed form from a contrastive variance objective, that keeps directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with other classes. **`CCS` beats every baseline steering method in all 12 model-domain settings across three LLMs and four domains**, with gains of 48 to 70% over the next-best method on `AxBench` and up to 151% over difference-of-means steering. A toy experiment with a planted topic nuisance, a human study with 23 raters on 296 generations, and a multi-turn extension in which `CCS` sustains concept expression and fluency as other methods drift support the main result.

papers.title: Pick the Mixture, Not the Samples: Combinatorial Data Selection for LLMs
papers.abstract: Data selection for LLM fine-tuning faces two facts about real training: data pools draw from many distinct domains, and evaluation spans diverse tasks. As a result, the same sample helps different tasks differently, and samples interact during training so that a subset's value is not the sum of its parts. Current data-selection methods leave these realities largely unaddressed. We formalize them as Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS), a framework that separates attribution (how samples are scored) from selection (which subset to pick) and models the non-additive interactions among samples. On a real instruction-tuning data pool, we find substantial cross-domain complementarity (joint utility exceeds the sum of singletons), alongside redundancy within domains. Inspired by this, we propose Mixture-then-Select, a two-stage algorithm that first decides how many samples to take from each domain, then ranks samples within each domain by attribution score. Theoretically, the gap to the optimal subset is linear in the selection size and independent of data pool size. Empirically, Mixture-then-Select outperforms strong baselines by 20 to 54%, is robust across attribution methods, and works across different models and data pool sizes. The framework also extends to the data purchasing problem under a budget constraint when sample prices vary. Our findings suggest that allocating selection across domains offers a promising path toward more efficient and effective data selection for modern LLMs.
papers.summary: Data selection for LLM fine-tuning has to cope with training pools drawn from many domains and evaluation spanning many tasks, so a sample's value varies by task and samples interact in ways that make a subset's utility non-additive. Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS) formalizes this by separating attribution, meaning how samples are scored, from selection, meaning which subset to pick, and a real instruction-tuning pool shows strong cross-domain complementarity alongside within-domain redundancy. The proposed `Mixture-then-Select` algorithm first decides how many samples to draw from each domain and then ranks samples within each domain by attribution score, with a gap to the optimal subset that is provably linear in selection size and independent of pool size. **`Mixture-then-Select` outperforms strong baselines by 20 to 54%**, is robust across attribution methods, models, and pool sizes, and extends to budgeted data purchasing when sample prices vary.

papers.title: Can We Trust This Evaluation? Instance-Level Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation commonly aggregates multiple judges' decisions into a majority vote, yet this panel decision process does not guarantee that the evaluation of an individual item is reliable. We propose Structured Cross-fitted Uncertainty Risk (SCUR), a label-free approach for estimating instance-level evaluation reliability based on the judge panel's behavior. A latent measurement model serves as the backbone for measurement system analysis, from which SCUR derives three complementary signals capturing panel uncertainty, measurement cross-entropy, and perturbation sensitivity. These three sources of evidence are combined into a risk score. We evaluate the SCUR approach on five real-world benchmarks using majority-vote error ranking, selective trust, and risk stratification. Furthermore, we show our approach to be more effective at detecting high-consensus risk items, which are the blind spots for many other LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methods.
papers.summary: LLM-as-a-judge pipelines typically aggregate several judges' decisions by majority vote, but agreement at the panel level does not guarantee that any individual item was evaluated reliably. Structured Cross-fitted Uncertainty Risk (SCUR) is a label-free method that fits a latent measurement model to the panel's behavior and derives three complementary signals, panel uncertainty, measurement cross-entropy, and perturbation sensitivity, which are combined into a per-instance risk score. Evaluated on five real-world benchmarks through majority-vote error ranking, selective trust, and risk stratification, **`SCUR` is especially effective at flagging high-consensus items that are nonetheless wrong**, the blind spot of most other LLM-as-a-judge reliability methods.

papers.title: Rotate the Loop: Blockwise Conformality for Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one shared block across many recurrent steps, so depth becomes a quantity that can be spent at runtime rather than a stack of distinct layers. Those extra steps help only if a write made on one recurrent step is still readable on later ones, and that depends on the linear map applied to the residual between recurrent steps. We show that whether the loop learns to track state is a geometric question about the form of this map, and we propose blockwise conformal injections: the residual splits into coordinate-aligned groups and rotates inside each one, so every group has its own timescale while the geometry stays exact within it. Our experiments show a performance increase on a demanding form of state tracking - last-token accuracy when the rest of the prefix is already correct - and on language modelling, where a signal written earlier has to be retrieved at the end of the sequence.
papers.summary: Looped transformers reuse a single shared block across many recurrent steps, turning depth into a runtime budget, but extra steps only help if information written to the residual stream on one step remains readable on later steps, which depends on the linear map applied to the residual between steps. Whether a loop learns to track state is framed as a geometric property of this map, motivating blockwise conformal injections: the residual is split into coordinate-aligned groups and rotated within each group, giving every group its own timescale while preserving exact geometry inside it. **Experiments show gains on a demanding state-tracking measure, last-token accuracy when the rest of the prefix is already correct**, and on language modeling tasks where a signal written early must be retrieved at the end of the sequence.

papers.title: PLDiv: Measuring Dataset Diversity and Semantic Collapse via Persistence Landscapes
papers.abstract: Modern data pipelines increasingly combine human-created and human-curated data with AI-generated data for model training and evaluation. As datasets grow, they often add semantically redundant samples rather than expanding semantic coverage, which deteriorates the quality of the whole dataset. Existing diversity metrics primarily summarize lexical variation, entropy, or pairwise similarity, but provide limited characterization of the shape of the underlying data distribution. In this paper, we propose PLDiv, a diversity metric derived from persistence landscapes that quantifies the structural organization of a dataset from its geometric representation. PLDiv summarizes how data neighborhoods evolve as nearby samples progressively connect, producing an interpretable scalar measure of structural diversity without requiring task-specific supervision. Whether measuring intrinsic diversity in text generations or image embeddings, or detecting semantic collapse in instruction datasets and reasoning trajectories, PLDiv performs competitively against evaluated baselines and aligns strongly with diversity labels during semantic collapse. Consequently, it effectively supports applications in synthetic data monitoring, dataset construction, data augmentation, and generative model evaluation.
papers.summary: Training and evaluation datasets increasingly mix human-created and AI-generated data, and as they grow they often add semantically redundant samples rather than broadening coverage, a form of semantic collapse that existing diversity metrics based on lexical variation, entropy, or pairwise similarity capture poorly because they say little about the shape of the data distribution. `PLDiv` is a diversity metric derived from persistence landscapes, a construction from topological data analysis, that summarizes how neighborhoods in an embedding space merge as nearby samples progressively connect, yielding a single interpretable scalar without task-specific supervision. **Across text generations, image embeddings, instruction datasets, and reasoning trajectories, `PLDiv` performs competitively against baselines and aligns strongly with diversity labels during semantic collapse**, supporting uses in synthetic-data monitoring, dataset construction, augmentation, and generative-model evaluation.

papers.title: A Geometric Perspective on Reward Function Updates in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved using Lagrangian optimisation, by jointly optimising a primal-dual problem with gradient descent to obtain the optimal reward function parameters and corresponding optimal policy. While this algorithmic view of IRL has been highly influential, gradient-based reward updates only paint a partial picture, largely ignoring the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. In this paper, we present an occupancy-space view of reward updates in IRL. We leverage the insight that both the optimal solution and its geometry in occupancy space are known, and show that the geometry along the e-geodesic (straight line in occupancy space) toward the optimal occupancy directly affects the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward parameter space. This perspective naturally suggests preconditioning the dual gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. We show that this preconditioned gradient is just a convex interpolation of the old reward and a new target reward, yielding efficient natural-gradient-style updates with little additional computational overhead. We then analyse these occupancy-space reward updates from a Mirror Descent (MD) perspective, and show that policy search over the resulting rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy. Finally, we conclude with convergence results of such geometry-aware IRL algorithms.
papers.summary: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved as a Lagrangian primal-dual problem with gradient descent over reward parameters, a view that largely ignores the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. Taking an occupancy-space perspective, the geometry along the e-geodesic, the straight line in occupancy space toward the known optimal occupancy, is shown to directly shape the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward-parameter space, which suggests preconditioning that gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. **The preconditioned update reduces to a convex interpolation between the old reward and a new target reward**, giving natural-gradient-style steps at little extra cost. A Mirror Descent (MD) analysis then shows that policy search over these rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy, and convergence results are given for the resulting geometry-aware algorithms.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning from Real-Robot Interaction without High-Quality State Estimates
papers.abstract: A longstanding goal for robot reinforcement learning (RL) is that robots learn from their own physical experience, as humans and animals do. A key obstacle to learning directly from physical experience, especially outside instrumented lab environments, is that the state of the world is usually unobservable to the learner and must be estimated from on-board sensing. Errors in that estimate corrupt both the policy input and potentially the reward signal. We study this challenge using the contact-rich task of a bipedal robot learning to score soccer goals. We estimate all key state variables on-board with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and no external instrumentation (e.g., motion capture or overhead cameras). Because the UKF may incorrectly estimate state when the ball is unobserved, we learn a new state representation with a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) that, critically, only corrects the RSSM's latent state when the ball is observed. Building on RLPD, we introduce RSSM-RLPD and apply it to the task of a NAO robot learning to dribble a soccer ball into a goal. We show that the robot learns to score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction, reaching 100% success against 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget. We complement our physical robot experiments with a simulation study and show that RSSM-RLPD learns policies that achieve a higher success rate than behavior cloning, a feed-forward, and GRU baseline. Taken together, our results show that the addition of a learned state representation to existing on-robot learning methods enables RL from real-robot data even with a high degree of partial observability.
papers.summary: Robots learning by reinforcement from their own physical experience outside instrumented labs must estimate world state from on-board sensors, and estimation errors corrupt both policy inputs and reward signals. Using a NAO bipedal robot learning to dribble a soccer ball into a goal, all key state variables are estimated on-board with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and no motion capture or overhead cameras, and because the filter drifts when the ball is out of view, a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) learns a latent state representation that is corrected only when the ball is actually observed. The resulting `RSSM-RLPD` method, built on `RLPD`, lets the robot **learn to score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction, reaching 100% success against 0% for a feed-forward policy** under the same training budget. A simulation study confirms higher success rates than behavior cloning, feed-forward, and GRU baselines.

papers.title: The Future of AI-assisted Physics: Discovering, Verifying and Organizing Results via Formalization
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in AI have opened a new era for physics, enabling unprecedented capabilities in research and discovery. However, these advances also bring challenges in verifying, trusting, and reusing the results they so rapidly produce. Formalization is a necessary part of the solution to these challenges. In this paper, as well as giving an overview of the role of AI and formalization in physics, we make the case that: (1) formalization is an essential layer for AI-driven discoveries in both computational and theoretical physics; (2) AI is lowering the barrier to, and increasing the efficiency of, formalization in physics, though it remains weaker at choosing definitions and designing libraries than at writing proofs; (3) the speed AI brings to formalization in physics currently comes at the cost of trust, credit, and community; (4) shared, community-reviewed formal libraries such as Physlib should be central in making progress in this field, both as a trusted, reusable foundation for physics results and as the environment in which AI systems can reason about physics; (5) formalizing physics raises challenges beyond those in mathematics, most importantly that a checked proof does not establish that its definitions faithfully capture the intended physics. We also give our perspectives on near-term and long-term directions in these areas.
papers.summary: Rapid AI progress in physics is producing results faster than they can be verified, trusted, and reused, and the argument advanced here is that formalization, meaning machine-checked definitions and proofs, is a necessary part of the answer for both computational and theoretical physics. AI is lowering the barrier to formalization and speeding it up, though it remains weaker at choosing definitions and designing libraries than at writing proofs, and that speed currently comes at the cost of trust, credit, and community. Shared, community-reviewed formal libraries such as `Physlib` are proposed as the central remedy, serving both as a reusable foundation for physics results and as the environment in which AI systems reason about physics. **A key challenge beyond those faced in mathematics is that a checked proof does not establish that its definitions faithfully capture the intended physics.**

papers.title: Auditing LLM Program Search for Bermudan Stopping with Primal--Dual Certificates
papers.abstract: LLM program-search agents are usually judged by the score that drives their search. We study LLM-driven search over Python exercise policies for Bermudan options, an optimal stopping problem where a trusted evaluator owns the simulation and a dual upper bound~$U$. For any policy, $0 \le V^\star - L_\pi \le U - L_\pi$; we report Monte Carlo estimates of both bounds with their sampling error. We audit 24 generation attempts from two pipelines, a six-pair feedback-representation ablation, and a holdout evaluated after selection was frozen. No selected generated program improves on Ridge LSMC consistently or by more than Monte Carlo uncertainty; holdout gap scores lie within $0.002$ of it. On six one-dimensional puts, a high-precision binomial reference places Ridge within Monte Carlo noise of optimal and attributes 99\% of the estimated gap to dual-bound looseness, so this dual audits validity but cannot certify progress at the search's scale. Structured memory showed no benefit over score-only memory in this ablation. Whether search ``worked'' depends on reporting rules: retaining the initial reference, freezing selection before holdout, and counting failures.
papers.summary: LLM program-search agents are usually judged by the very score that drives their search, so the question is whether that score reflects real progress. Here an LLM searches over Python exercise policies for Bermudan options, an optimal stopping problem in which a trusted evaluator owns the simulation and computes both a lower bound from the policy and a dual upper bound, so the gap between them bounds the policy's distance from optimal and both are reported with Monte Carlo error. Auditing 24 generation attempts from two pipelines, a six-pair feedback-representation ablation, and a frozen-selection holdout, **no selected generated program beats the `Ridge LSMC` baseline consistently or by more than Monte Carlo uncertainty**, with holdout gap scores within 0.002 of it. On six one-dimensional puts a high-precision binomial reference places `Ridge LSMC` within noise of optimal and attributes 99% of the estimated gap to dual-bound looseness, structured memory shows no benefit over score-only memory, and whether the search worked depends on reporting rules such as retaining the initial reference, freezing selection before holdout, and counting failures.

papers.title: Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue
papers.abstract: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.
papers.summary: As LLM agents enter high-stakes enterprise settings, privacy leakage in agent-to-agent dialogue depends on whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which the information was originally shared. `CIMemories` is extended into `CIMemories Dialogue`, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory, used to evaluate seven open-weight models from the `Qwen3` and `Llama 3.1` families at one and six conversation turns under three prompting conditions. **More capable models are systematically leakier, and no evaluated model decouples task capability from privacy leakage.** Thinking models leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, attributed to the larger reasoning surface of chain-of-thought, and leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from one to six turns.

papers.title: Is the Future Predictable? Modeling Future Predictability for Reliable Temporal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable when reasoning about the future. Existing models often overlook the difference among future states, committing to specific answers even when the queried facts are inherently volatile. To capture this challenge, we introduce ChronoRegime, a future-oriented temporal reasoning task that requires models to determine whether historical temporal evidence justifies commitment to a future answer. Furthermore, we propose Confidence-Aware Temporal Reasoning (CTR), a framework that estimates future predictability from temporal dynamics and regulates answer commitment accordingly. Rather than performing unconditional forecasting, CTR commits only when the reconstructed evidence supports the target future state. Across multiple LLMs, CTR improves strict overall accuracy by 6.7 percentage points and reduces hallucination rates by 18.4 percentage points on average over the plain QA baseline. These results demonstrate that explicit predictability assessment is an effective mechanism for safer and more reliable temporal reasoning under future uncertainty.
papers.summary: Large language models reason unreliably about the future because they commit to specific answers even when the queried fact is inherently volatile, ignoring the difference between future states that are predictable and those that are not. `ChronoRegime` is a future-oriented temporal reasoning task that asks whether historical temporal evidence justifies committing to a future answer, and Confidence-Aware Temporal Reasoning (CTR) is a framework that estimates future predictability from temporal dynamics and commits to an answer only when the reconstructed evidence supports the target future state. **Across multiple LLMs, `CTR` improves strict overall accuracy by 6.7 percentage points and cuts hallucination rates by 18.4 percentage points on average** relative to a plain question-answering baseline.

papers.title: One Model, Multiple Compute Budgets: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE for Flexible Compute Across Turns
papers.abstract: Large language models typically support different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations. In multi-turn interactions, however, compute demand can vary substantially across turns. Using a high-compute model for every turn wastes computation, while routing among independent models may require rebuilding model-specific history states after switches. We therefore ask whether a single shared model can support multiple compute budgets that can be flexibly assigned across turns. We introduce Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE, which jointly supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 (CR2/CR4/CR8) within a shared backbone. Lightweight full-token modules reduce compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers support distinct compression levels, and cross-ratio training enables mixed-ratio processing within the same context. Across PTBench and SFTBench, the three fixed modes outperform their compute-matched MoE baselines in all 6 comparisons while remaining competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists. On CodeChat and CoSQL, mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy--compute trade-off, outperforming the Large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while reducing FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE further reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models. These results demonstrate that a single shared model can provide multiple compute budgets for flexible compute allocation across turns.
papers.summary: Large language models usually offer different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations, but in multi-turn interactions the compute each turn needs varies, and switching among independent models forces model-specific history states to be rebuilt. `Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE` supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 within one shared backbone, using lightweight full-token modules to cut compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers for each compression level, and cross-ratio training so that different ratios can be mixed within the same context. On `PTBench` and `SFTBench` the three fixed modes beat compute-matched MoE baselines in all six comparisons while staying competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists, and on `CodeChat` and `CoSQL` mixed-ratio inference beats the large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while cutting FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%. **Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, the shared model reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models.**

papers.title: Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning for Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation: From Physical Alignment to Scene Aggregation
papers.abstract: Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) requires an agent to locate sound targets by jointly leveraging visual and auditory cues. While prior work has achieved notable success with static sound sources, real-world scenarios often involve moving targets, giving rise to the more challenging problem of \textbf{Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation (D-AVN)}. Existing approaches largely rely on semantic auditory features, which limits generalization to unheard sound categories and hinders fine-grained spatial reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel \textbf{Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning} framework for D-AVN. In the Physical Alignment stage, the proposed \textbf{Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder (ICGE)} performs physics-informed alignment of sound intensity with visual geometry to capture category-agnostic spatial correspondence. In the Scene Aggregation stage, a Transformer-based \textbf{Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator (CMSA)} dynamically integrates multi-modal features to construct a robust state representation for policy learning. Extensive experiments on Replica and Matterport3D demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art success rates, while significantly improving generalization and navigation efficiency in complex environments and under unheard sound scenarios.
papers.summary: Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) asks an agent to find a sound source using both sight and hearing, and the harder Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation (D-AVN) setting has the source moving, where prior methods that lean on semantic auditory features generalize poorly to unheard sound categories and struggle with fine-grained spatial reasoning. A two-stage framework first performs physical alignment with an Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder (ICGE) that matches sound intensity to visual geometry in a category-agnostic way, then uses a Transformer-based Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator (CMSA) to fuse multimodal features into a state representation for policy learning. **On `Replica` and `Matterport3D` the method achieves state-of-the-art success rates**, with improved generalization and navigation efficiency in complex environments and on unheard sounds.

papers.title: SAGE: Efficient Protected Vision-Language Inference on Smart Glasses
papers.abstract: Smart glasses are a promising platform for vision-language assistants, but private split inference remains expensive: protecting visual representations before transmission does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. We present SAGE (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding), a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses. SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, reduces visual input cost, executes shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets before transmission. Unlike efficiency methods optimized only for nominal model size, SAGE selects its operating point using downstream answer quality together with measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior on real Mentra Live glasses. On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces glasses inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility and comparable prompted containment. Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers across four additional VLM families. These results show that private wearable VLM inference must be optimized jointly across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than through model compression alone.
papers.summary: Vision-language assistants on smart glasses face expensive private split inference: protecting visual representations before they leave the device does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or execution that ignores the hardware. `SAGE` (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding) keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, trims visual input cost, runs shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into 256-dimensional INT8 packets, choosing its operating point from downstream answer quality together with latency, memory, and thermal measurements on real Mentra Live glasses. **On a matched `Qwen` workload, `SAGE` cuts glasses inference latency by 39.18%, sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56% while keeping 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility.** Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and lower median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms, and the compact protected interface transfers to four more VLM families.

papers.title: Pristine Models
papers.abstract: Training on broad, unfiltered data enables high-quality image generation, but can also teach models concepts that should not be generated; restricting the training data ensures safety, but reduces quality because examples containing unsafe concepts also provide useful knowledge that is not itself unsafe. Existing approaches largely address this trade-off post hoc through concept unlearning, which can lead to catastrophic forgetting as the number of concepts to remove grows. We instead ask whether unsafe concept knowledge can be compartmentalized during pretraining so that access to it can be disabled at inference. We introduce Pristine Models, a novel text-to-image generation architecture with an attention mechanism that encourages the separation of safe and unsafe knowledge into independently parameterized branches. The branch-specific parameters are learned during training, while the unsafe branch can be detached at inference. On ImageNet, Pristine Models enable safer generation while retaining much of the utility of full-data pretraining, achieving higher image quality and better text alignment than training only on safe data or applying post-hoc concept removal. We further scale our approach to CC12M, demonstrating that it remains effective in a substantially larger and more diverse open-world pretraining setting.
papers.summary: Text-to-image models trained on broad unfiltered data learn concepts they should never generate, while filtering the training set hurts quality and post-hoc concept unlearning risks catastrophic forgetting as the list of removed concepts grows. The authors instead compartmentalize knowledge during pretraining: the `Pristine Models` architecture uses an attention mechanism that routes safe and unsafe knowledge into separately parameterized branches, and the unsafe branch is simply detached at inference. On `ImageNet`, the approach **achieves higher image quality and better text alignment than either safe-data-only training or post-hoc concept removal** while retaining much of the utility of full-data pretraining, and it continues to work when scaled to the larger and more diverse `CC12M` dataset.

papers.title: Human Pose Estimation by Probabilistic Mixtures of Gaussian and Uniform Distributions
papers.abstract: Despite advancements in sub-pixel decoding, modern Human Pose Estimation (HPE) architectures remain constrained by deterministic coordinate extraction from discrete heatmaps, which systematically fails under dense occlusions and Out-of-Distribution (OoD) ambiguities. To address these limitations, we propose a post-hoc continuous probabilistic framework that intercepts raw heatmaps and models them as a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) augmented with a spatially agnostic uniform distribution, requiring no architectural modifications or retraining. This continuous representation allows us to comprehensively explore the distinct contributions of density modeling to HPE. We show that the spatial expectation of our fitted GMM achieves precision parity with leading sub-pixel decoders without heuristic post-processing. Leveraging this continuous space, our test-time augmentation aggregates probability distributions rather than discrete activations, mitigating multi-scale heatmap poisoning. Furthermore, because our multimodal GMM parameterization isolates competing spatial hypotheses, it naturally interfaces with geometric regularizers such as Markov Random Fields. However, our analysis exposes the inherent vulnerabilities of 2D kinematic priors under perspective foreshortening and visual degradation. Crucially, this density formulation yields significant improvements in uncertainty quantification: our calibrated geometric covariance volume outperforms standard peak-intensity heuristics in OoD anomaly detection under severe occlusion. For in-distribution calibration, dynamically fusing our geometric metric via Adaptive Softmax reduces or matches baseline Area Under the Sparsification Error (AUSE) across benchmarks and degradation levels. Finally, we establish that this continuous parameterization is extensible to multi-view 3D architectures, bypassing the $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ voxel memory bottleneck.
papers.summary: Human pose estimation (HPE) networks usually extract joint coordinates deterministically from discrete heatmaps, which breaks down under dense occlusion and out-of-distribution (OoD) inputs. The authors propose a post-hoc method that fits each raw heatmap with a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) plus a uniform background component, requiring no retraining, so that test-time augmentation can aggregate full distributions rather than discrete activations and competing spatial hypotheses can feed geometric regularizers such as Markov random fields. The GMM's spatial expectation matches leading sub-pixel decoders in precision, and **its calibrated geometric covariance outperforms peak-intensity heuristics at detecting OoD anomalies under severe occlusion**, with a fused uncertainty metric matching or reducing area under the sparsification error (AUSE) across benchmarks and degradation levels. The same continuous parameterization extends to multi-view 3D architectures without the cubic voxel memory cost, though the analysis also exposes weaknesses of 2D kinematic priors under perspective foreshortening.

papers.title: A Physics-Informed Hybrid Forward-Inverse Machine Learning Framework for High-Dimensional Sparse Recipe Reconstruction
papers.abstract: High-dimensional sparse recipe formulation in process industries involves nonlinear association of various covariates, bounded by sparsity constraints and multi-criteria tolerances. Traditional physics-based classical methods (such as Kubelka-Munk) fail to generate sparse candidate recipes properly due to their simplified assumptions and industrial process variations. This study proposes a hybrid physics-informed uncertainty-aware framework that is structured into three modules: (a) Module A, a multi-target forward quality model; (b) Module B, a sparse inverse reconstructor; and (c) Module C, a feasibility-constrained ranking layer. Then it has been validated in an industrial textile dyeing context with recipe-grouped cross-validation under multi-illuminant quality assessment comprising process and production information, target reflectance, K/S values, and spectral descriptors. Histogram Gradient Boosting (HGB) with spectral-only features ($R_\lambda$, K/S) and Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBDT) with recipe-process features outperforms other configurations with out-of-Fold MAE of 0.1655 and 0.1523 in the forward quality model. For inverse reconstruction, a component-wise median blend achieved a recipe-vector MAE of 0.0295. Exploratory conditional treatment effect (CATE) suggests an observational association that alkali adjustment reduces error for red and pale shades (CATE = -0.196). This framework provides a human-in-the-loop decision-support tool that minimizes costly laboratory trials across industrial formulation domains.
