papers.summary: Formulating sparse, high-dimensional recipes in process industries such as textile dyeing involves nonlinear interactions among many ingredients under sparsity and tolerance constraints that classical physics models like Kubelka-Munk handle poorly. The proposed framework chains a multi-target forward quality model, a sparse inverse recipe reconstructor, and a feasibility-constrained ranking layer, validated with recipe-grouped cross-validation on industrial dyeing data assessed under multiple illuminants. Gradient-boosted forward models reached out-of-fold mean absolute errors of roughly 0.15 to 0.17, and **a component-wise median blend achieved a recipe-vector mean absolute error of 0.0295** for inverse reconstruction, with an exploratory conditional treatment effect (CATE) analysis suggesting that alkali adjustment reduces error for red and pale shades.

papers.title: From Prototype to Massing: Learning Graph Correspondence for Scalable Facade Modeling
papers.abstract: Facade articulation at building scale is usually resolved manually or through parametric systems that encode design intent as explicit rules. This paper investigates a complementary workflow in which a designer-authored prototype supplies transferable articulation logic. Prototype and target massing are represented as heterogeneous attributed graphs, and a Siamese graph attention network with instance-local triplet supervision embeds their segments in a shared metric space. Many-to-one nearest-neighbor retrieval then routes prototype Patterns to the larger target. On the original 85/15 within-corpus holdout, prototype-to-massing top-1 accuracy reached 96.5%, compared with a reported 76.5% raw-feature baseline. A Rhino demonstrator converts predicted correspondence into reusable facade Patterns, and qualitative applications on four built projects show the workflow across distinct massing organizations. The contribution is not automated facade generation, but an authoring model in which resolved geometry serves as a computational specification for project-scale propagation.
papers.summary: Articulating building facades at project scale is typically done by hand or through parametric rule systems that must encode design intent explicitly. The authors instead let a designer-authored prototype supply transferable articulation logic: prototype and target massing are represented as heterogeneous attributed graphs, a Siamese graph attention network trained with instance-local triplet supervision embeds their segments in a shared metric space, and many-to-one nearest-neighbor retrieval maps prototype patterns onto the larger target. On an 85/15 within-corpus holdout, **prototype-to-massing top-1 accuracy reached 96.5% versus 76.5% for a raw-feature baseline**, and a `Rhino` demonstrator turns the predicted correspondences into reusable facade patterns on four built projects. The contribution is framed as an authoring model in which resolved geometry serves as a computational specification, rather than as automated facade generation.

papers.title: Fin_Agent at FinEval 2026: Task-Aware Methods for Multilingual Financial NLP
papers.abstract: We present Fin_Agent, our submission to the FinEval 2026 shared task on multilingual fi nancial language understanding. Our sys tems address Greek financial named-entity recognition, Japanese implicit communication recognition, and multilingual financial ques tion answering. For Greek NER, we com bine annotation-aware numeric rules with zero shot Qwen2.5-32B classification, achieving 0.9521 public F1 and 0.8884 private F1. For Japanese implicit communication, an inter pretable cue-based ordinal scorer achieves 98.0% test accuracy. For multilingual financial QA, BGE-M3retrieval with Qwen3-32B gen eration achieves 0.3023 and 0.3419 ROUGE-1 F1 on the public and private splits. Key limita tions include dataset-specific rules, handcrafted cues, and limited supervision. Implementa tion code is available https://github.com/ Rashidnira/finagent-fineval-2026.
papers.summary: The submission to the `FinEval 2026` shared task on multilingual financial language understanding covers three subtasks: Greek financial named-entity recognition (NER), Japanese implicit communication recognition, and multilingual financial question answering. Greek NER pairs annotation-aware numeric rules with zero-shot `Qwen2.5-32B` classification, Japanese implicit communication uses an interpretable cue-based ordinal scorer, and financial QA combines `BGE-M3` retrieval with `Qwen3-32B` generation. The Greek NER system reached **0.9521 public and 0.8884 private F1**, the cue-based scorer hit 98.0% test accuracy, and the QA pipeline scored 0.3023 and 0.3419 ROUGE-1 F1 on the public and private splits; the authors note dataset-specific rules, handcrafted cues, and limited supervision as the main limitations.

papers.title: Embodied Zero-Shot Task Planning via Hardware-Aware LLM-VLM Integration for Grounded Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models can translate natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but robotic execution requires physically grounded decisions that respect robot embodiment, workspace geometry, reachability, collision constraints, and grasp feasibility. This paper presents a hardware-aware large language model-vision-language model (LLM-VLM) manipulation framework for a simulated Franka Research 3 robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The framework separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and generates only symbolic task information, including the object to manipulate, target relation, approach preference, and objects to avoid. A local Qwen3-VL 8B VLM verifier supports semantic confirmation of ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. Both the LLM planner and the VLM verifier are prohibited from generating robot coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, trajectory waypoints, or success labels. Instead, these decisions are handled by deterministic grounding and execution modules that use the robot model, scene geometry, MoveIt 2 collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasp validation, release verification, and final visual assessment. Execution feedback is returned only as symbolic context for replanning. The framework is evaluated through simulated digital-twin trials involving pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.
papers.summary: Large language models can turn natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but real execution must respect robot embodiment, reachability, collisions, and grasp feasibility. The framework, built for a simulated Franka Research 3 arm in `NVIDIA Isaac Sim`, strictly separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and emits only symbolic decisions such as which object to move, the target relation, an approach preference, and objects to avoid, while a local `Qwen3-VL 8B` vision-language model (VLM) verifies ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. **Neither model is allowed to produce coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, waypoints, or success labels**; deterministic modules using the robot model, `MoveIt 2` collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasp validation, and release verification handle those, and execution feedback returns to the planner only as symbolic context for replanning. The system is evaluated in digital-twin trials covering pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.

papers.title: Does System One Transfer? Calibrated Typed-Decision Models, Label Budgets, and Translation for Indonesian Regional Languages
papers.abstract: Calibrated typed-decision ("System One") models return a label and a probability in a single forward pass at a small fraction of the cost of large language models (LLMs), yet their evaluation has been almost entirely English. We report a pre-registered evaluation of the commercial Jev model and the open Laya-multilingual model on Indonesian regional languages, using the parallel NusaX sentiment (12 languages) and NusaTranslation sentiment and emotion (7 languages) test sets. Jev is more often correct on sentences that are lexically closer to Indonesian in all three datasets, and presenting the human Indonesian translation instead raises its accuracy by up to 37.2 points, most in languages distant from Indonesian. Its expected calibration error does not grow on regional languages, but its ability to rank its own errors degrades in all three datasets. Retrained classifiers need more than 500 labels per language to match zero-shot Jev in 9 of 10 NusaX regional languages. A confidence-gated cascade that sends Jev's 10-30% least confident decisions to a local IndoBERT classifier matches or exceeds the better of the two systems, and routing to an LLM instead matches that LLM at 24-77% lower API cost. Of six further commercial LLMs (three Claude and three GPT models), five are 4-14 points more accurate than Jev, at several hundred times the API cost where it is reported, while the smallest (Claude Haiku) is less accurate. We release the pre-registration, code and all predictions.
papers.summary: Calibrated typed-decision models, which return a label and a probability in a single forward pass at a small fraction of the cost of large language models (LLMs), have been evaluated almost entirely on English. In a pre-registered study, the commercial `Jev` model and the open `Laya-multilingual` model are tested on Indonesian regional languages using the parallel `NusaX` sentiment set across 12 languages and the `NusaTranslation` sentiment and emotion sets across 7 languages. `Jev` is more accurate on sentences lexically closer to Indonesian, and **feeding it the human Indonesian translation raises accuracy by up to 37.2 points**, mostly for distant languages; its expected calibration error holds up on regional languages but its ability to rank its own errors degrades. Retrained classifiers need more than 500 labels per language to match zero-shot `Jev` in 9 of 10 `NusaX` languages, and a confidence-gated cascade that routes the 10-30% least confident decisions to a local `IndoBERT` classifier matches or exceeds either system alone, while routing to an LLM instead matches that LLM at 24-77% lower API cost.

papers.title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
papers.abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.
papers.summary: Data science agents built on large language models are usually evaluated on downstream predictive performance and code correctness, which can mask methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation. The authors evaluate agentic data science from three angles: a large-scale analysis of failure modes across common agent frameworks and models on 220 tasks, a reusable test suite of curated tasks that probe six specific failure types in a controlled way, and a qualitative comparison of agent pipelines against expert solutions on `Kaggle` competitions. **The majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode regardless of harness complexity or model capacity**, and data leakage failures correlate positively with predictive performance, so accuracy alone rewards the wrong behavior. The qualitative analysis finds that agents lack the problem-solving creativity and domain knowledge of competition-winning data scientists.

papers.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.
papers.summary: Post-training pipelines for agents that operate in sandboxed harness environments with file systems and shells are scarce and typically one-shot, relying on a stronger teacher model to synthesize tasks and on human researchers to read the evaluation results. `ClawLoop` closes this into a self-sustaining cycle with no external teacher: a task synthesis phase builds a diverse task pool through two construction routines, grows difficulty conditioned on diagnosis, and validates tasks both with and without the agent; a training phase updates the agent with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and/or reinforcement learning (RL); and a diagnosis phase analyzes rollouts into a capability report that steers the next round of task synthesis. With `Qwen3.6-27B` as the loop model, **the cycle yields consistent gains on `SkillsBench`, `Claw-Eval-Live`, and `ClawGym-Bench`**, and the refined tasks also improve smaller `Qwen3.5-4B` and `Qwen3.5-9B` models across all benchmarks, indicating that the data quality does not depend on the loop model.

papers.title: Early Detection of Pension-Sponsor Distress from Public Filings: A Sponsor Vulnerability Index, Stress-Augmented VaR, and Dynamic Self-Investment Caps
papers.abstract: A defined-benefit pension is only as safe as its sponsor, yet sponsor distress is under-instrumented relative to plan-side modelling. We present a transparent, reproducible early-warning pipeline built entirely on public data. A Sponsor Vulnerability Index (SVI), a gradient-boosted classifier over point-in-time SEC EDGAR balance-sheet fundamentals and two macro series, predicts a filings-based distress state one to two quarters ahead. On 36 U.S. sponsors in five sector groups (1,418 firm-quarters, 2015Q1-2025Q3) it reaches an out-of-fold AUC-ROC of 0.887 and PR-AUC of 0.711 (base rate 11.9%) under leave-one-firm-out cross-validation. A Monte Carlo VaR with a stylized transition-stress overlay shows that climate-type stress is negligible for a diversified plan but adds 20-43% to one-year 95% VaR when 22.5% of assets are held in sponsor securities. A dynamic self-investment cap maps the SVI to a limit that falls from 8% to below 1% in acute distress and recovers with the sponsor, which we illustrate on PG&E's 2019 bankruptcy and Boeing's persistent fragility. We report the method's failure modes alongside its results (book-equity labels that also fire on non-credit events such as spin-offs, positives concentrated in one firm, and stylized stress parameters) and release code, data and results under a concept DOI.
papers.summary: Defined-benefit pensions depend on the health of their sponsor, yet sponsor distress is far less instrumented than plan-side risk. The authors build a transparent early-warning pipeline on public data: a Sponsor Vulnerability Index (SVI), a gradient-boosted classifier over point-in-time `SEC EDGAR` balance-sheet fundamentals and two macro series, predicts a filings-based distress state one to two quarters ahead and **reaches an out-of-fold AUC-ROC of 0.887 and PR-AUC of 0.711** on 36 U.S. sponsors across 1,418 firm-quarters under leave-one-firm-out cross-validation. A Monte Carlo value-at-risk (VaR) with a stylized transition-stress overlay finds climate-type stress negligible for a diversified plan but adds 20-43% to one-year 95% VaR when 22.5% of assets sit in sponsor securities, and a dynamic self-investment cap tied to the SVI falls from 8% to under 1% in acute distress, illustrated on PG&E's 2019 bankruptcy and Boeing's persistent fragility. Failure modes such as book-equity labels firing on spin-offs and positives concentrated in one firm are reported alongside the results, with code and data released.

papers.title: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reasoning Systems for Knowledge-Grounded Material Substitution
papers.abstract: AI-assisted scientific discovery increasingly seeks to move beyond generating plausible ideas toward reproducible, constraint-aware workflows that can support practical engineering decisions. We present MARS, a hierarchical Multi-Agent Reasoning System for knowledge-grounded material substitution under scientific and manufacturing constraints. We apply MARS to replace per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), a demanding materials-design problem in which substitutes must satisfy functional performance, environmental, experimental, and processing requirements. MARS decomposes substitution into a closed-loop workflow comprising requirement analysis, grounded candidate generation, and manufacturability assessment with process design. The system integrates retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge-graph reasoning, a database of lab-available materials, persistent memory of intermediate results, and rejection-aware iterative feedback. In a PFAS-substitution case study, MARS generates structured material requirements, identifies an evidence-grounded substitute candidate, and develops a lab-scale manufacturing route. In a multi-seed ablation evaluation, MARS achieves the highest overall performance across all three subsystems, with gains that persist when the backbone model is held fixed. These results suggest that hierarchical decomposition, knowledge grounding, and manufacturability-aware refinement improve material-substitution reasoning beyond model capability alone.
papers.summary: AI-assisted scientific discovery increasingly needs reproducible, constraint-aware workflows rather than merely plausible ideas. `MARS`, a hierarchical multi-agent reasoning system, decomposes material substitution into a closed loop of requirement analysis, grounded candidate generation, and manufacturability assessment with process design, integrating retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge-graph reasoning, a database of lab-available materials, persistent memory of intermediate results, and rejection-aware iterative feedback. Applied to replacing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), the system produces structured requirements, an evidence-grounded substitute candidate, and a lab-scale manufacturing route, and **in a multi-seed ablation it achieves the highest overall performance across all three subsystems even when the backbone model is held fixed**, suggesting that decomposition and grounding contribute beyond raw model capability.

papers.title: The AI's Poker Face: Contrasting Persuasion and Sycophancy in Voice-Based Multi-Turn Conversations
papers.abstract: As interactions with large language models (LLMs) become increasingly routine, concerns about their capacity to influence users' beliefs grow. Yet how such influence unfolds in sustained dialogue remains insufficiently understood. We conduct a randomized controlled experiment (N=616) where participants engage in multi-turn, spoken dialogue with an LLM under three conditions: non-directive, and two directive conditions maintaining opposing stances on a polarizing topic (the merits of feminism). We examine opinion change, rhetorical strategies, and sycophancy, distinguishing the semantic content of LLM argumentation from the pragmatic strategies used to manage the interaction. Both directive conditions shifted opinions toward their assigned stances, but asymmetrically: shifts were larger for pro-feminist positions, which also elicited distinct rhetorical strategies. The non-directive condition, likewise shifted opinions pro-feminism. Social sycophancy, though near-universal, was not associated with opinion change; instead it shaped users' subjective experience. Our findings highlight distinct roles for argumentation and sycophantic accommodation in AI influence.
papers.summary: How large language models (LLMs) shift users' beliefs over sustained dialogue is poorly understood. In a randomized controlled experiment with 616 participants holding multi-turn spoken conversations with an LLM, three conditions were compared: a non-directive assistant and two directive assistants holding opposite stances on the merits of feminism, with analysis of opinion change, rhetorical strategies, and sycophancy that separates the semantic content of arguments from the pragmatic strategies used to manage the interaction. **Both directive conditions moved opinions toward their assigned stance, but asymmetrically, with larger shifts toward pro-feminist positions**, and even the non-directive condition shifted opinions in the pro-feminist direction. Social sycophancy was near-universal yet unrelated to opinion change, instead shaping users' subjective experience, pointing to distinct roles for argumentation and accommodation in AI influence.

papers.title: On physical implementability of reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning
papers.abstract: In the machine learning community, the reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning process has been intensively studied since around 2025. In this article, we present a negative result on the hardware implementation of this reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning process in a physical neural network model in the presence of a reward external potential energy for a given reward. In this hardware implementation, the existence of a chain of thought in dynamics contradicts the Lyapunov stability of the system.
papers.summary: Reinforcement-learning-driven reasoning, in which a model produces a chain of thought shaped by a reward signal, has been studied intensively since around 2025. The note considers implementing this process in a physical neural network model where the reward enters as an external potential energy, and presents a negative result: **the existence of a chain of thought in the dynamics contradicts the Lyapunov stability of the system**.

papers.title: A Stochastic Analysis Perspective on Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Generative modelling involves two complementary tasks: learning a probabilistic approximation of an unknown data distribution from observations, and designing a tractable mechanism for sampling from this approximation. We present a stochastic-analysis perspective on score-based generative models, connecting ideas from classical sampling theory, score estimation, and diffusion time reversal. We first explain how score functions link Langevin sampling with score matching, and how Gaussian smoothing leads to denoising score matching and multiscale sampling methods. We then emphasize the distinction between dynamics preserving a fixed distribution and dynamics transporting a prescribed family of marginals. This motivates a path-space treatment of diffusion time reversal. Finally, we connect the ideal reverse diffusion with practical generative algorithms.
papers.summary: Generative modelling combines learning a probabilistic approximation of an unknown data distribution with designing a tractable sampler for it. The exposition connects score-based generative models to classical sampling theory, score estimation, and diffusion time reversal: it shows how score functions tie Langevin sampling to score matching, how Gaussian smoothing leads to denoising score matching and multiscale sampling, and **why dynamics that preserve a fixed distribution must be distinguished from dynamics that transport a prescribed family of marginals**. That distinction motivates a path-space treatment of time reversal, which is then linked to the practical reverse-diffusion algorithms used in generation.

papers.title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.
papers.summary: Diffusion denoisers are trained on real images mixed with noise but at inference consume their own imperfect predictions from earlier steps, an exposure bias that accumulates error and may be one reason sampling often depends on classifier-free guidance (CFG). The proposed corrector takes the base denoiser's clean-sample prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target, making correction an explicit learning task; at sampling time it refines the prediction at each denoising step and can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs despite being trained only on base-model predictions. Across `DiT`, `SiT`, and `JiT`, **the authors report improved FID over previously published results for unguided and especially unconditional generation, reaching quality competitive with CFG**, and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation. The extra inference cost can be removed by distilling the refined predictions back into the base model.

papers.title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0: Automating Diverse Task Construction and Measuring Sustained Agent Progress
papers.abstract: Long-horizon terminal benchmarks measure whether an agent can sustain progress through extended workflows with process rewards, not only whether its final state passes a binary check. We present Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0 (LHTB 2.0), an extension of Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench that preserves its 46 original tasks while correcting task and evaluation-infrastructure defects and extending 31 tasks. LHTB 2.0 contains 77 tasks across 13 domains and eight task types. The extended tasks are produced through a systematic reconstruction-task pipeline. We start from a working scientific or engineering artifact, then use a parameterized reference implementation to generate multiple scenarios, reveal six as behavioral evidence, hold out three for evaluation, and use dense progress ladders to reward partial progress while preventing memorization of public outputs. We also extend the evaluation horizon from 90 minutes to three hours and record verifier checkpoints every 30 minutes, enabling direct measurement of sustained progress within a run. Across 1,145 scored model-task runs from 15 frontier models, GPT-6-astra leads with dense mean reward 0.69 and 37 tasks at R at least 0.95, followed by GPT-5.6-sol with dense mean reward 0.67 and 32 tasks at the same threshold. On the 30 reconstruction tasks, binary verifier scores average 0.221, whereas dense ladder scores average 0.653, showing that outcome-only evaluation discards substantial intermediate progress. LHTB 2.0 provides a broader, hardened, and process-aware testbed for studying reliable agent execution over hours.
papers.summary: Long-horizon terminal benchmarks test whether an agent can sustain progress through extended workflows using process rewards rather than a single binary final check. The second version of `Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench` keeps the original 46 tasks, fixes task and infrastructure defects, and adds 31 tasks built through a reconstruction pipeline that starts from a working scientific or engineering artifact, generates scenarios from a parameterized reference implementation, reveals six as behavioral evidence, holds out three for evaluation, and scores partial progress on dense ladders; the evaluation horizon grows from 90 minutes to three hours with verifier checkpoints every 30 minutes. Across 1,145 scored runs from 15 frontier models, `GPT-6-astra` leads with a dense mean reward of 0.69 followed by `GPT-5.6-sol` at 0.67, and on the 30 reconstruction tasks **binary verifier scores average 0.221 while dense ladder scores average 0.653**, showing that outcome-only evaluation discards most intermediate progress.

papers.title: VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
papers.abstract: VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework addresses the gap between AI advances in human medicine and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development.
papers.summary: Veterinary medicine and animal science lack the standardized, high-quality datasets that have driven AI progress in human medicine. `VETNET` is proposed as an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks assembled through multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors, with the stated aim of **closing the gap between human-medicine AI and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development**.

papers.title: Beyond Discrimination: Evaluating Probability Calibration in Radiomics-Image Fusion for Renal Cell Carcinoma Classification
papers.abstract: Reliable probability estimates are important for the clinical interpretation of machine-learning classifiers, yet radiomics--image fusion models for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) are commonly evaluated primarily by discrimination. Using 396 patients from the KiTS23 dataset, we evaluated whether adding radiomics to four image-model families improved probabilistic performance in addition to discrimination. Seventeen individual models and four probability-average ensembles were assessed using discrimination, probability calibration, and proper scoring measures. Across 12 matched image-only versus fusion comparisons, AUC and AP improved in all 12, while Brier score and negative log likelihood (NLL) improved in 11 of 12 and expected calibration error (ECE) in eight of 12. The 3D MedVAE gated-fusion model achieved the strongest overall individual-model profile. Probability averaging across concatenation, cross-attention, and gated fusion produced favourable point estimates across all five primary metrics relative to image-only models in all four families, although paired-bootstrap support was stronger for Brier score and NLL than for ECE. These findings show that radiomics--image fusion can improve probabilistic prediction quality beyond discrimination, while calibration behaviour varies across image architectures and fusion strategies. We show that our proposed probability-average ensemble models improve discrimination and calibration simultaneously across all architectures in the study.
papers.summary: Radiomics-image fusion models for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) classification are usually judged on discrimination alone, even though clinical use depends on reliable probability estimates. Using 396 patients from `KiTS23`, the authors test whether adding radiomics to four image-model families improves probabilistic performance, assessing seventeen individual models and four probability-average ensembles with discrimination, calibration, and proper scoring metrics. Across 12 matched image-only versus fusion comparisons, **AUC and average precision improved in all 12, Brier score and negative log likelihood (NLL) in 11, and expected calibration error (ECE) in 8**, with the 3D `MedVAE` gated-fusion model giving the strongest individual profile. Probability-averaging ensembles across concatenation, cross-attention, and gated fusion improved discrimination and calibration together in all four families, though paired-bootstrap support was weaker for ECE than for Brier score and NLL.

papers.title: Beyond Gate Weights: Decision-Level Interpretation of Radiomics-Image Feature Fusion for RCC Classification
papers.abstract: Gate coefficients describe how a fusion layer weights intermediate features, but they do not necessarily reflect the magnitude of branch contributions at the classifier output. We investigate this distinction in a fixed 3D MedVAE--radiomics model for clear cell versus non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma classification from contrast-enhanced CT. Because the model uses a linear classification head, the binary decision logit can be decomposed exactly into a gated image term, a direct radiomics term, and a bias. We define effective radiomics dominance as the direct radiomics term's share of the summed absolute non-bias branch contributions and compare it with structural radiomics weighting. Internally, mean structural radiomics weighting was 0.823, whereas mean effective radiomics dominance was 0.148, with a modest case-wise association (\r{ho} = 0.290). The gated image term retained substantially stronger discriminative ranking information than the direct radiomics term. The same structural-to-effective discrepancy was observed in exploratory external evaluation. Branch-targeted permutation, integrated-gradient, and Shapley-style analyses further identified radiomics descriptors influencing the direct radiomics term. Because radiomics also generates the gate, the gated image term remains radiomics-dependent, so additive branch contribution should not be interpreted as total input influence. These findings show that structural gate weighting and decision-level branch contribution represent distinct aspects of gated feature fusion and should be interpreted separately.
papers.summary: Gate coefficients in a fusion layer describe how intermediate features are weighted, but not how much each branch actually contributes at the classifier output. In a fixed 3D `MedVAE` plus radiomics model for clear cell versus non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma classification on contrast-enhanced CT, the linear classification head lets the decision logit be decomposed exactly into a gated image term, a direct radiomics term, and a bias, from which the authors define effective radiomics dominance as the direct term's share of the summed absolute branch contributions. **Mean structural radiomics weighting was 0.823 while mean effective radiomics dominance was only 0.148**, with a modest case-wise correlation of 0.290, and the gated image term carried far more discriminative ranking information; the same discrepancy appeared in exploratory external evaluation. Because radiomics also drives the gate, additive branch contributions should not be read as total input influence, so structural weighting and decision-level contribution must be interpreted separately.

papers.title: OpenMobile-2: Building Versatile Mobile Agents with Scalable Environments and App-Native Tools
papers.abstract: We introduce OpenMobile-2, a near-frontier mobile agent with fully open training environments and recipes. We make three key advances: (1) Diverse environments with simulated commercial apps: We build MobileGym++, featuring 35 realistic, functionally rich commercial-style apps with cross-app workflows, while preserving full controllability for reset and verification. Together with newly configured apps in Android emulators, this yields a diverse playground spanning over 110 apps. (2) Open training data at scale: Building on this foundation, we curate nearly 12K mobile interaction trajectories for supervised fine-tuning and the largest open collection of verifiable RL training data for mobile agents, comprising over 2K executable tasks with automatic rewards. (3) Hybrid GUI and app-native tool use: We explore an experimental mobile-use setting where apps expose selected functionalities as app-native tools alongside their GUIs, allowing agents to interleave GUI actions and tool calls within a task. We implement this setting in MobileGym++ with over 300 carefully scoped tools across 50+ apps. Additionally, we introduce MobileGym++ Bench for complex, long-horizon commercial mobile scenarios, supporting both GUI-only and hybrid GUI-tool evaluation on a shared task suite. OpenMobile-2 performs competitively across established benchmarks, including AndroidWorld (79.9) and MobileWorld (50.4), while showing promising transfer to real-device mobile use, nearly doubling SPA-Bench performance from 31.9 to 59.6. All resources are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OpenMobile2-Home/.
papers.summary: Mobile GUI agents have lacked open, controllable training environments that resemble real commercial apps. `OpenMobile-2` is a near-frontier mobile agent released with its full training environments and recipes: `MobileGym++` provides 35 realistic commercial-style apps with cross-app workflows and full reset and verification control, which together with newly configured Android emulator apps spans over 110 apps, and the training data comprises nearly 12K interaction trajectories for supervised fine-tuning plus over 2K executable tasks with automatic rewards for reinforcement learning. The authors also explore a hybrid setting in which apps expose selected functions as app-native tools alongside their GUIs, implemented as over 300 scoped tools across 50+ apps, with a companion `MobileGym++ Bench` for long-horizon commercial scenarios in both GUI-only and hybrid modes. The agent scores 79.9 on `AndroidWorld` and 50.4 on `MobileWorld`, and **nearly doubles real-device performance on `SPA-Bench` from 31.9 to 59.6**.

papers.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can sample tokens in parallel, but they lose quality when the number of sampling steps is cut, process the full sequence at every step, and need many passes over the data to train well. The authors propose a two-stage coarse-to-fine scheme: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting every code within a level in parallel. At matched parameter counts, `NCM` **beats the strongest DLM baseline on `LM1B` in generative perplexity while running 21 times faster**, stays competitive on `OpenWebText` at 10 times the speed, matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L on `XSum` at 31 times the speed, and outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines on Sudoku at every difficulty level with fewer function evaluations.

papers.title: AutoEnvScaling: Automating the Data Flywheel with Terminal Agents
papers.abstract: Terminal agents solve tasks in software engineering and scientific research by executing commands in a terminal. Training them via reinforcement learning (RL) requires diverse and verifiable environments, but these environments are still mostly designed by human researchers, so their supply grows only as fast as researchers can work. We introduce AutoEnvScaling, which treats environment design as a terminal task and uses agents to automate the data flywheel. A proposer agent builds new RL environments from the rollouts of the solver being trained, and the solver's new rollouts guide the next round. By turning environment generation into a terminal task, AutoEnvScaling increases the valid-environment rate by up to 25 times compared to prompt-only generation, at up to 75% lower cost per valid environment. We show that training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on AutoEnvScaling environments from GPT-5.6-sol improves its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score by 4.3 points over the matched Tmax baseline. The broader goal of AutoEnvScaling is to enable recursive self-improvement (RSI): by making both environment generation and solving terminal tasks, it lets one model co-evolve in both roles. We show that Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, acting in both roles, gains 12.2 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and raises its Terminal-Bench 4.0 score from 1.6 to 3.2. The pipeline also generalizes across agentic domains, generating environments for software engineering, computer use, professional work, and GPU kernel programming. Overall, these results show a path toward agents building their own training environments, reducing human reliance and taking a core step toward RSI.
papers.summary: Terminal agents that solve software-engineering and research tasks by running shell commands are trained with reinforcement learning (RL), but the diverse, verifiable environments they need are still mostly built by human researchers. `AutoEnvScaling` treats environment design itself as a terminal task: a proposer agent builds new RL environments from the rollouts of the solver being trained, and the solver's fresh rollouts steer the next round. Compared with prompt-only generation, this raises the valid-environment rate by up to 25 times at up to 75% lower cost per valid environment, and training `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` on environments proposed by `GPT-5.6-sol` adds 4.3 points on `Terminal-Bench 2.1` over a matched baseline. With `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` acting as both proposer and solver, a recursive self-improvement (RSI) setting, **the model gains 12.2 points on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`** and doubles its `Terminal-Bench 4.0` score from 1.6 to 3.2, and the pipeline also produces environments for computer use, professional work, and GPU kernel programming.

papers.title: Do you "see" what I "see"? A Multi-panel Visual Question Answer Dataset for Large Language Model Chart Analysis
papers.abstract: Digital libraries increasingly host scientific publications whose figures encode primary research findings, yet making this visual content searchable, accessible, and reusable remains an open challenge. Large language and multimodal models (LLMs/LMMs) provide the possibility to automate many figure parsing tasks such as determining data trends or extracting data from plots. In this work, we consider if these models can reliably support task-oriented visual data analysis when presented with synthetic, but realistic, scientific figures that contain multiple charts. Our Visual Question Answering (VQA) process scaffolds our tasks along a four-level description model from basic conceptual answers to interpretive and analytical understanding. Additionally, we outline our process for synthetically generating our single and multi-panel (charts in which there are multiple panels present) plots and testing the data with various LMMs using quantitative analysis. In general, we find LMMs become less accurate with increasing figure complexity as the number of panels, number of plot elements, and difficulty of questions increase. Finally, because LMM accuracy is expected to change rapidly, our analysis also considers cost relative to performance as a metric to inform future user decisions. We provide the detailed question-answer pairs used in this analysis, along with the code used to generate random plots, question-answer pairs and detailed bounding-box metadata for chart elements. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ReadingTimeMachine/LLM_VQA_MultiPanel and https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/visual\_qa\_multipanel
papers.summary: Scientific figures in digital libraries carry primary research findings, but making that visual content searchable and reusable is unsolved, and it is unclear how well large multimodal models (LMMs) handle realistic figures that contain several charts. The authors synthetically generate single- and multi-panel plots with bounding-box metadata for every chart element and build a Visual Question Answering (VQA) suite scaffolded on a four-level description model, from basic conceptual questions to interpretive and analytical ones, then test a range of LMMs quantitatively. **Accuracy falls as the number of panels, the number of plot elements, and question difficulty increase**, and because model accuracy is expected to shift quickly, the analysis also weighs cost against performance. The question-answer pairs, plot-generation code, and element-level bounding boxes are released.

papers.title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
papers.abstract: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. We evaluate twenty-six models, nineteen open-weight and seven closed, under a common harness, scorer and panel of LLM judges. Our main finding is that an open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, provided it is given enough turns. The benchmark's published limit on agent messages is a confound: a task that exhausts the limit scores zero on every checkpoint, including those it had already passed, so results at that limit partly measure which models finish in time. At the published limit the leading open-weight and closed models cannot be distinguished. With the limit relaxed, the models it was truncating recover, and the highest rewards belong to open-weight models. Among the leading models, price is a poor guide to capability: models with similar rewards differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. Because the benchmark's checkpoint scores largely record what an agent did or mentioned, we also introduce stage-level metrics that score what the agent submits, by executing its detection queries in the telemetry store and judging its outputs against the answer key. Rather than combining them into one more overall reward, we show that different models lead different stages, which suggests routing each stage of the workflow to the model that performs it best rather than choosing a single model by its overall score. We also report how many tokens each model generates, and find that the share of output spent on thinking does not track the reward.
papers.summary: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work must choose between open-weight models they can run and audit themselves and far more expensive closed frontier models. The study evaluates 26 models, 19 open-weight and 7 closed, on `CTI-REALM`, a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store, under a common harness, scorer, and panel of LLM judges. The main finding is that **an open-weight model can match the strongest closed models at less than a tenth of their cost, given enough turns**, and that the benchmark's published cap on agent messages is a confound, because a task that exhausts it scores zero on every checkpoint, so relaxing the cap lets truncated models recover and puts open-weight models at the top. New stage-level metrics that execute the submitted detection queries and judge outputs against an answer key show different models leading different stages, which argues for routing each workflow stage to its best model, while price is a poor guide to capability and the share of output spent on thinking does not track reward.

papers.title: ULPack: Reference-Conditioned Lossless Compression of Checkpoint Trajectories
papers.abstract: Studying model training requires checkpoint trajectories, whose storage cost limits temporal resolution. Although adjacent checkpoints are numerically close, existing lossless codecs either operate on XOR bit patterns or ignore trajectory-specific conditional structure. We show that a reference weight's exponent predicts the bit length of its displacement in ordered floating-point space without side information. We introduce \textbf{ULPack}, a lossless codec which exploits this dependence by conditioning entropy models of ordered-integer residuals on the reference exponent. Across bfloat16, float16, and float32 trajectories, ULPack reduces storage by up to 27\% against ZipNN, 21\% against zstd-19, and 11.5\% against FM-Delta. Across two dense trajectories, compression improves as updates shrink and reference conditioning strengthens, while near uniform low-order bits set the remaining compression floor and earlier checkpoints add little information.
papers.summary: Studying training dynamics needs dense checkpoint trajectories, but storage cost limits how often checkpoints can be kept, and existing lossless codecs either operate on XOR bit patterns or ignore the conditional structure between adjacent checkpoints. The authors show that a reference weight's floating-point exponent predicts the bit length of its displacement in ordered floating-point space without any side information, and `ULPack` exploits this by conditioning entropy models of ordered-integer residuals on that exponent. Across bfloat16, float16, and float32 trajectories it **cuts storage by up to 27% relative to `ZipNN`**, 21% relative to `zstd-19`, and 11.5% relative to `FM-Delta`, with compression improving as updates shrink, while near-uniform low-order bits set the remaining floor and earlier checkpoints add little information.

papers.title: Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function
papers.abstract: Could model-free reinforcement learning algorithms actually be learning a model of the environment? In this work, we apply counterfactual interventions which hold everything about a state fixed, besides a targeted change, to explore if the value function of a Proximal Policy Optimization agent forms a world model of the Crafter environment. Despite only being trained to optimize reward, we discover that the value function learns concepts such as the rules governing when a diamond is collectible, water and food having an impact on health, heuristics regarding inventory, and more. Finally, we discuss the safety implications of our visualizations and some shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents that will prevent us from building truly advanced machine intelligence.
papers.summary: The question is whether model-free reinforcement learning agents, trained only to maximise reward, end up learning a model of their environment anyway. The authors apply counterfactual interventions that hold a state fixed except for one targeted change and examine how the value function of a Proximal Policy Optimization (`PPO`) agent responds in the `Crafter` environment. **The value function encodes concepts such as the rules for when a diamond is collectible, the effect of water and food on health, and inventory heuristics**, despite never being trained on them directly. The paper closes by discussing safety implications of these visualisations and shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents that the authors argue block more advanced machine intelligence.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.
papers.summary: Explaining a vision-language model (VLM) prediction means tracing the influence of training examples down to the multimodal evidence that carries it, yet existing attribution methods mostly stop at the whole-sample level, and recent latent-mediated influence methods for language models lack multimodal and spatial structure. `MOSAIC` (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization) learns a shared sparse image-text latent space whose concepts are sparse within each modality, supported on contiguous image regions, aligned to descriptive phrases, and approximately decorrelated, then applies `EK-FAC` to decompose training-example influence through those concepts and localise it to text phrases and image regions. Evaluated on `Qwen` and `Gemma` across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering, the features are more localised and coherent without hurting task behaviour, and **ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency**. Visual evidence can substantially reorganise training-data attribution while preserving much of the shared latent structure.

papers.title: Simple Linear Corrections for Compression in Late Interaction
papers.abstract:
Late-interaction (multi-vector) models represent documents using a set of token-level vectors, providing a middle ground between cross-encoders and dense encoders in terms of quality and cost of embedding. However, compared to the latter, the indices are costly to store and score. Pooling and pruning based compression techniques are deployed widely but deteriorate in quality noticeably with aggressive compression. We investigate whether a lightweight change to the scoring function can recover retrieval quality after document-vector compression. For each combination of encoder, compressor, and vector budget, we learn a global linear correction by distilling the uncompressed model's score distributions over candidate documents. The encoder and compressor remain frozen, and the correction can be applied to each query at search time or once, offline, to the stored vectors.
  We evaluate the method with ColBERTv2 and Jina v4 on MS MARCO and BEIR, and with ColPali2 on the ViDoRe v3 visual document retrieval benchmark. Experiments cover four training-free compression methods, multiple vector budgets, in-domain adaptation, and transfer from MS MARCO to BEIR. In the in-domain setting, the correction improves over baseline compression in 154 of 160 BEIR settings, while transfer from MS MARCO is more variable across models and datasets. We also find that matrices trained with synthetic queries can improve over baseline compression on ViDoRe v3. These results show that a small learned correction can recover some of the quality lost to compression without retraining the encoder or recompressing the documents.
papers.summary: Late-interaction retrieval models such as `ColBERTv2` store a vector per document token, which costs far more to index and score than single-vector encoders, and the pooling and pruning techniques used to shrink those indices lose noticeable quality under aggressive compression. The authors learn a global linear correction to the scoring function for each combination of encoder, compressor, and vector budget by distilling the uncompressed model's score distributions over candidate documents, leaving the encoder and compressor frozen and applying the correction either per query at search time or once offline to the stored vectors. Tested with `ColBERTv2` and `Jina v4` on `MS MARCO` and `BEIR`, and with `ColPali2` on the `ViDoRe v3` visual document benchmark, across four training-free compressors and multiple budgets, **the correction beats baseline compression in 154 of 160 in-domain `BEIR` settings**, while transfer from `MS MARCO` is more variable and matrices trained with synthetic queries help on `ViDoRe v3`.

papers.title: Refined Grid Sampling for Efficient Implicit Neural Representations of Large-Scale Scientific Data
papers.abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a powerful framework for modeling high-dimensional physical fields, but their training remains inefficient because evaluating dense coordinate grids is computationally expensive. Existing coordinate-pruning strategies rely on local error functions that can oversample correlated points and incur substantial overhead from full-grid error evaluation. We introduce Refined Grid Sampling (RGS), which combines stratified grid sampling, error-based refinement, and dynamic grid-resolution adjustment. This design reduces spatial redundancy without evaluating errors over the full grid. On high-resolution Navier--Stokes fields, RGS achieves higher reconstruction accuracy within a fixed wall-clock budget and reaches the accuracy of full-grid training up to $6\times$ faster than the evaluated baselines.
papers.summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) can model high-dimensional physical fields, but training them is slow because evaluating dense coordinate grids is expensive, and existing coordinate-pruning schemes rely on local error functions that oversample correlated points and require full-grid error evaluation. Refined Grid Sampling (`RGS`) combines stratified grid sampling, error-based refinement, and dynamic adjustment of grid resolution to cut spatial redundancy without ever evaluating error over the full grid. On high-resolution Navier-Stokes fields it reaches higher reconstruction accuracy within a fixed wall-clock budget and **matches full-grid training accuracy up to 6 times faster** than the evaluated baselines.

papers.title: Token-Budgeted Candidate Retrieval for 3D Scene-Grounded VLMs: Category Names vs. Pairwise Geometry
papers.abstract: Under a fixed context budget, which objects and relations should a 3D scene-grounded VLM see first? On ScanNet indoor referring benchmarks (Dai et al., 2017), matching the query to object category names outperforms pairwise geometry scoring at every reported K. The gaps are largest at high recall. Analytic pairwise cues beat per-object cue scoring and query-agnostic kNN graphs, including on paraphrases. MiniLM and BGE-small still score higher on those splits. We evaluate token-budgeted candidate retrieval with axis-aligned boxes, a token-ratio metric, training-free baselines, two small encoders that match q to each object's category name, and QCRR (Query-Conditioned Relation Retrieval), a deterministic pairwise-geometry scorer. Across ScanRefer gt_val plus a custom 20% scan-id split of Nr3D and Sr3D (35,504 queries; not official ReferIt3D val), additive noun matching reaches R@10 0.864 on ScanRefer against QCRR's 0.626; MiniLM and BGE-small reach 0.911 to 0.913 on ScanRefer and 0.941 to 0.947 on Nr3D. A corrected 3DGraphLLM harness (native Acc@0.25 0.67 on the full graph, n=300 ScanRefer queries) shows that context selection changes downstream accuracy under a matched object budget (Random 0.44, QCRR 0.56, MiniLM 0.67, oracle 0.70). Semantic retrieval beats hand-designed geometry on that harness. We will release the protocol, retriever implementations, and per-query outputs so new selectors can be swapped in without rewriting the analysis.
papers.summary: When a 3D scene-grounded vision-language model has a fixed context budget, the question is which objects and relations it should be shown first. The study compares training-free candidate retrievers on `ScanNet` indoor referring benchmarks, including additive noun matching between the query and object category names, two small encoders (`MiniLM` and `BGE-small`), and `QCRR` (Query-Conditioned Relation Retrieval), a deterministic pairwise-geometry scorer, using axis-aligned boxes and a token-ratio metric across `ScanRefer` plus custom splits of `Nr3D` and `Sr3D` totalling 35,504 queries. Matching category names beats pairwise geometry at every reported K, with noun matching reaching R@10 of 0.864 on `ScanRefer` against 0.626 for `QCRR` and the small encoders scoring higher still, and on a corrected `3DGraphLLM` harness **context selection moves downstream accuracy from 0.44 with random selection to 0.67 with `MiniLM`, close to the oracle's 0.70**. The protocol, retriever implementations, and per-query outputs are to be released so new selectors can be swapped in.

papers.title: Should SLMs be in the Driver's Seat? A Study of Local Models as Interpreters in Cloud-Written Agent Programs
papers.abstract: The most accurate agents executing user-provided tasks are driven by large, cloud-hosted models, which solve them by reading the private data of the user. Agents powered by models small enough to run on edge devices keep that data local, but yield far worse results. A third option is to have cloud models write a program that devices execute: the data stays local, but as the program is written before any data is seen, it fails whenever a step depends on interpreting content that appears only at run time. We explore an intermediate architecture, in which the cloud-written program defers bounded questions over user data to a small local model through an ordinary function call. On AppWorld this improves the success rate of a code-only agent in all six combinations of backbone model and test partition we evaluate, by up to 14.9pp, recovering a substantial part of the gap to a cloud-hosted ReAct loop while keeping user data on the device.
papers.summary: The most capable task agents run on cloud-hosted models that read a user's private data, while agents small enough for edge devices keep data local but perform far worse, and having the cloud write a program for the device to run fails whenever a step depends on content that only appears at run time. The proposed architecture keeps the cloud-written program but lets it defer bounded questions about user data to a small local model through an ordinary function call, so the data never leaves the device. On `AppWorld`, this **raises the success rate of a code-only agent in all six backbone-and-partition combinations tested, by up to 14.9 percentage points**, recovering a substantial part of the gap to a cloud-hosted `ReAct` loop.

papers.title: Agreement versus Softmax under Spatial Disambiguation
papers.abstract: ScanRefer Multiple queries require spatial disambiguation: several instances of the target class are present, and the referencer must pick one. When per-query logits were never logged, a common substitute is cross-epoch agreement. On the full ScanRefer validation set (9,508 queries; GeoClassifier with ground-truth proposals), object-level softmax is similarly miscalibrated on Unique and Multiple (ECE 0.068 vs. 0.102; the scene-bootstrap gap interval includes zero). Fixed-final agreement on the same checkpoints reports ECE 0.041 vs. 0.272 (gap +0.231). Modal-vote agreement is 0.045 vs. 0.318. Most Multiple errors are same-class wrong-instance (45.6%); geometric miss (H2) is 59.6%, and wrong-category (H1) is 16.7%. A non-monotone H1 pattern does not appear under the default fixed-final protocol, and we retract it. Logit-free thresholds rank spatially hard queries poorly. If only agreement was logged, calibrate abstention on Multiple and report wrong-instance rates with H1.
papers.summary: Queries in the `ScanRefer` Multiple split require spatial disambiguation among several instances of the target class, and when per-query logits were never logged, cross-epoch agreement is a common stand-in for confidence. On the full 9,508-query validation set with a `GeoClassifier` on ground-truth proposals, object-level softmax is similarly miscalibrated on the Unique and Multiple splits, with expected calibration error of 0.068 versus 0.102 and a bootstrap gap interval that includes zero, whereas **fixed-final agreement on the same checkpoints shows a far larger gap of 0.041 versus 0.272**, and modal-vote agreement shows 0.045 versus 0.318. Most Multiple errors are same-class wrong-instance picks at 45.6%, and logit-free thresholds rank spatially hard queries poorly. A previously reported non-monotone wrong-category pattern does not appear under the default fixed-final protocol and is retracted, with the recommendation that agreement-only setups calibrate abstention on Multiple and report wrong-instance rates alongside wrong-category rates.

papers.title: Modeling the Arrival Time of Information-Bearing Events in Natural Language
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is distributed over time is fundamental to modeling natural language. While existing empirical studies primarily rely on post-hoc analysis of information-theoretic metrics, such as surprisal, little is known about the generation processes under the surface. We propose a novel approach for addressing this gap using the tool of neural temporal point processes (TPPs) by modeling the key information-bearing events in text sequences with learnable event intensity functions. Our model takes the history of event intervals and the contextual semantic representations from LLMs as input, and predicts the future arrival times for two types of events: new-word and high-surprisal-token. The experimental results reveal an interesting distinction in event intensities: LLMs tend to produce new words at significantly higher rates than humans, while high-surprisal tokens do not exhibit the difference. A decaying pattern of intensity over time is found in new-word events for both humans and LLMs, but not in high-surprisal-token events. Our findings revisit and extend previous studies that use simpler methods; provide supplementary evidence for theories about constrained context representation inherent in human language production; and find a new angle to view human and LLM generation differences.
papers.summary: How information is spread over time in text is usually studied through post-hoc analysis of metrics such as surprisal, leaving the generative process underneath largely unexamined. The authors model key information-bearing events in text with neural temporal point processes (TPPs), feeding the history of event intervals and contextual representations from LLMs into learnable intensity functions that predict when the next new word or high-surprisal token will arrive. **LLMs produce new words at significantly higher rates than humans, while high-surprisal tokens show no such difference**, and intensity decays over time for new-word events in both human and LLM text but not for high-surprisal-token events. The results extend earlier studies that used simpler methods and offer supporting evidence for theories of constrained context representation in human language production.

papers.title: Embedding Graph Kernel Entropy (EGKE): Fine-grained Hallucination Detection for LLMs from Embeddings
papers.abstract: Hallucination detection is critical for ensuring the reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world deployments. While recent works, such as Semantic Entropy (SE) and Kernel Language Entropy (KLE), identify hallucinations by measuring semantic disagreement across multiple generated responses using Natural Language Inference (NLI) models, these methods depend on separately loaded NLI classifiers to estimate pairwise semantic similarity, introducing significant computational overhead. We propose Embedding Graph Kernel Entropy (EGKE), a variant of Kernel Language Entropy (KLE) that replaces its NLI-derived semantic graph with a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel applied to dense sentence embeddings generated by a BGE embedding model, while retaining KLE's graph Laplacian, heat kernel, and von Neumann entropy formulation unchanged. By computing similarities directly in a continuous embedding space, the proposed method provides a symmetric and computationally efficient alternative to NLI-based semantic comparison. We evaluate our approach across 30 experimental setups (covering multiple question-answer datasets and open-weight LLM families) using both AUROC and AUARC, and demonstrate that this RBF-based method achieves competitive hallucination detection performance against state-of-the-art methods.
papers.summary: Hallucination detectors such as Semantic Entropy (`SE`) and Kernel Language Entropy (`KLE`) measure semantic disagreement across several sampled responses, but they depend on separately loaded Natural Language Inference (NLI) classifiers for pairwise similarity, which adds substantial compute. Embedding Graph Kernel Entropy (`EGKE`) keeps KLE's graph Laplacian, heat kernel, and von Neumann entropy formulation unchanged but replaces the NLI-derived semantic graph with a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel over dense sentence embeddings from a `BGE` model, giving a symmetric and cheaper similarity measure. Across 30 experimental setups spanning multiple question-answering datasets and open-weight LLM families, measured by AUROC and AUARC, **the embedding-based variant performs competitively with state-of-the-art detectors**.

papers.title: Cortex: Measurement-Gated Evolution and Pruning of Coding-Agent Skills and Rules
papers.abstract:
Coding agents such as Claude Code also follow text files that developers write for them: a project file, skills the agent may choose to open, and rules that load automatically when the agent reads matching files. We call these files the agent's harness. Developers add to it whenever they correct the agent, but one success proves little: the same agent can pass a task once and fail it the next time.
  We present Cortex, a tool that tests changes to the harness instead of trusting them. It saves fixes from the developer's sessions as replayable tasks, finds the corrections that recur, writes one skill or rule at a time, and keeps it only if repeated runs with and without it show a net gain and no task made noticeably worse. Existing text is tested the same way before it is deleted, and Cortex neither adds nor deletes text the agent never used.
  We tested Cortex with Claude Haiku 4.5 on a repository built for the purpose, with conventions the model tends to break, one area with nothing to learn, and a script playing the developer. On held-out tasks, the harnesses it built made the agent follow the conventions far more often than no skills or rules did, left the comparison area unchanged, and added no text read on every turn. Rules, which load automatically, did most of the work; skills helped only when offered with the files a task touches, and those offered on every turn were rarely opened. Cortex kept none of the useless or harmful suggestions we planted, but the agent never opened the useless ones or the harmful skills, and it reached no verdict on the harmful rules, so the test shows that Cortex keeps no unused text, not that it detects damage. Under the stronger Claude Sonnet 5 a single run's harness added little, and on a real open-source project, where the agent was rarely corrected, Cortex found nothing to learn. We release the tool, the lab and its data.
papers.summary: Coding agents such as `Claude Code` take direction from a harness of developer-written text, a project file, skills the agent may open, and rules that load automatically, and developers extend it after every correction even though one success proves little about whether an addition helps. `Cortex` saves fixes from developer sessions as replayable tasks, finds recurring corrections, writes one skill or rule at a time, and keeps it only if repeated runs with and without it show a net gain and no task gets noticeably worse, testing existing text the same way before deleting it. With `Claude Haiku 4.5` on a purpose-built repository, **the harnesses it built made the agent follow conventions far more often on held-out tasks** without adding text read on every turn, and rules did most of the work, since skills offered on every turn were rarely opened. Planted useless and harmful suggestions were discarded only because the agent never used them, so damage detection remains untested, and with the stronger `Claude Sonnet 5` or on a real open-source project with few corrections the tool found little or nothing to learn.

papers.title: Learnable Low-Rank Polynomial Sketch for Effective Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Softmax attention in Transformers suffers from quadratic complexity in sequence length, making it impractical for long-context applications. Linear attention alleviates this issue by replacing the exponential kernel with alternative functions that enable linear-time computation. Among existing linear attention approaches, recent studies have shown that polynomial kernels are particularly effective, as they exhibit sparse and spiky behavior similar to softmax attention, which emphasizes large dot products while suppressing irrelevant interactions. However, the exact computation of high-degree polynomial kernels is infeasible for high-dimensional representations. As a result, prior work relies on approximate polynomial kernels. This introduces a non-negligible approximation error. In this paper, we show that, from the perspective of polynomial kernel approximation, existing linear attention methods are still suboptimal. We propose \textbf{L}earnable \textbf{Lo}w-Rank \textbf{P}olynomial \textbf{S}ketch (LLoPS), a principled and flexible framework for approximating polynomial kernels with linear attention. Our method learns a low-rank polynomial sketch that provably achieves a strictly smaller approximation error than existing approaches. Experiment results show that LLoPS achieves the highest performance across extensive benchmarks, comparing with various linear attention baselines.
papers.summary: Softmax attention scales quadratically with sequence length, and linear attention swaps the exponential kernel for cheaper feature maps, among which polynomial kernels work well because they stay sparse and spiky like softmax, but exact high-degree polynomial kernels are infeasible in high dimensions and existing approximations carry non-negligible error. The authors argue that, viewed as polynomial kernel approximation, current linear attention methods are still suboptimal, and propose Learnable Low-Rank Polynomial Sketch (`LLoPS`), which learns a low-rank sketch of the polynomial kernel.
