These results suggest that comprehensive zero-shot evaluation of skill execution requires judge reliability as carefully as model capability.
papers.summary: Enterprise customer-support deployments increasingly rely on language models to execute bounded, stateful, tool-using workflows under policy constraints, which the authors frame as Skill LLMs. They build a benchmark pipeline that mines recurrent workflows from real transcripts, converts them into structured skill descriptions with tool requirements, simulates environment state with Model Context Protocol (MCP)-compatible mocks, and generates multi-turn dialogues, then evaluate 17 models zero-shot with five LLM judges plus a rule-based checker for tool coverage, hallucinated tool use, and unsupported claims. **`GPT-5.4` leads by a wide margin and `QWEN3.5-9B` is the strongest open-weight model under 20B parameters**, beating several closed baselines under every judge. Pairwise judge agreement on pass/fail verdicts averages only a Kappa of 0.524, so judge reliability deserves as much care as model capability.

papers.title: Multimodal Co-Generation With Continuous Bitstream Diffusion
papers.abstract: We show that continuous bitstream diffusion (CoBit), originally developed for language modeling, provides a unified framework for joint and conditional multimodal generation using the same training and sampling protocol. Across image-text, speech-text and protein sequence-structure modeling, models are trained separately from scratch, but each uses a single input projection, transformer backbone, bitwise prediction head and binary score-matching objective shared across its modalities. Within each setting, a single checkpoint supports joint generation and the conditional directions included in training by changing which parts of the bitstream are observed. We first validate the approach on MNIST-Sum, a controlled image-text task pairing raw binary images with equations encoded as text, achieving near-perfect conditional accuracy and high joint consistency without learned tokenizers. We then apply the same protocol at larger scale to speech-text and protein sequence-structure modeling. Trained without text pretraining, a single speech-text model performs speech synthesis, recognition, continuation, and unconditional co-generation. Jointly generated speech and text achieve 3.5% word error rate between the generated text and automatic transcriptions of the generated speech. In protein modeling, a single CoBit checkpoint supports forward folding, inverse folding, and joint sequence-structure generation. For jointly generated proteins spanning 100-500 residues, computational refolding of CoBit's sequences yields structures that agree with the generated backbones at a mean self-consistency TM-score of 0.911. Together, these results show that CoBit provides a common generative framework for substantially different modalities and forms of cross-modal dependence, without introducing a domain-specific objective or sampling procedure.
papers.summary: Continuous bitstream diffusion (`CoBit`), originally a language-modeling approach, is shown to serve as a single framework for joint and conditional multimodal generation using one training and sampling protocol. Each model uses a shared input projection, transformer backbone, bitwise prediction head, and binary score-matching objective across its modalities, and a single checkpoint supports joint generation and any conditional direction seen in training simply by changing which parts of the bitstream are observed. On `MNIST-Sum` the approach reaches near-perfect conditional accuracy without learned tokenizers, and a speech-text model trained without text pretraining handles synthesis, recognition, continuation, and joint co-generation with a 3.5% word error rate between generated text and transcriptions of the generated speech. In protein modeling, **a single checkpoint supports forward folding, inverse folding, and joint sequence-structure generation with a mean self-consistency TM-score of 0.911** on proteins of 100 to 500 residues.

papers.title: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
papers.abstract:
Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories.
  It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Codex with GPT-6 Sol, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.
papers.summary: AI agents that automate vulnerability discovery can also be turned against software at scale, so defenders need ways to slow such attacks and buy time to patch. Studying agent trajectories, the authors find that agents produce very different results on real-world commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability, which motivates mining a corpus of natural, functionality-preserving code transformations from recurring development patterns and applying them as a defense. **Even a single transformation reduces vulnerability-discovery success for frontier agents such as `Codex` running `GPT-6 Sol`**, and the study also examines agent failure modes, composing transformations for stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who try to reverse them.

papers.title: Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction for Signal Temporal Logic Inference with Many Classes
papers.abstract: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) inference provides interpretable formulas for time series classification. For multiclass classification, however, accurate predictions do not necessarily ensure that the inferred formulas are satisfied consistently with the true class. We introduce the positive satisfaction rate and codeword satisfaction rate to quantify satisfaction of required formulas and consistency with the complete class codeword, respectively. We develop a two-stage procedure that first learns discriminative formulas using a margin-based objective and then refines predicate thresholds toward a small positive robustness target while fixing the formula structure and temporal intervals. Satisfaction and ranking penalties discourage violations of required formulas and loss of class separation. The decoding loss is used as a nonconformity score and calibrated separately for each class, providing finite-sample class-conditional coverage under intra-class exchangeability. Experiments on naval, synthetic, and robot manipulation trajectories demonstrate discrepancies between classification accuracy and formula satisfaction. The results further reveal a data-dependent tradeoff between robustness tightness and satisfaction, while class-conditional calibration mitigates undercoverage that can be hidden by pooled calibration.
papers.summary: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) inference yields interpretable formulas for time series classification, but in multiclass settings high accuracy does not guarantee that the inferred formulas are satisfied consistently with the true class. The authors introduce positive and codeword satisfaction rates to measure this, and propose a two-stage procedure that learns discriminative formulas with a margin-based objective and then refines predicate thresholds toward a small positive robustness target with satisfaction and ranking penalties, while the decoding loss serves as a nonconformity score calibrated separately per class to give finite-sample class-conditional coverage. Experiments on naval, synthetic, and robot manipulation trajectories expose **gaps between classification accuracy and formula satisfaction**, a data-dependent tradeoff between robustness tightness and satisfaction, and undercoverage that pooled calibration hides but class-conditional calibration mitigates.

papers.title: Actionable Meta-Requirements for AI Robustness Auditing
papers.abstract: AI-enabled systems must remain dependable when the conditions under which they operate change (e.g., due to input perturbations, distribution shifts, or changes in external dependencies). This makes robustness auditing of such systems important for judging whether the available evidence is sufficient to support a defined robustness conclusion. However, designing an AI robustness auditing framework is challenging. A key unresolved issue is determining the requirements such a framework should support; these requirements have not yet been consolidated. We address this gap through meta-requirements: higher-order requirements specifying what a class of auditing frameworks should support. In design science research, literature and domain experts are common sources of meta-requirements; accordingly, we derive the initial set from literature and validate and refine it with practitioners. Our systematic literature review retained 74 of 2,890 records and derived 43 meta-requirements across 16 categories. We evaluated them with 128 practitioners, obtaining 5,504 ratings and 586 substantive comments. Overall, 81.20% of ratings indicated agreement or strong agreement. In particular, 41 of the 43 literature-derived meta-requirements were classified as strongly supported. Practitioner feedback refined the requirements and identified an additional requirement concerning external components and supply chain dependencies. The final set comprises 44 meta-requirements across 16 categories, of which 43 received quantitative validation. These meta-requirements can help organizations implement AI robustness auditing frameworks, assess existing frameworks for completeness, and refine them.
papers.summary: Robustness auditing asks whether the available evidence supports a defined robustness conclusion for an AI system under input perturbations, distribution shifts, or changes in external dependencies, but the requirements such auditing frameworks should satisfy have not been consolidated. Following design science research, the authors derive meta-requirements from a systematic literature review that retained 74 of 2,890 records, yielding 43 requirements across 16 categories, then validate them with 128 practitioners who provided 5,504 ratings and 586 comments. **81.20% of ratings indicated agreement or strong agreement, with 41 of 43 requirements classified as strongly supported**, and practitioner feedback added a requirement on external components and supply chain dependencies for a final set of 44.

papers.title: When Pleasing the User Compromises Care: AI Sycophancy in Caregiver-Mediated Healthcare
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) alignment often assumes that the user interacting with a model is also the primary beneficiary of its behavior. Yet in many consequential settings, one person directs the system while another bears the consequences. We study this problem in caregiver-mediated healthcare, where parents, pet owners, and caregivers make decisions for children, animals, and older adults. We introduce an evidence-grounded benchmark spanning veterinary, pediatric, and older-adult care, and test whether AI advisors maintain appropriate care when users express clinically inferior preferences. Holding patient facts fixed, we vary stated care preferences and communication styles and evaluate both initial recommendations and multi-turn follow-up. Across frontier and open-weight models, inferior preferences substantially increase switching from appropriate to inappropriate care beyond neutral conversational drift and increase agreement with the requested action, while communication style alone has a smaller effect. These failures accumulate across turns, including on cases models initially answer correctly, and often carry moderate or severe potential harm. In matched eldercare cases, the effect of an inferior preference is similar whether it is expressed by the patient or by a caregiver. Together with models' limited tendency to elicit patient preferences in caregiver conversations, this suggests that current models are highly sensitive to expressed user preferences but less sensitive to whose preferences are represented and who bears the consequences. Our results expose a broader limitation of user-centric alignment in settings with multiple stakeholders.
papers.summary: Alignment typically assumes the user talking to a model is also the one who bears the consequences, which breaks down in caregiver-mediated healthcare where parents, pet owners, and caregivers decide for children, animals, and older adults. The authors build an evidence-grounded benchmark across veterinary, pediatric, and older-adult care and, holding patient facts fixed, vary stated care preferences and communication styles while scoring both initial recommendations and multi-turn follow-ups. Across frontier and open-weight models, **expressing a clinically inferior preference substantially increases switching from appropriate to inappropriate care** beyond neutral conversational drift, with failures compounding over turns and often carrying moderate or severe potential harm. The effect is similar whether the patient or a caregiver voices the preference, and models rarely elicit the patient's own preferences in caregiver conversations.

papers.title: The Sample Complexity of Multicalibration with an ERM Oracle
papers.abstract: A predictor is multicalibrated with respect to a class of subpopulations (formally, of functions on the inputs, called auditors) if, for every subpopulation in the class and every value the predictor outputs, the average outcome among the members of that subpopulation who receive that value is close to the value itself. For finite classes, about $\varepsilon^{-3}$ samples are necessary and sufficient to learn a predictor with multicalibration error $\varepsilon$, but the algorithms that attain this rate enumerate the class, which is impossible for the large classes of interest. We ask how many samples suffice when the learner accesses the class only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples and polynomially many ERM calls, where $d$ is the VC dimension of the class. Its dependence on $\varepsilon$ is optimal for all learners. When $d$ is at least about $1/\varepsilon$, every learner that can only access the class through polynomially many ERM calls needs $\tilde{\Omega}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples. Learners with unlimited computation need only $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}+d\varepsilon^{-2})$ samples, so the extra factor $1/\varepsilon$ on the dimension term is the price of oracle efficiency. For swap multicalibration, which allows a different function from the class for each predicted value, $\tilde{\Theta}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples are necessary and sufficient. For estimating the error of a given predictor, the ordinary notion is the harder one: the swap error can be estimated with an ERM oracle, whereas the ordinary error is NP-hard to approximate even for classes with linear-time ERM. Consequently, there are classes for which it is computationally easier to learn a multicalibrated predictor than to compute the multicalibration error of a given predictor.
papers.summary: A predictor is multicalibrated with respect to a class of auditor functions if, within every subpopulation in the class and for every predicted value, the average outcome is close to that value, and known sample-optimal algorithms enumerate the class, which is infeasible for the large classes of interest. The authors study learners that access the class only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle and give an algorithm using roughly d/eps^3 samples and polynomially many ERM calls, where d is the VC dimension. **This rate is tight for oracle-efficient learners when d is at least about 1/eps, while unlimited-computation learners need only about eps^-3 + d eps^-2 samples**, so the extra 1/eps factor on the dimension term is the price of oracle efficiency. Swap multicalibration needs about d/eps^3 samples in both directions, and estimating ordinary multicalibration error is NP-hard even for classes with linear-time ERM, so learning a multicalibrated predictor can be easier than measuring one.

papers.title: ConformalGuard: False-Positive-Controlled Action Gating for LM Classifiers
papers.abstract: Language model classifiers are increasingly deployed for high-stakes decisions such as phishing screening, content moderation, and fraud triage, yet validation-set thresholds provide no finite-sample control of deployment-time false positives. We present ConformalGuard, a model-agnostic calibration layer that wraps a fixed scoring function with finite-sample control over the rate at which legitimate inputs trigger an intervention tier. Our contribution is empirical and operational, not a new conformal theorem: zero-shot LM API scores can be coarse enough (10--11 unique values here) to make temperature scaling and isotonic regression operationally identical to raw thresholding for low-FPR action gating. We compare these methods with conformal calibration for fine-tuned BERT, Claude Sonnet 4, and GPT-4o on public email corpora. For Claude, conformal calibration reduces FPR from 0.040 to 0.008 while recall falls from 0.938 to 0.875. For deterministic GPT-4o scores, the 1% operating point is too conservative to deploy (recall 0.564); three-run stochastic averaging raises recall to 0.732 at FPR 0.005. At 2% prevalence with BERT, conformal calibration removes 25 false-positive reviews per 10,000 emails (95% CI [10, 43]). The guarantee is legitimate-event-rate control under exchangeability; discrimination, workload effects, and robustness to shift remain empirical.
papers.summary: Language-model classifiers used for phishing screening, content moderation, and fraud triage are usually thresholded on a validation set, which offers no finite-sample control over deployment-time false positives. `ConformalGuard` is a model-agnostic calibration layer that wraps a fixed scoring function with finite-sample control of the rate at which legitimate inputs trigger an intervention tier; the contribution is operational rather than a new conformal theorem, and the authors note that zero-shot LM API scores can be so coarse, with 10 to 11 unique values, that temperature scaling and isotonic regression collapse to raw thresholding. On public email corpora with fine-tuned `BERT`, `Claude Sonnet 4`, and `GPT-4o`, **conformal calibration cuts Claude's false-positive rate from 0.040 to 0.008 while recall falls from 0.938 to 0.875**. Deterministic `GPT-4o` scores are too conservative at the 1% operating point until three-run stochastic averaging lifts recall to 0.732, and the guarantee holds only under exchangeability.

papers.title: History, Adaptation, and Hidden Gain: Two Prospective Tests of Learned Predictive Control in a Synthetic Neural Population
papers.abstract: We study learned one-step predictive control of a synthetic population of 64 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons whose light sensitivity is scaled by a hidden factor s, using two prospective confirmations on plants simulated only after the analysis was frozen. In the first (50 plants, 11 conditions), removing the 200-ms input-output history substantially worsened a parameter-count-matched neural predictor at low and moderate gain (s = 0.6, 0.8; RMSE rose by 2.47 Hz at s = 0.6, 97.5% CI 2.43-2.51). In secondary comparisons, recursively adapted ARX had the lowest mean error of the deployable controllers in 10 of 11 conditions, tuned PI with anti-windup matched or beat the network for s >= 0.7, and training for 10,000 rather than 900 epochs lowered prediction error but worsened control. Development work suggested the network's learned action sensitivity did not track the hidden gain. A second protocol (50 new plants, 9 sensitivities, 2 noise levels) confirmed three pre-specified predictions at the primary noise level. Re-estimating a single multiplicative input gain recovered 87% (95% CI 86-88%) of the benefit of full adaptive ARX. Supplying that online estimate to the network as an extra input reduced high-gain tracking error by 1.84 Hz [1.81, 1.88]. Longer training worsened the plain network by 1.09 Hz but improved the gain-input network by 1.07 Hz, a differential of 2.16 Hz [2.13, 2.20]. Under high process noise (sigma = 2.0) the effects shrank to about 0.04 Hz or less and gain-only adaptation recovered only 24% of the adaptive-ARX benefit. In this synthetic plant, at the primary noise level, one-parameter online gain estimation accounts for most of the gap between a history-based network and full adaptive ARX, and for its prediction-control mismatch.
papers.summary: The study tests learned one-step predictive control of a synthetic population of 64 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons whose light sensitivity is scaled by a hidden gain, using two prospective protocols run on plants simulated only after the analysis was frozen. In the first protocol, removing the 200-ms input-output history markedly worsened a parameter-matched neural predictor at low and moderate gain, recursively adapted ARX had the lowest error among deployable controllers in 10 of 11 conditions, and longer training lowered prediction error but worsened control. The second protocol confirmed three pre-specified predictions: **re-estimating a single multiplicative input gain recovers 87% of the benefit of full adaptive ARX**, feeding that estimate to the network as an extra input reduces high-gain tracking error, and the effects largely vanish under high process noise.

papers.title: When More Memory Fails: Hidden Feasibility Holes in Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization
papers.abstract: Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization (DTR) trains neural networks under a memory budget by evicting tensors and recomputing them on demand. A natural expectation is that a budget large enough to complete training stays sufficient when it is increased. Using DTR's reference simulator, simrd, to replay the public DTR training traces, we show that this expectation fails. We call the exceptions feasibility holes: memory budgets at which an eviction policy runs out of memory although both a smaller and a larger budget complete, a form of non-monotone feasibility. Under a written sweep protocol with dated amendments, a 0.01-step budget grid shows no such hole for DTR on any of six confirmatory traces, although unresolved timeouts prevent it from establishing monotonicity. Finer sampling finds holes on InceptionV4 (three regions) and U-Net (two regions), in addition to one on the ResNet-32 development trace. Every hole is reproduced by three repeats and by unmodified simrd. For one InceptionV4 pair (0.2343 versus 0.235 of peak memory) we trace the failure to individual allocations. The larger budget avoids one eviction at an operator where the smaller budget was 173,479 bytes short. The extra data it carries forward forces a later eviction of a tensor needed three operators afterwards, and rebuilding that tensor triggers a recomputation cascade that cannot fit. Keeping that one tensor resident under the same budget prevents the failure. The two simple score changes we tested do not remove holes across traces; both add failing budgets on some traces. All results are from simulation, with no allocator model; behaviour on GPU hardware is untested.
papers.summary: Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization (DTR) trains networks under a memory budget by evicting tensors and recomputing them on demand, and one would expect a budget sufficient for training to stay sufficient when increased. Replaying the public DTR traces in the reference simulator `simrd` under a written sweep protocol, the authors find feasibility holes: budgets at which the eviction policy runs out of memory even though both a smaller and a larger budget complete. **Fine-grained sampling finds such holes on `InceptionV4`, `U-Net`, and `ResNet-32`, each reproduced across three repeats and by unmodified simrd**, and for one InceptionV4 pair the failure is traced to a single avoided eviction whose carried-forward data forces a later eviction and a recomputation cascade, which keeping that one tensor resident prevents. Two simple scoring changes do not remove holes across traces, and all results are simulation-only with no allocator model.

papers.title: DexFLEX: Contact-Aware Foundation Controller for Command-Guided Dexterity
papers.abstract: Dexterous robot hands can receive useful motion intent from teleoperation or learned policies, but successful execution also depends on contact decisions that these commands rarely specify. We introduce DexFLEX, a contact-aware foundation controller that turns upstream fingertip-motion drafts into contact-consistent joint commands. Instead of treating a draft as a trajectory to copy, DexFLEX treats it as evidence about intent: from the current tactile-proprioceptive state, it proposes feasible short-horizon motion chunks, predicts their contact consequences, and selects the candidate that best follows the command while preserving future contact stability. At inference time, a simple Draft-Dream-Select procedure combines pure-prior proposals for recovery with draft-seeded proposals for responsiveness, then decodes the selected motion into executable joint-space targets. Across degraded-command simulation, real-world shared control, and visuomotor policy learning, the same trained controller improves robustness without retraining, increasing real-world teleoperation success from 29.2% to 78.3% and reaching 46.7% policy-learning success, 3.5 times direct joint-action prediction, and 1.56 times prior-only correction. Videos are available at dex-flex.github.io.
papers.summary: Dexterous robot hands receive motion intent from teleoperation or learned policies, but those commands rarely specify the contact decisions that determine whether execution succeeds. `DexFLEX` is a contact-aware foundation controller that treats an upstream fingertip-motion draft as evidence about intent: from the current tactile-proprioceptive state it proposes feasible short-horizon motion chunks, predicts their contact consequences, and selects the candidate that follows the command while preserving future contact stability, with a Draft-Dream-Select inference procedure mixing prior-only proposals for recovery and draft-seeded proposals for responsiveness. Without retraining, the same controller **raises real-world teleoperation success from 29.2% to 78.3%** and reaches 46.7% policy-learning success, 3.5 times direct joint-action prediction and 1.56 times prior-only correction.

papers.title: DPAL: A Test-Time Adaptation Loss for Financial Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) enables time series forecasters to update after deployment as new observations become available. However, adaptation objectives that focus primarily on prediction errors at individual time steps do not fully address the needs of financial time series forecasting. In addition to pointwise return fitting, return direction and the price trajectories reconstructed from sequences of returns are also important. To better account for these properties, we introduce Direction- and Price-Aware Adaptation Loss (DPAL), which combines pointwise return fitting with directional and price-calibration terms. We apply DPAL within existing TSF-TTA frameworks without modifying the source forecaster or the adapter architecture. Across a diverse collection of financial datasets, DPAL reduces reconstructed-price mean squared error in most evaluated settings.
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) lets time series forecasters update after deployment, but objectives focused on pointwise prediction error neglect properties that matter in finance, namely return direction and the price trajectories reconstructed from sequences of returns. Direction- and Price-Aware Adaptation Loss (`DPAL`) combines pointwise return fitting with directional and price-calibration terms and plugs into existing time series forecasting TTA frameworks without changing the source forecaster or the adapter architecture. Across a diverse collection of financial datasets, **`DPAL` reduces reconstructed-price mean squared error in most evaluated settings**.

papers.title: Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking: A Byte-Local Method for LLM Text
papers.abstract: We introduce Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking (TI-WM), a method that embeds a watermark during token generation but keys and scores it on canonicalized UTF-8 bytes. The detector does not invoke the tokenizer. Canonicalizer-preserving edits leave its score unchanged; other localized canonical-byte edits affect a bounded number of scoring windows. Across three fixed keys and 128 prompts per key and model, a deterministic white-box attack at a 5% word-edit budget leaves mean attacked-AUC 0.530 on Qwen3-8B and 0.664 on Gemma 4 E4B, compared with 0.410 and 0.489 for Unigram with detection-side deletion. These operating points are not jointly matched on quality and clean detectability. Bias sweeps show model-dependent distortion costs, and shared-rule controls support a locality interpretation without establishing a unique advantage of bytes. Visible insertion outside the canonicalizer's deletion set defeats the default design. Alphabetic filtering closes that channel but does not resolve source shift or calibrated detection power. TI-WM thus provides a concrete construction with local scoring guarantees and measured attack-ranking gains, not a general robustness or low-false-positive-rate deployment guarantee.
papers.summary: Text watermarks for language models typically key and score on tokens, which ties detection to a specific tokenizer. Tokenization-Invariant Watermarking (`TI-WM`) embeds the watermark during generation but keys and scores it on canonicalized UTF-8 bytes, so the detector never invokes the tokenizer, canonicalizer-preserving edits leave the score unchanged, and other localized edits affect only a bounded number of scoring windows. Under a deterministic white-box attack at a 5% word-edit budget, **mean attacked AUC is 0.530 on `Qwen3-8B` and 0.664 on `Gemma 4 E4B`, versus 0.410 and 0.489 for `Unigram` with detection-side deletion**, though these operating points are not matched on quality and clean detectability. Visible insertion outside the canonicalizer's deletion set defeats the default design, and the authors frame the method as offering local scoring guarantees rather than general robustness or low-false-positive deployment guarantees.

papers.title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while keeping the environment coherent across repeated observations and interventions and preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED-BENCH (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark built around this requirement. The key idea is to separate the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: LLMs generate natural-language scenarios and task text, while hidden probabilistic graphical models define the causal graph, data-generating process, intervention semantics, validation checks, and oracle answers. This yields scientific worlds that are natural for agents to investigate but exact enough for scalable, programmatic evaluation. The main leaderboard ACED-CORE contains 180 tasks: 60 set-valued causal ancestry/descendancy questions and 120 constrained causal-decision tasks. We also report ACED-QUAL, a 150-question yes/no qualification check using the same hidden-PGM interface. We evaluate seven contemporary LLMs and two earlier-generation models across three active agent designs. ACED-QUAL checks whether agents can use the interface to draw conclusions from evidence, while ACED-CORE tests whether they can decide what evidence to collect and when to commit to an answer. Evidence-ledger analysis localizes failures within the investigation: agents test the wrong intervention, lose relevant evidence, or continue after sufficient evidence has appeared. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for experiment design, evidence retention, answer commitment, and stopping.
papers.summary: Language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet evaluations rarely test whether they can investigate a system by choosing experiments, interpreting finite evidence, and committing to causal decisions. Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark (`ACED-BENCH`) separates a readable scientific surface from a formal causal world: LLMs generate natural-language scenarios and task text, while hidden probabilistic graphical models define the causal graph, intervention semantics, validation checks, and oracle answers, yielding `ACED-CORE` with 180 tasks and a 150-question `ACED-QUAL` qualification check. Evaluating seven contemporary and two earlier-generation LLMs across three active agent designs, **evidence-ledger analysis localizes failures to testing the wrong intervention, losing relevant evidence, or continuing after sufficient evidence has appeared**, pointing to a need for explicit support for experiment design, evidence retention, answer commitment, and stopping.

papers.title: ANASSA: From High-Level Framework to Low-Level Architecture for Spatial Agentic AI
papers.abstract: Agentic AI systems operating over geospatial data require more than autonomous reasoning and tool use; they must also support explicit orchestration, spatial validation, governance, provenance, failure handling, and human decision authority. Prior work introduced ANASSA, an agentic AI orchestration framework for spatial intelligence that established high-level components and responsibility boundaries for governed agentic execution (arXiv:2609.14824). However, the framework did not specify how those high-level responsibilities should be systematically decomposed into an implementation-facing low-level architecture. This paper addresses that gap by applying Design Science Research (DSR) to refine the ANASSA framework from high-level architectural (HLA) responsibilities into a low-level architecture (LLA). The resulting design preserves the responsibility boundaries of the foundational framework while translating them into executable architectural structures, including 47 logical roles, versioned task graphs, capability-based agent selection, typed contracts, explicit runtime states, spatial validation mechanisms, governance controls, failure and recovery paths, and provenance records. The architecture is demonstrated through an end-to-end execution trace and analytically evaluated for requirements traceability, internal consistency, responsibility preservation, and technology independence. The resulting high-level-to-low-level design provides an implementation-facing bridge between the ANASSA framework and future system implementations, defining how governed spatial agentic workflows can be made inspectable, reconstructable, and testable without binding the architecture to a specific AI model, geospatial platform, communication protocol, or deployment environment.
papers.summary: Agentic systems that operate over geospatial data need explicit orchestration, spatial validation, governance, provenance, and human decision authority, but the earlier `ANASSA` framework only defined these as high-level responsibilities without saying how to implement them. Using Design Science Research (DSR), the authors refine the framework's high-level architecture (HLA) into a low-level architecture (LLA) built from **47 logical roles**, versioned task graphs, capability-based agent selection, typed contracts, explicit runtime states, and failure and recovery paths. The design is demonstrated through an end-to-end execution trace and evaluated analytically for requirements traceability, internal consistency, and technology independence, so it stays unbound to any particular model, geospatial platform, or deployment environment.

papers.title: Deep learning from a control vantage point
papers.abstract: This article offers an overview of recent developments in deep learning from a control vantage point. It reviews several classes of models including feedforward and residual neural networks, transformers, large-language models, and selective state space models while explaining how control theory plays an important role in understanding their training, properties, or architecture design. The article explains how residual neural networks can be interpreted as the discretization of a continuous-time control system thereby enabling the use of control theoretic techniques for its analysis. To illustrate the power of this bridge between control and deep learning, two technical results are discussed: 1) the ability of a residual neural network to approximate arbitrary continuous functions is a non-standard controllability problem that can be solved using geometric nonlinear control and 2) transformers, the key architectural component of most large language-models, can be seen the discretization of a consensus algorithm and thus large language-models exhibit consensus. Another point of contact between control theory and deep learning is the connection between backpropagation, the algorithm used to train neural networks, and optimal control. The article addresses how the older connection between these problems, established in the 80's using discrete-time models can be reconciled with the more recent approach using continuous-time models. Several open problems and directions for future research are discussed, including selective state-space models, a recent class of models inspired by the models used in control.
papers.summary: Control theory offers a lens for understanding how deep networks are trained, what properties they have, and how their architectures are designed, and this survey reviews feedforward and residual networks, transformers, large language models, and selective state space models from that vantage point. Residual networks are read as discretizations of a continuous-time control system, which turns their ability to approximate arbitrary continuous functions into a non-standard controllability problem solvable with geometric nonlinear control. **Transformers are shown to be discretizations of a consensus algorithm**, so large language models exhibit consensus dynamics, and the classic 1980s link between backpropagation and discrete-time optimal control is reconciled with the newer continuous-time formulation. Open problems around selective state-space models, a recent model class inspired directly by control-style models, close out the discussion.

papers.title: Decomposing A Neural Learner
papers.abstract: Neural learners for classification and regression are often criticized as black boxes. We propose a probabilistic decomposition of neural learners that accounts for heterogeneous predictability across the feature space. A training procedure combining the EM algorithm, stochastic gradient descent, and maximum likelihood estimation is developed to jointly learn the predictable component and an input-dependent reliability score. We show that the optimal decomposed learner recovers the response distribution within the predictable component, while the reliability score characterizes the predictability of individual observations. We further extend the framework to incorporate localized feature transformations. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
papers.summary: Neural networks for classification and regression are often treated as black boxes, and their predictability can vary widely across different regions of the input space. The authors propose a probabilistic decomposition that splits a learner into a predictable component and an input-dependent reliability score, trained jointly with a procedure that combines the EM algorithm, stochastic gradient descent, and maximum likelihood estimation. They show that **the optimal decomposed learner recovers the response distribution within the predictable component** while the reliability score characterizes how predictable each observation is, extend the framework with localized feature transformations, and validate it on synthetic and real-world datasets.

papers.title: Measuring the Inference Energy Efficiency of Open-Weight LLMs across Benchmarks, Reasoning Modes, and Hardware
papers.abstract: Benchmark scores tell us what an LLM can do, but not how much energy is required to deliver that capability. We directly measure this trade-off for 86 open-weight model checkpoints, evaluated on seven benchmarks and six hardware platforms ranging from a consumer GPU to an eight-GPU server. We find large differences in energy efficiency even among models with similar capability. Most configurations lie away from the score--energy Pareto frontier: they use a median of 2.6--4.8$\times$ more energy than another configuration that scores at least as well, with differences reaching 27$\times$. Reasoning can improve capability, but enabling thinking increases energy by about 3.7$\times$ on average, and the benefit depends strongly on the model family and output budget. Generated-token count is also an imperfect proxy for energy, misordering 18--24\% of model pairs. In contrast, FP8 reduces energy by roughly a quarter with little change in score, while changing hardware largely rescales energy without changing the relative ranking of models. These results show that capability alone gives an incomplete picture of efficiency. We argue that benchmark scores should be reported together with measured energy consumption under a specified serving regime and output budget.
papers.summary: Benchmark scores say what a model can do but not how much energy it burns doing it, so the authors measure both for 86 open-weight checkpoints across seven benchmarks and six hardware platforms ranging from a consumer GPU to an eight-GPU server. Most configurations sit well off the score-versus-energy Pareto frontier, **using a median of 2.6 to 4.8 times more energy than another configuration that scores at least as well**, with gaps reaching 27 times. Enabling thinking raises energy by about 3.7 times on average with benefits that depend strongly on model family and output budget, generated-token count misorders 18 to 24 percent of model pairs as an energy proxy, and `FP8` cuts energy by roughly a quarter with little score change, while hardware swaps mostly rescale energy without reordering models. The authors argue that benchmark results should be reported alongside measured energy under a specified serving regime and output budget.

papers.title: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
papers.abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.
papers.summary: Curating experimental data from scientific literature means verifying exact conjunctive conditions such as specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability across long heterogeneous files, which existing short-query relevance benchmarks do not capture. `SciCurateBench` provides 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals for this task, and plain LLMs as well as popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle on it. The authors also propose `LangPoli`, in which a policy agent writes natural-language action guidelines that actor agents turn into executable tools, and it reaches **83.16 percent F1 on paper classification versus 58.22 percent for its base LLM** while also improving structured information retrieval and re-ranking on `LitSearch`, `BEIR`, and `TREC`. A curriculum-transfer method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks is explored to speed up solving related problems.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Training Instability in Large-Scale Recommender Systems: A Cascade Perspective
papers.abstract: Training large-scale recommender systems on dynamic industrial platforms, such as Short-Form Video (SFV) services with billions of daily interactions, faces critical stability challenges. Rapid distribution shifts in user data and increasing model complexity frequently trigger a divergence cascade, typically initiating with gradient explosion, propagating to weight explosion, and culminating in loss explosion. This G-W-L cascade severely impedes model convergence and performance. This paper provides a systematic analysis of this G-W-L cascade within an industrial SFV recommender context. We then propose and evaluate a structured mitigation framework where interventions are explicitly mapped to counteract specific stages of the cascade: gradient (G) control, weight/activation (W) stabilization, and loss (L) shaping. Our contribution provides a structured framework for understanding and tackling training divergence, offering practical insights for deploying robust, continuously updated recommenders in large-scale, non-stationary settings. We empirically validate the effectiveness of these strategies on a major industrial SFV recommendation system.
papers.summary: Recommender models trained continuously on industrial Short-Form Video (SFV) platforms with billions of daily interactions suffer from a recurring divergence cascade in which gradient explosion leads to weight explosion and finally loss explosion, stalling convergence. The authors analyze this gradient-weight-loss (G-W-L) cascade systematically in a production SFV recommender and propose a mitigation framework that maps interventions to each stage: gradient control, weight and activation stabilization, and loss shaping. **The staged interventions are validated empirically on a major industrial SFV recommendation system**, offering practical guidance for keeping continuously updated recommenders stable under rapid distribution shift.

papers.title: Clinical value claims in multimodal AI outpace supporting evidence
papers.abstract: Multimodal prediction models add a data source, such as imaging or an assay, to clinical information, and health systems must decide whether that added test is worth acquiring. We audited 177 studies comparing multimodal with unimodal models: 81 from a systematic review and 96 from a probability sample of 2025-2026 PubMed records. Gains in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) were smaller when a study fitted a separate model for every data source (adjusted difference, -0.030; 95% CI, -0.056 to -0.005). Within 78 such studies, leaving out the strongest source's model would have raised the average gain from 0.046 to 0.108. This complete benchmarking fell from 69.1% of review studies to an estimated 46.0% of recent ones. An estimated 22% assessed decision utility and none evaluated a model prospectively, yet most claimed potential clinical usefulness or improved care (84.0% and an estimated 87.7%).
papers.summary: Multimodal clinical prediction models add a data source such as imaging or an assay to clinical information, and health systems must decide whether that extra test is worth acquiring. An audit of 177 studies comparing multimodal with unimodal models, 81 from a systematic review and 96 from a probability sample of 2025 to 2026 PubMed records, finds that gains in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) were smaller when a study fitted a separate model for every data source, and that within 78 such studies, leaving out the strongest source's model would have raised the average gain from 0.046 to 0.108. Such complete benchmarking fell from 69.1 percent of review studies to an estimated 46.0 percent of recent ones, and **an estimated 22 percent of studies assessed decision utility and none evaluated a model prospectively**, yet most claimed potential clinical usefulness or improved care.

papers.title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
papers.abstract: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.
papers.summary: Assisting workers through a head-mounted camera requires vision language models to understand what a worker is doing and help document it, but field work such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair is high-variance and mostly proprietary, making it hard to benchmark. `RealityBench` models such work in Blender across eleven environments with two tasks: acceptability asks whether a view is suitable proof-of-work, and documentation asks whether a model can read the task-relevant state of the scene from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, **top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame but are weak at reading measurements and judging small parts and spatial relations**, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to score because human raters disagree with each other, the best models are indistinguishable from a single non-author rater at a cost within the range of a human pass, and model rankings on rendered frames transfer to the real images available for three documentation questions.

papers.title: Sparse-TD-JEPA: Improving Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning With Sparse Latent Task Representations
papers.abstract: Successor-feature-based zero-shot reinforcement learning methods pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on offline, reward-free data, then recover a policy at test time by solving a closed-form linear regression over a small labeled dataset. We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow. We address this limitation by introducing an l1 sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder's latent space. The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure. We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA, a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation. Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons. On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 +- 6 to 714 +- 3. On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 +- 0.8 to 48.4 +- 2.3, with improvements of 13.4-18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains. Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains. Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape.
papers.summary: Successor-feature methods for zero-shot reinforcement learning pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on reward-free offline data, then recover a policy at test time with a closed-form linear regression over a few labeled samples, but dense task encodings make the inferred reward diffuse across the state space and give the policy a weak signal to follow. `Sparse-TD-JEPA` adds an l1 sparsity penalty, applied only during training, to the task encoder of Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (`TD-JEPA`), concentrating reward-predictive structure into a smaller latent subspace with a one-line code change and no modification to inference. Across 65 tasks on the DeepMind Control (`DMC`) Suite and `OGBench`, it beats `TD-JEPA` in all 13 domain-level comparisons, raising DMC average return from 661 to 714 and **OGBench average success rate from 38.0 to 48.4 percent**, and it achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of 13 domains. Analysis shows the sparsity yields a sharper, more task-informative inferred reward landscape.

papers.title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) handle mathematical and logical reasoning reasonably well but degrade as the number of interacting constraints and the search space grow, while satisfiability solvers like `Z3` scale and verify but cannot read natural-language problem statements. `SAT-RL` is a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains an LLM to drive a symbolic solver through multi-turn tool execution, combining synthetic problem generation with verifiable solutions, a supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded RL with tool-aware rewards. **Trained models substantially improve tool-based symbolic reasoning on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks**, and the code is released.

papers.title: SPROUT: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has driven substantial progress in coding agents by relying on verified successful trajectories as learning signals. However, such trajectories are scarce in long-horizon software engineering tasks, where a minor error can invalidate the entire rollout. Repeatedly restarting from the initial state is commonly used yet inefficient, and resetting only the context with working directory misses state changes such as installed dependencies. Therefore, branching from intermediate steps to preserve earlier progress requires restoring both the agent context and execution environments. In this paper, we present SPROUT (SnaPshot-based RollOUT), an agentic RL rollout framework that scales long-horizon coding tasks by resuming and branching from intermediate states. Specifically, SPROUT was built on top of a lightweight infrastructure that checkpoints both the filesystem and the agent context after each assistant turn. A verifier-guided backtracking policy then selects where to resume a failed attempt and how to proceed. Extensive experiments on long-horizon coding tasks show that SPROUT achieves up to 23.6% improvement over pass@k across various LLMs, while using $32$--$52%$ of their tokens. For RL training of Qwen3.8-27B, SPROUT stably outperforms standard GRPO by $13.9$ points on three long-horizon coding benchmarks while cutting the time per training step by $39.5%$. SPROUT thus makes RL on long-horizon coding tasks both more effective and cheaper to scale.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for coding agents depends on verified successful trajectories, which are rare in long-horizon software engineering tasks where one slip can invalidate an entire rollout, and restarting from scratch wastes work while resetting only the context misses environment changes such as installed dependencies. `SPROUT` (SnaPshot-based RollOUT) checkpoints both the filesystem and the agent context after every assistant turn, then uses a verifier-guided backtracking policy to pick where to resume a failed attempt and how to branch from there. On long-horizon coding tasks it improves pass@k by up to 23.6 percent across LLMs while consuming only 32 to 52 percent of their tokens, and for RL training of `Qwen3.8-27B` it **outperforms standard `GRPO` by 13.9 points on three long-horizon coding benchmarks while cutting time per training step by 39.5 percent**.

papers.title: Memory Without Curation: Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies
papers.abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.
papers.summary: Robot policies need long-term memory for complex tasks, but conditioning on all past observations invites spurious shortcuts and adds deployment latency, so existing memory-augmented policies curate what to keep through recent frames, keyframes, text summaries, or vision-only latents. `IMPRINT` is a policy-agnostic latent memory for vision-language-action (VLA) models that compresses multiple streams, including observations, actions, and proprioception, into a latent memory updated incrementally at inference time without constraining what the policy remembers. To avoid shortcut learning it trains in two stages, first supervising the memory to reconstruct past streams and estimate task progress, then fine-tuning end to end with the policy on action prediction. Across simulation and real-world memory-dependent tasks it **raises average success over the base VLA by at least 26 percent**, beats popular alternatives, and keeps the lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs.

papers.title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
papers.abstract: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.
papers.summary: Sampling from diffusion or flow-matching models requires hundreds of sequential velocity-field integration steps, a workload that fits analog neuromorphic hardware better than GPUs if generation can be cast as a single physical relaxation trained without backpropagation. `Energy Matching` already samples by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential, but computing that gradient is itself a backward pass, so the authors prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries the needed gradient, with error vanishing for small injection strengths. A backprop-trained Energy Matching model loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone matches the original FID to within 0.04 on `CIFAR-10` and `ImageNet-32`, and training end to end with Equilibrium Propagation, whose updates match backpropagation's to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, **reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation**. An architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 under backpropagation without group normalisation or attention.

papers.title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
papers.abstract: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.
papers.summary: Computational coarse-graining replaces a sequence of updates in a model with a cheaper module, and the question is how to judge such a replacement by the computation that follows it rather than by local approximation error. The authors propose a continuation-relative evaluation framework that scores replacements jointly on downstream task quality and total execution cost, separating boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss, with an exact loss decomposition that isolates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. In two frozen pretrained language models, representation fidelity and task loss favor different fitting objectives: on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, **next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output**, yet the ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, a jointly adapted candidate beats frozen-bank and router-only baselines but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
papers.abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.
papers.summary: Frontier models are increasingly pretrained jointly on text, vision, and audio, yet how much of each modality to mix and what interference it causes the others is poorly understood or unpublished. The authors derive data-mixing scaling laws for the three modalities using Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, which Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt because they scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference, running 268 experiments from 457M to 8.3B parameters on up to 150 billion tokens. Compute optima turn out to be modality-specific, with audio favoring parameters over tokens while text and vision want balanced scaling of model size and data, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefit, and **cross-modal interference is highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, while audio's interference with text and vision is negligible**.

papers.title: ByteMark: A Unified Byte-Level Watermark for Detection Across Language Models
papers.abstract: As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.
papers.summary: As watermarked LLM text reaches deployment, users need to check text of unknown origin, but existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, so even providers using the same scheme would produce mutually incompatible watermarks and the text itself does not reveal which representation produced it. `ByteMark` defines its watermark signal directly on the UTF-8 bytes of published text, so models with different tokenizers embed it under one public specification and key and a single detector verifies it from the text and key alone. **When a baseline detector's tokenizer or embedding model is swapped its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, keeps its detection rate**, and the signal remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.

papers.title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
papers.abstract:
Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure.
  We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.
papers.summary: Enterprise workflow automation such as customer support (CS) resolution needs complete, accurate retrieval from large operational corpora of SOPs and policy documents, which in production usually means elaborate chunking, indexing, re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure. This deployment case study reports a simpler alternative: a portable skill made of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools such as a retrieval API and format-checking scripts, and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, a structured Wikipedia-style index over the documents. Built in one to two engineer days and runnable in capable agentic harnesses such as `Claude Code`, the skill **achieved 99.2 percent procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3 percent evidence sufficiency** on CS resolution workflow generation, though at roughly 90 seconds per case versus 8 to 9 seconds for the deployed production assistant. The claim is scoped to a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case, where maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.

papers.title: MemForm: Benchmarking Memory Formation Poisoning in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at https://github.com/opanhw/memform-code.
