papers.summary: Long-term memory lets LLM agents learn from past interactions but exposes the process by which memories are formed to adversarial influence, and prior taxonomies organized by attack channel, corruption pattern, or lifecycle stage leave those formation interfaces poorly characterized. The authors define Memory Formation Poisoning as manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent memory is produced and committed, and introduce `MemForm`, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five of them: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning, with the latter two isolating retention and consolidation-order effects respectively. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats find **broad susceptibility at all five interfaces**, and that authentic, successful experiences still yield undesirable downstream behavior when contextual support, retention, or consolidation order is altered, with consolidation order alone changing behavior on identical retained experiences. Interface applicability depends on memory architecture, Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater, and the evaluated defenses mitigate only partially and unevenly across interfaces.

papers.title: Design Choices for Multimodal Transformer Learning with Missing and Longitudinal Healthcare Data
papers.abstract: Multimodal learning offers the potential to improve predictions by integrating complementary information from heterogeneous data sources. However, multimodal datasets are frequently incomplete, raising important questions about how models should handle missing information. Although recent approaches increasingly rely on Transformer-based architectures for multimodal fusion, incomplete multimodal data introduces challenges such as missing modalities and intra-modal missingness, which motivate key architectural design choices, such as tokenization granularity. In addition, many datasets are longitudinal, with observations collected across multiple time points. The sequential nature of the Transformer architectures provides a natural framework for modeling such data, but introduces additional considerations, such as how temporal information should be represented. In this study, we systematically investigate these design choices using three different cancer datasets. We compare modality-level and feature-level tokenization and evaluate attention masking and imputation as strategies for handling missing information, both naturally occurring in the datasets and synthetically induced. We further investigate approaches for incorporating temporal information in our training process and how to model it. Experiments are conducted with unimodal and multimodal configurations, as well as different levels of missingness for binary survival classification and multiple time encoding strategies for discrete-time survival prediction. Our results show that while multimodal outperforms unimodal results, missing data heavily impacts predictions and thus effective design choices such as tokenization granularity, and intra-missing handling is essential for reliable prediction.
papers.summary: Multimodal models for healthcare can combine complementary data sources, but clinical datasets are often incomplete, with whole modalities or individual features missing, and longitudinal, with observations collected at multiple time points, raising design questions for Transformer-based fusion. Using three cancer datasets, the authors systematically compare modality-level versus feature-level tokenization, attention masking versus imputation for handling both naturally occurring and synthetically induced missingness, and several ways of encoding temporal information, across unimodal and multimodal configurations for binary survival classification and discrete-time survival prediction. **Multimodal models outperform unimodal ones, but missing data heavily degrades predictions**, so choices such as tokenization granularity and intra-modal missingness handling are essential for reliable prediction.

papers.title: From Transfer Probes to Expert Grouping: Evidence from LoRA Post-Training
papers.abstract: A platform that post-trains one base model for many business lines often has more lines than experts it can maintain, so lines must share experts, yet lines seldom come with a taxonomy saying which should share. We ask whether transfer probes (train on one source, measure paired changes on all sources) can discover a grouping when the standard one is unknown. To test probes against a reference, we use seven public sources that do have a label tree (five mathematics subfields and two kinds of programming, standing in for business lines) and treat the tree's grouping as a label reference that the evaluator holds and the method does not. With four LoRA experts under fixed per-source exposure and per-expert budgets, we compare a purely probe-derived grouping and an uninformed uniform default (whose tied routing serves every line from one expert) against this reference. Trained once for one interval from a shared warm-up state and routed by a rule fixed by each allocation, neither reached the prespecified practical gain of 2 percentage points, and both had lower overall utility than the reference ($-2.43$ and $-2.54$ pp; 95\% intervals below zero). In a post hoc comparison, the probe-derived grouping was indistinguishable from the uniform default ($+0.11$ pp, $[-1.25,+1.54]$). In fixed-budget LoRA post-training, a grouping built from initial-state single-source probes thus did not deliver the advantage predicted from the probes once carried to a later training state, a finite budget, and specified routing.
papers.summary: A platform that post-trains one base model for many business lines usually has more lines than experts it can maintain, so lines must share experts, yet there is rarely a taxonomy saying which should share. The authors test whether transfer probes, which train on one source and measure paired changes on all others, can discover a grouping, using seven public sources with a known label tree of five mathematics subfields and two kinds of programming as a reference the evaluator holds but the method does not, and comparing a probe-derived grouping and a uniform default against it with four `LoRA` experts under fixed per-source exposure and per-expert budgets. Neither grouping reached the prespecified practical gain of 2 percentage points, both had lower overall utility than the reference at minus 2.43 and minus 2.54 points with 95 percent intervals below zero, and **the probe-derived grouping was statistically indistinguishable from the uniform default**, differing by plus 0.11 points. Initial-state single-source probes thus did not deliver the predicted advantage once carried to a later training state, a finite budget, and specified routing.

papers.title: Neither True nor False: Do LLMs Represent Truth-Value Gaps in Plural Predication?
papers.abstract: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) genuinely grasp the truth conditions of plural descriptions, or do they force every sentence into true or false? We investigate the Homogeneity Gap, a semantic phenomenon where a plural definite (e.g., the kids laughed) and its negation (the kids didn't laugh) are both neither true nor false when only some of the kids laughed, whereas their quantified counterparts (all, not all) remain strictly bivalent. We introduce HomogeneityNLI, a diagnostic dataset of 1,000 minimal-pair items crossing determiner, polarity, and group composition across ten logical conditions. Evaluating seven open-weight models, we uncover a pervasive Bivalence Bias: models assign plural definites their homogeneous truth conditions, reading the kids as all of them and the kids didn't as none of them, yet collapse the truth-value gap into falsity. In the zero-shot setting, no model recognizes the gap for both polarities in more than 15% of scenarios, and negated definites are judged False in 84% of cases. Explicit linguistic rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts produce unstable, model-specific effects that often entrench the bias. Taken together, our findings indicate that current open-weight LLMs have acquired the truth conditions of plural predication but not its trivalent logic.
papers.summary: Plural definites like 'the kids laughed' and their negations are both neither true nor false when only some of the kids laughed, a phenomenon called the homogeneity gap, whereas quantified versions with 'all' and 'not all' stay strictly true or false. The authors build `HomogeneityNLI`, a diagnostic set of 1,000 minimal-pair items crossing determiner, polarity, and group composition across ten logical conditions, and test seven open-weight models on it. The models show a pervasive bivalence bias: they read 'the kids' as all of them and 'the kids didn't' as none of them, but collapse the truth-value gap into falsity, with **no model recognizing the gap for both polarities in more than 15% of zero-shot scenarios** and negated definites judged false 84% of the time. Linguistic rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts produce unstable, model-specific effects that often reinforce the bias.

papers.title: SceneForesee: Learning Scene Evolution for Spatiotemporal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to understand how entities move and interact as a scene develops. This requires following the same entities over time and relating their observed motion to subsequent changes. We formulate Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), a task for predicting and interpreting this change. Given observed video, a model estimates entity histories and predicts one scene continuation through future trajectories and Events, accompanied by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. We construct SceneForesee, a benchmark for evaluating entity continuity and scene evolution reasoning through paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities. It contains 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events paired with observed evidence. We propose a spatiotemporal reasoning framework, EvoSee, that learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment. It selects one continuation per entity from observation and uses the selected changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. On SceneForesee, EvoSee outperforms Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1. On the 4D reasoning benchmark Dyn-Bench, it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over their respective base systems. These results support scene evolution as both a prediction target and a dynamic representation that brings predicted entity changes into spatiotemporal reasoning.The project is available at https://github.com/mikubaka88/SceneForesee-Spatiotemporal-Reasoning.
papers.summary: Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to track the same entities across a video and relate their motion to what happens next. The authors define Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), where a model estimates entity histories from observed video and predicts one continuation as future trajectories and events backed by visual evidence, and release `SceneForesee`, a benchmark of 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K events with shared entity identities between observed and future scenes. Their `EvoSee` framework learns future geometry and event semantics jointly through shared candidate states and assignment, selecting one continuation per entity and feeding the selected changes back into entity refinement and scene representation. On `SceneForesee`, **`EvoSee` beats `Qwen3.5-9B` by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1**, and it improves question answering accuracy and grounding on the 4D reasoning benchmark `Dyn-Bench` by 4.8 and 3.58 points over the respective base systems.

papers.title: Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization (TETPO): Smooth Variance Control via Bridge Importance Sampling
papers.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models is computationally efficient but inherently off-policy: the learner updates on rollouts generated by a stale policy, while correcting this mismatch requires importance weights that can be extremely heavy-tailed. A small number of trajectories may then dominate an update, collapsing the effective sample size (ESS) and increasing the variance and instability of the resulting gradient estimates. Existing stabilizers apply fixed interventions regardless of the realized severity of weight concentration, either discarding selected samples or reweighting them without adapting the correction strength. We introduce \emph{Target--ESS Tempered Policy Optimization} (TETPO), which replaces each importance weight $\rho$ by $\rho^\alpha$ for a data-adaptive exponent $\alpha\in[0,1]$: $\alpha=1$ preserves the original importance weights, whereas $\alpha=0$ assigns uniform coefficients. For each prompt group, TETPO selects the largest $\alpha$ whose tempered weights satisfy a target ESS fraction $\kappa$, applying little tempering to healthy groups and stronger tempering when weight degeneracy is severe. At the population level, the tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between the sampler and learner policies. The exponent is efficiently found by one-dimensional bisection, while the resulting weights satisfy deterministic bounds on normalized-weight dispersion and weighted-gradient norm that are independent of policy drift, together with a fixed-$\alpha$ bound on bridge-target discrepancy. Power tempering also introduces no explicit zero-weight mask. On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, TETPO outperforms strong on- and off-policy baselines.
papers.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models updates on rollouts from a stale policy, and the importance weights that correct this mismatch can be so heavy-tailed that a few trajectories dominate an update and collapse the effective sample size (ESS). `TETPO` (Target-ESS Tempered Policy Optimization) replaces each importance weight rho with rho raised to a data-adaptive exponent alpha between 0 and 1, choosing per prompt group the largest alpha whose tempered weights meet a target ESS fraction, so healthy groups are barely tempered while degenerate ones are tempered hard. The tempered coefficients are exact importance weights for a geometric bridge between sampler and learner policies, the exponent is found by one-dimensional bisection, and the weights satisfy deterministic bounds on dispersion and gradient norm that do not depend on policy drift, with no zero-weight masking of samples. **On mathematical-reasoning benchmarks under high staleness, `TETPO` outperforms strong on-policy and off-policy baselines.**

papers.title: Evaluating Semantic Relation Knowledge through Bidirectional Relation Prediction from Gloss Pairs
papers.abstract: Semantic relations organise word senses and are fundamental to lexical semantics. In order to evaluate semantic relation knowledge of large language models (LLMs), we propose a challenging task in which an LLM predicts the relation between two glosses (definitions of senses) presented in two different orders. The predictions for the two orders are evaluated for consistency with the symmetry or asymmetry of semantic relations. Our task is designed for both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation, allowing us to examine whether relation knowledge remains accessible when the same senses are verbalised through glosses in different languages. We construct a dataset of 3,069 sense pairs, with each sense verbalised in English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese. Experiments with 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings reveal generally poor performance. In each setting, only eight LLMs achieve a macro-averaged F1 score significantly above a random baseline, and only one (zero-shot) and two (five-shot) significantly outperform a neural baseline. In particular, LLMs often fail to generate bidirectionally consistent predictions for hypernymy and to make correct predictions for holonymy in either direction. Our results suggest limitations in current LLMs' semantic relation knowledge, both in identifying relations and in respecting asymmetry.
papers.summary: The authors test whether large language models know the semantic relations between word senses by asking them to predict the relation between two glosses, or sense definitions, presented in both orders, and checking whether the two predictions respect the symmetry or asymmetry of the relation. They build a dataset of 3,069 sense pairs with each sense verbalised in English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese, supporting both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation, and run 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings. Performance is generally poor: **only eight models score a macro-averaged F1 significantly above a random baseline in each setting**, and only one zero-shot and two five-shot models significantly beat a neural baseline. Models often fail to give bidirectionally consistent predictions for hypernymy and to identify holonymy in either direction.

papers.title: Specification-Based Testing of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Model cards, system cards, and safety reports increasingly document LLM safety behaviors, yet safety evaluations typically start from predefined benchmarks rather than asking which documented claims those benchmarks actually test. We introduce LEST (LLM Evaluation through Specification-driven Testing), a framework that treats documented safety claims as specifications for black-box testing. In LEST, each claim determines which benchmark prompt tests it and whether a Refuse-to-Comply transition, where a model refuses a prompt but complies with its mutated version, counts as evidence against it. LEST mutates these prompts to search for counterexamples, manually validates each candidate, and traces validated counterexamples back to the claims they contradict. We evaluate LEST using the system cards of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 with 97 seed prompts from SORRY-Bench across Mental Health and Self-Harm, Harmful and Violent Content, and Fairness and Bias. Of 56 identified safety claims, 29 (51.8%) are prompt-testable, but only 17 (58.6%) are exercised by an applicable benchmark prompt. Both models refuse >95% of benchmark prompts. Evaluating 1,836 mutated prompts on both models reveals 312 candidate Refuse-to-Comply transitions flagged by automated response classifiers. However, human validation confirms only 19 (6.1%) as both intent-preserving and genuinely compliant, showing automated evaluation substantially overestimates behavioral failures. Tracing these 19 transitions back to the claims reveals counterexamples for 6 of 9 covered claims for which refusal is an applicable oracle. Our results show that benchmark prompts may not be sufficient to validate all documented LLM safety behavior, and automated failure detection requires manual validation. LEST provides end-to-end traceability from natural-language safety documentation to executable tests and human-validated counterexamples.
papers.summary: Safety evaluations usually start from a benchmark rather than asking which documented claims in a model card or system card the benchmark actually tests. `LEST` (LLM Evaluation through Specification-driven Testing) treats each documented safety claim as a specification: a claim determines which benchmark prompt tests it and whether a Refuse-to-Comply transition, where the model refuses a prompt but complies with a mutated version, counts as evidence against it, then mutates prompts to search for counterexamples, validates candidates manually, and traces them back to the claims they contradict. Applied to the system cards of `Claude Opus 4.8` and `GPT-5.5` with 97 seed prompts from `SORRY-Bench`, 29 of 56 safety claims were prompt-testable but only 17 were exercised by an applicable benchmark prompt, and both models refused over 95% of benchmark prompts. Across 1,836 mutated prompts, automated classifiers flagged 312 candidate transitions, but **human validation confirmed only 19 (6.1%) as intent-preserving and genuinely compliant**, which still yielded counterexamples for 6 of the 9 covered claims where refusal is an applicable oracle.

papers.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
papers.abstract: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.
papers.summary: Asynchronous rollout speeds up reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by filling in idle time during long-tail generation, but the sustained concurrency packs more context into each decode step and raises the key-value (KV) cache workload per step. The authors characterize this KV concentration and find that KV cache quantization accelerates rollout far more than weight-only or weight-activation quantization at matched workloads, though plain INT4 KV rollout can hurt learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). `KV4-RL` pairs calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context, which reduces sampler mismatch while keeping most of the speedup. Over 400 iterations of `GRPO` training on `Qwen3-8B-Base` it delivers **a 1.80x cumulative rollout speedup and 1.27x full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout**, and final six-benchmark mean accuracy under a BF16 evaluator stays within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both `Qwen3-4B-Base` and `Qwen3-8B-Base`.

papers.title: Jevolution: A Framework for Studying Communication and Collective Dynamics in AI Agents
papers.abstract: Experiments with remote decision-making agents depend on more than the policy: the world may change during inference, the simulator determines which actions are available, and births and immigration alter who can act. We present Jevolution, an instrumented spatial predator-prey framework that makes these dependencies explicit. Its reference implementation separates the evolving world, asynchronous request scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records. The model combines local observations, energy and resource constraints, predefined signals, and inherited scalar traits. We describe these mechanisms using the ODD protocol and distinguish implemented controls from research questions requiring additional interventions. Free synthetic fixtures exercise scheduling, signaling, and inheritance against the pinned implementation; they validate specified software behavior rather than model intelligence or ecological realism. A completed communication case study illustrates the end-to-end workflow using Jev to control both species. Across 6 complete habitat-seed pairs, the mean signals-on minus signals-off difference in normalized rabbit abundance was -0.0095 (nominal 95% pair-bootstrap interval [-0.0772, 0.0602]). This small study does not resolve the direction of the signal-system effect. The contribution is an inspectable experimental system and its evidence boundaries, not a new policy-learning algorithm or a demonstration of emergent language, adaptive selection, or biological predictive validity.
papers.summary: Experiments with remote decision-making agents depend on more than the policy: the world can change during inference, the simulator determines which actions exist, and births and immigration change who can act. `Jevolution` is an instrumented spatial predator-prey framework that makes these dependencies explicit by separating the evolving world, asynchronous request scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records, combining local observations, energy and resource constraints, predefined signals, and inherited scalar traits, all described using the ODD protocol. Synthetic fixtures validate specified software behavior for scheduling, signaling, and inheritance rather than model intelligence or ecological realism. In a communication case study using `Jev` to control both species across six habitat-seed pairs, **the mean signals-on minus signals-off difference in normalized rabbit abundance was -0.0095 with a bootstrap interval spanning zero**, so the direction of the signal-system effect remains unresolved, and the authors frame the contribution as an inspectable experimental system with stated evidence boundaries rather than a new learning algorithm.

papers.title: Learning to Extrapolate in Depth with Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse a single block across iterations, raising a natural question: how far can a block trained at one depth be safely extrapolated to greater depths? We study this question for all-pairs graph connectivity, where harder graphs require longer-range information propagation. We show that under exchangeability and symmetric positive initialization, population training at depth K converges to an update rule governed by a single effective parameter that balances graph propagation against fitting structure unresolved at training depth. This trade-off creates a finite extrapolation window: too few test-time loops provide insufficient propagation, while too many eventually create false connections. We derive explicit endpoints for this window and bound the graph hardness solvable beyond training as a function of training depth and hardness. In particular, a test depth chosen solely from the training distribution can guarantee recovery on substantially harder graphs, with a certified depth gain that grows exponentially as training depth outpaces training hardness. Experiments validate the predicted windows and show how compute budget and initialization affect the optimal training depth.
papers.summary: Looped transformers reuse one block across iterations, which raises the question of how far a block trained at one depth can be run for more iterations at test time. Studying all-pairs graph connectivity, where harder graphs need longer-range information propagation, the authors show that under exchangeability and symmetric positive initialization, population training at depth K converges to an update rule governed by a single effective parameter that trades off graph propagation against fitting structure left unresolved at training depth. This trade-off yields a finite extrapolation window: too few test-time loops propagate too little, while too many eventually create false connections, and the paper derives explicit endpoints for the window and bounds the graph hardness solvable beyond training. **A test depth chosen only from the training distribution can guarantee recovery on substantially harder graphs, with a certified depth gain that grows exponentially as training depth outpaces training hardness**, and experiments confirm the predicted windows and show how compute budget and initialization shape the optimal training depth.

papers.title: Re-executing Coding-Agent Evaluations: Unchanged Decisions and Unresolved Policy Risk
papers.abstract: Executable tests grade large language model (LLM) coding-agent patches for leaderboards, rewards and self-improvement. Two preregistered re-execution studies returned negative results. SWE-bench Pro v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration changed. Their exploratory, unweighted upper confidence limit is 4.95% under candidate independence, leaving a 3% exposed-patch risk unresolved; the preregistered estimator uses inverse sampling-probability weights. An extension was inconclusive. In a selected stratum, a reconstructed module cache built from the reference solution's dependencies rejected accepted alternatives from four models that passed with their own dependencies. Re-executing 1,929 selected agent-version/task evaluations from the Darwin G\"odel Machine's archive preserved best-agent selection and system-variant ranking, with search history and scores of evaluations not rerun fixed. Exploratory host, image and adapted-grader comparisons also preserved them. Seven of 23 disagreements with archived verdicts did not recur on a second host; rebuilt images changed 16 three-run majority verdicts (0.83%) under four-CPU execution. We provide an evidence-to-claim summary, lessons for grader audits and an anonymous replication package. These results concern accepted patches and fixed-history decisions; general policy safety and adaptive-learning robustness require broader evaluations.
papers.summary: Executable tests decide which coding-agent patches count as passing for leaderboards, rewards, and self-improvement loops, so the authors preregistered two re-execution studies to check whether those verdicts hold up when graders are rerun. Re-running `SWE-bench Pro` v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration had changed, leaving an exploratory upper confidence limit of 4.95% and roughly 3% of exposed-patch risk unresolved, while in one selected stratum a module cache rebuilt from the reference solution's dependencies rejected accepted patches from four models that had passed with their own dependencies. **Re-executing 1,929 selected evaluations from the `Darwin Gödel Machine` archive preserved best-agent selection and system-variant ranking**, though 7 of 23 disagreements with archived verdicts did not recur on a second host and rebuilt images flipped 16 three-run majority verdicts (0.83%). The paper offers an evidence-to-claim summary, lessons for grader audits, and a replication package, and notes that the results cover accepted patches and fixed-history decisions rather than general policy safety.

papers.title: Evaluating Bias in Chinese Large Language Models across Tasks and Registers: Task Operationalization Effects and Irony Classification Risks
papers.abstract: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.
papers.summary: Chinese content governance increasingly uses large language models to flag toxic and discriminatory expressions, but how a task is operationalized and whether the text is ironic can both shift the bias readings an audit produces. In a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of several Chinese LLMs, **the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% on formal text to 23.5% on the yinyang echoic-irony register**, a risk difference of 12.7 percentage points whose direction held under both adjudicated and majority-vote references, although lower inter-rater agreement on ironic items means part of the increase reflects label uncertainty. Explicit irony-aware prompts cut the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 points, and casting the same 29 proposition anchors as social consensus estimation, high-stakes decision, and controlled association rating tasks showed the decision and association forms diverging from the consensus form on irony-probe materials. The authors conclude that task operationalization effects on bias readings must be measured empirically and that the ironic register should be a standard test condition in safety evaluation.

papers.title: Co-adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining for Structured Knowledge Retrieval
papers.abstract: Structured knowledge retrieval acquires task-relevant evidence from structured knowledge sources for downstream tasks. Existing methods rely on unconstrained retrieval or predefined query-rule supervision, such as author-paper rules for scientific discovery and anatomy-drug rules for precision medicine. Such supervision is rarely available in practice. We propose Co-Adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining Retrieval (CoRE), which jointly learns which reasoning rule to assign to each query and how to retrieve evidence under that rule, without predefined query-rule pairs. A routing agent selects a rule, and its corresponding retriever traverses the knowledge base and ranks evidence that satisfies the rule's constraints. Because routing and retrieval are interdependent, CoRE alternates between reinforcement learning for the routing policy and contrastive learning for the rule-constrained retriever. The selected rules provide supervision for retriever training, while retrieval performance rewards the routing policy. This closed-loop process enables both components to co-adapt without explicit query-rule supervision. Experiments on STaRK-QA datasets across scientific discovery, biomedical reasoning, and e-commerce knowledge management demonstrate CoRE's effectiveness. Ablations show the benefit of co-adapting the router and retriever. Generation-based routing transfers across datasets and benefits from multi-domain pretraining followed by target-specific fine-tuning. Analysis of rule usage across queries also informs automatic rule refinement and discovery.
papers.summary: Structured knowledge retrieval pulls task-relevant evidence from knowledge bases, but existing methods either retrieve without constraints or depend on predefined query-rule supervision, such as author-paper rules for scientific discovery, which is rarely available in practice. `CoRE` (Co-Adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining Retrieval) learns jointly which reasoning rule to assign to each query and how to retrieve under that rule: a routing agent picks a rule, and the matching retriever traverses the knowledge base and ranks evidence satisfying the rule's constraints. Because the two are interdependent, training alternates between reinforcement learning for the router, rewarded by retrieval performance, and contrastive learning for the rule-constrained retriever, supervised by the selected rules. **On `STaRK-QA` datasets spanning scientific discovery, biomedical reasoning, and e-commerce, `CoRE` outperforms baselines**, ablations confirm the benefit of co-adaptation, generation-based routing transfers across datasets, and rule-usage analysis points toward automatic rule refinement.

papers.title: Diffusion-Based Auctions for Multi-Winner Banner Ads
papers.abstract: We propose a new framework for banner ad auctions, leveraging diffusion models to allow for multiple bidders to co-win a single banner ad opportunity, and in particular influence the ad shown on the banner depending on the strength of their bids, enabling a far richer outcome space compared to standard banner ad auctions, where there is a single winner who shows their ad. In our framework, the outcomes are images (what ad to show) and each bidder expresses their preferences over outcomes by declaring their value per unit of alignment between the image chosen by the mechanism and a textual description of their desired image. Our proposed mechanism combines the advertisers' bids and textual descriptions into a score that drives the reverse process of a diffusion model. This is used to sample a set of candidate images from which the welfare maximizing one is eventually chosen. Extensive experimentation evaluates our proposed mechanism around the following axes: (1) efficiency improvements of our allocation rule relative to the single-winner allocation rule; (2) monotonicity of our allocation rule; and (3) approximate incentive compatibility when combining our allocation rule with Myerson lemma-based or Clarke rule-based payments. Improvements along all these axes are shown with the number of Monte Carlo samples. Meanwhile, these benefits are attained while preserving the image quality.
papers.summary: Standard banner ad auctions pick a single winner who shows their own ad, so the authors propose a framework in which multiple bidders can co-win one banner opportunity and influence the generated image in proportion to their bids. Each bidder declares a value per unit of alignment between the displayed image and a textual description of their desired ad, and the mechanism combines bids and descriptions into a score that guides the reverse process of a diffusion model, samples candidate images, and selects the welfare-maximizing one. Experiments evaluate efficiency gains over the single-winner rule, monotonicity of the allocation rule, and approximate incentive compatibility when paired with Myerson-lemma or Clarke-rule payments, finding that **all three properties improve as the number of Monte Carlo samples grows** while image quality is preserved.

papers.title: RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation
papers.abstract: Medication recommendations seek to deliver personalized drug combinations based on patients' clinical information, where ensuring transparent decision-making and personalized safety are of paramount importance. However, existing approaches predominantly operate as ``black boxes'', offering limited interpretability and hindering clinician trust. Furthermore, they typically rely on fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints, neglecting the heterogeneity of risk tolerance across individuals, which poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. To address these gaps, we propose \textbf{RES-MR}, a novel Risk-aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation using LLMs. RES-MR follows a two-stage training paradigm: (1) an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage to elicit diagnostic capabilities by fine-tuning on synthesized reasoning trajectories, grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval; and (2) a risk-aware policy optimization stage to dynamically balance therapeutic efficacy with personalized safety. This stage employs disentangled drug factors to construct patient-specific reference prototypes that capture desired therapeutic drug features and risk features to avoid. These prototypes enable risk boundary calibration and guide the model toward safe recommendations via reward shaping and clipping. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RES-MR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, safety, and explainability. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/wangcong2001/RES-MR.
papers.summary: Medication recommendation systems propose drug combinations from a patient's clinical record, but existing models act as black boxes and apply fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints that ignore differences in individual risk tolerance. `RES-MR` (Risk-aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation) trains an LLM in two stages: an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage that fine-tunes on synthesized reasoning trajectories grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval, followed by a risk-aware policy optimization stage that balances therapeutic efficacy against personalized safety. The second stage uses disentangled drug factors to build patient-specific reference prototypes capturing desired therapeutic features and risk features to avoid, which calibrate risk boundaries and steer the policy through reward shaping and clipping. **On benchmark datasets, `RES-MR` outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, safety, and explainability**, and code and data are released.

papers.title: EdgeLLM-Nano: Auditing Polar-Guided Key-Cache Compression and Consistency-Anchored Pruning on a 33.6 MB On-Device Language Model
papers.abstract: Deploying language models (LMs) on the edge presents unique memory, latency, and power challenges absent in high-performance computing. KV-cache compression emerges as a promising approach to address these challenges. However, the effectiveness of current KV-cache compression methods has not been thoroughly examined on edge devices. Moreover, we show that existing evaluation methods do not always involve the KV-cache under test. We propose EdgeLLM-Nano, a measurement study of KV-cache compression using a nano-scale decoder-only LM (transformer) testbed that has 8.39M parameters, i.e., 33.6 MB, to enable end-to-end examination of each backend, seed, and power sample. Our results give a negative verdict for a polar-guided key-cache quantizer (round-to-nearest (RTN) control causes an order of magnitude less damage), as well as a consistency-anchored progressive weight pruner (one-shot magnitude-based pruning performs as well as, if not better). We also introduce Long-Context Decode Fidelity (LCDF) evaluation, a token-by-token examination of teacher-forced log-losses using the KV-cache under test. Unlike perplexity that gives the same 5.461 score to all methods, LCDF distinguishes different KV-cache compression backends thanks to its paired statistics across seeds and effect sizes. Our companion Raspberry Pi 5 measurement shows all compression backends we tested to be less energy-efficient per token compared to uncompressed FP16 inference. Except for KIVI that is close to lossless in terms of LCDF, our findings indicate KV-cache compression can be improved. LCDF offers a simple and effective way of shedding light on KV-cache compression methods, whose negative impacts have been overlooked by perplexity.
papers.summary: Running language models on edge devices brings memory, latency, and power limits that make key-value (KV) cache compression attractive, yet existing evaluations have not been checked on actual edge hardware and sometimes do not even exercise the KV cache under test. `EdgeLLM-Nano` is a measurement study built around an 8.39M-parameter, 33.6 MB decoder-only transformer testbed small enough to examine every backend, seed, and power sample end to end. It returns negative verdicts for a polar-guided key-cache quantizer, where round-to-nearest (RTN) control causes an order of magnitude less damage, and for a consistency-anchored progressive weight pruner, which one-shot magnitude pruning matches or beats, and it introduces Long-Context Decode Fidelity (`LCDF`), a token-by-token teacher-forced log-loss evaluation that distinguishes compression backends where perplexity assigns every method the same 5.461 score. **On a Raspberry Pi 5, every compression backend tested was less energy-efficient per token than uncompressed FP16 inference**, with only `KIVI` close to lossless under `LCDF`.

papers.title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. Standard representational similarity analysis (RSA) summarizes similarity across all stimulus pairs, potentially obscuring differences in alignment between nearby and distant inputs. Neighborhood-Weighted RSA (NW-RSA) addresses this limitation by weighting stimulus pairs according to their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale. Counterfactual RSA (CF-RSA) tests which linguistic properties support alignment by comparing intact representations in one model with representations under controlled linguistic perturbations in another. Across diverse language models, we find strong agreement in coarse representational geometry but substantial divergence in local neighborhoods. Alignment is observed both across broadly sampled natural text and within linguistic equivalence classes that preserve particular aspects of meaning or structure. Counterfactual analyses reveal selective sensitivity: changes to logical scope reduce alignment substantially more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure. Alignment also decreases when sentence structure or lexical meaning is disrupted in word lists and jabberwocky sentences, suggesting that the regularities of natural language support stronger convergence. These findings refine claims of representational universality by showing that strong overall similarity need not imply agreement in how models represent finer linguistic distinctions.
papers.summary: Aggregate similarity scores between language models can hide how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties drive it. The authors introduce Neighborhood-Weighted representational similarity analysis (`NW-RSA`), which weights stimulus pairs by their proximity in representational space to place local and global alignment on a common scale, and Counterfactual RSA (`CF-RSA`), which compares intact representations in one model against representations of controlled linguistic perturbations in another to identify what supports alignment. Across diverse models they find **strong agreement in coarse representational geometry but substantial divergence in local neighborhoods**, both over broadly sampled text and within linguistic equivalence classes. Counterfactual tests show that changes to logical scope reduce alignment far more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure, and alignment drops for word lists and jabberwocky sentences, so overall similarity does not imply agreement on finer linguistic distinctions.

papers.title: What Counts as the Same Task? Executable Contracts for Robustness Evaluation of Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Robustness tests for tool-using agents often change the agent's environment, for example by hiding a hostile note in an invoice, and then judge the agent by what it does. The result tells us about the original task only if the changed test case is still a valid test of that task. Many evaluations decide this with weak rules, such as accepting any well-formed edit or any edit that stays close to the original in embedding space. We propose executable task contracts. A contract states which facts define a task, which edits are allowed, and what finishing the task means, and it checks each changed test case before the agent runs. We compare validity rules by scoring the same 14,336 stored agent runs under each rule. Across four encoders, embedding thresholds allowed 75-100% of edits that changed the task, such as swapping the payee, yet rejected 24-45% of valid hostile notes. With a MiniLM cosine threshold, Mistral appeared vulnerable on all 64 tasks, but only 26 had a successful valid attack. Replaying a saved solution and allowing edits to benchmark fields fail in similar ways. Evaluations should state, and check, what counts as the same task.
papers.summary: Robustness tests for tool-using agents edit the environment, for instance by hiding a hostile note in an invoice, but the result only says something about the original task if the edited case is still a valid test of that task, and many evaluations settle this with weak rules like accepting any well-formed edit or anything close in embedding space. The authors propose executable task contracts that state which facts define a task, which edits are allowed, and what completing it means, and that check each edited case before the agent runs. Scoring the same 14,336 stored agent runs under different validity rules, **embedding thresholds across four encoders accepted 75-100% of edits that changed the task, such as swapping the payee, while rejecting 24-45% of valid hostile notes**. Under a `MiniLM` cosine threshold `Mistral` looked vulnerable on all 64 tasks, but only 26 had a successful valid attack, and replaying saved solutions or allowing edits to benchmark fields fail in similar ways.

papers.title: AphaVoice: Text-to-Speech Model for Aphasia Patient Simulation
papers.abstract: While language therapy is the primary treatment for post-stroke aphasia, limited clinical resources often restrict patient access to proper care. Addressing this gap requires reliable training simulations for medical professionals. However, current AI efforts focus almost exclusively on speech processing, leaving speech generation largely unexplored. This study introduces AphaVoice, a novel text-to-speech (TTS) framework explicitly engineered to synthesize highly realistic aphasic speech. Evaluated against state-of-the-art TTS systems, AphaVoice demonstrates a superior ability to capture the clinical feature of dysfluency, outperforming existing models in temporal metrics while consistently maintaining speaker identity. By leveraging latent space shifting, the model also supports multi-speaker generation without sacrificing phonetic realism. Ultimately, AphaVoice provides a scalable, high-fidelity tool for medical training and clinical simulation related to aphasia.
papers.summary: Language therapy is the main treatment for post-stroke aphasia, but limited clinical resources restrict access, and training simulations for clinicians need realistic synthetic aphasic speech that current AI work, focused almost entirely on speech processing, does not provide. `AphaVoice` is a text-to-speech (TTS) framework engineered to synthesize aphasic speech, using latent space shifting to support multiple speakers without losing phonetic realism. Compared with state-of-the-art TTS systems, **it better captures the clinical feature of dysfluency, outperforming existing models on temporal metrics while maintaining speaker identity**, and is positioned as a scalable tool for medical training and clinical simulation.

papers.title: AlignPoison: Conditional Targeted Poisoning of Generative Recommenders via Decoding-Aligned Prefixes
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation models based on autoregressive decoding have been adopted as alternatives to classical ranking-based systems. While their modeling flexibility has been widely studied, their resilience to data poisoning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we ask: how susceptible are generative recommenders to conditional targeted poisoning? Under a realistic setting where an adversary can inject limited malicious interactions and query a recommendation API as a black box, our empirical study shows that generative recommenders are vulnerable: injecting fewer than 1% synthetic interactions significantly increases the likelihood of promoting malicious targets under the trigger. To characterize this vulnerability, we analyze the synthesis of malicious interactions from two perspectives: (i) decoding alignment and (ii) prefix popularity. We observe that short, context-aligned prefixes that are both common under the model's induced transition dynamics and strongly linked to a frequent trigger consistently amplify targeted promotion. Motivated by this analysis, we develop AlignPoison, a black-box framework that discovers and samples context-aligned prefixes from API outputs. We conduct experiments on benchmarks in unimodal and multimodal generative recommendation settings. Results show that these prefixes outperform competitive baselines, improving ASR lift by up to 16.3 percentage points and highlighting a decoding-dependent, context-sensitive poisoning vulnerability in generative recommendation models.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders that produce item sequences by autoregressive decoding are replacing classical ranking systems, but their resilience to data poisoning has barely been studied. Under a realistic threat model where an adversary injects a limited number of malicious interactions and queries the recommendation API as a black box, the authors show that **injecting fewer than 1% synthetic interactions significantly raises the chance of promoting a malicious target under a trigger**. Analysis of decoding alignment and prefix popularity reveals that short, context-aligned prefixes that are common under the model's transition dynamics and strongly linked to a frequent trigger amplify targeted promotion, which motivates `AlignPoison`, a black-box framework that discovers and samples such prefixes from API outputs. On unimodal and multimodal generative recommendation benchmarks these prefixes beat competitive baselines, improving attack success rate lift by up to 16.3 percentage points.

papers.title: HiPPT: Physiology-Grounded Wearable PPG Representation Learning via Multi-Scope Text Alignment
papers.abstract: Reusable wearable PPG representations should capture local pulse morphology and broader physiological regularities. Existing pretraining objectives, however, usually apply supervision at the recording or pair level, overlooking that different concepts become reliable over different scopes of waveform evidence. We propose HiPPT, a physiology-grounded framework that matches each supervision source to its appropriate evidence scope. We construct a PPG-Text corpus of over 4 million wrist-worn recordings from 202K users, pairing recordings with waveform-derived morphology and metadata-derived context descriptions. HiPPT combines record-level morphology alignment, which grounds individual recordings in pulse characteristics, with cross-recording context alignment, which aggregates recordings sharing the same metadata tuple to capture context-consistent regularities. Waveform-guided text modeling further recovers masked contextual concepts from PPG patch representations, providing fine-grained waveform-text supervision. Across six downstream tasks spanning blood pressure, vascular stiffness, physiological attributes, and cross-dataset heart-rate estimation, HiPPT achieves the best result on the primary linear-probing metrics. The aligned space also supports zero-shot profiling of age group, sex, and BMI category, individually and jointly, with performance improving as more recordings are aggregated. These results show that evidence-scope matching yields transferable and semantically accessible wearable PPG representations. Code and pretrained weights will be released.
papers.summary: Reusable wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) representations should capture both local pulse morphology and broader physiological regularities, but existing pretraining objectives supervise at the recording or pair level and ignore that different concepts become reliable over different scopes of waveform evidence. `HiPPT` matches each supervision source to its evidence scope: record-level morphology alignment grounds individual recordings in pulse characteristics, cross-recording context alignment aggregates recordings sharing the same metadata tuple, and waveform-guided text modeling recovers masked contextual concepts from PPG patch representations. It is trained on a PPG-text corpus of over 4 million wrist-worn recordings from 202K users paired with waveform-derived morphology and metadata-derived context descriptions. **Across six downstream tasks covering blood pressure, vascular stiffness, physiological attributes, and cross-dataset heart-rate estimation, `HiPPT` achieves the best primary linear-probing results**, and the aligned space supports zero-shot profiling of age group, sex, and BMI category that improves as more recordings are aggregated.

papers.title: A Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM) for Physically-Interpretable Rainfall-Evapotranspiration-Runoff Simulation Across Diverse Hydroclimatic Regimes
papers.abstract:
Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships.
  We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks.
  GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows. Learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships governing snowmelt, runoff, seepage, and evapotranspiration. GCHM combines competitive predictive performance with mass conservation and interpretability, providing a foundation for hydrologic modeling and counterfactual analysis.
papers.summary: Machine learning has improved rainfall-runoff prediction, but most data-driven models are hard to interpret and do not enforce physical conservation laws. The Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (`GCHM`) is a mass-conserving architecture built on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP), with five storage states for canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation, and constrained gates that govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships. Evaluated on 50 `CAMELS` catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes with NOAA AORC forcing and remotely sensed land-surface data, using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, **`GCHM` reproduces streamflow dynamics across all regimes including arid catchments while keeping states and fluxes interpretable**. Ablations show simplified variants do fine in wet conditions but fail to capture flow persistence and recession in dry periods when groundwater sustains low flows, and the learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships.

papers.title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
papers.abstract: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.
papers.summary: Explainer videos are treated not as pixels to generate but as programs: a script, storyboard, and per-frame animation code that a deterministic renderer turns into frames, so the artifact can be read, diffed, tested, and audited. `Reels-RSI` is an open-source reel director for agent harnesses whose self-improvement happens at the program level: every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot, retrospectives pair each check finding with the diff that fixed it, lessons that a static check can catch are compiled into rules with must-fail and must-pass examples so the memory is unit-tested, and a bounded benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it. Across 111 reels, a rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after, rules served as a guard for a weaker director (thirty violations unguarded versus five), and lessons shortened revision loops without compounding or moving the judge. **The first playbook rewrite's 11-1 verdict turned out to be a position bias, with judges picking the second-shown reel 62-81% of the time**, masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft; four failure modes of the preference signal are documented along with which check caught each and the fixes.

papers.title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
papers.abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (DEFT), a plug-and-play adapter for EFM fine-tuning. DEFT encourages branch disentanglement of pretrained tokens into task-oriented content and subject-consistent style, then performs downstream prediction from the content branch. It instantiates this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones show that DEFT improves matched fine-tuning baselines. Further ablations and analyses support the intended content/style branch organization.
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models (EFMs) transfer representations learned from large multi-subject pretraining, but their embeddings retain substantial subject-specific variation that burdens downstream classifiers, especially in cross-subject settings. Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (`DEFT`) is a plug-and-play adapter that splits pretrained tokens into a task-oriented content branch and a subject-consistent style branch and predicts from content alone, implementing this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. **Across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones, `DEFT` improves over matched fine-tuning baselines**, and ablations support the intended content/style separation.

papers.title: Rethinking Activation Functions: Reducing Bias Can Improve Learning
papers.abstract: Many widely used activation functions, including ReLU, GELU, Swish, and Sigmoid, produce predominantly positive outputs, resulting in a nonzero post-activation mean that we term activation bias. Despite its ubiquity, the effect of activation bias on learning dynamics remains poorly understood. Using controlled models, we show that activation bias accelerates initial loss reduction but is accompanied by overshooting, non-smooth trajectories, and a steeper loss landscape. This early advantage also coincides with the model's use of task-relevant information encoded in the activation bias component. In contrast, reducing activation bias slows initial learning but ultimately yields a lower final loss. Experiments on larger vision and language models exhibit a similar pattern: smaller activation bias is associated with better late-stage performance. Thus, this seemingly minor property can substantially redirect learning and warrants explicit consideration in future activation function design.
papers.summary: Widely used activation functions such as `ReLU`, `GELU`, `Swish`, and `Sigmoid` produce mostly positive outputs, giving a nonzero post-activation mean the authors call activation bias, whose effect on learning dynamics has been poorly understood. Using controlled models, they show that activation bias accelerates initial loss reduction but brings overshooting, non-smooth trajectories, and a steeper loss landscape, with the early advantage coinciding with the model exploiting task-relevant information carried in the bias component. **Reducing activation bias slows initial learning but ultimately yields a lower final loss**, and larger vision and language models show the same pattern of smaller bias associating with better late-stage performance, suggesting this property deserves explicit consideration in activation function design.

papers.title: MontageFlow: Physically Valid High Fidelity EEG Generation
papers.abstract: Generative modeling offers a promising solution to the scarcity of labeled clinical electroencephalography (EEG) data under strict privacy constraints. Although recent generative models report substantial improvements in generation fidelity, we show that these gains conceal a categorical failure. EEG is not an arbitrary multichannel signal: each channel records the voltage difference between two scalp electrodes. So, real recordings satisfy exact linear identities among their channels. Current generators invariably violate these identities, yet this has gone unnoticed. We therefore propose MontageFlow, a flow-matching model that enforces these identities by restricting its output to signals that satisfy them. We find that ensuring validity improves fidelity too. Furthermore, to retain the EEG characteristics that oversmoothing washes out, we also condition the model on a physiological state vector encoded from the whole EEG window. For generation, this vector is drawn from a prior fitted in latent space. Across 3 large-scale benchmarks, our model improves TS-FID by 1.6-3.6$\times$ over the closest rival while ensuring validity.
papers.summary: Generative models could ease the scarcity of labeled clinical electroencephalography (EEG) data under privacy constraints, but each EEG channel records a voltage difference between two scalp electrodes, so real recordings satisfy exact linear identities among channels that current generators invariably violate without anyone noticing. `MontageFlow` is a flow-matching model that restricts its outputs to signals satisfying these identities, and it is further conditioned on a physiological state vector encoded from the whole EEG window, drawn at generation time from a prior fitted in latent space, to retain characteristics that oversmoothing washes out. **Across three large-scale benchmarks it improves `TS-FID` by 1.6-3.6x over the closest rival** while guaranteeing validity, and the authors find that enforcing validity itself improves fidelity.

papers.title: TartanMatch: Towards Universal Dense Correspondence Across Modalities
papers.abstract: Robotic platforms combine multi-modal sensors to operate across diverse conditions, but most dense correspondence methods are limited to RGB-RGB or a small set of modality pairs. Training a model for each modality pair scales poorly with the number of sensors and forgoes potential positive transfer across modality pairs. We introduce TartanMatch, a unified model for dense correspondence across all 25 ordered pairs among RGB, event, thermal, depth, and projected LiDAR. TartanMatch adapts an RGB-pretrained correspondence model to all modality pairs within one shared network using lightweight modality adaptation and a mixture of real and synthetic data. On zero-shot real-world benchmarks, TartanMatch reduces Endpoint Error (EPE) over the strongest baselines by 61.9% for cross-modal matching and 49.6% for same-modal matching. We further show that joint training across all modality pairs improves average matching accuracy over pair-specific training, especially on challenging cross-modal pairs. These results demonstrate that a single model achieves broad multi-modal coverage and state-of-the-art matching accuracy.
papers.summary: Robotic platforms fuse multi-modal sensors, yet most dense correspondence methods handle only RGB-RGB or a few modality pairs, and training a separate model per pair scales poorly and forgoes positive transfer. `TartanMatch` adapts an RGB-pretrained correspondence model into a single shared network covering all 25 ordered pairs among RGB, event, thermal, depth, and projected LiDAR, using lightweight modality adaptation and a mix of real and synthetic data. **On zero-shot real-world benchmarks it reduces Endpoint Error (EPE) by 61.9% for cross-modal and 49.6% for same-modal matching** relative to the strongest baselines, and joint training across all pairs improves average accuracy over pair-specific training, especially on hard cross-modal pairs.

papers.title: Compositional Concepts Erasing: Disentangling Object-Style via Domain Manifold Unlearning
papers.abstract: Diffusion models pose significant risks regarding the generation of illicit content and copyright violations. This has catalyzed the development of machine unlearning to erase harmful concepts or copyrighted styles from a model's generative repertoire without compromising its general performance. However, previous unlearning approaches on diffusion models have largely focused on either object-level or style-level removal and failed to address the challenge of object-style combination unlearning. At the same time, multiple unlearning requests often lead to catastrophic forgetting. To address these challenges, we propose Domain Manifold Unlearning (DMU), which uses an EMA-updated feature proxy extracted from intermediate diffusion features to represent the retained target-object direction. As a lightweight estimating representation of an object, DMU enables selective unlearning of domain-specific components in a specific object while preserving other semantic representations, thereby significantly enhancing robustness in multiple combination unlearning scenarios. Extensive experiments show that DMU significantly mitigates catastrophic forgetting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods of batch unlearning and sequential unlearning.
papers.summary: Machine unlearning for diffusion models has mostly targeted either objects or styles in isolation, leaving object-style combinations unaddressed, and sequences of unlearning requests tend to cause catastrophic forgetting. Domain Manifold Unlearning (`DMU`) builds an exponential-moving-average feature proxy from intermediate diffusion features to represent the retained target-object direction, enabling selective removal of domain-specific components of a particular object while preserving its other semantic representations. **In experiments, `DMU` substantially mitigates catastrophic forgetting and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both batch and sequential unlearning** scenarios.

papers.title: Query-Adaptive Neuron Steering for LLMs
papers.abstract: Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. This raises a natural question: Can internal steering in LLMs be made query-adaptive? In this work, we investigate whether query-induced internal activations can guide adaptive steering in LLMs. Our pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons can improve model performance. Based on these findings, we propose Q-NeuS, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that dynamically determines which neurons to modulate and by how much for each input. Specifically, Q-NeuS constructs a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and employs a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to generate neuron-wise modulation coefficients. To learn effective intervention strategies, we introduce Neu-GRPO, which adapts group-relative optimization to train the Query-Adaptive Gate using the relative performance of multiple neuron intervention configurations. The base LLM remains frozen throughout training and inference, and no task or subject labels are required at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Q-NeuS consistently improves model performance and exhibits broad applicability across model scales and strong cross-benchmark transferability.
papers.summary: Eliciting large language model (LLM) capabilities at inference time usually relies on context engineering or fixed activation steering, neither of which adapts to the knowledge and reasoning demands of individual queries. Pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons helps, motivating `Q-NeuS`, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that builds a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and uses a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to produce per-neuron modulation coefficients for each input. The gate is trained with `Neu-GRPO`, which adapts group-relative optimization to compare the outcomes of multiple intervention configurations, while the base LLM stays frozen and no task or subject labels are needed at inference. **Across multiple LLMs and benchmarks, `Q-NeuS` consistently improves performance** and transfers across model scales and benchmarks.

papers.title: Identication and Estimation of Nonsymmetric Determinantal Point Processes
papers.abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) provide tractable distributions for nite random sets, but the usual symmetric-kernel specication imposes nonpositive pairwise dependence. Statistical research on nonsymmetric DPPs, which can accommodate positive dependence, remains limited. We study identication and estimation for this class. First, we establish the equivalence of two sucient conditions for a nonsymmetric kernel to dene a valid DPP. Second, we develop the identication theory for nonsymmetric DPPs. Third, we develop cardinality-truncated maximum-likelihood estimation and estimation by averaged stochastic gradient descent. Under suitable identication and regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality for both estimators. Simulations examine identication, the eects of truncation, and the nite-sample performance of the estimators. We illustrate the methods with two cyber applications at markedly dierent sampling frequencies: weekly sector-by-breach data and second-by-second enterprise authentication data with more than ve million set observations.
papers.summary: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) provide tractable distributions over finite random sets, but the standard symmetric-kernel specification forces nonpositive pairwise dependence, and statistical theory for nonsymmetric DPPs that can accommodate positive dependence has been limited. The work proves the equivalence of two sufficient conditions for a nonsymmetric kernel to define a valid DPP, develops identification theory for the class, and proposes cardinality-truncated maximum-likelihood and averaged stochastic gradient descent estimators, **establishing consistency and asymptotic normality for both estimators** under suitable identification and regularity conditions. Simulations probe identification, truncation effects, and finite-sample behavior, and two cyber applications illustrate the methods at very different sampling rates: weekly sector-by-breach data and second-by-second enterprise authentication data with more than five million set observations.

papers.title: ScienceBuddy-PV: A Verifier-Governed Recursive Improvement Protocol for Panvascular Intervention Research
papers.abstract: ScienceBuddy-PV adapts the ScienceBuddy recursive-in-recursive design to panvascular intervention research through a structured evidence ledger, device-vessel ontology, abstention contract and retained failure bank.
