In `Von`, fixing a shared separator's position eliminates two eligibility-induced preference flips, and `Laya-typed` produces five passage swaps without strict binary flips on its default CUDA path, with both yearly action-change intervals including zero and its probability movement vanishing at four-decimal resolution in an FP32 rerun.

papers.title: PVFH-Bench: Benchmarking Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of multimodal tasks. However, object hallucination remains a persistent challenge, undermining model reliability in applications such as visual question answering, embodied agents, and human-AI decision support systems. In this paper, inspired by cognitive science studies on perceptual bias, we investigate a new failure mode termed Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination (PVFH). Specifically, PVFH refers to a premise-induced reasoning error in which models become anchored to visually confusable evidence, accept a false textual premise, and subsequently generate responses about an absent yet visually plausible object. To systematically study this phenomenon, we introduce PVFH-Bench, a benchmark that automatically constructs visually confusable but absent targets and pairs the core hallucination setting with diagnostic subsets to trace how models move from object recognition to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Experimental results on 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs demonstrate that all evaluated models are highly vulnerable to Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination. Moreover, we find that explicit chain-of-thought reasoning can further exacerbate this failure mode by encouraging models to overinterpret weak visual cues as supporting evidence for hallucinated objects.
papers.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) still hallucinate objects, and the authors characterize a failure mode they call Premise-Induced Visual Fixation Hallucination (PVFH), in which a model anchors on visually confusable evidence, accepts a false textual premise, and then describes an absent but visually plausible object. `PVFH-Bench` automatically constructs visually confusable but absent targets and pairs the core hallucination setting with diagnostic subsets that trace how models move from object recognition to the hallucination. **All 10 state-of-the-art LVLMs evaluated are highly vulnerable, and explicit chain-of-thought reasoning makes the failure worse** by encouraging models to overinterpret weak visual cues as evidence for the hallucinated object.

papers.title: PEARL: Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Agents
papers.abstract: Terminal rewards make multi-turn agents trainable without step-level annotations, but group-relative advantages provide little guidance about which intermediate decisions to adjust. Failed trajectories also contain reasonable actions, while unfavorable decision patterns can recur as training proceeds. We introduce PEARL (Process-Experience Aware Reinforcement Learning), which improves local credit assignment without an additional critic. Given two continuations from the same history with different outcomes, PEARL locates their first divergence and builds a feature representation of each branch's local decision. It clusters these decision features in recent failure and success memories to identify recurring local patterns. Using this pattern memory, PEARL selectively strengthens negative advantages at lower-reward decisions, while leaving positive advantages and the base policy optimizer unchanged. On AppWorld, PEARL improves over ARPO on Normal and Challenge tasks at both 4B and 8B scales. On ALFWorld, it achieves 97.9% mean success at 4B, 2.7 points above the strongest baseline, while remaining competitive at 8B. Ablations of shaping location, success-bank filtering, and memory window support the value of selective, recurring-pattern-based updates.
papers.summary: Multi-turn agents trained only on terminal rewards get little signal about which intermediate decision caused a failure, since group-relative advantages spread credit evenly across a trajectory and failed rollouts still contain reasonable actions. `PEARL` takes two continuations from the same history that ended differently, locates their first divergence, and builds features of each branch's local decision, then clusters those features against recent success and failure memories to spot recurring bad patterns. It uses that pattern memory to selectively strengthen negative advantages at lower-reward decisions, leaving positive advantages and the base policy optimizer untouched, so no extra critic is needed. On `ALFWorld` it reaches **97.9% mean success at 4B parameters, 2.7 points above the strongest baseline**, and it improves on `ARPO` across the Normal and Challenge splits of `AppWorld` at both 4B and 8B.

papers.title: AegisVox: Factorized Privacy and Clinical Preservation for Long-Form Speech
papers.abstract: Clinical speech reveals identity through both spoken identifiers and voice, yet its pauses, delivery, and speaker roles can also carry useful clinical evidence. Protecting that speech therefore requires more than preserving its words. We present AegisVox, a factorized framework that assigns consistent surrogate voices and edits identifier-bearing turns using document-consistent replacements. Across 390 public simulated or non-patient conversations totaling 63.6 hours, a matched comparison of two speech renderers separates replacement realization from retained identifiers, speaker linkage, and clinical preservation. Text-to-speech rendering realizes 535/601 planned replacements versus 453/601 for the codec-based speech editor. However, similar aggregate clinical preservation conceals more model-labeled contradictions, and conversation-wide speaker scores conceal greater edited-speech linkage under a score-direction sensitivity analysis. Fresh transcription of original audio provides a reference for interpreting the clinical measurement chain; an independent judge tests sensitivity to model-based assessment. Better replacement realization can therefore coexist with worse clinical or speaker-linkage measurements. AegisVox supports use-specific evaluation of those tradeoffs, not a guarantee of identifier removal or clinical safety.
papers.summary: Clinical conversations expose identity through both spoken identifiers and voice timbre, while pauses, delivery, and speaker roles can carry clinically useful evidence that blunt anonymization destroys. `AegisVox` factorizes the two concerns, assigning each speaker a consistent surrogate voice and rewriting identifier-bearing turns with document-consistent replacements, then compares two renderers over 390 simulated or non-patient conversations totaling 63.6 hours. Text-to-speech rendering realized **535 of 601 planned replacements, against 453 for the codec-based speech editor**, yet that better realization coincided with more model-labeled clinical contradictions and greater speaker linkage under a score-direction sensitivity analysis. The authors present the framework as a way to measure these tradeoffs for a specific use, not as a guarantee that identifiers are removed.

papers.title: Shaping Latent Mixture-of-Experts: From Expert Geometry to Layerwise Capacity Allocation
papers.abstract: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly increase expert count by narrowing each expert, treating expert shape as a by-product of routing granularity. LatentMoE moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space, exposing the input dimension and intermediate width of each expert as explicit design choices. We show that an expert's local Jacobian rank is jointly bounded by these two dimensions, and that balancing them maximizes the rank ceiling at fixed per-expert parameters. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities consistently favor near-square experts. We further use layerwise intrinsic dimension (ID) to guide capacity allocation across depth, co-varying the number and shape of experts while keeping per-layer parameter count, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant. Compared with layer-homogeneous baselines, our ID-guided allocation achieves lower validation loss and stronger downstream performance. These results establish expert shape and layerwise allocation as practical design axes for MoEs.
papers.summary: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models normally add experts by making each one narrower, treating expert shape as a by-product of routing granularity rather than a design choice. `LatentMoE` moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space so input dimension and intermediate width become explicit, and shows an expert's local Jacobian rank is bounded jointly by the two, meaning **balanced, near-square experts maximize the rank ceiling at a fixed per-expert parameter budget**. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities confirm that preference, and allocating capacity across depth using layerwise intrinsic dimension, while holding per-layer parameters, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant, yields lower validation loss and better downstream results than layer-homogeneous baselines.

papers.title: Prospective Forcing: Learning to Look Ahead for Autoregressive Long Video Diffusion
papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generators synthesize long videos through chunk-wise rollouts, yet they are typically trained to predict only the immediate future. This limited prediction horizon makes it challenging to maintain video quality over extended rollouts. To address this problem, we introduce Prospective Forcing, a multi-head prediction framework that injects long-range predictive signals into autoregressive video representations. Built on a rolling-window generator, Prospective Forcing attaches lightweight, offset-specific heads that share the same conditioning information and independently predict chunks at different future temporal offsets. By extending supervision beyond the next chunk, these heads encourage the shared history representation to retain information useful for longer-horizon prediction, supporting temporally consistent generation. At inference time, we accelerate sampling by using accepted future-chunk predictions to skip full-window backbone executions. We equip the head with learnable embeddings to generate multiple candidates for the next chunk, and a learned verifier either selects a candidate or rejects all and falls back to standard autoregressive generation.
papers.summary: Autoregressive video generators build long clips chunk by chunk but are trained to predict only the immediate next chunk, so quality degrades across extended rollouts. Prospective Forcing attaches lightweight offset-specific heads to a rolling-window generator that share the same conditioning and each predict a chunk at a different future time offset, which **pushes the shared history representation to retain information useful well beyond the next step**. Learnable embeddings let a head propose several candidate next chunks that a trained verifier either accepts or rejects in favor of standard autoregressive decoding, and accepted future-chunk predictions let the sampler skip full-window backbone passes at inference.

papers.title: RASSG: Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating for Streaming Tool Execution
papers.abstract: Streaming speech assistants can launch tools before users finish speaking, overlapping execution with incoming speech to reduce user waiting time. However, subsequent self-corrections can invalidate apparently stable arguments, causing stale execution whose irreversible effects persist even after the final call is corrected. We propose Repair-Aware Semantic Survival Gating (RASSG) to jointly control tool launch and cancellation during streaming speech. RASSG launches a tool when three consecutive speech recognition results arrive with identical nonempty arguments, then combines calibrated argument invalidity risk with execution costs to decide cancellation at the last feasible opportunity before effects become irreversible. Evaluation on ReCAST, FDB-v3, and Audio2Tool uses a controlled execution clock with fixed tool runtimes and cancellation parameters. On ReCAST's prospective-repair subset, RASSG reduces the stale execution rate from LocalAgreement-2's 50.00% to 3.15%, with a mean delay of 3.676s across successful trajectories. The stale reduction also holds against every early-execution baseline on both public speech datasets. Ablations with identical initial launches support active cancellation, showing the value of controlling ongoing calls before their effects become irreversible. Code and data are available at https://github.com/daijinhu/RASSG.
papers.summary: Streaming speech assistants cut waiting time by launching tool calls before the speaker finishes, but a later self-correction can invalidate arguments that looked settled, leaving behind an irreversible stale action. `RASSG` launches a tool only once three consecutive speech recognition results agree on identical non-empty arguments, then combines a calibrated estimate of argument-invalidity risk with execution costs to cancel at the last feasible moment before effects become permanent. On the prospective-repair subset of `ReCAST`, it cuts the stale execution rate from **50.00% for a LocalAgreement-2 baseline to 3.15%**, with a mean delay of 3.676 seconds across successful trajectories, and the reduction holds against every early-execution baseline on `FDB-v3` and `Audio2Tool`.

papers.title: Ascent Conditions for Length-Normalized Single-Rollout Policy Updates
papers.abstract: Dividing each trajectory's score contribution by its realized length can change the direction of a reward-centered policy update. In a finite trajectory model, we derive an exact ascent threshold for a three-outcome softmax policy and exhibit a binary-reward example in which the expected Euclidean update decreases task success. Natural-gradient ascent holds for fully controllable outcome distributions with deterministic binary labels, but can fail under a one-parameter restriction. A third-order U-statistic estimates the first-order return change without bias from independent current-policy trajectories, one per request. In the example, a same-sample plug-in estimator instead has the opposite sign in expectation for batch sizes two through forty-nine. Exact policy-grid enumeration confirms the local sign reversal. In a branching process, length-normalized learning initially loses return, then recovers and exceeds the unnormalized comparator. The analysis concerns the expected update field at the current policy.
papers.summary: Dividing each trajectory's score contribution by its realized length, a normalization common in policy-gradient training of language models, can reverse the direction of a reward-centered update. The analysis derives an exact ascent threshold for a three-outcome softmax policy and exhibits a binary-reward example where **the expected Euclidean update actually decreases task success**, with exhaustive policy-grid enumeration confirming the local sign reversal. Natural-gradient ascent still holds for fully controllable outcome distributions with deterministic binary labels but can fail under a one-parameter restriction, and a third-order U-statistic over independent current-policy trajectories estimates the first-order return change without bias, whereas a same-sample plug-in estimator carries the opposite sign in expectation for batch sizes from two to forty-nine.

papers.title: A Hybrid Kinematic GCN and Elastic Transformer for Efficient Indian Sign Language Recognition
papers.abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) presents complex challenges due to variable signing speeds and spatial intricacies. Specifically, Indian Sign Language (ISL) requires precise modeling of its inherently bimanual nature and is bottlenecked by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and the inability of standard models to handle irregular signing velocities. To address this, a structurally-aware hybrid framework for efficient, gloss ISL recognition is proposed. To minimize computational redundancy, an entropy-driven SVD sampler that dynamically extracts informative keyframes is used. Because this subsampling creates irregular physical time gaps, the proposed architecture employs a Continuous Dual Positional Encoding paired with a distance-aware Elastic Transformer to preserve natural signing rhythm. Spatially, a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN explicitly models bimanual geometry using unified bone-joint features. To validate our framework, a 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset is created. Augmented by Physical Node Dropout and ArcFace optimization to mitigate subject-specific memorization, our framework achieves a competitive 89.8% accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for complex sign language modeling.
papers.summary: Indian Sign Language (ISL) recognition is held back by inherently two-handed signs, irregular signing velocities, and a shortage of large-vocabulary benchmarks. The proposed pipeline picks informative keyframes with an entropy-driven singular value decomposition sampler, compensates for the uneven time gaps that subsampling creates using continuous dual positional encoding feeding a distance-aware Elastic Transformer, and models two-handed geometry with a kinematically conditioned adaptive graph convolutional network over unified bone-joint features. Trained on a newly built 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset with physical node dropout and `ArcFace` optimization to limit subject-specific memorization, it reaches **89.8% accuracy**.

papers.title: Triage-PiEvo: Evidence Admission for Principle-Evolving Scientific Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based AI Scientists advance scientific discovery, yet they suffer from inefficiencies due to noisy observations. Existing principle-evolving agents act on every anomaly, leaving its source unresolved: a new mechanism or an evaluation artifact, so invalid revisions bias evolution. To address this, we formulate revision as evidence admission: anomalies steer search immediately, but only independently verified evidence may rewrite persistent principles, and contradicted principles are retracted. We realize this in TRIAGE-PIEVO , which pairs an anomaly-responsive search portfolio with a staged verification gate that alone controls what enters principle state. Across four scientific tasks with three backbones, TRIAGE-PIEVO (1) attains the highest average solution quality with +7.5%~11.8% over the strongest baseline per backbone, matching the strongest baseline's full-budget quality with one-third of the evaluation budget on Qwen3-235B; and additional stress tests and cross-harness deployment demonstrate that (2) in constructed stress tests, it admits none of the corrupted, hidden-source, or exploit evidence that ungated variants admit, while missing no planted mechanism, and (3) plugged unchanged into three external research harnesses, it cuts false evidence admissions by over 60% and raises verified scores by 31%~43%.
papers.summary: Agents that evolve scientific principles from experiments tend to react to every anomaly without first deciding whether it reflects a real mechanism or an evaluation artifact, so invalid revisions accumulate and bias the search. `TRIAGE-PIEVO` reframes revision as evidence admission: anomalies may steer search immediately, but only independently verified evidence passing a staged verification gate can rewrite persistent principles, and contradicted principles are retracted. Across four scientific tasks and three backbones it improves average solution quality by **7.5% to 11.8% over the strongest baseline**, matching that baseline's full-budget quality on `Qwen3-235B` with a third of the evaluation budget. In stress tests it admitted none of the corrupted, hidden-source, or exploit evidence that ungated variants accepted, and dropped unchanged into three external research harnesses it cut false evidence admissions by over 60%.

papers.title: One-Way Coupling via Patchwise Adaptive Normalization in Transformer Surrogates
papers.abstract: Many physical systems exhibit one-way coupling: exogenous fields such as medium density or obstacle geometry influence the dynamics without being affected by them. We investigate how explicitly representing these fields can improve the accuracy and computational efficiency of transformer-based PDE surrogates. Building on spatially adaptive normalization, we introduce Patchwise Adaptive Normalization (PAdaNorm), which partitions exogenous fields into patches aligned with the state tokenization. We evaluate PAdaNorm on datasets from three different domains, using a Walrus-inspired transformer architecture. Across the three PDE families, PAdaNorm is on par with or up to 16% better than parameter-matched baselines in mean long-horizon variance-scaled RMSE on 60-step autoregressive rollouts. We also find that PAdaNorm better maintains hard physical constraints over long rollouts, such as preventing flow into impenetrable solid regions in porous media. When the conditioning is static, PAdaNorm caches the conditioning embeddings once and reuses them across the entire rollout, reducing inference FLOPs per step by up to 36% compared with parameter-matched baselines. An ablation over eight conditioning variants shows that modulating a single attention axis (temporal or spatial) suffices and that a lightweight shared MLP across blocks remains competitive with per-block projections.
papers.summary: Many physical systems have one-way coupling, where exogenous fields such as medium density or obstacle geometry drive the dynamics without being changed by them. Patchwise Adaptive Normalization (`PAdaNorm`) represents those fields explicitly by splitting them into patches aligned with the state tokenization and using them to modulate normalization inside a `Walrus`-inspired transformer surrogate for partial differential equations. Across three equation families it matches or beats parameter-matched baselines by **up to 16% on long-horizon variance-scaled error over 60-step autoregressive rollouts**, holds hard constraints such as no flow into impenetrable solid regions better, and when conditioning is static caches its embeddings once to cut per-step inference FLOPs by up to 36%.

papers.title: Accelerating Cross-Model LLM Inference via Attention Map Reuse
papers.abstract: LLM-augmented data workflows often involve multiple heterogeneous models operating over substantial shared context, such as schemas, tool specifications, interaction history, and intermediate results. Although prefix caching can reduce prefilling overhead, existing approaches are largely limited to reuse within the same model because KV states are tightly coupled to model-specific architectures. We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross-model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix-heavy data workflows. Our code is available: https://github.com/PKU-DAIR/MapFlow.
papers.summary: Workflows that route a request across several different language models share large blocks of context such as schemas, tool specifications, and history, but prefix caching cannot carry across models because key-value states are tied to one architecture. `MapFlow` reuses attention maps instead, on the argument that token dependency patterns transfer more readily than KV state, combining partial recomputation with a lightweight linear translation across layers and heads, plus block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel to make the approach workable on long contexts. Experiments report **lower prefilling latency and better end-to-end serving efficiency across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads** with generation quality preserved.

papers.title: DexCast: Learning Real-World Dexterous Control from Human Videos
papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) perception have opened new opportunities for learning dexterous robotic skills from human videos. However, existing dexterous imitation learning methods often rely on costly and manually teleoperated robot demonstrations, requiring substantial human effort. Therefore, we build DEXCAST, a framework that learns dexterous robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D videos by leveraging joint HOI reconstructions, without requiring any teleoperation. Furthermore, how to model high-dimensional robotic hand motion and extract temporal context to inform future action generation remains a key challenge. To this end, we propose a DexHand Motion Perception Module (DMPM) to capture inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies in compact latent representations that condition our diffusion policy. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that DEXCAST achieves exceptional performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.
papers.summary: Teaching robot hands dexterous skills usually depends on teleoperated demonstrations that take substantial human effort to collect. `DEXCAST` instead learns hand control from monocular RGB-D video of people manipulating objects, using joint 3D hand-object interaction reconstruction as its supervision and requiring **no teleoperated robot demonstrations at all**. A DexHand Motion Perception Module compresses inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies into compact latent representations that condition a diffusion policy, and the authors report strong results across a range of real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.title: AcrossVAM2.0: Conflict-Aware Point Supervision for Parameter-Efficient Video Diffusion Adaptation
papers.abstract: Explicit point correspondence is attractive for adapting video generators: it describes how visible surfaces move, but can overwrite the appearance prior learned by a large pretrained model. We study this tension in a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. ACROSSVAM2.0 combines a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad that removes only the auxiliary component opposing the primary flow-matching gradient on shared LoRA parameters. The design preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects its primary update during adaptation. In a four-way ablation trained for 1,000 steps with three independent seeds, the full method lowers KLT forward-backward cycle error in all three seeds relative to a matched flow-only continuation (mean seed-level difference -0.00711, SD 0.00505), while robust sharpness remains positive in all three. An expanded 24-prompt evaluation (216 videos) yields 9.7% lower aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error than the matched control and near-matched performance on six VBench dimensions; however, the seed-level tracking effect is heterogeneous and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022. These results support a bounded claim: conflict-aware adaptation improves correspondence consistency without broad perceptual degradation, but does not uniformly improve video quality. We release equations, pseudocode, matched outputs, source tables, and artifact provenance.
papers.summary: Supervising a video generator with explicit point correspondences describes how visible surfaces move, but it can overwrite the appearance prior the pretrained model already learned. Working inside a 5.01-billion-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer, `ACROSSVAM2.0` adds a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head, zero-initialized residual feedback, and an asymmetric variant of `PCGrad` that strips only the auxiliary gradient component opposing the primary flow-matching update on shared LoRA parameters. Across 24 prompts and 216 videos it reports **9.7% lower aggregate `CoTracker3` cycle error** than a matched flow-only control with near-matched scores on six `VBench` dimensions, though per-seed tracking gains are uneven and Fréchet video distance regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022, supporting only a bounded claim about correspondence consistency.

papers.title: VoTSpeech: Decoupling Voice Design from Speech Generation in Instruction-Following TTS
papers.abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (TTS) typically leaves voice design implicit, as conventional speaker embeddings encode reference audio rather than text-driven targets. We propose VoTSpeech, which decouples voice design from speech generation via an explicit intermediate voice latent. Built on a shared language model backbone, VoTSpeech first predicts a continuous voice latent from text instructions using a flow-based module. This latent serves as a shared condition for both the language model and the Acoustic DiT, guiding autoregressive sequence modeling and acoustic latent generation, respectively, before an audio VAE decoder converts the acoustic latents into waveforms. To capture speaker identity and complementary acoustic nuances, the voice latent is jointly supervised by speaker embeddings and temporally pooled audio VAE features. With task-specific adaptation, VoTSpeech performs strongly on InstructTTSEval-ZH, demonstrating competitive capabilities against strong open-source models while maintaining high naturalness. These results confirm that explicit voice latent design and its conditioning interface effectively empower text-driven voice design for controllable speech synthesis. Code, model, and audio samples are available at https://github.com/ywbn/VoTSpeech .
papers.summary: Instruction-following text-to-speech (TTS) leaves voice design implicit, because conventional speaker embeddings encode a reference recording rather than a voice described in text. `VoTSpeech` inserts an explicit intermediate voice latent, predicted from the text instruction by a flow-based module and then used as a shared condition for both a language model backbone and an acoustic diffusion transformer, whose latents an audio variational autoencoder decodes into waveforms. Supervising that latent jointly with speaker embeddings and temporally pooled audio features lets the system **perform competitively against strong open-source models on `InstructTTSEval-ZH`** while keeping naturalness high.

papers.title: Understanding Hidden Spatial Preferences in Bayesian Optimization
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization uses posterior uncertainty to decide where to explore, but this uncertainty is not spatially neutral. On bounded domains, Gaussian-process posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, giving variance-based acquisition functions a systematic boundary bias. This spatial preference is usually inherited from the surrogate rather than chosen as part of the exploration strategy. We separate these roles by keeping the predictive model fixed and modifying the spatial preference of the exploration term. We control the preference with spatial weight fields and amortize their construction with neural surrogates. Controlled experiments show that the Gaussian process' default boundary bias changes which parts of the domain are explored and which optima are reached. We compare three alternative exploration principles and find, across standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, that they can often lower regret, particularly early in the optimization. The spatial structure of posterior uncertainty is therefore not a neutral default: it shapes the exploration strategy and can materially affect optimization performance.
papers.summary: Gaussian process posterior variance on a bounded domain is larger near faces, edges, and corners, so variance-driven acquisition functions in Bayesian optimization inherit a boundary bias that was never chosen as part of the exploration strategy. The study separates the two roles by holding the predictive model fixed and changing only the exploration term's spatial preference, encoded as spatial weight fields whose construction is amortized with neural surrogates. Across standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, three alternative exploration principles **often reach lower regret, particularly early in the run**, showing the default boundary bias changes which regions get explored and which optima are found.

papers.title: AlignAudio: A Unified Dual-Alignment Framework for Noise-Robust Speech-Conditioned Generation
papers.abstract: Speech-conditioned generation maps speech signals to target audio outputs. Prior end-to-end speech-conditioned generative models achieve high fidelity in clean acoustic conditions, but their performance degrades substantially under environmental noise. While prior noise-robust approaches have achieved significant success in feature-level purification, maintaining consistent generation under clean and noisy conditioning remains a key challenge. To address this, we propose AlignAudio, a noise-robust generative framework based on dual alignment: (i) aligning the representations of clean and noisy speech to preserve semantic cues, and (ii) enforcing generation-level consistency within a flow matching paradigm to improve conditioning fidelity. Experiments on speech-to-audio (STA) and voice conversion (VC) tasks demonstrate that AlignAudio maintains performance comparable to baselines on clean speech while significantly outperforming them across various noisy conditions. Furthermore, the proposed dual-alignment strategy is applicable to both single- and multi-stream speech conditioning and can be integrated into different flow matching-based generation frameworks and post-training settings. Audio demonstrations and qualitative comparisons: \href{https://alignaudio.github.io/AlignAudio}{\textcolor{cyan}{\textit{https://alignaudio.github.io/AlignAudio}}}.
papers.summary: Models that generate audio conditioned on speech perform well in clean conditions but degrade substantially under environmental noise, and feature-level purification alone does not keep outputs consistent between clean and noisy conditioning. `AlignAudio` applies two alignments at once: matching representations of clean and noisy speech to preserve semantic cues, and enforcing generation-level consistency within a flow matching objective. On speech-to-audio and voice conversion tasks it **holds performance comparable to baselines on clean speech while clearly outperforming them under varied noise**, and the dual-alignment strategy carries over to single- and multi-stream conditioning and to different flow-matching frameworks and post-training setups.

papers.title: Joint Discrete and SE(3) Diffusion for Protein Interface Design
papers.abstract: The design of high-affinity, target-specific protein binders is central to the development of modern therapeutics. However, existing protein-generation methods remain limited in this setting, as many generated designs fail to simultaneously achieve geometric and physicochemical complementarity at binding interfaces. To address this challenge, we introduce PIDiff, a physicochemically enhanced multimodal diffusion framework for protein-protein complex design. PIDiff jointly designs target-conditioned protein sequences and structures by coupling diffusion in discrete sequence space with diffusion on the continuous (SE(3)) structural manifold. At its core, PIDiff employs PIFormer, a novel architecture that interleaves geometry-aware invariant point attention with global sequence self-attention. We further curate PIBench, a protein-protein complex dataset with diverse target scaffolds derived from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We first pretrain PIDiff on PIBench and subsequently fine-tune it for two therapeutically relevant applications: minibinder design and antibody design. PPFrame consistently outperforms baseline methods across sequence design success rate, structure binding energy, and sequence-structure co-designability on all tasks.
papers.summary: Designing protein binders that attach tightly and selectively to a chosen target requires geometric and physicochemical complementarity at the interface simultaneously, which existing generative methods often miss. `PIDiff` co-designs target-conditioned sequence and structure by coupling discrete diffusion over amino acid sequences with SE(3) diffusion on the continuous structural manifold, using an architecture that interleaves geometry-aware invariant point attention with global sequence self-attention. The authors curate `PIBench`, a protein-protein complex dataset with diverse target scaffolds drawn from the Protein Data Bank, pretrain on it, and fine-tune for minibinder and antibody design, reporting **gains over baselines on sequence design success rate, structure binding energy, and sequence-structure co-designability across all tasks**.

papers.title: DSABench: Benchmarking Source Discovery, Coordination, and Execution for Multi-Database Agents
papers.abstract: Most text-to-SQL benchmarks provide the target database. In a large data catalog, however, choosing the sources is part of the problem: an agent must find every database needed for a request, determine how their results fit together, and execute the resulting workflow. We present DSABench to evaluate these capabilities jointly. Its 815 human-reviewed tasks draw on Spider, BIRD, and LiveSQLBench; 618 require several databases to contribute, and 105 allow more than one interpretation of the required sources. Executable contracts define source participation, cross-source dependencies, and source-local execution, while RouteEnv lets agents inspect public catalog evidence without revealing the gold annotations. In our routing-only study across seven model backends, the highest RA-Set score is 60.55%, compared with a highest RA-Graph score of 34.66% when coordination requirements are included. The gap becomes more pronounced when execution is required. Across four backends, median non-privileged Route+Exec-Graph success ranges from 6.69% to 7.98% without clarification and from 11.44% to 13.25% with one clarification; the best observed clarified configuration reaches 16.99%. On ambiguous tasks, clarification improves exact branch-source recovery by 39.8-43.2 percentage points. These findings illustrate why retrieving plausible databases or producing correct local SQL is not enough: an agent must carry the right information through the entire multi-database workflow.
papers.summary: Text-to-SQL benchmarks normally hand the agent its target database, hiding the harder job of locating every source a request needs in a large catalog, working out how their results combine, and executing the resulting workflow. `DSABench` supplies 815 human-reviewed tasks drawn from `Spider`, `BIRD`, and `LiveSQLBench`, 618 of which require several databases, with executable contracts defining source participation and cross-source dependencies and an environment that exposes only public catalog evidence. In routing alone, the best of seven model backends scored 60.55% on set-level source recovery but **only 34.66% once coordination structure was also required**, and median end-to-end routed execution success ran from 6.69% to 7.98% without clarification, rising to roughly 11% to 13% when one clarifying question was allowed. On ambiguous tasks, that single clarification lifted exact branch-source recovery by around 40 percentage points.

papers.title: Towards Merging-conditional Backdoor Unalignment against Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Model merging has become widely adopted for enhancing the task-specific performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) without additional training. While the specialized model from third-party platforms may undergo safety audits (e.g., backdoor detection), we reveal a novel and critical threat: One-sided Merging-Conditional Backdoor (OMCB). OMCB remains dormant and undetectable within one standalone model but activates upon merging, triggering safety unalignment. We first theoretically analyze the existence and geometric location of OMCB, revealing that the parameter shift crossing safety decision boundaries is the main cause of backdoor activation. Building upon this insight, we propose SMOKE, a meta-learning-based attack framework. SMOKE implants OMCB via a bi-level optimization strategy: the inner loop synthesizes surrogate meta-vectors through random low-rank initialization and finite-step maximization, while the outer loop optimizes the target model by simulating the merging process. Furthermore, preliminary analysis shows that the injected OMCB has bounded generalization loss under unknown merging configurations. Extensive experiments across diverse model architectures and merging techniques validate the effectiveness of SMOKE and its resistance to existing backdoor detections, highlighting a significant yet previously overlooked vulnerability in the model merging paradigm.
papers.summary: Merging a third-party specialized model into your own is now routine, and the donor model may pass a safety audit on its own, yet the authors describe a one-sided merging-conditional backdoor that stays dormant and undetected in the standalone model and only undoes safety alignment once merging happens. They analyze where such a backdoor can sit in parameter space, attributing activation to the merge shifting parameters across safety decision boundaries, and build `SMOKE`, a meta-learning framework whose outer loop simulates the merging process while its inner loop synthesizes surrogate task vectors from random low-rank initialization. Across model architectures and merging techniques the implanted behavior **persisted through existing backdoor detection methods**, which points to a gap in the merging pipeline that per-model audits do not cover.

papers.title: Linear-Time Non-Local Codec Placement for Machine Learning Model Compression
papers.abstract: On-device inference imposes constraints on model storage and operand traffic and thus benefits from compressed operand representations, which mandate the use of encoding and decoding operators. However, na\"{\i}ve placement of codec operators can cancel the operand traffic gains sought from compression. In this work, I present an algorithm to place codec operators into a source computational graph to make it compatible with target hardware. The edges of the graph are colored so that each induced subgraph is weakly connected and has a maximal node that both postdominates all subgraph inputs and dominates all subgraph outputs; this unique node - dubbed the $\textit{absolute dominator}$ - is the natural location to observe the traffic flowing through the subgraph and learn parametric codec operators. The algorithm's time complexity is linear in the source graph's size. With respect to na\"{\i}ve local codec placement, the algorithm reduces modeled operand traffic by $24\%$-$44\%$ across four models, including $24\%$ on SigLIP and $34\%$ on SmolLM2.
papers.summary: On-device inference is bounded by model storage and operand traffic, which compressed tensor representations relieve only if the encode and decode operators are placed well, since naive local placement can cancel the savings entirely. The algorithm colors the edges of a computation graph so each induced subgraph is weakly connected and contains one node that postdominates all subgraph inputs and dominates all its outputs, making that node the natural place to observe traffic and learn parametric codec operators. Placement runs in **time linear in graph size and reduces modeled operand traffic by 24% to 44%** relative to naive local placement across four models, including 24% on `SigLIP` and 34% on `SmolLM2`.

papers.title: Lingdan-V2: Large language models for clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine
papers.abstract: Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. We develop a TCM language model family comprising models with 4 billion, 8 billion, and 14 billion parameters. The artificial intelligence contribution is a staged clinical alignment framework integrating large scale continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and prescription-centered reinforcement learning (RL). We further formulate herbal prescription generation as a structured RL problem with prescription-level feedback, enabling direct optimization of clinical decision outputs beyond knowledge reproduction and generic instruction following. The engineering application is TCM clinical decision support, particularly herbal prescription recommendation. We evaluate the models on a public benchmark containing 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 TCM knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks and on a private retrospective dataset of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease prescription cases. The 14 billion parameter reinforcement aligned model achieves a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 on the public benchmark, compared with 32.3 for DeepSeek-R1 with 671 billion total parameters, and a herb-level F1 of 52.8 on the clinical dataset with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training consistently improves prescription recommendation across all scales, while physician-source analysis shows that expert heterogeneity affects reward stability. These findings demonstrate a scalable pathway from domain grounding and reasoning supervision to clinically oriented prescription decision support.
papers.summary: Prescribing in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) means chaining syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herb composition, and dosage, which general medical language models handle poorly. The authors build 4B, 8B, and 14B parameter models through large-scale continued pretraining on TCM texts and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and reinforcement learning with prescription-level feedback so the clinical output itself is optimized rather than knowledge recall. On a public benchmark of 25,620 expert-verified items the 14B reinforcement-aligned model reaches **a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 against 32.3 for `DeepSeek-R1`, which has 671 billion total parameters**, and scores herb-level F1 of 52.8 on a private set of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease cases. The authors also note that disagreement between prescribing physicians destabilizes the reward signal.

papers.title: How to Build a Benchmark That Actually Measures Taste
papers.abstract: Expert-aligned "taste" benchmarks should reward craft judgment, not the ability to game the test. We introduce TasteBench, a pairwise good-vs-bad benchmark across visual, brand, book, and tech items under a frozen rubric with expert-only gold (panel n>=3; percent agreement >=0.60 primary gate; weak engagement labels train/analysis-only), together with a control protocol that separates craft judgment from test-gaming. Applying the protocol to a Round-1 pilot (primary_human_expert; three biological human experts; n=250 pairs) surfaces and quantifies three validity threats: two construction artifacts that inflate the trivial-baseline layer, and a difficulty ceiling that inflates every score. (1) Position: the preferred item is slot A with probability 0.956, so an always_item_a policy scores 0.956 (fair chance 0.5). (2) Lexical leakage: a filename token cue scores 0.912. (3) Difficulty ceiling: craft domains show near-ceiling human agreement (book/brand/tech 1.0), and even under A/B randomization (eval_assignment_seed7; gold_side_A ~0.47) all five VLM cards reach 1.0 on craft, with only visual separating (~0.84-0.91; a post-hoc hard subset, n=107, leaves craft at 1.0). The protocol (expert-only gold, a weak-label firewall, side randomization at construction, filename scrubbing, and hard filters) makes each artifact measurable and, for the two construction artifacts, correctable; we release a reference eval harness and a side-randomization tool, and show the tool removes the position skew (0.916 to 0.495/0.505). The result is a calibrated view of what the benchmark does and does not yet measure: position and leakage are fixable, whereas the craft-domain ceiling is a pair-difficulty limit that Round-2 must address. We do not evaluate engagement, era/circle conditioning, or calibration here, and we claim no general taste SOTA.
papers.summary: Pairwise benchmarks that ask a model to pick the better of two items can be gamed through construction artifacts rather than measuring craft judgment. `TasteBench` pairs good-versus-bad items across visual, brand, book, and tech domains with expert-only gold labels from panels of at least three people, and adds a control protocol of a weak-label firewall, side randomization, filename scrubbing, and hard filters to separate judgment from test-gaming. In a 250-pair pilot, **an always-pick-slot-A policy scored 0.956** because the preferred item almost always sat in the first slot, a filename token cue scored 0.912, and all five vision-language model cards reached 1.0 on the craft domains even after randomization, exposing a pair-difficulty ceiling. The released side-randomization tool removes the position skew to roughly 0.5, while the craft-domain ceiling is left for a second round to address.

papers.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.
papers.summary: Models deployed in assistants and recommendation systems need to infer a person's preferences and likely future actions from long behavior histories, yet they are trained on static text or synthetic data that do not capture how behavior evolves over time. `Vela` converts anonymized behavior records from 100,000 users into 100,000 tasks drawn from 91 real-world templates, then applies difficulty filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria to retain about 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` on these trajectories **improves user-related tasks by up to 11.5 points** and general benchmarks by an average of 4 points, and reinforcement learning after this fine-tuning beats reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points.
papers.highlight_summary:
Personal assistants and recommenders need LLMs that can infer one person's preferences and next actions from weeks or years of behavior history, a skill that training on static web text or synthetic data does not build. `Vela` treats a user's own subsequent behavior as the training signal, converting anonymized logs from 100,000 users of a social media platform into tasks whose answers are checked against what that user actually did next.

- Each history is cut into 72K to 120K-token segments with the first two-thirds visible and the rest hidden, and 91 templates across six behavior categories (views, searches, purchases, posts, follows, dislikes) produce Predictive questions scored by exact match or set-F1 against the hidden future and Rubric questions on profile summaries and behavior attribution scored by an LLM judge, giving 100,000 tasks.
- Tasks are kept only when the base model's mean score over four samples lands in [0.2, 0.8], and the best of four `Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B` trajectories is accepted only if it beats that mean, yielding about 75,000 examples for `Vela-Instruct` and, from self-generated `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` trajectories, 9,375 for `Vela-RFT`, though an ablation at 37.5K shows the difficulty filter adds just 1.1 points on user-related OOD and nothing in-domain.
- Fine-tuning `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` on `Vela-Instruct` lifts in-domain `VelaBench` from 51.5 to **63.0**, above the far larger `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` and `Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B` but still below `Kimi-K3` at 64.0, and raises the user-related OOD average by **6.2 points** (`AdRecommendation` +11.2, `ProfileSummary` +10.1) and the general OOD average by **4.0 points** (`IFBench` +6.7, `CL-bench Life` +5.6, `GPQA-Diamond` +4.6).
- Gains grow with data, from 59.2 on `VelaBench` at 4.7K examples to 63.0 at 75K with no plateau, and `GSPO` reinforcement learning started from the 18.8K-example SFT checkpoint beats RL from the base model by **7.7 points** on both `VelaBench` (66.2 vs 58.5) and `ProfileSummary` (37.6 vs 29.9), with RL from the base never catching the un-RL'd SFT checkpoint.
- The same 2.4T-parameter `Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B` serves as task composer, rubric scorer, trajectory teacher, and comparison baseline, and the self-distilled `Vela-RFT` gains only 2.0 on `VelaBench` and 0.0 on general OOD, so much of the "general intelligence" gain may be ordinary distillation from a stronger teacher rather than the behavior signal, while `PurchaseIntent` barely moves at +0.2 and only templates, prompts, and code are slated for release, not the single-platform behavior data.

papers.title: DeKoR: Decomposed Knowledge Routing for Efficient GNN--LLM Fusion
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for text-attributed graph learning by leveraging rich pre-trained knowledge and language understanding capabilities. Combining LLMs with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offers a promising paradigm for expanding the modeling capabilities of graph learning. However, LLMs and GNNs follow distinct learning paradigms, leading to a pronounced mismatch between their knowledge spaces. Such discrepancies make effective knowledge fusion nontrivial. Moreover, existing methods often incur substantial additional computation for only limited performance gains. To address these challenges, we propose DeKoR, an efficient framework for GNN and LLM knowledge fusion. To enable efficient knowledge transfer, DeKoR decomposes LLM knowledge into complementary local and global views and uses the LLM as an offline teacher to distill them into lightweight experts. To enable selective knowledge fusion, an adaptive router learns how much each node should rely on each expert. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DeKoR outperforms existing baselines on both node and subgraph classification, achieving superior effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.summary: Combining large language models (LLMs) with graph neural networks (GNNs) for text-attributed graphs is hampered by the mismatch between the two models' knowledge spaces and by the heavy extra computation that existing fusion methods spend for modest gains. `DeKoR` decomposes LLM knowledge into complementary local and global views, uses the LLM as an offline teacher to distill each view into a lightweight expert, and trains an adaptive router that decides per node how much to rely on each expert. Across multiple benchmarks, **it outperforms existing baselines on both node and subgraph classification** while reducing the cost of fusion.

papers.title: Multi-Token Random-Walk Learning via Meeting-Triggered Information Exchange
papers.abstract: Random walk (RW)-based algorithms are widely used in decentralized learning due to their low communication overhead and scalability. While most existing methods rely on a single token, multiple tokens can explore the network in parallel and exchange information upon meeting. However, the fundamental benefits of such meeting-triggered interactions remain unclear. In this work, we investigate multi-token RW learning under two information exchange policies: \textsc{Average-Gradient} and \textsc{Average-Model}, which average stochastic gradients and updated models, respectively, when tokens meet. We establish iteration complexity lower bounds for non-convex, convex, and strongly convex objectives on complete graphs, which apply to both exchange policies. Compared with single-token RW learning, the scaling factor in these bounds is reduced by a factor of $m^2$ for non-convex and convex objectives, and by an exponentially in $m$ for strongly convex objectives, where $m$ denotes the number of tokens. Numerical experiments reveal distinct behaviors of the two policies under two performance criteria: mean-token loss (the average loss across all tokens) and best-token loss (the minimum loss across all tokens). \textsc{Average-Model} achieves lower mean-token loss and is relatively insensitive to the network-to-token ratio $N/m$, where $N$ is the number of nodes. In contrast, \textsc{Average-Gradient} achieves lower best-token loss but exhibits a trade-off between parallel exploration and gradient interference as $N/m$ decreases.
papers.summary: Random walk (RW) algorithms for decentralized learning usually pass a single token around the network, and the benefit of letting multiple tokens explore in parallel and exchange information when they meet has been unclear. The authors study two exchange policies, `Average-Gradient` and `Average-Model`, which average stochastic gradients or updated models respectively on meeting, and derive iteration complexity lower bounds for non-convex, convex, and strongly convex objectives on complete graphs. Relative to single-token learning, **the scaling factor in the bounds shrinks by a factor of m² for non-convex and convex objectives** and exponentially in m for strongly convex ones, where m is the number of tokens. Experiments show `Average-Model` achieves lower mean-token loss and is insensitive to the node-to-token ratio, while `Average-Gradient` achieves lower best-token loss but trades parallel exploration against gradient interference as that ratio falls.

papers.title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
papers.abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.
papers.summary: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) requires recognizing known classes and detecting novel ones from an unlabeled test stream after deployment, but existing methods can only assign anonymous cluster labels to the classes they discover. `SEGA`, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework, uses a large language model to generate attribute-rich descriptions of known classes and builds an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG) describes an unknown sample relative to similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the language model for candidate concepts, reranks them in the learned space, and uses the chosen concept for confidence-guided semantic stabilization. **The approach improves over TTD baselines** while turning anonymous clusters into interpretable named concepts.

papers.title: Integrating AIRL-Based Reward Estimation into a Control Method Using Fuzzy Inference and Policy Gradient
papers.abstract: A method integrating policy gradient with fuzzy inference has been proposed. This method, hereafter referred to as the base model, has high flexibility with respect to the configuration of fuzzy inference rules and fuzzy representation. It can also automatically adjust the rule weights and the membership functions in the antecedent and consequent parts using the same framework for learning. In methods that integrate reinforcement learning with fuzzy inference, however, the reward function must be designed in advance. It is therefore useful to add learning-based reward estimation to the base model. This paper proposes a fuzzy control method that integrates a reward estimation mechanism based on the adversarial inverse reinforcement learning (AIRL) framework into the base model. The generative adversarial nets (GAN) framework adopted in AIRL, however, tends to suffer from unstable learning. To address this, the proposed method treats the policy of the base model as the generator and also uses the set of membership functions in the policy as the cost function of the discriminator. This configuration allows the discriminator update for reward estimation and the generator update for policy estimation to be performed simultaneously on the parameters shared by both, without estimating a value function. In simulations of an illustrative vehicle speed control task, the proposed method acquired policies with high generalization performance through stable and efficient learning.
papers.summary: A previously proposed controller that combines policy gradient learning with fuzzy inference can tune rule weights and membership functions automatically, but it still requires a hand-designed reward function. The authors add reward estimation based on adversarial inverse reinforcement learning (AIRL), and counter the instability of its underlying generative adversarial nets (GAN) training by treating the fuzzy policy as the generator and reusing the policy's membership functions as the discriminator's cost function. Because the two share parameters, the discriminator and generator updates run simultaneously without estimating a value function. In a simulated vehicle speed control task, **the method learned policies with high generalization through stable and efficient training**.

papers.title: MHWA: Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action Model
papers.abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.
papers.summary: Autoregressive world models enable sample-efficient decision making, but their open-loop rollouts drift and accumulate error even over short planning horizons, and prior hierarchical fixes add complexity that limits their gains over flat baselines. `MHWA` adds a strided high-level context channel that updates global context less often to curb compounding drift, plus a context-aware gating network that reconfigures a low-level mixture of experts from both the global context and the current observation, reducing the interference seen in static hierarchies. On a 14-game `Atari` subset with 10% subsampled offline data, **the 77M-parameter model reaches an interquartile-mean human-normalized score of 0.884 versus 0.529 for a matched `JOWA-70M` baseline**, and matches `JOWA-150M` with about half the parameters and roughly 71% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.

papers.title: Self-improving data synthesis can scale embedding models across domains and tasks
papers.abstract: Adapting embedding models to new tasks requires training data that reflect task-specific information needs and relevance criteria. However, manual data design is costly and difficult to scale. Here we introduce SYNTRA, a novel retrieval data synthesis method whose self-improvement loop iteratively refines reusable synthesis instructions using feedback on trial outputs. This process requires only an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs. Experiments across 24 retrieval datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate the effectiveness of the synthesized data. These data also improve widely used, strong embedding models on tasks with and without existing labelled training sets. Self-improvement enhances retrieval on all six evaluated tasks, outperforming human calibration on four. Moreover, retrieval performance continues to improve on MS MARCO as we scale the training dataset to 32 times its initial size. Overall, with minimal human intervention, SYNTRA enables scalable adaptation of embedding models across domains and tasks.
papers.summary: Adapting embedding models to new retrieval tasks requires training data that reflects task-specific relevance criteria, and designing such data by hand does not scale. `SYNTRA` synthesizes retrieval training data through a self-improvement loop that iteratively refines reusable synthesis instructions using feedback on trial outputs, needing only an unlabeled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs. Across 24 retrieval datasets spanning 15 domains, the synthesized data improves strong embedding models on tasks with and without existing labeled sets, and **self-improvement raises retrieval on all six evaluated tasks, beating human-calibrated instructions on four**. Performance on `MS MARCO` keeps rising as the synthetic training set grows to 32 times its initial size.

papers.title: VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval
papers.abstract: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. VitaBench contains a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier that composes them into generated customer-service-style interaction streams. We characterize lifecycle decision structure with three diagnostics: lifecycle headroom, measuring the advantage of adaptive choices over the best fixed strategy; horizon reversal, measuring when short-horizon decisions change under delayed consequences; and optimal-action diversity, measuring whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. Across both tiers, VitaBench exhibits substantial lifecycle structure: lifecycle headroom is 1.364 in Diagnostic and 1.405 in Naturalistic, and 60.2% and 56.5% of states, respectively, change their preferred action between short and full horizons. A learned delayed lifecycle policy further improves over the best fixed strategy on VitaBench-Naturalistic, reaching 101.5 versus 83.4 joint utility. These results show that retrieving past information and deciding how it should persist are distinct evaluation problems, and that lifecycle management requires evaluation of the delayed consequences of representation decisions.
papers.summary: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents test whether earlier information can be retrieved when relevant, but persistent memory systems must also decide, before future use is known, whether a memory should stay exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. `VitaBench` makes these lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation, with a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier of generated customer-service-style interaction streams. Three diagnostics quantify the structure: lifecycle headroom over the best fixed strategy is 1.364 and 1.405 across the two tiers, **60.2% and 56.5% of memory states change their preferred action between short and full horizons**, and optimal-action diversity checks whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. A learned delayed lifecycle policy reaches 101.5 joint utility against 83.4 for the best fixed strategy on the Naturalistic tier.

papers.title: Think in Strategies, Act with Tools: Traceable Agentic Optimization for Combinatorial Problems
papers.abstract: Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) directly leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate candidate solutions through natural-language prompting. However, OPRO's optimization process is difficult to track, which prevents LLMs from capturing useful information accumulated over previous iterations, thereby limiting solution quality. To address this limitation, we propose a Tool-Augmented Strategic Agent (TASA) which summarizes and exploits trajectory to improve solution quality. Specifically, TASA plans the strategy for each step based on the optimization trajectory, which decomposes the optimization process into traceable strategy selections. Moreover, we leverage LLM to construct problem-specific tools and introduce a strategy-guided adaptive tool planner, which efficiently utilizes the information of trajectory to update solutions. We establish local convergence under persistent exploration and evaluate the complete framework under a shared candidate-evaluation budget. The results support its solution quality and the traceability of strategy-guided search.
papers.summary: Optimization by PROmpting (`OPRO`) has large language models (LLMs) propose candidate solutions to combinatorial problems directly from prompts, but its search is hard to trace, so useful information accumulated over earlier iterations is lost. The Tool-Augmented Strategic Agent (`TASA`) plans a strategy at each step from a summary of the optimization trajectory, decomposing the search into traceable strategy selections, and has the LLM construct problem-specific tools that a strategy-guided adaptive planner invokes to update solutions. The authors establish local convergence under persistent exploration and, **evaluating under a shared candidate-evaluation budget, report results supporting its solution quality and the traceability of the strategy-guided search**.

papers.title: PTGPO: Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Training language agents on long-horizon interactive tasks is challenging because sparse terminal rewards provide weak credit signals for intermediate actions. Existing group-based methods either assign a shared trajectory-level advantage or estimate step-level advantages from state groups, which may conflate the current action with subsequent decisions. We propose Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization (PTGPO), a critic-free method that constructs prefix trees over trajectory suffixes within anchor-state groups. PTGPO assigns each tree edge a credit given by the difference between its child and parent empirical mean returns, capturing the conditional return change revealed by each additional action. These prefix-tree credits provide fine-grained learning signals without requiring a critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on interactive benchmarks ALFWorld, WebShop and Sokoban show that PTGPO consistently improves over RL baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness.
papers.summary: Training language agents on long-horizon interactive tasks is hard because sparse terminal rewards give weak credit to intermediate actions, and existing group-based methods either share one trajectory-level advantage or estimate step advantages that conflate an action with the decisions that follow it. Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization (`PTGPO`) is a critic-free method that builds prefix trees over trajectory suffixes within groups sharing an anchor state and credits each tree edge with the difference between its child's and parent's empirical mean returns, isolating the conditional return change from each added action. These credits require no critic or additional rollouts, and **the method consistently improves over reinforcement learning baselines on `ALFWorld`, `WebShop`, and `Sokoban`**.

papers.title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
papers.abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real-world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight-only vector quantization. First, Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation-weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction-codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation-weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance in the 2-bit quantization setting. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom-designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.
papers.summary: Weight-only quantization below 3 bits cuts deployment cost for large language models, and vector quantization (VQ) preserves accuracy better than scalar methods at that level, but existing VQ approaches still degrade substantially on real-world tasks. `SAGE` (Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy) adds Energy-Stratified Grouping, which mixes channels from different energy tiers within each subvector and uses activation-weighted fitting to protect sensitive channels, and Adaptive Bit Split, which chooses per matrix how to divide a fixed bit budget between direction-codebook capacity and radius precision. Across knowledge, math, code, instruction-following, and tool-use benchmarks it sets state-of-the-art 2-bit results, and **on `Qwen3-30B-A3B` it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average score**. A custom CUDA kernel delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16.

papers.title: More Domains, No Gains? FLO: Fast-Slow Reciprocal Learning for Multi-Domain Graph Pre-training
papers.abstract: Inspired by the great success of foundation models in the development of artificial general intelligence, Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently attracted significant attention and have the potential to advance graph intelligence. Exhibiting such intelligence requires effectively learning knowledge from large-scale, multi-domain graph data during pre-training. Increasing domain diversity during pre-training is expected to yield richer and more generalizable knowledge. Most existing methods pursue this goal by designing domain alignment strategies that help a single graph model learn from multiple domains. However, we observe that existing methods struggle to benefit from increasing domain diversity. Through empirical and theoretical analysis, we reveal two key limitations. Firstly, pre-training in most GFMs is confined to a single message-passing paradigm. Since propagation flattens relations among neighboring nodes, the graph model can hardly perceive the knowledge beyond propagation, namely the attribute-predictable component of these relations. Secondly, domain alignment strategies often rely on randomly initialized parameters that are jointly updated with the graph model using immediate loss feedback, leaving early knowledge acquisition vulnerable to cross-domain interference.
