To address these issues, we propose FLO, a Fast--sLow reciprOcal approach for multi-domain graph pre-training. Specifically, a propagation-free attribute branch predicts the graph model's relations without message passing and returns these predictions to refine the model. We further stabilize knowledge acquisition by pairing a fast process that adapts to the current domain with a slow process that integrates knowledge across domains. On 12 datasets, FLO benefits from increasing domain diversity and achieves the best average performance in cross-domain and cross-task transfer.
papers.summary: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) are expected to gain from pre-training on more diverse domains, yet existing domain-alignment methods fail to benefit as diversity grows. The authors trace this to two causes: pre-training stays within message passing, which flattens neighbor relations and hides their attribute-predictable component, and randomly initialized alignment modules are updated jointly with the graph model on immediate loss, leaving early learning exposed to cross-domain interference. `FLO` adds a propagation-free attribute branch that predicts the graph model's relations without message passing and feeds those predictions back to refine it, and pairs a fast process that adapts to the current domain with a slow process that integrates knowledge across domains. On 12 datasets, **it improves as domain diversity increases and achieves the best average cross-domain and cross-task transfer**.

papers.title: Equal-information evaluation of credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning is difficult to evaluate because an attributed signal may improve a component loss without adding decision-relevant information or improving economic outcomes. We propose an evaluation framework combining equal-information reconstruction controls, fixed-utility comparisons and prespecified downstream guardrails. The framework is instantiated in an attribution-guided modular trading architecture and tested in three controlled studies covering update allocation, supervision-target representation and portfolio risk control. We find that residual-based allocation is exactly reproduced by an ordinary loss-budget control under the disclosed interface; direct shortfall supervision improves component prediction but fails decoded-outcome preservation; and component-wise critic supervision worsens risk-condition certainty equivalent and drawdown relative to scalar supervision under fixed utility. These results identify three distinct evaluation failures: redundant attribution signals, representation-induced prediction trade-offs, and misalignment between component supervision and downstream risk outcomes. A preserved historical engineering case further shows why module-level learning claims require run-level provenance. The contribution is a reusable methodology for evaluating credit assignment in expert systems operating under partial observability, delayed feedback and economic risk constraints.
papers.summary: In modular reinforcement learning for trading, an attributed credit signal can lower a component's loss without adding decision-relevant information or improving economic outcomes, which makes credit assignment hard to evaluate. The proposed framework combines equal-information reconstruction controls, fixed-utility comparisons, and prespecified downstream guardrails, and is tested in three controlled studies on update allocation, supervision-target representation, and portfolio risk control within an attribution-guided modular trading architecture. **Residual-based allocation is exactly reproduced by an ordinary loss-budget control**, direct shortfall supervision improves component prediction but fails to preserve decoded outcomes, and component-wise critic supervision worsens certainty equivalent and drawdown relative to scalar supervision under fixed utility. A preserved engineering case shows why module-level learning claims need run-level provenance.

papers.title: Random Fourier Features in Near-Linear Time
papers.abstract: Random Fourier features approximate a shift-invariant kernel in $\mathbb{R}^d$, such as the Gaussian kernel $\exp(-\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2)$, using independent samples from its spectral measure to construct an unbiased estimator for the kernel value with subgaussian concentration. However, generating $m$ such features requires $O(md)$ time. A long line of work on structured random features has accelerated this computation for the Gaussian kernel and other radial kernels, albeit with weaker concentration guarantees. We close this gap by showing a random feature map that can be computed in near-linear time $O((d+m)\log d)$ and yields near-subgaussian concentration. We obtain it through a new and tighter analysis of the Fastfood feature map of Le, Sarl\'{o}s and Smola (ICML 2013), using Brascamp-Lieb inequalities and the Schoenberg representation of radial kernels.
papers.summary: Random Fourier features approximate shift-invariant kernels such as the Gaussian kernel with unbiased estimators that have subgaussian concentration, but generating m features in d dimensions costs O(md) time, and faster structured alternatives have only come with weaker concentration guarantees. Through a new, tighter analysis of the `Fastfood` feature map using Brascamp-Lieb inequalities and the Schoenberg representation of radial kernels, the authors show that **a feature map computable in near-linear O((d+m) log d) time achieves near-subgaussian concentration**, closing the gap between speed and concentration quality.

papers.title: GateSight: Recurrent Memory Anticipates Attention Memory for Query-Agnostic KV Eviction in Hybrid LLMs
papers.abstract: Hybrid language models interleave Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, whose recurrent memory has a fixed size, with full-attention layers, whose key-value (KV) cache grows with the context and dominates serving memory. In this paper, we ask whether the recurrent memory already knows what the attention memory will need. We first show that which GDN heads of Qwen3.8-27B keep long memories is fixed by the weights rather than by the document. Next, we define the future utility of a KV entry by how much removing it changes the attention output over the model's own continuations, and find that the write gate, decay and write magnitude that GDN layers emit during prefill anticipate this utility before any query is seen. Because the relation is spread across many GDN heads and layers, and a linear map recovers its trend but less of its high-utility tail than a nonlinear one, we propose GateSight, which learns it with lightweight per-head multilayer perceptrons that read these signals and no attention score. Their predicted utility decides which entries each attention layer keeps, and how much each layer keeps is set by the model's native attention output gate, whose mean differs by more than an order of magnitude across layers. Finally, at serving time, GateSight scores the cache once after prefill and physically releases discarded KV entries. Experimental results on SCBench and RULER-4096 with Qwen3.8-27B and, with the same recipe, the sparse-attention model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, up to the 262K-token limit of the models, show that with a tenth of the attention KV cache, GateSight is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three of the four model-benchmark pairs and leads KVzip on all four, by 9.5 to 47.2 points. Notably, it scores a full-length context with negligible overhead relative to prefill.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models interleave fixed-size Gated DeltaNet (GDN) recurrent layers with full-attention layers whose key-value (KV) cache grows with context and dominates serving memory. The authors show that which GDN heads of `Qwen3.8-27B` keep long memories is fixed by the weights, and that the write gate, decay, and write magnitude emitted during prefill anticipate a KV entry's future utility, defined by how much its removal changes attention output on the model's own continuations, before any query is seen. `GateSight` learns this relation with lightweight per-head multilayer perceptrons that read only these recurrent signals, sets each attention layer's retention budget from its native attention output gate, and physically releases discarded entries after a single post-prefill scoring pass. On `SCBench` and `RULER-4096` with `Qwen3.8-27B` and `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` up to 262K tokens, **keeping a tenth of the attention KV cache it beats `KVzip` on all four model-benchmark pairs by 9.5 to 47.2 points** and is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three of them.

papers.title: Amharic-English Cross-Language Question Answering Using Statistical Machine Translation, Named Entity Recognition, and Semantic Indexing
papers.abstract: The predominance of English-language Web content creates an information-access barrier for speakers of low-resource languages such as Amharic. This paper presents the design, imple-mentation, and evaluation of a bidirectional Amharic-English cross-language question answering (CLQA) system that allows a user to formulate a natural-language question in either Amharic or English and retrieve an answer from documents written in the other language. The system integrates a statistical machine translation (SMT) component for query translation, a maximum-entropy named entity recognition (NER) component for Amharic text processing, semantic-based indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction. A domain-diverse Amharic-English parallel corpus was used to train the SMT component, while monolingual cor-pora supported language modeling. Documents were normalized, tokenized, stemmed, indexed, and semantically enriched before retrieval. The original evaluation used precision and recall as the principal effectiveness measures. For Amharic-to-English retrieval, the system achieved 72% precision and 79% recall; for English-to-Amharic retrieval, it achieved 65% precision and 70% recall. These findings show that a modular translation-and-retrieval architecture can provide useful cross-language access even under low-resource conditions. This revised article preserves the original experimental claims while situating them in the context of subsequent multilingual transformer and Amharic QA research.
papers.summary: English dominates Web content, leaving speakers of low-resource languages such as Amharic with limited access to information. The bidirectional Amharic-English cross-language question answering (CLQA) system accepts a natural-language question in either language and retrieves answers from documents in the other by chaining statistical machine translation (SMT) for query translation, maximum-entropy named entity recognition (NER) for Amharic text, semantic indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction, with the SMT component trained on a domain-diverse parallel corpus. **Amharic-to-English retrieval reached 72% precision and 79% recall**, and English-to-Amharic reached 65% precision and 70% recall. This is a revised version of earlier work that keeps the original experimental claims while situating them alongside later multilingual transformer and Amharic QA research.

papers.title: Rethinking Opinion Measurement Interfaces for Human-in-the-Loop Optimization
papers.abstract: Human-in-the-loop optimization refers to systems that present choices to a human decision-maker and query their judgment to optimize system parameters iteratively. The user interface typically provides either an absolute rating scale or asks for a preferred option. However, these approaches can potentially suffer from calibration problems, inconsistencies, and completeness violations of user preferences in such a sequential evaluation. This paper revisits the design space of opinion measurement interfaces for human-in-the-loop optimization. We conducted a study (N=360) using text summarization and image color enhancement tasks to evaluate human sequential feedback in six representative opinion measurement interfaces. Based on our analysis, we recommend using a listwise approach to support sequential opinion measurement, which counterweighs individual rating and preferential choice limitations and conveys more information for subsequent use. We further discuss the trade-offs in different user interface designs and provide guidelines to inform future research.
papers.summary: Human-in-the-loop optimization iteratively presents choices to a person and uses their judgments to tune system parameters, usually through absolute rating scales or pairwise preference choices, both of which can suffer from calibration problems, inconsistency, and incomplete preference information across a sequence of queries. A study with 360 participants compared six opinion measurement interfaces on text summarization and image color enhancement tasks. **The authors recommend a listwise interface for sequential opinion measurement**, arguing it offsets the limitations of individual ratings and pairwise choices while conveying more information for downstream use, and they discuss trade-offs and offer design guidelines.

papers.title: The Constitution Speaks Nheengatu: An Open MT System and Reproducible Corpus Pipeline for the Amazonian L\'ingua Geral
papers.abstract:
Nheengatu (yrl), the Amazonian L\'ingua Geral, has 6--10 thousand speakers and is co-official in S\~ao Gabriel da Cachoeira (Brazil), yet remains poorly served by evaluated Portuguese--Nheengatu MT resources. We present the largest parallel corpus assembled for the language (14.5k Portuguese--Nheengatu pairs), anchored by the 2023 official translation of the Brazilian Federal Constitution; the first MT evaluation set built from transcribed spontaneous speech; and, to our knowledge, the first open-weight MT models dedicated to bidirectional Portuguese--Nheengatu translation.
  Three findings organize the paper. First, translation into Nheengatu on held-out constitutional articles plateaus on development data regardless of training length or model size, and much of the remaining error sits in conventional legal terms that the written sources do not attest consistently; a terminology success rate over a frozen lexicon shows that glossary mechanisms at training time and lexical constraints at decoding each raise term realization, the latter at a cost in repetitive output that chrF++ barely registers. Second, a corpus expansion that adds transcribed conversation raises speech chrF++ by 24--27 points while leaving written domains unchanged, a register gap that written-only benchmarks cannot see. Third, a larger NLLB model helps translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu on legal or speech text. For Portuguese-to-Nheengatu translation, our final systems reach 31.7--32.8 chrF++ on article-disjoint constitutional text, 64.1--64.5 on the near-domain set (62.1 after removing items with target-side content overlap), and 45.2--47.5 on speech.
papers.summary: Nheengatu, the Amazonian Língua Geral with 6 to 10 thousand speakers, lacks evaluated Portuguese-Nheengatu machine translation resources. The authors assemble the largest parallel corpus for the language, 14.5k sentence pairs anchored by the 2023 official translation of the Brazilian Federal Constitution, build the first evaluation set from transcribed spontaneous speech, and release open-weight bidirectional translation models. Translation into Nheengatu plateaus on held-out constitutional text regardless of training length or model size, with residual errors concentrated in legal terms the written sources attest inconsistently, and glossary mechanisms or lexical decoding constraints each raise term realization, the latter at a cost in repetitive output. **Adding transcribed conversation to the corpus raises speech chrF++ by 24 to 27 points while leaving written domains unchanged**, a larger `NLLB` model helps only when translating into Portuguese, and the final Portuguese-to-Nheengatu systems reach 31.7 to 32.8 chrF++ on article-disjoint constitutional text and 45.2 to 47.5 on speech.

papers.title: CrossMean: Model Merging by Pairing Merged and Expert Activations
papers.abstract: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one network without retraining, and closed-form methods compute each merged layer from statistics of its input activations. However, these statistics are measured on a single expert, while in the merged model, each layer receives activations from the merged layers that precede it. Recent work re-measures these statistics in the merged model but still forms them from a single network. We formulate closed-form methods as a linear system and show that they use the same matrix on both sides. We then introduce CrossMean, which replaces this matrix on one side with a bilinear statistic that pairs merged and expert activations. From the same statistics, we also derive a label-free criterion that indicates the task sets in which accounting for the merged activations improves the merge more. Empirically, task sets with a lower criterion value show a larger improvement. On the eight-task benchmark of each vision backbone that we tested and on BERT encoders, CrossMean improves on merging with statistics measured on the experts, and with all linear layers merged, it also improves on re-measuring these statistics in the merged model. These results suggest that merging benefits from pairing merged and expert activations.
papers.summary: Closed-form model merging computes each merged layer from statistics of its input activations, but those statistics come from a single expert even though each layer in the merged network actually receives activations from the merged layers before it. Formulating closed-form merging as a linear system shows that existing methods use the same matrix on both sides, and `CrossMean` replaces the matrix on one side with a bilinear statistic that pairs merged and expert activations. The same statistics yield a label-free criterion that predicts which task sets gain most from accounting for merged activations, and task sets with lower criterion values indeed show larger improvements. **On eight-task benchmarks across the tested vision backbones and on `BERT` encoders, it improves over merging from expert-only statistics**, and with all linear layers merged it also beats re-measuring those statistics inside the merged model.

papers.title: CUSE: Fine-Grained Multimodal Unlearning with Counterfactual Guidance and On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reproduce sensitive, copyrighted, or unsafe information from their training data. Effective unlearning must remove target information while preserving non-target content, even within the same response. Existing methods typically apply uniform forgetting objectives to complete responses and rely on fixed, off-policy supervision, resulting in coarse token control and misalignment with the model's current behavior. We propose CUSE, a Counterfactual-guided Unlearning framework via on-policy Self-distillation for multimodal large language models. It first constructs counterfactual inputs by removing target-related evidence and uses the resulting changes in token probabilities to identify which tokens require stronger forgetting. It then distills token-level forgetting and retention targets on responses sampled from the current policy, with a frozen copy of the original model serving as the teacher model augmented with the corresponding forgetting- and retention-oriented privileged contexts. This design jointly determines what to forget and what to preserve. On MLLMU-Bench, CUSE reduces forget-set ROUGE-L by 33.6% while achieving 1.2% higher retain-set ROUGE-L than the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can regurgitate sensitive, copyrighted, or unsafe training data, and existing unlearning methods apply uniform forgetting objectives to whole responses using fixed off-policy supervision, so they cannot selectively remove a target fact while keeping the surrounding content. `CUSE` builds counterfactual inputs with the target evidence removed and uses the resulting shifts in token probabilities to locate which tokens need stronger forgetting, then distills token-level forget and retain targets on responses sampled from the current policy, with a frozen copy of the original model acting as teacher under forgetting- and retention-oriented privileged contexts. On `MLLMU-Bench`, the method **reduces forget-set ROUGE-L by 33.6% while raising retain-set ROUGE-L 1.2% above the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: Last Secure Code Benchmark: Is the Code You Vibe Secure?
papers.abstract: AI coding agents now write much of the code that ships, yet whether that code is secure remains unclear. We introduce the Last Secure Code Benchmark, a comprehensive evaluation of secure code generation by coding agents. Built from 150 real vulnerabilities, its 450 tasks span seven widely used languages (Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Go), 24 CWEs including 21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25 and 8 of the Top 10 KEV weaknesses, more than any benchmark we compare with, and three vibe-coding scenarios: filling in a function, writing a file, and building a repository's source tree from scratch. Every task asks only for functionality, through a specification that never mentions security, and hidden functional and security tests grade the result. Across six frontier agents, 73.6% to 91.3% of tasks pass functionally, yet even the strongest, Claude Fable 5, produces code that is both functional and secure for only 25.1% of tasks, and the others for 16.4% to 24.7%. The best model only passes 12% of the vulnerability scenarios across all vibe coding setting, posing strong concern on the security of the code written by vibe coding.
papers.summary: Coding agents now produce much of the code that ships, but whether that code is secure is poorly measured. The `Last Secure Code Benchmark` derives 450 tasks from 150 real vulnerabilities across seven languages (Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Go) and 24 Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) categories, covering three vibe-coding scenarios: completing a function, writing a file, and building a repository source tree from scratch. Each specification asks only for functionality and never mentions security, with hidden functional and security tests grading the output. Across six frontier agents, 73.6% to 91.3% of tasks pass functionally, yet **even the strongest, `Claude Fable 5`, produces code that is both functional and secure on only 25.1% of tasks**, the others land between 16.4% and 24.7%, and the best model passes just 12% of vulnerability scenarios across all settings.

papers.title: Who Receives Respect? A Counterfactual Benchmark for Honorific Allocation Bias in Bengali
papers.abstract: Bengali has no grammatical gender, but honorificity is obligatory: every third-person reference must choose ordinary or respectful register. English has no such signal, so the system must choose a level of deference that the source never specified. We use this property to measure how large language models (LLMs) allocate respect in English--Bengali translation. Our evaluation set contains 2{,}016 sentences across 72 occupations. Each appears in seven sentence frames under four pronoun conditions. Masculine and feminine versions differ by one word, forming counterfactual pairs. We report a single Honorific Bias Score (HBS) for each model on a 0--100 scale, covering both the gender and occupation axes. A lower score means that respect is allocated more evenly. For the occupation analysis, we compute each occupation's honorific rate across the seven no-pronoun sentence frames. The standard deviation of these 72 occupation-level rates ranges from 17.2 to 35.5 percentage points across models, showing substantial variation in how honorifics are allocated across occupations. Occupation is associated with 3.2\% to 51.5\% of the variance in register choice, compared with at most 1.2\% for gender. Gender effects are much smaller overall: only two of the nine models show significant directional gender gaps, and they favor opposite genders. HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1 across the nine models, showing substantial variation in how evenly the models allocate respect.
papers.summary: Bengali lacks grammatical gender but requires every third-person reference to pick an ordinary or respectful register, a choice English source text never specifies, which makes English-to-Bengali translation a natural probe of how large language models (LLMs) allocate respect. The authors build 2,016 sentences spanning 72 occupations in seven sentence frames and four pronoun conditions, with masculine and feminine versions differing by a single word to form counterfactual pairs, and summarize each model with an Honorific Bias Score (HBS) on a 0-100 scale covering both gender and occupation. Across nine models, **occupation explains 3.2% to 51.5% of the variance in register choice versus at most 1.2% for gender**, the standard deviation of occupation-level honorific rates ranges from 17.2 to 35.5 percentage points, and only two models show significant directional gender gaps, in opposite directions. HBS values span 19.9 to 70.1 across the models.

papers.title: Prior-Fitted and Frozen Scorers for Multimodal Contrastive Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning typically relies on manually specified scoring functions, such as cosine similarity, to quantify the similarity between representations from different modalities. Several such functions have been recently proposed to extend contrastive learning beyond two modalities. In principle, however, any function that assigns high compatibility to matched samples and low compatibility to mismatched ones could serve as a scorer. Motivated by this broader view, we instantiate the scorer with a Transformer and find that even a randomly initialized model, when kept frozen, can outperform strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines, whereas optimizing the scorer jointly with the encoders is less effective. Building on this observation, we introduce the Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS): a Transformer scorer pre-trained on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model (SCM) priors before transferring it to real-world data. The SCM exposes the scorer to diverse dependency structures, including shared, pairwise, and private information, providing a structured prior over higher-order cross-modal similarity. Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive to contrastive baselines, and prior-fitting further improves the random initialization. More broadly, our results suggest that multimodal contrastive learning need not rely on manual similarity functions: Transformers can provide strong inductive biases, while causal pretraining can further shape these biases.
papers.summary: Multimodal contrastive learning usually scores cross-modal compatibility with a handcrafted function such as cosine similarity, and recent extensions beyond two modalities have added more hand-designed variants. Treating the scorer as any function that rates matched samples high and mismatched ones low, the authors instantiate it with a Transformer and find that **a randomly initialized, frozen Transformer scorer can outperform strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines**, whereas training the scorer jointly with the encoders works less well. They then introduce the `Prior-Fitted Scorer` (`PFS`), which pre-trains the scorer on synthetic multimodal data drawn from structural causal model (SCM) priors that expose shared, pairwise, and private dependency structures before transfer to real data; across four real-world datasets, prior-fitting further improves on the random initialization.

papers.title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
papers.abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.
papers.summary: Camera-first agents must act on a visual world that keeps changing, and the authors argue the limiting factor is not recognition, which multimodal models already handle well, but time: many visual targets appear, matter to a query, and vanish within a window shorter than a monolithic perceive-then-reason pipeline takes to finish. They formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract that separates a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, and propose a two-deadline architecture with an always-on bounded non-semantic fast path, an event-driven active remembering mechanism that commits moments to durable memory before they are overwritten, and a deferred deliberation layer built from a multimodal model plus tools. Instantiating the contract on real `MOT17` track windows and calibrating a single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency, they find **even a short answer takes 1.2 to 9.3 seconds**, with agentic identify-and-search taking longer still.

papers.title: ProgAgent: Learning Tool Orchestration through Programmatic Training
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to orchestrate diverse tools over long-horizon tasks. Existing agents typically use Direct Tool Calling (DTC), where the model invokes tools sequentially, and tool responses accumulate in the model context, which can lead to context rot and orchestration breakdown. In contrast, Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) invokes tools through executable code and stores intermediate results in runtime variables rather than appending them to the context. Prior work has explored PTC mainly as an inference-time optimization, but its benefits for agentic training remain unclear, and suitable verifiable training tasks are scarce. In this work, we introduce ProgAgent, a full PTC training stack, comprising a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long-horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two-stage training recipe. Using only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, ProgAgent yields higher pass rates than the evaluated baselines of comparable size across four benchmarks. On LOCA-bench, ProgAgent-14B achieves a 30.7% pass rate at a 64k-token environment state, where these baselines score zero. Cross-harness experiments show that PTC-trained models outperform DTC-trained models under both evaluation interfaces, suggesting that the benefits of PTC training extend beyond the interface.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) orchestrating many tools over long tasks usually rely on Direct Tool Calling (DTC), where every tool response is appended to the context and eventually degrades orchestration, whereas Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) invokes tools from executable code and keeps intermediate results in runtime variables. PTC has mostly been studied as an inference-time optimization, so `ProgAgent` supplies a full training stack: a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long-horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two-stage training recipe. Trained on only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, the models beat comparably sized baselines on four benchmarks, and **`ProgAgent-14B` reaches a 30.7% pass rate on `LOCA-bench` at a 64k-token environment state where those baselines score zero**. Cross-harness experiments show PTC-trained models outperform DTC-trained models under both evaluation interfaces, suggesting the gains are not tied to the interface itself.

papers.title: Training a Compact, Strong, and Realistic Text-to-Speech Model
papers.abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) systems are conventionally optimized for intelligibility and speaker similarity. However, neither objective captures the prosodic detail that distinguishes human performances from synthetic speech, leaving a realism gap that larger models and higher-quality data can narrow but not close. In the absence of an objective that directly targets this gap, realism remains a persistent challenge in TTS. We present Audio8-TTS, a compact 0.6B-parameter model for zero-shot voice cloning that achieves state-of-the-art performance in intelligibility and speaker similarity, with particularly strong results in perceptual naturalness. To align the training signal with human perception rather than signal-level fidelity, we construct a quality ladder from widely used open-source TTS systems and train a realism critic to assess generated speech against matched human recordings of the same sentences. An identity-erasure objective discourages the critic from relying on generator fingerprints. We train the model in three stages: multilingual supervised fine-tuning; group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) rewards; and GRPO guided by the realism critic. The final stage improves perceived prosodic naturalness and speaker similarity while preserving WER performance.
papers.summary: Text-to-speech (TTS) systems are usually optimized for intelligibility and speaker similarity, neither of which captures the prosodic detail separating human performances from synthetic speech, so a realism gap persists even as models and data scale. `Audio8-TTS` is a 0.6B-parameter zero-shot voice cloning model trained in three stages: multilingual supervised fine-tuning, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) rewards, and GRPO guided by a realism critic. The critic is trained on a quality ladder of open-source TTS systems to judge generated speech against matched human recordings of the same sentences, with an identity-erasure objective that stops it from keying on generator fingerprints. The authors report **state-of-the-art intelligibility and speaker similarity with particularly strong perceptual naturalness**, and the critic-guided stage improves prosodic naturalness and similarity without hurting WER.

papers.title: LYNX: Analytical Program Synthesis via Grounding and Closed-Loop Refinement
papers.abstract: LLM-powered data analytics aims to translate natural language instructions into executable analytical programs over underlying data. However, existing approaches, whether treating LLMs as intent-to-code translators or as standalone analytical engines, often fail to reliably align domain semantics with complex schemas and heterogeneous metadata, resulting in brittle execution and semantically inconsistent analytical outputs in real-world workloads. We present LYNX, a multi-agent framework that formulates LLM-driven analytics as a schema- and knowledge-constrained analysis problem rather than a single-pass generation task. LYNX organizes analytical synthesis into a closed-loop workflow of planning, generation, verification, and refinement through three role-specialized agents that collaboratively enforce schema grounding, semantic consistency, and execution correctness. To address domain ambiguity and schema misalignment, LYNX integrates Semantic-Structural Distillation and Stage-Aware Allocation (SSD-SAA). A delta-guided iterative revision continuously diagnoses and repairs semantic and execution-level failures, substantially improving synthesis robustness. We evaluate LYNX on two NL-to-SQL benchmarks, BIRD-SQL Mini-Dev and the more challenging Spider 2.0-Lite. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance and efficiency, achieving 10.66% to 59.54% execution accuracy across lightweight and commercial models, while reducing token consumption by 70.53% compared with the prior most efficient method. Our framework displays high generalization over different backbones, from open-source, lightweight models to the latest commercial models. Additional case studies on quantitative finance analytics and complex multi-relational SQL workloads further demonstrate the framework's robustness, scalability, and practical applicability in real-world analytical scenarios.
papers.summary: Translating natural language analytics requests into executable programs over real databases often breaks down because LLM-based systems fail to align domain semantics with complex schemas and heterogeneous metadata. `LYNX` reframes the problem as schema- and knowledge-constrained analysis rather than single-pass generation, running a closed loop of planning, generation, verification, and refinement across three role-specialized agents, with Semantic-Structural Distillation and Stage-Aware Allocation (SSD-SAA) to resolve domain ambiguity and a delta-guided iterative revision that diagnoses and repairs semantic and execution failures. On `BIRD-SQL Mini-Dev` and `Spider 2.0-Lite`, the framework reaches 10.66% to 59.54% execution accuracy across lightweight and commercial backbones while **cutting token consumption by 70.53% relative to the previously most efficient method**.

papers.title: Formalizing Forgetting: Theory of Forgetting for Online Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires a learner to acquire a sequence of tasks in a single pass over the data, and catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks remains its central challenge. Despite the many methods proposed to mitigate forgetting, the theoretical understanding of forgetting in OCL is still limited: existing analyses mostly focus on linear, overparameterized, or neural tangent kernel regimes, and it remains unclear which factors govern forgetting and how they affect it. To fill this gap, we analyze single-pass Shuffle SGD under strongly convex and general convex objectives and derive explicit upper bounds on the expected final forgetting. Further analysis of these bounds shows how the per-task data amount, task similarity, and task ordering enter them, and that their effects can differ across objective classes. Moreover, experiments with neural networks on Split-CIFAR-100 and PMNIST show that the trends suggested by our theory also appear in practice, indicating that these insights extend beyond the convex setting.
papers.summary: Online continual learning (OCL) asks a model to learn a sequence of tasks in a single pass over the data, and catastrophic forgetting remains the central obstacle, yet existing theory covers mostly linear, overparameterized, or neural tangent kernel regimes. The authors analyze single-pass shuffle SGD under strongly convex and general convex objectives and derive explicit upper bounds on expected final forgetting, showing how per-task data amount, task similarity, and task ordering enter the bounds and that **their effects can differ between the two objective classes**. Experiments with neural networks on `Split-CIFAR-100` and `PMNIST` reproduce the trends the theory predicts, indicating the insights carry beyond the convex setting.

papers.title: Training-Free BioNEL-RAG: Advancing Biomedical Entity Linking through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: Biomedical Named Entity Linking (BioNEL) is the task of mapping mentions extracted from biomedical texts to canonical entities or concepts in the standardized knowledge base. Although existing methods have achieved remarkable performance in mapping accuracy, most rely on training with domain-specific datasets, which fundamentally limits their cross-domain adaptability. To address this limitation, we propose BioNEL-RAG, a novel training-free framework that combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with large language models (LLMs). Within this framework, the RAG module focuses on retrieving candidate entities, while the large language model module plays the role of selecting the most appropriate candidate for entity normalization, which is based on the analysis of the mention's context, with the aid of its remarkable text comprehension capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that BioNEL-RAG achieves performance comparable to existing methods without requiring training on subdomain datasets, whereas these methods necessitate fine-tuning on specific subdomains such as genes, diseases, or chemical compounds.
papers.summary: Biomedical Named Entity Linking (BioNEL) maps mentions in biomedical text to canonical concepts in a knowledge base, and most high-performing systems depend on fine-tuning for a specific subdomain such as genes, diseases, or chemicals, which limits cross-domain use. `BioNEL-RAG` is a training-free pipeline in which a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module retrieves candidate entities and a large language model (LLM) selects the best candidate using the mention's surrounding context. The authors report **performance comparable to fine-tuned baselines without any subdomain-specific training**.

papers.title: Counterfactual Regret for Reflective Agents with Lean-Verified Guarantees
papers.abstract: Reflective language agents reuse feedback and memory to adapt across tasks without updating model weights. However, existing guarantees for policy selection and action generation do not by themselves establish when local reflection yields long-term performance guarantees for the complete agent under resource constraints. In this paper, we address this gap by deriving sufficient conditions for sublinear counterfactual regret from local generation and deployment guarantees, while retaining the native controller. Specifically, we establish a resource-sensitive transfer that bounds full-state deployment discrepancies along actual execution paths and preserves the own-history laws of both learner and comparator. Besides, local generation reliability yields a cumulative generation opportunity bound, linking policy acquisition to long-term performance through an explicit quality, coverage, and hard-budget tradeoff. To verify these guarantees, we formalize the conditional proof chain for all thirteen numbered theoretical results in Lean, including a native instance with repeated policy growth and imperfect validation.
papers.summary: Reflective language agents adapt across tasks by reusing feedback and memory rather than updating weights, but existing guarantees for policy selection and action generation do not establish when such local reflection yields long-term performance guarantees for the whole agent under resource limits. The authors derive sufficient conditions for sublinear counterfactual regret from local generation and deployment guarantees while keeping the agent's native controller, via a resource-sensitive transfer that bounds full-state deployment discrepancies along executed paths and a cumulative generation opportunity bound tying policy acquisition to an explicit quality, coverage, and hard-budget tradeoff. **All thirteen numbered theoretical results are formalized in `Lean`**, including a native instance with repeated policy growth and imperfect validation.

papers.title: GREAT-ESDD: Graph Edge Attention Network for Effectively Steered Delivery Decisions
papers.abstract: Online, same-day delivery requires operators to constantly update their routes, and the routing cost for deliveries increases with the number of customers. Out-of-home (OOH) delivery options can help companies handle increasing customer numbers while keeping delivery costs low. We develop a dynamic pricing-and-routing framework for this online ordering scenario with home and OOH delivery options. First, we develop a neural solver for the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) based on the Graph-Edge-Attention-Network (GREAT). We train it to solve CVRP with varying instance sizes and starting conditions, allowing it to reoptimize partially executed routes under changing conditions. It is fast while achieving solution quality competitive with traditional baselines. Our solver processes several CVRP instances in parallel in batches and we use it to solve the candidate routing problems that arise from an incoming customer's choice of home or OOH delivery. This provides an estimate of the delivery cost increase per option, which we use to set dynamic prices. Further, it directly provides the updated route once the customer decides. We trade off delivery fees against routing costs and steer customers toward OOH delivery when home delivery would be costly. However, effective steering requires us to know the customer preferences. To learn those online, we use Thompson sampling with a Laplace-approximated posterior. We call the resulting framework GREAT-ESDD (GREAT for Effectively Steered Delivery Decisions). Compared to a traditional routing solver, it increases profit by around 11% under a similar pricing decision time budget. Moreover, we show that we can estimate customer preferences successfully, outperforming a static pricing strategy after only 5 days of simulated operations.
papers.summary: Same-day delivery operators must reoptimize routes as orders arrive, and out-of-home (OOH) pickup options can absorb growing customer numbers at lower routing cost, but steering customers toward them requires knowing both the marginal routing cost and customer preferences. The authors train a neural capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) solver based on the Graph-Edge-Attention-Network (`GREAT`) that handles varying instance sizes and partially executed routes, evaluate the candidate routings for each incoming customer's home versus OOH choice in parallel batches to price each option dynamically, and learn preferences online with Thompson sampling over a Laplace-approximated posterior. In simulation, `GREAT-ESDD` **raises profit by about 11% over a traditional routing solver** under a similar pricing-time budget and overtakes a static pricing strategy after five simulated days.

papers.title: CESNET-TimeSeries26: A Multi-Year Network Traffic Time Series Dataset for Annual Seasonality, Concept Drift, and Long-Term Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Forecast-based models are fundamental to network traffic management and anomaly detection. However, it is essential to evaluate these forecasting models over extended periods of time in order to assess their adaptability to unexpected phenomena and shifts in underlying patterns. This kind of long-term evaluation requires multi-year data to account for yearly seasonality and behavioral drift. Existing public datasets are too short to support such long-horizon forecasting tasks. We introduce CESNET-TimeSeries26, comprising 995 days of continuous traffic time series from the CESNET3 network, together with a single subnet spanning approximately 4.5 years. The dataset captures 278,466 IP addresses, 285 institutions, and 566 institutional subnets at three aggregation intervals. The dataset provides a definitive longitudinal benchmark for evaluating forecasting models in both operational management and security monitoring. We demonstrate that annual seasonality is the dominant periodic component. Moreover, we show that a forecasting model can exploit the annual component only when its training window covers at least one complete annual cycle, which no sub-year dataset provides.
papers.summary: Forecasting models underpin network traffic management and anomaly detection, but judging how they cope with yearly seasonality and behavioral drift requires multi-year data that existing public datasets are too short to provide. `CESNET-TimeSeries26` contains 995 days of continuous traffic time series from the CESNET3 network plus one subnet spanning roughly 4.5 years, covering 278,466 IP addresses, 285 institutions, and 566 institutional subnets at three aggregation intervals. The authors show that annual seasonality is the dominant periodic component and that **a forecasting model can exploit it only when its training window covers at least one full annual cycle**, which no sub-year dataset allows.

papers.title: YOUDrive: Driving Style as a Composable Direction for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies can achieve strong task performance while offering limited control over their driving style. Driving style describes how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and maintains distance. Policies trained without explicit preference conditioning lack a direct mechanism for adjusting these behaviors at inference. We propose YOUDrive, a vision--language--action planner for continuous and composable driving-style control. Each teacher's behavior is distilled into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation. These directions can be scaled and combined at inference without retraining the backbone. Conditioned on these directions, a flow-matching decoder models a multimodal trajectory distribution and generates kinematically feasible motion alternatives. We introduce the Style Alignment Score (SAS) to describe human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating. On NAVSIM navtest, a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas, while PDMS remains above 0.90 across the tested individual and blended configurations, reaching 0.954. Further analyses reveal systematic policy-specific kinematics after controlling for scene context, whereas the evaluated discrete style labels provide limited additional explanatory power. Code, checkpoints, and the metric will be released.
papers.summary: End-to-end driving policies perform well on benchmarks but give little control over driving style, meaning how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and keeps distance, because they are trained without explicit preference conditioning. `YOUDrive` is a vision-language-action planner that distills each teacher's behavior into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation; these directions can be scaled and blended at inference without retraining the backbone, and a flow-matching decoder conditioned on them produces kinematically feasible trajectory alternatives. The authors also introduce the Style Alignment Score (SAS) for human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating, and on `NAVSIM navtest` **a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas while PDMS stays above 0.90**, peaking at 0.954.

papers.title: ASIWorld: Benchmarking Autonomous Agents in a Persistent Survival Sandbox
papers.abstract: Evaluating autonomous agents requires examining whether they can translate goals into coherent action across extended interactions. In persistent environments, this requires coordinating interdependent actions under incomplete observations, accounting for delayed effects, and adapting as earlier decisions shape subsequent opportunities. We introduce ASIWorld, a survival sandbox that combines persistent world and character state with character-scoped observations and a programmable asynchronous interface to study sustained goal execution. Agents pursue interdependent production and exploration tasks through direct actions or agent-authored programs that continue running between model calls. The evaluation assesses task success, the attainment of development achievements, and survival costs, complemented by an analysis of execution behavior. In an exploratory study of nine agent configurations using a common harness, eight complete the production task and six complete both tasks. Analyses of execution trajectories and performance across difficulty levels reveal different preparation, combat, and recovery behaviors among configurations with similar task outcomes. Incomplete preparation is associated with stalled progression, while configurations that complete the tasks differ in survival costs and the fulfillment of additional achievement criteria. These findings illustrate the value of assessing sustained goal execution through both task outcomes and the behaviors and costs associated with achieving them.
papers.summary: Evaluating autonomous agents on sustained goal execution requires persistent environments where actions are interdependent, observations are incomplete, and earlier decisions reshape later options. `ASIWorld` is a survival sandbox with persistent world and character state, character-scoped observations, and a programmable asynchronous interface through which agents act directly or author programs that keep running between model calls while pursuing interdependent production and exploration tasks, scored on task success, development achievements, and survival costs. In an exploratory study of nine agent configurations on a common harness, **eight complete the production task and six complete both tasks**, yet trajectories reveal distinct preparation, combat, and recovery behaviors among configurations with similar outcomes, with incomplete preparation associated with stalled progression.

papers.title: Groups Don't Move as One: A Bregman Clustering View of Linearized Group Influence
papers.abstract: Influence functions provide an efficient alternative to retraining for assessing the effects of removing or reweighting training data. For groups, however, the standard first-order estimate reduces individual contributions to a sum that can conceal substantial differences among members, including opposing effects that cancel. We establish a Bregman centroid formulation of the linearized group influence objective, interpreting this aggregate as a single representative and using Bregman information (BI) to quantify the variation it omits. Extending this formulation to multiple clusters reveals distinct contributions whose sum recovers the original estimate. We further propose an estimator that jointly optimizes the weights of these cluster contributions, rather than simply summing them. Experiments uncover cluster-specific influence patterns and a positive association between target-specific BI and approximation error. The proposed estimator achieves higher $R^2$ than standard group influence in predicting target changes under the nonlinear proximal Bregman response function. Simplified clustering and correction variants reduce computational cost. The centroid view thus explains what additive group influence leaves out and provides a basis for using that information to improve estimation.
papers.summary: Influence functions estimate the effect of removing or reweighting training data without retraining, but the standard first-order group estimate collapses members into a single sum that can hide large differences, including opposing effects that cancel. The authors recast the linearized group influence objective as a Bregman centroid problem, interpret the aggregate as one representative, and use Bregman information (BI) to quantify the variation it discards; extending to multiple clusters yields distinct contributions whose sum recovers the original estimate, and a proposed estimator learns weights for these cluster contributions instead of summing them. Experiments uncover cluster-specific influence patterns, a positive association between target-specific BI and approximation error, and **higher R-squared than standard group influence when predicting target changes under the nonlinear proximal Bregman response function**.

papers.title: KedgeFlow: A Programmable Control Plane for Enterprise AI Agents
papers.abstract: Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, concurrently reuse the same permission, or retry operations whose responses were lost. These failures arise when approval and resource execution lack a shared contract. KedgeFlow specifies language-independent contracts for trusted controllers to authorize state-changing operations and privileged gateways to enforce that authority independently of agent reasoning. Inspired by OpenFlow, it connects policy checks supported by evidence, signed permission for an exact action, a shared allowance that can be consumed only once, target-side conditions for applying the change, and retained outcome records. Under trusted issuance of exact-action authority, two conditional properties establish at most one successful claim per allowance and link every governed dispatch to a matching grant, claim, and subsequent dispatch authorization, even when the agent is compromised. A reference implementation exposes this execution path to agent systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In the single-resource evaluation, 6,560 concurrent ledger claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances. Boundary tests rejected unauthorized and altered requests before consumption. A 32-call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authorized an undesirable effect, exposing the limits of execution authorization. Evaluation uses three members of the etcd coordinated key-value store on one host, synthetic authentication and authorization inputs, and a mock target that rejects stale requests. Distributed reservations, enforcement of every production access route, native crash recovery, exactly-once effects at real targets, and interoperability between independent implementations remain untested.
papers.summary: Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, reuse a single permission concurrently, or retry operations whose responses were lost, failures that arise when approval and execution lack a shared contract. `KedgeFlow`, inspired by `OpenFlow`, specifies language-independent contracts in which trusted controllers issue signed permission for an exact action backed by policy evidence, a shared allowance can be consumed only once, target-side conditions gate the change, and outcome records are retained, with privileged gateways enforcing this independently of agent reasoning; a reference implementation exposes the path through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In an evaluation on three etcd members on one host with synthetic inputs and a mock target, **6,560 concurrent claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances**, a 32-call gateway race committed a single effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no extra dispatch. A deliberately permissive policy still authorized an undesirable effect, and distributed reservations, crash recovery, and exactly-once effects at real targets remain untested.

papers.title: Depth-progressive 3D seismic velocity model building via 2D generative diffusion models
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) velocity model building (VMB) remains computationally challenging with conventional approaches and native 3D neural networks, largely due to the prohibitive memory and training cost of full 3D formulations. Therefore, we introduce a depth-progressive framework that achieves 3D VMB using 2D generative diffusion models through a depth-as-channel formulation, in which the depth dimension of each 3D velocity patch is mapped to the channel dimension of a 2D U-Net. This allows the model to synthesize overlapping depth patches sequentially from shallow to deep while conditioning the prediction of the deeper patch on the shallower one, as well as on any available geophysical constraints, including well logs and structural attributes. During training, paired shallow-deep patch pairs with randomized overlaps are used to teach the network how deeper velocity structures relate to shallower information, and a classifier-free guidance strategy enables the model to handle missing constraints gracefully. At inference, starting from a shallow velocity prior, the model recursively generates deeper patches in a top-down manner, and a depth-attenuated Gaussian blending scheme merges overlapping predictions into spatially coherent 3D volumes while accounting for the progressive accumulation of uncertainty at greater depths. Numerical experiments on both in-distribution benchmark models, including Overthrust, SEAM Arid, and SEG/EAGE, and the out-of-distribution Marmousi model demonstrate that the method effectively propagates shallow velocity priors downward and produces high-quality 3D velocity volumes across a range of geological settings and conditioning scenarios. Compared to a 3D benchmark of equivalent architecture, the proposed method significantly reduces parameter count, training cost, and inference cost, while maintaining superior VMB accuracy.
papers.summary: Building three-dimensional (3D) seismic velocity models, known as velocity model building (VMB), is costly with conventional methods and with native 3D neural networks because full 3D formulations demand prohibitive memory and training compute. The proposed depth-progressive framework maps the depth axis of each 3D velocity patch onto the channel dimension of a 2D U-Net diffusion model, generating overlapping depth patches from shallow to deep while conditioning each deeper patch on the one above it and on available constraints such as well logs and structural attributes, with classifier-free guidance to tolerate missing constraints and depth-attenuated Gaussian blending to merge patches into coherent volumes. On the `Overthrust`, `SEAM Arid`, and `SEG/EAGE` benchmarks and the out-of-distribution `Marmousi` model, the method propagates shallow priors downward effectively and, **compared with a 3D network of equivalent architecture, substantially reduces parameter count, training cost, and inference cost while achieving higher VMB accuracy**.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Dengue Infection Using Clinical and Hematological Data from Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Benchmark and Extended Prediction Models
papers.abstract: Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV) and a major public health concern in Bangladesh, where symptom overlap with other febrile illnesses complicates early diagnosis. This study compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost to predict dengue from clinical and hematological data using two Bangladeshi hospital datasets (2024, n=1,511; 2025, n=1,283) with SMOTE. Extended models outperformed benchmarks within 2024 (Random Forest ROC-AUC 0.640 to 0.661), with RDW-CV the most consistently influential added predictor. 2025 benchmark performance was higher (ROC-AUC 0.904), unexplained by class imbalance and possibly reflecting data quality. External validation is needed.
papers.summary: Dengue, caused by the dengue virus (DENV), is a major public health burden in Bangladesh, where its symptoms overlap with other febrile illnesses and complicate early diagnosis. The study compares `Logistic Regression`, `Random Forest`, and `XGBoost` for predicting dengue from clinical and hematological data in two Bangladeshi hospital datasets (1,511 records from 2024 and 1,283 from 2025) with `SMOTE` oversampling, contrasting benchmark feature sets against extended ones. Within the 2024 data, extended models edged out benchmarks, with **`Random Forest` ROC-AUC rising from 0.640 to 0.661** and the red cell distribution width measure RDW-CV the most consistently useful added predictor, while the 2025 benchmark reached 0.904, a gap the authors attribute to possible data quality differences and flag as needing external validation.

papers.title: Seamless Deployment of Machine Learning Inference at the Far Edge: An Empirical AWS IoT Greengrass Architecture for Industrial Predictive Maintenance
papers.abstract: Industrial IoT sensors produce continuous, high-volume data streams that predictive maintenance needs to analyse in real time. Cloud-centric architectures send all raw telemetry to central servers, which costs latency, bandwidth and resilience. This paper presents a hybrid cloud-edge architecture for manufacturing predictive maintenance built on AWS IoT Core and AWS IoT Greengrass v2, with local machine learning inference at the edge and selective cloud synchronization. We deploy two configurations on real AWS infrastructure and compare them: a cloud-only baseline (Configuration A) and the proposed hybrid edge architecture (Configuration B). We measure end-to-end inference latency, bandwidth consumption and inference accuracy. Configuration B cuts cloud-bound bandwidth by 86.8% (63.6 KB to 7.2 KB per 200-reading window) and decision latency by 256x (23.1 ms cloud round trip to 0.09 ms local inference). At the edge, with no cloud involvement, it keeps an anomaly-class F1 score of 0.84 and 91% recall. The evaluation also instruments system uptime and Stream Manager queuing under cloud disconnection; the quantitative disconnection experiment is left as planned work. Our review of the literature points to four gaps that this work addresses: the lack of empirically validated Greengrass v2 deployments for predictive maintenance, unquantified bandwidth savings from selective edge synchronization, unmeasured resilience under cloud disconnection, and the open MLOps feedback loop at the edge.
papers.summary: Industrial Internet of Things (IoT) sensors emit continuous high-volume streams that predictive maintenance must analyze in real time, and shipping all raw telemetry to the cloud costs latency, bandwidth, and resilience. The authors build a hybrid cloud-edge architecture on `AWS IoT Core` and `AWS IoT Greengrass v2` with local machine learning inference and selective cloud synchronization, deploy it on real AWS infrastructure alongside a cloud-only baseline, and measure end-to-end latency, bandwidth, and accuracy. The hybrid configuration **cuts cloud-bound bandwidth by 86.8% and decision latency by 256x** (23.1 ms cloud round trip versus 0.09 ms local inference) while holding an anomaly-class F1 of 0.84 and 91% recall at the edge; uptime and queuing under disconnection are instrumented, but the quantitative disconnection experiment is left as planned work.

papers.title: Explore This! Beat and Downbeat Tracking From a Learned Tatum Grid
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art beat tracking is based on neural networks that model beats and downbeats as individual events, often followed by a separate Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) enforcing musical consistency. We propose a novel architecture that combines deep learning with differentiable theory-based modules: Specifically, we design a system that first predicts a tatum grid, then groups tatum events to beats and downbeats, explicitly modelling multiple options for the current tempo and time signature in a bar-pointer-like fashion. Our approach improves continuity metrics compared to existing DBN-free systems and is more versatile than the de-facto standard DBN, but still falls behind the best DBN-based methods on average. Given the many design choices and hyperparameters involved, we assume we have not yet explored the full potential of this idea and publish our code and invite others to explore this further.
papers.summary: Most neural beat trackers predict beats and downbeats as separate events and then rely on a Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) to impose musical consistency. The proposed architecture instead predicts a fine-grained tatum grid and groups those tatum events into beats and downbeats using differentiable, theory-based modules that explicitly track multiple hypotheses for the current tempo and time signature, in the manner of a bar-pointer model. It improves continuity metrics over existing DBN-free systems and adapts to more settings than the standard DBN post-processor, **but still trails the best DBN-based methods on average**; the authors release the code and invite others to explore the many untested design choices and hyperparameters.

papers.title: A Reference Architecture for Integrating Agentic AI into Enterprise Software: Responsibilities, Interactions, and Variability
papers.abstract: Agentic AI moves generative AI applications toward systems that coordinate reasoning, enterprise context, model inference, and external actions. Integrating these capabilities into enterprise software introduces diverse architectural concerns, from orchestration, knowledge and memory, and model access to tools and actions, security, runtime infrastructure, and evaluation. Existing research and industry architectures address many of these concerns but differ in scope, abstraction, responsibility organization, interaction representation, and assumptions about which capabilities are required. This paper presents a technology-neutral reference architecture for enterprise agentic AI integration. We synthesize architectural capabilities from research publications, industry architecture guidance, and interoperability specifications by architectural purpose, organize them into ten responsibilities, and define boundary invariants, typed cross-responsibility interactions, and variation points that distinguish responsibilities from condition-dependent capabilities and replaceable realization mechanisms. We instantiate the architecture as an ESG portfolio-analysis and pre-trade compliance agent over an existing service-oriented ESG metric computation and reporting system, and complement the case with a mapping of an independently published agentic architecture. The case realizes seven of the ten responsibilities; different questions take different interaction paths, controls activate only under their conditions, and the probed boundary invariants hold. The independent architecture maps onto the proposed responsibilities without requiring an additional one. These results provide initial evidence for the architecture's organization and applicability rather than its completeness. The deployment and recorded results are available as a replication package.
papers.summary: Integrating agentic capabilities into enterprise software raises a sprawl of concerns, from orchestration, knowledge and memory, and model access to tools, security, runtime infrastructure, and evaluation, and existing research and industry architectures disagree on scope, abstraction, and which capabilities are mandatory. The authors synthesize research publications, industry guidance, and interoperability specifications into a technology-neutral reference architecture organized around **ten responsibilities**, with boundary invariants, typed cross-responsibility interactions, and variation points that separate responsibilities from condition-dependent capabilities and replaceable realization mechanisms. They instantiate it as an ESG portfolio-analysis and pre-trade compliance agent over an existing service-oriented ESG reporting system, realizing seven of the ten responsibilities with the probed invariants holding and controls activating only under their conditions, and show that an independently published agentic architecture maps onto the responsibilities without needing an extra one. The results are presented as initial evidence of the architecture's organization and applicability rather than its completeness, with a replication package provided.

papers.title: AI-Native Product Management: A Vision
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support product management tasks. At the same time, AI-native research and development (R&D) may increase software realization capacity. Organizations may realize software faster than they can identify, qualify, and reconsider what should be realized. This paper asks how product management should be re-envisioned under these conditions. We synthesize research on software product management, product learning, human-AI collaboration, and the Product Management and R&D boundary. We propose a vision in which AI becomes a persistent participant in product work. The vision covers sensing, exploration, decision-making, realization, and learning. We propose six principles and make the vision tangible through an operating model grounded in human professionals, AI personas, agents, skills, and a shared product context. We further argue that AI-native Product Management and AI-native R&D can form a continuous product-learning process. Finally, we identify four AI-specific research directions that require empirical investigation.
papers.summary: As AI-native research and development (R&D) lets organizations realize software faster than they can identify, qualify, and reconsider what should be built, product management itself needs re-envisioning. Drawing on research in software product management, product learning, human-AI collaboration, and the boundary between product management and R&D, the authors propose a vision in which AI is a persistent participant across sensing, exploration, decision-making, realization, and learning. The vision is expressed as **six principles** and an operating model built from human professionals, AI personas, agents, skills, and a shared product context, with the argument that AI-native product management and AI-native R&D together form a continuous product-learning process; four AI-specific research directions are identified for empirical investigation.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual TTS for Indian Languages: A Benchmark and Inference-Time Duration Estimation Strategies
papers.abstract: Recent alignment-free Text-to-Speech (TTS) models achieve high synthesis quality by removing explicit alignment modules and simplifying training. However, they often struggle in cross-lingual scenarios due to differences in character durations across languages, leading to duration mismatch and degraded speech quality. Existing approaches typically address this issue using explicit duration predictors, increasing model complexity. Systematic evaluation of TTS performance for Indian languages in cross-lingual settings remains under-explored due to the lack of standardized evaluation benchmarks. In this work, we construct a cross-lingual evaluation benchmark covering English and nine Indian languages and propose a language-aware inference-time duration estimation strategy for alignment-free TTS that incorporates language-specific duration-per character statistics without retraining or architectural modifications. We further develop heuristic formulations that refine duration estimation based on language-dependent duration variations. Experiments on bilingual and multilingual A-DMA models demonstrate improved speech naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity while reducing duration mismatch.
papers.summary: Alignment-free text-to-speech (TTS) models synthesize high-quality speech without explicit alignment modules, but in cross-lingual settings they suffer from duration mismatch because characters take different amounts of time to pronounce across languages. The authors build a cross-lingual evaluation benchmark spanning English and nine Indian languages and propose a language-aware inference-time duration estimation strategy that plugs language-specific duration-per-character statistics into an alignment-free model without retraining or architectural changes, plus heuristic refinements for language-dependent duration variation. On bilingual and multilingual `A-DMA` models, the strategy **improves naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity while reducing duration mismatch**.

papers.title: EvoCowork: A Benchmark for Real-World Office Tasks
papers.abstract: Office workflows are a demanding testbed for self-improving agents because their deliverables must be correct, natively editable, and mutually consistent. A central question is whether gains on feedback tasks reflect reusable procedures rather than task-specific fixes. We introduce EvoCowork, a 240-task benchmark for evaluating harness-level recursive self-improvement across four office modalities, with model weights held fixed. The benchmark covers presentations, documents, spreadsheets, and cross-office workflows, and scores submitted artifacts for content, native structure, formulas, cross-file consistency, and visual quality where needed. Its protocol separates feedback, revision selection, and final testing: methods learn from single-modality tasks, then are evaluated on unseen single-modality tasks and cross-office workflows under a shared initial harness and explicit budgets. In static evaluations of two models and four harnesses, the best configuration scores 42.25 overall and 30.62 on cross-office tasks. Starting from the same MSA harness with GLM 5.3, ACE and AHE improve in-domain scores by 4.90 and 2.64 points, respectively, but change cross-office scores by only +0.03 and -1.72. Thus, gains on the file types that provide feedback do not necessarily transfer to coordinated workflows. EvoCowork makes this distinction explicit while recording the capability, transfer, and cost of harness evolution. Code and task packages: https://github.com/DeepThinkingZhouLiu/cowork-evolution-benchmark.
papers.summary: Office deliverables such as slides, documents, and spreadsheets must be correct, natively editable, and consistent with one another, which makes them a demanding test of whether an agent's self-improvement produces reusable procedures rather than task-specific fixes. `EvoCowork` is a 240-task benchmark for harness-level recursive self-improvement with model weights held fixed: methods learn from feedback on single-modality tasks, then are tested on unseen single-modality tasks and cross-office workflows under a shared initial harness and explicit budgets, with artifacts scored on content, native structure, formulas, cross-file consistency, and visual quality. The best static configuration among two models and four harnesses scores 42.25 overall and 30.62 on cross-office tasks, and starting from the `MSA` harness with `GLM 5.3`, the `ACE` and `AHE` methods raise in-domain scores by 4.90 and 2.64 points **but move cross-office scores by only +0.03 and -1.72**, showing that gains on the file types that supply feedback do not necessarily transfer to coordinated workflows.

papers.title: Sequence-Structured Decision Learning for Branch-and-Bound in Mixed-Integer Linear Programming
papers.abstract: Branch-and-bound (BnB) solves mixed-integer linear programs by constructing and exploring a search tree. Node selection and branching are two recurrent decisions that directly determine the tree. Learning-based approaches typically optimize either decision in isolation and condition on a mostly local view, leaving the coupled evolution of the search tree insufficiently modeled. This paper proposes Seq-BnB, a sequence-structured framework that learns branching and node selection from a shared global representation of the evolving BnB process.
