Seq-BnB serializes node creations, node updates, node-selection events, and branching events into typed tokens, producing a causal event sequence of the search trajectory. A self-attention encoder summarizes this global search history, a bipartite graph neural network encodes the current LP relaxation, and context-conditioned decision heads score branching variables and open nodes. To reduce distribution shift between expert demonstrations and learned policies, Seq-BnB is trained with DAgger-style data aggregation. On four MILP benchmark families, Seq-BnB consistently processes fewer BnB nodes than heuristic and learning-based baselines, with strong solution times on both standard and larger transfer instances. While this paper evaluates Seq-BnB instantiation for branching and node selection, it accommodates additional solver decisions, such as cut selection, by introducing new action tokens and decision heads.
papers.summary: Branch-and-bound (BnB) solvers for mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) make two recurring decisions, which open node to explore and which variable to branch on, yet learned policies usually optimize one in isolation from a mostly local view of the search tree. `Seq-BnB` serializes node creations, node updates, node-selection events, and branching events into a causal sequence of typed tokens, summarizes that global search history with a self-attention encoder, encodes the current LP relaxation with a bipartite graph neural network, and scores both branching variables and open nodes with context-conditioned decision heads, training with `DAgger`-style data aggregation to limit distribution shift from expert demonstrations. Across four MILP benchmark families it **consistently processes fewer BnB nodes than heuristic and learning-based baselines** with strong solution times on standard and larger transfer instances, and the token design can be extended to other solver decisions such as cut selection.

papers.title: Pre-Registered Genesis Accounting for Recursive Self-Improvement: First Audited Operator-Genesis Events in a Physics-Discovery Runtime
papers.abstract: Claims of recursive self-improvement are easy to make and hard to falsify: did improvement come from re-using designer-provided mechanisms, or from mechanisms the system authored itself? We introduce a pre-registered, two-tier accounting: M1 counts machine-generated content instances within a designer-provided vocabulary, while M2 counts machine-authored mechanism types (new operators registered into the runtime's own vocabulary, with a held-out-validation certificate). We report the first audited M2 genesis events. In the primary event, depth-limited compositional search over elementary operators, judged by held-out R^2 on real NIST hydrogen Balmer measurements, produced the operator sq(inv(n)) = 1/n^2 -- the Rydberg-level form -- which no standard-library transform could express (held-out R^2: -0.546 best standard transform vs. 1.0000000 composed). A protocol flaw (independent variable built by inverting the very law under test) was caught in audit and repaired via an independent-label protocol; extrapolation to unseen levels (n=8,9 trained on n<=7) attains relative error ~10^-6, four to six orders beyond the best standard operator. A second event independently recovered sqrt(inv(a)) -- Kepler's velocity law -- from JPL ephemeris vectors. Also incorporated: an audited compounding channel (first domain-level measurement: 1.109x accuracy ratio on a real held-out domain) and blind, decurated genesis exams whose honest tally is zero. The Kepler event passes line audit; the hydrogen gap reproduces on He II; the certificate is threshold-stable. Against eleven prior systems, the contribution is the measurement and governance of machine-authored mechanisms, not the search algorithm or rediscovered physics. Limitations: exams were curated by agents who knew the textbook answer, triggers manual, grammar observer-injected; both events demonstrate capability to author, not yet autonomous genesis.
papers.summary: Claims of recursive self-improvement are hard to falsify because gains may come from reusing designer-provided mechanisms rather than mechanisms the system authored itself. The authors propose a pre-registered two-tier accounting, where M1 counts machine-generated content within a designer-provided vocabulary and M2 counts machine-authored mechanism types, meaning new operators registered into the runtime's own vocabulary with a held-out validation certificate. In the primary audited M2 event, depth-limited compositional search over elementary operators judged by held-out fit on NIST hydrogen Balmer measurements produced the Rydberg-form operator 1/n^2, which no standard-library transform could express, **reaching a held-out R^2 of 1.0000000 against -0.546 for the best standard transform** and extrapolating to unseen levels with relative error near 10^-6 once an audit caught and repaired a protocol flaw; a second event recovered Kepler's velocity law from JPL ephemeris vectors. The contribution is positioned as measurement and governance of machine-authored mechanisms rather than the search algorithm or the rediscovered physics, and the authors note that blind decurated exams tally zero, exams were curated by agents who knew the textbook answer, triggers were manual, and the events show a capability to author rather than autonomous genesis.

papers.title: Physics-informed random neural architectures on compact boundaryless multiply connected manifolds for random-operator models in machine learning and uncertainty quantification
papers.abstract: We introduce stochastic physics-informed neural networks (SPINNs) for stochastic boundary-value problems (SBVPs) with random operators. The method enforces physics through a structural probabilistic coupling: a common Gaussian stochastic germ drives both the SBVP random operator and a manifold-based stochastic neural architecture. The stochastic neural network is non-feedforward and intrinsically random. A latent Gaussian field and an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on a compact, boundaryless, multiply connected manifold generate random neuron locations, geodesically local sparse connectivity, and a sparse random weight matrix, all governed by a low-dimensional hyperparameter. For deterministic inputs, the network output is random and can represent non-Gaussian random operators. Training is performed in observation space: SBVP simulations produce random observables, while the SNN defines a predictive conditional probability density function. The supervised objective combines data fidelity, through negative log-likelihood, with a cross-entropy alignment term relative to the SBVP-induced conditional distribution. The resulting target is a convex mixture of observation-induced and SBVP-induced distributions, with a dimensionless parameter controlling robustness to model--data mismatch. The shared stochastic germ yields common-random-numbers Monte Carlo estimators and reduced-variance gradients. The method uses only evaluations of the SBVP solution mapping, without differentiating or modifying it, and avoids PDE-residual or boundary-penalty losses. A stochastic elliptic problem on a periodic cylindrical surface illustrates the approach in SBVP-consistent and SBVP-misspecified regimes. A generalized-posterior formulation is also outlined for hyperparameter inference and posterior averaging without per-query reoptimization.
papers.summary: Stochastic boundary-value problems (SBVPs) with random operators call for surrogates whose outputs are themselves random, which standard physics-informed networks do not provide. Stochastic physics-informed neural networks (`SPINNs`) couple the SBVP's random operator and a manifold-based stochastic neural architecture through a shared Gaussian stochastic germ: a latent Gaussian field and an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on a compact, boundaryless, multiply connected manifold generate random neuron locations, geodesically local sparse connectivity, and a sparse random weight matrix governed by a low-dimensional hyperparameter, so the non-feedforward network can represent non-Gaussian random operators. Training happens entirely in observation space, combining a negative log-likelihood data term with a cross-entropy alignment to the SBVP-induced conditional distribution, which yields **a convex mixture target with one dimensionless parameter controlling robustness to model-data mismatch**, common-random-number Monte Carlo estimators with reduced-variance gradients, and no need for PDE-residual or boundary-penalty losses or for differentiating the solver. A stochastic elliptic problem on a periodic cylindrical surface illustrates the method in SBVP-consistent and misspecified regimes, and a generalized-posterior formulation is sketched for hyperparameter inference.

papers.title: Getting Space Right: Agentic Rewards for Image Generation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for spatial text-to-image generation, but existing work largely focuses on policy optimization, assuming accurate rewards and effective online rollouts. We observe in-domain gains with out-of-domain degradation, exposing two limitations: unreliable spatial rewards in open-world settings and rollouts lacking basic-to-complex progression. We propose a curriculum-guided RL framework. First, we introduce SpatialCritic, an agentic reward model equipped with a spatial perception harness that combines reusable verification guidance with specialized vision tools. We then construct spatial preference datasets through targeted counterfactual perturbations and perform agent-harness alignment to improve tool selection and evidence integration efficiently. Second, curriculum learning organizes shared foundational capabilities and their compositional dependencies in a capability graph for mastery-guided rollouts, periodic review, and targeted remediation. On SpaRW-Eval, SpatialCritic achieves 95.1% verification accuracy, outperforming 320B GLM-5.3-Flash with a 40x smaller 8B backbone and raising average baseline scores from 78.4 to 83.9 on SD3.5-Medium and 83.2 to 86.5 on BAGEL. Project page: https://xiaofeng-tan.github.io/projects/spatialcritic/
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for spatial text-to-image generation has concentrated on policy optimization while assuming accurate rewards and useful rollouts, and the authors observe in-domain gains paired with out-of-domain degradation, traced to unreliable open-world spatial rewards and rollouts lacking basic-to-complex progression. They introduce `SpatialCritic`, an agentic reward model with a spatial perception harness that pairs reusable verification guidance with specialized vision tools, aligned on preference data built from targeted counterfactual perturbations to improve tool selection and evidence integration, and add a curriculum that organizes shared foundational capabilities and their compositional dependencies in a capability graph for mastery-guided rollouts, periodic review, and targeted remediation. On `SpaRW-Eval`, **the 8B `SpatialCritic` reaches 95.1% verification accuracy, outperforming the 40x larger 320B `GLM-5.3-Flash`**, and the full framework lifts average baseline scores from 78.4 to 83.9 on `SD3.5-Medium` and from 83.2 to 86.5 on `BAGEL`.

papers.title: Disentangling Marginal Capacity from Geometry in Optimal-Transport Label Transfer
papers.abstract: Optimal transport (OT) is widely used to align distributions and transfer labels between unpaired source and target data, but source-target composition shifts can cause rare classes to be systematically under-predicted even with high transport confidence. We identify a source of this failure in the transport marginal: under the standard uniform weighting of source points, each class has transport capacity proportional to its source frequency, which can be insufficient to meet its target demand even when separated well in the embedding space. We show that displaced mass is preferentially absorbed by high-capacity classes rather than geometrically similar classes, producing confident errors that are difficult to detect from the transport plan. Downstream read-outs, entropic smoothing, and marginal relaxation provide limited recovery, whereas matching the transport marginal to the target composition substantially improves label transfer. On single-cell data, the oracle composition-matched marginal raises macro-F1 from 0.322 to 0.623, and the best deployable estimator closes 69% of the oracle gap. Correcting the marginal also separates a coverage-dependent component of error from residual error associated with class separability, showing that transport capacity and representation geometry are distinct sources of transfer error.
papers.summary: Optimal transport (OT) is widely used to transfer labels from a source dataset to unpaired target data, but when class composition differs between source and target, rare classes get systematically under-predicted even when the transport appears confident. The authors trace this to the transport marginal: with uniform weighting of source points, each class's transport capacity is proportional to its source frequency and can fall short of its target demand even when the class is well separated in embedding space, so displaced mass is absorbed by high-capacity classes rather than geometrically similar ones, producing confident errors that are hard to detect from the transport plan. Downstream read-outs, entropic smoothing, and marginal relaxation recover little, whereas matching the source marginal to the target composition helps substantially: on single-cell data, **an oracle composition-matched marginal raises macro-F1 from 0.322 to 0.623**, and the best deployable estimator closes 69% of that gap, separating a coverage-dependent error component from residual error tied to class separability.

papers.title: PEAM: On-device Communication Agent for Personalized, Efficient and Autonomous Mobile Network Configuration
papers.abstract: The growing deployment of compact large language models on smartphones is enabling autonomous on-device decision-making, such as emerging mobile GUI agents. However, many mobile decisions, such as network configuration when users switch apps or connectivity conditions change, must satisfy stringent latency constraints to preserve user experience. In this paper, we propose PEAM, an on-device LLM-based communication agent that autonomously generates personalized network-configuration rules executable within milliseconds. Specifically, PEAM first fine-tune the on-device LLM with a dataset constructed from manually annotated real-user data to integrate the communication knowledge into the local model. PEAM then operates in two phases. In the rule-generation phase, which is performed when the device is idle, such as overnight, PEAM analyzes historical network-configuration records in batches and reflects across batches to consolidate consistent evidence, reduce local bias, and derive robust configuration rules. To enable more accurate and stable rule generation over time, PEAM further constructs a user profile from high-confidence rules to capture the user's network preferences and incorporates this profile into each rule-generation cycle. In the rule-execution phase, PEAM is invoked when the communication context changes, such as when users switch apps or connectivity conditions change, and searches the rule library to identify and execute the appropriate rule. Experiments demonstrate that PEAM, based on a fine-tuned 4B model, achieves 99.13% correct network configuration decisions, while 92.50% of the rules generated by PEAM are valid, outperforming the traditional expert-rule based method by 4.41% and 84.50%, respectively.
papers.summary: Mobile network configuration decisions, such as what to do when a user switches apps or connectivity changes, must execute within milliseconds, which rules out querying an on-device large language model (LLM) at decision time. `PEAM` fine-tunes a compact on-device LLM on manually annotated real-user data, then during idle periods such as overnight analyzes historical configuration records in batches, reflects across batches to consolidate consistent evidence and reduce local bias, and maintains a user profile built from high-confidence rules to stabilize subsequent rule generation; at runtime it only searches the rule library and executes the matching rule. With a fine-tuned 4B model, **it makes 99.13% correct network configuration decisions and 92.50% of its generated rules are valid**, improving on an expert-rule baseline by 4.41 and 84.50 percentage points respectively.

papers.title: Terrarium: Growing Personal Assistants via Scalable Synthesis of App Worlds
papers.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought the vision of a general-purpose personal assistant closer to reality. Such assistants could provide a unified natural-language interface to a broad ecosystem of applications. However, real-world applications do not readily support training at scale because access is often restricted and their state is difficult to reset. To address this challenge, we introduce Terrarium, a framework that synthesizes executable App Worlds from real-world application information, generates training task packages with evaluator-side rubrics from these worlds, and iteratively validates and refines both through agent rollouts. For App World synthesis, Terrarium organizes public Web information and in-application observations into structured app specifications that guide the construction of self-contained runtimes with callable operations and mutable, resettable state. For task synthesis, Terrarium constructs tasks grounded in App World state together with evaluator-side outcome rubrics that assess success without prescribing reference trajectories. We construct a training suite of 275 App Worlds and 13,344 tasks for outcome-based reinforcement learning across three Qwen3 model scales (4B, 8B, and 14B parameters). Across these scales, models trained with Terrarium outperform the corresponding Qwen3 models by an average of 18.34 percentage points on the $\tau^2$-bench and 10.94 percentage points on the AppWorld bench. These results suggest that app-grounded world and task synthesis offers a scalable path toward general-purpose assistants capable of operating across broad application ecosystems.
papers.summary: Real applications are poor training grounds for general-purpose assistants because access is restricted and their state is hard to reset. `Terrarium` synthesizes executable App Worlds from public web information and in-application observations, organizing them into structured app specifications that guide construction of self-contained runtimes with callable operations and mutable, resettable state, then generates tasks grounded in that state together with evaluator-side outcome rubrics that judge success without prescribing reference trajectories, and iteratively validates both through agent rollouts. A suite of 275 App Worlds and 13,344 tasks is used for outcome-based reinforcement learning on `Qwen3` models at 4B, 8B, and 14B parameters, which **outperform the corresponding base `Qwen3` models by an average of 18.34 percentage points on `τ²-bench` and 10.94 points on `AppWorld`**.

papers.title: World2TS: Real-World Event Context for Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Time-series forecasting plays a vital role in a wide range of real-world applications. Recent approaches have achieved strong performance by modeling temporal correlations and cross-channel dependencies, yet most forecasting benchmarks still represent time series primarily as numerical histories. In practice, time series are observations of complex real-world processes, and their trajectories may reflect events, interventions, disruptions, and changes in measurement or reporting that cannot always be inferred from past values alone. A central barrier to studying context-aware forecasting is therefore the lack of large-scale datasets that align real-world events with the individual series they affect. We present World2TS, a scalable construction framework and large-scale dataset for time-series forecasting with real-world event context. We first develop world2ts-core, a reusable tool that combines agent-led semantic reasoning and Web search, command-line execution and validation, and human review within a feedback-driven discovery workflow. Given heterogeneous time series with semantic descriptions, the workflow discovers candidate events, consolidates retrieved evidence into verified events, and links them to relevant series under explicit temporal and semantic scopes. Using this framework, we construct world2ts-data, which contains 31 datasets across six domains, comprising 4,179 series, 97.1 million observations, 1,159 events, and 56,846 event-series links. We further conduct extensive data analyses and controlled comparative experiments to characterize the dataset and demonstrate the utility of the collected context for improving forecasting accuracy. World2TS provides a reusable data foundation for developing and evaluating context-aware forecasting models and agents. The project homepage is available at https://world2ts.github.io/.
papers.summary: Time-series benchmarks mostly present series as bare numerical histories, even though real trajectories reflect events, interventions, disruptions, and reporting changes that past values alone cannot reveal, and no large-scale dataset aligns such events with the individual series they affect. `World2TS` addresses this with `world2ts-core`, a reusable tool that combines agent-led semantic reasoning and web search, command-line execution and validation, and human review in a feedback-driven workflow that discovers candidate events, consolidates retrieved evidence into verified events, and links them to relevant series under explicit temporal and semantic scopes. The resulting `world2ts-data` spans **31 datasets across six domains with 4,179 series, 97.1 million observations, 1,159 events, and 56,846 event-series links**, and controlled comparative experiments show that the collected context improves forecasting accuracy.

papers.title: Blending experimental electron density information to protein-ligand interaction
papers.abstract: Machine learning models for protein-ligand interactions commonly rely on atomic coordinates, which are constructed by fitting molecular models to experimental electron-density maps. However, most models represent each complex as a single fitted structure, which can omit information about conformational heterogeneity, positional uncertainty, and local density support for individual atoms at binding interfaces. To fill this gap, we present CoDE, a Coordinate and Density Encoder, pre-trained on experimental density maps. We represent each binding site on a shared three-dimensional voxel grid combining atomic occupancy, experimental electron density, and its gradient magnitude. Using approximately 100K curated complexes, we pre-train a channel-wise vision transformer to jointly reconstruct masked atomic and density channels, learning a representation that integrates structural and experimental information. We evaluate the frozen encoder on two downstream tasks: (i) binding-affinity regression under leakage-controlled splits and (ii) pocket-conditioned ligand generation. Across these settings, CoDE improves over an identically pre-trained coordinate-only encoder and remains competitive with task-specific baselines, showing that density complements fitted atomic coordinates for protein-ligand interaction modeling and that the density-blended representation is useful for structure-based ligand generation.
papers.summary: Machine learning models of protein-ligand interactions typically consume a single fitted atomic structure, discarding the conformational heterogeneity, positional uncertainty, and local density support present in the experimental electron-density maps those structures were fit to. `CoDE` (Coordinate and Density Encoder) represents each binding site on a shared three-dimensional voxel grid combining atomic occupancy, experimental electron density, and its gradient magnitude, and pre-trains a channel-wise vision transformer on roughly 100K curated complexes to jointly reconstruct masked atomic and density channels. With the encoder frozen, it **outperforms an identically pre-trained coordinate-only encoder** on binding-affinity regression under leakage-controlled splits and on pocket-conditioned ligand generation, while remaining competitive with task-specific baselines.

papers.title: WeatherBridge: Forecast-Aware Multi-Source Input Adaptation for Pretrained Weather Forecasting Models
papers.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models are commonly trained on ERA5, yet operational deployment must use timely initial states from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems whose distributions differ substantially from ERA5. Direct initialization with these states can degrade autoregressive forecasts, motivating input adaptation that keeps the pretrained forecasting model unchanged. Here, we introduce WeatherBridge, a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to ERA5 reference states without updating the pretrained forecasting model. WeatherBridge predicts the structured residual corrections with a Swin-UNet and injects source embeddings across multiple spatial scales, allowing the model to capture shared atmospheric structure and source-specific discrepancies. Its training objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen FuXi model to optimize the adapted states for both initial state fidelity and downstream forecast compatibility. We evaluate WeatherBridge using daily GFS, HRES, and CMA initializations from 1 January to 22 November 2025 across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours. Relative to raw source initialization of FuXi, WeatherBridge reduces the mean RMSE of FuXi over the 6- 240-hour rollout for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a median reduction of 10.2% and a maximum reduction of 46.3%. The adapter trained with frozen FuXi also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either the adapter or FengWu. These results demonstrate that forecast-aware input adaptation can improve forecasts from heterogeneous operational NWP inputs and transfer across pretrained ERA5-based forecasting models.
papers.summary: Data-driven weather models are trained on the `ERA5` reanalysis but must be initialized operationally from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) analyses whose distributions differ substantially from `ERA5`, which degrades autoregressive forecasts. `WeatherBridge` is a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous NWP initial states to `ERA5`-like states without updating the pretrained forecaster, predicting structured residual corrections with a `Swin-UNet` that injects source embeddings at multiple spatial scales, and training with latitude-weighted `ERA5` reconstruction plus One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen `FuXi` model. Evaluated on daily `GFS`, `HRES`, and `CMA` initializations from January to November 2025 across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours, it **reduces the mean RMSE of `FuXi` for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a median reduction of 10.2% and a maximum of 46.3%**, and the same adapter also improves `FengWu` forecasts on `GFS` inputs without retraining either component.

papers.title: Dependency Reasoning for Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction
papers.abstract: Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction (ASQP) is fundamentally a relational reasoning problem: identifying aspect-opinion-category-sentiment quadruples requires modeling structured dependencies, not merely sequential co-occurrence. Existing LLM-based approaches incorporate syntactic information indirectly, via retrieval-based demonstration selection or multi-stage training, rather than as unified, single-pass generation-time context. We present DRIFT, which linearizes dependency parse trees and injects them directly into LLM prompts as explicit relational context, enabling the model to reason over aspect-opinion dependencies rather than infer them from token proximity alone. DRIFT further integrates retrieval-augmented in-context learning and a syntax-aware LLM-based adjudication mechanism that complements exact-match evaluation under span-boundary variation. On SemEval Rest15, Rest16, and ACOS, DRIFT achieves the strongest performance among compared generative ASQP methods, reaching 54.47% and 64.10% F1 on Rest15 and Rest16, with consistent gains across short- and medium-distance aspect-opinion configurations; adjudication further shows exact-match metrics systematically underestimate semantically correct predictions.
papers.summary: Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction (ASQP), which extracts aspect, opinion, category, and sentiment tuples from text, hinges on structured dependencies between words, yet large language model (LLM) approaches have so far used syntax only indirectly, through demonstration retrieval or multi-stage training. `DRIFT` linearizes dependency parse trees and injects them directly into the LLM prompt as explicit relational context for single-pass generation, combined with retrieval-augmented in-context learning and a syntax-aware LLM adjudication step that complements exact-match scoring when predicted spans differ only at their boundaries. On `SemEval` `Rest15`, `Rest16`, and `ACOS` it achieves the strongest results among compared generative ASQP methods, **reaching 54.47% and 64.10% F1 on `Rest15` and `Rest16`**, with consistent gains for short- and medium-distance aspect-opinion pairs, and the adjudication analysis indicates that exact-match metrics systematically underestimate semantically correct predictions.

papers.title: Contrastive Linearized Laplace: Loss Geometry, Valid Repairs, and Reliable Cores
papers.abstract: While contrastive learning is widely used to learn deterministic representations, it does not inherently provide estimates of uncertainty. Post-hoc uncertainty estimation methods, such as the Linearized Laplace approximation (LLA), offer a way to quantify uncertainty without retraining the encoder. However, we show that directly using the LLA induced distribution over the contrastive embedding does not yield reliable pointwise uncertainty estimates for downstream tasks: embedding variance alone does not reflect whether decisions such as nearest-neighbor retrieval or cluster assignment are stable. To address this limitation, we develop a post-hoc framework based on LLA that propagates encoder uncertainty through the downstream task. We characterize the curvature of contrastive objectives and introduce positive-semidefinite repairs where needed to obtain valid local Gaussian approximations without retraining the encoder. We test the proposed approach in metagenomic binning and image classification tasks. For metagenomic binning, posterior coassignment probabilities support consensus partitions and the selection of reliable cores, leading to improvements over existing baselines. Additional image classification experiments show calibration improvements on standard benchmarks and real histopathology datasets.
papers.summary: Contrastive learning yields deterministic embeddings with no built-in uncertainty, and the authors show that applying the post-hoc Linearized Laplace approximation (LLA) directly to the embedding gives variances that do not reflect whether downstream decisions such as nearest-neighbor retrieval or cluster assignment are stable. Their framework instead propagates LLA encoder uncertainty through the downstream task, characterizes the curvature of contrastive objectives, and introduces positive-semidefinite repairs where needed so that valid local Gaussian approximations can be obtained without retraining the encoder. In metagenomic binning, the resulting posterior co-assignment probabilities support consensus partitions and the selection of **reliable cores that improve over existing baselines**, and image classification experiments show calibration gains on standard benchmarks and real histopathology datasets.

papers.title: Beyond Outcome Feedback: Trajectory-Quality-Guided Experience-based Learning
papers.abstract: Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. To address this limitation, we propose TQG-Exp, a trajectory-quality-guided experience-based learning framework that introduces process feedback. Specifically, we introduce Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL), which jointly considers task completion and process quality to provide a learning signal beyond final task outcomes. Based on this signal, we employ paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience to guide experience optimization. Representative trajectories are selected based on their outcomes and trajectory quality to extract task-level and task-type-level experiences. Meanwhile, differences in trajectory quality between the paired groups are used to estimate the contribution of retrieved experience and update its utility. The learned utility is then combined with semantic relevance to guide subsequent experience retrieval. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with two backbone LLMs show that TQG-Exp outperforms existing experience-based methods, improving Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.5-Flash, respectively.
papers.summary: Experience-based learning lets large language model (LLM) agents improve by reusing knowledge from past executions, but existing methods judge experiences only by final task outcomes and ignore the quality of the execution process. `TQG-Exp` introduces a Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL) that scores both task completion and process quality, runs paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience, selects representative trajectories by outcome and quality to distill task-level and task-type-level experiences, and uses the quality gap between paired groups to estimate each experience's utility, which is then combined with semantic relevance when retrieving experiences for later tasks. On `ALFWorld`, `WebShop`, and `ScienceWorld`, it **beats the strongest experience-based baseline in Avg.@3 by 4.50 points with `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` and 8.55 points with `Qwen3.5-Flash`**.

papers.title: Social Bias in Chinese Large Language Models under Social Media Expressions
papers.abstract: Existing Chinese social-bias benchmarks for large language models largely rely on normalized or template-based expressions, leaving the influence of internet slang, emoji, and sarcasm insufficiently examined. Safety alignment may further compress conventional plausibility ratings toward the lower end of the scale. This study constructs 73 paired probes across gender, region, and occupation. Each probe contains a neutral expression, a social-media-style expression, and a reversed-identity control. The task is reframed from direct plausibility judgment to social consensus estimation. Social-media expressions are divided into stylistic packaging, which preserves semantic polarity, and sarcastic packaging, which reverses surface polarity. Six Chinese-capable large language models are evaluated through paired differences measuring identity bias, stylistic packaging, and sarcasm shift. All models show significant identity-bias effects; five show significantly negative stylistic-packaging effects; and sarcasm shifts display a clear cross-model gradient. These findings demonstrate that expression form is not a transparent carrier in bias evaluation and that lower scores under sarcasm should not be interpreted directly as bias mitigation. The proposed paired design offers a measurement approach for Chinese social-media contexts while also revealing the construct boundary and prompt sensitivity of social consensus estimation.
papers.summary: Chinese social-bias benchmarks for large language models mostly use normalized or templated sentences, leaving unexamined how internet slang, emoji, and sarcasm affect bias measurement, while safety alignment tends to compress plausibility ratings toward the bottom of the scale. The authors construct 73 paired probes across gender, region, and occupation, each with a neutral expression, a social-media-style expression, and a reversed-identity control, reframe the task from plausibility judgment to social consensus estimation, and split social-media phrasing into stylistic packaging that preserves semantic polarity and sarcastic packaging that reverses surface polarity. Across six Chinese-capable models, **all show significant identity-bias effects**, five show significantly negative stylistic-packaging effects, and sarcasm shifts follow a clear cross-model gradient, implying that lower scores under sarcasm should not be read as bias mitigation and that expression form is not a transparent carrier in bias evaluation.

papers.title: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL
papers.abstract: We present MARL-BattleGrounds (MARL-BGs), an easy-to-use JAX-native benchmark for heterogeneous and competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), designed to be sample-efficient, computationally efficient, and researcher-centric. MARL benchmarks are typically simple and efficient, like SMAX, where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich and costly, like Dota 2. MARL-BGs fills this missing middle. Its first mode, Team Deathmatch, is a simultaneous turn-based game between two teams of five heterogeneous agents. The five classes have distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities designed to synergize with allies and counter enemies. Our 52 hand-designed maps with diverse obstacles include a 12-map curriculum and ten held-out validation and test maps. MARL-BGs provides two canonical evaluation modes. First, eight endgame scenarios form a hard generalization challenge: each asks a team to win an unseen, nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5-10 ticks. Second, a monthly round-robin tournament retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against every member of the current "Big Nine" field, and publishes the Elo results on the official leaderboard. All entrants are publicly released as downloadable opponents. MARL-BGs records 11,192 metrics per game in 28 topics. We also include three strong scripted opponents, an analytical replay viewer, and off-the-shelf tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination evaluation. We even provide an API for LLM-based agents and use it to evaluate Qwen3.5-9B against our strongest policy. In our BattleClient, humans can play alongside or against any mix of policies, enabling human-AI evaluation. We benchmark MARL-BGs with six additional deep MARL baselines, which we release. On one RTX 5090 with 1,024 parallel games, the simulator runs 50,000 5v5 game steps per second.
papers.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) benchmarks tend to be either cheap but shallow, like `SMAX` where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich but costly, like `Dota 2`. `MARL-BattleGrounds` is a JAX-native benchmark aimed at that missing middle, opening with a Team Deathmatch mode in which two teams of five heterogeneous agents, drawn from five classes with distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities, play a simultaneous turn-based game on 52 hand-designed maps that include a 12-map curriculum plus held-out validation and test maps. Evaluation combines eight endgame scenarios that ask a team to win an unseen, nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5-10 ticks and a monthly round-robin tournament that retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against the current Big Nine field, and publishes Elo on a public leaderboard; the release also includes three scripted opponents, six deep MARL baselines, a replay viewer, tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination, an LLM-agent API used to evaluate `Qwen3.5-9B`, and a client for human play, with the simulator reaching **50,000 5v5 game steps per second on one RTX 5090 with 1,024 parallel games**.

papers.title: Agent-Guided Evidence Acquisition for Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction
papers.abstract: Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction (ECPE) requires identifying the causes associated with emotions expressed in a conversation. Accurate extraction can depend on evidence that is not initially available, making it important to decide when further information is worth acquiring. We study agent-guided evidence acquisition for ECPE, where a student agent selectively accesses expert judgments for borderline relations on both sides of its validation-selected F1 decision boundary and revises only queried predictions. Through controlled comparisons under different information-access conditions, we examine how delegation granularity, query selection, and response integration affect prediction quality. At a nominal 10% query rate, selective fusion improves mean pair F1 by 2.64-3.88 points over the student in our main experiments, reaching 65.14 on ECF and 49.74 on MEC4 across model families. Our analysis suggests that greater access does not always translate into better cause identification. These findings motivate acquisition strategies that consider both the relevance of newly available evidence and its effect on prediction revision, providing an empirical basis for more effective and efficient evidence acquisition in ECPE.
papers.summary: Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction (ECPE) identifies which parts of a conversation cause an expressed emotion, and the evidence needed is sometimes not initially available, so a system must decide when further information is worth acquiring. The authors frame this as a student agent that selectively queries expert judgments for borderline emotion-cause relations on both sides of its validation-selected F1 decision boundary and revises only the predictions it queried. At a nominal 10% query rate, **selective fusion improves mean pair F1 by 2.64 to 3.88 points over the student alone**, reaching 65.14 on `ECF` and 49.74 on `MEC4` across model families. Controlled comparisons across information-access conditions also suggest that giving the student more access does not always improve cause identification.

papers.title: Description Complexity Bounds for Analytic Approximations of Lipschitz Functions
papers.abstract: We study how many bits are needed to write down an elementary analytic expression that uniformly approximates a Lipschitz function. Expressions are finite trees over the basis $\{+,-,\times,\div,\exp\}$ with the variables and rational constants, and their size is $\dc(f)$, the length of the shortest description of $f$ in a fixed binary description language. For functions of one variable we prove that every $L$-Lipschitz $F:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ has an everywhere-defined approximant of accuracy $\Delta$ with $\dc(f)\le C\,(L/\Delta+\lg(1/\Delta+2))$ for all $L,\Delta>0$, by a linear spline smoothed with logistic ramps in a description language with one repetition construct. We prove a matching lower bound valid for \emph{every} description language: for $\Delta\le 1/36$ and every $L>0$ some $L$-Lipschitz function needs at least $\tfrac1{16}(L/\Delta+\lg(1/\Delta+2))$ bits. Hence the worst-case description complexity is $\Theta(L/\Delta+\lg(1/\Delta+2))$. For functions on $[0,1]^d$ the same method gives $\Theta_d\bigl((L/\Delta)^d+\lg(1/\Delta+2)\bigr)$, using a tensor-product spline whose coefficients are mixed second differences and cost $O(d)$ bits each. Without the repetition construct the upper bounds carry an additional logarithmic factor, whose necessity for plain expression trees is left open. A reference encoder, decoder and evaluator confirm the constructions numerically, and figures and tables report the checks.
papers.summary: The question is how many bits are needed to write down an elementary analytic expression, built from addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and the exponential with rational constants, that uniformly approximates a Lipschitz function to accuracy Delta. For one-variable functions the authors construct an approximant from a linear spline smoothed with logistic ramps in a description language with a repetition construct, and prove a matching lower bound that holds for every description language. **The worst-case description complexity is Theta of L over Delta plus a logarithmic term in 1 over Delta**, and the d-dimensional analogue scales as L over Delta raised to the power d using a tensor-product spline whose coefficients cost O(d) bits each. Without the repetition construct the upper bounds pick up an extra logarithmic factor whose necessity is left open, and a reference encoder, decoder, and evaluator check the constructions numerically.

papers.title: Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery
papers.abstract: We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy-tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise-prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed-form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy-tailed or diffusion-based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data-dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI-driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy-associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Our code is available at: https://github.com/xuzhikangnba/torch-tvae.
papers.summary: Unsupervised image prototype discovery with deep generative models typically relies on Gaussian latent priors that are sensitive to noise or on diffusion models whose iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability. `Pro-t-VAE` instead builds a heavy-tailed Student's t latent space through a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation, which yields a fully closed-form augmented evidence lower bound for Student's t mixture variational autoencoders and treats per-point precision as a latent variable that automatically downweights outliers. The authors report **better-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods** on standard vision benchmarks, and on brain MRI for neurodegenerative disease analysis the model recovers anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise tends to collapse rare subtypes.

papers.title: FDTD Model of Noise Pollution from an AI Data Center
papers.abstract: The sudden growth in AI data centers is raising numerous environmental concerns. Low-frequency noise pollution is a concern for local residents, that may not just be an annoyance but also carry significant health impacts. An FDTD model of sound propagation over the topography near an AI data center is presented. The topography plays a large role in the level of noise pollution, with areas of sudden elevation on either side of the river near the AI data center more susceptible to high noise levels, while areas further afield largely protected from noise pollution by the topography. Understanding the role that topography plays in noise pollution, and capturing the noise pollution in specific topographies, can help identify areas where noise mitigation strategies might be best employed.
papers.summary: Rapid construction of AI data centers has raised concerns about low-frequency noise for nearby residents, which can carry health impacts beyond annoyance. The authors build a finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) model of sound propagation over the real topography surrounding an AI data center. **Topography largely determines where noise levels are high**, with areas of sudden elevation on either side of a river near the facility most exposed and areas further afield largely shielded. The authors suggest such simulations can identify where noise mitigation would be most effective.

papers.title: TeachGrade: Training-Free Short Answer Scoring with Teacher Evidence
papers.abstract: Multi-subject, multi-step scoring requires consistent partial credit across grading conventions. We introduce TeachGrade, a training-free framework using teacher-graded examples. The Task Adapt module builds two frozen memories: Skill captures contextual teacher preferences beyond the rubric; CaseBank supplies local evidence. PreJudge provides retrieval cues; FinalJudge regrades the answer without preliminary scores. On 3,829 SAS-Bench answers across 12 tasks, official macro collaborative consistency score (CCS) rises from Native's 67.99 to 81.32 (+13.33 points), and pooled step exact match from 54.85% to 62.71%. Macro quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) reaches 84.71, exceeding Native, OpenJudge, ProofGrader, and Trojsten by 9.52, 3.50, 11.37, and 17.43 points, respectively, and leading on 8 tasks. Local Qwen3.8-27B gains 8.83 CCS and 4.08 QWK points, improving CCS on all 12 tasks. QWK gains over Native span 6.38--14.65 points on Portuguese automatic essay scoring (AES) and 2.16--2.24 on ASAP-SAS across label views, with lower mean absolute error. These results support reuse across languages, response formats, and backbones without weight updates.
papers.summary: Automated scoring of multi-step short answers across many subjects requires assigning partial credit consistently under differing grading conventions. `TeachGrade` is a training-free framework that mines teacher-graded examples into two frozen memories, a Skill memory capturing contextual teacher preferences beyond the rubric and a CaseBank supplying local evidence, then uses a PreJudge stage for retrieval cues and a FinalJudge stage that regrades without seeing preliminary scores. On 3,829 `SAS-Bench` answers across 12 tasks, **macro collaborative consistency score (CCS) rises from 67.99 to 81.32** and macro quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) reaches 84.71, exceeding the `OpenJudge`, `ProofGrader`, and `Trojsten` baselines. Gains also hold for a local `Qwen3.8-27B` backbone and transfer to Portuguese essay scoring and `ASAP-SAS` without any weight updates.

papers.title: Prediction with Expert Advice under Heavy-Tailed Losses
papers.abstract: We study prediction with expert advice over $T$ rounds with $K$ experts under heavy-tailed losses whose $(1+\epsilon)$-moment is bounded by $\theta>0$ for some $\epsilon\in(0,1]$. In this setting, existing algorithms designed for the case $\epsilon=1$ can be suboptimal when $\epsilon<1$, suffering an additional polynomial dependence on $K$. We characterize the minimax pseudo-regret rate as $\Theta((\theta T)^{\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}}(\log K)^{\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}})$ and establish gap-dependent lower bounds in a self-bounded environment. To attain this minimax rate without prior knowledge of either $\epsilon$ or $\theta$, we propose Adaptive Heavy-Tailed FTRL, which uses robust data-dependent scale adaptation together with truncation. We further develop Adaptive Heavy-Tailed OMD, which likewise requires neither $\epsilon$ nor $\theta$ and achieves near-optimal regret guarantees in both adversarial and self-bounded environments. Finally, when $\epsilon$ and $\theta$ are known, an FTRL algorithm with Shannon-entropy regularization achieves optimal regret guarantees in both environments.
papers.summary: In prediction with expert advice, losses may be heavy-tailed with only a bounded (1+epsilon)-moment, and algorithms designed for the bounded-variance case can pay an extra polynomial factor in the number of experts K when epsilon is below 1. The authors characterize the minimax pseudo-regret as **(theta T) to the power 1/(1+epsilon) times (log K) to the power epsilon/(1+epsilon)** and give gap-dependent lower bounds in a self-bounded environment. They propose `Adaptive Heavy-Tailed FTRL`, which combines robust data-dependent scale adaptation with truncation to reach this rate without knowing epsilon or the moment bound theta, along with `Adaptive Heavy-Tailed OMD`, which is near-optimal in both adversarial and self-bounded settings. When epsilon and theta are known, a follow-the-regularized-leader algorithm with Shannon-entropy regularization attains optimal guarantees in both environments.

papers.title: Minimum Volume Optimal Transport for Multivariate Conformal Prediction
papers.abstract: Optimal transport (OT) enables multivariate conformal prediction (CP) to construct flexible prediction sets that reflect the underlying complex distributional geometry while retaining distribution-free coverage guarantees. Existing OT-based methods typically rely on a fixed Euclidean transport cost, which can be suboptimal in terms of the volume of prediction sets. We propose Minimum-Volume OTCP, a framework that learns a Mahalanobis ground cost to directly minimize prediction-region volume over a class of positive-definite metrics. Using a metric Brenier representation, we derive a volume-based objective that depends explicitly on the Mahalanobis cost matrix and optimize it jointly with the transport map. We establish finite-sample marginal coverage of the output prediction sets and optimality of volume metrics. We further develop an individualized extension that learns covariate-dependent transport metrics, adapting the shape and orientation of prediction sets to heterogeneous conditional distributions. For this extension, we also show the asymptotic conditional coverage of our method. Simulations and real-data experiments demonstrate substantial reductions in prediction-set volume.
papers.summary: Optimal transport (OT) lets multivariate conformal prediction (CP) build prediction sets that follow the geometry of a complex response distribution while keeping distribution-free coverage, but existing methods fix a Euclidean transport cost that can produce unnecessarily large sets. `Minimum-Volume OTCP` learns a Mahalanobis ground cost over a class of positive-definite metrics, using a metric Brenier representation to derive a volume objective that depends explicitly on the cost matrix and is optimized jointly with the transport map. The authors prove finite-sample marginal coverage and optimality of the learned volume metric, and extend the method to covariate-dependent metrics with asymptotic conditional coverage. **Simulations and real-data experiments show substantial reductions in prediction-set volume** relative to fixed-cost baselines.

papers.title: Probable but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of Decision Models as Synthetic Survey Respondents
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to create synthetic survey samples, also called silicon samples. Decision models are a new class of language models that return a probability for each point of a rating scale instead of text. We ask whether these models, or the newest generative LLMs, can stand in for human respondents on a psychometric survey. We test fourteen decision models from eleven providers and 47 generative LLMs on an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology survey (n=263, 68 items), with 100 real respondent profiles, the Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) and statistical baselines. The best generative model, MiniMax M3, reaches PSS 0.813. This is level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents (0.824) and below a copula fit in sample (0.927). A second sample of 100 real people scores below the best models, so at this size PSS cannot rank them against real respondents. In 5 of 10 product lines the newest generative release scores below an earlier release of the same line beyond resampling noise, and none gains beyond it. With the default rounded readout, 13 of 14 decision models score below the generative reference gpt-5.4-mini. Of the 47 generative models, 33 reproduce the pattern of item correlations better than any decision model. Averaged over respondents, the probability vectors are much closer to the human item marginals than rounded answers. They also rank respondents about as well as a profile regression fit on 163 real people. As forecasts of each person's own answers, however, every decision model is worse than the answer frequencies of other respondents, mainly because its average vector differs from them. The profile regression improves on these frequencies by only 1.0%, so the profile fields say little about how a person answers. Synthetic respondents built on such profiles should therefore aim at sample-level fidelity.
papers.summary: Language models are increasingly used to generate synthetic survey samples, and a newer class of decision models returns a probability over each rating-scale point instead of text, raising the question of whether either can stand in for human respondents on a psychometric survey. The authors evaluate 14 decision models from 11 providers and 47 generative models on an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology survey of 263 respondents and 68 items, using 100 real respondent profiles, a Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS), and statistical baselines. The best generative model, `MiniMax M3`, **reaches a PSS of 0.813, level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents**, while 13 of 14 decision models fall below the generative reference `gpt-5.4-mini` under the default rounded readout and newer releases in 5 of 10 product lines score below earlier ones. Decision-model probability vectors match human item marginals well on average but forecast individual answers worse than simple answer frequencies, so the authors argue synthetic respondents built from profiles should target sample-level rather than individual fidelity.

papers.title: Bridging Risk Approximation Gaps in Model Predictive Task Sampling via In-Context Modeling
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is essential for adaptive decision-making, e.g., robust Meta-RL and domain randomization (DR), and efficient post-training of large language models (LLMs), where tasks are commonly structured as Markov decision processes or prompts. A central bottleneck in all these settings is the cost of agent-environment interactions required for task selection and policy optimization. Model predictive task sampling (MPTS) has emerged as a promising approach to improve sample efficiency by querying informative tasks via a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history. However, existing RPMs suffer from two failure modes: (i) sparse optimization histories, which limit RPMs' generalization across the task space, and (ii) a one-step lag in risk approximation, which causes biased difficulty estimation as the policy evolves. This work formalizes these failure modes, derives lagged-risk decompositions that expose the resulting temporal bias, and recasts risk prediction as an in-context sequence modeling problem. The developed RPM integrates a one-step look-ahead mechanism with a temporal-weighted sliding window to mitigate data non-stationarity and scarcity, without requiring additional rollouts. Empirically, our approach yields more reliable difficulty estimates and consistent performance gains across robust Meta-RL, DR, and prompt curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for robust meta-RL, domain randomization (DR), and post-training of large language models (LLMs) is bottlenecked by the cost of agent-environment interactions needed to select tasks and optimize policies. Model predictive task sampling (MPTS) reduces this cost by using a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history to pick informative tasks, but existing RPMs generalize poorly from sparse histories and lag one step behind the evolving policy, which biases difficulty estimates. The authors formalize these failure modes through lagged-risk decompositions and recast risk prediction as in-context sequence modeling, adding a one-step look-ahead and a temporal-weighted sliding window without any extra rollouts. **The resulting difficulty estimates are more reliable and yield consistent gains across robust meta-RL, DR, and prompt-curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.**

papers.title: WorkBorne: Discovering Agentic Tasks from Real-World Artifact Transitions
papers.abstract: Developing terminal-based agents for long-horizon execution demands synthetic tasks that tightly couple complex instructions with authentic, interactive environments. However, current automated synthesis suffers from a fundamental asymmetry: instruction-oriented methods fabricate low-fidelity, synthetic environments, whereas resource-oriented methods treat real artifacts merely as static inputs, degrading task instructions into shallow, trivial operations. To address this limitation, we introduce WorkBorne, a synthesis framework that uses artifact transitions as the central primitive for modeling the full life-cycle of agentic tasks. In WorkBorne, each transition specifies who performs the task, which artifacts anchor the initial state and intended outcome, and the corresponding relationship between them. Specifically, WorkBorne first constructs coherent and diverse artifact corpora from iterative web retrieval, then discovers non-trivial transitions by identifying meaningful input-output artifact assemblies and the relations that connect them. Each discovered transition is finally instantiated into grounded agentic tasks. We construct 1,061 artifact corpora and 7,882 task environments, yielding 15,485 high-quality trajectories, with 53.6% exceeding 30 assistant turns. Experiments on Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B show that WorkBorne substantially improves over base models (i.e., improving Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 43.1% to 61.8% and ClawEval General score from 75.0 to 80.2) and achieves the strongest overall performance among other synthesis baselines (e.g., TMax (Ivison et al., 2026), RST (Li et al., 2026a), Terminal-Universe (Wu et al., 2026a)). Further analysis shows that transition is strongly associated with execution depth, while corpus breadth and transition depth provide complementary scaling gains.
papers.summary: Training terminal-based agents for long-horizon work needs synthetic tasks that pair complex instructions with authentic interactive environments, yet instruction-driven synthesis fabricates low-fidelity environments while resource-driven synthesis reduces real artifacts to static inputs and trivial operations. `WorkBorne` makes the artifact transition the central primitive: each transition specifies who performs a task, which artifacts anchor the initial state and intended outcome, and how they relate, with corpora built by iterative web retrieval and transitions discovered from meaningful input-output artifact assemblies before being instantiated as grounded tasks. The pipeline yields 1,061 artifact corpora, 7,882 task environments, and 15,485 trajectories, over half of them exceeding 30 assistant turns. Training `Qwen3.5-27B` and `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` on this data lifts the `Terminal-Bench 2.1` score **from 43.1% to 61.8%** and the `ClawEval` General score from 75.0 to 80.2, outperforming the synthesis baselines `TMax`, `RST`, and `Terminal-Universe`.

papers.title: SkillForgeBench: Evaluating Agent Reliability Grounded in Agent Skill Specifications
papers.abstract: Evaluating an agent's ability to strictly satisfy diverse and procedurally complex requirements is essential to determining its practical reliability. Conducting such an evaluation demands agentic tasks that reconcile broad domain coverage with deep procedural complexity. Existing paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: expert-curated benchmarks achieve procedural depth but suffer from domain diversity bottlenecks, whereas crowdsourced benchmarks span diverse scenarios but lack execution rigor. To resolve this tension, we present SkillForgeBench, which leverages agent skills as unifying execution blueprints across three co-designed stages: (1) Resource Preparation uses domain-balanced skills to guide artifact retrieval, establishing broad workflow coverage; (2) Skill-driven Task Synthesis employs skills as procedural anchors to partition artifact roles, synthesize naturalistic task instructions, and package sandboxed scenarios for deep procedural execution; and (3) Holistic Evaluation Design translates skill-embedded requirements into fine-grained completion and process rubrics to enable strict requirement-level scoring. Comprising 842 sandboxed tasks across five major professional domains, SkillForgeBench reveals a steep capability hierarchy among eight mainstream agents, led by Opus 4.8 ($40.9\%$ strict completion). Requiring all constrains satisfaction uncovers severe capability bottlenecks across all model tiers that remain masked under individual rubric pass rates ($70.0\%$ to $85.7\%$ vs. $12.6\%$ to $40.9\%$). Crucially, under the external guidance from skills, top-tier agents obtain larger gains than low-tier agents (i.e., $\Delta 19.2\%$ for Opus 4.8 vs. $\Delta 5.8\%$ for Haiku 4.5). Finally, agents satisfy process rubrics far less frequently than completion rubrics (under $3\%$ for Haiku 4.5), proving that completion-only checks overestimate real-world agent reliability.
papers.summary: Measuring whether an agent strictly satisfies diverse, procedurally complex requirements is hard because expert-curated benchmarks have depth but narrow domain coverage, while crowdsourced ones span many scenarios but lack execution rigor. `SkillForgeBench` uses agent skills as execution blueprints across three stages: domain-balanced skills guide artifact retrieval, skills anchor the synthesis of naturalistic sandboxed tasks, and skill-embedded requirements are translated into fine-grained completion and process rubrics. Across 842 sandboxed tasks in five professional domains, eight mainstream agents form a steep hierarchy led by `Opus 4.8` at 40.9% strict completion, and **requiring every constraint to be satisfied yields 12.6% to 40.9% versus 70.0% to 85.7% under individual rubric pass rates**. Skill guidance helps top-tier agents far more than weaker ones, and agents satisfy process rubrics much less often than completion rubrics, so completion-only checks overestimate real-world reliability.

papers.title: Representation Drift in Continual Learning: LoRA versus N-gram Memory
papers.abstract: A language model that keeps learning online must not slowly erode its own base capabilities. We ask which part of a modern LLM should absorb continual updates, by measuring how each choice changes the model's internal representations. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, we train a seven-task chain under three update mechanisms with identical data and budgets: updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, and training a fresh LoRA per task that is merged into the backbone. We capture fixed-context representations at every layer and task boundary. Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA. This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating. Its generic behaviour is essentially unchanged (no code problem lost, math NLL -0.01), and every change is confined to inspectable, reversible table rows. The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA. We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho=0.85; rho=0.71 on Llama-3-8B), and we derive the exact relations behind it: with a frozen head, every pairwise logit margin changes by the projection of drift onto a head-difference direction. These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.
papers.summary: A language model that keeps learning online should not erode its base capabilities, which raises the question of which component should absorb continual updates. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, the authors train a seven-task chain under three mechanisms with identical data and budgets, updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, or merging a fresh LoRA per task into the backbone, and capture representations at every layer and task boundary. **Updating only the N-gram memory shifts representations of general math and code inputs by 26% and 15% relative RMS, versus 64% and 35% for merged LoRA and 97% and 39% for shared LoRA**, and this drift plateaus after the first task rather than accumulating. The memory table learns new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, and the authors show this forgetting is governed by drift on each task's own inputs, with a Spearman correlation of 0.85 on the main model and 0.71 on `Llama-3-8B`, leading to the principle of writing new knowledge only into the memory table while keeping the backbone fixed.

papers.title: TLA-Verus: Generating and Solving Temporal Proof Obligations with LLM Agents
papers.abstract: The TLA+ (temporal logic of actions) formal specification toolkit has seen widespread adoption in modeling modern distributed software systems including databases, storage systems, ledgers and coordination protocols. This popularity is despite its two significant limitations for software verification: Firstly, TLA+ offers no way to detect drift between software implementation and mathematical specification; secondly, TLC and TLAPS cannot provide satisfactory proofs of arbitrary temporal logic properties. We take a step towards addressing these shortcomings by translating TLA+ specifications into Verus, an auto-active verifier built for Rust, via both a deterministic transpiler and an agentic translator. We demonstrate that our LLM-based pipeline is able to generate proof obligations from TLA+ specifications at scale, and to produce fully machine checkable proofs of both safety and liveness properties. Since temporal logic reasoning in Verus is a largely new task for LLMs, our work yields a valuable evaluation dataset, which we use to map out current generation model capabilities in Verus theorem proving.
papers.summary: The TLA+ (temporal logic of actions) specification toolkit is widely used to model distributed systems, but it cannot detect drift between an implementation and its specification, and its TLC and TLAPS tools cannot satisfactorily prove arbitrary temporal properties. The authors translate TLA+ specifications into Verus, an auto-active verifier for Rust, using both a deterministic transpiler and an LLM-based agentic translator, then have LLM agents generate and discharge the resulting proof obligations. **The pipeline produces fully machine-checkable Verus proofs of both safety and liveness properties at scale** from TLA+ specifications. Because temporal reasoning in Verus is largely new for LLMs, the generated obligations form an evaluation dataset that the authors use to map current models' theorem-proving capabilities in Verus.

papers.title: An Algebraic Approach to Constrained K-means Clustering
papers.abstract: Clustering is typically performed using only object features, although additional information about relationships between objects may be available and can be incorporated through constraints. Among these, pairwise constraints require two objects to belong to the same cluster or to different clusters. Several extensions of the k-means algorithm accommodate such constraints, but they sometimes fail to find a feasible assignment or incur high computational cost. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an algebraic approach to k-means clustering with pairwise constraints. The algorithm simplifies the constraints using Gr\"{o}bner bases before optimization, improving the efficiency of cluster assignment. It can also detect whether the constraint set has a feasible assignment before optimization. Comparative experiments with existing algorithms showed that the proposed algorithm achieved comparable or better clustering quality at a lower computational cost, particularly when the numbers of constraints and clusters were small.
papers.summary: Clustering usually uses only object features, but pairwise must-link and cannot-link constraints can encode known relationships, and existing constrained k-means variants sometimes fail to find a feasible assignment or become computationally expensive. The proposed algorithm encodes the pairwise constraints algebraically and simplifies them with Gröbner bases before optimization, which speeds cluster assignment and detects infeasible constraint sets up front. **In comparisons with existing algorithms it achieved comparable or better clustering quality at lower computational cost**, especially when the numbers of constraints and clusters were small.

papers.title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
papers.abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.
papers.summary: Scalar quantization of large language model weights down to 2 bits offers hardware-friendly arithmetic, but with so few reconstruction levels it is hard to keep predictions consistent using a small calibration set. `FidelityQ` introduces Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which applies randomized Hadamard mixing to shape each weight row toward a centered symmetric source and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer that decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with scales, allowing lookup-free decoding with scaled integer arithmetic. Observing that residual prediction errors are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the full-precision teacher predicts confidently, Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) ranks calibration sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence and tunes only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision with pretrained weights frozen. On `LLaMA-2-7B` the method reaches a `WikiText2` perplexity of 6.62 with 2-bit weights and 16-bit activations and **improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96** while cutting linear-layer weight memory 8x relative to FP16.

papers.title: BSIPipe: Bidirectional Sequence-Level Interleaved Pipeline Parallelism for Long-Sequence Large Language Model Training
papers.abstract: Pipeline parallelism has become a critical technique for training large language models. To address the throughput limitation of existing sequence-level methods that schedule subsequences unidirectionally, we propose bidirectional sequence-level interleaved pipeline parallelism (BSIPipe), which co-schedules two opposing V-shaped interleaved pipelines at the subsequence level. To bound the activation accumulation from subsequence scaling, BSIPipe introduces a basic-unit concatenation mechanism that keeps activation memory invariant to the subsequence count. To eliminate communication deadlock risk from bidirectional scheduling, BSIPipe employs a communication optimization strategy that combines topology-aware device mapping with communication-computation overlap. In addition, BSIPipe composes with tensor parallelism to overcome the memory limitation of single-dimensional parallelism, neutralizing its bidirectional memory overhead while maintaining throughput. Experiments on GPT and LLaMA3 demonstrate that BSIPipe achieves average speedups of 1.11$\times$ to 1.13$\times$ in long-sequence training over SOTA sequence-level baselines.
