papers.summary: Pipeline parallelism is central to training large language models, but existing sequence-level schedules that process subsequences in one direction limit throughput on long sequences. `BSIPipe` co-schedules two opposing V-shaped interleaved pipelines at the subsequence level, adds a basic-unit concatenation mechanism that keeps activation memory invariant to the number of subsequences, and removes the deadlock risk of bidirectional scheduling through topology-aware device mapping combined with communication-computation overlap. It also composes with tensor parallelism to offset the memory overhead of bidirectional scheduling while maintaining throughput. On GPT and `LLaMA3` models it achieves **average speedups of 1.11x to 1.13x** over state-of-the-art sequence-level baselines in long-sequence training.

papers.title: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance
papers.abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page.
papers.summary: Diffusion policies can represent multimodal action distributions, which aids exploration, but optimizing them with reinforcement learning tends to collapse that diversity, and fine-tuning a pretrained policy can erase its acquired capabilities while action-space residuals lack the expressiveness for multimodal exploration. `CFG-Policy` is a plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and composes their score or velocity fields at sampling time through classifier-free guidance. For online RL a frozen exploration branch preserves diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards, and for offline-to-online RL a frozen pretrained branch is steered by a trainable one, in both cases leaving the underlying RL objective intact. Applied on top of `QSM` and `QVPO` on five `MuJoCo` tasks and `Flow-SDE` with PPO on four `RoboTwin` manipulation tasks, **the framework improves performance in both the online and offline-to-online settings**.

papers.title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
papers.abstract:
How do language models generalize from their training data? This is a central challenge for alignment: models reliably learn their training distribution given enough samples, but we want models that behave well when deployed in new contexts. We study out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of propensities. Our central experiment uses a range of elicitation techniques -- system prompting, few-shot learning, SFT on reference answers, and GRPO -- to increase a target propensity in a model, then measures how it spills over onto others across the resulting cross-elicitation matrices. We find that spillover is highly correlated between models when the same elicitation technique is used, but our SFT and GRPO runs induce different spillover profiles.
  Elicitation of benign traits can sometimes generalize towards undesired traits, for example a model trained to claim that it is sentient often becomes more power-seeking. We further find that spillover partially resembles trait correlations found in humans and identify three clusters of traits that account for about half of the variance using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Across many elicitation runs, we observe that models change in characteristic ways that don't depend on the targeted trait, a phenomenon we refer to as drift. Drift moves Qwen3.5-9B towards its base model.
  When investigating if LLMs are able to predict spillover, we find that Claude Opus 5.5 predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves, but worse than data-driven approaches using alternative elicitation methods or models. Overall, no single dominant predictor emerges, and generalization remains hard to predict. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nielsrolf/propensity-spillover.
papers.summary: Alignment depends on how a model's learned propensities generalize beyond the training distribution, since models reliably fit their training data but are deployed in new contexts. The authors use several elicitation techniques, including system prompting, few-shot learning, supervised fine-tuning on reference answers, and GRPO, to raise one target propensity and then measure how it spills over onto other traits in cross-elicitation matrices. Spillover is highly correlated across models under the same elicitation technique but differs between SFT and GRPO runs, and **eliciting benign traits can generalize toward undesired ones, for instance a model trained to claim it is sentient often becomes more power-seeking**. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) finds three trait clusters explaining about half the variance, many runs show a trait-independent drift that pulls `Qwen3.5-9B` toward its base model, and `Claude Opus 5.5` predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves but worse than data-driven predictors, so generalization remains hard to predict.

papers.title: VC-OPD: Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation for Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning
papers.abstract: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has advanced vision-language reasoning, but its sequence-level rewards provide limited credit assignment for individual reasoning tokens. On-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this issue by providing dense supervision on student-generated trajectories, yet standard OPD assigns similar importance to all teacher-preferred tokens, including template phrases and visually irrelevant continuations. We introduce Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation (VC-OPD), a grounding-aware distillation method that prioritizes tokens whose correctness depends on image-specific evidence. After a teacher-supervised warm start that stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts, VC-OPD performs on-policy distillation with two teacher evaluations for each student trajectory: one under the original image and one under a counterfactual image with corrupted instance-specific evidence. The original-image teacher distribution determines the distillation target, while the original--counterfactual teacher gap estimates token-level visual dependence and softly reweights the loss. To avoid unstable response-level update scales, VC-OPD further applies mass-preserving normalization to the token weights. This design preserves the dense supervision of OPD while shifting learning capacity toward visually grounded reasoning tokens. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that VC-OPD improves visual reasoning performance and produces more effective token-level distillation.
papers.summary: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has advanced vision-language reasoning, but its sequence-level rewards give weak credit assignment to individual tokens, and while on-policy distillation (OPD) supplies dense token-level supervision, it weights template phrases and visually irrelevant tokens as heavily as grounded ones. `VC-OPD` runs a teacher-supervised warm start, then performs on-policy distillation in which the teacher evaluates each student trajectory twice, once with the original image and once with a counterfactual image whose instance-specific evidence is corrupted. The original-image teacher distribution serves as the distillation target while the gap between the two teacher evaluations estimates each token's visual dependence and softly reweights the loss, with mass-preserving normalization keeping update scales stable. **On multimodal reasoning benchmarks the method improves visual reasoning performance over standard OPD** and shifts learning toward visually grounded tokens.

papers.title: Compositional Average Velocity Modeling for Efficient Diffusion Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for offline reinforcement learning, but their reliance on multi-step denoising introduces substantial computational overhead and requires backpropagation through time during training, limiting scalability and practical deployment. In this work, we propose \textbf{Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL)}, a single-step generative policy learning framework that retains the expressive capacity of diffusion models while eliminating iterative sampling and BPTT. InsQL builds on the flow-matching perspective of diffusion policies, but replaces marginal velocity parameterization with \emph{average-velocity} modeling and introduces a principled compositional mechanism, yielding a theoretically grounded objective that learns average velocity consistently across scales. This formulation provides a direct noise-to-action mapping and enables single-step action generation. InsQL further unifies compositional average-velocity modeling with behavior-regularized actor--critic optimization in a single framework, requiring only a single policy network and avoiding distillation, multi-stage procedures, and Jacobian computations during training. At inference time, actions are generated in a single forward pass and can be refined via value-guided candidate selection to improve performance. Extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show that InsQL matches or surpasses state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing both training and inference time. Overall, these results establish compositional average-velocity modeling as an efficient and scalable alternative to multi-step generative policies for offline RL.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based policies are strong for offline reinforcement learning, but multi-step denoising adds inference cost and requires backpropagation through time (BPTT) during training. `InsQL`, or Instant Flow Q-Learning, replaces the marginal velocity parameterization of flow-matching policies with average-velocity modeling and a compositional mechanism that learns the average velocity consistently across scales, giving a direct noise-to-action mapping and single-step action generation. The method pairs this with behavior-regularized actor-critic optimization using a single policy network, with no distillation, multi-stage training, or Jacobian computation, and can refine actions at inference through value-guided candidate selection. **On standard offline RL benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks it matches or surpasses state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing training and inference time.**

papers.title: Probabilistic Multi-Source Data Selection via Learnable Categorical Priors: Variance Reduction and Guaranteed Derandomization
papers.abstract: Bilevel data selection is a fundamental task with numerous applications in machine learning and statistics. A common strategy for tackling this problem is to relax the original bilevel combinatorial optimization into a continuous one. However, existing methods, including 0-1 relaxation and probabilistic relaxation, still suffer from several limitations, such as unstable gradient estimation and infeasible rounding. To address these issues, this paper proposes a new probabilistic relaxation for the multi-source bilevel data selection problem. Our key idea is to introduce multiple learnable categorical priors to parameterize a probability distribution supported only on feasible data subsets, thus naturally yielding a lossless rounding scheme. We further show that our proposed relaxation admits an effective two-point gradient estimator, which can simultaneously avoid the inverse-Hessian computation required by existing 0-1 relaxation and the unbounded score term appearing in prior probabilistic relaxation. Furthermore, we develop a reducible representation of this estimator, which substantially reduces the number of lower-level retrainings required for gradient computation. Built upon this reducible two-point estimator, we then design a novel stochastic gradient algorithm, termed ReSGD, for multi-source bilevel data selection problem, and establish a rigorous approximation guarantee for the subset returned by ReSGD under weak submodularity. Finally, extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our proposed ReSGD.
papers.summary: Bilevel data selection chooses a subset of training data from multiple sources so that a model retrained on it performs best on a downstream objective, and existing continuous relaxations suffer from unstable gradient estimates or rounding steps that produce infeasible subsets. The approach parameterizes a distribution supported only on feasible subsets with multiple learnable categorical priors, which makes rounding lossless, and derives a two-point gradient estimator that avoids both the inverse-Hessian computation of 0-1 relaxations and the unbounded score term of earlier probabilistic relaxations. A reducible form of the estimator cuts the number of lower-level retrainings needed per gradient step, and the resulting `ReSGD` algorithm comes with **an approximation guarantee under weak submodularity** for the returned subset, backed by experiments.

papers.title: Exact Phase-Type Point Processes for Certified Measurement and Prediction of Event Streams
papers.abstract: Temporal point processes are used both to measure market mechanisms, for example how fast prices absorb news and how much of the reaction is the market responding to itself, and to predict the next event. We show that one algebraic object, the phase-type (Erlang-chain) state space, serves both purposes with exact likelihoods. For measurement, we build a multiscale phase-type Hawkes process whose parameters all enter linearly. Its log-likelihood is concave, and we compute the global maximum together with a Fenchel duality-gap certificate. A Markov embedding gives the response to an exogenous shock, echoes included, in closed form, and this response is stable if and only if the spectral radius of the branching matrix is below one. Applied to six markets around 670 scheduled macroeconomic releases (2022-2026) with a built-in placebo test, the model shows that the direct reaction to CPI, payrolls, PPI and the FOMC statement is absorbed in about a second, while the market's own echoes stretch half of the response to 16-137 s. For prediction, we introduce EPT-X, a neural point process that adds a history-dependent mixture-of-Erlang renewal channel to a linear Hawkes backbone. Its intensity and compensator remain in closed form, its states follow an affine recursion that trains with a parallel scan, and it can start from the certified fit of the measurement model. EPT-X has the best test likelihood on all five LOBSTER order-book streams and on Retweet and Taobao, and is level with the best published model on StackOverflow. We also find that the EasyTPP implementation of IntensityFree clamps short inter-event times before scoring, and that the gaps of the EasyTPP Amazon data are uniform on two fixed intervals.
papers.summary: Temporal point processes are used both to measure how markets absorb news and to predict the next event in a stream, and the authors show that a single phase-type (Erlang-chain) state space supports both uses with exact likelihoods. For measurement, a multiscale phase-type Hawkes process has a concave log-likelihood with a certified global maximum, and applied to six markets around 670 scheduled macroeconomic releases it finds that the direct reaction to releases such as CPI and the FOMC statement is absorbed in about a second, while **the market's own echoes stretch half of the response to 16-137 seconds**. For prediction, `EPT-X` adds a history-dependent mixture-of-Erlang renewal channel to a linear Hawkes backbone, keeps intensity and compensator in closed form, and reaches the best test likelihood on all five `LOBSTER` order-book streams as well as `Retweet` and `Taobao`. Along the way the authors report that the `EasyTPP` implementation of `IntensityFree` clamps short inter-event times before scoring.

papers.title: Do Personalized LLMs Need the Whole Conversation? Matching the Full History with Only 5% of Its Text via Relevance-Filtered Context
papers.abstract: Personalized assistants accumulate long conversation histories, and passing the whole history to an LLM with every request is costly. We show that it is also unnecessary. On PersonaMem-v2 (180 questions), with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 as judges, a relevance-filtered context, built by sentence-level retrieval that ranks the history by similarity to the current request and stops at a fixed budget, matches full-history accuracy with only 5% of the text, cutting the judge's input about 20-fold. An LLM summary of the same length performs on par, but it needs an LLM to read the entire history, whereas retrieval needs only a small embedding model. While both sentence-level retrieval and LLM summary perform strongly, retrieval does so while placing the relevant evidence in the context for only 61% of the questions, and an oracle given only that evidence beats the full history by 15.6 points, making better context selection a promising path to surpassing the full history.
papers.summary: Personalized assistants accumulate long conversation histories, and sending the whole history to a large language model on every request is expensive. The authors test a relevance-filtered context built by sentence-level retrieval that ranks the history by similarity to the current request and stops at a fixed budget, evaluating on `PersonaMem-v2` with `GPT-5.6-terra` and `Claude Opus 5.5` as judges. **The filtered context matches full-history accuracy using only 5% of the text**, cutting judge input roughly 20-fold, and an equal-length LLM summary performs on par but requires an LLM to read the entire history rather than a small embedding model. Retrieval achieves this while placing the relevant evidence in context for only 61% of questions, and an oracle given just that evidence beats the full history by 15.6 points, suggesting better context selection could surpass the full history altogether.

papers.title: Counterfactual Rollouts for Offline Contrastive Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) learns goal-conditioned values by associating state--action pairs with the states subsequently reached, assuming that no unobserved variable jointly affects the recorded action and its outcome. When offline demonstrations come from a demonstrator with information hidden from the learner, this assumption fails and the critic absorbs spurious action--outcome associations. We formalize this setting with confounded Markov decision processes and introduce counterfactual transitions that separate what the data identify from what they do not; minimizing over all compatible transitions yields a worst-case occupancy that lower-bounds the true one. Causal Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CauCRL) learns a pessimistic counterfactual transition from positive and negative offline demonstrations and trains the critic on counterfactual rollouts, substantially improving success rates over standard CRL on confounded goal-reaching tasks.
papers.summary: Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) learns goal-conditioned values by associating state-action pairs with the states reached afterward, which assumes no hidden variable jointly influences the recorded action and its outcome. When offline demonstrations come from a demonstrator with information the learner cannot see, that assumption breaks and the critic absorbs spurious action-outcome associations. The authors formalize this with confounded Markov decision processes and introduce counterfactual transitions that separate what the data identify from what they do not, showing that minimizing over all compatible transitions yields a worst-case occupancy that lower-bounds the true one. `CauCRL` learns a pessimistic counterfactual transition from positive and negative demonstrations and trains the critic on counterfactual rollouts, **substantially improving success rates over standard CRL on confounded goal-reaching tasks**.

papers.title: MCPDisCo: Seesaw-Mitigated Tuning for MCP-Native Agents
papers.abstract: The Model Context Protocol provides a shared interaction substrate for the agentic web, allowing heterogeneous services to expose capabilities through a standardized interface. Learning to use this ecosystem entails a hierarchy of capabilities: tool-format skills, server-level transfer, and cross-server composition. We present MCPDisCo, an ecosystem-scale reinforcement learning framework for MCP-native agents. Using a Thought-Markov Decision Process (Thought-MDP), the framework explicitly represents internal reasoning alongside routing, execution, and termination and trains on real-server, long-horizon interactions spanning 70 MCP servers and 527 tools across six domains. We study the reasoning--tool seesaw, a joint-learning failure mode in which improvement in one objective can accompany deterioration in the other. To mitigate potential interference, MCPDisCo combines token-masked reward attribution with bidirectional gradient surgery: the former separates direct supervision for reasoning and action spans, while the latter removes conflicting components from both objective gradients in shared parameters. MCPDisCo achieves higher success with fewer chain-of-thought tokens. On the out-of-distribution MCP-Atlas and the GAIA benchmark, MCPDisCo maintains monotone gains, confirming that the learned behavior generalizes beyond the training server distribution and broader agentic tasks. Model weight and implementation are available.
papers.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives heterogeneous services a standardized interface for exposing tools to agents, and learning to use that ecosystem spans tool-format skills, server-level transfer, and cross-server composition. `MCPDisCo` is a reinforcement learning framework that models an agent's internal reasoning alongside routing, execution, and termination as a Thought-Markov Decision Process (Thought-MDP) and trains on real-server, long-horizon interactions across 70 MCP servers and 527 tools in six domains. The authors identify a reasoning-tool seesaw, where improving one objective degrades the other, and counter it with token-masked reward attribution that supervises reasoning and action spans separately plus bidirectional gradient surgery that removes conflicting gradient components in shared parameters. The resulting agent reaches **higher success with fewer chain-of-thought tokens** and keeps its gains on the out-of-distribution `MCP-Atlas` and `GAIA` benchmarks, with weights and code released.

papers.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
papers.abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.
papers.summary: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for agent skills, with past experiences stored as steering vectors, while facts and preferences about the user are assumed to require text. The authors test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM, where the shift an experience causes in late-layer states is stored under a whitened key for the conversation's gist and added back in a later session only when the gist matches, and they argue such a fixed average shift can only carry question-independent content because attention recomputes its effect for every question. In a pre-registered study on `Qwen3.5-2B` and `Qwen3.5-9B` with judges from four model families, the memory is selective, leaving about 98% of unrelated replies unchanged, but **stored facts are used cleanly at most 15% of the time versus 96-98% when given in context**. Leanings transfer only within a narrow strength window, and the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives, so a stored dislike is recalled as a like unless the opposite is subtracted.

papers.title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
papers.abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.
papers.summary: Formulaic alpha mining searches a vast, noisy space for executable expressions that capture predictive market signals, and prior LLM-based methods rely on prompting, iterative search, or evolving seed factors rather than learning to construct factors directly. `AlphaRLM` trains an LLM with reinforcement learning to build executable symbolic factors from financial literature without any input factor expressions, using Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO) to condition generation on literature-derived ideas and executable operators. The policy is aligned with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structure across factor quantiles. On `CSI 300`, `CSI 1000`, and `S&P 500`, the method **outperforms factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return**, and an 8B model shows strong cross-market performance.

papers.title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
papers.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.
papers.summary: Can an autonomous agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst, and does it work the same way? The authors compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE) by having nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scoring both with a common understanding rubric and recording every interaction with `IDA Pro`. The best agents, `GPT-5.5 Pro`, `Claude Opus 4.8`, and `Kimi K3`, **reach statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks**, with ablations showing that open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations while frontier models do not. Workflows differ sharply, since humans revisit functions and follow local program structure while strong agents exhibit greedy fetching, jumping across the binary and rarely returning to inspected code, and a context-saturation measurement over 4,000 real-world binaries shows that larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust even large windows, so scaling will need better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state.

papers.title: HiPAD: A Unified Gait, Audio-Visual, and Personality Fusion Network for Depression Detection, with a Hierarchical Personality Ablation and the Calibration Limits of Domain-Adapted LLMs
papers.abstract: We present HiPAD, a single fusion network submitted to all six sub-tracks of the MPDD-AVG 2026 depression-detection challenge, covering the Elder and Young cohorts and three modality sets (gait, audio-visual, and both), each combined with personality descriptions. The network encodes each available modality with a shared BiLSTM, zero-pads absent modalities, and applies cross-modal attention only when at least two of gait, audio and video are present. Personality, which dominates our results, is kept out of the attention and fused by concatenation. Because the architecture is identical in every sub-track, differences between them reflect the data rather than the model, and we use this to study three questions. Our main finding is that the personality description, roughly 150 tokens about who the subject is, carries more depression signal than audio, video, and gait combined: gait plus personality alone (TLS 0.647) beats every configuration that includes audio and video. First, a four-level ablation of the personality description (L0-L3) quantifies this: removing every personality-derived feature, including the Big Five scores that earlier MPDD ablations keep, lowers the Track-Level Score by 0.499 to 0.507 and leaves the model at chance. Second, domain-adapting the personality encoder with LoRA (7B) or QLoRA (72B) on PHQ-8/9 data raises binary Cohen's $\kappa$ by 0.13 but lowers the overall score by distorting the PHQ-9 regression; a frozen RoBERTa-large encoder does better at this sample size. Third, at fixed architecture, handcrafted clinical features (eGeMAPS, OpenFace action units) outperform generic deep features (wav2vec2, DenseNet) on the audio-visual tracks. The unified system reaches a cross-track G-Score of 0.482; with under 100 subjects per cohort, the limiting factors are the size of the representation and the calibration of the outputs, not the choice of architecture.
papers.summary: `HiPAD` is a single fusion network submitted to all six sub-tracks of the `MPDD-AVG 2026` depression-detection challenge, encoding gait, audio, and video with a shared BiLSTM, zero-padding absent modalities, applying cross-modal attention only when at least two are present, and fusing a personality description by concatenation. Because the architecture is identical across sub-tracks, differences reflect the data, and the main finding is that **a roughly 150-token personality description carries more depression signal than audio, video, and gait combined**, with gait plus personality alone (Track-Level Score 0.647) beating every configuration that includes audio and video. A four-level ablation shows that removing all personality-derived features, including Big Five scores, drops the score by about 0.5 to chance, and domain-adapting the personality encoder with LoRA or QLoRA on PHQ-8/9 data raises binary Cohen's kappa by 0.13 but lowers the overall score by distorting the PHQ-9 regression, so a frozen `RoBERTa-large` encoder does better at this sample size. Handcrafted clinical features (eGeMAPS, OpenFace action units) also beat generic deep features on the audio-visual tracks, and with under 100 subjects per cohort the limiting factors are representation size and output calibration rather than architecture.

papers.title: Cross-Material Magnetic Core Loss Prediction via Operating-Condition Matching and Partial Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Cross-material magnetic core loss prediction requires adapting to new material responses with limited measurements. Global feature alignment overlooks differences in source and target excitation coverage. This motivates selecting comparable samples and controlling each source measurement's alignment contribution. This paper proposes T-PCOT, a Transformer transfer method based on condition-supported partial optimal transport. Frequency, flux excursion, temperature, and waveform descriptors define a sparse graph of comparable operating conditions. A capacity-constrained transport plan distributes alignment across source measurements and leaves costly target mass unmatched. The plan is constructed from measured inputs before training and guides local waveform-feature consistency. An importance-weighted sampling scheme preserves both uniform source regression and the transport objective during minibatch optimization. Experiments on three material pairs and three target label budgets show that T-PCOT reduces mean relative error (MRE) and 95th-percentile error (P95) relative to Transformer-based multiple-kernel maximum mean discrepancy (T-MKMMD) in all nine comparisons. Macro MRE decreases from 12.60% to 9.65%, and macro P95 from 30.94% to 25.06%, corresponding to relative reductions of 23.41% and 19.01%. Controlled comparisons and ablations examine the roles of input processing, condition correspondence, and source capacity. The results demonstrate the predictive advantage of organizing cross-material alignment through operating-condition support over the compared global alignment method. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance in magnetic core loss transfer learning.
papers.summary: Predicting magnetic core loss for a new material requires adapting from well-measured source materials with only limited target measurements, and global feature alignment ignores differences in which excitation conditions the source and target data cover. `T-PCOT` is a Transformer transfer method based on condition-supported partial optimal transport, where frequency, flux excursion, temperature, and waveform descriptors define a sparse graph of comparable operating conditions, a capacity-constrained transport plan spreads alignment across source measurements while leaving costly target mass unmatched, and an importance-weighted sampling scheme preserves both the source regression and the transport objective during minibatch training. Across three material pairs and three target label budgets, it beats Transformer-based multiple-kernel maximum mean discrepancy (T-MKMMD) in all nine comparisons, **reducing macro mean relative error from 12.60% to 9.65%** and macro 95th-percentile error from 30.94% to 25.06%.

papers.title: SkillHorizon: Constructing Long-Horizon Agent Tasks through Skill Composition
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents must complete workflows in which later activities depend on earlier outputs and changes to shared state. A key challenge for evaluation is to expand task requirements and their dependencies while keeping tasks executable and outcomes verifiable. We introduce SkillHorizon, a benchmark that constructs long-horizon tasks through skill composition in seven business environments. Its generators use domain-specific rules to turn reusable skill procedures into concrete business activities. These activities are connected through input-output dependencies, shared resources, and state updates, allowing workload and coordination demands to grow together. Successful reference executions validate task feasibility and measure interaction workload, while programmatic evaluators assess local completion and whole-task success. We evaluate five language models on 1,050 tasks with reference interaction workloads ranging from 64K to 1M tokens. Across these scales, mean local-goal completion falls from 90.4% to 46.8%, as completed work fails to keep pace with growing requirements. At larger workloads, agents more often submit unsuccessful final answers with substantial work unfinished and tool-call allowance remaining. Trace analysis also identifies cases where scripts execute successfully but their outputs fail downstream business checks. SkillHorizon provides a configurable testbed for studying sustained progress, dependency coordination, and complete task delivery in growing workflows. Our code is available at https://github.com/KnowComp/SkillHorizon.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents must complete workflows where later steps depend on earlier outputs and on changes to shared state, and evaluating this requires growing task requirements and dependencies while keeping tasks executable and outcomes verifiable. `SkillHorizon` builds such tasks by composing reusable skill procedures into concrete business activities across seven business environments, linking them through input-output dependencies, shared resources, and state updates so that workload and coordination demands grow together, with reference executions validating feasibility and programmatic evaluators checking local completion and whole-task success. Evaluating five language models on 1,050 tasks whose reference interaction workloads range from 64K to 1M tokens, **mean local-goal completion falls from 90.4% to 46.8%** as workload grows. At larger scales agents more often submit unsuccessful final answers with substantial work unfinished and tool-call budget remaining, and trace analysis finds scripts that execute successfully yet fail downstream business checks.

papers.title: SEEK: Agentic Knowledge Graph Retrieval for Secure Code Generation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code while introducing exploitable security weaknesses, particularly when developers specify functionality without explicit security requirements. Recent state-of-the-art approaches mitigate this problem using external security knowledge, but largely rely on flat similarity-based retrieval over independent artifacts, making it difficult to infer the relevant vulnerability space and retrieve targeted knowledge when direct matches are unavailable. We propose SEEK, an agentic Graph RAG framework for secure code generation that constructs a security knowledge graph using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) taxonomy as its structural backbone and injects it with curated real-world CVE vulnerability-fix instances. At inference time, a Planner Agent predicts potential CWE weaknesses associated with the developer query, which guide Graph Scoping to restrict retrieval to relevant regions of the CWE taxonomy before deterministic multi-faceted candidate ranking. A Selection Agent subsequently validates the predicted weaknesses and retrieved candidates prior to code generation. Across five open-source LLMs, we evaluate SEEK in an out-of-distribution setting on CodeGuard+ and CyberSecEval, spanning C, C++, and Python. SEEK achieves the highest SecurePass@1 of 77.45% on CodeGuard+ and the highest aggregate ICD pass rate of 79.45% on CyberSecEval, surpassing prior approaches. Moreover, SEEK achieves 85.2% SecurePass@1 across 13 unseen CWE types with no directly linked vulnerability-fix instances, demonstrating strong generalizability, while maintaining acceptable inference latency costs.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often produce functionally correct code that contains exploitable weaknesses, especially when developers specify functionality without security requirements, and prior mitigations retrieve security knowledge through flat similarity search over independent artifacts that struggles when no direct match exists. `SEEK` is an agentic Graph RAG framework that builds a security knowledge graph with the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) taxonomy as its backbone and populates it with curated real-world CVE vulnerability-fix instances. At inference time a Planner Agent predicts likely CWE weaknesses for the query, which scope retrieval to relevant regions of the taxonomy before deterministic multi-faceted ranking, and a Selection Agent validates the predicted weaknesses and candidates before code generation. Across five open-source LLMs in an out-of-distribution setting on `CodeGuard+` and `CyberSecEval` spanning C, C++, and Python, it reaches **the highest SecurePass@1 of 77.45%** on `CodeGuard+` and a 79.45% aggregate ICD pass rate on `CyberSecEval`, and it holds 85.2% SecurePass@1 on 13 unseen CWE types that have no directly linked fix instances.

papers.title: FleetPilot: Fine-Grained Steering Empowers Real-World LLM Personalization
papers.abstract: With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.
papers.summary: Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from sparse, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories, and existing approaches based on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward models each carry recurring costs in context management, model deployment, or multi-candidate scoring. `FleetPilot` is a training-free steering framework that generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the forward pass, combining a match-contrast step that extracts user-relevant signals, a fine-grained steering component that hooks activations from attention and MLP layers, and a query-conditioned aggregation module that merges them into contextually relevant adjustments. Across scenarios including short-to-long text generation and web function calling, the method **consistently improves performance and is strongest in fast-shifting and data-sparse settings**, while avoiding training cycles and adding little storage or latency overhead.

papers.title: HodgePhaseNet: Discrete Hodge Decomposition of Semantic Flows in Transformer Attention
papers.abstract: WavePhaseNet introduced frequency-resolved semantic representations, QuantumPhaseNet introduced gauge-covariant phase connections, and ModularPhaseNet made a finite cyclic phase channel and its cycle holonomy computable in an ordinary Transformer. These constructions are complementary, yet they do not by themselves separate an observed collection of pairwise relations into a globally consistent direction, circulation around local compositions, and circulation that persists around a larger unfilled cycle. HodgePhaseNet addresses this separation by representing semantic transitions as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on a finite oriented simplicial complex. With vertex-edge incidence matrix $B_1$ and edge-face incidence matrix $B_2$, every such field has a unique orthogonal decomposition $\Omega = B_1^T\Phi + B_2\Psi + H$, where $B_1H=0$ and $B_2^TH=0$. The three component fields are unique even when their potentials are not. We give explicit projectors, a sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, a verified numerical example, and a redesigned attention interface. The attention bias is defined on allowed ordered query-key pairs, remains consistent under arbitrary choices of edge orientation, and preserves a decoder's causal information boundary by constructing its complex from the visible prefix. Gauge invariance of the attention output is conditional on using invariant or appropriately compensated features. A simple difference of vertex embeddings has no coexact or harmonic component; a genuine relation encoder is therefore indispensable. Local circulation is not automatically contradiction, and harmonic flow is not automatically missing knowledge. These interpretations and any reduction in factual error require controlled empirical evaluation. This paper presents a mathematical and architectural proposal, not external natural-language performance results.
papers.summary: Building on earlier PhaseNet constructions that gave Transformers frequency-resolved representations, gauge-covariant phase connections, and a finite cyclic phase channel, `HodgePhaseNet` addresses what those leave unseparated: splitting a collection of pairwise semantic relations into a globally consistent direction, circulation around local compositions, and circulation that persists around larger unfilled cycles. Semantic transitions are represented as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on a finite oriented simplicial complex, where the discrete Hodge decomposition splits every such field uniquely into gradient, curl, and harmonic components even when the underlying potentials are not unique. The authors provide explicit projectors, a sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, a verified numerical example, and an attention-bias interface that is consistent under arbitrary edge orientations and preserves a decoder's causal boundary by building the complex from the visible prefix. They note that a simple difference of vertex embeddings has no curl or harmonic component, so a genuine relation encoder is required, and **the work is a mathematical and architectural proposal with no natural-language performance results**.

papers.title: Metric-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Object Hallucination Reduction in LVLM-Based Image Captioning
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have excelled in joint visual and language understanding, particularly in image captioning. However, LVLMs remain prone to object hallucination, describing non-existent entities in the given image. Previous remedies, including dataset-enhanced supervised training and reinforcement learning from human feedback, show promise but rely heavily on costly human involvement, limiting scalability. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning framework to mitigate object hallucination in LVLM-based image captioning, driven entirely by natural language processing (NLP) metrics. While optimizing reinforcement learning solely on NLP metrics offers scalability, it also introduces pitfalls: reward hacking, sparse feedback, and costly training. Our framework sidesteps these by introducing an Object Consistency Score (OCS) capturing both correctness and coverage of objects, incorporating KL-regularization for denser token-level guidance, and designing a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters atop a frozen LVLM backbone, achieving efficiency and stability. Extensive experiments on the InstructBLIP baseline demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our framework, achieving a substantial hallucination reduction of up to 41\% on the COCO dataset and 29\% on the Visual Genome. Furthermore, the framework can enhance caption quality by incorporating complementary evaluation metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR. These results reveal a broader insight in multimodal learning: LVLMs can effectively self-correct hallucinations using metric feedback, motivating deeper exploration into scalable reinforcement frameworks that significantly reduce human effort.
papers.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) describe objects that are not present in images, and prior fixes such as dataset-enhanced supervised training or reinforcement learning from human feedback depend on costly human involvement. The proposed reinforcement learning framework is driven entirely by natural language processing (NLP) metrics and avoids reward hacking, sparse feedback, and expensive training by introducing an Object Consistency Score (OCS) that captures both correctness and coverage of mentioned objects, adding KL-regularization for denser token-level guidance, and using a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters on top of a frozen LVLM backbone. On an `InstructBLIP` baseline the framework **reduces object hallucination by up to 41%** on `COCO` and by 29% on `Visual Genome`, and incorporating complementary metrics such as `BERTScore` and `METEOR` also improves caption quality.

papers.title: Single-Sample Decoding of a Two-Layer Sound-Word Canvas Model for Thai Klon Pad
papers.abstract: We present a generator of Thai klon pad verse, one stanza from a short topic, and evaluate it against human verse on held-out topics. The generator is a masked language model initialised from WangchanBERTa over a fixed canvas with two layers: a sound layer of pronounced syllables, where rhyme, tone and syllable count are enforced as hard masks, and a word layer of whole words, so that no word is cut into written pieces. Decoding commits one cell at a time and samples at temperature 0.4; one sample is drawn per topic, with no selection, reranking or repair. On 78 held-out topics never used in development, judged by three independent runs of a frozen LLM judge in the same pools as the human stanzas from which the topics were written, 70.5% of the generated stanzas pass form, lexical cleanness of all four lines and topic alignment together, against 76.9% for the human stanzas (difference -6.4 points, 95% CI [-19.2, +6.4]). Cleanness is level with human (85.9% vs. 87.2%), and the stanzas pass form and cleanness together slightly more often than the human ones (+3.8 points, [-6.4, +14.1]); the difference lies in alignment (84.6% vs. 91.0%), on topics that were written from the human stanzas. The low temperature matters: at higher temperatures the same model passes clearly fewer of the same topics, because lexical errors lie in the model's lower-probability choices; sharpening the sampling distribution removes most of them, at a cost in vocabulary (7.5% rare words against 16.5% in the human stanzas) and diversity. The pre-registered target, all-three within 5 points of human, is missed by 1.4 points. KlonSuphap-LM, the only public klon pad generator we know of, passes none of the 78 held-out topics when judged in separate pools together with the method's and the human stanzas (form 19.2%, cleanness 3.8%).
papers.summary: The generator produces one stanza of Thai klon pad verse from a short topic using a masked language model initialised from `WangchanBERTa` over a fixed two-layer canvas, with a sound layer of pronounced syllables where rhyme, tone, and syllable count are enforced as hard masks and a word layer of whole words so no word is split into written fragments. Decoding commits one cell at a time, samples at temperature 0.4, and draws a single sample per topic with no reranking or repair. On 78 held-out topics judged by three runs of a frozen LLM judge alongside the human stanzas, **70.5% of generated stanzas pass form, lexical cleanness, and topic alignment together, against 76.9% for human verse**, with cleanness level with humans and the gap concentrated in topic alignment. The low temperature is essential because lexical errors sit in low-probability choices, though sharpening costs vocabulary and diversity, and the pre-registered target of all three metrics within 5 points of human is missed by 1.4 points, while the only other public generator, `KlonSuphap-LM`, passes none of the held-out topics.

papers.title: Fitting Every Hint Is Not Enough: Premature Floods in Recurrent Algorithmic Reasoners
papers.abstract: Recurrent algorithmic reasoners are trained with per-step hints on small graphs and run for many more steps on large ones. On breadth-first search in SALSA-CLRS, we find that a reasoner can reproduce every training hint and still fail on deep graphs: after some exact steps, it declares nodes reached before the search gets there. We call this a premature flood and trace two routes to it. In our GRU processor with a degree input, the flood is carried in the hidden state and set off when that input is in the tail of the training distribution. Setting the input higher at inference brings the flood sooner, and none of the six flooding models counts steps. Without the input, summing the neighbors' states instead of averaging them also breaks the processor. In the benchmark's own GIN and PGN, trained with its code, some seeds instead flood from a fixed step, on sparse and dense graphs alike. Clamping the degree input or adding 200 dense training graphs removes every failure of the GRU processor. Detaching the state between steps avoids the flood in that processor (0 of 23 seeds, against 6 under full backpropagation) but not with sums or a residual update, and two published remedies leave floods. None of the benchmark's test sets is both deep and dense, but its deepest one shows the second route: on its Delaunay graphs at 1,600 nodes, one GIN seed floods from step 18. We therefore recommend auditing the range of every input and aggregate, which catches the first route, and testing on deep graphs, which catches both.
papers.summary: Recurrent algorithmic reasoners are trained with per-step hints on small graphs and then run for many more steps on large ones, and on breadth-first search in `SALSA-CLRS` the authors find that a model can reproduce every training hint yet still fail on deep graphs by declaring nodes reached before the search arrives, a failure they call a premature flood. They trace two routes to it: in a GRU processor with a degree input, the flood is carried in the hidden state and triggered when that input falls in the tail of the training distribution, while in the benchmark's own GIN and PGN processors some seeds flood from a fixed step on sparse and dense graphs alike. **Clamping the degree input or adding 200 dense training graphs removes every failure of the GRU processor**, and detaching the state between steps avoids the flood in that processor for 0 of 23 seeds versus 6 under full backpropagation, though two published remedies still leave floods. The authors recommend auditing the range of every input and aggregate, which catches the first route, and testing on deep graphs, which catches both.

papers.title: Too Late to Prune: Generative AI, the Screen, and Team Creative Decisions
papers.abstract: Generative AI makes options cheap and shifts the bottleneck of creative work from generating options to screening them. We argue that AI's value depends on whether its options arrive before or after the team's screen. In our model, early options compete for a place in the portfolio; late options arrive after that competition and are kept unscreened. In a preregistered experiment, we randomly assigned 148 three-person teams to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. Moving the same 15 minutes of access from search to selection lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations, although teams used the model at similar rates. Platform logs locate the difference at the screen. Early access enlarged the pool of ideas fivefold, and teams pruned it. Late-access teams reached the screen with the same small pool as teams without AI and then searched again, devoting 29% of their selection-stage queries to generating new options, compared with 11% for teams with access throughout. Late access added breadth, not quality: these teams submitted 73% more proposals than did teams without AI. Language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.
papers.summary: Generative AI makes options cheap, shifting the bottleneck of creative work from generating ideas to screening them, and the authors argue that AI's value depends on whether its options arrive before or after a team's screening step. In a preregistered experiment, 148 three-person teams were randomly assigned to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. **Moving the same 15 minutes of access from the search stage to the selection stage lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations**, even though teams used the model at similar rates. Platform logs show early access enlarged the idea pool fivefold before pruning, while late-access teams arrived at the screen with the same small pool as no-AI teams, spent 29% of selection-stage queries generating new options, and submitted 73% more proposals without higher quality, and language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.

papers.title: Mixing Regularization for Average-Reward $Q$-Learning and $Q$-Planning
papers.abstract: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because its Bellman operator is known to contract in span only when the underlying Markov chain is mixing. Whereas existing work typically assumes a contraction property, e.g., through environment mixing, we consider the setting where we are given a reward-agnostic $m$-step mixing policy, and we control the contraction and exploration properties of the learned policy by regularizing toward the mixing policy. We provide finite-time analysis of $Q$-learning algorithms that can be instantiated with multiple choices of regularization, with guarantees measured with respect to the regularized fixed point. Our framework exposes novel regularizer-dependent objects that control contraction, exploration, and operator bias. In the one-step setting, our rates match the best known rates for $Q$-iteration and synchronous $Q$-learning, and for $m$-step mixing we derive new rates. We also study $Q$-planning variants, and show that planning acts as time-localized learning, where the planning horizon $H$ trades off the bias from the boundary value against the sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, and its advantage increases with bottleneck severity and, (ii) our theory predicts the convergence and bias rankings of regularizers from the $\alpha$-divergence family.
papers.summary: Average-reward reinforcement learning is difficult because its Bellman operator is only known to contract in span when the underlying Markov chain is mixing, and prior analyses typically assume such a contraction outright. The authors instead assume access to a reward-agnostic m-step mixing policy and regularize the learned policy toward it, which lets them control contraction and exploration, and they give a finite-time analysis of Q-learning algorithms under several choices of regularizer with guarantees relative to the regularized fixed point. The framework exposes regularizer-dependent quantities governing contraction, exploration, and operator bias, and **in the one-step setting the rates match the best known rates for Q-iteration and synchronous Q-learning**, while new rates follow for m-step mixing. Q-planning variants are shown to act as time-localized learning where the planning horizon trades boundary-value bias against sample complexity, and numerical studies confirm that a strong mixing policy helps more as bottlenecks worsen and that the theory predicts convergence and bias rankings across the alpha-divergence family of regularizers.

papers.title: Characterizing the Separability Gap in Prior-Data Fitted Networks
papers.abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are transformers pretrained on simulated datasets to approximate Bayesian posterior predictive distributions. Standard PFN theory assumes a separable task prior, under which the feature distribution and the mechanism generating labels from features are independent. We show that common PFN priors are non-separable, even in simple settings. Consequently, standard pretraining targets a predictive distribution based on a task posterior updated using both the labeled context and the query features. We characterize its difference from the predictive based on the context posterior alone and show that this difference vanishes under posterior concentration. Under misspecification (i.e., when the true joint distribution lies outside the prior's support), however, prior non-separability can favor better feature fit at the expense of conditional label fit. We illustrate the consequences for feature attribution, Bayesian optimization, and martingale checks of Bayesian behavior. The same dependence also enables PFNs to learn from additional unlabeled observations. We demonstrate this with SemiTabICL, a PFN explicitly pretrained to use these observations, which improves accuracy over a matched supervised baseline. Our findings highlight the need for explicit rules on unlabeled data use in PFN evaluation and establish the dependence between feature and label distributions as a consequential prior design choice.
papers.summary: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are transformers pretrained on simulated datasets to approximate Bayesian posterior predictive distributions, and standard PFN theory assumes a separable task prior in which the feature distribution and the label-generating mechanism are independent. The authors show that common PFN priors are non-separable even in simple settings, so standard pretraining actually targets a predictive distribution whose task posterior is updated using the query features as well as the labeled context. They characterize the gap from the context-only posterior, show it vanishes under posterior concentration, and show that under misspecification non-separability can trade conditional label fit for better feature fit, with consequences illustrated for feature attribution, Bayesian optimization, and martingale checks of Bayesian behavior. The same dependence lets PFNs learn from unlabeled observations, demonstrated by `SemiTabICL`, a PFN pretrained to use them that **improves accuracy over a matched supervised baseline**, which motivates explicit rules on unlabeled data use in PFN evaluation.

papers.title: Certify the Decision, Not Every Score: Exact Top-k Selection from Few Evaluations
papers.abstract: Choosing a few robust algorithms or schedules can require evaluating every candidate under many adverse scenarios, even though an agent only needs to identify the winners. A predictor may suggest those winners, but cannot rule out a surprise in an unevaluated scenario. We introduce Certified Adaptive Selection (CAS), which returns the exact top-$k$ set as soon as remaining uncertainty cannot change it. CAS keeps guaranteed lower and upper bounds on Expected Shortfall (ES), the average loss in the worst scenarios. Its stopping test compares the worst admissible selected candidate with the best admissible excluded one; for information-disjoint Cartesian intervals this one-cut test is necessary and sufficient. Prediction has a separate role: selecting the next outcome to evaluate, never authorizing the decision. For empirical ES with exact unit-cost queries, we compute in polynomial time the fewest evaluations that could have proved the realized decision in hindsight. Our prediction-guided agent CAS-PG is exact for every predictor, including adversarial ones. On two public algorithm-selection matrices, CAS-PG certifies the exact top three after 630 of 3150 and 981 of 2200 replayed queries, or $1.14$ and $1.18$ times that hindsight minimum. Without historical outcomes, its transcript-only variant requires $1.28$ and $1.37$ times the minimum, outperforming the tested non-predictive certified policies. Separately, a prediction-free CAS policy avoids $93.0\%$ of exact recourse solves in synthetic energy scheduling. One certificate thus supports several acquisition policies and separately proved risk/cost extensions: prediction changes the work, not the justified choice.
papers.summary: Choosing the top-k most robust algorithms or schedules normally means evaluating every candidate under every adverse scenario, even though only the identity of the winners matters. Certified Adaptive Selection (`CAS`) keeps guaranteed lower and upper bounds on each candidate's Expected Shortfall (ES), the average loss in the worst scenarios, and stops once the worst admissible selected candidate beats the best admissible excluded one. A predictor only chooses which evaluation to run next and never authorizes the decision, so the prediction-guided variant `CAS-PG` is exact for every predictor, including adversarial ones. On two public algorithm-selection matrices, `CAS-PG` certifies the exact top three after **630 of 3150 and 981 of 2200 replayed queries, about 1.14 to 1.18 times the hindsight minimum**, and a prediction-free policy avoids 93% of exact recourse solves in synthetic energy scheduling.

papers.title: Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and, like most transformers, they tie computational depth to the number of independently parameterized layers. We ask whether the ICL stage of such a model needs a distinct set of parameters for every layer, or only depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, which replaces the 12 untied ICL blocks of TabICLv2 with 4 tied blocks applied $k$ times and changes nothing else: the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior and training recipe are shared with an untied baseline trained for the same compute. At matched pretraining compute (18.2 EFLOP) and matched inference compute (12 block applications), Tab-Loop matches the baseline with 62\% fewer parameters (10.4M vs.\ 27.6M): held-out log loss is 0.4583 vs.\ 0.4588, mean accuracy on 200 TALENT datasets is 84.10\% vs.\ 83.92\%, and Elo on 38 TabArena datasets is 1409 vs.\ 1396. A 4-block untied control with Tab-Loop's parameter count, which sees 32\% more training tables for the same compute, trails both (83.46\%; Elo 1343). Because weights are shared, depth becomes a choice made at inference. Accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops extends the useful range, reaching the baseline's stage-2 scores at 4--5$\times$ its inference compute. At this scale, the ICL stage of a tabular foundation model needs depth more than it needs distinct parameters.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and like most transformers they tie computational depth to the number of separately parameterized layers. `Tab-Loop` replaces the 12 untied ICL blocks of `TabICLv2` with 4 weight-tied blocks applied repeatedly, keeping the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior, and training recipe identical to an untied baseline trained for the same compute. At matched pretraining and inference compute it matches that baseline with **62% fewer parameters (10.4M vs. 27.6M)**, with near-identical held-out log loss, mean accuracy on 200 `TALENT` datasets, and Elo on `TabArena`, while a 4-block untied control of the same size trails both. Because weights are shared, depth becomes an inference-time choice: accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops extends the useful range further.

papers.title: DiffGA: Steering Frozen Diffusion Models for Materials Design via Evolutionary Search
papers.abstract: Steering candidate generation toward user-defined objectives is central to inverse materials design, yet remains difficult when objectives are black-box, changing, or non-differentiable, as in many simulation- and experiment-derived properties. Generative models offer a solution but typically require retraining or fine-tuning for each new objective, demanding labeled data and substantial compute, or rely on differentiable guidance that is brittle to gradient noise and undefined for many practical targets. We present DiffGA, a retraining-free framework that injects evolutionary search into the sampling trajectory of a retrained diffusion model, evolving partially denoised states under an arbitrary black-box oracle. Because oracle evaluation often dominates campaign cost, we couple DiffGA with an on-the-fly Bayesian surrogate that reuses representations from state-of-the-art machine-learned force fields (MLFFs). A Gaussian process is fit during the campaign on the force fields's graph embeddings and, once it demonstrably ranks an unseen generation, replaces expensive property evaluations under an uncertainty-aware acquisition rule, reducing oracle cost with negligible loss of accuracy. Across three crystal-design tasks using a frozen MatterGen backbone, DiffGA outperforms diffusion-only, compute-matched, purely evolutionary, and fine-tuned baselines in oracle-assessed rates of stable, unique, and novel hits. Rather than proposing scientific compounds, we use density functional theory to quantify MLFF oracle fidelity, showing that it is a faithful proxy in key regimes but systematically biased in others, delineating when proxy-driven generative discovery can be trusted. On a representative sample, DiffGA's top hits survive first principles re-evaluation as physically realistic hits, while the surrogate-accelerated pipeline preserves this fidelity at a fraction of the cost.
papers.summary: Steering generative models toward materials-design objectives is hard when those objectives are black-box, non-differentiable, or change between campaigns, since retraining is costly and gradient guidance is brittle or undefined. `DiffGA` injects evolutionary search into the sampling trajectory of a frozen diffusion model, evolving partially denoised states under an arbitrary black-box oracle, and pairs it with a Gaussian-process surrogate on machine-learned force field (MLFF) embeddings that takes over expensive property evaluations once it demonstrably ranks unseen generations. Across three crystal-design tasks on a frozen `MatterGen` backbone, it **outperforms diffusion-only, compute-matched evolutionary, and fine-tuned baselines** in oracle-assessed rates of stable, unique, and novel hits. Density functional theory checks show the MLFF oracle is a faithful proxy in some regimes but systematically biased in others, and top hits survive first-principles re-evaluation while the surrogate-accelerated pipeline keeps that fidelity at a fraction of the cost.

papers.title: DisCo Algebra: Why Disintegration and Combination Are Not Inverses
papers.abstract: We present DisCo algebra---a compositional framework for joint probability built from a symmetric cooperad (disintegration) and a symmetric operad (combination) on the bare family $\mathcal{P}_n=\mathrm{Prob}([0,1]^n)$. No probability integral transform, no external summary functions, no enrichment of objects with conditional kernels. The disintegration side uses block-wise joint CDFs as intrinsic, measure-determined 1D summaries, yielding a lossy compression. The combination side reads the same summaries and reconstructs via regular conditional measures, yielding a lossless embedding. We prove that combination followed by disintegration is the identity on admissible inputs, but disintegration followed by combination is not---the information loss is exactly the conditional KL divergence between the true conditional distribution and the conditionally independent product. This asymmetry reveals a hard limit on how much cross-block dependence can be captured by scalar block summaries.
papers.summary: Joint probability distributions over several blocks of variables can be compressed into per-block summaries and then reassembled, but how much the round trip loses has not been pinned down. The `DisCo` algebra formalizes this with a symmetric cooperad for disintegration, which reduces a joint measure to block-wise joint cumulative distribution functions, and a symmetric operad for combination, which reconstructs via regular conditional measures, without probability integral transforms or external summary functions. Combination followed by disintegration is the identity on admissible inputs, but disintegration followed by combination is not: **the information lost is exactly the conditional KL divergence between the true conditional distribution and the conditionally independent product**. This asymmetry sets a hard limit on how much cross-block dependence scalar block summaries can capture.

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Preference Models? Stackelberg Games for Alignment
papers.abstract: Language models are frequently aligned to human preferences via imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization. We train policies to search for comparisons on which an evaluator may reverse the underlying preference, providing candidates for additional supervision. Since human preferences are unavailable during policy training, we use disagreement among an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for prediction error. We formulate this search as a zero-sum Stackelberg game between two opposing policies, a Leader which tries to minimize disagreement, and a Follower which maximizes it. For a general class of finite contextual Stackelberg games, we establish equilibrium existence and, under regularization, uniqueness and a closed-form characterization. We introduce Stackelberg Mirror Descent-Ascent (SMIDA), a two-timescale algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence in the tabular setting, and develop a neural policy-gradient analogue. Experiments with a synthetic oracle support disagreement as an informative proxy for prediction error. On held out data the trained policies outperform reference policies and increase the fraction of comparisons that exceed a disagreement threshold and reverse the oracle's preference.
papers.summary: Language models are aligned to human preferences through imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization, and human labels are unavailable to catch this while the policy trains. The approach trains two opposing policies to search for comparisons on which a preference model may be wrong, using disagreement within an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for error: a Leader minimizes disagreement while a Follower maximizes it in a zero-sum Stackelberg game. For a general class of finite contextual Stackelberg games they prove equilibrium existence and, under regularization, uniqueness in closed form, and introduce Stackelberg Mirror Descent-Ascent (`SMIDA`), a two-timescale algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence in the tabular setting and a neural policy-gradient analogue. With a synthetic oracle, disagreement proves an informative proxy for prediction error, and on held-out data the trained policies **surface more comparisons that exceed a disagreement threshold and reverse the oracle's preference** than reference policies.

papers.title: On the Complexity Gap Between POMDPs and Multi-Environment POMDPs
papers.abstract: Multi-environment POMDPs (ME-POMDPs) generalize POMDPs by encoding a finite set of possible environments, capturing model uncertainty.
