The finite-horizon robust reward maximization problem for a ME-POMDP asks for a policy that maximizes reward in the worst environment, and recent work has shown this problem to be $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete. We expand the complexity landscape of ME-POMDPs by identifying which subclasses retain this $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness. In particular, we take subclasses of POMDPs that are tractable in the single-environment case, and investigate the computational complexity of these classes when extended to the multi-environment setting. We first prove the $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of multi-environment blind MDPs and deterministic POMDPs using a certain closure-under-mixture condition. We then prove $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness for a range of subclasses that do not satisfy that closure condition, yielding new complexity results for multi-observation POMDPs. Finally, we show existential theory of the reals ($\exists \mathbb{R}$)-completeness for numerous ME-POMDP problems under time-dependent Markovian policies or finite-state controllers that are $\mathsf{NP}$-complete for standard POMDPs. These results reveal a subtle relationship between POMDP and ME-POMDP complexity that depends heavily on the subclasses involved.
papers.summary: Multi-environment partially observable Markov decision processes (ME-POMDPs) extend POMDPs with a finite set of candidate environments, and finding a policy that maximizes worst-case finite-horizon reward across them is known to be PSPACE-complete. The work maps which subclasses keep that hardness by taking POMDP subclasses that are tractable with a single environment and asking what happens with several. Multi-environment blind MDPs and deterministic POMDPs are NP-complete under a closure-under-mixture condition, while **a range of subclasses that violate that condition, including multi-observation POMDPs, remain PSPACE-complete**. Under time-dependent Markovian policies or finite-state controllers, several ME-POMDP problems that are NP-complete for ordinary POMDPs become complete for the existential theory of the reals, so the gap between the two models depends heavily on the subclass.

papers.title: Conformal Sequential Decision Making With Cost and Sublinear Policy Regret Guarantees
papers.abstract: Automated decision makers, such as AI agents that control robots or network devices, must often satisfy hard cost constraints while maintaining competitive performance. In such settings, a cost measure, such as a safety violation rate, energy consumption, or a distortion level, must stay within a given budget in every episode of operation. Furthermore, a cumulative reward metric, accounting for per-step performance, must stay close to the reward of a meaningful reference policy. We formulate this setup as an episodic sequential decision problem in which the state sequence is arbitrary, and the reward and cost may depend on past actions within the same episode. We propose the online conformal episodic agent (OCEA), a policy that selects one candidate action per episode using a regret-controlled algorithm, and switches to a zero-cost action when the remaining budget cannot absorb the maximum cost of one more round. We prove that OCEA satisfies per-episode cost constraints for every state sequence and for every realization of its internal randomness, while achieving a sublinear expected policy regret with respect to the best action sequence in hindsight from a comparator class satisfying the same per-episode cost constraints. We apply OCEA to risk-averse control and online compression with distortion guarantees.
papers.summary: Automated decision makers such as agents controlling robots or network devices must often keep a cost like safety violations, energy use, or distortion within a budget in every episode while staying competitive with a reference policy. The setting is an episodic sequential decision problem with arbitrary state sequences, in which reward and cost may depend on earlier actions within the same episode. The online conformal episodic agent (`OCEA`) picks one candidate action per episode with a regret-controlled algorithm and switches to a zero-cost action whenever the remaining budget cannot absorb the maximum cost of one more round. It **provably satisfies the per-episode cost constraint for every state sequence and every realization of its internal randomness** while achieving sublinear expected policy regret against the best cost-feasible action sequence in hindsight, and it is applied to risk-averse control and online compression with distortion guarantees.

papers.title: Algorithmic Fairness Over Time: Advances & Prospects
papers.abstract: In the presence of feedback loops, algorithmic decisions at one time step can influence observed data in subsequent steps, potentially introducing selection bias or shifts in data distribution. Research has demonstrated that ignoring these effects can lead to unfairness, which may worsen over time as the model remains deployed within society. This raises important questions of how to measure and ensure fairness of algorithmic decision-making models over time. In this short paper, we present a taxonomy that distinguishes between different types of static and temporal fairness notions in recent advancements. We then suggest prospects for future research by identifying common implicit temporal assumptions, open questions to enhance our temporal understanding of fairness, and other open challenges.
papers.summary: When deployed models influence the data they later observe through feedback loops, decisions at one step can introduce selection bias or distribution shift at the next, and ignoring these effects can produce unfairness that worsens the longer a model stays in use. The authors present a taxonomy that separates static from temporal fairness notions across recent work. They then **identify common implicit temporal assumptions** in existing methods and lay out open questions and challenges for measuring and ensuring fairness over the lifetime of a deployed system.

papers.title: PATTERN Can Be Solved from Memory: Generator-Aware Baselines for Synthetic Node Classification
papers.abstract: PATTERN, a synthetic node-classification benchmark still used to rank graph networks, plants a random subgraph in a random host graph and asks which nodes belong to it. Its generator draws 100 patterns once and plants the same ones in every split, so each test graph carries a pattern that also appears in 100 training graphs. A matcher that reads these patterns off the training labels and looks them up in each test graph reaches 99.2 class-weighted accuracy with no trained parameters, against 89.8 for the best published model. Inference under the generator without the patterns reaches 86.8. Two published models, CKGConv and GRIT, score lower on patterns they have not seen: on new graphs with fresh patterns both fall below this pattern-blind predictor, and withholding patterns from CKGConv's training lowers its accuracy on the test graphs that carry them. Training CKGConv with a new pattern in every graph raises its accuracy on fresh patterns by about 2 points, to the level of the pattern-blind predictor, at some cost on the reused patterns. The same kind of inference under the generator matches the best published result on CLUSTER and, without any training, scores above every published result we found on Minesweeper's released board. We recommend that synthetic benchmarks report scores on fresh templates beside reused ones, publish baselines built from their generators, and state how their metric is weighted and pooled.
papers.summary: `PATTERN`, a synthetic node-classification benchmark still used to rank graph networks, plants a random subgraph in a random host graph and asks which nodes belong to it. Its generator draws 100 patterns once and reuses them in every split, so a parameter-free matcher that reads the patterns off training labels and looks them up in test graphs reaches **99.2 class-weighted accuracy against 89.8 for the best published model**, while inference under the generator without the patterns reaches 86.8. Published models `CKGConv` and `GRIT` fall below this pattern-blind predictor on graphs with fresh patterns, and training `CKGConv` with a new pattern in every graph lifts fresh-pattern accuracy by about 2 points at some cost on reused ones. The same generator-aware inference matches the best published result on `CLUSTER` and, without training, beats every published result found on `Minesweeper`'s released board, so the authors recommend reporting scores on fresh templates, publishing generator-based baselines, and stating how metrics are weighted and pooled.

papers.title: UltraBERT: Beyond the Limit of BERT Pre-Training
papers.abstract: Recent bidirectional encoders have been modernized with innovations from causal large language models (LLMs). However, the pretraining recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions, leaving encoders underoptimized, with no single model performing competitively across both classification and retrieval tasks. In this work, we investigate how far encoder performance can be pushed by revisiting core design choices in training, revealing three key findings: (1) Encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, indicating that additional compute past this point does not help. (2) Across model sizes, lower masking ratios benefit classification while higher ones benefit retrieval, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models. (3) Distillation with pruning improves classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, a single encoder that assigns separate LM heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts the distillation objective to the low ratio. To our knowledge, UltraBERT is the first encoder to achieve state of the art on both classification and retrieval tasks, reaching 91.0 on GLUE and 47.7 on BEIR. Together, these results show how far encoder performance can be pushed and provide a principled basis for compute allocation, masking ratio design, and knowledge transfer in bidirectional models.
papers.summary: Bidirectional encoders have absorbed architectural ideas from causal large language models (LLMs), but their pretraining recipes still follow small-scale conventions, and no single encoder has been competitive on both classification and retrieval. Revisiting core training choices yields three findings: encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, lower masking ratios help classification while higher ones help retrieval across model sizes, and distillation with pruning helps classification at low masking ratios but hurts retrieval at high ones. `UltraBERT` acts on these by assigning separate language-modeling heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricting the distillation objective to the low ratio. It reaches **91.0 on `GLUE` and 47.7 on `BEIR`**, which the authors report as the first encoder to reach state of the art on both classification and retrieval.
papers.highlight_summary:
Modernized bidirectional encoders have borrowed architecture from decoder LLMs but still inherit a BERT-era pre-training recipe, leaving every existing model strong on either classification or retrieval but not both. By training to saturation at trillion-token scale, the authors show the two task families want opposite masking ratios, then reconcile them in one encoder by mixing 5% and 50% masked sequences in each batch with a separate LM head per ratio and distilling only on the low-ratio sequences.

- Training 150M and 1.3B encoders on up to **8.8T tokens** shows downstream scores on `GLUE`, `SQuAD 2.0`, and `BEIR` plateau around 1–2T tokens (BEIR is flat after 275B) even as training and validation loss keep falling, whereas the `SmolLM2` 1.7B decoder keeps improving after instruction tuning.
- At saturation, classification degrades monotonically as the masking ratio rises across 150M, 380M, and 1.3B models, contradicting prior small-budget findings that larger models prefer higher ratios, while retrieval peaks at **50% masking**, and raising effective rank artificially with a `KoLeo` regularizer at 6% masking helps BEIR less than 50% masking does while hurting GLUE.
- `UltraBERT` mixes 5% and 50% masked sequences at a 4:1 ratio within each batch and assigns each ratio its own LM head because the heads trained at the two ratios take visibly different geometries, giving a 150M model **89.4 GLUE / 45.1 BEIR** against 89.5 at pure 6% and 45.0 at pure 50%, while uniform ratio sampling collapses to the 30% result (88.0 / 44.2) and decaying schedules help neither task.
- Pruning the 1.3B teacher to 380M with logit distillation improves GLUE at 15% masking (90.2 to 90.8) but degrades BEIR at 50% (47.2 to 46.5), so the KL distillation loss is applied only to the 5% head and the 50% head trains with plain MLM.
- Trained on 2T tokens with native 32K context, `UltraBERT-380M` reaches **91.0 GLUE and 47.7 BEIR** and `UltraBERT-150M` reaches 89.5 and 45.2 with the largest gains on `RAR-b` code and math retrieval (7–8 points over the runner-up), though it trails `LFM2.5-Encoder` 350M on `MLDR` at medium size, is not best on `MultiCoNER v2` at base size, and the paper leaves unexplained why distillation hurts at high masking and whether effective rank causally drives retrieval.

papers.title: Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion-parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, for 24-class disease classification on the Symptom2Disease benchmark. Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. This improves upon the reported zero-shot baselines of 61.67% for a remote API and 65.00% for a local unadapted initialization, and outperforms the ClinicalBERT baseline (90.90%). By evaluating candidate logits in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, inference takes under 80 milliseconds per record on a single GPU, yielding a reported 31-fold speedup over generative LLM baselines. To examine symptom-level evidence, we introduce a Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual perturbation framework. Removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example reduces predicted-class confidence from 100.00% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo with 99.59% confidence, while removing secondary systemic symptoms produces less than 0.01% change in confidence. These findings suggest that decision-based architectures can combine the linguistic capabilities of large foundation models with low-latency inference and symptom-level interpretability for clinical triage.
papers.summary: Classifying diseases from patient-reported symptoms must trade the speed of small discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency of autoregressive large language models (LLMs), and decision foundation models sidestep this by scoring candidate classes directly without generating text. The authors adapt `Clef-Flash`, a 9-billion-parameter decision model on a `Qwen3.5` backbone, with 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) and differential learning rates for 24-class classification on `Symptom2Disease`. It reaches **95.42% accuracy and a macro F1 of 0.9551**, versus 61.67% and 65.00% for zero-shot baselines and 90.90% for `ClinicalBERT`, with single-forward-pass inference under 80 milliseconds per record that the authors report as a 31-fold speedup over generative baselines. A Leave-One-Symptom-Out (`LOSO`) counterfactual framework shows that removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example drops confidence from 100% to 0.12% and flips the prediction to impetigo, while removing secondary systemic symptoms changes confidence by under 0.01%.

papers.title: InCLAD: A Continual Learning Benchmark for Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks have advanced rapidly, yet they remain largely static and therefore underrepresent deployment settings in which inspection systems must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. In our setting, continual industrial anomaly detection is framed as a task-incremental problem: each component defines a task, while the learning objective remains semi-supervised. The goal extends beyond conventional anomaly detection, since models should preserve their performance on all components as they are sequentially exposed to new components. This framing is especially relevant because many existing industrial pipelines either assume fully supervised defect labels or study only isolated datasets, leaving open the question of how semi-supervised anomaly detectors behave across a sequence of heterogeneous components. We address this gap by organizing the benchmark as a sequence of related component-level tasks and by defining multiple scenarios, including random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy. In addition to single-dataset continual scenarios, we propose challenging scenarios spanning across multiple datasets. We further evaluate continual performance from two complementary perspectives: image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization. By recasting industrial anomaly detection as a continual benchmark rather than a static train/test problem, our work establishes a concrete path toward studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial environments.
papers.summary: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks are static, so they miss deployments where an inspection system must be extended from one component to the next over time. `InCLAD` frames continual industrial anomaly detection as a task-incremental problem in which each component is a task, supervision stays semi-supervised, and models must retain performance on earlier components as new ones arrive. The benchmark orders component-level tasks under random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy scenarios, adds harder scenarios spanning multiple source datasets, and **evaluates both image-level detection and pixel-level localization** throughout the sequence. The result is a concrete setting for studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization of semi-supervised anomaly detectors across sequences of heterogeneous components.

papers.title: What Drives AI Citations? Content, Retrieval and Model Knowledge in Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
papers.abstract: Generative search engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity now decide which Web pages users see as sources, and a growing industry of generative engine optimization advises publishers on how to earn these citations. We study what shapes citation in two 90-day collections of answers to commercial questions in contrasting markets: 158,099 answers with 468,037 citations. Comparing pages of the same website, content matters in one way: pages whose title and paragraphs match the questions people ask are cited more, whereas FAQ blocks, structured data, summary boxes and page speed appear effective only across websites. Page properties nevertheless explain little of the variation between pages of a website. Replaying the questions through the engines' APIs shows why. Every page ChatGPT cites is one its own search retrieved, and which pages that search retrieves, for sub-queries the model rewrites on every answer and that rarely coincide with Google's or Bing's results, explains far more of the variation than page properties (32% against 2.8%). Content acts mainly through this step, by matching the engine's queries in meaning. The model's own knowledge shapes it too: ChatGPT writes brands it knows into its searches, prefers websites it knows, and names brands without any supporting page, and controlled experiments show that brand names reorder its rankings of products with identical facts. Pages are thus cited when searched; brands are also named when remembered. The findings replicate in a market of small B2B vendors. We release data and code.
papers.summary: Generative search engines such as `ChatGPT`, `Gemini`, and `Perplexity` now decide which web pages users see as sources, and a generative engine optimization (GEO) industry advises publishers on earning those citations. Across two 90-day collections of answers to commercial questions, totaling 158,099 answers and 468,037 citations, pages whose titles and paragraphs match the questions people ask are cited more than sibling pages on the same site, while FAQ blocks, structured data, summary boxes, and page speed only appear effective across sites. Replaying the questions through the engines' APIs shows why page properties explain so little: every page `ChatGPT` cites was retrieved by its own search, and **which pages that search retrieves explains 32% of citation variation against 2.8% for page properties**, with the model's rewritten sub-queries rarely matching Google or Bing results. The model's knowledge also matters, since `ChatGPT` writes brands it knows into its searches, prefers websites it knows, names brands without any supporting page, and in controlled experiments reorders products with identical facts by brand name, a pattern that replicates among small B2B vendors.

papers.title: Sparsity Saves Compute, Not Samples: Oracle Inequalities for Dense and Sparse Mixture of Experts
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized experts through an input-dependent routing mechanism, and their sparse variants underpin many modern large-scale systems. Yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing remains only partially understood. We study the estimation error of least-squares MoE estimators when both the experts and the gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters. We represent each MoE as a gate--expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space, whose norm $\|\cdot\|_\Delta$ separates the contributions of routing and expert discrepancies. Using its empirical representation, we derive an oracle inequality with a fast rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big((Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}+d_{\mathrm{pr},g})/n\big)$ for dense MoEs with $K$ experts. For sparse Top-$k$ and Top-$p$ routing, the selection map is discontinuous in the gating parameters. We handle this by partitioning the gating class according to the selection patterns it induces on the sample. The resulting bounds match the dense rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector. We show that such a routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped: Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice. For linear softmax gating, the routing cost is of the same order as the gating term. Finally, for linear experts, we establish a matching minimax lower bound of order $Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}/n$, showing that the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each input to specialized experts, and their sparse variants underpin many large systems, yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing is only partly understood. The analysis studies least-squares MoE estimators whose experts and gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters, representing each model as a gate-expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space whose norm separates routing and expert discrepancies. Dense MoEs with K experts obtain an oracle inequality at a fast rate scaling as K expert dimensions plus one gating dimension over n samples, and **sparse Top-k and Top-p routing match that rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector**. The routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped, since Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice, and for linear experts a matching minimax lower bound shows the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Foundations of Online Temperature Sampling
papers.abstract: Repetitive, degenerate generation is a persistent failure of LLM decoding, and the standard remedies (temperature, nucleus, and top-$k$ sampling) are static heuristics. By Kac's lemma and the AEP, a stationary source takes time exponential in its entropy to repeat a block. We therefore maximize the entropy of the sampling distributions under one cross-entropy budget that keeps the output plausible under the model. Offline, the solution is temperature sampling, with the inverse temperature as the budget's Lagrange multiplier. \emph{Our contribution is the online problem}: the conditionals $p_1, p_2, \dots$ are revealed one at a time, and the sampling distribution $q_t$ must be chosen causally from $p_1, \dots, p_t$ while the budget couples the entire horizon. The optimal temperature is thus a global shadow price that must be estimated from a prefix. We propose Entropic Online Sampling (EOS), which re-solves for the temperature on each prefix. We prove it loses $O(R\log n)$ entropy against the offline optimum while overshooting the budget by $O(R\log n)$, with $R$ an instance-dependent drift parameter. A budget-tightened variant is exactly feasible at the same rate. Conversely, every exactly feasible online algorithm must lose $\Omega(R)$, so EOS is optimal up to a $\log n$ factor. When the conditionals are drawn from a finite mixture, $R=\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. Experiments confirm that EOS tracks the offline temperature and beats fixed-temperature sampling in entropy.
papers.summary: Repetitive, degenerate text is a persistent failure of large language model (LLM) decoding, and standard fixes such as temperature, nucleus, and top-k sampling are static heuristics. Because a stationary source takes time exponential in its entropy to repeat a block, the approach maximizes sampling entropy under one cross-entropy budget that keeps outputs plausible, which offline recovers temperature sampling with the inverse temperature as the budget's Lagrange multiplier. Online, the conditionals arrive one at a time while the budget couples the whole horizon, so the optimal temperature is a global shadow price that Entropic Online Sampling (`EOS`) re-estimates on every prefix. `EOS` provably **loses only O(R log n) entropy against the offline optimum while overshooting the budget by the same order**, with R an instance-dependent drift parameter, any exactly feasible online algorithm must lose order R, and experiments confirm it tracks the offline temperature and beats fixed-temperature sampling in entropy.

papers.title: PAT: A Personality-Driven Augmentation and Transfer Learning Framework for Depression Detection on Social Media
papers.abstract: Depression is a prevalent mental disorder that affects millions worldwide, with early detection crucial for effective intervention. While exist?ing methods have achieved promising results in automated depression detection, they face two key limitations: (1) noise in post screening: symptom-based semantic screening is easily misled by superficial lexical patterns, thereby introducing false-positive posts; (2) weak op?timization of the post encoder: relying solely on coarse user-level supervision signals pre?vents models from capturing depressive cues within individual posts. To address these limita?tions, we propose PAT, a Personality-driven Augmentation and Transfer learning frame?work. In the first phase, PAT optimizes a post?level encoder via a fine-grained contrastive learning objective, utilizing LLM-based data augmentation driven by classic personality the?ories to alleviate data scarcity. In the second phase, the trained post-level scorer is deployed for high-quality post filtering, while its en?coder parameters are seamlessly transferred for user-level tasks. Extensive experiments demon?strate that PAT significantly outperforms exist?ing methods. Furthermore, PAT delivers multi?granular interpretability by tracing post-level mental-state trajectories and highlighting key symptoms, thereby offering reliable diagnostic evidence for clinical practice.
papers.summary: Automated depression detection from social media suffers from noisy post screening, where symptom-based semantic filters are fooled by surface lexical patterns, and from weak training of the post encoder, which sees only coarse user-level labels. `PAT` first trains a post-level encoder with a fine-grained contrastive objective, using LLM-generated augmentations driven by classic personality theories to counter data scarcity. The trained post scorer then filters posts for quality and its encoder weights transfer directly to user-level classification. The authors report that `PAT` **significantly outperforms existing depression detection methods** and offers multi-granular interpretability by tracing post-level mental-state trajectories and highlighting key symptoms.

papers.title: Belief Embedding Tree Search
papers.abstract: Beliefs in a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) are posterior distributions over the hidden state given the agent's history of actions and observations. They summarize everything the history says about the state, so planning in a POMDP is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs. Belief MDPs have continuous state spaces even for finite POMDPs, and exact planning in them is intractable in general. Planners must therefore approximate beliefs and estimate values. Monte Carlo planners do both inside a search tree, with an approximate belief at every node and a value estimate at every leaf. Approximations usually consist of sets of sampled states, with leaf values coming from rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks. Policies and values computed from these approximations are limited by their quality, and prior methods with learned networks rely on hand-chosen summaries of the sampled states. A belief representation should be computable from the parent node's representation through the POMDP's dynamics, let the search sample from it, and be learned so that it provides the information that policies and value functions need. We present Belief Embedding Tree Search (BETS), a Monte Carlo planner that meets these requirements by representing each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) while updating it through the POMDP dynamics. BETS trains its belief model alongside its policy and value networks through experience, with the realized hidden state of the POMDP as the belief model's training target. We evaluate BETS on six configurations of RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan against BetaZero and three planners without learned components. BETS is competitive or leading on all six, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one. Where beliefs are highest-dimensional, it outperforms them by a large margin, even without search.
papers.summary: Planning in a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) amounts to planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs, whose state space is continuous even for finite POMDPs. Monte Carlo planners therefore approximate each node's belief with sampled states and estimate leaf values with rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or networks fed hand-chosen summaries, which caps the quality of the resulting policies. Belief Embedding Tree Search (`BETS`) instead represents each node's belief with a learned generative distribution embedding (GDE) that is updated from the parent through the POMDP dynamics, can be sampled during search, and is trained alongside the policy and value networks with the realized hidden state as its target. On six configurations of `RockSample`, `LightDark`, and `PocMan`, `BETS` is **competitive or leading against `BetaZero` and three planners without learned components, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one**, and where beliefs are highest-dimensional it wins by a large margin even without search.

papers.title: Trace Evolution Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Improve from Their Own Environment Traces
papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint Gain: held-out success after an update minus success before. That difference can credit a frozen rescore as evolution. We introduce Trace Evolution Bench (TEB), a protocol that separates that rescore from a context or weight update, together with three frozen 80/20/40 packs. An update is accepted only when validation does not fall, held-out identifiers never enter the update, and a text update is not ranked with a weight update. The primary scoreboard is coding, graded by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace. On that pack (40 held-out tasks, one family), DeepSeek v4 Pro under no_evolve never changes its policy yet moves 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds. Of nine text-update cells inspired by GEPA, ACE, and ExpeL, seven have positive excess above that seed's own band, and one gepa_llm seed moves down by the width of its band (-12.5, regression 0.48). GLM and MiniMax do not reproduce that seven-of-nine pattern. No method stays above its own band on every seed of all three models: GLM has two paired cells above their own bands, and MiniMax expel_llm seed 44 is a third (regression 0.30). The methods were fixed on a validation screen before held-out was read. Office, graded by rule-bounded delivery, and manufacturing table QA are separate packs: office DeepSeek does not exceed its own bands (widest 17.5 points), and manufacturing has no paired positive excess beyond its seed band.
papers.summary: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint gain, held-out success after an update minus success before, but that difference can credit the random rescoring of a frozen policy as evolution. Trace Evolution Bench (`TEB`) separates that rescore from genuine context or weight updates using three frozen 80/20/40 task packs, accepting an update only when validation does not fall, keeping held-out identifiers out of the update, and never ranking text updates against weight updates. The primary pack is coding graded by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace, where `DeepSeek v4 Pro` with no evolution at all **moves by 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds**, setting the noise band any method must clear. Seven of nine text-update cells inspired by `GEPA`, `ACE`, and `ExpeL` exceed that band for `DeepSeek`, but `GLM` and `MiniMax` do not reproduce the pattern, no method clears its band on every seed of all three models, and the office and manufacturing packs show no paired excess beyond their bands.

papers.title: Select or Rewrite: Oracle-Guided Fine-Tuning for Generative ASR Post-Editing from N-Best Hypotheses
papers.abstract: Large language models can post-edit ASR by using linguistic context to compare N-best hypotheses and rewrite the transcript when needed, often improving WER without retraining the recognizer. However, prompt-only correction is brittle: it may over-edit when top-1 is correct and hallucinate when the reference is absent, and often needs very large models. We propose oracle-guided fine-tuning that turns N-best lists into supervision via three curated pools: corrections (reference in the list but not top-1) to teach selection, regularizers (top-1 correct) to discourage unnecessary rewrites, and hard negatives (reference absent) to suppress hallucination. Fine-tuning on this data provides more effective supervision than random subset fine-tuning for learning a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy, with the clearest gains from around 3B parameters on the proprietary dataset but less conclusive results on CommonVoice, a divergence suggesting that public read-speech text may overlap with LLM pretraining and mask genuine post-editing gains.
papers.summary: Large language models can post-edit automatic speech recognition (ASR) output by comparing N-best hypotheses in linguistic context and rewriting when needed, but prompt-only correction over-edits when the top hypothesis is already right, hallucinates when the reference is absent, and often needs very large models. Oracle-guided fine-tuning turns N-best lists into supervision through three curated pools: corrections where the reference is in the list but not top-1 to teach selection, regularizers where top-1 is correct to discourage needless rewrites, and hard negatives with no reference present to suppress hallucination. This curated data yields a **more effective select-or-rewrite policy than random-subset fine-tuning, with the clearest gains from about 3B parameters** on a proprietary dataset. Results on `CommonVoice` are less conclusive, which the authors attribute to possible overlap between public read-speech text and LLM pretraining data masking genuine post-editing gains.

papers.title: The Optimal Decoder is Tilted Temperature
papers.abstract: Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{\eta V}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. The optimum still needs the unknown verifier potential, which we estimate using two design approaches. In the online setting, our J-EOS algorithm jointly tracks the two constraint multipliers and learns the verifier potential from binary pass/ fail feedback alone. In the offline setting, we show that when the model is calibrated, its log-probability tracks correctness up to an affine map. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.
papers.summary: Larger sample budgets favor higher sampling temperatures in large language models (LLMs), but what temperature tuning optimizes and why has been unclear. Posing decoding as pass@k maximization under an entropy floor against diversity collapse and a cross-entropy ceiling against implausibility yields a closed-form rule, the tilted temperature, which exponentially tilts the model distribution by a verifier potential measuring how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass and then applies a temperature. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies are special cases, and **under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with k, the optimal temperature provably increases with the sample count**. The verifier potential is estimated online by `J-EOS` from binary pass/fail feedback or offline by Calibrated Temperature Decoding (`CTD`), which exploits model calibration to fit one scalar with no extra inference cost, and a resulting code-generation decoder beats standard and adaptive baselines on `HumanEval` and `MBPP`.

papers.title: Deep Learning-based Semantic Segmentation of Dental Radiographs: Comparative Evaluation of PSPNet, DeepLabv3, UNet, and UNet++
papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient analysis of dental radiographs has become increasingly important for disease diagnosis and clinical decision making. In particular, dental radiographs segmentation plays a critical role as it is challenging due to several reasons, such as low contrast, noise in the images, variations in the image quality, etc. Previous studies have primarily addressed these challenges using convolutional neural networks (CNN)-based models. However, direct comparison of these segmentation models is still challenging due to the variations among the experimental settings. Therefore, we mainly compared four segmentation models, including Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet), DeepLabV3, UNet, and UNet++, through a fair, controlled experimentation setting under varying conditions such as image sizes and batch sizes. For this, we used 1269 dental radiography images, and prior to training, we implemented a series of preprocessing techniques. To assess the models, we used several metrics, including Dice coefficient (DICE), Intersection over Union (IoU), accuracy, precision, training and validation losses. According to our results, UNet++ demonstrated the highest IoU score of 0.6719, and a DICE value of 0.7869, showing superior results in terms of segmentation, specifically when configured with an image size of 300x300 and a batch size of 16. In addition, we also explored the effect of image resolutions and batch sizes on model performance and accuracy under different architectures. Therefore, this study provides insights into the strengths of different segmentation models and the potential of deep learning-based semantic segmentation methods for improving automated dental radiograph analysis.
papers.summary: Segmenting dental radiographs is difficult because of low contrast, noise, and variable image quality, and prior convolutional neural network (CNN) results are hard to compare across inconsistent experimental setups. The authors benchmark Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (`PSPNet`), `DeepLabV3`, `UNet`, and `UNet++` under one controlled protocol on 1269 preprocessed dental radiographs, sweeping image resolution and batch size and reporting Dice coefficient, Intersection over Union (IoU), accuracy, and precision. **`UNet++` scored highest with an IoU of 0.6719 and a Dice of 0.7869** at 300x300 resolution and batch size 16, and the study documents how resolution and batch size shift results across the four architectures.

papers.title: Exposing AI Inference as a Telco Network API over the 5G User Plane
papers.abstract: Supporting edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference as a network service is challenging because current mobile systems can transport tensors but do not expose or understand the inference context that gives those tensors operational meaning. Prior studies have addressed this gap through dynamic partitioning, collaborative inference, and split pipelines; however, these solutions remain application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. This work proposes Inference on Demand (IoD), an inference-on-demand abstraction that exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like Application Program Interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band across the 5G user plane path. We evaluate the IoD on a programmable user plane function (UPF)-based testbed using a partitionable visual AI workload, showing that adaptive split selection can operate as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static configurations. Including our findings, split inference becomes more than offloading when the service intent, runtime partitioning, and tensor transport are made visible to the mobile data plane. This opens a path toward network-native AI services, in which programmable telco infrastructure coordinates computation, context, and connectivity for user-facing applications.
papers.summary: Mobile networks can carry tensors between devices and edge servers but have no notion of the inference context that gives those tensors meaning, so prior split-inference schemes stay application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. The authors propose Inference on Demand (`IoD`), which exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like Application Program Interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band across the 5G user plane. On a testbed built around a programmable user plane function (UPF) running a partitionable visual AI workload, **adaptive split selection operates as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static split configurations**, which the authors present as a path toward network-native AI services coordinated by programmable telco infrastructure.

papers.title: Toward a Multimodal Foundation Model for Plasma State Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Plasma experiments observe coupled physical states through sparse, heterogeneous, and incomplete diagnostics. We present a proof of concept toward a multimodal foundation model for plasma state reconstruction during magnetic reconnection, motivated by the Facility for Laboratory Reconnection Experiments (FLARE). Using 250 synthetic VPIC simulations at fixed reference electron beta $\beta_{e0}=0.2$, with 225 training runs and 25 disjoint validation runs, we train a 5.5M-parameter residual 3D U-Net to reconstruct three magnetic-field components and electron density from incomplete observations. The model combines spatial-only pooling, which preserves all 24 temporal frames, with global spatiotemporal self-attention and rotary positional encoding. Independently masking magnetic and density modalities across random, grid, block, and temporal patterns enables sparse sensing, cross-modal completion, density super-resolution, and temporal completion with a single set of weights and no task-specific retraining. With density fully hidden, just 0.1% magnetic spatial visibility reduces median density NRMSE from approximately 0.9 to 0.1. Conversely, observed density improves current-density reconstruction when magnetic data are absent or extremely sparse. With no magnetic observations, roughly 1% density visibility approaches the density reconstruction accuracy achieved with fully observed magnetic fields, although current structure remains more dependent on direct magnetic measurements. Full magnetic conditioning also stabilizes completion of missing future density frames. These results demonstrate bidirectional cross-modal predictive coupling within this simulation regime. Generalization across plasma regimes or to experimental measurements remains untested.
papers.summary: Laboratory plasma experiments observe coupled physical fields only through sparse, heterogeneous, and incomplete diagnostics. Motivated by the Facility for Laboratory Reconnection Experiments (FLARE), the authors train a 5.5M-parameter residual 3D U-Net with global spatiotemporal self-attention and rotary positional encoding on 250 synthetic `VPIC` magnetic reconnection simulations, masking magnetic-field and electron-density inputs independently under random, grid, block, and temporal patterns so that one set of weights handles sparse sensing, cross-modal completion, density super-resolution, and temporal completion. **With density fully hidden, only 0.1% magnetic spatial visibility cuts median density normalized root-mean-square error from roughly 0.9 to 0.1**, and observed density likewise improves current-density reconstruction when magnetic data are absent or extremely sparse. Generalization across plasma regimes or to real experimental measurements remains untested.

papers.title: On the Theoretical Limits of Learning Unconstrained Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) accelerate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations by learning the energies and forces that govern atomic motion. Recent work has shown that relaxing physical inductive biases can improve computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, raising the question of whether energy-and-force matching alone is sufficient to ensure accurate sampling. We show that, for unconstrained hypothesis classes, the relationship between prediction error and sampling accuracy is exponentially ill-conditioned in dimension. In particular, prediction errors that decay exponentially with dimension can coexist with nearly maximal total variation distance between the learned and target distributions. We identify two failure mechanisms. The first is kinetic trapping, where relaxation to an accurate learned equilibrium requires exponentially long times, even when simulations are initialized from training configurations at which energies and forces are matched exactly. The second is equilibrium mismatch, where the learned stationary distribution itself remains far from the target. Under explicit assumptions, we show that equilibrium mismatch can persist even in local, symmetry-preserving models, where small per-atom errors coexist with a distributional discrepancy that approaches its maximum as system size increases. Finally, we establish global energy-control conditions that guarantee equilibrium accuracy and identify additional conditions required for rapid relaxation.
papers.summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) speed up molecular dynamics (MD) by predicting energies and forces, and recent evidence that dropping physical inductive biases improves efficiency and accuracy raises the question of whether energy-and-force matching alone guarantees accurate sampling. The authors prove that for unconstrained hypothesis classes the relationship between prediction error and sampling accuracy is exponentially ill-conditioned in dimension: **prediction errors that decay exponentially with dimension can coexist with nearly maximal total variation distance between learned and target distributions**. Two failure mechanisms are identified, kinetic trapping, where relaxation to the learned equilibrium takes exponentially long even from exactly matched training configurations, and equilibrium mismatch, where the learned stationary distribution stays far from the target and can persist even in local, symmetry-preserving models as system size grows. The paper closes with global energy-control conditions that guarantee equilibrium accuracy and additional conditions needed for rapid relaxation.

papers.title: Knowledge transfer between simple discrete worlds
papers.abstract: Adapting to a new world and reasoning correctly about which outcomes are possible under rules one has not met before is a basic capacity underlying general intelligence. We study it in small discrete worlds: sets of grid configurations consistent with a shared set of rules, concretely Sudoku-like puzzles built from a common base and a handful of extra rules. We train a single depth-recurrent model on many combinations of rules and test it at four levels of novelty: a new puzzle, a new combination of known rules, a pairing of rules never seen together, and a rule instance not seen at all during training. The model receives the active rules either as a symbolic description or as two solved examples, and a model that gets no rule information is used as a baseline. At recombining rules it was trained on, the description matches or exceeds examples ($99\%$ against $95\%$ on new combinations). On rule instances whose components never co-occurred in training, the description falls below the no-information baseline while examples stay above it. The framework allows us to test many such generalization regimes in more systematic way than benchmarks such as ARC-AGI and provides new ground for evaluating depth-recurrent reasoning models, which are typically tested on saturated Sudoku benchmarks.
papers.summary: Adapting to unfamiliar rules and reasoning correctly about which outcomes they permit is a basic ingredient of general intelligence, and the authors study it in small discrete worlds: Sudoku-like puzzles sharing a common base plus a handful of extra rules. A single depth-recurrent model is trained on many rule combinations and tested at four levels of novelty (a new puzzle, a new combination of known rules, rules never paired in training, and a rule instance never seen at all), receiving the active rules either as a symbolic description or as two solved examples, with a model given no rule information as the baseline. Descriptions match or beat examples when recombining trained rules (99% versus 95% on new combinations), but **on rule instances whose components never co-occurred in training, descriptions fall below the no-information baseline while examples stay above it**. The framework is offered as a more systematic testbed for generalization regimes than `ARC-AGI` and as new ground for depth-recurrent reasoning models that are usually evaluated on saturated Sudoku benchmarks.

papers.title: GAMW: Generation-Aware Mel-Domain Watermarking for TTS Traceability
papers.abstract: As text-to-speech (TTS) systems continue to advance, provenance tracking and security verification of synthesized speech have become increasingly important. Audio watermarking provides active provenance by embedding imperceptible, machine-recoverable information into speech. However, existing post-hoc methods typically modify the waveform after synthesis, leaving the watermark vulnerable to compound perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose GAMW, a watermark injection framework integrated into the TTS generation process. Before waveform synthesis, GAMW embeds a content-adaptive multi-bit watermark residual into the generated representation, and its decoding objective combines focal modulation with dynamic per-bit weighting. We train and evaluate GAMW separately on two TTS backbones. With a 16-bit payload, GAMW improves decoding accuracy over the strongest baseline by 9.2 and 23.5 percentage points under individual and compound perturbations, respectively, while maintaining competitive speech quality. Reliable clean-speech decoding is also retained at higher payloads. Code is available at https://github.com/ZConJugaTe/GAMW.
papers.summary: Post-hoc audio watermarks that alter the waveform after text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis break down under compound perturbations, weakening provenance tracking for synthesized speech. `GAMW` moves watermark injection inside the TTS generation process, embedding a content-adaptive multi-bit watermark residual into the generated representation before waveform synthesis, with a decoding objective that combines focal modulation and dynamic per-bit weighting. Trained and evaluated separately on two TTS backbones with a 16-bit payload, **decoding accuracy improves over the strongest baseline by 9.2 percentage points under individual perturbations and 23.5 points under compound perturbations** while speech quality stays competitive, and clean-speech decoding remains reliable at higher payloads. Code is released.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Visual Agent via Margin Reward
papers.abstract: Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation have posed a promising direction for multimodal tasks. However, learning effective tool invocation usually relies on curated question-answer pairs or expert demonstrations at scale, which are expensive to acquire. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple-yet-effective self-evolution approach that enables learning tool invocation from unlabeled images. Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning. To encourage effective tool invocation, a good training question should be difficult enough to warrant tool use, yet remain within the solver's capabilities. To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver's performance difference with and without access to tools. With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation. Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1\% --- demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision.
papers.summary: Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation usually learn tool use from large curated question-answer sets or expert demonstrations, which are expensive to collect. `Marvo` learns from unlabeled images instead, using a challenger agent that generates question-answer pairs from the images and a solver agent trained by reinforcement learning to answer them through tool calls. The challenger is rewarded with a margin reward, defined as the solver's performance gap with and without tool access, so it produces questions hard enough to warrant tools yet still within the solver's reach, forming an adaptive curriculum. **Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, average accuracy rises by up to 7.1%** without any human supervision.

papers.title: Have You Been Convinced? A Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning Approach to Detecting Persuasiveness in ChangeMyView Discussions
papers.abstract:
Argument structures represent how individual arguments interact within a discourse. However, leveraging these structures to infer meaningful knowledge remains challenging, as it requires a formal representation of how argumentative influence propagates across the structure. We propose Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning System (NARS) for performing persuasiveness detection directly from online discussions. The neural component employs retrieval-augmented iterative LLM reasoning to extract bipolar argument structures, while the symbolic component applies gradual argumentation semantics to propagate argumentative influence over the structure.
  Using the Webis-CMV-20 corpus, we construct CMV2BAS, a dataset of long, multi-threaded ChangeMyView discussions annotated with LLM-derived bipolar argument structures and labeled with delta events (view change vs.\ no change). We investigate whether gradual argumentation semantics can effectively detect persuasiveness, whether augmenting them with argument quality and graph-based centrality improves performance, and whether symbolic reasoning remains necessary in the presence of modern LLMs. NARS achieves F1=0.57 and AUC=0.56 under its best configuration, outperforming zero-shot Qwen3.6:27B and GPT-oss:20B. We identify support-dominant discussions and long argumentative chains as key failure modes limiting attack influence propagation. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of operationalizing formal gradual argumentation semantics over noisy real-world discourse for scalable macro-level persuasion analysis, while highlighting key challenges and directions for future research in neuro-symbolic argumentation reasoning. We release both CMV2BAS dataset and the NARS framework for public use.
papers.summary: Argument structures describe how the individual arguments in a discussion support or attack one another, but using them to predict outcomes requires a formal account of how argumentative influence propagates through the structure. The Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning System (`NARS`) pairs a neural component, retrieval-augmented iterative LLM reasoning that extracts bipolar argument structures, with a symbolic component that applies gradual argumentation semantics to propagate influence over the graph. It is evaluated on `CMV2BAS`, a new dataset of long multi-threaded ChangeMyView discussions built from the `Webis-CMV-20` corpus, annotated with LLM-derived argument structures and labeled by whether a delta (view change) occurred. **`NARS` reaches an F1 of 0.57 and AUC of 0.56 in its best configuration, outperforming zero-shot `Qwen3.6:27B` and `GPT-oss:20B`**, with support-dominant discussions and long argumentative chains identified as the main failure modes, and both the dataset and framework are released.

papers.title: VLCQ: Post-training quantization for deep neural networks using variable length coding
papers.abstract: Quantization plays a crucial role in efficiently deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. Post-training quantization does not require access to the original dataset or retraining the full model. Current methods that achieve high performance close to baseline results typically require INT8 fixed-point integers. However, achieving higher model compression with lower bit-widths often leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we propose VLCQ, a post-training quantization method that relaxes the fixed-point encoding constraint, enabling more flexible exploration of quantization techniques through variable-length encoding. This approach achieves competitive or improved performance while reducing bit-widths, without requiring access to training data or model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on image classification, segmentation, and object detection demonstrate that VLCQ improves model compression and accuracy compared with state-of-the-art post-training quantization approaches. For per-channel quantization, VLCQ surpasses FP32 accuracy and Piece-Wise Linear Quantization (PWLQ) on most evaluated models, achieving up to 6x compression compared with FP32 and up to 1.7x compared with PWLQ. When prioritizing compression with limited accuracy loss, VLCQ achieves up to 12.25x compression compared with FP32 with less than 4% performance degradation. For per-tensor quantization, VLCQ is competitive with Data-Free Quantization (DFQ), while providing greater flexibility to achieve lower bit rates across different tasks and models.
papers.summary: Post-training quantization lets deep networks run on resource-constrained devices without retraining or access to the original dataset, but methods that stay close to baseline accuracy generally need INT8 fixed-point integers, and pushing below that degrades performance sharply. `VLCQ` relaxes the fixed-point constraint by encoding quantized values with variable-length codes, widening the design space while still needing no training data or fine-tuning. On image classification, segmentation, and object detection, per-channel `VLCQ` exceeds FP32 accuracy and Piece-Wise Linear Quantization (`PWLQ`) on most models with up to 6x compression over FP32 and 1.7x over `PWLQ`, and **when compression is prioritized it reaches up to 12.25x compression over FP32 with under 4% performance degradation**. Per-tensor results are competitive with Data-Free Quantization (`DFQ`) while offering more flexibility to hit lower bit rates.

papers.title: TurnCost: Turns, Not Observations: Cache-Aware Loop Engineering for Coding Agents
papers.abstract:
AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching.
  We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.
papers.summary: Coding agents work in loops of editing code, running tools, inspecting output, and deciding what to do next, and most efficiency work either compresses tool observations or routes some turns to cheaper models without establishing how much those levers are worth. Analyzing 600 public coding-agent trajectories across two scaffolds and two language models, the authors find that median observations hold only 118 to 286 tokens, the large build logs often cited to motivate compression sit near the 99th percentile, and 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overstates loop cost by roughly 7x under near-ideal caching. A closed-form, empirically validated break-even condition shows model delegation raises cost in half the evaluated settings, and **turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost versus 4% for mean observation size**, pointing to unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though the paper does not show turns can be removed without hurting task success. `TurnCost`, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies, is released.

papers.title: Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families
papers.abstract: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. We present SwaT (Swarm Telepathy), the first cross-family KV-cache transfer method that allows prefill-free communication in multi-family multi-agent systems. In an agent-to-agent communication setting, combining SwaT with recent advances in KV-cache compaction beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of $40\%$ higher accuracy and a mean of $4\times$ faster wall-clock time. Experiments show SwaT achieves high performance on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs and 6 families. Additionally, given a sender Vision-Language Model (VLM), SwaT is able to transfer the vision capabilities to a text-only receiver LLM exceeding text-to-text communication despite SwaT being trained on text-only data. SwaT keeps both sender and receiver models frozen without fine-tuning and only requires $<50M$ tokens and $<1$ GPU-day to train.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems communicate through text, which confines every exchange to discrete tokens, wastes compute on re-prefilling, and limits bandwidth, while prior KV-cache transfer methods either require sender and receiver from the same model family or cannot carry context without the receiver prefilling text. Swarm Telepathy (`SwaT`) is a cross-family KV-cache transfer method that enables prefill-free communication between frozen models from different families, requiring under 50M training tokens and under one GPU-day with no fine-tuning of either model. Combined with recent KV-cache compaction, **agent-to-agent communication through `SwaT` beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of 40% higher accuracy and 4x faster wall-clock time**, with results reported on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs from 6 families. A vision-language sender can also pass visual capability to a text-only receiver, exceeding text-to-text communication despite training on text only.

papers.title: Anchors Enhance Controllability and Reasoning of Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer new opportunities for controllable text generation. However, their controllability, defined as the ability to satisfy task constraints while preserving their original capabilities, remains underexplored. DLMs' bidirectional attention allows control tokens to guide generation from arbitrary positions in the output sequence, but effective guidance depends on the compatibility between their content and placement. To this end, we propose AnchorDLM, a framework in which an anchor generator produces an anchor consisting of a short output fragment and its position for each query. The anchor is placed as control tokens at the specified position to initialize the output sequence of a frozen DLM and guide subsequent denoising. We train the anchor generator with reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize anchor content and placement, using rewards computed from the DLM's generated outputs based on answer correctness and constraint satisfaction. Moreover, through the lens of discrete flow matching (DFM), we interpret anchor placement as helping to reshape the initial velocity field that guides generation. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning across five DLM backbones show that AnchorDLM improves controllability and further yields gains in reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) attend bidirectionally, so control tokens can steer generation from any position in the output, but their controllability, meaning the ability to satisfy task constraints while keeping their original capabilities, is underexplored and depends on both the content of the control tokens and where they are placed. `AnchorDLM` trains an anchor generator that produces, for each query, a short output fragment and a position, and the anchor is written into the initial output sequence of a frozen DLM to guide the subsequent denoising. The generator is optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using rewards for answer correctness and constraint satisfaction computed from the DLM's outputs, and the authors interpret anchor placement through discrete flow matching (DFM) as reshaping the initial velocity field that drives generation. **On code generation and mathematical reasoning across five DLM backbones, `AnchorDLM` improves controllability and also raises reasoning performance** across diverse benchmarks.

papers.title: Random Feature Pruning for Multi-Class Classification
papers.abstract: Weighted sums of random kitchen sinks (W-RKS) is a commonly used feature extraction technique for supervised learning tasks. A major drawback of this method is the redundancy and ineffectiveness of many extracted random features. This paper investigates efficient methods for reducing such redundancy in multi-class classification problems. We specifically formulate feature selection as a variant of the sequentially nested model selection problem and introduce the Successive Empirical Excess Risk Difference Maximization (SEED-MAX) algorithm. It recursively computes empirical risks to identify the most parsimonious yet informative set of features. We derive an analytical lower bound for the probability of correct feature selection by the SEED-MAX algorithm. This lower bound on the probability of correct feature selection can be made arbitrarily close to one by increasing the training dataset size. To further enhance the rate of pruning, we evaluate the features retained by SEED-MAX using the Fisher test (F-Test). Empirical evaluations on UCR time-series classification datasets show that the sequential application of SEED-MAX with the Fisher test achieves approximately 92 percent rate of pruning with negligible degradation in classification accuracy. Implementations of the SEED-MAX and SEED-MAX-F-Test methods are available at https://github.com/OmidiAmin/seed-max-ftest.
papers.summary: Weighted sums of random kitchen sinks (`W-RKS`) are a common random-feature extraction technique for supervised learning, but many of the generated features are redundant or uninformative. The authors cast feature selection for multi-class classification as a variant of sequentially nested model selection and introduce Successive Empirical Excess Risk Difference Maximization (`SEED-MAX`), which recursively computes empirical risks to find the most parsimonious informative feature set, backed by an analytical lower bound on the probability of correct selection that approaches one as the training set grows. A Fisher test (F-test) applied to the retained features prunes further. **On UCR time-series classification datasets, `SEED-MAX` followed by the F-test prunes roughly 92% of features with negligible loss in classification accuracy**, and implementations are released.

papers.title: RegExtract: A Benchmark for PFAS Regulatory Information Extraction with LLMs
papers.abstract: Extracting structured information from regulatory documents is a critical but challenging task. Relevant facts are scattered across long, legally dense texts, and traceability of extracted facts to their source is essential for verification. With increasing awareness of the environmental and health impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), regulatory documents have expanded significantly, varying in scope and product relevance, making interpretation challenging for manufacturers and policymakers. We introduce RegExtract, a benchmark for structured information extraction from PFAS regulatory documents, comprising 488 human-annotated field instances across 20 US state documents and 46 regulations. Each field instance includes a value and a provenance entry, yielding 976 entries in total. We define a typed, multi-field schema targeting key elements such as material definitions, permitted uses, and product exemptions, and propose provenance-aware evaluation metrics tailored to regulatory text. Through experiments with open- and closed-source LLMs across prompting strategies, document condensing methods, and schema partitioning approaches, we find that document identification fields remain challenging, and that field-specific few-shot examples improve extraction. This work lays the groundwork for AI tools for hazardous substance identification, question answering, and compliance monitoring. The code and data are available at https://github.com/IBM/PFAS-regulations.
papers.summary: Extracting structured facts from regulatory text is hard because relevant details are scattered across long, legally dense documents and every extracted value must be traceable to its source, and regulations on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) have grown rapidly while varying in scope and product relevance. `RegExtract` is a benchmark of 488 human-annotated field instances, each paired with a provenance entry for 976 entries in total, drawn from 20 US state documents spanning 46 regulations, with a typed multi-field schema covering material definitions, permitted uses, and product exemptions plus provenance-aware evaluation metrics tailored to regulatory text. Experiments with open- and closed-source LLMs across prompting strategies, document condensing methods, and schema partitioning show that **document identification fields remain the hardest to extract, while field-specific few-shot examples improve extraction**. Code and data are released.

papers.title: RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
papers.abstract: Latent recursion repeatedly processes internal representations through the same neural network. Recent work has shown this approach to be effective on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. However, whether latent recursion can support neural routing remains unclear. We introduce RELAGRAM (Recursive Latent Graph Model), a novel approach that brings latent recursion to graph combinatorial optimization. RELAGRAM encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens; a compact transformer recurrently updates the latent representations of these tokens. An output head maps the answer state to an edge heatmap, from which an autoregressive decoder constructs a feasible solution. On CVRP-100 instances, the 0.53M-parameter RELAGRAM achieves gaps to a PyVRP reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% under greedy decoding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search, respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, RELAGRAM generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000, achieving gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search. Together, these results demonstrate that latent recursion is a promising approach to neural routing.
papers.summary: Latent recursion, which repeatedly passes internal representations through the same network, has worked on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving, but whether it can support neural routing was unclear. The Recursive Latent Graph Model (`RELAGRAM`) encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens, recurrently updates their latent representations with a compact transformer, maps the answer state to an edge heatmap, and builds a feasible solution with an autoregressive decoder. **With only 0.53M parameters, it reaches gaps to a `PyVRP` reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% on CVRP-100** under greedy decoding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, it generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000 with gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search.

papers.title: Structural Chain-of-Thought: Reasoning with Executable Computational Graphs
papers.abstract:
Chain-of-thought prompting enables reasoning in large language models but produces explanations that are difficult to verify, expensive to generate, and not always faithful. We introduce a Structural Chain-of-Thought framework where models generate executable computational graphs instead of free-form reasoning. The final answer is obtained by deterministically executing the graph. The model is trained using graph-based reinforcement learning that rewards structural validity, answer correctness, and node overlap with reference graphs.
  Experiments across five benchmarks and four model families show that our method consistently improves accuracy over supervised graph training and can reduce generation length by up to 5-6x compared with standard GRPO and chain-of-thought supervised training. Our faithfulness experiments reveal that models trained with our approach tend to rely on deriving their answers from the generated graphs rather than producing post-hoc rationalizations as usually in chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought prompting produces reasoning traces that are hard to verify, expensive to generate, and not always faithful to how the answer was actually reached.
