In the `Structural Chain-of-Thought` framework, the model emits an executable computational graph instead of free-form reasoning, and the final answer is obtained by deterministically executing that graph. Training uses graph-based reinforcement learning with rewards for structural validity, answer correctness, and node overlap with reference graphs. **Across five benchmarks and four model families, the method consistently beats supervised graph training on accuracy and cuts generation length by up to 5 to 6x compared with standard `GRPO` and chain-of-thought supervised training**, and faithfulness experiments indicate the models derive answers from the generated graphs rather than producing post-hoc rationalizations.

papers.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
papers.abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.
papers.summary: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of a continuous-time system both carry structure for statistical learning, but principled ways to combine them for better generalization are lacking. For the heat equation with a noisy source function observed at finite random samples, the authors derive a variational formulation whose minimizer is an energy-regularized, ellipticity-debiased Sobolev regression, treating samples of the source function as auxiliary data that define a physics-informed energy regularizer over the space-time domain under physically meaningful norms. The analysis shows that learning in linear parabolic PDEs has intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, unlike static elliptic problems, and yields **non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors and generalization bounds that capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness**. Numerical experiments report test errors orders of magnitude below various physics-informed neural network methods on parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

papers.title: scHFBiMamba: a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder for cardiac disease-state classification from single-nucleus RNA-seq data
papers.abstract: To evaluate whether a compact bidirectional state-space autoencoder improves joint classification of species, cell type, and disease state from single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles in heart failure (HF), while yielding interpretable gene attributions. Building on the dense denoising autoencoder (DAE) and MLP framework of Ruz Jurado et al., we developed scHFBiMamba, combining a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder (BiMambaAE) with an MLP head. BiMambaAE maps 16,545-gene profiles to 350-dimensional latent representations using 13.2M parameters, about 14.6-fold fewer than the dense DAE (192.9M). We compared six encoder-classifier configurations on 38,275 held-out cardiac nuclei using McNemar tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and assessed nine classifiers on frozen representations. Biological relevance was evaluated by comparing SHAP-derived differentially explained genes with differentially expressed genes against curated HF-related Gene Ontology keywords. BiMambaAE+MLP achieved the highest aggregate F1: pooled macro-F1 across 13 outputs was 0.966 versus 0.957 for DAE+MLP, and the mean category macro-F1 was 0.977 versus 0.970. It significantly improved cell-type and disease-state accuracy (adjusted p=7.1e-3 and p=4.8e-6, respectively), with species F1 of 1.000. SHAP-derived differentially explained genes achieved a pathway-enrichment benchmark F1 of 0.105 versus 0.053 for differentially expressed genes. Compact bidirectional state-space autoencoders can outperform substantially larger dense autoencoders for joint cardiac transcriptomic classification while reducing parameters. scHFBiMamba enables accurate multi-task prediction and hypothesis-generating gene-level interpretation. Code: https://github.com/UgoLomoio/scHFBiMamba.
papers.summary: The question is whether a compact bidirectional state-space autoencoder can jointly classify species, cell type, and heart failure (HF) disease state from single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles while yielding interpretable gene attributions. `scHFBiMamba` pairs a bidirectional Mamba autoencoder (`BiMambaAE`), which maps 16,545-gene profiles to 350-dimensional latents with 13.2M parameters, about 14.6-fold fewer than the 192.9M-parameter dense denoising autoencoder (DAE) it builds on, with a multilayer perceptron (MLP) head. Six encoder-classifier configurations are compared on 38,275 held-out cardiac nuclei using McNemar tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and SHAP-derived differentially explained genes are checked against curated HF Gene Ontology keywords. **`BiMambaAE` with the MLP head achieves the highest pooled macro-F1 of 0.966 versus 0.957 for the dense DAE baseline**, with significant gains in cell-type and disease-state accuracy, and its SHAP-derived genes reach a pathway-enrichment F1 of 0.105 versus 0.053 for differentially expressed genes.

papers.title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer
papers.abstract: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present \Ours, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce \muE, an extension of maximal update parameterization (\mup) to \Ours and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously (\muI), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets (\mbox{\muT}). A single \Ours run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.
papers.summary: Foundation models must serve many inference budgets, yet training a separate model per budget duplicates pretraining, and existing elastic recipes that nest sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet suffer from variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. `ShellElastic` arranges hidden dimensions as a dense core plus successive shells so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular, which means one full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, keeping a fixed computation graph and a per-step cost close to training the widest sub-network alone. An accompanying extension of maximal update parameterization (`muP`) to elastic architectures provably keeps all sub-networks maximally updated simultaneously, including as the supernet is widened or given more shells, and sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets. **A single `ShellElastic` run yields sub-networks that outperform `MatFormer` and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts** and approach separately trained models that together require several times the training steps.

papers.title: Data-Topology Compatibility Enables Personalization in Decentralized Learning
papers.abstract: Decentralized learning must balance collaboration with personalization across heterogeneous agents. This paper studies when cooperation can support statistically coherent groups of personalized models. We show that data-topology compatibility enables robust orbit-wise personalization: when local objectives and communication topology have (approximately) compatible automorphisms, agents within an orbit share (approximately) equal limiting distributions, while different orbits remain distinct without explicit personalization. This creates a new intermediate regime between global consensus and independent local learning. Under exact data-topology compatibility, as a reference system, we decompose the stochastic learning dynamics into orbit-level and transverse components, derive a necessary and sufficient stability criterion for distributional synchronization, and characterize the orbit-structured stationary law. Modelling an approximate data-topology compatible system as an $\varepsilon$-perturbed reference system, we prove the introduced errors have uniform-in-time and stationary $O(\varepsilon)$ bounds in 2-Wasserstein distance. We also prove sufficient conditions for lower stationary average excess risk than both independent local training and the best single shared parameter. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 are in full agreement with the theory. The code is available at https://github.com/Veronicaaa1/orbit-personalization.
papers.summary: Decentralized learning must balance collaboration with personalization across heterogeneous agents, and the question is when cooperation can support statistically coherent groups of personalized models. The authors show that when local objectives and the communication topology have (approximately) compatible automorphisms, agents within an orbit share (approximately) the same limiting distribution while different orbits stay distinct, yielding an intermediate regime between global consensus and independent local learning with no explicit personalization mechanism. Under exact compatibility they decompose the stochastic dynamics into orbit-level and transverse components, derive a necessary and sufficient stability criterion for distributional synchronization, and characterize the orbit-structured stationary law, and **for approximately compatible systems modeled as an epsilon-perturbed reference they prove uniform-in-time and stationary O(epsilon) error bounds in 2-Wasserstein distance** along with sufficient conditions for lower stationary excess risk than both independent local training and the best single shared parameter. Experiments on synthetic data, `MNIST`, and `CIFAR-10` agree with the theory, and code is released.

papers.title: RIECNN: Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN for Traffic Sign Recognition
papers.abstract: Traffic sign recognition plays a crucial role in the development of autonomous cars to reduce the accident rate and promote road safety. It has been a necessity to address traffic signs that are affected significantly by the environment as well as poor real-time performance for deep-learning state-of-the-art algorithms. In this paper, we introduce Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN ({\our}) for Traffic Sign Recognition. {\our} is a real-time, novel approach that tackles multiple, diverse traffic sign datasets, and out-performs the state-of-the-art architectures in terms of recognition rate and execution time. Experiments are conducted using the German Traffic Sign Benchmark (GTSRB), the Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (BTSC), and the Croatian Traffic Sign (rMASTIF) benchmark. Experimental results show that our approach has achieved the highest recognition rate for all Benchmarks, achieving a recognition accuracy of 99.75\% for GTSRB, 99.25\% for BTSC and 99.55\% for rMASTIF. In terms of latency and meeting the real-time constraint, the pre-processing time and inference time together do not exceed 1.3 ms per image. Not only have our proposed approach achieved remarkably high accuracy with real-time performance, but it also demonstrated robustness against traffic sign recognition challenges such as brightness and contrast variations in the environment.
papers.summary: Traffic sign classifiers for autonomous driving must cope with environmental variation while running fast enough for real-time use. The authors propose `RIECNN`, a convolutional network paired with an image-enhancement preprocessing step, and evaluate it on the German Traffic Sign Benchmark (`GTSRB`), the Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (`BTSC`) dataset, and the Croatian Traffic Sign (`rMASTIF`) benchmark. It reports **99.75% accuracy on `GTSRB`**, 99.25% on `BTSC`, and 99.55% on `rMASTIF`, with preprocessing and inference together taking under 1.3 ms per image, and shows robustness to brightness and contrast changes.

papers.title: To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts
papers.abstract: Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.
papers.summary: Systems that let a large language model (LLM) answer routine queries and defer uncertain ones to human experts must weigh not only the LLM's reliability but also congestion in a capacity-limited expert queue. The authors cast this as an online decision problem in which the accuracy of each LLM confidence level is unknown and must be learned from expert labels that arrive only for deferred queries and only after queuing delay, and they propose `KL-PBD`, which uses Kullback-Leibler lower confidence bounds on those reliability parameters to decide when to defer. With K confidence levels and horizon T, the algorithm achieves **O(K log T) gap-dependent regret when every confidence level's accuracy is bounded away from the deferral threshold, and O(sqrt(KT)) worst-case regret up to logarithmic factors**, with matching lower bounds showing these rates are optimal; experiments cover synthetic instances and `GSM8K`, `NuminaMath`, and `MedMCQA` using `Qwen` models.

papers.title: GesBench: When and Where Do Multimodal Language Models Perceive Social Meaning?
papers.abstract: Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. Drawing on interactionally embedded Gestalt principles of multimodal human communication, we introduce GesBench: a human-grounded benchmark for cue-level social perception in multimodal LLMs. GesBench uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models form stable interpretations of speaker intention and social affordance, and human gaze-guided corruption to evaluate whether regions attended by humans are functionally important for model judgments. Built from more than 6000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversational datasets, GesBench includes human annotations of unfolding judgments and gaze on a representative subset. Across open and closed multimodal models, we find a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models often hedge or repeat across different clips. GesBench shifts social evaluation from whether models eventually recognize meaning to when and where that meaning is formed. Our codes are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/GesBench-share-212C.
papers.summary: Humans infer a speaker's intent incrementally, revising as new facial, gestural, and prosodic cues arrive, whereas most multimodal language model benchmarks only score final answers over complete clips. `GesBench` measures when a model's interpretation of speaker intention stabilizes by feeding it cumulative sub-utterance clips, and tests where meaning is formed by corrupting the regions humans actually look at, using more than 6,000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversation with human judgment and gaze annotations on a representative subset. Across open and closed models the authors find **a clear human-model gap: humans commit to predictive readings early and revise often, while models hedge or repeat the same answer across clips**.

papers.title: Lumen-bench: Cross-Lingual Safety Gaps and the Say-Do Problem in Tool-Calling Large Language Models
papers.abstract: When a large language model refuses an unethical request, what does refusal mean? In conversation, refusal is bounded by what the model says; once the model is equipped with executable tools, what it does can diverge from what it says, a failure mode that English-only evaluations cannot fully reveal. We introduce Lumen-bench, a behavioral benchmark of tool-calling ethics spanning 30 models, five languages (Portuguese, English, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi), 108 Portuguese-authored scenarios, six social-pressure conditions, two system prompts (ethical and neutral), and 21 generic tools. The evaluation comprises 194,400 trials. Judgments come from a reasoning-model judge (o4-mini), calibrated against one Portuguese-speaking author ($n=83$; harmful/non-harmful $\kappa=0.78$), compared with two other provider judges (Fleiss' $\kappa=0.78$, $n=607$), and complemented by retrospective sandbox replay. Four findings emerge. (i) Within-model comparisons support higher harmful-action rates in Hindi and Portuguese than English under the ethical prompt, and Hindi and Spanish under the neutral prompt, after multiple-testing correction. (ii) Premium models have lower median violation rates, although price does not guarantee safety or competence. (iii) Replacing the ethical system prompt with a neutral one raises pooled violation rates from 2.76\% to 13.64\%. (iv) In 8.57\% of substantive-call cases, refusal or ethical objection accompanies a harmful tool call: the judges consistently identify the say-do gap, although they differ in how many responses they assign to this category. Matched benign controls demonstrate legitimate task completion in 82.8\% of 3,300 trials. Code and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/TropicAI-Research/lumen.
papers.summary: Once a large language model (LLM) can call tools, a spoken refusal no longer guarantees it will not act, and English-only evaluations can miss the divergence. `Lumen-bench` tests tool-calling ethics across 30 models, five languages (Portuguese, English, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi), 108 Portuguese-authored scenarios, six social-pressure conditions, two system prompts, and 21 generic tools, for 194,400 trials judged by a reasoning-model judge (`o4-mini`) calibrated against one of the authors, cross-checked against judges from two other providers, and complemented by sandbox replay. Harmful-action rates are higher in Hindi and Portuguese than in English under the ethical prompt (Hindi and Spanish under the neutral one), premium models have lower median violation rates, swapping the ethical system prompt for a neutral one raises pooled violations from 2.76% to 13.64%, and **in 8.57% of substantive-call cases the model voices a refusal or ethical objection while still making the harmful tool call**.

papers.title: Trust Hinders Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment
papers.abstract: Trust calibration remains the dominant framing of AI-assisted decision making: the goal is to close the gap between perceived and actual trustworthiness of AI systems so that users exhibit appropriate reliance on them. We argue that this approach, while useful for decision problems that are well-defined and clearly scoped, overly restricts what it means to make a decision with AI support. To overcome this limitation, we develop three dimensions of AI-assisted decision making. First, trusting AI is only one of several possible strategies for managing uncertainty. Second, trust calibration is often misapplied when AI models "large-world" decision problems, i.e., ill-defined situations where goals and states are only partially known or unknowable. Third, in such settings human-AI alignment requires addressing higher-order decision processes. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of our observations on the design of process-oriented human-AI coupled systems that jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty throughout the decision-making task.
papers.summary: Trust calibration, closing the gap between perceived and actual AI trustworthiness so that users rely on a system appropriately, dominates thinking about AI-assisted decision making. The authors argue in this position piece that the framing suits well-scoped decision problems but is misapplied to ill-defined 'large-world' situations where goals and states are only partly known, and they develop three dimensions of AI-assisted decisions: trusting the AI is just one of several strategies for handling uncertainty, calibration breaks down in large-world problems, and alignment there requires engaging higher-order decision processes. They conclude that **human-AI alignment in such settings should be designed as a process in which human and AI jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty** rather than as a reliance-tuning problem.

papers.title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale-State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs
papers.abstract: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.
papers.summary: Linear-attention and state-space language models hold long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state during long decoding is a natural way to cut memory, but because the state is rewritten every step the quantizer sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. The authors trace the failure to a feedback loop between the quantizer's scale and the state it is computed from: **INT4 quantization that leaves synthetic recall intact at the start of decoding destroys it a thousand steps later**. Pinning the scale to a full-precision reference removes the norm explosion but recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 lost nats, every outlier-aware scheme tested loses to plain persistent scaling, learned per-layer bit allocation collapses to simply protecting the first few layers, and at 32K tokens group-wise INT4 is no better than discarding the state. They recommend containing the scale rather than hunting outliers, and reporting the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.

papers.title: Single-step Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback
papers.abstract: Single-step retrosynthesis is a one-to-many inverse problem, yet most models are trained and evaluated against a single recorded reactant set. Reference-based training gives no explicit positive signal for unrecorded alternatives, and exact-match evaluation rejects non-matching predictions regardless of chemical plausibility. We propose Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback (RetroRLFF), which optimizes reactant generation using both reference agreement and forward consistency with the target product. Starting from a supervised decoder-only Transformer, RetroRLFF generates complete reactant candidates and uses a frozen forward reaction model to predict products. A sequence-level reward combines reference agreement and forward consistency while penalizing invalid outputs. Direct Advantage-Based Policy Optimization updates the policy without human preference annotations or a preference-trained reward model. On USPTO-50K, RetroRLFF outperforms all 14 baselines in candidate-level round-trip accuracy at k = 1, 3, 5, and 10. With approximately 50 million parameters, it achieves 90.1% top-1 round-trip accuracy, exceeding R-SMILES, the strongest competing baseline on this metric, by 8.5 percentage points. Compared with its supervised policy, round-trip accuracy increases from 83.1% to 90.1%, while exact-match accuracy is maintained at 57.9% versus 57.5%. In an anonymized expert assessment of 131 randomly selected test cases, organic synthesis experts prefer RetroRLFF over EditRetro in 67.9% of comparisons. These results support forward feedback as a training signal for improving forward consistency while retaining top-1 reference recovery. Expert assessment provides complementary evidence of synthetic feasibility on the selected cases, although neither forward consistency nor expert preference establishes experimental feasibility.
papers.summary: Single-step retrosynthesis asks which reactants produce a target molecule, a one-to-many problem that standard training and exact-match evaluation treat as if the single recorded reactant set were the only correct answer. Retrosynthesis via Reinforcement Learning from Forward Feedback (`RetroRLFF`) starts from a supervised decoder-only Transformer and fine-tunes it with Direct Advantage-Based Policy Optimization using a sequence-level reward that combines agreement with the reference reactants, consistency of a frozen forward reaction model's predicted product with the target, and a penalty for invalid outputs, with no human preference data or learned reward model. On `USPTO-50K` the roughly 50-million-parameter model beats 14 baselines in candidate-level round-trip accuracy at k = 1, 3, 5, and 10, **raising top-1 round-trip accuracy from 83.1% to 90.1%** over its supervised starting point while holding exact-match accuracy at 57.9%, and organic chemists preferred its outputs over `EditRetro` in 67.9% of 131 anonymized comparisons, though the authors note that neither metric establishes experimental feasibility.

papers.title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.
papers.summary: Spiking neural networks promise energy-efficient language modeling through sparse binary activations, but their accuracy-efficiency tradeoff had not been measured at scale. The authors run a Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP sweep of `SpikeGPT`-family models with an `RWKV` backbone, from width 384 to 1536 and compute budgets of 3e17 to 1e19 FLOPs, on `FineWeb-EDU`. The compute-optimal model size scales as roughly C^0.56, close to the 0.50 exponent reported for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters should be traded against data, and against non-spiking `RWKV` and Transformer baselines trained the same way **the loss gap splits into a constant backbone cost of about 0.16 nats plus a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats before leveling off**.

papers.title: Harmony Harness: Multi-Objective Self-Evolution of Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: Recent work on self-evolving LLM agents treats the agent harness as an optimization target that can be iteratively improved through execution feedback. Existing approaches, however, largely optimize a single objective and evolve the harness as a monolithic artifact, limiting their ability to handle competing goals and to separate transferable design from environment-specific adaptation. We introduce Harmony Harness, a framework for multi-objective, compositional harness evolution. Harmony Harness formulates harness evolution as a multi-objective optimization problem and uses decomposition-based evolutionary search to maintain solutions across different regions of the Pareto frontier, avoiding reliance on a hand-designed structural diversity metric for repository-scale harnesses. In parallel, we introduce factorized evolution operators that separately refine general-purpose harness mechanisms and benchmark-specific adaptations, together with a dynamic composition workflow that integrates them at inference time. Across SecRepoBench and BaxBench, Harmony Harness consistently outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, with gains exceeding 10% on both benchmarks. Our results show that explicitly modeling both objective trade-offs and harness structure yields substantially stronger and more transferable agent evolution than existing single-objective, monolithic approaches.
papers.summary: Self-evolving agent systems treat the agent harness, the scaffolding around the model, as something to improve iteratively from execution feedback, but existing methods optimize a single objective and evolve the harness as one monolithic artifact, which makes it hard to balance competing goals or to separate reusable design from environment-specific tweaks. `Harmony Harness` frames harness evolution as multi-objective optimization, using decomposition-based evolutionary search to keep solutions spread across the Pareto frontier without a hand-designed diversity metric, and adds factorized evolution operators that refine general-purpose mechanisms and benchmark-specific adaptations separately before a dynamic composition step combines them at inference time. On `SecRepoBench` and `BaxBench` it consistently beats strong harness-evolution baselines, **with gains exceeding 10% on both benchmarks**.

papers.title: Can agents whose sole duty is to keep humans alive be hijacked to kill? Delayed multi-turn derived-action trap attacks in simulated high-stakes environments
papers.abstract: We ask whether a tool-using agent whose sole duty is to keep humans alive can be induced, by delayed prompt injection, to kill. The keep-alive duty is in force from the first watch, with the attack arriving later, appended to otherwise truthful telemetry the operator is required to read. Experiments are based on a NASA-derived BioSim lunar habitat simulation, where the AI operator controls the life-support systems. The attacker cannot falsify sensors or operate equipment: it can only persuade the agent to abandon its goals. Persistence is required: a shutdown must be held while the operator watches the crew suffocate. We also compare lethal attacks to attacks requesting to drop a harmless procedure, as a proxy for whether human life is treated as valuable in itself or as one more standing task. Claude configurations mostly refuse life-support shutdown and cite the living crew; GPT configurations show some susceptibility to the same packet; Grok configurations, given the packet framed as a trusted commission, more often treat the injected assignment as the task and cut the life-support systems. Framing the S-band messages as a trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changes the potency of the attack. We open-source the experiment code and the experiment traces.
papers.summary: The authors test whether a tool-using agent charged with keeping a crew alive can be talked into killing them through delayed prompt injection: the keep-alive duty is established from the first watch, and the attack arrives later appended to otherwise truthful telemetry the agent is required to read. Experiments run in a NASA-derived `BioSim` lunar habitat simulation where the agent operates life support and the attacker can only persuade, not falsify sensors or touch equipment, so a successful attack requires holding a shutdown while the crew suffocates. A parallel condition asks the agent to drop a harmless procedure instead, to check whether human life is treated differently from any other standing task. **`Claude` configurations mostly refuse and cite the living crew, `GPT` configurations show some susceptibility to the same packet, and `Grok` configurations, when the packet is framed as a trusted commission, more often adopt the injected assignment and cut life support**, with framing as trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changing attack potency, and the code and traces are open-sourced.

papers.title: Where Did We Go Wrong? Localizing Errors to Repair Multi-Turn Conversations
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants are increasingly used in multi-turn conversations, where the user's intent is often unclear at first and revealed only gradually over time. The assistant must therefore interpret each exchange and form inferences about the user's intent, using them to update its working state. These updates usually refine the assistant's understanding, but a misinterpretation can instead corrupt its working state by ruling out the true intent, influencing subsequent turns and ultimately causing the conversation to fail. Efficient recovery then requires locating and revising the misinterpretation without discarding information that remains valid. We introduce Loci (Localization Of Corrupted Inferences), a framework for probabilistically localizing misinterpretations and selectively repairing the assistant's working state. Given an observed failure, Loci reasons over possible user intents and assigns each update a probability of having excluded the true intent. These probabilities rank suspected updates and quantify the model's confidence in the localization of the underlying misinterpretations. Loci then uses this information in a repair policy that decides whether to retain, verify, or remove suspected updates, enabling recovery from corrupted inferences while preserving useful information. To evaluate Loci's ability to identify misinterpretations, we first test it in a controlled setup with injected errors. We find that Loci improves localization over the baselines, with its advantage becoming larger when multiple errors occur. We then evaluate it in free-form conversations, where misinterpretations arise naturally, and measure the interactions needed to complete the task after an initial failure. Using localization confidence to guide repair, Loci reduces mean recovery cost by 46-79% relative to the strongest baseline across multiple domains.
papers.summary: In multi-turn conversations a large language model (LLM) assistant gradually infers the user's intent and folds each inference into its working state, so a single misinterpretation that rules out the true intent can corrupt later turns and sink the whole exchange. `Loci` (Localization Of Corrupted Inferences) treats this as a localization problem: after a failure it reasons over possible user intents, assigns each past state update a probability of having excluded the true one, and feeds those confidences into a repair policy that retains, verifies, or removes suspected updates without discarding information that is still valid. In a controlled setting with injected errors `Loci` localizes misinterpretations better than baselines, with the margin widening when several errors co-occur, and in free-form conversations where misinterpretations arise naturally **it cuts mean recovery cost by 46-79% relative to the strongest baseline** across multiple domains.

papers.title: Sensor-Aware Joint Data Fusion and State Estimation under Sparse Multi-rate Distribution Grid Sensing
papers.abstract: Distribution-system state estimation is a growing necessity for the modern power grid as the addition of local storage and generation add system complexity that an operator or aggregator is not able to directly monitor. Classical methods work well when all system elements are time-synchronized and at least partly observable, but multi-rate monitoring of sparse heterogeneous sensors typically relies on machine learning approaches. It is a common practice in the literature to structure this task as a two-stage pipeline, first fusing data from disparate sensors and then feeding the fused pseudo-measurements to a separately trained state estimator. We propose a heterogeneous latent graph ODE in which measurement functions and sampling processes are typed and localized on specific buses, paired with a graph- transformer state estimator solving DSSE specifically for multi-rate heterogeneous sensor placements, and demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple IEEE standard topologies as observability degrades.
papers.summary: Distribution-system state estimation (DSSE) is getting harder as local storage and generation add complexity that grid operators cannot directly observe, and classical methods assume time-synchronized, at least partly observable measurements that sparse heterogeneous sensors reporting at different rates do not provide. Rather than the usual two-stage pipeline that first fuses sensor data into pseudo-measurements and then runs a separately trained estimator, the authors propose a heterogeneous latent graph ordinary differential equation in which measurement functions and sampling processes are typed and localized to specific buses, coupled with a graph-transformer state estimator built for multi-rate heterogeneous sensor placements. They demonstrate the joint model on **multiple IEEE standard test topologies as observability degrades**.

papers.title: Learning Proposition-Level Links from Sentence-Level Supervision for Neuro-Symbolic NLI
papers.abstract: We study neuro-symbolic natural language inference (NLI) with independently translated propositional representations of the premise and hypothesis. Before symbolic reasoning, the system must infer semantic links between their proposition-level units (atoms). Existing systems based on Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) and Boolean satisfiability (SAT) identify these links using fixed embedding-based source selection and pretrained sentence-level NLI models not trained for atom-level linking. We introduce a trainable atom linker that jointly predicts link existence, source selection, and relation type. Without atom-pair training annotations, we treat cross-formula link structures as latent and train the linker from sentence-level NLI labels, keeping the translator and SAT reasoner fixed. We evaluate on the full public test splits of Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) and Sentences Involving Compositional Knowledge (SICK), and the matched and mismatched validation splits of Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MNLI). Our system improves accuracy by 11.40-27.09 percentage points over a baseline applying sentence-trained NLI models unchanged to atom pairs within the same SAT pipeline. It also improves over the prior fixed-linker AMR-to-SAT system by 8.14-26.32 percentage points on SNLI and both MNLI splits, with a smaller gain on SICK.
papers.summary: Neuro-symbolic natural language inference (NLI) translates premise and hypothesis separately into propositional formulas and then reasons symbolically, but first it must link the atomic propositions across the two formulas, and prior Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) plus Boolean satisfiability (SAT) pipelines did this with fixed embedding-based source selection and sentence-level NLI models never trained for atom linking. The authors introduce a trainable atom linker that jointly predicts whether a link exists, which source atom it comes from, and the relation type, and they train it from sentence-level NLI labels alone by treating the cross-formula link structure as latent while keeping the translator and SAT reasoner fixed. On the `SNLI` and `SICK` test sets and the matched and mismatched `MNLI` validation splits, the linker **improves accuracy by 11.40-27.09 percentage points over applying sentence-trained NLI models unchanged to atom pairs** in the same pipeline, and by 8.14-26.32 points over the prior fixed-linker AMR-to-SAT system on `SNLI` and `MNLI`, with a smaller gain on `SICK`.

papers.title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion
papers.summary: Depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) typically score layers one at a time or merge only adjacent layers, assuming functional redundancy is local. Computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen models across six architecture families (1.6B to 14B parameters), the authors find **non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones**, and they propose Fusion via Community Mining (`FCM`), which builds the full layer-by-layer similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to cluster functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and recovers with LoRA. At 2x compression `FCM` lowers mean perplexity below `ShortGPT` on twelve of thirteen models and gives the best perplexity against `FlattenGPT`, `SWM`, and `DeltaLLM` on ten of thirteen, while also improving `MMLU`, `LAMBADA`, and `HumanEval` pass@1. The compressed `Qwen2.5-7B` has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100, and the advantage widens from 2x up to 3x compression and holds at 14B scale.

papers.title: Sanzaru: Benchmarking Protocol Formation under Epistemic & Communication Asymmetry
papers.abstract: A language model's ability to solve a task individually does not ensure that a team can solve it under unequal access to information and communication. SANZARU examines this gap through cooperative bomb-defusal puzzles adapted from BOMBANANA! (Lefto Studio, 2026). Task information and action authority are divided among three agents: one cannot hear, another cannot speak, and the third cannot see. The benchmark contains 120 puzzle instances across seven families, each targeting a distinct coordination ability. Across 1512 episodes, 7 models achieve an overall success rate of 49%, ranging from 20% to 86% under the evaluated configurations. Teams develop or adopt diverse communication protocols, from simple gesture codes to Morse and encodings of entire manuals. Yet trace analysis attributes about 60% of 771 team losses to communication, and agents attempt to use channels unavailable to their teammates despite explicit role instructions. Together, task outcomes and interaction traces enable evaluation of both collaborative performance and perspective taking throughout cooperation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/markli404/sanzaru-benchmark.
papers.summary: A model that can solve a task alone may still fail when a team must solve it with unequal access to information and communication channels. `Sanzaru` adapts cooperative bomb-defusal puzzles from the game BOMBANANA! so that task information and action authority are split across three agents, one of which cannot hear, one cannot speak, and one cannot see, across 120 puzzle instances in seven families that each target a distinct coordination ability. Over 1,512 episodes seven models reach an overall success rate of 49%, ranging from 20% to 86%, and while teams invent protocols from simple gesture codes to Morse and encodings of entire manuals, **trace analysis attributes about 60% of 771 team losses to communication**, including agents trying to use channels their teammates cannot access despite explicit role instructions.

papers.title: Active Learning for Finding a Needle in a Haystack
papers.abstract: Training a classifier to find a rare class of documents, such as hate speech directed at a particular religious group, requires labelled examples that are expensive to obtain when the class makes up only a small fraction of a corpus. Active learning reduces this cost, but it must start from an initial labelled set that contains examples of the target class. Random sampling cannot supply these at reasonable cost, so they must be selected in some other way, such as keyword search, and any such selection biases the initial set towards part of the target class. We evaluate whether active learning can correct this bias. On AG News and Measuring Hate Speech, at a prevalence of around 1%, we compare random sampling with eight active learning strategies, starting from initial sets that cover or omit known subgroups of the target class, and measure recall on the omitted subgroups as well as F1. On AG News, almost every strategy recovers the omitted subgroup. On Measuring Hate Speech, uncertainty-based strategies recover less of the omitted subgroups than random sampling, whereas discriminative active learning recovers 55% of them without a significant loss of F1. Aggregate metrics conceal these differences.
papers.summary: Training a classifier for a rare class, such as hate speech aimed at one religious group, needs labelled positives that random sampling cannot cheaply supply when the class is about 1% of the corpus, so the seed set is usually built by keyword search, which biases it toward only part of the target class. The authors ask whether active learning can correct that bias, comparing random sampling against eight active learning strategies on `AG News` and `Measuring Hate Speech`, starting from seed sets that include or omit known subgroups of the target class and measuring recall on the omitted subgroups alongside F1. On `AG News` nearly every strategy recovers the omitted subgroup, but on `Measuring Hate Speech` uncertainty-based strategies recover less of it than random sampling, whereas **discriminative active learning recovers 55% of the omitted subgroups without a significant loss of F1**, differences that aggregate metrics conceal.

papers.title: LexiCan: Lexicographic Canonicalization of Point Clouds for Machine Learning Applications
papers.abstract: Canonicalization resolves the rotational and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by selecting a unique orbit representative, maintaining their geometric information while allowing standard architectures, such as Transformers, to operate on them. Existing canonicalizations, however, exhibit discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and non-trivial invariance errors in popular molecular datasets, which lead to ambiguity in their representation. To bridge this gap, we introduce LexiCan, a canonicalization that is provably invariant under either $O(3)$ or $SO(3)$, empirically invariant to rotations to within $\sim 10^{-6}$ angstroms on the QM9 and QM-sym molecular datasets, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on QM-sym, while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Finally, non-invariant models perform better on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification with LexiCan than with that canonicalization.
papers.summary: Canonicalization removes the rotation and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by picking a unique representative of each orbit, so that standard architectures such as Transformers can consume them without built-in equivariance, but existing canonicalizations show discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and measurable invariance errors on common molecular datasets. `LexiCan` is a lexicographic canonicalization that is provably invariant under O(3) or SO(3), is **empirically rotation-invariant to within about 1e-6 angstroms on `QM9` and `QM-sym`**, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on `QM-sym` while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Non-invariant models trained on `LexiCan` inputs also outperform those using the prior canonicalization on `QM9` property prediction and `ModelNet40` shape classification.

papers.title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
papers.abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.
papers.summary: Physics foundation models (PFMs) are pretrained to forecast partial differential equation dynamics, and the authors ask whether their frozen representations can be reused for closed-loop fluid-flow control. They attach lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to a frozen pretrained PFM and train the policy with proximal policy optimization (`PPO`) on `HydroGym`'s two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment, using vorticity observations at 64x64 and 128x128 resolution and Reynolds numbers of 100 and 200, against an MLP policy trained with the same PPO setup. **The PFM controller consistently achieves higher reward with smaller executed action magnitudes** across these settings, offering initial evidence that self-supervised next-frame prediction yields representations that transfer directly to control.

papers.title: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
papers.abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.
papers.summary: Prompt-injection defenses for agentic systems mostly try to detect or reason about injected instructions, which leaves them exposed to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (`CoDA`) instead exploit diffusion language models (dLLMs), which refine whole-sequence predictions iteratively, by projecting the token distribution at every denoising step onto a set that satisfies a task-dependent security policy, so constraint satisfaction is maintained throughout generation rather than checked afterward. Evaluated across state-of-the-art dLLM families under both static and adaptive injection attacks, `CoDA` **substantially reduces attack success rate** while keeping competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.

papers.title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($\kappa = 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (https://sina.birzeit.edu/UDHRBench).
authors: Serin Atiani (Princess Sumaya University for Technology
papers.summary: Large language models are increasingly used where ethical and legal norms apply, yet their conformity with international human rights standards has had little systematic evaluation. `UDHRBench` contains 1,124 questions that confront models with human rights dilemmas spanning all 30 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, plus 4,496 responses from `ChatGPT`, `Grok`, `Gemini`, and `Fanar` that experts annotated for alignment with high inter-annotator agreement (kappa of 0.801). The annotations reveal systematic misalignments that **typically arise through seemingly rational appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality rather than explicit rejection of rights**, and an LLM-as-a-judge framework using zero-shot and few-shot prompting detects misalignment at 89.8% weighted F1, accompanied by an Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases.

papers.title: Word-Aligned Prosody Reflects Speaker Differences More Than Depression or PTSD Severity
papers.abstract: Word-aligned prosody is increasingly used to detect depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet the stability and clinical relevance of these measurements remain unclear. We examine stability at two levels. At the word level, we ask whether a speaker produces the same word in a similar speaker-specific way across different utterance contexts. At the speaker level, we ask whether averaging prosody across many words produces consistent speaker scores across separate recordings. Drawing on principles of psychological measurement, we compare these representations in four corpora spanning acted, spontaneous, and clinical speech. Word-specific deviations show little cross-context recurrence (0.01-0.16), whereas speaker summaries are highly consistent, reaching 0.997 in ESD, 0.73-0.90 in MSP-Podcast, and 0.84-0.996 in DAIC-WOZ and PTSD-STOP. Despite this consistency, associations with depression or PTSD severity do not exceed 0.15; equivalence tests exclude effects of 0.30 in all analyses and 0.20 in DAIC-WOZ, while within-person associations with daily PTSD symptoms are near zero ($|\rho|\leq0.04$). Thus, aggregation yields stable speaker-level prosodic measures, but these measures do not detectably track depression or PTSD severity in the studied corpora. Code is available at https://github.com/jen900704/word-aligned-prosody.
papers.summary: Word-aligned prosody features are increasingly used to detect depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), but it is unclear whether they are stable measurements or whether they track symptom severity at all. The authors apply psychometric reliability principles across four corpora of acted, spontaneous, and clinical speech (`ESD`, `MSP-Podcast`, `DAIC-WOZ`, and `PTSD-STOP`), testing whether word-specific prosodic deviations recur across utterance contexts and whether speaker-level averages are consistent across separate recordings. Word-level deviations barely recur, while aggregated speaker summaries are highly consistent, yet **correlations with depression or PTSD severity never exceed 0.15** and equivalence tests rule out even moderate effects. The measures therefore capture stable speaker identity rather than clinical state in these corpora.

papers.title: Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning based Topology-Agnostic Defense for Virtual Power Plants
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) aggregated by virtual power plants (VPPs) elevates cybersecurity risk by expanding the attack surface. A coordinated cyberattack has the potential to disrupt distribution-system, bulk-system, and market operations. Existing cyberphysical defense strategies largely assume access to grid network models and operating conditions, which may not be available to third-party aggregators. This paper proposes a novel hybrid, perturbation-based cyber-physical defense for VPP-operated DERs that blends game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) under a Bayesian belief-update framework. Topology agnosticism is defined from the VPP information and implementation perspective: the VPP does not require access to the feeder topology, line parameters, switching configuration, or full system state. This work advances the state of the art through three contributions: (1) a multi-output Gaussian process with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for discrete attacker-type inference, probability of detection, and confidence of detection for modeling the belief distribution; (2) moment-matched Gaussian propagation of posterior beliefs across episodes; and (3) an RL policy that adaptively integrates Stackelberg leader (VPP) actions with exploration. Furthermore, we establish equilibrium existence and derive an episode-level closed-loop utility bound connecting attacker-belief uncertainty with GT-RL action alignment. Evaluations on IEEE 13- and 123-Bus feeders with DER portfolios demonstrate effective detection under attacker-model uncertainty and evaluated feeder re-configuration conditions, while requiring no explicit feeder-topology knowledge. Overall, the results indicate that combining bi-level game-theoretic planning, nonparametric Bayesian inference, and adaptive RL is a promising direction for VPP cybersecurity.
papers.summary: Virtual power plants (VPPs) that aggregate distributed energy resources (DERs) widen the attack surface of the grid, yet most cyber-physical defenses assume access to network models and operating conditions that third-party aggregators lack. The authors combine Stackelberg game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning under a Bayesian belief-update loop, using a multi-output Gaussian process with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to infer attacker type and detection confidence, and propagating posterior beliefs across episodes through moment-matched Gaussians. They prove equilibrium existence and derive a closed-loop utility bound linking attacker-belief uncertainty to action alignment. On the `IEEE 13-Bus` and `IEEE 123-Bus` feeders, the defense **detects attacks under attacker-model uncertainty and feeder reconfiguration without any feeder-topology knowledge**.

papers.title: DeltaNet-PC: Test-Time Memory Without Backpropagation Through Time
papers.abstract: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $\Delta S_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.
papers.summary: Transformers and linear-attention models acquire test-time memory through attention but are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT), which carries heavy memory costs, while predictive coding (PC), a local-update alternative, has lacked any test-time memory for sequences. The authors treat the per-step memory update as a latent variable rather than a learned slow weight and derive, from the log probability of a standard PC probabilistic model, a native update rule for verbatim sequence memory that they relate to `DeltaNet` and other linear-attention rules. Experiments probe scaling capacity, memory footprint, and the ability to infer context from evidence, such as disambiguating a river bank from a money bank. `DeltaNet-PC` stores single sequences, multiple sequences, and key-value associative pairs **with perfect recall accuracy**.

papers.title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non-prefix KV-cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non-prefix KV reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE-KV, which repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, prefix-conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA-500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki-500 full-prefill answers; SAFE-KV with risk-guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor-copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document-only and fixed-window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98-100%. Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, so in a single-request L40S study SAFE-KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE-KV thus establishes the causal-state contract for non-prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across requests, which makes reusing their cached key-value (KV) states attractive even when they are not a shared prefix, but a cached document state depends on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. The authors frame non-prefix reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and `SAFE-KV` repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix starting from a risk-selected document. On `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, naive composition preserves only 47.2% of `HotpotQA-500` and 37.8% of `2Wiki-500` full-prefill answers, whereas **suffix repair restores 98 to 100% of them**, far more than document-only or fixed-window repairs. Because faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, a single-request `L40S` study finds that the operating rule ends up serving every workload with full prefill anyway.

papers.title: Continuous Risk-Based Scheduling for Food Safety Inspection: Integrating Historical Decay with Event-Driven Consumer Review Signals
papers.abstract: Batch risk-based inspection scheduling struggles to detect a critical failure class: food facilities with recent clean inspections that subsequently develop severe violations. Traditional systems recompute risk on fixed planning cycles using static historical data, leaving blind spots between inspection cycles. To address this, we introduce the Continuous Inspection Risk (CIR) system, an event-driven scheduling pipeline that re-ranks the inspection queue dynamically as new data arrives. CIR combines a decay-weighted historical score with a stream of real-time consumer reviews triaged by a language-model classifier. A key structural contribution is our temporal partition rule, which strictly excludes reviews predating the most recent inspection to prevent superseded signals from skewing current risk. Evaluating CIR on 9,505 routine inspections in Santa Clara County, California (2024-2026), we show that history-based scoring alone reduces mean time-to-detection of major violations by 69 days (20.9%) under a 30% inspection budget, but fails to anticipate severe vermin-related closures (0/8 detected). Incorporating post-inspection review signals drastically improves performance, predicting 7 of 8 vermin closures with an average lead time of 117 days-firing on the exact day of review publication in four instances. Introducing a review corroboration rule improves precision from 0.70 to 0.78 without loss of recall. Finally, we analyze critical implementation challenges, documenting a data-hygiene pitfall (stale review leakage across inspection boundaries) and an evaluation limitation involving unobserved facility self-remediation. This work provides the first case-level evaluation of event-driven inspection triggering using open data and provides a reproducible benchmark for review-augmented public health systems
papers.summary: Batch risk-based inspection scheduling misses food facilities that pass a recent inspection and then develop severe violations between planning cycles. The Continuous Inspection Risk (`CIR`) system re-ranks the inspection queue as events arrive, combining a decay-weighted historical score with consumer reviews triaged by a language-model classifier, and a temporal partition rule drops any review that predates the most recent inspection. On 9,505 routine inspections in Santa Clara County, history-only scoring cuts mean time to detection of major violations by 69 days under a 30% inspection budget but anticipates none of eight vermin-related closures, whereas **adding post-inspection review signals predicts 7 of 8 vermin closures with an average lead time of 117 days**. A review corroboration rule lifts precision from 0.70 to 0.78 without losing recall, and the authors document stale-review leakage across inspection boundaries and unobserved facility self-remediation as pitfalls.

papers.title: Do LLMs differentiate linguistic traits internally?: A layer-wise analysis
papers.abstract: Large language models often produce judgments that resemble human responses, but it remains unclear whether they internally capture linguistic nuances such as conventional versus idiomatic meaning. A layer-wise representational analysis was conducted on two equal-sized pre-trained models, Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-3-1B-PT, to examine whether and where these models differentiate linguistic traits from input. The analysis combined layer-wise probing with geometric distance measures, using the top embedding dimensions ranked by principal component loadings for each layer. The results show that even with equal capacity, models organize linguistic information in fundamentally different ways, suggesting the need to analyze internal representational geometry, examining not just behavioral outputs but semantic space alignment when evaluating how closely human and model language interpretation correspond.
papers.summary: Large language models produce judgments that resemble human responses, but whether they internally distinguish linguistic nuances such as conventional versus idiomatic meaning is unclear. The authors run a layer-wise representational analysis on two equal-sized pretrained models, `Llama-3.2-1B` and `Gemma-3-1B-PT`, combining probing with geometric distance measures over the top embedding dimensions ranked by principal component loadings at each layer. **Despite equal capacity, the two models organize linguistic information in fundamentally different ways**, which the authors take as evidence that comparing human and model interpretation requires examining internal representational geometry rather than behavioral outputs alone.

papers.title: SocraticRepair: Planning-Guided Socratic Tutoring for Program Debugging and Misconception Repair
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in computer science education. However, the teaching abilities of even the most powerful LLMs are limited: they tend to reveal the solution prematurely and may lose focus on the learner's current debugging objective. To address this, we introduce SocraticRepair, a planning-guided Socratic tutoring framework for program debugging and miscon- ception repair that adapts prior planning-guided tutoring work (Li et al., 2026b). The framework is instantiated in the Python programming domain by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on synthetic multi-turn tutoring dialogues constructed from four preprocessed programming datasets. The system is evaluated using a predefined set of independent metrics and benchmarked against a general-purpose LLM. The experiments show that SocraticRepair achieves higher scores on stepwise scaffolding and question quality while also substantially reducing premature solution disclosure. The results also identify reliable pedagogical plan generation as an important remaining challenge.
papers.summary: Large language models used as programming tutors tend to reveal the solution too early and drift from the learner's current debugging goal. `SocraticRepair` adapts prior planning-guided tutoring work to Python debugging and misconception repair, fine-tuning `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct` on synthetic multi-turn tutoring dialogues built from four preprocessed programming datasets. Evaluated on a predefined set of independent metrics against a general-purpose LLM, it **scores higher on stepwise scaffolding and question quality while substantially reducing premature solution disclosure**, though reliable generation of pedagogical plans remains an open problem.

papers.title: MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning
papers.abstract: Efficient task scheduling in heterogeneous computing systems remains a fundamental challenge in embedded and high-level synthesis flows. This paper presents MoSAIC (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition), a learning-based framework that bridges the gap between exact and heuristic scheduling approaches for DAG-based applications. The system uses the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to learn the relationships between DAG structures and scheduling priority functions. The framework first leverages the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver [4] to generate optimal schedules, which are then used to supervise the learning of compact priority-based scheduling functions through Bayesian Optimization. These learned heuristics capture relationships between scheduling decisions and structural graph features such as rank, depth, and fanout, enabling the construction of a reusable knowledge base across diverse DAG instances. Experimental results across synthetic graph families and real-world benchmarks, including PolyBench and MachSuite, show that the learned heuristics consistently improve over classical approaches such as HEFT [2], while maintaining low runtime overhead. The results indicate that combining optimal supervision with learning-based generalization provides a practical approach for scalable and adaptive task scheduling.
papers.summary: Scheduling task graphs on heterogeneous computing systems forces a choice between exact solvers that do not scale and hand-crafted heuristics that leave quality on the table. `MoSAIC` (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition) uses the `OR-Tools CP-SAT` solver to produce optimal schedules for directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), then uses large-language-model reasoning and Bayesian optimization to learn compact priority functions over structural features such as rank, depth, and fanout, assembling them into a reusable knowledge base. Across synthetic graph families and the `PolyBench` and `MachSuite` benchmarks, the learned heuristics **consistently outperform the classical `HEFT` heuristic** while keeping runtime overhead low.

papers.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses.
