To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking
papers.summary: Depth-based dynamic inference lets a large language model emit outputs from intermediate layers to fit a compute budget, but its effect on resistance to jailbreak attacks, where adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment, had not been examined. The authors mount adversarial-suffix attacks against models with multiple exit depths and measure attack success, optimization loss, and utility at each exit. They find that **shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreaks than deeper ones**, that deeper exits let the adversarial suffix reach lower attack loss, and that the suffix degrades utility uniformly across depths. The results are offered as guidance for designing dynamic-inference schemes that preserve safety.

papers.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
papers.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.
papers.summary: Deep-research agents must carry investigation state across many model calls and catch errors before they propagate into later steps. `PANINI-DR` is a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from research and verification of individual subquestions, using a shared workspace built on the `Generative Semantic Workspace` representation to record subquestions, dependencies, findings, and evidence, with a dedicated verification agent checking each proposed answer against its evidence. Compared with seven deep-research harnesses sharing the same language-model backbone and frozen corpora on `BrowseComp-Plus`, `FRAMES`, and `MoNaCo`, it has the strongest average performance and **reaches 73.3% on `BrowseComp-Plus`, 16.0 points above the next-best harness**, with its largest edge on hard questions. It also retains the most evidence from which answers can be recovered, and accounting for evidence support widens its lead.

papers.title: Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.abstract: A recurrent-depth language model reuses one block of weights several times in a row. The number of repetitions, which we call loops, is chosen when the model runs, not when it is trained, and running fewer is cheaper and faster, so a deployment may choose to do it. Running fewer loops also makes these models less safe, and the loss of safety is larger than the loss of anything else we measured. We study four released Ouro checkpoints and Huginn-0125. At half of its trained depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking still solves 0.692 of the GSM8K maths problems, against 0.775 at full depth, keeping 89% of its accuracy. Over the same reduction, the rate at which it helps with harmful requests rises from 0.038 to 0.205, 5.3 times higher. The information is not lost: a linear classifier reads whether a request is harmful from the model's internal state after a single loop, with an ROC AUC of 0.967 against 0.986 at full depth. What the missing loops remove is the refusal that should follow. We measure the effect with four instruments, one generating no text at all, and reproduce it on a second model family. Removing a single direction from Ouro-1.4B's internal state at full depth drops its refusal rate on harmful prompts from 0.950 to 0.130, identifying what the shallow model is missing. Two run-time repairs do not help: the models' early-exit rules do not spend more loops on harmful requests, and choosing a depth per request does not recover the loss. Changing the training does. Standard safety training makes the shallow model safe only by refusing 0.865 of harmless requests, while training at randomly chosen depths reaches a separation of +0.399 between harmful and harmless refusal at one loop, against +0.118. On Huginn-0125 it keeps harmful help at or below 0.040 at every depth from 1 to 32 loops, where standard training reaches 0.194, and it costs no accuracy at full depth.
papers.summary: Recurrent-depth language models reuse one block of weights for a number of loops chosen at inference time, and running fewer loops is a cheap deployment knob whose safety cost had not been measured. The authors evaluate four `Ouro` checkpoints and `Huginn-0125` with four instruments, including one that generates no text, and find that at half its trained depth `Ouro-1.4B-Thinking` keeps 89% of its `GSM8K` accuracy while **its rate of complying with harmful requests rises from 0.038 to 0.205**. A linear probe still reads harmfulness from the internal state after a single loop, and ablating one direction at full depth collapses refusal from 0.950 to 0.130, so what shallow runs lose is the refusal behavior rather than the harm detection. Early-exit rules and per-request depth selection do not fix this, but training at randomly chosen depths keeps harmful help at or below 0.040 at every depth from 1 to 32 loops on `Huginn-0125` with no accuracy cost at full depth, whereas standard safety training only makes the shallow model safe by refusing most harmless requests.

papers.title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
papers.abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.
papers.summary: Agents can improve by using environment feedback to revise their harness, the software that manages model inputs, tools, memory, and execution, but prior work optimizes a single agent, and in a multi-agent system (MAS) a single global optimizer faces growing context and may be barred from seeing other agents' internals. `HarnessNet` builds the system from `Agentrons`, each pairing an evolvable harness and a frozen foundation model with a local optimizer that can only observe and edit that harness, arranged in a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward so each upstream optimizer receives node-specific feedback from the layer below. On `AgentBench` with several foundation models, **it matches the gains of a single global optimizer while keeping access local and using fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call**. A migration study shows the evolved harnesses stay jointly effective after the underlying models are swapped.

papers.title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Has Many Edges of Stability
papers.abstract: Recent observations that deep learning models train at the edge of stability have renewed interest in understanding stability properties of classical optimization algorithms. For quadratic objectives, standard gradient descent has a sharp stability threshold: it converges from every initialization when $\eta<2/L$, diverges from almost every initialization when $\eta>2/L$, and diverges from every nonzero initialization when $\eta>2/\mu$. For non-Euclidean gradient descent, the corresponding known guarantees are weaker: convergence holds for every initialization when $\eta<2/S$, where $S$ is the generalized sharpness, while every nonzero initialization diverges when $\eta>2/\mu$. The behavior in the intermediate regime $2/S<\eta<2/\mu$ is not fully characterized. We show that Hilbertian norms are the only ones for which $2/S$ is an almost-everywhere sharp threshold for every positive-definite quadratic objective. Using linear conjugacy between non-Euclidean and Euclidean gradient descent, we show that for general norms the intermediate regime can contain arbitrarily many edges of stability associated with distinct attracting directions. We identify a forward-invariant region of exponentially divergent directions beyond the generalized stability threshold. When the directions of minimum curvature are finite and nondegenerate, we prove that, sufficiently close to $2/\mu$ from below, only their invariant directions remain convergent. We give smooth two-dimensional constructions with arbitrarily many distinct thresholds, arbitrarily large relative threshold separation and show these properties to be stable.
papers.summary: For quadratic objectives, Euclidean gradient descent has a sharp stability threshold at a step size of 2/L, but for non-Euclidean gradient descent only a weaker picture was known: convergence below 2/S, where S is the generalized sharpness, and divergence above 2/μ, with the regime in between uncharacterized. The authors show that Hilbertian norms are the only norms for which 2/S is an almost-everywhere sharp threshold for every positive-definite quadratic, and through linear conjugacy to Euclidean descent they prove that **for general norms the intermediate regime can contain arbitrarily many distinct edges of stability**, each tied to its own attracting direction. They identify a forward-invariant region of exponentially divergent directions beyond the generalized threshold, show that when the minimum-curvature directions are finite and nondegenerate, only their invariant directions remain convergent near 2/μ, and give smooth two-dimensional constructions with arbitrarily many well-separated thresholds that are stable under perturbation.

papers.title: Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning of LLMs in Learnable Low-Rank Subspaces
papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). However, ZO optimization suffers from high variance in high-dimensional parameter spaces. While recent methods restrict perturbations to random low-rank subspaces, these subspaces often misalign with task-specific descent directions. We propose AdaSub-ZO, a novel forward-only fine-tuning framework in learnable low-rank subspaces. Instead of relying on fixed random matrices, AdaSub-ZO iteratively learns layer-wise projection matrices directly from finite-difference feedback to track task-aware descent directions. Furthermore, AdaSub-ZO incorporates a subspace momentum acceleration mechanism to smooth noisy gradient estimates across evolving subspace bases. Extensive experiments on natural language understanding tasks demonstrate that AdaSub-ZO outperforms existing ZO baselines, substantially reducing gradient estimation variance and accelerating convergence.
papers.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization fine-tunes large language models with forward passes only, saving memory, but its gradient estimates are high-variance in high dimensions, and restricting perturbations to random low-rank subspaces often misaligns them with the task's descent directions. `AdaSub-ZO` learns layer-wise projection matrices directly from finite-difference feedback so the subspace tracks task-aware descent directions, and adds subspace momentum to smooth noisy estimates across evolving bases. On natural language understanding tasks it **outperforms existing ZO baselines with substantially lower gradient-estimation variance and faster convergence**.

papers.title: Understanding Unified VLMs: From Attention Probing to Guidance Tuning for Multimodal Generation
papers.abstract: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) perform both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one shared Transformer backbone, yet how the backbone processes the condition in either direction remains poorly understood. We study this question from the perspective of conditional guidance: we probe every attention head to show the activation difference between two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) with different conditional guidance. On two unified VLMs of autoregressive and masked-diffusion paradigms, the probing reveals a subset of heads that are more sensitive to the change of condition while others are agnostic to it. This characteristic pattern holds in both T2I and I2T generation and is largely stable across data samples, demonstrating the internal mechanism of unified VLMs. Motivated by this, we propose a new inference-time intervention approach for unified multimodal generation, named \textit{HeadTuned-CFG}, which uses the probed condition-change awareness to select and tune the conditional guidance at the attention-head level. Experiments show consistent benefits in both multimodal generation directions of unified VLMs without additional training, and in particular substantial improvements over strong baselines in T2I generation. These results further support the key finding of our probing analysis: the observed pattern of functional specialization is an intrinsic property of unified VLMs.
papers.summary: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) handle both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one Transformer backbone, but how that backbone processes the conditioning signal in either direction is poorly understood. The authors probe every attention head for the activation difference between the two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) on an autoregressive and a masked-diffusion unified VLM, finding a subset of heads that are sensitive to the condition while the rest are agnostic, a pattern that holds in both directions and is stable across samples. Building on this, `HeadTuned-CFG` selects and tunes conditional guidance at the head level at inference time with no extra training, and **yields consistent gains in both directions with substantial improvements over strong baselines in T2I generation**.

papers.title: Words to World: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physical Environments
papers.abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.
papers.summary: Large language models can now invoke tools and operate devices, yet existing benchmarks score them on static text, offline tool calls, or simulations rather than on acting in the physical world. The authors present a closed-loop benchmark in which a model drives a harness connected to real robotic arms, cameras, and sensors, and must issue instructions, read physical feedback, interpret the resulting state, and adapt, exercising grounded perception, planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, and recovery from execution uncertainty. Experiments with representative models reveal **recurring failure modes of hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans**.

papers.title: Using Evidence-Centered Design to Guide Prompt Engineering in Measurement: An Illustration with Automated Essay Scoring
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models, particularly large language models (LLMs), are increasingly used in educational settings for tasks such as item generation, automated scoring, and feedback delivery. The quality of these outputs depends not only on the AI model but also on how users construct the prompts that guide model behaviors. Current prompt engineering practices are largely ad hoc, relying on trial and error rather than principled design. This lack of structure introduces validity threats including construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and limited reproducibility. We propose that Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), a framework in educational measurement for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, can serve as a principled foundation for prompt engineering in educational applications. We map the three core ECD models, the student model, the evidence model, and the task model, onto the components of educational prompt design, and describe a workflow for ECD-based prompt engineering. We derive five design principles from this mapping and present an empirical study contrasting ECD-designed prompts with state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting baselines on an automated scoring task. Our empirical study demonstrates the usefulness of this framework on automated scoring. Results suggest that treating prompting as assessment design rather than informal instructions strengthens the validity, reliability, and fairness of AI-generated educational outputs.
papers.summary: Prompt engineering for educational uses of large language models, such as automated scoring and feedback, is largely ad hoc, which threatens validity through construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and poor reproducibility. The authors propose Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), an educational-measurement framework for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, as a foundation for prompt design, mapping its student, evidence, and task models onto prompt components and deriving five design principles and a workflow. An empirical study on automated essay scoring contrasts ECD-designed prompts with state-of-the-art prompting baselines and **reports that treating prompting as assessment design improves the validity, reliability, and fairness of the scores**.

papers.title: MoMaTune: Model, Match, Then Tune Language Models for Numerical Records
papers.abstract: Despite remarkable progress in language understanding and generation, decoder language models continue to exhibit striking failures on numerical data. Numerical examples are typically serialized as text by concatenating feature names with their values (e.g., fat:3.4), while conventional task adaptation applies loss only to the downstream prediction target. This leaves two structures weakly supervised: within-value sensitivity, where digit position determines numerical magnitude, because token cross-entropy contains no explicit numerical metric; and across-field structure, where measurements in the same record are statistically dependent, because target-only tuning provides no direct loss on the measurements or their dependencies. We introduce MoMaTune (Model, Match, then Tune), a two-stage post-training strategy organized around these supervision gaps. Stage 1 applies Model, ordinary next-token prediction densely over label-free serialized records, and optionally adds Match, a same-record consistency objective that aligns representations of different partial views of the same example. Stage 2 applies Tune, supervised fine-tuning for downstream target prediction. We evaluate MoMaTune on 169,285 records from eight public datasets, with 339 of 340 input fields numerical. At 1.5B parameters, Model raises the eight-dataset masked-value imputation aggregate from 0.106 to 0.401, while the three-dataset correct-context gain rises from 0.058 to 0.167. On diagnostics, Model also increases sensitivity to numerically consequential digit changes, while Match improves robustness to informative partial views. Adding Tune yields higher target-supervised embedding aggregates for each tested Stage-1 parent, and the two-stage recipes obtain higher aggregate scores than Tune alone. The same pattern is observed at 4B, 9.6B, and 27B parameters when model embeddings are used for downstream prediction.
papers.summary: Decoder language models still fail badly on numerical records, which are usually serialized as feature-name and value pairs while fine-tuning applies loss only to the prediction target, leaving digit-position magnitude and cross-field dependencies unsupervised. `MoMaTune` (Model, Match, then Tune) first trains with dense next-token prediction over label-free serialized records, optionally adding a same-record consistency objective that aligns representations of different partial views of one example, and then applies supervised fine-tuning on the downstream target. On 169,285 records from eight public datasets at 1.5B parameters, **the `Model` stage raises the masked-value imputation aggregate from 0.106 to 0.401**, the `Match` objective improves robustness to partial views, and the two-stage recipes beat `Tune` alone, with the same pattern holding at 4B, 9.6B, and 27B parameters when embeddings are used for prediction.

papers.title: Framework for an AI-Ready ARPES Community Database
papers.abstract: Condensed matter stands to gain profoundly from widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). However, its current means of data organization impedes this endeavor. As a premier measure of electronic structure underlying material properties, Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) has accumulated over four decades of spectra, yet the community's publication-centered workflow preserves only a highly selected fraction of its experimental record. A shared data ecosystem could transform these fragmented measurements and their contexts into a persistent, collective scientific memory, creating immediate value for reproducibility and reuse while laying the foundation for AI-enabled discovery. In this Perspective, we report outcomes of a recent community workshop and propose a practical path toward such an ecosystem. Its benefits unfold along three timescales. In the near term, standardized, searchable, and citable datasets strengthen analysis pipelines independently of AI. In the intermediate future, community-validated tools operating across laboratories could enable broader reuse and increasingly closed-loop automated experiments. In the long term, a diverse corpus of measured electronic spectra could support foundation models for quantum matter. Looking forward, a diverse corpus of measured electronic spectra could support foundation models for quantum matter and new discoveries. We discuss lessons from existing scientific databases, the current state of AI in ARPES, as well as areas of community convergence on data organization, access, credit, governance, and a staged pilot program.
papers.summary: Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES), a central probe of electronic structure in condensed matter, has produced four decades of spectra, but a publication-centered workflow preserves only a small, selected fraction of that record, which blocks adoption of artificial intelligence in the field. The authors report outcomes of a community workshop and propose a shared data ecosystem whose payoff unfolds across three horizons: standardized, searchable, citable datasets in the near term, community-validated cross-laboratory tools and closed-loop automated experiments in the medium term, and **a diverse corpus of measured spectra that could support foundation models for quantum matter in the long term**. They draw lessons from existing scientific databases and lay out areas of convergence on data organization, access, credit, governance, and a staged pilot program.

papers.title: ClinEdge: An Expert-Graded Benchmark of Real Patient Edge Cases Where Frontier Multimodal Models Fail
papers.abstract:
Most benchmarks for large language models in medicine are built from licensing examinations and theoretical questions. The few that draw on real clinical data do so only in part, and rarely require a model to read a patient's own imaging. ClinEdge addresses this gap with 32 real, de-identified patient cases from active clinical practice, each evaluated across seven frontier systems for a total of 224 expert-graded evaluations. Each case pairs primary imaging with a short vignette, contains a feature known to defeat pattern-matched reasoning, and is scored against the patient's documented clinical course. The suite is built for depth rather than volume. Grading followed a two-stage expert process. First, a senior orthopaedic surgeon graded all 224 responses on a weighted rubric and a pass-or-fail verdict. Second, a panel of nineteen physicians, largely senior specialists at teaching medical colleges, independently reviewed every case and every one of the 224 grades. All seven production systems were evaluated through their public interfaces, and all 224 conversations are preserved as replayable links.
  Performance was poor across all systems, and the failures were shared: different vendors missed the same findings and converged on the same wrong plans. From the experts' notes we catalogue 18 recurring failure modes in five families. The models stop reading an image at the first finding. They give generic plans and lean toward over-treatment. They trust a misleading history over correct imaging. Their answers vary across systems and runs, and change with question format. Failing answers were delivered fluently and without any expressed uncertainty. Four cases are released in full; the remaining 28 are held out, and we invite frontier AI labs and healthcare AI companies to evaluate their models against them (research@futrbridge.com)
papers.summary: Medical benchmarks for large language models are mostly built from licensing exams and rarely require reading a patient's own imaging, so `ClinEdge` assembles 32 de-identified real cases, each pairing primary imaging with a short vignette and containing a feature designed to defeat pattern-matched reasoning, scored against the patient's documented clinical course. Seven frontier systems were queried through their public interfaces, every response was graded by a senior orthopaedic surgeon on a weighted rubric with a pass-or-fail verdict, and every grade was reviewed by a panel of nineteen physicians. **All seven systems performed poorly and failed in the same ways**, and from the experts' notes the authors catalogue 18 recurring failure modes in five families, including stopping at the first imaging finding, defaulting to generic over-treatment plans, trusting a misleading history over correct imaging, and delivering wrong answers fluently with no expressed uncertainty. Four cases are released in full and the remaining 28 are held out for labs to evaluate against.

papers.title: Explicit Bounds on Hoffman Constants for Sparse Polyhedral Regularizers
papers.abstract: Hoffman constants quantify the distance to the solution set of a polyhedral system in terms of its residual; they control error bounds, geometric conditioning, the convergence rate of first-order iterative algorithms, and the stability of regression estimators to target perturbations. Despite their importance, explicit values of Hoffman constants are rarely available due to their computational complexity. In this paper, we derive explicit bounds on the Hoffman constant for a class of structured polyhedral systems arising in sparse regularization. We show that the constants admit a decomposition into spectral, geometric, and interaction components, which together determine their scaling behavior. This framework explains the gap between worst-case dimension-dependent bounds and the favorable conditioning observed empirically in structured problems. As a primary application, we analyze $\ell_1$-regularized least squares, demonstrating that the effective constants depend on low-dimensional active subspaces rather than the ambient dimension. We then extend to the elastic net and adaptive $\ell_1$-regularized formulations, demonstrating how the underlying optimization geometry is altered by the $\ell_2$ penalty and reweighting scheme. Furthermore, we relate our results to classical statistical assumptions and show that the restricted eigenvalue condition bounds only the primal curvature of the active set, leaving the dual interaction geometry unconstrained and is thus insufficient alone for fast theoretical convergence rates. We further show standard $\ell_\infty$ coherence conditions do not yield dimension-independent Euclidean bounds to close this gap. Our theoretical results show that Hoffman constants admit explicit, interpretable forms in structured regression settings and, in practice, provide actionable tools for post-hoc feature pruning and a priori optimal hyperparameter selection.
papers.summary: Hoffman constants bound the distance from a point to the solution set of a polyhedral system by its residual, governing error bounds and first-order convergence rates, yet explicit values are rarely available because they are hard to compute. The work derives explicit bounds for structured polyhedral systems arising in sparse regularization, decomposing the constants into spectral, geometric, and interaction components that explain why structured problems are better conditioned than worst-case dimension-dependent bounds suggest. For L1-regularized least squares, **the effective constants depend on a low-dimensional active subspace rather than the ambient dimension**, with extensions to the `elastic net` and adaptive L1 formulations showing how the L2 penalty and reweighting alter the geometry. The analysis also shows that the restricted eigenvalue condition constrains only primal curvature of the active set and that L-infinity coherence conditions do not yield dimension-independent Euclidean bounds, while offering practical tools for post-hoc feature pruning and a priori hyperparameter selection.

papers.title: EvolvAttack: Backdooring self Evolving VLM Agents
papers.abstract: Self-evolving mechanisms let vision-language model (VLM) agents continually adapt through evolving memory, but they also allow malicious behavior to emerge only after deployment. We introduce a new attack surface, the self-evolving backdoor, whose payload stays dormant in the initial agent and is progressively activated as the agent evolves. Unlike conventional backdoors, which can be exposed by testing triggered inputs on a static model, our attack requires both a visual trigger and a sufficiently evolved memory state; static scanning with clean memory thus yields near-zero attack success and may deem the agent benign. We realize this through memory-aware backdoor training, which couples trigger activation with the agent's evolving memory while preserving benign behavior unless the trigger co-occurs with payload-related memory. Across three VLM backbones, four agent pipelines, and recency-, semantic-, and reward-based memory evolution, the attack preserves normal functionality and stays nearly inactive before evolution (0.5% attack success rate), yet exceeds 95% attack success within 100 interactions, revealing a stealthy threat unique to self-evolving agents.
papers.summary: Self-evolving vision-language model (VLM) agents adapt after deployment through evolving memory, which opens a route for malicious behavior to appear only once the agent has been in use. The work introduces the self-evolving backdoor, implanted via memory-aware backdoor training so that the payload fires only when a visual trigger co-occurs with payload-related content in the agent's evolved memory, leaving static scans on clean memory ineffective. Across three VLM backbones, four agent pipelines, and recency-, semantic-, and reward-based memory evolution, the attack holds a 0.5% success rate before evolution yet **exceeds 95% attack success within 100 interactions** while preserving benign functionality.

papers.title: ObsSpec: Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents alternate between model generation and tool execution, waiting for each tool call to complete before starting the next generation. This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi-turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec, an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co-training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal-use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at https://github.com/kylemontgomery1/verl-recipe/tree/obsspec/obsspec.
papers.summary: Tool-using agents must wait for each tool call to finish before generating the next turn, and this serial pattern dominates the cost of agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which needs large batches of multi-turn rollouts. `ObsSpec` runs a small co-trained world model that predicts tool outputs while the real environment executes, letting the policy start generating early and keeping the speculative work only when the prediction matches the actual observation exactly, so rollout collection stays lossless. On terminal-use tasks, a 0.6B world model matches real observations exactly in 66.4% of attempts and returns about 16 times faster, **cutting agent latency by 9.3% for an 8B policy and 14.2% for a 32B policy**. Because generation overlaps with tool execution, the approach composes with existing RL acceleration techniques.

papers.title: Correlation-Aware Reconstruction for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Reconstruction-based detectors for multivariate time series anomaly detection typically learn a single entangled representation of normal behavior and flag anomalies based on reconstruction error. However, real-world anomalies are not only isolated spikes in a single channel but also disruptions in the relationships between channels, where each sensor individually appears normal, but their joint behavior deviates from the norm. Because these models compress both temporal evolution and inter-channel structure into this single space, they lack an explicit mechanism to isolate such inter-channel dependencies from normal temporal dependencies, leading to lower detection rates for cross-channel anomalies. We propose CARMA (Correlation-Aware Reconstruction for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection), which is a reconstruction-based variational autoencoder with two complementary latent spaces: a temporal latent that captures sequential dynamics, and a correlation latent that is trained to reconstruct the window's pairwise Pearson correlations. Both representations are fused in the signal decoder, and anomalies are detected from the reconstruction error. We evaluate CARMA on the TSB-AD-M benchmark suite (17 datasets, 180 series) against 29 baseline methods, and show that it significantly outperforms all of them across multiple threshold-free and range-aware metrics, achieving a VUS-PR of 0.4929. Ablations show that removing the correlation branch degrades performance, that adding a second latent without supervision recovers only part of the gain, and that supervising the correlation latent with an explicit correlation target accounts for the rest and produces a sharper error response at anomalies.
papers.summary: Reconstruction-based anomaly detectors for multivariate time series learn a single entangled representation of normal behavior, which leaves them weak at catching anomalies where each channel looks normal but the relationships between channels break. `CARMA` is a variational autoencoder with two latent spaces, one for temporal dynamics and one trained to reconstruct the window's pairwise Pearson correlations, fused in a shared signal decoder that scores anomalies by reconstruction error. On the `TSB-AD-M` benchmark suite of 17 datasets and 180 series, it **outperforms all 29 baselines across threshold-free and range-aware metrics**, reaching a VUS-PR of 0.4929. Ablations show that removing the correlation branch degrades results and that explicitly supervising it with a correlation target accounts for most of the gain over an unsupervised second latent.

papers.title: Sequent-Prover: Training Agents for Formal, Checkable SMT-based Reasoning
papers.abstract: We introduce Sequent-Prover, a family of verifier-using language-model agents, and the post-training framework that produces them. Agents reason in an executable SMT-LIB scratchpad: they write complete SMT-LIB programs, query Z3 across turns, inspect solver feedback, repair formalizations, and terminate with an explicit answer. Our recipe, verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, bootstraps from a noisy teacher proposal policy by sampling multi-turn trajectories, retaining the successful tail that is correct, non-trivial, grounded, and executable, then applying supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level preference optimization. Because solver success alone does not guarantee semantic faithfulness, we evaluate task accuracy, k-sample reliability, and SMT program quality. Across 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per model family, post-training raises the 4B model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and four-sample all-correct reliability (pass^4}) from 64.1% to 91.7%. It also reduces average SMT calls from 4.10 to 2.52 and tokens per attempt from 18.97k to 12.72k. Sequent-Prover agents give answers backed by executable formal artifacts.
papers.summary: `Sequent-Prover` is a family of language-model agents that reason inside an executable satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) scratchpad, writing complete SMT-LIB programs, querying the `Z3` solver across turns, repairing formalizations from solver feedback, and ending with an explicit answer. The post-training recipe, verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, samples multi-turn trajectories from a noisy teacher, keeps only those that are correct, non-trivial, grounded, and executable, then applies supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level preference optimization. Since solver success does not guarantee semantic faithfulness, evaluation covers accuracy, multi-sample reliability, and SMT program quality across 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per model family. Post-training **lifts the 4B model's per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0%** and four-sample all-correct reliability from 64.1% to 91.7%, while reducing average solver calls from 4.10 to 2.52 and tokens per attempt from roughly 19k to 12.7k.

papers.title: RECAP: Calibrating Low-Bit Reasoning Models on the History They Read
papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the cost of serving reasoning models but can substantially degrade long chains of thought. Each step reads cached keys and values spanning thousands of tokens, allowing quantization errors to accumulate along the trajectory. Standard calibration operates on short segments that omit the earlier context needed by later reasoning steps. Even when this context is retained, cache reconstruction error alone does not capture how quantization errors affect subsequent attention. We present RECAP, a post-training quantization method that calibrates reasoning models on the history they read. Dynamic-prefix calibration separates long historical context from short-block reconstruction. It regenerates prefix keys and values with the current quantizer and rotates the active block to supervise every position along the trajectory. Prefix read geometry further supervises historical cache errors according to their effects on attention outputs, weighting key and value errors asymmetrically. With both components applied only during calibration, RECAP outperforms the baseline across multiple reasoning models and quantization settings. Under W4A4KV4, RECAP improves accuracy over the baseline by 13.3 percentage points on MATH500 with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 15.8 points on AIME-120 with Qwen3-4B. These results highlight the importance of preserving historical dependencies during calibration for low-bit reasoning.
papers.summary: Low-bit quantization makes reasoning models cheaper to serve but can badly degrade long chains of thought, because each step reads cached keys and values spanning thousands of tokens and quantization errors accumulate along the trajectory, while standard calibration on short segments omits that history. `RECAP` is a post-training quantization method with two calibration-only components: dynamic-prefix calibration regenerates long prefix keys and values with the current quantizer and rotates the supervised block to cover every position, and prefix read geometry weights key and value errors asymmetrically according to their effect on attention outputs. Under 4-bit weights, activations, and KV cache, it **improves accuracy over the baseline by 13.3 points on `MATH500` with `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B`** and by 15.8 points on `AIME-120` with `Qwen3-4B`.

papers.title: LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics for World Models
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models directly in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. On conservative and actuated visual pendulum environments, LeHami substantially improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA world model and empirically maintains constant latent volume where the baseline contracts. The learned flow also supports accurate integration at unseen sub-frame step sizes and numerical time reversal. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.
papers.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors can contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (`LeHami`) replaces the predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a position-momentum latent state integrated by an exactly symplectic leapfrog step, which preserves phase-space volume and so rules out uniform contraction, stable fixed points, and merging of distinct states regardless of learned parameters or action sequence. On conservative and actuated visual pendulum environments, it **substantially improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA world model** and maintains constant latent volume where the baseline contracts, while also supporting integration at unseen sub-frame step sizes and numerical time reversal.

papers.title: Do correct answers have stable latent knowledge support?
papers.abstract: Large language models are typically evaluated in terms of the correctness of their output. However, output correctness alone does not confirm whether the latent knowledge supporting an answer has stable internal representations. We therefore propose latent state stability (LSS) and knowledge topology stability (KTS) to investigate the stability of individual knowledge states and their relational structure, respectively. Specifically, we first separately average the model's internal representations of the same knowledge under each elicitation condition. Using the mean representation under the baseline condition as a reference, we remove shared shifts to obtain corrected representations. We then formulate LSS as the distance between each corrected representation and its reference representation, normalized against the typical distance between knowledge items of the same type. We formulate KTS as the cross-condition consistency of the ordered pairwise representation distances among knowledge items of the same type. Next, we construct EpiStableBench, which comprises 4,411 items spanning factual knowledge and mathematical reasoning, with 76,766 controlled queries. Across 16 LLMs from four families, representation stability varies substantially even among items answered correctly under the base condition. Within models, higher stability generally corresponds to higher accuracy under held-out elicitation conditions; across models, stability does not consistently increase with model size or overall accuracy. Meanwhile, we present LatentDPO to learn a knowledge-editing policy that accounts for the stability of latent knowledge. Experimental results show that integrating LatentDPO with multiple existing editing methods consistently improves editing success and generalization across different expressions.
papers.summary: Output correctness does not reveal whether the internal representations supporting an answer stay stable when the same knowledge is elicited in different ways. The work defines latent state stability (LSS), the normalized drift of a knowledge item's corrected mean representation across elicitation conditions, and knowledge topology stability (KTS), the cross-condition consistency of pairwise representation distances among related items, and measures both on `EpiStableBench`, 4,411 factual and mathematical items with 76,766 controlled queries. Across 16 LLMs from four families, **stability varies substantially even among items answered correctly**, higher stability within a model predicts accuracy under held-out elicitation conditions, and stability does not consistently grow with model size or overall accuracy. A stability-aware knowledge-editing policy, `LatentDPO`, consistently improves editing success and generalization when combined with existing editing methods.

papers.title: GeoBridge: Evolving Transferable Decoder Topologies for Geometric Vision
papers.abstract: Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction share a need for multi-scale feature processing, yet use different prediction interfaces and training objectives. Whether a decoder's internal computation can be optimized once and reused across these systems remains a structural design question. Search over primitive configurations alone leaves the organization of transformations fixed. To address this gap, we propose GeoBridge, an evolutionary framework for transferable decoder topologies. First, GeoBridge makes stage-internal topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of configurable primitives. Shape-preserving composition retains the stage interfaces of a fixed multi-scale scaffold. Second, a functional-tree encoding supports stage-aware crossover and hierarchical mutation, while a gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy evaluates candidates without training. Multi-objective evolution balances this proxy with computation and parameter cost. Third, selected topologies are instantiated and trained in target systems with task-specific prediction interfaces. A single source search takes approximately 12 GPU hours. GeoBridgeNet-A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines under a common encoder and training protocol on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI. The same topology reaches 27.11 dB PSNR in Gaussian novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K, and its refined representations support open-vocabulary segmentation on LERF. These results support decoder topology as a reusable design object across the evaluated geometric vision systems. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/EMI-Group/GeoBridge-NAS.
papers.summary: Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction both need multi-scale feature decoding but differ in prediction interfaces and training objectives, raising the question of whether a decoder's internal topology can be optimized once and reused across them. `GeoBridge` makes stage-internal topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of primitives inside a fixed multi-scale scaffold, encodes candidates as functional trees for stage-aware crossover and mutation, and ranks them with a training-free gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy under multi-objective evolution against compute and parameter cost. A single search takes about 12 GPU hours, and the resulting `GeoBridgeNet-A3` **achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines on `NYU Depth V2` and `KITTI`** under a shared encoder, while the same topology reaches 27.11 dB PSNR for novel-view synthesis on `RealEstate10K` and supports open-vocabulary segmentation on `LERF`.

papers.title: Imperfect Verifiers, Exact Targets: Inference-Time Scaling for Continuous Generation
papers.abstract: Verifier-guided inference-time scaling uses additional computation to score intermediate states and steer generation toward better outputs. However, imperfect intermediate verifiers can distort sampling, and repeated refinement alone does not ensure recovery of the desired reward-tilted distribution. We introduce Continuous-State Verifier-Guided Backtracking (CS-VGB), an inference-time scaling method for sampling from reward-tilted distributions with continuous generative models through repeated denoising and renoising. With correctly paired denoising and renoising transitions, the stationary distribution of CS-VGB at the clean checkpoint equals the desired reward-tilted target, even when intermediate verifiers are inaccurate. Under stated regularity conditions, CS-VGB converges exponentially to the target despite verifier error, and the expected number of updates needed to reach a clean sample grows only linearly with the number of checkpoints. In analytically tractable settings, we empirically demonstrate that CS-VGB recovers the desired reward-tilted distribution despite verifier error, whereas the compared verifier-based sampling methods fail to recover the target under the same verifier errors. We also instantiate the framework with diffusion models and one-step stochastic posterior maps. Across prompt-guided ImageNet generation, facial-attribute generation on CelebA, and multi-robot planning, recurrent CS-VGB search improves reward and task success as inference budgets grow, with image-generation rewards continuing beyond the observed plateaus of denoising-only baselines.
papers.summary: Verifier-guided inference-time scaling scores intermediate states to steer generation, but inaccurate intermediate verifiers can distort sampling, and repeated refinement alone does not guarantee recovery of the intended reward-tilted distribution. Continuous-State Verifier-Guided Backtracking (`CS-VGB`) samples from reward-tilted targets with continuous generative models by alternating denoising and renoising, and with correctly paired transitions **its stationary distribution at the clean checkpoint equals the desired target even when intermediate verifiers are inaccurate**, with exponential convergence under regularity conditions and expected update counts growing only linearly in the number of checkpoints. In analytically tractable settings it recovers the target where compared verifier-based samplers fail, and instantiated with diffusion models and one-step stochastic posterior maps on prompt-guided `ImageNet` generation, `CelebA` attribute generation, and multi-robot planning, reward and task success keep improving with inference budget beyond the plateaus of denoising-only baselines.

papers.title: North or South? Diagnosing LLMs' Understanding of North Korean Language, Society, and Knowledge
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in multilingual question answering, yet their ability to understand low-resource sociolinguistic contexts remains under-explored. We study North Korea as a unique testbed where decades of division have produced distinct differences from South Korea in vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse. We introduce LENS (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society), a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 questions evaluating LLMs across three dimensions: linguistic robustness, sociocultural perspective alignment, and domain-specific knowledge. Evaluating diverse recent LLMs, we find a modest performance drop on North Korean language inputs, a larger gap in sociocultural perspective alignment, and severe limitations on domain-specific knowledge. Qualitative analysis reveals that models often conflate formal institutions with lived realities, project liberal-democratic assumptions, or rely on coarse stereotypes. Our results demonstrate that linguistic similarity alone does not guarantee sociocultural or domain-specific understanding, highlighting the critical need for grounded evaluation resources for underrepresented cultural and political contexts.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) handle multilingual question answering well, but their grasp of low-resource sociolinguistic contexts is largely untested, and North Korea offers a case where decades of division have produced distinct vocabulary, orthography, norms, and ideological discourse relative to South Korea. `LENS` (Language and sociocultural Evaluation for North Korean Society) is a human-validated benchmark of 1,765 questions covering linguistic robustness, sociocultural perspective alignment, and domain-specific knowledge. Recent LLMs show a modest drop on North Korean language inputs, a larger gap in perspective alignment, and **severe limitations on domain-specific knowledge**, with qualitative analysis showing models conflating formal institutions with lived realities, projecting liberal-democratic assumptions, and relying on coarse stereotypes.

papers.title: What a Data Release Must Preserve for Off-Policy Evaluation
papers.abstract: In off-policy evaluation, merging decision-time histories that matter differently for a specified policy value or comparison can make that evaluation unidentified, even with observed actions and outcomes and known behavior and target policies. We characterize which distinctions must be preserved: identification holds if and only if the action-specific evaluation weights are constant within each released record, and the coarsest exact release groups histories by these weights. For normalized outcomes, the largest sharp width induced by the release equals a behavior-weighted within-record radius of these weights. The same radius becomes a release-design objective when each record may be refined into at most $m$ categories. The optimum has an exact $m$-center characterization. When behavior does not vary within a released record, we give a finite-data repair algorithm whose maximum evaluation-weight radius is at most twice the finite-data optimum. For a fixed action-outcome distribution within a released record, a distinct sharp-identification problem remains. Under the same condition, the action-specific outcome distributions are identified, and optimizing over their couplings gives the sharp interval. We construct an AIPW envelope containing this sharp interval; it matches the interval for all such outcome distributions exactly when the extreme within-record action-coefficient vectors take at most two values in each action coordinate. In 24 KuaiRec tasks, the repair algorithm yields a 93% median reduction in mean pairwise sharp width at $m=64$ relative to the unrepaired release.
papers.summary: In off-policy evaluation, a data release that merges decision-time histories which matter differently for the target policy can leave the policy value unidentified even when actions, outcomes, and both behavior and target policies are known. The work characterizes exactly which distinctions a release must preserve: identification holds if and only if the action-specific evaluation weights are constant within each released record, the coarsest exact release groups histories by those weights, and for normalized outcomes the largest sharp interval width equals a behavior-weighted within-record radius of the weights. That radius becomes a design objective when each record may be split into at most m categories, admitting an exact m-center characterization and a finite-data repair algorithm within a factor of two of optimal, alongside an AIPW envelope that contains the sharp identification interval. On 24 `KuaiRec` tasks, **the repair algorithm reduces median mean pairwise sharp width by 93% at m=64** relative to the unrepaired release.

papers.title: FragFlex: Fragment-Based Flexible Molecular Generation for Exploring Vast Chemical Space
papers.abstract: Drug discovery requires efficient exploration of an astronomically large chemical space. Molecular graph diffusion models offer a promising approach to this task, but many require graph size to be fixed before generation. Although atom-level insertion and deletion can enable flexible-size generation, jointly modeling molecular size, atom types, and bonds while maintaining chemical validity remains challenging. We introduce FragFlex, a flexible-length discrete diffusion model that performs node insertion and deletion at the fragment level. During denoising, FragFlex jointly learns the size, fragment identities, and inter-fragment connectivity of the fragment graph. A neural attachment-site predictor and valence-aware assembler then convert the generated fragment graph into an atom-level molecule. In large-scale experiments generating 10 million molecules, FragFlex achieves near-perfect chemical validity while maintaining high uniqueness, demonstrating a strong balance between the two.
papers.summary: Molecular graph diffusion models are a promising route to exploring chemical space for drug discovery, but many require the graph size to be fixed in advance, and atom-level insertion and deletion struggle to jointly model size, atom types, and bonds while keeping molecules chemically valid. `FragFlex` is a flexible-length discrete diffusion model that inserts and deletes nodes at the fragment level, jointly learning fragment-graph size, fragment identities, and inter-fragment connectivity during denoising, after which a neural attachment-site predictor and valence-aware assembler convert the fragment graph into an atom-level molecule. In experiments generating 10 million molecules, it **achieves near-perfect chemical validity while maintaining high uniqueness**.

papers.title: Protein Crystallization Segmentation and Classification Using Subordinate Color Channel in Fluorescence Microscopy Images
papers.abstract: The accuracy of detecting protein crystals for fluorescence microscopy images is very critical for high throughput and automated systems. Although the trace fluorescent labeling method could highlight protein crystals, reflection and emission from the fluorescence dye is not always due to crystal regions. Therefore, the analysis of the peak wavelength in the emission spectra of a fluorophore may not always yield effective results. In this paper, we show that using the subordinate color intensity corresponding to longer wavelengths than the peak wavelength of the emission spectra could improve the accuracy of protein crystal detection. Hence, we have built a segmentation method based on the percentile intensity of the subordinate color for trace fluorescently labeled (TFL'd) protein crystallization trial images. Compared to using the dominant color channel, our segmentation method on subordinate color channel was able to reduce the misclassification rate of likely-leads or crystals as non-crystals by the percentage of from 9.71% to 2.02% depending on the classifier. Similarly, the accuracy of classifiers were increased by the percentage of from 1.77% to 5.53%. Our method reached around 94% accuracy while keeping misclassification of likely-leads and crystals as non-crystals below 1%. Moreover, to evaluate the generalizability of our method, we have conducted new wet lab experiments on two proteins, Concanavalin A (Con A) and Ab inorganic pyrophosphate (AbIPPase), and the misclassification rate was below 1%. Our experiments show that using the subordinate channel may be more helpful for TFL'd protein trial image classification.
papers.summary: Automated detection of protein crystals in fluorescence microscopy images is complicated because trace fluorescent labeling highlights crystals but dye reflection and emission also occur outside crystal regions, so relying on the peak emission wavelength is unreliable. The work segments trace fluorescently labeled crystallization trial images using percentile intensity in the subordinate color channel, corresponding to wavelengths longer than the emission peak, instead of the dominant channel. Compared to the dominant channel, this **reduces misclassification of crystals and likely leads as non-crystals by 2.02% to 9.71% depending on the classifier** and raises classifier accuracy by 1.77% to 5.53%, reaching around 94% accuracy, with new wet-lab trials on Concanavalin A and an inorganic pyrophosphatase keeping misclassification below 1%.

papers.title: Co-DSL: Human-LLM Co-design of Reusable Spatial Concepts for Layout Generation
papers.abstract: We present Co-DSL, a framework in which users and LLMs co-design reusable spatial concepts for layout generation. In the first stage, our system allows users to create a library of personalized operations. To add a concept, a user provides a description, which the LLM converts into an initial implementation. The user can then observe the concept's execution behavior over example scenarios and provide lightweight feedback to the LLM, which revises the concept's implementation logic. In the second stage, given a library, an LLM can author a layout program that meets a new layout request from a user. Executing a layout program instantiates a concept-graph, a declarative composition of library concepts. In this way, we require the LLM only to specify which concepts should hold, while we use a solver to search for a layout that satisfies them. Across five spatial layout domains, we find that Co-DSL libraries let LLMs capture layout patterns that are challenging for prior fixed-operation systems, and demonstrate that our concept-graph representation is needed for LLMs to reliably compose concepts together. We further find that Co-DSL lets LLMs author generative layout programs that expose high-level parametric controls users can manipulate to explore a distribution of related layouts without re-prompting.
papers.summary: Layout generation systems that hand an LLM a fixed set of spatial operations struggle to capture patterns outside that vocabulary. `Co-DSL` lets users and an LLM co-design a library of reusable spatial concepts: the user describes a concept, the LLM implements it, and the user refines it with lightweight feedback after watching it execute on example scenarios. Given a library, the LLM then writes a layout program whose execution yields a concept-graph, a declarative composition of concepts, and a solver searches for a layout satisfying them, so the LLM only has to specify which concepts should hold. Across five spatial layout domains, **the co-designed libraries let LLMs capture layout patterns that prior fixed-operation systems miss**, the concept-graph representation proves necessary for reliable composition, and the resulting programs expose parametric controls for exploring related layouts without re-prompting.

papers.title: OntoAR-HAR: Ontology-Guided Agentic RAG with Personalized Memory for Human Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly support sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) by linking motion signals with activity semantics and physical knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds decisions in sensor examples and domain features, enabling training-free target-user inference with less dependence on raw numerical arrays. However, existing LLM/RAG-based HAR typically searches single-level activity spaces using static population knowledge. Consequently, they compare many unrelated candidates using the same static population evidence and overlook personalized motion patterns. We propose OntoAR-HAR, an ontology-guided agentic RAG framework combining static population and personalized knowledge. Its tree-structured activity ontology decomposes classification into local decisions among semantically related activities. The static store supplies node-constrained examples, while offline-discovered executable signal features provide numerical evidence for local distinctions. During inference, the personalized store collects selected user observations, which the LLM integrates with static knowledge and signal features while traversing the ontology to an activity label. Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments show complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across multiple LLM backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance. By explicitly modeling hierarchical relations across activity granularities, OntoAR-HAR also addresses the long-overlooked semantic inclusion problem and avoids treating related labels as independent categories.
papers.summary: LLMs increasingly support sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR), and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds their decisions in sensor examples and domain features, but existing approaches search a flat activity space with static population knowledge, comparing many unrelated candidates and ignoring individual motion patterns. `OntoAR-HAR` is an ontology-guided agentic RAG framework whose tree-structured activity ontology breaks classification into local decisions among semantically related activities, drawing on a static store of node-constrained examples and offline-discovered executable signal features plus a personalized store of selected observations from the target user. Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments show **complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across multiple LLM backbones**, reaching state-of-the-art accuracy while explicitly modeling semantic inclusion among activity labels at different granularities.

papers.title: HGA-Quant: Heterogeneity-Aware Quantization for AutoRegressive Visual Generation Models
papers.abstract: Recently, AutoRegressive Visual Generation (ARVG) models have emerged as a competitive paradigm for high-quality image synthesis. However, their substantial computational and memory demands make them difficult to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) provides a promising solution to reduce the computational and memory costs of ARVG models, yet existing methods often suffer from substantial image quality degradation under low-bit quantization. In this paper, we propose a training-free PTQ framework for ARVG, consisting of Tail-Aware Bounded-init Grid Refinement (T-BGR) and Coarse-to-Fine Activation Precision Scheduling (CAPS). T-BGR introduces a tail-aware reconstruction objective for weight quantizer calibration, assigning greater importance to distribution-tail coefficients and preserving fine-grained information without introducing additional parameters or high-precision branches. CAPS performs coarse-to-fine activation precision scheduling by jointly considering the importance and computational cost of different generation stages, enabling efficient mixed-precision allocation under a given bit budget. Extensive experiments on multiple ARVG backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently improves robustness under aggressive low-bit quantization. Notably, on Infinity, our framework achieves near full-precision image generation quality at an effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while existing methods at W4A6 still exhibit noticeable quality degradation or inconsistent performance. Code is available at https://github.com/lxm-lc/HGA-Quant.
papers.summary: AutoRegressive Visual Generation (ARVG) models produce high-quality images but their compute and memory demands hinder deployment on edge devices, and existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods degrade image quality sharply at low bit widths. `HGA-Quant` is a training-free PTQ framework with two parts: Tail-Aware Bounded-init Grid Refinement (T-BGR) calibrates weight quantizers with a reconstruction objective that emphasizes distribution-tail coefficients without extra parameters or high-precision branches, and Coarse-to-Fine Activation Precision Scheduling (CAPS) allocates mixed activation precision across generation stages by weighing their importance against computational cost under a bit budget. On the `Infinity` backbone, it **reaches near full-precision image quality at an effective W4A5.6 precision**, whereas existing methods at W4A6 still show noticeable degradation or inconsistent results.

papers.title: CHEAR: Confusion-Hierarchy Evidence-Aware Reasoning for Cost-Efficient Human Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a new approach to wearable-sensor-based human activity recognition. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) further introduces similar motion examples and discriminative sensor knowledge, enabling decisions grounded in observations relevant to the current query. More evidence, however, does not necessarily mean better-organized evidence. When online prompts and LLM agents primarily orchestrate inference, decisions about which activities to compare and when to invoke discriminative knowledge remain concentrated at inference time. As the activity vocabulary grows, the model must repeatedly process more candidates and associated knowledge, whereas pruning candidates too early risks excluding the true activity. We propose confusion-hierarchy evidence-aware reasoning (CHEAR), which moves part of this knowledge organization offline. CHEAR constructs and validates an activity hierarchy from recurrent cross-subject retrieval errors and builds corresponding activity-pair knowledge. At inference time, the hierarchy orders candidate comparisons; the LLM retains candidates progressively, and local discriminative knowledge is accessed only for the remaining activities. Across eight datasets, CHEAR achieves 86.79\% mean cross-subject accuracy, a 75.91\% candidate reduction rate, and 96.44\% true-activity retention. Per-sample token use is 85.15\% lower on average than in a variant without the hierarchical structure. Mean accuracy across eight cross-dataset transfer directions is 88.81\%. These results show that organizing candidates and discriminative knowledge around observed activity confusions reduces online LLM input while maintaining recognition performance.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can classify wearable-sensor activities from similar motion examples and discriminative knowledge, but when candidate selection and knowledge lookup happen entirely at inference time, prompt size grows with the activity vocabulary while pruning candidates early risks dropping the true activity. Confusion-hierarchy evidence-aware reasoning (`CHEAR`) moves part of this organization offline by building and validating an activity hierarchy from recurrent cross-subject retrieval errors along with activity-pair knowledge; at inference the hierarchy orders comparisons, the LLM retains candidates progressively, and local discriminative knowledge is loaded only for the remaining activities. Across eight datasets it reaches 86.79% mean cross-subject accuracy with a 75.91% candidate reduction rate and 96.44% true-activity retention, **cutting per-sample token use by 85.15% on average** relative to a variant without the hierarchy, and averages 88.81% accuracy across eight cross-dataset transfer directions.

papers.title: WisdomNet: trustable machine learning toward error-free classification
papers.abstract: Misclassification is a critical problem in many machine learning applications. Since even the classifier models with high accuracy (e.g., > 95%) still introduce some misclassification error, it may not be possible to rely on the output of a classifier. In this paper, we introduce trustable learning, which prompts the learning model to yield only the true output, thus avoiding misclassifications. Whenever the model cannot decide the output accurately, the learning model should indicate that there could be a misclassification error if it is forced to classify, and hence, it should reject to make a decision or defer it to a human expert. Therefore, we develop a methodology for trustable learning and apply it to artificial neural networks and show that it is possible to develop a classifier with 0% misclassification error. We propose a novel neural network architecture named WisdomNet that could provide zero prediction error by introducing an additional neuron named as conjugate neuron that would indicate whether the network is able to classify the data correctly or not. The WisdomNet architecture can be applied to any previously built model, and we have evaluated WisdomNet with several network architectures such as multilayer perceptron, convolutional neural network, and deep network on different data sets. The results show that the WisdomNet is able to reduce the classification error rate to 0%, while labeling the data is difficult to classify as `reject' at a low percentage of within around 10%.
papers.summary: Even highly accurate classifiers still make some errors, which limits how far their outputs can be trusted in critical applications. The work proposes trustable learning, in which a model outputs only answers it can make correctly and otherwise rejects or defers to a human expert, and realizes it in `WisdomNet`, a neural network architecture that adds a conjugate neuron signaling whether the network can classify a given input correctly. The architecture can be attached to previously built models, and evaluations on multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and deeper networks across several datasets show it **reducing the classification error rate to 0% while rejecting roughly 10% of inputs** as too difficult to classify.

papers.title: FENAS: A Few-Shot Meta-Ensembling Framework for Efficient Neural Architecture Search with Synergized Zero-Cost Proxies
papers.abstract: Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. Existing zero-cost proxies (ZCPs) provide fast training-free signals, but each proxy usually captures only a partial property of an architecture, leading to unstable rankings across datasets and search spaces.
