In contrast, GNN-based predictors can improve accuracy, but often depend on labeled architectures, graph encoders, and costly representation learning, which makes them less suitable for extreme few-shot settings. We propose FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework that turns complementary initialization priors into robust ranking signals. Its core component, CAST, is a feature pipeline that combines copula alignment and synergy transformation. CAST maps heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold, enabling lightweight meta-learners to produce reliable rankings from scarce supervision. On NAS-Bench-201, with only 0.5% labeled samples, FENAS achieves a Kendall's Tau ($\tau$) of 0.70, outperforming representative topology-based few-shot predictors in this low-label regime. In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test accuracy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architectures under limited evaluation budgets.
papers.summary: Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) needs accurate performance estimates under tight evaluation budgets, but zero-cost proxies (ZCPs) each capture only a partial property of an architecture and rank unstably across datasets and search spaces, while GNN-based predictors need labeled architectures and costly representation learning that suits few-shot settings poorly. `FENAS` is a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework whose core feature pipeline, `CAST`, combines copula alignment and synergy transformation to map heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold from which lightweight meta-learners produce rankings with scarce supervision. On `NAS-Bench-201` with only 0.5% labeled samples, it **achieves a Kendall's tau of 0.70**, beating representative topology-based few-shot predictors in that regime, and evaluates the full search space in about 1138 seconds while reaching competitive test accuracy.

papers.title: Accuracy and Uncertainty in Machine Deception Detection (Research White Paper)
papers.abstract: A deception detector is only as useful as the trust its alarms deserve. Like a polygraph, detectors that read a language model's internal activations can catch deceptive responses that look honest. Yet current detectors depend on which layers they read, weaken on broader tests, and do not state how certain their alarms are. This white paper proposes the Machine Deception Detector, which targets both detection accuracy and the uncertainty of detector scores. The detector reads every layer of the language model, learns which tokens carry evidence of deception using only response labels, and calibrates its alarm threshold so that its false--positive rate stays below a prescribed level. An ensemble of such detectors measures the uncertainty of each score and raises an alarm only when its members agree, with a confidence level that sets how certain each alarm must be. The proposed evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements, tests on five unseen deceptive tasks of Liars' Bench read by six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, and is designed to also show which layers carry the deception feature and how this changes with model size.
papers.summary: Probes that read a language model's internal activations can flag deceptive responses that look honest, but existing detectors depend on which layers they read, weaken on broader tests, and give no sense of how confident their alarms are. The proposed `Machine Deception Detector` reads every layer, learns which tokens carry evidence of deception from response-level labels alone, and calibrates its threshold so the false-positive rate stays below a prescribed level; an ensemble of such detectors measures score uncertainty and raises an alarm only when its members agree at a chosen confidence level. The planned evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements and tests on **five unseen deceptive tasks from `Liars' Bench` across six `Qwen3` models from 0.6B to 32B parameters**, aiming to also show which layers carry the deception signal and how that shifts with model size.

papers.title: SuperAI: Merging Capabilities Across Heterogeneous Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Enabling the reuse and composition of knowledge and capabilities distributed across foundation models is an important step toward building scalable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. However, architectural differences and incompatible representations make it difficult to transfer and integrate these capabilities through a unified cross-model interface. To address this challenge, we propose SuperAI, a cross-architecture multi-model fusion framework that integrates complementary capabilities from multiple source models into a host model through orthogonal alignment of low-dimensional task-relevant representations. Specifically, we first extract task-relevant representations from the source models and the host model using shared anchor samples, and apply principal component analysis (PCA) to construct low-dimensional functional subspaces with the same dimensionality. Next, we use orthogonal Procrustes mappings to align the source and host coordinate systems, establishing cross-model correspondences while preserving the internal geometry of each source subspace. Finally, we train a lightweight residual multilayer perceptron (MLP) with joint supervision on task outputs and source-model increments, learning input-dependent residual increments that are injected into the host model for multi-model capability fusion. Experiments on three host models across 15 capability domains show that SuperAI achieves higher average domain scores than the evaluated cross-architecture fusion methods and better preserves general capabilities as the number of source models increases. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of orthogonal alignment, nonlinear residual mapping, and joint supervision.
papers.summary: Reusing capabilities spread across foundation models with different architectures is hard because their internal representations are incompatible. `SuperAI` extracts task-relevant representations from several source models and a host model on shared anchor samples, reduces them with principal component analysis (PCA) to subspaces of equal dimension, aligns source and host coordinates with orthogonal Procrustes mappings, and trains a lightweight residual multilayer perceptron (MLP) that injects input-dependent increments into the host, supervised jointly on task outputs and source-model increments. **Across three host models and 15 capability domains it achieves higher average domain scores than the compared cross-architecture fusion methods** and preserves general capabilities better as more source models are added, with ablations supporting the orthogonal alignment, nonlinear residual mapping, and joint supervision.

papers.title: Deep Neural Mixed Models for Nonlinear Longitudinal Prediction with Subject-Specific Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Longitudinal health data often exhibit within-subject correlation, subject-specific heterogeneity, and complex nonlinear predictor--response relationships that may not be adequately captured by conventional mixed models. We propose a Deep Generalized Neural Network Mixed Model (DGNMM) that extends the GLMM framework by using a deep neural network to learn nonlinear population-level relationships while incorporating directly trainable, regularized subject-specific effects to capture individual heterogeneity. The model is estimated using prediction-oriented stochastic optimization with separate regularization of the neural-network parameters and subject-specific effects. This formulation allows us to investigate when increased nonlinear representation capacity provides additional predictive benefit in the presence of subject-specific heterogeneity. A simulation study varies population-level nonlinearity and subject-specific heterogeneity and compares DGNMM with GLMM, artificial neural network (ANN), Maity--Pal (MP), and GNMM alternatives for continuous and binary longitudinal outcomes. In the real-data application, DGNMM achieved the lowest MSPE for continuous depression and anxiety prediction, while alternative models remained competitive for binary outcomes. Exploratory subject-level analyses showed heterogeneous predictive gains across individuals, but the magnitude of the estimated subject-specific effects was not significantly associated with predictive gain. Overall, increased nonlinear representation capacity was most beneficial for continuous prediction under nonlinear response structures, while greater subject-specific heterogeneity did not systematically yield larger predictive gains.
papers.summary: Longitudinal health data combine within-subject correlation, individual heterogeneity, and nonlinear predictor-response relationships that conventional generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) capture poorly. The `Deep Generalized Neural Network Mixed Model` (`DGNMM`) replaces the population-level component with a deep neural network while keeping directly trainable, regularized subject-specific effects, fitted by prediction-oriented stochastic optimization with separate regularization for the two parts. In simulations that vary nonlinearity and heterogeneity and in a real study of depression and anxiety outcomes, **the model achieved the lowest mean squared prediction error for continuous outcomes**, while `GLMM`, plain neural networks, and `GNMM` alternatives stayed competitive for binary outcomes, and greater subject-specific heterogeneity did not systematically translate into larger predictive gains.

papers.title: CIViC: Evidence Gates for Audio-Conditioned Visual Prediction on Proxy Tasks
papers.abstract: Removing audio can shift a visual predictor's output without showing whether the task uses the intended audio information. We introduce Conditional Input and Visual Interpretation Checks (CIViC), a four-gate protocol that links an interpretation to an intervention, held-out task comparison, or endpoint control. We demonstrate CIViC on actor-disjoint face-raster tests, a synthetic audio-feature mixture, and source-video-disjoint SpeakerVid proxy tasks. In the static face-raster test, cross-actor audio replacement meets the registered detection rule with a small effect; on a separate temporal endpoint, constant-audio fits score better than audio-trained fits in four matched seeds. In the synthetic mixture, the condition-augmented fit has higher 1,000-step RMSE than the audio-only fit (0.1807 vs. 0.1707), with the gap shrinking during training. In the SpeakerVid proxy, the five-feature-zero fit (five low-level audio summaries zeroed; identity, dialogue, and condition inputs retained) has lower whole-frame grayscale RMSE than aligned audio across four held-out conditions and five paired seeds, while aligned audio has lower segment-drift error. The results show that output activation, held-out error, and endpoint controls support different interpretations across these proxy tasks.
papers.summary: Removing the audio input to an audio-conditioned visual predictor can shift its output without revealing whether the model actually uses the intended audio information. `CIViC` (Conditional Input and Visual Interpretation Checks) is a four-gate protocol that ties each interpretation to an intervention, a held-out task comparison, or an endpoint control, demonstrated on actor-disjoint face-raster tests, a synthetic audio-feature mixture, and source-video-disjoint `SpeakerVid` proxy tasks. The gates often disagree: on the `SpeakerVid` proxy, **zeroing five low-level audio summaries gives lower whole-frame grayscale error than aligned audio across four held-out conditions and five paired seeds**, even though aligned audio yields lower segment-drift error, showing that output activation, held-out error, and endpoint controls support different conclusions.

papers.title: Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum: A Fully Unmasked Non-LLM Curriculum for Craftax
papers.abstract: We introduce Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum (AHC), a domain-informed, rule-based training system for Craftax-Full. AHC combines achievement-oriented tasks, harvested initial-state progress, difficulty adaptation, bounded selection, and original-task practice. It uses no LLM inference and keeps all 43 actions available. At 2,005,401,600 PPO rollout transitions, three primary AHC runs obtain native-task return $46.70\pm0.57$ (sample SD), compared with $41.91\pm1.01$ for fresh native PPO-GTrXL with the same student architecture and evaluation protocol. Evaluation uses ten stochastic rollouts on each of 1024 fixed worlds per model. An additional cohort of three AHC runs reaches $46.08\pm1.23$. Two single-component ablations retain similar mean returns, while jointly freezing difficulty and removing inherited progress gives $45.14\pm2.79$. All-67-achievement profiles show that most of the return difference comes from Intermediate achievements, while the deepest-floor achievements remain unsolved. A Skill-Preflight diagnosis with a 14B teacher shows how prerequisite and floor-access constraints restrict practice. AHC and three 14B diagnostic configurations reach aggregate returns near the reported 80B DiCode mean of 45.88 and below the 235B mean of 48.55. These results show that an explicit curriculum without LLM inference can reach returns comparable to those reported for LLM-generated curricula on Craftax-Full, without action masking.
papers.summary: Curricula for the open-ended `Craftax-Full` benchmark have recently been generated by large language models, raising the question of whether a hand-designed rule-based curriculum can do as well. `Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum` (`AHC`) combines achievement-oriented tasks, harvested initial-state progress, difficulty adaptation, bounded task selection, and practice on the original task, with no LLM inference and all 43 actions left unmasked. After about two billion `PPO` transitions, **three `AHC` runs reach a native-task return of 46.70 versus 41.91 for fresh `PPO-GTrXL` with the same architecture**, near the reported mean of the 80B-parameter `DiCode` LLM-curriculum result and below the 235B one, with most of the gain coming from intermediate achievements while the deepest achievements remain unsolved.

papers.title: Full Waveform Inversion with a Learned Preconditioner
papers.abstract: Full-waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful approach for reconstructing subsurface velocity models, but its practical performance is limited by ill-conditioning, sensitivity to the update direction, and the high cost of curvature-based methods. In this project, we investigate whether a neural operator trained on reverse-time-migration (RTM) images can provide a useful learned preconditioner for FWI. We compare projected FWI against neural-preconditioned FWI using either a standard Fourier neural operator (FNO) or a Jacobian-informed FNO (JI-FNO). The neural preconditioner applies the normal operator of the learned RTM map to modify the true Devito FWI gradient. Our experiments show that the JI-FNO preconditioner achieves the lowest model error while maintaining data-residual decay comparable to baseline projected FWI. In contrast, the standard FNO preconditioner is unstable and gives worse model recovery, despite using the same neural-preconditioning framework. We also identify a failure mode of a nonlinear neural Gauss Newton-type inner solve: directly matching the neural RTM output to the FWI gradient creates an objective-space mismatch and does not yield a reliable descent direction. These results suggest that forward RTM-image prediction alone is insufficient for learned preconditioning; accurate learned derivatives and objective-consistent use of the neural operator are critical for producing useful inversion updates.
papers.summary: Full-waveform inversion (FWI) reconstructs subsurface velocity models but suffers from ill-conditioning, sensitivity to the update direction, and the expense of curvature-based solvers. The authors test whether a neural operator trained to predict reverse-time-migration (RTM) images can serve as a learned preconditioner, applying the normal operator of the learned map to the true `Devito` FWI gradient and comparing a standard `Fourier neural operator` (`FNO`) with a Jacobian-informed variant (`JI-FNO`) against projected FWI. **The `JI-FNO` preconditioner achieves the lowest model error while matching the baseline's data-residual decay**, whereas the standard `FNO` preconditioner is unstable and degrades recovery, and a nonlinear Gauss-Newton-style inner solve that matches the neural RTM output directly to the gradient fails to give a reliable descent direction, suggesting accurate learned derivatives matter more than forward-image prediction alone.

papers.title: ZOIF: Zeroth-Order Influence Function Estimation for LLM Data Selection Using Only Forward Passes
papers.abstract: Influence functions enable principled data selection for large language models (e.g., identifying influential training samples for model editing, debugging, or efficient fine-tuning). However, scaling IFs to LLMs is hindered by the intractability of billion-scale Hessian matrices and the prohibitive memory overhead of backpropagation (BP). While many classical IF approximations reduce Hessian complexity, they still rely on BP for gradient computation, requiring massive storage for intermediate activations that impedes practical data selection at scale. To address this, we propose ZOIF, a zeroth-order framework for influence estimation that operates entirely via forward passes, enabling memory-efficient data selection under resource constraints. ZOIF decomposes influence estimation into three BP-free stages: (1) approximating the average proxy gradient via zeroth-order estimation; (2) reformulating and solving the inverse Hessian-vector product as an auxiliary zeroth-order optimization to bypass explicit inversion; and (3) deriving per-sample influence scores via a forward finite difference along the previously computed parameter update direction. Experiments show that ZOIF selects data subsets with downstream utility competitive with, and in some cases exceeding, the evaluated baselines, yet at substantially lower peak memory cost and with comparable overall computation time.
papers.summary: Influence functions can identify which training samples matter most for a large language model, but computing them requires inverting billion-scale Hessians and running backpropagation, whose stored activations make data selection impractical at scale. `ZOIF` estimates influence entirely through forward passes in three stages: a zeroth-order estimate of the average proxy gradient, an auxiliary zeroth-order optimization that solves the inverse Hessian-vector product without explicit inversion, and a forward finite difference along the resulting update direction to score each sample. **The selected subsets match or exceed the downstream utility of the evaluated baselines at substantially lower peak memory**, with comparable total computation time.

papers.title: CoLA: Multi-VLA Coordination via Learned Adapters
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per-arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two-arm and three-arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two-arm task's wrist-only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine-tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models usually run as isolated single-agent policies, and it is unclear when agents sharing a workspace need explicit messages rather than just observing each other. `CoLA` (Coordination via Learned Adapters) keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel plus a per-arm diffusion action head, with fully decentralised execution. Across three handover tasks the channel matters only when information is private: **on an occluded tray handover where only one agent can see the box's colour marker, success is 76.0% versus 1.3% with messages zeroed**, while with a shared overhead camera removing messages makes no measurable difference, and with a frozen `π0.5` backbone `CoLA` matches a `LoRA`-fine-tuned baseline using a fraction of the trainable parameters.

papers.title: MultiFlow: Vision-Driven Multimodal fMRI Encoding via Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Current fMRI encoding models frame prediction as deterministic regression, yet identical stimuli evoke a distribution of neural responses (arising from physiological noise, hemodynamic variability, and cognitive fluctuations) that a single point estimate cannot capture. This work introduces MultiFlow, a generative fMRI encoding framework based on Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) and a formulation termed Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching (SISFM). SISFM generalises CFM by conditioning the source distribution on the stimulus: a learnable temporal convolution shapes the source mean with an HRF-length receptive field, while a variance head shrinks its scale, shortening the expected transport path. SISFM is instantiated with a Diffusion Transformer (DiT-X) decoder parameterising the velocity field, with sub-layer Attention Residuals, heterogeneous fusion of ten frozen vision, audio, language, and audiovisual backbones, and per-subject Yeo-network heads. On the Algonauts 2025 dataset, a single MultiFlow checkpoint recovers most of the benefit of large deterministic ensembles: it trails the 1000-model TRIBE ensemble in-distribution by 0.003 PCC (0.3163 vs. 0.3195), and the strongest in- and out-of-distribution ensembles (VIBE-20, MedARC-50) by 0.010 and 0.009 PCC, using a single trained model rather than an ensemble of 20-1000. The same checkpoint also provides stimulus-conditioned uncertainty estimates and sample-based diversity.
papers.summary: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) encoding models usually predict a single deterministic response even though identical stimuli evoke a distribution of neural responses. `MultiFlow` treats encoding as generation using Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) and a variant called Stimulus-Informed Source Flow Matching (SISFM), which conditions the source distribution on the stimulus through a learnable temporal convolution and a variance head to shorten the transport path, with a `DiT-X` decoder fusing ten frozen vision, audio, language, and audiovisual backbones. On `Algonauts 2025`, **a single checkpoint trails the 1000-model `TRIBE` ensemble by only 0.003 Pearson correlation in-distribution (0.3163 vs. 0.3195)** and the strongest ensembles out of distribution by about 0.01, while also providing stimulus-conditioned uncertainty estimates.

papers.title: StimFlow: Synthesizing Brain Activity from Images via Stimulus-conditioned Flow Matching
papers.abstract: The inherent variability of fMRI responses across trials encourages a generative view of the stimulus-to-response mapping. Prior generative encoders often operate in compressed latent spaces and condition predominantly on semantic features, which provide limited low-level cues for early visual cortex. We propose StimFlow, which synthesizes fMRI directly in native voxel space using conditional flow matching with a linear path. This design aligns training and inference distributions, enabling competitive performance with a single sample and reducing reliance on averaging. To match the visual hierarchy, StimFlow combines structural DINOv2 features with semantic CLIP features, which prove complementary along the cortical processing stream. With a single sample, StimFlow achieves a per-voxel Pearson correlation of 0.371, matching baselines that average five draws. Generation in voxel space allows direct ROI analysis and concept localization without a decoder. Furthermore, it recovers over half of full-data performance from just one hour of scans, supporting efficient cross-subject adaptation.
papers.summary: Trial-to-trial variability in fMRI responses motivates generative rather than point-estimate encoders, but prior generative approaches work in compressed latent spaces and lean on semantic features that give early visual cortex few low-level cues. `StimFlow` synthesizes fMRI directly in native voxel space with conditional flow matching along a linear path, conditioning on structural `DINOv2` features and semantic `CLIP` features that prove complementary along the cortical hierarchy. **With a single sample it reaches a per-voxel Pearson correlation of 0.371, matching baselines that average five draws**, allows direct region-of-interest analysis without a decoder, and recovers over half of full-data performance from one hour of scans for cross-subject adaptation.

papers.title: Across Viewpoints and Time: Trajectory-Generalizable Physical Attacks on World Models and Video Understanding Models
papers.abstract: World models and video understanding models are increasingly deployed in dynamic visual environments, yet their robustness to physical adversarial threats remains largely underexplored. We study whether a single physical adversarial texture can mislead the victim model across different real-world scenarios where observing viewpoints vary along uncontrolled object--camera trajectories. We identify that heterogeneous video semantics and trajectories induce poorly aligned gradients for optimizing the adversarial texture. To address that, we propose the Trajectory-aware adversarial Alignment and Refinement Attack (TARA), which incorporates trajectory-aware optimization to capture the evolving geometric variations of a printed texture under real-world scenarios. To improve cross-instance optimization compatibility, TARA incorporates trajectory-aware contrastive alignment to encourage attacked representations from diverse video--trajectory instances to approach a shared adversarial region and then performs trajectory-aware task refinement to translate the aligned representation into task-level prediction errors. For reproducible evaluation, we develop a geometry-grounded tracking pipeline that provides physically plausible adversarial regions with temporally consistent trajectories on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and Something-Something V2. We further collect real-world print-and-recapture videos to validate attack effectiveness under physical deployment conditions. Together, the annotated benchmarks and real-world captured data form a reproducible testbed for future evaluation. Notably, our results reveal that a single printable adversarial texture can persistently disrupt world models and video understanding models under physical conditions, highlighting the fundamental security challenge.
papers.summary: World models and video understanding models are rarely tested against physical adversarial objects whose appearance changes as the camera moves along uncontrolled trajectories. The `Trajectory-aware adversarial Alignment and Refinement Attack` (`TARA`) optimizes a single printable texture with trajectory-aware contrastive alignment, which pulls attacked representations from diverse video-trajectory instances toward a shared adversarial region, followed by task-level refinement that converts that alignment into prediction errors. Using a geometry-grounded tracking pipeline on `EPIC-KITCHENS-100` and `Something-Something V2` plus real print-and-recapture videos, **a single texture persistently disrupts both world models and video understanding models under physical conditions**, and the annotated benchmarks are released as a reproducible testbed.

papers.title: CodeWalk: Generating Coding Benchmarks by Walking a Problem Graph
papers.abstract: High-quality coding problems are expensive to collect. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench rely on substantial human curation, while synthetic alternatives typically rely on costly model generation and validation. In this work, we show that new coding problems can be created at almost no cost by composing existing ones. We formulate problem generation as code composition: verified atomic problems are combined into level-$N$ tasks, and a task is kept only if every atomic problem remains unsolved and a joint reference solution passes the same check used at evaluation time. The entire task-construction process is programmatic and requires no language-model generation or validation. We instantiate this approach in four coding settings: multi-bug repair, proof completion, complexity analysis, and clone equivalence. The generated tasks are challenging for frontier models, which all degrade as compositional depth increases. The generated tasks are also useful as training data: rejection-sampling fine-tuning on them improves Qwen3.5-9B at every composition level.
papers.summary: High-quality coding problems are costly to curate by hand or to synthesize with model generation and validation. `CodeWalk` instead composes verified atomic problems into level-N tasks programmatically, keeping a task only if every atomic problem remains unsolved and a joint reference solution passes the same check used at evaluation time, with no language-model generation or validation anywhere in the construction. Instantiated for multi-bug repair, proof completion, complexity analysis, and clone equivalence, **the generated tasks cause every frontier model tested to degrade as compositional depth increases**, and rejection-sampling fine-tuning on them improves `Qwen3.5-9B` at every composition level.

papers.title: Gugak-VocalSet: A Multi-Genre Studio-Quality Dataset of Korean Traditional Singing with Sigimsae Annotations
papers.abstract: We present Gugak-VocalSet, the first publicly available audio dataset for Korean traditional singing with dense annotations of sigimsae, a structured pitch contour system of vocal expressions. Gugak-VocalSet contains 24.5 hours of unaccompanied solo vocal recordings across 305 tracks of representative repertoire curated by the National Gugak Center, performed by 20 professional singers in a controlled studio environment with fixed key and tempo. In addition to genre, lyrics, and mood/timbre tags, the dataset provides a unified sigimsae ontology and approximately 68,000 segments (71,700 instances including multi-label) of audio-grounded sigimsae annotations; the ontology adopts a functional-position-based hierarchy designed for consistent application across genres, and 14 expert annotators specializing in Korean traditional music performed segment-level labeling accordingly. Baseline experiments on sigimsae classification and event detection show that domain-informed F0 representations remain competitive with, and on classification surpass, frozen probing of a general-purpose music foundation model, while pitch and spectral cues play complementary roles in event-level detection. Companion page: https://www.danbinaerin.com/Gugak-VocalSet/
papers.summary: No public audio dataset has existed for Korean traditional singing with annotations of sigimsae, the structured pitch-contour system of vocal ornamentation. `Gugak-VocalSet` provides 24.5 hours of unaccompanied solo recordings across 305 tracks by 20 professional singers, curated by the National Gugak Center, with genre, lyrics, and mood tags plus a unified sigimsae ontology and about **68,000 expert-labeled segments of audio-grounded sigimsae annotations**. Baseline experiments show that domain-informed fundamental-frequency representations remain competitive with, and on classification surpass, frozen probes of a general-purpose music foundation model, while pitch and spectral cues play complementary roles in event detection.

papers.title: Siam-ALS: An Explainable Siamese Deep Learning Framework for Early ALS Detection Using EEG and Eye-Tracking Signals
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) diagnosis remains challenging due to heterogeneous symptoms and reliance on clinical assessment, underscoring the need for objective, data-driven approaches that leverage patient-generated physiological signals. We propose Siam-ALS, an explainable Siamese deep learning framework that jointly models synchronized electroencephalography (EEG) and eye-tracking (ET) signals. EEG captures ALS-related changes in brain activity, while ET provides information about oculomotor control, allowing the model to learn complementary patterns associated with ALS. The framework employs two modality-specific encoders: a convolutional EEG encoder that captures spatiotemporal neural patterns and an MLP-based ET encoder that models oculomotor dynamics. These modality-specific features are processed through weight-sharing Siamese branches and fused into a compact 64-dimensional joint embedding. A lightweight classifier is used to predict ALS, while pairwise metric learning helps the model learn more effective patterns from the small, diverse ALS datasets. Performance was evaluated on the public EEGET-ALS dataset using strict subject-level cross-validation, where Siam-ALS achieved an accuracy of 0.988 and an AUROC of 0.998, demonstrating strong performance compared with classical machine learning, DL, and non-Siamese fusion approaches. Cross-dataset evaluation on the independent BigP3BCI dataset achieved an AUROC of approximately 0.98, supporting the generalization capability of Siam-ALS across different BCI paradigms. To enhance interpretability, six XAI methods were evaluated in the learned embedding space, with SHAP achieving the highest, though statistically comparable, fidelity in identifying important EEG and ET patterns that contribute to ALS predictions. Overall, Siam-ALS provides an accurate, generalizable, and explainable framework for multimodal ALS detection.
papers.summary: Diagnosing amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) relies on clinical assessment of heterogeneous symptoms, motivating objective signal-based approaches. `Siam-ALS` pairs a convolutional electroencephalography (EEG) encoder with a multilayer perceptron eye-tracking (ET) encoder, passes both through weight-sharing Siamese branches into a 64-dimensional joint embedding, and trains with pairwise metric learning alongside a lightweight classifier to cope with small datasets. Under subject-level cross-validation on `EEGET-ALS` it reaches **0.988 accuracy and 0.998 AUROC**, transfers to the independent `BigP3BCI` dataset at roughly 0.98 AUROC, and among six explainability methods `SHAP` gives the highest, though statistically comparable, fidelity in identifying influential EEG and ET patterns.

papers.title: JSIR: An Audio-Aligned, Multi-Task Dataset of Jazz Standard Recordings
papers.abstract: Beat tracking, chord estimation, and structure analysis are staple tasks of music information retrieval. Their datasets are drawn largely from Western popular music, and jazz remains a repertoire on which state-of-the-art systems underperform. We present JSIR, the Jazz Standards dataset for Information Retrieval. Its 267 recordings of 44 jazz standards span 25.6 hours, 3.7 times the audio of JAAH, the closest existing resource. For each recording, we provide annotations for beat and downbeat positions, chords, and sections, all produced by a jazz musician and revised in several passes. In baseline experiments, models trained with JSIR also improve on other jazz datasets: the downbeat F-measure of a state-of-the-art beat tracker rises from 87.7% to 89.2%, and the seventh-chord accuracy of a pop-trained chord estimator on JAAH from 34% to 41%. We publicly release the annotations, the annotation tool used to create them, and a web application that displays them in sync with the audio.
papers.summary: Beat tracking, chord estimation, and structure analysis datasets skew toward Western popular music, and jazz remains a repertoire where state-of-the-art systems underperform. `JSIR` (Jazz Standards dataset for Information Retrieval) covers 267 recordings of 44 jazz standards totaling 25.6 hours, 3.7 times the audio of `JAAH`, with beat, downbeat, chord, and section annotations produced by a jazz musician and revised over several passes. Training on the dataset helps on other jazz data too: **a state-of-the-art beat tracker's downbeat F-measure rises from 87.7% to 89.2%** and a pop-trained chord estimator's seventh-chord accuracy on `JAAH` rises from 34% to 41%, with the annotations, annotation tool, and a synced web viewer released publicly.

papers.title: Adversarial Detection for Pre-trained Classifiers via Lipschitz-Margin Analysis with Certification
papers.abstract:
Deep classifiers deployed in safety-critical services like autonomous-driving perception remain vulnerable to small adversarial perturbations. Certified $\ell_2$ defenses today face a costly trade-off: randomized smoothing (RS) requires hundreds of noisy queries per input, while Lipschitz networks (LN) constrain the architecture and sacrifice clean accuracy. We take a detection-oriented approach instead: rather than certifying that predictions are invariant inside an $\ell_2$ ball, we certify that adversarial inputs within an $\ell_2$ ball are \emph{detected} --- a guarantee aligned with security-critical deployments where missing an attack is costlier than flagging a clean input.
  To realize this, we prove a Lipschitz-margin reduction from certified $\ell_2$ robustness to certified detection, which reduces the problem to handling a single Lipschitz constant $L$. We introduce two detector families: $\mathbb{D}_{Adv}$, which estimates $L$ from a single defender-side perturbed pair, and $\mathbb{D}_{lc}$, which augments that pair with a local margin centroid to keep the estimate above what the certificate requires. Both deploy on any pretrained classifier without retraining. With a valid global bound, the detector is fully certified at that radius; with a local estimate $L'$, certification is sample-wise and applies only when our certified condition holds.
  Across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-1k on four backbones (LeNet-5, VGG16, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16), our detectors match or outperform five baselines (CTT, SortNet, CRM, ContraNet, A$^2$D). For CIFAR-10 with 1-Lipschitz SortNet, our reduction delivers $100\%$ certified detection at the lowest FPR among compared certified detectors; on the standard CIFAR-10 VGG16, our detectors reject all evaluated in-budget adversarial examples, with 62-82\% both rejected and formally certified.
papers.summary: Certified defenses against small L2 adversarial perturbations either need hundreds of noisy queries per input, as in randomized smoothing, or constrain the architecture and hurt clean accuracy, as in Lipschitz networks. The authors instead certify that adversarial inputs within an L2 ball are detected, proving a Lipschitz-margin reduction from certified robustness to certified detection that hinges on a single Lipschitz constant, and build two detector families, one estimating that constant from a single defender-side perturbed pair and one adding a local margin centroid, both attachable to any pretrained classifier without retraining. Across `MNIST`, `CIFAR-10`, and `ImageNet-1k` on `LeNet-5`, `VGG16`, `ResNet-50`, and `ViT-B/16`, the detectors match or beat five baselines including `SortNet` and `ContraNet`, and **on a standard `CIFAR-10` `VGG16` they reject all evaluated in-budget adversarial examples, with 62-82% both rejected and formally certified**.

papers.title: TRACE: Temporal Risk Assessment and Concept Editing for Safer Language Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can produce harmful content while generating a response. A useful safeguard should not only detect this risk during generation but also intervene while leaving safe responses largely unchanged and provide an auditable record of the internal patterns supporting its decisions. We propose TRACE (Temporal Risk Assessment and Concept Editing), a framework that tracks harmful-response risk during generation, selectively edits token activations, and leaves an auditable trace of its detection and steering decisions. TRACE learns a codebook of recurring activation patterns, with each codebook vector representing a latent concept. At inference time, it assigns each token activation to the nearest codebook vector to obtain the corresponding concept. A gated recurrent unit (GRU) processes the activations and their assigned concept features to predict completed-response harmfulness and a monotone cumulative streaming risk. During steering, activations assigned to harmful concepts are steered along directions defined by nearby benign targets. An external LLM labels the learned concepts post hoc, making detection sequences and harmful-to-benign edit records interpretable. Experiments across three generators and the WildGuard and S-Eval benchmarks show that TRACE improves streaming F1 over Kelp in five of six comparisons while remaining competitive on completed-response detection. TRACE's selective steering reduces Harmbench attack success with little change in refusal on originally safe responses. The post-hoc audit reveals recurring semantic structure in the learned concepts and distinct traces associated with harmful detection, safe generation, and activation edits.
papers.summary: Safeguards for large language models (LLMs) should detect harmful content while it is being generated, intervene without disturbing safe responses, and leave an auditable record of why they acted. `TRACE` (Temporal Risk Assessment and Concept Editing) learns a codebook of recurring activation patterns treated as latent concepts, assigns each token activation to its nearest concept, and feeds activations plus concept features to a gated recurrent unit (GRU) that predicts completed-response harmfulness and a monotone cumulative streaming risk; during steering, activations assigned to harmful concepts are pushed toward nearby benign targets, and an external LLM labels the concepts post hoc. Across three generators on `WildGuard` and `S-Eval`, **`TRACE` improves streaming F1 over `Kelp` in five of six comparisons**, and its selective steering lowers `HarmBench` attack success with little change in refusals on originally safe responses.

papers.title: ANTE: Anticipate, Then Execute -- Learning Internal World Models for Coding Agents from Verified Beliefs
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.
papers.summary: Coding agents in containerized environments rarely anticipate the consequences of their actions, and a sparse terminal reward cannot attribute failure to the early edit that corrupted the repository. `ANTE` (Anticipate, Then Execute) has the policy state an internal belief about what each action will do, verifies that prediction against real execution, and uses `Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization` (`BAPO`) to turn the settled forecasts into per-step credit for both actions and trust-or-abstain decisions, while a test-time optimization step selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. **The method raises `Qwen3-32B` from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on `SWE-bench Verified`, 6.2% above a matched `GRPO` baseline without the belief state**, the internal world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains.

papers.title: A Sovereign, Indic-First, Reasoning Model
papers.abstract:
Gnani-Evon-v3.3-30B-A3B is a long-context hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model for reasoning, instruction following, and tool use in English and eight Indian languages. Starting from NVIDIA's Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B checkpoint, it retains the 52-layer backbone and changes the vocabulary, training data, and post-training objectives. An in-place expansion from 131,072 to 163,072 tokens reduces mean Indian-language fertility by 38.6%. The new embedding rows are initialized from their upstream decompositions and warmed before the backbone is updated. Continual pretraining then adds broad English-Indic data, high-quality annealing, and direct training at a 131,072-token sequence length.
  The central result appears after post-training. Reinforcement learning across four verifiable task environments improves mathematics, graduate-level science, and instruction following, but degrades Indic extractive question answering because the rewards do not require an answer in the requested language. The share of Indic extraction items answered in English rises from 8.7% to 91.7%. Accuracy conditional on answering in the target script roughly doubles, which is consistent with preserved reading ability but is measured on a self-selected subset.
  Two unreleased studies test repairs. A scoped Indic reward restores the language convention. A 26B-A4B generative judge outperforms a 235B-parameter model on RM-Bench, and distillation restores 81% of the capabilities displaced by optimizing against it.
  Relative to the architecture-identical starting checkpoint, the released model gains 5.2 points on an Indic aggregate while giving up 1.7 points of English retention. The unreleased Indic-aware branch trades further, gaining 14.6 Indic points at a cost of 5.4 in English. A planned FP8 release reduces the artifact to 32GB with near-zero mean change across 32 paired benchmarks.
papers.summary: `Gnani-Evon-v3.3-30B-A3B` is a long-context hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model for reasoning, instruction following, and tool use in English and eight Indian languages, built from NVIDIA's `Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B` by expanding the vocabulary from 131,072 to 163,072 tokens, which cuts mean Indian-language fertility by 38.6%, followed by continual pretraining and direct training at 131,072-token sequence length. The central finding is that reinforcement learning on four verifiable task environments improves math, science, and instruction following but breaks the language convention, because rewards never require the requested language: **the share of Indic extractive question-answering items answered in English rises from 8.7% to 91.7%**. A scoped Indic reward restores the convention in an unreleased branch, a 26B-A4B generative judge beats a 235B model on `RM-Bench`, and the released model gains 5.2 points on an Indic aggregate while giving up 1.7 points of English retention relative to its starting checkpoint.

papers.title: Fewer Bits, More Tries: Recovering Capability Under Memory Constraints
papers.abstract: Large language models are generally more capable than smaller ones, but their memory requirements can make local deployment difficult. We ask whether part of this capability gap can instead be recovered by running a smaller or more compressed model multiple times and selecting among its outputs using public or model-generated tests. Single-user local inference can leave hardware underutilized, allowing parallel candidate generation to trade additional test-time computation for accuracy at modest latency cost. Across four code-generation benchmarks, verified retry recovers substantial accuracy lost to model size or compression. A 7B Qwen model with eight parallel attempts essentially matches a 32B model on MBPP+ and exceeds it on the other three benchmarks, while using about $4\times$ less model memory, running up to $6\times$ faster, and using less energy, as measured on Nvidia GPU. We observe similar tradeoff across model sizes, compression levels and hardware choices, although exact benefit depends on the hardware profile and problem setting. These results show that model capacity can be traded for verified test-time computation when correct solutions remain reachable within a modest retry budget.
papers.summary: Larger language models are more capable but often will not fit in local memory, so the question is whether a smaller or more compressed model can close part of the gap by generating several candidates in parallel and selecting one with public or model-generated tests. Single-user local inference typically leaves hardware underutilized, which makes parallel sampling cheap in latency. Across four code-generation benchmarks, **a 7B `Qwen` model with eight parallel attempts essentially matches a 32B model on `MBPP+` and exceeds it on the other three**, using about four times less model memory, running up to six times faster, and consuming less energy on an Nvidia GPU, with similar tradeoffs across model sizes, compression levels, and hardware whenever correct solutions are reachable within a modest retry budget.

papers.title: In-Place Indic Tokenizer Expansion and Continual Pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B
papers.abstract: We adapted Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B for eight Indian languages without changing its backbone architecture. We expanded the vocabulary in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix rebalancing, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%. We initialized new input and output rows by averaging their original constituent rows, then trained them on 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone. Continual pretraining then progressed through broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens. The annealed checkpoint gained 12.9 points on the Indic MILU benchmark but lost 3.4 on English MMLU. We also report practical negative results. Direct token addition underperformed continued byte-pair encoding. AdamW weight decay changed rows intended to stay fixed. Perplexity on an Indic-heavy holdout did not select the learning rate that best preserved English performance.
papers.summary: Adapting a large model to new languages usually means a new tokenizer and a fresh backbone, so `Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B` was instead extended in place for eight Indian languages. The vocabulary grew from 131,072 to 163,072 entries through continued byte-pair encoding with `AdaptMix` rebalancing, cutting tokens per word by 38.6%; new input and output rows were initialized by averaging their original constituent rows and trained on mostly Indic text before the backbone was updated, followed by continual pretraining through broad, annealing, and long-context stages over roughly 1.27 trillion tokens. The annealed checkpoint **gained 12.9 points on the Indic `MILU` benchmark while losing 3.4 points on English `MMLU`**. Reported negative results include direct token addition underperforming continued byte-pair encoding, AdamW weight decay altering rows meant to stay fixed, and holdout perplexity failing to select the learning rate that best preserved English.

papers.title: LiveAnon: Improving Privacy and Utility in Streaming Speaker Anonymization with Codec Language Models
papers.abstract: Speaker anonymization (SA) aims to conceal speaker identity while preserving linguistic content and emotion, but existing streaming systems often lose emotion information through discrete content bottlenecks or require emotion-specific modeling. We present LiveAnon, a voice-conversion-based streaming SA system that directly conditions an autoregressive codec language model on hidden features from a pretrained streaming ASR encoder, preserving emotion without emotion-specific supervision. To reduce codec-generation latency, we introduce capped RVQ decoding, which preserves dependencies among coarse codebooks while predicting the remaining codebooks in parallel. Under VPC24, LiveAnon improves intelligibility and emotion preservation over fixed-target Stream-Voice-Anon (SVA), a strong prior streaming SA system, matches emotion-prompted SVA in emotion preservation, and achieves the strongest semi-informed privacy among streaming systems. Under VPC26, it ranks second across all metrics among the evaluated anonymization systems, demonstrating a strong privacy-utility balance.
papers.summary: Streaming speaker anonymization hides who is talking, but current systems route audio through discrete content bottlenecks that strip emotion unless emotion is modeled explicitly. `LiveAnon` does voice conversion by conditioning an autoregressive codec language model directly on hidden features from a pretrained streaming speech-recognition encoder, keeping emotion without emotion-specific supervision, and its capped residual vector quantization decoding predicts the later codebooks in parallel to cut generation latency. Under the `VPC24` setup it improves intelligibility and emotion preservation over fixed-target `Stream-Voice-Anon`, matches the emotion-prompted variant on emotion, and reaches **the strongest semi-informed privacy among streaming systems**; under `VPC26` it ranks second across all metrics.

papers.title: Analyzing the Dynamics of WSBM-based Echo State Networks using InputDSA
papers.abstract: Bridging the structural gap between biological brains and artificial neural networks presents a pathway to altered computational dynamics. This paper introduces a Reservoir Computing framework that replaces random networks with biologically realistic modularity by applying the Weighted Stochastic Block Model (WSBM) to Echo State Networks (ESNs). This topological parameterization constructs reservoirs reflecting latent functional sub-circuits. Furthermore, the integration of Input Dynamical Similarity Analysis (InputDSA) provides a mechanism to isolate and compare how structural priors modulate intrinsic recurrent dynamics versus external inputs. By evaluating these architectures, we establish that structural diversity does not necessarily predicts behavioral diversity across the selected network subset. Furthermore, our demixed analysis confirms Anna Karenina principle of dynamics, demonstrating that environmental constraints enforce dynamical convergence in successful agents, while failing networks degenerate into idiosyncratic trajectories.
papers.summary: Reservoir computing normally wires its recurrent layer at random, so the question here is what changes when that wiring carries brain-like modularity. Echo state networks were built with reservoirs sampled from a weighted stochastic block model, giving latent functional sub-circuits, and Input Dynamical Similarity Analysis (`InputDSA`) was used to separate how structural priors reshape intrinsic recurrent dynamics from how they reshape input-driven dynamics. Across the networks tested, **structural diversity did not predict behavioral diversity**, and the demixed analysis found that environmental constraints pushed successful agents toward convergent dynamics while failing networks degenerated into idiosyncratic trajectories.

papers.title: E8 Lattice Key Quantization for Low-Bit KV-Cache Compression
papers.abstract: Compressing the key-value (KV) cache is essential for serving long-context large language models (LLMs) under memory constraints. While current scalar quantization methods achieve significant compression, they typically face a quality-fidelity trade-off, either suffering from performance instability at 2-bit precision or necessitating 3-bit keys to maintain model quality. In this work, we demonstrate that a uniform low-bit k2v2 configuration (2-bit keys and 2-bit values) can preserve near-baseline quality by using vector quantization (VQ) based on the $E_8$ lattice for KV keys. We show that structured VQ exploits correlations across adjacent dimensions to achieve signal-to-quantization-noise ratios (SQNR) higher than those of independent scalar quantization at the same key payload rate. To ensure practical utility, we adapt a table-based asymmetric scoring algorithm that avoids explicit codebook dequantization during attention computation and preserves decode-throughput parity with scalar baselines. Across five LLM families, our $E_8$ k2v2 approach yields \textasciitilde$6\times$ KV compression, roughly 20\% smaller than scalar k3v2 (3-bit keys and 2-bit values), while retaining near-baseline long-context perplexity. In our full-suite perplexity evaluation, $E_8$ improves over scalar k3v2 in 80\% of model--dataset--context settings. These results indicate that $E_8$ lattice VQ improves quality per byte while keeping throughput at parity, suggesting that structured key quantization is a useful primitive for KV-compression stacks. Overall, our work provides a low-overhead primitive for expanding the quality-memory frontier in long-context LLM inference.
papers.summary: Serving long-context models under memory limits means shrinking the key-value cache, but scalar quantization is unstable at 2 bits and typically needs 3-bit keys to hold quality. Quantizing keys with vector quantization on the `E_8` lattice exploits correlations across adjacent dimensions, giving a higher signal-to-quantization-noise ratio than independent scalar quantization at the same bits per key, while a table-based asymmetric scoring algorithm avoids dequantizing the codebook during attention so decode throughput stays level with scalar baselines. Across five model families the resulting 2-bit-key, 2-bit-value setup yields **roughly 6x cache compression, about 20% smaller than scalar 3-bit keys, and beats that scalar configuration on long-context perplexity in 80% of model-dataset-context settings**.

papers.title: Approximation in Contrastive Representation Learning
papers.abstract:
Contrastive representation learning (CRL) is a fundamental paradigm for
  learning transferable representations. Recent work
  identifies its population target as the pointwise mutual information (PMI)
  $\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)}$
  between two modalities $X,Y$, where $p$ is the joint density function and
  $p_X,p_Y$ are the marginals. However, it remains unclear why standard inner-product scores $f(x)^\top g(y)$ can effectively approximate a generally nonseparable population target PMI. In this paper, we address this question from the aspect of approximation for CRL. By linking PMI to a compact operator, we show that $D$-dimensional inner-product models perform rank-$D$ spectral approximation, with error controlled by the spectral tail. We then study neural network realizations: in general settings, we show that deep neural network scoring functions are universally consistent, and the approximation error rates depend on the smoothness of the PMI function; under structured low-rank data models we obtain improved rates attained by moderate-width encoders. Finally, we establish a fast calibration rate from contrastive excess risk to downstream retrieval error under a density-ratio Tsybakov noise condition.
papers.summary: Contrastive representation learning is known to target the pointwise mutual information between two modalities, yet that target is generally not separable, leaving it unclear why a simple inner product of two encoders approximates it well. Linking pointwise mutual information to a compact operator shows that a D-dimensional inner-product model performs rank-D spectral approximation, with **error controlled by the spectral tail**. Deep network scoring functions are shown to be universally consistent, with approximation rates set by the smoothness of the target and improved rates from moderate-width encoders under structured low-rank data models. A fast calibration rate then carries contrastive excess risk through to downstream retrieval error under a density-ratio Tsybakov noise condition.

papers.title: From Acoustic Sensing to Physical Actions: A Comprehensive Survey of Security Risks in Edge-Deployed Audio LLM-Based Agents
papers.abstract: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.
papers.summary: Audio large language models now sit inside smart-home, vehicle, wearable, and embodied agents, where sound entering the microphone can reach persistent state and trigger real-world actions, yet existing surveys treat acoustic security, agent security, and edge deployment separately. An Acoustic Sensing-to-Action system model traces that influence along the full path from sensing to external execution, accounting for split edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformations, and is used to organize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods from all three literatures. The synthesis argues that **weaknesses arise not only inside components but at the transitions between stages, so a protection validated at one stage gives no end-to-end assurance**, motivating evaluation that follows acoustic influence through persistent state, system boundaries, and shifting deployment conditions.

papers.title: DC-Flow: Target-Conditioned Cyclic Peptide Design via Delayed-Coupling Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Target-conditioned cyclic peptide design requires coordinating interfacial side chains with macrocyclic closure. Existing end-to-end generators concurrently update geometric and chemical variables from noise, assigning residues to disordered coordinates. Meanwhile, predictor-assisted workflows often get stuck in local traps because they lack feedback in the propose-and-filter stage and ignore 3D structural proposals during sequence search. To overcome the drawbacks of these two paradigms, we propose DC-FLOW, a staged generative framework built around Delayed-Coupling Flow Matching. In principle, DC-FLOW postpones sequence and side-chain activation until a target-conditioned backbone takes shape, resolving structural ambiguity before chemical assignment. Then, it feeds delayed activations back into the backbone, achieving co-evolution of backbone geometry and emerging residue identities by coupling their flows. This mechanism enables more reliable macrocyclic closure and favorable interface packing. For predictor-assisted workflows, DC-FLOW supplies 3D proposals with in-trajectory guidance, enabling cascaded test-time scaling to prune redundant backbones and terminate unpromising refinement early. Extensive experiments show that DC-FLOW improves cyclization fidelity, diversity, and interface energetics, substantially increasing the yield of confident cyclic peptide binders under a fixed final-candidate budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/mianqiu00/DCFlow.
papers.summary: Designing a cyclic peptide for a protein target means getting interface side chains and macrocyclic ring closure right together; end-to-end generators update geometry and chemistry simultaneously from noise, assigning residues to coordinates that are still disordered, while propose-and-filter pipelines search sequences without 3D feedback. `DC-Flow` stages the process with delayed-coupling flow matching: sequence and side-chain activation is postponed until a target-conditioned backbone has formed, then fed back so backbone geometry and emerging residue identities co-evolve through coupled flows. The same trajectories supply 3D proposals with in-trajectory guidance, letting predictor-assisted workflows prune redundant backbones and stop unpromising refinement early. Reported improvements cover cyclization fidelity, diversity, and interface energetics, with **a substantially higher yield of confident binders under a fixed final-candidate budget**.

papers.title: WUSPruner: Second-Moment-Optimal Transforms for Structured Pruning
papers.abstract: Structured pruning is typically formulated as identifying which model dimensions to remove, often within the model's original representation. However, the effect of coordinate deletion fundamentally depends on the basis in which pruning is performed. This raises a more fundamental question: how should the basis be chosen specifically for coordinate deletion? We introduce WUSPruner, a transform-based framework for structured pruning of large language models. We formulate basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem that directly minimizes the reconstruction loss induced by pruning. Inspired by the second-moment transformation in WUSH, we consider a WUS transform constructed jointly from activation and weight statistics. We show that under positive-definite second moments, WUS transform minimizes the local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis. In the resulting basis, the activation and weight second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, causing the deletion error to decompose into independent spectral contributions and yielding a principled criterion for coordinate selection. Guided by this result, we develop a scalable pruning method based on blockwise WUS transformations and compact input projections. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models from 8B to 72B parameters show consistent improvements over structured pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation benchmarks, while also delivering practical reductions in inference latency and memory usage.
papers.summary: Structured pruning is usually framed as choosing which dimensions to delete, but the damage deletion does depends on the basis it happens in, which is normally just the model's native one. `WUSPruner` casts basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem and uses a transform built jointly from activation and weight second moments, proving that under positive-definite second moments this **transform minimizes local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis**. In that basis both second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, so deletion error decomposes into independent spectral contributions and gives a direct coordinate-selection criterion, made scalable through blockwise transforms and compact input projections. Experiments on `Llama` and `Qwen` models from 8B to 72B parameters improve on structured-pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code, with measured latency and memory reductions.

papers.title: GA-SVD: Generation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for LLM Compression
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. However, existing SVD-based methods primarily target multiple-choice benchmarks and often fail to preserve performance on generation tasks. Moreover, their rank allocation strategies are typically heuristic. We propose GA-SVD, a generation-aware low-rank compression framework for LLMs. First, we introduce Generation-Aware Weight Whitening (GAWW), which leverages gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation to construct whitening transformations aligned with generative behavior. Second, we develop an evolutionary global rank allocation method that searches for effective layer-wise rank allocation under a given global compression ratio. Across extensive experiments on Mistral-7B, Qwen3 series, and Llama-3.3 models, evaluated on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, GA-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD-based baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) results. We further demonstrate scalability by applying our method to models with up to 70B parameters.
papers.summary: One-shot low-rank compression shrinks a model without retraining, but existing singular value decomposition methods are tuned on multiple-choice benchmarks, degrade on open-ended generation, and allocate per-layer ranks heuristically. `GA-SVD` adds generation-aware weight whitening, which builds whitening transforms from gradients of on-policy knowledge distillation so they align with generative behavior, plus an evolutionary search over layer-wise rank allocations under a fixed global compression ratio. On `Mistral-7B`, `Qwen3`, and `Llama-3.3` models it **outperforms prior singular-value-decomposition baselines on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks**, and scales to 70B parameters.

papers.title: Harnessing VLM in Embodied RL: From Reward Regressor to Success Detector via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating
papers.abstract: VLMs provide promising solutions to embodied reward design. Most current methods that train VLMs as reward regressors not only require extensive annotations but are also primarily designed for finetuning pretrained policies, and perform less well in the more challenging from-scratch RL setting. This issue stems from a fundamental mismatch: regressing precise rewards is misaligned with what VLMs naturally excel at. We posit that it is more aligned with VLMs' inherent multi-modal VQA capabilities for the models to function as success detectors, and propose VLM success reward via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating (VLMeg) to well harness VLM for embodied reward design. As the core of VLMeg, the proposed exploration-augmented key-observation gating first determines whether the current RL episode is judgment-worthy based on its similarity to a generated success trajectory. Then, the key observation with the lowest confusion from the judgment-worthy episode will be selected for VLM evaluation as episodic reward. This gating mechanism not only avoids redundant calls but also enables higher detection accuracy of VLM. Considering the sparsity of judgment-worthy episodes, the advanced exploration incentives based on the generated trajectory are introduced, enabling more efficient exploration toward judgment-worthy trajectories for more VLM reward triggers and thus gaining higher RL efficiency. Extensive experiments in MetaWorld demonstrate VLMeg achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL, outperforming advanced VLM-based baselines on 12 challenging reward-free tasks. Furthermore, VLMeg also enables effective RL without any ground-truth reward in 3 challenging real-world experiments. Code will be open after acceptance at https://github.com/Raina915/VLMeg.
papers.summary: Vision-language models are an appealing source of reward for embodied reinforcement learning, but training them to regress dense rewards needs heavy annotation and mostly helps when finetuning an already pretrained policy rather than learning from scratch. `VLMeg` uses the model as a success detector instead, which sits closer to its native visual question answering ability: exploration-augmented key-observation gating first decides whether an episode is judgment-worthy by comparing it to a generated success trajectory, then sends the least confusing observation from that episode for a single episodic reward judgment, reducing calls and raising detection accuracy. Because judgment-worthy episodes are rare, exploration incentives derived from the generated trajectory steer the agent toward them and so toward more reward triggers. On 12 reward-free `MetaWorld` tasks it **sets the best from-scratch reinforcement learning results against vision-language-model reward baselines**, and also trains three real-world tasks with no ground-truth reward.

papers.title: A Decade of PhotoMappers: A Longitudinal Study of Crowdsourced Disaster Photos Geolocalization with Vision-Language Models and Geospatial Reasoning
papers.abstract: Crowdsourced disaster imagery provides timely, ground-level observations when conventional disaster mapping is delayed or incomplete, yet its geographic value depends on where observations are produced, how they are interpreted, and whether they can be reliably located as actionable Geospatial Intelligence (GEOINT). Using more than a decade of PhotoMappers, a crowdsourced disaster-mapping initiative, this study examines the changing geography of disaster information and asks how emerging GeoAI models compare with human geographic interpretation. We combine longitudinal spatial analysis with cross-view geolocalization using street view imagery (SVI) and remote sensing imagery (RSI), and evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) reasoning through 30 indicators spanning geographic cues and reasoning evidence. The results reveal a geographically and temporally uneven archive shaped by changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities. Integrating VGI, SVI, and RSI with Sinkhorn re-ranking achieves 40.90% R@1, 61.10% R@5, and 69.45% R@10, while yearly R@1 varies markedly from 25.00% to 65.07%. Geographic reasoning is similarly uneven: Qwen3.6-27B achieves an overall agreement of 67% compared with 51% for InternVL3-8B, with both models showing greater difficulty with localized and place-specific evidence than broad spatial configurations. We argue that the value of GeoAI lies less in replacing volunteered geographic interpretation than in complementing it, scaling candidate retrieval while retaining human judgment for ambiguous and consequential cases. This provides a pathway toward more human-centered and responsible GeoAI for disaster mapping. All data and code are openly available at https://github.com/bobleegogogo/PhotoMappers-VLM.
papers.summary: Crowdsourced disaster photos fill gaps when official mapping lags, but their value as intelligence depends on whether they can be reliably located, which invites a comparison between geospatial AI and human geographic interpretation. More than a decade of the `PhotoMappers` volunteer disaster-mapping archive was analyzed longitudinally and paired with cross-view geolocalization against street-view and remote-sensing imagery, plus an assessment of vision-language model reasoning across 30 indicators of geographic cues and evidence. Combining volunteered, street-view, and satellite imagery with Sinkhorn re-ranking reached **40.90% recall at rank 1 and 69.45% at rank 10, though yearly recall at rank 1 ranged from 25.00% to 65.07%**. `Qwen3.6-27B` agreed with human interpretation 67% of the time against 51% for `InternVL3-8B`, with both weaker on localized, place-specific evidence than on broad spatial configuration, supporting a complementary rather than substitutive role.

papers.title: State Representation Shapes Long-Horizon Agent Learning and Transfer: An Empirical Study
papers.abstract: An end-to-end success rate alone cannot distinguish failure to learn an action from failure to apply it as task state changes. We study this distinction in deterministic tool workflows that provide the current artifact state and candidate action recipes. Using 1.7B, 8B, and 27B Qwen models, we compare supervised learning across workflow horizons and cross the state representation used for training with the one used at evaluation. Horizon-matched supervision yields high completion, but an H4-trained 1.7B model transfers poorly to longer workflows under full-state observations. In an H16 crossover, compact-trained 1.7B adapters complete 50/50 held-out tasks in compact view and 0/50 in full view for each of three paired training seeds; full-trained outcomes vary across seeds. A separate 8B adapter pair shows a similar asymmetry. The view dependence also appears in paired-choice tasks where both candidate calls are executable and the correct choice depends on table contents; here, the compact mask does not consult the target action. An explicit relevance cue improves full-view execution but does not close the gap for the tested checkpoint. In a separate 27B ScienceWorld study, compact-state training improves local accuracy under both views, indicating that the transfer pattern depends on the task and observation construction.
