Together, these experiments identify representation-sensitive transfer as a bottleneck in the controlled workflows, without isolating content reduction from other changes to the observation.
papers.summary: An end-to-end success rate cannot distinguish an agent that never learned an action from one that learned it but fails to apply it as task state changes, so this study separates the two in deterministic tool workflows that expose the current artifact state and candidate action recipes. `Qwen` models at 1.7B, 8B, and 27B were supervised across workflow horizons, crossing the state representation used for training against the one used at evaluation. Horizon-matched supervision gave high completion, but the representation mismatch dominated: at 16-step horizons, **compact-state-trained 1.7B adapters completed 50 of 50 held-out tasks in the compact view and 0 of 50 in the full view** across three paired seeds, with a similar asymmetry at 8B and in paired-choice tasks where the right call depends on table contents. An explicit relevance cue improved full-view execution without closing the gap, while a 27B `ScienceWorld` study saw compact-state training help under both views, so the pattern depends on how the observation is constructed.

papers.title: CoverSynth: Coverage-Guided Generation of Retrieval Evaluation Sets
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents need retrieval evaluation sets that expose domain-specific failures and guide developers towards efficient deployment tradeoffs. Neither expert-human-authored sets nor current synthetic generation methods provide a methodology for achieving the necessary coverage, reliability, efficiency, and discriminability required for such decision-making. Simultaneously, the field does not have an assessment framework for determining when an evaluation set has satisfied these properties. We introduce an evaluation set assessment framework for these criteria and CoverSynth -- a generator specifically designed to satisfy these criteria without incurring the high cost of human expert labeling. Starting from an unannotated corpus, CoverSynth targets coverage across retrieval demands and system capabilities. Deterministic checks locate evidence quotes in their sources, while model-based checks assess semantic validity to guarantee reliable ground truth. Across five public enterprise-style corpora, our method provides informative variation in difficulty, revealing unseen failure modes such as an inability of agents to handle underspecified or ambiguous requests. On the RepLiQA corpus, 91\% of human-generated queries can be answered by all members on a panel of 12 retrieval systems, compared to only 12\% of CoverSynth-generated queries. Finally, in a repeated TechQA/RepLiQA study, 12 of 12 within-harness model contrasts have positive nominal 95\% intervals on generated sets, compared with 4 of 12 on human sets. CoverSynth makes coverage and evidence quality explicit construction objectives, producing corpus-grounded evaluations that reveal retrieval headroom and differences between agent configurations.
papers.summary: Teams building enterprise retrieval agents need evaluation sets that expose domain-specific failures, but neither expert-authored nor current synthetic sets come with a method for guaranteeing coverage, reliable ground truth, efficiency, and the power to separate system configurations. `CoverSynth` generates queries from an unannotated corpus while deliberately targeting coverage over retrieval demands and system capabilities, using deterministic checks to locate evidence quotes in their sources and model-based checks for semantic validity, and is paired with a framework for judging when an evaluation set satisfies those criteria. On the `RepLiQA` corpus **91% of human-written queries were answerable by every member of a 12-system retrieval panel, against only 12% of generated ones**, and generated sets exposed failures such as agents mishandling underspecified or ambiguous requests. In a repeated `TechQA`/`RepLiQA` study, 12 of 12 within-harness model contrasts had positive nominal 95% intervals on generated sets versus 4 of 12 on human sets.

papers.title: From Candidate Tokens to Final Outcomes: Decoding Relative Long-Horizon Candidate Value from Reasoning Model Representations
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models generate reasoning trajectories token by token. At a given prefix, multiple next-token candidates may be plausible, yet shape subsequent reasoning and differ in their chances of leading to the correct answer. Whether these differences are reflected in internal representations remains unclear. To study this question, we define relative long-horizon candidate value to quantify within-prefix differences and construct the Reasoning Candidate-Token Value (RCTV) dataset, pairing mathematical reasoning prefixes with plausible next-token candidates and their empirical long-horizon candidate values. Using RCTV, we examine hidden states, multilayer perceptron outputs, and attention outputs at candidate positions with sparse linear probes. Experimental results provide evidence that relative long-horizon candidate value is linearly decodable from these representations at multiple layers. Candidate-value probes can also outperform probability- and embedding-based baselines. Furthermore, a controlled online intervention experiment shows that using the decoded signals to guide token selection during generation can improve the chances of eventual success. Our findings provide evidence that internal representations encode information about relative long-horizon candidate value, offering insights into how local candidate-level representations relate to long-horizon reasoning outcomes.
papers.summary: At any point in a reasoning trace several next tokens look plausible, yet they steer subsequent reasoning differently and differ in their odds of reaching the right answer; whether a model's own activations register that difference was unclear. Relative long-horizon candidate value is defined to quantify these within-prefix differences, and the `RCTV` dataset pairs mathematical reasoning prefixes with plausible next-token candidates and their empirical long-horizon values. Sparse linear probes on hidden states, multilayer perceptron outputs, and attention outputs recover that value **linearly at multiple layers, outperforming probability- and embedding-based baselines**, and a controlled online intervention that uses the decoded signal to guide token selection raised the chance of eventually answering correctly.

papers.title: Sensitivity or Criterion? Measuring and Moving When Language Models Act
papers.abstract: Before an agent acts, it must decide whether action is warranted. A single accuracy cannot distinguish failure to recognize a warranted action from reluctance to act. Signal-detection theory separates sensitivity from criterion, but criteria estimated from authored binary labels depend on each benchmark's example mix. We introduce FlipAct, a diagnostic of tool use in physical states. A rule over annotated tool properties computes each answer and a graded evidence score, fixing the Yes/No boundary at zero across models. Questions form 2-by-2 quads that hold required knowledge fixed while the state flips. The slope of the fitted Yes-rate curve measures sensitivity; its crossing at one half measures criterion. Across 44 open models, sensitivity rises with size within a family, and its ranking agrees with three of four external when-to-act benchmarks. Models respond to evidence sign rather than magnitude, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, most models are conservative across rephrasings; in some, this partly reflects a preference for No. Criterion is not determined by size. Activation steering shifts criterion with weights fixed; distillation from a model's own steered copy puts the shift into its weights without a significant sensitivity change. The distilled shift transfers to six external benchmarks, including two without Yes/No answers, while criterion-free AUC is preserved on the five benchmarks where it is available. Accuracy improves where models start conservative and declines or remains within error where they start permissive. Project page: https://sixundong.com/projects/flipact
papers.summary: A single accuracy figure cannot separate a model that fails to recognize an action is warranted from one that recognizes it and holds back, and criteria estimated from authored yes/no labels shift with each benchmark's example mix. `FlipAct` fixes the boundary instead: a rule over annotated tool properties computes both the answer and a graded evidence score, pinning the yes/no threshold at zero, and questions form two-by-two quads that hold required knowledge fixed while flipping physical state, so the fitted yes-rate curve's slope measures sensitivity and its crossing at one half measures criterion. Across **44 open models, sensitivity rises with size within a family while criterion is not determined by size**; models respond to the sign of evidence rather than its magnitude, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones, and most lean conservative about acting. Activation steering moves criterion with weights frozen, and distilling from a model's own steered copy writes the shift into the weights, transferring to six external benchmarks without significant sensitivity change or loss of criterion-free discrimination.

papers.title: SpecFit: Not All Draft Tokens Cost the Same in Offloaded MoE Inference
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, but when their expert weights are offloaded to host memory, host-to-device (H2D) expert transfers enter the critical path of decoding. Speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens in one forward pass, yet in an MoE model each verified token activates its own experts, so a larger draft tree transfers more experts. Because of this H2D cost, speculative decoding commits several tokens per verification cycle yet is sometimes even slower than autoregressive decoding. Based on this observation, we propose SpecFit, which chooses the verified draft subtree to maximize predicted throughput rather than acceptance length. SpecFit estimates the expected number of committed tokens from draft path probabilities and predicts cycle time from the node count and the per-layer union of the experts the subtree activates; this union is a monotone submodular coverage function, so each node pays only for the experts it adds. An exact search over ancestor-closed subtrees returns the subtree with the highest predicted throughput; run after each draft level, the same search also decides when to stop drafting, and the unmodified target verifies the result. On CNN/DailyMail summarization and a GSM8K subset with Qwen3-30B-A3B, SpecFit decodes 21.6% and 7.0% faster than EAGLE-3 with the same expert cache and 1.97x and 1.72x as fast as vanilla EAGLE-3. Code is available at https://github.com/Chlience/SpecFit.
papers.summary: When a mixture-of-experts model keeps expert weights in host memory, every verified token pulls its own experts over the host-to-device link, so speculative decoding can commit several tokens per cycle and still be slower than plain autoregressive decoding. `SpecFit` chooses which draft subtree to verify by predicted throughput rather than acceptance length, estimating committed tokens from draft path probabilities and cycle time from node count plus the per-layer union of experts the subtree activates; since that union is a monotone submodular coverage function, each node only pays for the experts it adds. An exact search over ancestor-closed subtrees returns the highest-throughput subtree and, run after each draft level, also decides when to stop drafting, with the target model left unmodified. With `Qwen3-30B-A3B` it is **21.6% and 7.0% faster than `EAGLE-3` using the same expert cache on `CNN/DailyMail` summarization and a `GSM8K` subset, and up to 1.97x faster than vanilla `EAGLE-3`**.

papers.title: Riemannian Graph Tokenizer for Structural Knowledge Transfer
papers.abstract: Foundation models are at the forefront of artificial intelligence. A tokenizer, converting the raw input into discrete representations that the model can understand, plays an important role to the success of foundation models. Unlike the text tokenizer that is well studied in large language models, graph tokenizer is still at its early stage, facing the challenges of tackling the non-Euclidean structures and capturing the structural semantics. How to design a graph tokenizer for structural knowledge transfer? To this end, we propose a Riemannian Graph Tokenizer (RGT) that bridges the structural knowledge and quantized representations to support cross-domain structural knowledge transfer. The connection is established by Riemannian geometry. Specifically, we first define the geometric vocabulary (trees, cycles and sequences), which captures fundamental structural patterns and reflects the intrinsic geometry of graph. Second, we construct a Riemannian quantizer with Riemannian Straight-Through Estimator to tokenise graph structures across multiple domains into discrete tokens. To ensure consistency and transferability across diverse geometric spaces, RGT further incorporates a geometry-aligned decoder that projects manifold-specific tokens into a unified tangent space. The theoretical analysis and geometric interpretations are provided to support the effectiveness of our proposed method. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that RGT significantly enhances structural knowledge transferability across graph domains.
papers.summary: Text tokenizers are well understood, but graph tokenizers must handle non-Euclidean structure and capture structural semantics, which limits how well structural knowledge transfers across graph domains. The `Riemannian Graph Tokenizer` defines a geometric vocabulary of trees, cycles, and sequences to capture fundamental structural patterns, quantizes graph structure into discrete tokens using a Riemannian quantizer with a Riemannian straight-through estimator, and adds a geometry-aligned decoder that projects manifold-specific tokens into a shared tangent space for consistency across geometries. Theoretical analysis and geometric interpretation accompany experiments across diverse datasets reporting **significantly improved transfer of structural knowledge between graph domains**.

papers.title: Pessimistic Latent Task-aware Optimization for Robust Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Context-based offline meta-reinforcement learning (COMRL) has advanced almost entirely through better task representations, which separate task identity from artifacts of the behavior policy so that the latent reflects the task alone. The implicit expectation has been that a clean representation will transfer to out-of-support (parameter-extrapolation) tasks. On such a task, however, the encoder produces a latent outside the training support, where the policy has never been trained. We address this gap with Pessimistic Latent Task-aware Optimization (PLATO), which exposes the policy to off-support latents during training. PLATO assumes a mild manifold hypothesis: task latents lie on a low-dimensional manifold, and out-of-support tasks lie farther from the training centroid. It exploits this geometry by perturbing inferred latents outward from the centroid to synthesize counterfactual tasks. A learned decoder ensemble then rolls out short trajectories at each perturbed latent, and the policy is updated on the imagined transitions under a pessimism weight that down-weights steps on which the ensemble disagrees. We prove that the perturbation leaves the training support by a controllable margin and that the out-of-support generalization gap is bounded by the same perturbation reach, and we give explicit conditions, verified empirically, under which the epistemic disagreement at the perturbed latent stays bounded away from zero. On eight MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, PLATO consistently improves out-of-support returns over strong COMRL baselines while remaining competitive on in-distribution tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/deephoony/plato.
papers.summary: Context-based offline meta-reinforcement learning has progressed mainly by cleaning up task representations, on the assumption a clean latent will transfer to tasks outside the training range; in practice the encoder maps such a task to a latent the policy has never been trained on. `PLATO` exposes the policy to those off-support latents during training, assuming task latents lie on a low-dimensional manifold with out-of-support tasks farther from the training centroid, so perturbing inferred latents outward synthesizes counterfactual tasks; a learned decoder ensemble rolls out short imagined trajectories there and updates are down-weighted where the ensemble disagrees. The authors prove the perturbation leaves the training support by a controllable margin and that the out-of-support generalization gap is bounded by the same reach, with conditions keeping epistemic disagreement away from zero. On **eight `MuJoCo` continuous-control benchmarks, out-of-support returns consistently improve over strong baselines** while in-distribution performance stays competitive.

papers.title: World Modeling through Spectral Alignment
papers.abstract: How do we tell a world model what information to preserve? We study this question through the lens of spectral representation learning. We introduce SpecWM, a JEPA framework that explicitly specifies desired relationships between observations through a target similarity kernel and trains the encoder to reproduce those relationships in its embedding geometry. Different kernels provide different supervision, ranging from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel requiring only the ordering of observations within trajectories. We characterize the global optima of the objective, establish conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and connect temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure under an idealized setting. Empirically, the choice of kernel strongly controls which physical quantities are recoverable from the representation. More importantly, temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel from 52% to 68% on OGBench Cube, 49% to 77% on OGBench Scene, and 29% to 51% on CALVIN. These results suggest that explicitly specifying representation geometry provides a simple way to steer what latent world models preserve for control.
papers.summary: Latent world models need some way of being told what information to preserve, and `SpecWM` supplies it by specifying desired relationships between observations as a target similarity kernel and training a joint-embedding predictive encoder to reproduce those relationships in its embedding geometry. Kernels range from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel needing only the ordering of observations within a trajectory; the work characterizes the objective's global optima, gives conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and connects temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure. Empirically the kernel choice determines which physical quantities are recoverable, and temporal spectral alignment lifts cross-entropy-method planning success over `LeWorldModel` **from 52% to 68% on `OGBench` Cube, 49% to 77% on `OGBench` Scene, and 29% to 51% on `CALVIN`**.

papers.title: Harnessing SPAD Noise: Test-Time Gated Attention for Indoor Depth Estimation
papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) has emerged as a cost-effective alternative to hardware-dependent 3D sensing modalities, yet predicting precise metric depth remains a persistent challenge due to intrinsic scale ambiguity, edge bleeding, and limited zero-shot generalization in unseen environments. Recent multi-modal approaches incorporate 1D/3D Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) data to resolve these ambiguities, but they mainly treat SPAD noise as a harmful artifact required for denoising or leave the noise ignored. In this paper, we present an essentially different insight: native SPAD noise is an informative prior that implicitly encodes deterministic environmental characteristics. Driven by this paradigm shift, we introduce a novel, lightweight Test-Time Gated Attention framework by Harnessing SPAD Noise, therefore dubbed HSN. Tailored for indoor scenarios, HSN leverages the synergistic combination of 1D SPAD histograms and Gate Adapters (GAs). Through three complementary optimization phases, it generates channel-wise gated attention vectors to dynamically adjust encoder feature maps at inference time, effectively resolving ambiguous scale and boundary challenges without the heavy computational overhead or dense 3D modalities that other TTA methods suffer from. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world indoor benchmarks show that HSN achieves state-of-the-art metric depth accuracy in in-domain settings, while exhibiting even greater potential under zero-shot generalization to unfamiliar environments. Furthermore, interpretability analysis reveals that the proposed gated attention mechanism adaptively shifts attention toward deeper semantic layers under intensifying SPAD noise. Code will be made publicly available.
papers.summary: Monocular depth estimation is cheap compared with dedicated 3D sensing but struggles with scale ambiguity, edge bleeding, and unfamiliar scenes; adding single-photon avalanche diode measurements helps, though prior work treats the sensor's noise as an artifact to denoise or simply ignores it. `HSN` instead treats that native noise as an informative prior encoding deterministic properties of the environment, combining 1D photon histograms with lightweight gate adapters that produce channel-wise gated attention vectors to adjust encoder feature maps at inference time, across three complementary optimization phases and without dense 3D input or the cost of heavier test-time adaptation. On real-world indoor benchmarks it reports **state-of-the-art metric depth accuracy in-domain and larger relative gains under zero-shot transfer to unseen environments**, and interpretability analysis shows attention shifting toward deeper semantic layers as noise intensifies.

papers.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Advancing Harmful Content Understanding via Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play
papers.abstract: Despite significant advances in language understanding, Large Language Models (LLMs) can still miss meaning hidden in plain sight, failing to identify harmful intent in expressions readily understood by humans. Malicious users exploit this gap by strategically disguising harmful content to evade automated moderation, posing a serious threat to online platform safety. The vulnerability reflects a fundamental cognitive asymmetry between human readers, who integrate contextual, phonetic, and visual cues to decipher the intent behind deliberate obfuscation, and text-based LLMs, which rely primarily on token sequences and have limited exposure to evolving evasions. To bridge this asymmetry, we propose PASP (Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play), which combines multi-perceptual views with adversarial self-play to improve understanding of harmful intent as evasions evolve. Specifically, PASP constructs textual, phonetic, and visual views of each input, preserving its original context while exposing pronunciation and glyph cues obscured in token space. During adversarial self-play, an attacker uses defender feedback to generate intent-preserving evasions, while the defender is trained using an intent-invariance reward to understand harmful intent across changing surface forms. Extensive experiments show that PASP reduces adaptive attack success rates by up to 73.71% and 74.49% on ChineseHarm-Bench and EvoHarmBench, respectively, preserves model capabilities with minimal degradation, and effectively interprets real-world evasive expressions in e-commerce.
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail to recognize harmful intent in text that has been deliberately obfuscated with phonetic substitutions or look-alike glyphs, a gap that malicious users exploit to slip past automated moderation. `PASP` (Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play) builds textual, phonetic, and visual views of each input, then trains a defender against an attacker that uses defender feedback to generate intent-preserving evasions, with an intent-invariance reward pushing the defender to recognize harm across changing surface forms. The authors report that the method **reduces adaptive attack success rates by up to 73.71%** on `ChineseHarm-Bench` and by up to 74.49% on `EvoHarmBench`, with minimal degradation of general capabilities, and that it correctly interprets real-world evasive expressions collected from e-commerce platforms.

papers.title: BridgeCodec: Mamba Enhanced Neural Audio Codec with Schr\"odinger Bridge at Low Bitrate
papers.abstract: Neural audio codecs achieve remarkable performance but operate as closed ecosystems with rigidly co-trained encoderdecoder pairs, severely hindering interoperability. To resolve this, we propose BridgeCodec, a versatile framework that decouples these pairs by translating latent representations between mismatched, frozen endpoints. We formulate this cross-codec translation as a Schr\"odinger Bridge optimal transport problem, enabling robust mapping between disparate distributions without predefined noise priors. To efficiently capture longrange speech temporal dependencies, we integrate a Mambaenhanced U-Net architecture. We validate BridgeCodec on an extreme deployment scenario: mapping a lightweight 8 kHz source encoder directly to a 48 kHz target decoder at an ultralow bitrate of 1 kbps. Experimental results demonstrate that BridgeCodec achieves superior wideband reconstruction and high perceptual quality, successfully bridging heavily bottlenecked, heterogeneous codecs.
papers.summary: Neural audio codecs are trained as tightly coupled encoder-decoder pairs, so the encoder from one codec cannot be used with the decoder of another. `BridgeCodec` translates latent representations between mismatched, frozen endpoints by framing the problem as Schrödinger Bridge optimal transport, which maps between the two latent distributions without a predefined noise prior, and it uses a Mamba-enhanced U-Net to capture long-range temporal structure in speech. In the test scenario, **a lightweight 8 kHz source encoder is bridged directly to a 48 kHz target decoder at 1 kbps**, and the authors report superior wideband reconstruction and high perceptual quality despite the heavily bottlenecked, heterogeneous pair.

papers.title: Personalized Physiological-Model-Based Neural Network for Glucose Forecasting in Type 1 Diabetes
papers.abstract: Accurate, physiologically consistent glucose forecasts could help people with type 1 diabetes respond to impending excursions. We applied our physiological-model-based neural network (PMB--NN) framework to glucose forecasting. A temporal convolutional network (TCN) used 180 min of history, constrained during training by a personalized four-parameter physiological model. The main PMB--NN combined forecast and neural--physiological agreement losses; a three-term variant additionally fitted physiological predictions to measured glucose. Data comprised 6--8 weeks of continuous glucose monitoring, pump, and meal records from 25 AZT1D participants. Person-specific models used chronological 70/10/20 train/validation/test splits and 30-, 60-, and 120-min horizons. Median mean absolute errors were 16.24, 25.00, and 30.20 mg/dL with basal insulin records and 15.38, 24.21, and 31.79 mg/dL before these records became available. In the latter setting, PMB--NN had the lowest median error at 30 and 60 min; it outperformed the physiological model alone in all six settings. In input-increase tests, glucose predictions changed in the expected direction for 85\% of correction boluses and 100\% of carbohydrate rescues, versus 57\% for active insulin and 56\% for active carbohydrates. Most standalone physiological fits showed locally distinguishable parameter effects, with glucose-related coefficients more stable under resampling than insulin- or carbohydrate-related coefficients. The three-term variant improved hyperglycaemia accuracy with basal records, but did not significantly change overall MAE and reduced directional plausibility in three tests. PMB--NN combines personalized forecasting with an explicit physiological model, allowing assessment of predictive accuracy, physiological response behavior, and participant-specific coefficients.
papers.summary: People with type 1 diabetes could respond earlier to glucose excursions if forecasts were both accurate and physiologically consistent. The physiological-model-based neural network (`PMB-NN`) framework trains a temporal convolutional network (TCN) on 180 minutes of history while constraining it with a personalized four-parameter physiological model, and the authors fit person-specific models for 25 participants in the `AZT1D` dataset using 6 to 8 weeks of continuous glucose monitoring, pump, and meal records at 30, 60, and 120 minute horizons. Median mean absolute errors were 16.24, 25.00, and 30.20 mg/dL with basal insulin records available, and the neural model **outperformed the standalone physiological model in all six settings** while shifting predictions in the expected direction for 85% of correction boluses and 100% of carbohydrate rescues. A three-term variant that also fit physiological predictions to measured glucose improved hyperglycaemia accuracy but did not change overall error significantly and reduced directional plausibility in three tests.

papers.title: Split Conformal Interval Length under Huber Contamination
papers.abstract: Existing analyses of interval length in split conformal prediction largely focus on clean data. However, how contamination at the training and calibration stages alters interval length relative to the corresponding clean population oracle remains understudied. In this paper, we consider Huber contamination and derive a finite-sample upper bound that holds uniformly over contaminating distributions, with leading terms scaling as $L(\delta_1+n_1^{-1/2}) +(n_2^{-1/2}+\delta_2)/((1-\delta_2)r_0)$, in addition to a clean-sample estimation term. We further establish a minimax lower bound matching the upper-bound rate up to constant factors on a regular asymmetric location submodel. For calibration contamination, we obtain an exact worst-case characterization of the population interval-length deviation. We also extend the upper-bound results to conformalized quantile regression and adaptive residual scores. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets provide empirical support for our theoretical findings on training and calibration contamination.
papers.summary: Analyses of prediction interval length in split conformal prediction have mostly assumed clean data, leaving open how contamination during training or calibration changes interval length relative to the clean population oracle. The authors adopt the Huber contamination model and derive a finite-sample upper bound on the deviation that holds uniformly over contaminating distributions, with a training term that grows with the contamination fraction and the inverse square root of the training size, and a calibration term driven by the calibration contamination fraction, the calibration sample size, and the density at the target quantile. They also **prove a minimax lower bound matching the upper-bound rate up to constant factors** on a regular asymmetric location submodel, give an exact worst-case characterization of interval-length deviation under calibration contamination, extend the bounds to conformalized quantile regression and adaptive residual scores, and confirm the predicted behavior on synthetic and real datasets.

papers.title: When Messages Go Wrong: Understanding Communication Faults in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) use specialized agents that exchange messages to accomplish complex tasks. Their reliance on networked protocols, remote tools, and model endpoints exposes communication to message loss, delay, and context expiration. Because agents often exchange open-ended natural language, anomalies can alter task-relevant information while leaving messages processable, allowing semantic errors to propagate through subsequent interactions. Systematic studies of faults in inter-agent communication remain limited. This paper presents a large-scale empirical study of how communication faults manifest, propagate, and affect task outcomes in LLM-MAS. We construct a cross-layer taxonomy linking lower-stack disturbances to application-visible faults and develop a fault-injection and tracing pipeline. Our evaluation covers more than 29,000 executions across 100 tasks, five domains, three workflow topologies, and three model configurations. We find that 20.7% of failures with complete detection records occur without an immediate failure signal, reaching 76.2% for partial-content faults. Flat maintains 53.0% task success under communication faults, compared with 3.3% and 3.2% for Sequential and Hierarchical, respectively. This advantage primarily arises when an alternative information path preserves the evidence required by downstream agents. We also evaluate execution-side and evidence protection mechanisms and find that they recover different failure cases. Evidence recovery depends on whether trustworthy information remains accessible through an unaffected path. These observations provide empirical insights into communication-fault propagation, workflow resilience, and protection design for LLM-MAS.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems built from large language models exchange natural-language messages over networked protocols, remote tools, and model endpoints, so message loss, delay, and context expiration can corrupt task-relevant information while leaving messages perfectly processable. The authors build a cross-layer taxonomy linking lower-stack disturbances to application-visible faults, develop a fault-injection and tracing pipeline, and run more than 29,000 executions across 100 tasks, five domains, three workflow topologies, and three model configurations. About 20.7% of failures with complete detection records showed no immediate failure signal, rising to 76.2% for partial-content faults, and **a flat topology kept 53.0% task success under communication faults versus 3.3% and 3.2% for sequential and hierarchical workflows**, mainly because an alternative information path preserved the evidence downstream agents needed. Execution-side and evidence-protection mechanisms recovered different failure cases, with evidence recovery hinging on whether trustworthy information remained reachable through an unaffected path.

papers.title: Scalable Robust MCTS with Anytime Deterministic Optimality Guarantees
papers.abstract: MDP planners often rely on nominal transition models that may differ from the true dynamics. Robust MDP planning accounts for this uncertainty through a set of admissible models, but doing so with limited online computation is challenging: the search tree grows exponentially with the horizon and each robust backup requires an additional optimization. Existing online robust methods remain limited in scale and offer at most probabilistic guarantees. We introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first deterministic anytime guarantees for robust online MDP planning. We restrict computation to the sampled search tree while deterministically bounding the contribution of unsampled trajectories. For any fixed policy, we derive lower and upper bounds on the gap between its projected and true robust values under rectangular and non-rectangular uncertainty sets. Under rectangular uncertainty, we propagate these bounds through the robust Bellman operator to bound the optimal robust value. These bounds are computable from the current sampled tree, hold at every node, tighten as the sampled support expands, and converge to the robust values as full support is recovered. We develop CAR-MCTS, a bound-guided MCTS planner that uses these deterministic bounds to guide exploration, prune provably suboptimal branches, and terminate once the optimal root action is certified. The fixed-policy bounds also yield an anytime policy-evaluation mechanism that certifies the robust value of any policy, independent of how it was obtained. Experiments verify the deterministic bounds, their tightening under support expansion, substantial branch pruning, root-action certification, and convergence to the optimal robust policy. To our knowledge, this is the first scalable robust MCTS framework with anytime deterministic guarantees for both online planning and policy evaluation, without enumerating the full state space.
papers.summary: Online planners for Markov decision processes (MDPs) usually trust a nominal transition model, and robust planning over a set of admissible models is expensive because the search tree grows exponentially with the horizon and each robust backup needs an inner optimization. The authors restrict computation to the sampled search tree, derive deterministic lower and upper bounds on the gap between a policy's projected and true robust values under rectangular and non-rectangular uncertainty sets, and propagate those bounds through the robust Bellman operator to bound the optimal robust value from the current tree. The resulting `CAR-MCTS` planner uses the bounds to guide exploration, prune provably suboptimal branches, and stop once the root action is certified, and the fixed-policy bounds double as an anytime certificate for the robust value of any policy regardless of how it was obtained. Experiments confirm that the bounds tighten as sampled support expands and show substantial pruning and convergence to the optimal robust policy, which the authors present as **the first scalable robust Monte Carlo tree search with anytime deterministic guarantees** that avoids enumerating the full state space.

papers.title: MemeLogos: Knowledge-Driven Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for Harmful Meme Detection
papers.abstract: With the rapid proliferation of social media, harmful memes have become a growing threat to online ecosystems. Their harmfulness is often implicitly conveyed through complex interactions among visual, textual, and contextual cues, making accurate detection challenging. Recent studies have introduced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and external knowledge into harmful meme detection. However, existing methods mainly retrieve similar instances or auxiliary information, limiting their ability to capture reusable harmfulness knowledge and underlying reasoning mechanisms, and thus constraining both detection performance and interpretability. To address these challenges, we propose MemeLogos, a knowledge-driven retrieval-augmented reasoning framework for harmful meme detection. MemeLogos abstracts recurring harmfulness patterns and reasoning structures from diverse harmful cases into reusable knowledge units and organizes them into a dedicated star-shaped knowledge graph. By combining structured knowledge retrieval with an explicit multi-stage reasoning process inspired by cognitive mechanisms, MemeLogos leverages retrieved knowledge to guide harmfulness reasoning, improving both detection reliability and interpretability. Extensive experiments show that MemeLogos consistently outperforms existing harmful meme detection methods while generating more coherent and interpretable reasoning, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured harmfulness knowledge for multimodal content understanding.
papers.summary: Harmful memes convey their intent through interactions among visual, textual, and contextual cues, and prior retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches to detecting them mostly retrieve similar instances or auxiliary facts rather than reusable knowledge about why content is harmful. `MemeLogos` abstracts recurring harmfulness patterns and reasoning structures from diverse harmful cases into knowledge units, organizes them in a star-shaped knowledge graph, and retrieves from that graph to drive an explicit multi-stage reasoning process modeled on cognitive mechanisms. The authors report that it **consistently outperforms existing harmful meme detectors** while producing more coherent and interpretable reasoning.

papers.title: SkillFusion: Towards Reliable Multi-Skill Composition for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Independently authored skills can impose incompatible requirements, competing preferences, and redundant instructions when jointly loaded by an LLM agent. We propose SkillFusion, an offline compiler that reconciles these interactions into a reusable merged skill. Its central idea is to make composition decisions explicit through typed, scoped constraints linked to their source directives. A type-scope gate selects candidate interactions, while selective fallback revisits pairs potentially missed by structural pruning. A classifier identifies interaction types, and an adversarial verifier re-examines uncertain judgments. The resolver applies conditional routing or explicit priorities to hard conflicts, verified abstraction to soft conflicts, and deduplication to redundant instructions. Source-linked checks guide synthesis and compression, and metadata synthesis supports discovery of the merged skill. The resulting artifact retains associated scripts and resources and can be reused across tasks and executor models. SkillFusion achieves the highest mean Success among evaluated non-oracle methods on all three agent benchmarks and on both transfer benchmarks across three executor models. At the largest tested instruction configurations, it achieves over 2.5 times the Success of unresolved multi-skill loading, highlighting the growing value of reconciliation as composition becomes more demanding. The code will be open-sourced after the review process concludes.
papers.summary: When an LLM agent loads several independently authored skills at once, their instructions can impose incompatible requirements, competing preferences, and redundant directives. `SkillFusion` is an offline compiler that reconciles those interactions into a single reusable merged skill by making every composition decision explicit as a typed, scoped constraint linked to its source directive: a type-scope gate selects candidate interactions with a selective fallback for pairs that structural pruning might miss, a classifier labels interaction types with an adversarial verifier rechecking uncertain cases, and a resolver applies conditional routing or explicit priorities to hard conflicts, verified abstraction to soft conflicts, and deduplication to redundancy. The merged artifact keeps its scripts and resources and transfers across tasks and executor models, and it achieves the highest mean success among non-oracle methods on three agent benchmarks and two transfer benchmarks with three executor models, reaching **over 2.5 times the success of unresolved multi-skill loading** at the largest instruction configurations.

papers.title: Security in LLM-Assisted Coding: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: Large Language Models accelerate software development but introduce severe security vulnerabilities. This systematic review investigates security risks in automated coding, benchmark limitations, and the role of human developers. Findings indicate that models frequently generate insecure code and faulty patches due to training data biases. Additionally, the models themselves are susceptible to direct attacks. Current evaluation methods suffer from data contamination and lack robust security metrics. Consequently, human oversight remains essential. Safer integration of automation will require more security-aware model architectures, stronger security-specific benchmarks, and more effective human-AI collaboration frameworks to mitigate these systemic risks.
papers.summary: Large language models speed up software development but also introduce security vulnerabilities into the code they produce. This systematic literature review surveys the security risks of automated coding, the limitations of existing benchmarks, and the role human developers play in mitigating those risks. It finds that **models frequently generate insecure code and faulty patches, which the reviewed work attributes to biases in training data**, that the models themselves are susceptible to direct attacks, and that current evaluations suffer from data contamination and lack robust security metrics. The authors conclude that human oversight remains essential and call for security-aware model architectures, stronger security-specific benchmarks, and better human-AI collaboration frameworks.

papers.title: AlphaPilot: Multi-Turn Tool-Using LLM Agents for Adaptive Alpha Mining with Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks interpretable expressions that rank assets by future returns. The task is challenging because it demands simultaneous processing of unstructured market descriptions, historical data, and quantitative evaluation of candidate factors, yet most existing methods exploit only a subset of these signals. We introduce AlphaPilot, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents for adaptive alpha mining. The agent conditions on market descriptions, proposes factor expressions, queries real-data evaluator feedback, and updates a retained factor pool across turns. This design jointly leverages market text, LLM financial knowledge, real data, and evaluation feedback. At inference time, AlphaPilot performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to shifting market regimes. Across three independent runs in out-of-sample rolling backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, AlphaPilot achieves mean total returns of 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively. It attains the highest mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the evaluated methods on both universes.
papers.summary: Formulaic alpha mining searches for interpretable expressions that rank assets by expected future return, and most existing methods use only a subset of the available signals among market text, historical data, and quantitative factor evaluation. `AlphaPilot` trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents with reinforcement learning: the agent conditions on market descriptions, proposes factor expressions, queries an evaluator that scores them on real data, and updates a retained factor pool across turns, then at inference time repeats the search and pool updates day by day to track shifting market regimes. In out-of-sample rolling backtests averaged over three runs, it reached **mean total returns of 42.93% and 54.19%** on `CSI300` and `CSI500` with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, the highest total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the compared methods on both universes.

papers.title: When Skills Remain But Access Fails: Factorized Skill Memory for Continual Skill Internalization
papers.abstract: Skill internalization aims to convert externally specified procedural skills into persistent model capabilities, allowing language-model agents to execute them without retrieving or reinjecting skill descriptions at inference time. Yet when new skills are learned continually, whether previously internalized skills remain usable is still poorly understood. We study forgetting in continual skill internalization and uncover a clear hierarchical structure. Early in subsequent training, a model may lose the ability to invoke an old skill from the raw request, while supplying only the correct canonical skill name substantially restores the learned behavior; with further optimization, this conditional execution also degrades. We call these two stages skill-addressing forgetting and skill-execution forgetting. Guided by this finding, we introduce Factorized Skill Memory (FSM), which separates continual skill memory into a plastic Address Memory and a stable Execution Memory. At each stage, FSM trains a new LoRA executor using only current-stage data, freezes it after acquisition, and appends it to Execution Memory; in parallel, Address Memory incrementally learns to map current requests to executors without replaying historical requests or execution trajectories. At inference time, Address Memory selects one executor from the raw request, and only that frozen executor performs a single language-model generation. On a five-stage benchmark built from 100 TaskBench skills, FSM achieves 65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% addressing accuracy across two task orders, improving over the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline by 14.3 percentage points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay, which retains historical training examples.
papers.summary: Skill internalization trains procedural skills into a language-model agent's weights so it can execute them without being handed the skill description at inference time, but it has been unclear whether earlier skills survive when new ones are learned continually. The authors find a two-stage forgetting pattern: early in subsequent training the model loses the ability to invoke an old skill from a raw request even though supplying the canonical skill name largely restores the behavior, and only with further optimization does execution itself degrade. Factorized Skill Memory (`FSM`) separates a plastic address memory, which incrementally learns to route requests to executors without replaying historical requests or trajectories, from a stable execution memory of frozen per-stage LoRA executors, so inference picks one executor and runs a single generation. On a five-stage benchmark built from 100 `TaskBench` skills, `FSM` reaches **65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% addressing accuracy** across two task orders, 14.3 points above the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline and within 1.9 points of full replay.

papers.title: RF Fingerprinting of DSP Implementations using Machine Learning: An Over-the-Air Case Study
papers.abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting aims to identify transmitters by exploiting small differences in the emitted signal waveform. Common approaches exploit hardware-dependent imperfections for that purpose. This work instead investigates whether differences between digital signal processing implementations of a transmitter can be identified from their radiated signals. As a practical case study, five different software-based DSP implementations for generating a 2-FSK RTTY communication waveform are considered. In a monitoring receiver, a classifier can identify these DSP implementations using convolutional neural networks that are trained on augmented software-generated signals represented as raw IQ, power spectrum or instantaneous frequency. The trained networks are evaluated on over-the-air recordings obtained using a shortwave transceiver and a software-defined radio receiver. The best neural network combines IQ and the power spectrum representation and achieves an accuracy of up to 90%. The study further examines the influence of the signal SNR and the observation bandwidth on the classification accuracy. The results demonstrate that DSP implementations leave distinguishable characteristics in the transmitted signals and suggest that DSP-dependent fingerprinting can provide complementary information for specific emitter identification systems.
papers.summary: Radio frequency fingerprinting usually identifies transmitters by hardware imperfections, and this study asks instead whether different digital signal processing (DSP) software implementations of the same waveform leave their own detectable traces. Using five software implementations of a 2-FSK radioteletype (RTTY) waveform, the authors train convolutional neural networks on augmented software-generated signals represented as raw IQ samples, power spectra, or instantaneous frequency, then test them on over-the-air recordings captured with a shortwave transceiver and a software-defined radio receiver. **The best network, combining IQ and power-spectrum inputs, reaches up to 90% accuracy** at identifying the implementation, with accuracy depending on signal-to-noise ratio and observation bandwidth, suggesting DSP-dependent features can complement hardware-based emitter identification.

papers.title: Concept Representations in Vector Space: Quantifying Sharedness and Idiosyncrasy of Meaning
papers.abstract: Concepts are the basic units through which we navigate the world and communicate meaning. But do you and I really mean the same thing when we think or speak about a concept? The present study develops a measurement framework for modeling and analyzing interindividual variation in concept representations through sentence embeddings, dense vector representations mapping entire utterances into a shared geometric space. The framework is developed in a theoretical argument and validated, demonstrated, and subjected to robustness checks in a pre-registered study. Short personal definitions, elicited from $N = 125$ participants, are encoded as sentence embeddings and submitted pairwise to a crossed random effects model yielding two concept-level quantities: sharedness ($S_b$), the expected dissimilarity between two randomly drawn individuals, and idiosyncrasy ($I_b$), the person-specific share of total dyadic variance. Two validity tests support the approach: the embedding space fully recovers concept and domain organization from participant definitions even with the target word excluded, and a parameter-free classifier achieves 0.630 accuracy in a within-participant extensional prediction task against a chance baseline of 0.500 and a consistency ceiling of 0.893. The framework finds theoretically interpretable variation in $S_b$ and establishes $I_b$ as a reliable source of dyadic variance across concepts. Results replicate across three encoders varying in architecture and capacity, providing a reproducible and scalable instrument for the empirical study of meaning variation.
papers.summary: Whether two people mean the same thing by a concept is hard to measure, and this pre-registered study builds a framework for quantifying interindividual variation in concept representations using sentence embeddings. Short personal definitions elicited from 125 participants are embedded and compared pairwise in a crossed random effects model, yielding two concept-level quantities: sharedness, the expected dissimilarity between two randomly drawn individuals, and idiosyncrasy, the person-specific share of total dyadic variance. Validation shows the embedding space recovers concept and domain organization from definitions even with the target word removed, and **a parameter-free classifier reaches 0.630 accuracy on a within-participant extensional prediction task** against a 0.500 chance baseline and a 0.893 consistency ceiling, with results replicating across three encoders of differing architecture and capacity.

papers.title: Revisited Support Vector Machines: A Unified Joint Optimization Framework with Nystr\"om Approximation for Scalable Adaptive Learning
papers.abstract: The theoretical elegance of Support Vector Machines (SVMs), grounded in statistical learning theory, establishes them as a reference for robust classification. However, in the era of Big Data, classical SVMs face two major bottlenecks: the prohibitive cubic complexity $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ of training and the rigidity of static kernels. Traditional methodologies treat kernel selection as a discrete, "brute-force" GridSearch problem, effectively decoupling the learning of data representation from the optimization of the decision boundary. This paper proposes a paradigm shift with a so-called "Revisited SVM", a unified framework that recasts the learning process as a continuous %bi-level joint optimization problem. We derive a novel objective function $J(\alpha, \theta)$ that allows for the simultaneous optimization of dual Lagrange multipliers and kernel hyper-parameters. To solve this challenging non-convex problem efficiently, we introduce a hybrid Block Coordinate Ascent (BCA) algorithm, tightly integrated with Nystr\"om-based low-rank approximation, which drastically reduces computational complexity to $\mathcal{O}(Nm)$. Extensive experiments conducted across four heterogeneous domains (Bioinformatics, Finance, Cybersecurity, and Computer Vision) demonstrate that our approach not only matches but often exceeds exhaustive GridSearch accuracy, while delivering training speedups of up to 100x. Notably, on the complex NSL-KDD intrusion detection dataset, our adaptive kernel approach achieves 96.25\% accuracy compared to a mere 50\% for standard baselines, proving its unique ability to model complex non-linear manifolds in high-dimensional spaces. We validate our results using rigorous statistical tests and provide a theoretical convergence analysis of the proposed algorithm.
papers.summary: Classical support vector machines (SVMs) suffer from cubic training complexity in the number of samples and from static kernels whose hyperparameters are chosen by discrete grid search, which decouples representation learning from decision-boundary optimization. The proposed Revisited SVM recasts training as a joint optimization over the dual Lagrange multipliers and the kernel hyperparameters, solved by a hybrid block coordinate ascent (BCA) algorithm integrated with a Nyström low-rank approximation that reduces complexity to linear in the sample size times the approximation rank. Across datasets from bioinformatics, finance, cybersecurity, and computer vision, the authors report accuracy matching or exceeding exhaustive grid search with **training speedups of up to 100x**, including a claimed 96.25% accuracy on the `NSL-KDD` intrusion detection dataset versus 50% for standard baselines, backed by statistical tests and a convergence analysis.

papers.title: The Imperishable Record, Forgiveness, and the Future of Criminal Justice
papers.abstract: Digital technologies can preserve records of wrongdoing indefinitely, and AI can give those records continuing influence over a person's future. We describe this condition as the eternal data present and argue that it threatens the possibility of forgiveness. In criminal justice, formal punishment has an end, whereas the harms caused by the continued use of criminal records may not. Drawing on Hegel's account of the "hard heart" and Arendt's account of the irreversibility of action, we distinguish two dangers that digital systems can combine. People may be permanently identified with what they have done, and acts that cannot be undone may continue to determine what happens to them. We propose a right to remain unfinished, supported by rights to limits on the weight given to older records, to re-evaluation in light of personal change, to reassessment of inferences that affect their lives, and to time limits on the use of records in specified decisions. These proposals extend the ethics of AI beyond accuracy, transparency, and non-discrimination to address how long past wrongdoing should be allowed to govern a person's life.
papers.summary: Digital records of wrongdoing can persist indefinitely, and AI systems can keep those records shaping a person's opportunities long after formal punishment has ended, a condition the authors call the eternal data present. Drawing on Hegel's account of the hard heart and Arendt's account of the irreversibility of action, the essay distinguishes two dangers that digital systems combine: people being permanently identified with what they have done, and irreversible acts continuing to determine what happens to them. The authors propose **a right to remain unfinished**, supported by rights to limits on the weight given to older records, re-evaluation in light of personal change, reassessment of inferences that affect a person's life, and time limits on using records in specified decisions, extending AI ethics beyond accuracy, transparency, and non-discrimination.

papers.title: Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models as Single-Pass Decision Makers
papers.abstract: Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new-schema tests with held-out human-labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182-fold speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new-schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning's accuracy advantage while generating 27-58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.
papers.summary: Language models typically make classification-style decisions by generating tokens, which costs decoding time and hides the probability over options, while task-specific classifiers need per-task training and do not generalize to unseen label schemas. Large Decision Models (LDMs) repurpose a language model to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time in a single prefill forward pass, trained first with Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS) over varied domains, rules, and labels, then with Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD), which has a frozen teacher generate tasks, filters them for answer consistency, and distills label distributions from repeated teacher reasoning. On the `DecisionVista` benchmark across three base models the recipe improves accuracy by 1.8 and 1.5 points over a step-matched baseline on new-schema and held-out human-labelled tests, with a **182-fold latency speedup** over reasoning rollouts on `Gemma-4-31B`; because reasoning still wins on new schemas, a confidence router that sends uncertain cases to reasoning recovers a median 92% of its accuracy advantage while generating 27 to 58% of its tokens.

papers.title: Data Portability Revisited: Toward the Human-Centric, AI-Driven Data Ecosystems of Tomorrow
papers.abstract: This Article critically examines the contemporary regulatory framework and discourse surrounding data portability in the United States. Using recent regulatory developments in the European Union as an illustration, this Article suggests that although data access and portability are identified as vital issues in multiple policy instruments, in its current iteration, at least, legal conceptions of portability continue to reinforce the interests of service providers and data controller enterprises rather than individual end users. This Article argues that a paradigm shift toward a more human-centric data approach to data governance must occur, under which data would be recognized as fundamental to an individual's identity in a digital age. Therefore, it should be placed in the hands of individuals rather than service providers or data controller enterprises. This Article considers technical and market trends in the European Union that reveal and facilitate such a change. It suggests that regulatory frameworks should better align with these technological and market developments to encourage change-inducing trends among market actors. In short, this Article identifies a transformative approach to data portability that empowers individuals with the freedom and ability to aggregate their data in secure personal spaces under their control or dominion. Such a human-centric perspective on data portability is crucial in building Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered applications for individual consumers that can pave the way for the human-centric, AI-driven data ecosystems of the future.
papers.summary: Data access and portability are named as vital issues in multiple policy instruments, yet this legal article argues that current United States conceptions of portability still serve service providers and data controllers rather than individual end users. Using recent European Union regulatory developments as illustration, it calls for a human-centric paradigm in which data is treated as fundamental to individual identity in the digital age and is placed in the hands of individuals. The article points to technical and market trends in the European Union that already move in this direction and argues regulation should align with them so that **individuals can aggregate their data in secure personal spaces under their own control**, which it presents as a precondition for consumer-facing AI applications built on personal data.

papers.title: CacheLink: Functional KV Transport for Zero-Prefill Cross-Model Context Handoff
papers.abstract: KV caches make long-context serving efficient by reusing past computation, but model switching breaks this reuse and forces the receiver to prefill the context again. We study \emph{zero-prefill cross-model context handoff}: translating a sender cache into a receiver-compatible state so that the receiver can continue directly without prefilling same context. Existing affine transport methods show that receiver KV states can be substantially reconstructed from sender caches. However, through extensive analyses, we find that reconstruction fidelity is a poor proxy for receiver utility. Similar K/V reconstruction errors can lead to substantially different attention patterns, predictive distributions, and downstream accuracy, because conventional reconstruction objectives overlook the query-dependent functional importance of K and V in receiver attention. We thus introduce CACHELINK, which learns a coupled K/V correction through the receiver behavior directly. Across four independently trained sender--receiver pairs and seven evaluation panels, CACHELINK improves the equal-weight mean over all methods for every pair. In matched diagnostics, CACHELINK changes K/V squared error by less than 0.4% while substantially changing receiver attention and next-token behavior. At 32K context, it reduces handoff latency by up to $7.27\times$ relative to receiver re-prefill. Our findings verify that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient and that preserving the receiver computation induced by the transported cache is important for effective cross-model KV transport.
papers.summary: Key-value (KV) caches let long-context serving reuse past computation, but switching to a different model forces the new model to prefill the whole context again. The authors study zero-prefill cross-model context handoff, translating a sender model's cache into a state the receiver can continue from, and find that the reconstruction fidelity targeted by existing affine transport methods is a poor proxy for receiver utility because similar K/V reconstruction errors can yield very different attention patterns, predictive distributions, and downstream accuracy. `CacheLink` instead learns a coupled K/V correction supervised through the receiver's own behavior, and across four independently trained sender-receiver pairs and seven evaluation panels it improves the equal-weight mean over all compared methods for every pair while changing K/V squared error by less than 0.4%. At 32K context, **handoff latency drops by up to 7.27 times relative to re-prefilling the receiver**.

papers.title: REPRO: Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimizer for Automated LLM Red-Teaming
papers.abstract:
Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass their safety training. Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. We present REPRO (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization), a pure black-box framework that discovers adversarial prompts through evolutionary optimization driven entirely by a compressed open-weight 7B reflective model on a single consumer GPU. REPRO introduces two mechanisms absent from prior work, both isolated in a component ablation: semantic crossover, an LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator, and Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling informed by structured failure analysis.
  We catalog REPRO's behavior on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench across 36 target models from 11 families, including GPT-5-nano, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4.1. Under our protocol REPRO reaches 100\% attack success rate (ASR) on every evaluated target in a single turn, at a median of 24 target queries per behavior. Two properties of the protocol qualify that figure. The judge scoring candidates during optimization also produces the reported ASR, and search halts when it accepts, so ASR reports whether search succeeded within the iteration budget rather than success at a fixed budget. All baseline figures are transcribed from their original papers, which use different judges, budgets, and model versions. We therefore present this as a catalog of model coverage under one protocol rather than a head-to-head ranking, and develop both qualifications in the paper.
papers.summary: Safety-aligned language models remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts, and existing automated red-teaming methods either need privileged model access, hand-built per-model templates, or single-objective optimization without population diversity. `REPRO` (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization) is a pure black-box evolutionary search driven by a compressed open-weight 7B reflective model on a single consumer GPU, adding two mechanisms isolated in ablations: semantic crossover, an LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator, and Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling informed by structured failure analysis. On `AdvBench`, `JailbreakBench`, and `HarmBench` the authors catalog behavior across **36 target models from 11 families**, including `GPT-5-nano`, `Claude-3.5-Sonnet`, `Gemini-2.5-Pro`, and `Grok-4.1`, reporting 100% attack success rate (ASR) on every target in a single turn at a median of 24 queries per behavior. They qualify that figure explicitly: the judge scoring candidates during search also produces the reported ASR and search halts on acceptance, and baseline numbers are transcribed from papers using different judges, budgets, and model versions, so the results are presented as a coverage catalog under one protocol rather than a head-to-head ranking.

papers.title: SARATHI: Decoupled Data-Free Probing and Adaptive Reconstruction for Structured LLM Pruning
papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces the inference cost of large language models (LLMs) by permanently removing neurons and weight rows, yielding dense, hardware-agnostic speedup. Existing post-training methods couple neuron selection and weight reconstruction through a shared calibration dataset, introducing domain bias and out-of-memory failures at high sparsity. We propose SARATHI, a framework that decouples these two stages. A data-free \emph{NMF Residual Subspace Probe} scores neurons using intrinsic weight geometry, without accessing any calibration data, and carries a formal connection to Robust PCA. \emph{Adaptive OBS} then reconstructs the pruned weights with a localized calibration batch, operating in $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ peak memory per layer and eliminating the global memory bottleneck of coupled methods. A \emph{Bias Shift Compensation} step corrects systematic activation drift in post-LayerNorm architectures that would otherwise cause perplexity collapse at high sparsity. Experiments across six models from two architecture families (gated and non-gated FFN) at 15--40\% sparsity show that SARATHI achieves competitive perplexity and matches or exceeds existing structured pruning baselines on zero-shot accuracy.
papers.summary: Structured pruning removes whole neurons and weight rows from large language models (LLMs) to get dense, hardware-agnostic speedups, but existing post-training methods tie neuron selection and weight reconstruction to a shared calibration set, which introduces domain bias and causes out-of-memory failures at high sparsity. `SARATHI` decouples the two stages: a data-free NMF residual subspace probe scores neurons from the geometry of the weights alone, with a formal connection to robust PCA, and an adaptive OBS step reconstructs the pruned weights from a localized calibration batch in quadratic memory per layer, while a bias shift compensation step corrects systematic activation drift in post-LayerNorm architectures that would otherwise collapse perplexity. Across six models from gated and non-gated feed-forward families at 15 to 40% sparsity, the method **achieves competitive perplexity and matches or exceeds existing structured pruning baselines on zero-shot accuracy**.

papers.title: OceanFlow: Coherent Flow Matching for Probabilistic Ocean Modeling
papers.abstract: Probabilistic ocean modeling is essential for risk-aware marine operations, climate analysis, and scientific decision-making, where downstream decisions depend on the conditional distribution of future ocean states rather than a single deterministic trajectory. Recent data-driven ocean models have made deterministic global ocean modeling increasingly accurate and efficient, but probabilistic ocean modeling remains underdeveloped. Specifically, perturbation-driven ensembles can create spread without explicitly optimizing the joint distribution of their members, often yielding poor calibration and physical inconsistency. To address these issues, we propose OceanFlow, a coherent flow matching framework for probabilistic global ocean modeling. OceanFlow first establishes a sharp, stable mean anchor for the conditional ensemble. Flow matching then learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law that jointly reshapes the residual distribution around this anchor at each transition, preserving the predictive center while refining state-dependent uncertainty. We further introduce a Factorized Dynamics Operator (FDO), which combines factorized transitions with a learned state-conditioned response to parameterize the mean anchor and residual-flow velocity. Extensive experiments show that OceanFlow improves ensemble-mean accuracy, probabilistic reliability, and physical-consistency diagnostics over competitive baselines, supporting coherent flow matching as an effective route toward data-driven probabilistic ocean modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/YuanGao-YG/OceanFlow.
papers.summary: Risk-aware marine operations and climate analysis need the conditional distribution of future ocean states, but existing data-driven ocean models are mostly deterministic, and perturbation-based ensembles create spread without optimizing the joint distribution of their members, giving poor calibration and physically inconsistent forecasts. `OceanFlow` first fits a sharp, stable mean anchor for the conditional ensemble, then uses flow matching to learn a state-conditioned pathwise law that reshapes the residual distribution around that anchor at each transition, preserving the predictive center while refining state-dependent uncertainty. A Factorized Dynamics Operator (FDO) combines factorized transitions with a learned state-conditioned response to parameterize both the mean anchor and the residual-flow velocity. **The method improves ensemble-mean accuracy, probabilistic reliability, and physical-consistency diagnostics over competitive baselines**, and code is released.

papers.title: Improving the Bounds on Approximating Weighted Maximin Share for Chores
papers.abstract: We investigate the problem of allocating indivisible chores among agents with arbitrary positive weights and additive nonnegative cost functions. An allocation is said to be $\alpha$-weighted-maximin-share (WMMS) fair if the cost incurred by each agent is at most $\alpha$ times her weighted maximin share. We establish that every instance admits a $4.124234528$-WMMS allocation. Moreover, for instances in which all weights and costs are rational numbers represented in binary, we give an algorithm that computes a $4.12424$-WMMS allocation in time polynomial in the number of agents, the number of chores, and the total binary encoding length of the input. Complementing these upper bounds, we construct a family of instances with strictly positive, identically ordered costs for which the optimal WMMS approximation factors converge to $e$. Together, our results substantially narrow the previously best-known gap of $[2,12]$ established by Li et al.~\cite{LWX26} to $[e,4.12424]$.
papers.summary: The setting is allocating indivisible chores to agents with arbitrary positive weights and additive nonnegative costs, where an allocation is alpha-weighted-maximin-share (WMMS) fair if each agent's cost is at most alpha times that agent's weighted maximin share. The authors show that every instance admits a roughly 4.1242-WMMS allocation, and for inputs with rational weights and costs in binary they give an algorithm computing a 4.12424-WMMS allocation in time polynomial in the number of agents, the number of chores, and the input encoding length. They also construct a family of instances with strictly positive, identically ordered costs whose optimal approximation factors converge to Euler's number e. **Together these results narrow the previously best-known gap of [2, 12] to [e, 4.12424].**

papers.title: A Step in the Right Place: Understanding and Optimizing Timestep Placement in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models represent an emerging paradigm for language modeling. They generate text in parallel by iteratively refining continuous representations and mapping them back to tokens through a decoder. However, realizing the efficiency advantage of parallel generation requires maintaining generation quality with only a few denoising steps. Even when the number of steps is fixed, their placement along the denoising trajectory remains flexible. In this paper, we demonstrate that changing timestep placement alone can substantially alter the final latent representations and thereby affect the decoded token distributions. Building on these findings, we introduce StepTune, an algorithm that searches for timestep placements that improve generation quality.
