A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.
papers.summary: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model multi-agent decision-making in which agents assign local variables subject to shared constraints, but many solvers rely on broad repeated peer-to-peer messaging and react to conflicts without strategic coordination or learning. `DCC-Incomplete` is a repair-based solver that groups the unsolved part of a problem into conflict clusters, restricts communication to agents within the same conflict region through a coordination layer, and adds a memory-guided restart that lets agents and clusters pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. On distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments, **memory-guided restart raises the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%**, lowers median runtime from 0.565 s to 0.367 s, and roughly halves median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint.

papers.title: Testing Central Structure for Complex Networks
papers.abstract: Centrality measures rank nodes even when the observed differences can be explained by ordinary structural variation. We therefore study a preceding question: whether a network contains a statistically identifiable central structure at all. We formulate this question as a network-level hypothesis testing issue using the adjacency spectral radius as the test statistic and estimate an empirical p-value from randomized networks generated under a specified null model. The framework is evaluated using G(N,M), Chung-Lu, and two implementations of the configuration model on simulated benchmarks and 55 real networks. Controlled experiments further vary the number and connection weights of designated central nodes while holding network size and density fixed. The results show a clear negative association between central-structure strength and the empirical p-value. They also demonstrate that rejection decisions depend substantially on the structural properties preserved by the null model: the detected network sets are not simply nested across models.
papers.summary: Centrality measures always produce a ranking of nodes, even when the observed differences could arise from ordinary structural variation. The authors instead ask whether a network contains a statistically identifiable central structure at all, framing it as a network-level hypothesis test that uses the adjacency spectral radius as the statistic and estimates an empirical p-value from randomized networks drawn under a chosen null model. Evaluations with `G(N,M)`, `Chung-Lu`, and two configuration-model nulls on simulated benchmarks and 55 real networks show a clear negative association between central-structure strength and the p-value, and **the networks flagged as having central structure depend substantially on which structural properties the null model preserves**, with detected sets not simply nested across models.

papers.title: Feedback as an Interface: Controlling Form and Detail in LLM Translation Refinement
papers.abstract: Feedback presentation shapes how LLMs use evaluator judgments during translation refinement. We introduce a machine translation protocol that keeps the evaluator score, main issue, and recommendation fixed while varying feedback form and supporting detail. Across seven models and six translation directions, low-load feedback outperforms high-load feedback in all 42 translator-direction settings under xCOMET. On the 29,400-record rewriting subset, mean xCOMET scores multiplied by 100 are 83.30 for low-load feedback and 80.67 for high-load feedback; the full-matrix original-translation reference mean is 83.46. MetricX-24 supports the low-load advantage on a stratified subset. A no-feedback second pass yields a small improvement over the original translations, and direct evaluator prompting reproduces the low-load advantage without a separate rewriting stage. These results show that compact feedback limits the quality loss from evaluator-guided refinement in the evaluated high-resource MT settings.
papers.summary: How evaluator feedback is presented shapes how large language models use it when refining machine translations. The authors introduce a protocol that holds the evaluator's score, main issue, and recommendation fixed while varying the form and amount of supporting detail, and run it across seven models and six translation directions. **Low-load feedback beats high-load feedback in all 42 translator-direction settings under `xCOMET`**, with mean scores of 83.30 versus 80.67 on a 29,400-record rewriting subset against 83.46 for the original translations, and `MetricX-24` supports the same advantage on a stratified subset. A no-feedback second pass yields only a small gain, and prompting the evaluator directly reproduces the low-load advantage without a separate rewriting stage, suggesting compact feedback limits the quality loss from evaluator-guided refinement in high-resource settings.

papers.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.
papers.summary: Generative policies give online reinforcement learning (RL) expressive action distributions, but diffusion- and flow-based policies usually require costly iterative sampling. `DriftSpread` is a one-step generative policy built on `Drifting` for maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL: from an energy-based view, the authors derive a critic-guided Drift update and an entropy-induced Spread update from the negative MaxEnt objective, learn them sequentially in the same actor through action regression and distribution matching, and avoid sampling from the critic-defined Boltzmann target or estimating policy densities or scores. They prove convergence to the Boltzmann target under exact fitting with a fixed critic, and on `MuJoCo` **the method attains the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods** while beating diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

papers.title: A Persian Vision-Language-Action Dataset and Benchmark for Ambiguity- and Infeasibility-Aware Instruction-to-Plan Grounding
papers.abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. We introduce the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task: 258 instances over 230 real household/office photographs, annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and an auto-generated chain-of-thought rationale for training. Using this resource, we ablate retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and an agentic disambiguation step, evaluated with an LLM-as-judge protocol and a new metric, PGOS-FA, extending prior work (PG2S) with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired statistical testing across 36 comparisons shows retrieval-augmentation is a large, robustly significant effect, while finer-grained additions are directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from noise at this scale, and the LLM-judge metric has near-zero power where PGOS-FA succeeds. A blind human-correlation study on 79 real outputs shows PGOS-FA tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM-judge. Testing generalization beyond the ablation's single backbone, we find that most of the gap between an open-weight and a substantially stronger closed planner is attributable to open-weight model generation rather than to the closed model's capability specifically, and that our best configuration significantly outperforms an independently reproduced external baseline despite a weaker backbone. The dataset, PGOS-FA implementation, and evaluation code will be made available upon reasonable request.
papers.summary: Turning a natural-language instruction plus a scene image into an executable action plan is central to embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks are English-only, simulated or video-based, and assume instructions are clear and feasible. The authors release the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task, 258 instances over 230 real household and office photographs annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and auto-generated chain-of-thought rationales, and they propose `PGOS-FA`, a metric that extends `PG2S` with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired tests across 36 comparisons show **retrieval augmentation is a large and robustly significant effect, while chain-of-thought prompting and agentic disambiguation are not distinguishable from noise at this scale**, and the LLM-as-judge metric has near-zero statistical power where `PGOS-FA` succeeds. A blind study on 79 real outputs finds `PGOS-FA` tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM judge, and most of the gap between an open-weight and a stronger closed planner is attributed to open-weight generation quality rather than the closed model's capability.

papers.title: Rate-Resolved Text Evaluation with Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: A single evaluation score can rank generation systems but rarely reveals what failed. We propose rate-resolved text evaluation, which turns the masking rate of masked diffusion language models into a diagnostic axis. By reconstructing text under different fractions of masked tokens, one diffusion score becomes a vector of band-conditioned scores that reflect reconstruction difficulty at varying levels of visible context. On SummEval, preserving this rate structure yields complementary signal: the best masking-rate band improves fusion with autoregressive likelihood over a collapsed diffusion scalar, survives a sample-shuffle control that breaks rate ordering, and adds residual signal to a fixed prompted judge. A second diffusion model reproduces the effect more weakly. On WMT MQM zh-en, roundtrip mask-and-reconstruct probing produces a tunable localization curve in which ranking-oriented AUROC and span-detection F1 peak at different masking rates. Factuality benchmarks bound the interpretation: band semantics are model- and task-dependent, so each application requires empirical validation.
papers.summary: A single evaluation score can rank text generation systems but rarely shows what went wrong. Rate-resolved evaluation turns the masking rate of a masked diffusion language model into a diagnostic axis: by reconstructing text under different fractions of masked tokens, one diffusion score becomes a vector of band-conditioned scores that reflect reconstruction difficulty at different levels of visible context. On `SummEval`, **the best masking-rate band improves fusion with autoregressive likelihood over a collapsed diffusion scalar**, survives a sample-shuffle control that breaks rate ordering, and adds residual signal to a fixed prompted judge, though a second diffusion model reproduces the effect more weakly. On `WMT MQM` Chinese-to-English, a roundtrip mask-and-reconstruct probe yields a tunable localization curve in which ranking AUROC and span-detection F1 peak at different masking rates, and factuality benchmarks show that band semantics are model- and task-dependent, so each application needs empirical validation.

papers.title: ProtoPur: Prototype-Purity Pseudo-Labeling for Weakly Supervised Instance Learning in Pathology
papers.abstract: Weak bag-level labels are widely available in computational pathology, whereas reliable instance-level annotations for whole-slide images remain expensive and ambiguous. Weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) achieves strong bag-level classification, but instance-level supervision from attention scores, model predictions, negative bags, or spatial refinement may fail to identify class-specific local evidence. We propose ProtoPur, a prototype-purity pseudo-labeling method for weakly supervised instance-level learning in pathology whole-slide images. ProtoPur estimates class-balanced local purity over prototype regions constructed from frozen foundation-model features, and assigns pseudo-labels to high-purity regions strongly associated with a target class. This purity-first design separates class-specific evidence from negative or shared morphology, with coverage used only to ensure sufficient pseudo-label assignment. We provide a PAC-style analysis showing that the risk of an instance classifier trained with ProtoPur pseudo-labels can be decomposed into a standard uniform-convergence term and a ProtoPur-specific pseudo-label noise term, comprising selected-region mismatch and a coverage residual. Experiments on three public whole-slide image datasets with two pathology foundation encoders show that ProtoPur consistently improves instance-level performance across multiple MIL backbones while maintaining competitive bag-level performance. Pseudo-label quality comparisons on two public datasets further demonstrate that prototype-purity selection provides stronger instance supervision. These results suggest that the foundation-model features contain exploitable instance-level supervision signals, and ProtoPur is a way to reveal and use these signals from weak bag labels without requiring dense instance annotations.
papers.summary: Computational pathology has abundant slide-level labels but few reliable instance-level annotations, and weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) often fails to pinpoint class-specific local evidence when instance supervision is derived from attention scores, predictions, negative bags, or spatial refinement. `ProtoPur` builds prototype regions from frozen pathology foundation-model features, estimates class-balanced local purity over those regions, and assigns pseudo-labels only to high-purity regions strongly tied to a target class, using coverage solely to guarantee enough assignments. A PAC-style analysis decomposes the instance classifier's risk into a standard uniform-convergence term plus a pseudo-label noise term made of selected-region mismatch and a coverage residual, and experiments on three public whole-slide image datasets with two foundation encoders show **consistent instance-level gains across multiple MIL backbones** while bag-level performance stays competitive.

papers.title: Knowledge Interaction in Hypernetwork-based Continual Learning: Conflict and Composition
papers.abstract: Continual learning aims to adapt pretrained large language models (LLMs) to evolving data while preserving their pretrained capabilities. A central challenge is catastrophic forgetting: adaptation to new data can impair performance on previously learned knowledge. Since continual learning commonly changes model parameters, the model's predictions may draw on knowledge from the base model, the parameter update, and the input context. Understanding how these sources interact is essential: conflicts reveal whether new knowledge can override outdated knowledge, while multi-hop reasoning tests whether new knowledge can be composed with existing knowledge to support generalization. We study these interactions in a hypernetwork-based adaptation framework, where a shared network generates adapters from context, allowing a frozen base model to adapt without task-specific updates. We find that, under knowledge conflict, models preferentially follow the context, and their choices depend more on where knowledge is presented than on its content. We also show that context and adapter knowledge perturb the base model's representations along directions orthogonal to its clean hidden states, enabling us to derive steering vectors that control which source the model follows. In multi-hop reasoning, we find that models fail to reliably compose knowledge across the three sources, with the key breakdown arising from the interaction of the hypernetwork with both the base model and the context. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/missswiftie/Knowledge-Interaction-in-CL
papers.summary: Continual learning adapts pretrained large language models (LLMs) to evolving data while trying to avoid catastrophic forgetting, so a model's predictions may draw on the base model, the parameter update, and the input context at once. The authors study how these three sources interact in a hypernetwork-based framework, where a shared network generates adapters from context for a frozen base model, probing both knowledge conflicts and multi-hop composition. **Under conflict, models preferentially follow the context, and their choice depends more on where knowledge is presented than on its content**; context and adapter knowledge perturb hidden states along directions orthogonal to the clean representations, which yields steering vectors that control which source the model follows. In multi-hop reasoning, models fail to reliably compose knowledge across the three sources, with the key breakdown traced to the hypernetwork's interaction with both the base model and the context.

papers.title: The Mathematical Collective Unconscious: Jungian Archetypes within the Latent Space
papers.abstract: Carl Jung theorised that the human psyche contains an inherited framework, the collective unconscious, populated by universal archetypes. As large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast corpora of textual data, this paper investigates whether they spontaneously construct distinct archetype-like regions within their high-dimensional latent spaces. The paper proposes that these regions function as spatial constraints that naturally organise semantically related narratives. To evaluate this, we applied cosine similarity and angular distance metrics across thirteen experiments utilising OpenAIs text-embedding-3-small model. The paper contains two experimental sections the first section explores these ideas using synthetically constructed narratives, the results of which act as a baselines for experiments conducted in the second section where the synthetic data is replaced by human-authored literature (Shmoop corpus), unedited dream reports (DreamBank corpus), and culturally distilled folklore (Andrew Langs Fairy Books). The results show that archetypal roles occupy distinct, measurable regions in the latent space. Crucially, these regions remain compact and consistent because of narrative structure rather than simple word overlap. Additionally, text category dictates spatial distribution: dream reports concentrate within Trickster and Shadow regions, while traditional folklore distributes evenly across all tested archetypes. We conclude that transformer latent spaces encode stable regions which appear to correspond to recognised Jungian archetypes.
papers.summary: Tests whether large language model (LLM) embedding spaces spontaneously organise narratives into regions resembling Carl Jung's universal archetypes, such as the Trickster and the Shadow. Thirteen experiments apply cosine similarity and angular distance to `text-embedding-3-small` embeddings, first on synthetically constructed narratives as a baseline and then on human-authored literature from the `Shmoop` corpus, unedited dream reports from `DreamBank`, and folklore from Andrew Lang's Fairy Books. **Archetypal roles occupy distinct, compact regions whose coherence comes from narrative structure rather than simple word overlap**, and text category shapes the spatial distribution, with dream reports concentrating in Trickster and Shadow regions while folklore spreads evenly across all tested archetypes.

papers.title: Rethinking Human Intent-to-CAD: Parametric CAD Model Generation via Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Parametric Computer-Aided-Design (CAD) modeling from human intent remains challenging, particularly during the conceptual design stage, where design goals are expressed through incomplete and unstructured modalities (e.g., hand-drawn sketches and textual descriptions). In this work, we rethink the human intent-to-CAD pipeline and propose a unified method that directly maps multi-level human intents to executable codes, without assuming the prior existence of target CAD models. To support our study, we construct HiCAD, the first large-scale dataset aligning hand-drawn sketches, textual descriptions, and parametric CAD codes. Based on this, we introduce HiCAD, a two-stage framework comprising Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment to bridge the representational gap between heterogeneous inputs, and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning to enforce geometric and topological consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines across multiple tasks, validating its effectiveness and robustness in transforming heterogeneous human intents into high-fidelity parametric CAD models. Our project page: https://zqwlearning.github.io/HiCAD.
papers.summary: Generating parametric Computer-Aided Design (CAD) models from early-stage design intent is hard because that intent arrives as incomplete hand-drawn sketches and text rather than finished geometry. The authors build `HiCAD`, a large-scale dataset aligning sketches, textual descriptions, and parametric CAD code, plus a two-stage framework of the same name that uses Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment to bridge the heterogeneous inputs and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning to enforce geometric and topological consistency, mapping intent directly to executable code without assuming a target model already exists. **The method significantly outperforms existing baselines across multiple intent-to-CAD tasks**, which the authors read as evidence of robustness in turning heterogeneous human intent into high-fidelity parametric models.

papers.title: Radioactive Feedback: Tracing Models Trained by Label-Only LLM Supervision
papers.abstract: Conventional distillation transfers capability through teacher-generated demonstrations. LLM-as-a-Judge knowledge distillation offers a distinct and increasingly practical alternative. In the label-only variant studied here, the student generates every response and improves from scalar scores alone. Prior work shows that this non-demonstrative feedback can improve student capability, but it creates a fundamentally different provenance problem. No teacher-generated answer enters the student's training set, so any evaluator-specific trace must pass through a low-bandwidth reward signal rather than copied text. Existing watermarks and distillation detectors do not cover this score-only channel. We introduce Radioactive Feedback, which encodes a registered pattern of behavioral preferences in the rewards themselves. The evaluator applies bounded pointwise adjustments to quality-qualified responses, allowing repeated optimization to transfer the pattern to a student trained by another party. Experiments on code and mathematics show that the registered preferences transfer through scores alone and across datasets, enabling black-box detection against a fixed reference pool.
papers.summary: In label-only LLM-as-a-Judge distillation the student generates every response and learns from scalar scores alone, so no teacher text ever enters its training set and existing watermarks and distillation detectors cannot trace the evaluator's influence. `Radioactive Feedback` embeds a registered pattern of behavioral preferences into the reward signal itself: the evaluator applies bounded pointwise score adjustments to quality-qualified responses so that repeated optimization transfers the pattern to a student trained by another party. **On code and mathematics tasks the registered preferences transfer through scores alone and across datasets**, enabling black-box detection against a fixed reference pool.

papers.title: Towards Autopilot Labeling for Short Video Content Governance
papers.abstract: The explosive growth of short videos has presented significant challenges to content governance. Traditional manual labeling is inefficient, slow to iterate, and costly. Therefore, we explore and develop a multi-stage autopilot labeling framework aimed at progressively increasing the level of automation in short video content annotation. To move beyond the heavy reliance on human expert labeling at the initial L0 stage, we first introduce a discriminative MLLM labeler at the L1 stage, which is fine-tuned with supervised data to directly predict labels for short videos. Advancing to the L2 stage, we shift to a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short video data and use it for zero-shot labeling, enabling flexible generalization without task-specific supervision. In the L3 stage, we propose an agentic annotation workflow, and equip the agent with several key tools, which empower the agent to handle complex, unfamiliar, or vaguely defined cases, significantly reducing the need for human intervention. We conduct extensive experiments across various content issues, and results demonstrate that each stage of the autopilot labeling framework progressively improves labeling accuracy, and has significantly reduced manual labor costs in real-world applications by up to 85%.
papers.summary: Manual labeling of short videos for content governance is slow, costly, and hard to iterate, so the authors propose a staged framework that progressively automates annotation. Starting from human expert labeling (L0), they add a supervised multimodal large language model (MLLM) labeler fine-tuned to predict labels directly (L1), then a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short video data for zero-shot labeling (L2), and finally an agentic workflow equipped with tools to handle complex, unfamiliar, or vaguely defined cases (L3). Experiments across a range of content issues show each stage improves labeling accuracy, and **real-world deployment cut manual labor costs by up to 85%**.

papers.title: When do explicit penalties improve flow matching?
papers.abstract: Flow matching can learn structure directly from data, raising the question of when additional constraints improve generation. We study penalties that encode such constraints, with physics-informed flow matching as a motivating example. Satisfying a constraint more closely need not make the generated distribution more accurate. We therefore compare penalised and unpenalised generative modelling through their expected squared $2$-Wasserstein error. Our analysis covers both vector-valued and functional data in a Hilbert-space setting. We first derive geometric criteria that account for constraint violations and the distribution of samples after projection onto the constraint set. We then solve the statistical comparison explicitly for specific velocity-field classes and constraints via flow matching. In this model, penalisation improves accuracy exactly when the reduction in estimation variance outweighs the increase in squared bias. The resulting formula shows how this trade-off depends on sample size, the model class, the noise schedule, and the penalty weight.
papers.summary: Adding penalties that encode known constraints, such as physical laws, to flow matching does not automatically make the generated distribution more accurate, so the authors ask when it actually helps. They compare penalised and unpenalised generative modelling through expected squared 2-Wasserstein error in a Hilbert-space setting that covers both vector-valued and functional data, first deriving geometric criteria that account for constraint violations and the distribution of samples after projection onto the constraint set, then solving the statistical comparison explicitly for specific velocity-field classes and constraints. **Penalisation improves accuracy exactly when the reduction in estimation variance outweighs the increase in squared bias**, and the resulting formula shows how that trade-off depends on sample size, model class, noise schedule, and penalty weight.

papers.title: Notes on Uniform Policy Score Bounds and Lipschitz Continuity for Truncated Gaussian, Product Cauchy, Boltzmann, and Softmax Policies
papers.abstract: We establish uniform score bounds and Lipschitz continuity for truncated Gaussian, Cauchy, Boltzmann, and softmax policies under explicitly stated parameterizations.
papers.summary: These notes establish **uniform bounds on the policy score function and Lipschitz continuity for four policy families used in reinforcement learning (RL): truncated Gaussian, product Cauchy, Boltzmann, and softmax policies**. The results are stated and proved under explicitly specified parameterizations of each class.

papers.title: FARL: A Fully Automated Pipeline of RL Interface and Solver Design
papers.abstract: Existing reinforcement learning (RL) largely focuses on optimizing learning algorithms within a pre-defined task formulation, while applying RL to new tasks still relies heavily on human expertise to design the learning pipeline: what an agent observes, how it is rewarded, which algorithm it uses, and how training is configured. Automating these choices is challenging because they are tightly coupled. We introduce FARL (Fully Automated Reinforcement Learning), a framework that automates RL design by jointly searching observation and reward programs, learning algorithms, and training settings. FARL uses training statistics and observed behavior to diagnose failures, propose changes, and test whether they improve learning. Its search preserves diverse candidates and the controls needed for these tests, using a staged budget to screen designs before investing in longer training. Experimental memory records each finding together with its conditions, so an unsuccessful component can be reconsidered in a different combination. Across expert-withheld and expert-available settings, FARL outperforms the evaluated automated baselines on challenging navigation, locomotion, and manipulation tasks. On Adroit Hand Relocate, FARL achieves 97.1% success at 5M training steps per policy, compared with 0% for Eureka and LiMEN and 1.0% for native Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) under the same policy training budget.
papers.summary: Applying reinforcement learning (RL) to a new task still relies on human experts to decide what the agent observes, how it is rewarded, which algorithm it uses, and how training is configured, and these choices are tightly coupled. `FARL` (Fully Automated Reinforcement Learning) jointly searches observation and reward programs, learning algorithms, and training settings, using training statistics and observed behavior to diagnose failures, propose changes, and test whether they help, while a staged budget screens candidates before longer runs and an experimental memory records each finding with its conditions so a rejected component can be reconsidered in a new combination. It beats the evaluated automated baselines on navigation, locomotion, and manipulation tasks in both expert-withheld and expert-available settings; **on Adroit Hand Relocate it reaches 97.1% success at 5M training steps per policy versus 0% for `Eureka` and `LiMEN` and 1.0% for native Proximal Policy Optimization (`PPO`)** under the same budget.

papers.title: Do LLM Tutors Actually Teach? A Process-Centered Synthesis of the Tutoring Loop
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent tu- toring dialogue, but whether they actually help students learn remains unclear. We present a process-centered synthesis of LLM tutoring that follows the path from learner-state infer- ence to pedagogical action, tutor training, eval- uation, and student simulation. This view ex- poses a central gap: implementing a tutoring component does not establish that it works or that its outputs meaningfully affect later stages. A structured study-level audit shows that peda- gogical evaluation is common, while evidence becomes much thinner for learner-conditioned intervention, human learning gains, and espe- cially transfer or delayed retention. Human studies nevertheless provide a conditional posi- tive result: LLM tutors can improve learning, but benefits depend on pedagogical structure, learner engagement, and how learning is mea- sured. We argue that progress requires validat- ing the interfaces between tutoring stages, not only improving individual components.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent tutoring dialogue, but whether students actually learn from them remains unclear. The authors synthesize the literature along the tutoring loop, from learner-state inference to pedagogical action, tutor training, evaluation, and student simulation, and run a structured study-level audit of what evidence exists at each stage, exposing the gap between implementing a component and showing that it works or affects later stages. **Pedagogical evaluation is common, but evidence thins sharply for learner-conditioned intervention, measured human learning gains, and especially transfer or delayed retention**; human studies do show LLM tutors can improve learning, yet the benefit depends on pedagogical structure, learner engagement, and how learning is measured, leading the authors to argue for validating the interfaces between stages rather than only improving individual components.

papers.title: DRanker: A Transformer-Based Multi-Task Ranking Model for the Disney+ Homepage
papers.abstract: We present DRanker (Disney+ Ranker), a transformer-based multitask ranking model serving personalized recommendations on the Disney+ homepage. We describe the encoder-only architecture over enriched engagement-history sequences paired with a lightweight causal debiasing mechanism, and the inference stack that enables transformer-based ranking at scale. Through iterative development, we systematically evaluated more complex alternatives and found that simpler designs consistently outperformed them on offline metrics, qualitative behavioral evaluation, and in production. Deployed globally, DRanker drives over 1% lift in our key engagement metric and 0.5% lift in daily active users across all experiences powered by the ranker. We share practical lessons on data engineering, debiasing, and architectural choices that shaped our ranking system at scale.
papers.summary: Serving personalized recommendations on the Disney+ homepage calls for transformer ranking over long engagement histories at production scale. `DRanker` answers this with an encoder-only multi-task architecture over enriched engagement-history sequences, a lightweight causal debiasing mechanism, and an inference stack built to run transformer ranking globally. Through iterative development the team repeatedly found that simpler designs beat more complex alternatives on offline metrics, qualitative behavioral evaluation, and in production, and **deployed worldwide it drives over 1% lift in the key engagement metric and 0.5% lift in daily active users**, with the paper sharing lessons on data engineering, debiasing, and architectural choices.

papers.title: TabMosaic: Unified In-Context Diffusion for Tabular Generative Tasks
papers.abstract: Generative modeling for tabular data has advanced to the point where models can synthesize realistic records, recover missing values, and generate samples conditioned on class labels or observed attributes. Despite recent advances, existing approaches either require table-specific training or restrict in-context learning to single-cell prediction. In this work, we formulate these tabular generative tasks as a single problem: modeling the joint conditional distribution of an arbitrary set of target cells given the observed cells of an unseen table. To this end, we turn to diffusion, whose denoising objective is defined jointly over all target cells rather than one cell at a time. Under the pretraining distribution, this objective is minimized by the posterior predictive distribution over the target set. Building on this, we propose TabMosaic, a unified in-context diffusion model for generating mixed-type target cells in unseen, potentially incomplete tables without table-specific training. We further show that its pretraining objective bounds the conditional negative log-likelihood and the divergence from the posterior predictive for arbitrary target sets, extending the Bayesian account of in-context learning from a single-value prediction to joint multi-cell generation. Across 48 real-world tables, TabMosaic ranks first on all evaluated generative tasks against 20 baseline approaches
papers.summary: Existing tabular generative models either need table-specific training or restrict in-context learning to predicting a single cell at a time. The authors reframe synthesis, imputation, and conditional generation as one problem, modeling the joint conditional distribution of an arbitrary set of target cells given the observed cells of an unseen table, and solve it with `TabMosaic`, an in-context diffusion model whose denoising objective is defined jointly over all target cells and is minimized by the posterior predictive distribution under the pretraining distribution. They further show the pretraining objective bounds the conditional negative log-likelihood and the divergence from the posterior predictive for arbitrary target sets, extending the Bayesian account of in-context learning to multi-cell generation, and **across 48 real-world tables `TabMosaic` ranks first on every evaluated generative task against 20 baselines**.

papers.title: RespFocus: Learning Temporal Evidence for Weakly Supervised Respiratory Sound Classification
papers.abstract: Respiratory auscultation provides a low-cost means of assessing pulmonary function, yet transient crackles and sustained wheezes can be difficult to recognize in noisy clinical recordings. Conventional deep learning classifiers often operate as black boxes, offering limited insight into the temporal acoustic evidence supporting their predictions. We present RespFocus, a weakly supervised framework that uses multiple instance learning (MIL) to learn inspectable temporal evidence from cycle-level labels and integrate it into classification. We also introduce PedResp2026, a multicenter pediatric respiratory sound cohort collected in routine clinical environments with adjudicated cycle-level annotations. In classification experiments, RespFocus achieves four-class Scores of 69.55\% on public ICBHI 2017 and 72.91\% on PedResp2026. Evidence diagnostics and matched temporal interventions support the functional contribution of the learned evidence to model predictions. Together, these findings highlight RespFocus's potential as a tool for automated respiratory sound diagnosis.
papers.summary: Transient crackles and sustained wheezes in lung auscultation recordings are hard to recognize in noisy clinical environments, and conventional deep classifiers offer little insight into which parts of the recording support their predictions. `RespFocus` uses multiple instance learning (MIL) to learn inspectable temporal evidence from cycle-level labels and integrate it into classification, and the authors also introduce `PedResp2026`, a multicenter pediatric respiratory sound cohort collected in routine clinical settings with adjudicated cycle-level annotations. **It achieves four-class Scores of 69.55% on `ICBHI 2017` and 72.91% on `PedResp2026`**, and evidence diagnostics with matched temporal interventions indicate that the learned evidence functionally contributes to the predictions.

papers.title: bharatSetu: a 1M x 22 bridge for indic translation
papers.abstract: India's Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages, yet parallel data is uneven across them, and many language pairs, especially among lower-resource languages such as Bodo, Dogri, Santali and Kashmiri, lack direct bitext. We present BharatSetu 22-Indic 1M, a row-aligned table of 984,764 English sentences, each paired with machine translations into all 22 scheduled languages (21,664,808 Indic cells), generated with the sarvamai/sarvam-translate model family. Because every Indic cell in a row translates the same English sentence, any two columns form a translation pair: 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 including English, without direct bitext. We call these pivot-derived pairs and propose a confidence layer that lets users choose how strictly each pair is connected. The corpus is machine-generated and not human-verified; quality is expected to vary by language, domain and sentence style, and pivot-derived pairs can inherit errors from both sides. We therefore release BharatSetu as a machine layer and propose a human-correction layer keyed to the same row identifiers, so that each corrected column upgrades every pair that uses it, together with an evaluation protocol. We report no translation-quality results.
papers.summary: Parallel data across India's 22 constitutionally scheduled languages is uneven, and many pairs among lower-resource languages such as Bodo, Dogri, Santali, and Kashmiri have no direct bitext at all. `BharatSetu 22-Indic 1M` is a row-aligned table of **984,764 English sentences each machine-translated into all 22 languages with the `sarvam-translate` model family, giving 21,664,808 Indic cells**; because every cell in a row translates the same English sentence, any two columns form a pivot-derived translation pair, yielding 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs or 506 including English. The corpus is machine-generated and not human-verified, so the authors release it as a machine layer with a confidence layer for choosing how strictly pairs are connected, propose a human-correction layer keyed to the same row identifiers so that each corrected column upgrades every pair using it, and explicitly report no translation-quality results.

papers.title: Generalizable Model Editing Could Be More Than Direct Generalization
papers.abstract: A central desideratum in model editing is generalization to complex tasks, which prior work formalizes under a direct generalization paradigm: treating and evaluating LLM behavior as an input-output mapping and expecting a factual update to alter outputs on reasoning tasks. Yet despite substantial empirical effort, the field consensus remains that such generalization is highly challenging and elusive. However, when we deploy the latest models in an in-the-wild chatbot-user setting, we surprisingly find that even classical editing methods exhibit remarkably fluent generalization behavior. This motivates us to revisit the obstacles to generalization and the limitations of the prevailing paradigm. We find that direct generalization is fundamentally constrained both theoretically and practically: theoretically, it suffers from an identifiability issue; and practically, existing approaches attempting to circumvent this are further hindered by the ambiguity of their constructed biases and by vulnerability to being overridden by other factors such as optimization dynamics. We instead identify compositional generalization, empowered by the increasingly strong reasoning and composition abilities of modern LLMs, as a theoretically grounded and empirically validated alternative. We validate this phenomenon across multiple models and editing methods, showing that such generalization behavior is widespread. Overall, we argue that generalizable model editing could be more than direct generalization, and call for a paradigm shift toward more generalizable and practically deployable knowledge update techniques.
papers.summary: Model editing research has judged generalization under a direct paradigm that treats large language model (LLM) behavior as an input-output mapping and expects a factual update to alter outputs on downstream reasoning tasks, a goal the field broadly regards as elusive. Deploying recent models in an in-the-wild chatbot setting, the authors find that even classical editing methods generalize fluently, and they argue that direct generalization is fundamentally limited by an identifiability issue in theory and, in practice, by the ambiguity of the biases existing workarounds construct and their vulnerability to being overridden by optimization dynamics. **They identify compositional generalization, powered by modern LLMs' reasoning and composition abilities, as a theoretically grounded alternative and show the behavior is widespread across multiple models and editing methods**, calling for a shift toward more practically deployable knowledge-update techniques.

papers.title: SpecForge: Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents via Behavioral Specifications
papers.abstract: Coding agents based on frozen language models can improve their performance by refining the external context they rely on, without updating model weights. We study recursive self-improvement through behavioral specifications: natural-language code documentation that describes the behavior of program entities and guides agents in generating correct code. We formulate a self-improvement loop in which an agent generates code from its current specifications, evaluates it with execution-verified tests, and refines the specifications based on observed failures. The improved specifications then guide subsequent generation, progressively improving the agent's understanding of the codebase. However, recursive refinement is challenging because program entities are interdependent. Improving the specification of one entity can inadvertently degrade the correctness of others, a phenomenon we call output coupling. This creates a whack-a-mole effect in which local improvements cause regressions elsewhere, preventing consistent progress. We introduce SpecForge, a multi-frontier tree search framework that addresses this challenge with three mechanisms: (i) Pareto-guided state selection preserves complementary specification states and prevents premature commitment; (ii) dependency-constrained entity selection prioritizes callee-before-caller refinement; and (iii) error-diversified expansion explores multiple refinements using different subsets of test failures. On DevEval+, SpecForge achieves the best performance across five backbone models, including a 94.9% solve rate with Claude-4.5-Sonnet and a 5.7-percentage-point average improvement over the strongest baseline. The improved specifications also make the agent better at tasks outside the loop: they transfer to cross-language translation and to new-feature implementation, where they outperform the benchmark-provided requirement documents.
papers.summary: Coding agents built on frozen language models can improve by refining the external context they rely on, and the authors study a loop in which an agent generates code from natural-language behavioral specifications of program entities, evaluates it with execution-verified tests, and rewrites the specifications based on observed failures. Because entities are interdependent, improving one specification can silently break others, an effect they call output coupling that produces whack-a-mole regressions; `SpecForge` counters it with a multi-frontier tree search combining Pareto-guided state selection, dependency-constrained callee-before-caller entity selection, and error-diversified expansion over different subsets of test failures. **On `DevEval+` it achieves the best results across five backbone models, including a 94.9% solve rate with `Claude-4.5-Sonnet` and a 5.7-percentage-point average gain over the strongest baseline**, and the refined specifications also transfer to cross-language translation and new-feature implementation, where they outperform the benchmark-provided requirement documents.

papers.title: Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization
papers.abstract: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.
papers.summary: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is rewritten at every step, so quantizing that state to low precision causes rounding errors that accumulate across steps, unlike one-shot quantization of weights or key-value caches. The authors show these errors are highly coherent over time, mainly because small updates vanish in rounding, and propose two training-free fixes: Low-Rank Bypass (`LRB`) accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges sufficiently large elements into the state, while Bounded Directional Rounding (`BDR`) rounds elements that would otherwise move opposite to their update toward the update direction without extra storage. Although `BDR` enlarges the single-step rounding error it improves the model, suggesting update direction matters more than per-step error, and **across `Gated DeltaNet`, `GLA`, `Mamba2`, and `RetNet` the method substantially outperforms INT4 while cutting state memory by up to 5.3x and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9x relative to FP32 states**.

papers.title: Suggested Is Not Superseded: A Pre-Registered Evaluation of a System-One Model as a Memory-Retirement Gate
papers.abstract: Long-term memory for assistants needs a gate that decides when a new utterance retires an old stored claim. Benchmark labels for this step mark a pair as changed or not, so they cannot tell a gate that acts on established change from one that acts on a hint. We write a task contract that separates the two (SUPERSEDED vs. NEEDS-CONFIRMATION vs. COMPATIBLE), label 500 test pairs built from STALE (change pairs plus same-user controls) with three LLM annotators and two human adjudicators (one author and a second annotator; provenance reported), and evaluate Jev, a typed "System One" decision model, under pre-registered hypotheses. Of the 179 test pairs STALE marks as changed, 72 meet the contract's bar for an established change. Jev never retired a claim on 141 same-conversation non-changes. Its failure is premature retirement: the binary gate retires 39.2% of claims whose change is only suggested. A three-way decision cuts this to 15.5% at a 15.3-point detection cost, which misses our pre-registered 10-point budget, and it lands on the binary gate's own threshold frontier; these verdicts hold under three readings of the gold labels. On a held-out vault scored against a second annotator's labels, a cascade that escalated uncertain cases to a reasoning model and looked best on development data was indistinguishable from simply raising the threshold (premature retirement 26.8% vs. 6.5% on dev). Part of the gap comes from the gold labels: relative to that annotator's reading, LLM-majority gold shares most of its errors with a same-family escalation model, and an identity for binary labels says how much such shared errors hide. The rest is small-sample selection on development data. For builders this means a binary score should not be wired to delete: route suggested changes to pending evidence, and do not trust a cascade selected on development data of this size.
papers.summary: Assistants with long-term memory need a gate that decides when a new user utterance retires a stored claim, but existing benchmark labels only mark a pair as changed or not and so cannot separate a gate that acts on established change from one that acts on a hint. The authors write a three-way task contract (SUPERSEDED, NEEDS-CONFIRMATION, COMPATIBLE), label 500 test pairs built from `STALE` with three LLM annotators and two human adjudicators, and evaluate `Jev`, a typed 'System One' decision model, under pre-registered hypotheses. `Jev` never retired a claim on 141 same-conversation non-changes, but **as a binary gate it prematurely retired 39.2% of claims whose change was only suggested**; a three-way decision cut this to 15.5% at a 15.3-point detection cost that missed the pre-registered 10-point budget, and a cascade escalating uncertain cases to a reasoning model, which looked best on development data, was indistinguishable on a held-out vault from simply raising the threshold. For builders the conclusion is that a binary score should not be wired to delete, suggested changes should be routed to pending evidence, and cascades selected on development sets this small should not be trusted.

papers.title: What DNA Foundation Models Learn Beyond Sequence Composition
papers.abstract: Do genomic foundation models (FMs) provide predictive information beyond simple sequence composition? We evaluate frozen representations from five DNA FMs against normalized k-mer frequencies across 57 genomic classification datasets and two exploratory gene-expression regression tasks. Simple k-mer features remain competitive with most models, whereas NTv3 shows a consistent advantage; the ranking is robust to globally fixed and multi-scale k-mer baselines and alternative downstream probes. To test incremental predictive utility directly, we compare global 6-mer features with their concatenation with each FM embedding under a matched Random Forest protocol. NTv3 improves 46 of 57 datasets (mean $\Delta$MCC = +0.072), while Caduceus provides smaller gains and the other models do not improve mean MCC. We separately decompose embeddings into a component linearly predictable from 6-mer frequencies and a ridge residual, finding that linear recoverability does not reliably indicate downstream utility. Exact 6-mer-preserving shuffles further reveal task-relevant sequence-order sensitivity, most pronounced for NTv3, although order sensitivity alone does not guarantee predictive improvements. Our results establish compositional features as essential controls and offer complementary diagnostics for evaluating the added value of frozen genomic representations, without making claims about fine-tuning capacity.
papers.summary: The question is whether frozen representations from genomic foundation models (FMs) carry predictive information beyond simple sequence composition. The authors benchmark five DNA FMs against normalized k-mer frequency baselines on 57 genomic classification datasets and two exploratory gene-expression regression tasks, finding that k-mer features remain competitive with most models while `NTv3` shows a consistent advantage that holds under fixed and multi-scale k-mer baselines and alternative probes. **Concatenating each embedding with global 6-mer features under a matched Random Forest protocol, `NTv3` improves 46 of 57 datasets with a mean Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) gain of 0.072, `Caduceus` yields smaller gains, and the other models do not improve mean MCC**. Decomposing embeddings into a 6-mer-predictable component and a residual shows linear recoverability does not track downstream utility, and 6-mer-preserving shuffles reveal task-relevant order sensitivity, strongest for `NTv3`, that alone does not guarantee gains.

papers.title: TL;QR: Querying Temporal Discursive Patterns in Textual Corpora
papers.abstract: Many questions about large textual corpora concern patterns that unfold over time, such as a political group whose stance on a topic drifts from support to criticism over several years of debates. We present TL;QR (Too Long; Query with logical temporal Reasoning), a declarative query language and open-source engine for finding such temporal discursive patterns. In TL;QR, a single query combines natural-language predicates, whose truth is judged by a Large Language Model (LLM), with regular expressions and the operators of a temporal logic. The LLM answers only local questions about individual text passages; a symbolic engine then aggregates these judgments over time and links every match to the recorded passages and predicate decisions behind it. With this division of labor, the temporal and relational reasoning stays exact and auditable even over long time horizons. In addition, when a query includes a regular-expression pre-filter, only a small fraction of the corpus ever reaches the LLM. On a suite of controlled synthetic benchmarks with temporally and semantically complex patterns, TL;QR is substantially more accurate than LLM-only baselines. In a case study on ten years of European Parliament debates (442,593 multilingual speeches), TL;QR identifies candidate shifts in the political groups' stances on the GDPR privacy regulation.
papers.summary: Many questions about large text corpora concern patterns that unfold over time, such as a political group whose stance on a topic drifts from support to criticism across years of debate. `TL;QR` (Too Long; Query with logical temporal Reasoning) is a declarative query language and open-source engine in which a single query combines natural-language predicates judged by a Large Language Model (LLM), regular expressions, and temporal logic operators. The LLM answers only local questions about individual passages while a symbolic engine aggregates those judgments over time and links every match to the passages and decisions behind it, keeping temporal reasoning exact and auditable, and a regex pre-filter means only a small fraction of the corpus ever reaches the LLM. **On controlled synthetic benchmarks with temporally and semantically complex patterns it is substantially more accurate than LLM-only baselines**, and a case study over ten years of European Parliament debates (442,593 multilingual speeches) surfaces candidate shifts in political groups' stances on the GDPR privacy regulation.

papers.title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation
papers.abstract: Healthcare agents must transform longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, conditions under which model-centric systems may lose context, misuse tools, fail to verify consequential transitions, or cross authorization boundaries. Existing medical-agent benchmarks primarily emphasize terminal task outcomes, making it difficult to determine whether execution failures arise from the agent model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. We present the Medical Harness Protocol, an outcome-preserving framework that independently evaluates seven healthcare-specific process dimensions: Care Action Fulfillment, Clinical Resource Competence, Patient-Evidence Alignment, Clinical Workflow Continuity, Clinical Auditability, Closed-Loop Verification, and Clinical Conduct Boundaries. A normalized intervention trace further tracks whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into subsequent behavior. We instantiate the protocol as MedHarnessBench, comprising 342 executable tasks across FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. Across more than 16,000 controlled task executions, MedHarness yields broad improvements in terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and healthcare-specific process quality. We further evaluate MedHarness against multiple general-purpose harnesses and use controlled single-fault perturbations to verify the sensitivity and discrimination of the seven-dimensional evaluation. These results demonstrate that healthcare-specific runtime support can substantially improve both task completion and execution quality, while revealing failures that terminal outcomes alone cannot capture. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Tomry1114/Awesome-Agent-Harness-for-Healthcare.
papers.summary: Healthcare agents must turn longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, yet existing medical-agent benchmarks score only terminal outcomes and so cannot tell whether failures come from the model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. The Medical Harness Protocol independently evaluates seven process dimensions, among them care action fulfillment, clinical workflow continuity, auditability, closed-loop verification, and conduct boundaries, and traces whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into later behavior; `MedHarnessBench` instantiates it with 342 executable tasks spanning FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. **Across more than 16,000 controlled executions, healthcare-specific runtime support broadly improves terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and process quality**, and controlled single-fault perturbations confirm the seven dimensions discriminate failures that outcome metrics alone miss.

papers.title: History Replays Itself: Unleashing Long-Context Capability in Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Linear attention promises the efficiency needed for long-context language modelling, yet its fixed-size recurrent state must simultaneously support ongoing computation and preserve information from an ever-growing history. This coupling has reinforced a prevailing view that the state's memory capacity defines the model's long-context capability. We challenge this presumed ceiling: \emph{recurrent computation need not bear the full burden of long-term storage}. We introduce NoteBank, a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, uses the backbone's native features for writing and addressing, and reads retrieved evidence through its native forward computation via replay. This \emph{training-free, plug-and-play} interface requires no external embedding model, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader. At one million tokens, it raises Gated DeltaNet's mean accuracy across six RULER retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no observed significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens. This recovery adds $\leqslant$0.025% to analytical FLOPs, with persistent context storage approximately 1/2,600 that of a Transformer's full MHA KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Experiments extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to Mamba-2-8B and post-trained Qwen3.5-9B, demonstrating gains on LongBench v1/v2 and MemoryAgentBench. Together, these results show that sparse evidence storage and native replay can substantially expand the long-context capability of pretrained linear attention models while retaining the efficiency of recurrent computation.
papers.summary: Linear attention models keep a fixed-size recurrent state that must both drive ongoing computation and preserve an ever-growing history, which has entrenched the view that state capacity caps long-context ability. `NoteBank` decouples the two roles with a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, writes and addresses entries using the backbone's own features, and reads retrieved evidence back through the model's native forward computation via replay, all training-free and without any external embedding model, trained retriever, or separate reader. **At one million tokens it raises `Gated DeltaNet`'s mean accuracy across six `RULER` retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%** with no significant degradation from 4K to 1M tokens, adding at most 0.025% to analytical FLOPs and storing persistent context at roughly 1/2,600 the size of a Transformer's full multi-head attention KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Gains extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to `Mamba-2-8B` and a post-trained `Qwen3.5-9B` on `LongBench` v1/v2 and `MemoryAgentBench`.

papers.title: To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse
papers.abstract: Cross-model KV cache sharing reduces prefill computation by allowing a receiver model to reuse prefix KV states generated by a related sender model. Existing methods optimize such reuse for latency and generation quality, but its safety implications remain unclear. In this work, we systematically evaluate this issue across diverse sender-receiver pairs and reuse configurations. We refer to deviations from the receiver's native safety behavior as safety incompatibility. Our study shows that both the direction and magnitude of safety incompatibility depend on the model pair and reuse configuration, with value reuse causing substantially larger deviations than key reuse across all evaluated pairs. Furthermore, we propose VReparo, a technique that learns per-layer and per-KV-head affine maps offline to align reused sender value tensors with their receiver-native counterparts before decoding. Across two model pairs under full KV reuse and the state-of-the-art selective reuse setting, VReparo reduces the average HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21% and the average StrongREJECT score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 upon our benchmarks, while retaining an average Time to First Token (TTFT) reduction of 85.62%.
papers.summary: Cross-model KV cache sharing lets a receiver model reuse prefix key-value states computed by a related sender model to cut prefill cost, but its effect on safety behavior had not been studied. The authors evaluate many sender-receiver pairs and reuse configurations, defining safety incompatibility as deviation from the receiver's native safety behavior, and find that reusing value tensors causes far larger deviations than reusing keys. They propose `VReparo`, which learns per-layer, per-head affine maps offline to align reused sender values with receiver-native ones before decoding. **It cuts the average `HarmBench` attack success rate (ASR) from 57.28% to 39.21%** and the `StrongREJECT` score from 0.4215 to 0.2163 while keeping an 85.62% reduction in time to first token (TTFT).

papers.title: Adaptive Robust Confidence Sets in High Dimensions
papers.abstract:
We study adaptive confidence sets for mean vectors of multivariate Gaussians with identity covariance under Huber contamination when the contamination proportion is unknown. We show that an information-theoretically optimal adaptive confidence set can be constructed by simultaneously quantifying uncertainty across all one-dimensional projections. The resulting confidence set achieves the optimal diameter and reveals a substantial adaptation cost compared with the minimax estimation error.
  Although statistically optimal, this construction is computationally infeasible. We establish a Statistical Query (SQ) lower bound showing that achieving diameter $O(m^{-1/2})$ requires either exponentially many queries or query tolerance $d^{-\Omega(m)}$. Thus, in contrast to robust mean estimation, adaptation to the unknown contamination proportion incurs both a statistical cost and a computational barrier within the SQ framework.
  Finally, we give a low-degree moment-matching algorithm that constructs an adaptive confidence set using $d^{O(m)}$ samples and time. Its diameter bound contains an additional $O(m^{-1/2})$ term beyond the information-theoretic rate, matching the dependence on $m$ in the SQ lower bound. Together, these results characterize the statistical limits of adaptive robust confidence sets under Huber contamination and quantify a computational barrier within the SQ framework.
papers.summary: The question is how to build confidence sets for the mean of a Gaussian with identity covariance when an unknown fraction of samples is adversarially corrupted under Huber contamination. The authors show an information-theoretically optimal adaptive confidence set can be built by quantifying uncertainty across all one-dimensional projections, but this construction is computationally infeasible, and they prove a Statistical Query (SQ) lower bound showing that **adapting to the unknown contamination level incurs both a statistical cost and a computational barrier**, unlike plain robust mean estimation. A low-degree moment-matching algorithm produces an adaptive set in d^O(m) samples and time, with an extra diameter term that matches the dependence on m in the lower bound.

papers.title: Uncovering the Generative Landscape of Diffusion Models: A Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion Framework
papers.abstract: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models have emerged as powerful generative priors across domains ranging from molecular design to high-resolution image synthesis. However, standard diffusion sampling is inherently biased toward high-likelihood regions, often limiting the diversity of outputs. In many domains, a single, high-likelihood sample is insufficient. Instead, diverse portfolios of high-performing solutions are required, motivating methods that uncover a model's full expressive range. Here we show that integrating Quality-Diversity (QD) optimisation with diffusion models enables the discovery of diverse, high-performing outputs. We first propose Quality-Diversity Diffusion, a framework that adapts QD to diffusion models by directly optimising the model's latent noise and conditioning embeddings and leveraging embedding models to quantify diversity. Second, we introduce a novel h-space Spectral Mutation operator, which guides search along directions of maximal semantic sensitivity by analysing principal singular vectors of the model's input-to-activation Jacobian. We evaluate our combined approach, Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion, on text-to-image generation. Against 12 baselines, our method consistently achieves the lowest FID score, demonstrating an excellent balance of image quality and diversity.
papers.summary: Standard diffusion sampling concentrates on high-likelihood regions, which limits output diversity in settings such as molecular design where a portfolio of varied, high-performing samples is needed. The authors adapt Quality-Diversity (QD) optimisation to diffusion models by directly optimising latent noise and conditioning embeddings, using embedding models to measure diversity, and add an h-space Spectral Mutation operator that follows the principal singular vectors of the model's input-to-activation Jacobian to search along directions of maximal semantic sensitivity. On text-to-image generation, the combined `Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion` method **achieves the lowest FID score against 12 baselines**, balancing image quality with diversity.

papers.title: SkillMarker: A KGW-Based Watermarking Method for Agent Skill Ownership Verification
papers.abstract: Agent skills encode operational procedures and domain expertise as reusable knowledge assets, yet their distribution in plaintext exposes them to unauthorized copying and leakage. However, practical mechanisms for skill ownership verification and leakage tracing remain underdeveloped. Watermark embedding before distribution offers a potential solution, but structured, compact skill instructions impose stringent requirements for factual and procedural accuracy. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillMarker, a KGW-based watermarking method that jointly targets functionality preservation and strong watermark embedding. SkillMarker unifies quality-constrained rewriting with signal-oriented candidate search. The former separates essential knowledge from flexible expression to preserve instruction fidelity; the latter explores alternative expressions to obtain a stronger watermark signal under preservation constraints. We release an open-source toolkit that integrates watermark embedding, quality auditing, and detection to support the protection of agent skills. SkillMarker targets ownership verification and leakage tracing in distributed skill ecosystems, where content may be copied in whole or in part, or incorporated into other skills.
papers.summary: Agent skills are distributed as plaintext instruction files, which makes them easy to copy or leak, and there is no established way to verify ownership or trace leaks. `SkillMarker` applies a KGW-based watermark through a rewriting step that separates essential knowledge from flexible phrasing, then searches among alternative expressions for the one carrying the strongest watermark signal while preserving the skill's factual and procedural content. **The method is designed to survive partial copying or incorporation into other skills**, and the authors release an open-source toolkit covering embedding, quality auditing, and detection.

papers.title: A Dependency-Aware Multi-GPU Training Framework for Temporal Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) achieve superior performance in many dynamic graph learning tasks. These models use node state vectors (i.e., memories) to capture and record graph changes (i.e., events), and then exploit these memories to assist prediction. However, this memory-centric design makes multi-GPU training challenging because predictions for later events often depend on memory updates from earlier events. To maintain model quality, existing multi-GPU TGNN training schemes strictly preserve all event dependencies, which limits parallelism and causes expensive cross-GPU memory synchronization. In this work, we observe that many of these dependencies can be handled more flexibly without harming training quality. Specifically, (a) dependencies in TGNN training have high locality in both time and graph topology, (b) the short-range dependencies missed within a large batch can often be recovered cheaply, and (c) many memory updates are not immediately needed. Based on these observations, we propose DepBloom to accelerate multi-GPU TGNN training with three techniques: (1) temporally bounded spatial partitioning to reduce unnecessary cross-GPU synchronization and improve parallelism; (2) intra-batch memory refinement to recover missing short-range temporal dependencies inside enlarged batches; and (3) critical-path optimization to prioritize urgent memory updates while deferring non-critical work during multi-GPU pipeline execution. Experimental results across representative models and diverse datasets show that DepBloom achieves an average speedup of 2.84$\times$ and up to 5.16$\times$ over state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining comparable or better model accuracy.
papers.summary: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) keep per-node memory vectors updated by a stream of events, and because later predictions depend on earlier memory updates, existing multi-GPU training schemes preserve every dependency, which limits parallelism and forces costly cross-GPU synchronization. The authors observe that these dependencies are local in time and topology, that short-range dependencies missed inside a large batch can be recovered cheaply, and that many memory updates are not needed immediately. `DepBloom` exploits this with temporally bounded spatial partitioning, intra-batch memory refinement, and critical-path scheduling that prioritizes urgent updates, yielding **an average 2.84 times speedup and up to 5.16 times** over state-of-the-art methods with comparable or better accuracy.

papers.title: NepPlural: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Persona Annotation in Nepali Migration Discourse
papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment asks that language models faithfully represent a society's diverse, competing values rather than collapse them into one dominant viewpoint, yet flagship pluralistic-alignment datasets remain heavily skewed toward Western respondents. We introduce NepPlural, a human-anchored benchmark for modelling competing socio-cultural personas in Nepali public discourse on youth migration and brain drain. We curate 2,148 code-mixed (Devanagari, Romanized Nepali, English) YouTube comments, annotate them along a four-axis persona taxonomy (Intent, Primary Driver, Value Orientation, Affect) plus an explicit No-Persona class, and build a 300-comment gold set labelled independently by three native Nepali speakers (mean Fleiss' $\kappa \approx 0.55$). Using this gold set to audit automatic annotation, we find that LLM annotation reliability is driven by protocol. Labels collected in batches through chat interfaces reach only near-chance inter-model agreement ($\kappa \approx 0.17$). Annotating one comment at a time raises agreement above the native-speaker level ($\kappa \approx 0.72$), but consistency is not validity: under a forced-choice schema, models agree on personas for the 39% of comments native speakers judge to express none, keeping macro-F1 against human gold near 0.50. Allowing abstention resolves this: models recover No-Persona comments with F1 of 0.79 to 0.87 and, against leave-one-annotator-out references, match or exceed individual native speakers (macro-F1 0.75 to 0.86 vs. 0.75). Encoders fine-tuned on the batched labels reach only 0.34.
