The authors run an industry-scale comparison of single-head autoregressive decoding with constrained beam search against multi-token prediction (MTP), where dedicated heads predict all SID tokens in parallel, adding a new auxiliary ranking loss over the joint SID score to train the MTP objective inside a multi-task LLM that does personalized retrieval, content question answering, and instruction following over a large streaming-media catalog. **Single-head beam search beats MTP on most product-critical metrics, namely ranking and content QA, and trains at roughly 2.6 times lower dollar cost at `Qwen3-8B` scale**, with MTP winning only on raw inference throughput. Against the previous non-SID baseline with an auxiliary ranking head, the stack delivers +77% item cold-start ranking, +22% content-QA accuracy, and 2.8 times faster training, and a language-metric regression traced to SID vocabulary expansion is repaired with reinforcement learning post-training.

papers.title: Unchecked or Falsely Accused? Evaluating AI-Generated Text Detectors on Kazakh
papers.abstract: AI-text detectors are already applied to Kazakh writing, yet no study reports how often publicly available detectors flag Kazakh text whose human authorship is dated before ChatGPT. We present AINA-KK: 3,811 human passages from encyclopedic, news, web and educational pages that provably existed before ChatGPT, and 5,597 machine and gray-zone passages from 9 generators, including the Kazakh-built KazLLM and Sherkala, with script and length stress tests. Five English-trained detectors from the Hugging Face Hub flag up to 81.4% of human passages and 79.6% of published student essays; recalibrated, they catch at most 1.3% of machine text. Calibrated zero-shot detectors catch at most 50.3% of machine text from in-distribution generators. Fine-tuned encoders rank text almost perfectly, but mDeBERTa at its default threshold flags 24.4% of 50-word human excerpts, partly because machine outputs are shorter than human text; calibrated, it catches only 47.1% of KazLLM and 62.7% of Sherkala passages. Without script handling, machine-transliterated Latin-2021 text defeats every detector. Fixes that need no new data (calibration, script canonicalization, script-augmented and length-matched training, and an OR with a zero-shot scorer) form AINA-KK-Det. On test it flags 0.9% of human passages (95% CI 0.4-2.7; 1.5% on development data) and catches 85.2% of machine text from known generators, 92.9% from two unseen Gemini-family Gemma-4 models and 61.3% from the Kazakh-built ones; its configuration was chosen with test results in view. We release the data, code and detector at https://github.com/ozxmn/aina-kk.
papers.summary: AI-text detectors are already applied to Kazakh writing, yet no study has measured how often public detectors flag Kazakh text whose human authorship predates ChatGPT. `AINA-KK` pairs 3,811 human passages from encyclopedic, news, web, and educational pages that provably existed before ChatGPT with 5,597 machine and gray-zone passages from nine generators, including the Kazakh-built `KazLLM` and `Sherkala`, plus script and length stress tests. **Five English-trained detectors from the Hugging Face Hub flag up to 81.4% of human passages and 79.6% of published student essays, and once recalibrated catch at most 1.3% of machine text**, fine-tuned encoders rank text almost perfectly but `mDeBERTa` at its default threshold flags 24.4% of 50-word human excerpts, and machine-transliterated Latin-script text defeats every detector without script handling. Combining calibration, script canonicalization, script-augmented and length-matched training, and an OR with a zero-shot scorer yields `AINA-KK-Det`, which flags 0.9% of human passages and catches 85.2% of machine text from known generators, 92.9% from two unseen `Gemma-4` models, and 61.3% from the Kazakh-built ones, with the authors noting that its configuration was chosen with test results in view.

papers.title: Entropy-Regularized Mean-Field Games with Average-Reward Criterion: Span-Seminorm Contractions and Model-Free Learning
papers.abstract: We study stationary discrete-time mean-field games with finite state and action spaces under the average-reward criterion, with an entropy-regularized objective and population-dependent dynamics and rewards. Under a minorization condition, the soft Q-operator is a span-seminorm contraction for the full transition kernel, so relative value iteration does not require the minorizing measure. When the Lipschitz constant of the kernel is below the minorization mass and the temperature exceeds an explicit threshold, the equilibrium fixed-point operator is a contraction: an equilibrium exists, its population distribution is unique, and a fixed-point iteration converges to it geometrically. We then learn the equilibrium model-free from a simulator, combining soft Q-learning at a fixed population distribution with an empirical transition kernel. We prove a finite-sample bound for soft Q-learning in the span seminorm, with temperature-independent constants, and derive convergence rates for the learned population distribution and policy. A congestion-aware routing game illustrates the results.
papers.summary: Stationary discrete-time mean-field games with finite state and action spaces are studied under the average-reward criterion, with an entropy-regularized objective and dynamics and rewards that depend on the population distribution. Under a minorization condition the soft Q-operator is a span-seminorm contraction for the full transition kernel, so relative value iteration needs no minorizing measure, and when the kernel's Lipschitz constant is below the minorization mass and the temperature exceeds an explicit threshold the equilibrium fixed-point operator is a contraction, so **an equilibrium exists, its population distribution is unique, and fixed-point iteration converges to it geometrically**. The equilibrium is then learned model-free from a simulator by combining soft Q-learning at a fixed population with an empirical transition kernel, with a finite-sample bound in the span seminorm whose constants do not depend on temperature and convergence rates for the learned population distribution and policy, illustrated on a congestion-aware routing game.

papers.title: Engram Injection: A Study of Temporal Validity in Parametric Language-Model Memory
papers.abstract: A stored fact may stop being valid when a user changes a preference or an event replaces an earlier one. We study whether a language model can learn these changes in its parameters and answer correctly from only a question and the current time. Engram Injection stores facts in LoRA adapters and supplies the clock through FiLM conditioning on a frozen Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model. We compare it with additive clock conditioning, prompting with the full dated history, and retrieving four dated records. We train six matched adapters across three seeds after fixing a sampler that could admit test-age examples into training. The training audit reports no such examples among 127,760 evaluated training inputs. On 62 pairs of questions asked before and after an update, at an elapsed age of seven days excluded from training, both adapter methods answer zero pairs correctly under the primary blinded assistant review with order code 1 held fixed. Full-history prompting answers 59/62 pairs correctly, and retrieval answers 62/62. Separate experiments show that adapters can store facts and that removable memory units can support local deletion. Combining fact selection with time-based version selection remains unsuccessful. These results separate learning a fact from learning when to use it.
papers.summary: A fact stored in a language model can stop being valid when a user changes a preference or a later event supersedes an earlier one, and the question is whether a model can learn such changes in its parameters and answer correctly given only a question and the current time. `Engram Injection` stores facts in LoRA adapters and supplies the clock through FiLM conditioning on a frozen `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct`, and it is compared with additive clock conditioning, prompting with the full dated history, and retrieving four dated records, using six matched adapters across three seeds after fixing a sampler that could leak test-age examples into training. On 62 question pairs asked before and after an update at a seven-day elapsed age held out of training, **both adapter methods answer zero pairs correctly, while full-history prompting answers 59 of 62 and retrieval answers 62 of 62** under a blinded assistant review. Separate experiments show adapters can store facts and that removable memory units support local deletion, but combining fact selection with time-based version selection remains unsuccessful, which separates learning a fact from learning when to use it.

papers.title: What the Model Cannot See: Covert and Provable Text Invisibility in LLMs
papers.abstract: Text wrapped in a trigger can be made behaviorally invisible to a language model: omitted from summaries and quotations, ignored in question answering, and left unflagged by downstream filtering. We study this selective blindness as a dual-use information-flow primitive, a supply-chain backdoor, and a white-box auditing problem. We first implement it exactly as a serving-time span veto: blocking information flow out of a marked span makes every outside activation bit-identical under same-length substitution of the span's content, a noninterference property we verify across ten models, seven mixer families, and 0.5B-120B parameters. The veto serves as a deployable quarantine, an exact reference for calibrating leakage, and a teacher. Distilled into weights, it yields a backdoor: checkpoints trained on six model families from 4B to 120B ignore marked context at little benchmark cost, and their outputs show no measurable semantic trace of the suppressed content above the veto reference on our held-out suite; an in-domain variant suppresses planted vulnerabilities during AI code review. Detection is therefore a white-box problem. Simpler backdoors remain internally transparent -- linear probes recover suppressed content at 0.57-0.79 accuracy versus 0.025 chance -- but hardening the attack until probes reach chance collapses attention from outside the span into it below the range of base models. Across the attacks we evaluate, probe visibility trades off against routing visibility; we do not establish that this tradeoff is fundamental.
papers.summary: Text wrapped in a trigger phrase can be made behaviorally invisible to a language model, so it is dropped from summaries, ignored in question answering, and never flagged by downstream filters. The authors first implement this as an exact serving-time span veto that blocks information flow out of a marked span, verifying bit-identical outside activations across ten models from 0.5B to 120B parameters, then distill the veto into weights to produce a backdoor across six model families that ignores marked context at little benchmark cost. **An in-domain variant of the backdoor suppresses planted vulnerabilities during AI code review**, and because outputs show no semantic trace of the hidden content, detection becomes a white-box problem. Linear probes recover suppressed content from simpler backdoors at 0.57 to 0.79 accuracy versus 0.025 chance, but hardening the attack until probes fail collapses attention into the span below base-model levels, suggesting a tradeoff between probe visibility and routing visibility that the authors do not claim is fundamental.

papers.title: RetryBench: Separating Retry Permission from Recovery Outcomes in GPT Tool Use
papers.abstract: False retry permission (FRP) occurs when an agent retries a timed-out tool call without support from the visible contract. RetryBench separates this error from realized recovery. Successful protected recovery does not imply reliable rejection of unsupported retries. In a 720-response key control, valid keys usually enabled safe progress, but offered changed keys elicited unsupported retries in Sol (1/80), Terra (55/80), and Luna (60/80). A later 240-response control removed the candidate and required models to supply a key. Luna still made 8/80 unsupported dispatches; Sol and Terra made none in 80 responses each. Accepting a displayed bad key therefore cannot explain all observed errors, although changed output requirements and conditions preclude a pure display-effect comparison. Removing the weak-contract label increased retries in Sol and Terra's coded-action conditions in a six-endpoint study. A separate 1,536-response canonical-action block also found a positive Terra contrast (115/128 versus 124/128 retries), concentrated in two task/order conditions; the other five contrasts remained unresolved after multiplicity correction. An explicit-contract cue control elicited deferral in all 762 returned responses, leaving recovery unresolved. These results support reporting permission and recovery together across declared interface variants. The evidence covers four purposive tasks, fixed GPT endpoints, and one recovery decision; it identifies neither internal mechanisms nor episode-level safety.
papers.summary: False retry permission (FRP) is the error of an agent retrying a timed-out tool call when the visible interface contract does not support doing so, and `RetryBench` measures it separately from whether recovery actually succeeds. Using fixed GPT endpoints referred to as `Sol`, `Terra`, and `Luna` on four tasks, the authors run key-control experiments in which valid keys enable safe progress but offered changed keys elicit unsupported retries. **Unsupported retries ranged from 1 of 80 responses for `Sol` to 60 of 80 for `Luna`**, and `Luna` still made 8 unsupported dispatches when no candidate key was displayed, so accepting a shown bad key cannot explain all errors. Several contrasts remain unresolved after multiplicity correction, and the authors argue that permission and recovery should be reported together across declared interface variants.

papers.title: Comparative Study of Canvas- and Coordinate-Based Geometry-Conditioned Neural Networks for Real-Time Prediction of Indoor Environments with Varying Room Dimensions
papers.abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is computationally expensive for iterative building design. Deep learning surrogates offer faster predictions, but generalization across varying room dimensions remains challenging. This study compares two geometry-conditioned neural network surrogate models for rapid indoor airflow and temperature field prediction under varying room sizes. During the architectural design stage, this method is relevant for real-time assessment of whether conditioned supply air will effectively provide fresh and cool air throughout rooms with varying heights and lengths. The canvas-based neural network (CaNN) explicitly encodes room size by preserving different occupied regions within a fixed canvas, whereas the coordinate-based neural network (CoNN) uses normalized coordinate channels. Both employ U-Net autoencoders to separately predict airflow and temperature fields. Evaluation uses simplified rooms with varying heights and lengths as a controlled benchmark. The results show that CaNN achieves higher agreement with CFD results than CoNN, demonstrating its potential to support performance-driven building design.
papers.summary: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is too slow for iterative building design, and deep learning surrogates struggle to generalize across rooms of different sizes. Two geometry-conditioned U-Net surrogates for predicting indoor airflow and temperature are compared: a canvas-based neural network (`CaNN`) that places rooms of varying dimensions inside a fixed canvas, and a coordinate-based neural network (`CoNN`) that uses normalized coordinate channels. On a controlled benchmark of simplified rooms with varying heights and lengths, **`CaNN` matches the CFD reference more closely than `CoNN`**, supporting its use for real-time assessment of whether supply air reaches all parts of a room during early-stage design.

papers.title: Variance-Optimal State Resampling for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards spends much of its rollout budget on states that yield no learning signal. We recast this as a question about the sampling distribution itself: under a fixed rollout budget, which distribution over states minimizes the variance of the policy-gradient estimator? The answer admits a closed-form Neyman allocation, $\mu_{\mathrm{var}}^\pi(s) \propto d^\pi(s)\,\sigma_\pi(s)$, which connects naturally to GRPO's group-relative advantage and induces an emergent reverse curriculum as the policy improves, with no externally imposed schedule. Building on this principle, we propose VSR (Variance-driven State Resampling), a plug-in modification to GRPO using a prefix replay buffer and a zero-cost variance proxy. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks and long-horizon agentic tasks (Sokoban, BabyAI), VSR outperforms GRPO and GiGPO on most benchmarks with fewer generated tokens per update.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards wastes much of its rollout budget on states that produce no learning signal because every sample yields the same reward. The authors ask which distribution over states minimizes the variance of the policy-gradient estimator under a fixed budget and derive a closed-form Neyman allocation proportional to state visitation times the per-state reward standard deviation, which ties directly to the group-relative advantage in `GRPO` and induces a reverse curriculum without any imposed schedule. Building on this, `VSR` (Variance-driven State Resampling) adds a prefix replay buffer and a zero-cost variance proxy as a plug-in to `GRPO`. **On math reasoning benchmarks and long-horizon `Sokoban` and `BabyAI` tasks, `VSR` outperforms `GRPO` and `GiGPO` on most benchmarks while generating fewer tokens per update.**

papers.title: Learning Multimodal Sensor Fusion with JEPA Representations for Breathing Activity and Pose Recognition
papers.abstract: Predictive video representations do not by themselves specify how a multimodal system should handle missing sensors. We transfer frozen V-JEPA2 features to a set of heterogeneous sensors comprised by RGB video, depth video, and radar time series. A shared fusion model uses modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit availability to classify breathing activity and pose from all seven non-empty sensor subsets. The contribution is a controlled evaluation of subset supervision, pooling capacity, and representation transfer on 39 OMuSense-23 subjects with five subject-group folds and three seeds. With matched downstream parameter counts, the final model reaches recording-level activity macro-F1 of $75.23%\pm0.60$ averaged across seven subsets. Supervising all subsets in each batch improves the matched query-pooling control by 1.923 percentage points (conditional 95% subject-bootstrap interval [0.647, 3.209]), while query pooling shows no clear advantage over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision. Radar probes support transfer beyond pooled wavelet pixels, 64-token inference approximately preserves mean activity performance, and the tested Consensus-JEPA loss adds no measured benefit against its exact control.
papers.summary: Predictive video representations do not specify how a multimodal classifier should behave when some sensors are missing. Frozen `V-JEPA2` features are transferred to RGB video, depth video, and radar time series, and a shared fusion model with modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit availability flags classifies breathing activity and pose across all seven non-empty sensor subsets on 39 subjects from `OMuSense-23`. **The final model reaches a recording-level activity macro-F1 of 75.23% averaged across the seven subsets**, and supervising all subsets in every batch improves over a matched query-pooling control by about 1.9 percentage points. Query pooling shows no clear advantage over mean pooling under balanced supervision, 64-token inference roughly preserves accuracy, and the tested `Consensus-JEPA` loss adds no measurable benefit.

papers.title: Minimax Rates and Improved Spectral Convergence for Multi-Manifold Clustering
papers.abstract: We study eigenpair estimation for the tensorized, density-weighted Laplace--Beltrami operator from $n$ independent data points sampled from a multi-manifold mixture distribution where manifolds may intersect. Let $d$ denote the largest intrinsic dimension of the manifold components and $s\geq2$ the smoothness of the sampling densities. For simple, nontrivial eigenpairs, we establish the minimax rate $n^{-s/(d+2s)}$ for approximating the eigenvalue and eigenfunction of the tensorized Laplace--Beltrami operator, and show that a continuum plug-in estimator based on kernel density estimation attains the same rate when the supporting manifolds are known. We further analyze a manifold-agnostic graph Laplacian estimator and prove that its eigenpairs converge to those of the tensorized Laplace--Beltrami operator at rate $n^{-1/(2.5d-1)}$, up to logarithmic factors, improving upon previously known spectral convergence rates for multi-manifold learning. Numerical experiments on synthetic multi-manifold data corroborate the rates guaranteed by our theorems. These results characterize the information-theoretic difficulty of multi-manifold spectral estimation and quantify the additional cost of learning without oracle component information.
papers.summary: The work studies how well eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the tensorized, density-weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator can be estimated from n points drawn from a mixture of possibly intersecting manifolds, the setting underlying spectral multi-manifold clustering. For simple nontrivial eigenpairs, **the minimax rate is n^(-s/(d+2s))**, where d is the largest intrinsic dimension and s the density smoothness, and a kernel-density plug-in estimator attains it when the manifolds are known. A manifold-agnostic graph Laplacian estimator is shown to converge at rate n^(-1/(2.5d-1)) up to logarithmic factors, improving on previously known spectral convergence rates, with synthetic experiments corroborating both rates and quantifying the cost of not knowing the component manifolds.

papers.title: Make Every Expansion Count: Learning to Search Efficiently in LLM Code Repair
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) code-repair systems fix faulty programs by repeatedly generating and testing revisions. Each revision is costly, making the choice of which repair to pursue important for efficiency. Existing search policies rely on test pass rates and search statistics, ignoring the details of test failures and proposed edits. We introduce CodeTriage, a learned policy that prioritizes edits before their revised programs are generated and tested. Its 0.6B-parameter model reads the test output, failure diagnosis, and proposed edit, then predicts a distribution over the number of repair steps needed to reach a fix through that edit. These predictions prioritize all pending edits across programs before generating and testing the revised code. On held-out repair tasks, CodeTriage finds fixes with 21% fewer program revisions and 12% fewer output tokens than the strongest baseline on each metric. Without retraining, it achieves the highest average success across search budgets for each of 11 unseen repair LLMs. Ablations show that both the failure context and edit text, as well as comparisons across programs, improve search. We also release a corpus of 12.2 million program versions from four LLMs, organized into repair trees with proposed edits and test results.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) code-repair systems iterate by generating and testing revisions, and each revision is expensive, so choosing which candidate edit to pursue matters for efficiency. `CodeTriage` is a learned 0.6B-parameter policy that reads the test output, a failure diagnosis, and a proposed edit, then predicts a distribution over how many further repair steps that edit would need, ranking all pending edits across programs before any code is generated or tested. **On held-out repair tasks it reaches fixes with 21% fewer program revisions and 12% fewer output tokens than the strongest baseline**, and without retraining it gives the highest average success across search budgets for each of 11 unseen repair LLMs. Ablations show that failure context, edit text, and cross-program comparison all help, and the authors release a corpus of 12.2 million program versions organized into repair trees.

papers.title: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
papers.abstract: Qwen3-8B reviewing Llama-3.1-8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3-8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is that the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator. Code and per-question results: https://github.com/Kamilaabb/verification-or-capability-transfer
papers.summary: Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator, which conflates true verification, where the pair beats either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer merely supplies answers it could have produced on its own. For example, `Qwen3-8B` reviewing `Llama-3.1-8B` on math adds 33.2 points, yet `Qwen3-8B` alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the reviewed result. Across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models from 3B to 72B on math, knowledge, code, and reasoning, **review beats the stronger model alone in only 9 of 96 review directions**, and does worse as the capability gap widens because the reviewer tends to follow the generator and discard its own correct answers. Review also costs 2.6 to 2.8 times the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate and cheaper, so the authors argue verification studies should report the stronger model alone as a baseline.

papers.title: Lightweight Scheduling Policies for Continuously Batched LLLM Serving Across GPU Architectures
papers.abstract: Large language model serving is increasingly limited not only by model size and GPU speed, but also by scheduling during autoregressive decoding, where continuous batching interleaves requests at token granularity as sequences arrive and finish. We study whether lightweight scheduling policies can improve latency-throughput tradeoffs without changing model architectures, kernels, or deploying learned schedulers. We implement a Python/PyTorch continuous-batching testbench with real Hugging Face execution and evaluate eight policies across 1,152 GPU-model-scheduler-workload runs using ShareGPT-derived traffic, six Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral models, and Modal L40S, A100, and H100 GPUs. Scheduler choice changes throughput, TTFT, completion latency, and tail behavior under fixed model, GPU, workload, batch size, and prefill budget. Aging shortest-prompt-first is the strongest practical baseline in many L40S and mixed-workload settings, while oracle remaining-length scheduling shows that job-size knowledge alone is insufficient because batching and hardware effects also shape performance. The custom dataset has been uploaded to Hugging Face.
papers.summary: Large language model serving is increasingly bounded by how requests are scheduled during continuous batching, where sequences join and leave the batch at token granularity. The authors build a Python/PyTorch continuous-batching testbench running real Hugging Face models and evaluate eight lightweight scheduling policies across 1,152 runs spanning six `Qwen`, `Gemma`, and `Mistral` models, `ShareGPT`-derived traffic, and L40S, A100, and H100 GPUs, without changing kernels or training a learned scheduler. Scheduler choice measurably shifts throughput, time to first token, completion latency, and tail behavior at fixed model, hardware, and workload. **Aging shortest-prompt-first is the strongest practical baseline in many L40S and mixed-workload settings**, while an oracle that knows remaining lengths shows that job-size knowledge alone is insufficient because batching and hardware effects also shape performance.

papers.title: Gen Through the Lens: Camera-Controllable Video Generation via Cross-Coordinate Conditioning Fusion
papers.abstract: We present Gen Through the Lens, a camera-controllable image-to-video generation framework that synthesizes videos from a given reference image while enabling realistic and physically consistent camera operations. Unlike previous models that treat camera motion as abstract conditioning or rely on a single coordinate system, our approach explicitly decomposes and fuses control signals across three coordinate spaces: the camera coordinate (modeled by intrinsic parameters), the world coordinate (represented by spatial geometry hints), and the object coordinate (described by 3D bounding boxes of target subjects). Through cross-coordinate conditioning fusion, these heterogeneous cues are unified to guide the generative process, enabling precise control of camera motion, focus, and framing while preserving temporal and spatial coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces controllable and visually consistent results across diverse camera operations, outperforming existing approaches in both realism and editability.
papers.summary: Camera-controllable image-to-video generation aims to animate a reference image while obeying realistic, physically consistent camera operations. Rather than treating camera motion as abstract conditioning in a single coordinate system, the framework decomposes control signals into three spaces: camera coordinates from intrinsic parameters, world coordinates from spatial geometry hints, and object coordinates from 3D bounding boxes of target subjects, then fuses them through cross-coordinate conditioning fusion to guide generation. **The authors report precise control of camera motion, focus, and framing with preserved temporal and spatial coherence, outperforming prior approaches in realism and editability.**

papers.title: LURE: a Phase-Labelled Synthetic Corpus of Online-Grooming Exchanges
papers.abstract: Phase-annotated conversational data is essential for studying the progression of online grooming of minors and for developing early warning tools. However, the only publicly available source (i.e., Perverted-Justice archive, which contains a subset coded using ChatCoder) is small, outdated, and frozen. We present a synthetic corpus of groomer-victim exchanges, generated using a retrieval-augmented pipeline running on institutional hardware. This pipeline uses an openly available, eight-billion-parameter, refusal-ablated language model. The corpus was created using the five stages of the responsible-generation protocol for synthetic datasets: ontology-driven design based on the ChatCoder luring-communication scheme (eight communicative tags mapped onto four grooming phases); multi-model prompt testing; human-in-the-loop supervision; semantic and feature-level validation; and modality-aware documentation. The released corpus contains 2,121 unique exchanges across seven tags and four phases, each accompanied by a Plutchik emotion field. Validation quantifies the integrity and lexical profile of the corpus, as well as the reproduction of real seed lines, in-domain label recoverability (tag accuracy: 0.85; phase accuracy: 0.93) and its transfer to real ChatCoder offender lines, which were coded automatically at the eight-tag level (31,640 lines) and by human coders at the three-construct level (10,876 posts). Accuracy was measured for lexical and sentence-embedding features, while a real-versus-synthetic discriminator was able to separate the two domains with 91% accuracy. The scope of the corpus includes controlled, phase-conditioned experimentation, pipeline development and augmentation alongside real data and awareness material. The corpus, its datasheet and the audit code are released with vetted access.
papers.summary: Phase-annotated conversations are needed to study how online grooming of minors progresses and to build early-warning tools, but the only public source, the Perverted-Justice archive partly coded with `ChatCoder`, is small and frozen. The authors generate a synthetic corpus of groomer-victim exchanges with a retrieval-augmented pipeline built on an openly available eight-billion-parameter refusal-ablated model, following a five-stage responsible-generation protocol covering ontology-driven design, multi-model prompt testing, human supervision, validation, and documentation. **The released corpus holds 2,121 unique exchanges across seven communicative tags and four grooming phases**, each with a Plutchik emotion field, with in-domain label recoverability of 0.85 tag accuracy and 0.93 phase accuracy and transfer tested on real `ChatCoder` offender lines. A real-versus-synthetic discriminator separates the domains with 91% accuracy, and the corpus, datasheet, and audit code are released under vetted access.

papers.title: Two Linear Programs are Better than One
papers.abstract:
The extension complexity $\operatorname{xc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$ is the minimum number of facets of a polytope that projects onto it. Motivated by the complexity of neural networks, Hertrich and Loho introduced the virtual extension complexity $\operatorname{vxc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$, which is the minimum of $\operatorname{xc}(Q) + \operatorname{xc}(R)$ among all polytopes $Q$ and $R$ such that $P+Q=R$. We show the following results pertaining to virtual extension complexity.
  First, we resolve the core open problem on the topic by showing the virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity. Second, we show there are matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity by adapting a semi-algebraic counting argument by Hrube\v{s} that extends the counting arguments of Rothvoss. Finally, we show that the maximum virtual extension complexity of a polygon with $n$ vertices is $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$. This resolves an analogue of a question on extension complexity of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary in 2011 in the case of virtual extension complexity.
papers.summary: The extension complexity of a polytope is the minimum number of facets of a polytope projecting onto it, and the virtual extension complexity, introduced by Hertrich and Loho with neural network complexity in mind, is the minimum total extension complexity of polytopes Q and R with P + Q = R. **The central open question is settled by showing that virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity.** The authors also adapt a semi-algebraic counting argument of Hrubeš, extending Rothvoss's techniques, to exhibit matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity, and prove that the maximum virtual extension complexity of an n-vertex polygon is Θ(√n), resolving the virtual analogue of a 2011 question of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary.

papers.title: RIVO: Lightweight Adaptive Rerouting for Deep Research Agents
papers.abstract: Deep Research agents rely on long-horizon reasoning and iterative tool use to solve complex information-seeking tasks. However, adaptive decision-making over these trajectories remains challenging, as agents may stop prematurely when further evidence is needed, continue unnecessarily after sufficient evidence has been gathered, or fail to redirect unproductive trajectories. Existing solutions either require costly model retraining and dense turn-level supervision, or rely on heuristic control rules that are not directly optimized for downstream research utility. This motivates a lightweight, utility-aware alternative for Deep Research control. We formulate adaptive rerouting in long-horizon Deep Research as a state-conditioned trajectory correction problem. Based on this view, we introduce RIVO, a lightweight plug-in framework for adaptive trajectory correction. The agent estimates its research state from lightweight signals and determines whether trajectory redirection is needed. Once triggered, the plug-in modifies the Host token logits to steer generation toward a more promising research direction. Theoretical analysis shows that, under a value-alignment condition and bounded local curvature, a sufficiently small logit intervention can locally improve expected downstream research utility. We further construct BrowseCore, a curated dataset with a paired local corpus, for efficient and controlled Deep Research experimentation. Building on this resource, the plug-in is trained from downstream outcomes, enabling it to learn corrections that improve subsequent research and final task performance. Extensive experiments across multiple Deep Research benchmarks and control settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showing that lightweight logit intervention can improve long-horizon research without retraining the underlying Host model.
papers.summary: Deep Research agents that chain long-horizon reasoning with iterative tool use often stop too early, continue after gathering enough evidence, or fail to redirect unproductive trajectories, and existing fixes either require retraining with dense turn-level supervision or rely on heuristics not optimized for research utility. `RIVO` reframes this as state-conditioned trajectory correction: a lightweight plug-in estimates the agent's research state from cheap signals, decides whether redirection is needed, and if so modifies the host model's token logits to steer generation toward a more promising direction. A theoretical analysis shows that under a value-alignment condition and bounded local curvature, a sufficiently small logit intervention locally improves expected downstream utility. The authors also build `BrowseCore`, a curated dataset with a paired local corpus, train the plug-in from downstream outcomes, and report **improved long-horizon research performance across multiple Deep Research benchmarks without retraining the host model**.

papers.title: More Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Executing Clinical Guidelines with LLMs and Rules
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in clinical decision support. However, existing approaches often rely on multi-step reasoning or multi-agent collaboration to execute clinical guidelines, introducing substantial computational overhead without reliably preventing decision errors. To address these limitations, we propose a framework for Medical Decision Execution (MedDEx) that integrates structured patient states with deterministic rule execution to support guideline-based treatment planning. MedDEx separates clinical record interpretation from guideline execution, leveraging LLMs to extract patient information and generate treatment plans while assigning guideline-defined decision logic to a rule executor. Experiments across multiple clinical guideline benchmarks demonstrate that MedDEx improves decision accuracy while reducing inference costs. Further analyses highlight the critical roles of structured patient representations and deterministic rule execution, suggesting that additional LLM reasoning does not necessarily translate into better guideline adherence.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are promising for clinical decision support, but existing systems execute clinical guidelines through multi-step reasoning or multi-agent collaboration, adding compute cost without reliably preventing decision errors. `MedDEx` (Medical Decision Execution) separates record interpretation from guideline execution: LLMs extract structured patient states and draft treatment plans, while a deterministic rule executor applies the guideline-defined decision logic. **Across multiple clinical guideline benchmarks, `MedDEx` improves decision accuracy while reducing inference cost**, and ablations indicate that structured patient representations and deterministic rule execution drive the gains, with additional LLM reasoning not translating into better guideline adherence.

papers.title: Sample-Optimal Multi-Group Learning with an ERM Oracle
papers.abstract: In multi-group learning, a single predictor must perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in a class on every group in a rich, possibly infinite and overlapping, collection of subpopulations. The known algorithms with the optimal sample complexity keep track of every pair of a group and a hypothesis, which is impossible for the large classes of interest, and the known oracle-based algorithms have a worse rate. We ask whether the optimal rate can be attained by a learner that accesses the classes only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples and polynomially many calls to a weighted ERM oracle over pairs of a group and a hypothesis, where $d_G$ and $d_H$ are the VC dimensions of the group and hypothesis classes and $\varepsilon$ bounds the excess risk on every group, weighted by its probability. We also show a matching lower bound of $\Omega((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples for every learner even with unlimited computation, so oracle efficiency costs no additional samples. We also consider a natural special case in which every input belongs to at most $k$ groups and these groups can be listed. In this case, an ERM oracle for the hypothesis class alone suffices, with $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples in the agnostic setting and $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon)$ samples when every group has a hypothesis that is correct on it.
papers.summary: In multi-group learning, one predictor must perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in a class on every group in a rich, possibly infinite and overlapping collection of subpopulations. Existing sample-optimal algorithms track every group-hypothesis pair, which is infeasible for large classes, while oracle-based algorithms have worse rates. **The authors give an algorithm using Õ((d_G + d_H)/ε²) samples and polynomially many calls to a weighted empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle over group-hypothesis pairs**, where d_G and d_H are the VC dimensions of the group and hypothesis classes, and prove a matching Ω((d_G + d_H)/ε²) lower bound for any learner, so oracle efficiency costs no extra samples. When each input lies in at most k listable groups, an ERM oracle for the hypothesis class alone suffices, with Õ((d_H + log k)/ε²) samples in the agnostic case and Õ((d_H + log k)/ε) when every group has a hypothesis that is correct on it.

papers.title: RINO: Renormalization Group Distillation with No Labels
papers.abstract: Supervised machine learning in high-energy physics (HEP) requires training on labeled simulations of particle collisions, which are known to be unfaithful to the underlying physics. This leads to significant inaccuracies and biases in the transfer of trained models to real data, limiting the power of deep learning methods. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a promising alternative for pretraining directly on real, unlabeled data. However, existing techniques largely operate with inductive biases inspired by domains such as images and natural language. We propose RINO (Renormalization Group DIstillation with NO Labels), which, for the first time, exploits the fundamentally multi-scale renormalization group structure of high-energy jet formation as a physically grounded source of SSL views. We define teacher-student representations across energy scales using different levels of hierarchical clustering, aligned via DINO-style self-distillation. To mirror the background-dominated nature of real collider data, RINO pretrains exclusively on jets from quantum chromodynamics (QCD) processes and is evaluated on out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer to rare signal classes. In our controlled data-efficiency study, RINO matches fully supervised training on JetNet after finetuning on only 1% of the labeled data. With the full labeled dataset, RINO improves OOD classification accuracy on top-quark jets by 5.9% and, without retraining, improves AUC on the unseen Higgs boson decay channel $H \to 4q$ by 4.1% over the strongest SSL baseline. Scale-structure diagnostics reveal that DINO-style self-distillation permits our backbone to retain scale-dependent structure. Ablation studies show that this accounts for an 8.6% OOD accuracy gap with respect to alternative SSL paradigms such as SimCLR. Code is available at https://github.com/zichunhao/RINO.
papers.summary: Supervised learning in high-energy physics (HEP) depends on labeled simulations of particle collisions that are known to be unfaithful to real physics, biasing models when transferred to real data, while self-supervised learning (SSL) methods mostly borrow inductive biases from images and text. `RINO` (Renormalization Group Distillation with No Labels) instead uses the multi-scale renormalization-group structure of jet formation as the source of SSL views, defining teacher and student representations at different levels of hierarchical clustering and aligning them with `DINO`-style self-distillation, pretraining only on background quantum chromodynamics (QCD) jets. **After finetuning on just 1% of labels, `RINO` matches fully supervised training on `JetNet`**, and with full labels it improves out-of-distribution top-quark jet accuracy by 5.9% and AUC on the unseen Higgs to four-quark decay channel by 4.1% over the strongest SSL baseline. Diagnostics attribute an 8.6% out-of-distribution accuracy gap over `SimCLR`-style alternatives to the backbone retaining scale-dependent structure.

papers.title: Fast and Accurate: Improving Personalized LLM Performance by Semantic Concentration Inspired Workload Split between RAG and Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: With ever increasing personalized large language model (LLM) services, the next question to answer is how to improve the quality of services/users' experiences, which is indicated by personalized LLM generation accuracy/quality and inference latency. Although state-of-the-art designs, e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or Full PEFT+RAG, can help, they largely ignore the heterogeneous semantic concentrations of users' historical data and cannot fully unleash the potential of personal data for personalized LLM performance enhancement. In this paper, we propose PEFT Union RAG (PUR), a novel ``fast and accurate'' approach that exploits the semantic concentration of users' personal historical data to split workload between PEFT and RAG, aiming to improve personalized LLM performance in terms of better generation accuracy/quality and lower inference latency. Briefly, PUR partitions user's personal historical data and assigns semantic concentrated ``core'' information to PEFT for offline parametric fine-tuning, while retaining dispersed information for RAG. During the online LLM inference, PUR directly generates responses for ``core'' queries covered by the PEFT region and invokes RAG only for sporadic ``peripheral'' queries. Experimental results show that, by appropriately splitting workload between PEFT and RAG, PUR consistently achieves the best generation accuracy/quality for various users across multiple tasks, while reducing inference latency by 14.4%--46.6% compared with the best performed method.
papers.summary: Personalized large language model (LLM) services are judged on generation quality and inference latency, but parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and their combination ignore how unevenly a user's history is concentrated semantically. `PUR` (PEFT Union RAG) partitions each user's historical data, assigning semantically concentrated core information to offline PEFT and leaving dispersed information to RAG, so that at inference time core queries are answered directly from the fine-tuned weights and RAG is invoked only for sporadic peripheral queries. **Across multiple users and tasks, `PUR` achieves the best generation quality while cutting inference latency by 14.4% to 46.6%** relative to the best-performing baseline.

papers.title: Frequency-Step Cache: Separating Synchronization and Repair for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video generation enables long-horizon synthesis but requires repeated forward passes through large diffusion transformers. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing intermediate computation, yet existing controllers often couple two decisions: when to synchronize the cache exactly and how much computation to repair between synchronizations. We introduce Frequency-Step Cache (FSC), which separates these roles. FSC schedules exact full-computation anchors on a dense-to-sparse trajectory, while a lightweight latent-space risk based on frequency-resolved drift and token age controls inter-anchor repair through whole-step replay, selective token recomputation, or full repair. On SkyReels-V2, whole-step reuse provides most of the acceleration, while selective token computation is most effective as fidelity repair. A controlled ablation shows that using one reactive signal for both synchronization and repair reduces fidelity at matched latency, with the same separation advantage observed on FramePack and Matrix-Game. Across multiple autoregressive video backbones, FSC improves speed-quality trade-offs. On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed reaches 2.36x speedup versus MotionCache's 2.275x while improving SSIM by 0.019 and PSNR by 0.5 dB. At MotionCache-matched speed, FSC-Quality improves SSIM by 0.031 and PSNR by 1.0 dB and lowers LPIPS by 0.024. Without retuning, FSC-Quality transfers to SkyReels-V2 14B at 2.12x speedup versus 1.79x for MotionCache.
papers.summary: Autoregressive video diffusion enables long-horizon generation but requires repeated forward passes through large diffusion transformers, and existing training-free caching schemes couple two decisions: when to resynchronize the cache exactly and how much to recompute in between. Frequency-Step Cache (`FSC`) separates them, scheduling exact full-computation anchors on a dense-to-sparse trajectory while a lightweight latent-space risk score based on frequency-resolved drift and token age chooses between whole-step replay, selective token recomputation, or full repair. **On `SkyReels-V2`, `FSC-Speed` reaches a 2.36x speedup versus 2.275x for `MotionCache` while improving SSIM by 0.019 and PSNR by 0.5 dB**, and at matched speed `FSC-Quality` improves SSIM by 0.031 and PSNR by 1.0 dB. A controlled ablation shows that using one reactive signal for both roles lowers fidelity at matched latency, with the same pattern on `FramePack` and `Matrix-Game`, and `FSC-Quality` transfers to the 14B `SkyReels-V2` model without retuning.

papers.title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments
papers.abstract:
Agent environments are essential for large language model (LLM) development. They use programmatic verifiers to turn complex outcomes into rewards. Verifiers can be attacked into awarding full credit to cheating agents without completing the intended task, causing inaccurate evaluation and misalignment in training. As agent environments scale in numbers and difficulty, so must the repairing of exploitable verifiers. To this end, we ask whether today's model with scaled compute can automatically harden agent environments to prevent potentially stronger future models from reward hacking. We introduce a scalable, fully automatic approach to weak-to-strong verifier hardening. It first sets up an isolated verifier sandbox that agents cannot directly modify, then uses a hacker-fixer loop to find and repair remaining verifier vulnerabilities.
  We apply this loop to Terminal Bench, KernelBench, and SETA, substantially reducing attack success across these agent environments. The iterative design scales with the hardening budget, producing progressively stronger defenses as the number of loop iterations increases and outperforming the static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of our hacker-fixer loop has been adopted by the official Terminal Bench repository as a way to audit exploits in its environments. Project page: https://verifier-hardening.github.io/.
papers.summary: Agent environments for large language model (LLM) development rely on programmatic verifiers to convert task outcomes into rewards, and those verifiers can be exploited so that cheating agents receive full credit, corrupting both evaluation and training. The authors ask whether current models with scaled compute can automatically harden environments against stronger future models, proposing a fully automatic weak-to-strong approach that first isolates the verifier in a sandbox agents cannot modify and then runs a hacker-fixer loop to find and patch remaining vulnerabilities. **Applied to `Terminal Bench`, `KernelBench`, and `SETA`, the loop substantially reduces attack success**, with defenses growing stronger as the number of iterations increases and outperforming a static, non-iterative baseline. An earlier version of the loop has been adopted by the official `Terminal Bench` repository to audit exploits in its environments.

papers.title: Multi-Horizon Explainable Queue Forecasting and Resource-Aware Decision Support for Intelligent Border Control Using LightGBM
papers.abstract: Border crossing points are stochastic service systems in which traffic demand, traveler categories, registration status, inspection requirements, staffing, and lane availability interact on multiple time scales. This paper extends an earlier multimodal queue-management framework by introducing an implementation-oriented, multi-horizon forecasting and decision-support architecture based on Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) models. In contrast to a single forecasting block, the proposed approach constructs horizon-specific regressors for 15, 30, 60, and 120 min forecasts and jointly estimates future waiting time and queue lengths. The models operate on temporally lagged traffic, service, density, and queue features, while an operational layer incorporates lane compatibility, officer availability, possibly degraded resources, traveler category, preregistration information, and human-approval constraints. Quantile LightGBM models provide 95\% prediction intervals for waiting-time forecasts. Beyond prediction, the framework produces machine-readable recommendations, alerts, aggregate key performance indicators, confidence information, and integration outputs suitable for border resource-management and decision-support systems. The results establish a reproducible synthetic-data baseline and a practical interface for subsequent validation with operational border-crossing data.
papers.summary: Border crossing points are stochastic service systems where traffic demand, traveler categories, registration status, inspection needs, staffing, and lane availability interact across time scales. Extending an earlier multimodal queue-management framework, the work builds horizon-specific Light Gradient Boosting Machine (`LightGBM`) regressors for 15, 30, 60, and 120 minute forecasts that jointly estimate waiting time and queue length from lagged traffic, service, density, and queue features, with quantile models supplying 95% prediction intervals. An operational layer accounts for lane compatibility, officer availability, degraded resources, traveler category, preregistration, and human-approval constraints, and emits machine-readable recommendations, alerts, and key performance indicators. **The results establish a reproducible synthetic-data baseline** and an interface intended for later validation on operational border-crossing data.

papers.title: Mesh-Free Convolution: Learned Spectral Attenuation and Transport
papers.abstract:
Learning solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) requires models that can represent spatial structure across grids and scales. This becomes especially important in time-dependent problems, where the learned operator is often used autoregressively: each predicted state is fed back as input to predict future states. In this setting, small spatial errors can be repeatedly propagated through the learned dynamics, leading to instability and drift, vitiating long-term solution fidelity.
  We propose Mesh-Free Convolutions (MFCs), filters defined in continuous space and discretized only at evaluation time. This allows the same learned filters to be applied across resolutions. Rather than imposing a grid-dependent stencil or a fixed spectral cutoff, MFCs learn smooth scale-dependent filtering and include directional terms for transport-like behavior.
  Across fluid-dynamics and weather-forecasting benchmarks, MFC-based models produce stable long-horizon rollouts, transfer reliably across resolutions, and better preserve long-time statistics. These results suggest that continuous, mesh-free filtering is a useful inductive bias for PDE operator learning, especially in autoregressive prediction.
papers.summary: Neural operators for time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) are usually applied autoregressively, feeding each predicted state back as input, so small spatial errors compound into drift and instability over long rollouts. `Mesh-Free Convolutions` (`MFCs`) are filters defined in continuous space and discretized only at evaluation time, letting the same learned filters run at any resolution, with smooth scale-dependent attenuation and directional terms for transport-like behavior instead of a grid-dependent stencil or fixed spectral cutoff. Across fluid-dynamics and weather-forecasting benchmarks, **MFC-based models produce stable long-horizon rollouts, transfer reliably across resolutions, and better preserve long-time statistics**, supporting continuous mesh-free filtering as an inductive bias for operator learning.

papers.title: DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies
papers.abstract: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires learning and representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions, something conventional neural policies struggle to achieve. Diffusion models offer a natural solution, but standard diffusion training requires direct samples from a fixed target distribution, which are generally unavailable under iterative game-solving updates. We propose a diffusion-based framework for equilibrium computation that enables diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Our approach derives a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without requiring direct samples from each updated policy. Our main method, DiffNash, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer. To correct the resulting distribution shift from sample reuse, we derive an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential provides a tractable proxy for the corresponding importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.
papers.summary: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires representing rich multi-modal strategy distributions, which conventional neural policies handle poorly, while diffusion policies normally need direct samples from a fixed target distribution that iterative game-solving updates never provide. The authors derive a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without such samples, enabling diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). `DiffNash` combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions from a replay buffer, correcting the resulting distribution shift with an unbiased estimator of the gap between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential stands in for the importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. On forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games it **reduces the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%**, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: Error-Based Bidirectional Predictive Coding Enables Deep, 4-Bit Predictive Coding Networks
papers.abstract: Predictive coding networks (PCNs) promise properties not offered by backpropagation-trained networks: learning from purely local information, a single network that both discriminates and generates, and flexible inference by energy minimization. However, their iterative inference is expensive, making hardware acceleration desirable, and a useful, efficient accelerator needs both depth and aggressive quantization. Canonical state-based PC delivers neither: its inference signal decays exponentially with depth, so deep models fail to train, and low precision makes it worse. We show that pairing two recent methods carries the full PCN property set into the deep, 4-bit regime: bidirectional PC (bPC), which unifies discrimination and generation, and the error-based reparameterization (ePC), which optimizes prediction errors rather than states during inference. Error optimization delivers the output signal to every layer in a single backward pass, removing the signal decay; one additional element, global-norm clipping of the error gradients, stabilizes the error dynamics at depth. The resulting ePC+bPC model trains stably up to at least eight layers and retains its full-precision accuracy and clean class-conditional generation under W4A4E4 quantization-aware training, across FP4 and three posit formats. On six-layer networks, where state-based bPC collapses to chance, ePC+bPC classifies more than 50 accuracy points above it after one epoch of training, with class-conditional generations 5-9x better in RMSE. 4-bit quantization is nearly free: full-precision and 4-bit accuracies differ by at most ~5 points, and by under two in the best-performing formats. We characterize the two failure modes the method overcomes, bounded signal decay in state-based PC and error divergence in unregularized error optimization, and discuss implications for a 4-bit-native PCN accelerator.
papers.summary: Predictive coding networks (PCNs) promise purely local learning, a single network that both discriminates and generates, and flexible inference by energy minimization, but their iterative inference is expensive and canonical state-based predictive coding cannot train deep models because its inference signal decays exponentially with depth, a failure that low precision worsens. The authors pair bidirectional predictive coding (`bPC`), which unifies discrimination and generation, with the error-based reparameterization (`ePC`), which optimizes prediction errors rather than states so the output signal reaches every layer in a single backward pass, and add global-norm clipping of the error gradients to keep the error dynamics stable at depth. The resulting `ePC+bPC` model trains stably to at least eight layers and keeps its full-precision accuracy and clean class-conditional generation under 4-bit weight, activation, and error quantization-aware training across FP4 and three posit formats. On six-layer networks where state-based `bPC` collapses to chance, **`ePC+bPC` classifies more than 50 accuracy points higher after one epoch**, and 4-bit accuracy trails full precision by at most about 5 points and by under two in the best formats.

papers.title: The Anatomy of a Blind Spot: What an LLM Judge Must Be Shown, and How Much
papers.abstract: Evaluation of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is increasingly delegated to LLMs acting as judges, yet what such a judge must be shown remains unresolved. We treat a judge whose reports are acted on as a regulator, in the sense of cybernetics, and ask what it must be shown, how much, in what form, and what its reports must get right. On seven public benchmarks we varied only what the judge was shown. Across three judges whose prices differ 10- to 17-fold, what the judge was shown mattered more than which judge it was. When a system revised its answers on feedback from a judge denied the material they had to respect, it ended below its starting point on instruction following and question answering. On instruction following the loss grew with each round, and it persisted when the judge saw the user's request but not the constraints and with a second judge family. On news summarisation, a correct reference summary beside the source undid most of the source's contribution, whereas on single-answer questions a reference helped. About a tenth of the source did almost all of its work, and a small entailment graph matched an LLM judge at finding errors in grounded text. We committed 83 testable clauses before running; of the 81 that ran, 32 met their bar and 50 went in the predicted direction, and most quantitative predictions from the theory failed. We report every shortfall and derive design rules tied to measured effects.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to judge text generated by other LLMs, yet what a judge must be shown remains unresolved, so the authors treat a judge whose reports are acted on as a regulator in the cybernetic sense and vary only its inputs across seven public benchmarks and three judges whose prices differ 10- to 17-fold, finding that **what the judge was shown mattered more than which judge it was**. A system that revised its answers on feedback from a judge denied the constraints it had to respect ended below its starting point on instruction following and question answering, with the loss growing each round and persisting under a second judge family. On news summarisation a correct reference summary beside the source undid most of the source's contribution, whereas on single-answer questions a reference helped, about a tenth of the source did almost all of its work, and a small entailment graph matched an LLM judge at finding errors in grounded text. Of 83 testable clauses committed before running, 81 ran, 32 met their bar, and 50 went in the predicted direction, with most quantitative predictions from the theory failing, and the authors report every shortfall alongside design rules tied to measured effects.

papers.title: Natural Language Processing for Aligning Readings with Learning Objectives and Assessing Topic Balance in Dental Education
papers.abstract: Curriculum teams often lack time to check whether assigned readings support learning objectives (LOs) and whether topic coverage is balanced. We present a natural language processing (NLP) workflow to support evidence-informed curation of reading lists. The workflow combines PubMedBERT sentence embeddings and cosine similarity for retrieval, natural language inference (NLI) for evidence checking, and topic modeling for coverage analysis. We tested the approach in dental education using 13 course-level LOs and a PubMed-derived corpus of 3,837 LO-abstract pairs. Median cosine similarity ranged from 0.86 to 0.91 across the 13 LOs, showing generally high semantic similarity. Topic modeling showed broad but uneven coverage, with one or two dominant topics per domain. Similarity alone was not enough for selecting readings: among high-similarity pairs (cosine 0.90-1.00), 22.9% were classified by NLI as neutral or contradictory. In a 49-pair expert-labeled validation set, cosine-based retrieval (cosine >= 0.90) achieved 0.69 accuracy, while the combined cosine and NLI approach achieved 0.73 accuracy against expert alignment labels. Overall, the workflow shows how AI can support curriculum alignment by reducing false positives and helping select readings that better match intended LOs.
papers.summary: Curriculum teams often lack time to check whether assigned readings support stated learning objectives (LOs) or whether topic coverage is balanced. The natural language processing (NLP) workflow combines `PubMedBERT` sentence embeddings with cosine similarity for retrieval, natural language inference (NLI) for evidence checking, and topic modeling for coverage analysis, tested on 13 dental course LOs and a PubMed-derived corpus of 3,837 LO-abstract pairs. Median cosine similarity ranged from 0.86 to 0.91 and topic modeling showed broad but uneven coverage, yet similarity alone was insufficient, since 22.9% of high-similarity pairs were classified by NLI as neutral or contradictory. On a 49-pair expert-labeled validation set, **combining cosine retrieval with NLI raised alignment accuracy from 0.69 to 0.73**.

papers.title: Physics-guided machine learning for saturation control across variable hydraulic conditions in heap leaching
papers.abstract: Heap-leaching hydraulics vary between regions of an ore bed, motivating fast prediction models that accommodate different material properties. This study develops a parameter-conditioned physics-guided machine-learning (PGML) surrogate and demonstrates its use in simulated saturation control. A dataset of 4096 numerical Richards-equation trajectories was divided into 2867 training, 614 validation and 615 evaluation cases. The network predicts hourly saturation profiles from the current profile, irrigation rate and four hydraulic parameters, and is trained with an approximate Gardner mass-balance penalty. A daily predictive controller compared 200 constant irrigation rates over a 24-hour horizon. Across the evaluation cases, the median full-cycle tracking deviation was 4.9% of a 0.70 saturation target, equal to that of a tuned proportional-integral (PI) controller, while the PGML controller reached the target without overshoot in the median and applied approximately 4% less irrigation. Moderate physics guidance reduced long-horizon prediction error by approximately 30% relative to data-only training and reduced irrigation-bound activity, but slightly worsened closed-loop tracking. For a matched prediction workload, the surrogate was approximately 70 times faster than the numerical solver, and batched evaluation cost under 2 ms per column for 5000 columns. The results support a reusable physics-guided surrogate for large-scale saturation control in simulation.
papers.summary: Hydraulic conditions vary across regions of a heap-leach ore bed, so fast prediction models must accommodate different material properties. A parameter-conditioned physics-guided machine-learning (PGML) surrogate predicts hourly saturation profiles from the current profile, irrigation rate, and four hydraulic parameters, trained on 4,096 numerical Richards-equation trajectories with an approximate Gardner mass-balance penalty, and feeds a daily predictive controller that compares 200 constant irrigation rates over a 24-hour horizon. Across evaluation cases the controller matched a tuned proportional-integral (PI) controller's median tracking deviation of 4.9% of a 0.70 saturation target while reaching the target without overshoot and applying about 4% less irrigation, and **the surrogate was roughly 70 times faster than the numerical solver**, under 2 ms per column in batched evaluation. Moderate physics guidance reduced long-horizon prediction error by about 30% relative to data-only training but slightly worsened closed-loop tracking.

papers.title: Vision: "What Don't I Know About User's Preferences?" How Uncertainty Estimation Improves Proactive Assistant Alignment
papers.abstract: Proactive Smart Assistants (PSAs) increasingly use general knowledge, learned patterns from group-level data, patterns from individual user's data, and recent sensor observations to anticipate which action a user may prefer. Existing systems typically select actions from predicted user preference likelihoods, but these likelihoods alone do not reveal how reliable the prediction is, which evidence supports it, or why ambiguity remains. In this vision paper, we argue that uncertainty estimation can provide this missing information and substantially change appropriate downstream behavior. Using the example of a home assistant, we introduce the questions that uncertainty estimation aims to answer, i.e. how sure is the assistant about the predicted preference likelihood, whether the confidence come from group-level assumptions or individual's data, and whether likelihood ambiguity reflect the user's intrinsic preference variability or insufficient data for the particular situation. We further introduce uncertainty estimation applications in neighboring domains, such as human trajectory prediction, personalized activity recognition, information-collection, and model-based control. Finally, we draw on insights from neighboring domains to envision how future uncertainty-aware proactive assistants may address key challenges in proactive interaction.
papers.summary: Proactive Smart Assistants (PSAs) anticipate which action a user may prefer from general knowledge, group-level patterns, individual history, and recent sensor observations, but the predicted preference likelihoods they act on do not reveal how reliable a prediction is, which evidence supports it, or why ambiguity remains. The authors argue that uncertainty estimation can supply this missing information and substantially change appropriate downstream behavior, using a home assistant example to pose three questions: how sure the assistant is about the predicted likelihood, whether confidence comes from group-level assumptions or the individual's own data, and whether ambiguity reflects intrinsic preference variability or insufficient data for the situation. They review uncertainty estimation in neighboring domains such as human trajectory prediction, personalized activity recognition, information collection, and model-based control, and **draw on those insights to envision how uncertainty-aware proactive assistants could address key challenges in proactive interaction**.

papers.title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.
papers.summary: Ransomware causes growing financial and data losses, and increasingly sophisticated attacks defeat traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis. The proposed framework couples software-level scanning with hardware-level monitoring of microprocessor activity for real-time detection, hardens the static analysis against obfuscation through adversarial training, and applies neural architecture search (NAS) to tailor detection models for stronger generalizability. The authors report that **the approach substantially improves detection accuracy and reduces latency compared with existing methods** while providing trace-level interpretability of its decisions.

papers.title: Small area learning
papers.abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop standard and cross-fitted estimators for low-complexity and flexible learners, unifying synthetic, model-based, and fully residual-corrected estimation. For area means, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality and provide variance estimators and confidence intervals. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals a bias--variance trade-off: partial residual correction can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to working-model misspecification, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34\%--49\% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. An empirical application favours a cross-fitted estimator using a flexible learner under the chosen validation criterion. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.
papers.summary: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model, tying estimates to that model's assumptions. The learner-agnostic `SAL` framework recasts SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem with outcome prediction as a nuisance task, allows unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift across areas, and provides standard and cross-fitted estimators for both low-complexity and flexible learners that unify synthetic, model-based, and fully residual-corrected estimation.
