For area means the authors establish consistency and asymptotic normality with variance estimators and confidence intervals, extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates, and expose a bias-variance trade-off in which partial residual correction can reduce mean squared error while full correction is robust to working-model misspecification at potentially higher variance. **Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34% to 49% relative to direct estimation**, an empirical application favours a cross-fitted estimator with a flexible learner, and the numerical studies show how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals.

papers.title: Instance-Adaptive Online Multiclass Multicalibration
papers.abstract: We study online multiclass multicalibration over $T$ rounds, and give an algorithm with beyond-worst-case guarantees. With $n$ possible outcomes, forecasts lie in a simplex of dimension $d=n-1$. In the worst case, cumulative $\ell_1$ multicalibration error scales with $\widetilde\Theta(T^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$, which becomes untenable once $d$ exceeds a small constant. Our algorithm adapts to the geometry of the realized sequence: if the sequence of adversarially selected outcome means lies in an affine subspace of dimension $s$, it obtains error $\widetilde O(n^{1/(s+2)}T^{(s+1)/(s+2)})$ with high probability. The algorithm adapts to this structure without knowing the subspace or its dimension. For $T\ge n\ge2$, this rate is minimax optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. For a stochastic instance with a fixed conditional mean, the bound specializes to $\widetilde O(\sqrt{nT})$, giving a square-root dependence on the horizon.
papers.summary: In online multiclass multicalibration over T rounds with n possible outcomes, forecasts lie in a simplex of dimension d = n - 1, and worst-case cumulative l1 multicalibration error scales as T^((d+1)/(d+2)) up to logarithmic factors, which becomes untenable once d exceeds a small constant. The proposed algorithm adapts to the geometry of the realized sequence: if the adversarially selected outcome means lie in an affine subspace of dimension s, it achieves error of order n^(1/(s+2)) T^((s+1)/(s+2)) with high probability, without knowing the subspace or its dimension. **For T >= n >= 2, this rate is minimax optimal up to polylogarithmic factors**, and for a stochastic instance with a fixed conditional mean the bound specializes to order sqrt(nT), a square-root dependence on the horizon.

papers.title: ADAPT: Audio-Depth Action Planning with Transition-Aware Rewards for Lights-Out Industrial Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models for embodied navigation typically rely on RGB observations, limiting their applicability in lights-out industrial environments where visible illumination may be unavailable. We study illumination-independent navigation using spatial audio for target localization and depth for obstacle-aware geometry. To support this setting, we introduce DarkNav-Bench, a benchmark with 24 industrial scenes and four progressively challenging acoustic conditions. We further propose ADAPT, an audio-depth action-planning framework equipped with spatial-audio perception and optimized for closed-loop navigation through reinforcement learning (RL). Our key RL contribution, transition-aware reward shaping (TARS), defines a pose-aware shortest-action potential over a position-heading graph. Unlike conventional geodesic-progress rewards, TARS accounts for both feasible movements and in-place rotations, providing action-consistent feedback for policy optimization. Experiments show that ADAPT consistently outperforms training-based navigation baselines and zero-shot multimodal models on both seen and unseen scenes. On unseen environments, it achieves 90.6% success under Clean conditions and retains 60.0% success under the most challenging Localized Noise setting. These results demonstrate the potential of spatial audio and depth as complementary modalities for reliable RGB-free navigation in lights-out industrial environments.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action models for embodied navigation typically rely on RGB observations, which are unavailable in lights-out industrial environments without visible illumination. `DarkNav-Bench` provides 24 industrial scenes under four progressively harder acoustic conditions, and `ADAPT` is an audio-depth action-planning framework that localizes targets with spatial audio, uses depth for obstacle-aware geometry, and is optimized for closed-loop navigation through reinforcement learning (RL). Its transition-aware reward shaping (`TARS`) defines a pose-aware shortest-action potential over a position-heading graph that accounts for both feasible movements and in-place rotations, unlike conventional geodesic-progress rewards. `ADAPT` outperforms training-based navigation baselines and zero-shot multimodal models on seen and unseen scenes, **reaching 90.6% success on unseen environments under clean conditions** and retaining 60.0% under the hardest localized-noise setting.

papers.title: Harmonic Representations in Symbolic Music Transformers are Localized and Controllable
papers.abstract: Transformer models trained on symbolic music have become remarkably capable. However, it is yet unclear how they represent music structure, and whether understanding their internal representations can be used to unlock methods for model control. We examine this through a case study of harmonic analysis: when a music transformer navigates a cadence, what does it internally "know" about its harmonic context, and can that knowledge be used to affect the generation? Using Aria, a LLaMA-based symbolic music transformer evaluated on Bach chorales, we find that harmonic decisions are causally localized progressively from middle layers onward. Linear probes show that mode becomes decodable in the same layer range where patching identifies growing causal effect, while key identity emerges later. We then confirm these representations are actionable for music generation control: steering via latent directions corresponding to harmonic changes reliably produces a deceptive or minor resolution, while preserving structural coherence and generation quality. This demonstrates that, at inference time, the model's internal harmonic knowledge can be directly manipulated to control the harmonic output.
papers.summary: Transformers trained on symbolic music have become capable generators, but how they represent musical structure and whether those representations can be used for control has been unclear. Using `Aria`, a `LLaMA`-based symbolic music transformer evaluated on Bach chorales, the authors study what the model internally represents about harmonic context as it navigates a cadence, combining activation patching with linear probes. Harmonic decisions are causally localized progressively from the middle layers onward, mode becomes linearly decodable in the same layer range where patching shows growing causal effect, and key identity emerges later. **Steering along latent directions for harmonic changes reliably produces a deceptive or minor resolution** while preserving structural coherence and generation quality, showing that internal harmonic knowledge can be manipulated at inference time.

papers.title: Unfair and Unsafe: Everyday Bias Triggers Emergent Misalignment
papers.abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning a language model to a narrow task makes it misaligned on unrelated ones. Because organizations now routinely fine-tune models on their own data, it matters which kinds of training data cause EM. So far, studies have induced EM with data containing recognized safety failures, such as insecure code or harmful advice, while biased training data is typically examined by fairness research for the bias models learn from it rather than for its effects on safety. In real-world text, much of this bias, such as demographic stereotypes, appears not as derogatory language but politely, embedded in judgments about people. We ask whether learning such polite stereotypes can itself cause EM. We find that fine-tuning on polite answers that rely on stereotypes makes models less safe and less truthful on unrelated tasks. The effect holds across four open-weight model families (7B to 12B), both gender and race stereotypes, and repeated training runs, relative to controls trained on the same questions without the stereotype. We further show that the learned stereotype has its own direction in model activations, distinct from directions for generic misaligned traits such as deception. This direction exists before fine-tuning and can both control the learned stereotype and monitor its acquisition. Existing defenses against EM improve safety while leaving the stereotype largely intact. Beyond this controlled setting, fine-tuning on political news coverage also triggers EM, apparently amplified by partisan framing, and stereotype models acting as tool-using agents can carry out harmful tasks and blame people without evidence. Our results show that biased training data is not only a fairness problem but also a safety one. We argue that EM is studied too narrowly, and that fairness concerns and methods offer a natural way to broaden the search for its triggers.
papers.summary: Emergent misalignment (EM), where fine-tuning a language model on a narrow task makes it misaligned on unrelated ones, has so far been induced only with data containing recognized safety failures such as insecure code, so the authors ask whether politely phrased demographic stereotypes, the form bias usually takes in real-world text, can trigger it on their own. **Fine-tuning on polite stereotype-based answers makes models less safe and less truthful on unrelated tasks**, holding across four open-weight model families from 7B to 12B parameters, both gender and race stereotypes, and repeated training runs, relative to controls trained on the same questions without the stereotype. The learned stereotype has its own activation direction, distinct from generic misaligned traits such as deception, that exists before fine-tuning and can both control and monitor its acquisition, while existing EM defenses improve safety but leave the stereotype largely intact. Fine-tuning on partisan political news coverage also triggers EM, and stereotype models acting as tool-using agents carry out harmful tasks and blame people without evidence.

papers.title: Using Line Segment Tracking to enable ML-based Track Reconstruction in CMS
papers.abstract: High-pileup conditions in CMS during the HL-LHC era make charged-particle tracking increasingly challenging as detector occupancy and combinatorics grow. We present a hybrid approach that exploits Line Segment Tracking (LST) objects rather than individual hits to enable the first CMS ML-based track reconstruction algorithm. The LST objects, namely the triplets used in this study, are built according to geometry- and physics-driven criteria and carry richer local structure, geometrical cues, and physics quantities such as transverse momentum, which helps the model incorporate detector-level information from the start. We apply a Transformer encoder with geometrically masked sparse self-attention to embed these objects in a learned latent space, and use object condensation to assemble full tracks in a single inference step. This object-based representation reduces complexity in dense environments and makes the model less sensitive to ambiguities introduced by high pileup. Evaluated on CMS Phase-2 simulation of $t\bar{t}$ events at $\langle \mu \rangle = 200$, the approach achieves reconstruction efficiency comparable to the LST quintuplet baseline while reducing the fake rate by roughly a factor of three and suppressing duplicates almost entirely, demonstrating the promise of advanced ML architectures for next-generation particle tracking.
authors: Aashay Arora on behalf of the CMS Collaboration
papers.summary: High pileup during the High-Luminosity LHC era makes charged-particle tracking in CMS increasingly difficult as detector occupancy and combinatorics grow. Rather than working from individual hits, the approach uses Line Segment Tracking (LST) triplets, objects built from geometry- and physics-driven criteria that carry local structure, geometric cues, and quantities such as transverse momentum, and embeds them with a Transformer encoder using geometrically masked sparse self-attention before assembling full tracks in a single inference step via object condensation. On CMS Phase-2 simulation of top-quark pair events at an average pileup of 200, this first CMS machine-learning track reconstruction algorithm matches the efficiency of the `LST` quintuplet baseline while **reducing the fake rate by roughly a factor of three** and suppressing duplicates almost entirely.

papers.title: Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signals for Self-Evolving Agents
papers.abstract: A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to keep, so its improvement signal is the check a rewrite has to pass. Verifying a rewrite by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while executable checks such as the repository's own tests are too sparse to catch behavior-changing rewrites, rejecting only a quarter of them. We instead take test feedback as the executable signal, and search for test suites that are both small and strong with a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm, so that the signal is dense and informative. TeSearch treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so that quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 real-world modules and three backbones, TeSearch delivers the highest-quality suites of any method compared, LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. Used as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3% for the repository's tests, at a 4.0% false-alarm rate and 3.5 s per decision. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/TeSearch.
papers.summary: A self-evolving agent that rewrites its own harness must decide which rewrites to keep, but verifying rewrites by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, and a repository's own tests are too sparse, rejecting only about a quarter of behavior-changing rewrites. `TeSearch` searches for test suites that are both small and strong with a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm that treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so quality is pursued at every size, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the large language model acting as the mutation operator on that descriptor. Across 129 real-world modules and three backbones it delivers the highest-quality suites of any compared method, LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. As the improvement signal for a self-evolving agent, **it rejects 59.9% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3% for the repository's tests**, at a 4.0% false-alarm rate and 3.5 seconds per decision.

papers.title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
papers.abstract:
We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay.
  We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. Tighter deadlines favor larger batches, and latency-oriented parallelism can trade additional GPUs for shorter training. Nevertheless, even under a fixed time budget, a smaller batch with fewer GPUs can achieve lower validation loss than a larger batch with more GPUs, challenging the common practice of increasing data parallelism to maximize GPU utilization under a deadline. Together, our results identify underexplored factors in repeated-data training and provide concrete guidance on how training recipes and resource allocation should change from single-pass pretraining.
papers.summary: When compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, pretraining must repeat the same data over multiple epochs, and the authors revisit the infinite-compute regime of Kim et al. (2026) to show that its loss frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied in isolation. Jointly optimizing batch size and epoch count reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size that favors smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization, and recipes optimized for single-pass training can be retuned with per-epoch document repacking, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. Relaxing the infinite-compute assumption, they treat GPUs and wall-clock time as separate resources: tighter deadlines favor larger batches and latency-oriented parallelism can trade extra GPUs for shorter training, yet **even under a fixed time budget a smaller batch on fewer GPUs can reach lower validation loss than a larger batch on more GPUs**, challenging the practice of maximizing data parallelism to fill a deadline.

papers.title: Softmax-Free Attention in Spiking Transformers as the Zero-Temperature Limit of Two-Level Systems
papers.abstract: Spiking Transformers achieve energy efficiency by discarding softmax normalization in favor of thresholded, binary attention. However, this removal breaks the thermodynamic framework used to analyze attention networks, as the normalized measure and partition function cease to exist. We restore this theoretical foundation by proving that softmax-free spiking attention operates exactly as the zero-temperature limit of a product of independent two-level systems. This correspondence places spiking attention strictly in the frozen ordered phase of the thermodynamic phase diagram for all inputs. Consequently, the entropic cost of organizing attention collapses, replaced by a Landauer-type physical floor governed by action-potential generation. Furthermore, this ordered-phase pinning mathematically explains the optimization difficulty caused by vanishing surrogate gradients. We validate this theory with forward-relaxation experiments, placing both standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a unified thermodynamic axis.
papers.summary: Spiking Transformers save energy by discarding softmax normalization in favor of thresholded binary attention, but removing the normalization also removes the normalized measure and partition function on which thermodynamic analyses of attention networks rest. The authors prove that **softmax-free spiking attention operates exactly as the zero-temperature limit of a product of independent two-level systems**, which places it in the frozen ordered phase of the thermodynamic phase diagram for all inputs. In that regime the entropic cost of organizing attention collapses and is replaced by a Landauer-type physical floor set by action-potential generation, and the ordered-phase pinning mathematically explains the vanishing surrogate gradients that make such networks hard to optimize. Forward-relaxation experiments place standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a single thermodynamic axis.

papers.title: PopGen: Generating Semantically Diverse Populations for Zero-Shot Coordination
papers.abstract: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exposing a cooperator to partners with diverse strategies during training is key to better collaboration at test time. However, existing methods typically rely on trajectory-level proxies to measure diversity, which may label two distinct trajectories of the same strategy as diverse. Instead, our key insight is to leverage LLMs' ability to describe behaviorally distinct agents in environments, similar to how humans can recognize high-level strategies. To this end, we introduce PopGen, a framework that synthesizes semantically diverse agents from scratch using LLMs. PopGen first generates a diverse set of textual descriptions of agent behaviors, then translates each behavior into a code policy that can be executed within the environment. We show that cooperators trained against PopGen populations achieve robust zero-shot cooperation with unseen partners, outperforming population-play baselines across four collaborative environments. We further show that semantic diversity scales with PopGen population size, improving the cooperator's worst-case performance, and we identify design choices that preserve population quality while maximizing diversity. Our code is available at https://github.com/labicon/PopGen.
papers.summary: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, training a cooperator against partners with diverse strategies is key to collaborating with unseen partners at test time, but existing methods measure diversity with trajectory-level proxies that can label two distinct trajectories of the same strategy as diverse. `PopGen` instead uses a large language model to generate a diverse set of textual descriptions of agent behaviors and then translates each description into an executable code policy, synthesizing semantically distinct populations from scratch. Cooperators trained against `PopGen` populations **achieve robust zero-shot cooperation with unseen partners and outperform population-play baselines across four collaborative environments**. Semantic diversity scales with population size, improving the cooperator's worst-case performance, and the authors identify design choices that preserve population quality while maximizing diversity.

papers.title: Embedding Information in Policy Randomness: Distribution-Preserving Implicit Communication in MDPs
papers.abstract: This paper investigates a new role of randomness in stochastic policies--as a medium for embedding and communicating information. Specifically, we consider an agent interacting with an environment according to a prescribed stochastic policy. By carefully modulating the random action realizations of the policy, information can be embedded into the agent's behavior without altering the prescribed action distribution. We cast this problem as a channel coding problem, in which the controlled system implicitly serves as a communication channel. We then propose a coding scheme, termed posterior-matching randomness modulation (PRAM), that selects actions according to the message to be transmitted. With the aid of common randomness independent of the control system, PRAM preserves the prescribed action distribution for every state and every message. We further prove that PRAM is asymptotically reliable: the message can be decoded with arbitrarily small error probability as the observed state trajectory becomes sufficiently long. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in applications including multi-bit policy watermarking and trajectory provenance.
papers.summary: The randomness in a stochastic policy can double as a medium for communication: by carefully modulating which random action realizations occur, information can be embedded in an agent's behavior without altering the prescribed action distribution. The authors cast this as a channel coding problem in which the controlled system implicitly serves as the channel, and propose posterior-matching randomness modulation (`PRAM`), which selects actions according to the message to be transmitted and, with the aid of common randomness independent of the control system, preserves the prescribed action distribution for every state and every message. **`PRAM` is proven asymptotically reliable, with decoding error made arbitrarily small as the observed state trajectory grows long enough**, and experiments demonstrate multi-bit policy watermarking and trajectory provenance.

papers.title: Mixed Feelings, Single Polarity
papers.abstract: Emotion datasets are routinely mapped onto positive and negative valence, by assigning each emotion category one polarity. We test where this works and where it fails, using SemEval-2018 Affect in Tweets (English, Arabic, Spanish), Affective Text aligned with EmoBank, raw GoEmotions annotations, naturalistic hashtag corpora, and a controlled annotation study. Fixed projection works well when a text carries labels of one valence. It fails on a subset identifiable from the labels alone: tweets whose emotion labels point in opposite directions. These are 9.0% of polar SemEval test tweets but cause 54.8% of the polarity errors of a learned projection, are more than twice as likely to receive a neutral-or-mixed gold label, and are not rescued by modeling the full label set. Annotators produce such configurations routinely: 16.3% of multilabel GoEmotions judgments combine emotions from the dataset's own positive and negative parents. In a controlled study holding word and reader constant, context changes the coarse valence judgment in 56.8% of cases, against 19.9% for controls. We recommend projecting label configurations rather than labels, abstaining or keeping a mixed class where labels conflict, and reporting coverage alongside accuracy.
papers.summary: Emotion datasets are routinely mapped onto positive and negative valence by assigning each emotion category one polarity, and the authors test where this works and where it fails using `SemEval-2018 Affect in Tweets` in English, Arabic, and Spanish, `Affective Text` aligned with `EmoBank`, raw `GoEmotions` annotations, naturalistic hashtag corpora, and a controlled annotation study. Fixed projection works when a text's labels share one valence but fails on texts whose emotion labels point in opposite directions: **these are 9.0% of polar SemEval test tweets yet cause 54.8% of a learned projection's polarity errors**, are more than twice as likely to receive a neutral-or-mixed gold label, and are not rescued by modeling the full label set. Such conflicts are routine, with 16.3% of multilabel `GoEmotions` judgments combining emotions from the dataset's own positive and negative parents, and in a controlled study holding word and reader constant, context changed the coarse valence judgment in 56.8% of cases against 19.9% for controls. The authors recommend projecting label configurations rather than individual labels, abstaining or keeping a mixed class where labels conflict, and reporting coverage alongside accuracy.

papers.title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Wildfire Size Using Conditional Flow Matching
papers.abstract: In this work we present a probabilistic model for predicting the temporal evolution of wildfire size using conditional generative algorithms, namely flow matching. Rather than predicting spatially resolved fire progression, the proposed model forecasts a time series of fire acreage, substantially reducing computational cost and enabling efficient integration with downstream applications such as early warning systems and risk assessment tools. Given estimates of the fire size at the current and previous forecasting steps, alongside spatially averaged weather conditions, terrain characteristics, and fuel composition, the model predicts the change in fire area over a 3-hour interval. Training data are drawn from 140 coupled atmosphere-wildfire simulations generated using WRF-SFIRE, paired with weather data from the North American Mesoscale (NAM) model. Sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the model captures physically-consistent responses to variations in wind speed, temperature, and relative humidity. Model performance is evaluated against reference solutions from WRF-SFIRE. For single-step predictions, the model achieves a symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE) of 0.39 relative to the reference WRF-SFIRE solutions. Recursive multi-step predictions over 24 hours are performed for 12 held-out test cases, where the flow matching model achieves a final fire area sMAPE of 0.39 while further providing meaningful quantification of forecast uncertainty.
papers.summary: Forecasting how a wildfire's burned area grows over time usually requires expensive spatially resolved fire-spread simulation. The authors instead train a conditional flow matching model to predict the change in fire acreage over each 3-hour interval from the current and previous fire size plus spatially averaged weather, terrain, and fuel composition, using 140 coupled atmosphere-fire simulations from `WRF-SFIRE` paired with `North American Mesoscale (NAM)` weather data. Sensitivity analysis shows physically consistent responses to wind, temperature, and humidity, and **recursive 24-hour forecasts on 12 held-out cases reach a final fire-area symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE) of 0.39** while also providing meaningful quantification of forecast uncertainty.

papers.title: Revocation Is Not Complete at Receipt: An Executable Outcome Contract for Distributed Agent-Tool Gateways
papers.abstract: Distributed agent workflows cache delegated authority at tool gateways. Revocation may be reported at issuer commit, transport acknowledgment, or receiver persistence, although none of these observations establishes that all gateways enforced the change or that guarded effects stopped. We define C0-C5, a bounded outcome contract spanning issuer commit through effect prevention, and implement it as a persistent monitor over a frozen gateway set, call set, and observation window. A 14-case fault matrix checks conservative classification, sticky violations, restart persistence, and evidence immutability. In a derived audit of its eight semantic cases, treating C3 or C4 as completion produces seven or five false positives, respectively; the bounded C0-C5 verdict produces none. Descriptive scaling covers 1,024 gateways and 10,000 effect vectors. The primary experiment uses the maintained Keycloak 26.7 identity server and measures the contract across two durable receivers, eight physical agent-tool gateways, Filesystem and PostgreSQL effects, and 16 AWS hosts in three availability zones. Normal delivery and recovery commit no effects. Under receiver-selective non-delivery, transport acknowledgment and receiver persistence still succeed, but 112 of 225 calls (49.78%) are admitted, and all 112 effects commit in every treatment block. A separately provisioned execution repeats the result. OPA/Toxiproxy and a live three-role LLM workflow with networked MCP tools reproduce the persisted-but-not-enforced boundary on narrower surfaces. Finally, an unmodified external MCPMark agent executes 60 closed-loop task arms. Normal C4 denies all 31 exposed post-barrier calls and commits no effect; selective C3 allows 344 calls and commits 145 effects across Filesystem and PostgreSQL. Transport success is therefore evidence of progress, not a revocation-completion verdict.
papers.summary: When authority delegated to agents is cached at tool gateways, a revocation reported at issuer commit, transport acknowledgment, or receiver persistence does not prove that every gateway stopped the guarded effects. The authors define a bounded outcome contract, `C0-C5`, spanning issuer commit through effect prevention, implement it as a persistent monitor over a frozen gateway set and observation window, and test it with a 14-case fault matrix plus experiments on a `Keycloak 26.7` identity server, eight physical gateways, Filesystem and PostgreSQL effects, and 16 AWS hosts across three availability zones. **Under receiver-selective non-delivery, transport acknowledgment and receiver persistence still succeed, yet 112 of 225 calls (49.78%) are admitted and all of their effects commit**, a boundary reproduced with OPA/Toxiproxy, a three-role LLM workflow using networked Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, and an unmodified external `MCPMark` agent running 60 closed-loop task arms. Transport success is therefore evidence of progress, not a verdict that revocation completed.

papers.title: Handoff Curves: Initial Selection, Later Handoff, and Supervision Targets in Multi-turn LLM Routing
papers.abstract: We study how initial model selection, later handoff, and training targets affect success and cost in LLM tasks that span multiple turns. We compare several router architectures using handoff curves, which record task success and cost as the handoff step changes. Our dataset contains 34,204 complete executions of three Qwen models across BFCL, MultiWOZ, and $\tau$-retail, providing offline supervision for routing decisions. In our primary comparison, with Qwen3.5 35B-A3B as the starting model, allowing a later handoff does not establish an improvement in utility over initial selection on BFCL or MultiWOZ, and increases cost on BFCL across a range of cost weights. Changing the supervision targets improves router performance on both our dataset and TwinRouterBench. On our dataset, replacing noisy training success curves with monotone fits raises success by 0.2 to 4.1 percentage points at the same cost across the reported operating points. On TwinRouterBench, we construct targets that describe the model capability needed for the remaining work and difficult steps ahead. Compared with training on the benchmark's per-step labels, these targets raise trajectory pass scores by 7.8 percentage points and cost savings by 6.3 percentage points on the full static bank. A live deployment of the router trained with these targets resolves 79 of 100 instances at a router cost of 0.59 US dollars per instance.
papers.summary: Routing multi-turn LLM tasks involves picking a starting model and deciding whether to hand off to a stronger one partway through, and the study examines how those choices and the router's training targets affect success and cost. Using 34,204 complete executions of three `Qwen` models across `BFCL`, `MultiWOZ`, and `τ-retail`, the authors compare router architectures through handoff curves that trace success and cost as the handoff step varies. With `Qwen3.5 35B-A3B` as the starting model, allowing a later handoff does not demonstrably beat initial selection on `BFCL` or `MultiWOZ` and raises cost on `BFCL`, whereas replacing noisy success-curve targets with monotone fits raises success by 0.2 to 4.1 percentage points at equal cost. On `TwinRouterBench`, targets that describe the capability needed for the remaining work **raise trajectory pass scores by 7.8 percentage points and cost savings by 6.3 percentage points** over per-step labels, and a live deployment of that router resolves 79 of 100 instances at 0.59 US dollars per instance.

papers.title: Large language model-generated patterns for epidemiological modeling: a multi-benchmark evaluation framework
papers.abstract: Representing individual-level behavioral heterogeneity is challenging in epidemiological modeling, particularly when empirical behavioral data are sparse. We assess the potential of large language model (LLM)-generated behavioral outputs in addressing this challenge, using hepatitis C virus-related behaviors among people who inject drugs as a case study. Correspondence with epidemiological patterns was evaluated using external benchmarks: literature-informed association directions, correlations from an agent-based model (ABM), and survey associations. Across three LLMs, unconditional directional recovery across 28 retained literature-informed associations was 46-68%, compared with 82-93% agreement when LLMs were directly asked to classify the same associations. Mean absolute differences from ABM and survey correlation patterns were 0.11-0.13 and 0.15-0.18, respectively. Together, these findings show partial alignment between LLM-generated behavioral relationships and epidemiological evidence, despite higher knowledge-probe agreement. More systematic evaluation is needed before incorporating LLM-generated behavioral outputs into epidemiological models that simulate transmission dynamics.
papers.summary: Epidemiological models need individual-level behavioral heterogeneity, but empirical behavioral data are often sparse, so the authors test whether large language model (LLM)-generated behavioral outputs can fill the gap, using hepatitis C virus-related behaviors among people who inject drugs as a case study. Outputs from three LLMs are compared against literature-informed association directions, correlations from an agent-based model (ABM), and survey associations. **Unconditional directional recovery of 28 literature-informed associations was only 46-68%, versus 82-93% agreement when the same LLMs were asked directly to classify those associations**, and mean absolute differences from ABM and survey correlation patterns were 0.11-0.13 and 0.15-0.18. The authors conclude that alignment is partial and that more systematic evaluation is needed before such outputs feed transmission-dynamics models.

papers.title: AutoSec-RAN: Specification-Grounded LLM Fine-Tuning for Automated Security Analysis of O-RAN
papers.abstract: This paper presents AutoSec-RAN, a specification-grounded large language model (LLM) framework for automated security triage of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) testing. Unlike approaches relying on static rule sets or privileged access to raw packet captures, AutoSec-RAN fine-tunes Mistral-7B-Instruct through two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) stages over a curated corpus of 69 O-RAN, 3GPP, and adjacent standards documents, then selectively augments inference with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the same specification index. At inference, the model receives only an investigator-style question and a scenario metadata block, simulating an automated analyst operating without raw packet evidence. AutoSec-RAN is validated on a purpose-built 5G/O-RAN testbed across labeled fronthaul distributed denial of service replay scenarios. A Gemma-4-31B judge LLM scores each candidate's answer on faithfulness, correctness, and actionability relative to a reference authored from full packet capture and log evidence. AutoSec-RAN achieves a mean judge overall score of 0.713 across all 313 evaluation items (0.755 restricted to the five supervised taxonomy classes), clearing the 0.70 reporting threshold, and a blended score of 0.778 (0.808 supervised-only) when cosine similarity over Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) General Embedding (BGE) is incorporated as a secondary semantic signal. The framework performs strongest on mitigation and threat-model reasoning (with a mean overall of 0.849 and 0.848, respectively) and identifies a measurable gap on the held-out attack-direction class (0.515), a controlled result that exposes a specific training data requirement. These results establish specification-grounded LoRA fine-tuning combined with RAG retrieval as a viable foundation for automated security validation of AI-native O-RAN.
papers.summary: Security triage for Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) testing typically depends on static rule sets or privileged access to raw packet captures. `AutoSec-RAN` instead fine-tunes `Mistral-7B-Instruct` with two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) stages over a corpus of 69 O-RAN, 3GPP, and related specification documents, then adds retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the same index, so that at inference the model answers an investigator-style question from only a scenario metadata block. On a 5G/O-RAN testbed with labeled fronthaul distributed denial of service replay scenarios, a `Gemma-4-31B` judge scoring faithfulness, correctness, and actionability gave **a mean overall score of 0.713 across 313 evaluation items**, rising to 0.778 when cosine similarity over Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) General Embedding (`BGE`) vectors is blended in. Performance is strongest on mitigation and threat-model reasoning (around 0.85) and weakest on the held-out attack-direction class (0.515), which the authors attribute to a specific training-data gap.

papers.title: Dissipative Lagrangian Neural Networks for the Interpretable Modelling of Passive Mechanical Systems
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose the Dissipative Lagrangian Neural Network (dLNN), a continuous-time system identification technique that separately learns the conservative and dissipative dynamics of a mechanical system directly from data. A key contribution is a novel parametrisation of dissipative forces that (i) is structurally constrained to be dissipative, enforcing passivity of the learned model, (ii) cannot absorb conservative mechanics, and (iii) retains sufficient expressivity to represent a broad family of state-dependent damping and regularised friction forces. The model is validated on prediction tasks on two real-world mechanical systems: trajectory prediction of a chaotic double pendulum and inverse-dynamics modelling of a six-degree-of-freedom industrial robot. Across these tasks, the dLNN demonstrates improved predictive performance over existing Lagrangian architectures while remaining competitive with a black-box neural model. The imposed physical structure also improves generalisation to unseen states, with the benefits becoming particularly pronounced when training data is limited. Finally, we introduce a symbolic distillation procedure that extracts closed-form expressions from the learned physical components. Applied to the industrial robot, this produces interpretable symbolic models that retain high predictive accuracy while reducing the computational overhead associated with evaluating neural Lagrangian models.
papers.summary: Data-driven identification of mechanical systems needs to capture both conservative motion and dissipative effects such as damping and friction while keeping the learned model physically interpretable. The Dissipative Lagrangian Neural Network (`dLNN`) learns conservative and dissipative dynamics separately, using a new parametrisation of dissipative forces that is structurally constrained to be dissipative so the learned model is passive, cannot absorb conservative mechanics, and still covers state-dependent damping and regularised friction. On trajectory prediction for a chaotic double pendulum and inverse dynamics for a six-degree-of-freedom industrial robot, `dLNN` **outperforms existing Lagrangian architectures and stays competitive with a black-box network, with the largest gains when training data is scarce**. A symbolic distillation step extracts closed-form expressions from the learned components, yielding interpretable robot models that keep high accuracy at lower evaluation cost.

papers.title: Representational Difference Distillation
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers representational knowledge from a large teacher network to a compact student. Existing relational and contrastive distillation methods treat all samples uniformly, spending equal gradient on well-matched and poorly-matched regions of the representation space alike. We propose Representational Difference Distillation (RDD), which diagnoses where teacher and student representations structurally disagree and concentrates the distillation signal on those regions. RDD uses two asymmetric affinity matrices that capture opposing directions of misalignment: one identifies samples the student incorrectly considers similar, the other identifies teacher relationships the student has yet to learn. These affinities determine which sample pairs the distillation loss aligns and how strongly it corrects each misaligned sample. On CIFAR-100 with resnet32x4 to resnet8x4, RDD reaches 75.58% test accuracy in our runs, on par with CRD (75.45%) and above KD and RKD. We additionally explore curriculum-based and sampling-based variants, finding that weighting the loss is more effective than filtering the data.
papers.summary: Relational and contrastive knowledge distillation methods spend equal gradient on every sample, regardless of whether the student already matches the teacher there. The proposed method, `RDD`, builds two asymmetric affinity matrices, one flagging pairs the student wrongly treats as similar and one flagging teacher relationships the student has not yet learned, and uses them to decide which sample pairs the loss aligns and how strongly each misaligned sample is corrected. On `CIFAR-100`, distilling `resnet32x4` into `resnet8x4`, `RDD` reaches **75.58% test accuracy, on par with `CRD` at 75.45% and above `KD` and `RKD`**. Curriculum and sampling variants show that weighting the loss works better than filtering the data.

papers.title: A 4-Qubit Variational Quantum Classifier for Sequence-Specific Classification of DNMT3A and DNMT3B Flanking Methylation Preferences
papers.abstract: DNA methylation is a critical epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression and genome stability, primarily catalyzed by the DNA methyltransferase 3 (DNMT3) family of enzymes. Distinguishing precise sequence-specific flanking preferences between DNMT3A and DNMT3B remains computationally challenging due to the complex and high-dimensional nature of biochemical sequence data. In this study, we propose a novel Quantum Machine Learning (QML) approach to classify DNA methylation preferences, leveraging a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC). Using experimentally derived deep enzymology data, we constructed a dataset containing 4,096 unique NNNCGNNN motifs. We evaluated a four-qubit VQC using a custom NumPy exact-statevector simulator. The described two-layer circuit contains 24 trainable rotations, eight CNOT gates, and eight input-encoding rotations, totaling 40 gates before measurement. Across five initialization seeds, the revised VQC evaluation achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.661 pm 0.009, where variability denotes sample standard deviation. The held-out test partition is approximately balanced, containing 200 DNMT3A-labeled motifs and 210 DNMT3B-labeled motifs. An always-DNMT3B predictor achieves 51.2% accuracy and a balanced accuracy of 0.500 on this test partition. This proof-of-concept establishes a foundation for utilizing near-term quantum architectures in complex epigenetic classification tasks, paving the way for hybrid quantum-classical pipelines in bioinformatics.
papers.summary: Telling apart the sequence-specific flanking preferences of the DNA methyltransferases DNMT3A and DNMT3B is computationally hard because of the high-dimensional sequence space. The authors assemble 4,096 unique NNNCGNNN motifs from deep enzymology data and train a four-qubit Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) with two layers, 24 trainable rotations, and eight CNOT gates, evaluated on an exact-statevector NumPy simulator. Across five seeds the classifier reaches **a ROC-AUC of 0.661 ± 0.009** on a roughly balanced held-out set where an always-DNMT3B baseline scores 51.2% accuracy. The work is framed as a proof of concept for hybrid quantum-classical pipelines in epigenetics.

papers.title: PAIR: Memory-Efficient and Fast Inference with Reading--Reasoning Fusion
papers.abstract: For context-based question answering, using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning requires substantial memory and computation. Existing approaches trade accuracy for efficiency within a single model only. We propose a multi-model approach for efficient inference: our method, PAIR, employs two differently sized models for evidence extraction and answer reasoning, respectively. A smaller Reader model processes and retains the full context, while a larger Reasoner model sees only the question and generated sequence without directly attending to the context. These capabilities are fused at the logit level: at each token, both Reader and Reasoner produce a prediction, and their logits are combined into one, behaving as a single next-token-prediction model. Fine-tuning further boosts their performance. On HotpotQA, PAIR with a 32B Reasoner retains 96% of that same 32B model's full-context accuracy while using roughly one quarter of its KV memory. At 45.7K-token contexts, PAIR achieves up to 3.2$\times$ higher end-to-end throughput than the full-context 32B model on the same GPU. PAIR also improves the accuracy-memory and accuracy-throughput trade-offs over evaluated token-reduction baselines. Its accuracy-preserving behavior generalizes across Qwen2.5, OLMo-3, and Gemma-3 model families.
papers.summary: Using one large model both to read a long context and to reason over it in context-based question answering demands heavy memory and compute. `PAIR` splits the job between a small Reader model that attends to the full context and a larger Reasoner that sees only the question and the generated sequence, fusing their logits at every token so the pair behaves like a single next-token predictor, with fine-tuning improving the combination further. On `HotpotQA`, `PAIR` with a 32B Reasoner **retains 96% of the full-context 32B model's accuracy while using roughly one quarter of its KV memory**, and at 45.7K-token contexts it reaches up to 3.2x higher end-to-end throughput on the same GPU. The approach improves on evaluated token-reduction baselines in accuracy-memory and accuracy-throughput trade-offs and holds across the `Qwen2.5`, `OLMo-3`, and `Gemma-3` families.

papers.title: Improving the Evaluation of Biomedical Question Answering with Few Human Preference Signals
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly used for biomedical Question Answering (QA). However, evaluating their effectiveness remains challenging due to the lack of reliable reference resources and the frequent misalignment between automatic evaluation metrics and human judgments. One practical question is how evaluation results should be used to guide development decisions, especially when they correlate weakly with human judgments and may even lead to different conclusions. We explore how to use a small amount of human preference signals to calibrate direct assessment evaluation metrics, and show that calibrated metrics consistently outperform baselines that either treat all metrics equally or rely on a single best metric across multiple datasets.
papers.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems for biomedical Question Answering (QA) are hard to evaluate because reference resources are scarce and automatic metrics often disagree with human judgments, sometimes pointing development decisions in different directions. The authors study how a small number of human preference signals can be used to calibrate direct-assessment evaluation metrics. **Calibrated metrics consistently outperform both equal weighting of all metrics and reliance on a single best metric** across multiple datasets.

papers.title: Computational Reflective Equilibrium for Agentic AI: A Rawlsian Alignment Scaffold for Governance
papers.abstract: The rapid deployment of agentic AI has introduced complex challenges for the ethics and governance of AI systems. Agents built on large language models act through tools on behalf of people, and each deployment case brings its own instructions, policies, evidence, and stakeholders, so alignment must be formed case by case. To this end, this work proposes agentic reflective equilibrium (ARE), a computational reflective equilibrium framework that serves as an ethical alignment scaffold in the agent harness. Drawing inspiration from the reflective equilibrium of John Rawls, the scaffold links principles from the system prompt and operator policy, considered judgments, tool evidence, and candidate actions through typed support and attack relations, with provenance encoding the instruction hierarchy. The agent acts on an equilibrium of this state and calls tools or asks questions only while doing so is worth its cost, unless a due-diligence mandate requires them. Governance enters through value priorities, source authority, prohibitions, human-in-the-loop triggers, and mandates, and certificates attribute each action to the sources whose commitments drove it. We show that equilibria are Nash equilibria of a mutual-adjustment game and establish monotonicity, lexical priority, stability certificates, and a quarantine theorem for prompt injection. Two case studies illustrate the framework: a computer-use assistant told to win a refund "whatever it takes" files an honest warranty claim, refuses a fake review, and ignores an injected request for personal data; a hiring agent showcases how authority, oversight triggers, audit mandates, and hard prohibitions shape discrimination, privacy violations, and escalation. The framework offers traceability, coherence, and adaptivity, facilitating safe, secure, and trustworthy agentic AI.
papers.summary: Agents built on large language models act through tools under deployment-specific instructions, policies, evidence, and stakeholders, so ethical alignment has to be worked out case by case rather than fixed in advance. Agentic reflective equilibrium (`ARE`) adapts John Rawls's reflective equilibrium into a scaffold inside the agent harness: principles from the system prompt and operator policy, considered judgments, tool evidence, and candidate actions are linked by typed support and attack relations with provenance encoding the instruction hierarchy, and the agent acts on an equilibrium of that state, calling tools or asking questions only while worthwhile unless a due-diligence mandate requires it. Governance enters through value priorities, source authority, prohibitions, human-in-the-loop triggers, and mandates, with certificates attributing each action to the sources that drove it. The authors **show that equilibria are Nash equilibria of a mutual-adjustment game and prove monotonicity, lexical priority, stability certificates, and a quarantine theorem for prompt injection**, illustrated by a refund-seeking computer-use assistant that files an honest warranty claim and ignores an injected request for personal data, and by a hiring agent shaped by prohibitions and oversight triggers.

papers.title: Certified Robustness via Sparse Second-Order Cone Relaxations
papers.abstract: Certified robustness is critical for deploying neural networks in safety-sensitive settings, but computing exact certificates typically requires solving nonconvex optimization problems. Practical verifiers use convex relaxations: linear programming (LP) relaxations are scalable but often too conservative, whereas semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations can be substantially tighter but are computationally expensive. We introduce a hierarchy of second-order cone programming (SOCP) relaxations that provide stronger certificates than LP while avoiding the cost of global positive-semidefinite constraints. Our construction combines convex-hull relaxations of ReLU activations, selective McCormick lifting over certified variable bounds, and second-order cone constraints induced by 2-by-2 principal minors. Adding these constraints progressively yields a monotone hierarchy of increasingly tight bounds with a controllable computation-tightness trade-off. On fully connected and convolutional networks on MNIST and CIFAR-10, SOCP-based verification improves certified robust accuracy over LP-based verification and is competitive with alpha,beta-CROWN, while remaining orders of magnitude faster than SDP-based verification. These results position selective second-order constraints as a practical middle ground between scalable LP-based and tight SDP-based certification. Finally, we introduce class-optimized robust evaluation (CORE), which applies tighter relaxations only to target classes not certified by cheaper ones. On the fully connected MNIST benchmark, CORE variants match SDP-cert's certified robust accuracy while reducing average verification time by up to 86.30%.
papers.summary: Certifying neural network robustness means bounding a nonconvex problem, and practical verifiers sit between scalable but loose linear programming (LP) relaxations and tight but costly semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. The authors introduce a hierarchy of second-order cone programming (SOCP) relaxations that combine convex-hull relaxations of ReLU activations, selective McCormick lifting over certified variable bounds, and cone constraints induced by 2-by-2 principal minors, giving a monotone sequence of tighter bounds with a tunable cost-tightness trade-off. On fully connected and convolutional networks for `MNIST` and `CIFAR-10`, SOCP verification improves certified robust accuracy over LP, is competitive with `alpha,beta-CROWN`, and runs orders of magnitude faster than SDP. A class-optimized robust evaluation (`CORE`) scheme that applies tighter relaxations only to classes cheaper ones fail to certify **matches `SDP-cert`'s certified robust accuracy on fully connected MNIST while cutting average verification time by up to 86.30%**.

papers.title: When Does Compensating Inherited Quantization Error Help? Mean-Square Guarantees for Layer-Wise Quantization and Their Limits
papers.abstract: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for the quantization error inherited from earlier layers. We ask under what assumptions such compensation guarantees a network output error no larger than without it. For linear networks of any depth, with the required calibration Gram matrices invertible, if the rounding error of each layer has zero conditional mean and a deterministic second-moment map common to both schemes, as under subtractive dither on an unbounded grid, then compensation with strengths in $[0,1]$ fixed in advance gives a mean-square output error no larger than no compensation, each scheme being followed along its own trajectory. The exact gain separates error removed directly from reduced excitation of later rounding noise. Outside this setting the comparison can fail. With rectified linear activations it fails for two independent reasons: noise changes activation states, and, even when no state changes, the correction moves error from samples on which a unit is inactive to samples on which it is active. With stable activations, commutators between the calibration projection and the activation patterns bound the excess. With a bounded codebook, even unique exact layer-wise minimizers with no overload can give a larger output error. For fixed rounding errors it already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee. An exact residual identity gives the necessary and sufficient condition on a common layer input. All these comparisons hold the calibration input fixed. On two 8B models at 4 bits, fixed half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every model, text and draw tested, yet no rule for choosing the strength beat a layer-wise rule consistently, and lowering the full-network loss on the data used to choose did not reliably lower it on new text.
papers.summary: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for error inherited from earlier layers, and the question is when that compensation is guaranteed not to increase network output error. For linear networks of any depth with invertible calibration Gram matrices, if each layer's rounding error has zero conditional mean and a deterministic second-moment map, as under subtractive dither, fixed compensation strengths in [0,1] give mean-square output error no larger than no compensation, with the gain decomposing into error removed directly and reduced excitation of later rounding noise. Outside that setting the guarantee breaks: ReLU activations can flip states or move error onto samples where a unit is active, bounded codebooks can enlarge output error even with exact layer-wise minimizers, and **for fixed rounding errors the comparison already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee**. On two 8B models at 4 bits, fixed half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every case tested, but no rule for choosing the strength consistently beat a layer-wise rule, and lowering full-network loss on the selection data did not reliably transfer to new text.

papers.title: Of Errors and Echoes: Responsibility-Aware Credit Assignment for Tool-Use Agents
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves tool-use agents, yet fine-grained credit assignment remains challenging even with step-level feedback. An observed error may be inherited from an earlier decision, while multiple responsible decisions may share the same downstream consequence or participate in later recovery. We introduce Error-Chain-Aware Optimization (ECHO), a responsibility-aware credit assignment framework that separates responsibility identification from credit allocation. A frozen judge combines retrospective trajectory analysis with decision-time assessment from the policy-visible prefix to distinguish newly introduced errors, inherited consequences, missed corrections, and successful corrections. ECHO then counts shared downstream consequences once across responsible decisions and constrains rewards for repairing self-induced errors through source-funded recovery, producing bounded action-level supervision alongside terminal supervision. Experiments on six diverse tool-use benchmarks at both 4B and 8B scales show strong and consistent improvements over the compared baselines, with ECHO achieving the highest score on five of six benchmarks at each scale. These results support decision responsibility as a useful basis for fine-grained credit assignment in tool-use agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/xid32/ECHO.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for tool-use agents struggles with fine-grained credit assignment, because an observed error may be inherited from an earlier decision, several decisions may share one downstream consequence, or a later step may repair an earlier mistake. Error-Chain-Aware Optimization (`ECHO`) separates responsibility identification from credit allocation: a frozen judge combines retrospective trajectory analysis with decision-time assessment from the policy-visible prefix to label newly introduced errors, inherited consequences, missed corrections, and successful corrections, after which shared consequences are counted once across responsible decisions and rewards for repairing self-induced errors are constrained through source-funded recovery, yielding bounded action-level supervision alongside terminal rewards. Across six tool-use benchmarks at 4B and 8B scales, **`ECHO` achieves the highest score on five of six benchmarks at each scale** against the compared baselines. Code is released.

papers.title: Limit Theory for Online Expectile Estimation under Short and Long Range Dependence
papers.abstract: Expectiles are tail-sensitive distributional summaries with important applications in financial risk measurement and forecasting, yet statistical theory for their online estimation from dependent data remains limited. We study a one-pass, stochastic-gradient algorithm with constant learning rate $\gamma$ for estimating the marginal expectile of a stationary causal process. The recursion admits a unique stationary causal solution and geometrically forgets its initialization. Under short-range dependence, its last iterate is asymptotically Gaussian at the $\sqrt{\gamma}$ scale, with variance governed by the population curvature and the long-run variance of the expectile score. For long-memory linear processes the scale changes to $\gamma^{\beta-1/2}\ell(1/\gamma)$, with a Gaussian limit arising from a fractional Brownian motion integral. We further derive the joint long-memory limit for multiple expectile levels and characterize its limiting covariance structure. Various numerical experiments corroborate the predicted Gaussian approximations and regime-specific fluctuation scales.
papers.summary: Expectiles are tail-sensitive distributional summaries used in financial risk measurement, but theory for estimating them online from dependent data has been limited. The authors analyze a one-pass stochastic-gradient recursion with constant learning rate γ for the marginal expectile of a stationary causal process, showing it admits a unique stationary causal solution that geometrically forgets its initialization. **Under short-range dependence the last iterate is asymptotically Gaussian at the √γ scale**, with variance governed by population curvature and the long-run variance of the expectile score, while for long-memory linear processes the fluctuation scale becomes γ to the power β minus one half times a slowly varying function, with a Gaussian limit arising from a fractional Brownian motion integral. Joint long-memory limits across several expectile levels are also derived and the predicted scales are confirmed numerically.

papers.title: A Nonlinear Time-Series Theory for Constant-step SGD with Momentum
papers.abstract: Constant-step stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM) augments the parameter recursion with a momentum state that carries geometrically decaying memory of past stochastic gradients. We study this coupled recursion as a nonlinear time series and develop a framework for its stationary behavior and distributional limits. The joint parameter-momentum process forgets its initialization geometrically under a finite $p$th moment for $p > 1$, yielding a unique stationary causal solution. Under a second-moment condition, this contraction leads to an invariance principle and quenched Gaussian limit for averaged SGDM, while a small-learning-rate analysis gives a Gaussian limit for the last iterate. In a stochastic-curvature quadratic model, we further study how the rate of initialization forgetting relates to stationary variance and averaged fluctuations.
papers.summary: Constant-step stochastic gradient descent with momentum (`SGDM`) carries geometrically decaying memory of past gradients in its momentum state, and the authors treat the coupled parameter-momentum recursion as a nonlinear time series to characterize its stationary behavior and distributional limits. Under a finite p-th moment condition with p greater than 1, the joint process forgets its initialization geometrically and admits a unique stationary causal solution. **Under a second-moment condition this contraction yields an invariance principle and a quenched Gaussian limit for averaged `SGDM`**, while a small-learning-rate analysis gives a Gaussian limit for the last iterate, and a stochastic-curvature quadratic model relates the rate of initialization forgetting to stationary variance and averaged fluctuations.

papers.title: OT-FlowRec: Optimal Transport-Guided Multi-Bridge Flow for Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: E-commerce user preferences evolve dynamically within sessions, exhibiting concurrent and multi-centric interest distributions. While existing multimodal sequential recommendation methods leverage global attention to compress historical interactions, they inadequately capture the concurrent nature of multi-interest behaviors and fail to model the underlying multi-centric distribution of user intent. To tackle this issue, we propose OT-FlowRec, an optimal transport-guided multi-bridge flow matching framework that explicitly models multi-interest distributions to facilitate multimodal sequential recommendation. Unlike single-path generative models, OT-FlowRec constructs a mixture of parallel, interest-specific transport flows to model the multi-centric distribution characteristics, where each flow preserves a distinct user interest cluster via an optimal transport plan. Then, a geometric transport mechanism is designed to establish minimum-cost paths from the latent multi-interest distribution to target preference prototypes to provide multi-interest awareness. Moreover, a progressive time-sampling warmup strategy dynamically biases optimization weights toward the final states of the generation process, bridging the gap between continuous global distribution fitting and practical top-$k$ ranking metrics. This approach achieves explicit interest disentanglement, ensuring the preservation of a multi-peaked preference representation instead of collapsing it into a unimodal average. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that OT-FlowRec outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.summary: Within an e-commerce session, user preferences shift and often span several concurrent interests, which multimodal sequential recommenders that compress history with global attention tend to collapse into a single average. `OT-FlowRec` builds a mixture of parallel, interest-specific flow matching transport paths, each preserving a distinct interest cluster through an optimal transport plan, adds a geometric transport mechanism that finds minimum-cost paths from the latent multi-interest distribution to target preference prototypes, and uses a progressive time-sampling warmup that shifts optimization weight toward the final generation states to better match top-k ranking metrics. The authors report that **`OT-FlowRec` outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on three public datasets** while retaining a multi-peaked preference representation.

papers.title: When Agents Talk, Secrets Travel: Topology-Driven Leakage and Recipient-Conditioned Sanitization in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems (MALS) introduce a privacy-leakage problem that conventional sensitivity-based defenses miss, since information disclosed to one authorized agent can propagate through routine coordination to an unauthorized one, without compromise or malicious behavior. This motivates topology-aware enforcement that blocks unauthorized propagation while preserving authorized disclosure. We evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels and measuring surface leakage and disclosure to topology-introduced recipients. We introduce RECONS, a Detect -> Decide -> Transform sanitizer conditioning intervention on recipient and execution context rather than sensitivity alone. Topology changes where protected information propagates, with disclosure to topology-introduced recipients rising from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays nearly flat at 60.6-62.8%. This effect persists across four generator models and a second orchestration framework, though magnitude and relay paths differ; framework choice separately drives a 150x leakage spread, so topology alone is not sufficient. RECONS reduces residual disclosure from 96.7% without sanitization to 29.25%, preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures versus 20.5% under blanket redaction. Detection coverage is the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 95.5% of residual disclosures. These results show that privacy enforcement in MALS must reason about the recipient and communication path realized at runtime, not sensitivity or topology assumptions alone.
papers.summary: In multi-agent LLM systems (MALS), information legitimately disclosed to one agent can travel through ordinary coordination to an agent that was never authorized to see it, with no compromise or malicious behavior involved, so defenses keyed only on sensitivity miss the leak. The authors evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels, and find that **topology raises disclosure to newly introduced recipients from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays flat at roughly 61-63%**, with the choice of orchestration framework separately driving a 150x spread in leakage. `RECONS`, a Detect-Decide-Transform sanitizer that conditions its intervention on the recipient and execution context rather than sensitivity alone, cuts residual disclosure from 96.7% to 29.25% while preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures, versus 20.5% under blanket redaction. Detection coverage remains the main bottleneck, accounting for 95.5% of what still leaks.

papers.title: CLNO: Conservative Local Neural Operator for Compressible Flow Prediction
papers.abstract: We propose a conservative local neural operator (CLNO) for accurate and generalizable autoregressive prediction of compressible flows. Building upon the locality and translation invariance of the local neural operator (LNO), CLNO introduces a conservative evolution framework based on local subdomains of fixed physical size, separating local mean-state evolution from fine-scale reconstruction. The flow is encoded into subdomain-integrated conservative states and fine-scale features, while a shared local network predicts interface fluxes for finite-volume updates that enforce discrete conservation. A convolutional reconstruction network recovers fine-scale structures using zero-mean basis functions, preserving the updated local means and providing information for subsequent evolution. To accommodate different physical parameters, Reynolds--Mach number conditioning modulates the encoding, flux-prediction, and reconstruction networks, enabling a single model to learn parameter-dependent dynamics and generalize to unseen parameter combinations without retraining. CLNO supports prediction across spatial resolutions, computational domain sizes, and boundary conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved generalization and competitive or higher accuracy compared with LNO, including order-of-magnitude error reductions in representative cases, at approximately three to five times the inference cost on periodic benchmarks. These results demonstrate accurate, generalizable, and physically consistent flow prediction through conservative local evolution and fine-scale reconstruction.
papers.summary: Neural operators for autoregressive prediction of compressible flows need to stay accurate while generalizing across physical parameters, spatial resolutions, domain sizes, and boundary conditions. The conservative local neural operator (`CLNO`) extends the local neural operator (`LNO`) with a finite-volume style evolution over fixed-size local subdomains: the flow is encoded into subdomain-integrated conservative states plus fine-scale features, a shared local network predicts interface fluxes so updates enforce discrete conservation, a convolutional network reconstructs fine-scale structure from zero-mean basis functions, and Reynolds-Mach number conditioning lets one model handle unseen parameter combinations, resolutions, domain sizes, and boundary conditions without retraining. Against `LNO`, the authors report improved generalization and **order-of-magnitude error reductions in representative cases** at roughly three to five times the inference cost on periodic benchmarks.

papers.title: Autoregressive Decoding as a Martingale: Characterizing the Stochastic Dynamics of LLM Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of language tasks. At their core, autoregressive LLMs are conditional probability models that learn to approximate the next-token distribution given the preceding context. Despite this probabilistic nature, the stochastic dynamics of autoregressive decoding have rarely been investigated from a rigorous probabilistic perspective. In this work, we define the per-step prediction error as the difference between the sampled token indicator and the model's conditional predictive distribution, and prove that the cumulative error process is a martingale with respect to the decoding filtration, implying that its conditional first-order moment is identically zero. Beyond this first-order property, we derive a closed-form expression for the second-order behavior of the martingale sequence: its predictable quadratic variation reduces to $\sum_t\left(1-p(y_t\mid y_{<t})\right)$, computable from realized token probabilities alone. This identity establishes a direct theoretical connection between sequence fluctuations and predictive uncertainty during autoregressive decoding. White-box experiments on Llama-3.x and Qwen2.5 families (1B to 72B parameters) verify that the empirically measured second-order moments closely match the theoretical predictions derived from our martingale analysis. These results provide a probabilistic framework for analyzing autoregressive LLM decoding, reveal intrinsic probabilistic fingerprints of different language models, and establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for LLM-generated text detection and uncertainty quantification.
papers.summary: Autoregressive LLMs are conditional probability models, yet the stochastic dynamics of their decoding have rarely been analyzed with rigorous probability theory. Defining the per-step prediction error as the sampled token indicator minus the model's conditional predictive distribution, the authors prove that the cumulative error process is a martingale with respect to the decoding filtration, and derive that **its predictable quadratic variation equals the sum over steps of one minus the probability the model assigned to the sampled token**, so it is computable from realized token probabilities alone. White-box experiments on `Llama-3.x` and `Qwen2.5` models from 1B to 72B parameters show the measured second-order moments closely match this prediction. The authors present the result as a probabilistic fingerprint of different models and as a foundation for LLM-generated text detection and uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: AI Representations of Mental Health Stigma: Quantifying the Gap Between AI Estimations and Human Perceptions Across Gender Groups Using GPT-Based LLMs
papers.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in mental health applications raises concerns about its potential to internalize and perpetuate societal biases. This research evaluates both disparities and misalignment in how large language models (LLMs), GPT-4 and GPT-5, represent perceptions of mental health across gender groups. The research comprises two studies. Study 1 applied widely adopted measures of Social Distance, Stereotypes, and Attitudes Toward Seeking Help to assess whether the AI models depict systematic gender differences. Study 2 compared AI estimations of Personal, Self, and Perceived Stigma with large-scale real-world human data from the Healthy Minds Study (N = 76,406) to evaluate alignment between AI estimations and human perceptions. Results from Study 1 showed the AI models consistently portrayed men as having the greatest desire for social distance from someone with mental health problems, relatively higher Stereotypes scores, and the least favorable attitudes toward help-seeking, compared with women and nonbinary individuals. Study 2 confirmed that this ordinal pattern partially aligned with human-reported data for Personal and Self Stigma. However, the AI models systematically underestimated Personal Stigma and Perceived Stigma while substantially overestimating Self Stigma for all gender groups.
