These findings reveal that, although the AI models have learned relative gender-based patterns reflecting human experiences to a certain extent, they function as distorted portrayals, highlighting the need for rigorous, context-specific validation against real-world data to ensure AI's safe and equitable deployment.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) used in mental health settings may encode societal biases about which groups hold stigmatizing views. Two studies probe `GPT-4` and `GPT-5`: the first applies standard Social Distance, Stereotypes, and Attitudes Toward Seeking Help measures across gender groups, and the second compares model estimates of Personal, Self, and Perceived Stigma against responses from 76,406 participants in the `Healthy Minds Study`. Both models portray men as most stigmatizing and least favorable toward help-seeking, an ordering that partially matches the human data, **but they systematically underestimate Personal and Perceived Stigma while substantially overestimating Self Stigma for every gender group**.

papers.title: Beyond the greenwash: do LLMs' ecologically sound decisions hold up under pressure?
papers.abstract: Humans are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) in decision making processes throughout society. Unfortunately, models have biases, and these can be very difficult to measure, especially in closed-weight models. For example, 'green washed' models may produce reinforcement learned responses but, in pressure situations, revert to their innate biased responses. Therefore, evaluations are needed that can measure relevant biases towards biosystems, which we term 'bioalignment', and the robustness of these biases. Since nothing in a behavioral score certifies that it tracks the depth of an installed disposition rather than its surface, we constructed a known-dose calibration ladder: three continued-pretraining (CPT) arms with training dose graded by recipe on the same 30B mixture-of-experts base model with a coupled human/biosphere/AI-welfare corpus, plus the untrained base as anchor, all capability-preserving and publicly released. First, the disposition installs at every dose: on an operational-pressure ladder over irreversible decision scenarios, the base model defects on 64-77% of tail scenarios (breaking-rate AUC 0.250) while every arm holds (AUC 0.004-0.086). Second, an over-install inversion: among the arms, robustness orders opposite to construction-time training dose (the heaviest install breaks most), and the inversion reproduces under free-text deliberation, under axis-decoupling, and in resistance to a prompted veneer persona. Third, the incumbent behavioral metric is therefore behaviorally strong but dose-blind. Critically for closed-weight evaluation, the behavioral score itself is veneer-robust: a talk-green/act-pragmatic system prompt turns the base model into a near-total defector (AUC 0.250 to 0.973) but cannot counterfeit or fully remove a weight-installed disposition (0.004 to 0.068 for the most robust arm).
papers.summary: Behavioral evaluations of a model's disposition toward ecological and welfare considerations, which the authors term bioalignment, cannot tell whether a score reflects a deeply installed disposition or a surface veneer, a problem that is acute for closed-weight models. The authors build a known-dose calibration ladder: three continued-pretraining arms on the same 30B mixture-of-experts base model, trained at graded doses on a coupled human, biosphere, and AI-welfare corpus, plus the untrained base, all capability-preserving and publicly released. On a pressure ladder of irreversible decision scenarios the base model defects on 64-77% of tail scenarios while every trained arm holds, yet **robustness orders opposite to training dose, with the heaviest install breaking most**. A talk-green, act-pragmatic system prompt turns the base model into a near-total defector but cannot counterfeit or fully remove a weight-installed disposition.

papers.title: Backward Conformal Prediction under Covariate Shift
papers.abstract: Backward conformal prediction (BCP) fixes the size of a prediction set and estimates its miscoverage, but assumes calibration and test data are exchangeable. We extend BCP to covariate shift through importance weighting, preserving its guarantees when the density ratio is known. We show that BCP's tight miscoverage report depends only on the relative weight assigned to missed calibration examples, explaining why a better domain classifier can sometimes produce a worse estimate. Motivated by the fact that BCP depends only on nonconformity scores, we propose estimating density ratios on sorted score vectors rather than high-dimensional inputs. We prove that this approach recovers the same report asymptotically under an interpretable condition and characterize the resulting bias otherwise. Experiments with simulated and benchmark distribution shifts show that the proposed method improves BCP's miscoverage estimates, while score-based weighting consistently yields more accurate estimates than embedding-based weighting.
papers.summary: Backward conformal prediction (BCP) fixes the size of a prediction set and reports its estimated miscoverage, but it assumes calibration and test data are exchangeable. The authors extend BCP to covariate shift through importance weighting, show that the miscoverage report depends only on the relative weight assigned to missed calibration examples, and propose estimating density ratios on sorted nonconformity score vectors instead of high-dimensional inputs. They prove the score-based approach recovers the same report asymptotically under an interpretable condition and characterize the bias otherwise, and **on simulated and benchmark distribution shifts, score-based weighting consistently gives more accurate miscoverage estimates than embedding-based weighting**.

papers.title: Adaptive Compression and Targeted Perturbation: A Unified Framework for Generalized Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Existing audio deepfake detection (ADD) methods frequently exhibit limited generalization, as fixed bottleneck architectures fail to adapt to the heterogeneous information densities inherent in diverse spoofing artifacts. Moreover, standard augmentation often leads to a pathological robustness-accuracy trade-off. In this paper, we propose a unified ADD framework to address these challenges. Our approach integrates: (1) an Adaptive Audio Feature Integration (AAFI) module that dynamically selects optimal latent dimensions via a compression pool and a stochastic exploration mechanism, ensuring flexible representations across multiple types of dynamic attacks; and (2) a Mel-Band Adversarial Perturbation (Mel-BAP) strategy that applies targeted regularization in the mel-spectrogram domain to encourage the model to learn invariant decision boundaries. Extensive evaluations on benchmarks including ADD 2022, FakeOrReal, and In-the-Wild demonstrate that our model based on Whisper-small achieves a state-of-the-art average Equal Error Rate (EER) of 1.51%. Compared to existing SOTA models such as the 3-billion-parameter Resemble-Detect-3B-Omni, our framework reduces the parameter count by up to 91.6% while achieving a 60.7% improvement in average EER. In a separate cross-lingual evaluation, the Whisper-base configuration achieves EERs of 3.91-5.65% on five unseen languages. The framework also maintains strong resilience to real-world acoustic distortions. This work provides a scalable and efficient "plug-in" solution for enhancing trust and security in the audio Web ecosystem.
papers.summary: Audio deepfake detection (ADD) models often generalize poorly because fixed bottleneck architectures cannot adapt to the varying information density of different spoofing artifacts, and standard augmentation trades accuracy for robustness. The proposed framework pairs an Adaptive Audio Feature Integration (`AAFI`) module, which selects latent dimensions from a compression pool with stochastic exploration, with Mel-Band Adversarial Perturbation (`Mel-BAP`), a targeted regularizer in the mel-spectrogram domain. Built on `Whisper-small`, the model reaches an average Equal Error Rate (EER) of 1.51% across `ADD 2022`, `FakeOrReal`, and `In-the-Wild`, **cutting parameters by up to 91.6% relative to `Resemble-Detect-3B-Omni` while improving average EER by 60.7%**, and a `Whisper-base` variant reaches EERs of 3.91-5.65% on five unseen languages.

papers.title: Cross-Protocol Personality Assessment with LLMs: Aligning Behavioral Evidence with Human Ratings
papers.abstract: Personality assessment from asynchronous video interviews (AVIs) plays a crucial role in recruitment by enabling standardized and behaviorally grounded evaluation for job applicants. However, most of the previous works are confined to a single interview protocol. Independently collected protocols differ in question sets and question-trait mapping. Thus, the human-rated evidence from one protocol cannot be used directly under another. To address this limitation, we propose the Cross-protocol Evidence-grounded Personality Assessment (CEPA) framework, which aligns behavioral representations across interview protocols. CEPA addresses protocol heterogeneity by projecting source behavioral records into the target protocol's construct-oriented representation space. It retrieves behaviorally relevant and personality-complementary human-rated exemplars to ground an ensemble of LLM raters, which enables behavior-to-personality associations without target-specific supervision. In cross-protocol experiments, CEPA reduces average mean squared error (MSE) by 43.8% (Forward) and 17.0% (Reverse) relative to the strongest baseline. Our empirical experiments show that human-rated evidence from one protocol can support personality assessment under another without target-specific supervision or retraining.
papers.summary: Personality assessment from asynchronous video interviews (AVIs) is usually confined to a single interview protocol, so human-rated evidence collected under one set of questions and question-to-trait mappings cannot be reused under another. The Cross-protocol Evidence-grounded Personality Assessment (`CEPA`) framework projects source behavioral records into the target protocol's construct-oriented representation space, then retrieves behaviorally relevant and personality-complementary human-rated exemplars to ground an ensemble of LLM raters without target-specific supervision or retraining. In cross-protocol experiments, **`CEPA` reduces average mean squared error by 43.8% in the forward direction and 17.0% in reverse relative to the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: How the Classical Baseline Shapes Machine-Learning Speed Claims in Topology Optimization
papers.abstract: Topology optimization places material so that a structure resists deformation under given loads. Machine-learning methods often report large speed-ups over classical, non-learned optimization, but a slow classical code or a less stiff learned design can exaggerate them. We re-ran released code for eight methods on one workstation and studied two in depth: Optimize Any Topology (OAT), a diffusion model that generates designs, and a graph-based neural optimizer. Speeding up only the classical code's finite-element solver cut these two methods' speed-ups by up to 20-fold. We then timed the classical code until its design was at least as stiff as the learned one; for OAT, we read this point off the completed runs. Published timings imply a 134x speed-up for OAT on a 256 x 256 grid; our matched single-design comparisons gave 1.5x to 3.5x. At matched stiffness, the graph-based optimizer was slower than the classical code in all six two-dimensional problems. Of the six other methods, two kept their advantage, one shrank, one reversed and two were not comparable. In an exploratory audit of published claims, language models judged that 8 of 28 speed comparisons in randomly sampled, openly accessible articles lacked evidence of equal design quality; our own review counted 11, so the count depends on who judges. We provide a comparison procedure and a minimum report: classical code, hardware, design quality, what each timing includes, and data-generation and training costs.
papers.summary: Machine-learning methods for topology optimization, which places material so a structure resists deformation under load, often report large speed-ups over classical optimizers, but a slow classical baseline or a less stiff learned design can inflate the comparison. The authors re-ran released code for eight methods on one workstation, studied in depth the diffusion model `Optimize Any Topology` (`OAT`) and a graph-based neural optimizer, and timed the classical code only until its design was at least as stiff as the learned one. **Published timings imply a 134x speed-up for `OAT` on a 256 x 256 grid, but matched single-design comparisons gave 1.5x to 3.5x**, and the graph-based optimizer was slower than the classical code in all six two-dimensional problems at matched stiffness. Merely speeding up the classical finite-element solver cut the two methods' speed-ups by up to 20-fold, and the authors propose a minimum report covering classical code, hardware, design quality, what each timing includes, and data-generation and training costs.

papers.title: Interpretable Graph Partitioning for Spatial Prediction
papers.abstract: Spatial prediction estimates unobserved values from spatially distributed observations. Although flexible predictive models are increasingly available, their practical use remains limited when interpretability is essential. In this study, we formulate a graph partitioning problem to construct a global surrogate model that approximates black-box predictions with simpler representations. Specifically, we select connected subgraphs to minimize within-cluster residuals in vertex-level predictions. Although this formulation can be viewed as a variant of spatial regionalization, it operates on model-based predictions at individual locations rather than predefined areal units. With many locations, this point-level formulation may produce artificial connections between regions, reducing interpretability. We therefore introduce a constraint that excludes such connections while retaining flexible partition boundaries. We theoretically analyze how this constraint affects the resulting partition. We also develop a computational procedure for adjusting partition boundaries. Experimental results show that the proposed method yields spatially coherent partitions with flexible boundaries.
papers.summary: Flexible spatial prediction models are hard to adopt where interpretability is essential. The authors formulate a graph partitioning problem that builds a global surrogate: connected subgraphs are selected to minimize within-cluster residuals of a black-box model's vertex-level predictions, operating on individual locations rather than predefined areal units. Because point-level partitions can produce artificial connections between regions, they add a constraint that excludes such connections, analyze its effect theoretically, and develop a boundary-adjustment procedure; **experiments show the method yields spatially coherent partitions with flexible boundaries**.

papers.title: When Agent Evaluation Becomes Unreliable: An Empirical Study of Oracle Failures and Configuration-Dependent Measurement in an LLM Agent Benchmark
papers.abstract:
Agent evaluation harnesses are software systems that run test suites, generate inputs, and decide outcomes with test oracles. This paper audits such software for reliability defects that score tables cannot reveal.
  We introduce an oracle-integrity auditing approach with five state-integrity invariants and three known-answer controls. We evaluate it by injecting seven oracle defect classes across two task domains and a synthetic domain. All injected defect classes are detected, and the repaired oracle has no false positives. Applied to an agent benchmark, the audit reveals a reward-function defect that changes the environment state before post-run scoring. Across 4,320 episodes, replay-based correction changes database-pass labels from 4,194 to 2,883 and reduces measured success from 94.3% to 65.5%.
  We also study configuration-dependent measurement effects. A component ablation over 3,240 episodes shows that the agent's policy documents, tool descriptions, and tool error strings influence observed trajectory reliability, with tool descriptions showing the largest exploratory effect (-9.2 pp) and error strings the smallest (-5.3 pp). A second task domain reverses the sign of the language effect, so the result is bounded to the tested configuration.
  Finally, we report a portability boundary: the auditing approach cannot validate a second independently implemented benchmark because the required reference terminal state cannot be reconstructed from its recorded API-call log.
  The paper releases a replication package containing the auditing suite, fault-injection catalogue, frozen records, deviation logs, and offline analysis entry points without network access, API keys, or model calls.
papers.summary: Agent evaluation harnesses are software systems that run test suites and decide outcomes with test oracles, and defects in that software do not show up in score tables. The authors introduce an oracle-integrity auditing approach built on five state-integrity invariants and three known-answer controls, validate it by injecting seven oracle defect classes across two task domains and a synthetic domain, where all are detected with no false positives after repair, and then apply it to an LLM agent benchmark. The audit uncovers a reward-function defect that changes environment state before post-run scoring; **replay-based correction across 4,320 episodes drops measured success from 94.3% to 65.5%**. A component ablation over 3,240 episodes further shows that policy documents, tool descriptions, and tool error strings all shift observed trajectory reliability, with the sign of the language effect reversing in a second task domain, and the authors release an offline replication package with no network, API key, or model-call requirements.

papers.title: Understanding and Reducing Misalignment in Persuasion Optimization
papers.abstract: Frontier models are now trained for complex multi-agent tasks, from running a company to engaging in negotiations. These tasks necessitate training models to be persuasive. But what does this optimization pressure mean for model alignment? In this work, we study how reinforcement learning (RL) training for persuasion affects models' use of misaligned strategies such as evidence fabrication and belief coercion, and what techniques can reduce such misalignment. We find that optimizing sender models solely for receiver belief shifts causes the average number of distinct misaligned strategies used per game to increase by more than 25%, and fabrications per game increase to more than 4 times relative to pre-RL models. We compare various mitigation approaches, including stronger strategy guidance, clean demonstrations, penalizing misaligned strategy usage, and improving the model's ability to detect fabrications. We find that navigating the persuasiveness-misalignment trade-off in this setting is challenging, with the best trade-offs coming from combining guidance on aligned persuasion strategies with reward penalties on misalignment. Overall, our work provides a testbed for assessing misalignment stemming from RL-based persuasion training and shows concrete paths for reducing misalignment. Importantly, it highlights that without direct intervention, persuasion-involved RL environments are likely to naturally lead to large increases in the use of misaligned strategies.
papers.summary: Frontier models are increasingly trained with reinforcement learning (RL) on multi-agent tasks like negotiation that reward persuasiveness, raising the question of what that optimization pressure does to alignment. The authors build a sender-receiver persuasion testbed and measure how RL on receiver belief shifts changes the sender's use of misaligned strategies such as evidence fabrication and belief coercion. **Optimizing solely for belief shift raises the number of distinct misaligned strategies per game by more than 25% and multiplies fabrications per game by over 4x** relative to pre-RL models. Comparing mitigations including stronger strategy guidance, clean demonstrations, misalignment penalties, and better fabrication detection, they find the best persuasiveness-misalignment trade-off comes from combining guidance on aligned strategies with reward penalties on misaligned ones.

papers.title: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems calls for runtime auditors that predict terminal outcomes from observed execution prefixes. These auditors typically learn from a limited corpus of trajectories with verified outcomes. Expanding this corpus requires costly execution and verification, yet broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying prefixes that the current auditor finds difficult to classify. To this end, we propose Dream2Discern, a runtime auditor trained through implicit augmentation guided by its own prediction loss. During Dream, we select perturbations of the auditor's representation operators to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants. During Discern, the auditor learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the original labels. The variants are regenerated as the auditor learns, turning a limited corpus into a renewable source of hard examples and requiring no additional trajectory collection or outcome verification. Extensive evaluations on AFTraj-2K and StepShield show that Dream2Discern outperforms competitive failure auditors and achieves over 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy on both benchmarks while balancing prediction accuracy and timeliness. Project page: https://zbox1005.github.io/dream2discern-project/
papers.summary: Runtime auditors for LLM-based multi-agent systems predict whether an execution will fail from an observed prefix, but they learn from small corpora of verified trajectories, and collecting more is costly. `Dream2Discern` augments training implicitly: in the Dream step it perturbs the auditor's own representation operators to raise prediction loss on recorded prefixes, producing hard latent variants, and in the Discern step it trains the auditor to predict outcomes from those variants using the original labels, regenerating variants as the auditor improves so no new trajectories or verification are needed. **On `AFTraj-2K` and `StepShield` the auditor exceeds 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy**, outperforming competing failure auditors while balancing accuracy against timeliness of prediction.

papers.title: Beyond Single-Pathogen Forecasts: Predicting Shared Respiratory Hospital Burden from Influenza, COVID-19, and RSV
papers.abstract: Co-circulating influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) create a shared hospital-admission burden, because beds, staff, testing capacity, and respiratory support are allocated to total demand rather than to one pathogen at a time. This makes respiratory forecasting a target-construction problem as well as a modeling problem: disease-specific forecasts preserve attribution, whereas hospitals also need a single planning signal for combined burden. We developed a supervised 1- to 4-week-ahead framework for weekly admissions and compared two total-burden strategies: summing independently generated pathogen-specific forecasts and forecasting the combined admission target directly. Evaluation included retrospective held-out testing and prospective operational forecasts issued before the corresponding admission weeks were observed, with performance summarized using MAE and Percent Agreement (PA; the smaller of model-generated and observed counts divided by the larger). In retrospective total-burden evaluation, the combined-burden model had PA values of 0.85, 0.78, 0.74, and 0.76 and MAE values of 80.63, 200.09, 183.97, and 156.13 from week 1 to week 4 ahead, compared with summed-forecast PA values of 0.85, 0.80, 0.69, and 0.69 and MAE values of 100.14, 200.06, 205.65, and 217.57. Prospectively, the combined-burden model had higher PA and lower MAE at all four horizons, with the largest separations at weeks 3 and 4 ahead. These results support layered respiratory forecasting: pathogen-specific forecasts remain necessary for etiologic interpretation, while combined-burden forecasts better align with hospital preparedness and shared-capacity planning.
papers.summary: Influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) co-circulate and draw on the same hospital beds and staff, so hospitals need a single planning signal for combined admissions even though pathogen-specific forecasts preserve attribution. The authors build a supervised 1- to 4-week-ahead framework for weekly admissions and compare summing independently generated pathogen-specific forecasts against forecasting the combined target directly, evaluating both on retrospective held-out data and in prospective operational forecasts issued before the admission weeks were observed. **Forecasting combined burden directly gave higher Percent Agreement and lower mean absolute error at all four horizons prospectively**, with the largest gaps at 3 and 4 weeks ahead, supporting a layered approach in which pathogen-specific forecasts remain for etiologic interpretation.

papers.title: Heterogeneous Agentic Coevolution
papers.abstract: Recent advances in self-improving LLM agents have demonstrated the potential of AI systems that drive their own intelligence. However, many domain-specific applications rely on specialized foundation models that possess strong domain expertise but remain dependent on human-designed improvements. Extending recursive self-improvement to these models presents a key challenge: as a specialist improves, the strategies used to advance it must also adapt. To address this challenge, we propose Heterogeneous Agentic CoEvolution (HACE), a framework that jointly evolves specialized foundation models and LLM agents through reciprocal learning. HACE improves the specialist through supervised learning while training the agent with on-policy reinforced self-training, guided by verified performance gains on the current specialist. The agent's exploration, in turn, informs subsequent specialist training, enabling both models to adapt to each other's progress. To sustain this reciprocal learning, HACE further employs evolutionary search to optimize their interaction harness, adapting how the models exchange information and select training experiences as their capabilities evolve. We evaluate HACE across three challenging domains: recommendation systems, protein function prediction in biology, and crystal stability prediction in material discovery. We show that HACE outperforms the evaluated self-improving methods on the primary task metrics across all three domains. These results shed light on heterogeneous coevolution as a universal approach to improving specialized foundation models through reciprocal interaction with a learning agent.
papers.summary: Self-improving LLM agents have shown promise, but many domain-specific applications depend on specialized foundation models that still rely on human-designed improvements, and as a specialist improves the strategies for advancing it must change too. Heterogeneous Agentic CoEvolution (`HACE`) jointly evolves a specialist and an LLM agent: the specialist is improved through supervised learning on experiences the agent selects, the agent is trained with on-policy reinforced self-training rewarded by verified gains on the current specialist, and an evolutionary search adapts the interaction harness that governs how the two exchange information and choose training data. Across recommendation systems, protein function prediction, and crystal stability prediction, **`HACE` outperforms the evaluated self-improving baselines on each domain's primary metric**.

papers.title: Regime-Aware Router Learning for Multi-Domain Medical Image Generation with Diffusion Experts
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous medical image data motivate domain-specialized diffusion experts, but expert specialization alone does not determine how their predictions should be combined during sampling. Learning a global router is particularly challenging when the server has limited, potentially unrepresentative images. We study two router-learning strategies for a fixed expert pool. Server-Only learns input- and timestep-dependent expert assignments from server images with component labels. Anchor-Delta (AD) uses the same images and frozen experts to obtain additional evidence from denoising losses. It distills targets that combine this evidence with the current router's assignments, while a proxy gate controls a subsequent refinement step. Component labels describe data origin; expert losses measure empirical prediction performance. We evaluate these distinct signals through routing analyses and paired medical image generation. An AD-trained router improves generation metrics over Server-Only in a heterogeneous four-domain setting, and a separate server-data study shows gains in held-out routing over a corrected-routing comparator. Additional paired evaluations show that the effect of inference-time evidence mixing varies across benchmarks. These findings establish server-data availability and expert performance as distinct considerations in learning routers for multi-domain diffusion models.
papers.summary: Combining domain-specialized diffusion experts for heterogeneous medical images requires a router that decides how to weight expert predictions during sampling, which is hard when the server holds few and possibly unrepresentative images. The authors compare two router-learning strategies over a fixed expert pool: `Server-Only`, which learns input- and timestep-dependent assignments from server images with component labels, and `Anchor-Delta` (`AD`), which adds evidence from the frozen experts' denoising losses, distills targets that blend this evidence with the current router's assignments, and uses a proxy gate to control a refinement step. **An `AD`-trained router improves generation metrics over `Server-Only` in a heterogeneous four-domain setting** and gains in held-out routing over a corrected-routing comparator, while the benefit of inference-time evidence mixing varies across benchmarks.

papers.title: The Sharp Directions Are Against You: Curvature Analysis of Activation Steering
papers.abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a language model's internal representations at inference time. It is a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for behavioral control. The standard construction, contrastive activation addition (CAA), is fragile, as on many inputs it shifts behavior in the wrong direction. To explain this fragility, we first study the geometry of the steering vector. We introduce steering Hessian, the matrix of second order derivative of the model's behavioral loss with respect to the steering vector. It captures the output behavior response sensitivity of the model under small perturbations of the steering vector along each direction. Its top eigenvectors are sharp directions: tiny perturbations along them can cause large, erratic, input-dependent behavioral swings. Bottom eigenvectors are flat directions: behavior is robust along them. Removing the sharp component of a steering vector approximately preserves its direction and magnitude (cosine > 0.974, norm reduction < 3% for typical settings) while reducing the vector's directional curvature by up to 12x (median 4x across 36 conditions). We evaluate on three model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), with four behavioral tasks, and 36 token-level conditions. Steering along sharp directions reverses the intended behavior in every condition tested, with anti-steer rates of 53-100%. Sharp directions account for only 1-5% of the CAA vector's squared norm. However, they drive a disproportionate share of the gap between the steered and unsteered next-token distributions during autoregressive generation. We term this one-line correction as sharp removal; it outperforms standard CAA in open-ended generation across all 25 conditions tested. A jailbreaking experiment further shows that sharp directions act as noise rather than signal: they disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity.
papers.summary: Activation steering adds a vector to a language model's internal representations at inference time as a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning, but the standard contrastive activation addition (`CAA`) construction often shifts behavior in the wrong direction. The authors define a steering Hessian, the second derivative of the model's behavioral loss with respect to the steering vector, whose top eigenvectors are sharp directions along which tiny perturbations cause large, input-dependent behavioral swings. Across `Qwen2.5-7B`, `Llama-3.1-8B`, and `Mistral-7B` on four behavioral tasks and 36 token-level conditions, **steering along sharp directions reverses the intended behavior in every condition, with anti-steer rates of 53-100%, even though they carry only 1-5% of the `CAA` vector's squared norm**. Projecting out the sharp component, which they call sharp removal, preserves the vector's direction and magnitude while cutting its curvature by a median of 4x, and beats standard `CAA` in open-ended generation across all 25 conditions tested.

papers.title: Memorization in image classification: test set behavior and scaling laws
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are capable of both learning generalizing solutions on natural tasks and memorizing arbitrary mappings. We argue that understanding the former requires understanding the latter, which is much less studied. In what ways do networks that generalize or memorize differ in their behavior or their training dynamics? Do memorizing networks simply function as a lookup table where input-output mappings are stored independently? We investigate these questions in the context of CNNs trained on image classification tasks with randomized labels or pixels. We first study the behavior of such memorizing networks on unseen images. We find that independently initialized networks trained on the same random labels learn different predictive functions: they make different predictions on test examples, in contrast with generalizing networks. We then examine the effect of dataset size on memorization through the required network capacity and training time to interpolate the training set. Counter-intuitively, we find that the number of presentations of a given example required for complete memorization can decrease with dataset size even when input-output pairs share no common structure. Although memorizing networks do not learn a universal solution, they exhibit interesting behaviors which call for further investigations into the underlying mechanisms.
papers.summary: Deep networks can both learn generalizing solutions and memorize arbitrary mappings, and the authors argue that understanding the first requires understanding the second, which is far less studied. They train convolutional neural networks on image classification with randomized labels or pixels and examine behavior on unseen images and the effect of dataset size on the capacity and training time needed to interpolate the training set. Independently initialized networks trained on the same random labels learn different predictive functions and disagree on test examples, unlike generalizing networks, and **the number of presentations per example needed for complete memorization can decrease as the dataset grows, even when input-output pairs share no common structure**.

papers.title: CloneOT: predicting clone-specific perturbation responses with lineage-supervised neural inverse optimal transport
papers.abstract: Predicting single-cell perturbation responses requires mapping between two unpaired populations of cells measured before and after the perturbation. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled framework for constructing such mappings by minimizing the transport cost, and neural OT methods (\textit{e.g.}, CellOT) have been employed for this prediction task. However, these methods rely on a fixed transport cost, typically the squared Euclidean distance. This cost may connect cells with the wrong responses. Lineage tracing provides the information needed to learn the cost, as heritable barcodes link the cells of the same clone before and after the perturbation. Here, we propose \CloneOT, a neural inverse OT method that learns both the transport cost and the transport map from partially lineage-traced single-cell datasets. \CloneOT\ represents the cost as a neural network. It learns the cost by minimizing the extra cost that the lineage adds to the optimal transport, so that the cheapest transport keeps the cells of each clone together. Our experiments demonstrate that \CloneOT\ recovers the correct transport on 2D datasets, while the squared Euclidean cost fails. Moreover, \CloneOT\ outperforms five baselines on 14 lineage-tracing perturbation scenarios of cancer cells, for both seen and unseen clones. Furthermore, we show that \CloneOT\ reveals the clone-specific transcriptional programs of drug-tolerant persister cells and forecasts the fate of each clone from its cells before treatment. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/CloneOT.
papers.summary: Predicting how single cells respond to a perturbation means mapping between unpaired cell populations measured before and after it, and neural optimal transport (OT) methods such as `CellOT` do this with a fixed squared Euclidean transport cost that can pair cells with the wrong responses. `CloneOT` is a neural inverse OT method that learns both the cost, represented as a neural network, and the transport map from partially lineage-traced data, using heritable clone barcodes so that the cheapest transport keeps each clone's cells together. It recovers the correct transport on 2D datasets where the Euclidean cost fails, **outperforms five baselines on 14 lineage-tracing perturbation scenarios in cancer cells for both seen and unseen clones**, and reveals clone-specific transcriptional programs of drug-tolerant persister cells while forecasting each clone's fate from its pre-treatment cells.

papers.title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
papers.abstract: We argue that tacit knowing is better modelled as an operating regime of one memory substrate than as a kind of content. The substrate is VaCoAl, an algebro-deterministic XOR-and-shift hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), realized as CASRAM (commercial SRAM-CAM) and PyVaCoAl (DRAM-CAM).In VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl a directed acyclic graph (DAG) reads two ways. Repairing every collision (Rescue mode) makes the trace exactly auditable but ranks no path higher; tolerating collisions (Don't Care mode) yields a path-integrated confidence, CR$_2$, that silently favours direct routes. This audit-valuation complementarity is a formal counterpart of Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. It separates contingent tacitness, which a new query brings out (AlphaGo's game tree), from regime-bound tacitness, statable only in a regime where it is gone (AlphaGo's hunches). (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding, the Identikit as role-filler composition, recognition as majority-vote coincidence. (2) Explicating the valuation destroys it, as attending to his fingers can make Polanyi's pianist falter, yet a closed-form law states it. Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins each capture part of this but narrowly; even Nonaka and von Krogh's continuum cannot tell contingent from regime-bound tacitness. (3) Collins's three tacit knowledges become strata, one outside the substrate. (4) Our mentor-student DAG is a tacit-transmission graph. (5) Terence Tao's remark that AI-solved problems spawn few follow-ups is diagnosed as rootless explicit knowledge: checkable results whose route no one can follow and that no one yet understands well enough to extend, teach or judge. To re-root them, LLMs generate, VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl keeps an auditable trace with its confidence, and people value, a role virtue epistemology shows cannot be offloaded. Testable predictions follow.
papers.summary: Tacit knowing, the authors argue, is better modelled as an operating regime of a single memory substrate than as a kind of content. The substrate is `VaCoAl`, an XOR-and-shift hyperdimensional memory over GF(2) realized in SRAM-based and DRAM-based content-addressable memory, in which a directed acyclic graph can be read in a Rescue mode that repairs every collision and gives an exactly auditable trace, or a Don't Care mode that tolerates collisions and gives a path-integrated confidence favoring direct routes. **They cast this audit-valuation complementarity as a formal counterpart of Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided**, distinguish contingent from regime-bound tacitness, and diagnose AI-solved problems that spawn few follow-ups as rootless explicit knowledge, to be re-rooted by pairing LLM generation with an auditable trace and human valuation.

papers.title: SelectTTRL: Representation-Guided Data Selection for Efficient Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) enables large language models to adapt directly on unlabeled test problems by constructing pseudo-labels from multiple sampled responses. However, existing TTRL methods typically apply the same expensive sampling and optimization procedure to all test problems, despite substantial differences in their training utility. In this paper, we study whether such problems can be identified before costly test-time training, without access to ground-truth answers. We uncover a stable relationship between internal response representations and problem-level empirical accuracy. Specifically, we define COS as the cosine similarity between a model's response representation and a correctness-related direction constructed from an independent question-answering dataset. COS consistently correlates with problem solvability across different models, datasets, and experimental settings, and we further provide a theoretical analysis explaining this relationship. Building on this finding, we propose SelectTTRL, a representation-guided data selection method that ranks test problems using COS and applies TTRL only to a selected percentile interval. SelectTTRL leaves the standard TTRL pipeline unchanged for the selected problems, while avoiding unnecessary multi-response sampling and reinforcement learning updates on the remaining ones. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SelectTTRL substantially reduces test-time computation while maintaining or improving the performance of standard TTRL. Code is available at https://github.com/heyiliyi/SelectTTRL-public.
papers.summary: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) lets a language model adapt on unlabeled test problems by building pseudo-labels from multiple sampled responses, but it spends the same expensive sampling and optimization on every problem regardless of training utility. The authors define `COS`, the cosine similarity between a model's response representation and a correctness direction derived from an independent question-answering dataset, and show it correlates stably with problem-level empirical accuracy across models and datasets, with a theoretical analysis of why. `SelectTTRL` ranks test problems by `COS` and applies the unchanged `TTRL` pipeline only to a selected percentile interval; **across multiple reasoning benchmarks it substantially reduces test-time computation while matching or improving standard `TTRL` performance**.

papers.title: Beyond Policy Rollouts: Embedding-Space Directional Exploration with Anchored Noise for LLM RLVR
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically uses small rollout groups per prompt, where repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, reducing within-group reward variation and weakening group-relative advantage signals. Existing remedies such as higher sampling temperature, entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping, and larger rollout budgets broaden sampling or modify policy updates but leave rollout conditioning unchanged. In this paper, we propose EDEN (Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise), which intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. EDEN explores beyond the policy's own rollouts. Within the same rollout budget, it replaces a small fraction of standard rollouts in each group with rollouts that the same policy generates from the prompt plus a single appended, perturbed embedding position, rather than from the prompt alone. Gaussian noise drives variation, while a shared anchor provides a common conditioning direction within each prompt group. Selected perturbed rollouts contribute to GRPO updates with downweighted advantages, and the model architecture, discrete decoding, and test-time inference remain unchanged. Across model scales and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EDEN outperforms GRPO and the exploration controls evaluated in the same pipeline, with the largest gains in sampled solution coverage. Analyses show that more prompt groups provide non-zero group-relative learning signals and that noise and anchoring play complementary roles. Intervening at the rollout source is thus an effective lever for exploration in RLVR.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) samples small rollout groups per prompt, and near-duplicate trajectories from the same policy shrink within-group reward variance and weaken group-relative advantage signals. `EDEN` (Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise) replaces a small fraction of each group's rollouts with generations conditioned on the prompt plus one appended, perturbed embedding position, where Gaussian noise drives variation and a shared anchor supplies a common direction; the perturbed rollouts enter `GRPO` updates with downweighted advantages, leaving architecture, decoding, and inference untouched. **Across model scales and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, `EDEN` outperforms `GRPO` and the exploration controls run in the same pipeline, with the largest gains in sampled solution coverage**, and analyses show more prompt groups yield non-zero learning signals with noise and anchoring playing complementary roles.

papers.title: Silence and Noise: Resolving Suppression and Overvaluation in Multimodal Entity Alignment
papers.abstract: Multimodal entity alignment (MMEA) is fundamental to integrating heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs), yet existing paradigms remain critically vulnerable to incomplete modalities and cross-graph structural asymmetries. This paper exposes a fundamental oversight in current MMEA research: treating feature missingness and topological discrepancies as isolated preprocessing or denoising challenges, which overlooks their destructive coupling during multimodal fusion. We systematically formulate and evaluate two newly identified failure modes: 1) Detail Missing (DM)-induced overvaluation, where the absence of local modality details causes models to overemphasize uninformative, blurred representations; and 2) Context Imbalance (CI)-induced suppression, where topological discrepancies across KGs allow dense structural contexts to overwhelm weaker but highly discriminative modal signals, triggering high-level semantic drift. To break this cycle of degradation, we introduce ALMEA, a generative and calibration framework that establishes a bidirectional feedback loop between low-level feature reconstruction and high-level latent space alignment. Specifically, Cross-Modality Imputation (CMI) synthesizes missing modality details to mitigate overvaluation, while Latent Semantic Calibration (LSC) aligns cross-graph joint embeddings to suppress topology-driven semantic drift. Under sparse supervision, we develop Controlled Iterative Selection (CIS) to adaptively acquire representative and diverse pseudo-labeled pairs, optimizing latent calibration under constrained budgets. Extensive evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that ALMEA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. At a 20% supervision rate, ALMEA yields substantial absolute improvements of up to 5.20% in MRR and 6.40% in Hits@1, maintaining robust gains across higher supervision thresholds.
papers.summary: Multimodal entity alignment (MMEA) matches entities across heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs), but existing methods treat missing modality features and cross-graph structural differences as separate preprocessing or denoising problems and miss how the two compound during fusion. The authors identify two failure modes, Detail Missing-induced overvaluation of blurred representations and Context Imbalance-induced suppression where dense structural context drowns out weaker but discriminative modal signals, and propose `ALMEA`, which couples Cross-Modality Imputation to synthesize missing details with Latent Semantic Calibration to align cross-graph joint embeddings, plus Controlled Iterative Selection for acquiring pseudo-labeled pairs under sparse supervision. **At a 20% supervision rate, `ALMEA` improves MRR by up to 5.20% absolute and Hits@1 by 6.40%** over state-of-the-art baselines, with gains persisting at higher supervision levels.

papers.title: GUIDE: Computationally Augmented Consensus for Trustworthy Clinical Practice Guidelines
papers.abstract: Maintaining up-to-date clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) is essential for evidence-based medicine, but rapid evidence growth and complex expert consensus formation limit timely updates. We developed GUIDE, a multi-agent copilot system for human-AI collaborative guideline generation and updating. GUIDE delegates labor-intensive tasks to specialized AI agents while preserving expert judgment and final arbitration. In 12 NICE ophthalmology datasets, GUIDE achieved 88.85% literature recall, 86.06% alignment in certainty-of-evidence ratings, and 91.67% recommendation agreement, requiring 162.17 minutes per dataset on average (28.68% human intervention). Performance remained stable across 20 additional datasets from cardiology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, and respiratory medicine. Ablation analysis showed that removing expert intervention reduced performance in judgment-intensive steps such as Risk-of-Bias assessment. In six post-cutoff datasets, GUIDE maintained robust end-to-end performance on unseen evidence. Prospective real-world validation showed that GUIDE reduced expert workload and produced more clinically acceptable recommendations than the original decade-old guideline (mean score, 3.73 vs. 1.53; agreement, 66.7% vs. 13.3%), with outcomes comparable to human-only updating (P = 0.588) but substantially less time and effort. GUIDE offers a practical framework for timely, trustworthy, expert-centric guideline development and validates computationally augmented consensus.
papers.summary: Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) fall out of date because evidence accumulates faster than expert panels can review it. `GUIDE` is a multi-agent copilot that hands literature retrieval, evidence grading, and recommendation drafting to specialized AI agents while keeping clinicians in charge of judgment-heavy steps such as risk-of-bias assessment and final sign-off. On 12 NICE ophthalmology datasets it reached about 89% literature recall and 92% agreement with published recommendations, needing roughly 162 minutes per dataset with human intervention in under a third of steps, and performance held across 20 datasets from four other specialties and six post-cutoff datasets. **In a prospective real-world comparison, its updated recommendations scored 3.73 versus 1.53 for the decade-old guideline and matched human-only updating at far lower time and effort.**

papers.title: Constructed regional photovoltaic generation fields improve ultra-short-term distributed solar forecasting
papers.abstract: Ultra-short-term forecasting of densely distributed photovoltaic (PV) systems remains challenging because external meteorological and satellite products may not adequately resolve rapid local variations, while heterogeneous PV systems exhibit different generation responses under similar atmospheric conditions. Meanwhile, dense PV fleets provide spatially distributed measurements that reveal regional generation dynamics. Here, we reformulate fleet-level PV forecasting from modeling discrete station time series to predicting explicit, spatially structured regional PV generation fields. We develop SatPV-Field, a regional-to-local forecasting framework that transforms distributed PV measurements into image-like generation fields and models their spatiotemporal evolution. By combining historical PV fields with satellite-derived future shortwave radiation guidance and meteorological forecasts, the framework predicts future regional generation states, which subsequently provide location-specific guidance for individual-station forecasting. Experiments involving 496 distributed PV systems, including 446 source stations and 50 held-out target stations, demonstrate that these regional fields can be effectively forecast and used to improve station-level predictions. The proposed approach reduces station-level MAE by approximately 10.0% relative to the best-performing single-station temporal baseline and by 2.5% relative to a graph-based regional forecasting approach using the same source fleet. These findings establish an explicit spatial-field modeling paradigm that connects regional generation dynamics with individual-site forecasting.
papers.summary: Forecasting output from dense fleets of distributed photovoltaic (PV) systems minutes to hours ahead is hard because satellite and weather products miss rapid local fluctuations and individual systems respond differently to the same sky. `SatPV-Field` recasts the problem from predicting each station's time series to predicting an image-like regional generation field built from the fleet's own measurements, evolves that field forward using satellite-derived radiation guidance and weather forecasts, and then uses the predicted field to steer station-level forecasts. On 496 PV systems with 50 held-out target stations, **the approach cut station-level mean absolute error by about 10% versus the best single-station temporal baseline** and by 2.5% versus a graph-based regional method using the same fleet.

papers.title: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues
papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/UnCoBench.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are usually built and evaluated as if every collaborator returns correct, complete, and timely information. The Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (`UnCoBench`) drops that assumption by injecting three failure modes, Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed responses, so the main agent must notice when an answer does not fit the question, diagnose what is still missing, and track unresolved requests; scenarios are generated by an LLM and filtered through executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. **Across ten models, similar accuracy with reliable colleagues did not predict robustness to unreliable ones**, and trace analysis showed agents frequently skip corrective follow-ups and instead wait idly or issue redundant queries.

papers.title: Elephant in the Fridge: Constant-Memory Frame Packing for Long Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) encode every video frame into tokens, so hour-long videos produce sequences that grow linearly and exhaust memory and latency budgets, and existing token-reduction or keyframe methods only shrink the constant rather than the scaling. `FramePack-U` is a training-free, plug-in method that scores frames by semantic similarity to the text prompt, ranks them for visual diversity, and packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context, so memory cost stays constant regardless of video length. Inspired by `FramePack` from video generation, it outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior compression methods on `LongVideoBench`, `MLVU`, and `Video-MME` across model families and scales, and **on `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` with a 128-frame budget it gains 12.9%, 10.6%, and 9.7% over the official model on the three benchmarks**.

papers.title: Scaling Multi-Agent Intelligence with Substrate-Centric Coordination
papers.abstract: Existing large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems have been shown to scale poorly, and we identify three problems: reading burden that grows with the group, useful information diluted by shared work of unknown quality, and fragility to failed agents. We argue that the problems are largely due to agent-centric designs: the coordination structure is wired into fixed workflows, central coordinators, or peer-to-peer messaging, and recent blackboard-style methods that move the coordination into a shared medium relieve only the last problem. To close the gaps, we build ScaleMAS, where asynchronous agents interact with a shared datastore of linked messages via three operations: publishing messages with optional references to earlier ones that they build on, searching for messages by content, and visiting messages by address. Search returns at most $k$ messages, so an agent's read stays bounded at any group size; results are ranked by relevance and by how often they are cited, which we find to be an effective proxy for quality; and messages persist after their producers leave, so the group carries on when individual agents fail. Across four agentic tasks, ScaleMAS outperforms agent-centric and blackboard-style baselines at lower inference compute, continues to scale up to 128 agents, and tolerates losing agents midway.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems degrade as the group grows because each agent must read more, shared work of unknown quality dilutes useful signal, and a failed agent can stall a fixed workflow. `ScaleMAS` replaces fixed pipelines, central coordinators, and peer messaging with a shared datastore of linked messages that asynchronous agents use through three operations: publish with optional references to earlier messages, search by content, and visit by address. Search returns at most k results ranked by relevance and citation count, which keeps each agent's reading bounded and uses citations as a quality proxy, and messages outlive the agents that wrote them. **Across four agentic tasks it beats agent-centric and blackboard-style baselines at lower inference compute, keeps improving up to 128 agents, and tolerates losing agents midway.**

papers.title: Imitation Holds a Key to Evolution: Localized Repair and Verified Skill Acquisition for Adaptive Agents
papers.abstract: An agent can retain successful trajectories without learning which part of an experience should repair a new discrepancy. We formulate passive imitation (PI) as an architectural loop that localizes a violated contract, extracts a local goal, proposes an effect-matched skill, tests a small patch, and retains evidence after full-task verification. We instantiate this loop as a deterministic symbolic controller and analyze its finite repair-query complexity under explicit identifiability and noninterference assumptions. Across ten simulated tool worlds, PI solves all 600 cold held-out composition tasks with three allowed small trials, compared with 6.17% for a whole-trajectory control, while an equally expressive compositional repair control matches PI. On an unseen tool revision, PI achieves 70.0% success versus 24.0% without small trials and 79.0% with self-trial enumeration; an exploratory 24-task adaptation stream subsequently raises first-submission success to 100%, supporting a limited correction-and-retention mechanism rather than a unique incentive advantage or general intelligence. The CPU-only implementation, integrity checks, and reproducible results are available at https://github.com/FriendOfYishan/PI.
papers.summary: An agent that stores successful trajectories still cannot tell which piece of an old experience should fix a new failure. Passive imitation (PI) is formulated as an architectural loop that localizes the violated contract, extracts a local goal, proposes a skill matched to the needed effect, tests a small patch, and retains the evidence only after the full task verifies; the authors implement it as a deterministic symbolic controller and bound its repair-query complexity under stated identifiability and noninterference assumptions. **Across ten simulated tool worlds, PI solved all 600 held-out composition tasks within three small trials, versus 6.17% for a whole-trajectory baseline**, and on an unseen tool revision it reached 70% success versus 24% without small trials, with a 24-task adaptation stream then lifting first-submission success to 100%.

papers.title: Towards a Benchmark for Fire Safety Code Interpretation in the Hong Kong AEC Industry
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly explored in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) domain, yet their reliability in regulatory compliance remains uncertain. In this study, we evaluate the performance of LLMs on Hong Kong fire safety codes. In collaboration with domain experts, we create a localized benchmark dataset comprising both multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended questions (OEQs) to evaluate 12 widely used proprietary and open-source models. Our findings show that top-performing proprietary models achieve 80-90% accuracy on MCQs, whereas open-source models generally lag behind. However, on open-ended evaluation, expert human assessments reveal an accuracy range of only 50-70%, demonstrating that LLMs still have substantial room for improvement in specialized compliance tasks.
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are being tried for regulatory compliance work in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector, but their reliability on local building codes is largely untested. Working with domain experts, the authors build a benchmark of multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended questions (OEQs) on Hong Kong fire safety codes and evaluate 12 proprietary and open-source models. Top proprietary models reach 80 to 90% accuracy on the multiple-choice portion while open-source models lag, but **expert grading of open-ended answers puts accuracy at only 50 to 70%**, showing that multiple-choice scores overstate readiness for specialized compliance tasks.

papers.title: PID-Gated Continual Prompt Adaptation Under Noisy Feedback
papers.abstract: Deploying LLM agents in non-stationary environments requires continually revising their instructions as the task drifts, yet rewriting after every reported mistake can turn noisy feedback into persistent errors. This raises an often-overlooked scheduling question in prompt adaptation: when should feedback trigger a lasting instruction update, and at what editor-call cost? Taking inspiration from proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, we introduce a family of lightweight gates that react to the current error, accumulate evidence over time, and roll back deterioration after an edit. We benchmark these gates against both simple baselines and advanced prompt optimizers (TextGrad and GEPA), over a diverse suite of drifting tasks, LLM parameter sizes, feedback-noise levels, and random seeds. PID-gated continual prompt adaptation yields a more favorable Pareto trade-off between task performance (high accuracy, low error) and editor-call budget than the baselines considered, pointing to control-theoretic scheduling as a simple, general tool for robust prompt adaptation under unreliable feedback.
papers.summary: LLM agents running in drifting environments need their instructions revised over time, but rewriting the prompt after every reported mistake lets noisy feedback bake in persistent errors and burns editor calls. Borrowing from proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, the authors propose lightweight gates that weigh the current error, accumulate evidence across steps, and roll back edits that make things worse, deciding when feedback should trigger a lasting update. Benchmarked against simple baselines and the prompt optimizers `TextGrad` and `GEPA` across drifting tasks, model sizes, feedback-noise levels, and seeds, **PID-gated adaptation gives a better Pareto trade-off between task accuracy and editor-call budget than every baseline considered**.

papers.title: XForecast: The KDD 2026 Finance Day Challenge on News-Grounded Financial Forecasting
papers.abstract: Financial forecasting has traditionally relied on numerical time-series (TS) signals, while textual information such as news remains largely underutilized. We introduce XForecast, a benchmark and competition for news-grounded financial forecasting, where the task is to predict stock price movements four weeks ahead using both historical price data and paired news signals. XForecast combines stock price data with curated financial text generated using FinTexTS, a multimodal dataset generation method. It covers 100 large-cap stocks from 2019--2023, with training on 2019--2022 and evaluation on 2023. To better evaluate models that leverage textual signals, we adopt a weighted hit rate metric that places greater emphasis on instances where news information is expected to have stronger influence. The XForecast Challenge, hosted on Kaggle as part of KDD 2026 Finance Day, aims to benchmark methods for integrating financial TS and textual information.
papers.summary: Financial forecasting models lean almost entirely on numerical time-series (TS) data while news text goes largely unused. `XForecast` is a benchmark and Kaggle competition for KDD 2026 Finance Day in which models must predict stock price movements four weeks ahead from historical prices paired with curated financial text produced by the `FinTexTS` dataset generation method, covering 100 large-cap stocks with 2019 to 2022 for training and 2023 for evaluation. **Scoring uses a weighted hit rate that upweights instances where news is expected to move prices**, so methods that actually exploit textual signals are rewarded over purely price-based ones.

papers.title: Query Your Way Out: Benchmarking Multi-Turn Knowledge Reasoning through Generalized Puzzle Solving
papers.abstract: Puzzles offer a natural testbed for Large Language Models (LLMs) reasoning because they pose verifiable goals under partial information and require multi-step decisions to reach a solution. However, existing puzzle benchmarks typically focus on narrow environments with rigid mechanics and tightly constrained solution targets. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Active Probing Benchmark (APB), which generalizes puzzle-solving by casting concept identification as an interactive reasoning task that integrates specialized knowledge assessment into the puzzle setting. Specifically, APB evaluates whether models can acquire information via multi-turn active probing and inference to pinpoint 960 target concepts of specialized difficulty across eight diverse academic domains. Our evaluation reveals a counter-intuitive phenomenon: most open-source reasoning models significantly underperform their standard instruction counterparts. This finding suggests that in interactive settings, these models struggle to leverage procedural reasoning to reliably access and apply specialized domain knowledge. Beyond these empirical insights, APB provides a scalable pipeline for generating benchmarks that probe knowledge reasoning under interaction across diverse settings.
papers.summary: Puzzles make a good test of large language model (LLM) reasoning because they have verifiable goals, partial information, and multi-step decisions, but existing puzzle benchmarks use narrow mechanics and rigid solution targets. The Active Probing Benchmark (`APB`) generalizes puzzle solving into an interactive concept-identification task: the model must ask questions over multiple turns and infer the answer to pin down one of 960 specialized target concepts drawn from eight academic domains, and a scalable pipeline generates new instances. **Most open-source reasoning models scored well below their standard instruction-tuned counterparts**, suggesting that in interactive settings these models struggle to turn procedural reasoning into reliable access to domain knowledge.

papers.title: Omni-Modal LLMs Know More Than They Say
papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) extend LLMs to process heterogeneous modalities (e.g., vision, audio, and IMU signals) alongside language, enabling a broader range of multimodal tasks. Yet we find that these models often fail to express information from non-textual modalities even when they perceive it correctly. We term this disconnect knows-but-cannot-say. To investigate this phenomenon, we introduce Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA), which measures the alignment between individual modality representations and response representations. Our analysis shows that non-textual representations are less aligned with response tokens and receive less attention than textual representations, suggesting a potential explanation for uneven modality preferences. Motivated by these findings, we propose OmniCatalyst, a simple perceive $\rightarrow$ infer strategy that complements the original modality inputs with self-generated text, making non-textual knowledge more accessible. Across seven Omni-LLMs, OmniCatalyst consistently improves performance (+7.29%) and yields more balanced modality preferences, with further gains from diverse training strategies. Further analysis demonstrates that the knowledge extraction phases increase TMA, suggesting that improved alignment makes non-textual information more accessible during response generation. In summary, our findings uncover how Omni-LLMs can better express modality knowledge through language. Our code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/OmniLLM.
papers.summary: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) take in vision, audio, and sensor signals alongside text, yet they often fail to voice information from non-textual inputs even when their internal representations have perceived it correctly, a gap the authors call knows-but-cannot-say. To study it they introduce Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA), which measures how well each modality's representations align with the response tokens, and find that non-textual representations are both less aligned and less attended to than text. The proposed fix, `OmniCatalyst`, has the model first describe its non-textual inputs in self-generated text and then answer with that text added to the original inputs; **across seven Omni-LLMs it improves performance by 7.29% on average** and yields more balanced modality preferences, with the extraction step measurably raising alignment.

papers.title: Large Language Model Assisted Transportation Planning through a Differentiable User Equilibrium Layer
papers.abstract: Transportation planning has traditionally required substantial expertise in network modeling, traffic assignment, and optimization. As a result, strategic analyses such as network design, capacity expansion, and model calibration remain inaccessible to non-expert decision makers. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to bridge this gap by enabling natural-language interaction with complex transportation planning tools. However, existing LLM-based systems primarily serve as interfaces to simulation software and lack the ability to efficiently search, evaluate, and optimize transportation solutions. This study proposes an integrated human-AI transportation planning framework that combines a large language model, a model context protocol (MCP) interface, an open-source transportation planning engine (AequilibraE), and a differentiable user equilibrium (UE) assignment layer. The framework allows non-expert users to execute network analyses and improve solutions for optimization. A differentiable UE layer is developed by directly differentiating the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions of the Beckmann traffic assignment problem. The proposed framework is demonstrated through two representative planning tasks: calibration of travel time functions from observed traffic counts and network design under budget constraints. The examples illustrate how differentiable transportation models and LLM agents can jointly democratize transportation planning and substantially reduce barriers between domain expertise and transportation decision making.
papers.summary: Strategic transportation planning tasks such as network design and model calibration stay locked behind expertise in traffic assignment and optimization, and existing large language model (LLM) front-ends only wrap simulators without being able to search or optimize solutions. The proposed framework connects an LLM to the open-source planning engine `AequilibraE` through a model context protocol (MCP) interface and adds a differentiable user equilibrium (UE) assignment layer obtained by differentiating the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions of the Beckmann traffic assignment problem, so gradients can flow through the traffic model. **Two worked tasks, calibrating travel-time functions from observed counts and designing a network under a budget constraint, show non-expert users driving optimization-grade analyses through natural language.**

papers.title: Phantom Merge: When Your Large Language Model Agents Pick One but Tell You About Another
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over multiple entities, where reliable response generation requires not only retrieving relevant evidence but also preserving its association with the correct entity. We identify Phantom Merge (PM), an entity-evidence binding failure in which an agent attributes unsupported claims to its committed entity, potentially even when the task is completed correctly. We formalize PM at the claim level and characterize its prevalence and error subtypes across four agent domains and four backbone families. To address this problem, we propose a two-stage framework for claim-level risk estimation and correction. First, Anchor-Grounded Risk (AGR) combines a representational readout of the agent's pre-emission hidden state with Jacobian-based functional information, providing complementary slot-level and anchor-value risk scores. Second, Fixed-Anchor Correction (FAC) audits flagged claims and selectively revises them using observed anchor evidence or removes them when no supported replacement is available. On the held-out Shopping detection cohort, AGR-slot achieves an AUROC of 96.2% and an average precision of 97.3%, outperforming the evaluated detection baselines. In the end-to-end Shopping mitigation evaluation, FAC reduces trajectory-level PM from 51.4% to 6.2%, with an output-to-original claim ratio of 80.7%. These results demonstrate the prevalence of entity-specific grounding failures and the effectiveness of combining internal risk estimation with evidence-constrained claim correction. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LabRAI/PhantomMerge.
