papers.summary: LLM agents that work over many entities, such as products in a shopping task, must keep each piece of retrieved evidence bound to the right entity, and they often do not. The authors name this failure Phantom Merge (PM), where an agent attributes unsupported claims to the entity it committed to, sometimes even while completing the task correctly, and characterize it at the claim level across four agent domains and four model families. Their fix pairs Anchor-Grounded Risk (AGR), which scores claims by reading the agent's pre-emission hidden state together with Jacobian-based functional information, with Fixed-Anchor Correction (FAC), which audits flagged claims and rewrites or removes them based on observed evidence. On a held-out shopping cohort the slot-level risk detector reaches an AUROC of 96.2%, and **end-to-end correction cuts trajectory-level Phantom Merge from 51.4% to 6.2%** while retaining about 81% of the original claims.

papers.title: Distributional Regression for Arbitrary Response Variables Using ReLU Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for distributional regression with arbitrary response variables. Rather than relying on scalar thresholds or Euclidean structure, we model conditional event probabilities indexed by measurable sets, which extends distributional regression to general response spaces while retaining a direct connection to classical event-based formulations. Within this framework, we study two complementary estimators: a preliminary estimator based on separate regression of event indicators, and a constrained estimator that enforces inclusion-consistent predictions through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over a finite set family. We establish general error bounds for both estimators and further specialize the results to dense ReLU networks, yielding explicit convergence rates overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Simulation studies and real-data experiments further demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed framework.
papers.summary: Distributional regression usually predicts a conditional distribution over a scalar or Euclidean response, which limits it when the response lives in a more general space. The framework here instead models conditional probabilities of events indexed by measurable sets, so arbitrary response spaces fit while the link to classical threshold-based formulations is retained, and it studies two estimators: separate regressions of event indicators, and a constrained version that enforces consistency between nested events through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over a finite family of sets. **Error bounds for both estimators specialize to dense ReLU networks with explicit convergence rates that overcome the curse of dimensionality**, and simulations plus real-data experiments back up the theory.

papers.title: Hashrope: A Persistent Data Structure for Mechanisms of LLM Context Management
papers.abstract: Serving stacks for large language models manage context through four recurring mechanisms: incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, identification of reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding of repeated segments. Each mechanism is served today by a different specialist structure. We show that all four reduce to a single persistent weight-balanced rope whose every node carries a polynomial hash of its subtree over a Mersenne prime, so that the structure supports logarithmic edits and logarithmic verified content-identity queries at the same time. We validate each mechanism with pre-registered, replicated experiments, then compare against a deployed specialist per mechanism: the Ropey editing library, a faithful PagedAttention copy-on-write block table, and the vendored SGLang radix matcher. On workloads that interleave edits with identity queries, Hashrope is net-superior to Ropey by a factor that grows without bound (369.7x at one million characters). Against the radix matcher on a live vLLM stack serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M on four A100 GPUs, Hashrope identifies a one-million-token shared prefix exactly and 1.20x faster, at a context length the dense engine cannot even prefill.
papers.summary: LLM serving stacks juggle four context-management jobs, incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, finding reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding repeated segments, and each is handled today by a different specialized structure. `Hashrope` shows all four reduce to one persistent weight-balanced rope in which every node stores a polynomial hash of its subtree modulo a Mersenne prime, giving logarithmic-time edits and logarithmic-time verified content-identity queries from the same structure. In pre-registered experiments against a deployed specialist for each mechanism, the `Ropey` editing library, a copy-on-write block table modeled on `PagedAttention`, and the `SGLang` radix matcher, it wins on mixed edit-and-query workloads by a margin that grows with input size, and **on a live `vLLM` stack serving `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M` across four A100 GPUs it identifies a one-million-token shared prefix exactly and 1.20 times faster than the radix matcher**.

papers.title: Pollard: Governed Semantic Execution Trees for Framework-Independent AI Agent Control and Replay
papers.abstract: Agent frameworks can persist checkpoints, trace tool calls, and limit resource use, but these facilities often assign different identities to execution, governance, and replay. We present Pollard, a framework-independent runtime based on governed semantic execution trees. A step identity commits to canonical input, kind, attempt, and parent identity; the same tree records completion, refusal, resource settlement, and branch history. Strict replay returns a verified stored result without invoking the wrapped operation, while a transactional store coordinates reservations across concurrent workers. Under a signed deterministic freeze, two state-model replicas each executed the evaluation transitions without an invariant violation, retained-lease PostgreSQL groups were tested against exact limits, strict replay avoided external calls, and all semantic mutations were detected with no false alarms on the controls. A multi-pair framework matrix preserved reference behavior and verified the trees. A separate cost-capped hosted study exercised live provider paths, and every completed Pollard trial produced a verified tree. Together, the studies support the core mechanisms under explicit lease, boundary, and seal-custody assumptions.
papers.summary: Agent frameworks can checkpoint state, trace tool calls, and cap resource use, but they typically give the execution, its governance, and its replay separate identities, so the three can drift apart. `Pollard` is a framework-independent runtime built on governed semantic execution trees: each step's identity is derived from its canonical input, kind, attempt number, and parent, and the same tree records completion, refusal, resource settlement, and branch history, so strict replay can return a verified stored result without calling the wrapped operation while a transactional store coordinates resource reservations across concurrent workers. Under a signed deterministic freeze, two independent replicas ran the evaluation transitions without any invariant violation, PostgreSQL-backed leases held at exact limits, and **every semantic mutation of a recorded tree was detected with zero false alarms on controls**; a cost-capped study against live model providers produced a verified tree for every completed trial.

papers.title: Unravel: Recovering an Interactive 3D Scene from a Single Image
papers.abstract: We present Unravel, a training-free framework that turns a single image into an interactive 3D scene, where every object is an independent and movable asset. Existing generators either produce one entangled geometry in which no object can be moved, or predict all objects in one feed-forward pass, where a wrong guess cannot be detected or repaired. Unravel instead takes a different approach: it first takes the scene apart, and then puts it back together. Starting from the input image, an agentic harness that iteratively peels the image layer by layer, and adopts point cloud as major modality for spatial relationship recovery. Specifically, a vision-language model plans which objects are fully visible, an image editor removes them and restores the occluded regions. Every edit is verified before being incorporated into the reconstruction. This process gradually turns occluded parts of the scene into direct observation, allowing objects to be reconstructed when they are best exposed rather than hallucinated from the original image alone. The scene is then rebuilt in reverse removal order, so that the supporting objects are naturally placed before the objects they support. Since a single-view image only reveals part of an object, we treat the observed points as a lower bound on its size: an asset may grow to cover its points, but can not shrink away from them. Finally, we physically settle the reconstructed scene to remove floating objects and interpenetrations, followed by an agentic audit that corrects remaining placement errors. Extensive experiments on diverse indoor scenes show that Unravel recovers more objects, places them more faithfully, and produces scenes that are more physically-plausible than existing methods.
papers.summary: Turning a single photograph into a 3D scene usually yields either one fused geometry where nothing can be moved or a single-shot prediction of all objects in which mistakes cannot be caught or repaired. `Unravel` is a training-free agentic pipeline that disassembles the scene before rebuilding it: a vision-language model picks out fully visible objects, an image editor removes them and inpaints what was behind, each edit is verified, and the process repeats layer by layer so occluded objects are reconstructed once directly observed rather than hallucinated. The scene is then reassembled in reverse removal order so supports are placed before what rests on them, each object is sized to cover at least its observed points, and a physics settling step plus an agentic audit remove floating objects and interpenetrations. **On diverse indoor scenes it recovers more objects, places them more faithfully, and produces more physically plausible layouts than existing methods.**

papers.title: BARTER: Compact Dynamic Sparse Training with Standard Dense Kernels
papers.abstract: Dynamic sparse training (DST) aims to reduce training costs while maintaining accuracy. Existing DST methods mask out parameters but keep matrix dimensions unchanged. Training speedups therefore depend on specialized support, such as sparse kernels. We introduce BARTER, a structured DST framework that reduces training cost using standard dense kernels by keeping training tensors physically compact while dynamically reallocating capacity across layers. Unlike existing works that require computing gradients for all parameters, BARTER instead uses statistics collected only from active units during ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate fixed global budgets. At each topology update, it resizes the affected parameter tensors and remaps their optimizer states, so subsequent training steps operate directly on the compact model. Training and fine-tuning experiments with Transformer-based vision models on two image classification benchmarks at densities from $0.1$ to $0.7$ show competitive Top-1 accuracy relative to full-tensor DST baselines. On an NVIDIA L40, BARTER achieves speedups of up to $6.29\times$ in measured training segments and reduces peak allocated GPU memory by up to $81.3\%$ relative to these implementations. An iPhone 13 Pro Max training benchmark additionally shows a $2.78\times$ speedup over the full-tensor DST baseline.
papers.summary: Dynamic sparse training (DST) cuts training cost by masking parameters, but because tensor shapes stay the same, real speedups depend on specialized sparse kernels. `BARTER` instead keeps training tensors physically compact: using statistics gathered only from active units during ordinary backpropagation, it prunes and clones attention heads and feed-forward channels under fixed global budgets, then resizes the affected tensors and remaps optimizer states so subsequent steps run on the smaller model with standard dense kernels. On Transformer-based vision models across two image classification benchmarks at densities from 0.1 to 0.7 it matches the Top-1 accuracy of full-tensor DST baselines, and **on an NVIDIA L40 it trains up to 6.29 times faster in measured segments while cutting peak GPU memory by up to 81.3%**, with a 2.78 times speedup on an iPhone 13 Pro Max training benchmark.

papers.title: Equilibrium Learning in Unbounded Stochastic Games with Gaussian Transitions
papers.abstract: Learning equilibria from data is difficult when several decision makers interact indefinitely and the system state has no prescribed bounds. We examine discounted general-sum stochastic games with compact action sets and an unknown nonlinear drift observed through Gaussian transition noise. The proposed procedure uses a single uninterrupted trajectory to update Gaussian-process models of the drift and to solve successively refined finite games. We prove a perturbation result showing that stability of equilibrium selection, together with uniform KL accuracy of Gaussian transition models, is sufficient for regional uniform convergence of the induced values and approximate Nash behavior in the original game. The region specifies where the guarantees are evaluated; strategies and dynamics continue to act on the entire Euclidean state space. For GP estimators, simultaneous confidence bounds yield a rate controlled by posterior uncertainty, kernel information gain, and joint-state dimension. Numerical studies illustrate how kernel choice and dimension appear in the predicted convergence behavior.
papers.summary: Learning equilibrium strategies is hard when several players interact indefinitely in a system whose state is unbounded and whose dynamics are unknown. The setting is discounted general-sum stochastic games with compact action sets and an unknown nonlinear drift observed through Gaussian noise; the procedure uses one uninterrupted trajectory to fit Gaussian-process models of the drift and repeatedly solves finite approximations of the game. **A perturbation theorem shows that stable equilibrium selection plus uniformly accurate transition models in KL divergence suffice for the induced values to converge uniformly on a region and for the learned strategies to be approximately Nash in the original game.** Gaussian-process confidence bounds then yield rates governed by posterior uncertainty, kernel information gain, and joint-state dimension, and numerical studies show how kernel choice and dimension shape convergence.

papers.title: WildTrace: Evaluating Training Data Detection in Realistic Large-Scale LLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: Although post-training significantly enhances model performance, the use of massive undisclosed data raises concerns about benchmark contamination and copyright infringement. This drives growing interest in training data detection for post-trained models. Existing evaluations for training data detection often leverage benchmarks constructed post hoc, which can introduce distribution shifts. Alternatively, controlled evaluations rely on small-scale training setups that diverge from realistic post-training settings. As a result, their reported performance may not faithfully reflect the effectiveness of detection methods in real-world scenarios. To this end, we introduce \textsc{\method}, a reliable benchmark designed to evaluate detection methods in realistic, large-scale post-training settings. Built on a multi-stage pipeline, \method\space encompasses stage-specific models throughout the post-training lifecycle, spanning SFT, DPO, and RL. To perform a reliable evaluation, we construct model-specific evaluation sets across four diverse tasks, featuring distribution-matched members and non-members with verifiable membership labels. Our results reveal that even the best-performing method achieves an average AUC of only 0.529 on our benchmark, which approaches random-guessing level (0.5). Furthermore, our analysis suggests that evaluation protocols can significantly affect measured detection performance. These findings highlight the significant potential for developing effective, practical, and robust detection methods under realistic scenarios.
papers.summary: Post-training on massive undisclosed data raises worries about benchmark contamination and copyright, which has spurred methods for detecting whether a given example was in a model's post-training data, but existing evaluations either build benchmarks after the fact with distribution shift or use small-scale training setups. `WildTrace` evaluates detection methods on realistic, large-scale post-training by producing stage-specific models across the full pipeline of supervised fine-tuning, DPO, and RL, with model-specific evaluation sets over four tasks whose members and non-members are distribution-matched and carry verifiable labels. **Even the best detection method reaches an average AUC of only 0.529, barely above the 0.5 of random guessing**, and the analysis shows that evaluation protocol choices substantially change measured detection performance.

papers.title: Uncovering Robustness Weaknesses in LLM Agents via Persona Evolution with Task-Integrity Constraints
papers.abstract: Interactive-agent evaluations commonly rely on standardized LLM-based user simulators that exhibit broadly cooperative behavior, potentially overlooking failures that arise under diverse but realistic user interactions. This can lead to overly optimistic estimates of agent robustness and provide limited failure signals for training agents that generalize across users. Existing approaches largely rely on predefined user behaviors, which may miss agent- or domain-specific weaknesses, while failure-oriented search can reduce task success by invalidating the underlying task rather than exposing genuine robustness failures. To fill this gap, we introduce TIPER, a task-integrity-preserving persona evolution method that automatically discovers agent-specific user policies exposing robustness weaknesses while keeping the underlying task valid and solvable. TIPER evolves persistent user personas through reflection-guided behavioral mutations and task-wise Pareto selection under a task-integrity constraint. Across four interactive-agent benchmarks, TIPER yields lower held-out avg@3 scores in all 12 GPT-5.4 settings, with observed reductions of 5.8 to 33.7 percentage points, and in all 28 agent-domain pairs spanning seven agents, with a median observed reduction of 22.9 points. Further analysis yields a behavior-to-failure taxonomy that connects discovered user behaviors to recurring agent failure modes. Together, these results show that TIPER enables more diagnostic robustness evaluation of interactive agents and provides informative failure analysis for future agent robustness improvement. Code repository: https://github.com/UCSB-NLP-Chang/TIPER.
papers.summary: Evaluations of interactive agents usually pair them with cooperative large language model (LLM) user simulators, which can hide failures that realistic, less accommodating users would trigger, while failure-seeking alternatives often cheat by making the task itself unsolvable. `TIPER` evolves persistent user personas through reflection-guided behavioral mutations and task-wise Pareto selection, constrained to keep the underlying task valid and solvable, so the discovered user policies expose genuine weaknesses. Held-out scores dropped in all 12 `GPT-5.4` configurations tested, by 5.8 to 33.7 percentage points, and in all 28 agent-domain pairs spanning seven agents, with a **median observed reduction of 22.9 points**. The authors also derive a behavior-to-failure taxonomy linking the discovered user behaviors to recurring agent failure modes.

papers.title: Fisher information and the geometry of memorization in neural networks
papers.abstract: A fruitful approach towards understanding generalization in machine learning involves characterizing how models separate generalizable structure from idiosyncratic or even corrupted features of training data. Fisher information has emerged as a diagnostic tool for this separation, leveraging loss geometry to distinguish generalization from memorization. Here we investigate this connection in vision models trained on CIFAR-10 with controlled noise that can be learned only through memorization. We show that projecting model weights onto the top Fisher eigenvectors decouples general task performance from noisy sample memorization, and we investigate how this decoupling presents differentially across layers. We show that the same phenomena are present in small transformers trained to solve a synthetic in-context learning task, and are reproduced in closed form in a simple, analytically solvable linear model. Our results reveal that Fisher information captures aspects of the geometric structure underlying how neural networks allocate capacity between generalization and memorization.
papers.summary: Separating what a network generalizes from what it merely memorizes is central to understanding generalization, and Fisher information has been proposed as a loss-geometry diagnostic for that split. Vision models trained on `CIFAR-10` with injected noise that can only be fit by memorization show that **projecting weights onto the top Fisher eigenvectors decouples general task performance from memorization of noisy samples**, with the effect appearing unevenly across layers. The same behavior shows up in small transformers trained on a synthetic in-context learning task and is reproduced in closed form in an analytically solvable linear model, suggesting Fisher information captures real geometric structure in how capacity is split between generalization and memorization.

papers.title: Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.
papers.summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems normally exchange plain text, which both limits what can be transferred and forces every downstream model to re-prefill the conversation; sharing key-value (KV) caches directly avoids this, but prior methods needed a trained fusion adapter for each pair of models. `CacheFuse` drops the training step entirely, augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache by linear interpolation, which consistently beats what the downstream model achieves alone. Across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks it gains up to 8.6 percentage points in accuracy and delivers **up to a 12.2x speedup in time to first token** compared with text-based communication.

papers.title: Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting under Moving-Solid Interaction
papers.abstract: We propose the task of Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting: predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of a future dense 3D liquid velocity field conditioned on how a solid object moves through it. This task provides an upstream physical forecasting primitive for systems that need to reason about motion-conditioned liquid response, including robotic liquid manipulation, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation. Existing works have made efforts in predicting flow around static or prescribed solid geometries and synthesizing visually plausible fluid motion. Yet these approaches provide limited coverage for interactive liquid dynamics, as they are not capable of forecasting how a moving solid induces a future full-domain liquid response. In this forecasting scenario, the hydrodynamic effect is condensed near an evolving liquid-solid interface, but the prediction target is a global spatiotemporal rollout. To address this challenge, we propose a two-level recurrent forecasting framework, TIDE/TIDES: TIDE isolates localized interface-driven forecasting, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization to reduce accumulated rollout error. Across adapted neighboring baselines, controlled component ablations, motion/size OOD tests, and long-horizon evaluation, TIDES achieves the best forecasting performance and the ablations identify localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization as the key contributors. Together, our task formulation, benchmark, and TIDE/TIDES study establish a controlled foundation for moving-solid-conditioned dense liquid forecasting. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jongwonryu/TIDE-TIDES.
papers.summary: Forecasting how a liquid responds to a solid moving through it is posed here as a new task: predict the future dense three-dimensional liquid velocity field across the whole domain, conditioned on the solid's motion, as an upstream primitive for robotic liquid manipulation, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation. Existing methods handle flow around static or prescribed geometry, or synthesize visually plausible motion, neither of which produces a full-domain response to a moving solid, where the hydrodynamic effect concentrates near an evolving liquid-solid interface. A two-level recurrent framework addresses this: `TIDE` isolates the localized interface-driven forecasting, and `TIDES` adds transport-aware coupling plus explicit stabilization to limit error accumulated over rollouts. **`TIDES` performs best across adapted baselines, out-of-distribution motion and size tests, and long-horizon evaluation**, with ablations crediting localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization.

papers.title: DeepThink: A Conceptual Model for Knowledge-Addressable Recurrent Language Modeling
papers.abstract: This manuscript presents DeepThink, a knowledge-addressable framework for recurrent language modeling. A Knowledge Bank stores typed Knowledge Units, a Knowledge Activator selects units from the current execution state, Knowledge Assembly produces an executable configuration, and a Shared Thinking Operator updates that state. An output stage then organizes generation. This organization exposes knowledge capacity, activation width, and recurrent depth as separate design variables, supporting both complete parameter packages and fine-grained expert or low-rank modules. We formalize the interfaces and their execution semantics, including state-dependent selection, parameter-space assembly, and thinking followed by generation. For compatible templates and complete runtime-state configurations, we establish an exact Fixed-Schedule Realization of an existing fixed-depth model. Exact shared-base reparameterization and pretrained output-tail reuse provide complementary initialization constructions. Together, these results define a route from pretrained models to dynamically selected and assembled recurrent computation. A synthesis of conditional computation, recurrent models, modular parameters, and knowledge interfaces positions DeepThink within the research landscape and identifies the design questions arising from their integration.
papers.summary: `DeepThink` is a conceptual architecture for recurrent language modeling in which computation is addressed by knowledge: a Knowledge Bank holds typed Knowledge Units, an activator selects units from the current execution state, an assembly step turns them into an executable parameter configuration, and a shared thinking operator iterates that state before a separate output stage generates text. The design separates knowledge capacity, activation width, and recurrent depth into independent variables, accommodating both complete parameter packages and finer-grained expert or low-rank modules. The authors formalize the interfaces and their execution semantics and establish an **exact Fixed-Schedule Realization showing the framework can reproduce an existing fixed-depth model**, with exact shared-base reparameterization and reuse of a pretrained output tail as complementary initialization routes. The contribution is formal rather than experimental, and situates the framework against work on conditional computation, recurrent models, and modular parameters.

papers.title: EventLens: Event-Structure Reinforcement Learning for Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong results on video question answering, yet often fail to recover the temporal structure that makes a video coherent. They may merge neighboring events, miss single-event progression, or infer implausible relations across events. We study structured temporal understanding as the ability to recover event structure from visual evidence, including event boundaries, single-event progression, and multi-event relations. We argue that this gap arises from a mismatch between current post-training objectives and temporal reasoning, where caption-style supervision allows models to rely on language shortcuts rather than visual temporal grounding. To address this, we propose EventLens, a vision-centric reinforcement learning framework that learns video understanding through event-structure recovery. Instead of reconstructing captions, EventLens trains models to recover temporal structure under controlled perturbations, such as altered temporal granularity, reversed progression, and shuffled event order. We instantiate this framework with a three-level temporal ontology and derive three verifiable task families: event segmentation, progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning. These tasks admit deterministic rewards, enabling task-specialized GRPO training without human preference labels or learned reward models. We further introduce multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MT-OPD) to consolidate specialized policies into a unified model. Experiments on Qwen3-VL backbones show consistent improvements on temporal grounding and event-sensitive reasoning benchmarks, while preserving general video-QA performance. Learning curves further demonstrate that EventLens achieves comparable downstream transfer with significantly reduced training cost compared to direct mixed RL optimization.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer video questions well while still failing to recover temporal structure, merging adjacent events, missing progression within a single event, or inferring implausible relations between events; the authors attribute this to caption-style post-training that rewards language shortcuts over visual grounding. `EventLens` instead trains models to reconstruct event structure from video perturbed in controlled ways, such as altered temporal granularity, reversed progression, and shuffled event order. A three-level temporal ontology yields three task families with deterministic, verifiable rewards, so `GRPO` training needs no human preference labels or learned reward model, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation folds the specialized policies back into one model. On `Qwen3-VL` backbones this improves temporal grounding and event-sensitive reasoning while preserving general video question answering, and **reaches comparable downstream transfer at significantly lower training cost than direct mixed reinforcement learning**.

papers.title: ProCARE: Real-World Study Automation via Profile-Grounded Evidence Contracts
papers.abstract: Real-world studies (RWS) analyze routinely collected healthcare data, such as electronic health records and insurance claims, to estimate treatment effects, monitor safety, and identify risk factors outside randomized trials. Automating RWS with large language model agents is appealing but brittle: valid analyses depend on dataset-specific clinical semantics, including index dates, follow-up windows, patient/event-level units, and outcome boundaries that are often implicit in observational data. This leads to schema mismatches, temporal errors, inconsistent analytical granularity, and unsupported clinical claims. We present ProCARE, a profile-grounded framework that reformulates RWS automation as constrained compilation. ProCARE converts heterogeneous data profiles into Evidence Contracts specifying available variables, temporal attributes, distributions, and evidentiary limits, and compiles study objectives into RWS-IR, a strongly typed intermediate representation for variables, time relations, analysis units, and statistical tasks. Deterministic validation and localized repair then check and revise generated workflows across schema mapping, cohort construction, variable derivation, analysis, and interpretation. On 36 EHR-based benchmark tasks, ProCARE outperforms strong LLM-agent baselines in code executability, semantic consistency, and conclusion traceability, with automated violation diagnoses showing moderate-to-substantial agreement with blinded expert review.
papers.summary: Real-world studies reuse routinely collected healthcare data such as electronic health records (EHR) and insurance claims to estimate treatment effects and monitor safety. Automating them with large language model agents is brittle, because the clinical semantics that make an analysis valid, including index dates, follow-up windows, patient- versus event-level units, and outcome boundaries, are left implicit in observational data. `ProCARE` recasts the job as constrained compilation: data profiles become Evidence Contracts stating available variables, temporal attributes, distributions, and evidentiary limits, study objectives compile into `RWS-IR`, a strongly typed intermediate representation for variables, time relations, analysis units, and statistical tasks, and deterministic validation with localized repair checks each stage from schema mapping through interpretation. **Across 36 EHR-based benchmark tasks it beats strong agent baselines on code executability, semantic consistency, and conclusion traceability**, with automated violation diagnoses agreeing moderately to substantially with blinded expert review.

papers.title: Label-Centric Knowledge Retrieval for Zero-Shot Text Classification
papers.abstract: Flagship large language models (LLMs) offer rich general knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but their high inference cost and latency limit their use for large-scale data labeling. We study zero-shot text classification with semantically meaningful labels and task descriptions, without task-specific labeled examples or classifier feedback. We propose \textbf{SLKR} (Semantic Label Knowledge Retrieval), a label-centric retrieval-augmented generation framework that separates offline knowledge construction from lightweight online inference. Offline, a flagship LLM independently generates label definitions, retrieval keywords, and boundary rules for potentially confusable label pairs, forming a reusable label-knowledge store. Because this construction operates over the label space rather than the input corpus, its one-time flagship cost can be amortized across large-scale inference. Online, hybrid semantic and lexical retrieval first identifies the top-$K$ candidate labels and then selects up to $M$ input-relevant boundary rules connecting candidate-label pairs. A lightweight LLM performs the final classification in a single call using the retrieved definitions and rules. Across three public benchmarks and a real-world multilingual book-classification dataset, SLKR achieves the best results on all four datasets with Qwen3.5-4B and on three of four with Ministral-3-3B, while using compact input contexts and no task-specific labeled examples. Boundary ablations further show that retrieving a small set of input-relevant rules preserves performance close to using all boundaries with substantially less context, supporting efficient reuse of flagship-generated label knowledge for lightweight classification.
papers.summary: Flagship large language models (LLMs) label text well but cost too much and run too slowly for large-scale annotation, so `SLKR` (Semantic Label Knowledge Retrieval) moves the expensive reasoning offline and into the label space instead of the corpus. A flagship model generates label definitions, retrieval keywords, and boundary rules for potentially confusable label pairs once, forming a reusable store whose cost amortizes across inference; online, hybrid semantic and lexical retrieval narrows to the top-K candidate labels and a few input-relevant boundary rules, and a lightweight model classifies in a single call. **It wins on all four evaluated datasets with `Qwen3.5-4B` and three of four with `Ministral-3-3B`**, using compact contexts and no task-specific labeled examples, and ablations show a small set of input-relevant rules nearly matches using every boundary rule.

papers.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees
papers.abstract: Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm's final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm's returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.
papers.summary: Regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization usually bound cumulative regret across all queries, which says little about the single point the algorithm finally recommends, the quantity that matters most when evaluations are noisy. The proposed remedy is a drop-in exploration strategy that occasionally substitutes an exploration query for the usual acquisition query, supported by an analysis bounding the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, a measure of the largest unexplored region. **That bound yields upper bounds on inference regret, the gap between the global optimum and the value at the returned point**, and empirically the strategies improve the final recommendations of existing Bayesian optimization algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.

papers.title: Correct Choices, Failed Sequences: Choice2Seq Benchmarks Correctness Retention Across Output Interfaces
papers.abstract: A model may select the correct answer yet fail to construct it through a sequence of local decisions. We introduce Choice2Seq, a diagnostic benchmark that measures correctness retention across complete-answer selection and sequential construction in independent runs on the same problems and candidate sets. Sequence Composition Rate (SCR) measures the fraction of correctly selected items that are also answered correctly through local construction. Jev achieves 97.1% and 99.5% selection accuracy on arithmetic and lexical retrieval, yet retains only 33.0% and 2.1% of those correct choices under serial construction, respectively. Substantial gaps also emerge for StartLux and Qwen, including when Qwen emits characters directly. Restricting local options to candidate-supported characters improves construction, while explicit position indexing improves copying fidelity, even for incorrect selections. These interventions distinguish task correctness, plan fidelity, and output compliance. Matched dialogue-state evaluations reveal that local field construction largely preserves Jev's correct states but reduces Qwen's mean-turn accuracy, highlighting task- and interface-dependent differences. Sequence-level confidence and request-cost analyses further characterize completed outputs.
papers.summary: Selecting a correct complete answer and building that same answer through a sequence of local decisions turn out to be different abilities, and `Choice2Seq` measures the gap by running both formats independently on identical problems and candidate sets. Its Sequence Composition Rate reports what fraction of correctly selected answers survive serial construction, and the loss is severe: `Jev` selects correctly 97.1% of the time on arithmetic and 99.5% on lexical retrieval, yet **retains only 33.0% and 2.1% of those correct choices under step-by-step construction**. Comparable gaps appear for `StartLux` and `Qwen`, including when `Qwen` emits characters directly. Restricting local options to candidate-supported characters improves construction and explicit position indexing improves copying fidelity, which lets the authors separate failures of task correctness, plan fidelity, and output compliance.

papers.title: MSC: Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control Framework with Uncertainty-Aware NMPC and RL-based Execution Layer
papers.abstract: Freely swiveling casters are widely adopted in industrial AMRs/SDVs for their mechanical simplicity and load capacity. However, caster misalignment during low-speed or high-curvature maneuvers induces strong contact nonlinearities, widening the planning-execution gap between commanded $(v, \omega)$ and realized motion. Existing caster-aware strategies are highly sensitive to state-estimation reliability, causing unstable execution in uncertain transition regimes. To address this, we present Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control (MSC), a planning-execution integrated hierarchical framework featuring two core mechanisms. First, an uncertainty-aware NMPC (CU-MPC) dynamically schedules caster-aware costs and input regularization using predictive uncertainty to suppress overly aggressive maneuvers. Second, a reinforcement learning-based execution layer estimates and predicts caster states under partial observability, transforming high-level velocity commands into physically executable wheel speeds adapted to current contact conditions. Validations in Isaac Sim and real robots demonstrate that MSC offers a clear comparative advantage over existing decoupled compensation approaches by significantly improving caster-state estimation accuracy, minimizing misalignment, and enhancing tracking robustness in caster-sensitive maneuvers.
papers.summary: Freely swiveling casters keep industrial autonomous mobile robots mechanically simple and load-bearing, but during low-speed or high-curvature maneuvers the casters misalign, introducing contact nonlinearities that make realized motion diverge from commanded linear and angular velocity, and existing caster-aware controllers degrade when state estimation is unreliable. Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control joins planning and execution in two layers: an uncertainty-aware nonlinear model predictive controller that schedules caster-aware cost terms and input regularization according to predictive uncertainty, damping overly aggressive maneuvers, and a reinforcement learning execution layer that estimates and predicts caster states under partial observability to convert velocity commands into physically achievable wheel speeds. Tests in `Isaac Sim` and on real robots report **better caster-state estimation, less misalignment, and more robust tracking than decoupled compensation approaches**.

papers.title: L\"ushi-1840: Building and Probing a Knowledge Cutoff for a Classical Chinese Language Model
papers.abstract: Language models trained only on text from before a given year are useful for studying hindsight and historical language, but the open collections of pre-modern Chinese carry no publication dates and unreliable dynasty labels. We present L\"ushi-1840, a 983M-parameter model trained from scratch on 12,262 books (1.28B characters) selected as composed before 1840. A first corpus, dated by a common heuristic, in effect ended at 1644 while containing twentieth-century material. We describe the re-dating and cleaning pipeline that replaced it and an audit with markers the pipeline did not use, which still finds later material. On the model side we measure surprisal, relative to a modern reference, on annals compiled after the cutoff. For events after 1840 against events up to 1820 the ratio is 1.38 (95% interval 1.33-1.44), against about 1.00 for modern general-purpose models. In a series of 294M models, adding the later court records lowers the ratio from 1.33 to 1.16, and the two models diverge from the 1820s, where the added records begin. The probe tracks the coverage of sources and does not establish a single cutoff year; none of our probes exposes the audited contamination. Model, book list and scripts will be released.
papers.summary: Language models restricted to text written before a chosen year are useful for studying historical language and hindsight, but open collections of pre-modern Chinese carry no publication dates and unreliable dynasty labels. `Lüshi-1840` is a 983M-parameter model trained from scratch on 12,262 books, about 1.28 billion characters, judged to have been composed before 1840, after a re-dating and cleaning pipeline replaced a first corpus whose common dating heuristic effectively stopped at 1644 while still admitting twentieth-century material. Measuring surprisal against a modern reference model on annals compiled after the cutoff gives a **ratio of 1.38 for post-1840 events versus events up to 1820, against roughly 1.00 for modern general-purpose models**, and in a 294M-parameter series adding later court records pulls the ratio from 1.33 down to 1.16, with the two models diverging from the 1820s where those records begin. The authors caution that the probe tracks source coverage rather than establishing a single cutoff year, and that none of their probes detected the later material their own audit found.

papers.title: MP-MNCA: Morphology-Prior Masked Neighbor Cross-Attention for Efficient Spatial Domain Identification
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics jointly captures molecular state, tissue morphology, and spatial organization, yet spatial-domain methods are typically compared only at late training checkpoints, obscuring differences in convergence efficiency. We introduce MP-MNCA, a morphology-prior masked neighbor cross-attention framework that preserves the full 3,000 dimensional highly-variable-gene representation while selectively routing molecular information across spatial neighbors, with histological similarity incorporated as a continuous attention prior under a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective. Across 12 heterogeneous human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) sections, MP-MNCA is evaluated against established spatial-domain baselines using both convergence trajectories and epoch-wise spatial-domain visualizations. Our results show that MP-MNCA (i) reaches coherent spatial-domain structure in substantially fewer training epochs, as reflected quantitatively by convergence curves and qualitatively by progressive spatial grids, and (ii) maintains strong clustering quality, achieving a mean peak refined ARI of 0.546 versus 0.549 for the strongest baseline (STAIG), while attaining the highest mean refined NMI of 0.657 versus 0.640. Moreover, MP-MNCA outperforms STAIG on 7 of 12 sections in ARI and 11 of 12 in NMI, demonstrating faster convergence without sacrificing spatial-domain quality.
papers.summary: Spatial transcriptomics captures molecular state, tissue morphology, and spatial organization together, yet methods for identifying spatial domains are typically compared only at late training checkpoints, which hides differences in how fast they converge. `MP-MNCA` keeps the full 3,000-dimensional highly-variable-gene representation and selectively routes molecular information across spatial neighbors, folding histological similarity in as a continuous attention prior under a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective. Across 12 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex sections it **reaches coherent spatial-domain structure in substantially fewer training epochs**, essentially matching the strongest baseline `STAIG` on refined adjusted Rand index (0.546 versus 0.549) and leading on refined normalized mutual information (0.657 versus 0.640), winning on 7 of 12 sections by the first measure and 11 of 12 by the second.

papers.title: SafeDSE: Joint Exploration of Safety Architecture Patterns, Mapping, and Scheduling for Dataflow Applications With Safety Arguments (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: Embedded platforms increasingly host safety-related streaming functions next to less critical ones. Whether a safety architecture pattern, such as a doer/checker pair, protects a function depends on the cores that run its components. Their schedule must meet the throughput requirement, and mixing safety integrity levels (SILs) on one core raises development cost. This report presents SafeDSE, a design space exploration framework for synchronous dataflow applications. One declarative constraint model decides the pattern of each actor, the placement that the fault model requires, the static-order schedule, and the platform, and prices SIL promotion. Guards activate the chosen patterns in a fixed graph that holds all of them, and node potentials encode throughput. An independent verifier re-checks every solution, and a generator turns its checks into evidence of a safety argument in Goal Structuring Notation. On 9 benchmark instances under period bounds, no rule that fixes patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive under conservative pricing, while joint exploration was. In the generated arguments, 49 to 62% of the leaves cite verifier checks; the rest are claims a mapping cannot discharge. Optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs with up to 16 actors. This extended version adds the full model, the verifier and generator in detail, the complete catalog and parameters, and a proof of the potential characterization. It also reports every experiment per instance, a mutation analysis of the verifier, and the negative results of the development.
papers.summary: Embedded platforms increasingly run safety-related streaming functions next to less critical ones, and whether a safety architecture pattern such as a doer/checker pair actually protects a function depends on which cores host its components, on meeting the throughput requirement, and on the development cost of mixing safety integrity levels (SILs) on one core. `SafeDSE` folds all of that into a single declarative constraint model for synchronous dataflow applications, deciding each actor's pattern, the placement the fault model requires, the static-order schedule, and the platform, while pricing SIL promotion; guards activate the chosen patterns inside one fixed graph holding all of them, and node potentials encode throughput. An independent verifier re-checks every solution and a generator converts its checks into a safety argument in Goal Structuring Notation, where 49 to 62% of leaves cite verifier checks and the rest are claims a mapping cannot discharge. **On 9 benchmark instances, no rule that fixed patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive under conservative pricing, whereas joint exploration was**, and optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs up to 16 actors.

papers.title: OneShot: Label-Efficient Detector Weighting for Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Time series (TS) anomaly detection (AD) lacks a universal detector, with the best choice determined by the series rather than by the algorithm. Existing methods therefore either select one detector for each series or average a pool of them. However, both assume that no label ever arrives, while a deployed monitor does receive them, since an operator confirms the alarms it raises. In this paper, we propose ONESHOT, which uses a single confirmed anomaly to weight the pool rather than to choose one detector from it. Specifically, we score each detector on the confirmed anomaly, and those scores become the weights of a soft mixture over the whole pool. We show that a single confirmed anomaly is enough to come close to the best detector for the series. Across 152 univariate and 73 multivariate series, ONESHOT outperforms the strongest single detector, averaging the whole pool, and even picking the best detector on the confirmed event. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/one_shot.
papers.summary: No single time series anomaly detector wins everywhere, so existing systems either pick one detector per series or average a whole pool, both assuming labels never arrive; in practice a deployed monitor does receive them, because an operator confirms the alarms it raises. `ONESHOT` uses exactly one confirmed anomaly, scoring every detector in the pool on that event and turning those scores into weights for a soft mixture rather than selecting a single winner. Across 152 univariate and 73 multivariate series it **beats the strongest single detector, averaging the whole pool, and even picking the best detector on the confirmed event**, indicating one confirmed anomaly is enough to come close to the best detector for a given series.

papers.title: When Participant Disjoint Validation Is Not Enough to Establish Generalization in Parkinson's Gait Classification
papers.abstract: Participant-disjoint cross-validation prevents direct participant overlap, but it may still produce optimistic estimates when acquisition site and diagnosis are structurally dependent. We examined Parkinson's disease classification using 159 pressure-walkway summary features from 133 WearGait-PD participants, including 65 participants with Parkinson's disease and 68 controls. The cohort was non-factorial: two sites contained only one diagnostic group, whereas VA-Seattle was the only site containing both groups. In repeated participant-level nested cross-validation, site alone achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.955 plus or minus 0.003, exceeding the gait-feature model (0.882 plus or minus 0.014). Under the evaluated logistic-regression pipelines, adding gait features to site, age, and sex produced no measurable improvement in pooled discrimination. More site-controlled evaluations produced lower and imprecise estimates: VA-Seattle same-site AUC was 0.668 (95% bootstrap confidence interval 0.477 to 0.836), and the JHOC + Bayview-to-VA-Seattle transport stress test achieved 0.576 (0.375 to 0.770). Supporting within-diagnosis site-prediction and site-conditioned permutation analyses showed that the gait representation retained substantial acquisition-site structure. These findings indicate that participant-disjoint pooled validation did not isolate disease-related discrimination from site-associated variation. They encourage careful examination of site-label dependence and, where possible, support for pooled results through within-site or independent validation before broader claims are made about generalization across institutions.
papers.summary: Participant-disjoint cross-validation prevents the same person appearing in training and test data, but it can still flatter a model when acquisition site and diagnosis are structurally dependent. In a cohort of 133 `WearGait-PD` participants described by 159 pressure-walkway gait features, two sites contained only one diagnostic group each and a single site contained both, and **site identity alone classified Parkinson's disease with an area under the curve of 0.955, above the gait-feature model's 0.882**; adding gait features to site, age, and sex gave no measurable improvement in pooled discrimination. Site-controlled evaluations collapsed, to 0.668 within the one mixed site and 0.576 when transporting a model trained elsewhere, both with wide bootstrap intervals, and supporting analyses showed the gait representation itself retains substantial site structure. The authors conclude pooled participant-disjoint validation did not isolate disease-related signal from site variation, and urge within-site or independent validation before claiming generalization across institutions.

papers.title: Look Back to Move Forward: Learning to Revisit for Agentic Compositional Image Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-image models have made remarkable progress in visual fidelity and instruction following, yet complex compositional generation remains challenging. Existing agentic approaches address this limitation through iterative generation and editing, adapting their actions based on interaction history. However, they typically fix the continuation state (i.e., the image from which refinement proceeds) to the latest image. Since iterative editing is not necessarily monotonic, the agent may continue refining from the latest image even when it has already degraded. In this work, we introduce GenRevisit, an agentic framework that extends action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection. The agent can not only use interaction history to adjust editing instructions but also select an image candidate to edit, jointly deciding where to continue from and how to refine. We train GenRevisit with SFT followed by agentic reinforcement learning. To address the coarse credit assignment of final outcome reward in GRPO, which assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, we further propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to redistribute positive advantage according to each action's contribution to reducing the remaining objective. On GenEval2, GenRevisit achieves GM scores of 84.3 and 74.4 with Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo, surpassing the strongest baselines using the same generators by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively. GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2 among baselines.
papers.summary: Agentic text-to-image systems handle complex compositional prompts by iterating generation and editing, but they almost always continue from the latest image, which is a problem because editing is not monotonic and the latest image may already have degraded. `GenRevisit` widens the action space so the agent jointly chooses which candidate image to continue from and how to refine it, trained by supervised fine-tuning followed by agentic reinforcement learning. Because outcome-only rewards in `GRPO` hand every action in a trajectory the same advantage, the authors add Normalized Action Credit Assignment, redistributing positive advantage according to how much each action reduced the remaining objective. On `GenEval2` it scores 84.3 with `Qwen-Image-2512` and 74.4 with `Z-Image-Turbo`, **surpassing the strongest same-generator baselines by 12.7 and 10.9 points**, with state-of-the-art results also on `GenEval` and `GenEval++`.

papers.title: NetRL: Powering Network Decisions via NetGRPO-Driven Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract:
Network decision-making tasks, including adaptive bitrate streaming, load balancing, and congestion control, require
  policies to process heterogeneous states and actions while balancing near- and long-term consequences. Existing solutions
  generalize poorly across network tasks, require substantial task-specific redesign, and lack reliable evaluation of long-
  horizon action consequences. Methods that learn through online interaction additionally face unstable optimization. We
  present NetRL, a two-stage LLM-based reinforcement learning framework that combines supervised fine-tuning on
  demonstration trajectories with online policy optimization. A universal mixed-embedding interface combines textual task
  descriptions with precise numerical states, while a network action head produces valid decisions. At its core, NetGRPO
  evaluates candidate actions over multiple future trajectories, directs deeper search toward uncertain alternatives
  through confidence-aware budgeting, and performs group-relative, clipped, and KL-regularized updates. NetRL achieves
  23.6% higher QoE than NetLLM, 12.2% lower job completion time than Genet, and 24.1% higher network utility than Orca,
  yielding state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods. Confidence-aware budgeting reduces end-to-end training
  time by 27.1% without reducing validation QoE. NetRL also converges stably and generalizes to unseen network traces
  without retraining. Code and model weights are available at the repository linked in this paper.
papers.summary: Network decision tasks such as adaptive bitrate streaming, load balancing, and congestion control each tend to get a bespoke policy, generalize poorly across tasks, and are hard to train online, since long-horizon consequences of an action are difficult to evaluate and online optimization is unstable. `NetRL` fine-tunes a large language model on demonstration trajectories and then optimizes it online, feeding it a universal mixed-embedding interface that combines textual task descriptions with precise numerical state and emitting choices through a network action head that enforces validity. Its `NetGRPO` objective scores candidate actions by rolling out several possible futures, concentrating deeper search on alternatives the model is least confident about, and applies group-relative, clipped, KL-regularized updates. Reported results are **23.6% higher quality of experience than `NetLLM`, 12.2% lower job completion time than `Genet`, and 24.1% higher network utility than `Orca`**, with confidence-aware budgeting cutting end-to-end training time 27.1% at no cost in validation quality and the policy transferring to unseen network traces without retraining.

papers.title: Learning to GUIDE the Group: Self-Learning LLM Facilitation Across Multi-Party Tasks
papers.abstract: As large language models are increasingly adopted as multi-party communication facilitators, there is a growing demand for agents capable of balancing diverse group dynamics across contexts. However, existing LLM facilitators are often fine-tuned for task-specific objectives; generalized LLM-based facilitation methods that can adapt to different types of tasks and diverse group dynamics are underdeveloped. To address this gap, we present GUIDE (Generalized Unified Intervention for Dynamic Exchanges, a framework for developing generalized LLM-based facilitators across different multi-party contexts. GUIDE evaluates facilitation across both objective task outcomes and subjective metrics, including psychological safety and perceived friction. Within this framework, we study whether LLMs can self-learn generalized facilitation strategy offline to real-time interventions. We first collect multi-party human interactions guided by task-specific expert LLM facilitators (N=432 conversations). We then employ a self-learning method in which an LLM induces an actionable strategic playbook from conversations and iteratively refines it using feedback from an LLM judge aligned with human annotators (N=20), developing a single generalized facilitator that outperforms the three task-specific expert facilitators on held-out conversations 61.4% win rate. Finally, we evaluate these improvements empirically; in a real-time online empirical study, the self-learned generalized facilitator preserves facilitator performance and group productivity, improves speaking comfort and reduces interpersonal friction, while using 24.7% fewer turns and 29.0% fewer words than the expert prompts. These findings provide empirical evidence that LLMs can learn generalizable, task-agnostic social facilitation from task-specific human interactions, on-par with hand-crafted task-specific prompts across diverse group settings.
papers.summary: As large language models take on facilitating conversations among several people, they are typically fine-tuned for one task's objective rather than adapting to different task types and group dynamics. `GUIDE` scores facilitation on task outcomes together with subjective measures such as psychological safety and perceived friction, then asks whether a model can learn a general strategy offline: from 432 multi-party human conversations run by task-specific expert facilitators, a model induces an actionable strategic playbook and refines it iteratively using feedback from an LLM judge aligned with 20 human annotators. The resulting single generalized facilitator **beat all three task-specific expert facilitators on held-out conversations with a 61.4% win rate**, and in a real-time online study it preserved facilitator performance and group productivity while improving speaking comfort, reducing interpersonal friction, and using 24.7% fewer turns and 29.0% fewer words than the expert prompts.

papers.title: AutoNovo: Agentic Program Search Discovers Transferable Nucleic Acid Design Algorithms
papers.abstract: In-silico optimization of nucleic acids relies on predictive oracles that imperfectly capture biological function, so sequences optimized against one model may exploit model-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to independent models. Recent studies have shown that not all designers generalize equally well to independent models. In this work, we use agentic program search to iteratively propose, execute, evaluate, and revise code for nucleic-acid designers. We describe the successful strategies used to prompt the search. AutoNovo designers achieved the best observed mean among the evaluated methods on 3/3 DNA-design tasks in terms of in-silico performance, and 6/6 transfer tasks in terms of independent models. The designers come from a family of discovered nucleic acid designers rather than a single universal best designer. We plan to release the resulting designers. These results are the first steps in creating nucleic acid designers that maximize cross-model generalization, and thus improving the odds that in-silico designed sequences reflect real biology.
papers.summary: Computational design of nucleic acid sequences leans on predictive oracles that capture biological function imperfectly, so sequences optimized hard against one model may be exploiting that model's artifacts and fail when scored by an independent one, and prior work shows designers differ in how well they transfer. `AutoNovo` turns agentic program search on the design algorithms themselves, having a model iteratively propose, execute, evaluate, and revise designer code, and the authors document the prompting strategies that made the search productive. The discovered designers **achieved the best observed mean among the evaluated methods on all three DNA design tasks and all six transfer tasks scored by independent models**, emerging as a family of complementary designers rather than one universal best, which the authors plan to release.

papers.title: From Simulated Fluids to Living Tissue: Zero-Shot Foundation Model Transfer to Perturbed Embryos
papers.abstract:
Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics.
  We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17{\deg}C and 27{\deg}C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development.
  Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.
papers.summary: Video of developing embryos under genetic and environmental perturbations is scarce, which makes it hard to train models that generalize beyond wild-type conditions. The authors finetune `Walrus`, a continuum dynamics foundation model pretrained on a broad set of simulated physical systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos, then test autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot on unseen temperature and mutant conditions. A `Fourier Neural Operator` trained from scratch wins in-distribution on VRMSE, but **Walrus is the strongest model on CRPS under the most severe distribution shift to mutated embryos and unseen temperatures**, and its predictions capture the mean tissue velocity trajectory, its separation between 17°C and 27°C, and the timing of the peak at germ band extension onset. The authors present this as preliminary support that representations learned from other continuum systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in low-data regimes.

papers.title: Reflected Proximal Dynamics for Accelerated High-Accuracy Log-Concave Sampling
papers.abstract: We study sampling from $\pi(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ is $\alpha$-strongly convex and $\beta$-smooth with condition number $\kappa=\beta/\alpha$. For this problem, the proximal sampler preserves the target exactly and recovers overdamped Langevin dynamics in the small-step limit, but its Gaussian resampling step discards directional information. Underdamped Langevin dynamics retains such information through momentum to accelerate exploration, motivating a proximal construction that combines target preservation with directional persistence. We introduce \textit{reflected proximal dynamics}, which combines proximal sampling with an exact reflection of the auxiliary variable, conditional kinetic motion, and controlled refreshment. We develop two realizations: a flux-resampled underdamped half-turn and a persistent-momentum quarter-turn. From a warm start with constant $\chi^2$ divergence, both methods achieve total variation error $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde O(\sqrt{\kappa}d^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. We further remove the supplied warm-start assumption by combining either sampler with existing posterior samplers in a proximal initialization stage with an optimized coarse step size. Accounting for both initialization and sampling yields $\widetilde O(\kappa^{6/7}d^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. In both regimes, the dependence on the target accuracy $\varepsilon$ is $\mathrm{polylog}(1/\varepsilon)$, making reflected proximal dynamics a promising framework for accelerated high-accuracy log-concave sampling.
papers.summary: Sampling from a strongly log-concave density is well served by the proximal sampler, which preserves the target exactly but discards directional information in its Gaussian resampling step, whereas underdamped Langevin dynamics keeps momentum for faster exploration. The authors introduce `reflected proximal dynamics`, which pairs proximal sampling with an exact reflection of the auxiliary variable, conditional kinetic motion, and controlled refreshment, realized as a flux-resampled underdamped half-turn and a persistent-momentum quarter-turn. **From a warm start, both samplers reach total variation error epsilon using on the order of the square root of the condition number times the fourth root of the dimension in expected oracle queries**, and dropping the warm-start assumption via a proximal initialization stage with an optimized coarse step size gives a bound of order condition number to the 6/7 times the fourth root of the dimension. In both regimes the dependence on the target accuracy is only polylogarithmic.

papers.title: Avoiding What Your Teacher Already Knows: Entity Familiarity for Deep-Search Distillation
papers.abstract: Deep-search agents are commonly trained by distilling tool-use trajectories from stronger teacher models. However, structurally complex questions may remain relatively easy for teachers familiar with key entities in the underlying entity graph, resulting in lower search demand and weaker supervision. We refer to this teacher-specific variation in question difficulty as teacher-relative difficulty and investigate entity familiarity as an early predictor. We first introduce Evidence-Verified Entity Familiarity (EVF), which estimates familiarity by verifying a teacher-generated factual brief against online evidence. Across multiple teachers, EVF is significantly correlated with teacher-relative difficulty with AUCs of 0.60--0.70. However, its high cost makes it impractical for constructing entity graphs at scale. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Reported Entity Familiarity (SEF), a lightweight gating signal that directly asks a teacher whether it is familiar with an entity before admitting that entity into the graph. Across multiple teachers, trajectories from SEF-gated synthesis exhibit greater observed search demand and yield higher downstream student accuracy than those from ungated synthesis. Because familiarity is teacher specific, we further study cross-teacher reuse. We screen graphs collected for other teachers using Kimi-K3's SEF judgments and use the retained graphs to produce 5,411 additional trajectories. Combined with 2,200 trajectories from newly constructed, SEF-gated graphs, these data improve Qwen3.8-27B's accuracy from 44.10% to 66.41% on a BrowseComp subset, and achieving state-of-the-art performance among models of comparable size on BrowseComp, SEAL-0, HLE-text, and xbench. Overall, SEF provides a low-cost way to synthesize more informative supervision for deep-search distillation.
papers.summary: Deep-search agents are usually trained by distilling tool-use trajectories from a stronger teacher, but questions whose key entities the teacher already knows well require little searching and so produce weak supervision. The authors call this teacher-relative difficulty and propose two predictors: Evidence-Verified Entity Familiarity (EVF), which checks a teacher-written factual brief against online evidence and correlates with difficulty at AUCs of 0.60 to 0.70 but is expensive, and Self-Reported Entity Familiarity (SEF), a cheap gate that simply asks the teacher whether it knows an entity before admitting it into the question graph. SEF-gated synthesis yields trajectories with more observed search demand and higher student accuracy than ungated synthesis, and reusing graphs screened by `Kimi-K3` judgments plus newly gated graphs **raises `Qwen3.8-27B` from 44.10% to 66.41% on a `BrowseComp` subset**, with state-of-the-art results among similar-size models on `BrowseComp`, `SEAL-0`, `HLE-text`, and `xbench`.

papers.title: ScreenASR-Bench: A Tiered Benchmark for Speech Recognition with Visual Context
papers.abstract: Current ASR models perform well on general benchmarks but still struggle with acoustically ambiguous words. Visual context can aid recognition in screen-based scenarios, yet existing benchmarks provide limited insight into the benefits of different types of visual evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ScreenASR-Bench , a tiered benchmark with three progressively challenging levels: Explicit Textual Evidence (ETE), based on direct on-screen text; Explicit Visual Evidence (EVE), using visible content rather than on-screen text; and Implicit Semantic Evidence (ISE), requiring scene-level inference. Extensive experiments on ASR models, Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) and Omni models show that incorporating visual context substantially improves recall over the audio-only setting across all three model families. The gains are largest for ETE and smallest for ISE, indicating that models leverage direct visual evidence more effectively than indirect semantic cues. To facilitate future research on visually grounded speech recognition, we publicly release ScreenASR-Bench.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) models still stumble on acoustically ambiguous words that on-screen context could disambiguate, yet existing benchmarks say little about which kinds of visual evidence actually help. `ScreenASR-Bench` is organized into three tiers of increasing difficulty: Explicit Textual Evidence (ETE), where the answer appears as on-screen text; Explicit Visual Evidence (EVE), where visible content rather than text carries the cue; and Implicit Semantic Evidence (ISE), which demands scene-level inference. Across conventional ASR models, Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs), and omni models, **adding visual context substantially improves recall over audio-only input in all three model families**, with the largest gains on the textual tier and the smallest on the semantic tier. The benchmark is publicly released.

papers.title: Hardware-Friendly Token-Group Activation Quantization for Low-Bit Mamba Super-Resolution
