papers.abstract: Mamba-based super-resolution models are efficient alternatives to Transformer-based restoration backbones, but their low-bit post-training quantization remains challenging because selective scan, Mamba's input-dependent state-space operator, induces different activation ranges across spatial tokens. Thus, a single layer-wise clipping range poorly matches all tokens. We propose Token-Group Quantization, a hardware-friendly activation PTQ framework that statically approximates a hardware-unfriendly post-scan grouping oracle, where tokens with similar preferred clipping ranges are assigned to the same group. To avoid runtime post-scan grouping in static low-bit inference, a lightweight predictor infers the groups from pre-scan features available before the quantized scan path. During calibration, we form pseudo-labels by clustering post-scan activation descriptors that capture similar rounding--clipping behavior. At inference, the frozen predictor maps pre-scan features to groups and selects entries from offline-calibrated group-wise clipping-bound tables, without runtime statistics collection, dynamic clipping updates, or post-scan group assignment. To address low-bit restoration degradation, we further introduce a Frequency-Preserving Refinement (FPR) objective for clipping-bound calibration. FPR aligns Fourier amplitude and phase between full-precision teacher and quantized student outputs to preserve high-frequency structures. Across PTQ protocols, bit-widths, backbones, and tasks, our method consistently outperforms prior Mamba and SR PTQ baselines, transfers to Transformer SR and Vision Mamba classification, composes with rotation-based quantization, and achieves 2.23x speedup on Jetson Orin Nano over FP16. Code is available here.
papers.summary: Mamba-based super-resolution models are efficient alternatives to Transformer restoration backbones, but their selective scan produces activation ranges that vary across spatial tokens, so a single layer-wise clipping range quantizes poorly at low bit-widths. `Token-Group Quantization` is a post-training quantization (PTQ) scheme that statically approximates a post-scan grouping oracle: during calibration, tokens are clustered by their rounding and clipping behavior into pseudo-labels, and a lightweight predictor learns to assign groups from pre-scan features so inference needs no runtime statistics or dynamic clipping. A Frequency-Preserving Refinement (FPR) objective calibrates clipping bounds by aligning Fourier amplitude and phase between the full-precision teacher and quantized student to keep high-frequency detail. The method outperforms prior Mamba and super-resolution PTQ baselines across protocols, bit-widths, and backbones, transfers to Transformer super-resolution and `Vision Mamba` classification, composes with rotation-based quantization, and **achieves a 2.23x speedup over FP16 on a Jetson Orin Nano**.

papers.title: Spectral Considerations on Unsupervised Time-domain EEG Representation Learning with Deep Networks
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a non-invasive, scalable source of quantitative biomarkers for the early diagnosis of brain disorders, and deep representation learning has become a powerful paradigm for extracting information-rich latent features from raw signals. However, neural networks tend to under-represent high-frequency information, a concern that is especially acute for EEG given its oscillatory nature and characteristic $1/f^\chi$ power decay, which risks masking disease-relevant high-frequency signatures. In this study, we systematically investigate the spectral constraints of unsupervised time-domain feature extraction across three autoencoder architectures (LSTMVAE, VAEEG, Transformer) and a state-of-the-art EEG foundation model. Using synthetic experiments and empirical validation, we show that while autoencoders capture macro-scale shifts such as alpha slowing, they remain biased against higher frequencies due to a magnitude-driven masking effect induced by the Mean Squared Error loss under 1/f-decaying spectra. Increasing latent dimensionality mitigates this attenuation but sacrifices latent compactness and generative stability. We argue that, as the field advances toward large-scale foundation-level feature extractors, it is imperative to move beyond simple time-domain reconstruction and to integrate spectral-domain loss terms and gradient-balancing techniques, so that the subtle high-frequency transients critical for diagnosing complex brain disorders are preserved in the latent representation.
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals have a characteristic 1/f power decay, and deep networks tend to under-represent high frequencies, which risks hiding disease-relevant high-frequency signatures in learned features. The authors probe the spectral limits of unsupervised time-domain feature extraction across three autoencoders (`LSTMVAE`, `VAEEG`, and a Transformer) and a state-of-the-art EEG foundation model using synthetic experiments and empirical validation. **Autoencoders capture macro-scale shifts such as alpha slowing but remain biased against higher frequencies, because under a 1/f spectrum the mean squared error loss lets large low-frequency magnitudes mask small high-frequency ones**, and raising latent dimensionality reduces the attenuation only at the cost of compactness and generative stability. They argue that foundation-scale EEG extractors should add spectral-domain loss terms and gradient balancing rather than rely on plain time-domain reconstruction.

papers.title: Error Correction in Trained TTT Layers
papers.abstract: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update fast-weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient-based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction-derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot-product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction-error residual and establish conditions under which inner-loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective used by TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero-epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per-token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8-2.9% on TTT-Linear-760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2-4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta-rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction-derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test-time memory.
papers.summary: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update a fast-weight memory with gradient steps while reading a sequence, but a gradient update alone does not say how the memory revises an existing association. The authors analyze released TTT implementations: for dot-product objectives they show there is no prediction-error residual and that inner-loop ascent and descent coincide after reparameterization, and for the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective of `TTT-Linear` and `TTT-MLP` they derive the inner gradient and find a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization. Measured on three trained checkpoints, removing the normalized prediction's contribution while keeping the LayerNorm Jacobian cuts the gradient norm ratio to 0.25 to 0.32, and on 100,303 tokens of `War and Peace` **this intervention raises perplexity by only 2.8 to 2.9% on `TTT-Linear-760M` and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it 4.2 to 4.5 times**. The authors conclude that implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to judge what test-time memory actually contributes.

papers.title: Deep learning methods for gamma event selection in TAIGA-IACT image analysis in stereo-mode
papers.abstract: In astrophysical complex TAIGA there are four Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs), located at a distance of 300-500 m from each other, due to which extensive air showers (EAS) generated by cosmic and gamma radiation are recorded by a single telescope or by multiple telescopes simultaneously (stereo-mode). The analysis of EAS images from two or more Cherenkov telescopes together is of particular interest, since for this approach the reconstruction of physical parameters of the primary gamma ray is much more accurate than in mono-observations. However, the gamma-ray event reconstruction strongly depends on the quality of the hadron background suppression of the classifier, therefore, the gamma event selection stage is one of the important ones in the further analysis of IACT data. We propose and study several neural network methods for gamma event selection in joint TAIGA-IACT image analysis. Neural network methods we suggested involves a single-stage analysis of IACT images from two telescopes, while the second method considers the formation of autoencoder-derived essential features that contain the EAS physical parameters, including the type of primary particle.
papers.summary: The TAIGA astrophysical complex operates four Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs) spaced 300 to 500 m apart, so extensive air showers (EAS) from cosmic and gamma radiation can be captured by several telescopes at once in stereo mode, which allows far more accurate reconstruction of the primary gamma ray than single-telescope observation. Because reconstruction quality hinges on suppressing the hadron background, the authors propose neural network methods for selecting gamma events from joint two-telescope image analysis. **One approach classifies image pairs from two telescopes in a single stage, while a second first derives autoencoder features that encode the shower's physical parameters, including the primary particle type**.

papers.title: Deep Speech Representations Track Word Timing along a Low-Dimensional Circular Trajectory
papers.abstract: Speech timing is fundamental for speech models to recognize words accurately, but how word-timing information is represented in speech models remains underexplored. We study this question using the framework of representational geometry, which investigates whether and how concepts are represented in low-dimensional subspaces of the representation space. Prior work in cognitive neuroscience has shown that when HuBERT feature sequences are averaged across words of the same duration, they form near-circular trajectories from word onset to word offset in a two-dimensional "temporal subspace." Here we show that this circular structure of word timing is a general property of deep speech representations, by demonstrating its emergence in nine additional speech models covering both supervised and self-supervised. We then move beyond averaged word segments and show that in HuBERT, the circular trajectories are consistent enough at the level of individual words to perform word segmentation. Our approach, Rotary Segmentation (RoSeg), achieves 64.3% boundary F-score on Librispeech by detecting word boundaries when cycles complete in the temporal subspace. Although supervision is needed to identify a good subspace, nevertheless this result demonstrates much stronger implicit word knowledge in HuBERT than has previously been shown.
papers.summary: How speech models encode word timing is poorly understood, though prior cognitive neuroscience work found that `HuBERT` features averaged over words of equal duration trace near-circular paths from onset to offset in a two-dimensional temporal subspace. Using the representational geometry framework, the authors show this circular structure appears in nine additional supervised and self-supervised speech models, suggesting it is a general property of deep speech representations. They then show that in `HuBERT` the trajectories are consistent enough at the level of individual words to drive segmentation: their method, Rotary Segmentation (`RoSeg`), marks a word boundary whenever a cycle completes in the temporal subspace and **reaches a 64.3% boundary F-score on `Librispeech`**. Supervision is still needed to find the right subspace, but the result reveals more implicit word knowledge in `HuBERT` than previously shown.

papers.title: A Survey of Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. We organize the literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled (e.g., action policies, value critics, transition dynamics) and the mechanism of RL signal integration (e.g., energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization). Furthermore, we survey emerging frontiers such as discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, provide a systematic comparative analysis against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and outline critical open problems. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational roadmap for the next generation of generative reinforcement learning and alignment.
papers.summary: Flow Matching (FM) has become a popular way to parameterize expressive, multimodal policies for reinforcement learning (RL), using ordinary differential equation (ODE) sampling with learned velocity fields instead of the stochastic denoising chains of diffusion policies, which lowers inference latency and eases the integration of RL objectives. The survey organizes a fast-growing and fragmented literature along two axes: **what distribution is modeled (action policies, value critics, or transition dynamics) and how the RL signal is injected (energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, or group relative policy optimization)**. It also covers discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, compares flow-based methods systematically against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and lays out open problems across offline control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment.

papers.title: agent-risk: Risk Assessment for Changes to AI Agents
papers.abstract: Before changing a deployed AI agent (a stricter safety gate, a new model), organizations must approve the change, starting from existing logs. Extending classical risk analysis to partial records and partial changes to running systems, agent-risk replays logged episodes, assuming nothing else changes and the agent does not anticipate the change. The log settles episodes acting as before, a declared stop value settles stopped ones, and the rest need logged support, a saved-state rerun, or a bound. We prove what logs must record for exact replay and which saved states serve a gate family. For independent episodes, we bound the reruns a decision needs and tolerable drift from live behavior. In a bash sandbox, a 7,200-episode log alone decided neither of two retry gates, which let the agent act after refusals the log never shows. Rerunning only each gate's blocked episodes from saved states reached both live decisions at half the agent calls of a live test sized post hoc for them, given the log. Without per-step harm, a stopping gate's certified harm ceiling rose up to 2.5-fold, since the log hides whether harm preceded the stop. Approval thus needs evidence designed in advance: log fields, saved states, targeted reruns.
papers.summary: Before changing a deployed AI agent, say by adding a stricter safety gate or swapping the model, an organization must approve the change from the logs it already has, so `agent-risk` replays logged episodes under the assumption that nothing else changes and the agent does not anticipate the change: episodes where the agent would act as before are settled by the log, stopped episodes by a declared stop value, and the rest need logged support, a saved-state rerun, or a bound. The authors prove what a log must record for exact replay, which saved states serve a family of gates, and, for independent episodes, how many reruns a decision needs and how much drift from live behavior is tolerable. In a bash sandbox, **a 7,200-episode log alone could decide neither of two retry gates**, which let the agent act after refusals the log never shows, while rerunning only each gate's blocked episodes from saved states reached both live decisions at half the agent calls of a post-hoc live test. Without per-step harm records, a stopping gate's certified harm ceiling rose up to 2.5-fold because the log hides whether harm preceded the stop, so approval needs evidence designed in advance: log fields, saved states, and targeted reruns.

papers.title: RelLedger: Relational Information Governance for LLM Agent Organizations
papers.abstract: In LLM agent organizations, shared records determine which facts are available for later decisions. A sender consults interaction histories before deciding whether to report an event. A delivery gap across histories does not show whose relationship drove the choice or whether the resulting record matters downstream. We introduce RelLedger to audit these links. It holds the event, evidence, risk, and message fixed while crossing the sender's histories with the event target and an unrelated actor. Role reassignment and history rewrites locate the controlling cue. Message and cost interventions show when the effect appears. An attribution ledger maps each claim to its required response cells and separates missing interventions from sampling uncertainty. Recipient replay follows delivered information into downstream decisions. Executable workflows for a simulated one-person company extend the audit to retrieved histories, tool calls, and shared ledger updates. Across GPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, and Qwen, the audit reveals model-specific control paths and smaller relation gaps under explicit loss rules. Claude sends the same factual notice 62.22 percentage points more often with conflict histories than with friendly histories. In executable workflows, strained histories reduce recipient review rates by 45.83 points relative to warm histories for Claude.
papers.summary: In organizations of large language model (LLM) agents, a sender consults its interaction histories before deciding whether to report an event, and a delivery gap alone does not reveal which relationship drove the choice or whether the record matters downstream. `RelLedger` audits these links by holding the event, evidence, risk, and message fixed while crossing the sender's histories with the event target and an unrelated actor, using role reassignment and history rewrites to locate the controlling cue, message and cost interventions to show when the effect appears, an attribution ledger that maps each claim to its required response cells, and recipient replay that follows delivered information into later decisions. Across `GPT`, `Gemini`, `Claude`, `DeepSeek`, and `Qwen`, the audit finds model-specific control paths and smaller relation gaps under explicit loss rules. **`Claude` sends the same factual notice 62.22 percentage points more often after conflict histories than after friendly ones**, and in executable workflows for a simulated one-person company, strained histories cut `Claude` recipients' review rates by 45.83 points relative to warm histories.

papers.title: Moment-Based Anomaly Detection in High-Dimensional Mixed Data
papers.abstract: We propose an anomaly detection method for high-dimensional mixed-type data that maps heterogeneous features to a common scale via standardized moment-based transformations, yielding interpretable feature-level anomaly scores. These scores are combined through a dependence-aware aggregation step to construct the Mixed-data Influence (MDI) score, accounting for correlations across features and providing a unified measure of how strongly an observation departs from the reference data distribution. By incorporating higher-order moments, the MDI can detect anomalies that arise not only from location shifts, but also from changes in variability, skewness, and other distributional characteristics. The aggregation mechanism allows our method to capture both sparse anomalies concentrated in a small number of features and weak, coordinated deviations distributed across many features. We empirically investigate the distribution and thresholding behavior of the MDI score across different sample sizes, dimensions, dependence structures, and data types. Simulation experiments and two real-data applications, to multi-omics and ESG data, evaluate finite-sample calibration, detection performance, and feature-level interpretability.
papers.summary: Anomaly detection in high-dimensional data with mixed feature types is hard because heterogeneous features lack a common scale and anomalies may show up as shifts in variability or skewness rather than location. The method maps each feature through standardized moment-based transformations to produce interpretable feature-level anomaly scores, then combines them with a dependence-aware aggregation step into the Mixed-data Influence (MDI) score, which accounts for correlations across features and measures how far an observation departs from the reference distribution. **Because it uses higher-order moments and a correlation-aware aggregation, the MDI score can flag both sparse anomalies confined to a few features and weak, coordinated deviations spread across many**. Simulations across sample sizes, dimensions, dependence structures, and data types, plus applications to multi-omics and ESG data, examine calibration, detection performance, and feature-level interpretability.

papers.title: REVEAL: Reverse Engineering Agentic Latents from Frontier-Model Traces
papers.abstract: Frontier LLM agents perform complex interactive tasks, but their inference costs motivate transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents. Distillation and latent communication typically require target-model training or access to source-model internals. We study how textual frontier-model trajectories can provide reusable local controls for a frozen agent. Inspired by protocol reverse engineering, we introduce $\textit{Agentic Latents}$, comprising anchored states and dynamic profiles of feedback--response cycles elicited by replay in the target model. Our training-free framework, $\textbf{REVEAL}$ ($\textbf{REV}$erse $\textbf{E}$ngineering $\textbf{A}$gentic $\textbf{L}$atents), uses these profiles and trajectory outcomes to match and select local events from successful and failed rollouts of the same task and source model. Their response-transition contrasts yield a target-specific steering direction, applied before each response. Within-benchmark evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity's Last Exam with tools report higher accuracy than unmodified agents across three targets. Representation analyses and behavioral case studies support reusing frontier-model experience as local activation control.
papers.summary: Frontier LLM agents are expensive to run, and transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents usually requires training the target model or access to the source model's internals. Borrowing from protocol reverse engineering, the authors define `Agentic Latents`, consisting of anchored states and dynamic profiles of feedback-response cycles obtained by replaying textual frontier-model trajectories through the frozen target model. The training-free `REVEAL` (Reverse Engineering Agentic Latents) framework uses these profiles and trajectory outcomes to match local events from successful and failed rollouts of the same task, and the contrast in their response transitions yields a target-specific steering direction applied before each response. **Across three target models, steered agents score higher than unmodified agents on `Terminal-Bench 2.1` and on `Humanity's Last Exam` with tools**, and representation analyses and case studies support reusing frontier experience as local activation control.

papers.title: Fast Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss Transforms
papers.abstract:
Quantization has emerged as one of the primary techniques for reducing the memory footprint of large language models during inference. A prominent example is Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss (QJL), which compresses KV caches using 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products required by the attention mechanism. Recent theoretical and practical work aims at replacing the dense Gaussian projections used by the aforementioned transforms with more structured embeddings $-$ such as compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms $-$ while retaining the same embedding dimension.
  In this paper, we introduce two constructions based on a composition of randomized Hadamard transforms, albeit with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage. The first adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, while the second inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance structure of the resulting Gaussian measurements.
  We prove embedding-dimension and running-time guarantees analogous to those of Fast JL in the non-quantized setting. The first construction achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(d/\delta))$, while the second achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d/\delta))$ under a restriction on $m$. Both constructions can be applied in $O(d\log d)$ time.
papers.summary: Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss (QJL) transforms compress key-value caches for LLM inference with 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products attention needs, but they rely on dense Gaussian projections that are slow to apply. The authors propose two constructions built from compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage: one adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, the other inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance of the Gaussian measurements. **Both can be applied in O(d log d) time, with the first achieving embedding dimension proportional to log²(d/δ)/ε² and the second the tighter log(d/δ)/ε² under a restriction on the embedding dimension**, matching the guarantees of `Fast JL` in the unquantized setting.

papers.title: SLDBench v2: Active Scaling Law Discovery
papers.abstract: Scaling laws predict large-model performance from small experiments, but finding a reliable law itself requires costly experiments. SLDBench tests whether language-model agents can discover scaling laws when all experimental results are given upfront. We introduce SLDBench v2 with two extensions. First, we expand the corpus from 8 to 127 scenarios spanning language-model pretraining, downstream performance, and vision-language transfer, and select 30 challenging scenarios on which a reference power-law fit reaches $R^2 \le 0.8$; they represent at least $1.09 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs of source-reported training compute. Second, we introduce active scaling law discovery: an agent chooses which experiments to run, pays each one's recorded cost (e.g., training FLOPs), and revises its law as outcomes arrive, and is scored on the same hidden extrapolation targets as in the passive setting. Across 8 frontier agent systems, median $R^2$ drops from 0.72-0.75 (passive) to 0.24-0.57 (active), and prediction error rises 1.5-4.7 times, depending on the system. Agents favor cheap experiments, spending 8-44% of the full-pool cost on average; low-cost acquisition can yield strong predictions, but cheap purchases also leave experimental conditions needed for extrapolation unobserved. Experimental planning thus remains a key open challenge for agents that assist model development in the prevailing AI-for-AI study.
papers.summary: Scaling laws let practitioners predict large-model performance from small runs, but discovering a reliable law is itself expensive, and `SLDBench` tested whether language-model agents could do so when every experimental result was handed over upfront. `SLDBench v2` expands the corpus from 8 to 127 scenarios spanning pretraining, downstream performance, and vision-language transfer, selects 30 hard scenarios where a reference power-law fit gets R² at or below 0.8 (representing at least 1.09 × 10²³ FLOPs of reported training compute), and adds an active setting in which the agent chooses which experiments to buy at their recorded cost and revises its law as results arrive. **Across 8 frontier agent systems, median R² falls from 0.72 to 0.75 in the passive setting to 0.24 to 0.57 in the active one**, with prediction error rising 1.5 to 4.7 times. Agents favor cheap experiments, spending 8 to 44% of the full-pool cost on average, and while cheap acquisition can work, it often leaves the conditions needed for extrapolation unobserved.

papers.title: Memory-Efficient Integer-Only Training of Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Training neural networks in reduced precision can yield significant efficiency gains, yet all existing methods that scale to standard computer vision benchmarks retain floating-point in at least one stage, typically the weight update or optimizer state. We present a training algorithm that scales to modern deep neural networks, in which every tensor (weights, gradients, and activations) is stored as INT8, and every operation (forward pass, backward pass, weight update, optimizer update) is performed in integer arithmetic. Specifically, tensors are stored as signed integer mantissas paired with explicit power-of-two exponents, on which integer-only operations are performed using five custom composable building blocks (products, sums, divide-by-constant, nonlinear functions, and weight updates). This allows complete implementation of trainable integer layers, including convolutions, batch and layer normalization, softmax, and GELU. A per-group velocity mechanism with independent exponent tracking preserves gradient precision across neurons and channels with diverse magnitudes. As every tensor fits in INT8, training memory is roughly 4x smaller than the FP32 baseline. We validate our training algorithm on CNNs (ResNet-18/34/50/101, MobileNetV2) and Vision Transformers (ViT-Ti / B), demonstrating for the first time that training neural networks with INT8 tensors and integer arithmetic can achieve competitive accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet at a reduced memory budget.
papers.summary: Reduced-precision training promises large efficiency gains, but every prior method that scales to standard vision benchmarks keeps floating point somewhere, usually in the weight update or optimizer state. The authors present a training algorithm in which every tensor (weights, gradients, activations) is stored as INT8 and every operation, including the forward pass, backward pass, weight update, and optimizer update, runs in integer arithmetic: tensors are signed integer mantissas with explicit power-of-two exponents, five composable integer building blocks implement products, sums, divide-by-constant, nonlinearities, and updates, and a per-group velocity mechanism with independent exponent tracking preserves gradient precision across channels of differing magnitude. This yields trainable integer convolutions, batch and layer normalization, softmax, and GELU, with **training memory roughly 4x smaller than an FP32 baseline**. Experiments on `ResNet-18/34/50/101`, `MobileNetV2`, and `ViT-Ti/B` show competitive accuracy on `CIFAR-10`, `CIFAR-100`, and `ImageNet`, which the authors describe as the first demonstration of fully integer INT8 training at this scale.

papers.title: FON: A Draft-Revise Dual-Organ Language Model without Sequence-Level Quadratic Attention
papers.abstract: Self-attention assigns two functions to one mechanism-where to read and how to mix-at the price of O(L^2) training, an O(T) decode state, and position signals bound to the training length. Existing attention-free alternatives all optimize the single function of generation. We propose FON (Fusion-Organ Network), which differentiates one weight stack into a drafting organ (multi-tap learnable delays + content-adaptive recursion; causal, O(S) training, O(1) decode state, no sequence-level quadratic attention) and a revision organ that re-processes the written prefix through multi-scale ripple kernels injected via weak gates, never generating. At 30M parameters, iso-parameter and iso-token budget, FON reaches perplexity 131.03 on WikiText-103, beating Transformer (197.73) and Mamba2 (152.53); the advantage persists under all depth-aligned baselines and at the 70M tier (-20.8%). At 8x length extrapolation FON degrades by ~8-9% without positional-encoding engineering, between ALiBi and RoPE. The revision channel provides a structural pathway for in-domain infilling that causal architectures lack in principle (+19% over on-demand coupling), at a perplexity cost indistinguishable within measurement precision. We report all costs and boundaries: impaired long-range retrieval, synthetic-task disadvantages, weaker out-of-domain code infilling than a same-recipe Transformer, and a 6.5-12.3x wall-clock gap.
papers.summary: Self-attention bundles two jobs, deciding where to read and how to mix, into one mechanism that costs quadratic training time, a decode state that grows with sequence length, and position signals tied to the training length, while existing attention-free alternatives optimize only for generation. `FON` (Fusion-Organ Network) splits one weight stack into a drafting organ built from multi-tap learnable delays and content-adaptive recursion (causal, linear-time training, constant decode state) and a revision organ that re-reads the written prefix through multi-scale ripple kernels injected via weak gates but never generates. **At 30M parameters under matched parameter and token budgets, `FON` reaches 131.03 perplexity on `WikiText-103` versus 197.73 for a `Transformer` and 152.53 for `Mamba2`**, the advantage holds at the 70M tier, and 8x length extrapolation degrades by about 8 to 9% without positional-encoding engineering. The revision channel enables in-domain infilling that causal architectures lack, but the authors also report impaired long-range retrieval, weaker synthetic-task and out-of-domain code infilling results, and a 6.5 to 12.3x wall-clock gap.

papers.title: ATTCK-R: Knowledge-Aware Long-Horizon Jailbreaking for Protected LLMs
papers.abstract: As large language models are deployed behind increasingly sophisticated safety mechanisms, evaluating their robustness under realistic adversarial conditions becomes increasingly difficult and critical. Existing jailbreaking evaluations often rely on static prompts, limited interaction horizons, or lightly protected systems, failing to reflect protected deployment settings with prompt-based safety protections. We show that the introduction of a prompt-based safety protection reduces the average attack success rate of a strong multi-turn baseline from 0.896 to 0.608 (32.1\% relative), demonstrating that unprotected evaluations substantially overestimate real-world vulnerabilities. We propose Adaptive Traceback and Tactic Curation for Knowledge-based Red-teaming (ATTCK-R), a planning-driven multi-turn red teaming framework designed for protected black-box systems. ATTCK-R models jailbreaking as a long-horizon trajectory optimization problem using a structured belief state, introduces optimization-based tactic curation to abstract reusable strategies from prior successes and failures, and employs informed traceback to resume attacks from strategically meaningful states rather than restarting. Evaluated across 9 widely used LLMs configured with a single prompt-based safety protection layer, ATTCK-R consistently outperforms strong recent multi-turn jailbreaking frameworks. Ablation results confirm that long-horizon planning and tactic curation improve attack effectiveness, while adaptive traceback improves efficiency through structured recovery from conversational failure.
papers.summary: Jailbreak evaluations typically use static prompts, short interactions, or lightly protected models, so they overstate the vulnerability of deployed systems that sit behind prompt-based safety protections. The authors first show that adding a single prompt-based protection layer **drops the average attack success rate of a strong multi-turn baseline from 0.896 to 0.608**, a 32.1% relative reduction. They then propose `ATTCK-R` (Adaptive Traceback and Tactic Curation for Knowledge-based Red-teaming), which treats jailbreaking as long-horizon trajectory optimization over a structured belief state, curates reusable tactics from prior successes and failures, and uses informed traceback to resume from strategically useful conversational states instead of restarting. Across 9 widely used LLMs with a prompt-based safety layer, `ATTCK-R` outperforms recent multi-turn jailbreaking frameworks, with ablations attributing effectiveness to planning and tactic curation and efficiency to traceback.

papers.title: Narrative Paradoxes in LLM Inference: Shaping Reasoning Trajectories toward Misalignment
papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often associated with reliability, yet it can still pose risks when a model infers harmful goals under a benign context. We identify a distinct challenge: ensuring the safety of the \emph{multi-step reasoning process} itself, where locally coherent steps may still lead to globally harmful outcomes. To explore this vulnerability, we propose PDRA (Paradox-driven Reasoning-based Attack), a novel attack method that programs a harmful reasoning trajectory. PDRA first constructs a paradoxical narrative core by pairing a malicious actor (e.g., a terrorist) with a benign task (e.g., writing a safety bulletin). It then embeds this core into a structured analytical framework that forces the model through a mandatory three-stage analysis -- surface purpose, latent intent, and operational reconstruction -- guiding it to produce detailed harmful content while maintaining narrative coherence. Mechanistically, we show PDRA steers the model's internal representations away from refusal-related patterns, suppressing safety-triggering lexicons while activating planning-oriented terms. Empirically, PDRA achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates across diverse LLMs with high efficiency. \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Warning:} This paper may contain sensitive content.}
papers.summary: Explicit reasoning is often treated as a reliability feature, yet a chain of locally coherent steps can still carry a model to a globally harmful output when it infers harmful goals from a benign-looking context. `PDRA` (Paradox-driven Reasoning-based Attack) builds a paradoxical narrative core by pairing a malicious actor, such as a terrorist, with a benign task, such as writing a safety bulletin, then wraps it in an analytical framework that forces a mandatory three-stage analysis of surface purpose, latent intent, and operational reconstruction, steering the model toward detailed harmful content while preserving narrative coherence. Mechanistically, the attack **pushes internal representations away from refusal-related patterns, suppressing safety-triggering vocabulary while activating planning-oriented terms**. The authors report state-of-the-art attack success rates across diverse LLMs with high efficiency.

papers.title: ReTAC: Residual Test-Time Agentic Computation for Video Spatial Reasoning
papers.abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.
papers.summary: Adding planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection at test time can help multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on video spatial reasoning, but applying extra computation indiscriminately can redo already-solved work, inject noisy evidence, and overturn correct predictions. `ReTAC` is a training-free multi-agent framework that spends computation only on requirements the base model leaves unresolved: it plans ordered steps to gather missing spatial evidence, combines the observations with compatible native evidence, uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning, and after a failure recomputes only the dependent states while reusing the rest. **It achieves the highest overall score among compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely used benchmarks**, and further analysis shows the gains depend on where computation is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved, not just on how much is spent.

papers.title: Strong yet Controllable LLM Abstention without Learning to Abstain
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reduce hallucination by abstaining from questions they would likely get wrong. Abstention can be implemented outside the model (selective answering) using a confidence threshold that controls the answer rate (coverage), or learned inside it (abstention training), which can perform better but fixes coverage once trained. To compare the two, we match their coverage and decompose risk (error rate) into answering ability and distinguishing ability, i.e., how well the model answers and how accurately it abstains, respectively. The decomposition shows that abstention training performs better mainly by answering better: with strong confidence estimators, the two have nearly equal distinguishing ability. This motivates Train for Accuracy, then Post-hoc Select (TAPS), a modular approach that keeps coverage controllable, needs only standard post-training and an off-the-shelf confidence estimator, and benefits from advances in either component. Across three LLMs and three factual QA benchmarks, TAPS with a probing-based confidence estimator attains 1.5--9.4 percentage points lower mean risk than three representative abstention training methods at matched coverage. Within TAPS, accuracy training often weakens the model's own confidence signals, yet refitting the estimator largely preserves distinguishing ability. Together, these results establish TAPS as a strong yet controllable baseline and raise the bar for future abstention training: sacrificing control over coverage should yield gains beyond what can be achieved by optimizing answering and abstaining separately.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can cut hallucinations by abstaining on questions they are likely to get wrong, either through a post-hoc confidence threshold that controls the answer rate or through abstention training that bakes a fixed coverage level into the model. By matching coverage and decomposing risk into answering ability and distinguishing ability, the authors find that abstention training wins mainly by answering better, since with strong confidence estimators both approaches separate answerable from unanswerable questions about equally well. Their proposed `TAPS` (Train for Accuracy, then Post-hoc Select) trains only for accuracy and adds an off-the-shelf confidence estimator, and with a probing-based estimator it **reaches 1.5 to 9.4 percentage points lower mean risk than three abstention training methods at matched coverage** across three LLMs and three factual QA benchmarks. Accuracy training tends to degrade a model's own confidence signals, but refitting the estimator recovers most of the distinguishing ability.

papers.title: HyWe: Unifying Search and Operation for Real-World Hybrid Web Tasks
papers.abstract: Real-world hybrid web tasks need both information gathering and page interaction, yet search-based and operation-based agents are developed and evaluated separately. To bridge this gap, we introduce HyWe, a framework that unifies both capabilities within one model and trajectory. Its two modes use dedicated prompts and tool sets to sustain sub-goal execution; explicit switching selects the needed capability, and shared history lets each mode build on the other's findings. To provide demonstrations of these behaviors, we develop HyWeCollector, a fully automatic pipeline that uses task prototypes, four switching patterns, and multi-agent synthesis to produce verified hybrid trajectories. We train HyWe-35B on these demonstrations to unify efficient information gathering and browser interaction in a single 35B web agent. To evaluate hybrid task completion, we introduce HyWeBench: 100 human-written tasks on websites distinct from training, with human-written sub-goal checklists and an outcome-based evaluation pipeline. Hybrid training enables HyWe-35B to achieve 47.0% success on this benchmark, improving on the untrained base model by 19.0 percentage points and outperforming existing search-based and operation-based agents. Even before training, the same base model solves 28.0% of tasks with HyWe, versus 11.0% with all tools under one prompt. Beyond hybrid tasks, HyWe-35B achieves 59.0% and 88.3% success on Online-Mind2Web and WebVoyager, outperforming existing open-source baselines and cutting action cost per successful task by 48.3% and 51.9% compared with Fara-7B.
papers.summary: Real-world web tasks often require both searching for information and operating on pages, yet search-based and operation-based agents are typically built and evaluated in isolation. `HyWe` puts both capabilities in one model and one trajectory, with two modes that have dedicated prompts and tool sets, explicit switching between them, and shared history, while an automatic pipeline called `HyWeCollector` synthesizes verified hybrid trajectories from task prototypes and four switching patterns. The resulting `HyWe-35B` reaches **47.0% success on the new 100-task `HyWeBench`, 19.0 percentage points above its untrained base**, and also posts 59.0% on `Online-Mind2Web` and 88.3% on `WebVoyager` while roughly halving the action cost per successful task compared with `Fara-7B`. Even without training, the same base model solves 28.0% of hybrid tasks under the mode-switching design versus 11.0% with all tools in a single prompt.

papers.title: BehaviorFormer: Discovering Behavioral Patterns via Clusterable Next-Token Prediction
papers.abstract: Discovering behavioral patterns in open-ended games is challenging due to the lack of clear objectives or ground-truth annotations. In this work, we extend a next-token prediction Transformer with the deep clustering algorithm DCSS to learn meaningful representations with well-separated clusters. In a controlled Minecraft session with 26 players, the method discovers 23 distinct behavioral patterns that generalize across the studied players, further refining structures present in self-supervised representations into clearly separable clusters. We group the clusters into seven interpretable categories covering stationary, roaming, travel, mining, base work, logging, and farming behavior.
papers.summary: Open-ended games lack clear objectives or ground-truth annotations, which makes discovering player behavioral patterns difficult. The authors extend a next-token prediction Transformer with the deep clustering algorithm `DCSS` so that the learned representations form well-separated clusters, refining structure already present in self-supervised features. On a controlled `Minecraft` session with 26 players, the method **discovers 23 distinct behavioral patterns that generalize across the studied players**, which the authors group into seven interpretable categories covering stationary, roaming, travel, mining, base work, logging, and farming behavior.

papers.title: When a Conceptor Complement Becomes Gain: Operator Geometry and Behavioral Attribution in Language Models
papers.abstract: When a steering intervention changes a language model's behavior, which part of the intervention deserves the credit? We test this question for a target-centered, scaled conceptor complement by removing its fitted covariance filter while preserving the same target-specific center and gain. At the original aperture $\alpha=.05$ and gain $\beta=2$, all 21 fitted maps across three models and seven targets expand every direction at the generation intervention layers. The matrix correction is $0.093\%$--$7.815\%$ of the matched-control displacement on held-out extraction activations. In 480 paired comparisons within a 1,920-response study, retaining the matrix changes many individual texts but does not establish a consistent additional target-suppression benefit on the four-target panel. A geometric aperture sweep shows that the operating regime changes with the filter setting. Separately, an invertible soft filter preserves what an unrestricted affine readout can recover, whereas dedicated erasure methods reduce prediction by newly fitted probes. Together, the results show why a whole-intervention comparison cannot by itself attribute generated behavior to the fitted matrix: analyze the complete transformation, hold shared components fixed, and test its output consequences directly.
papers.summary: When a steering intervention changes a language model's behavior, it is unclear which part of the intervention deserves the credit. The authors test a target-centered, scaled conceptor complement by removing its fitted covariance filter while keeping the same target-specific center and gain, and find that at the original aperture and gain settings all 21 fitted maps across three models and seven targets expand every direction at the generation intervention layers, with the matrix correction amounting to only **0.093% to 7.815% of the matched-control displacement** on held-out activations. In 480 paired comparisons from a 1,920-response study, retaining the matrix changes many individual texts but does not establish a consistent additional target-suppression benefit on the four-target panel, an aperture sweep shows the operating regime shifts with the filter setting, and an invertible soft filter preserves what an unrestricted affine readout can recover whereas dedicated erasure methods do reduce prediction by newly fitted probes. The authors conclude that a whole-intervention comparison cannot by itself attribute generated behavior to the fitted matrix, and that one should analyze the complete transformation, hold shared components fixed, and test output consequences directly.

papers.title: Probabilistic Simulation of Gas-Liquid Interfaces with Coupled Flow Matching on Spherical Harmonics
papers.abstract: Bubbly flows involve strongly coupled bubble motion, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions, making high-fidelity simulation computationally expensive. We propose a neural surrogate that jointly predicts bubble trajectories and interface deformation in a compact, shared representation, replacing costly mesh-resolved simulation with fast generative inference. Because two-phase flow dynamics is nonlinear and chaotic, we treat forecasting as a conditional generative problem rather than deterministic regression, predicting entire future windows in a single pass. We train and evaluate the surrogate on BubbleSH, a Front-Tracking dataset of rising deformable bubble swarms, assessing performance using trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics over kinematic, morphological, and interaction-based properties. The surrogate reproduces key flow statistics while running several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.
papers.summary: High-fidelity simulation of bubbly flows is expensive because bubble motion, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions are tightly coupled. The proposed neural surrogate jointly predicts bubble trajectories and interface deformation in a compact shared spherical-harmonics representation, and because two-phase flow is nonlinear and chaotic it treats forecasting as conditional generation with flow matching, producing entire future windows in a single pass rather than deterministic regression. Trained and evaluated on `BubbleSH`, a Front-Tracking dataset of rising deformable bubble swarms, the surrogate **reproduces key flow statistics while running several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying direct numerical simulation solver** on trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics.

papers.title: Explicitly Aligned Multi-View Breast Cancer Risk Prediction from Variable-Length Screening Histories
papers.abstract: Accurate breast cancer risk prediction from screening mammography is essential for improved risk stratification and personalized screening. It can benefit from both temporal breast tissue changes across longitudinal examinations and complementary anatomical information from craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) views. Leveraging longitudinal information requires identifying corresponding tissue regions across examinations, yet most approaches rely on implicit feature alignment without explicitly enforcing spatial consistency. Recent work has demonstrated the benefits of explicit temporal alignment; however, existing methods model each view independently, preventing them from exploiting complementary CC and MLO information. Furthermore, explicit approaches have been limited to a single prior examination. To fill these gaps, we propose (github.com/sot176/FlexLMV-Net), a breast-wise longitudinal multi-view framework that jointly models CC and MLO views across screening examinations while accommodating a variable number of prior examinations. FlexLMV-Net explicitly aligns longitudinal feature maps and integrates complementary views through cross-view temporal fusion and a dual-stream attention block. Evaluated on EMBED and CSAW-CC, FlexLMV-Net consistently outperforms existing approaches across breast density, cancer subtypes, and demographic subgroups, highlighting the benefits of explicit longitudinal alignment, multi-view modeling, and flexible use of available screening history. We further introduce (github.com/sot176/BCRBench), an open-source benchmark that unifies state-of-the-art single- and multi-timepoint breast cancer risk prediction models under standardized preprocessing, training, inference, and evaluation protocols, enabling fair and reproducible comparison of existing methods.
papers.summary: Breast cancer risk prediction from screening mammography can draw on both tissue changes across longitudinal exams and complementary anatomy from craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) views, but prior methods either align exams only implicitly, model each view independently, or handle just a single prior exam. `FlexLMV-Net` is a breast-wise longitudinal multi-view framework that explicitly aligns feature maps across a variable number of prior exams and fuses CC and MLO views through cross-view temporal fusion and a dual-stream attention block. **On `EMBED` and `CSAW-CC` it consistently outperforms existing approaches** across breast density, cancer subtypes, and demographic subgroups. The authors also release `BCRBench`, an open-source benchmark that standardizes preprocessing, training, inference, and evaluation for single- and multi-timepoint risk prediction models.

papers.title: BAT3R: Robust Online 3D Reconstruction with Bayesian Adaptive State Updates
papers.abstract: Feed-forward transformer models have driven remarkable progress in 3D vision,yet their quadratic complexity renders them impractical for long video sequences. Streaming 3D reconstruction addresses this bottleneck by processing frames sequen?tially with constant memory. However, existing recurrent architectures inevitably suffer from progressive degradation over long sequences, as they fail to account for the intrinsic reliability of observations and the accumulated confidence of the historical state, leading to severe error accumulation. To address these issues, we introduce BAT3R, a training-free Bayesian adaptation framework comprising two synergistic modules: State Innovation Gating (SIG) and Bayesian-guided Adaptive State Updating (BASU). SIG acts as a distributional regularizer that anchors state evolution to its geometric initialization, effectively arresting representational drift during long-term inference. Building on this, BASU reformulates state update as a recursive Bayesian inference process within a Kalman filtering framework. By jointly modeling the temporal reliability of observations via information-theoretic gain and spatial relevance via cross-attention maps, BASU achieves an asymmetric spatio-temporal state fusion: well-consolidated historical regions are protected from redundant updates, while genuinely novel scene content is aggressively incor?porated. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks (7-Scenes, TUM, ScanNet, KITTI, etc.) demonstrate that BAT3R consistently outperforms state-of-the-art online 3D reconstruction methods, with the most significant gains observed on long sequences and complex scenes.
papers.summary: Streaming 3D reconstruction processes video frames sequentially with constant memory, but existing recurrent architectures degrade over long sequences because they ignore the reliability of each observation and the accumulated confidence of the historical state. `BAT3R` is a training-free Bayesian adaptation with two modules: State Innovation Gating (SIG), which anchors state evolution to its geometric initialization to arrest representational drift, and Bayesian-guided Adaptive State Updating (BASU), which recasts the state update as recursive Bayesian inference in a Kalman filtering framework using information-theoretic gain for temporal reliability and cross-attention maps for spatial relevance. This yields asymmetric fusion in which well-consolidated regions are protected from redundant updates while genuinely novel content is incorporated aggressively. **On `7-Scenes`, `TUM`, `ScanNet`, `KITTI`, and other benchmarks it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art online reconstruction methods**, with the largest gains on long sequences and complex scenes.

papers.title: TRAP: Tool-result Replay Attack for Probing Misbinding in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: As AI agents increasingly act through external tools, tool results are no longer simple outputs but execution artifacts that must remain correctly associated with the context that produced them. Yet as results persist across caches, recovery mechanisms, and shared runtime state, this association can break, causing a real and unmodified result to be consumed in an incompatible execution context and lead the agent to an unsafe action. We characterize this failure as tool-result misbinding. To systematically study this failure, we introduce ReplayBench, a benchmark that uses controlled tool-result replay to evaluate misbinding across 19 representative agent scenarios, 4 failure properties, and 3 replay mechanisms. Across eight LLMs, three agent frameworks, and diverse stateful workflows, we find widespread replay-induced failures, with a mean Final-State Error Rate of 0.649 under cross-task replay. Stage-wise analysis localizes these failures to model-side action generation. Further analyses show that replay susceptibility varies with task similarity, shows little dependence on object similarity, and remains high under result staleness and implicit environment changes. These findings motivate runtime validity mechanisms that eliminate final-state errors in our evaluated settings while preserving legitimate recovery. The results call for explicit contextual binding in tool-using agent runtimes. Our work is public at https://github.com/Phitooo/Replaybench.
papers.summary: As agents act through external tools, each tool result must stay correctly bound to the execution context that produced it, yet caches, recovery mechanisms, and shared runtime state can cause a genuine, unmodified result to be consumed in an incompatible context and push the agent toward an unsafe action, a failure the authors call tool-result misbinding. `ReplayBench` uses controlled tool-result replay to evaluate this failure across 19 representative agent scenarios, 4 failure properties, and 3 replay mechanisms, and across eight large language models (LLMs) and three agent frameworks replay-induced failures are widespread, with **a mean Final-State Error Rate of 0.649 under cross-task replay**. Stage-wise analysis localizes the failures to model-side action generation, and susceptibility rises with task similarity, shows little dependence on object similarity, and stays high under stale results and implicit environment changes. Runtime validity mechanisms eliminate the final-state errors in the evaluated settings while preserving legitimate recovery, motivating explicit contextual binding in tool-using agent runtimes.

papers.title: WorldRoPE: Probabilistic World-Centric Rotary Embedding for Multi-View Attention
papers.abstract: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) is widely used to encode relative positions in Transformers. In multi-view settings, however, patch coordinates are defined independently in each image: the same 3D point can therefore have different coordinates across views, making them insufficient for establishing cross-view correspondences. We introduce WorldRoPE, a probabilistic world-centric RoPE for multi-view attention. At each layer, WorldRoPE back-projects each patch token into a set of volumetric Gaussian primitives in a shared world frame. These primitives represent multiple plausible 3D supports for a token, jointly capturing alternative depth hypotheses, depth uncertainty, and the finite spatial extent of its patch frustum. When a key token's support is projected into a query view, it induces a distribution over where that key may appear in the query image. WorldRoPE integrates the rotary operator over this distribution in closed form, combining rotations at the projected primitive centers according to their mixture weights with covariance-dependent attenuation. This makes attention less sensitive to uncertain key locations in the query view, without rasterizing or warping token features. The formulation reduces to deterministic RoPE when the support collapses to a point. Across layers, the predicted geometry guides cross-view attention, while the updated features refine the geometry used at the next layer. Experiments on novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRoPE for multi-view Transformers.
papers.summary: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) encodes relative positions within a single image, but in multi-view settings the same 3D point receives different patch coordinates in each view, so per-image positions cannot establish cross-view correspondence. `WorldRoPE` back-projects each patch token at every layer into a set of volumetric Gaussian primitives in a shared world frame, capturing alternative depth hypotheses, depth uncertainty, and the finite extent of the patch frustum. Projecting a key token's primitives into the query view induces a distribution over where that key may appear, and the rotary operator is integrated over this distribution in closed form with covariance-dependent attenuation, which reduces to ordinary deterministic RoPE when the support collapses to a point. Predicted geometry guides cross-view attention while updated features refine the geometry at the next layer, and **experiments on novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction demonstrate its effectiveness for multi-view Transformers**.

papers.title: Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning via Confidence-Guided Adaptive Debate
papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate has shown promise for improving the reasoning of large language models, yet recent theory suggests its benefits are highly regime-dependent. While interaction can amplify informative signals under corrective conditions, symmetric debate dynamics are neutral in expectation, often making majority voting preferable. We reconcile these views by arguing that debate is effective only when invoked at the right time and with appropriate structure. Based on this insight, we propose LASE: Leader-Adaptive Structured Engagement, a leader-centric multi-agent debate framework that selectively engages interaction only in non-neutral regimes. LASE introduces an asymmetric leader-supporter architecture that enables directed information flow and selective signal amplification, while defaulting to simple aggregation otherwise. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks show that LASE achieves multi-agent-level performance with near single-agent token cost, substantially improving efficiency over static debate and voting baselines.
papers.summary: Multi-agent debate can improve large language model reasoning, but recent theory indicates that symmetric debate is neutral in expectation and often loses to simple majority voting, with gains appearing only under corrective conditions. `LASE` (Leader-Adaptive Structured Engagement) reconciles this by invoking debate only when confidence signals indicate a non-neutral regime, using an asymmetric leader-supporter architecture for directed information flow and selective signal amplification, and defaulting to plain aggregation otherwise. Across diverse reasoning benchmarks it **matches multi-agent-level accuracy at close to single-agent token cost**, substantially improving efficiency over static debate and voting baselines.

papers.title: ChronoScribe: Semantic-Numerical Specialization for Instruction-Driven Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Recent advances in instruction-driven time series forecasting highlight a fundamental tension: systems must simultaneously master natural-language instruction following and precise numerical prediction. Current approaches often force a compromise. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret unstructured requests but may be inaccurate when asked to produce forecast values directly, whereas time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide numerical forecasts but typically require structured inputs specifying the target series, context window, and horizon. We present ChronoScribe, which applies semantic-numerical specialization to this workflow. A LoRA-adapted LLM proposes an execution path and context length; deterministic rules resolve the executable configuration. On the specialist path, a frozen TSFM produces quantile trajectories for the task-specified horizon. Deterministic trajectory summaries condition the response, while the LLM neither generates nor revises predicted values. We evaluate a Qwen3.5-9B--Chronos-2 implementation across 23 evaluation dimensions and 30 public datasets against eleven proprietary direct LLMs and three open TSFMs. ChronoScribe has the lowest error on sMAPE, MASE, WAPE, RMSE, and MAE among all evaluated systems, including fixed-context controls. Across these metrics, even the lowest direct-LLM error remains 2.0--2.7 times the corresponding ChronoScribe error. At the system level, ChronoScribe achieves a Task-Level Score (TLS) of 65.5, 10.6 points above the strongest direct-LLM baseline. The results support ChronoScribe's division of labor, in which the LLM handles interpretation, configuration, and communication while the TSFM handles numerical forecasting.
papers.summary: Instruction-driven time series forecasting must both follow natural-language requests and produce precise numbers, but large language models (LLMs) are often inaccurate when asked to emit forecast values directly, while time series foundation models (TSFMs) need structured inputs specifying the target series, context window, and horizon. `ChronoScribe` divides the labor: a LoRA-adapted LLM proposes an execution path and context length, deterministic rules resolve the executable configuration, a frozen TSFM produces quantile trajectories for the task horizon, and deterministic trajectory summaries condition the LLM's response so that it never generates or revises predicted values. A `Qwen3.5-9B` plus `Chronos-2` implementation evaluated across 23 dimensions and 30 public datasets **has the lowest sMAPE, MASE, WAPE, RMSE, and MAE of all evaluated systems, including eleven proprietary direct LLMs and three open TSFMs**, with even the best direct LLM at 2.0 to 2.7 times its error. Its Task-Level Score of 65.5 is 10.6 points above the strongest direct-LLM baseline.

papers.title: Rescuing Points Trapped Inside Incorrect Decision Regions: A target for Evaluating and Improving Forward-Forward Learning
papers.abstract: Forward-Forward learning replaces end-to-end backpropagation with local, layer-wise training objectives. Its variants are evaluated primarily by classification accuracy, often measured with linear probes trained on their representations. We show that this evaluation can over-credit the learning method: a linear probe on the representations of an untrained convolutional neural network already reaches accuracy well above chance. Moreover, a single accuracy value does not reveal which datapoints become correctly classified after training and which remain misclassified. To examine what learning contributes beyond the random, untrained baseline, we present an analysis methodology built on the Boundary Proximity Index (BPI), a multiclass margin normalized by a class-centroid reference. We apply our analysis to seven Forward-Forward variants and related layer-local methods and find that initially misclassified points near the probe's decision boundary generally have higher rescue rates than those farther inside incorrect decision regions. Rescue rates vary substantially across methods, with some correcting a substantial fraction of these deeply embedded points. Together, these analyses offer a way to evaluate representation learning beyond accuracy and identify the rescue of points far inside incorrect decision regions as a target for improving local learning methods.
papers.summary: Forward-Forward learning replaces end-to-end backpropagation with local, layer-wise objectives, and its variants are usually judged by linear-probe accuracy on their representations. The authors show that this metric can over-credit the learning method, since **a linear probe on an untrained convolutional neural network already scores well above chance**, and a single accuracy number hides which datapoints get fixed by training and which stay misclassified. They introduce an analysis built on the Boundary Proximity Index (BPI), a multiclass margin normalized by a class-centroid reference, and apply it to seven Forward-Forward variants and related layer-local methods, finding that initially misclassified points near the probe's decision boundary are rescued at higher rates than points deep inside incorrect regions, with rescue rates varying substantially across methods. Rescuing those deeply embedded points is proposed as a concrete target for improving local learning methods.

papers.title: DWI Connectome-based Sex Classification in Young using Supervised Variational Autoencoder
papers.abstract: During adolescence, significant changes in brain development are influenced by hormonal changes that impact both the body and the brain. This study presents sex classification in 787 young adults having age range of 15-25 years using Diffusion-weighted (DWI) structural connectome, focusing on 82 Desikan-Killiany atlas ROIs. A supervised variational autoencoder (SVAE) is used to extract latent space features from DWI connectome data. Although several studies explored differences in brain structure and function between sexes, the main contribution of this study lies in incorporating SVAE to learn a compact, regularized latent representation for the task of sex classification. Initial exploratory data analysis shows that these features can capture the differences in sex-specific latent space patterns. Subsequently, the learned latent space SVAE features are fed to different ML models for sex classification. Among the considered ML classifiers, the multi-layer perceptron yields the highest accuracy of 80% in classifying sex. This demonstrates the effectiveness of SVAE in learning compact, informative representations from DWI connectome for sex classification. The present work highlights the potential of using DWI brain connectomics and deep learning to differentiate sex, paving the way for future research on diverse populations that may include transgender individuals, to better understand sex-related variations in brain structure.
papers.summary: Adolescent brain development is shaped by hormonal changes that affect both body and brain, motivating a study of sex differences in structural connectivity. Using diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) structural connectomes over 82 Desikan-Killiany atlas regions from 787 participants aged 15 to 25, a supervised variational autoencoder (SVAE) learns a compact, regularized latent representation, and exploratory analysis shows sex-specific patterns in that latent space. The latent features are then fed to several machine learning classifiers, and **a multi-layer perceptron reaches the highest accuracy at 80%** for sex classification.

papers.title: RIFT: Token Influence Follows the Path of Least Resistance
papers.abstract: Which context tokens drive a language model's answer? Graph-based tools such as attention rollout and attention flow answer this from a single forward pass, yet their faithfulness in decoder-only models is rarely tested against interventions. We view the layers of a decoder as a causal network whose conductances are attention weights, and read a token's influence on the answer from the resistance between them. We propose RIFT (Resistance-based Information Flow in Transformers), which scores a token by the series resistance of its path of least resistance to the answer, found exactly by a classic shortest-path dynamic program. On synthetic in-context retrieval tasks and extractive question answering over Wikipedia paragraphs, RIFT predicts the effect of replacing a token with a Spearman correlation of 0.52-0.68; predicting a single replacement, it reaches 77-96% of the agreement between two different random replacements. It needs no gradients and no extra forward passes, scoring every token of a prompt in 0.9-3.4 ms on one CPU thread, whereas the replacement experiment needs a forward pass per token. On 576 held-out prompts from four models of two families (Qwen3 and Llama 3.2), it outperforms token distance, attention rollout and attention flow in every pre-specified comparison, by 0.23 to 0.88 in mean Spearman correlation, and it is the best or tied-best of all attention-based scores we test. Aggregates that add up all routes (attention flow, effective resistance and rollout) instead mostly encode token position: as a simple proposition shows, early tokens have many more parallel routes to the answer.
papers.summary: Graph-based attribution tools such as attention rollout and attention flow estimate which context tokens drive a decoder-only language model's answer from a single forward pass, but their faithfulness is rarely checked against interventions. `RIFT` (Resistance-based Information Flow in Transformers) treats the decoder's layers as a circuit whose conductances are attention weights and scores each token by the series resistance along its path of least resistance to the answer, computed exactly with a classic shortest-path dynamic program, needing no gradients or extra forward passes and scoring every prompt token in 0.9 to 3.4 ms on one CPU thread. On synthetic in-context retrieval and extractive question answering over Wikipedia paragraphs, it predicts the effect of replacing a token with Spearman correlations of 0.52 to 0.68, and **on 576 held-out prompts from `Qwen3` and `Llama 3.2` models it beats token distance, attention rollout, and attention flow in every pre-specified comparison**, by 0.23 to 0.88 in mean Spearman correlation. The authors also show that aggregates summing all routes mostly encode token position, since early tokens have many more parallel routes to the answer.

papers.title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation.
