We present a method for deriving queryable knowledge graphs from clinical narratives, conforming to the Extended Grammar of SNOMED CT across multiple ontologies. The method specifies how entities should be annotated and related. It defines five relation classes, each bound to a construction rule that assembles the entities and relations into post-coordinated expressions. A deterministic implementation, UNIGRAPHE, applies those rules to construct knowledge graphs from annotated text. Applied to expert-annotated real-world oncology documentation, UNIGRAPHE reconstructed 5,299 annotations into 2,196 post-coordinated expressions and shows that relation structure is the missing piece to make clinical narrative formally queryable.
papers.summary: Decisive information in oncology documentation sits in free text, so cohort identification depends on incomplete diagnostic codes or manual review, and coding individual terms captures what a document mentions rather than what it asserts. The method derives queryable knowledge graphs from clinical narrative that conform to the Extended Grammar of `SNOMED CT` across multiple ontologies, specifying how entities are annotated and related through five relation classes, each tied to a construction rule for assembling post-coordinated expressions. A deterministic implementation, `UNIGRAPHE`, applied to expert-annotated real-world oncology records **reconstructed 5,299 annotations into 2,196 post-coordinated expressions**, supporting the claim that relation structure is what makes narrative formally queryable.

papers.title: XAI-Guided Fourier Domain Generalisation for Pure-Simulation Sim-to-Real Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for vision-based autonomous driving, but policies trained in simulation often suffer severe performance degradation when deployed in the real world. Existing sim-to-real methods commonly address this gap through image-transfer-based domain adaptation or policy-agnostic domain randomisation. However, the former requires laborious acquisition of target-domain data and is often limited to the deployment domain, whereas the latter introduces unguided perturbations that may not reflect the underlying sim-to-real discrepancy, leading to suboptimal transfer performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose XFD, an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-guided Fourier domain generalisation framework for pure-simulation sim-to-real reinforcement learning. The proposed framework extracts explainability attribution maps from simulated observations, and converts these attributions into policy-conditioned Fourier-domain interventions. By perturbing appearance-sensitive spectral components while preserving task-defining spatial structures, XFD constructs robustness-enhancing visual domains entirely within simulation. Subsequently, the proposed robust policy optimisation guides the policy towards attending to task-critical features while suppressing sensitivity to irrelevant visual information. Extensive experiments in simulation and zero-shot real-world deployment demonstrate that XFD consistently improves traveled distance and reward over standard policy and randomly domain-randomised baseline, especially on unseen maps with cluttered backgrounds. Attribution-based analysis further proves that the proposed policy preserves more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and real-world observations.
papers.summary: Vision-based driving policies trained with deep reinforcement learning degrade sharply in the real world, and existing fixes either need target-domain images or apply unguided domain randomisation that may not reflect the actual sim-to-real discrepancy. `XFD` extracts explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) attribution maps from simulated observations and turns them into policy-conditioned Fourier-domain interventions that perturb appearance-sensitive spectral components while preserving task-defining spatial structure, generating robustness-enhancing visual domains entirely in simulation. A robust policy optimisation step then pushes the policy to attend to task-critical features and ignore irrelevant visual detail. In simulation and zero-shot real-world deployment, **`XFD` consistently improves travelled distance and reward over standard and randomly domain-randomised policies**, with the largest gains on unseen maps with cluttered backgrounds, and attribution analysis shows the policy keeps more consistent task-relevant evidence across simulated and real observations.

papers.title: PXRD-Bench: How Close Are We to Determining Crystal Structures from Powder Diffraction?
papers.abstract: Determining crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) would enable routine characterization of newly synthesized materials, including those absent from reference databases. Generative models offer a promising approach, but existing evaluations remain fragmented and largely assume single-phase samples with known composition. To fill this gap, we introduce PXRD-Bench, a unified benchmark that extends evaluation to unknown per-element atom counts and recovery of both structures in two-phase mixtures. It provides approximately 4.1 million training structures with simulated PXRD, tests generalization to unseen compositions and structural prototypes, and evaluates recovery from experimental PXRD after excluding structurally matching training entries. To provide a strong reference baseline, we also introduce Bragglite, a PXRD-to-structure model developed through a systematic study of PXRD modeling choices. It achieves a 44.2\% Top-1 match rate on experimental RRUFF patterns with known composition, 24.6\% above the strongest prior baseline. Further analysis yields several key findings: some models fail to benefit from experimental PXRD, while generalization to unseen structural prototypes and recovery from two-phase mixtures remain challenging. Together, our benchmark, systematic studies, and Bragglite clarify the capabilities and limitations of current PXRD-to-structure models.
papers.summary: Determining crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) would allow routine characterisation of newly synthesised materials absent from reference databases, but existing evaluations of generative models are fragmented and mostly assume single-phase samples of known composition. `PXRD-Bench` extends evaluation to unknown per-element atom counts and to recovering both structures in two-phase mixtures, supplying roughly 4.1 million training structures with simulated patterns, tests on unseen compositions and structural prototypes, and experimental recovery tests that exclude structurally matching training entries. The accompanying `Bragglite` model, designed through a systematic study of PXRD modelling choices, reaches **a 44.2% Top-1 match rate on experimental `RRUFF` patterns with known composition, 24.6% above the strongest prior baseline**. Further analysis finds that some models fail to benefit from experimental patterns and that generalisation to unseen prototypes and two-phase recovery remain hard.

papers.title: SLEM: Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory, resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per input but must keep all expert parameters in memory, and existing expert-merging compression methods interpolate directly in parameter space, which need not interpolate expert functions meaningfully, and typically estimate merging coefficients from calibration data. Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (`SLEM`) is calibration-free: it encodes expert weights into a structured latent space with a VAE, groups experts within and across layers by latent similarity, derives merging coefficients from the weight spectra, performs geometry-aware interpolation in the latent space, and decodes the result into merged weights. Against existing merging methods, `SLEM` **matches or exceeds performance on general knowledge benchmarks and achieves higher average scores on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks**.

papers.title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. GrowRL freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and a feed-forward network branch at each Transformer layer. Zero-initialized output projections preserve the pretrained policy at initialization, and RL updates only the added pathways. The learned pathways remain explicit after training, allowing transfer to structurally compatible target models and subsequent adaptation with the target backbone frozen. The architecture also supports sequential transfer of additional pathways. By keeping the learned attention and feed-forward computation separate from the pretrained weights, GrowRL provides an explicit structure for preserving and reusing the outcome of an RL run. Experiments across five backbones show competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with a small number of trainable parameters. Learned pathways provide immediate gains across all three transfer directions, with performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case. These results support computational pathways as parameter-efficient and reusable units of reinforcement learning adaptation.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve LLM reasoning but is expensive, and the resulting updates are normally locked into one model's weights. `GrowRL` freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and feed-forward branch at every Transformer layer, with zero-initialised output projections so the initial policy is unchanged, and RL updates only these added pathways. Because the pathways stay explicit, they can be transferred to structurally compatible target models, adapted further with the target backbone frozen, and stacked sequentially. Across five backbones the method gives competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution results with few trainable parameters, and transferred pathways yield immediate gains in all three transfer directions, with **performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case**.

papers.title: Communication, Vocalisation, and Language
papers.abstract: The contention is that the current batch of Large Language Models don't *understand* language, but they *do* it. Rather than LLMs forming some kind of ``distributed representation'' of symbols, the claim is that LLMs are capturing ``Cultural Intelligence'' and grounding symbols in what the sociologists call practices.
papers.summary: A position piece contending that the current generation of large language models does not understand language but does do it. Instead of attributing to LLMs a distributed representation of symbols, the author argues that **they capture 'cultural intelligence' and ground symbols in what sociologists call practices**.

papers.title: Drafting Agents, Not Just Tokens: Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version can exhaust the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. We introduce Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), which drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while requiring complete verification before adoption. Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. Group Verification Optimization (GVO) learns the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison, terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%--40.0%. Additional evaluations show that SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone--task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85%--2.38% in macro-average system score across twenty backbones. Coding-validation success reaches 69.4% versus HGM's 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.
papers.summary: Improving an agent through successive revisions means balancing exploration against evaluation under a fixed budget, since a narrow search misses useful edit sequences while fully evaluating every intermediate version exhausts the budget first. Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (`SpecRSI`) drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated but requires complete verification before any version is adopted. Verification-Aware Tree Search (`VATS`) allocates budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation, and Group Verification Optimization (`GVO`) trains the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison **terminal gains exceed `Janus` by 33.3% to 40.0%**, with wins on all 50 scientific backbone-task pairs, a 1.85% to 2.38% macro-average edge over `MetaRSI-v1` across twenty backbones, and 69.4% coding-validation success versus 64.3% for `HGM` at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.

papers.title: From Caricature to Collective Artifact: How Persona Construction Drives Polarization in Generative Social Simulations
papers.abstract: Generative Social Simulation (GSS) leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to create sophisticated personas that define agents with demographics, emotions, and political opinions. While prior work shows that personas compress outputs into stereotypical caricatures, there is no comprehensive study of how these caricatures evolve into collective artifacts when they interact. Using a Twitter-like GSS platform with personas derived from the American National Elections Study (ANES), we ablate three layers of partisan identity: affective polarization markers, party identification, and vote choice, while retaining demographics, ideological positioning and important issues. We find that collective outcomes depend heavily on how survey responses are translated into personas. Removing a few explicitly partisan statements moves the network from near-complete segregation to cross-party ties approaching those of real Twitter networks. We argue that matching one outcome is not evidence for behavioral validity and point to salience as a possible explanation. Surveys ask for a position on every question regardless of its importance to the respondent, and persona construction turns each answer into a direct behavioral instruction. We conclude with a checklist for more comprehensive evaluation of personas in future works.
papers.summary: Generative Social Simulation (GSS) uses large language models to build agent personas with demographics, emotions, and political opinions, and earlier work showed such personas collapse into stereotypical caricatures, but how those caricatures aggregate into collective outcomes when agents interact had not been studied. On a Twitter-like GSS platform with personas derived from the American National Elections Study (`ANES`), the authors ablate three layers of partisan identity, namely affective polarization markers, party identification, and vote choice, while keeping demographics, ideological positioning, and salient issues. **Removing a few explicitly partisan statements moves the network from near-complete segregation to cross-party ties approaching those of real Twitter networks**, showing that collective outcomes hinge on how survey answers are translated into personas. They attribute the effect to salience, since surveys demand a position on every question regardless of its importance to the respondent and persona construction turns each answer into a behavioral instruction, and they close with an evaluation checklist for personas.

papers.title: KARAMEL: Knowledge-Aware Ranking for Multimodal Entity Linking in the Arts via Heterogeneous Graphs
papers.abstract: Discovering and disambiguating entities from multimodal and heterogeneous data is a key challenge in discovery science, where relevant knowledge is often implicit and distributed across modalities. We present KARAMEL, a framework for multimodal entity linking (MEL) - the task of aligning visual and textual mentions to entities in a knowledge base - in the cultural heritage domain. Unlike prior vision-language models that primarily rely on surface-level multimodal alignment, our approach incorporates sociohistorical and contextual knowledge through a knowledge-aware architecture that fuses a vision-language encoder with a heterogeneous graph neural network. This design enables contextual reasoning over complex relational structures and supports robust entity disambiguation under ambiguous or underspecified evidence. To benchmark multimodal discovery in this setting, we introduce WikiMuSA (Wikidata-based Multimodal Semantic data for Art), a new dataset that links artworks to Wikidata entities via images, textual descriptions, and structured contextual knowledge. Experimental results show that KARAMEL surpasses strong baselines, particularly on implicit or abstract mentions, while ablation studies highlight the critical role of domain-specific, structured context in learning expressive representations. While instantiated in the cultural heritage domain, KARAMEL addresses a general knowledge discovery problem and applies to other scientific settings involving multimodal observations and heterogeneous background knowledge. Both the dataset and source code are made publicly available.
papers.summary: Multimodal entity linking (MEL), the task of aligning visual and textual mentions to entities in a knowledge base, is hard in cultural heritage because the relevant knowledge is implicit and spread across modalities. `KARAMEL` fuses a vision-language encoder with a heterogeneous graph neural network so that sociohistorical and contextual knowledge can inform disambiguation of ambiguous or underspecified mentions, rather than relying on surface-level multimodal alignment alone. The authors also release `WikiMuSA`, a dataset linking artworks to Wikidata entities through images, descriptions, and structured context. `KARAMEL` surpasses strong baselines, **with the largest gains on implicit or abstract mentions**, and ablations show that domain-specific structured context is critical to the learned representations.

papers.title: pi-Net: Empirical Latent Representations for Differentiable Physics Heads in Data-Scarce Systems
papers.abstract: Developing reliable predictive models for multi-physics systems often forces a compromise between computationally demanding physical simulators and data-hungry, opaque machine learning (ML) algorithms. While incorporating dimensional analysis into directed computation graphs offers a structurally sound alternative to explicitly solving partial differential equations (PDEs), such formulations typically yield underdetermined systems that act as imperfect simulators. We introduce pi-Net, a physics-informed latent variable model that resolves these imperfect simulators. The hybrid pi-Net architecture consists of an encoder that maps inputs into physically normalized latent space, which are then decoded into final predictions by a differentiable physics head. Evaluated on a real-world, data-scarce Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) case study, the framework achieves an R2 of 0.864 with only 60 experimental samples. The results demonstrate that pi-Net significantly outperforms purely data-driven baselines in data-scarce regimes while providing causal, process-level explainability.
papers.summary: Predictive models for multi-physics systems usually force a choice between costly physical simulators and data-hungry, opaque machine learning, and dimensional-analysis computation graphs, while structurally sound, tend to be underdetermined and act as imperfect simulators. `pi-Net` is a physics-informed latent variable model in which an encoder maps inputs into a physically normalised latent space that a differentiable physics head decodes into predictions, resolving those imperfect simulators. On a real-world, data-scarce Gas Metal Arc Welding (`GMAW`) case study it reaches **an R2 of 0.864 from only 60 experimental samples**, well ahead of purely data-driven baselines, while offering causal, process-level explanations.

papers.title: Boosting the Learning for Ranking Patterns
papers.abstract: Pattern mining is a valuable tool for exploratory data analysis, but identifying relevant patterns for a specific user is challenging. Various interestingness mea- sures have been developed to evaluate patterns, but they may not efficiently estimate user-specific functions. Learning user-specific functions by ranking patterns has been proposed, but this requires significant time and training samples. In this paper, we present a solution that formulates the problem of learning pattern ranking functions as a multicriteria decision making problem. Our approach uses Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to elicit weights for different interestingness measures based on user preference. We also propose an active learning mode with a sensitivity-based heuristic to minimize user ranking queries while still providing high-quality results. Experiments show that our approach significantly reduces running time and returns precise pattern ranking while being robust to user error, compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
papers.summary: Pattern mining surfaces many candidate patterns, and generic interestingness measures rarely match what a particular user finds relevant, while learning a user-specific ranking function has required many training samples and considerable time. The authors cast learning a pattern ranking function as a multicriteria decision-making problem and use the Analytic Hierarchy Process (`AHP`) to elicit weights over interestingness measures from user preferences, adding an active learning mode with a sensitivity-based heuristic to minimise the number of ranking queries. Experiments show the approach **substantially reduces running time while returning precise rankings and staying robust to user error** compared with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Intent-Triggered Anchoring for Multi-Token Format Units in Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: In parallel decoding, diffusion language models commit several tokens per forward pass, so co-committed tokens cannot see each other, breaking multi-token format units that parsers need. On ECHO, an open-weight one-step chest X-ray (CXR) report generator, 32.7-36.7% of evaluation reports lack a parseable Impression heading and score as empty. We propose intent-triggered anchoring, a training-free decoding rule that completes a format unit once the model commits its first token, inserting only units with a unique, content-free completion; fallbacks write the unit when the model stops or loops without starting it. On three CXR evaluation sets, the rule raises readable rates from 63.3-67.3% to 100.0% with no regressions and a 95th-percentile latency ratio of 0.68-1.28 against official decoding. Broken headings state findings absent from the reference; adding the heading at the end leaves them in 15.5-31.0% of reports, our rule in at most 0.6%. For math answer markers, the rule raises accuracy in the most parallel setting of five diffusion language models by 5.8-20.8 points on GSM8K and 5.1-17.1 on GSM-Symbolic, held out from tuning. With lenient answer extraction, gains are 3.3-12.5 and 2.7-6.3 points; the rule adds 1.4-8.6 points over a stop-only fallback for four of the five models.
papers.summary: In parallel decoding, diffusion language models commit several tokens per forward pass, so tokens committed together cannot condition on each other and multi-token format units such as section headings or answer markers get broken, leaving outputs that parsers reject. The proposed fix, `intent-triggered anchoring`, is a training-free decoding rule that completes a format unit as soon as the model commits its first token, inserting only units with a unique content-free completion, with fallbacks that write the unit if the model stops or loops without starting it. On three chest X-ray (CXR) report sets generated by `ECHO`, the rule **raises the readable-report rate from 63.3-67.3% to 100.0%** with no regressions and keeps 95th-percentile latency within 0.68-1.28 times official decoding. For math answer markers, it improves accuracy of five diffusion language models in their most parallel setting by 5.8-20.8 points on `GSM8K` and 5.1-17.1 points on `GSM-Symbolic`, a set held out from tuning.

papers.title: Trust-Calibrated VLA Policy Post-Training with Evolving Imagination
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage. Existing refinement paradigms expose a reliability--efficiency tension: model-free refinement avoids simulator bias but is interaction-intensive, whereas model-based refinement can exploit unreliable imagination even as its simulator adapts. We propose Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a trust-calibrated framework that couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator comprising a world model and a reward proxy head. Across stages, simulator reliability controls the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon; within rollouts, chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight. For recursive imagination without exact grounded continuations, a residual predictor estimates trust without querying future ground truth. On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, MERL reaches 79.7% average success, improves high-threshold learning speed by 10.9% over the matched model-free control, and outperforms same-protocol external baselines across three training seeds. Fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task achieves 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models pretrained by imitation learning need reinforcement learning (RL) post-training once deployment leaves demonstration coverage, but model-free refinement is interaction-hungry while model-based refinement can exploit an unreliable learned simulator even as that simulator adapts. `MERL` (Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning) couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator made of a world model and a reward proxy head, letting simulator reliability set the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon across stages while chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight within rollouts, and a residual predictor estimates trust for recursive imagination without querying future ground truth. On perturbed `LIBERO-PRO` tasks it **reaches 79.7% average success**, speeds high-threshold learning by 10.9% over a matched model-free control, and beats same-protocol baselines across three seeds, while fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task reaches 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.

papers.title: Asymptotic Risk of Learning-Rate Schedules for Least-Squares Regression with Discretely Distributed Features
papers.abstract: We study the last iterate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on streaming least squares with discretely distributed features (Slock's model), which decouples the dynamics across eigendirections. Under power-law source and capacity conditions, we derive the exact finite-time risk and asymptotic equivalents of constant and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedules. With a tuned base learning-rate, the resulting scaling law decays as $\Theta(T^{-q})$, where $T$ is the horizon, and $q$ is independent of the cooldown length $c \in (0,1]$ but is strictly smaller for the constant schedule: any cooldown of fixed relative length $c > 0$, however short, improves the risk by a polynomial factor, while its length only affects the constant, which is minimized by linear decay ($c = 1$). Finally, we show that the optimal risk depends on the batch size $b$ and horizon $T$ only through $bT$, up to a critical batch size.
papers.summary: The analysis studies the last iterate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on streaming least squares with discretely distributed features, a model that decouples the dynamics across eigendirections, in order to compare constant and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) learning-rate schedules. Under power-law source and capacity conditions it derives the exact finite-time risk and asymptotic equivalents of both schedules. With a tuned base learning rate the risk scales as T to the power minus q in the horizon T, and **any cooldown of fixed relative length, however short, improves the risk over the constant schedule by a polynomial factor** because its decay exponent is strictly larger, while the cooldown length only affects the constant, which is minimized by linear decay over the full horizon. The optimal risk depends on batch size and horizon only through their product, up to a critical batch size.

papers.title: Learning Reachability-Based Safety Representations for Real-Time Robot Navigation in Unknown and Dynamic Environments
papers.abstract: Safe robot navigation in unknown, dynamic environments requires more than geometric collision checking: a robot still far from an obstacle may be unable to avoid it because of its speed, orientation, or the obstacle's motion. Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis captures this in a value function whose sign separates states that admit a safe continuation from those where collision is unavoidable, but computing it online for every newly observed environment is too expensive. This dissertation trains neural implicit representations offline on reachability solutions to give optimization-based controllers this information in real time. Since the value function never exceeds the constraint, it equals a directly computed constraint, such as a signed distance, minus a nonnegative dynamics correction. Learning only this correction keeps represented obstacles outside the predicted safe set despite approximation errors. The first two of five methods use the learned function as a terminal constraint in model predictive control, for static local environments and predicted obstacle motion. The next two use it as a barrier candidate in control barrier function safety filters, for static environments and, through pairwise barriers in relative coordinates, for a varying number of moving obstacles. Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show better collision avoidance than geometric and hand-designed baselines, especially for short horizons and moving obstacles. The fifth method replaces the grid-based offline solver, which limits the first four to low-dimensional models. For control-affine dynamics with polytopic inputs, the HJ Hamiltonian is maximized at a vertex, so a parallelizable tree search over vertex inputs can generate training labels. With a loss from the HJ variational inequality, these labels yield barrier candidates for systems with up to 13 states.
papers.summary: Safe navigation in unknown dynamic environments needs more than geometric collision checks, since a robot's speed, orientation, or an obstacle's motion can make a collision unavoidable while still far away; Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability captures this in a value function, but computing it online for each new environment is too expensive. This dissertation trains neural implicit representations offline on reachability solutions, learning only a nonnegative dynamics correction subtracted from a directly computed constraint such as a signed distance, so represented obstacles stay outside the predicted safe set despite approximation error. Four methods use the learned function as a terminal constraint in model predictive control or as a barrier candidate in control barrier function safety filters, for static and moving obstacles, and **simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show better collision avoidance than geometric and hand-designed baselines**, especially for short horizons and moving obstacles. A fifth method replaces the grid-based offline solver with a parallelizable tree search over vertex inputs for control-affine dynamics with polytopic inputs, yielding barrier candidates for systems with up to 13 states.

papers.title: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents
papers.abstract: Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. Prior work mainly addresses the resulting instability through reward shaping or denser supervision, while treating these components as fixed. We instead introduce EAU, a meta-agent framework for environment--agent--user co-evolution. During training, EAU monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics; diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions; and proposes targeted modifications to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration. Validated changes are hot-swapped into the ongoing run, allowing the training setup to evolve together with the policy. These adaptations also persist across runs, so later training can build on previously discovered improvements rather than restarting from a fixed setup. We enable this process through an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics, while the agent remains a neural LLM optimized with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models, EAU consistently outperforms prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7--15.0% and increasing successful task completion on ColBench by up to 36.7%, showing that co-evolving the training system with the policy can substantially improve multi-turn RL.
papers.summary: Training large language model agents for multi-turn interaction with users is unstable because the learning signal also depends on the user simulator and the environment, which may involve stochastic users, unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers; prior work treats these components as fixed and compensates with reward shaping or denser supervision. `EAU` is a meta-agent framework for environment-agent-user co-evolution that monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics during reinforcement learning, diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions, and proposes targeted changes to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration, hot-swapping validated changes into the ongoing run and persisting them across runs. This relies on an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics while the agent itself stays a neural LLM trained with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models it beats prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7-15.0% and **raising successful task completion on `ColBench` by up to 36.7%**.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning with Hawkes-Structured Networks for Market Making
papers.abstract: Market making under realistic order-flow dynamics is challenging due to the clustered, self-exciting nature of order arrivals, which are naturally modeled by non-Markovian Hawkes processes. We propose a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) framework for market making with general Hawkes order-flow dynamics. We first establish non-asymptotic performance bounds that quantify the loss incurred by approximating the infinite-dimensional Hawkes state using a finite collection of exponentially weighted features. Guided by this analysis, we introduce the Hawkes-Structured Network (HSN), a novel neural architecture that encodes historical order flow through a learnable mixture-of-exponentials filter. HSN is trained end-to-end using model-free RL, jointly optimizing the feature representation and quoting policy directly from reward feedback. Experiments on single- and multi-asset market-making problems with mixture-of-exponentials, power-law, and regime-switching kernels demonstrate that HSN outperforms general-purpose neural architectures, achieving higher trading rewards while implicitly recovering the underlying order-flow intensities.
papers.summary: Market making under realistic order flow is hard because order arrivals cluster and self-excite, which is naturally modeled by non-Markovian Hawkes processes whose state is infinite-dimensional. The work proves non-asymptotic bounds on the performance lost by approximating the Hawkes state with a finite collection of exponentially weighted features, then introduces the Hawkes-Structured Network (`HSN`), which encodes order-flow history through a learnable mixture-of-exponentials filter and is trained end to end with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) so that the feature representation and quoting policy are optimized jointly from reward feedback. On single- and multi-asset market-making problems with mixture-of-exponentials, power-law, and regime-switching kernels, **`HSN` earns higher trading rewards than general-purpose neural architectures** while implicitly recovering the underlying order-flow intensities.

papers.title: Support or Magnitude? Characterizing Neuron Relevance for Instruction Data Selection
papers.abstract: Model-internal signals, such as neuron activations and gradients, have been used for instruction data selection, yet how neuron relevance should be characterized remains underexplored. In particular, should selection prioritize the magnitude of relevance or how broadly it is distributed across neurons? To investigate this question, we construct sample-level relevance profiles using AttnLRP-guided attribution and introduce two complementary criteria: Effective Relevance Support (ERS), which measures the effective support of positive relevance, and Positive Relevance Magnitude (PRM), which captures its average strength. Our analyses reveal that these characterizations produce distinct sample rankings and selection preferences despite sharing the same underlying relevance profiles. On Qwen2 models, PRM exhibits stronger associations with activation-based selection, whereas ERS produces substantially different rankings. These differences extend to task composition, within-task sample preferences, and semantic selection patterns, with varying degrees of agreement across backbones. Experiments across three language models and five downstream benchmarks demonstrate the practical value of relevance-guided selection, with ERS achieving the best overall average performance rank among the evaluated methods. Our findings highlight that how neuron relevance is distributed and characterized, rather than its magnitude alone, matters for instruction data selection.
papers.summary: Model-internal signals such as neuron activations and gradients are used to select instruction-tuning data, but it is unclear whether selection should prioritize how strong a sample's neuron relevance is or how broadly it is spread across neurons. Using `AttnLRP`-guided attribution to build sample-level relevance profiles, the authors define Effective Relevance Support (`ERS`), which measures the effective support of positive relevance, and Positive Relevance Magnitude (`PRM`), which captures its average strength, and show that the two produce distinct sample rankings and selection preferences from the same profiles; on `Qwen2` models `PRM` tracks activation-based selection while `ERS` diverges substantially, with differences extending to task composition, within-task preferences, and semantic selection patterns. Across three language models and five downstream benchmarks, **`ERS` achieves the best overall average performance rank** among the evaluated selection methods, suggesting that how relevance is distributed matters more than its magnitude alone.

papers.title: Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? We investigate this question through the spectral structure of LLM gradients and find that gradient energy progressively concentrates into a shrinking effective subspace, which is characteristic of RLVR, as it is absent under supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and is largely removed when the verifiable reward is replaced by a random one. Moreover, the rank required to capture a fixed fraction of gradient energy steadily decreases over training, revealing that the effective dimensionality of useful updates itself evolves with training. These findings motivate a new optimization principle: rather than prescribing the update rank externally, an optimizer should adapt its rank to the evolving spectral structure of the gradient. We introduce Ares (Adaptive Rank-Effective Spectral Optimization), which estimates the effective update rank from the gradient's spectral energy distribution, tracks its evolution, and confines the gradient signal driving each update to the resulting low-rank subspace. Across LLMs of different scales, Ares improves accuracy over widely used optimizers and generalizes across RLVR algorithms and tasks. Results suggest that effective optimization may require optimizers to be designed around the geometry and dynamics of the training process. We release the code and data at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Ares.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard way to give large language models (LLMs) reasoning ability, yet the optimizers used were inherited from teacher-forcing training, raising the question of whether RLVR has its own optimization geometry. Analyzing the spectral structure of LLM gradients, the authors find that **gradient energy progressively concentrates into a shrinking effective subspace under RLVR**, a pattern absent under supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and largely gone when the verifiable reward is replaced by a random one, with the rank needed to capture a fixed fraction of gradient energy falling steadily over training. They introduce `Ares` (Adaptive Rank-Effective Spectral Optimization), which estimates the effective update rank from the gradient's spectral energy distribution, tracks its evolution, and confines each update's gradient signal to the resulting low-rank subspace. Across LLMs of different scales `Ares` improves accuracy over widely used optimizers and generalizes across RLVR algorithms and tasks, with code and data released.

papers.title: Does the Explanation Drift Before the Guarantee? Label-Free Early Warning on Evolving Graphs
papers.abstract: Deployed models can fail silently as the world they describe evolves. Attribution drift has served as an early warning in tabular data; we ask whether, in graph streams, a model's own explanations can forewarn the loss of nominal conformal coverage. Doing so requires repairing the naive drift statistic twice. A vanishing edge loses mask mass regardless of whether the model relied on it, so we condition the importance on edge presence. Evolving graphs also break edge identity: a relabelling that changes nothing shifts the identity-based statistic by 0.69 on synthetic graphs and 0.83 on real ego-networks, whereas aggregating over structural roles brings both to 0.0 and stays well-defined when the support changes. We test six pre-registered regimes on thirty seeds each. A two-channel monitor, tracking conditional mask mass and its distribution over roles, precedes coverage collapse by 8 to 14.5 steps across four gradual regimes (node addition, removal, replacement, and edge thinning), all surviving Holm correction. A sudden knockout yields the expected zero lead, and a harmless change triggers no alarm. Leads track the length of the transitional phase (Spearman 0.79 over 150 runs). On real transaction ego-networks, the untuned mass channel forewarns staged drift by 27 steps and is the only channel, attributional or structural, that never alarms on a stationary stream. The main limitation is that the mass channel is blind to covariate drift, which breaks the guarantee in every run; the distributional channel detects it and also rescues the rewiring regime, so we report the two channels separately rather than as a union.
papers.summary: Deployed graph models can fail silently as the graph they describe evolves, and the question is whether a model's own explanations can give early warning before conformal prediction loses its nominal coverage. The naive attribution-drift statistic must be repaired twice for graph streams: importance is conditioned on edge presence so that a vanishing edge does not lose mask mass regardless of whether the model relied on it, and importance is aggregated over structural roles rather than edge identities, which removes a spurious shift of 0.69 on synthetic graphs and 0.83 on real ego-networks caused by harmless relabelling. Across six pre-registered regimes with thirty seeds each, a two-channel monitor tracking conditional mask mass and its distribution over roles **precedes coverage collapse by 8 to 14.5 steps in four gradual drift regimes**, surviving Holm correction, while a sudden knockout gives the expected zero lead and a harmless change triggers no alarm. On real transaction ego-networks the untuned mass channel forewarns staged drift by 27 steps and never alarms on a stationary stream, but it is blind to covariate drift, which only the distributional channel detects, so the two channels are reported separately.

papers.title: Learning, Compression, and Meta-Complexity
papers.abstract: The idea that learning is closely tied to compression has long served as both a powerful principle and, at times, an informal analogy across machine learning and learning theory. Here we focus on settings in which that intuition can be made mathematically precise, surveying formal connections among learning algorithms, data compression, and computational complexity theory, with an emphasis on recent progress and current frontiers. We describe how techniques from complexity theory can guide the design of both supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms with provable guarantees, and conversely, how learning algorithms can yield new insights and results in complexity theory. A central theme is the role of data compression as a bridge between learning and complexity, especially through an area called meta-complexity, which studies the computational difficulty of compression problems and time-bounded variants of Kolmogorov complexity.
papers.summary: The link between learning and compression has long served as both a formal principle and an informal analogy, and this survey concentrates on settings where it can be made mathematically precise, mapping connections among learning algorithms, data compression, and computational complexity theory with emphasis on recent progress and current frontiers. It describes how complexity-theoretic techniques guide the design of supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms with provable guarantees, and conversely how learning algorithms yield new insights and results in complexity theory. **The central bridge is meta-complexity**, the study of the computational difficulty of compression problems and of time-bounded variants of Kolmogorov complexity.

papers.title: Learning Graded Sparse Mechanisms: A Representation Theorem and Certified Generalization
papers.abstract: In a variety of multi-agent and physical environments, an element's update depends strongly on a few other elements and weakly on many, and both the identity and the number of the elements that matter change with the state of the system. Such graded sparse mechanisms are common, for instance, in flocks, crowds, learned particle simulators and the neighborhood aggregation of graph networks, yet they have received little systematic study as a class of functions with the grading given. In this paper we study the supervised learning of the mechanism when the grading is provided by the environment, as a weight on every element. First, we define the class by axioms, where each element's influence is capped by its weight, the dependence on the weights is regular, and no element is distinguished, and prove a representation theorem: the class is exactly the Lipschitz ball of a transport metric on weighted multisets, and the metric is forced by the axioms. Next, the geometry of the representation gives generalization bounds that depend on the data in two ways. One is via the sparsity profile of the data -- the law of how many elements matter and by how much -- which bounds the rate over all designs with that profile, with an exponent from the profile and no dependence on the number of elements. In a number of natural cases we also show matching lower bounds, up to constants in the exponent. The other is empirical: due to the representation result, classical empirical discrepancy bounds apply to the class as they stand, and the resulting bound is the transport distance between the two halves of the sample in the class's own metric, computed exactly by a matching, with an additional concentration term. Finally, we study a simulated Vicsek flock under four interaction rules at two noise levels, and show that the certificate is non-vacuous, a small fraction of the trivial value on every rule.
papers.summary: In flocks, crowds, learned particle simulators, and the neighborhood aggregation of graph networks, each element's update depends strongly on a few other elements and weakly on many, with the identity and number of relevant elements changing with the system state; such graded sparse mechanisms have not been studied systematically as a function class when the grading is supplied by the environment as a weight on each element. The work defines the class by axioms, where each element's influence is capped by its weight, dependence on the weights is regular, and no element is distinguished, and proves a representation theorem: **the class is exactly the Lipschitz ball of a transport metric on weighted multisets, with the metric forced by the axioms**. This geometry yields generalization bounds whose rate depends on the data's sparsity profile and not on the number of elements, with matching lower bounds in several natural cases, plus empirical discrepancy bounds that reduce to the transport distance between the two halves of a sample, computed exactly by a matching. On a simulated Vicsek flock under four interaction rules and two noise levels the certificate is non-vacuous, a small fraction of the trivial value on every rule.

papers.title: PatTransBench: an ipc-stratified, multi-dimensional benchmark for patent machine translation evaluation
papers.abstract: We present PatTransBench, a 12,000-item Chinese-English/Japanese/Korean patent machine translation (PatMT) benchmark with a four-dimensional evaluation protocol. The benchmark comprises 6,000 short-text (sentence/claim) and 6,000 long-text (paragraph) pairs, evenly split across three language pairs and both translation directions, built via IPC-section-stratified sampling and dualthreshold quality gating from upstream patent-family parallel corpora. The evaluation protocol spans literal n-gram overlap (BLEU, ROUGE-L, chrF), cross-lingual semantic textual similarity (CLSTS), 38-probe-language consistency testing, and serving performance under concurrency. A case study on PatMT2-7B and its fp8/AWQ4/AutoRound-4bit variants reveals direction-dependent quantization effects masked by aggregate scores and non-monotonic language-failure patterns across quantization schemes that are invisible to single-metric evaluation. We plan to release the benchmark, protocol, and case-study results upon publication to support reproducible PatMT evaluation.
papers.summary: Patent machine translation (PatMT) lacks a benchmark that covers technical domains evenly and evaluates beyond a single aggregate score. `PatTransBench` contains 12,000 Chinese-English, Chinese-Japanese, and Chinese-Korean items, split evenly between 6,000 sentence or claim pairs and 6,000 paragraph pairs across both translation directions, sampled with stratification over patent classification sections and filtered by dual-threshold quality gating from patent-family parallel corpora. Its four-dimensional protocol combines n-gram overlap metrics (`BLEU`, `ROUGE-L`, `chrF`), cross-lingual semantic textual similarity (CLSTS), 38-probe-language consistency testing, and serving performance under concurrency. A case study of `PatMT2-7B` and its fp8, AWQ 4-bit, and AutoRound 4-bit variants **reveals direction-dependent quantization effects masked by aggregate scores** and non-monotonic language-failure patterns across quantization schemes that single-metric evaluation cannot see.

papers.title: Neural Network Preconditioning: A Case Study for the Solution of the Parametric Helmholtz Equation
papers.abstract: This work presents a hybrid numerical approach for solving linear systems arising from the discretization of the two-dimensional parametric Helmholtz equation. A convolutional neural network based on the U-Net architecture is trained in an self-supervised manner (i.e., without explicitly generating reference solutions) to approximate the inverse of the discretized Helmholtz operator, using a loss function involving the residual norm of the linear system. The trained network is used as a nonlinear preconditioner within the flexible GMRES (FGMRES) algorithm. Numerical experiments show that while the neural network is not accurate enough to act as a standalone solver, it significantly improves the convergence of FGMRES when employed as a preconditioner. The neural preconditioner demonstrates robust performance and generalization capabilities with respect to variations in the velocity field and the domain size. Comparisons with algebraic preconditioners, based on LU factorizations of approximations of the original system matrices, indicate the superior efficiency of the neural approach under equivalent conditions. We believe that the proposed method is not tied to a specific neural architecture and can be extended to other parametric PDEs.

papers.summary: Linear systems from discretizing the two-dimensional parametric Helmholtz equation are expensive to solve, and this case study tests a hybrid approach in which a `U-Net` convolutional network approximates the inverse of the discretized operator. The network is trained in a self-supervised manner, without generating reference solutions, using a loss on the residual norm of the linear system, and is then used as a nonlinear preconditioner inside the flexible GMRES (`FGMRES`) solver. **The network is not accurate enough as a standalone solver but substantially accelerates `FGMRES` convergence as a preconditioner**, generalizes across velocity fields and domain sizes, and is more efficient than algebraic preconditioners built from LU factorizations of approximate system matrices under equivalent conditions, with the authors arguing the approach is not tied to a particular architecture and can extend to other parametric PDEs.

papers.title: Overtaught, Underlearned: Learner-Centered Distillation from Multi-Agent Discussion
papers.abstract: Multi-agent discussion produces reasoning collaboratively, while deployment still relies on a smaller student that must answer alone. Full-graph distillation transfers such discussions by treating each correct solution as a separate training target, but what teachers provide need not match what the student learns. This mismatch appears in two ways: several correct solutions may amount to the same lesson in the student's representation (over-teaching), while some training questions remain missed after learning (under-learning). We quantify both with rates that are high on discussion graphs. To address them, we introduce FAR (Fold--Attempt--Revisit), a learner-centered distillation procedure that organizes supervision around the student's own state. Before training, FAR folds solutions within each discussion state into representative lessons. After training, the student's own attempts identify missed questions, while poorly represented clusters indicate where folding may have lost useful variation; FAR then writes targeted lessons from retained discussion contexts. Across two students and four reasoning tasks, FAR outperforms full-graph distillation with far fewer training targets and lower under-learning. Further analyses examine the behavior of FAR and the sources of its gains. Overall, the results show that organizing discussion supervision around the student can make distillation both more effective and more efficient.
papers.summary: Multi-agent discussion produces reasoning collaboratively, but deployment relies on a smaller student that answers alone, and full-graph distillation treats every correct solution in a discussion as a separate training target. The authors quantify two mismatches between what teachers provide and what the student learns, over-teaching, where several correct solutions reduce to the same lesson in the student's representation, and under-learning, where training questions remain missed after training, and find both rates high on discussion graphs. `FAR` (Fold-Attempt-Revisit) folds the solutions within each discussion state into representative lessons before training, then uses the student's own attempts to find missed questions and poorly represented clusters where folding may have lost useful variation, writing targeted lessons from retained discussion contexts. Across two students and four reasoning tasks, **`FAR` outperforms full-graph distillation with far fewer training targets** and lower under-learning.

papers.title: Heuristics are Not Enough: Calibrated and Corrected Caching for Video Diffusion Acceleration
papers.abstract: Feature caching has become a mainstream training-free strategy for accelerating video diffusion models by reusing intermediate outputs across denoising steps. However, existing adaptive methods rely on heuristic difference measures misaligned with actual generation quality, employ a single global threshold that ignores heterogeneous phase dynamics, and never validate their budget estimates against true approximation error, allowing systematic bias to propagate uncorrected. We propose \textbf{AlignCache}, a closed-loop caching framework that directly aligns scheduling decisions with their true influence on the final generated video through three tightly coupled components: (1) phase-adaptive budget routing that partitions the denoising trajectory into structurally distinct phases, each governed by an independent threshold and a staleness-aware guard; (2) closed-loop threshold calibration that exploits counterfactual error measurement at the classifier-free guided output level to adjust decision boundaries online via an EMA feedback loop; and (3) momentum-augmented draft synthesis combining direction-magnitude gated residual extrapolation with anchor-guided unconditional correction. By transforming scheduling from a static risk accumulator into a feedback-driven, self-correcting controller, AlignCache consistently achieves superior acceleration-quality trade-offs across state-of-the-art video generation models. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiangjyjy/AlignCache.
papers.summary: Feature caching accelerates video diffusion models by reusing intermediate outputs across denoising steps, but existing adaptive schemes rely on heuristic difference measures that are misaligned with generation quality, use one global threshold that ignores phase-dependent dynamics, and never check their budget estimates against true approximation error, so systematic bias goes uncorrected. `AlignCache` is a closed-loop framework with three coupled parts: phase-adaptive budget routing that splits the denoising trajectory into structurally distinct phases, each with its own threshold and a staleness-aware guard; closed-loop threshold calibration that measures counterfactual error at the classifier-free guided output and adjusts decision boundaries online through an EMA feedback loop; and momentum-augmented draft synthesis that combines direction-magnitude gated residual extrapolation with anchor-guided unconditional correction. By turning scheduling from a static risk accumulator into a feedback-driven, self-correcting controller, **`AlignCache` achieves better acceleration-quality trade-offs than prior caching methods across state-of-the-art video generation models**, with code released.

papers.title: DeepFlow: Two Convergent Differentiable Approaches for Pairwise Conditional Random Fields
papers.abstract: Basic probabilistic models form the basis of modern deep learning largely by defining the final activation layer of a network and allowing the networks outputs to be interpreted through a probabilistic lens. By increasing the complexity of these final activation layers to include features such as spatial regularisation, allow for these models to improve in performance without requiring significantly more data. The challenge however is to ensure that these more complex probabilistic graphical models adapt well to being used in tandem with deep learning, that is, ensuring they converge and have meaningful derivatives. The goal of this paper is to show two algorithms with provable convergence properties to allow this type of regularisation for image and signal classification models. Through both rigorous mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, we can show the differing performance between these solution types.
papers.summary: Basic probabilistic models underpin deep learning largely by defining the final activation layer so that network outputs can be read as probabilities, and making that layer richer with features such as spatial regularisation, as in pairwise conditional random fields, can improve image and signal classifiers without much more data, provided the inference converges and has meaningful derivatives when embedded in a network. The work presents two differentiable algorithms for pairwise conditional random fields, each with **provable convergence guarantees**, so that this kind of structured regularisation can be trained end to end with a deep model. Rigorous mathematical analysis and in silico experiments compare the behaviour and performance of the two solution types.

papers.title: Know Yourself and Know Your Neighbour: A Syntactically Informed Self-Supervised Compositional Sentence Representation Learning Framework using a Recursive Hypernetwork
papers.abstract: Sentence representation learning is still an open challenge in Natural Language Processing. In this work, we propose a new self-supervised framework for learning sentence representations, using a special type of neural network called a recursive hypernetwork. Our proposed model composes the representation of a sentence from representations of words by applying a recursive composition through the parse tree. We maintain a separate syntactic and semantic representation, and the semantic composition is guided by the information from the syntactic representation. To train this model, we introduce a novel set of six self-supervised tasks. By analysing the performance on 7 probing tasks, we validate that the generated sentence representation encodes richer linguistic information than both averaging baselines and state-of-the-art alternatives. Furthermore, we assess the impact of the six proposed self-supervised training tasks through ablation studies. We also demonstrate that the representations generated by our model are stable for sentences of varying length and that the semantic composition operators adapt to different syntactic categories\footnote{Code available: https://github.com/vasudev2020/codi/tree/main}.
papers.summary: Sentence representation learning remains an open problem, and this self-supervised framework builds a sentence vector by recursively composing word representations along the parse tree using a recursive hypernetwork, which generates the composition operators. Separate syntactic and semantic representations are maintained, with the semantic composition guided by the syntactic one, and training uses a novel set of six self-supervised tasks. On 7 probing tasks **the learned representations encode richer linguistic information than averaging baselines and state-of-the-art alternatives**; ablations assess each of the six training tasks, and the representations are shown to be stable across sentence lengths, with composition operators that adapt to different syntactic categories.

papers.title: Making Language the Low-Rate Code of Vision: Successive Refinement from Words to Pixels
papers.abstract: An ordered visual code lets a short prefix stand in for an image, and the training loss decides what that prefix contains. Under pixel reconstruction the first bits go to the directions of highest variance, and we prove that a caption can then be independent of the entire first half of a code that is rate-optimal for pixels at every length. In the rate-distortion sense a caption is therefore not the low-rate code of its image, unless the code is built to make it one. We study that construction and what it costs. We cast captioning and text-to-image generation as successive refinement under a distortion measure that changes along the code, from caption log-loss in the early stages to pixel distortion in the last, so that each stage is compared with its own optimum. Putting words first then costs nothing among the caption stages exactly when the captions form a summarization chain, and it costs the pixels at most the caption uncertainty left in a pixel-optimal reconstruction, which is large for short prefixes and small at full length. We build RUNG, an ordered code whose prefixes are supervised by a summarization ladder of captions and whose full length reconstructs the image; generation extends the code past the prompt and captioning truncates it. With data and capacity held fixed, ordering by language instead of reconstruction raises prefix-caption information 2.9 times and GenEval from 0.76 to 0.83, at a measured cost of 2.8 dB PSNR at a quarter of the code and 0.1 dB at full length. RUNG-XL (3.4B) reaches 0.88 GenEval and 87.6 DPG-Bench in 32 network evaluations and 0.91 GenEval when errors are redrawn at the rung where they appear; its coarse and fine captions agree 94.1% of the time, and it edits images without inversion.
papers.summary: An ordered visual code lets a short prefix stand in for an image, and the training loss decides what that prefix contains: under pixel reconstruction the first bits go to the highest-variance directions, and the authors prove a caption can be independent of the entire first half of a code that is rate-optimal for pixels at every length, so a caption is not the low-rate code of its image unless the code is built to make it one. They cast captioning and text-to-image generation as successive refinement under a distortion measure that shifts along the code from caption log-loss early to pixel distortion late, show that putting words first costs nothing among the caption stages exactly when the captions form a summarization chain, and build `RUNG`, an ordered code whose prefixes are supervised by a ladder of captions and whose full length reconstructs the image, so generation extends the code past the prompt and captioning truncates it. With data and capacity fixed, ordering by language instead of reconstruction raises prefix-caption information 2.9 times and `GenEval` from 0.76 to 0.83 at a cost of 2.8 dB PSNR at a quarter of the code and 0.1 dB at full length. **`RUNG-XL` at 3.4B parameters reaches 0.88 on `GenEval` and 87.6 on `DPG-Bench` in 32 network evaluations**, rising to 0.91 `GenEval` when errors are redrawn at the rung where they appear, and it edits images without inversion.

papers.title: AI Discovery in Combinatorics: From Problems to Solutions and Back to Bigger Problems
papers.abstract: We introduce $qt$Bench, a benchmark of 29 open problems in algebraic combinatorics. These problems ask for a simple combinatorial algorithm that explains given polynomial coefficients or identities. To help AI agents search for such algorithms, we provide a scaffold for playing with combinatorial objects, countering cheating attempts, and testing candidate solutions. To explore how far frontier AI systems can go on these problems, we collaborated with OpenAI, whose researchers obtained proposed solutions to several of them. This highlights bigger meta-problems: is AI discovery at scale ethical? How should these results be released? How should proof digestion be organized? We discuss these questions and give our views.
papers.summary: `qtBench` is a benchmark of 29 open problems in algebraic combinatorics, each asking for a simple combinatorial algorithm that explains given polynomial coefficients or identities. To let AI agents search for such algorithms, the authors provide a scaffold for manipulating combinatorial objects, countering cheating attempts, and testing candidate solutions. In a collaboration with OpenAI, **researchers obtained proposed solutions to several of the open problems**, which raises meta-questions the authors discuss and take positions on: whether AI discovery at scale is ethical, how such results should be released, and how digestion of the resulting proofs should be organized.

papers.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.
papers.summary: In image-goal navigation the target usually lies outside the current field of view, so an agent must model environment dynamics and also keep a persistent spatial memory; existing methods either fine-tune pretrained models on the target task, underusing their spatial priors, or depend on external 3D reconstruction that is too expensive for real-world deployment. The Geometry Grounded World Action Model (`G2WAM`) encodes spatial cues with a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, jointly predicts future states and actions so that no cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning is needed, and operates entirely in latent space to avoid pixel-level reconstruction. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks it reduces the average ATE and RPE trajectory error metrics by 40.1% and 35.2%, and in closed-loop navigation it **raises the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%** while remaining efficient.

papers.title: Scalable Identification of Physics-Based and Neural Dynamics from Partial Measurements
papers.abstract: We present a scalable method for identifying nonlinear dynamics from partial measurements, supporting physics-based, neural-network, and gray-box models. We use the Prediction Error Method (PEM) coupled with state estimation performed by a Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) scheme, which can account directly for general nonlinear dynamics. This results in a bi-level optimization problem that scales poorly with increasing model parameters. To improve computational efficiency, we derive a reformulation that avoids explicit parameter-wide sensitivity matrices and exploits the temporal structure of the underlying optimization problem. Numerical comparisons show up to a $215\times$ speedup in hypergradient evaluation. Racing-vehicle simulations demonstrate accurate prediction and physical-parameter recovery in tire-force identification. Real-world data show that the gray-box model improves prediction accuracy with a neural residual while retaining physical interpretability.
papers.summary: Fitting nonlinear dynamical models from partial state measurements usually means solving a bi-level problem: the Prediction Error Method (PEM) tunes model parameters while a Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) scheme reconstructs unobserved states, and the cost grows badly with the number of parameters. The authors reformulate the hypergradient computation to avoid parameter-wide sensitivity matrices and exploit the temporal structure of the inner optimization, which lets the same machinery fit physics-based, neural-network, and gray-box models. Numerical comparisons show **up to a 215x speedup in hypergradient evaluation**, racing-vehicle simulations recover physical tire-force parameters accurately, and on real data a gray-box model with a neural residual improves prediction while keeping the physical part interpretable.

papers.title: Optimal Transport PAC-Bayes Bounds
papers.abstract: PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds are among the strongest distribution-dependent guarantees in statistical learning and are typically expressed in terms of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between a prior and posterior distribution. While analytically convenient, the KL divergence requires the posterior to be absolutely continuous w.r.t. the prior, imposing support constraints that can substantially restrict the choice of posterior. Moreover, the KL divergence does not account for the underlying geometry of the probability space. In this work, we derive new PAC-Bayesian bounds replacing the KL divergence with general optimal transport (OT) distances, including the total variation and Wasserstein-$p$ distances.
papers.summary: PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds are usually written in terms of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between a prior and a posterior over hypotheses, which forces the posterior to be absolutely continuous with respect to the prior and ignores any geometry on the hypothesis space. The authors derive new PAC-Bayesian bounds that replace the KL term with general optimal transport (OT) distances, including total variation and Wasserstein-p distances. **The resulting bounds lift the support constraint on the posterior and account for the geometry of the underlying probability space**, widening the family of posteriors for which such guarantees can be stated.

papers.title: The Language of Looking: Motion Tokens Reveal Domain-Dependent Local Structure in Gaze Sequences
papers.abstract: Human gaze is the primary high-bandwidth interface through which we parse the semantics of our environment. While often modeled as a sequence, the degree to which gaze exhibits transferable local structure across domains remains underexplored. Using motion tokenization as a diagnostic lens across four diverse datasets, we investigate the transferability of local sequence structure. We demonstrate that while gaze can share a reusable motion-token vocabulary, identical motion tokens are organized into different local transition patterns depending on the dataset and task context. Our results show the limitations of naive data-pooling under low-semantic motion-token representations and provide a framework for evaluating behavioral sequences through information-theoretic diagnostics.
papers.summary: Human gaze is often modeled as a sequence, but it is unclear how much of its local structure transfers from one task or dataset to another. The authors use motion tokenization as a diagnostic across four gaze datasets, quantizing movements into a shared vocabulary and then comparing the local transition statistics of those tokens with information-theoretic measures.
