They find that **a single motion-token vocabulary can be reused across datasets, yet the same tokens are organized into different local transition patterns depending on the dataset and task**, which exposes the limits of naively pooling gaze data under low-semantic token representations.

papers.title: VLA-GAUGE: Systematically Evaluating Generalization and Robustness in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have achieved high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, yet it remains unclear whether such scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization and perturbation robustness. Existing evaluation frameworks provide limited capability-level diagnosis and combinatorial perturbation coverage, often without connecting diagnosis to targeted model refinement. We introduce VLA-GAUGE, a diagnostic framework that unifies both evaluations under a shared executable task representation. It combines (1) paired in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites, (2) single-factor sensitivity analysis with combinatorial perturbation screening and evaluation, and (3) diagnosis-driven refinement through targeted data augmentation and model fine-tuning. We evaluate 12 VLAs spanning different model sizes and action-modeling paradigms under a unified protocol. We find that (1) The mean Zero-Shot Score on VLA-GAUGE is only 22.3%, with SimpleVLA-RL scoring 8.0% and ranking second to last among the evaluated models. (2) Under three representative combinatorial perturbation configurations, the mean R-Score is 9.3. (3) Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves $\pi_{0.5}$'s zero-shot generalization and robustness under a selected perturbation combination on held-out scenarios by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively; the latter exceeds the 10.9-point gain from LIBERO-Plus single-factor fine-tuning despite fewer successful training trajectories. These results show that high reported success rates on familiar manipulation tasks do not guarantee strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or robustness to combinatorial perturbations, while diagnostic evaluation provides actionable signals for targeted model improvement.
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models score well on familiar manipulation tasks, but those scores say little about zero-shot generalization or robustness to combined perturbations. `VLA-GAUGE` is a diagnostic framework built on a shared executable task representation that pairs in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites, runs single-factor sensitivity analysis plus combinatorial perturbation screening, and feeds the diagnosis back into targeted data augmentation and fine-tuning. Across 12 VLAs of varying size and action-modeling paradigm, **the mean zero-shot score is only 22.3% and the mean robustness score under combinatorial perturbations is 9.3**, with `SimpleVLA-RL` ranking second to last. Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning raises `π0.5`'s held-out zero-shot generalization and robustness by 72.4 and 31.8 points respectively, the latter beating the 10.9-point gain from `LIBERO-Plus` single-factor fine-tuning despite using fewer successful trajectories.

papers.title: From a Large-Scale Teacher to Efficient Multimodal Students for Search Relevance Prediction
papers.abstract:
Relevance prediction between user queries and items is a fundamental component of e-commerce search systems. Traditionally, high-quality relevance labels are obtained through human judgment, which is reliable but expensive, slow, and difficult to scale. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) enable automated relevance judgment at scale, achieving performance comparable to human annotators. However, such systems often rely on large commercial LLMs with complex prompts, resulting in high inference costs and limited throughput.
  In this work, we propose a framework that bridges this gap by distilling a high-performing LLM-based relevance judgment system into efficient multimodal student models. We first curate a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset to serve as ground truth. Using this dataset, we develop a reliable LLM-as-a-judge pipeline through careful prompt engineering and iterative refinement. This pipeline is then used to generate large-scale relevance labels, which serve as training data for compact multimodal models. Our distilled models achieve performance close to the teacher system while significantly improving latency, cost, and scalability. This approach enables practical deployment of high-quality relevance prediction systems in production environments.
papers.summary: E-commerce search needs query-item relevance labels at scale, and while large commercial language models can now judge relevance about as well as human annotators, running them with complex prompts in production is slow and expensive. The authors curate a small human-labeled gold set, iterate on an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline until it agrees reliably with that set, then use the pipeline to label a large corpus and distill it into compact multimodal student models that see both text and item images. **The distilled students approach the teacher's relevance accuracy while cutting latency and cost enough for production deployment**, replacing the large commercial model in the serving path.

papers.title: $\texttt{NFDiag}$: High-dimensional MCMC Convergence Diagnosis with Normalizing Flows
papers.abstract: Accurately assessing the convergence of Monte Carlo Markov Chains is crucial for ensuring their validity in Bayesian inference problems. However, convergence assessment in high dimensions is known to be difficult, due to most convergence diagnostics becoming insensitive beyond a few dozen parameters. Conventional convergence statistics analyze marginal distributions which in high dimensions neglects increasing levels of information from the joint and conditional probability distributions. Thus we propose $\texttt{NFDiag}$, which taps into the information of the full multivariate joint posterior with a normalizing flow (NF). Our convergence diagnostic thereby also analyzes information from conditional distributions. In other words, by working in the full multivariate space, it is sensitive with respect to the geometry of the chain in high dimensions. Our diagnostic utilizes that NFs assume independent and identically distributed (iid) training samples, which is a testable assumption that will be violated by a non-converged or strongly correlated chain. Our diagnostic trains NFs on separate parts of a chain, and then assesses whether these correspond to the same multivariate target distribution. We test our diagnostic in up to 250 dimensions, and demonstrate it is universal and unbiased, and detects problematic chain quality also when Gelman-Rubin $\hat{R}$ and the multivarite effective sample size do not.
papers.summary: Standard Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence diagnostics such as Gelman-Rubin R-hat examine marginal distributions, which makes them insensitive once a posterior has more than a few dozen parameters. `NFDiag` instead trains normalizing flows (NFs) on separate segments of a chain and tests whether those segments were drawn from the same joint multivariate target, exploiting the fact that flows assume independent and identically distributed training samples, an assumption a non-converged or strongly autocorrelated chain violates. Tested in up to 250 dimensions, **the diagnostic is universal and unbiased and flags problematic chains in cases where R-hat and the multivariate effective sample size do not**, because it is sensitive to the geometry of the full joint and conditional distributions.

papers.title: Variational Filtering for Bayesian Last Layers with an Independent Binary Probit Surrogate
papers.abstract: Modern deep classifiers trained by gradient descent need many passes over the data to become accurate, and even then are not always well calibrated; post-hoc temperature scaling corrects calibration after training but cannot influence training-time accuracy or convergence. We propose a variational filtering algorithm for the last layer of deep classifiers, whose parameters are treated as the latent state of a linear-Gaussian state-space model. Each mini-batch is assimilated by an exact prediction step followed by a closed-form variational update, made conjugate by an independent binary probit (IBProbit) surrogate for the categorical likelihood. The filter's process noise stabilises the updates under feature drift and keeps the predictive distribution from collapsing to a point estimate, allowing the same procedure to be used for linear probing on a frozen backbone and for full-network fine-tuning. We evaluate on DINOv3 backbones against two baselines tuned under an identical protocol: AdamW with cross-entropy and post-hoc temperature scaling, and Variational Bayesian Last Layers (VBLL). As a linear probe on frozen features, IBProbit attains the best accuracy and negative log-likelihood on all five downstream tasks at the largest backbone, and on two of the five at the smallest. In out-of-distribution detection with CIFAR probes on the largest backbone, IBProbit reduces the false-positive rate at 95\% true-positive rate by a factor of 1.4 to 3.2 relative to the better of the two baselines, on all three dataset pairs. When the whole network is fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k, IBProbit reaches the final performance of the cross-entropy baseline in half the wall-clock time.
papers.summary: Deep classifiers trained with gradient descent need many epochs to reach good accuracy and still end up poorly calibrated, and post-hoc temperature scaling cannot help training-time accuracy or convergence. The authors treat the last layer's weights as the latent state of a linear-Gaussian state-space model and run a variational filter over mini-batches, using an independent binary probit (`IBProbit`) surrogate for the categorical likelihood so that each update is closed-form and conjugate, with process noise that handles feature drift and prevents the predictive distribution from collapsing. On `DINOv3` backbones compared against tuned AdamW with temperature scaling and `VBLL`, the filter gives the best accuracy and negative log-likelihood on all five downstream tasks as a linear probe at the largest backbone, and **cuts the out-of-distribution false-positive rate at 95% true-positive rate by 1.4x to 3.2x on all three `CIFAR` dataset pairs**. When fine-tuning the full network on `ImageNet-1k`, it reaches the cross-entropy baseline's final performance in half the wall-clock time.

papers.title: LLM-HB: Language-Aware LLM-Guided Hotword Biasing for Code-Switching ASR
papers.abstract: Code-switching (CS) speech, characterized by language alternation within a single utterance, is prevalent in multilingual communities and poses challenges to automatic speech recognition (ASR) due to rapid language transitions. We propose LLM-HB, a language-aware large language model-guided hotword biasing framework for code-switching ASR (CS-ASR). The framework incorporates a mixture-of-experts (MoE) adaptor and an auxiliary language prediction head to better capture and differentiate multilingual representations, while hotwords are injected through LLM-based prompting. Experiments on the ASRU2019 code-switching challenge test set demonstrate that LLM-HB achieves a 20.30% relative reduction in mixed error rate (MER) over the baseline, reaching 5.85% MER under a 15-distractor hotword setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate LLM-guided biasing into code-switching ASR. We further release the extracted ASRU2019 hotword list to support future research.
papers.summary: Code-switching speech, where speakers alternate languages within one utterance, trips up automatic speech recognition (ASR) because of rapid language transitions. `LLM-HB` adds a mixture-of-experts (MoE) adaptor and an auxiliary language-prediction head to separate multilingual representations, and injects hotwords such as names and domain terms through prompts to a large language model that guides decoding. On the `ASRU2019` code-switching test set, **the system reduces mixed error rate (MER) by 20.30% relative to the baseline, reaching 5.85% MER with 15 distractor hotwords**; the authors describe it as the first use of LLM-guided biasing for code-switching ASR and release the extracted hotword list.

papers.title: Characterizing and Mitigating Distributional Bias in Physics-Informed Generative Models
papers.abstract: Physics-informed generative models augment a data-fitting objective with residual penalties that encourage physical constraints to hold in generated samples. However, improving constraint satisfaction need not improve fidelity to the data distribution. We study this conflict in residual-regularized diffusion models and identify two possible consequences. First, the same prediction error can incur different residual costs near different feasible states, preferring states with lower residual sensitivity (avoidance). Second, this preference can extend to feasible states outside the data support, where the residual also vanishes (leakage). Motivated by this analysis, we propose a data-anchored penalty that weights prediction errors by the residual Jacobian at the clean training sample and normalizes the resulting magnitude. This removes the incentive to relocate to less sensitive states without changing the model architecture or sampling procedure. Experiments on a controlled synthetic system, three PDE systems, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching demonstrate the benefits of anchoring. Code is available at https://github.com/TanjaBien/anchored_diffusion.
papers.summary: Physics-informed generative models add a residual penalty so that samples satisfy physical constraints, but satisfying constraints better does not necessarily mean matching the data distribution better. Analyzing residual-regularized diffusion models, the authors identify two failure modes: avoidance, where the same prediction error is cheaper near feasible states with lower residual sensitivity so the model drifts toward them, and leakage, where that preference extends to feasible states outside the data support where the residual also vanishes. They propose a data-anchored penalty that weights prediction errors by the residual Jacobian evaluated at the clean training sample and normalizes the magnitude, **removing the incentive to relocate toward less sensitive states without changing the architecture or sampler**, and show benefits on a synthetic system, three partial differential equation systems, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching.

papers.title: OctMole: Multiscale 3D Molecular Generation with Hierarchical Spatial Flows
papers.abstract: Generating accurate 3D molecules requires jointly determining a variable number of atoms, their identities, and geometry across spatial scales: global shape emerges coarsely, whereas chemical bonds demand fine local precision. Existing atom-based diffusion and flow models operate largely at a single scale, while dense spatial fields become costly at high resolution. We introduce OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. A hierarchical occupancy flow progressively resolves sparse molecular support from coarse to fine, and a joint atom flow assigns atom types and continuous in-cell offsets to occupied leaves. This decomposition combines efficient global structure with subcell geometric precision, while cell corruption improves robustness to generated support. On QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, OctMole achieves strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality, with particularly clear gains over Uni-3DAR on GEOM-DRUG and substantial efficiency gains over dense 3D generation. As an additional capability, intermediate occupancy states and selected regions provide spatial conditioning without task-specific retraining, supporting multiscale shape conditioning, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation. Code and pretrained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/octree-nn/octmole and https://huggingface.co/Disembo/octmole, respectively.
papers.summary: Generating 3D molecules means jointly choosing how many atoms there are, their types, and their positions, where global shape is coarse but bond geometry needs fine precision; atom-based diffusion and flow models work at one scale and dense voxel fields get expensive at high resolution. `OctMole` uses a hierarchical occupancy flow over an octree that resolves the sparse molecular support from coarse to fine, paired with a joint atom flow that assigns atom types and continuous in-cell offsets to occupied leaves, with cell corruption during training to tolerate imperfect generated support. On `QM9` and `GEOM-DRUG` it reaches strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality, with **clear gains over `Uni-3DAR` on `GEOM-DRUG` and substantially lower cost than dense 3D generation**, and its intermediate occupancy states double as spatial conditioning for shape-conditioned generation, regional editing, linker design, and shape interpolation without retraining.

papers.title: Code-Interactive Visual Reasoning for Financial Candlestick Understanding
papers.abstract: Financial candlestick understanding requires locating visual elements, aligning them across trading dates and panels, and combining observations through numerical and financial reasoning. Answer accuracy alone does not reveal whether predictions are supported by chart evidence. We introduce Code-Interactive Financial Candlestick Reasoning and present Fin-Thinker, a model based on Qwen3.5-9B that generates and executes code to acquire evidence and perform computations. The model uses the returned observations to guide subsequent reasoning. To train these capabilities, we construct FinKLine-32K with 32,184 replay-verified code-observation trajectories collected through teacher-guided student exploration. These include successful solutions with and without error recovery. Our three-stage training framework combines foundational visual-code fine-tuning, financial process supervision of successful reasoning and corrective continuations, and execution-feedback reinforcement learning. For evaluation, we introduce FinKLineBench with 1,200 questions across 138 financial task types to assess answer correctness, code execution, and evidence grounding separately. On FinKLineBench, Fin-Thinker improves strict accuracy by 13.1 and 33.2 percentage points over the best-performing direct-answer baseline among those evaluated and its base model with sandbox access, respectively. Training-stage ablations further show that financial process supervision and execution-feedback reinforcement learning yield successive improvements in both answer accuracy and GPT-5.6-judged grounded accuracy.
papers.summary: Reading financial candlestick charts requires locating visual elements, aligning them across dates and panels, and combining what is seen with numerical and financial reasoning, and a correct final answer does not show whether the model actually used chart evidence. `Fin-Thinker`, built on `Qwen3.5-9B`, writes and executes code to extract evidence and compute values, then conditions its subsequent reasoning on the returned observations; it is trained on `FinKLine-32K`, a set of 32,184 replay-verified code-observation trajectories gathered by teacher-guided student exploration that include both clean solutions and error-recovery traces, through a three-stage pipeline of visual-code fine-tuning, process supervision, and execution-feedback reinforcement learning. On the new `FinKLineBench` of 1,200 questions over 138 task types, which scores answer correctness, code execution, and evidence grounding separately, **strict accuracy improves by 13.1 points over the best direct-answer baseline and by 33.2 points over the base model given sandbox access**, with ablations showing process supervision and execution-feedback RL each adding to both answer accuracy and judged grounded accuracy.

papers.title: HyBRA-EEG: Hyperbolic Global-Local Brain-Region Aggregation for Self-Supervised EEG Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) representation learning is challenged by noisy signals, inter-subject variability, and heterogeneous electrode montages in different datasets and recording settings. Recent self-supervised EEG pretraining methods improve transferability by converting heterogeneous recordings into unified token or sequence representations, but channel-aware designs may still encode montage- or dataset-specific regularities. We propose HyBRA, a self-supervised framework based on hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation. HyBRA maps heterogeneous channel observations into a fixed regional token space by combining electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances. A channel-evidence injection branch preserves fine-grained discriminative cues during aggregation. The resulting tokens are processed by a Region-Time Transformer and pretrained with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals. HyBRA outperforms the compared methods in average balanced accuracy on six benchmark datasets. Under a controlled six-fold evaluation on OpenBMI-MI, HyBRA matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 percentage points and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, and uses 96.8\% fewer parameters. Matched comparisons on TUAB and TUEV show higher balanced accuracy for hyperbolic matching than for Euclidean distance or cosine similarity.
papers.summary: Self-supervised pretraining for electroencephalography (EEG) must cope with noisy signals, variation across subjects, and electrode montages that differ between datasets, and channel-aware tokenizers can quietly memorize montage-specific regularities. `HyBRA` maps heterogeneous channels into a fixed set of brain-region tokens by combining electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances, keeps fine-grained cues through a channel-evidence injection branch, and pretrains a Region-Time Transformer with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals. It achieves the best average balanced accuracy across six benchmark datasets, and in a controlled six-fold evaluation on `OpenBMI-MI` it **matches `CSBrain` in balanced accuracy while improving AUROC by 1.84 points and AUPRC by 5.23 points with 96.8% fewer parameters**; matched comparisons on `TUAB` and `TUEV` favor hyperbolic matching over Euclidean distance or cosine similarity.

papers.title: JtT: Rethinking Point Trajectory Diffusion for Diverse and Rigid Motion from an Image
papers.abstract:
We study forecasting rigid-body motion from a single image: generating diverse and physically plausible future trajectories for arbitrary points in a scene, without building rigidity into the architecture or relying on geometric inputs such as depth. Like video generators, recent trajectory generators fail at this task, even in simple synthetic Kubric scenes, despite scaling up model size and training on real data.
  We show how to solve this with the right architecture and parameterization. Our model, JtT, is a simple diffusion transformer that operates directly in coordinate space and decodes arbitrary and dense query patterns, without the trajectory VAEs or fixed grids assumed in prior work. Through a systematic study of the design space of point trajectory diffusion, we find that diffusing per-frame velocities is the only parameterization that captures rigidity, that it must be paired with the right timestep schedule, and that adding full-resolution RGB at the query points resolves the boundary failures of prior methods.
  However, evaluating such 2D models rigorously is itself non-trivial. To our knowledge, we are the first to observe that physical plausibility and diversity do not improve together during training: larger models, as used in prior work, memorize the single ground-truth future per training image, becoming more rigid while covering fewer possible futures.
  Yet prior work has paid little attention to this, so we show how model rankings depend on model size, metric, and stopping time, and adopt a stricter, checkpoint-averaged evaluation protocol. Under this protocol, JtT improves over prior methods on both distributional and rigidity metrics and approaches ground-truth rigidity, with only about 50M parameters.
papers.summary: Forecasting rigid-body motion from a single image means generating diverse yet physically plausible future trajectories for arbitrary scene points without hard-coding rigidity or using depth, and both video generators and recent trajectory generators fail at this even on simple synthetic `Kubric` scenes. `JtT` is a plain diffusion transformer that works directly in coordinate space and decodes arbitrary dense query patterns without the trajectory VAEs or fixed grids of prior work; a systematic design-space study finds that diffusing per-frame velocities is the only parameterization that captures rigidity, that it needs a matching timestep schedule, and that full-resolution RGB at the query points fixes boundary failures. The authors also observe that **physical plausibility and diversity do not improve together during training, since larger models memorize the single ground-truth future per image and become more rigid while covering fewer futures**, so they adopt a stricter checkpoint-averaged evaluation protocol under which the roughly 50M-parameter `JtT` beats prior methods on distributional and rigidity metrics and approaches ground-truth rigidity.

papers.title: Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.
papers.summary: In agentic reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models, multi-turn rollouts keep issuing new prefill requests, so prefill and decode work coexist throughout rollout rather than arriving in a single burst as in conventional RL. The authors show that prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design borrowed from online LLM serving, speeds up such rollouts by reducing interference between data-parallel attention modules, allowing stage-specific parallelism, and shortening trajectory completion, but that a fixed split of workers between the two roles loses these gains as the workload mix shifts across tasks and over time. `Prorsa` tracks the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand, then uses those forecasts to reallocate workers and switch rollout engines between roles, **delivering end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x to 4.05x over prefill-decode colocation** in both synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings.

papers.title: Double-Rollout Reinforcement Learning with Sampling-based Reward Estimation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) implemented with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has driven substantial progress in training reasoning language models. However, verifiable outcome rewards provide an imperfect measure of reasoning quality: a correct final answer may not be supported by the reasoning trace, whereas an incorrect rollout may contain a nearly correct reasoning trajectory. We present empirical evidence for this mismatch and hypothesize that the resulting reward noise contributes to instability in reinforcement learning for both reasoning accuracy and token efficiency. To address this credit assignment challenge, this paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning. For each sampled rollout, we truncate its reasoning trace, sample multiple continuations from the truncated prefix, and replace the original reward with the mean continuation reward, yielding a more robust estimate of reasoning quality. This double-rollout algorithm incurs only a moderate increase in compute cost and yet reaches substantially higher accuracies across math and coding tasks and across Qwen and Nemotron models than baseline algorithms with fewer RL steps. For example, using only DAPO data it trains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B to reach 95.4% on AIME 2026, versus 91.5% by GRPO and substantially above state of the art for this model size, within 30 RL steps. When combined with length-based rewards, the same algorithm further improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier over existing efficiency optimizations. These findings suggest that the double-rollout reward estimation is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve both the accuracy and token efficiency of reasoning RL.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`), a correct final answer can sit on top of flawed reasoning and a wrong answer can follow a nearly correct trace, and the authors present evidence that this reward noise destabilizes both accuracy and token efficiency. Their double-rollout method truncates each sampled reasoning trace, samples several continuations from the truncated prefix, and replaces the rollout's reward with the mean continuation reward as a more robust estimate of the reasoning's quality. At moderate extra compute, the method reaches higher accuracy on math and coding tasks across Qwen and Nemotron models in fewer RL steps than baselines; **using only `DAPO` data it takes `Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B` to 95.4% on `AIME 2026` within 30 RL steps, versus 91.5% with `GRPO`**, and combined with length-based rewards it pushes out the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier beyond existing efficiency methods.

papers.title: Towards Modality-Agnostic Seizure Classification: A Unified Deep Learning Framework for Heterogeneous EEG and Intracranial EEG Signals
papers.abstract: Seizure prediction and detection, essential for clinical treatment of epilepsy, remain the crucial task of this neurological disease. EEG and iEEG are widely used to analyze epilepsy due to its capability of capturing discriminative brain activities at high time resolution. However, existing works generally analyze either EEG or iEEG seizure activity separately, where EEG analysis has been well-researched, while more and more works consider iEEG for its higher specificity at the spatial level and signal quality. Currently, most of the existing seizure prediction systems are single-modal in nature, which limits its application to a variety of clinical conditions. Therefore, a common framework to analyze seizures with both EEG and iEEG signals needs to be developed. This paper presents a new framework of multimodal seizure classification integrating the heterogeneous EEG and iEEG recordings from different subjects and sources. A specific framework, called Unified Multimodal Signal Harmonization (UMSH), is developed for harmonizing signals with varied sampling rates and recording conditions. Moreover, to handle the extremely class-imbalanced problem in the data sets, we use a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) based data augmentation technique to generate synthetic samples to balance the class distribution. The proposed framework uses the EEGNet-Vision Transformer (EEGNet-ViT) as the feature extraction and classification network to learn the local discriminative patterns as well as global contextual information in the multimodal seizure data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for robust seizure classification, emphasizing the potential of integrated EEG-iEEG multimodal learning in advancing next-generation epilepsy monitoring and clinical decision-support systems.
papers.summary: Seizure detection and prediction systems for epilepsy typically handle either scalp electroencephalography (EEG) or intracranial EEG (iEEG) alone, which limits where they can be deployed. The authors propose a Unified Multimodal Signal Harmonization (UMSH) stage that reconciles recordings with different sampling rates and recording conditions from multiple subjects and sources, balance the heavily skewed class distribution with synthetic samples from a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN), and classify with an `EEGNet-ViT` hybrid that pairs local pattern extraction with a Vision Transformer for global context. **Experiments indicate robust seizure classification when EEG and iEEG are pooled under the harmonized framework**, which the authors present as a step toward epilepsy monitoring tools that work across clinical recording setups.

papers.title: DEFlow: Deep Equilibrium Flow Maximum-Entropy Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Expressive flow policies can represent multiple high-value actions, but sampling them with few integration steps while retaining tractable action densities remains challenging. We introduce DEFlow, a deep equilibrium flow policy that replaces explicit Euler sampling with implicit Euler integration and solves all intermediate actions jointly as an equilibrium system. We combine implicit differentiation with a discrete change-of-variables formula for the final-action density, enabling off-policy training within soft actor-critic without backpropagating through solver iterations. DEFlow achieves an average relative improvement of approximately 10% in mean successful coverage over the strongest baseline across four Multi-Goal docking variants. It also achieves the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks, while remaining broadly competitive across five MuJoCo tasks. These results support implicit flow policies for tasks requiring both diversity and precision, at the cost of additional nonlinear and linear solves. Primary
papers.summary: Flow-based policies can represent several high-value actions at once, but sampling them in a few integration steps while keeping a tractable action density is hard. `DEFlow` replaces explicit Euler sampling with implicit Euler integration and solves all intermediate actions jointly as a deep equilibrium system, combining implicit differentiation with a discrete change-of-variables formula for the final-action density so the policy can be trained off-policy inside soft actor-critic (`SAC`) without backpropagating through solver iterations. The policy yields **roughly 10% higher mean successful coverage than the strongest baseline across four Multi-Goal docking variants**, the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks, and competitive results on five `MuJoCo` tasks, at the cost of extra nonlinear and linear solves per action.

papers.title: MixLID: Token-Level Language Identification in Mixed-Language Text
papers.abstract: Processing multilingual text requires both identifying a broad range of languages and distinguishing the language of each token in inputs containing multiple languages. We introduce MixLID, a token-level language identification model supporting 111 language-script combinations. MixLID follows a two-stage training process: it first learns to distinguish individual languages using the language labels of monolingual examples, then continues training on mixed-language data. The second stage uses concatenated examples from existing code-switching data alongside augmented examples created through word substitution based on correspondences between English source words and loanwords. For monolingual identification, MixLID outperforms all baselines in both accuracy and macro F1 on four benchmarks within the language coverage shared with each baseline. For mixed-language identification, it outperforms the baselines in identifying the language of individual tokens on every evaluated language pair. MixLID achieves high performance across a broad range of languages in both monolingual and mixed-language settings. The model is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/nlpai-lab/MixLID.
papers.summary: Multilingual text processing needs to identify a wide range of languages and, within mixed-language inputs, label the language of each token. `MixLID` is a token-level language identifier covering 111 language-script combinations, trained first on monolingual examples and then on mixed-language data built from concatenated code-switching examples plus augmented sentences created by substituting English words with their loanword counterparts. **It beats all baselines in accuracy and macro F1 on four monolingual benchmarks within shared language coverage and outperforms them on token-level identification for every evaluated mixed-language pair**; the model is released publicly.

papers.title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
papers.abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
papers.summary: Visual token compression lowers the inference cost of Vision-Language Models by keeping only a subset of image tokens, and existing methods choose tokens by text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed mix of the two that ignores the input. Grid-searching the best relevance-diversity weight per benchmark shows large cross-task variation, and recovering per-sample oracle weights by maximizing answer likelihood shows high variance even within a single benchmark. `SAVER` infers a sample-specific weight at inference time from a Geometric Intent Prior based on how spatially concentrated the text-relevant tokens are, then selects tokens jointly using a Weighted Text Centroid for relevance and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain for diversity, with no additional training; it **retains 96.5% of full-model performance on `LLaVA-1.5-7B` with only 11.1% of the visual tokens** and transfers to `LLaVA-NeXT` and `Mini-Gemini`.

papers.title: DR-APO: Decoupled-Representation Advantage-Guided Policy Optimization from Continuous Control to Embodied Navigation
papers.abstract: Policy representations in reinforcement learning have expanded beyond Gaussian policies to diffusion and flow-matching based generative policies. However, existing RL methods remain representation-specific, lacking a unified optimization interface for emerging generative policies. In particular, extending likelihood-based objectives to multi-step generative policies couples optimization to their internal generation process, where accumulated likelihood ratios can weaken the update signal. Meanwhile, generative-policy-specific methods often rely on multi-candidate generation and critic-based selection, improving overall return while providing limited improvement to the policy itself. We introduce DR-APO (Decoupled-Representation Advantage-Guided Policy Optimization), which decouples policy improvement from policy representation through advantage-guided target improvement and representation-compatible direct action fitting, providing a shared optimization principle for Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies. Across five MuJoCo-v5 tasks, DR-APO remains competitive with SAC for Gaussian policies and achieves the best aggregate policy-only performance for both diffusion and flow-matching policies. NavDP post-training improves the Success Rate (SR) from 70.33% to 89.55% in simulation and from 25% to 65% in real-world navigation. These results demonstrate a unified policy-improvement principle across Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies, from continuous-control learning to embodied-policy post-training.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning policies now include diffusion and flow-matching generators alongside Gaussian ones, but optimization methods remain tied to a particular representation: likelihood-based objectives couple to the multi-step generation process and accumulate ratios that weaken updates, while generator-specific methods lean on sampling many candidates and picking by critic score, which improves returns without much improving the policy itself. `DR-APO` separates policy improvement from representation by first constructing an advantage-guided improved target action and then fitting the policy to it with a representation-compatible direct action loss, giving Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies one shared update rule. On five `MuJoCo-v5` tasks it stays competitive with `SAC` for Gaussian policies and gives the best aggregate policy-only performance for diffusion and flow policies, and post-training `NavDP` with it **raises navigation success rate from 70.33% to 89.55% in simulation and from 25% to 65% on a real robot**.

papers.title: Weak Segmentation-Guided GAN for~Realistic Color Edition
papers.abstract: Editing the color of images in a realistic way finds many applications such as changing the perception of an image, data augmentation or film post processing. The design of an automatic tool is a complex and long addressed challenge. In particular, two properties are difficult to meet altogether: generating realistic results without artifacts and the possibility to precisely choose the future color. Conventional methods using segmentation and histogram matching maximize the controllability but also introduce a lack of realism or are complex to automate. On the contrary, GANs that specialize in realism are difficult to control. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel GAN architecture leveraging any differentiable segmentation model. We demonstrate the genericness of our framework that presents state of the art results on different use cases. It generates images that look realistic while offering a precise color control.
papers.summary: Realistic image color editing has to satisfy two competing demands: results free of artifacts, and precise control over the target color. Segmentation-plus-histogram-matching pipelines deliver control but look unrealistic or are hard to automate, while generative adversarial networks (GANs) produce realistic output that is hard to steer. The authors propose a GAN architecture that can be guided by any differentiable segmentation model and report **state-of-the-art results across several color-editing use cases** while keeping exact control over the chosen color.

papers.title: Answer It or Not? Towards Prompt-Adapted Adversarial Images on Vision Language Models
papers.abstract: With the advancement in language modeling, research on adversarial images has recently shifted from image classifiers to vision-language models (VLMs). Despite the new, text-prompt-driven nature of VLMs, we find that existing VLM adversaries have largely overlooked the dynamics of text prompts. In a typical use case, adversarial images can protect visual privacy by rejecting VLMs from answering questions about the image. However, existing protections are prompt-agnostic, i.e., indiscriminately rejecting any question, including those for potential legitimate use of the image. To address this limitation, we propose Prompt-Adapted (ProAda) adversarial images, which are optimized to balance the rejection of harmful prompts and the correct response of legitimate prompts. In particular, to achieve a more accurate adversarial direction, the text prompt is also iteratively updated with a simple classifier judging whether the harmfulness of the prompt remains. Extensive experiments on visual-privacy-related datasets validate that ProAda can reject over 90% of harmful prompts while allowing over 90% of legitimate ones, demonstrating superior overall performance compared to existing prompt-agnostic VLM adversaries. In addition, our ProAda achieves competitive overall cross-model transferability and improved robustness against countermeasures.
papers.summary: Adversarial images are one way to stop vision-language models (VLMs) from answering questions about a private photo, but existing methods are prompt-agnostic and block every question, including legitimate ones. `ProAda` (Prompt-Adapted adversarial images) optimizes the perturbation to reject harmful prompts while still permitting benign ones, iteratively updating the text prompts during optimization with a small classifier that judges whether each prompt remains harmful. On visual-privacy datasets the method **rejects over 90% of harmful prompts while allowing over 90% of legitimate ones**, with competitive cross-model transfer and better robustness to countermeasures than prompt-agnostic baselines.

papers.title: LATCH: LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness for Post-Route FPGA Optimisation
papers.abstract: Post-route FPGA timing closure remains expert-dependent and computationally expensive. We present LATCH (LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness), a two-layer framework that separates large language model (LLM) orchestration from deterministic FPGA implementation and evaluation. Across sixteen designs and seven LLMs, a single-iteration study compares three agent control granularities - expert-written recipes, direct EDA operations and LLM-constructed procedures - to ask how much control an agent needs per attempt. Functional-pass rates are 98.2%, 71.4% and 17.9%, respectively; yet direct operations give slightly larger 3.4% median Fmax gains when passing, versus 3.2% for recipes. This exposes a trade-off between execution reliability and timing improvement. Informed by this trade-off, a multi-iteration study fixes the action tier at expert recipes to ask how repeated attempts are best organised, comparing a fitted deterministic heuristic with sequential LLM reasoning, branching exploration and knowledge base-guided exploration within 12 checkpoints per run. Branching raises mean maximum-frequency improvement from 10.5% (sequential) to 16.0%, and the knowledge base to 20.3%, improving 15 of 16 designs. Characterisation across 2,421 recipe attempts profiled their gain and validation rates, showing hard-block re-placement gives the largest cumulative mean gain at 41.4MHz.
papers.summary: Closing timing on a routed FPGA design is slow and depends on expert intuition. `LATCH` separates large language model (LLM) orchestration from a deterministic implementation-and-evaluation layer and uses it to compare three levels of agent control across 16 designs and seven LLMs: expert-written recipes, direct electronic design automation (EDA) operations, and LLM-built procedures. Recipes pass functional checks far more reliably (98.2% versus 71.4% and 17.9%) at only a slight cost in frequency gain, and in a multi-iteration study **knowledge-base-guided exploration raises the mean maximum-frequency improvement from 10.5% to 20.3%**, improving 15 of 16 designs. Profiling 2,421 recipe attempts shows hard-block re-placement gives the largest cumulative gain.

papers.title: Integrating Feature Understandability into Feature Selection for Human-Centred Tabular Explanations
papers.abstract: Existing human-centred XAI research predominantly evaluates explanations after they have been generated. However, this fails to provide actionable insights into improving accessibility. This study incorporates human-based feature understandability into feature selection to improve the generation of human-centred explanations. Natural language explanations for machine learning models trained on tabular data often cite influential features in the input data to explain a given decision. As a consequence, users' ability to understand the produced explanation hinges on their understanding of the cited features. To quantify this natural-language feature understandability, Rossberg et al. proposed the Feature Understandability Scale, which assigns numerical `understandability scores' to features based on user feedback. To evaluate the degree to which these scores can improve machine learning explanation quality, this study collects understandability scores across two datasets, proposes an understandability-aware feature selection algorithm to select features that are both understandable and informative, and trains a random forest based on these feature subsets. The SHAP-based explanations generated by this model are evaluated using user feedback, and changes in explanation quality are assessed. The individual evaluation of the explanations showed that while the understandability-based explanations scored higher on average, the difference was not statistically significant. In contrast, the comparative evaluation found that participants preferred these explanations significantly more frequently than expected at the chance level. It is concluded that the integration of understandability can yield more understandable explanations at minimal cost to classification performance, although changes to quality require elucidation in larger cohorts.
papers.summary: Natural-language explanations of tabular models cite influential input features, so an explanation is only as understandable as the features it names. The study collects Feature Understandability Scale scores from users for two datasets, proposes an understandability-aware feature selection algorithm that trades off informativeness against those scores, trains a random forest on the chosen features, and evaluates the resulting `SHAP` explanations with human feedback. Explanations from the understandability-selected models scored higher on average but not significantly so in isolation, yet **participants preferred them significantly more often than chance in head-to-head comparisons**, at minimal cost to classification accuracy.

papers.title: AeroChem: Closed-loop Physics-Informed State Space Modeling for Long-term Chemically-Reactive Air Quality Forecasting--Extended Version
papers.abstract: Accurate long-term air quality forecasting is challenging due to long-range transport, meteorological variability, and nonlinear chemical reactions underlying secondary pollutant formation. Purely data-driven models often suffer from long-horizon drift and lack physical consistency, while existing physics-informed approaches commonly follow open-loop designs that fuse neural and physical components only at the output level. We propose AeroChem, a closed-loop physics-informed state space framework for chemically reactive air quality forecasting. AeroChem adopts a two-branch co-correction design: a UDE-based process branch provides a structured but imperfect physical prior, while a Mamba-based virtual measurement branch captures long-range temporal context and produces probabilistic virtual observations. Neural Kalman Fusion couples the two branches by correcting the latent physical state at each forecasting step and feeding the posterior state back into the simulator, reducing long-horizon drift. We further introduce HanoiAir, a real-world dataset integrating pollutant concentrations, meteorology, and emission inventories. Experiments on HanoiAir and a public benchmark show that AeroChem improves long-horizon stability and sudden-change forecasting.
papers.summary: Long-horizon air quality forecasting is hard because of long-range pollutant transport, variable weather, and nonlinear chemistry producing secondary pollutants, and purely data-driven models drift over long horizons. `AeroChem` pairs a universal differential equation (UDE) process branch, which supplies an imperfect physical prior, with a `Mamba`-based branch that produces probabilistic virtual observations from long temporal context; a Neural Kalman Fusion step corrects the latent physical state at each forecasting step and feeds the posterior back into the simulator, closing the loop. The authors also release `HanoiAir`, a real-world dataset combining pollutant concentrations, meteorology, and emission inventories, and report **improved long-horizon stability and sudden-change forecasting** on it and on a public benchmark.

papers.title: REEL: Learning to Retrieve, Evaluate, and Evolve Visual Memory for Any Long-Horizon Multi-Shot Video Generation
papers.abstract: Memory-based long-video generation aims to combine user control with long-range visual consistency. We organize this process into three functional components: a planner, an adapter, and a generator. Representative multi-shot systems couple memory to generator-specific interfaces or use predefined agent workflows, rather than independently training a memory policy for cross-shot objectives. We introduce REEL, a general-purpose visual-memory planner. Through a unified tool interface, REEL learns to retrieve references, create missing visual evidence, and update persistent memory. Backend-specific adapters translate its evidence plans into supported conditioning inputs, allowing the same policy to guide different black-box video generators. To train REEL, we construct two high-quality datasets, REEL-SFT-4k and REEL-RL-1k, covering diverse interaction patterns and prompt types. Training proceeds in three stages: supervised fine-tuning, single-shot Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and multi-shot GRPO. Multi-shot GRPO carries policy-generated memory across consecutive shots, so later outcomes guide earlier reference selection and memory updates. REEL-Bench tests identity preservation and intended state changes under text-only requests and timed reference-image uploads. On JoyAI-Echo~1.5 and MiniMax-H3, REEL improves cross-shot consistency on ST-Bench by 15.1\% and 20.7\%, and Core-100 on our proposed REEL-Bench by 2.41 and 8.32 points, respectively, over the no-memory baseline.
papers.summary: Memory-based long video generation needs to keep characters and objects consistent across shots while following user instructions. `REEL` is a general-purpose visual-memory planner that, through a unified tool interface, learns to retrieve reference images, generate missing visual evidence, and update a persistent memory; backend-specific adapters translate its evidence plans into conditioning inputs for different black-box video generators. It is trained with supervised fine-tuning on `REEL-SFT-4k`, then single-shot and multi-shot Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on `REEL-RL-1k`, where multi-shot GRPO carries policy-generated memory across shots so later outcomes shape earlier reference choices. On `JoyAI-Echo 1.5` and `MiniMax-H3` it **raises cross-shot consistency on `ST-Bench` by 15.1% and 20.7%** over a no-memory baseline, with further gains on the authors' `REEL-Bench`.

papers.title: ACED: Reference-Anchored Aggregation of Natural-Language and Executable Evidence for Mathematical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Natural-language self-consistency and executable programs provide complementary test-time evidence for mathematical reasoning, yet either channel may support the same semantic error. Thus we propose ACED, a reference-anchored framework that treats the self-consistency answer as the default and executable outputs as supporting evidence rather than interchangeable votes. ACED converts source-specific answer counts into smoothed supports, combines them through a weighted logarithmic pool, and overrides the reference only when a calibrated relative-evidence margin is exceeded. The same rule supports both candidate selection and admission of executable-only answers. Across five math word-problem benchmarks, ACED matches or outperforms the corresponding baselines. On GSM8K, ACED-CANDIDATE recovers 89.7% of the attainable candidate-set gain with only three damaging overrides, while ACED-ALL reaches 86.9% accuracy versus 82.6% for direct Program-of-Thought aggregation. These results show that preserving evidence provenance enables more reliable integration of natural-language and executable reasoning.
papers.summary: Majority voting over natural-language chains of thought and executing generated programs give complementary evidence for math word problems, but both can agree on the same wrong answer. `ACED` treats the self-consistency answer as a reference and executable outputs as supporting evidence: it converts per-source answer counts into smoothed supports, combines them with a weighted logarithmic pool, and overrides the reference only when a calibrated relative-evidence margin is exceeded, using the same rule to select candidates and to admit executable-only answers. Across five benchmarks it matches or beats the baselines; on `GSM8K` the full variant **reaches 86.9% accuracy versus 82.6% for direct Program-of-Thought aggregation**, and the candidate-selection variant recovers 89.7% of the attainable gain with only three damaging overrides.

papers.title: SuPER-Mamba: Surprisal Prioritization for Extended-Context Routing in Mamba
papers.abstract: State space models provide efficient linear-complexity processing for long sequences, but their performance frequently degrades as context length grows. We propose SuPER-Mamba, a training-free framework that uses Surprisal as a model-intrinsic signal for long-range state routing in pretrained Mamba models. SuPER-Mamba computes position-wise Surprisal from next-token predictions, aggregates neighboring responses through Local Pooling, and uses the resulting scores to prioritize Global-Channel updates without query-dependent scoring or additional training. We evaluate SuPER-Mamba on three state-space models across the LongBench-E benchmark. The results show that SuPER-Mamba improves the average score from 8.06 to 15.69, corresponding to a 94.7% relative gain over the Base Models and a 13.1% improvement over the state-of-the-art prior baseline. Ablation and length-wise analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed routing framework.
papers.summary: State space models process long sequences in linear time, but pretrained `Mamba` models often degrade as context grows. `SuPER-Mamba` is a training-free method that uses surprisal from the model's own next-token predictions as a routing signal: position-wise surprisal is pooled over local neighborhoods, and the resulting scores prioritize which positions drive global-channel state updates, with no query-dependent scoring or extra training. On three state space models evaluated on `LongBench-E`, it **lifts the average score from 8.06 to 15.69**, a 94.7% relative gain over the base models and 13.1% over the prior best baseline.

papers.title: Learning Deployable Causal Action Geometry under Temporal Non-Stationarity
papers.abstract: Learning a response law for continuous decisions from observational time series is central to many real-world decision systems, yet temporal non-stationarity poses a fundamental challenge: as outcomes drift over time, naively pooled models can conflate action effects with shifting baselines and even reverse action rankings. Even when the one-step response is identifiable, unrestricted cross-time generalization remains fundamentally ill-posed. We therefore seek the part of the response that remains stable for decisions even when outcome levels do not. We propose deployable causal action geometry: the action-response shape that remains after anchoring away action-independent level shifts on a selected link scale and profiling out positive amplitude variation. Building on this target, we develop a two-stage orthogonal estimator that first obtains cross-fitted pilot estimates of anchored responses and then performs honest profiled selection over link, representation, and shape classes. The resulting estimator admits oracle guarantees for the restricted target and, under approximate persistence, produces decision rules that remain near optimal in future periods. Experiments on synthetic data and Dominick's support the proposed target and its transfer behavior. In a randomized Taobao A/B test, the deployed system improves GMV and purchase counts by \(1.16\%\) and \(1.70\%\).
papers.summary: Learning how continuous actions such as prices affect outcomes from observational time series is confounded by non-stationarity: outcome levels drift, so pooled models can mistake baseline shifts for action effects and even reverse action rankings. The authors define a deployable causal action geometry, the response shape that survives after anchoring away action-independent level shifts on a chosen link scale and profiling out positive amplitude changes, and estimate it with a two-stage orthogonal procedure that cross-fits pilot estimates and then performs honest selection over link, representation, and shape classes. The estimator has oracle guarantees for this restricted target and yields near-optimal future decisions under approximate persistence; beyond synthetic data and `Dominick's`, **a randomized Taobao A/B test raised gross merchandise value by 1.16% and purchases by 1.70%**.

papers.title: Learning Incompressible 3D Flows from Sparse Samples: A Set Transformer Approach to Divergence-Free Kernel Fitting
papers.abstract: Recovering divergence-free velocity fields from sparse and corrupted observations requires reconciling physical consistency, expressive representations, and robustness to missing data. We introduce DFK-Former, a set-to-field transformer that reconstructs divergence-free velocity fields from sparse, noisy, and irregularly sampled 3D observations. The model is inherently invariant to the number and ordering of input samples and predicts the parameters of a divergence-free kernel representation, producing continuous, mesh-free velocity fields that satisfy incompressibility exactly by construction rather than approximately through soft constraints or projection operators. Unlike existing divergence-free kernel approaches, which estimate kernel coefficients via a separate optimization for each field, DFK-Former predicts these coefficients directly in a single forward pass. This eliminates costly iterative fitting while providing a learned prior that enables accurate reconstruction even when observations are insufficient to uniquely determine the field. To enhance representational power, we introduce adaptive and anisotropic divergence-free kernels that preserve exact incompressibility guarantees while capturing more complex flow structures. Extensive experiments across varying levels of sparsity, noise, and occlusion, including transfer to real Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) turbulence data, demonstrate substantial gains in both accuracy and efficiency. DFK-Former reduces endpoint error by up to 4.6x compared to per-field divergence-free-kernel optimization, while reconstructing each field in 7.5 ms instead of 9.8 s, yielding a speedup of more than three orders of magnitude. These results establish direct, feed-forward prediction of divergence-free kernel parameters as a practical and effective paradigm for physically consistent velocity-field reconstruction from sparse observations.
papers.summary: Reconstructing incompressible 3D velocity fields from sparse, noisy, irregular samples requires physical consistency, expressiveness, and robustness to missing data. `DFK-Former` is a set-to-field transformer, invariant to the number and order of input samples, that directly predicts the coefficients of a divergence-free kernel representation in one forward pass, so the output field is mesh-free and exactly incompressible by construction; adaptive, anisotropic kernels extend what the representation can capture. Across sparsity, noise, and occlusion settings, including transfer to real Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) turbulence data, it **cuts endpoint error by up to 4.6x while reconstructing a field in 7.5 ms instead of 9.8 s** compared with per-field kernel optimization.

papers.title: SIREN: Situation-aware Index for Response and Emergency ActioNability in Crisis Translation
papers.abstract: Machine translation (MT) is increasingly utilized in multilingual crisis communication, yet conventional evaluation does not directly assess whether translated emergency messages preserve their actionability. We introduce SIREN (Situation-aware Index for Response and Emergency ActioNability), a human evaluation framework assessing whether translation choices compromise protective action, directive force, and urgency of the source text. We evaluate SIREN in two complementary settings. At the error level, we apply it to HOPE-annotated Italian--English translations produced by ChatGPT-4o and Google Translate: 31.63\% and 48.73\% of errors, respectively, compromise actionability, predominantly by affecting the protective action. At the message level, we evaluate English--French translations produced by TranslateGemma-4B and Google Translate, with actionability preserved in 85.34\% and 92.67\% of translations, respectively. TranslateGemma-4B failures predominantly weaken directive force, whereas Google Translate failures more often compromise protective actions and receive Major impact ratings. These findings show that translation systems can differ not only in how often actionability is lost, but also in the nature and functional impact of these failures. Alongside SIREN, we contribute an English--French crisis-translation resource with human actionability annotations and post-edited reference translations, supporting further research on function-oriented evaluation for crisis communication. Our experimental data is available at https://github.com/mcstaiano/SIREN.
papers.summary: Machine translation (MT) is increasingly used for multilingual emergency messaging, yet standard evaluation never asks whether a translated warning still tells people what to do. `SIREN` is a human evaluation framework that checks whether translation choices compromise the protective action, directive force, or urgency of a message. Applied at the error level to Italian-English output from `ChatGPT-4o` and `Google Translate`, **31.63% and 48.73% of errors respectively undermined actionability**, mostly by altering the protective action; at the message level, `TranslateGemma-4B` and `Google Translate` preserved actionability in 85.34% and 92.67% of English-French translations, with the former mainly weakening directive force and the latter more often damaging the protective action. An English-French crisis-translation resource with actionability annotations and post-edited references is released.

papers.title: IND-Eval: Aligning Evaluation and Simulation for Industrial Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: We introduce IND-Eval, a public benchmark that organizes industrial time series across domains into source-specific forecasting tasks. Relative to established benchmarks such as GIFT-Eval, it emphasizes finer sampling resolutions and a greater prevalence of multivariate forecasting. Evaluating Chronos-2, TiRex-2, and TimesFM-3, we find that TimesFM-3 achieves the lowest source-balanced aggregate nMASE and nCRPS and leads seven of nine sources under each metric; source-specific exceptions reinforce the need for domain-representative evaluation for model selection. These findings also motivate improving domain alignment during pretraining, where real industrial data are often too scarce to close domain-specific gaps directly; we therefore investigate whether a domain's statistical structure can guide simulator design. In a case study on two offshore well-monitoring regimes, we improve a general simulator's coverage using an oscillator-augmented simulation pipeline. This lowers forecasting error in the target domain but reduces performance on the subset of GIFT-Eval with natively univariate targets. A 50/50 mixture of the general and augmented simulation recipes achieves the lowest error among the three training recipes for all four event-metric pairs in the case study while recovering most of the lost GIFT-Eval performance. Together, these results illustrate how domain-representative evaluation can guide model selection and the composition of simulated data while revealing a trade-off between specialization and generality.
papers.summary: Time series foundation models are usually judged on general benchmarks that under-represent the fine sampling rates and multivariate structure of industrial data. `IND-Eval` organizes industrial series from several domains into source-specific forecasting tasks; evaluating `Chronos-2`, `TiRex-2`, and `TimesFM-3` on it, **`TimesFM-3` achieves the lowest source-balanced nMASE and nCRPS and leads on seven of nine sources**, though per-source exceptions show that model choice depends on the domain. A case study on offshore well monitoring then uses the target domain's statistics to design an oscillator-augmented simulator for pretraining; the augmented data lowers in-domain error but hurts `GIFT-Eval` performance, and a 50/50 mix of general and augmented simulation gives the best case-study results while recovering most of the lost generality.

papers.title: Counting with Attention and LayerNorm: Norm Scaling and Representation Geometry
papers.abstract: Counting is a simple task on which transformers can nevertheless fail at long sequence lengths. We study the cost of counting in a single attention layer, up to a maximum length $L$, focusing on how softmax attention and layer normalization shape the representation from which the count is recovered. We mainly focus on regression read-out but also consider classification read-out. For regression, we show unnormalized linear attention counts exactly at parameter norms independent of $L$. For softmax attention, regression cannot count exactly with finite parameters; it recovers the count after rounding, but only when the vector parameter norms grow with $L$. We measure this cost by $B_{\min}$, the smallest bound that can be placed on every trainable vector to ensure exact counting after rounding, and derive tight rates. At fixed model dimension, $B_{\min}$ grows as $L$ without normalization, as $L^{3/2}$ under bare post-normalization, and as $L^{3/4}$ with learned post-normalization. The last rate is unexpected: post-normalization discards the magnitude that carries the count and might be expected to make counting harder, yet with a learnable gain it counts at a smaller norm than softmax without normalization. Bare pre-normalization is different: it bounds the attention scores, so beyond a finite length no parameter norm suffices. A classification read-out keeps every norm bounded under every placement, but a dense head stores one output vector per count and costs more in storage. Experiments on the post-normalized model reproduce this split between the two read-outs. Together, our theoretical and empirical findings characterize how self-attention, layer-normalization placement, and read-out choice shape the representation geometry and parameter cost of counting in the minimal single-head architecture studied here.
papers.summary: Transformers can fail at counting once sequences get long, and the work analyzes why in a single attention layer with a regression or classification read-out, up to a maximum length L. Unnormalized linear attention counts exactly with parameter norms independent of L, whereas softmax attention can only count after rounding and needs vector parameter norms that grow with L; the minimum such bound grows as L without normalization, as L^(3/2) under bare post-layer-normalization, and **only as L^(3/4) with a learnable post-normalization gain**, so normalization with a learned gain unexpectedly makes counting cheaper. Bare pre-normalization bounds the attention scores, so beyond some length no finite norm suffices, while a classification read-out keeps norms bounded at the cost of storing one output vector per count; experiments on the post-normalized model reproduce this split between the two read-outs.

papers.title: Guidance Without Labels: Flow Matching from Coupled Gaussian Mixtures
papers.abstract: Flow matching models are typically trained to transport a Gaussian source to the data distribution, with source and target samples paired independently. We replace the source with a fitted Gaussian mixture and couple each data point to a mixture component through an entropic optimal transport problem. We show that the resulting transport reduces to the standard Gaussian-source problem up to a guidance-like correction, which enables the reuse of a pretrained velocity field. This correction is a closed-form function of the fitted mixture plus a term that we learn with a small correction network. We test our model on published checkpoints for CIFAR-10 and CelebA-HQ. It improves FID at every step count, and on CelebA-HQ it reaches the quality of the baseline with about half the steps. The closed-form term alone, with no training, already delivers most of this improvement; the small correction network accounts for the rest.
papers.summary: Flow matching models normally transport a single Gaussian to the data distribution with source and target samples paired at random. Replacing the source with a fitted Gaussian mixture and coupling each data point to a mixture component via entropic optimal transport, the authors show the resulting transport equals the standard Gaussian-source problem plus a guidance-like correction, so a pretrained velocity field can be reused; the correction has a closed form in terms of the fitted mixture plus a residual learned by a small network. On published `CIFAR-10` and `CelebA-HQ` checkpoints it improves FID at every step count, and **on `CelebA-HQ` it matches baseline quality in about half the sampling steps**, with the training-free closed-form term alone providing most of the gain.

papers.title: Does a Hosted Decision Model Respect Irrelevant Alternatives? A Pre-Registered Test of Option-Set Dependence in Jev
papers.abstract: Decision APIs that return a probability for each option are routinely used as if those probabilities were properties of the options themselves. That reading is valid only if the model satisfies independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): adding an option that is neither the right answer nor its strongest rival should leave the odds between those two unchanged. We test this in a pre-registered study of jev-1.13.0, a hosted decision model, using 299,463 calls on intent classification (BANKING77, CLINC150) and topic classification (AG News). Every added option moves the log-odds between the gold label and the strongest wrong label: the root-mean-square systematic shift is 0.20-0.52 nats, 1.2 to 3 times the run-to-run variation, even when the added option takes at most 0.1% of the probability mass. The shifts are directional. An option similar to the wrong answer draws probability from it (+0.10 nats toward the gold label). A paraphrase of the wrong answer produces an intermediate pattern: the gold label's probability is almost conserved, but the paraphrase receives only about a third of the wrong answer's share rather than the half that strict substitution implies. The distortion grows steadily with the logarithm of the number of options, reaching about 1 nat at 255 options, and off-domain padding pushes the odds against the gold label. In contrast, questions packed into one call do not interact (bias < 0.001). Scoring each option with an independent yes/no question removes the option-set dependence but picks the right answer 8.7 points less often. Jev sits between two local baselines, an option-independent scorer and a prompt readout. Its probabilities are best read as relative to the option list they were computed over.
papers.summary: Decision APIs return a probability per option, and treating those as properties of the options assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): adding an option that is neither correct nor the top rival should not change the odds between the two. A pre-registered study of the hosted model `jev-1.13.0` across 299,463 calls on `BANKING77`, `CLINC150`, and `AG News` finds that **every added option shifts the gold-versus-strongest-wrong log-odds by 0.20 to 0.52 nats root-mean-square**, one to three times the run-to-run noise, even when the added option receives almost no probability mass. The shifts are directional, grow with the logarithm of the option count to about 1 nat at 255 options, and vanish when multiple questions are packed into one call; scoring each option with an independent yes/no question removes the dependence but costs 8.7 accuracy points. The model's probabilities should be read as relative to the option list they were computed over.

papers.title: RFWeave: Learning Wireless Propagation Across Scenes and Transceiver Configurations
papers.abstract: Wireless propagation modeling is foundational to the evaluation and design of modern communication systems. To achieve accurate wireless propagation prediction, recent learning-based approaches leverage scene geometry and materials, demonstrating promising generalization across transceiver locations and unseen scenes. However, these approaches remain largely confined to a fixed configuration of array size, receiver orientation, and transmit beam. In this work, we introduce RFWeave, a learned wireless propagation model designed to generalize across scenes, transceiver locations, and transceiver configurations. To accommodate varying array structures, RFWeave incorporates variable-length transceiver tokens that represent antenna elements individually.
