Furthermore, to capture the geometry between transmit and receive antenna elements, RFWeave aggregates their pairwise spatial relations into propagation tokens. A configuration-conditioned decoder predicts the spatial spectrum and received power. RFWeave is trained on a large-scale simulated dataset spanning 10,000 indoor scenes and more than 5 million channel records under diverse transceiver configurations. Extensive evaluations show that RFWeave achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated generalization settings, improving spatial spectrum structural similarity (SSIM) by up to 15.7% and reducing received power mean absolute error (MAE) by up to 35.4% over the strongest baselines on unseen scenes. Additional experiments on measured DICHASUS data and in beam management further demonstrate RFWeave's broader applicability to real-world channels and downstream wireless tasks.
papers.summary: Learned wireless propagation models generalize across scene geometry and transceiver positions but are typically tied to a fixed antenna array size, receiver orientation, and transmit beam. `RFWeave` represents each antenna element as its own token so arrays of any size fit, aggregates pairwise transmit-receive spatial relations into propagation tokens, and decodes the spatial spectrum and received power with a configuration-conditioned decoder. Trained on 10,000 simulated indoor scenes and more than 5 million channel records, it **improves structural similarity (SSIM) of predicted spatial spectra by up to 15.7% and cuts received-power mean absolute error (MAE) by up to 35.4%** over the strongest baselines on unseen scenes, and it transfers to measured `DICHASUS` channels and a beam management task.

papers.title: Compression Through Time: An Interplay of Separability, Stationarity and Capacity
papers.abstract: Information-theoretic and geometric compression have been widely studied as possible explanations for generalization. Yet their temporal dynamics in recurrent networks remain largely unexplored. Using discretized LSTMs, whose finite embedding space enables direct estimates of information quantities, we observe pronounced compression across the final timesteps of many datasets. We explain this effect through three competing mechanisms: (i) class separability permits stronger compression at the final timestep; (ii) shared recurrent dynamics propagate this pressure across timesteps with similar activation states, making its extent depend on temporal stationarity; and (iii) limited representational capacity opposes prolonged compression because it restricts information available for subsequent computation. We systematically test these mechanisms through controlled synthetic interventions and real-world sequence tasks. Our results identify class separability, temporal stationarity, and network capacity as key determinants of temporal compression, and suggest that compression acts as a regularizer-potentially beneficial when excess capacity is available, but harmful to generalization when it consumes memory needed for the task.
papers.summary: Compression of representations has been proposed as a driver of generalization, but how it unfolds over time in recurrent networks is little studied. Using discretized LSTMs, whose finite embedding space allows direct estimates of information quantities, the authors observe strong compression over the final timesteps on many datasets and attribute it to three interacting mechanisms: class separability permits more compression at the last step, shared recurrent dynamics spread that pressure to earlier steps with similar activations so the extent depends on temporal stationarity, and limited capacity resists prolonged compression because it removes information needed later. Controlled synthetic interventions and real sequence tasks support this account, suggesting **compression acts as a regularizer that helps when spare capacity exists but hurts when it consumes memory the task needs**.

papers.title: Structural Baselines Matter for Agent Failure Detection and Attribution
papers.abstract: An LLM agent using tools can fail silently. It stops before the task is done, raises no error, and answers fluently. Two kinds of monitor address this, one deciding whether a run failed and the other naming the step where failure became unavoidable. Much of the reported performance on both tasks comes from regularities that need no model. Failing runs are longer, and the step labelled decisive is usually the last. A rule that always names the last step is correct $67\%$ to $96\%$ of the time here, without reading the run at all. That ceiling reflects how the labels were written, not how agents break. On failures whose decisive step replay can confirm, it falls to near chance. Reporting gain over that rule therefore changes what a score means. Under that correction, methods tested here gain nothing on give-up failures, while several published systems keep a clear advantage on other splits. For detection, the agent's internal states beat transcript length and text similarity on the agent benchmark, and hold up where the text baseline does not. Precision stays low when failures are rare, so such a monitor should rank runs for review, not replace it.
papers.summary: Tool-using LLM agents can stop early, raise no error, and still answer fluently, so monitors are built to flag failed runs and to name the step where failure became unavoidable. The authors show that much of the reported performance on both tasks comes from label regularities: failed runs are longer, and the annotated decisive step is usually the last one, so **a rule that always blames the final step is right 67% to 96% of the time without reading the transcript**, yet it drops to near chance on failures whose decisive step can be confirmed by replay. Measured as gain over that rule, the tested methods add nothing on give-up failures while several published systems retain an advantage on other splits. For failure detection, the agent's internal states outperform transcript length and text similarity and remain useful where text baselines break, though low precision on rare failures means such monitors should rank runs for review rather than replace it.

papers.title: Making LoRA Identifiable: Orthogonal Alignment for Continual Learning
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in applying Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) to Continual Learning, as it enables faster training, mitigates catastrophic forgetting, and facilitates better adaptation to new tasks. Prior approaches have explored a range of strategies, including extending new LoRA branches for each incoming task, training under orthogonal loss objectives across all task-specific LoRA modules, and employing gating mechanisms to integrate new and existing LoRA modules. However, these methods incur memory costs that grow linearly with the number of tasks, limiting their scalability. More recent approaches investigate training a single LoRA by leveraging asymmetries in its parameterization; however, they often suffer from insufficient representational alignment across the LoRA parameter space. To address these limitations, we propose Stiefel Optimization and Aligned Rotation (SOAR), a two-stage framework for continual LoRA learning. First, we constrain the A matrix to lie on the Stiefel manifold, thereby reducing coordinate misalignment to the space of orthogonal rotation matrices. Second, we introduce an Orthogonal Procrustes alignment procedure for the B matrix to estimate the optimal rotation, coupled with a per-rank retention merging strategy that quantifies directional agreement between representations of new and previously learned tasks. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks, demonstrating that SOAR achieves strong continual learning performance without incurring additional memory overhead.
papers.summary: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) is attractive for continual learning, but adding a LoRA branch per task makes memory grow linearly, and single-LoRA methods suffer from misaligned representations across tasks. `SOAR` (Stiefel Optimization and Aligned Rotation) constrains the LoRA A matrix to the Stiefel manifold, which reduces coordinate misalignment between tasks to an orthogonal rotation, then estimates that rotation for the B matrix with an Orthogonal Procrustes alignment and merges updates with a per-rank retention rule based on directional agreement between new and old task representations. Across multiple models and benchmarks the method **achieves strong continual learning performance with no additional memory overhead** as tasks accumulate.

papers.title: Amortized Variational Inference of Latent Intensities from Replicated Point Patterns
papers.abstract: Bayesian inference for latent point process intensities often relies on per-dataset sampling or optimization, making repeated inference computationally expensive. We propose a neural-network-based amortized variational framework that learns a reusable inference rule mapping a variable number of replicated point patterns to a distribution over their shared latent intensity. Trained from event times using the point process likelihood, the model learns an amortized inference rule without ground-truth intensity supervision. At test time, it performs inference of the latent distribution in a forward pass. On synthetic data, additional realizations improve intensity recovery and yield narrower credible intervals with broadly stable coverage. Our method is tested on bicycle-sharing data and achieves the highest mean held-out log likelihood among the evaluated methods while requiring substantially less inference time than the Log-Gaussian Cox Process baseline.
papers.summary: Bayesian inference of a latent intensity for point processes typically requires sampling or optimization for each new dataset. The proposed amortized variational method trains a neural network that maps a variable number of replicated point patterns to a distribution over their shared latent intensity, using only the point process likelihood of observed event times, so inference at test time is a single forward pass. On synthetic data, more replicates improve intensity recovery and tighten credible intervals with stable coverage, and on bicycle-sharing data the method **attains the highest held-out log likelihood among the compared methods while running much faster than a Log-Gaussian Cox Process baseline**.

papers.title: Spectral Costs of Multinomial and Residual Resampling in High-Dimensional Particle Ensembles: A Free-Probability Analysis
papers.abstract: Resampling is the standard remedy against weight degeneracy in particle filters, yet its effect on the spectrum of the particle second-moment matrix is poorly understood. We study a single resampling step for a d-dimensional ensemble of N particles with d/N -> c. For any unbiased scheme, the resampled empirical second-moment matrix dominates its pre-resampling counterpart in conditional convex order, while the conditional mean is preserved; the excess second spectral moment equals the Frobenius energy of the resampling perturbation. For multinomial resampling, the empirical count law converges to the mixed-Poisson law determined by the limiting weight law. For residual resampling, the count law is determined by the joint limit of floor-fraction pairs: we classify all residual limits of weight sequences converging to delta_1 in law as a one-parameter family between the deterministic identity and the full multinomial count law. Each count law feeds a common covariance-side spectral map, yielding exact consequences: a closed-form zero-eigenvalue mass, a rank-and-spectral-gap transition with a universal lower edge benchmark, computable regular edges, unbounded right support, and scheme-specific second-moment costs. The effective sample size determines one bulk statistic but cannot determine the limiting spectrum. Pre-registered numerical experiments confirm the theory at every level.
papers.summary: Resampling is the standard fix for weight degeneracy in particle filters, but its effect on the spectrum of the particle second-moment matrix has been poorly understood. The authors analyze a single resampling step for a d-dimensional ensemble of N particles in the proportional limit where d/N tends to a constant, showing with free-probability tools that any unbiased scheme leaves the conditional mean unchanged while the resampled second-moment matrix dominates its predecessor in conditional convex order, with the excess second spectral moment equal to the Frobenius energy of the resampling perturbation. For `multinomial resampling` the particle-count law converges to a mixed-Poisson law, while `residual resampling` limits form a one-parameter family between the deterministic identity and the full multinomial law, and both feed a common spectral map that yields a closed-form zero-eigenvalue mass, a rank and spectral-gap transition, computable edges, and scheme-specific second-moment costs. **The effective sample size pins down one bulk statistic but cannot determine the limiting spectrum**, and pre-registered numerical experiments confirm the theory at every level.

papers.title: EHR-Bench: A Chinese Multi-Task Benchmark for Recruitment AI
papers.abstract: Recruitment applications span diverse operations, from drafting job descriptions and interpreting queries to organizing profiles, assessing fit, and recommending candidates and jobs. Systematic LLM evaluation therefore requires task coverage that reflects this range of business needs. We introduce EHR-Bench, an open Chinese benchmark comprising twelve tasks across six capability families and five recruitment scenarios. The tasks cover generation, extraction, classification, retrieval, semantic similarity, and reciprocal ranking within one evaluation framework. An internal recruitment dataset guides task definitions, the occupation taxonomy and sampling targets, output requirements, and scoring protocols. Following these specifications, we construct 8,336 task instances from public materials and controlled augmentation, with source-aware expert review and documented provenance. We evaluate twelve LLMs through task-level, capability-level, and aggregate comparisons. Closely ranked models exhibit distinct task strengths, and performance varies across input sources, reference evidence, and candidate pools. Five shared models retain the same observed Overall ordering on a private operational reference, with variation in capability and task correspondence. EHR-Bench provides a reproducible foundation for systematic model assessment, task-specific model selection, and further research on LLMs for recruitment. The project repository is available at https://github.com/EhrBench/EHR-Bench.
papers.summary: Recruitment work spans drafting job descriptions, interpreting queries, organizing candidate profiles, assessing fit, and recommending candidates and jobs, so evaluating large language models (LLMs) for this domain calls for task coverage that matches that range. `EHR-Bench` is an open Chinese benchmark with twelve tasks across six capability families (generation, extraction, classification, retrieval, semantic similarity, and reciprocal ranking) and five recruitment scenarios, built from **8,336 task instances** drawn from public materials and controlled augmentation with source-aware expert review, using an internal recruitment dataset to guide task definitions, occupation taxonomy, and scoring protocols. Evaluating twelve LLMs at task, capability, and aggregate levels, the authors find that closely ranked models have distinct task strengths and that performance shifts with input source, reference evidence, and candidate pool, while five shared models keep the same overall ordering on a private operational reference set.

papers.title: Feature-Context Consistency: Unsupervised Adversarial Detection with Drift Stability on Attributed Graphs
papers.abstract: Adversarial detection on evolving attributed graphs faces two challenges: fraud labels arrive late or not at all, and natural distributional drift erodes any trained decision boundary. Modern detectors can reach strong detection rates when labels are available and the distribution is stationary; sustaining that quality without labels and under drift is the open problem. We identify feature-context consistency -- the alignment between a node's attributes and its aggregated neighborhood attributes -- as a single structural signal that addresses both. We formalize it as the Context Boost (CB) score within a Restricted Boltzmann Machine framework (CB-RBM) and prove two complementary worst-case guarantees: a strict separation between the expected CB of legitimate and adversarial nodes, with gap growing linearly in model capacity, whenever the adversary's context stays far enough from legitimate neighborhood context; and a Wasserstein-Lipschitz bound on how far the CB distribution moves under natural drift. We validate on XBlock Ethereum phishing (~153K nodes) and Reddit banned-user detection (~11K nodes), with two further datasets in the appendix spanning diverse domains. With zero labels, CB-RBM achieves AUROC >= 0.96 on four adversarial attacks and keeps FPR close to its calibrated 5% target under drift -- outperforming supervised GNNs (hundreds of labels), unsupervised graph-anomaly baselines, and a standard RBM whose FPR collapses to 89-100%. What typically requires separate mechanisms -- label-free operation and drift stability -- here follows from a single structural regularity of the data. Code: https://github.com/serval-uni-lu/CB-RBM.
papers.summary: Detecting adversarial nodes such as fraudsters on evolving attributed graphs is hard because labels arrive late or never, and natural distribution drift erodes any trained decision boundary. The authors identify feature-context consistency, the alignment between a node's own attributes and its aggregated neighborhood attributes, as a single structural signal that addresses both problems, formalizing it as a Context Boost (CB) score inside a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) framework called `CB-RBM`, and they prove a worst-case separation between legitimate and adversarial nodes that grows linearly with model capacity plus a Wasserstein-Lipschitz bound on how far the score distribution moves under drift. On the `XBlock` Ethereum phishing graph of about 153K nodes and a Reddit banned-user dataset of about 11K nodes, `CB-RBM` reaches **an area under the ROC curve of at least 0.96 across four adversarial attacks using zero labels** and keeps its false-positive rate near the calibrated 5% target under drift, beating supervised graph neural networks trained on hundreds of labels, unsupervised graph-anomaly baselines, and a standard RBM whose false-positive rate collapses to 89 to 100%.

papers.title: Universal Distributed Feature Extraction Complementary to Side Information via H-Score
papers.abstract: This paper considers a distributed estimation system where edge nodes transmit averaged features to a center node for parameter estimation. A key challenge arises when the center node possesses auxiliary side information: how to design local extractors that are universally optimal for any downstream task, while avoiding redundancy with the side information. To tackle this problem, we orthogonally decompose the joint function space and demonstrate in the weak-dependence regime that the modal decomposition of the canonical dependence kernel's conditional-additive component yields optimal, task-independent features. We construct a distributed nested H-score to learn this decomposition and show that, under a limited feature budget, the mean-squared error (MSE) gap to the best task-specific features is determined solely by the task's alignment with the discarded, least informative modes, and vanishes to leading order for every square-integrable task once the budget is sufficient.
papers.summary: In a distributed estimation system, edge nodes send averaged features to a center node for parameter estimation, and the challenge is to design local feature extractors that are universally optimal for any downstream task while not duplicating auxiliary side information the center node already holds. The authors orthogonally decompose the joint function space and show, in the weak-dependence regime, that the modal decomposition of the conditional-additive component of the canonical dependence kernel gives optimal task-independent features, which they learn with a distributed nested `H-score`. Under a limited feature budget, **the mean-squared error (MSE) gap to the best task-specific features is determined solely by the task's alignment with the discarded, least informative modes**, and it vanishes to leading order for every square-integrable task once the budget is sufficient.

papers.title: Attention-Graph Curvature for the Verification of Mathematical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Language models have recently solved open Erd\H{o}s problems and achieved gold-medal level performance on International Mathematical Olympiad problems. But their solutions, written in natural language, cannot yet be verified by proof assistants. An erroneous reasoning step can invalidate every step that comes after, so it is advantageous to detect errors early. Several methods have been proposed to detect erroneous reasoning quickly based on the features of the forward pass of the language model that performs reasoning. In this work, we study whether the directed Forman curvature of that model's attention graph, a local quantity computed at an edge from the attention weights around it, carries information about a step's correctness. To do so, we evaluate four per-step verifiers on ProcessBench with and without the curvature appended to their input. Appending curvature values improves the overall mean performance of all four verifiers. ReProbe, the verifier that takes every token of a step as input, shows the largest improvement. Adding the curvature increases the time of the language model's forward pass by 18% on average.
papers.summary: Language models now produce natural-language solutions to open Erdős problems and olympiad-level mathematics that proof assistants cannot yet check, and since one wrong step invalidates everything after it, cheap early error detection matters. The authors ask whether the directed Forman curvature of the reasoning model's attention graph, a local quantity computed at each edge from the attention weights around it, carries information about a step's correctness, and they test this by appending curvature values to the inputs of four per-step verifiers evaluated on `ProcessBench`. **Appending curvature improves the mean performance of all four verifiers**, with the largest gain for `ReProbe`, the verifier that takes every token of a step as input, at the cost of an average 18% increase in the language model's forward-pass time.

papers.title: Audit Before You Distill: A Controlled Workflow for Reasoning Transfer into Compact Medical Language Models
papers.abstract: Teacher rationales can help a smaller model answer health professions questions, but they can also reinforce errors. We examined when they help and how this evidence can guide training using Brazilian Portuguese questions from medical and multiprofessional residency examinations. First, we measured how a teacher rationale changed the student's probability of selecting the correct answer and compared this effect with rationales drawn from other questions. The complete rationale increased this probability by 21~p.p. when the teacher was correct and decreased it by 14~p.p. when the teacher was wrong. By intervening on the reasoning content, we showed that shuffled rationales did not produce the same pattern. Guided by this result, we trained only with rationales attached to correct teacher answers and compared answer-only training, step-by-step distillation, and our proposed Distill-SFT method. Distill-SFT showed a modest advantage over step-by-step distillation on previously missed questions under reasoning, while using fewer training instances by combining the answer and rationale into a single target. We also investigated catastrophic forgetting using the out-of-domain ENEM dataset. Answer-only training reduced reasoning accuracy by 12~p.p. relative to baseline, compared with approximately 4~p.p. for either rationale-based training method. Together, these findings support a workflow that audits rationale content before distillation, verifies teacher answers before supervision, and trains compact models efficiently for health professions question answering.
papers.summary: Teacher rationales can help a compact student model answer health professions exam questions, but they can also reinforce the teacher's errors, so the authors examine when they help and how that evidence should shape training, using Brazilian Portuguese questions from medical and multiprofessional residency examinations. They first measure how a teacher rationale changes the student's probability of picking the correct answer: **a complete rationale raised that probability by 21 percentage points when the teacher was correct and lowered it by 14 points when the teacher was wrong**, a pattern that shuffled rationales did not reproduce. Guided by this audit, they train only on rationales attached to correct teacher answers and compare answer-only training, step-by-step distillation, and a proposed `Distill-SFT` method that merges answer and rationale into a single target, finding a modest edge for `Distill-SFT` on previously missed questions with fewer training instances, and on the out-of-domain `ENEM` dataset answer-only training cut reasoning accuracy by about 12 points versus roughly 4 points for either rationale-based method.

papers.title: What Is the "Self" of a Large Language Model?
papers.abstract: What could the "self" of a large language model be, if it is neither a particular word nor a single privileged layer? We propose a relational account: a functional self is an actor-centered organization of information that distinguishes the model's recorded actions from externally supplied material while content and reasoning operations change. Its representational candidate is a family of layer-specific source-binding components, rather than one unchanged vector throughout the network. Preliminary observations from a 27B BF16 model provide a geometric starting point. Across 150 matched message bodies, 450 role conditions, and a 75/75 discovery-held-out split, the combined Assistant-versus-external displacement transfers strongly across bodies and positions. Selected early components place User and System closer to one another than to Assistant, whereas this full-space distance relation does not persist throughout depth. These findings motivate a layered account: an early source-encoding candidate can be combined with role-specific information use and continuation preparation at later depths, without requiring monotonic overwriting of the common displacement. We connect this account to dynamic reasoning, historical continuity, and a computational model separating content operations, source binding, authority, and output. The reported evidence establishes a reproducible role-conditioned geometry; the proposed interpretation is that functional selfhood may reside in persistent relations among changing representations.
papers.summary: If a large language model has a self, it is neither a particular word nor a single privileged layer, so the authors propose a relational account: a functional self is an actor-centered organization of information that distinguishes the model's own recorded actions from externally supplied material even as content and reasoning operations change. Its representational candidate is a family of layer-specific source-binding components rather than one unchanged vector, and preliminary experiments on a 27B-parameter BF16 model, using 150 matched message bodies, 450 role conditions, and a 75/75 discovery and held-out split, show that **the combined Assistant-versus-external displacement transfers strongly across message bodies and positions**. Selected early components place User and System roles closer to each other than to Assistant, a distance relation that does not hold at every depth, which motivates a layered account in which early source encoding combines with role-specific information use and continuation preparation later in the network, and the authors connect this to dynamic reasoning, historical continuity, and a computational model separating content operations, source binding, authority, and output.

papers.title: Learn from Move: the Next Step for GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Existing benchmarks for GUI agents primarily focus on increasing task difficulty by extending task horizons. Besides, enabling agents to explore unfamiliar environments and successfully complete tasks within them is also a critical yet challenging problem. We introduce LatentGUIWorld, a benchmark of six tasks in three matched pairs organized by the evidence needed for control: $I_0$ uses prior knowledge and available observations, $I_1$ requires interaction that directly reveals hidden semantics, and $I_2$ identifies dynamics from action-response relationships. Frontier models struggle especially on $I_2$ tasks. We introduce MOVE, which separates movement from button events and exposes intermediate visual feedback, together with demonstrations of iterative exploration and control. Ablations show that both action granularity and multi-step demonstrations improve performance. After SFT, LatentLearner-9B achieves 50.0% overall success on LatentGUIWorld, comparable to several frontier models. Joint RL further raises egocentric Drag and Ten-Choice success to 92.0% and 75.3%. Behavioral analysis reveals multi-step exploration. In egocentric Drag, RL increases Pearson correlation between error-normalized commands and ideal gain compensation from 0.610 to 0.803. Together, these behaviors show that models learn to explore through interaction and adapt their control to environment dynamics. The same format improves GUI grounding after RL, reaching 67.37% mean accuracy across five benchmarks versus 66.72% for conventional RL.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for graphical user interface (GUI) agents mostly raise difficulty by lengthening task horizons, leaving open whether agents can explore an unfamiliar environment and learn how it responds. `LatentGUIWorld` is a benchmark of six tasks in three matched pairs organized by the evidence needed for control: I0 tasks solvable from prior knowledge and visible observations, I1 tasks that require interaction to reveal hidden semantics, and I2 tasks that require identifying dynamics from action-response relationships, where frontier models struggle most. The authors also introduce `MOVE`, an action format that separates movement from button events and exposes intermediate visual feedback, together with demonstrations of iterative exploration and control, and ablations show that both the action granularity and the multi-step demonstrations help. After supervised fine-tuning, `LatentLearner-9B` reaches 50.0% overall success on `LatentGUIWorld`, comparable to several frontier models, and **joint reinforcement learning further raises egocentric Drag and Ten-Choice success to 92.0% and 75.3%**, while the same format also improves GUI grounding after RL to 67.37% mean accuracy across five benchmarks versus 66.72% for conventional RL.

papers.title: Lost in Contrast: Instruction-Preserving Decoding for Reliable Visual Question Answering
papers.abstract: Visual contrastive decoding corrects answers using the prediction difference between the original image and a reference condition, yet the same contrast also turns supported abstentions into incorrect answers. We find that abstentions are lost at two stages: contrastive decoding with candidate filtering can exclude the abstention token before any comparison takes place, and the reference branch's response to the abstention instruction is removed when the reference prediction is subtracted. We therefore propose instruction-preserving decoding, which keeps the effect of the abstention instruction on the original-image prediction intact while leaving the contrast strength freely adjustable. Using a perturbed image and an image-free prediction as references, we obtain IP-VCD and IP-M3ID. On decision utility (DU), which credits both correct answers and supported abstentions, both methods outperform all compared non-IP baselines on every one of nine models on VizWiz, and IP-VCD also leads on eight of nine models on Food-101. Candidate measurements and paired per-question comparisons show that computing the instruction effect and the visual contrast term separately lets contrastive decoding support both correct answers and supported abstentions.
papers.summary: Visual contrastive decoding corrects vision-language answers using the difference between predictions on the original image and on a reference condition, yet the same contrast turns supported abstentions into incorrect answers. The authors find that abstentions are lost at two stages: candidate filtering can exclude the abstention token before any comparison happens, and subtracting the reference prediction removes the reference branch's response to the abstention instruction. Their instruction-preserving decoding keeps the abstention instruction's effect on the original-image prediction intact while leaving contrast strength freely adjustable, giving `IP-VCD` with a perturbed-image reference and `IP-M3ID` with an image-free reference. On decision utility (DU), which credits both correct answers and supported abstentions, **both methods outperform all non-instruction-preserving baselines on every one of nine models** on `VizWiz`, and `IP-VCD` also leads on eight of nine models on `Food-101`.

papers.title: Trace-to-Architecture: Capability Bottleneck Diagnosis for Harness Revision
papers.abstract: Improving an LLM agent requires knowing what to change when it fails. Similar failures can require different fixes, and resolving one problem can expose another. We introduce Trace-to-Architecture (T2A), a framework that uses execution trajectories to determine what to change in an agent's harness and when those changes apply. A development agent diagnoses failures using execution evidence from successful and failed tasks, revises the corresponding harness components, and then checks whether target tasks improve, selected successful tasks remain successful, and the edits are actually triggered. New execution evidence guides subsequent diagnosis and revision. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and AppWorld, T2A achieves the highest aggregate score for all three evaluated task agents, exceeding their respective strongest baselines by 6.2--30.3 points. We also integrate T2A's diagnosis and validation procedures into Meta-Harness, improving the resulting harnesses' mean ScienceWorld score by 21.6 points from the same starting harness.
papers.summary: Improving a large language model (LLM) agent requires knowing what to change in its harness when it fails, yet similar failures can need different fixes and resolving one problem can expose another. Trace-to-Architecture (`T2A`) has a development agent diagnose failures from execution trajectories of both successful and failed tasks, revise the corresponding harness components, and then check that target tasks improve, selected successful tasks still succeed, and the edits are actually triggered, with the new execution evidence guiding the next round of diagnosis and revision. Across `ALFWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, and `AppWorld`, `T2A` achieves **the highest aggregate score for all three evaluated task agents, exceeding their strongest baselines by 6.2 to 30.3 points**, and integrating its diagnosis and validation procedures into `Meta-Harness` improves that system's mean `ScienceWorld` score by 21.6 points from the same starting harness.

papers.title: Queue-Aware Token Communications: Bridging AI Representation and Wireless Service
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models and edge intelligence is transforming wireless networks from data-oriented communication systems into artificial intelligence (AI)-native service platforms. Token communications (TokenCom) has emerged as a promising paradigm that directly transmits task-oriented AI representations. However, existing studies typically assume that generated tokens can be transmitted immediately, overlooking the queueing dynamics arising from the mismatch between token workload generation and time-varying wireless service capability. To address this limitation, we introduce Queue-Aware TokenCom, which explicitly incorporates token queues into the AI service pipeline. We present an end-to-end architecture integrating AI representation generation, token workload management, wireless transmission, and downstream task inference. We then discuss two key design directions: budget-aware token representation optimization and queue-aware token service optimization, with the token budget serving as a critical interface between AI performance and communication efficiency. Moreover, we investigate fixed and adaptive token budget strategies to characterize the fundamental tradeoff between AI performance and communication efficiency in dynamic wireless environments. Finally, we outline research directions toward closed-loop, task-aware, and scalable TokenCom systems.
papers.summary: As foundation models and edge intelligence turn wireless networks into artificial intelligence (AI)-native service platforms, token communications (TokenCom) proposes transmitting task-oriented AI representations directly, but existing studies assume generated tokens can be sent immediately and overlook the queues that build up when token generation outpaces time-varying wireless capacity. The authors introduce Queue-Aware TokenCom, an end-to-end architecture that integrates AI representation generation, token workload management, wireless transmission, and downstream task inference, with the token budget serving as the interface between AI performance and communication efficiency. They discuss two design directions, budget-aware token representation optimization and queue-aware token service optimization, **compare fixed and adaptive token budget strategies to characterize the tradeoff between AI performance and communication efficiency in dynamic wireless environments**, and outline research directions toward closed-loop, task-aware, and scalable systems.

papers.title: VAttnPO: Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards commonly assigns one sequence advantage to an entire response. This outcome-level signal distinguishes overall response quality but leaves changes in visual-evidence use across generated tokens implicit. We introduce VAttnPO (Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization), which uses answer-conditioned visual attention to refine token-level credit while preserving the verifier-derived trajectory-mean advantage. A frozen old policy constructs a visual reference by teacher forcing the known correct answer and produces a visual distribution for each rollout token. VAttnPO measures their agreement in visual-attention space using Jensen--Shannon divergence, rather than reading guidance from teacher output-token distributions or introducing an attention-matching objective. Trajectory centering, relative-position weighting, and credit balancing turn this agreement into a zero-mean, position-aware correction to the GRPO sequence advantage. Token intervention, visual-index permutation, and trajectory analysis provide diagnostic evidence linking this signal to model behavior, visual correspondence, and generation position. On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, VAttnPO raises six-task image AVE from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50 and scores higher on every reported structured, video, and MME metric. Gains over GRPO also hold on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL3-8B-Instruct.
papers.summary: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards usually assigns one sequence-level advantage to a whole response, which separates good from bad responses but leaves changes in visual-evidence use across generated tokens implicit. Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization (`VAttnPO`) refines token-level credit while preserving the verifier-derived trajectory-mean advantage: a frozen old policy teacher-forces the known correct answer to build a visual reference, each rollout token's visual attention distribution is compared with it using Jensen-Shannon divergence, and trajectory centering, relative-position weighting, and credit balancing turn that agreement into a zero-mean, position-aware correction to the `GRPO` sequence advantage. Token intervention, visual-index permutation, and trajectory analysis link the signal to model behavior, visual correspondence, and generation position. On `Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct`, `VAttnPO` lifts the six-task image average over `GRPO` **from 70.97 to 73.50**, scores higher on every reported structured, video, and `MME` metric, and the gains also hold on `Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct` and `InternVL3-8B-Instruct`.

papers.title: Amortised adaptive importance sampling
papers.abstract: Monte Carlo sampling algorithms aim to produce samples from a target distribution with a given unnormalised probability density function. The high cost of running Monte Carlo algorithms, with many simulation steps or particles needed to obtain a good empirical approximation to the target, can be reduced by introducing learnable components into the sampler -- a form of amortisation. Once these components are trained, amortised samplers can produce high-quality samples with less computation at sampling time than training-free algorithms would require. We propose an amortised sampler built upon the framework of adaptive importance sampling -- a hierarchical importance sampling procedure where the proposal is iteratively adapted. Our amortised adaptive importance sampling algorithm fits a lightweight neural network that adapts the proposal using information obtained over the course of sampling. By training our sampler over many different targets taken from the same family of distributions, we obtain a sampler that can adapt to a specific target at sampling time without a priori access to the target's parameters. We show that our procedure can efficiently sample from targets within the family the sampler was trained on, giving improvements over target-specific amortised samplers and training-free adaptive importance sampling algorithms. We also explore the potential for generalisation, where the trained sampler is used to sample from targets outwith its training family.
papers.summary: Monte Carlo samplers draw from a target known only through an unnormalized density, and their cost in simulation steps or particles can be reduced by adding learnable components that are trained once and reused, a form of amortization. The authors build an amortized sampler on adaptive importance sampling, the hierarchical procedure in which the proposal is iteratively adapted, by fitting a lightweight neural network that adjusts the proposal using information collected during sampling, and they train it across many targets from one family so it can adapt to a specific target at sampling time without prior access to that target's parameters. **The trained sampler improves over both target-specific amortized samplers and training-free adaptive importance sampling on targets within its training family**, and the paper also explores generalization to targets outside that family.

papers.title: CopyQuad: Quadrupedal Skill Transfer from a Single Side-View Video Without a Depth Model
papers.abstract: Video-to-robot pipelines for quadrupedal imitation insert a learned lifting stage, either a monocular depth model or a per-clip 3D reconstruction, to recover the one axis a side-view camera cannot see. We present CopyQuad, which omits that stage and pins the missing axis to the robot's own stance width instead. The setting is side-view footage of sagittally dominated motion, where limb motion is almost entirely in the image plane. A frozen 2D keypoint detector and a fixed analytic retargeting then turn a single uncalibrated clip into a robot reference whose foot targets are reachable by construction, so no per-clip trajectory optimization is needed. One phase-indexed reward structure, whose only per-behavior freedom is three scalars from a shared sweep, learns a dog walk, a horse walk, a horse trot and two non-periodic gestures, all deployed zero-shot on hardware. We then measure what omitting the axis costs. In a training-free rigidity test, a video depth model varies the distance between the animal's hips by $40$ to $107\%$ of its own mean and a single-image metric model by $22$ to $58\%$, though that distance cannot move. Motion capture puts the true lateral paw travel of a dog walk at $4.5$ cm peak to peak, a mean deviation near $1.4$ cm against the $3.5$ cm of lateral foot error our policies already leave, so the discarded axis sits below the pipeline's resolution. Depth repaired to feasibility never beats the constant, and the unrepaired estimates put the robot on the ground.
papers.summary: Video-to-robot pipelines for quadruped imitation usually insert a learned lifting stage, either a monocular depth model or a per-clip 3D reconstruction, to recover the one axis a side-view camera cannot see. `CopyQuad` omits that stage and pins the missing axis to the robot's own stance width, targeting side-view footage of sagittally dominated motion where limb movement is almost entirely in the image plane: a frozen 2D keypoint detector and a fixed analytic retargeting turn a single uncalibrated clip into a robot reference whose foot targets are reachable by construction, and one phase-indexed reward with only three per-behavior scalars learns a dog walk, a horse walk, a horse trot, and two non-periodic gestures, all deployed zero-shot on hardware. Measuring what omitting the axis costs, the authors show that a video depth model varies the animal's fixed hip-to-hip distance by 40 to 107% of its mean and a single-image metric model by 22 to 58%, while motion capture puts true lateral paw travel of a dog walk at 4.5 cm peak to peak, **a mean deviation near 1.4 cm against the 3.5 cm of lateral foot error the policies already leave, so the discarded axis sits below the pipeline's resolution**. Depth estimates repaired to feasibility never beat the constant, and the unrepaired ones put the robot on the ground.

papers.title: Before Attention Sinks Form: Hidden-State Geometry Reveals and Modulates Their Formation
papers.abstract: Attention sinks are usually studied after they have formed. We ask whether a measurable hidden-state change appears beforehand and whether changing that geometry alters what happens later. To remove network depth as a shortcut, we compare prompts in the same model and at the same layer. When sink timing varies across prompts, simple spectral summaries of the hidden states add information beyond current attention, with the clearest prompt-specific signal in a short window about two to three layers before sink formation. The predictive strength varies across cohorts, so we treat the spectrum as a readout of a pre-sink state change rather than a universal warning statistic. The signal is broader than one measured extreme activation. We then modify only the singular values of the post-layer hidden states after current attention has already been computed. These interventions change later sink behavior in Qwen2.5, GLM-Z1, and GPT-OSS relative to norm-matched random spectral perturbations. In Qwen2.5, the immediate suppressive effect is accompanied by a reduction in next-layer query--key preference for position~0, and the learned spectral directions remain stable when estimated from substantially less training data. Together, the results show that attention sinks are preceded by a short spectral reorganization of hidden states, and directly perturbing this geometry can causally alter subsequent sink formation.
papers.summary: Attention sinks are usually studied after they have formed, so the authors ask whether a measurable hidden-state change appears beforehand and whether altering that geometry changes what happens later. To remove network depth as a shortcut, they compare prompts within the same model at the same layer and find that simple spectral summaries of the hidden states add information about sink timing beyond current attention, with the clearest prompt-specific signal in a window about two to three layers before sink formation, though predictive strength varies across cohorts, so they treat the spectrum as a readout of a pre-sink state change rather than a universal warning statistic. They then modify only the singular values of the post-layer hidden states after attention has already been computed, and these interventions **causally change later sink behavior relative to norm-matched random spectral perturbations** in `Qwen2.5`, `GLM-Z1`, and `GPT-OSS`, with the suppressive effect in `Qwen2.5` accompanied by reduced next-layer query-key preference for position 0 and learned spectral directions that stay stable when estimated from much less training data.

papers.title: NFMap: Topographic 2D Manifold Learning with Invertible Normalizing Flows
papers.abstract: We present NFMap, a dimensionality reduction method for 2D visualisation that extends Generative Topographic Mapping (GTM) with a bijective normalizing flow. Like GTM, NFMap places a fixed mixture grid prior over a 2D latent map, giving a parametric embedding, an explicit likelihood, and the ability to project new points onto an existing map; the likelihood is an effective out-of-distribution signal on chemical datasets. Unlike GTM, whose latent-to-data mapping is an RBF network of bounded flexibility, NFMap's mapping is a normalizing flow, and is therefore fully invertible: any location on the map can be carried back to data space. To alleviate map crowding on large datasets, NFMap additionally supports heavy-tailed Student-t mixture components. NFMap maps data to a latent space of the same dimension, split into a 2-dimensional navigable map and an off-manifold residual. Because the flow is bijective and its objective penalises volume contraction, variance squeezed out of the residual must reappear in the navigable map. The residual scale is the main control between local neighbourhood fidelity and global distance fidelity; its effect depends on the dimensionality of the data and is coupled to the extent of the latent grid.
papers.summary: `NFMap` is a dimensionality reduction method for 2D visualisation that extends Generative Topographic Mapping (GTM) by replacing its radial basis function mapping of bounded flexibility with a bijective normalizing flow. Like `GTM`, it places a fixed mixture grid prior over a 2D latent map, giving a parametric embedding, an explicit likelihood that serves as an effective out-of-distribution signal on chemical datasets, and the ability to project new points onto an existing map, and to relieve crowding on large datasets it also supports heavy-tailed Student-t mixture components. Because the flow is invertible, **any location on the map can be carried back to data space**, and the data are mapped to a latent space of the same dimension split into a 2D navigable map and an off-manifold residual. Since the objective penalises volume contraction, variance squeezed out of the residual must reappear in the navigable map, making the residual scale the main control between local neighbourhood fidelity and global distance fidelity, with an effect that depends on data dimensionality and is coupled to the extent of the latent grid.

papers.title: The Multilingual Artificial Hivemind: Do All LLMs Think Alike in Every Language?
papers.abstract: Text generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) often remains limited in diversity compared to that produced by humans. Recent advances demonstrate the presence of inter- and intra-model collapse in open-ended generation of English text, raising concerns about the long-term homogenization of LLM, and more importantly, human thought. However, our understanding of whether this homogenization extends to languages beyond English is limited. In this work, we investigate the role of language on output diversity. Specifically, we aim to understand whether multilingual LLM-generated text is also homogeneous, and whether this homogeneity matches what we observe in humans. Across 23 open-weight models and 13 languages, we find that the artificial hivemind effect is pervasive but uneven in its extent. The intra-model effect holds in three different embedding spaces and under a lexical metric that uses no embedding model, so it is not an artifact of how diversity is measured. The size of the homogenization gap is associated with a model's competence in a language, measured on a held-out translation benchmark, robustly across embedding spaces. Thus, we demonstrate a performance-diversity tradeoff in multilingual LLMs.
papers.summary: Text generated by large language models (LLMs) is less diverse than human writing, and prior work has shown inter- and intra-model collapse in open-ended English generation, raising concerns about long-term homogenization of LLM and ultimately human thought, but whether this extends to other languages was unknown. Across 23 open-weight models and 13 languages, the authors find that the artificial hivemind effect is pervasive but uneven in extent, and the intra-model effect holds in three different embedding spaces and under a lexical metric that uses no embedding model, so it is not an artifact of how diversity is measured. **The size of the homogenization gap is associated with a model's competence in a language**, as measured on a held-out translation benchmark and robust across embedding spaces, which the authors characterize as a performance-diversity tradeoff in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Is the Platform Part of the Measurement? A Protocol and Simulation Study for Cross-Platform Equivalence of Machine-Labelled Policy Sentiment
papers.abstract: Comparing machine-labelled sentiment across social media platforms is now routine: differences in classifier scores between platforms are read as differences in public opinion. These comparisons rest on an assumption that the classifier measures the same construct, on the same scale, on every platform. Some studies check a classifier's validity platform by platform, but to our knowledge none has modelled the platform as a facet of the classifier's measurement. We adapt the psychometric equivalence toolkit (generalizability theory, measurement invariance and differential item functioning, and score linking) to machine-labelled policy sentiment, treating the platform as a survey mode, and specify a six-step protocol with anchor events fixed in advance, an anchor-density audit, and a two-classifier convergence control. A simulation with known ground truth illustrates what the assumption can cost in one generating configuration fixed in advance: across 500 replications, because the platforms measure through different functions, a pooled index that takes platform scores at face value reports the wrong sign of aggregate sentiment on nearly a quarter of days, whereas an index adjusted with each platform's known measurement function does so on under one day in sixty on average. A case study of the instrument from the first author's MSc dissertation, a fine-tuned BERT classifier over 255,446 UK economic-policy comments from Twitter/X, Reddit, YouTube, and Quora, motivates the design and illustrates the instrument-dependence the protocol addresses. The full four-platform application, under fresh collection with the pre-specified design, is the designated follow-up study. The protocol lets a researcher test whether pooling platforms is defensible in a given corpus, or whether platform scores must be linked before any average is taken.
papers.summary: Comparing machine-labelled sentiment across social media platforms is routine, but it assumes the classifier measures the same construct on the same scale on every platform, and no prior study has modelled the platform as a facet of the classifier's measurement. The authors adapt the psychometric equivalence toolkit of generalizability theory, measurement invariance and differential item functioning, and score linking to machine-labelled policy sentiment, treating the platform as a survey mode, and specify a six-step protocol with anchor events fixed in advance, an anchor-density audit, and a two-classifier convergence control. In a simulation with known ground truth over 500 replications, **a pooled index that takes platform scores at face value reports the wrong sign of aggregate sentiment on nearly a quarter of days**, whereas an index adjusted with each platform's known measurement function does so on under one day in sixty on average. A case study of a fine-tuned `BERT` classifier over 255,446 UK economic-policy comments from Twitter/X, Reddit, YouTube, and Quora motivates the design, with the full four-platform application under fresh collection designated as the follow-up study.

papers.title: Separating Prompt Harmfulness from Interaction Safety via Partial Generation
papers.abstract: LLM-based information systems need safety guardrails. Most guardrails classify the prompt alone. If the prompt looks harmful, the system rejects it before any answer is generated. This is costly. Many rejected prompts would have received a safe response. Users lose help they should have received from the information system. This cost grows as conversational and generative search becomes common. Prompt-level labels treat harm as a property of the query. But harm depends on what the model actually writes. Existing input-output guards do look at responses. But they judge a finished response, so the decision comes after full generation. However, we observe that safety of model interaction with the input prompt can be inferred early with only partial output. So the system can start generating, watch the partial response, and stop only if it turns harmful. We test this idea in three steps. First, we build a dataset of 41,944 prompt-response pairs with seven open weights LLMs from three families: Llama, Gemma, and Qwen. Second, we show that prompt harmfulness and interaction safety differ. Prompt labels and response labels agree on only 50.46\% of items (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.06). Of the prompts that make any model respond harmfully, only 3.5\% do so for all seven LLMs. Third, we show that partial responses carry most of the signal. Fine-tuned classifiers predict response-level harm well (best AUPRC 0.885, F1 0.807). About one third of the response tokens recover almost full-response AUPRC.
papers.summary: Most guardrails for large language model (LLM) based information systems classify the prompt alone and reject anything that looks harmful before generation, which discards many prompts that would have received a safe response, while existing input-output guards judge only a finished response after full generation. The authors observe that the safety of a model's interaction with a prompt can be inferred early from partial output, so a system can start generating, watch the partial response, and stop only if it turns harmful. On a dataset of 41,944 prompt-response pairs from seven open-weight models in the `Llama`, `Gemma`, and `Qwen` families, **prompt-harm labels and response-harm labels agree on only 50.46% of items, with Cohen's kappa of 0.06**, and only 3.5% of the prompts that make any model respond harmfully do so for all seven. Fine-tuned classifiers predict response-level harm well, with a best area under the precision-recall curve of 0.885 and F1 of 0.807, and about one third of the response tokens recover almost the full-response score.

papers.title: Relational Learning as World Modeling
papers.abstract: Relational learning typically predicts from a database state, but decision making asks a different question: how will that state change under an action? In operational systems, the answer depends on system-specific dynamics that may not be visible in the database itself. We view each such system as a relational "world" and ask whether a model can infer how it behaves from observed executions. We introduce TabWM (Tabular World Model) and WorldRel, a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining. Given executions from an unseen world, TabWM uses them as context to predict the sparse structured edits caused by a new action without parameter updates. Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no observed executions to 0.685 with 64, where a correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Because these predictions are explicit relational edits, they can be applied recursively to imagine candidate futures and compare actions before they are taken. Broader search over these predicted futures improves the realized return of selected action sequences. Together, these results suggest that relational dynamics can be learned in context, broadening relational learning from modeling system state to modeling how that state changes under action.
papers.summary: Relational learning typically predicts from a database state, but decision making asks how that state will change under an action, which depends on system-specific dynamics that may not be visible in the database itself. The authors treat each operational system as a relational world and introduce `TabWM` (Tabular World Model) together with `WorldRel`, a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining, so that given observed executions from an unseen world as context, `TabWM` predicts the sparse structured edits a new action will cause without any parameter updates. **Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no observed executions to 0.685 with 64**, where a correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Because the predictions are explicit relational edits, they can be applied recursively to imagine candidate futures and compare actions before taking them, and broader search over these predicted futures improves the realized return of selected action sequences.

papers.title: Geospatial Vector Geometry as a Native Spatial Modality for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Geospatial reasoning links VLMs to real-world action and decision making. Reliable reasoning requires accurate spatial information and effective spatial representations. However, current VLMs obtain this information mainly from language and vision. At larger geographic scales, limited visual observations make it difficult to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. This leads to a bottleneck for VLM spatial perception and reasoning. This paper proposes that geospatial vector geometry can become a native spatial modality within a VLM and introduces GeoVec-VLM. First, we develop a structured geometry representation that preserves the spatial structure and arrangement of vector objects, building an explicit spatial basis. Second, we introduce a geometry interaction strategy that brings this basis into multimodal computation, where it interacts with visual content and language references according to the queried spatial relations. Together, these designs allow perception and reasoning to operate on shared geometric references. Across five spatial reasoning tasks, GeoVec-VLM improves mean accuracy by about 11\% relative to the strongest baseline, maintains its gains under geographic transfer, and shows greater geometric consistency. Our results show that geospatial vector geometry offers a promising internal spatial basis for VLM spatial reasoning. https://github.com/TXFR/GeoVector-VLM
papers.summary: Vision-language models (`VLMs`) struggle with geospatial reasoning at large geographic scales, where sparse visual observations make it hard to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. `GeoVec-VLM` treats geospatial vector geometry as a native input modality, pairing a structured geometry representation that preserves the arrangement of vector objects with an interaction strategy that lets this geometric basis engage with visual content and language references according to the queried relation. Across five spatial reasoning tasks the model **improves mean accuracy by about 11% over the strongest baseline**, keeps its gains under geographic transfer, and shows greater geometric consistency.

papers.title: Game-Creation-Agents: Autonomous Game Production
papers.abstract: Game-Creation-Agents (GCA) turns a natural-language request into a runnable Phaser 4 browser game. The pipeline first builds a multimodal game design document that couples mechanics and scene contracts to grounded visual references. It then projects that document into a runtime scaffold, machine-readable contracts, and deterministic tests. Eight specialized agents next carry out production: scenes are implemented serially, assets are produced in parallel, and one reduced manifest joins the two branches into a single build. Build-linked real-UI checks and a code-blind critic then verify that build and decide whether the game may ship. Each blocker returns to the agent that owns the affected artifact for a bounded repair, and the game is released once all the gates pass. We evaluate finished games separately, through their rendered interfaces alone, over prompt-matched tasks run under a common protocol. GCA achieves stronger requirement satisfaction, core mechanics, content depth, and functional visuals than a comparable open pipeline. In a side-by-side human study, raters also score GCA's games higher on every dimension and prefer them overall.
papers.summary: `Game-Creation-Agents` (`GCA`) is a multi-agent pipeline that converts a natural-language request into a runnable `Phaser 4` browser game. It first builds a multimodal design document tying mechanics and scene contracts to grounded visual references, projects that document into a runtime scaffold with machine-readable contracts and deterministic tests, then has eight specialized agents implement scenes serially and assets in parallel before merging them into one build. Build-linked real-UI checks and a code-blind critic gate release, routing each blocker back to the owning agent for a bounded repair. Evaluated through rendered interfaces alone on prompt-matched tasks, GCA beats a comparable open pipeline on requirement satisfaction, core mechanics, content depth, and functional visuals, and **human raters prefer its games on every dimension**.

papers.title: PrivacyGuard: Source-Linked Sanitization and Locally Resolvable PII References for Cloud GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Cloud graphical user interface (GUI) agents send instructions and screenshots to remote planners, exposing personally identifiable information (PII). Existing placeholder defenses mask detected spans and reuse exact strings. Fragmented or changed forms can expose PII or break entity continuity across turns. PrivacyGuard addresses this private reference problem with source-linked sanitization (SAN) and a structured reference lifecycle (REF). SAN reconstructs fragmented or overlapping evidence and rewrites the complete source extent. REF links changed appearances to session entities and supports locally resolvable references without returning raw values to the upload path. In five-turn sessions scored against common gold, PrivacyGuard reduces audited source-value leakage by 33.55\%--82.60\% relative to the closest prior full-pipeline system in all four reader--language combinations. REF raises strict cross-form continuity from 0.04 under exact-value reuse to 0.81. In reference-required Android tasks, verified completion rises from 8/30 and 7/30 to 17/30 and 20/30. On AndroidLab, PrivacyGuard achieves the highest or tied-highest task-success point estimate among protection pipelines for all four planners. On PrivScreen, it reduces fixed-reader field exposure by 62.72\%--62.84\% relative to the same baseline. PrivacyGuard lowers upload exposure while preserving a locally resolvable task path.
papers.summary: Cloud graphical user interface (`GUI`) agents upload instructions and screenshots to remote planners, which exposes personally identifiable information (`PII`), and existing placeholder defenses that mask detected spans and reuse exact strings fail when PII appears fragmented or in changed forms across turns. `PrivacyGuard` combines source-linked sanitization (`SAN`), which reconstructs fragmented or overlapping evidence and rewrites the full source extent, with a structured reference lifecycle (`REF`) that links changed appearances to session entities and resolves references locally without sending raw values upstream. In five-turn sessions it **reduces audited source-value leakage by 33.55% to 82.60%** relative to the closest prior full-pipeline system, raises strict cross-form continuity from 0.04 to 0.81, and roughly doubles verified completion on reference-required Android tasks. On `AndroidLab` it achieves the highest or tied-highest task-success estimate among protection pipelines for all four planners, and on `PrivScreen` it cuts fixed-reader field exposure by about 63%.

papers.title: A Bethe-Ansatz Source of Early Token Correlations: A marginal-preserving construction for parallel proposals
papers.abstract: Parallel token proposals in language-model decoding need a joint law, not merely accurate token marginals. We construct a family of coordinate-Bethe-ansatz laws from the periodic XXZ chain and compare each with its maximum-entropy pairwise projection at identical one- and two-site moments. In the eight-site, three-excitation sector, symmetry makes their entire probability-law difference one-dimensional, determined by a contiguous three-site moment. Along the Bethe branch, this gap varies with anisotropy, changes sign, and vanishes exactly at $\Delta=(3+\sqrt{3})/2$, where the eigenstate law becomes exactly pairwise. A nonlinear readout transfers a nonzero gap into the first two token positions while preserving their separate marginals. At $\Delta=1.5$ the deterministic binary token laws differ by 0.02654573 in total variation. Exact speculative verification then gives a strict accepted-prefix advantage for a constructed target and a neighborhood within targets sharing its first-token marginal. This is a mathematical existence result. It does not establish a language-model gain or wall-clock speedup.
papers.summary: Parallel token proposals in language-model decoding need a joint distribution over positions, not just accurate per-token marginals. The authors construct a family of coordinate-Bethe-ansatz probability laws from the periodic `XXZ` spin chain and compare each with its maximum-entropy pairwise projection at matched one- and two-site moments; in the eight-site, three-excitation sector the difference is one-dimensional, varies with anisotropy, and **vanishes exactly at Δ = (3 + √3)/2**, where the law becomes exactly pairwise. A nonlinear readout carries a nonzero gap into the first two token positions while preserving their marginals, giving binary token laws that differ by about 0.027 in total variation at Δ = 1.5 and a strict accepted-prefix advantage under exact speculative verification for a constructed target. The authors state this is a mathematical existence result that does not establish a language-model gain or wall-clock speedup.

papers.title: LIBERO-Industry: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation under Industrial Process Constraints
papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.
papers.summary: Flexible manufacturing such as high-mix, low-volume (`HMLV`) electronics assembly imposes process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances, that existing robot-policy benchmarks do not systematically capture. `LIBERO-Industry` extends the `LIBERO` benchmark with three scenarios, Static-to-Dynamic loading, Dynamic-to-Static unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic transfer, totaling 216 tasks that vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and acceptance-region size. Across five generalist policies, including vision-language-action and world-action models, **performance degrades progressively as constraints are introduced and combined**, and co-training on the new suite yields higher target-transfer completion than training on the original benchmark alone.

papers.title: InfoVis: Unified Slide Image Generation and Editing
papers.abstract: Generating and editing presentation slides requires models to combine accurate text rendering, instruction following, visual grounding, aesthetic design, and precise editing within one canvas. Existing work covers only subsets of these capabilities and lacks large-scale slide-native supervision and diagnostic evaluation. We formulate four slide-centric tasks and build a scalable data engine with over 13M continual-pretraining records and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records. We also introduce VisSlideBench, a benchmark of 1,527 manually screened instances that covers all four tasks with task-specific, multidimensional evaluation. Its automatic rankings agree with blinded, dimension-wise human rankings. Using these resources, we train InfoVis, a unified 9B slide generation and editing model. On VisSlideBench, InfoVis leads every evaluated open-source model on all eleven metrics and scores 7.94 overall against 7.99 for Nano-Banana-2. Starting from FLUX.2-klein-base-9B, slide-specific post-training adds 1.6 points overall, with the largest generation gains in content faithfulness; the remaining gap to proprietary models is smallest in content faithfulness and largest in aesthetic quality. Built on InfoVis, our document-to-slide workflow achieves the second-highest Aesthetics score on the external SlidesGen-Bench. We will release the model, code, data, and benchmark.
papers.summary: Generating and editing presentation slides requires accurate text rendering, instruction following, visual grounding, aesthetic design, and precise editing within a single canvas, and existing work covers only subsets of these with little slide-native supervision. The authors define four slide-centric tasks, build a data engine with over 13M continual-pretraining and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records, and release `VisSlideBench`, a 1,527-instance benchmark whose automatic rankings agree with blinded human rankings. The resulting 9B model `InfoVis`, post-trained from `FLUX.2-klein-base-9B`, **leads every evaluated open-source model on all eleven metrics and scores 7.94 overall against 7.99 for `Nano-Banana-2`**, with the remaining gap to proprietary models smallest in content faithfulness and largest in aesthetics. A document-to-slide workflow built on it places second on aesthetics on the external `SlidesGen-Bench`.

papers.title: Logit Leakage through Floating-Point Bias Addition
papers.abstract: Language model APIs can expose token-specific biases while withholding logits and token probabilities. Existing bias-based extraction recovers relative logits, leaving a common additive component undetermined in ideal arithmetic. We identify a numerical side channel in floating-point bias addition that exposes information about this component through token identities alone. The channel distinguishes score vectors with identical complete unperturbed log probabilities. Our method exploits changes in representable spacing at binary exponent boundaries. Under the stated binary32 arithmetic assumptions and a known reachable score interval, it recovers a logit pair and its unknown tie-breaking priority exactly in at most 52 token queries. Given complete relative logits, one recovered anchor determines the original logit vector. We evaluate recovery across 11 public checkpoints from seven model families and extend the local method with adaptive interval search and anchor selection. In end-to-end experiments with vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp, adaptive recovery succeeds on all 128 Qwen3-0.6B inputs per system, including 64 held-out inputs. A separate token-only experiment extracts a pretrained small model's complete output-head representation up to an invertible hidden-basis transformation. We also establish a sufficient condition for suppressing common-shift disclosure by subtracting the maximum before bias addition. In controlled experiments, this mitigation eliminates all observed distinctions between common-shift variants and preserves token decisions under the tested random biases.
papers.summary: Language-model APIs that accept per-token logit biases while withholding logits let existing attacks recover only relative logits, leaving a common additive shift undetermined under ideal arithmetic. The authors identify a numerical side channel in floating-point bias addition: changes in representable spacing at binary exponent boundaries make the returned token identities depend on that shift, and under stated binary32 assumptions the method **recovers a logit pair and its tie-breaking priority exactly in at most 52 token queries**, which together with relative logits pins down the full logit vector. Adaptive recovery succeeds on all 128 `Qwen3-0.6B` inputs per system in end-to-end runs against `vLLM`, `SGLang`, and `llama.cpp`, and a token-only experiment extracts a small model's complete output-head weights up to an invertible basis change. Subtracting the maximum logit before adding biases is shown to suppress the disclosure while preserving token decisions in controlled tests.

papers.title: Efficient Preconditioned Optimization Methods with Frequent Directions
papers.abstract: Adaptive optimization methods have received considerable attention in recent years due to their strong empirical performance.
