However, they generally require maintaining a preconditioning matrix, which incurs prohibitive computational overhead in large-scale applications. To address these limitations, we investigate the acceleration of preconditioned optimization methods through frequent directions (FD), a widely used matrix sketching technique. We first propose FTSL by integrating FD with adaptive subgradient methods under the primal-dual framework and adding back the cumulative information discarded by FD. FTSL obtains a tighter regret bound than existing state-of-the-art results. We then apply a doubling trick that further reduces the time complexity of FTSL, while maintaining the same regret guarantee. We also consider optimization over matrix-valued decision variables and exploit their structural properties to construct sketched preconditioners. We develop FTSL-Shampoo by adapting FD to Shampoo and give a novel analysis under the primal-dual framework. To further mitigate its computational complexity, we design one-sided variants of FTSL-Shampoo under both mirror descent and primal-dual frameworks. Our algorithms not only reduce the computational cost of FTSL-Shampoo, but also achieve tighter regret bounds. We extend our methods to offline stochastic convex optimization and exploit smoothness to achieve faster convergence rates. Finally, we introduce practical variants of our algorithms and empirically demonstrate their efficiency and effectiveness across a broad range of tasks.
papers.summary: Adaptive optimizers that maintain a full preconditioning matrix become prohibitively expensive at scale. The authors use frequent directions (`FD`), a matrix sketching technique, to build `FTSL`, which integrates FD with adaptive subgradient methods under the primal-dual framework while adding back the cumulative information the sketch discards, and they pair it with a doubling trick that lowers time complexity without weakening the guarantee. They then adapt FD to `Shampoo` for matrix-valued variables as `FTSL-Shampoo`, derive one-sided variants under mirror descent and primal-dual frameworks that are cheaper still, and extend everything to offline stochastic convex optimization with faster rates under smoothness. **FTSL obtains a tighter regret bound than existing state-of-the-art sketched methods**, and practical variants are shown to be efficient across a range of tasks.

papers.title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning
papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language-model reasoning. While \emph{value evolution along trajectory} characterizes relative token-level credit, yet standard critics often fail to track it under sparse terminal rewards. To model this evolution, we analyze the relation between successive prefix values and show that they admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space. We use this additive structure to construct Tracking-Value PPO (\method), a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits. These outputs are learned through terminal-outcome supervision on the reconstructed values. \method improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively, while improving out-of-distribution generalization. Gains extend to Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B and to countdown, and scientific coding tasks. Further analysis shows more accurate tracking of value evolution and more reliable advantage estimates. Our code is publicly available in https://github.com/LINs-lab/TPPO.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, Proximal Policy Optimization (`PPO`) critics often fail to track how value evolves along a reasoning trajectory under sparse terminal rewards, which weakens token-level credit assignment. The authors show that successive prefix values admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space, and use this to build `TPPO`, a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits trained from terminal outcomes. **TPPO improves aggregate math reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on `Qwen3-4B-Base` and `Qwen3-8B-Base`**, improves out-of-distribution generalization, and extends to `Qwen3-4B`, `Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B`, `Qwen3.5-9B`, countdown, and scientific coding tasks, with analysis showing more accurate value tracking and more reliable advantages.
papers.highlight_summary:
Standard `PPO` critics for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards predict each prefix value independently and fail to track how value changes along a reasoning trajectory: on `Qwen3-8B-Base`, sign agreement between critic-predicted and Monte Carlo value changes sits near chance and falls from 50.34% to 45.91% over training. `TPPO` exploits the fact that, under binary terminal rewards, each prefix value is a success probability whose Bayesian update is additive in log-odds space, so the critic sums per-position scalar outputs into a value logit.

- The critic emits one scalar per token, cumulatively sums them into a logit, applies a sigmoid to reconstruct the prefix value, and trains with binary cross-entropy against the terminal outcome only, after which the values feed unchanged into GAE and the PPO clipped objective with no extra rollouts or process labels (the paper explicitly does not claim the learned increments recover true log-likelihood ratios).
- With 8 rollouts per prompt on `Polaris` math data, the in-domain average over seven math benchmarks rises **+7.0** points on `Qwen3-4B-Base` (41.6 vs 34.6) and **+8.4** on `Qwen3-8B-Base` (45.9 vs 37.5) over `PPO`, ahead of `GRPO`, `VAPO`, and `SPPO`, with out-of-domain averages on `ARC-C`, `AGI-Eval`, and `BBH` also improving on both base models.
- Gains persist with a single rollout per prompt (+7.5 on `Qwen3-8B-Base`, +10.1 on `Qwen3-4B`), transfer to `Countdown` on `Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B` (+4.6 on 3–4 numbers, +3.2 on 5), and to scientific coding on `Qwen3.5-9B` (+7.0 average, **+15.5** on `LiveCodeBench` v6, though part of that delta reflects `PPO` regressing below the base model there).
- Against Monte Carlo references on `Qwen3-8B-Base`, value-change sign agreement is 3.9–6.8 points above `PPO` and advantage sign accuracy 15.3–19.9 points above across the last four checkpoints, and ablations show `PPO`+BCE helps but trails while `TPPO`+MSE collapses, so the cumulative parameterization rather than the loss is the main driver.
- Limitations include models no larger than 9B, only verifiable domains, a formulation that assumes binary terminal rewards with γ=1, MC diagnostics restricted to 64 prompts at nine anchors that miss within-interval swings, and a fixed-actor controlled comparison that lifts sign accuracy only to about 53% from 51%, still close to chance.

papers.title: One-Layer Transformers Provably Learn In-Context K-Nearest Neighbor Prediction with Chain-of-Thought
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enables transformers to solve complex reasoning tasks by generating intermediate reasoning steps. Despite strong empirical success, the mechanisms by which such reasoning abilities emerge during training remain poorly understood, particularly from a theoretical perspective. In this work, we study this question in a stylized yet fully analyzable setting: in-context $\mathrm{K}$-nearest-neighbor ($\mathrm{K}$-NN) prediction with a one-layer transformer. Earlier work has demonstrated that one-layer transformers can be trained to perform $1$-NN without CoT (Li et al., 2024a) by having the softmax attention attend to the nearest neighbor in context. However, this result on $1$-NN cannot be extended to $\mathrm{K}$-NN for $K>1$, as softmax attention is much less naturally suited to attending to the 2nd through $K$-th nearest neighbors. We first give a rigorous negative result showing that this limitation already appears on a well-separated class of binary classification tasks for odd $K>1$. We then give an explicit construction of a one-layer transformer, and show that it can solve $\mathrm{K}$-NN via CoT reasoning. We further prove that, under a stylized training setup, gradient descent can recover this construction, thereby showing that transformers can acquire the capability to solve $\mathrm{K}$-NN through training. In addition, we show that the resulting trained model applies to a broader test class than that assumed in the training analysis. Our results shed light on how CoT expands the ability of transformers to learn and solve tasks that are otherwise hard to solve.
papers.summary: Chain-of-Thought (`CoT`) prompting empirically helps transformers reason, but the training mechanisms behind this ability are poorly understood theoretically. The authors study in-context K-nearest-neighbor (`K-NN`) prediction with a one-layer transformer, where prior work showed 1-NN is learnable without CoT because softmax attention can focus on the single nearest neighbor. They first prove a negative result: for odd K greater than 1, a one-layer transformer without CoT fails on a well-separated class of binary classification tasks, since softmax attention is ill-suited to attending to the 2nd through K-th neighbors. They then give an explicit one-layer construction that solves K-NN via CoT and **prove that gradient descent recovers this construction under a stylized training setup**, with the trained model generalizing to a broader test class than the training analysis assumes.

papers.title: When Repeated Measurements Hurt Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on IID benchmarks, but how do they respond to repeated measurements at the same inputs? Across six TFMs, synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments show that additional measurements can improve predictions at measured inputs while degrading them elsewhere. Harm is most frequent at low noise, and irrelevant features amplify it in several models; real repeated-measurement datasets show similar patterns. Statistically, the IID rule targeted by PFN pretraining treats each repeated input as fresh evidence about the input distribution. When the prior links this distribution to the response function, the resulting protocol mismatch can outweigh the benefit of additional measurements, even under exact inference. Computationally, interventions identify row-count dependence in TabPFN-v3's attention scaling as a contributor to harm. Resetting the count largely reverses distortion in a noiseless linear diagnostic and attenuates amplification by irrelevant features. Finally, we evaluate ways to retain the benefits of repeated measurements while limiting their harm. Averaging measurements usually outperforms supplying them separately at larger repetition counts, whereas count reset can suppress both harm and useful gains. Code, saved results and reproduction instructions are available at https://github.com/drizmiz/PFN-Repeated-Measurement-Supp
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (`TFMs`) excel on IID benchmarks, but their behavior when the same input is measured repeatedly has not been examined. Across six TFMs, synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments show that extra measurements can improve predictions at the measured inputs while **degrading predictions elsewhere, most often at low noise and amplified by irrelevant features**, with real repeated-measurement datasets showing similar patterns. The authors trace this to a protocol mismatch, since the IID rule targeted by prior-fitted network (`PFN`) pretraining treats each repeat as fresh evidence about the input distribution, and computationally to row-count dependence in `TabPFN-v3` attention scaling, which resetting the count largely reverses. Averaging repeated measurements usually beats supplying them separately at larger repetition counts, whereas the count reset suppresses both the harm and the useful gains.

papers.title: Predicting Audio Popularity: A Comparative Study of Metadata and Acoustic Features Across Music and Sound Effects
papers.abstract: This study addresses the prediction of audio popularity on an online sharing platform by leveraging both metadata and acoustic feature representations. Two distinct categories of audio content are considered: music and sound effects. Popularity is formulated as a supervised classification task based on two target variables: the number of downloads and the average user rating. We conduct a comparative evaluation of multiple machine learning models, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and a Neural Network model. Experiments are performed across different feature sets, including metadata, platform-provided descriptors, and eGeMAPS acoustic features. Results indicate that metadata consistently provide the most informative representation for predicting popularity. Nevertheless, acoustic features alone achieve performance significantly above chance level, demonstrating that intrinsic properties of the audio signal contribute to popularity prediction.
papers.summary: The study predicts audio popularity on an online sharing platform for two content types, music and sound effects, framing it as supervised classification on download counts and average user rating. It compares `Random Forest`, `XGBoost`, and a neural network across feature sets drawn from metadata, platform-provided descriptors, and `eGeMAPS` acoustic features. **Metadata consistently provides the most informative representation**, while acoustic features alone still perform significantly above chance, indicating that intrinsic signal properties contribute to popularity.

papers.title: DASS: A Solver-Adaptable Dynamic Auxiliary Search Strategy for Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) aims to discover interpretable mathematical expressions from data and plays a key role in scientific discovery. However, existing methods face a common bottleneck: the enormous search space and severe combinatorial explosion make it difficult to achieve a favorable trade-off between accuracy and algorithmic efficiency. We argue that, in addition to designing increasingly complex solver-specific SR strategies, an equally promising direction is to equip them with a shareable auxiliary strategy that can provide reliable search guidance. To this end, we propose DASS, a solver-adaptable Dynamic Auxiliary Search Strategy that improves SR by constructing and refining a high-potential auxiliary search subspace. DASS represents the auxiliary search space as a functional subspace spanned by a set of high-potential basis function terms. It estimates term utility through multi-environment evaluation, filters unstable guidance, and updates term potential scores with a Gibbs posterior, thereby calibrating the subspace to provide more reliable guidance for downstream solvers. The high-quality solutions produced by the solver are used to update the set of basis terms. This forms a virtuous closed-loop optimization process: the subspace guides the downstream solver, and the solver feedback reshapes the subspace for subsequent exploration. DASS can be easily integrated with various types of SR solvers. Extensive experiments on LLM-SRBench show that DASS significantly improves the accuracy of original solvers with a manageable increase in runtime.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression (`SR`) searches for interpretable mathematical expressions from data, but the combinatorial size of the expression space forces a poor trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. `DASS` is a solver-agnostic auxiliary strategy that maintains a functional subspace spanned by high-potential basis terms, estimates term utility through multi-environment evaluation, filters unstable guidance, and updates term scores with a Gibbs posterior, while the solver's best solutions in turn refresh the basis set in a closed loop. It can be attached to various SR solvers, and on `LLM-SRBench` it **significantly improves the accuracy of the original solvers with a manageable increase in runtime**.

papers.title: Carve VFM: Carving Specialists out of Generalists, Automatic Task-Specific Compression of Vision Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Vision foundation models (VFMs) provide transferable visual representations, but their inference cost limits deployment in many settings. Fine-tuning specializes a VFM without shrinking it; distillation shrinks it, but through expensive teacher-guided training. Structured pruning offers a more direct route by extracting a compact subnetwork from the VFM. However, as compression gets aggressive, existing methods fail because they treat subnetwork selection and recovery as separate axes. Across layers, capacity must follow task sensitivity rather than spread uniformly. Within a layer, a removal cannot be judged by importance alone; its impact also depends on how well the lost contribution can be recovered from what remains. Selection and recovery must therefore be decided jointly. We introduce Carve VFM, which resolves this interdependence. Given a VFM, a calibration set, and a parameter budget, it (i) searches for task-specific capacity allocations across layers; (ii) guides the search via an adaptive recovery-aware fitness criterion; and (iii) reconstructs removed behavior through iterative closed-form low-rank corrections merged into the surviving weights. The result is a dense encoder produced in minutes on a single GPU without backbone retraining. Across twelve benchmarks and four models from DINOv3 and MetaCLIP-2, Carve VFM achieves the highest reported mean accuracy in seven of eight backbone-budget configurations among the evaluated dense structured-pruning methods. Further fine-tuning surpasses the strongest evaluated edge model (88.1% vs. 85.8%), and carved models cut compute and memory while delivering 1.3-2.0x higher GPU throughput than the uncompressed one. These results show that the compact model you need is inside the VFM; it only has to be carved out.
papers.summary: Vision foundation models (`VFMs`) offer transferable representations but are costly to run, and existing structured pruning fails under aggressive compression because it decides which subnetwork to keep separately from how to recover the lost contribution. `Carve VFM` treats selection and recovery jointly: given a model, a calibration set, and a parameter budget, it searches for task-specific capacity allocations across layers, scores candidates with a recovery-aware fitness criterion, and reconstructs removed behavior through iterative closed-form low-rank corrections merged into surviving weights, producing a dense encoder in minutes on one GPU without backbone retraining. Across twelve benchmarks and four `DINOv3` and `MetaCLIP-2` models it **achieves the highest mean accuracy in seven of eight backbone-budget configurations** among dense structured-pruning methods, and carved models deliver 1.3 to 2.0 times higher GPU throughput with further fine-tuning surpassing the strongest edge model at 88.1% versus 85.8%.

papers.title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.
papers.summary: Large language models (`LLMs`) used as judges to produce scalar scores for tasks like paper review are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection hidden in the evaluated content, and existing defenses modify the judge itself, tying safety to a specific model and requiring rework whenever the judge changes. `StableJudge` externalizes the defense as a reusable pre-scoring step built around a **compact 0.13B `Sentry` model that localizes injected spans and sanitizes them before evaluation**, trained against adversarially evolving attacks, and it derives deterministic fine-grained scores from the judge's output distribution to stabilize measurement. On held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants it improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose judging performance.

papers.title: On the Calibration of Crowdsourcing Aggregators
papers.abstract: Calibration has been extensively studied for classifiers, but remains largely unexplored for crowdsourcing aggregation methods, which are increasingly used for making probabilistic decisions. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first theoretical and empirical study of calibration in label aggregation. To our great surprise, we find that widely used aggregation methods can be severely miscalibrated, and in opposite directions: Majority Vote is underconfident while model-based aggregators are overconfident. We prove that the Bayesian aggregator is perfectly calibrated under its data-generating model. We also show that exact calibration of weighted majority votes requires highly restrictive conditions, which helps explain why Majority Vote is generally miscalibrated in realistic crowds. Empirically, we study calibration across $39$ human crowdsourcing datasets and LLM-based crowds. In both cases, we observe systematic miscalibration for aggregation models such as Majority Vote, Dawid--Skene, GLAD, and CrowdFM. Finally, we propose a post-hoc calibration procedure that \emph{aggregates the aggregators}: for any aggregation function $\phi$, we introduce a transformation that first combines its predictive distribution with those of complementary aggregators, before applying temperature scaling. This simple and interpretable transformation makes temperature scaling more effective than when applied directly to $\phi$. It improves calibration, especially in the high-redundancy regime where there are many annotations per item, while generally preserving or even improving accuracy.
papers.summary: Calibration is well studied for classifiers but largely unexplored for crowdsourcing label aggregators, which increasingly feed probabilistic decisions. The authors show theoretically and empirically that common aggregators are miscalibrated in opposite directions, with **`Majority Vote` underconfident and model-based aggregators such as `Dawid-Skene`, `GLAD`, and `CrowdFM` overconfident**, prove that the Bayesian aggregator is perfectly calibrated under its generative model, and show that exact calibration of weighted majority votes requires highly restrictive conditions. Across 39 human crowdsourcing datasets and LLM-based crowds the miscalibration is systematic. A post-hoc fix that first combines an aggregator's predictive distribution with those of complementary aggregators and then applies temperature scaling improves calibration, especially with many annotations per item, while generally preserving or improving accuracy.

papers.title: Statistical Downscaling of Daily Precipitation from ERA5 Atmospheric Fields to IMERG over West Africa
papers.abstract: Global reanalyses are too coarse to resolve the convective systems that produce most West African monsoon rainfall. In this work, we use U-Net based architectures to downscale daily ERA5 fields (0.25{\deg}) to IMERG V07 satellite precipitation (0.1{\deg}) over West Africa for the June to October seasons of 2000 to 2024, using geopotential, temperature, humidity and wind at three pressure levels together with elevation and land fraction. Adding ERA5 precipitation as input slightly improves performance for this particular challenging region. We find that all the deterministic networks investigated for this work are too dry and lose almost all observed variance below a few hundred kilometers, which motivated our use of a GAN-based alternative. We also investigated permutation importance for the U-Net that ranks 500 hPa specific humidity first, consistent with the sensitivity of deep convection to mid-tropospheric moisture.
papers.summary: Global reanalyses are too coarse to resolve the convective systems behind most West African monsoon rainfall. The authors train U-Net based networks to downscale daily `ERA5` fields at 0.25 degrees to `IMERG V07` satellite precipitation at 0.1 degrees for June to October of 2000 to 2024, using geopotential, temperature, humidity, and wind at three pressure levels plus elevation and land fraction, with ERA5 precipitation as an extra input giving a slight gain. **All deterministic networks are too dry and lose nearly all observed variance below a few hundred kilometers**, which motivated a GAN-based alternative, and permutation importance ranks 500 hPa specific humidity as the top predictor, consistent with deep convection's sensitivity to mid-tropospheric moisture.

papers.title: Growing to See: Efficient Pretraining of Self-Supervised Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Progressive depth growth builds large networks by starting with shallow models and inserting layers during training. Recent advances in large language models have renewed interest in this longstanding approach, demonstrating benefits for training efficiency and reasoning alongside changes in internal computations. However, how growing affects representation quality and computational patterns in self-supervised vision transformers remains unclear. In this work, we systematically investigate progressive depth growth in two popular self-supervised families, namely masked autoencoders (MAE) and DINOv3, and analyze how growing affects downstream performance, intermediate representations, and internal computations. Across global and dense tasks, we show that growing improves downstream performance while reducing training FLOPs by 13.9--24.8%, with ImageNet linear-probe accuracy gains of up to 3.36 percentage points. Growing also improves downstream performance at intermediate layers and reshapes internal computational patterns, introducing recurring alternations between global and localized attention in MAE and earlier local-to-global attention progression in self-distilled DINOv3. Together, these findings establish progressive depth growth as an effective and efficient pretraining strategy for improving downstream performance across global and dense visual tasks with less computation, and advance our understanding of how growing shapes visual computation.
papers.summary: Progressive depth growth trains a shallow network and inserts layers over time, an approach recently revived for large language models, but its effect on representation quality in self-supervised vision transformers was unclear. The authors systematically apply growth to masked autoencoders (`MAE`) and `DINOv3` and analyze downstream performance, intermediate representations, and attention patterns. Growing **improves downstream performance while cutting training FLOPs by 13.9% to 24.8%**, with `ImageNet` linear-probe gains of up to 3.36 percentage points, and it also improves intermediate-layer features and reshapes computation, introducing alternating global and local attention in MAE and an earlier local-to-global progression in DINOv3.

papers.title: Calibrated $\alpha$-Barycenters for Multiobjective $f$-Divergence Optimization
papers.abstract: Matching one distribution to many targets can require repeated evaluations of every target. CAL-$\alpha$-MODM aggregates a nonlinear predictor into one barycenter, calibrates its residual derivatives, and checks steps against the original $f$-divergence objective. Under smoothness assumptions, calibration controls parameter-step model error without requiring targets to be close to the model. Exact-oracle stationarity and local convergence guarantees are established. At common matching, canonical geometry cancels the leading quadratic iteration error, giving cubic convergence with second-order calibration and sufficiently accurate inner solves. High-precision experiments support this prediction. Sensitivity-based initialization also accelerates preference continuation along regular stationary branches. On 300-target Jensen--Shannon problems, CAL-p2 achieves median paired speedups of $3.15\times$ over L-BFGS and $1.10\times$ over second-order Direct-TR, across 23/25 and 24/25 objective-comparable stationary pairs. The savings arise when cheaper predictor queries offset calibration overhead.
papers.summary: Matching one distribution to many target distributions under f-divergence objectives can require repeatedly evaluating every target. `CAL-α-MODM` aggregates a nonlinear predictor into a single barycenter, calibrates its residual derivatives, and checks each step against the original objective, with calibration controlling model error without requiring targets to be near the model. The authors establish exact-oracle stationarity and local convergence, show that at common matching the canonical geometry cancels the leading quadratic error to give cubic convergence with second-order calibration, and confirm this in high-precision experiments. On 300-target Jensen-Shannon problems the `CAL-p2` variant achieves **median paired speedups of 3.15 times over L-BFGS** and 1.10 times over a second-order trust-region method, with savings arising when cheaper predictor queries offset calibration overhead.

papers.title: Sample-Size Extrapolation in Simulation-Based Inference via Statistical Scaling
papers.abstract: In simulation-based inference (SBI), neural posterior estimators trained on a bounded range of sample sizes can become inaccurate on larger datasets because their parameterizations do not specify how posterior location, uncertainty and shape must change as observations accumulate. We propose center-estimated NPE (CE-NPE), which combines a statistical center with an explicit contraction rate and learns a local center correction and residual densities in posterior-scale coordinates. The center is a statistical estimate, such as a closed-form statistic or a simulator-based moment match, which does not require an evaluable likelihood. Our analysis explains how contraction amplifies center error and decomposes Gaussian posterior error into shape, mean and covariance contributions. On six regular benchmarks, CE-NPE gives the best reference-posterior agreement of all tested amortized estimators at every out-of-range size, up to five times the largest training size, without retraining; it also fits better within the training range on most of them. Matched controls and nonregular examples characterize the scope of these gains and identify the conditions on which they depend: an appropriate contraction rate, an accurate center, and a stable residual representation.
papers.summary: In simulation-based inference (`SBI`), neural posterior estimators (`NPE`) trained on a limited range of sample sizes degrade on larger datasets because nothing in their parameterization dictates how posterior location, uncertainty, and shape should change as observations accumulate. Center-estimated NPE (`CE-NPE`) pairs a statistical center estimate, such as a closed-form statistic or simulator-based moment match that needs no evaluable likelihood, with an explicit contraction rate, and learns a local center correction and residual densities in posterior-scale coordinates. On six regular benchmarks it gives **the best reference-posterior agreement of all tested amortized estimators at every out-of-range size, up to five times the largest training size**, without retraining, and usually fits better within the training range too, while matched controls and nonregular examples show the gains depend on an appropriate contraction rate, an accurate center, and a stable residual representation.

papers.title: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. The key difficulty is that neural architectures are operation-labeled DAGs: edge direction defines computational flow, but existing predictors often treat direction as a local structural cue. We propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer based on encoder-wide directional consistency, which preserves directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature update. DTA-GT realizes this principle with direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative sequence-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and Magnetic spectral controls show that the improvements come from coordinated direction-aware stages and edge-orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics confirm that the modules exhibit the intended directional behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation.
papers.summary: Neural architecture search relies on attribute predictors that estimate accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates, but architectures are directed graphs of labeled operations whose edge direction defines computational flow, and existing predictors treat that direction only as a local structural cue. `DTA-GT` keeps directional semantics consistent across the whole encoder through direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a direction-sensitive mixture-of-experts feed-forward layer. On accuracy and latency prediction for `NAS-Bench-101` and `NAS-Bench-201`, **it consistently outperforms sequence-based, graph-network, Transformer, and hybrid predictors under limited evaluation budgets**, and ablations with Magnetic spectral controls attribute the gains to the coordinated direction-aware stages and orientation-sensitive spectral information.

papers.title: Mean Accuracy Is the Wrong Estimand for a Release Decision
papers.abstract: A release decision about a fine-tuned model is an operational commitment about the \emph{next} rerun of its training recipe. Yet standard benchmark reporting gives only the mean accuracy of past seeds. These target fundamentally different questions: release decisions depend on catastrophic tail risk, whereas standard evaluation reports only central tendency. Because fine-tuning induces bimodal mode collapse, high average accuracy frequently conceals severe failure rates. Auditing $2\,124$ fine-tuned models across eleven language models, we show that shipping models based on mean accuracy violates a $10\%$ deployment failure budget $48.0\%$ of the time. Common heuristics like $\bar b - 2\sigma$ prove equally dangerous: by underestimating variance on small samples, they become most permissive when evidence is weakest. We introduce \textbf{recipe cards}, an evaluation framework that directly certifies rerun tail failure rates using exact finite-sample binomial bounds. Recipe cards reduce held-out budget violations to $0.6\%$, enforce a mathematical sample floor ($N \ge 22$) that prevents certification on thin evidence, and explicitly refuse unverified claims under domain and task shifts.
papers.summary: Deciding whether to release a fine-tuned model is a commitment about the next rerun of its training recipe, yet standard reporting gives only the mean accuracy across past seeds, which measures central tendency rather than the catastrophic tail risk a release decision depends on. Because fine-tuning induces bimodal mode collapse, an audit of 2,124 fine-tuned models across eleven language models finds that **shipping on mean accuracy violates a 10% deployment failure budget 48.0% of the time**, and the common mean-minus-two-standard-deviations heuristic is most permissive exactly when evidence is thinnest because it underestimates variance on small samples. The proposed `recipe cards` certify rerun tail failure rates with exact finite-sample binomial bounds, cutting held-out budget violations to 0.6%, enforcing a sample floor of at least 22 runs, and explicitly refusing unverified claims under domain and task shifts.

papers.title: Unsupervised Data Drift Monitoring for Deployed Deepfake Speech Detectors
papers.abstract: Deepfake speech detectors are typically evaluated as binary classifiers on fixed benchmarks, but deployed systems face evolving attacks, codecs, speakers, and recording conditions, with labels unavailable during operation. This makes it difficult to know when a detector operates in familiar conditions and can be relied on. We propose an unsupervised drift monitor that operates on the internal embeddings of a deployed detector. The monitor compares each input against bona fide and spoof references using regularized Mahalanobis distances. These distances define trusted, ambiguous, and novel regions of the detector embedding space, allowing unfamiliar inputs to be routed for review. We evaluate the monitor on four modern detectors on three datasets. The monitor raises alerts for dataset mismatches and substantially reduces the security-critical case of accepting deepfakes at the cost of reduced automatic coverage. The results also show that drift affects both classes: bona fide recordings can move away from the training reference, increasing alert rates even in in-domain settings. Our findings suggest that deployed deepfake speech detectors should be treated not only as a binary classification, but also as a reliability problem.
papers.summary: Deployed deepfake speech detectors face shifting attacks, codecs, speakers, and recording conditions without any labels, so it is hard to know when their outputs can be trusted. The proposed monitor works unsupervised on a detector's internal embeddings, comparing each input against bona fide and spoof references with regularized Mahalanobis distances to carve the embedding space into trusted, ambiguous, and novel regions and route unfamiliar inputs for human review. Across four modern detectors and three datasets, the monitor flags dataset mismatches and **substantially reduces the security-critical case of accepting deepfakes**, at the cost of reduced automatic coverage, and it reveals that bona fide recordings also drift away from the training reference even in in-domain settings.

papers.title: The Bell Boundary of Shared Representations
papers.abstract: When does a shared representation become insufficient for jointly supporting multiple tasks? This question lies at the heart of multi-task learning models. Although task interference in shared representations has been widely observed, its onset, measurable form, and capacity boundary remain poorly understood. In this paper, we revisit this problem through the lens of Bell's theorem. We show that if four binary task outcomes can be jointly represented by a common shared representation, their correlations must satisfy the classical CHSH bound $|S|\leq2$. We introduce NCnet, a controlled multi-task model for studying how representational capacity affects task compatibility. Experiments reveal a clear capacity-dependent transition. Once nontrivial task fitting emerges, constrained capacity can yield $|S|>2$. As capacity further increases, these exceedances progressively disappear and $S$ returns to the bounded region. This systematic pattern provides evidence that limited representational capacity is an important source of the observed incompatibility. We observe similar transitions across CNNs, PLMs, and LLMs, suggesting that the phenomenon extends beyond the controlled NCnet setting. We refer to this capacity-dependent transition as the Bell Boundary, providing a measurable diagnostic for representation bottlenecks, task incompatibility, and capacity allocation in multi-task models.
papers.summary: Task interference in shared multi-task representations is widely observed, but when it sets in and how to measure its capacity boundary remain poorly understood. Borrowing from Bell's theorem, the authors show that if four binary task outcomes can be jointly represented by a common shared representation, their correlations must satisfy the classical CHSH bound of |S| at most 2, and they introduce `NCnet`, a controlled multi-task model for varying representational capacity. Experiments reveal **a capacity-dependent transition in which constrained models exceed the bound once nontrivial task fitting emerges, with the violations vanishing as capacity grows**, a pattern that also appears across CNNs, pretrained language models, and large language models and that the authors name the Bell Boundary, offering a measurable diagnostic for representation bottlenecks and task incompatibility.

papers.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
papers.abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.
papers.summary: Syntactic language models (SLMs), which generate sentences together with their syntactic trees, have mostly been evaluated at small scale on narrow task suites, leaving the design space of tree linearizations and attention masks underexplored. The study trains 12 controlled configurations, one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants, at up to 1B parameters and 100B tokens and evaluates them on 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. SLM variants using standard causal attention match or beat structural-mask variants while needing no architectural changes and staying compatible with `FlashAttention`, but **at the 1B-parameter scale the best SLM no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline**, suggesting SLMs become less competitive as scale grows.

papers.title: Same Operation, Different Permission: Evaluating Whether Guardrails Honor Authorization
papers.abstract: As language-model agents write code, move money and change records on behalf of users, deciding whether an action is authorized has become a central safety problem. Guardrails are often placed in front of these actions, yet few evaluations ask whether their decisions follow authorization: blocking unauthorized actions while still allowing the same actions under valid permission. We introduce \bench{}, a benchmark that contrasts authorization evidence for the same operation in its language track. It combines expert-annotated natural-language scenarios with executed and verified operations, plus externally sourced native-policy requests. \bench{} checks each decision for correctness, usability and resulting effect, and tracks each request across guardrail changes. Our experiments show that many blocked operations stem from failed reviews, not correct denials. Repairing the output format restores usable decisions but changes which authorized requests are honored, and adding a second reviewer removes some errors while rejecting valid authorization. Guardrails should therefore be evaluated on both the unauthorized actions they stop and the authorized actions they let through.
papers.summary: As language-model agents write code, move money, and change records, guardrails placed in front of those actions are rarely tested on whether they actually follow authorization, meaning they block an unauthorized operation while still allowing the identical operation under valid permission. The authors build a benchmark whose language track contrasts authorization evidence for the same operation, combining expert-annotated natural-language scenarios with executed and verified operations plus externally sourced native-policy requests, and it scores each guardrail decision on correctness, usability, and resulting effect while tracking requests across guardrail versions. **Many blocked operations turn out to stem from failed reviews rather than correct denials.** Repairing the output format restores usable decisions but shifts which authorized requests are honored, and adding a second reviewer removes some errors while rejecting valid authorization.

papers.title: Label Collapse in Diffusion Language Model In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) applies large language models to new tasks by prepending a few labeled demonstrations to a query. Prior work has studied how demonstration ordering affects ICL, but the interaction between label arrangement patterns and model biases has not been systematically examined. We define label collapse as the failure mode in which the model generates query-independent labels, and show that it is architecturally universal at the tested 8-9B scale: five models spanning autoregressive (Llama-3, Qwen3.5) and discrete diffusion (LLaDA, iLLaDA, LLaDA-Instruct) families all exhibit label collapse even under the class-balanced alternating arrangement, with some label word pairs collapsing in virtually every tested condition and others flipping their collapse direction with arrangement. Critically, accuracy alone cannot detect this collapse: models can achieve near-chance accuracy while generating query-independent labels, a score indistinguishable from balanced performance, so the failure can persist undetected in deployment. We measure separation, the log-odds of the two label words at the query position (the quantity that label-bias calibration operates on), as a complementary diagnostic that exposes collapse hidden beneath surface accuracy, together with a measurement protocol that guards label extraction against tokenizer and formatting artifacts. For autoregressive models, collapse persists where the majority-label-bias account does not apply, and arrangement patterns can reverse the collapse direction; for diffusion models, we present a systematic evaluation of ICL failure modes, complementing contemporaneous studies of dLLM context comprehension and demonstration-order sensitivity, and identify open questions about how iterative denoising interacts with label biases.
papers.summary: In-context learning (ICL) prepends a few labeled demonstrations to a query, and the authors study a failure mode they call label collapse, where the model emits query-independent labels regardless of input. Testing five 8-9B models from the autoregressive `Llama-3` and `Qwen3.5` families and the discrete diffusion `LLaDA`, `iLLaDA`, and `LLaDA-Instruct` models, they find **collapse in every architecture even under class-balanced alternating demonstration arrangements**, with some label-word pairs collapsing in nearly every condition and others flipping direction with the arrangement. Because collapsed models can score near-chance accuracy indistinguishably from balanced performance, they propose measuring separation, the log-odds between the two label words at the query position, along with an extraction protocol robust to tokenizer and formatting artifacts, and they note that for autoregressive models the collapse persists where majority-label-bias explanations do not apply.

papers.title: Few-for-Many Best-Arm Identification in Multi-Objective Bandits
papers.abstract: Real-world systems often serve many objectives but can deploy only a few options, whose performance must be learned from noisy feedback. Modeling each option as an arm in a multi-objective bandit, we introduce \emph{few-for-many best-arm identification}, which seeks a small set of arms minimizing the worst weighted degradation from the objective-wise optima, rather than the best arm for every objective. We consider both known objective groups and latent groups specified only by a representative budget, and propose \textsc{GFM-Elim} and \textsc{AFM-Elim} with instance-dependent sample-complexity guarantees. For Gaussian rewards, we further derive a lower bound for the latent-group setting and show that it is asymptotically attainable with high probability by an oracle-based Track-and-Stop procedure. Our results show that sharing observations across objectives and ignoring irrelevant objective-wise distinctions can substantially reduce the sampling cost, as confirmed by experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks.
papers.summary: Real-world systems often serve many objectives but can deploy only a few options whose quality must be learned from noisy feedback. Framing each option as an arm in a multi-objective bandit, the authors define few-for-many best-arm identification, which seeks a small set of arms that minimizes the worst weighted degradation from each objective's optimum, and they propose `GFM-Elim` and `AFM-Elim` for known and latent objective groups with instance-dependent sample-complexity guarantees. For Gaussian rewards they derive a lower bound for the latent-group setting that an oracle-based Track-and-Stop procedure asymptotically attains with high probability, and experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks confirm that **sharing observations across objectives and ignoring irrelevant objective-wise distinctions substantially reduces sampling cost**.

papers.title: Feature Normalization under Finite Training Budgets
papers.abstract: Standardizing a rare feature can help stochastic gradient descent learn its effect within a finite budget, but it also changes the noise cost of learning. We characterize the lowest rare-subgroup risks attainable by standardized and unscaled training when each chooses a nonnegative constant learning rate and a deterministic stopping time under the same observation cap. For two independent binary features, we derive both optimized risks as prevalence vanishes while the expected number of rare observations remains finite. Uniform control over rates and stopping times reduces each limiting oracle to a scalar minimization. With positive noise, the preferred scaling changes exactly once as we move signal to the rare feature while the limiting risk at initialization stays fixed and positive. The formulas also explain how noise and budget affect the comparison. Separate finite-prevalence bounds favor standardization on a rare-dominant signal family and unscaled training on a common-dominant family. The results concern final iterates with population preprocessing and fresh observations. Exact-moment searches assess the approximation at finite prevalence. In a controlled study, both orderings persist under observation reuse, estimated preprocessing, and intercept fitting when tuning choices are fixed before evaluation. Selecting a predictor after observing training can reverse an ordering, even when selection uses exact population risk.
papers.summary: Standardizing a rare binary feature can help stochastic gradient descent learn its effect within a limited sample budget, but it also changes the noise cost of learning. The authors characterize the lowest rare-subgroup risk attainable by standardized versus unscaled training when each picks a constant learning rate and deterministic stopping time under the same observation cap, deriving both optimized risks for two independent binary features as prevalence vanishes while the expected number of rare observations stays finite. **With positive noise, the preferred scaling switches exactly once as signal shifts toward the rare feature**, finite-prevalence bounds favor standardization on rare-dominant signals and unscaled training on common-dominant ones, and a controlled study shows these orderings persist under observation reuse and estimated preprocessing but can reverse when a predictor is selected after observing training.

papers.title: Radial Tail Repair: Post-Training Correction for Diffusion and Flow Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching models may struggle to accurately represent distributional tails, especially for heavy-tailed data. Existing approaches often use heavy-tailed noise or modify the generative dynamics, requiring dedicated retraining and more difficult estimation. We take a simpler approach: rather than relearning the full distribution, we correct only the model's behavior in the extreme regime. Our method builds on the radial-angular decomposition of multivariate heavy tails, where radius and direction become asymptotically independent. This allows us to preserve the directional structure learned by the pretrained model and correct only its radial tail. We estimate the tail onset from reference and generated samples, then rescale generated extremes so that their radial survival matches the target distribution. The resulting method is a lightweight post-training correction applied to a frozen diffusion or flow-matching model, requiring neither retraining nor changes to its sampling dynamics. Experiments on challenging synthetic heavy-tailed distributions and real weather and wildfire datasets show that this simple correction substantially improves extreme-tail coverage using only a small number of fitting samples.
papers.summary: Diffusion and flow-matching models often misrepresent distributional tails on heavy-tailed data, and existing fixes use heavy-tailed noise or altered generative dynamics that require retraining and harder estimation. Instead of relearning the whole distribution, the proposed post-training correction uses the radial-angular decomposition of multivariate heavy tails, under which radius and direction become asymptotically independent, so the pretrained model's directional structure is kept and only the radial tail is corrected by estimating the tail onset from reference and generated samples and rescaling generated extremes to match the target's radial survival function. Applied to frozen models without retraining or changes to sampling, the method **substantially improves extreme-tail coverage using only a small number of fitting samples** on synthetic heavy-tailed distributions and real weather and wildfire datasets.

papers.title: Towards Cost-Efficient Video Dataset Construction with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Research on video classification models has witnessed significant growth recently, accompanied by a significant increase in the demand for datasets to train such models. Existing video dataset curation approaches share a common bottleneck: candidate videos must be downloaded before any relevance judgment is made, which results in storage, time and annotation costs. In this work, we present a filtering step, using Large Language Models (LLMs) to pre-screen videos based on their metadata, before actually downloading these videos, thereby saving on these costs. We evaluate the LLMs against a strict human majority vote derived from four independent annotators and validate the reliability of the annotations through inter-annotator agreement analysis (Gwet's AC1). We compare the LLM pre-filter against two no-LLM baselines, namely two keyword heuristics. Via a Leave-One-Rater-Out (LOO) mechanism and an Add-One-Rater-In (AORI), we evaluate the performance of the LLMs as virtual annotators. Finally, we report cost comparisons relative to existing approaches. To ensure reproducability, we made our implementation available on github.
papers.summary: Building video classification datasets normally requires downloading candidate videos before judging their relevance, incurring storage, time, and annotation costs. The authors insert a pre-download filtering step in which large language models screen candidates from metadata alone, and they evaluate it against a strict human majority vote from four independent annotators, checking annotation reliability with Gwet's AC1 inter-annotator agreement. Compared with two keyword-heuristic baselines, and using Leave-One-Rater-Out (LOO) and Add-One-Rater-In (AORI) analyses that treat the LLM as a virtual annotator, they **report the LLM pre-filter's reliability as an annotator and its cost savings relative to existing curation approaches**, with the implementation released publicly.

papers.title: ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one: developers also constrain how the task must be carried out-modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.
papers.summary: For coding agents working inside repositories, a functionally correct patch may still be unacceptable because developers also constrain how the work is done, including modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting, a capability the authors call engineering constraint following that current evaluations largely ignore. `ANCHOR` builds on naturalistic multilingual repository tasks across eight language groups, pairing a taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf constraint types distilled from real developer interactions with an automated pipeline that instantiates atomic constraints and composes them into AND, THEN, and PRIORITY relations, then checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory using rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest system, `Claude Opus 4.8` under `Cline`, reaches 70.1% atomic and 63.7% relation compliance, yet **only 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item**, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, while adding constraints changes task completion by only +0.7 points on average.

papers.title: GpFlash: Maximizing Speed and Minimizing Memory for Gaussian Process Training and Prediction
papers.abstract:
This paper presents GpFlash, a Gaussian process library that is focused on fast training and posterior evaluations, minimal memory usage, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. GpFlash was compared to the popular GP libraries scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT on a MacBook Pro and the supercomputer Trillium. GpFlash was found to use less memory and to be faster for training and posterior evaluations relative to the other GP libraries for all cases considered. For example, when using $
x = 10^4$ training points in a 10-dimensional space GpFlash required 9.6 to 35 times less memory and was 2.6 to 54 times faster than the other GP libraries for the evaluation of the marginal log likelihood and its gradient. The memory reduction was achieved by only using one matrix of size $
x 	imes 
x$ to store different symmetric matrices in its lower and upper triangular entries. The computational speedup was the result of designing algorithms to access memory efficiently, using BLAS and LAPACK methods extensively, and factoring kernel equations so that expensive exponential calculations could be reused. GpFlash was more than 440 times faster than all of the other GP libraries considered when evaluating the posterior mean together with its gradient for the case with $10^4$ training points and 10 dimensions. GpFlash is available at https://github.com/marchildon/gpflash.
papers.summary: `GpFlash` is a Gaussian process library built for fast training and posterior evaluation, minimal memory use, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. Benchmarked against `scikit-learn`, `GPy`, `GPflow`, `GPyTorch`, and `SMT` on a MacBook Pro and the Trillium supercomputer, it used less memory and ran faster in every case considered, and with 10,000 training points in 10 dimensions it **needed 9.6 to 35 times less memory and was 2.6 to 54 times faster at evaluating the marginal log likelihood and its gradient**, with a more than 440-fold speedup for the posterior mean and its gradient. The savings come from storing different symmetric matrices in the lower and upper triangles of a single n-by-n matrix, memory-efficient algorithms that lean heavily on BLAS and LAPACK, and factored kernel equations that reuse expensive exponential calculations.

papers.title: Better together? A performance theory of human-machine skill policies under generalization difficulty
papers.abstract: Organizations pairing a human and a machine on a task decide, often by default, which executes each instance and what happens when both do. We account for what this attains under the squared rule, with performance distributed over instances to capture generalization difficulty. A gross stake lies between the skills' mean and best per instance. It splits at the best single skill into a systematic part, known from separate assessments and secured by commitment, and a residual, the expected value of perfect information on which skill each instance favors, known only from paired observation and split further by classes. Skills set the stake; workflows decide the take, via two channels. Routing directs work, weighting or selecting responses; with binary truth it is capped by the best skill per instance. Reading responses as joint evidence is not routing; what they jointly reveal caps it. Synergy lets skills interact before responding; bounded by no skill either way, its lift over independent responses must clear a break-even and can fall below one. As algorithms, arrangements form a ladder stating what each reads, holds and records, and a procedure whose checks keep earlier gains when class means are known and lose little on finite records given a margin. The theory extends to many skills, each worth what it adds where it beats all others held, and to competing skills, where at parity a single failure's allowed cost decides. In a public chest-radiograph study with 227 radiologists, they are near parity with the model and the stake is mostly residual; assisted reading, no better on average originally, returned less than averaging both responses; recalibrating the model alone beats any deployable arrangement of raw responses. Organizations can learn from their records what is at stake, which arrangement collects it and what evidence each step needs; pricing costs and errors is future work.
papers.summary: Organizations that pair a human and a machine on a task must decide which one handles each instance and how to combine them when both respond, and the paper develops a performance theory of these arrangements under squared error with per-instance performance distributions capturing generalization difficulty. The attainable gain over the best single skill splits into a systematic part knowable from separate assessments and a residual equal to the expected value of perfect information about which skill each instance favors, learnable only from paired observation, while workflows collect that value through routing, which is capped by the best skill per instance, or through synergy, whose lift must clear a break-even and can fall below one. In a public chest-radiograph study with 227 radiologists, **the radiologists sit near parity with the model, assisted reading returned less than simply averaging both responses, and recalibrating the model alone beat any deployable arrangement of raw responses**.

papers.title: Efficient Resource-Shiftable RL Post-training with Generative Rewards
papers.abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with generative reward models (GenRM) has become a central recipe for improving large language models (LLMs), and it is also increasingly resource-intensive: policy rollout, GenRM-based reward evaluation, and policy training all compete for GPU resources. However, existing colocated and disaggregated systems rely on static resource allocation for these roles. Such allocation cannot adapt as each role's workload changes during RL and therefore leaves a role's resources underutilized.
  We present PivotRL, an RL post-training system that dynamically shifts resources among different roles according to their runtime demands. PivotRL introduces a resource-shiftable runtime built on a Global Parameter Storage, together with a unified mechanism that efficiently shifts role-specific context. A shift-aware scheduler enables sequence migration upon a shift, while a planner considers the aggregate throughput benefit and the shift overhead to determine when and how to shift. We evaluate PivotRL on a 128-GPU cluster using four model groups spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. PivotRL enables resource shifting within seconds and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.81-2.05 times over colocated deployment and 1.50-1.95 times over disaggregated deployment, while preserving RL convergence.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models with generative reward models (GenRM) splits GPU resources among policy rollout, reward evaluation, and policy training, but existing colocated and disaggregated systems allocate resources statically even though each role's workload shifts during training. `PivotRL` dynamically moves resources among roles using a resource-shiftable runtime built on a Global Parameter Storage, a unified mechanism for transferring role-specific context, a shift-aware scheduler that migrates in-flight sequences, and a planner that weighs aggregate throughput gains against shift overhead. On a 128-GPU cluster across four dense and mixture-of-experts model groups, it shifts resources within seconds and **raises end-to-end throughput 1.81 to 2.05 times over colocated and 1.50 to 1.95 times over disaggregated deployments** while preserving RL convergence.

papers.title: Davinci-Tool: Scaling Agentic Tool-Use Supervision with Verifiable Executable Environments
papers.abstract: Reliable agentic tool use requires training data that pair diverse multi-step workflows with executable evidence that the requested outcomes were achieved. Scaling either trajectory coverage or verification alone is insufficient as new environments introduce distinct states, rules, and dependencies that must also be reflected in the success criteria. To address this challenge, we introduce Davinci-Tool, a 30B tool-use model, and Davinci-ToolData, an execution-grounded dataset designed to scale environment coverage and outcome verification together. Davinci-ToolData preserves restorable states, execution traces, outcomes, and verifiers as a unified substrate for supervision. Two complementary pipelines populate this substrate: Execution-Grounded Task Synthesis (EGTS) derives verified demonstrations from independently authored systems, and Executable Environment Synthesis (EES) synthesizes auditable environments, state-grounded tasks, and executable verifiers across single and coordinated domains. These pipelines yield 30,395 verified trajectories spanning 2,260 invoked tool names. We first train on these demonstrations with supervised fine-tuning, then reuse EES states and verifiers to compare alternative actions and construct outcome-grounded preferences for Direct Preference Optimization. Davinci-Tool improves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct from 52.4 to 88.2 on $\tau^2$-bench, from 30.4 to 62.8 on BFCL v4 multi-turn, and from 16.9 to 56.2 on MCP-Atlas, outperforming Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct on all three benchmarks with only 1/16 of its total parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/MassLab-SII/Davinci-Tool.
papers.summary: Training reliable tool-using agents needs data that pairs diverse multi-step workflows with executable evidence that the requested outcomes were achieved, and scaling trajectory coverage or verification alone fails because each new environment brings its own states, rules, and success criteria. `Davinci-ToolData` stores restorable states, execution traces, outcomes, and verifiers as a single supervision substrate, populated by Execution-Grounded Task Synthesis (EGTS), which derives verified demonstrations from independently authored systems, and Executable Environment Synthesis (EES), which synthesizes auditable environments, state-grounded tasks, and executable verifiers, yielding 30,395 verified trajectories over 2,260 tool names. After supervised fine-tuning on these demonstrations and Direct Preference Optimization on outcome-grounded preferences built from EES states, the resulting 30B `Davinci-Tool` lifts `Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct` from 52.4 to 88.2 on `τ²-bench`, 30.4 to 62.8 on `BFCL v4` multi-turn, and 16.9 to 56.2 on `MCP-Atlas`, **outperforming `Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct` on all three benchmarks with one sixteenth of its parameters**.

papers.title: From Parallel to Sequential: Small-Batch Noise Restores Simplicity Bias of Muon
papers.abstract: Simplicity bias, which can arise from sequential feature learning during training, has been proposed as a general explanation for the success of deep learning. An important driver of this phenomenon is saddle-to-saddle behavior, in which the gradient flow trajectory remains close to a sequence of saddle manifolds while learning one feature at a time. However, Muon, a state-of-the-art optimizer based on spectral descent, does not exhibit such dynamics in the full-batch setting and instead learns features in parallel. How is it then that Muon is so successful in deep learning settings? We show that stochastic gradient noise fundamentally changes this behavior: small-batch noise restores sequential feature learning, providing a mechanism for simplicity bias that is absent from full-batch Muon. We explain this transition through stochastic smoothing of the spectral descent operator underlying Muon. When gradients are small relative to the noise scale, the expected spectral update becomes approximately proportional to the actual gradient, which restores gradient-flow-like dynamics. We formalize this mechanism for deep linear models by deriving the effective continuous dynamics of noisy spectral descent. Experiments on low-rank matrix reconstruction, vision transformers, and large language models (LLMs) support these findings.
papers.summary: Simplicity bias, in which networks learn features sequentially along saddle-to-saddle gradient-flow trajectories, has been proposed as a general explanation for deep learning's success, yet the spectral-descent optimizer `Muon` learns features in parallel under full-batch training, raising the question of why it works so well. The authors show that **small-batch gradient noise restores sequential feature learning in Muon**, explaining the transition through stochastic smoothing of the spectral descent operator: when gradients are small relative to the noise scale, the expected spectral update becomes approximately proportional to the true gradient, recovering gradient-flow-like dynamics. They formalize this by deriving the effective continuous dynamics of noisy spectral descent for deep linear models, and experiments on low-rank matrix reconstruction, vision transformers, and large language models support the mechanism.

papers.title: SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications?
papers.abstract: As coding agents become more capable, tests remain the primary evidence for judging whether their code is correct. Yet passing available tests does not establish that an implementation satisfies its natural language specification. Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the specification and scenarios that thoroughly exercise the code, but current benchmarks provide limited insight into whether agents can construct such evidence themselves. We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories, covering 8 types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. Given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising executable checks and test scenarios. The checks should reject implementations that violate the specification while accepting those that satisfy it, and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise the code. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, none constructs a harness scored as faithful on the benchmark's implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The bottleneck lies less in exploring test scenarios than in constructing checks that faithfully reflect the specification. Specifically, the agents show a clear tendency to write checks that mirror the reference implementation rather than the specification, and therefore reject implementations that the specification permits.
papers.summary: Tests are the main evidence for judging code written by coding agents, but passing available tests does not show that an implementation meets its natural-language specification, and existing benchmarks say little about whether agents can build such validation evidence themselves. `SpecGuardBench` contains 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories covering 8 kinds of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols, and asks an agent, given a specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, to construct a validation harness of executable checks and test scenarios that reject violating implementations, accept conforming ones, and exercise the code thoroughly. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, **none produces a harness scored as faithful on more than 63% of tasks**, and the bottleneck is check construction rather than scenario exploration: agents tend to write checks that mirror the reference implementation instead of the specification, rejecting implementations the specification permits.

papers.title: CLIVO: Differentiable Cluster-Based Instruction Mixing with Learned Validation Objectives
papers.abstract: Target-aware multimodal instruction selection requires useful examples and an appropriate balance of supervision. Sample-level rankings can overrepresent similar content without optimizing this balance; group-level methods face coarse units, predefined set-level validation signals, and costly or inaccurate mixture search. We propose CLIVO, a target-aware framework connecting fine-grained semantic allocation, automatically learned validation objectives, and differentiable mixture search. Specifically, semantic clusters provide independently adjustable shares at the hundred-cluster scale. Correlations between per-example merged-proxy losses and real probe performance identify target-relevant validation examples; learned nonnegative weights combine their losses into an objective. A single backward pass through the merged proxy supplies gradients for all shares, avoiding an additional mixture-response regression model. Selecting 100K instructions from an 8M pool, CLIVO attains 97.2% of the full-data four-target average score with only 1.25% of the data. It improves on the strongest evaluated selection baseline by 1.16 points using random within-cluster sampling; combining learned quotas with sample ranking increases this advantage to 1.55 points. Analyses show that finer units benefit most targets, short-trained experts preserve mixture responses, sample weighting retains useful validation information, and direct search consistently reduces the learned objective. CLIVO also supports interpretable allocation, modular selection, and reuse across targets and granularities.
papers.summary: Selecting multimodal instruction-tuning data for a target task requires both useful examples and the right balance of supervision, but sample-level rankings overrepresent similar content while group-level methods suffer from coarse units, hand-defined validation signals, and costly or inaccurate mixture search. `CLIVO` allocates data shares across hundreds of semantic clusters, identifies target-relevant validation examples by correlating per-example losses on a merged proxy model with real probe performance, learns nonnegative weights that combine those losses into an objective, and obtains gradients for every cluster share from a single backward pass through the proxy rather than a separate mixture-response regression model.
