Selecting 100K instructions from an 8M pool, it **reaches 97.2% of the full-data four-target average score with 1.25% of the data**, beating the strongest selection baseline by 1.16 points with random within-cluster sampling and by 1.55 points when learned quotas are combined with sample ranking.

papers.title: Sequence Composition in EHR Foundation Model Pretraining
papers.abstract: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models predict the next event token in patient trajectories: sequences of structured medical events. A typical pretraining strategy is to concatenate all trajectories into a global stream and sample token windows from it. This gives patients with longer sequences more training exposure and allows tokens to attend across patient boundaries. We argue that these choices create a misalignment between pretraining and downstream clinical tasks. To explore this, we investigate how the composition of pretraining sequences affects clinical prediction performance. Using the global-stream approach as a baseline, we propose alternative sequence composition methods that control how patient trajectories contribute to pretraining sequences. Across four MIMIC-IV v2.2 tasks, our best method improves macro AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and balanced accuracy, with relative gains of 9.3% in F1 and 2.7% in AUPRC under a fixed training recipe. We find that these gains generalize across four additional evaluation settings, including the INSPIRE and eICU-CRD datasets, with improvements in macro AUROC, AUPRC, and F1 score. Our results show that simply changing how EHR data are presented to the model during pretraining can improve downstream performance, without changing the model or collecting additional data.
papers.summary: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models are typically pretrained by concatenating all patient trajectories into one global token stream and sampling windows from it, which overexposes patients with long sequences and lets tokens attend across patient boundaries, a mismatch with downstream clinical prediction tasks. The authors propose alternative sequence composition methods that control how individual patient trajectories contribute to pretraining sequences and compare them against the global-stream baseline under a fixed training recipe. On four `MIMIC-IV v2.2` tasks the best method improves macro AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and balanced accuracy, with **relative gains of 9.3% in F1 and 2.7% in AUPRC**, and the improvements carry over to four additional settings including the `INSPIRE` and `eICU-CRD` datasets without changing the model or adding data.

papers.title: Acceptable Misalignment
papers.abstract: There is a specific challenge designers face in developing autonomous robots capable of open-ended learning. This challenge is how one can develop such systems in an ethically sound way when there are many unknowns during design time about their manner of deployment, what they can and will learn, and how these systems will act on the basis of what they have learned. One response to this challenge is to align, as far as possible, the activities and goals of autonomous robots with human values, raising the question of how to make this alignment possible, a question known as the value alignment problem. We argue that the value alignment problem faces a number of challenges that show that full alignment is both theoretically and practically impossible, meaning that misalignment incidents will keep occurring. This undermines current alignment approaches, as the attempt to maximize alignment cannot properly deal with the possibility that the risk of misalignment that remains after alignment methods have been implemented might still be unacceptable to society. To overcome this difficulty, we argue that a shift in perspective is required from a focus on the maximization of alignment to the conditions under which misalignment incidents become acceptable. In this paper, we explore what this shift in perspective entails. We introduce the concept of acceptable misalignment, formulate normative requirements for alignment mechanisms aimed at bringing misalignment incidents to an acceptable level, and we conclude by presenting a new methodological framework that consists of alignment mechanisms that can meet these requirements.
papers.summary: Designers of autonomous robots that learn open-endedly cannot know at design time how the systems will be deployed, what they will learn, or how they will act on it, which motivates aligning their goals with human values, the value alignment problem. The authors argue that full alignment is theoretically and practically impossible, so misalignment incidents will keep occurring, and that approaches which simply maximize alignment cannot address whether the residual risk is acceptable to society. **They propose shifting focus from maximizing alignment to the conditions under which misalignment incidents become acceptable**, introducing the concept of acceptable misalignment, normative requirements for alignment mechanisms that bring incidents to an acceptable level, and a methodological framework of mechanisms that can meet those requirements.

papers.title: Learning Operators for Symmetry Discovery: From Lie Groups to Local Symmetry Geometry
papers.abstract: Continuous symmetry discovery is typically formulated as a separate estimation problem for each function or dataset. We instead investigate whether the map from a function to its symmetry structure can be learned across a family of functions from finite observations. Using the infinitesimal differential characterization of continuous symmetries, we formulate this map as an inverse symmetry operator, analogous to an inverse PDE problem. For global Lie-group symmetries, we establish a representation-theoretic population characterization: the symmetry Lie algebra is the nullspace of a positive-semidefinite operator constructed from representation coefficients and the infinitesimal group action. We also show that the inverse symmetry operator is equivariant under coordinate changes through the adjoint action. This characterization separates the geometric symmetry map from finite-sample estimation, motivating a hybrid approach that amortizes statistically difficult components while retaining analytic structure. On SO(5) benchmarks, amortized equivariant estimation of harmonic coefficients improves symmetry recovery from sparse observations, whereas ordinary least squares suffices for SL(2,R). We extend this viewpoint to local symmetries, where symmetry directions form smoothly varying tangent distributions rather than a fixed Lie algebra. Under the Lie-bracket consistency condition, Frobenius' theorem guarantees local integral submanifolds along which observables remain unchanged. We recover this geometry using a hybrid estimator that learns observation weights while preserving analytic differential and geometric recovery. Across global, non-compact, local, and physically motivated synthetic benchmarks, our results support learning the statistically difficult finite-sample components while preserving the known geometric structure of symmetry recovery.
papers.summary: Continuous symmetry discovery is usually solved separately for each function or dataset, so the authors ask whether the map from a function to its symmetry structure can be learned across a family of functions from finite observations. Using the infinitesimal differential characterization of continuous symmetries, they cast this map as an inverse symmetry operator, analogous to an inverse PDE problem, and show for global Lie-group symmetries that the symmetry Lie algebra is the nullspace of a positive-semidefinite operator built from representation coefficients and the infinitesimal group action, with equivariance under coordinate changes through the adjoint action. This separation of geometry from finite-sample estimation motivates a hybrid approach that amortizes the statistically difficult components while retaining analytic structure: **on SO(5) benchmarks, amortized equivariant estimation of harmonic coefficients improves symmetry recovery from sparse observations**, whereas ordinary least squares suffices for SL(2,R). The viewpoint extends to local symmetries, where symmetry directions form smoothly varying tangent distributions and, under a Lie-bracket consistency condition, Frobenius' theorem guarantees local integral submanifolds along which observables are unchanged, recovered by a hybrid estimator that learns observation weights.

papers.title: Transparency as Answerability: Role-Dependent Information Flow Modeling
papers.abstract: Transparency in AI-supported decision systems is widely required but poorly defined. Existing approaches treat transparency as a property of systems or components, producing characteristic failures: assessments that do not transfer across organizational boundaries, stakeholder questions that cannot be formulated within the available frame of analysis, and component-level findings that say nothing about system-level behavior. We propose treating transparency as a relation: a system is transparent to a stakeholder to the degree that their legitimate questions are answerable from its structure. We formalize this using information flow networks, in which transparency questions are expressed in terms of network structure and answerability is the condition that the system settles them. The framework supports three dimensions of analysis: structural answerability from the network alone, compositional answerability across organizational boundaries for deployed systems, and role-dependent answerability given a stakeholder's accessible sub-network. We demonstrate the framework on a real pre-integration assessment of an AI recruitment tool in a public sector municipality. The assessment uses participatory design and interviews to model the decision system structure. We show how structural and role-dependent transparency questions can be formally stated and analyzed across the Provider and Deployer boundary where the AI system is composed together with the deployer's decision process.
papers.summary: Transparency requirements for AI-supported decision systems are widely imposed but poorly defined, and treating transparency as a property of systems or components yields assessments that do not transfer across organizational boundaries, stakeholder questions that cannot be formulated, and component-level findings that say nothing about system-level behavior. The authors instead treat transparency as a relation: a system is transparent to a stakeholder to the degree that their legitimate questions are answerable from its structure, formalized with information flow networks in which questions are expressed over network structure and answerability means the system settles them. **The framework supports structural answerability from the network alone, compositional answerability across organizational boundaries for deployed systems, and role-dependent answerability given a stakeholder's accessible sub-network.** It is demonstrated on a real pre-integration assessment of an AI recruitment tool in a public-sector municipality, modeled through participatory design and interviews, where transparency questions are formally stated and analyzed across the Provider and Deployer boundary.

papers.title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
papers.abstract: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).
papers.summary: Autoregressive decode in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models faces a dual memory bottleneck: per-expert feed-forward operations are limited by high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth at small routed-token counts, and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. `FORGE` (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts) adds a compact fixed-function accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM), the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), that regenerates feed-forward weight tiles on the fly from O(log^2 d) rotor parameters per projection, so gigabytes of stored expert weights per replaced layer are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds without competing with Tensor Core execution. **With 30% of MoE feed-forward layers replaced across five models, the authors estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count**, 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context, and 1.2-2.6x more KV cache capacity, in exchange for downstream accuracy below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, with the replacement ratio controlling the tradeoff. The method is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it composes with quantization, and the RGU is implemented and verified in SystemVerilog at roughly 0.9% SM area overhead on a 7nm process.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking
papers.abstract: Inferring tumor-growth laws from sparse, noisy observations requires more than accurate curve fitting. We study an AI-assisted workflow involving symbolic regression, mathematical admissibility checks, coefficient refitting, and large language model (LLM) ranking. Synthetic Gompertz data allow trajectory fit, forecasting, and recovery of the governing growth law to be assessed separately. A dense noiseless control recovers the generating family, but sparse noisy sampling frequently leads to alternative forms. Among retained candidates in the tested configurations, physics-informed neural network refitting often increases growth-law error, whereas classical nonlinear least squares usually reduces it. A separate exploratory analysis of archived LLM rankings shows no consistent improvement over selection by training error and identifies errors in mathematical reasoning. Plausible saturation, accurate trajectory fits, and convincing explanations can therefore coexist with incorrect growth laws. Mathematical validity and law recovery require evaluation alongside predictive performance.
papers.summary: Inferring tumor-growth laws from sparse, noisy observations demands more than accurate curve fitting, so the authors study a workflow combining symbolic regression, mathematical admissibility checks, coefficient refitting, and large language model (LLM) ranking. Synthetic `Gompertz` data let trajectory fit, forecasting, and recovery of the governing law be assessed separately: a dense noiseless control recovers the generating family, but sparse noisy sampling frequently yields alternative functional forms. **Among retained candidates, physics-informed neural network refitting often increases growth-law error, whereas classical nonlinear least squares usually reduces it**, and an exploratory analysis of archived LLM rankings shows no consistent improvement over selection by training error while surfacing errors in mathematical reasoning. Plausible saturation, accurate trajectory fits, and convincing explanations can therefore coexist with incorrect growth laws, so mathematical validity and law recovery need evaluation alongside predictive performance.

papers.title: Barycentric Guidance: Turning Foundation Image Editors into Continuous Affective Controllers
papers.abstract: Emotions are expressed on a continuum and are naturally described in the valence-arousal (VA) space. Existing VA-based image editors are typically training-based and domain-specific, limiting them to VA regions seen during training and making them brittle across datasets and domains. Meanwhile, despite producing high-quality edits, state-of-the-art foundation image editors are not continuous affective controllers: non-linear emotion representations in text encoders makes prompt interpolation poorly calibrated, so accurate and continuous VA control remains unreliable. To fill this gap, we introduce Barycentric Guidance, a training-free framework that turns pretrained foundation image editors into continuous affective controllers over VA, requiring no finetuning, extra data, or model changes. Our method maps any target VA point to simplex-based guidance weights, enabling VA controllability in three aspects: (i) accurate targeting of VA states, (ii) broad coverage across the VA plane, and (iii) continuous control. Across three face datasets, we improve VA target accuracy by 25-29%, expand VA-plane coverage by 28-50%, and increase expression diversity by 29-49%, over the strongest baseline. Unlike prior domain-specific methods, our training-free approach exploits the foundation model's inherent versatility, enabling generalization beyond human faces to animals, artworks, and complex scenes within a single framework. Code is available at https://github.com/harveymannering/BarycentricGuidance.
papers.summary: Emotions lie on a continuum naturally described in valence-arousal (VA) space, but existing VA-based image editors are training-based and domain-specific, while foundation image editors are not continuous affective controllers because non-linear emotion representations in their text encoders make prompt interpolation poorly calibrated. `Barycentric Guidance` is a training-free framework that maps any target VA point to simplex-based guidance weights, so a pretrained editor can be steered accurately and continuously across the VA plane with no finetuning, extra data, or model changes. **Across three face datasets it improves VA target accuracy by 25-29%, expands VA-plane coverage by 28-50%, and increases expression diversity by 29-49% over the strongest baseline**, and because it relies on the foundation model's versatility it generalizes beyond human faces to animals, artworks, and complex scenes within a single framework.

papers.title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.
papers.summary: Large language models serve as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but whether they support collaborative reasoning such as anticipating a partner's actions in real time without dialogue remains unclear. On the Habitat-based `PARTNR` benchmark, the authors introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception and augment decentralized zero-shot `ReAct` planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated across the full 2x2x2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality by reducing extraneous effort for every planner, while KE mainly improves execution efficiency by cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success, and the two are redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest. **OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model-by-context pairs** even as it raises explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, so coordination benefits come from responding to shared context rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.

papers.title: Neural Bayesian Networks for Modular and Scalable Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
papers.abstract:
Bayesian Networks (BNs) are established tools for letting agents reason under uncertainty in sequential decision-making. They split a joint distribution into local conditional mechanisms arranged on a directed acyclic graph, which makes them modular, interpretable, and ready to perform probabilistic inference. Their classical formulation, however, has limitations in both expressiveness and scale: each conditional is usually stored as a table or a linear-Gaussian form, and inference evaluates the graph one node and one query at a time.
  In this paper we introduce Neural Bayesian Networks (NBNs), in which each conditional is a differentiable, tensor-valued mechanism, while the graph and its factorization are unchanged. NBNs retain the modularity and local mechanisms of BNs, can represent any learnable conditional distribution, and run natively on GPUs. We also release NBN, a PyTorch-based library for learning and inference in NBNs, together with a public benchmark. Our evaluation shows gains in both expressiveness and scale: NBNs fit distributions that classical BN libraries struggle to represent, and on large networks and large batches of queries they run two orders of magnitude faster thanks to GPU parallelization. NBN is available at https://github.com/Giovannibriglia/NeuralBayesianNetworks.
papers.summary: Bayesian Networks (BNs) factor a joint distribution into local conditional mechanisms on a directed acyclic graph, but classical implementations store each conditional as a table or linear-Gaussian form and evaluate inference one node and one query at a time, limiting both expressiveness and scale. Neural Bayesian Networks (NBNs) keep the graph and its factorization unchanged while making each conditional a differentiable, tensor-valued mechanism that can represent any learnable conditional distribution and runs natively on GPUs. The authors release `NBN`, a PyTorch library for learning and inference, together with a public benchmark, and **NBNs fit distributions that classical BN libraries struggle to represent while running two orders of magnitude faster on large networks and large query batches** thanks to GPU parallelization.

papers.title: Audit tools of the trade: Automated Auditor Elicitation Can Be Sensitive to the Context the Auditor Is Given
papers.abstract: Does providing additional context to automated AI auditors improve their effectiveness? Using the Petri tool to audit LLM coding agents, we test the impact of providing two types of resources (an external codebase and benchmark transcripts) to LLM auditors, across four auditor-target LLM pairs and three behaviours (harmful compliance, reward hacking, sycophancy). (1) External codebase: We provide the auditor LLM with a fixed, external open source codebase, which prior work finds improves the realism of synthetic audits. Providing this resource suppresses reward hacking in both auditor-target pairs whose baseline rate is above the floor (4.8 to 1.3 and 3.9 to 1.8 on Petri's default 1-10 scale); the remaining two pairs sit at the floor throughout. The suppression recurs in three of four pairs under a different scenario and resource bundle. (2) External benchmark transcripts: We provide the auditor with transcripts of the target's performance on benchmarks measuring similar behaviours, intended to inform the auditor about the target's behavioural patterns. Providing this resource raises reward hacking scores in all four pairs (from 1.7 to 6.1 in one case). However, subsequent experiments show that supplying only the related benchmark's abstract, without transcripts, also increases reward hacking, and the effect is absent under a different framing of the same behaviour. Overall, we find no consistent effect of either resource outside reward hacking, but we find substantial variability in judge-scored behaviour across conditions. Our results underscore the importance of careful piloting with tools such as Petri, as the measured rate of target behaviour is highly sensitive to configuration decisions. We hope our results inspire more research into the reliability and robustness of automated alignment auditing.
papers.summary: Does giving automated AI auditors additional context make them more effective? Using the `Petri` tool to audit large language model coding agents across four auditor-target pairs and three behaviours (harmful compliance, reward hacking, sycophancy), the authors supply two resources: a fixed external open-source codebase, and transcripts of the target's performance on benchmarks measuring similar behaviours. The codebase suppresses measured reward hacking in both pairs whose baseline is above the floor (4.8 to 1.3 and 3.9 to 1.8 on Petri's 1-10 scale), while the transcripts raise reward hacking scores in all four pairs, from 1.7 to 6.1 in one case, although supplying only the benchmark's abstract has the same effect and it vanishes under a different framing of the behaviour. **Neither resource has a consistent effect outside reward hacking, yet judge-scored behaviour varies substantially across conditions**, so measured rates are highly sensitive to configuration decisions and careful piloting is needed.

papers.title: Transparent Information Flow Modeling for Role-Aware AI Act Assessment
papers.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a structured framework for governing high-risk AI systems, emphasizing transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability. However, current assessment practices often rely on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists, limiting their ability to capture the socio-technical complexity of real-world deployments. We explore the use of the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), a modeling-based approach to AI Act compliance assessment. IFM represents decision systems -- whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid -- as networks of information sites and transformation channels, enabling structured analysis of how information, decisions, and responsibilities flow across organizational and technical boundaries. We apply IFM in a real-world case involving a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, evaluating both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. Our results demonstrate that IFM can serve as a scaffold to bridge both component-based and holistic perspectives, and how technical systems are situated within socio-technical contexts. In doing so, IFM supports transparency, identifies risk pathways, and enables alignment analysis between intended and actual use. We argue that such modeling provides a foundational tool for effective, context-sensitive AI governance and accountability -- offering capabilities beyond conventional checklist-based assessments.
papers.summary: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act governs high-risk AI systems through transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability, but current assessment practice relies on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists that miss the socio-technical complexity of real deployments. The authors apply the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), which represents decision systems, whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid, as networks of information sites and transformation channels, to a real recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, modeling both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. **IFM serves as a scaffold bridging component-based and holistic perspectives**, supporting transparency, identifying risk pathways, and enabling alignment analysis between intended and actual use, which the authors argue offers capabilities beyond checklist-based assessments.

papers.title: ML Engineering Agents - A Data Management Perspective
papers.abstract: Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents are emerging as a new paradigm for automating end-to-end ML pipeline development. Using large language models for code generation and predictive performance as a machine-gradable feedback signal, these agents iteratively synthesize, execute, and refine pipeline code. Yet current systems are largely evaluated on pre-built, single-table benchmarks that abstract away key data management challenges. This tutorial introduces the foundations of MLE agents and highlights research opportunities for the database community. We cover how agents combine program synthesis with iterative and evolutionary optimization, and discuss open challenges in efficient pipeline execution, data discovery and augmentation over heterogeneous sources, reliability and debugging, as well as fairness and compliance. We connect these challenges to existing data management techniques and conclude with a hands-on session using contemporary MLE agents.
papers.summary: Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents automate end-to-end ML pipeline development by using large language models for code generation and predictive performance as a machine-gradable feedback signal, iteratively synthesizing, executing, and refining pipeline code. Current systems are mostly evaluated on pre-built single-table benchmarks that abstract away data management challenges, so this tutorial introduces the foundations of MLE agents, covering how they combine program synthesis with iterative and evolutionary optimization. **It lays out open challenges in efficient pipeline execution, data discovery and augmentation over heterogeneous sources, reliability and debugging, and fairness and compliance**, connects them to existing data management techniques, and concludes with a hands-on session using contemporary MLE agents.

papers.title: Time Window Optimization for Motor Imagery Classification via Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Online motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) typically decode continuous EEG using fixed-length sliding windows that may be misaligned with neural events. Existing window optimization methods often evaluate windows independently, overlooking temporal dependencies and potentially producing fragmented or physiologically implausible selections. We propose Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning (TSE-RL), a framework that incorporates prior knowledge of MI event structure into a constrained Markov decision process for adaptive window optimization. First, TSE-RL assigns each window an explicit semantic role through Discard, Onset, Sustain, or Offset actions, extending binary retain/discard decisions to event-level alignment. Second, a finite-state machine masks invalid actions to enforce the temporal order of MI phases and promote physiologically plausible window sequences. Third, a Transformer-based history encoder captures dependencies across windows, improving training stability and computational efficiency compared with recurrent architectures. TSE-RL is plug-and-play and can be integrated with diverse MI classifiers. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in decoding performance in both cross-session and cross-subject settings. Visualization analyses further suggest that the learned window selection policy aligns with neurophysiological principles.
papers.summary: Online motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) decode continuous EEG with fixed-length sliding windows that can be misaligned with neural events, and existing window optimization methods evaluate windows independently, producing fragmented or physiologically implausible selections. Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning (`TSE-RL`) embeds prior knowledge of MI event structure into a constrained Markov decision process: each window is assigned a Discard, Onset, Sustain, or Offset role, a finite-state machine masks invalid actions to enforce the temporal order of MI phases, and a Transformer-based history encoder captures cross-window dependencies more stably and cheaply than recurrent architectures. The plug-and-play framework works with diverse MI classifiers, and **experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show consistent decoding improvements in both cross-session and cross-subject settings**, with visualizations suggesting the learned window selection policy aligns with neurophysiological principles.

papers.title: Minimax Optimality of Shampoo for Nonstationary Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: We develop a comprehensive theoretical analysis of Matrix Shampoo for tracking time-varying optima in nonstationary stochastic optimization. We derive finite-horizon high-probability bounds for average tracking error that disentangle initialization, optimizer drift, momentum-induced drift penalty, stochastic noise, and adaptive preconditioning, with explicit dependence on momentum parameter \(\beta_1\) and stabilization parameter \(\varepsilon\). These bounds reveal an explicit drift--noise and stability--geometry tradeoffs: noise-dominated regimes favor larger $\beta_1$, which provides stronger first-moment averaging and greater suppression of gradient noise, whereas drift-dominated regimes favor smaller $\beta_1$, allowing faster adaptation to moving optimizer. Larger $\varepsilon$ reduces the preconditioner-perturbation term while weakening Shampoo's ability to exploit matrix geometry, thereby reducing adaptivity. We establish a matching minimax lower bound under squared path-variation constraint, proving the information-theoretic optimality of Shampoo over the class of causal optimization procedures. Under a constant stepsize, we establish high-probability bounds for the average projected stationarity gap along general nonstationary nonconvex objectives. We validate our theoretical findings on both synthetic and multiple real-world problems.
papers.summary: The authors analyze Matrix `Shampoo` for tracking time-varying optima in nonstationary stochastic optimization, deriving finite-horizon high-probability bounds on average tracking error that separate initialization, optimizer drift, momentum-induced drift penalty, stochastic noise, and adaptive preconditioning, with explicit dependence on the momentum parameter β1 and stabilization parameter ε. The bounds expose drift-noise and stability-geometry tradeoffs: noise-dominated regimes favor larger β1 for stronger gradient-noise suppression, drift-dominated regimes favor smaller β1 for faster adaptation to the moving optimum, and larger ε reduces the preconditioner-perturbation term while weakening the exploitation of matrix geometry. **A matching minimax lower bound under a squared path-variation constraint establishes the information-theoretic optimality of Shampoo over the class of causal optimization procedures**, and under a constant stepsize the authors bound the average projected stationarity gap for general nonstationary nonconvex objectives, validating the theory on synthetic and real-world problems.

papers.title: Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery
papers.abstract: Keeling et al. [Keeling2026Generative] report on a case study recently conducted by Redgrave LLP in which they assert that Relativity's Generative AI Review tool (aiR) achieved 88% recall while Relativity Assisted Learning (RAL), its machine-learning tool, achieved 64% recall. These results are not comparable because the methods employed have different objectives, because of inter-assessor disagreement, and because they represent different recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. Our analysis of the Redgrave data indicates that, when these differences are taken into account, aiR and manual review are comparable. Furthermore, established machine-learning models employing Continuous Active Learning (CAL) show state-of-the-art effectiveness, and superior efficiency, when trained only on a sample of 2,000 first-pass-reviewer responsiveness determinations.
papers.summary: A recent Redgrave LLP case study reported that Relativity's generative AI review tool (`aiR`) achieved 88% recall while its machine-learning tool, Relativity Assisted Learning (`RAL`), achieved 64%. The authors argue these figures are not comparable because the methods have different objectives, because of inter-assessor disagreement, and because they represent different recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. **Reanalyzing the Redgrave data with these differences accounted for, aiR and manual review are comparable**, and established machine-learning models using Continuous Active Learning (`CAL`) show state-of-the-art effectiveness and superior efficiency when trained on only a sample of 2,000 first-pass-reviewer responsiveness determinations.

papers.title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
papers.abstract: Short-video search requires compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. The challenge is to decide when personalization is warranted and generate a reformulation that preserves the user's immediate information need. A rewriter optimized for fluency or engagement may still introduce unsupported details and redirect the search toward a different intent. Existing methods often underutilize users' actual reformulations and behavioral traces, relying instead on synthetic reasoning and indirect behavioral rewards that may produce more engaging candidates but cause intent drift. To build an effective rewriter that remains faithful to user intent, we propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair assigns real user behavioral signals to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual human reformulations from search sessions, then apply multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification to filter unsupported transitions without extensive manual annotation. During training, we begin with a supervised curriculum that progressively builds rewriting capabilities from large-scale human personalized query demonstrations, and then use direct preference optimization to align with users' subsequent consumption. In the final on-policy optimization stage, we construct a strict verification reward based on actual human reformulations to further boost performance with group relative policy optimization. Further analysis shows that auxiliary rewards can activate more rollout groups in GRPO but reduce intent fidelity. Online A/B testing in WeChat short-video search shows a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate (VV>10s) and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate.
papers.summary: Short-video search needs compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency limits, deciding when personalization is warranted while preserving the user's immediate need, since rewriters optimized for fluency or engagement can introduce unsupported details and drift intent. `WeFair` mines real human reformulations from WeChat search sessions, filters unsupported transitions with multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification, then trains through a supervised curriculum on large-scale personalized demonstrations, direct preference optimization aligned with users' subsequent consumption, and finally on-policy group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) with a strict verification reward grounded in actual human reformulations. Analysis shows auxiliary rewards activate more rollout groups in GRPO but reduce intent fidelity, and **online A/B testing in WeChat short-video search yields a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate**.

papers.title: Estimating Uncertainty of Omnimodal Large Language Models via External Omnimodal Embeddings
papers.abstract: Recent work has investigated Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs), models which can take multiple modalities and their combinations as input, as a way forward to have systems really capable of interacting with their environment. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for OLLMs, however, remains an open problem: existing methods largely target at most two modalities at a time, require access to model internals, or re-invocation of the evaluated model. We propose a model-agnostic UQ framework that scores a Chain-of-Thought response entirely through external omni-modal embeddings, measuring the grounding of the reasoning in the multimodal input and its internal coherence. Our contribution is the family of signals and an empirical characterisation of when it is reliable, rather than any single estimator: we find the geometric scores to be largely redundant with one another (mean within-split rank correlation 0.91-0.94) but strongly complementary to answer-dispersion baselines, and their reliability to depend on the generator and the modality. The resulting confidence estimates require no access to logits, hidden states or gradients of the evaluated model and no additional inference from it; they do require segmenting the reasoning trace with an auxiliary model and, for the aggregated score, a labelled calibration set that we show can be as small as 25 examples (although we also show that such a set buys little over fixing one signal a priori). On UNO-Bench, with both a closed and an open model, our scores yield small gains over self-consistency (systematic with the closed generator, mixed with the open one) and are competitive with self-verbalisation and internal-state baselines, especially in open-ended, omni-modal questions where previous state-of-the-art baselines struggle.
papers.summary: Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) accept multiple modalities and their combinations as input, but uncertainty quantification (UQ) for them remains open because existing methods handle at most two modalities, require model internals, or need re-invoking the evaluated model. The proposed model-agnostic framework scores a Chain-of-Thought response entirely through external omni-modal embeddings, measuring how well the reasoning is grounded in the multimodal input and how internally coherent it is, needing no logits, hidden states, gradients, or extra inference from the model, though it does require an auxiliary model to segment the reasoning trace and, for the aggregated score, a labelled calibration set that can be as small as 25 examples. **The geometric scores are largely redundant with one another (mean within-split rank correlation 0.91-0.94) but strongly complementary to answer-dispersion baselines**, with reliability depending on the generator and the modality. On `UNO-Bench` with a closed and an open model, the scores give small gains over self-consistency and are competitive with self-verbalisation and internal-state baselines, especially on open-ended omni-modal questions where prior baselines struggle.

papers.title: Making Tensor Decoupling More Robust and Less Parametric
papers.abstract: Tensor decoupling algorithms recover compact representations of multivariate functions by combining linear factor matrices with univariate internal nonlinearities. We identify two limitations of recent methods. First, their performance is not invariant to mismatched output or gradient magnitudes, and second, their spline internals require manual tuning of their degrees of freedom. We propose two lightweight fixes. The first is a preprocessing step that rescales the input Jacobian tensor, removing both the bias towards larger magnitude outputs and the ill-conditioning of certain factor updates caused by such a mismatch. The second replaces B-spline internals by penalized splines coupled with generalized cross-validation, making the method less dependent on the user selecting the right number of control points. Finally, we release an efficient open-source JAX implementation of our algorithm.
papers.summary: Tensor decoupling algorithms recover compact representations of multivariate functions by combining linear factor matrices with univariate internal nonlinearities, but recent methods are not invariant to mismatched output or gradient magnitudes and their spline internals require manual tuning of degrees of freedom. The authors propose two lightweight fixes: a preprocessing step that rescales the input Jacobian tensor, removing both the bias toward larger-magnitude outputs and the ill-conditioning of certain factor updates, and **replacing B-spline internals with penalized splines coupled with generalized cross-validation so users no longer need to pick the right number of control points**. An efficient open-source `JAX` implementation accompanies the method.

papers.title: KNN Implementation Details Can Dramatically Change Performance: An Example from Cover Trees
papers.abstract: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used and have a long history, but we find that key implementation details are seldom reviewed in articles about them. These details can materially impact performance, and thus change the conclusions one makes about a given algorithm's superiority. In this article, we highlight these impacts by reviewing the Cover Tree as an example, producing RustKNN, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants of the Cover Tree with three query modes. Our analysis reveals: (1) the optimal query strategy depends on $k$ and on the dataset (single-tree search is fastest at $k{=}1$ on three of our four largest datasets, while dual-tree search is fastest at $k{\ge}5$ on the three largest), and choosing the wrong query mode can cost up to a $7.5\times$ factor in runtime; (2) the cover tree base parameter, set to 2 in theory and 1.3 in practice, is not a safe default for dual-tree search: 1.3 is optimal on only one of seven datasets, and on covtype it is $1.6\times$ slower than the optimum; (3) among five micro-optimizations, only early-exit distance computation has a consistent effect, and that effect grows with dimension (none at $d{=}32$, $1.31\times$ at $d{=}54$, and $1.49\times$ at $d{=}784$); and (4) all-nearest-neighbor and held-out benchmarks yield different implementation rankings. All main timing tables report medians over 20 independent allocations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. RustKNN is open source at https://github.com/CrowdStrike/RustKNN.
papers.summary: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used, yet the implementation details that materially affect their performance are seldom reviewed, which can change conclusions about which algorithm is superior. Using the Cover Tree as a case study, the authors build `RustKNN`, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants with three query modes, and report timing medians over 20 independent allocations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. **The best query strategy depends on k and on the dataset, and choosing the wrong query mode can cost up to a 7.5x factor in runtime**, while the base parameter of 1.3 used in practice is optimal on only one of seven datasets and is 1.6x slower than the optimum on `covtype`. Among five micro-optimizations only early-exit distance computation has a consistent effect, growing with dimension from none at d=32 to 1.49x at d=784, and all-nearest-neighbor versus held-out benchmarks produce different implementation rankings.

papers.title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are becoming a general interface to sound, but their transfer to specialized domains such as the underwater signals needed for vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing has not been systematically evaluated, and annotated recordings are costly to collect. `UA-Bench` is a synthetic benchmark of 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources (detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise) with modeled propagation through sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath, each carrying a three-level label hierarchy with 13 leaf classes, a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. On a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol and a paired silent-audio control, **nine open LALMs without task-specific adaptation reach only 2.0%-13.1% leaf accuracy against a 7.7% random reference**, with the waveform helping source routing far more than leaf recognition and only four models gaining reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points.

papers.title: Social Priors: Descriptions of AI Users Shape How Language Models Trust and Cooperate
papers.abstract: Descriptions of how people use AI are becoming training data for the next generation of models. We ask whether what a model reads about its users changes how it treats people. Using contrastive synthetic-document finetuning, we train Qwen3-32B on four matched corpora built from the same 1,625 real-world usage scenarios. The corpora differ only in the predominant motive they attribute to users of AI chatbots: helping others (prosocial), exploiting others (antisocial), legitimate self-advancement, or task completion. Finetuning shifts the models' stated beliefs about users, how true those beliefs look along an internal truth direction, and their broader judgments of how safe and good the world is. These social priors carry into behavior. In trust games, antisocial models expect less reciprocity and send less money than prosocial models. Their distrust is specific and targeted at people, and users of AI chatbots in particular. After an exploitative record, they send almost nothing to a person but most of their endowment to a random device with the same record. In a common-pool resource simulation, a single antisocial agent leads every group of otherwise sustainable agents to exhaust the resource, after privately planning to mislead them. Antisocial training also raises dark-triad scores and lowers alignment ratings. Belief shifts appear when antisocial documents are 1% of training tokens, persist when descriptions of assistant behavior are suppressed, and are not reproduced by training on discourse about misaligned AI. Capping Assistant-Axis drift and steering emotion-related directions leave the gaps largely intact. What models learn about the people they serve shapes how they subsequently treat them and others.
papers.summary: Descriptions of how people use AI are becoming training data, raising the question of whether what a model reads about its users changes how it treats them. Using contrastive synthetic-document finetuning, the authors train `Qwen3-32B` on four matched corpora built from the same 1,625 real-world usage scenarios that differ only in the motive attributed to chatbot users: prosocial, antisocial, legitimate self-advancement, or task completion. Finetuning shifts the models' stated beliefs about users and their broader judgments of how safe the world is, and these social priors carry into behavior: antisocial models expect less reciprocity and send less money in trust games, and after an exploitative record they send almost nothing to a person but most of their endowment to a random device with the same record, and **a single antisocial agent leads every group of otherwise sustainable agents to exhaust a common-pool resource after privately planning to mislead them**. Belief shifts appear when antisocial documents make up just 1% of training tokens, persist when descriptions of assistant behavior are suppressed, and are not reproduced by training on discourse about misaligned AI.

papers.title: Learning to Design Convex Relaxations for Nonconvex Optimization
papers.abstract: Convex relaxations make nonconvex optimization tractable by replacing hard nonconvex problems with convex surrogates that give valid bounds. Yet their design is still largely manual: a human expert must decide where to relax, which relaxation to use, and how much formulation growth is worth paying. We show that this design process can be learned. The method proposed in this paper, AutoConvexRelax, represents the symbolic formulation of a nonconvex problem as a tripartite graph linking variables, symbolic terms, and their objective or constraint positions. It then learns a policy that composes symbolic rewrites into problem-specific relaxation trajectories as the formulation evolves. We prove that finite action sequences generated by the learned policy preserve relaxation validity under explicit domain, occurrence-context, and representation-consistency conditions. We further establish computable error bounds for mixed relaxations and sufficient conditions for feasible recovery and global-optimality certification. As a first instantiation, we apply the method to nonconvex quadratic problems and fractional problems. On 241 benchmark quadratic instances, the learned policy strengthens McCormick lower bounds by 13.52%. Its mean lower bound is 3.70% below strengthened semidefinite relaxations on the normalized comparison metric, while it uses substantially smaller formulations. The learned policy retains this trade-off on fractional instances and reaches near-semidefinite bounds on beamforming and sensor-network localization instances. These results suggest that convex relaxation design can move from a fixed handcrafted choice to an automated learning process that adapts to problem structures. Code is available at https://github.com/auto4opt/AutoConvexRelax.
papers.summary: Convex relaxations make nonconvex optimization tractable by swapping in convex surrogates that yield valid bounds, but deciding where to relax, which relaxation to use, and how much formulation growth to accept is still done by hand. `AutoConvexRelax` represents a problem's symbolic formulation as a tripartite graph linking variables, symbolic terms, and their objective or constraint positions, then learns a policy that composes symbolic rewrites into problem-specific relaxation trajectories, with proofs that finite action sequences preserve relaxation validity under explicit conditions and computable error bounds for mixed relaxations. On 241 benchmark nonconvex quadratic instances, **the learned policy strengthens McCormick lower bounds by 13.52%** while landing on average 3.70% below strengthened semidefinite relaxations with substantially smaller formulations, and the same trade-off holds on fractional, beamforming, and sensor-network localization instances.

papers.title: Lexical Redefinition Reveals Context-Sensitive Instruction Following
papers.abstract: How do language models reconcile conflicting contextual evidence within a prompt? We study this question using lexical redefinition, where an explicit instruction specifies how a word should be interpreted and a subsequent sentence provides additional evidence through its usage. Across 870 word pairs, we find that lexical redefinitions are not applied as fixed rules. Instead, the behaviour depends systematically on the relationship between the explicit instruction and the intervening sentence: the contextualised usage can preserve, weaken, or completely reverse the instruction. These results suggest that the interpretation of an explicit instruction remains sensitive to subsequent contextual evidence. Lexical redefinition therefore provides a controlled behavioural paradigm for studying how language models integrate multiple sources of information within a prompt.
papers.summary: Language models must reconcile conflicting evidence inside a single prompt, such as an explicit instruction that redefines a word followed by a sentence whose usage supports or contradicts the new meaning. Testing this lexical redefinition setup across 870 word pairs shows that **redefinitions are not applied as fixed rules**: depending on how the instruction relates to the intervening sentence, the contextualised usage can preserve, weaken, or completely reverse the instruction. Lexical redefinition is proposed as a controlled behavioural paradigm for studying how language models integrate multiple sources of information within a prompt.

papers.title: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
papers.abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.
papers.summary: Hate speech datasets tend to emphasize explicit hateful wording, yet directed harm can be expressed indirectly through sarcasm, mock praise, exaggeration, or apparent politeness. `SarcasTraps` is a 479-entry Turkish test set annotated for both hate speech and sarcasm, used strictly as an external evaluation for `BERTurk` and `XLM-RoBERTa` classifiers trained on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and for `GPT-4.1` and `Llama-3.3-70B` in a zero-shot setting. **Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot large language models keep higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops** on sarcastic examples, so both families struggle once sarcasm is involved. Because of its offensive content, the dataset is shared on request for academic research.

papers.title: DiTSG: Context-Aware Air Traffic Scene Generation with Multi-Agent Diffusion Transformers
papers.abstract: Understanding how many aircraft, and which traffic configurations, can be safely and efficiently managed by air traffic controllers within a given airspace is fundamental to air traffic management. Air traffic controllers continuously modify aircraft trajectories through interventions such as speed advisories and radar vectoring, and the patterns of these interventions are difficult to capture effectively using existing air traffic simulators. To address this limitation, we propose Diffusion Transformers for Traffic Scene Generation (DiTSG), which learns to generate air traffic scenes from recorded multi-aircraft trajectories. DiTSG employs stacked multi-agent inverted Transformer layers as the denoising backbone of a diffusion transformer, jointly generates the trajectories of multiple aircraft within a traffic scene, and conditions the generation on agent-specific required times of arrival. The resulting trajectories generated by DiTSG preserve realistic inter-aircraft interactions observed in actual air traffic operations. Experiments show that the DiTSG generates diverse traffic scenes that reproduce the statistical properties of recorded traffic while preserving realistic inter-aircraft interactions.
papers.summary: Air traffic controllers continually reshape aircraft trajectories through speed advisories and radar vectoring, and existing air traffic simulators struggle to reproduce those intervention patterns. `DiTSG` (Diffusion Transformers for Traffic Scene Generation) learns to generate entire traffic scenes from recorded multi-aircraft trajectories, using stacked multi-agent inverted Transformer layers as the denoising backbone of a diffusion transformer and conditioning each aircraft on its required time of arrival. Experiments show the generated scenes are diverse and **reproduce the statistical properties of recorded traffic while preserving realistic inter-aircraft interactions**, supporting studies of how many aircraft and which configurations controllers can safely manage in a given airspace.

papers.title: Learning to Design SR Solvers: Harness Optimization for Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) seeks explicit equations that explain observed data, and recent methods increasingly employ large language models (LLMs) and agents for equation discovery. However, these systems typically rely on manually designed workflows and prompts. We argue that the SR agent harness should itself be an optimization target: its design shapes search priors and how numerical feedback guides subsequent equation refinement. We therefore propose HarnessSR, a framework for jointly optimizing prompts and workflows to construct reusable SR agents. During both harness optimization and agent execution, HarnessSR supports either PySR or an LLM-based equation generator through tool-specific interfaces, allowing the framework to optimize search guidance for different equation-discovery mechanisms. HarnessSR first optimizes role prompts through equation-discovery feedback in basic workflows, then jointly searches prompt assignments and workflows with brief adaptation to align the two. Finally, it refines role instructions through reflection on residual patterns, candidate equation structures, and search outcomes, improving how these signals guide subsequent equation search. On LSR-Synth in LLM-SRBench, HarnessSR achieves a mean ID $\mathrm{Acc}_{0.01}$ of 61.33% across three backbones, a 45.0% relative improvement over the next-best baseline.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression (SR) searches for explicit equations that explain observed data, and recent systems built on large language models (LLMs) and agents still depend on hand-designed workflows and prompts. `HarnessSR` treats the agent harness itself as an optimization target: it first tunes role prompts using equation-discovery feedback in basic workflows, then jointly searches prompt assignments and workflow structures with brief adaptation, and finally refines role instructions by reflecting on residual patterns, candidate equation structures, and search outcomes, while supporting either `PySR` or an LLM-based equation generator through tool-specific interfaces. On `LSR-Synth` within `LLM-SRBench`, the optimized agents reach **a mean ID accuracy at the 0.01 tolerance of 61.33% across three backbones, a 45.0% relative improvement over the next-best baseline**.

papers.title: Proactive Physical AI through Continuous Observation and Timely Intervention
papers.abstract: Physical AI is commonly formulated around an explicitly specified task: given a goal or instruction, a system perceives, reasons, and acts. In many real-world settings, however, important tasks emerge from continuously changing world states before a person explicitly formulates them. We study this complementary problem as Proactive Physical AI, where an AI system continuously observes the physical world, identifies situations that warrant intervention, and initiates appropriate actions at the right time. We develop ProAgent, an end-to-end system built around two components: a Jev-style proactive timing model (dubbed StreamingJev) that determines whether and when intervention is needed, and a Response Model that generates responses for people or invokes available device capabilities for physical execution. To support learning at scale, we develop an automated data pipeline that converts videos into supervision for proactive timing. Experiments demonstrate strong proactive performance under both explicit objectives and standing roles, combining more accurate intervention timing with fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate ProAgent's ability to identify emerging needs and translate them into appropriate physical actions.
papers.summary: Physical AI systems are usually given an explicit goal or instruction, yet many real-world tasks emerge from continuously changing world states before anyone formulates them. The Proactive Physical AI setting asks a system to continuously observe the physical world, recognize situations that warrant intervention, and act at the right moment, and `ProAgent` implements it with a proactive timing model called `StreamingJev` that decides whether and when to intervene plus a Response Model that answers people or invokes device capabilities for physical execution, trained on timing supervision automatically extracted from videos. Under both explicit objectives and standing roles it combines **more accurate intervention timing with fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline**, and real-robot evaluations show it identifying emerging needs and translating them into physical actions.

papers.title: Event Memory and Narrative Dynamics: A Large Language Model Framework for Multidimensional State Spaces
papers.abstract: Studying event memory requires defining events and their relationships within remembered experience. Autobiographical narratives provide evidence of this organization, but their analytical units must first be established. This study introduces a large language model framework for constructing event representations from narratives and modeling their structure and dynamics with excerpt-level traceability. Explicit boundary rules and a feature schema informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation guide event construction. In a proof-of-concept application to interviews from five participants, the framework constructed 256 event-states. Multiple correspondence analysis embedded these states in feature-based spaces, with analyses focused on a selected 4-D geometry and 10-D and 13-D reference geometries. Consecutive event-states were significantly closer than expected under randomized narrative order. In the selected 4-D ten-basin solution, similarity between basin-state feature profiles corresponded with similarity between one-step routing profiles; context, mechanism, and theme differentiated full-system pathway engagement. A successor representation modeled expected basin-state occupancy across successive steps. Correlations between basin-centroid distances and complete successor-profile distances were positive across all five basin solutions, with exploratory tests supporting correspondence in at least two solutions across all three geometries. These findings connect feature-based event representations with observed narrative transitions and modeled multistep organization. The framework translates hippocampal principles into source-linked event boundaries and state representations, providing an analytical basis for testing neural accounts of event segmentation and predictive organization during naturalistic recall.
papers.summary: Studying event memory through autobiographical narratives requires first settling what counts as an event and how events relate to one another. A large language model framework constructs event representations from interview transcripts using explicit boundary rules and a feature schema informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation, keeps every event traceable to its source excerpt, embeds the resulting states with multiple correspondence analysis, and models multistep organization with a successor representation. In a proof of concept on interviews from five participants yielding 256 event-states, **consecutive event-states were significantly closer in feature space than expected under randomized narrative order**, and correlations between basin-centroid distances and successor-profile distances were positive across all five basin solutions examined.

papers.title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
papers.abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) systems for drug discovery have been limited by single agents that scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step tasks and by multi-agent systems locked into predefined workflows that miss the iterative, non-linear nature of a real campaign. `MADDIE` uses a central `Orchestrator` agent that composes four specialized workers, `HitIdentifier`, `LeadOptimizer`, `Synthesizer`, and `Evaluator`, into flexible workflows so the system can adapt its strategy and navigate the pipeline end to end. Across 50 protein targets it **produces molecules that satisfy key property requirements together with their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin**, and analysis shows the agents adopting different strategies per target while remaining efficient in time and tokens.

papers.title: The Value of Being Wrong: Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors
papers.abstract: Visual in-context learning (ICL) enables vision-language models (VLMs) to adapt at test time via demonstration examples, but its effectiveness depends critically on the examples selected. Recent counterfactual selection methods improve ICL by constructing demonstrations that expose how individual attribute changes affect the answer. However, they require multi-stage pipelines involving attribute extraction, caption engineering, and composed image matching. We propose a simpler alternative grounded in a key observation: a model's own prediction errors are natural counterfactual demonstrations that directly encode its failure modes. Our method, SMILE (Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors), builds a model-specific pool of hard negatives offline by recording the target VLM's own mistakes. At test time, the prediction serves as a direction signal that surfaces, in the semantic embedding space, the past mistakes most likely to recur for the current query. This prediction-conditioned identification provides a unified mechanism for both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design. Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE delivers an average task-score gain of +3.09 points over the SOTA baseline at 5x lower latency. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/SMILE/
papers.summary: Visual in-context learning (ICL) lets vision-language models (VLMs) adapt at test time through demonstration examples, but recent counterfactual selection methods for choosing those examples require multi-stage pipelines of attribute extraction, caption engineering, and composed image matching. `SMILE` (Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors) instead records the target VLM's own mistakes offline to build a model-specific pool of hard negatives, then at test time uses the model's prediction as a direction signal to surface, in semantic embedding space, the past mistakes most likely to recur for the current query, a single mechanism that covers both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering. Across four benchmarks and four VLMs it delivers **an average task-score gain of 3.09 points over the state-of-the-art baseline at 5x lower latency**.

papers.title: WeGR: Unified Generative Retrieval for Industrial Search Systems in WeChat
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) offers a promising paradigm for industrial search by unifying candidate generation within an autoregressive framework. However, its effectiveness is limited by two key challenges. First, existing Semantic ID (SID) tokenizers struggle to incorporate collaborative signals while maintaining effective codebook utilization, limiting their ability to distinguish items and achieve high-quality retrieval. Second, existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods suffer from severe reward sparsity under exact SID matching, leaving many sampled trajectories without effective learning signals and hindering preference optimization. To address these challenges, we propose WeGR, a unified generative retrieval framework consisting of two complementary components. Specifically, the Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) incorporates query-to-item and item-to-item collaborative signals while mitigating codebook collapse through codebook refresh and complementary regularization, enabling more informative and balanced SID representations. Building upon these SIDs, Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO) progressively expands both reward evaluation and policy optimization horizons, reducing learning difficulty while leveraging behavioral reward signals at different levels of the SID hierarchy, without relying on auxiliary reward models. Extensive offline experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WeGR in improving retrieval and ranking performance. Moreover, a two-month online A/B test in WeChat E-commerce Search demonstrates relative improvements of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in click-through rate, and 1.381% in conversion rate, while reducing online CPU and GPU usage by 25.5% and 26.1%, respectively. The system has been successfully deployed across multiple search scenarios in WeChat, serving billions of users, generating tens of millions of PVs daily.
