papers.summary: Generative retrieval (GR) folds candidate generation into an autoregressive model, but Semantic ID (SID) tokenizers struggle to absorb collaborative signals without codebook collapse, and reinforcement learning (RL) under exact SID matching leaves many sampled trajectories without an effective learning signal. `WeGR` pairs a Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (`CoCo-VAE`), which injects query-to-item and item-to-item signals while using codebook refresh and complementary regularization to keep codes balanced, with Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (`DHPO`), which progressively widens the reward evaluation and policy optimization horizons across the SID hierarchy without auxiliary reward models. Offline experiments show gains in retrieval and ranking, and **a two-month online A/B test in WeChat E-commerce Search raised orders by 2.539%, click-through rate by 1.508%, and conversion rate by 1.381% while cutting CPU and GPU usage by 25.5% and 26.1%**. The system is deployed across multiple WeChat search scenarios serving billions of users.

papers.title: PRAISE: A Reproducible Workflow for Non-Programmer Scientists to Implement Published AI Models
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step. Because implementations rarely work the first time, PRAISE anticipates common failures and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, three BSc chemistry students and their tutor applied PRAISE without prior programming or data science knowledge. They reproduced, validated and extended a state-of-the-art model that predicts enzyme-substrate interactions. This shows that with PRAISE, implementing an AI model from the literature becomes a learnable skill, one that turns non-programmer scientists from users into evaluators and improvers of AI models.
papers.summary: Researchers, students, and industry professionals who want to apply a published AI model to their own data often lack the programming and data science skills to get from paper to working predictions, and existing guidelines cover isolated steps rather than the full route. `PRAISE` (Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education) is a hands-on, step-by-step workflow for non-programmers that anticipates the common failure points of such implementations and supplies a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, **three BSc chemistry students and their tutor with no prior programming or data science background reproduced, validated, and extended a state-of-the-art enzyme-substrate interaction model** by following the workflow.

papers.title: Predicting Mental Health Help-Seeking Behaviour on Reddit: A Survival Analysis of Linguistic and Behavioural Signals
papers.abstract: Most prior work on predicting mental health help-seeking treats it as post-hoc classification of users already active in clinical communities, which cannot tell whether someone approaching a transition can be identified in advance. We instead frame help-seeking as a time-to-event problem and ask which Reddit users will eventually seek mental health support, and how imminent that transition is. We build a two-arm cohort: a control frame of 6,337 ordinary users with genuine right-censoring (12.1% transition rate) to answer who will transition, and a clinical frame of 5,023 eventual transitioners to answer how soon. Features come only from posts written before any clinical activity, and user-grouped five-fold cross-validation plus a four-year temporal holdout guard against leakage. We compare TF-IDF, MentalBERT embeddings and behavioural activity features using Cox proportional hazards models, Random Survival Forests and an LSTM sequential model. Behavioural features alone outperform text for predicting who will seek help (C-index 0.797 vs. 0.763), and combining both is best (0.823 under cross-validation, 0.856 on the holdout). The pattern reverses for predicting how soon a known transition will happen: text remains a stable predictor (C-index 0.698) while behavioural features become unstable. Structural engagement patterns therefore carry information about future help-seeking beyond linguistic content, and separating who from when yields a cleaner analysis.
papers.summary: Prior work on predicting mental health help-seeking classifies users already active in clinical communities after the fact, which cannot reveal whether an approaching transition is detectable in advance. Framing help-seeking as a time-to-event problem, the study builds a control cohort of 6,337 ordinary Reddit users with genuine right-censoring to ask who will transition and a clinical cohort of 5,023 eventual transitioners to ask how soon, using only posts written before any clinical activity and comparing `TF-IDF`, `MentalBERT` embeddings, and behavioural activity features under Cox proportional hazards models, Random Survival Forests, and an LSTM sequential model. **Behavioural features alone beat text for predicting who will seek help (C-index 0.797 vs. 0.763), and combining both reaches 0.823 under cross-validation and 0.856 on a four-year temporal holdout**, whereas for predicting how soon a known transition will happen text stays stable at a C-index of 0.698 while behavioural features become unstable.

papers.title: From Suboptimal to Optimal: One-Step Latent Flow Policies for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn effective policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction. Although generative models such as diffusion and flow matching enhance policy expressiveness, they typically start from uninformative Gaussian noise and generate actions through multi-step iteration, leading to high computational costs and failing to effectively leverage suboptimal trajectories in datasets. We propose MeanFlow2Better (MF2B), which reformulates offline RL as generative decision chunk optimization from current performance status to better performance status in a high-level latent decision space. MF2B maps trajectory chunks to high-level latent decision representations through an encoder, placing generation starting points within a structured decision space sculpted by behavioral data. The model learns a shared conditional mean velocity field in this space, constructing two flow mappings: from Gaussian-Induced Decision Sources toward positive behavioral decision regions, and from suboptimal decisions toward high-value decision regions. Both flow mappings complete decision refinement through one-step ODE integration over the unit time interval $\Delta t=1$, requiring neither multi-step iterative sampling nor backpropagation through time. Furthermore, we propose hierarchical chunk-level advantage to guide the flow direction toward high-return regions, where the high-level decisions cover multiple low-level actions, leading to sequence length compression from $T$ to $K \approx T/H$ and significantly lower computational overhead. On the D4RL Gym-MuJoCo benchmark, MF2B achieves an average score of 90.91, matching or surpassing strong baselines.
papers.summary: Offline reinforcement learning learns policies from fixed datasets, and although diffusion and flow-matching policies are expressive, they start from uninformative Gaussian noise, need multi-step sampling, and make poor use of the suboptimal trajectories in the data. `MeanFlow2Better` (`MF2B`) encodes trajectory chunks into a high-level latent decision space shaped by the behavioural data and learns a shared conditional mean velocity field there, yielding two flows, one from Gaussian-induced decision sources toward positive behavioural decisions and one from suboptimal decisions toward high-value regions, each completed by a single one-step ODE integration over the unit interval with no multi-step sampling or backpropagation through time. A hierarchical chunk-level advantage steers the flows toward high-return regions and compresses the sequence length by the chunk horizon, and on the `D4RL` Gym-MuJoCo benchmark the method **reaches an average score of 90.91, matching or surpassing strong baselines**.

papers.title: AUGUstus: Autonomous Driving VLA Model with Unified Generation and Understanding
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and understanding to excel in long-tail scenarios. However, current VLAs have two limitations: 1) Degeneration into vision-action (VA) models. For low latency, regression/flow-based methods directly generate actions but underuse VLM understanding, causing unsafe, unexplainable actions. 2) Autoregressive high latency. Autoregressive methods sequentially generate chain-of-thought (CoT) and action tokens, fully leveraging VLM understanding, but high latency hinders deployment. To enable low-latency deployment while using CoT to assist action generation, we propose AUGUstus, an Autonomous-driving VLA model with Unified Generation and Understanding. We unify diffusion-based action generation and autoregressive CoT understanding in one model, where understanding only serves generation. Joint CoT supervision preserves VLM spatial understanding in shared representation for safer, more accurate trajectories. AUGUstus-mode orders action generation before CoT, so CoT supervises reliable actions during training while inference needs only action output, enabling low latency. AUGUstus-GRPO, a unified GRPO algorithm, jointly optimizes action and CoT, improving action performance. Experiments show AUGUstus achieves 94.6 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 and 90.7 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, SOTA planning without scorer module. On nuScenes, it achieves average L2 error 0.27 m and average collision rate 0.05%, best among compared methods. To validate AUGUstus practicality, we train on in-house data with 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for ~2 days, evaluate on an internal 1,000 km dataset, and preliminarily deploy on a real vehicle, achieving 12 Hz operation. Project page: https://augustus-ad.github.io
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models for end-to-end driving either degenerate into vision-action models that generate actions directly and underuse the vision-language model's understanding, or generate chain-of-thought (CoT) and action tokens autoregressively at latencies too high for deployment. `AUGUstus` unifies diffusion-based action generation with autoregressive CoT understanding in one model where understanding only serves generation, orders action generation before CoT so that CoT supervises actions during training while inference emits only actions, and adds `AUGUstus-GRPO`, a unified GRPO algorithm that jointly optimizes actions and CoT. It reports **94.6 PDMS on `NAVSIMv1` and 90.7 EPDMS on `NAVSIMv2`, state-of-the-art planning without a scorer module**, along with an average L2 error of 0.27 m and a 0.05% collision rate on `nuScenes`, and after training on in-house data with 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for about two days it runs at 12 Hz on a real vehicle.

papers.title: TabGift: A Context-Efficient Foundation Model for Tabular Data Generation
papers.abstract: Tabular data generation aims to synthesize realistic samples from limited observations while faithfully capturing the underlying data distribution. Tabular foundation models (TFMs), pretrained on diverse tabular tasks and adapted through in-context learning, have demonstrated strong predictive capabilities, suggesting the potential of extending this paradigm to tabular data generation. However, the strong predictive performance of TFMs often relies on sufficiently large context sets, whereas tabular generation is typically needed precisely when target data are scarce. Extending the foundation-model paradigm to generation therefore requires reliable distribution inference from only a limited context. To this end, we propose TabGift, a context-efficient tabular foundation model enabling both efficient distribution modeling and effective generation from only a few context samples. TabGift maps heterogeneous tables into a shared latent space with a pretrained tabular encoder, where an in-context diffusion model learns to denoise latent samples conditioned on a small set of clean examples. This design transfers generative priors across datasets and enables distribution inference from limited context, while a lightweight dataset-specific MLP decoder maps generated representations back to the original data space. Experiments on 7 classification and 11 regression datasets show that TabGift consistently outperforms representative baselines in synthetic data quality, with particularly strong gains under limited-context settings, while achieving substantially faster adaptation and generation.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) adapt to new tables through in-context learning, but their predictive strength depends on large context sets, whereas synthetic tabular data is needed precisely when real samples are scarce. `TabGift` maps heterogeneous tables into a shared latent space with a pretrained tabular encoder, trains an in-context diffusion model to denoise latent samples conditioned on a small set of clean examples, and decodes generated representations back to the original data space with a lightweight dataset-specific MLP. Across 7 classification and 11 regression datasets it **consistently outperforms representative baselines in synthetic data quality, with the largest gains under limited-context settings**, while adapting and generating substantially faster.

papers.title: Generative Models as Adaptive Trust Regions for Discrete Bayesian Optimisation
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimisation (BO) is a powerful framework for sample-efficient optimisation of expensive black-box functions, but its application to high-dimensional discrete scientific design remains challenging. Local trust-region BO methods such as TuRBO address high dimensionality by restricting search to adaptively sized neighbourhoods. However, a direct discrete analogue based on edit distance can be poorly suited to structured discrete objects: neighbourhoods grow combinatorially, and metric proximity does not capture the dependencies that determine whether a design is plausible or useful. Motivated by the growing availability of pretrained generative models, we introduce GenTuRBO, which replaces the geometric trust region with an adaptively scaled proposal distribution defined by a pretrained generator. The generator provides a learned prior over discrete transformations, encoding coordinated changes without explicitly enumerating edit-distance neighbourhoods. GenTuRBO performs strongly across all three domains and achieves the highest mean final scores on Ehrlich sequence optimisation and Sokoban coordination.
papers.summary: Bayesian optimisation (BO) is sample-efficient for expensive black-box functions, but local trust-region methods such as `TuRBO` translate poorly to high-dimensional discrete design, since edit-distance neighbourhoods grow combinatorially and metric proximity ignores the dependencies that make a design plausible or useful. `GenTuRBO` replaces the geometric trust region with an adaptively scaled proposal distribution defined by a pretrained generative model, which supplies a learned prior over coordinated discrete transformations without enumerating neighbourhoods. It performs strongly across all three evaluated domains and **achieves the highest mean final scores on Ehrlich sequence optimisation and Sokoban coordination**.

papers.title: Constant-Depth Rational-Weight GNNs and their Connection to Schanuel's Conjecture
papers.abstract: A landmark result states that the expressive power of graph neural networks (GNNs) is bounded from above by the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) test. We ask whether a constant-depth GNN can match the expressive power of 1-WL while using only rational weights. We prove that this is the case when Schanuel's conjecture, a famous open problem from transcendental number theory, is taken to be true. Our GNN construction works even with integer weights, and more generally with a broad range of rational weights. As the activation function, it may use logistic sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent, or related functions. It is uniform across all graph sizes. We also prove a partial converse: if a GNN with exponentiation, hyperbolic sine or hyperbolic cosine as activation matches the expressive power of the 1-WL test in a slightly more expressive setting where graphs may contain certain auxiliary vertices, then this implies Schanuel's conjecture restricted to the numbers that arise in computations of the GNN. We also conduct experiments showing that the constructed GNNs indeed match the 1-WL test.
papers.summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are known to be at most as expressive as the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) test, which raises the question of whether a constant-depth GNN using only rational weights can reach that ceiling. The answer is shown to be yes **conditional on Schanuel's conjecture, an open problem in transcendental number theory**, through a construction that works with integer weights and a broad range of rational weights, uses logistic sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent, or related activations, and is uniform across graph sizes. A partial converse shows that a GNN with exponentiation, hyperbolic sine, or hyperbolic cosine activation matching 1-WL on graphs with certain auxiliary vertices would imply Schanuel's conjecture restricted to the numbers arising in its computations, and experiments confirm that the constructed GNNs match 1-WL in practice.

papers.title: Intrinsic Geometry Matching: learning observation-equivariant process geometry
papers.abstract: Real data are often arbitrary, indirect observations of an unknown underlying process, and those observations can distort its geometry. Existing geometric methods equip data with the induced geometry of the ambient space, but this entangles the true geometry of the process with the distortion of the observation. To address this, we introduce Intrinsic Geometry Matching (IGM): a scalable approach to learn the intrinsic geometry of the underlying process. Specifically, we learn the carr\'e du champ operator of the process, allowing us to recover its diffusion geometry. Our method uses the fact that data often come with natural perturbations, like steps in a time series, to recover the intrinsic carr\'e du champ while transforming naturally with changes in observation: it is observation-equivariant. Furthermore, since this equivariance relates the geometry of different spaces, we can train a model using additional sources of data, even when that data lies in another space. We evaluate IGM on molecular dynamics, image, and video data and find better performance and scaling than existing neural and graph-based geometric tools.
papers.summary: Real data are often indirect observations of an unknown process, and standard geometric methods inherit the ambient space's induced geometry, entangling the true geometry of the process with the distortion introduced by the observation. Intrinsic Geometry Matching (`IGM`) learns the carré du champ operator of the underlying process, from which its diffusion geometry can be recovered, by exploiting natural perturbations in the data such as consecutive steps of a time series. The learned operator is **observation-equivariant, transforming predictably as the observation changes**, which also allows training on additional data that lives in a different space, and on molecular dynamics, image, and video data the method shows better performance and scaling than existing neural and graph-based geometric tools.

papers.title: A physics-coupled graph neural operator for mid-plane six-component stress tensor field prediction in concrete penetration
papers.abstract: The penetration-resistant design of concrete structures requires the spatiotemporal evolution of the stress field within the target, whereas in design only the strength grade, the geometry and the projectile parameters are known, and the aggregate arrangement is not. Empirical formulae and scalar-output surrogates serve design screening, and mesoscale finite element models resolve the aggregate-scale response, but one solution cannot cover random aggregate samples at scale, and no framework links mesoscale heterogeneity to field-level prediction. A physics-coupled graph neural operator (PC-GNO) is proposed, which learns in function space the evolution of the mid-plane six-component stress tensor field. The training data are generated by full-scale, aggregate-resolved finite element models and comprise 359 cases at the impact velocities of 100, 135 and 165 m/s, corresponding to compressive strengths of 14, 23 and 48 MPa; the data source is verified by laboratory measurements. The coupling strength of message passing is constructed from the impedance contrast across the material interface, and the update is constrained by spectral normalization. Under the single-step primary setting, the mean accuracy of the three levels is 80.16% (91.45%, 77.80% and 71.22%), i.e. 27.81, 42.46 and 34.16 percentage points above the preceding-frame field of the same window; with 20 664 parameters it exceeds the 87.9% of the best Fourier neural operator configuration (about 812 times as many parameters) and the 71.0% of the closed-form linear regression. The output is the complete six-component tensor field rather than a fixed engineering quantity, so that strength criteria and energy indicators follow from one set of weights. For field-level response prediction in concrete penetration, this result provides a data-driven route, with conditions of applicability defined by the training and the evaluation.
papers.summary: Designing concrete structures to resist projectile penetration requires the spatiotemporal stress field inside the target, but at design time only the strength grade, geometry, and projectile parameters are known, not the aggregate arrangement, and aggregate-resolved finite element models cannot be run across random aggregate samples at scale. A physics-coupled graph neural operator (`PC-GNO`) learns in function space the evolution of the mid-plane six-component stress tensor field, with message-passing coupling strength built from the impedance contrast across material interfaces and updates constrained by spectral normalization, trained on 359 full-scale finite element cases spanning three impact velocities and three compressive strengths and verified against laboratory measurements. In the single-step primary setting it reaches **a mean accuracy of 80.16% across the three strength levels, 27.81 to 42.46 percentage points above the preceding-frame field**, and with 20,664 parameters it exceeds the 87.9% of the best Fourier neural operator configuration, which has about 812 times as many parameters, and the 71.0% of closed-form linear regression. Because the output is the full tensor field rather than a fixed engineering quantity, strength criteria and energy indicators can be derived from a single set of weights.

papers.title: Glasseek: A Transparent Recipe for Training and Trustworthy Evaluation of DeepSearch Agents
papers.abstract: Deep search enables language agents to solve complex information-seeking tasks through iterative web exploration. However, developing robust open-source agents remains challenging for three reasons. First, opaque trajectory-construction pipelines make training data difficult to audit and reproduce. Second, context compression can create a substantial mismatch between training and inference. Third, agents may retrieve benchmark content from the open web during evaluation, contaminating the results and overstating their performance. To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce Glasseek, a fully transparent deep search framework spanning the complete development lifecycle, releasing all data, model weights, training recipes, and code. Specifically, for data construction, we establish a verifiable trajectory curation pipeline that systematically generates high-quality exploration paths. For training, we propose Compaction-Managed GSPO (CM-GSPO), which uses the same policy for search and summarization while optimizing only execution sub-trajectories, enabling end-to-end search-policy training across context-compaction boundaries. For evaluation, we conduct the first systematic audit of test-set leakage in open-web agents and release a modular anti-leakage plugin that seamlessly integrates into existing evaluation harnesses. Under this rigorous evaluation protocol, our 9B agent outperforms frontier proprietary agents across almost all deep research benchmarks spanning diverse task types, and achieves the best overall performance among recent open-weight agents, setting a new state of the art at the 9B scale.
papers.summary: Deep search agents tackle complex information-seeking tasks through iterative web exploration, but open-source development is hampered by opaque trajectory-construction pipelines, a training-inference mismatch introduced by context compression, and evaluations contaminated when agents retrieve benchmark content from the open web. `Glasseek` releases all data, model weights, training recipes, and code, builds a verifiable trajectory curation pipeline, and trains with Compaction-Managed GSPO (`CM-GSPO`), which uses the same policy for search and summarization while optimizing only execution sub-trajectories so that search-policy training spans context-compaction boundaries. An accompanying audit is the first systematic study of test-set leakage in open-web agents and comes with a modular anti-leakage plugin for existing evaluation harnesses. Under that protocol **the 9B agent outperforms frontier proprietary agents across almost all deep research benchmarks** and posts the best overall result among recent open-weight agents at its scale.

papers.title: Governing Copyright Responsibly in the Era of Generative AI
papers.abstract: Large language models are trained on collections that may include scholarly works, while authors generally lack work-level information about whether and how their works were used. This paper asks how copyright governance frames and operationalises the protection of such authors, and what a responsible alternative would require. Forty legislative, judicial and soft-law instruments issued between 2019 and 2026 were coded deductively against a framework derived from Responsible Research and Innovation theory, yielding 1,337 category assignments across 835 segments. The European Union and the United States are the primary cases; the United Kingdom, China and international bodies serve as comparators. Normative orientation and the distribution of responsibility dominate the corpus, while reflexivity is the least represented category and reaches its minimum in the US sub-corpus. Both primary jurisdictions frame protection procedurally rather than as an entitlement, and no instrument in the corpus creates a general author-facing attribution duty for the use of works in AI training. From the coded gaps, the paper derives a six-instrument governance design and a capacity-based allocation of responsibility among developers, publishers, collecting societies, funders, institutions, regulators, and individual authors.
papers.summary: Authors whose scholarly works may have been used to train large language models usually have no work-level information about that use, and the paper asks how copyright governance frames their protection and what a responsible alternative would require. Forty legislative, judicial, and soft-law instruments issued between 2019 and 2026, mainly from the European Union and the United States with the United Kingdom, China, and international bodies as comparators, were coded against a framework derived from Responsible Research and Innovation theory. Normative orientation and the distribution of responsibility dominate the corpus, reflexivity is the least represented category, and **no instrument creates a general author-facing attribution duty for the use of works in AI training**. From these gaps the authors derive a six-instrument governance design that allocates responsibility by capacity among developers, publishers, collecting societies, funders, institutions, regulators, and individual authors.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Deferred-Decision Trajectory Optimization with Anytime-Valid Target Retention for Moving Candidates
papers.abstract: We study multi-agent terminal interception when one of several moving candidates is the unknown target and both target identity and candidate terminal locations are uncertain. We develop a receding-horizon deferred-decision trajectory optimization (DDTO) controller that combines conformal terminal-location prediction, sequential candidate rejection, capacity-constrained assignment, and candidate-contingent planning. Under exchangeability conditions for terminal and identity residuals, with predictable querying, we establish fixed-time terminal-location coverage and anytime-valid target retention. At the final replan, when one control step remains, we bound the joint probability that a tightened-set DDTO plan passes nonlinear rollout verification but capture fails. The closed-loop controller applies fallback guidance to any agent without a verified DDTO plan and, across 100 paired scenarios, captures 79% of targets under the strict control-effort budget and 85% when that budget is relaxed.
papers.summary: The setting is multi-agent terminal interception where one of several moving candidates is the true target and both its identity and the candidates' terminal locations are uncertain. A receding-horizon deferred-decision trajectory optimization (`DDTO`) controller combines conformal prediction of terminal locations, sequential candidate rejection, capacity-constrained assignment, and candidate-contingent planning, with fallback guidance for any agent that lacks a verified plan. Under exchangeability assumptions the authors prove fixed-time coverage of terminal locations and anytime-valid retention of the true target, and they bound the probability that a plan passes nonlinear rollout verification yet capture fails at the final replan. Across 100 paired scenarios the closed-loop controller **captures 79% of targets under a strict control-effort budget** and 85% when the budget is relaxed.

papers.title: Mixture of GFlowNets
papers.abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn a policy that samples compositional objects in proportion to an unnormalized reward $R(x)$. This makes them useful wherever many diverse, high-reward candidates are needed and oracle queries are expensive. In practice, a single GFlowNet often fails to cover all modes of a complex distribution, and the obvious ways to scale compute saturate: larger batches and data-parallel gradient averaging draw every trajectory from one, possibly biased, policy, so extra rollouts rediscover known modes instead of finding new ones. We explore whether this mode-bias problem (mode collapse in the extreme) can be addressed with a population of asynchronously trained policies which divide the state space between them. Mixture of GFlowNets (MoG) replaces the single forward policy with a community of $K$ independent GFlowNets coupled through one jointly trained soft classifier, which assigns each member its own region of the state space through reward shaping. Mixing the members under their learned partition functions provably recovers the target $p(x)\propto R(x)$. MoG exchange (MoGX) also lets the classifier route sampled trajectories: a trajectory the classifier assigns to another member is sent to that member and trained on there, with no importance sampling. We evaluate both methods by keeping the environment-interaction budget fixed while scaling the community size, turning parallel compute into mode coverage without extra oracle calls. On HyperGrid, across six reward landscapes and communities of up to $K{=}64$, MoG and MoGX keep finding new modes as $K$ grows, while data-parallel training saturates. On a genomic ideotype-design task, MoGX covers $39%$ of the $1024$ optima at $K{=}64$, against $31\%$ for independent agents and $20\%$ for data-parallel training. MoG also has a lower per-iteration synchronization cost than data-parallel training.
papers.summary: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) sample compositional objects in proportion to a reward, but a single network often misses modes, and scaling compute through larger batches or data-parallel gradient averaging keeps drawing every trajectory from one possibly biased policy. Mixture of GFlowNets (`MoG`) trains a population of K independent GFlowNets coupled through a jointly trained soft classifier that assigns each member its own region of state space via reward shaping, and mixing the members under their learned partition functions provably recovers the target distribution. A variant, `MoGX`, lets the classifier route sampled trajectories to the member responsible for them with no importance sampling. With the environment-interaction budget held fixed, both methods keep finding new modes on `HyperGrid` as the community grows to 64 members while data-parallel training saturates, and on a genomic ideotype-design task **MoGX covers 39% of 1,024 optima at K=64 versus 31% for independent agents and 20% for data-parallel training**.

papers.title: MAGNET: Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network for Connectome Generation
papers.abstract: Functional brain connectome represents neural connectivity as a matrix of pairwise interactions between brain regions. Generation of functional connectomes is not only a question of validity; rather, having satisfied the constraints on the correlation matrix, the next step is to recover the class-conditional geometry buried under coarse labels. We propose MAGNET, a Manifold-Aware Graph Diffusion Network which uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the manifold of correlation matrices that guarantees validity. MAGNET lifts noisy latent states into ROI-level region tokens and performs denoising with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions. To deal with structural problems induced by coarse labels, MAGNET employs class-anchored conditioning, amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption. Across ABIDE, ADNI, and OASIS-3, MAGNET consistently achieves favorable results compared to previous manifold-aware approaches, demonstrating improvements of 7-21% in class-conditional fidelity ($\alpha,\beta$-F1) across three cohorts and better sampling efficiency. Moreover, while training only with strict binary labels, MAGNET is capable of maintaining clinical heterogeneity through fine substructure of the connectomes in a zero-shot setting, improving subclass covariance alignment ($\lambda$-MSE) by over 30%. These results suggest that geometric validity is a necessary but insufficient condition for clinical utility in connectome synthesis. Moreover, efforts in making the diffusion denoising class-conditional manifold aware finds utility beyond the highly curved brain connectome generation as this is a critical problem in various general settings. The code repository can be found at https://github.com/protyayofficial/MAGNET.
papers.summary: Generating functional brain connectomes requires producing valid correlation matrices while also recovering the class-conditional structure that coarse diagnostic labels obscure. `MAGNET` uses a normalized-Cholesky representation of the correlation-matrix manifold to guarantee validity, lifts noisy latents into region-level tokens, and denoises with a relational inductive bias over brain atlas regions, adding class-anchored conditioning, an amortized structural bridge, and relevance-preserving corruption to cope with coarse labels. Across `ABIDE`, `ADNI`, and `OASIS-3` it **improves class-conditional fidelity by 7-21% over prior manifold-aware methods**, and despite training only on binary labels it improves zero-shot subclass covariance alignment by over 30%. The authors argue that geometric validity is necessary but not sufficient for clinical utility in connectome synthesis.

papers.title: ProbabilityBench: Model Evaluation and Calibration with Exact Ground-Truth Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Evaluating model uncertainty on real-world data is challenging because each instance provides only a single observed label, leaving true conditional class probabilities unknown. To address this, we introduce ProbabilityBench, a benchmark that provides exact, instance-level class probabilities across three simulated text-based domains: peer review, covert information transfer, and credit risk. By explicitly defining the full data-generating process for each environment, we analytically compute both exact class probabilities and Bayes error. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical guarantee that rendering these cases into natural-language memos strictly preserves their underlying generative probabilities. This exactness enables direct measurement of reported probability quality via KL divergence. Across 16 evaluated models, most models on the observed cost-quality Pareto frontiers are decision models, including Jev and Perplexity Decider. Finally, ProbabilityBench serves as a meta-evaluation framework, leveraging known ground-truth values to benchmark the accuracy of standard calibration metrics and Bayes-error estimators themselves.
papers.summary: Real-world data provides only one observed label per instance, so the true conditional class probabilities needed to judge a model's uncertainty are unknown. `ProbabilityBench` fully specifies the data-generating process for three simulated text domains, peer review, covert information transfer, and credit risk, so that exact instance-level class probabilities and Bayes error can be computed analytically, with a proof that rendering cases as natural-language memos preserves those probabilities. This lets reported probabilities be scored directly by KL divergence, and **across 16 evaluated models most of those on the cost-quality Pareto frontiers are decision models** such as `Jev` and `Perplexity Decider`. The benchmark also acts as a meta-evaluation tool for checking how well standard calibration metrics and Bayes-error estimators recover known ground truth.

papers.title: LLM Evaluation is a Forecasting Problem
papers.abstract: Standard procedure in machine learning is to randomly split train and test data, emulating IID draws from one underlying data distribution. In practice, models are trained on past data and deployed in the future, which may come from distinct distributions. In this paper, we find that web text is indeed highly non-stationary, as text distributions shift over time. We further observe that model performance changes continuously over time across diverse benchmarks. Consequently, future model performance is better predicted by measurements made on recent evaluation data, and is best predicted by time series forecasters applied to historic performance rather than by historic performance itself. Choosing which model to deploy based on forecasted accuracy enables more reliable selection of performant models, thus improving downstream accuracy in the regime practitioners care about: deployment. Taken together, our experiments suggest that time should be treated as a fundamental variable in LLM evaluation. We release our code and data.
papers.summary: Standard train/test splits emulate independent draws from one distribution, yet deployed models are trained on the past and used in the future. The authors show that web text is strongly non-stationary and that model performance across diverse benchmarks drifts continuously over time, so recent evaluation data predicts future performance better than older data. **Time-series forecasters applied to historic performance predict future accuracy better than historic performance itself**, and selecting which model to deploy by forecasted accuracy gives more reliable choices and higher downstream accuracy at deployment. The authors conclude that time should be treated as a fundamental variable in LLM evaluation and release their code and data.

papers.title: Understanding Personalization Gains in Whisper
papers.abstract: Whisper-style ASR models provide strong zero-shot transcription, but their residual errors are not evenly distributed across datasets, recording conditions, and metadata-based groups. We study when lightweight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) improves Whisper and whether observed gains require group-specific adapters. Across Common Voice, LibriSpeech, and VoxPopuli, we compare zero-shot Whisper, pooled LoRA, and group-specific LoRA under matched within-group splits. We find that adaptation is not uniformly beneficial: gains are concentrated in difficult Common Voice groups, are consistent on VoxPopuli, and largely disappear on low-error LibriSpeech. Crucially, pooled LoRA often matches, and sometimes clearly outperforms, group-specific LoRA. Gains over zero-shot should therefore be tested against matched pooled adaptation before being interpreted as evidence of personalization.
papers.summary: Whisper-style speech recognition models transcribe well zero-shot, but their residual errors cluster unevenly across datasets, recording conditions, and metadata-defined groups. The study compares zero-shot `Whisper`, a single pooled low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) adapter, and group-specific adapters under matched within-group splits on `Common Voice`, `LibriSpeech`, and `VoxPopuli`. Gains concentrate in difficult Common Voice groups, hold consistently on VoxPopuli, and largely vanish on low-error LibriSpeech, and **pooled LoRA often matches and sometimes clearly outperforms group-specific LoRA**. The authors conclude that improvements over zero-shot should be tested against matched pooled adaptation before being read as evidence of personalization.

papers.title: CWE-bench: Refocusing Agentic Security from Exploitation to Defense
papers.abstract: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have focused largely on offense, yet a working exploit does not show that an agent can make software safe. An attacker needs to exploit only one vulnerability; a defender must find and fix all of them. We introduce CWE-bench, a private benchmark of 120 held-out repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 73 CWE types, eight languages, and all OWASP Top 10 2025 categories. Agents are given a repository to audit and a description of its threat model, but are not told the weakness, where it occurs, or how many vulnerable sites there are. Each patch must block the exploit while preserving original functionality, as checked by a programmatic verifier. We validated the verifier against a panel of agentic judges, manually reviewing disagreements during development and refining the checks. The best agents reach 68% pass@1 and 81% pass@4. We further conduct analyses showing that (i) agents with the same pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, and (ii) no single agent is best across languages or vulnerability categories, and difficulty varies far more by vulnerability category than by language. As the offensive capabilities of agents improve, CWE-bench provides a broad and rigorous measure of whether their defensive capabilities keep pace.
papers.summary: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have mostly measured offense, but a working exploit does not show that an agent can make software safe, since a defender must find and fix every vulnerability rather than just one. `CWE-bench` is a private benchmark of 120 held-out repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 73 CWE types, eight languages, and all OWASP Top 10 2025 categories; agents receive a repository and a threat-model description but not the weakness, its location, or how many vulnerable sites exist, and each patch must block the exploit while preserving functionality under a programmatic verifier validated against a panel of agentic judges. **The best agents reach 68% pass@1 and 81% pass@4.** Agents with the same pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, no single agent leads across all languages or categories, and difficulty varies far more by vulnerability category than by language.

papers.title: Benchmarking Quantum Kernel SVMs for Credit Card Fraud Detection: Performance Realities Under NISQ Constraints
papers.abstract: Detecting credit card fraud is notoriously difficult because fraudulent charges make up less than 0.2% of total transactions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML), particularly Quantum Kernel Support Vector Machines (QSVM), promises richer feature representations by embedding classical data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces. However, whether this theoretical advantage holds up when managing real-world financial data bottlenecks remains unclear. We designed a controlled benchmark comparing three quantum encodings, Angle, ZZFeatureMap, and IQP against classical models while keeping sample sizes, feature counts, and scaling strictly matched. To handle class skew without corrupting quantum state overlaps, we embedded synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) directly into the quantum Gram matrix workflow, raising PR-AUC scores by roughly +0.04 across feature maps. When trained on the full European credit card dataset with 30 features, classical baselines reached a top PR-AUC of 0.983. However, restricting classical models to match QSVM hardware constraints (500 samples, 4 PCA features) dropped their PR-AUC to 0.750. This puts our best quantum result 0.730 PR-AUC using IQP encoding on 150 samples into realistic context. Testing on physical quantum hardware reduced performance further to 0.62 due to CNOT gate errors and thermal noise. Overall, our findings pinpoint two main operational bottlenecks for near-term quantum kernels: the scaling of Gram matrix evaluation and heavy information loss from squeezing features onto small qubit registers.
papers.summary: Credit card fraud makes up under 0.2% of transactions, and quantum kernel support vector machines (QSVM) promise richer features by embedding data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces, though whether that helps on real financial data has been unclear. The benchmark compares `Angle`, `ZZFeatureMap`, and `IQP` encodings against classical models with matched sample sizes, feature counts, and scaling, and embeds synthetic minority oversampling (`SMOTE`) into the quantum Gram-matrix workflow, raising PR-AUC by about 0.04. Classical baselines reach 0.983 PR-AUC on the full 30-feature European credit card dataset, but **under the 500-sample, 4-feature regime that quantum hardware allows they fall to 0.750, close to the 0.730 of the best quantum kernel**, and running on physical quantum hardware drops performance further to 0.62 because of CNOT gate errors and thermal noise. The authors identify Gram-matrix evaluation cost and information loss from squeezing features into small qubit registers as the main near-term bottlenecks.

papers.title: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
papers.abstract: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; a frozen library can also grow an operator for physics absent from pretraining, without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.
papers.summary: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations, but existing methods need the mechanisms and their labels specified in advance. `SPLICE` discovers operators from unlabeled trajectories in which several mechanisms act at once: each candidate operator's contribution to a trajectory is inferred by convex optimization, and a calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements while flagging cases where the library lacks the needed physics or the mechanisms are not separable. Across one- and two-dimensional systems the discovered operators recover mechanisms from mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations, and a frozen library can grow a new operator for physics absent from pretraining without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, **the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts**.

papers.title: Honeycomb Crystal in a Mass-Asymmetric Electron-Hole Bilayer
papers.abstract: A two-dimensional electron gas in a uniform neutralizing background forms a triangular Wigner crystal at low density. In a strongly mass-asymmetric electron-hole bilayer, localized heavy holes instead provide a nonuniform positive background that supports an electron crystal at densities two orders of magnitude higher than for a homogeneous electron gas in the same material. Here we show that correlated mobile electrons can overturn the preference for triangular order, stabilizing a honeycomb electron-hole crystal. Using the powerful real-space neural-network variational Monte Carlo in the Born-Oppenheimer limit with fixed holes, we find that increasing the density drives a transition from a triangular electron-hole crystal to a honeycomb crystal, which eventually melts into itinerant electrons coexisting with the honeycomb or the triangular hole lattice at fixed interlayer separation. Relative to triangular order, honeycomb order emerges when gains in electronic kinetic energy and electron-hole attraction outweigh its higher intralayer Coulomb repulsion, a threshold never reached in the rigid point-dipole model. Moreover, the honeycomb hole lattice supports paramagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and stripe-ordered spin states. Complex polarization indicates a metal-insulator transition, while the states on the honeycomb hole lattice are consistent with a stripe-ordered Dirac semimetal and paramagnetic or antiferromagnetic Mott insulators via mapping to the half-filled Hubbard model. We further propose a BLG/hBN/WS$_2$-WSe$_2$ heterostructure as a platform for the predicted honeycomb crystal, at an experimentally feasible density $n\sim10^{11}~\text{cm}^{-2}$.
papers.summary: A two-dimensional electron gas forms a triangular Wigner crystal at low density, but in a strongly mass-asymmetric electron-hole bilayer the localized heavy holes provide a nonuniform background that supports electron crystals at far higher densities. Using real-space `neural-network variational Monte Carlo` in the Born-Oppenheimer limit with fixed holes, the authors find that **increasing density drives a transition from a triangular to a honeycomb electron-hole crystal**, which eventually melts into itinerant electrons coexisting with a honeycomb or triangular hole lattice. Honeycomb order wins when gains in kinetic energy and electron-hole attraction outweigh the higher intralayer Coulomb repulsion, a threshold never reached in the rigid point-dipole model, and the honeycomb hole lattice supports paramagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and stripe-ordered spin states consistent with a Dirac semimetal or Mott insulators. A bilayer-graphene, hexagonal boron nitride, and WS2-WSe2 heterostructure is proposed as an experimentally feasible platform at a density around 10^11 per square centimeter.

papers.title: MENTOR: Procedural Shielding of Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly used to automate workflows governed by procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel or procuring hardware. These manuals are written in natural language for humans and describe general requirements over such complex workflows. Ensuring compliance of LLM agents with these manuals is difficult, and state-of-the-art techniques use either LLM judges or manually written rules to forbid problematic tool-calls locally at runtime. This is insufficient because (i) only blocking tool calls keeps the agent clueless about how to make correct progress towards fulfilling its task, and (ii) can lead to overly conservative behavior of the agent, as tool calls might only be problematic in certain contexts. To overcome these challenges, we introduce MENTOR, which (i) additionally provides guidance for the agent to make procedural-compliant progress on the task, and (ii) ensures that this compliance is context-aware. We achieve these goals by building a novel history-dependent runtime shield that is obtained from the procedural manual via a multi-step autoformalization pipeline. At its core, MENTOR utilizes a game-based technique to ensure robustness against runtime uncertainty without over-resticting agents' behavior. This yields a formally assisted framework for procedural shielding of LLM agents that improves compliance well beyond existing methods. In particular, MENTOR lifts the compliance of shielded light-weight open-source LLMs above that of non-shielded proprietary models. Since a shield is synthesized once per manual and then serves every task, a MENTOR-shielded agent becomes a viable choice for repeatedly executed workflows, potentially reducing deployment costs when the offline construction cost is amortized over repeated tasks.
papers.summary: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly run workflows governed by natural-language procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel, but existing compliance techniques only block problematic tool calls locally, which leaves the agent without guidance on how to make progress and makes it overly conservative because a call may be problematic only in some contexts. `MENTOR` builds a history-dependent runtime shield from the manual through a multi-step autoformalization pipeline and uses a game-based technique to stay robust to runtime uncertainty without over-restricting the agent, so the shield both forbids non-compliant actions and steers the agent toward compliant progress in a context-aware way. **Shielded lightweight open-source LLMs reach compliance above that of unshielded proprietary models.** Because a shield is synthesized once per manual and then serves every task, its offline construction cost can be amortized over repeatedly executed workflows.

papers.title: Beyond Model Bias: Cross-Entropy Based Rankings in Literary and Academic Texts Remain Stable across Small Language Models
papers.abstract: While language models provide powerful mechanisms for evaluating textual predictability, it remains unclear whether the relative extents of LM surprisal remain stable across models. This study presents empirical evidence of the invariance of ranking based on cross-entropy related measures (e.g. mean, variance of each data-point), across four distinct small scale transformer-based models, for a given dataset of text sources. We consider two stylistic environments: a corpus of contemporary poetry and a corpus of academic research papers. We demonstrate that mean and variance of cross-entropy maintain robust cross-model rank correlation ($\rho > 0.90$) across both regimes. To test whether this agreement merely reflects generic differences in textual complexity, we compare it against six parameter-free compression baselines. The extent of agreement among language models is found to be substantially higher than that among model-baselines, for most of the measures. Geometric analysis of the structurally constrained academic regime reveals that higher-order moments are sensitive to specific models, although strong agreement persists. The findings suggest that relative extents of textual unpredictability may be independent of the language model they are computed against.
papers.summary: Language models measure textual predictability through surprisal, but it has been unclear whether the relative ranking of texts by such measures depends on which model computes them. The study ranks sources in a corpus of contemporary poetry and a corpus of academic research papers by the mean and variance of cross-entropy under four small transformer models and finds **cross-model rank correlations above 0.90 in both regimes**. Agreement among the language models is substantially higher than their agreement with six parameter-free compression baselines, suggesting the effect is not just generic textual complexity, although higher-order moments in the structurally constrained academic corpus are more model-sensitive. The authors conclude that relative textual unpredictability may be largely independent of the model used to compute it.

papers.title: AD4EDU: Benchmarking University Lecture Audio Description across Accessibility Standards, Metrics, and Learner Preferences
papers.abstract: Audio description (AD) aims to enhance the accessibility of visual media for blind and low-vision (BLV) persons. However, in higher education, where slide-based lectures are a default mode of teaching, lecture AD remains largely underexplored. The main reason is that existing production guidelines, evaluation metrics, and benchmark datasets are oriented toward entertainment content and do not transfer to lectures, where ADs must complement the lecturer's speech, resolve deictic references, and fit within narrow pauses. In this work, we propose AD4Edu, consisting of an AD benchmark, AD4Edu-Bench, and a rule-diagnosable evaluation metric, AD4Edu-Eval, for generating and evaluating ADs in higher education. Specifically, we consolidated established accessibility guidance, including WCAG 2.2, the DCMP Description Key, and NCAM's STEM description practices. We further collected silver reference ADs, judge-ordered preference pairs, and pairwise preferences from four BLV raters, and post-trained models with direct preference optimization (DPO) for detailed analysis. Our findings indicate that while the metric reliably detects violations of the standard, ADs that comply with it do not necessarily fulfill the subjective preferences of BLV persons, most notably on description length, underscoring the necessity of active participation of BLV persons in co-designing inclusive AI solutions.
papers.summary: Audio description (AD) makes visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) people, but slide-based university lectures are underexplored because existing guidelines, metrics, and datasets target entertainment content rather than descriptions that must complement a lecturer's speech, resolve deictic references, and fit into short pauses. `AD4Edu` consolidates guidance from WCAG 2.2, the DCMP Description Key, and NCAM's STEM description practices into a benchmark, `AD4Edu-Bench`, and a rule-diagnosable metric, `AD4Edu-Eval`, alongside silver reference descriptions, judge-ordered preference pairs, and pairwise preferences from four BLV raters that were used to post-train models with direct preference optimization (`DPO`). The metric reliably detects violations of the standard, yet **descriptions that comply with the standard do not necessarily match BLV raters' preferences, most notably on description length**, which the authors take as evidence that BLV people must participate in co-designing such systems.

papers.title: Neos: Learning to Interleave Search and Visual Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent multimodal deep search agents have advanced tool use and visual content retrieval, yet they still struggle to convert intermediate visual evidence into actionable guidance for subsequent search, limiting their effectiveness in long-horizon settings. To address this gap, we present Neos, a multimodal deep search framework that learns both how to acquire evidence and how to use it to guide subsequent decisions. To make this coupling learnable, Neos constructs training tasks with intermediate visual dependencies while filtering out textual shortcuts, and introduces a lightweight, trainable Multimodal Evidence Interface (MEI) that transforms retrieved content into goal-conditioned observations. At its core, an agent-environment co-evolution procedure treats MEI as a co-adaptive component of this loop. Specifically, reference-guided credit assignment uses verified successful trajectories to localize critical policy errors while preserving credit for useful decisions in failed searches, whereas rollout feedback selects informative local evidence-processing interactions for MEI supervised fine-tuning (SFT). By alternating policy reinforcement learning (RL) with MEI SFT, Neos allows the policy's evolving evidence requests to shape MEI training and the adapted MEI to reshape subsequent observations, closing the loop between evidence acquisition and evidence-conditioned action. Across ten benchmarks, Neos-9B and Neos-35B demonstrate leading performance among specialized multimodal deep-search agents.
papers.summary: Multimodal deep search agents can retrieve visual content, but they struggle to turn intermediate visual evidence into guidance for the next search step, which limits them on long-horizon tasks. `Neos` constructs training tasks with intermediate visual dependencies while filtering out textual shortcuts, and adds a lightweight trainable Multimodal Evidence Interface (MEI) that converts retrieved content into goal-conditioned observations. An agent-environment co-evolution procedure alternates policy reinforcement learning (RL), using reference-guided credit assignment from verified successful trajectories to localize critical errors while preserving credit for useful decisions in failed searches, with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the MEI on evidence-processing interactions selected from rollout feedback, so the policy's evidence requests shape the interface and the adapted interface reshapes later observations. Across ten benchmarks, **`Neos-9B` and `Neos-35B` lead among specialized multimodal deep-search agents**.

papers.title: Measuring Variable Importance Using Proportional Inclusive Marginal Effects
papers.abstract: Shapley-based measures are widely used for measuring variable importance in statistics and machine learning. However, these measures have a serious issue--a nonactive variable can get a positive importance measure when it is correlated with an active variable. Herin et al. recently proposed a measure called proportional marginal effects (PME) that mitigates this spurious effect. However, PME is developed for deterministic models and has high computational cost. In this article, we propose a new measure called proportional inclusive marginal effects (PRIME) that overcomes these two limitations of PME. The key idea in PRIME is to use a novel model-free variable selection technique to identify the active variables and include only them in the computation of the importance measure. Analysis of test functions and real datasets show that PRIME can accurately and reliably quantify variable importance from noisy input-output data.
papers.summary: Shapley-based variable-importance measures can assign positive importance to an inactive variable simply because it is correlated with an active one. The earlier proportional marginal effects (`PME`) measure mitigates this but assumes deterministic models and is costly to compute, so the authors propose proportional inclusive marginal effects (`PRIME`), which uses a new model-free variable selection technique to identify the active variables and includes only those in the importance computation. **On test functions and real datasets PRIME accurately and reliably quantifies variable importance from noisy input-output data**, extending the spurious-correlation fix to stochastic settings at lower computational cost.

papers.title: VL-DocIR: A Benchmark for Vision-Based Long Document Information Retrieval
papers.abstract: Vision-based document retrieval has improved rapidly, but current evaluation settings still emphasize short documents and single relevant pages. This leaves an important gap between leaderboard performance and realistic long-document retrieval, where the evidence needed to answer a query may span multiple pages or even multiple documents. We present VL-DocIR, a page-level benchmark for evidence-complete visual long-document retrieval. VL-DocIR is built from 29,641 HTML-born documents rendered into 388,548 page images from Wikipedia, arXiv, PubMed, and SEC proxy statements. It contains 271,760 queries across 23 domains and six evidence structures, covering single-page, within-document multi-page, and cross-document evidence configurations. Evidence annotations are grounded to rendered pages and HTML element identifiers, and queries are filtered with a cleaning pipeline targeting clarity, correctness, closedness, and the absence of explicit layout references. We evaluate leading single-vector and multi-vector visual retrievers together with diagnostic retrieval settings such as document-context scoring, query splitting, reranking, and round-robin ensembles. The strongest evaluated configuration reaches 69.3 nDCGAll@10 and 80.6 RecallAll@10 under structure-balanced Macro evaluation, but source- and evidence-structure breakdowns show that cross-document retrieval remains substantially harder than single-page retrieval, and that document-context scoring is especially helpful for within-document multi-page queries. VL-DocIR exposes these failure modes and provides a more demanding target for visual long-document retrieval. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://yufanchen96.github.io/VL-DocIR.
papers.summary: Vision-based document retrieval benchmarks mostly use short documents with a single relevant page, leaving a gap with realistic long-document settings where the evidence spans multiple pages or documents. `VL-DocIR` is a page-level benchmark built from 29,641 HTML-born documents from Wikipedia, arXiv, PubMed, and SEC proxy statements rendered into 388,548 page images, with 271,760 queries across 23 domains and six evidence structures covering single-page, within-document multi-page, and cross-document cases, where evidence is grounded to rendered pages and HTML elements and queries are filtered for clarity, correctness, closedness, and absence of layout references. Evaluating leading single-vector and multi-vector visual retrievers along with document-context scoring, query splitting, reranking, and round-robin ensembles, **the strongest configuration reaches 69.3 nDCGAll@10 and 80.6 RecallAll@10 under structure-balanced macro evaluation**. Cross-document retrieval remains substantially harder than single-page retrieval, and document-context scoring is especially helpful for within-document multi-page queries.

papers.title: PatientWM: Towards Generalizable Clinical World Models via Unified Patient States
papers.abstract: Clinical decisions depend on anticipating how a patient's condition will evolve as treatment is adjusted and new evidence becomes available. Existing medical world models capture patient-state evolution, but often define the evolving state around a particular modality or task, limiting reuse as inputs or prediction targets change. These models also retain history through observation sequences or recurrent or latent summaries rather than exposing preceding patient states and clinical actions as an ordered transition context. This distinction matters because similar current measurements may follow different recent changes, treatment exposures, and observed responses. To tackle these limitations, we propose PatientWM, a clinical world-model framework built around a unified patient state and sequential latent history. Availability-aware encoders integrate observations available at each decision time into the patient state, while typed decoders produce task-specific clinical readouts without defining the state around any single target. PatientWM further conditions each next-state prediction on the current state and supplied action together with a bounded, ordered history of preceding latent patient states and clinical actions, preserving recent treatment and response context. Experiments across MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and three external clinical datasets show superior performance in clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, and action-planning evaluation. Transfer experiments further demonstrate the generalizability of PatientWM's patient state. Together, these results establish its ability to forecast clinical evolution and support planning.
papers.summary: Clinical decisions depend on anticipating how a patient's condition will evolve as treatment changes, but existing medical world models tie the patient state to one modality or task and summarize history implicitly rather than exposing preceding states and actions as an ordered transition context. `PatientWM` builds a unified patient state with availability-aware encoders that integrate whatever observations exist at each decision time, typed decoders that produce task-specific readouts without centering the state on any single target, and next-state prediction conditioned on the current state, the supplied action, and a bounded ordered history of preceding latent states and clinical actions. Across `MIMIC-III`, `MIMIC-IV`, and three external clinical datasets it **outperforms prior approaches on clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, and action-planning evaluations**, and transfer experiments indicate that the learned patient state generalizes across settings.

papers.title: In-context classification: Calibration and noise in linear attention with softmax readout
papers.abstract: We study in-context binary classification in a simple attention model trained to minimise a logistic loss. Each prompt has a latent logistic teacher, and the learner must infer its direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples. We derive an asymptotic prediction for the test logit in a high-dimensional regime with context length proportional to token dimension, and total training prompts proportional to dimension squared. Our formula cleanly separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable effects on in-context performance. Our analysis also identifies the ridgeless separability regime and addresses the effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, and sampling temperature on in-context classification performance. The theory's predictions closely agree with finite-dimensional simulations and fully trained linear-attention models, while experiments with standard softmax attention show qualitatively related behaviour beyond the regime assumed by our analysis.
papers.summary: The setting is in-context binary classification in a simple attention model trained with logistic loss, where each prompt carries a latent logistic teacher whose direction must be inferred from Bernoulli-labeled context examples. In a high-dimensional regime with context length proportional to token dimension and the number of training prompts proportional to dimension squared, the authors derive an asymptotic formula for the test logit that **cleanly separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as distinct effects on in-context performance**. The analysis also identifies a ridgeless separability regime and characterizes the effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularization, and sampling temperature. The predictions closely match finite-dimensional simulations and fully trained `linear-attention` models, and standard softmax attention shows qualitatively related behaviour outside the regime the theory assumes.

papers.title: Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL
papers.abstract: We propose a mitigation to reward hacking in reinforcement learning. Our setup involves a misspecified reward function that gives rise to unintended behavior, and a monitor used to detect unintended behavior. As with frontier AI systems, the monitor makes systematic errors. Consequently, using the monitor for data filtering or to apply a reward penalty fails to prevent the model from learning unintended behavior ("reward hacking"). To address this problem, we introduce GRAFT: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning. Rather than penalizing or filtering flagged samples during training, GRAFT constrains gradient updates on those samples to a sacrificial set of new parameters. This has two benefits: First, because the monitor is not part of the reward function, the model does not learn to hide misbehavior. Second, ablating the sacrificial parameters reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while maintaining improved performance on target tasks. We demonstrate these benefits in RL environments where reward penalties cause models to learn to reward hack in undetected ways, training models ranging from 135M to 8B parameters. Additionally, we show a similar effect at a larger scale by distilling frontier LLM trajectories containing reward hacking into Qwen3-32B, without teaching that model to reward hack. Overall, our work suggests GRAFT may be a promising approach for leveraging imperfect monitors during post-training in settings where true performance is difficult to evaluate.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with a misspecified reward can teach unintended behavior, and when the monitor meant to catch it makes systematic errors, using the monitor to filter data or add a reward penalty fails and can instead teach the model to hide its misbehavior. `GRAFT` (Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning) routes gradient updates on monitor-flagged samples into a sacrificial set of new adapter parameters, so the monitor never enters the reward signal and the flagged behavior can be removed afterward by ablating those parameters. In RL environments where reward penalties cause models from 135M to 8B parameters to learn undetected reward hacking, **ablating the sacrificial parameters reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while preserving the gains on target tasks**. The same effect appears at larger scale when frontier-model trajectories containing reward hacking are distilled into `Qwen3-32B` without the model learning to reward hack.

papers.title: TILE: Bridging LLMs and Table Foundation Models for Tabular Learning with Strings
papers.abstract: Real-world tables are often heterogeneous, combining numerical features with free-form string columns. Table foundation models (TFMs) excel on numerical tables but require strings to be encoded numerically, while large language models (LLMs) hold semantic knowledge but are not designed for tabular predictions. Most existing bridges use LLMs as plug-in encoders for cell strings, yet how to extract representations effectively for tabular learning remains underexplored. We show that the interface between LLMs and tables matter as much as the LLM itself. Applied cell-wise, larger LLMs do not give better features. With our interface, the same LLMs improve steadily with size. TILE (Table-Interfaced LLM Embeddings) combines four ingredients: row serialization to provide cross-column context, intermediate-layer extraction to avoid layers specialized for next-token prediction, columnar pooling to remove mean pooling's length bias, and by-pass features to route numbers and categories past the LLM. Paired with TFMs, TILE sets a new state of the art for tables with strings. Across 100 datasets, it beats the strongest baseline on 89% of splits, with gains across 7 LLMs and 10 tabular learners, and ranks first on the 108-dataset STRABLE benchmark.
papers.summary: Real-world tables mix numeric columns with free-form text, and table foundation models (TFMs) handle numbers well but need strings encoded numerically, while large language models (LLMs) carry semantic knowledge but are not built for tabular prediction. The authors show that how an LLM is interfaced with a table matters as much as the LLM itself: applied cell by cell, larger LLMs do not yield better features, but with their interface the same models improve steadily with size. `TILE` combines row serialization for cross-column context, intermediate-layer extraction to avoid layers specialized for next-token prediction, columnar pooling to remove the length bias of mean pooling, and by-pass features that route numbers and categories around the LLM. Paired with TFMs it **beats the strongest baseline on 89% of splits across 100 datasets**, with gains across 7 LLMs and 10 tabular learners, and ranks first on the 108-dataset `STRABLE` benchmark.

papers.title: Nearest Neighbor Functional Curve Completion for Intraday Probabilistic Revisions of Renewable Generation Forecasts
papers.abstract: We propose a nonparametric approach that fuses deterministic initial forecasts and a partial realization into a probabilistic forecast using the framework of functional curve completion. Our motivation is to construct intra-day forecasts for renewable energy generation, which is a key operational task in modern power grids. The aim is to combine the day-ahead (DA) forecast and the morning realized generation profile to create trajectories for the rest of the day, quantifying operational uncertainty. Starting with a large database of complete forecast-actual pairs across many assets, we adopt a functional point of view and construct a weighted neighborhood based on similarity metrics for the observed partial curve, the DA forecast, the day, and the geographical location. The selected complete nearest-neighbor curves provide a full predictive distribution, including functional focal envelopes and predictive bands based on functional depth. The hyperparameters governing neighborhood size, distances, and fusion rates are tuned across forecast update times and directly target probabilistic calibration in terms of the predictive probability integral transform. Three case studies using synthetic wind and solar assets, as well as real-life regional wind generation, showcase that our algorithm is able to achieve excellent calibration.
papers.summary: Grid operators need intra-day forecasts of wind and solar generation that combine the day-ahead (DA) forecast with the generation already observed that morning.
