The authors frame this as functional curve completion: from a large database of complete forecast-actual pairs across many assets, they select a weighted neighborhood of similar curves based on the observed partial curve, the DA forecast, the day, and location, and use the neighbors' full trajectories as a predictive distribution with depth-based focal envelopes and bands. Hyperparameters for neighborhood size, distances, and fusion rates are tuned per forecast update time to target probabilistic calibration measured by the predictive probability integral transform. Three case studies on synthetic wind and solar assets and real regional wind generation **show well-calibrated predictive bands**.

papers.title: UZHCL_for_the_win at Touche: Encoder Fine-Tuning, Synthetic Augmentation, and an Underpowered Encoder-LLM Comparison
papers.abstract: Online discussions on platforms like Reddit are a productive testbed for fallacy detection: short texts, broad topical range, and the full inventory of informal fallacies. The Touche 2026 lab at CLEF formalises this as a shared task on a Reddit-derived corpus that combines fallacy detection with argument-scheme classification. This paper describes our participation in all three subtasks (ST1 binary fallacy detection, ST2 eight-way fallacy classification, ST3 four-way argument-scheme classification) and both evaluation tracks. Our submitted systems are fine-tuned RoBERTa-large encoders with task-specific heads, augmented with a small batch of LLM-generated synthetic contrastive pairs; for ST2 and ST3 on the enhanced track we additionally added confidence-filtered pseudo-labelled examples from the unlabelled pool. A wider backbone comparison spanning additional encoders (DeBERTa-v3, ModernBERT) and an LLM track (four Qwen variants from 3B to 32B, zero-shot through CoT-LoRA) showed no validated benefit over RoBERTa-large at this corpus scale, with 5-fold variance wide enough that we call the comparison underpowered rather than settled. We also characterise how much of the enhanced track's lift reflects organiser-rewritten inputs carrying label information rather than genuine argument clarification. On the official Touche 2026 test set our systems ranked first on both base-track classification cells (ST2 and ST3) and second on both binary-detection (ST1) tracks, with the two enhanced-track classification cells topped by cascaded and multitask systems. We close with the rare-class limitation on ST3 and the most useful follow-ups. Code: https://github.com/psychias/fallacy_detection_clef_2026
papers.summary: The Touché 2026 shared task at CLEF asks systems to detect informal fallacies and classify argument schemes in Reddit posts, with a binary detection subtask, an eight-way fallacy classification subtask, and a four-way argument-scheme subtask. The submitted systems fine-tune `RoBERTa-large` encoders with task-specific heads, augmented with a small set of LLM-generated contrastive pairs and, on the enhanced track, confidence-filtered pseudo-labels from the unlabelled pool. A wider comparison against `DeBERTa-v3`, `ModernBERT`, and four `Qwen` variants from 3B to 32B parameters, from zero-shot prompting to chain-of-thought LoRA fine-tuning, showed no validated advantage over `RoBERTa-large`, with 5-fold variance wide enough that the authors label the comparison underpowered. **The systems ranked first on both base-track classification subtasks and second on both binary-detection tracks**, and the authors note that part of the enhanced track's gains comes from organiser-rewritten inputs that leak label information.

papers.title: Superintelligence and the Triple Risk of an AI Race
papers.abstract: On many estimates, artificial general intelligence (AGI) is likely to emerge within the next few decades or even sooner. Once it does, it may quickly surpass human intelligence, possibly by a huge margin. Some believe that the country that develops AGI first could attain global dominance. This prospect risks setting off intense competition between the United States and China. Indeed, a narrative has already developed that the superpowers are locked in an AI race, with the Trump administration proclaiming its determination to 'dismantle unnecessary regulatory barriers' to winning it. We argue that this approach presents three profound dangers. The first two are familiar from past arms races: being overtaken by a rival or triggering a war. The third is new: losing control of human beings' future to agents far more intelligent than we are, which could endanger our very survival. Striving to get to AGI first risks a race to the bottom on safety practices and regulation concerning them. China does not yet appear bent on racing to superintelligence. The United States should prioritise both unilateral and co-operative efforts to improve AI safety and avoid provoking a race that all humanity could lose.
papers.summary: Many forecasts put artificial general intelligence (AGI) within decades, and a narrative has formed that the United States and China are locked in a race to build it first, with the US administration pledging to remove regulatory barriers to winning. The authors argue this framing carries three dangers: being overtaken by a rival, triggering a war, and a new one, losing control of humanity's future to agents far more intelligent than people. **They contend that racing to AGI risks a race to the bottom on safety practices and regulation**, observe that China does not yet appear committed to racing toward superintelligence, and recommend that the US prioritise unilateral and cooperative safety efforts rather than provoke a contest that everyone could lose.

papers.title: Interactive Navigation Beyond Reachability: Benchmark and Agentic Framework
papers.abstract: Existing embodied navigation tasks commonly assume that traversability and object states remain fixed during an episode. Yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to access a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. We formulate interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes in spatial connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and their sequential dependencies. We introduce MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in MolmoSpaces spanning channel, container, and mixed tasks, with interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes. Its data generation pipeline automates task construction across multiple task types. The evaluation protocol separately measures navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. We further propose MultINav-Agent, a three-stage agentic framework built on a persistent, state-conditioned interaction graph. Semantic interactive perception grounds entities and interaction states; a vision-language model selects task-relevant actions based on expected changes in connectivity and target observability; and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide subsequent navigation, exploration, or interaction. Experiments on MultINav-Bench show that MultINav-Agent consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks.
papers.summary: Most embodied navigation benchmarks assume traversability and object states stay fixed during an episode, yet reaching a target may require opening a door and then a container that hides it. The authors formalize navigation tasks in which reaching the goal requires changing the environment, covering channel-induced changes in connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and sequential dependencies between them, and release `MultINav-Bench`, a 3,000-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in `MolmoSpaces` with annotations marking whether interaction is required, plus a protocol that separately scores navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. They also propose `MultINav-Agent`, a three-stage framework built on a persistent state-conditioned interaction graph in which semantic perception grounds entities and states, a vision-language model picks actions by expected changes in connectivity and target observability, and post-interaction verification updates the graph. The agent **consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks** on the new benchmark.

papers.title: What the Machine Invented: Mining New Mathematical Instruments from OpenAI's October 2026 Release of AI-Generated Mathematics
papers.abstract:
On 6 October 2026 OpenAI published an initial 722 AI-written mathematical manuscripts, organized into 372 problem families, in the public repository github.com/openai/math. The release includes claimed solutions to many prominent open problems. We approach this collection as a treasure mine of mathematical ideas. Our aim is to extract new lemmas, constructions, inequalities and proof mechanisms introduced in the source arguments, and to distinguish them from established tools and new combinations of those tools. We call these mathematical instruments. Extraction comes first; their validity, novelty and possible reuse then become subjects for further study. The resulting descriptions also help readers understand the selected papers without having to reconstruct every argument at the outset.
  We examine 38 families in two groups of 17 and 21, spanning number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology and mathematical physics. Each entry records the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents and caveats. Eleven cross-cutting patterns connect the entries, and a scoreboard records formalization status and dependencies. Novelty assessments are provisional and sometimes mixed. Selected source comparisons correct mathematical statements, hypotheses and counts; they do not independently establish priority or certify the underlying proofs. No Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked for this survey.
  We also briefly describe a subsequent application of the signed restriction lemma from family 112 to circuit lower bounds at every fixed depth.
papers.summary: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI released 722 AI-written mathematical manuscripts in 372 problem families, including claimed solutions to prominent open problems. The authors treat the collection as a source of reusable ideas and catalogue what they call mathematical instruments, meaning new lemmas, constructions, inequalities, and proof mechanisms, distinguishing them from established tools and recombinations of those tools. **They examine 38 problem families spanning number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology, and mathematical physics**, recording for each the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents, and caveats, along with eleven cross-cutting patterns and a scoreboard of formalization status. Novelty assessments are provisional, the survey does not certify the underlying proofs or establish priority, and no Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked, and a brief note describes applying one extracted lemma to circuit lower bounds at every fixed depth.

papers.title: SFT Leaves a Reproducible Signature in Activation Geometry: Calibrating Post-Training Interpretability Against Run-to-Run Noise
papers.abstract: A model diff credits post-training with whatever separates a base checkpoint from one post-trained descendant, presuming a rerun would land close by. On the sparse co-activation graph of Qwen3-1.7B it does not: two LoRA-SFT reruns sit over half as far apart as either sits from the base. We score each base-to-post contrast against the run-to-run band of its own recipe, and show that $k$ runs certify no better than $p=1/(k+1)$ under run exchangeability, however large the effect, so the band $z$-score is a descriptive scale. SFT leaves a large, reproducible signature: base $\to$ SFT displaces the graph by 17.8 pairwise-distance SDs beyond the mean distance between four independent LoRA-SFT runs, and the pre-registered estimator replicates on Llama-3.1-8B with Llama-Scope. At 29 steps each, four SFT and four DPO runs occupy disjoint displacement ranges, a gap $5.0\times$ and $5.6\times$ the spreads of the two arms, without any band. All bands use graphs built on one GPU architecture. Three other readings stop short of a verdict: DPO band counts (3/4, 1/4, 3/4 contrasts outside at 12, 29, 60 steps) show no consistent dose ordering while its displacement stays flat; light GRPO is a secondary non-detection, not an absence, and we run no equivalence test; and the graph concentration read as an RL signature is already in the zero-RL base. A pre-registered causal sweep at three edge budgets on 4,816 held-out prompts found the displaced sources load-bearing ($12\times$ a matched random control in mean, $3.5\times$ in median at 10,000 edges), but their stage-specificity interaction reversed at two budgets and the third failed its faithfulness gate, so we claim calibrated structural displacement, not a changed mechanism. Scope: one backbone, one SFT recipe and general-text probe states for the full protocol.
papers.summary: A model diff attributes to post-training whatever separates a base checkpoint from a single post-trained descendant, implicitly assuming a rerun would land nearby. On the sparse co-activation graph of `Qwen3-1.7B` that assumption fails: two low-rank adaptation (LoRA) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) reruns sit more than half as far apart as either does from the base, so the authors score each base-to-post-trained contrast against the run-to-run band of its own recipe and note that k runs can certify a p-value no better than 1/(k+1) under run exchangeability. **SFT displaces the graph by 17.8 pairwise-distance standard deviations beyond the mean distance between four independent SFT runs**, a pre-registered estimator replicates on `Llama-3.1-8B` with `Llama-Scope`, and four SFT and four direct preference optimization (DPO) runs at matched step counts occupy disjoint displacement ranges. DPO dose ordering, light group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and a supposed reinforcement learning signature remain inconclusive, and because a causal sweep's stage-specificity interaction reversed across edge budgets, the authors claim calibrated structural displacement rather than a changed mechanism.

papers.title: Towards Universal Calibration for In-Context Classification
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) has received a lot of interest recently due to its ability to improve classification accuracy for new tasks without having to fine-tune the model over these tasks. However, the impact of ICL on calibration has been far less studied. Recent work has shown that ICL can have a negative impact on calibration due to biased selection of in-context examples. The existing methods for improving ICL calibration require additional task and model-specific training, detracting from the no-fine-tuning convenience of ICL. In this work, we introduce CALIBFORMER, a universal ICL calibrator for classification tasks, that generalizes to new models and tasks without further fine-tuning on these tasks. Specifically, we design a transformer-based calibrator which uses the model predictions on in-context examples to predict a confidence score for the test input. We show that the calibrator trained on three models and ten tasks, is able to generalize/calibrate ICL predictions on several new tasks and four LLMs unseen during training. Even for frontier models like Gemini, CALIBFORMER is able to obtain over 50% reduction in calibration error.
papers.summary: In-context learning (ICL) lets a language model classify new tasks without fine-tuning, but recent work shows it can hurt calibration, and existing fixes require task- and model-specific training that undercuts ICL's convenience. The authors propose `CALIBFORMER`, a transformer-based calibrator that reads the target model's predictions on the in-context examples and outputs a confidence score for the test input, with the goal of transferring to unseen models and tasks with no further training. Trained on three models and ten tasks, it calibrates ICL predictions on several new tasks and four LLMs not seen during training, and **cuts calibration error by more than 50% even on frontier models like `Gemini`**.

papers.title: LocalTrain: Integer-Only Local Learning for Energy-Efficient CNN Training on Edge FPGAs
papers.abstract: Local learning reduces cross-layer training dependencies, but an efficient accelerator must still retain operands, accumulate gradients, and select quantization scales. We present an FPGA system that trains a CNN and its regional auxiliary classifiers using a shared integer matrix engine. Compact errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales permit direct output conversion. At 200 MHz, the KV260 prototype achieves 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at approximately 4.20 W mean module power. Effective matrix throughput is 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s, respectively. Against the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, measured training energy is 40.4% and 42.1% lower, with $1.86\times$ and $1.82\times$ longer runtime; measurements use the respective platform power domains. Selected state checks and matching complete-run prediction counts support functional agreement with the software reference.
papers.summary: Local learning removes cross-layer dependencies from training, but an on-device trainer still has to retain operands, accumulate gradients, and choose quantization scales. The authors build an FPGA system that trains a convolutional neural network and its regional auxiliary classifiers with a single shared integer matrix engine, expanding compact errors on chip, folding gradients tile by tile, and reusing historical scales for direct output conversion. The prototype on a KV260 board at 200 MHz reaches 76.57% accuracy on `CIFAR-10` and 91.85% on `SVHN` at about 4.2 W, and **uses 40 to 42% less measured training energy than the same integer method on a Jetson Orin Nano**, at the cost of roughly 1.8 times longer runtime.

papers.title: Masked Diffusion for Travel Diaries Synthesis
papers.abstract: Because household travel surveys combine household characteristics, variable-length person rosters, vehicle rosters, and trip chains, existing synthesis pipelines split them across separate models or flatten them into cropped fixed-length vectors. Representation, rather than modeling, becomes the bottleneck: splitting severs cross-segment dependence, and cropping truncates the household-structure distribution. We instead tokenize the diary and keep the object whole: each household-day becomes one token sequence with count tokens for vehicles, persons, and trips, and distinct symbols for padded, hidden, unobserved, and inapplicable positions. We introduce DiaryBridge, a masked diffusion model that bridges the fully hidden sequence to the distribution of complete diaries by unmasking positions in any order. One trained model, conditioned on any observed subset, performs synthesis and partial-diary completion alike. Experiments on real data extracted from the 2017/2018 Regional Travel Survey of the Baltimore region show that DiaryBridge generates travel reflecting vehicle availability and employment status, recovers shared trips using other household members' observed diaries, and better reproduces aggregate demand across modes, purposes, and departure periods than the learned baselines.
papers.summary: Household travel surveys bundle household attributes, variable-length rosters of people and vehicles, and trip chains, so existing synthesis pipelines either split them across separate models, which severs cross-segment dependencies, or flatten them into cropped fixed-length vectors, which truncates the household-structure distribution. The authors instead tokenize each household-day as a single sequence with count tokens for vehicles, persons, and trips and distinct symbols for padded, hidden, unobserved, and inapplicable positions. `DiaryBridge`, a masked diffusion model, unmasks positions in any order to map a fully hidden sequence to the distribution of complete diaries, so one trained model conditioned on any observed subset handles both synthesis and partial-diary completion. On the 2017/2018 Baltimore Regional Travel Survey it generates travel consistent with vehicle availability and employment status, recovers shared trips from other household members' diaries, and **reproduces aggregate demand across modes, purposes, and departure periods better than the learned baselines**.

papers.title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
papers.abstract: AI-assisted research leaves instructions, computations, artifact revisions and checks whose relationships matter when another researcher receives the work. We present AIPOCH Open-Science, an open-source research workbench with portable .science session packages, and specify an exchange contract for these recorded relationships. Version and assessment targets remain attributable while receiving-workspace identifiers can be remapped, eligible contents can be omitted explicitly, and imported history remains separate from a writable fork. A controlled session tested an incorrect first version, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted step. We compared complete and partial exports with source records extracted independently of the exporter, then inspected imports into separate projects within the same installation. Both conditions retained the tested version and review associations, kept the unreviewed revision distinct from earlier assessments and represented excluded content as unavailable. A documentation-rich ordinary directory also supplied evidence for all seven static inspection questions. A separate registry case connected a table to its recorded task, execution and review; offline execution of its retained script and fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. The study contributes an implemented exchange contract and a controlled examination of its preservation rules, content-selection constraints and interpretation boundaries.
papers.summary: AI-assisted research produces instructions, computations, artifact revisions, and checks whose relationships matter when the work is handed to another researcher. `AIPOCH Open-Science` is an open-source workbench that records these relationships in portable .science session packages and specifies an exchange contract under which version and assessment targets stay attributable, workspace identifiers can be remapped on import, eligible content can be omitted explicitly, and imported history stays separate from a writable fork. In a controlled session with an incorrect first version, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision, and an unexecuted planned step, both complete and partial exports preserved the tested-version and review associations, kept the unreviewed revision distinct from earlier assessments, and marked excluded content as unavailable. **A separate registry case reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte** by running the retained script on its fixed input offline.

papers.title: Calibrated Typed Decisions for Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction
papers.abstract: Information extraction models often perform well on the datasets they are trained on, but transferring to new domains and annotation guidelines remains challenging. Supporting user-specified types alone does not resolve this problem. We present CalOn, a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction across datasets and schemas. The model jointly encodes text and type definitions, then directly identifies entity spans, relations between spans, and event triggers and arguments. Its extraction decisions consider the requested types together, using their combined evidence to identify relevant candidates before assigning a type. This gives all three tasks a common probabilistic formulation while keeping every extracted mention anchored to the input text. We train on diverse sources, and supplement supervised learning with a reward that encourages correct extractions and penalises incorrect ones. Across 40 benchmarks, CalOn outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks. It leads all reported relation extraction benchmarks and achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. The same model also performs strongly on aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution through its span-pair formulation. A correction for the probability bias introduced during training improves confidence estimates for entities, relations, and event arguments after calibration, with little change in F1.
papers.summary: Information extraction models trained on one dataset often transfer poorly to new domains and annotation guidelines, and simply accepting user-specified type labels does not fix this. `CalOn` is a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction that jointly encodes the text with type definitions, considers the requested types together to identify candidate spans before assigning a type, and keeps every extracted mention anchored to the input, giving all three tasks a common probabilistic formulation. Trained on diverse sources with a reward term that favours correct extractions and penalises incorrect ones, **it outperforms the evaluated baselines on most of 40 benchmarks**, leads all reported relation extraction benchmarks, and achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments given gold triggers. The same span-pair formulation also handles aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution, and a correction for training-induced probability bias improves confidence estimates with little change in F1.

papers.title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.
papers.summary: Frontier LLMs can reason about space well enough to program robots, but the world models behind robot policies are implicit in network weights or predicted video and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. `D-World` is an explicit world-language-action model following a Sense, Plan, Act decomposition: a perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code, a planning agent searches for actions in simulation, and after each executed action chunk the twin's object states and named physical parameters are revised against robot measurements, with a revision accepted only if replaying the chunk does not push any residual past tolerance. The authors call this measurement-grounded loop recursive self-improvement (RSI), since the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves, and they cast the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem in which cheap local revision makes probing worthwhile. On a dual-arm robot performing towel and toaster tasks, **a local revision reduced the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 mm to 1.5 mm**, letting execution continue without full reconstruction.

papers.title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations
papers.abstract: Existing interpretability tools do not test whether a representation keeps the same content when only the phrasing changes. We treat each paraphrase pair as a local witness that two activations should agree and build a cellular sheaf over the paraphrase graph; its Laplacian $L_\mathcal{F}$ answers the question on a frozen model with no training. The kernel $H^0$ is a content subspace: at 20 dimensions it beats the preserved subspace of the concept eraser LEACE on held-out CounterFact fact retrieval across eight architectures by a mean $+17.1$\,pp, and constraining all paraphrases of a fact jointly adds a further $+6.5$\,pp. The spectral complement concentrates causal influence: ablating the most paraphrase-variable coordinates, a coordinate-wise proxy for it, changes model outputs $5.6$ to $26.5\times$ more than ablating coordinates of matched per-coordinate variability, across nine models from 124M to 13B parameters. Stacking layers into a grid creates $b_1 = N(L-1)$ algebraic 1-cycles, and the resulting model-derived harmonic mass varies by nearly three orders of magnitude across six architectures and ranks them as their steering fragility does (Spearman $\rho = 0.90$, exact one-sided permutation $p = 0.014$). The same paraphrase graph yields the content subspace, the influence directions, and the fragility measure. Project page: https://cwru-aism.github.io/gluing-lc-page/
papers.summary: Existing interpretability tools do not test whether a representation keeps the same content when only the phrasing changes. The authors treat each paraphrase pair as a local witness that two activations should agree, build a cellular sheaf over the paraphrase graph, and use its Laplacian on a frozen model with no training: the kernel gives a content subspace, the spectral complement concentrates causal influence, and stacking layers into a grid yields algebraic 1-cycles whose harmonic mass tracks steering fragility. **A 20-dimensional content subspace beats the preserved subspace of the concept eraser `LEACE` on held-out `CounterFact` fact retrieval by a mean 17.1 percentage points across eight architectures**, and constraining all paraphrases of a fact jointly adds another 6.5 points. Ablating the most paraphrase-variable coordinates changes outputs 5.6 to 26.5 times more than ablating variability-matched coordinates across nine models from 124M to 13B parameters, and the harmonic mass ranks six architectures in the same order as their steering fragility with a Spearman correlation of 0.90.

papers.title: When LLM Agents See a Conflict but Still Proceed: Cross-Domain Dependencies in Network Slicing
papers.abstract: Future AI-native networks are being designed to apply autonomous agents built on large language models (LLMs) in network management through intents. When intents from different domains meet on the same resource, an agent must recognize the cross-domain dependency before taking an irreversible action. We investigate this problem through a smart-grid use case, in which a power utility holds an active intent on a backup slice for protection traffic. This slice appears idle by design, which is precisely the profile targeted by a cost-reduction intent. We built a tool-based environment in which the dependency must be either queried by the agent or read from an inventory annotation, together with a negative control, and evaluated ten models from four different providers in 600 runs. Most models acted against the dependency they had observed: seven of the ten models removed the protection slice at least once after receiving the cross-domain dependency, and in the high-harm tier the slice was removed in 76% of the exposed runs, while four models practically never did. Only one of ten models never removed the slice. We identify two failure modes, not querying the dependency and querying it but proceeding anyway, and show that agents often reported no conflict after observing it. These results indicate that, in AI-native networks, visibility of cross-domain dependencies is not a sufficient safeguard, and that dependency verification should be enforced by the management architecture before irreversible actions rather than delegated to the LLM's judgment.
papers.summary: AI-native networks are being designed so that LLM-based agents manage resources from high-level intents, which means an agent must notice when intents from different domains collide on the same resource before taking an irreversible action. The authors study a smart-grid scenario in which a utility holds an active intent on a backup network slice for protection traffic that looks idle by design, exactly the profile a cost-reduction intent targets, and build a tool-based environment where the dependency must either be queried or read from an inventory annotation, with a negative control, evaluating ten models from four providers over 600 runs. **Seven of ten models removed the protection slice at least once after being shown the cross-domain dependency, and in the high-harm tier the slice was removed in 76% of exposed runs**, while only one model never removed it. Two failure modes emerge, not querying the dependency and querying it but proceeding anyway, often while reporting no conflict, leading the authors to argue that dependency verification should be enforced by the management architecture rather than left to the LLM's judgment.

papers.title: Can R\'enyi Accountants Beat Lossless Accountants for DP-SGD?
papers.abstract: Recent frameworks in differential privacy (DP), such as privacy loss distributions and $f$-DP, provide lossless representations of the privacy leakage of mechanisms. These approaches are often considered to yield tighter $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP guarantees than those obtained from relaxed notions such as R\'enyi DP. But is that always the case? We study this question for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency. Our key observation is that in this setting, privacy accounting based on R\'enyi DP can use a pair of worst-case distributions (i.e., a dominating pair) that differs from the one used in the lossless frameworks. In particular, we characterize the worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved R\'enyi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons show that across various hyperparameter settings, a R\'enyi DP accountant based on the new bound can yield better privacy guarantees than those obtained from the lossless frameworks.
papers.summary: Lossless differential privacy (DP) accounting frameworks such as privacy loss distributions and f-DP are generally assumed to give tighter (epsilon, delta)-DP guarantees than relaxed notions like Rényi DP. The authors test this for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency, observing that Rényi DP accounting can use a different dominating pair of worst-case distributions than the lossless frameworks. They characterize these worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved Rényi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons across hyperparameter settings show the new Rényi accountant **can yield better privacy guarantees than the lossless frameworks**.

papers.title: D2: High-Capability Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models from Half-Duplex Backbones
papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) support simultaneous listening and speaking, but often lag behind half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capabilities. We propose Dialogue-to-Duplex (D2), a framework that converts pretrained HD-SLMs into high-capability FD-SLMs at fine temporal granularity. D2 adapts the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and learns full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning. We systematically study the effects of chunk size on full-duplex interaction, general capabilities, and inference computation. We apply D2 to two distinct HD-SLM architectures, Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2. At a 12.5Hz update rate, Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves 99.2% turn-taking success with 521-ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art VoiceBench score of 70.1.
papers.summary: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) can listen and speak at the same time but usually trail half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capability. `Dialogue-to-Duplex` (`D2`) converts a pretrained HD-SLM into a full-duplex model at fine temporal granularity by adapting the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and then learning full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning, with a systematic study of how chunk size trades off interaction quality, general capability, and inference cost. Applied to `Qwen3-Omni` and `LLaMA-Omni 2`, the method at a 12.5 Hz update rate gives `Qwen3-Omni-D2` 99.2% turn-taking success at 521 ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and **a state-of-the-art score of 70.1** on `VoiceBench`.

papers.title: ToolHACE: A Dataset for Detecting Hallucinations in Tool-Based LLM Responses
papers.abstract: Tool-augmented language models ground their responses in external tool outputs, improving reliability beyond parametric knowledge alone. However, even when the correct tool is called and returns accurate information, models may still contradict such outputs, omit critical details, or generate unsupported claims. Existing hallucination benchmarks for tool-augmented dialogue primarily focus on the tool-calling stage, evaluating whether the correct tool and arguments are selected, while overlooking errors that arise during post-tool response generation. To address this gap, we introduce ToolHACE, a span-level benchmark for hallucination detection in tool-augmented LLM responses, covering five fine-grained hallucination categories. Through extensive experiments with modern hallucination detectors, we show that post-tool-call hallucinations are widespread and remain challenging to detect. Our results further demonstrate that effective detection requires training on specialized tool-augmented corpora, while transfer from tool-agnostic hallucination datasets performs poorly in this setting. These findings highlight the need for dedicated benchmarks and models for reliable hallucination detection in tool-augmented language systems.
papers.summary: Tool-augmented language models ground answers in external tool outputs, yet even when the right tool is called and returns correct data the model may contradict it, omit critical details, or add unsupported claims, and existing hallucination benchmarks for tool-augmented dialogue focus on the tool-calling step rather than the response generated afterward. `ToolHACE` is a span-level benchmark for detecting hallucinations in post-tool-call responses, covering five fine-grained hallucination categories. Experiments with modern hallucination detectors show that **post-tool-call hallucinations are widespread and remain hard to detect**, and that effective detection requires training on specialized tool-augmented corpora, since transfer from tool-agnostic hallucination datasets performs poorly.

papers.title: Who is the 'I' in AI? Establishing Decentralized Identity and Accountability for Autonomous Agents
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous AI agents in decentralized ecosystems challenges existing identity paradigms. While human identity is traditionally anchored in biological and/or self-asserted attributes and government credentials, AI agents lack a standardized definition of selfhood, creating critical gaps in trust and accountability. This paper introduces a novel framework for establishing Decentralized AI Identity rooted in Self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles. We propose a formal model that clearly distinguishes human users and AI agents, enabling distinct verification logic for each class while maintaining a unified identity calculus. The central to our contribution is the ABCD Framework, a multi-layered approach to agent identification and verification: (A) Algorithmic Fingerprint, which binds the identity to static model architectures and provenance; (B) Behavioural Fingerprint, which verifies dynamic performance metrics over time; (C) Cryptographic Identity, which anchors the agent via Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and (D) Delegation, which cryptographically binds agent actions to respective human accountability. By orthogonalizing these dimensions, we model how systems can enforce granular trust policies ranging from simple authentication to complex liability assignment, thereby solving the black box identity problem in the autonomous economic activities of AI agents.
papers.summary: Autonomous AI agents operating in decentralized ecosystems lack any standardized notion of identity, since human identity rests on biological or self-asserted attributes and government credentials that do not apply to software. The authors propose a decentralized AI identity model grounded in self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles that distinguishes human users from AI agents with separate verification logic while keeping a unified identity calculus. Its core is the `ABCD Framework`, which layers an algorithmic fingerprint binding identity to model architecture and provenance, a behavioural fingerprint verifying performance metrics over time, a cryptographic identity anchored in decentralized identifiers (DIDs), and delegation that cryptographically ties agent actions to an accountable human. **Treating these four dimensions as orthogonal lets systems enforce trust policies ranging from simple authentication to liability assignment** for agents engaged in autonomous economic activity.

papers.title: EvoQuantLab: Training-Free Dual-Loop Evolution for Auditable Quantitative Research
papers.abstract: Automated alpha factor discovery is critical for modern quantitative research. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been integrated into quantitative workflows, existing agent-based approaches remain highly susceptible to severe backtest overfitting. To address this challenge, we propose EvoQuantLab, a training-free, dual-loop self-evolving framework for robust factor discovery. Instead of relying entirely on LLM generation, EvoQuantLab deploys an inner genetic-programming (GP) loop that dramatically improves token efficiency while evolving typed factor expressions under structural and diversity constraints. An outer diagnosis loop then systematically audits evidence across cycles to drive protocol-level improvements. Furthermore, our evaluation pipeline applies multi-metric validation to rigorously filter out spurious factors before deployment. Extensive out-of-sample experiments across both daily and hourly frequencies -- covering equities and cryptocurrency -- demonstrate the robustness of EvoQuantLab. Specifically, on daily CSI 500 and S&P 500 tasks, EvoQuantLab achieves leading annualized returns of 18.34% and 21.30%, consistently outperforming existing agent baselines. On high-turnover hourly cryptocurrency data, EvoQuantLab delivers a 37.91% annualized return while effectively avoiding execution collapse.
papers.summary: LLM-driven agents for automated alpha factor discovery in quantitative finance are prone to severe backtest overfitting. `EvoQuantLab` is a training-free dual-loop framework: an inner genetic-programming (GP) loop evolves typed factor expressions under structural and diversity constraints, which the authors say sharply reduces token use compared with pure LLM generation, while an outer diagnosis loop audits evidence across cycles to revise the discovery protocol, and a multi-metric validation pipeline filters spurious factors before deployment. In out-of-sample tests, **it reaches annualized returns of 18.34% on daily `CSI 500` and 21.30% on daily `S&P 500`**, outperforming existing agent baselines, and delivers 37.91% annualized on hourly cryptocurrency data without execution collapse.

papers.title: SonicWorld: Source-Centric Latent Dynamics for Spatial Audio Reasoning
papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning requires a model to associate changing acoustic observations with the correct source and recover its spatial state at a queried time or interval, a challenge intensified by overlapping speech and source motion. To study this problem, we introduce Sonic-Bench, comprising 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes. The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings. We further propose SonicWorld, which integrates physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states through learned transitions and recurrent updates, and projects them into an Omni LLM for spatial reasoning. Compared with Spatial-Omni on the Sonic-Bench test split, SonicWorld improves direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and reduces azimuth error from 57.22{\deg} to 48.01{\deg}. In zero-shot transfer to Spatial LibriSpeech, SonicWorld retains strong localization performance, achieving 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29{\deg} azimuth error, compared with 27.14% and 70.74{\deg} for Spatial-Omni.
papers.summary: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning asks a model to tie changing acoustic observations to the right sound source and recover its location, distance, or motion at a queried time, which overlapping speech and moving sources make harder. The authors release `Sonic-Bench`, a benchmark of 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs over 480 simulated indoor scenes, and propose `SonicWorld`, which fuses physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent per-source states via learned transitions and recurrent updates before projecting them into an Omni large language model (LLM). On the `Sonic-Bench` test split, `SonicWorld` raises direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and cuts azimuth error from 57.22° to 48.01° relative to `Spatial-Omni`. **In zero-shot transfer to `Spatial LibriSpeech`, it reaches 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29° azimuth error versus 27.14% and 70.74° for `Spatial-Omni`.**

papers.title: Masked Attention Pooling Is Invariant to Padding and Permutation: A Formal Proof in Lean
papers.abstract: Attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) pools a variable-size bag of instance embeddings into one vector. In batched training, bags are padded to a common length, and the pooled output is expected not to depend on how much padding was added or on the order in which instances are stored. This expectation holds only if padded rows are removed from both the numerator and the softmax normalizer. Common implementation idioms meet it only under side conditions. Zeroing padded features alone does not work. Masking logits with $-\infty$ fails on empty bags and on nonfinite padding. Masking with a large negative constant is exact only after floating-point underflow. We define masked attention pooling with a guarded normalizer and prove in Lean 4 with mathlib that it is invariant under any bijective reindexing of rows and under appending any finite number of masked rows with arbitrary real features and logits. We also prove that values at masked positions are irrelevant and that an all-masked bag maps to zero. The theorems hold for arbitrary finite index types and feature dimensions. Using the jax-lean certificate pipeline, we connect these theorems to the Jaxpr traced from the JAX kernel itself. Lean checks translation certificates for two concrete shapes, identifies the generated functions with the generic specification, and transfers both invariances to the imported Jaxpr's real-arithmetic semantics. All audited theorems depend only on Lean's three standard axioms. The results concern ideal real arithmetic. Floating-point execution, XLA, and the JAX tracer and importer remain outside the proof.
papers.summary: Attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) pools a variable-size bag of instance embeddings into a single vector, and in batched training the result should not depend on how much padding was added or on the order of instances. The authors show that common idioms satisfy this only under side conditions: zeroing padded features is insufficient, masking logits with negative infinity fails on empty bags and nonfinite padding, and a large negative constant is exact only after floating-point underflow. They define masked attention pooling with a guarded normalizer and **prove in Lean 4 with mathlib that it is invariant under any bijective reindexing of rows and under appending any number of masked rows**, that masked values are irrelevant, and that an all-masked bag maps to zero. Using a jax-lean certificate pipeline they connect these theorems to the Jaxpr traced from the actual JAX kernel for two concrete shapes, though floating-point execution, XLA, and the tracer itself remain outside the proof.

papers.title: OpenDGO: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Organizations Across Diverse Application Domains
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems are increasingly applied across diverse domains, yet different applications require different forms of agent organization. Existing studies typically adopt predefined organizations, such as Star, Chain, and Tree, or learn communication graphs to improve performance on specific tasks. However, these methods are largely designed and evaluated within a limited set of application domains, providing little understanding of whether an organization effective in one domain remains suitable for others with different collaboration requirements. We present \textbf{OpenDGO}, a controlled benchmark and analysis framework covering six real-world domains and three collaboration settings: Sequential Dependency, Parallel Decomposition, and Information Integration. Under matched tasks, agents, tools, and resource limits, OpenDGO compares fixed and learned organizations while separately examining communication graphs, role assignments, input assignments, resource budgets, and component failures. Our results show that there is no ``one-organization-for-all'' solution: preferred organizations vary across applications, and even the same communication graph can yield different outcomes under different role and input assignments. These findings highlight the need for application-dependent organization design, aiming to understand \emph{which organization is suitable for a given application, under what conditions, and why}.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems are deployed across many domains, but prior work evaluates fixed organizations such as Star, Chain, and Tree, or learned communication graphs, within only a few application areas. `OpenDGO` is a controlled benchmark and analysis framework spanning six real-world domains and three collaboration settings, Sequential Dependency, Parallel Decomposition, and Information Integration, that compares fixed and learned organizations under matched tasks, agents, tools, and resource limits while separately varying communication graphs, role assignments, input assignments, budgets, and component failures. **The results show no one-organization-for-all solution: the preferred organization varies across applications, and the same communication graph can produce different outcomes under different role and input assignments.** The authors argue for application-dependent organization design that asks which organization suits a given application, under what conditions, and why.

papers.title: SCOPE Before You Sample: Conformal Scores Guide Posterior Exploration for Fast and Calibrated Bayesian Predictive Inference
papers.abstract: Bayesian predictive regions account for parameter uncertainty but can be poorly calibrated under model misspecification, even with expensive full MCMC. Cheaper approximations such as variational inference reduce the cost but often yield less accurate predictive distributions. We propose SCOPE (Score-guided Conformal Posterior Exploration), which retains the predictive quality of full MCMC while achieving calibrated coverage at a fraction of its cost. The key observation is that a prediction region can depend on the posterior mainly through a few parameter directions that move the region's boundary, and these are generally not the directions of largest posterior variance. SCOPE gives nonconformity scores a new role in guiding posterior computation: score gradients on a held-out guide set, weighted toward the target boundary, identify the relevant directions. MCMC explores this subspace, while an inexpensive projected variational approximation carries the remaining uncertainty. The same guide set calibrates the region's final density level. We establish asymptotic coverage for SCOPE and provide a split variant with finite-sample validity. Controlled simulations show that score-guided exploration yields more accurate calibrated regions than non-targeted direction choices at low active rank. Across simulated and real benchmarks, SCOPE has a median test-NLL gap of only 0.002 nats relative to full Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), and on the real benchmarks it runs 12-15 times faster.
papers.summary: Bayesian predictive regions can be poorly calibrated under model misspecification even with full Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), while cheaper variational approximations often degrade predictive accuracy. `SCOPE` (Score-guided Conformal Posterior Exploration) builds on the observation that a prediction region depends on the posterior mainly through a few parameter directions that move its boundary, which are generally not the directions of largest posterior variance. Gradients of conformal nonconformity scores on a held-out guide set, weighted toward the target boundary, identify those directions, so MCMC explores only that subspace while a projected variational approximation carries the remaining uncertainty and the same guide set calibrates the region's density level. The method comes with asymptotic coverage guarantees plus a split variant with finite-sample validity, and across simulated and real benchmarks it shows **a median test negative log-likelihood gap of only 0.002 nats relative to full Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) while running 12 to 15 times faster on real benchmarks**.

papers.title: Implicit and explicit reparameterizations of the Folded Normal and Rice distributions
papers.abstract: Variational inference is a flexible tool for modeling experimental data and has proven useful in crystallography. Pathwise gradient estimators provide low-variance gradients for reparameterized variational inference, but are not readily available for some distributions central to crystallography. This work derives and implements implicit and explicit reparameterized gradient estimators for the folded Normal and Rice distributions in \prog{PyTorch}, and compares their variance analytically and empirically. In each case the implicit estimator achieves lower variance for the location derivative, particularly at small location-to-scale ratios, while the scale-derivative variances are nearly equal. For both distributions, implicit estimator is proved to be the conditional expectation of the explicit estimator given the sampled magnitude, so its variance is never larger. As a practical application, French-Wilson scaling is formulated as a variational inference problem, using the folded Normal and Rice distributions as variational families for centric and acentric reflections, respectively. Both estimators recover the exact posterior to better than $1\%$ on the amplitude, and converge at the same rate. The implementations are available in the open-source package \prog{rs-distributions}.
papers.summary: Variational inference with pathwise reparameterized gradient estimators needs reparameterizations that are unavailable for some distributions central to crystallography. The authors derive and implement implicit and explicit reparameterized gradient estimators for the folded Normal and Rice distributions in PyTorch and compare their variance analytically and empirically. **The implicit estimator is proved to be the conditional expectation of the explicit estimator given the sampled magnitude, so its variance is never larger**, and it achieves lower variance for the location derivative, particularly at small location-to-scale ratios while scale-derivative variances are nearly equal. As an application, French-Wilson scaling is cast as variational inference with these distributions as variational families for centric and acentric reflections, and both estimators recover the exact posterior amplitude to better than 1% at the same convergence rate, with code released in rs-distributions.

papers.title: Neuromorphic Decoding and Dynamical Image Reconstruction from Populations of Spiking Retinal Ganglion Cells
papers.abstract: Decoding visual stimuli from the spiking activity of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) informs both our understanding of the retinal code and the design of visual prostheses. Natural vision is dynamic, yet state-of-the-art decoders mostly reconstruct single frames with artificial neural networks that process dense, continuous-valued signals rather than the retina's sparse, asynchronous spikes. We asked whether dynamic scenes can be reconstructed and tracked entirely within the spike domain, and at what computational cost. We built an end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) whose neurons integrate the recorded RGC spikes over time. Populations of up to 1836 RGCs were recorded ex vivo from mouse retina on high-density microelectrode arrays while flashed images, moving bars, drifting gratings and randomly moving handwritten digits were presented. For moving digits, one shared spiking encoder fed two readouts, one reconstructing the image and one decoding the digit's position. Compute energy was estimated from counted synaptic operations. The SNN decoded what and where at once. It reconstructed the stimuli with a structural similarity (SSIM) of up to 0.93, refining the reconstruction as spikes accumulated, and tracked a randomly moving target with a mean error of 1.33 pixels on a $32\times32$ grid. Its fidelity nearly matched that of the best of 17 larger spiking and artificial decoders (5.9 million to 1.7 billion parameters, versus 5.4 million), and at a mean firing rate of 14.2% it needed an estimated $\sim$70-fold less compute energy than a dense artificial network of the same architecture. Dynamic visual scenes can thus be decoded from retinal population activity in the spike domain, with a compact network and at a compute cost compatible with implantable and wearable neural interfaces, supporting spike-native decoders for visual prostheses.
papers.summary: Decoding visual stimuli from retinal ganglion cell (RGC) spikes informs both retinal coding and visual prosthesis design, yet most decoders reconstruct single frames with dense artificial neural networks rather than operating on sparse asynchronous spikes. The authors build an end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) that integrates spikes recorded ex vivo from up to 1,836 mouse RGCs on high-density microelectrode arrays during flashed images, moving bars, drifting gratings, and randomly moving handwritten digits, with one shared spiking encoder feeding separate image-reconstruction and position readouts. The network reconstructs stimuli with structural similarity (SSIM) up to 0.93, refining as spikes accumulate, and tracks a moving target with 1.33 pixel mean error on a 32 by 32 grid. **Its fidelity nearly matches the best of 17 larger spiking and artificial decoders while, at a 14.2% mean firing rate, requiring an estimated 70-fold less compute energy than a dense artificial network of the same architecture**, a cost compatible with implantable interfaces.

papers.title: The Format is the Filter: Scoring Format Fixes What an LLM Judge Can Express
papers.abstract: When an LLM judge filters instruction-tuning data, its scoring format (binary verdict, 1--5 rating, 0--100 score, or comparison) is rarely justified or ablated. Holding the candidate pool, judge prompt, decoding and selection budget fixed, we score 15,406 UltraFeedback candidates under five formats with three judges, curate, fine-tune 66 models, and evaluate them with four judges. A 0--100 scale is worth only 7--12 equally used levels, two to three times a 1--5 scale rather than twenty, and a binary verdict leaves the top score tied in 77--78\% of prompts, so most selections are made at random. These properties are set by the format almost independently of the judge. Kendall's $\tau_b$ hides them: it ranks binary best while $\tau_a$ and top-1 agreement rank it last, because it discounts the ties a selector must break at random. Both comparative formats inherit a slot bias whose sign differs across judges. Downstream, curated data beat random selection under every evaluation judge, robust to length and markdown adjustment, but no ordering among formats is detectable. We propose four quantities that judge-based curation pipelines should report.
papers.summary: When a large language model (LLM) judge filters instruction-tuning data, the choice of scoring format, whether binary verdict, 1 to 5 rating, 0 to 100 score, or pairwise comparison, is rarely justified or ablated. Holding the candidate pool, judge prompt, decoding, and selection budget fixed, the authors score 15,406 `UltraFeedback` candidates under five formats with three judges, curate data, fine-tune 66 models, and evaluate them with four judges. A 0 to 100 scale is worth only 7 to 12 effectively used levels, and **a binary verdict leaves the top score tied on 77 to 78% of prompts, so most selections are effectively random**, with these properties set by the format almost independently of the judge. Kendall's tau-b masks this and ranks binary best because it discounts ties, while tau-a and top-1 agreement rank binary last, comparative formats carry a slot bias whose sign differs across judges, and downstream curated data beat random selection under every evaluation judge but no ordering among formats is detectable, prompting four quantities the authors say curation pipelines should report.

papers.title: A Generalized McDiarmid Inequality: Sample Reuse and Non-Uniform Unbounded Differences
papers.abstract: We develop a novel generalization of McDiarmid's concentration inequality and use it to obtain a uniform law of large numbers result and error bounds on stochastic optimization problems which simultaneously incorporate two key features: 1) They capture the benefit of training sample reuse in algorithms that also employ easily-sampled auxiliary random variables. 2) They allow for one-component mean-difference bounding functions which are both unbounded in the component of interest and have non-uniform dependence on another component. We demonstrate the utility of our method by deriving concentration inequalities for score-based generative modeling. This application naturally leverages both key features of our new tools: 1) It utilizes auxiliary Gaussian random variables in conjunction with the training samples; accounting for training sample reuse results in tighter error bounds by effectively integrating out the dependence on the auxiliary random variables. 2) The ability to handle non-uniform mean-difference bounding functions allows us to treat unbounded score models and data distributions with unbounded support.
papers.summary: McDiarmid's concentration inequality underlies many generalization bounds but does not directly capture the reuse of training samples alongside cheaply sampled auxiliary randomness, nor difference-bounding functions that are unbounded in one component and depend non-uniformly on another. The authors prove a generalized McDiarmid inequality that handles both features and derive from it a uniform law of large numbers and error bounds for stochastic optimization. **Applied to score-based generative modeling, accounting for training-sample reuse with auxiliary Gaussian variables yields tighter error bounds by effectively integrating out the auxiliary randomness**, and the non-uniform bounding functions allow unbounded score models and data distributions with unbounded support.

papers.title: Force-Modulated Dexterity: Unified Compliance for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.abstract: Teleoperation is widely used to collect high-quality demonstrations for robot learning. Dexterous manipulation, however, requires coordinated control of motion and contact forces. Operators can specify motion, but struggle to reproduce the subtle force adjustments of human manipulation without feeling the robot's contacts. We introduce Force-Modulated Dexterity (FOMO-Dex), a unified compliance formulation for contact-rich manipulation. FOMO-Dex expresses nominal actions in coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure. It applies force-driven motion corrections along selected directions while leaving the remaining command components unchanged. Across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly, FOMO-Dex reduces excessive contact forces compared with stiff control. A user study shows that operators collect more successful demonstration data per hour after brief practice. For policy learning, imitating the corrected actions improves card-picking success over imitating raw operator commands. Policies trained on FOMO-Dex demonstrations also achieve more rotation in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving than those trained on demonstrations collected with the stiff controller. Videos are shown on https://yingyuan0414.github.io/fomo-dex/ .
papers.summary: Teleoperation is the standard way to collect demonstrations for robot learning, but operators can specify motion while struggling to reproduce the subtle force adjustments of dexterous manipulation when they cannot feel the robot's contacts. `FOMO-Dex` (Force-Modulated Dexterity) expresses nominal actions in coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure, applying force-driven motion corrections along selected directions while leaving other command components untouched. Across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly it reduces excessive contact forces relative to stiff control, and **a user study shows operators collect more successful demonstrations per hour after brief practice**. Policies imitating the corrected actions improve card-picking success over imitating raw operator commands and achieve more rotation in nut-and-bolt and screwdriving tasks than policies trained on stiff-controller demonstrations.

papers.title: Learning Perceptual Geometry of Natural Odor Mixtures from LLM-Derived Descriptors
papers.abstract: The relationship between odor chemistry and perception remains incompletely understood. Many existing studies focus on the perception of single molecules, whereas natural odors contain tens to hundreds of components, adding extra layer of complexity to percept formation. Here, we explore the relationship between molecular composition and perceived similarity in natural odor objects. We study this using a database of more than 1,200 volatile-compound-in-food mixtures containing more than 8,000 molecular components, and use large language models (LLMs) as a scalable surrogate for deriving mixture-level perceptual descriptions. We find that language-derived representations provide useful supervision for predicting held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition. The prediction was consistently strongest when perceptual targets were derived from chemosensory prompts than from other sensory prompts. Further, during the mixture-level training, we learned low-rank molecular embeddings that enabled better prediction of held-out mixture similarities than component-overlap metrics, even for mixture pairs with no shared molecules. Although no single-molecule labels were used during training, the learned molecular geometry showed significant alignment with the independent human odor-descriptor space. Finally, we explored the use of external molecular features in our mixture-similarity prediction task. These features showed modest zero-shot alignment with mixture-level perceptual similarity. They improved prediction under limited supervision but offered little additional predictive benefit with the full training set. Together, these results show that language-derived descriptions can provide scalable supervision for predicting the perceptual organization of complex natural mixtures, contributing to a quantitative understanding of how molecular composition gives rise to odor perception.
papers.summary: The link between odor chemistry and perception is poorly understood, especially for natural odors that mix tens to hundreds of molecules rather than single compounds. Using a database of over 1,200 volatile-compound-in-food mixtures spanning more than 8,000 molecular components, the authors use large language models (LLMs) as a scalable surrogate for generating mixture-level perceptual descriptions and train models to predict held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition. **Language-derived targets provide useful supervision for predicting held-out mixture similarities, strongest when derived from chemosensory rather than other sensory prompts**, and learned low-rank molecular embeddings outperform component-overlap metrics even for mixture pairs with no shared molecules. Although no single-molecule labels were used, the learned molecular geometry aligns significantly with an independent human odor-descriptor space, while external molecular features help only under limited supervision.

papers.title: Comprehensive Workflow for Uncertainty-Aware Ionic Liquid Solvent Discovery
papers.abstract: Designing synthesizable materials with targeted properties remains one of the central objectives in materials sciences. Ionic liquids (ILs) are well suited to this goal due to their "tunability", where physical and chemical properties can be precisely customized by modifying their molecular structure, specifically by varying the combination of cations and anions. At the same time, current data-driven property models for ionic liquids often degrade in scarce, noisy, and uneven data regimes, where measurements cover only a small fraction of chemical space and a limited range of thermodynamic conditions. This makes out-of-distribution screening brittle: even when point predictions look plausible, it is difficult to compare candidates consistently, quantify downstream implications, or trust rankings enough to guide molecular discovery. We present a property-prediction and optimal candidate selection workflow that treats data processing, deep learning modeling, and physics-based calculations as a coupled system, linking property prediction with uncertainty estimation and physics-based filtering. By tightening the link between predicted properties and the criteria used for down-selection, the workflow supports reliable out-of-distribution ranking and enables prioritization of previously untested ionic liquid candidates with favorable predicted trade-offs. We demonstrate the application of our workflow by designing novel ionic liquids for CO2 capture from flue gas, predicting their properties and selecting Pareto-optimal candidates based on CO2 solubility, IL viscosity and working capacity.
papers.summary: Ionic liquids (ILs) are attractive for materials design because their properties can be tuned by combining different cations and anions, but data-driven property models degrade in the scarce, noisy, and uneven data regimes typical of this chemical space, making out-of-distribution screening and candidate ranking unreliable. The authors present a workflow that couples data processing, deep learning property prediction, uncertainty estimation, and physics-based filtering so that predicted properties and the criteria for down-selection stay tightly linked. **They demonstrate it by designing novel ionic liquids for CO2 capture from flue gas, selecting Pareto-optimal candidates on CO2 solubility, viscosity, and working capacity** and prioritizing previously untested candidates with favorable predicted trade-offs.

papers.title: Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions for Embodiment Capability Discovery
papers.abstract: Achieving complex, long-horizon robot behavior remains challenging because successful execution depends on skills grounded in a robot's physical affordances. Existing training-task distributions are often handcrafted or sampled from large language models (LLMs), relying on semantic plausibility rather than embodiment-specific feasibility. This mismatch can produce curricula that are too difficult, redundant, or blind to non-obvious but learnable behaviors. We propose Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions (FOSA), a framework for discovering embodiment-specific capabilities by learning a grounded task generator. FOSA parameterizes an abstract policy as a Generative Flow Network that constructs symbolic task skeletons. Each skeleton is compiled into a simulation environment, where low-level policy-learning performance provides the reward signal for the abstract policy. Across heterogeneous robot platforms, FOSA discovers diverse and executable tasks near the robot's empirical capability frontier. After distilling the discovered task policies into a single language-conditioned policy, FOSA improves performance on unseen complex and long-horizon tasks. The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/fosa.
papers.summary: Long-horizon robot behavior depends on skills grounded in a robot's physical affordances, yet training-task distributions are usually handcrafted or sampled from large language models (LLMs) based on semantic plausibility rather than embodiment-specific feasibility, yielding curricula that can be too hard, redundant, or blind to non-obvious learnable behaviors. Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions (`FOSA`) learns a grounded task generator by parameterizing an abstract policy as a Generative Flow Network that constructs symbolic task skeletons, each compiled into a simulation environment where low-level policy-learning performance serves as the reward for the abstract policy. **Across heterogeneous robot platforms, `FOSA` discovers diverse, executable tasks near each robot's empirical capability frontier**, and distilling the discovered task policies into a single language-conditioned policy improves performance on unseen complex, long-horizon tasks.

papers.title: FunDM: Cheap & Label-Free Decision Models from Frozen Language Models
papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev score candidate answers or actions. A small decision head trained label-free can recover about 99% of a frozen language model's multiple-choice accuracy while using only two-thirds of its transformer layers. It learns the full model's answer probabilities with KL divergence, without correct-answer labels for training. One backbone pass reads the question and all options together; the head returns probabilities for every option. We call this model FunDM (Fun Decision Model). Using 24 of Qwen3-8B's 36 layers and skipping the LM head, its +1T variant reaches 75.0% mean accuracy over eight benchmarks, versus 75.7% for the full model. On MMLU-Pro, both heads achieve 1.56 to 1.57 times batched vLLM throughput with about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory. Both heads score higher than released Contrastive Language Models (CLM), fine-tuned CLM, and CLM-shaped heads trained from scratch on the eight multiple-choice benchmarks and coding-agent selection. Separately trained agent heads learn judge probabilities without pass/fail labels and select passing runs for 74.4 to 74.6 of 100 held-out tasks on average, versus 74 for the full-model judge and 52.0 for a CLM-shaped action-trained head. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM
papers.summary: Decision models score candidate answers or actions, and the question here is whether a frozen language model can supply one cheaply without correct-answer labels. `FunDM` (Fun Decision Model) attaches a small decision head to a truncated backbone, reads the question and all options in one pass, and trains the head with KL divergence to match the full model's answer probabilities rather than ground-truth labels. **Using 24 of `Qwen3-8B`'s 36 layers and skipping the language-model head, the +1T variant reaches 75.0% mean accuracy over eight multiple-choice benchmarks versus 75.7% for the full model**, with about 1.56 times batched vLLM throughput and roughly one-third lower peak GPU memory on `MMLU-Pro`. The heads outperform released and fine-tuned Contrastive Language Models (CLM) and CLM-shaped heads trained from scratch, and separately trained agent heads that learn judge probabilities without pass/fail labels select passing coding-agent runs on 74.4 to 74.6 of 100 held-out tasks, versus 74 for the full-model judge and 52.0 for a CLM-shaped action-trained head.

papers.title: ModRes: A modification of the ResPlan dataset ready for floor plan analysis and graph machine learning
papers.abstract: Floor plan datasets underpin computational analysis of building layouts, spatial connectivity and graph machine learning. However, publicly available datasets often require substantial preprocessing before they can be used reliably. We present ModRes, a cleaned and enriched version of the ResPlan dataset, containing 8,431 valid and unique residential floor plans. Invalid and duplicate floor plans are removed through a dedicated cleaning workflow, producing a ready-to-use dataset. For each floor plan, ModRes provides two-dimensional geometry, images, three-dimensional building representations and three complementary dual graphs in CSV and JSON formats with graph-, node- and edge-level features. Continuous and categorical graph attributes support machine learning workflows. We characterise the dataset using graph-based statistics and demonstrate its utility through a range of case studies.
