Evaluating individual vs. compositional strengths across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, we find them largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method-family) settings, individual strength does not translate into compositional advantages, and the coupling is weakest among general-purpose models that practitioners are most likely to deploy. Standalone benchmarks are therefore often poor proxies for models' value in collaborative systems. We then propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome produced by the system as a whole, rather than the policy's correctness in isolation. The leave-one-out baseline in Shapley values cancels under a group policy gradient, so this needs no additional rollout cost beyond RL on the collaborative system's outcome and never requires running a coalition without the policy. Across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings, lifting collaborative performance by +4.0 to +5.4 pts on average (~3x the gain of baselines), up to +13.1 pts.
papers.summary: Language models are increasingly deployed in ensembles, debates, routers, and other multi-model systems, yet they are benchmarked alone. The authors define a model's compositional strength as its Shapley value in a cooperative game over coalitions from a model pool, approximated by a leave-one-out contribution that needs n+1 rather than 2^n system evaluations, and measure it across five pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets. **In 12 of 15 pool and method-family settings, individual strength does not predict compositional advantage**, and the link is weakest for the general-purpose models practitioners most often deploy. They then propose compositional reinforcement learning (`C-RL`), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system on the reward of the whole system's output; because the leave-one-out baseline cancels under a group policy gradient it adds no extra rollout cost, and it produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings with average gains of 4.0 to 5.4 points, roughly three times the baselines.

papers.title: BrowseSafe++: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detection Across Web Contexts, Languages, and Browser Views
papers.abstract: Browser agents need to make decisions and execute actions on behalf of users while consuming untrusted webpages, creating opportunities for malicious instructions embedded in webpages to redirect legitimate tasks. We introduce BrowseSafe++, which extends BrowseSafe from 14,719 pages to 38,675 pairs of pages. Most of its prompt injections were observed in the wild on production websites. We keep each injection unchanged and rewrite the sensitive parts of the page around it to protect privacy. Each attacked page has a clean copy of the same page as its control. Both are provided as HTML, Markdown, an accessibility tree, and a screenshot. Every pair includes a user task and its expected answer. The benchmark includes twelve types of websites, from news articles to shared documents and forums, with 24 attack types appearing in 18 different locations on a page. We use these paired pages to train BrowseSafe-Guard, two 0.8B-parameter detectors for text and screenshots. Both achieve higher F1 scores than the detector based on frontier models, while keeping false-positive rates on benign pages and inference cost low. BrowseSafe-Adapt revises benchmark injections from browser-agent feedback, and attacks that succeed on only a few percent of tasks when replayed directly reach up to 95.41% success once adapted.
papers.summary: Browser agents read untrusted web pages while acting on a user's behalf, so instructions planted in a page can hijack the task. `BrowseSafe++` extends `BrowseSafe` from 14,719 pages to 38,675 page pairs, most containing injections observed in the wild on production sites, each paired with a clean control copy of the same page and provided as HTML, Markdown, accessibility tree, and screenshot along with a user task and expected answer; it spans twelve website types, 24 attack types, and 18 page locations. The paired data trains `BrowseSafe-Guard`, two 0.8B-parameter detectors for text and screenshots, **which score higher F1 than a frontier-model-based detector while keeping false positives and inference cost low**. A companion method, `BrowseSafe-Adapt`, revises injections using browser-agent feedback, raising attacks that succeed on only a few percent of tasks when replayed directly to up to 95.41% success.

papers.title: Selective Inference for Clustering Under Unknown Covariance
papers.abstract: Unsupervised clustering is widely used to discover underlying group structure, after which researchers often seek to validate these groups via post-hoc hypothesis testing on the population means. However, using the same data both to form clusters and to test for a difference in means inflates the Type I error rate. Recent work in selective inference has proposed solutions when the underlying data are drawn from a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a known covariance matrix or an unknown isotropic covariance matrix. We propose a new selective test for the difference in means between two clusters that provably controls the Type I error rate under an arbitrary unknown covariance matrix. Our test statistic does not require estimating the feature covariance matrix; instead, it leverages a Monte Carlo sampling procedure over the set of orthogonal matrices. We show that this new selective test can be computed efficiently, and we derive closed-form solutions when clusters are formed using k-means or hierarchical clustering. In simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed p-value controls the selective Type I error rate and achieves substantial power, and we illustrate its application on gene expression and drug review data sets.
papers.summary: Clustering data and then testing whether the discovered clusters have different means on the same data inflates the Type I error rate, and prior selective-inference fixes assume a Gaussian model with known covariance or unknown isotropic covariance. The proposed selective test for the difference in means between two clusters **provably controls the Type I error rate under an arbitrary unknown covariance matrix** without estimating that covariance, instead using Monte Carlo sampling over the set of orthogonal matrices. The test is computationally efficient, with closed-form solutions when clusters come from k-means or hierarchical clustering. Simulations show it controls selective Type I error with substantial power, and it is demonstrated on gene expression and drug review data.

papers.title: Distilling Text LMs into Speech-to-Speech LMs by Matching Internal Text Predictions
papers.abstract: Text language models (LMs) acquire broad linguistic and factual capabilities through large-scale pretraining, while comparable capabilities remain difficult to learn from speech alone. Recent work has shown that knowledge distillation from pretrained text LMs offers a promising way to transfer their linguistic and factual capabilities to speech models. However, existing distillation approaches have largely focused on speech-input, text-output models. This idea has yet to be explored for {\it speech-to-speech} models, which operate on both speech input and speech output. In this work we introduce a speech-to-speech pretraining method that creates an internal text interface for knowledge transfer while preserving the speech-only input and output. The model first consumes speech context without its transcription, switches to text prediction, and then uses the predicted text to lead future speech generation word by word. It also provides an interface for knowledge distillation: the internal text predictions can be directly distilled from the base text LM. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of text LM distillation to a speech-to-speech LM. Under matched training conditions, the proposed sequence construction substantially improves the generative perplexity of spoken continuations over speech-only and interleaved speech-text models, approaching the performance of a text-leading inner-monologue model with external ASR prompt transcription. More importantly, distillation improves factual performance under both text and speech evaluation, indicating better retention of knowledge from the base text language model.
papers.summary: Speech-to-speech language models struggle to learn the linguistic and factual knowledge that text language models (LMs) acquire from large-scale pretraining, and existing distillation from text LMs has targeted only speech-input, text-output models. The proposed pretraining recipe builds an internal text interface: the model consumes speech context without a transcript, switches to predicting text, and then uses its own predicted text to lead speech generation word by word, so those internal text predictions can be distilled directly from the base text LM. Under matched training conditions this sequence construction substantially lowers the generative perplexity of spoken continuations compared with speech-only and interleaved speech-text models, approaching an inner-monologue model that relies on external ASR transcripts. **Distillation further improves factual performance under both text and speech evaluation**, indicating better retention of the text model's knowledge.

papers.title: An FPGA-Based Spiking Neural Network for Spatiotemporal Pattern Learning and Classification
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient spatiotemporal pattern recognition at the edge, but efficient deployment and on-device adaptation require specialized hardware. In this work, we present an FPGA implementation of multilayer SNNs for spatiotemporal pattern classification, in which both inference and training take place on the same hardware. Our design adopts a temporal-forward-only training algorithm that avoids the memory and latency overhead associated with traditional Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT). A mixed-precision scheme balances training stability with resource efficiency, and architectural optimization maximizes hardware and memory utilization. We further identify and resolve hazards that arise when inference and learning share the same memory, including port conflicts between the forward and backward access patterns and read-after-write dependencies in floating-point potential accumulation. Experimental evaluations on MNIST and five multivariate time-series classification datasets demonstrate that, with fully on-chip training, our SNN model achieves accuracy comparable to SNN or LSTM trained with BPTT. Compared to CPU and GPU based implementations, our FPGA design delivers 2.5 to 6 times higher throughput while consuming an order of magnitude less energy per sample.
papers.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) suit energy-efficient spatiotemporal pattern recognition at the edge, but on-device training and inference need dedicated hardware. The design implements multilayer SNNs on an FPGA with both inference and training on-chip, using a temporal-forward-only learning rule that avoids the memory and latency costs of Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT), a mixed-precision scheme for stable yet cheap training, and fixes for port conflicts and read-after-write hazards that arise when forward and backward passes share memory. On `MNIST` and five multivariate time-series classification datasets, fully on-chip training reaches accuracy comparable to SNNs or LSTMs trained with BPTT. **Relative to CPU and GPU implementations, the FPGA delivers 2.5 to 6 times higher throughput at an order of magnitude less energy per sample.**

papers.title: Efficient Fr\'echet Distributional Decoder Alignment for Latent Generative Models
papers.abstract: Fr\'echet Distributional (FD) objectives provide an effective distribution-level signal for post-training generative models. For latent generative models, however, existing FD-based post-training methods optimize only the latent generator while keeping the decoder frozen: the decoder is trained on reconstruction latents obtained from real images but deployed on generator-produced latents at generation time. When these latent distributions differ, this \textbf{decoder train-generation mismatch} means that the decoder is deployed on inputs drawn from a distribution it was not directly trained on. We introduce \textbf{Fr\'echet Distributional Decoder Alignment (FDDA)}, an efficient post-training method that freezes the latent generator and directly optimizes the decoder on generation-time latents using an FD objective. A single epoch of FDDA consistently improves gFID and gFDr$^6$ across diverse flow-based and autoregressive latent generative models. Across all 11 evaluated models, FDDA reduces gFDr$^6$ by 34.0-59.6\% from the original pretrained models and provides a further 10.2-57.2\% reduction after generator-side FD post-training. FDDA also reduces total wall-clock time by factors of $3.6\times$-$328.7\times$ relative to generator-side FD post-training across these models. These results show that generator-side post-training alone does not exhaust the benefits of FD optimization, and that further gains can be obtained by adapting the decoder at substantially lower cost.
papers.summary: Fréchet Distributional (FD) objectives are used to post-train generative models at the distribution level, but for latent generative models existing methods tune only the latent generator while the decoder stays frozen, even though the decoder was trained on reconstruction latents from real images and is deployed on generator-produced latents. Fréchet Distributional Decoder Alignment (`FDDA`) does the reverse: it freezes the generator and optimizes the decoder on generation-time latents with an FD objective. **A single epoch of FDDA cuts the gFDr^6 metric by 34.0 to 59.6% across all 11 flow-based and autoregressive models tested**, and by a further 10.2 to 57.2% on top of generator-side FD post-training, while also improving gFID. FDDA is 3.6 to 328.7 times cheaper in wall-clock time than generator-side FD post-training.

papers.title: From Orbit Matching to Docking: A Hierarchical Reinforcement-Learning Approach to Multiphase Rendezvous Trajectory Design
papers.abstract: As the complexity of space missions increases, autonomous spacecraft guidance must accommodate transitions between mission phases with distinct dynamics, objectives, and constraints. Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are particularly challenging because they span multiple operating regimes, from orbital-scale matching and far-range approach to close-range maneuvering and terminal docking. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches generally address only a subset of this sequence or rely on manually defined switching conditions between controllers. This study presents a hierarchical reinforcement-learning framework for autonomous, three-degree-of-freedom RPO that spans the complete trajectory from orbit matching to docking. Five specialized policies are trained for orbit matching, far-range approach, mid-range approach, close-range approach, and docking. A learned high-level manager policy then selects among these phase-specific controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state. The hierarchical approach is evaluated over the full end-to-end rendezvous sequence and compared with a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic to assess trajectory performance and transition behavior. Training and inference metrics are also analyzed for the individual phase policies and the complete hierarchical system.
papers.summary: Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) span regimes with distinct dynamics and constraints, from orbit matching through far-, mid-, and close-range approach to docking, and prior reinforcement-learning work covers only parts of the sequence or hand-codes the switching between controllers. The framework trains five phase-specific policies for three-degree-of-freedom RPO plus a learned high-level manager that selects among them based on the current spacecraft state. **The hierarchical system is evaluated over the full end-to-end rendezvous sequence and compared against a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic** for trajectory performance and transition behavior, with training and inference metrics reported for each phase policy and the complete system.

papers.title: Assessing the Performance of AI Models in Misinformation Detection Using Predefined Social Noise Constructs
papers.abstract: Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated content that often obscure meaningful discourse, a phenomenon conceptualized as social noise. While existing misinformation detection methods primarily focus on factual verification, they largely overlook the role of social noise in amplifying misinformation. This study assesses the performance of six text-based models and a graph neural network (GNN) in mitigating the effects of misinformation using predefined social noise constructs. The dataset consists of 500,000 tweets collected from the X platform using the Ukraine hashtag during the Russia-Ukraine conflict from March 2024 to March 2025. Advanced machine learning models achieve strong performance, with accuracies ranging from 79.94% to 97.17%. RoBERTa demonstrates the highest performance, with an accuracy of 97.17%, Cohen's kappa of 0.9660, MCC of 0.9660, and AUC of 0.9977. The GNN achieves an accuracy of 64.52% and an AUC of 0.899, demonstrating performance above random-chance classification by exploiting the relational structure between tweets. All text-based models achieve kappa values greater than 0.75, indicating substantial overall agreement. Explainable AI analysis using LIME reveals that 89.6% of predictive weight is attributed to contextual features rather than isolated keywords. The findings highlight that integrating social noise into AI pipelines enhances misinformation detection and supports more effective mitigation strategies in large-scale social media environments.
papers.summary: Misinformation detectors usually focus on factual verification and ignore social noise, the flood of user-generated content that obscures meaningful discourse and amplifies misinformation. The study evaluates six text-based classifiers and a graph neural network (GNN) on 500,000 tweets collected under the Ukraine hashtag between March 2024 and March 2025, using predefined social noise constructs as labels. `RoBERTa` performs best, **reaching 97.17% accuracy** with Cohen's kappa and MCC of 0.9660 and AUC of 0.9977; text models range from 79.94% to 97.17%, and the GNN reaches 64.52% accuracy with AUC of 0.899 by exploiting relations between tweets. `LIME` explanations attribute 89.6% of predictive weight to contextual features rather than isolated keywords.

papers.title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems promise a new axis for scaling inference: rather than having one agent think longer or sample more attempts, a task is split across many agents that work in parallel and coordinate. However, in practice, more agents can easily produce duplicate work, coordination failures, and higher costs. We therefore formulate team design as a compute allocation problem: starting from a solo agent, where should additional inference compute go to reach the reward-cost Pareto frontier? We build a minimal multi-agent harness from the ground up and trace this frontier by varying, one at a time, the workflow stage at which a lead delegates to its workers (planning, implementation, or verification), the models that form the team, and the number of workers. On ProgramBench, teams outperform solo agents but cost three to seven times as much. With the right compute allocation, however, a heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost. This efficiency stems from three findings. First, planning is the most valuable use of workers: in a homogeneous team whose lead decides how many workers to spawn, a lead that delegates only planning to its workers, and then implements and verifies the code itself, matches the reward of a lead that delegates to workers throughout planning, implementation, and verification, at half the cost. Second, cheap models pay off as planners but not as implementers: a strong lead with cheap planners recovers 47.5% of the reward gain of an all-strong team for only 13.9% of its additional cost, whereas cheap implementers lower reward. Third, planners keep improving reward as the team grows, whereas implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers. Together, our results offer a guide to spending an agent budget where it counts, given the task, cost, and latency constraints a user has.
papers.summary: Splitting a task across many coordinating agents is a new axis for scaling inference compute, but naively adding agents produces duplicated work, coordination failures, and higher cost. The authors treat team design as a compute allocation problem, build a minimal multi-agent harness, and trace the reward-cost Pareto frontier on `ProgramBench` by varying which workflow stage the lead delegates (planning, implementation, or verification), the mix of models, and the number of workers. Teams beat solo agents but cost three to seven times more; **a well-allocated heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost**. Three findings drive this: delegating only planning matches full delegation at half the cost, cheap models work as planners but hurt as implementers, and planners keep adding reward as the team grows while implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers.

papers.title: REA: From Correct LLM Judgments to Safe Decision Delivery
papers.abstract: Generative safety guards must classify requests correctly and return outputs that applications can parse. Reasoning guards can improve classification accuracy while producing outputs that applications cannot parse. When applications cannot extract a correct prediction, fallback handling can allow harmful requests or block safe ones. We introduce Resolve--Express--Act (REA), a framework that traces judgments through parsing and fallback to application actions. Experiments on classifiers and safety guards show that correct predictions can appear in incorrectly formatted outputs. Parsing the safety verdict preserves the reasoning guard's accuracy advantage, while stricter explanation requirements reject additional correct predictions. Accepting formatting variations recovers most rejected correct predictions. Held-out tests confirm that output requirements and generation limits affect whether correct predictions can be parsed. In our fail-open replay, matching the parser to the output and fixing formatting reduced the fraction of harmful requests allowed despite correct guard judgments from 95.5% to 0%. A fixed-output comparison shows that model-based extraction can preserve guard verdicts, but is not automatically reliable; deterministic normalization already repairs the observed native-format failures. Fallback replay shows that the same correct prediction can lead to different safety actions depending on the parser and fallback policy, including allowing requests the guard correctly identifies as harmful.
papers.summary: Generative safety guards must not only judge requests correctly but emit outputs an application can parse, and reasoning guards in particular can improve accuracy while producing verdicts that fall through to fallback handling, which may allow harmful requests or block safe ones. Resolve-Express-Act (`REA`) traces each judgment through parsing and fallback to the resulting application action. Experiments show correct predictions often sit inside malformed outputs: parsing just the verdict preserves the reasoning guard's accuracy edge, stricter explanation requirements reject more correct predictions, and tolerating formatting variations recovers most of them. **In a fail-open replay, matching the parser to the output and fixing formatting reduced harmful requests allowed despite correct guard judgments from 95.5% to 0%**, while deterministic normalization repaired the observed native-format failures and model-based extraction proved not automatically reliable.

papers.title: Structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics for partial differential equations
papers.abstract: Machine learning surrogates of partial differential equations (PDEs) are commonly trained on data generated by numerical solvers. Therefore, the training data obey not the PDE but the modified equation of the numerical scheme, and the test loss, computed on data from the same solver, cannot distinguish a model that learned the physics from one that learned the discretization error. Here, we show that the difference is nevertheless visible in the trained model. We propose a suite of structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics, simple scores that measure whether a learned model respects one known property of the physics, such as a conserved quantity, a symmetry or a Hamiltonian structure, without access to the training data or the governing equation. Over five systems, the diagnostics track the error with respect to the true dynamics with a rank correlation of up to $0.94$, while the test loss is uncorrelated or anti-correlated with it. For the Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries and Navier-Stokes equations, the diagnostics separate numerical schemes that the test loss ranks as equivalent, including schemes of the same order. order.
papers.summary: Machine-learning surrogates for partial differential equations (PDEs) are trained on numerical-solver output, which obeys the scheme's modified equation rather than the true PDE, so test loss on same-solver data cannot tell a model that learned the physics from one that learned the discretization error. The proposed structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics are simple scores that check whether a trained model respects a known physical property such as a conserved quantity, a symmetry, or a Hamiltonian structure, requiring neither the training data nor the governing equation. **Across five systems the diagnostics track error against the true dynamics with a rank correlation of up to 0.94**, while test loss is uncorrelated or anti-correlated with it. For the Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries, and Navier-Stokes equations, the diagnostics separate numerical schemes that test loss ranks as equivalent, including schemes of the same order.

papers.title: A Time-Synchronous Prequential Evaluation Framework for Next-Week Student Disengagement Prediction from Moodle LMS Logs
papers.abstract: Retrospective evaluation of early-warning models may not reflect information available when predictions are issued and outcomes become observable. We developed a time-synchronous prequential framework for online prediction of next-week student disengagement, operationalised as inactivity onset, from Moodle logs. Ordered by calendar time, models were updated only with available outcomes and remained unchanged for all predictions at each prediction cutoff; development, calibration and evaluation were chronologically separate. We compared stochastic gradient descent logistic regression (SGD-LR), online sequential extreme learning machine (OSELM) and echo state network (ESN) across predictive performance, fixed, frozen and rolling threshold policies, calendar-time variation and four behavioural feature sets. Held-out evaluation comprised 49,329 predictions with 37.68% inactivity-onset prevalence. Discrimination was similar (average precision 0.665-0.679; ROC-AUC 0.755-0.774). OSELM had the highest recall, SGD-LR the highest precision and specificity, and ESN the highest Matthews correlation coefficient and balanced accuracy. Lower thresholds increased recall and alert volume, whereas rolling adaptation did not improve MCC over frozen thresholds. Weekly performance and calibrated-probability distributions varied without sustained deterioration. During model selection, cumulative-and-temporal features achieved the highest individual-set AP, with modest gains from combining all feature groups. These findings indicate that streaming early-warning evaluation should consider calibration, threshold-dependent performance, alert burden and calendar-time variation alongside aggregate discrimination.
papers.summary: Early-warning models for student disengagement are usually evaluated retrospectively, which can leak information that would not have been available when a prediction was actually issued. The authors build a time-synchronous prequential framework over Moodle learning-management-system logs, in which models are updated only with outcomes already observable at each weekly cutoff and development, calibration, and evaluation are chronologically separated. Comparing `SGD-LR` (stochastic gradient descent logistic regression), `OSELM` (online sequential extreme learning machine), and `ESN` (echo state network) on 49,329 held-out predictions, they find **similar discrimination across models (average precision 0.665 to 0.679)** but different precision-recall tradeoffs, with threshold choice driving alert volume and rolling threshold adaptation offering no gain over frozen thresholds. They argue that streaming evaluations should report calibration, alert burden, and calendar-time variation alongside aggregate metrics.

papers.title: VeriPIE: Checkable Query Plans and Evidence-Guided Selection for Text-to-SQL
papers.abstract: Financial Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance and model risk management (MRM) emphasize independent validation, transparency, and effective challenge of AI-generated computations. Text-to-SQL translates natural-language questions into Structured Query Language (SQL), but queries that agree on one database can still express different computations. We present VeriPIE, a neurosymbolic framework combining language-model generation with symbolic checks. It ensembles direct SQL generation with QuerySketch, a structured plan language checked by a backend implemented in Lean, a theorem prover and programming language. Plan diagnostics guide repair before SQL generation, while execution agreement and bounded searches for distinguishing databases inform candidate selection. These checks expose malformed plans and hidden disagreement without proving agreement with the user's intent. In single-run experiments on the complete Spider development set, VeriPIE achieves 72.05% test-suite accuracy (745/1,034), compared with DeepEye's 65.67% (679/1,034). Its two-query shortlist covers 78.43% (811 questions), compared with 74.66% for DIN-SQL (772) and 69.05% for DeepEye (714). On BIRD, VeriPIE reaches 68.90% execution accuracy and 73.73% two-query coverage. The central benefit is reviewable evidence about the generated computation: explicit plan checks, repair diagnostics, and concrete disagreements that support safer financial analysis.
papers.summary: Text-to-SQL systems can produce queries that return the same answer on one database yet encode different computations, which is a problem for financial model risk management (MRM) settings that demand independent validation of AI-generated calculations. `VeriPIE` is a neurosymbolic framework that ensembles direct SQL generation with `QuerySketch`, a structured plan language whose plans are checked by a backend written in the `Lean` theorem prover; plan diagnostics drive repair before SQL generation, and execution agreement plus bounded searches for databases that distinguish candidates guide final selection. **On the `Spider` development set it reaches 72.05% test-suite accuracy versus 65.67% for `DeepEye`**, with a two-query shortlist covering 78.43% of questions, and it reaches 68.90% execution accuracy on `BIRD`. The checks surface malformed plans and hidden disagreement among candidates but do not prove agreement with the user's intent.

papers.title: Longitudinal Learner Participation Profiling in Online Learning: Heterogeneous Consensus Clustering under Unequal Observation Windows
papers.abstract: Learning management system traces are clustered to identify participation profiles, but unequal observation windows may cause profiles to reflect duration rather than participation alone. Using 16,448 complete learner--course sequences from 4,599 learners across 152 courses at a South African public university, we evaluated eight participation measures. All remained related to observation-window length even when expressed as rates or shares. Course-grouped adjustment reduced these relationships. Five retained measures were evaluated using K-means, Gaussian mixtures, Ward agglomerative clustering and K-medoids, with standardised measures and principal-component summaries. Evidence supported a broad two-profile grouping and a more detailed adjusted four-profile consensus: Gradually declining, Early-concentrated, Cyclical variable and Sustained active. Profile membership accounted for 2.87% of the variation in duration in the primary consensus, versus 38.18% using original measures. Mean assignment support was 0.739; 8.35% of assignments fell below 0.50, with greatest uncertainty in Sustained active. Two week-by-week sequence analyses agreed strongly with each other but only modestly with the four-profile consensus, indicating that the profiles combined multiple aspects of participation rather than distinct sequence patterns. Profiling should therefore assess duration effects, compare clustering methods and participation summaries, and report assignment consistency.
papers.summary: Clustering learning-management-system traces into participation profiles can be confounded by unequal observation windows, so that profiles mostly reflect how long a learner was observed. Using 16,448 learner-course sequences from a South African public university, the authors show that all eight candidate participation measures remain correlated with window length even as rates or shares, apply course-grouped adjustment, and run `K-means`, Gaussian mixtures, Ward agglomerative clustering, and `K-medoids` on the retained measures. The adjusted four-profile consensus (gradually declining, early-concentrated, cyclical variable, sustained active) **explains only 2.87% of variation in duration, versus 38.18% with unadjusted measures**, though 8.35% of assignments have support below 0.50 and week-by-week sequence analyses agree only modestly with the profiles. They recommend that profiling studies test for duration effects and report assignment consistency.

papers.title: A Sense of Proprioception in Language Models
papers.abstract: In humans, proprioception corresponds to the sense of self-movement or position, e.g. understanding the position of one's arm. This sense is often less well-understood and in popular understanding sometimes conflated with introspection. But, notably, proprioception is a separate sense, with dedicated receptors and verifiable outcomes. On the other hand though, language models cannot observe their own internal states during training (and for example answer the question which experts activated in a certain layer of an MoE) and so cannot accurately report on them. Yet, such information is, by virtue of being internal to the model, both accessible, and readily constructed into verifiable signals. We argue that this provides the basis for a digital analog of proprioception. As such, we train models through SFT and on-policy training to equip them with this ability. We show that modern models can be trained to understand a range of subtypes of proprioception, such as routing decision awareness, token entropy, decision depth or logit lens information, without affecting model capabilities. We then run these models through a broad evaluation of situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality, to evaluate in what ways access to proprioception changes model behavior.
papers.summary: Language models cannot observe their own internal states during training, so they cannot accurately answer questions such as which experts fired in a given mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer, even though that information is internal to the model and can be turned into verifiable training signals. Drawing an analogy to human proprioception, the sense of one's own body position and movement, the authors use supervised fine-tuning and on-policy training to teach models to report on subtypes of their own computation, including routing decisions, token entropy, decision depth, and logit-lens readouts. **Modern models can learn to report on these internal signals without degrading their general capabilities**, and the authors then evaluate how this access changes model behavior along situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality.

papers.title: Foundation Models for Event Prediction Across Heterogeneous Event Logs
papers.abstract: Event logs are ubiquitous across real-world domains, including business processes, manufacturing workflows, healthcare, and many other operational systems. Yet event logs can differ substantially in their event semantics, label spaces, interaction patterns, and temporal scales, making it difficult to build a single foundation model that generalizes directly to previously unseen systems. We address this challenge with the Foundation Event Predictor (FEP), a simple and scalable in-context architecture that performs next-event prediction through learned, event-level nonparametric inference. Causal self-attention encodes context and target histories into key and query representations, respectively, while the observed next context events are encoded as values. Cross-attention then performs learned, relevance-weighted aggregation of next-event outcomes over all context transitions, allowing the entire nonparametric prediction procedure to be expressed as standard attention operations and efficiently parallelized with modern kernels such as FlashAttention. To promote cross-system generalization, we introduce permutation-robust embedding learning and random fixed embeddings to decouple event IDs from persistent semantics, together with empirical quantile transforms and robust normalization to handle diverse temporal scales. We pretrain FEP on 696 real-world event datasets spanning heterogeneous event systems and evaluate it on 50 held-out datasets unseen during pretraining. Across these datasets, FEP generalizes effectively to new event systems without parameter adaptation, frequently approaching the performance of strong models trained separately on each target dataset while substantially outperforming existing foundation-model baselines, particularly on challenging prediction tasks.
papers.summary: Event logs from business processes, manufacturing, healthcare, and other operational systems differ in event semantics, label spaces, and temporal scales, which makes a single next-event foundation model hard to build. The `Foundation Event Predictor` (`FEP`) frames next-event prediction as learned nonparametric inference expressed entirely in attention: causal self-attention encodes context and target histories into keys and queries, observed next events become values, and cross-attention performs relevance-weighted aggregation over all context transitions, so the whole procedure runs on standard kernels such as `FlashAttention`. Permutation-robust embedding learning, random fixed embeddings, and quantile-based time normalization decouple event IDs and timescales from persistent semantics. **Pretrained on 696 real-world event datasets and evaluated on 50 unseen ones, `FEP` often approaches models trained separately per dataset without any parameter adaptation** and substantially outperforms existing foundation-model baselines.

papers.title: Merit: Making every modality earn its contribution in multimodal attention decoding
papers.abstract: More than 1.5 billion people have hearing loss. When several people talk at once, hearing aids amplify every voice alike. Auditory attention decoding (AAD) aims to solve this by reading a listener's brain signals to find the attended talker, letting the device amplify only them. A real device will not see the brain alone; smart glasses and earbuds also track eyes, head, and scene. These behavioral signals help, as people often look at who they listen to. However, they show where a listener looks, not whom they hear. A decoder relying heavily on them fails when a listener cannot move their head or listens without looking - exactly when a brain-based device is needed. A multimodal decoder must use these signals without letting them replace the electroencephalogram (EEG). Accuracy alone cannot show whether it does. We present MERIT, a decoder and evaluation method asking: how much accuracy does each input earn? MERIT shuffles each input stream across test examples, measures the accuracy drop, and splits the result across streams using Shapley values. It also blocks two shortcuts: candidate audio is checked before training so it cannot reveal the answer, and the scoring function cannot beat chance if it ignores the brain. On a public dataset with EEG, eye tracking, head motion, and scene video, MERIT improves on the published benchmark, reaching 0.82 four-way accuracy within listeners and 0.74 on unseen listeners (chance is 0.25). The measurement reveals what accuracy hides: adding behavioral streams raises overall accuracy but almost halves the brain's share of it. On two other datasets, the same tests find a label imbalance in a widely used benchmark and flag results that accuracy alone would report as brain decoding.
papers.summary: Auditory attention decoding (AAD) reads a listener's brain signals to identify which of several simultaneous talkers they are attending to, so a hearing aid can amplify only that voice. Real devices also carry eye, head, and scene sensors that correlate with attention but reveal where someone looks rather than whom they hear, so a decoder that leans on them fails exactly when brain decoding is needed. `MERIT` is a multimodal decoder plus an evaluation method that shuffles each input stream across test examples and attributes the resulting accuracy drop to streams via Shapley values, while blocking shortcuts such as candidate audio that leaks the answer. On a public dataset with electroencephalogram (EEG), eye tracking, head motion, and video it reaches 0.82 four-way accuracy within listeners and 0.74 on unseen listeners, but **adding behavioral streams raises accuracy while nearly halving the EEG's share of it**, and the same tests expose a label imbalance in a widely used benchmark.

papers.title: C{\AE}NL: Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning with Objective-Aligned Representation Control
papers.abstract: Active learning changes the representations used to acquire subsequent labels. We study this interaction through Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning (C{\AE}NL), which separates acquisition, Dynamic Collapse Regularization (DCR), and its coefficient policy. DCR penalizes a normalized within-class to between-class scatter residual above a frozen reference, with a separate class-separation safeguard. Fixed, scheduled, deterministic-feedback, and learned-feedback policies apply this objective. The analysis establishes scatter invariances, conditional local descent, and coefficient bounds, and shows why clean geometry alone cannot guarantee input robustness. Six-seed classification comparisons are complemented by a 104-run study with separate control selection and ten-seed evaluations on each of two backbones. At 60% annotations on ImageNet-100, entropy acquisition with DCR and MACC-Lite reaches 73.420 +/- 0.512% accuracy on ResNet-50 and 73.086 +/- 0.397% on ResNet-18 (mean +/- seed SD), exceeding entropy alone by 1.742 and 1.834 percentage points. Both gains survive Holm correction under paired-t and exact sign-flip tests, with unchanged feedback settings across backbones. Independently tuned constants attain slightly higher mean accuracy; the paired comparisons establish neither adaptive superiority nor equivalence. Separate six-seed spectral studies yield a small fixed-regularization C4 loss reduction, worse CIFAR-10 diffusion FID, and inconclusive AudioCaps captioning effects. Earlier classification studies find near-zero AutoAttack accuracy at L-infinity radius 8/255 and no added benefit from learned control. The results support the evaluated combined classification treatment and identify the task dependence of geometry-informed regularization.
papers.summary: Active learning reshapes the feature representations that are then used to choose the next labels, and this interaction is rarely controlled. `CÆNL` (Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning) separates the acquisition rule from `Dynamic Collapse Regularization` (`DCR`), which penalizes normalized within-class to between-class scatter above a frozen reference with a class-separation safeguard, and from the policy that sets the DCR coefficient, which can be fixed, scheduled, or driven by deterministic or learned feedback. **At 60% annotations on `ImageNet-100`, entropy acquisition with DCR and `MACC-Lite` reaches 73.4% on `ResNet-50` and 73.1% on `ResNet-18`, about 1.7 to 1.8 points above entropy alone**, with gains surviving Holm-corrected paired tests across ten seeds. Spectral studies on diffusion, captioning, and adversarial robustness are small, negative, or inconclusive, and the authors frame the regularizer's benefit as task dependent.

papers.title: YUBI-Real2Sim: 3DGS Scene Verification for Reliable Policy Evaluation
papers.abstract: Evaluating VLA policies on real robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce, making real-to-sim simulation essential for scalable evaluation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables rapid real-to-sim scene generation, the reconstruction quality required for reliable policy evaluation remains unquantified. In particular, policies relying on wrist-mounted fisheye cameras (e.g., YUBI handheld gripper data) are heavily exposed to visual artifacts (holes, floaters) in wide-angle views, directly degrading task performance. To address this, we present YUBI-Real2Sim, a unified framework for 3DGS-based scene reconstruction and real-to-sim policy evaluation under dual fisheye wrist views. We develop an integrated pipeline combining 200-degree fisheye camera capture, 3DGS training, 3D foundation models for object modeling, and MuJoCo-based physical simulation, reproducing the observed real-world policy ordering in eight of nine scene-task comparisons. Using this framework, we construct a benchmark across two bimanual robot platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and dual pi0.5-based policies. This systematically measures real-to-sim rank agreement and evaluates policy sensitivity against counterfactual 3DGS artifacts (ceiling holes, floaters, warping) and capture disturbances. We further analyze whether novel-view quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability under a scene-held-out evaluation protocol. The results show task-dependent performance and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction, highlighting the need to assess reconstruction quality when using Real2Sim for policy evaluation. These results do not yet establish a generally reliable scene-acceptance rule. Project Page: https://yubi-real2sim.airoa.io.
papers.summary: Evaluating vision-language-action (VLA) robot policies on physical hardware is slow and hard to reproduce, and while 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes real-to-sim scene reconstruction fast, nobody has quantified how much reconstruction quality is needed for simulated evaluations to be trustworthy, especially for policies using wide-angle wrist cameras that are sensitive to holes and floaters. The authors build a pipeline combining 200-degree fisheye capture, 3DGS training, 3D foundation models for object modeling, and `MuJoCo` physics, then construct a benchmark across two bimanual platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and two `pi0.5`-based policies that measures real-to-sim rank agreement and sensitivity to injected artifacts and capture disturbances. **The pipeline reproduces the real-world policy ordering in eight of nine scene-task comparisons**, but novel-view quality scores are only a weak predictor of ranking reliability under a scene-held-out protocol, and the authors do not yet offer a general scene-acceptance rule.

papers.title: Enhanced Detective: A Dual-Stage Proactive Defense Against Internal Poisoning Attacks in Financial Fraud Detection Using Federated Learning
papers.abstract: With recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the adoption of distributed learning paradigms such as Federated Learning (FL) has emerged. In simple terms, FL enables multiple entities to collaboratively train AI models without sharing local data. The FL paradigm is particularly valuable in privacy-sensitive settings, such as financial services, because it enables institutions to collaboratively improve fraud-detection models while keeping sensitive transaction data local. However, FL schemes are prone to security vulnerabilities, where malicious clients can poison local data or model updates and degrade the global model, and hence the performance of the resulting model might be affected. Therefore, in this work, we propose Enhanced Detective, a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that combines Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), distance-based update filtering, and FedMedian aggregation. Experiments on an imbalanced credit card dataset evaluate targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds. With 40% malicious clients, Enhanced Detective achieves an AUPRC of 0.796 and a Recall of 0.847.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) lets financial institutions jointly train fraud-detection models without sharing transaction data, but malicious participants can poison their local data or model updates to degrade the shared model. `Enhanced Detective` is a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that filters client updates using Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) and distance-based outlier detection before combining the survivors with `FedMedian`. In experiments on an imbalanced credit card fraud dataset under targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds, **the method sustains an AUPRC of 0.796 and recall of 0.847 with 40% of clients malicious**.

papers.title: Box-WAM: Box Trajectories as Compact State Representations for World Action Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) are a category of policy models that ex- plicitly predict both actions and future world states. They have been shown to outperform action-only models across various robotic manipulation tasks. How- ever, representing the future with full-frame video prediction can be computation- ally expensive during both training and inference. This raises a central question: what compact state representation preserves the planning and supervision bene- fits of future prediction? In this paper, we propose BoxWAM, which replaces dense future frames with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant ob- jects. By explicitly imagining object-centric future motion, our method provides a lightweight prediction target that captures the key physical changes induced by robot actions. We show that box trajectory prediction substantially reduces com- putational cost while improving action prediction performance, suggesting that object-centric compact states can serve as an efficient alternative to video-based world action modeling for robotic manipulation. Result videos can be found on https://box-wam.github.io
papers.summary: World action models (WAMs) predict future world states alongside actions and outperform action-only policies on manipulation tasks, but generating full future video frames is expensive at both training and inference time. `BoxWAM` replaces dense frame prediction with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant objects, so the policy imagines object-centric future motion as a lightweight target that still captures the physical changes caused by the robot's actions. **Box trajectory prediction substantially cuts computational cost while improving action prediction accuracy**, suggesting compact object-centric states can stand in for video-based world action modeling in robotic manipulation.

papers.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
papers.abstract: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune.
papers.summary: Large-model training recipes are hand-tuned for one model, cluster, and workload, and existing automated tuners search fixed knob spaces while only checking that a job runs, missing configurations that silently change what is being trained. `ATTUNE` is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe unattended within a user-set GPU-hour budget, diagnosing each run, changing one lever at a time guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and shipping a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate that checks for objective-altering settings and compares the loss curve against the baseline. **On held-out models at 64 to 128 GPUs it raises mean throughput by 6.7% on `Llama-3.1-405B` and 33.9% on `GLM-4.5` over the strongest public recipe**, beats `OptiCo`, Bayesian optimization, and random search under a common budget, and its gate rejects no legitimate run while catching 16 of 24 faulty ones. The authors release the code and `TrainingThroughputBench`, a leaderboard of the fastest verified recipes for mixture-of-experts models up to 744B parameters.

papers.title: Towards Green AI: Evaluating Energy Efficiency for Quantized LLM Inference
papers.abstract: While it is known that quantization of large language models (LLMs) reduces memory usage via lower-bit weights, studies quantifying the resulting impact on energy usage and carbon intensity are scarce. We present the first unified evaluation of weight-only quantization strategies for LLM inference across varying input/output lengths and GPUs, highlighting differences in energy efficiency in addition to accuracy degradation and runtime. We study quantized inference on Llama 2 7B, Phi 3.5 Mini Instruct, OLMo 1B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Qwen 2.5 14B across GLUE MNLI, MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K datasets, evaluating 10 post-training quantization (PTQ) strategies on NVIDIA H100, A6000, A100, and L4 GPUs. We identify a novel trend showing that quantization techniques tend to exhibit peak energy efficiency relative to full-precision baselines when inputs are sufficiently long and outputs are short. Furthermore, we show that quantization strategies become marginally more energy-efficient relative to full-precision models as batch sizes increase, though gains are modest. Notably, fused-kernel implementations such as EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8 offer the highest energy savings, up to 4x compared to FP32 on short text generation, with negligible accuracy loss. Finally, we observe that energy usage closely tracks runtime on our evaluated benchmarks, indicating that, in practice, latency optimization can serve as a reliable proxy for reducing the environmental footprint of LLM services. We conclude with suggested directions for strategically selecting low-carbon quantization strategies based on specific inference requirements.
papers.summary: Quantization is known to shrink large language model (LLM) memory footprints, but its effect on inference energy use and carbon intensity has rarely been measured. The authors evaluate ten post-training quantization (PTQ) strategies on `Llama 2 7B`, `Phi 3.5 Mini Instruct`, `OLMo 1B`, `Qwen 2.5 7B`, and `Qwen 2.5 14B` across `MNLI`, `MMLU`, `HumanEval`, and `GSM8K`, on NVIDIA H100, A100, A6000, and L4 GPUs, varying input and output lengths and batch sizes. Quantized models are most energy-efficient relative to full precision when inputs are long and outputs short, gains grow only modestly with batch size, and **fused-kernel int8 implementations such as `EETQ` and `Bitsandbytes` save up to 4x energy versus FP32 on short generation with negligible accuracy loss**. Energy closely tracks runtime, so latency optimization serves as a reliable proxy for reducing an LLM service's environmental footprint.

papers.title: Everyone Was Right: Lexical Representations in Language Models Are Both Abstract and Holistic
papers.abstract: Lexical representations can encode both abstract information and information specific to particular contexts. We investigate how these forms of information are organized in language models by decomposing contextual word representations into item, class, and word-class interaction components. Across six pretrained transformers and two linguistic categories, we find that the interaction is consistently present, grows across layers, and contains information associated with both item and class. Unlike the nearly orthogonal item and class effects, the interaction overlaps with both and encodes class information beyond the shared class effect. An interaction also emerges in artificial-language learners even when the input contains only additive structure. Together, these findings show that lexical representations combine abstract information with structure specific to particular word-class combinations.
papers.summary: Word representations in language models can carry both abstract, context-independent information and information tied to particular contexts, and how these are organized is unresolved. The authors decompose contextual word representations into item, class, and item-class interaction components and analyze them across six pretrained transformers and two linguistic categories. **The interaction component is consistently present, grows across layers, and overlaps with both item and class effects while encoding class information beyond the shared class effect**, unlike the nearly orthogonal item and class components themselves. An interaction also emerges in artificial-language learners trained on purely additive input, supporting the view that lexical representations are simultaneously abstract and holistic.

papers.title: TacitVLA: Reasoning Vision-Language-Action Models Without Reasoning Latency
papers.abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models improve when they reason in text before acting, but every action that conditions on that text must wait for autoregressive decoding. `TacitVLA` keeps the reasoning supervision during training but lets the action expert never attend to the reasoning generated for the current call, on the premise that the supervision already improves the shared backbone; on long-horizon tasks where reasoning text serves as episodic memory, each entry can be generated during execution rather than before it. Across `RoboMME`, `RMBench`, `LIBERO`, and `PhysicalAI-AV`, **it matches its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency** and matches the latency of a no-reasoning model with up to 17.1 points higher success. It also sets new published highs on the `RoboMME` Counting suite (82.7% vs 66.8%) and `RMBench` (77.5% vs 56.5%).

papers.title: Convex-Analytic View of Query Selection for Safety Verification of Markov Decision Processes
papers.abstract: Safety verification of a Markov decision process (MDP) asks whether the probabilities of reaching several failure states jointly lie in a convex safe region under every scheduler. Watanabe and Unno (2026) prove safety by refining an outer approximation of the failure probabilities, where each query bounds a nonnegative weighted sum of the probabilities. Their rule selects weights by the largest Euclidean violation. We present a unified framework to measure violation in an explicitly chosen error unit: directions are scored by the support-function gap between the outer approximation and the safe region, normalized by the support function of the unit. We show that the maximal score, when positive, equals the smallest enlargement of the safe region in multiples of that unit that contains the outer approximation. The Euclidean unit recovers the earlier rule; two new rules are generated by the unit cube and the safe region itself. We experimentally evaluate how the choice of measurement rule affects the performance of safety verification for MDPs.
papers.summary: Safety verification of a Markov decision process (MDP) asks whether the joint probabilities of reaching several failure states stay inside a convex safe region under every scheduler, and a recent approach by Watanabe and Unno refines an outer approximation through queries that bound nonnegative weighted sums of those probabilities, choosing weights by the largest Euclidean violation. The authors generalize this into a framework that scores candidate directions by the support-function gap between the outer approximation and the safe region, normalized by the support function of a chosen error unit. **The maximal score, when positive, equals the smallest enlargement of the safe region in multiples of that unit that contains the outer approximation**; the Euclidean unit recovers the original rule, while the unit cube and the safe region itself yield two new rules whose verification performance is compared experimentally.

papers.title: Many Steps into One: Reasoning Contraction and the Limits of Safe Memory Reuse for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories and caches turn many reasoning steps into one. We call this reasoning contraction. A contracted memory saves reasoning steps and errors until its facts change, then quietly answers wrong. Most systems trust memories by counting successes and failures. We prove that such counters are badly tuned change detectors: a symmetric counter notices a partial change only after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped one may never notice it. On five LLMs answering multi-hop questions over edited facts, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters serve 7.0-13.5x more stale answers than certified memories given the same information, and on code tasks with an exact verifier 35-73x more. Safety also has a price. When facts change and each memory is judged only by its own verified outcomes, one number, the certification load, sets how much reasoning any safe memory can skip, and under Zipf demand it yields a scaling law. Our recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies its utility against live reasoning, and restarts the certificate when facts change, with the likelihood-ratio detector as the safety net for unannounced changes; for large edits it also invalidates the memory.
papers.summary: Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories, and caches compress many reasoning steps into one reused answer, which the authors call reasoning contraction; such a memory saves work until the facts behind it change, after which it quietly answers wrong. They prove that the success-and-failure counters most systems use to trust memories are poorly tuned change detectors: a symmetric counter notices a partial change only after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped one may never notice at all. **On five LLMs answering multi-hop questions over edited facts, `ExpeL`- and `ACE`-style counters serve 7.0 to 13.5x more stale answers than certified memories, and 35 to 73x more on code tasks with an exact verifier.** Their recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies its utility against live reasoning, and restarts certification when facts change, and they show that a single certification-load quantity bounds how much reasoning a safe memory can skip, yielding a scaling law under Zipf demand.

papers.title: Reference Wording Shapes Retrieval of Robot Task Instructions
papers.abstract: Identifying a robot task from a short instruction is sensitive to which descriptions are available for retrieval. We investigate this effect in the natural-language instructions included with the RLBench manipulation benchmark. We extract 296 fixed descriptions from 62 publicly available task files and compare five training-free lexical rankers over 80 random choices of one indexed description per task. Exact strings assigned to conflicting task labels are excluded from the primary score. Character n-gram TF-IDF achieves 61.3% mean top-1 accuracy on the resulting held-out instructions, compared with 55.6% for BM25 and 54.9% for word TF-IDF. Across gallery choices, character TF-IDF ranges from 55.2% to 66.8%; its 5th-95th percentile range is 56.9%-64.8%. Adding a second indexed description improves character TF-IDF by 7.0 percentage points on matched queries. These results quantify the influence of reference wording and representation choice on instruction-to-task retrieval under a consistent evaluation protocol.
papers.summary: Matching a short natural-language instruction to the robot task it names depends on which reference descriptions are indexed for retrieval. Using 296 fixed descriptions extracted from 62 task files in the `RLBench` manipulation benchmark, the authors compare five training-free lexical rankers over 80 random choices of one indexed description per task. **Character n-gram `TF-IDF` achieves 61.3% mean top-1 accuracy, versus 55.6% for `BM25` and 54.9% for word `TF-IDF`**, but its accuracy swings from 55.2% to 66.8% depending on which description is indexed, and adding a second description improves it by 7.0 points. The results quantify how strongly reference wording and representation choice shape instruction-to-task retrieval.

papers.title: FlashVSR+: Efficient Video Super-Resolution via Hybrid Attention and Reward-Yield Distribution Matching
papers.abstract: Recent video super-resolution (VSR) models achieve efficient one-step generation through diffusion distillation. However, high-resolution inference remains costly, and distilled models are difficult to align with human preferences. These challenges call for improvements in both model architecture and training strategy. We present \textbf{FlashVSR+} to address both limitations. On the architecture side, we introduce hybrid attention based on the strong locality observed in pretrained VSR models, while retaining sparse global interaction for long-range consistency. It achieves up to $2\times$ DiT speedup and 45\% lower peak memory, enabling spatially untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090. On the training side, we propose Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD) for preference-aligned one-step generation. Ry-DMD uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts to incorporate black-box rewards into distribution matching, without backpropagating through the reward model. We further show that Ry-DMD generalizes beyond VSR to T2I generation. Together, FlashVSR+ delivers stronger restoration quality and substantially improves high-resolution efficiency, with consistent gains in user preference. We release our code, models, and training data at \href{https://www.flashvsr.tech}{\textcolor{FlashBlue}{\textbf{www.flashvsr.tech}}}.
papers.summary: One-step diffusion-distilled video super-resolution (VSR) models are fast but still costly at high resolution, and distilled models are hard to align with human preferences. `FlashVSR+` introduces hybrid attention that exploits the strong locality observed in pretrained VSR models while keeping sparse global interaction for long-range consistency, and `Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation` (`Ry-DMD`), which folds black-box rewards into distribution matching through reward-weighted teacher rollouts without backpropagating through the reward model. **The architecture delivers up to 2x DiT speedup and 45% lower peak memory, enabling untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090**, and the training recipe improves restoration quality and user preference while also transferring to text-to-image generation. Code, models, and training data are released.

papers.title: EdgeWise: Bringing Long-Horizon Agents to the Edge via Selective Cloud Delegation
papers.abstract: Complex and long-horizon agent tasks often rely on frontier models deployed in the cloud to achieve strong performance. However, using these models for every step of a long-horizon trajectory incurs substantial inference cost, even though not all steps may require the same level of model capability. In this paper, we find that allocating the LLM to only a small subset of key steps can achieve performance comparable to full LLM execution while significantly reducing inference cost. Motivated by this observation, we propose EdgeWise, an edge-cloud collaboration framework that deploys an SLM on the local device as the primary solver and selectively delegates critical steps to a cloud LLM when stronger model capacity is needed. To enable autonomous delegation without additional models at inference time, we introduce a step-level RL method that jointly optimizes task solving and delegation, with fine-grained credit assignment for individual delegation decisions. We also introduce an external judge-based delegation strategy and use it to systematically investigate key design choices in edge-cloud collaboration, including when to delegate, how delegation decisions should be made, what context should be shared, and how frequently the cloud LLM should be invoked. Experiments show that EdgeWise matches or outperforms pure-LLM execution while reducing inference cost up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. We further deploy EdgeWise on a local workstation, demonstrating comparable cost savings in a practical edge-cloud setting.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agent tasks typically route every step through a frontier cloud model, even though many steps do not need that level of capability. The authors find that invoking the large language model (LLM) on only a small subset of key steps matches full-LLM performance, and build `EdgeWise`, an edge-cloud framework where a small language model (SLM) on the local device is the primary solver and delegates critical steps to a cloud LLM; a step-level reinforcement learning method jointly trains task solving and delegation with fine-grained credit assignment for each delegation decision, and a judge-based delegation strategy is used to study when to delegate, what context to share, and how often to call the cloud. **`EdgeWise` matches or exceeds pure-LLM execution while cutting inference cost by up to 62% on `SWE-Rebench` and 34% on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`**, and a deployment on a local workstation shows similar savings in practice.

papers.title: Benchmarking Self-Supervised 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models and Transferability Estimation
papers.abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has expanded the pool of 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols. Models also differ in architecture, pretraining objective and data, while downstream targets range from voxel-level masks to patient-level diagnoses and outcomes. As a result, published findings provide little directly comparable evidence for choosing a model for a new task. Direct comparison of adaptation performance requires fine-tuning candidates on labelled target data, at substantial computational cost. We benchmark 23 candidates across the same 14 segmentation, classification and regression tasks spanning multiple anatomies and modalities. No candidate ranked among the top three across all segmentation tasks or across all classification and regression tasks; a convolutional encoder could outperform a transformer trained with the same objective on one task but underperform it on another. We benchmark transferability estimators against the fine-tuned rankings and find that their agreement varies across dense segmentation, classification and regression. InsightRank uses task-appropriate frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons to rank candidates before fine-tuning. Across the 23-model pool, mean Kendall tau-b was 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for classification and regression. The segmentation Top 3 contained a task winner on four of nine tasks; the image-level Top 3 contained none on the five tasks, despite better full-ranking agreement than the matched conventional estimators. A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks. Together, the benchmark provides a common reference for model selection and InsightRank offers a lower-cost way to prioritize fine-tuning, with shortlist performance that differs by target type.
papers.summary: Self-supervised pretraining has produced many 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints, and fine-tuning protocols, so practitioners have little comparable evidence for picking one, and fine-tuning every candidate is expensive. The authors benchmark 23 models on the same 14 segmentation, classification, and regression tasks across multiple anatomies and modalities, and propose `InsightRank`, a transferability estimator that ranks candidates from frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons before any fine-tuning. **No model ranked in the top three on every segmentation task or on every classification and regression task**, and a convolutional encoder could beat a transformer trained with the same objective on one task and lose on another. `InsightRank` reached mean Kendall tau-b of 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for image-level tasks, and a three-model shortlist cut extraction-plus-training time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks, though its top-3 shortlist missed the winner on all five image-level tasks.

papers.title: Dissociating Answerability from Extraction in LLM Question Answering over Radiology Reports
papers.abstract: Answering questions from radiology reports involves two decisions: whether the report contains an answer and which span gives it. A false answer presents an unsupported claim as fact; an over-abstention hides what the report says. Yet RadQA results are reported as a single F1 that merges both. We propose an evaluation method that separates them, reporting false-answer and over-abstention rates beside F1 and splitting F1 changes into extraction and answerability terms. We apply it to 13 LLMs on the RadQA test set, zero-shot and with three cumulative demonstration sets, the last adding an unanswerable example. Models with similar F1 differed more than twofold in false-answer rate. The unanswerable example changed when models answered, not how well they extracted: 12 of 13 models abstained more often, and three-quarters of the answers they withdrew had F1 $\geq$ 0.5. Within models, false answers showed no clear association with extraction quality, but acting on the decision itself helped: keeping an answer only when enough other models also answered lowered the zero-shot false-answer rate by 4 points without a detectable F1 change. Because the two decisions can change independently, we suggest radiology QA evaluations report them separately, not through F1 alone.
papers.summary: Extractive question answering over radiology reports involves two separate decisions, whether the report contains an answer at all and which span supplies it, yet standard evaluation collapses both into a single F1 score. The authors propose reporting false-answer and over-abstention rates alongside F1 and decomposing F1 changes into extraction and answerability components, then apply this to 13 large language models on the `RadQA` test set under zero-shot and cumulative few-shot prompting. **Models with similar F1 differed more than twofold in false-answer rate**, and adding an unanswerable demonstration changed when models answered rather than how well they extracted, with 12 of 13 models abstaining more often. A simple consensus filter that keeps an answer only when enough other models also answered cut the zero-shot false-answer rate by 4 points without a detectable F1 change.

papers.title: Risk-Averse Inference-Time Diffusion Model Alignment with Finite-Sample Guarantees
