On `ALFWorld`, `PaperSearchQA`, and `BFCLv3`, **`DeltaTTG` improves the average score over `GRPO` by 5.7 points with `Qwen3-4B` and 7.2 points with `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`**, beats all compared RL baselines on average with actor-training GPU-hours close to `GRPO`, and shows better sample efficiency, out-of-domain performance, and usefulness for test-time action selection.

papers.title: PrT-Flow: Probability-Tractable Flow Matching for Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Diffusion models and Flow Matching can represent flexible distributions over robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also require the probability of each action. We introduce PrT-Flow (Probability-Tractable Flow Matching), which computes probability density while retaining multimodal, multi-step action generation. Its Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) makes each sampling step invertible and enables efficient computation of its Jacobian determinant. We train these finite steps with Conditional Euler-step Training (CET), which supervises their displacement over one step during sampling rather than their instantaneous velocity. We prove that, under certain assumptions, CET has the same minimizers as fitting the Euler-solver updates of Flow Matching. PrT-Flow achieves 96% success on Robomimic Lift after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion policy reference, and 96% success on OGBench Cube-Triple after 600k online steps. These results demonstrate that invertible networks with tractable probability densities can learn effective robot policies and support SAC-style actor-critic training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sunlight-zero/PrT-Flow .
papers.summary: Diffusion and flow-matching policies can represent multimodal distributions over robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also need the probability density of each sampled action, which these models do not provide. Probability-Tractable Flow Matching (`PrT-Flow`) keeps multi-step, multimodal action generation while making each sampling step invertible through a Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) whose Jacobian determinant is cheap to compute, and trains the steps with Conditional Euler-step Training (CET), which supervises per-step displacement rather than instantaneous velocity and is proven under certain assumptions to share minimizers with fitting flow-matching Euler updates. `PrT-Flow` **reaches 96% success on `Robomimic Lift` after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion-policy reference**, and 96% on `OGBench Cube-Triple` after 600k online steps, showing that invertible networks with tractable densities support SAC-style actor-critic training.

papers.title: Cowork-Gym: Synthesizing Interactive Work Environments at Scale
papers.abstract: Cowork agents navigate dependencies across tools and files while adapting to changing user requirements and edits to shared workspaces. Scaling such environments requires maintaining consistency among task objectives, executable resources, user behavior, and success criteria. We introduce Cowork-Gym, a framework that synthesizes Cowork environments through a build-execute-revise loop that uses execution evidence and review feedback to validate and repair generated environments. To capture realistic Cowork dynamics, a stateful user simulator responds to the agent's actions through dialogue and direct edits to the shared workspace. We synthesize 64.9K environments across 14 application scenarios and use them to post-train 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B Qwen models with supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation. Averaged across six agentic benchmarks, these models outperform their corresponding base checkpoints by 8.7, 6.4, and 4.1 points, respectively. Ours-27B ranks second overall among the evaluated models and achieves the highest average scores on PawBench and ClawEval, outperforming models with over 100B total parameters on both benchmarks.
papers.summary: Agents that work alongside people must track dependencies across tools and files while adapting to changing requirements and edits to shared workspaces, and scaling such environments requires keeping task objectives, executable resources, user behavior, and success criteria consistent. `Cowork-Gym` synthesizes these environments through a build-execute-revise loop that uses execution evidence and review feedback to validate and repair generated environments, paired with a stateful user simulator that reacts to the agent through dialogue and direct workspace edits. The authors synthesize 64.9K environments across 14 application scenarios and post-train 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B `Qwen` models with supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation, gaining 8.7, 6.4, and 4.1 points over the base checkpoints averaged across six agentic benchmarks, with **the 27B model ranking second overall and topping `PawBench` and `ClawEval` ahead of models with over 100B total parameters**.

papers.title: Encounter-Driven City-Scale Human Mobility Generation with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for human mobility generation by modeling individual routines, activities, and mobility preferences. However, existing approaches remain largely resident-centric: generating realistic individual trajectories does not necessarily recover the encounters that emerge when multiple residents co-occur at the same place and time. To this end, we study encounter-aware human mobility generation, which jointly preserves individual mobility and population-level interaction structure. We propose EncounterMob, an encounter-driven LLM framework consisting of a coarse-to-fine Encounter Generator and an Iterative Coupling Framework. The Encounter Generator first captures city-level encounter rhythms and then instantiates participant-time-venue encounters, while the Iterative Coupling Framework coordinates these encounters with personal mobility behavior through successive refinement. We further introduce an encounter recovery protocol covering encounter marginal and joint distributions over residents, times, and venues. Experiments on the Japan and NYC datasets show that EncounterMob outperforms all external baselines on all seven encounter metrics and all six personal mobility metrics. Compared with ELLMob, it reduces the participant-time-venue joint error by 40.4%/41.7% and the mean personal mobility error by 58.8%/32.7% on Japan/NYC, respectively.
papers.summary: Large language models can generate realistic individual human mobility trajectories, but resident-centric generation does not recover the encounters that arise when multiple people co-occur at the same place and time. `EncounterMob` pairs a coarse-to-fine Encounter Generator, which first captures city-level encounter rhythms and then instantiates participant-time-venue encounters, with an Iterative Coupling Framework that reconciles those encounters with individual mobility behavior through successive refinement, and the authors add an encounter recovery protocol covering marginal and joint distributions over residents, times, and venues. On Japan and NYC datasets, `EncounterMob` outperforms all external baselines on all seven encounter metrics and six personal mobility metrics, and compared with `ELLMob` it **cuts the participant-time-venue joint error by 40.4% and 41.7%** while reducing mean personal mobility error by 58.8% and 32.7%.

papers.title: RALI@iKAT 2026: Retrieval-aware User Profile Denoising via Personalized Conversational Dense Retrieval
papers.abstract:
Modern conversational information access systems continuously extract user information from conversations to build user profiles for personalized retrieval. As user profiles accumulate over time, they inevitably become noisy, making effective user profile denoising a fundamental challenge. Existing personalized conversational query reformulation methods rely on the black-box reasoning capability of LLMs to expand the original query with relevant user profile phrases, producing a verbose query for retrieval. Such rewrite-then-retrieve pipelines reduce user profile denoising to the explicit selection of profile phrases in the sparse token space, separating personalization from downstream relevance modeling. Consequently, they often fail to identify user information that is truly beneficial for retrieval.
  To enable retrieval-aware user profile denoising, we propose Personalized Conversational Dense Retrieval (PCDR), which learns to jointly project the conversation history and user profile into a latent embedding space dedicated to retrieval. By inheriting the context denoising capability from conversational dense retrievers, PCDR requires only a handful of personalized relevance annotations for training. We evaluate PCDR on the iKAT 2026 tasks, where it serves as the core retrieval component of a conversational AI agent assisting users with complex information needs.
papers.summary: Conversational information access systems accumulate user profiles that grow noisy over time, and existing personalized query reformulation methods rely on black-box LLM reasoning to splice profile phrases into a verbose rewritten query, which separates personalization from relevance modeling and often misses the profile information that actually helps retrieval. Personalized Conversational Dense Retrieval (`PCDR`) instead learns to jointly project the conversation history and user profile into a latent embedding space dedicated to retrieval, inheriting context-denoising ability from conversational dense retrievers so that **only a handful of personalized relevance annotations are needed for training**. The method serves as the core retrieval component of a conversational agent submitted to the `iKAT 2026` tasks.

papers.title: Dynamic K-Head: Difficulty-Supervised Budget Selection for Continuous Latent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning but incurs substantial autoregressive rationale cost. Continuous CoT moves intermediate computation into recurrent hidden states, yet typically uses a fixed number of updates even though the best budget varies across questions and accuracy need not improve monotonically with $K$. We introduce Dynamic K-Head, a question-conditioned, pre-rollout budget selector. It is jointly trained with the reasoner under selected budgets, using difficulty supervision based on scores assigned from the question alone. We also show that latent-update count can misrepresent end-to-end cost because a short latent rollout can shift computation into a longer explicit continuation. We therefore count latent updates, implementation-specific special tokens, and all decoded text. Instantiated with CoDI on Llama 3.2 1B and GSM8K, Dynamic K-Head reaches 54.44% exact-match accuracy at 12.03 average reasoning/output tokens, compared with 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed-$K=6$ CoDI---a 2.12-point gain with 20.9% lower token cost. Across three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets, it reduces cost by 19.3--25.7% while improving accuracy by 0.30--2.22 points. These results demonstrate that difficulty-supervised budget selection can improve both accuracy and efficiency, while stable budget selection remains a central challenge.
papers.summary: Continuous chain-of-thought moves intermediate reasoning into recurrent hidden states instead of generated text, but it typically uses a fixed number of latent updates even though the best budget varies by question and accuracy does not improve monotonically with it. `Dynamic K-Head` is a question-conditioned selector that picks the latent budget before rollout, trained jointly with the reasoner using difficulty supervision derived from scores assigned to the question alone, and the authors argue that end-to-end cost must count latent updates, special tokens, and all decoded text since a short latent rollout can push computation into a longer explicit continuation. Instantiated with `CoDI` on `Llama 3.2 1B` and `GSM8K`, it **reaches 54.44% exact-match accuracy at 12.03 average tokens versus 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed-budget `CoDI`**, and on three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets it cuts cost by 19.3 to 25.7% while adding 0.30 to 2.22 accuracy points, though stable budget selection remains an open challenge.

papers.title: Deficit-Driven Stratified Acquisition for Building STRATA-S12: An Open SAR-Optical Corpus for Self-Supervised Learning
papers.abstract: Building a co-registered SAR-optical corpus for self-supervised Earth Observation is above all an acquisition problem, yet the main multi-modal datasets are collected opportunistically, with no per-stratum quota control and no mechanism against the geographic dropout that non-uniform cloud cover leaves behind. We present Deficit-Driven Stratified Acquisition (DDSA), an algorithm that treats building a co-registered Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 corpus as a constrained maximum-coverage problem over a hemisphere-corrected (class x season x region) stratification, enforces strict temporal pairing and a multi-stage quality gate, and closes the loop during acquisition with a human-in-the-loop deficit-repair stage. Measured on its own product, the algorithm yields three results a single-pass acquisition cannot report. Deficit-driven ordering makes a partial run a covering one: it holds every one of the 192 strata populated from the first few percent of the budget, where an abundance-first order leaves most strata empty until the end. Whether a failed attempt can be recovered depends on the temporal persistence of its cause, not the kind of defect: geometric failures such as nodata are among the most repairable (eta = 41.4%) while cloud is among the least (eta = 18.8%), because a cloudy location is cloudy on most dates of its season. The repair loop supplies 39.5% of the released pairs at no measurable quality cost, with 89.8% surviving manual review. The quality guarantee has a price: 2,928,370 acquisition attempts produced 740,746 released pairs. We release the corpus, STRATA-S12, with STAC/PDS4-aligned FAIR sidecars, and a pre-registered linear-probe check confirms it is fit for self-supervised pre-training. A metadata-level coverage comparison against SSL4EO-S12 and SEN12MS situates the corpus over a shared frame; systematic cross-corpus and cross-method comparison is left to follow-up work.
papers.summary: Building a co-registered SAR-optical corpus for self-supervised Earth observation is primarily an acquisition problem, yet existing multi-modal datasets are collected opportunistically with no per-stratum quotas and no defense against the geographic gaps that uneven cloud cover leaves. Deficit-Driven Stratified Acquisition (`DDSA`) treats building a Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 corpus as a constrained maximum-coverage problem over a hemisphere-corrected class-by-season-by-region stratification, enforces strict temporal pairing and a multi-stage quality gate, and adds a human-in-the-loop deficit-repair stage during acquisition. Deficit-driven ordering keeps all 192 strata populated from the first few percent of the budget, repairability depends on the temporal persistence of a failure's cause so nodata gaps are far more recoverable than clouds, and the repair loop supplies 39.5% of released pairs with 89.8% surviving manual review, though **2,928,370 acquisition attempts were needed to produce 740,746 released pairs**; the resulting `STRATA-S12` corpus is released with FAIR metadata sidecars and a pre-registered linear-probe check, with coverage compared at the metadata level against `SSL4EO-S12` and `SEN12MS`.

papers.title: LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures. Experiments on the benchmark show that action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations, whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96. Existing guardrail methods largely overlook such risks unless they are explicitly applied to workflow states. Case studies on a commercial deployed scenario further show that the safety metrics embedded in the benchmark provide a more realistic measure of safety for enterprise agents. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/LatentRiskBench.
papers.summary: Existing safety benchmarks for enterprise agents mostly evaluate action-local risks, missing failures where the same action is safe in one workflow state but violates policy in another. `LatentRiskBench` pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant state, forcing evaluators to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues, and introduces a suite of residual risk (RR) metrics for state-dependent risk. On the benchmark, **action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96**, existing guardrails largely miss such risks unless applied explicitly to workflow states, and case studies on a commercially deployed scenario suggest the metrics give a more realistic measure of enterprise agent safety; the dataset and code are released.

papers.title: Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?
papers.abstract: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.
papers.summary: Long contexts let large language models (LLMs) condition on more information, but inference cost grows steeply with length, and the emerging alternative of encoding context as temporary weight updates at test time blends the new material into general knowledge so the model may not treat it as context. The authors attach an identifier to each context during encoding so the model can later recite the encoded material on demand, and add a prompting framework that explicitly directs the model to use the recalled information as context rather than as background knowledge. Across controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, the method **outperformed a baseline that relies only on off-the-shelf LLMs** at context encoding.

papers.title: Stable Token-level Scheduling for Serverless LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. We observe that LLM inference comprises a computation-intensive prefill stage and a bandwidth-bound decode stage, where admitting new requests can disrupt ongoing decoding and increase latency. To address this, we propose Token Window Pacing (TWP), a closed-loop scheduling framework that leverages runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate request admission at the token level instead of the batch level. TWP dynamically adjusts a selfregulating token window and incorporates chunk-based prefill to minimize interference from incoming requests. Experiments on realistic serverless workloads show that TWP delivers stable TTFT, significantly reduces latency spikes, lowers P99 tail latency, minimizes ITL variation, and improves throughput by up to 45% over ServerlessLLM and 58% over conventional schedulers. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven tokenlevel scheduling enables stable, high-throughput serverless LLM inference without modifying the underlying model.
papers.summary: Serverless deployment of large language models (LLMs) scales elastically and shares GPUs, but existing schedulers optimize time to first token (TTFT) while ignoring inter-token latency (ITL), which degrades when the compute-heavy prefill of newly admitted requests interrupts the bandwidth-bound decode stage of requests already running. `Token Window Pacing` (`TWP`) is a closed-loop scheduler that uses runtime feedback on ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to admit work at the token level through a self-regulating window, combined with chunked prefill to limit interference. On realistic serverless workloads it stabilizes TTFT, cuts tail latency and ITL variation, and **improves throughput by up to 45% over `ServerlessLLM`** and 58% over conventional schedulers without modifying the model.

papers.title: MedEvo: Medical Reasoning Evolution through Knowledge Navigation
papers.abstract: Medical multimodal reasoning models are typically trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories, while general-domain correction methods offer little guidance for errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. We propose MedEvo, which uses medical knowledge, namely a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis, to navigate both trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error and provides a minimal, answer-free hint; the same student retains the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, MedEvo identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions for new rollouts and repairs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on the multimodal track of MedXpertQA (MedXpertQA-MM)), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively. Our analyses show that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.
papers.summary: Medical multimodal reasoning models are usually trained on teacher-written rationales, discarding the valid reasoning inside a student's own failed attempts, and generic self-correction methods give little guidance on errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. `MedEvo` uses a medical tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis to steer both trajectory repair and data selection: a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error in a failed rollout and gives a minimal answer-free hint, the same student keeps the valid prefix and regenerates the rest, and after each round capability gaps across tags on a held-out feedback set decide which questions get new rollouts. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, **`Qwen3.5-9B` mean accuracy across seven benchmarks rises from 65.57% to 69.12%**, beating teacher-distillation SFT at 66.93%, with similar gains for `Qwen3.5-35B` and `Qwen3.5-397B`. The analyses argue that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth keeping, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.

papers.title: HelpMeOut: A Neuropsychology-Grounded Benchmark for Error-Aware Monitoring of Household Task Execution
papers.abstract: We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.
papers.summary: Embodied household benchmarks usually assume the human performs tasks correctly, which does not hold for cognitively impaired people or older adults whose everyday activities contain structured execution errors. `HelpMeOut` turns neuropsychological research on everyday action errors into **20,000 paired activity episodes spanning nine error categories**, in which an agent watches a streaming human activity trajectory and must flag and diagnose errors as early as possible. Learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines all perform poorly, frequently missing the moment execution goes wrong, which the authors read as a gap left by goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks.

papers.title: zPocket: Better Pocket Finding with Frozen Co-Folding Features
papers.abstract: Identifying protein-ligand binding sites (pockets) is important for understanding protein function and developing drugs. However, no public method has leveraged co-folding models for novel pocket prediction; furthermore, this task lacks a suitable benchmark as existing benchmarks are within the training distribution of co-folding models. We therefore developed PocketWatch,a curated dataset of biologically relevant ligand pockets. The PocketWatch test set consists of unseen pockets stratified by sequence similarity, structural similarity, and crypticity to enable evaluation of generalization to novel and challenging pockets. Using this dataset, we develop zPocket, a method that trains pocket-prediction heads on top of frozen features from co-folding models. We show that zPocket heads outperform baseline methods across all stratifications. Our best zPocket model achieves overall per-target AUPRC of 0.745 compared to 0.598 and 0.595 for the strongest baselines, VN-EGNN and UniSite-1D retrained on the PocketWatch split (0.559 and 0.531 when using the published weights); the widely used P2Rank reaches 0.477. We further show that zPocket can be used to outperform baseline methods on top-N+2 recall of predicted pocket centroids through clustering per-residue predictions or using zPocket to rescore centroids proposed by other models. Finally, we explore two applications of zPocket: crystallographic fragment screens and a proteome-scale scan for uncharacterized pockets on human proteins. Together these results suggest that zPocket heads built on co-folding trunk features can greatly advance ligand binding site prediction.
papers.summary: Predicting where ligands bind on proteins matters for understanding function and for drug design, but no public method has exploited co-folding models for novel pocket prediction, and existing benchmarks overlap with those models' training data. The authors build `PocketWatch`, a curated dataset whose test set holds unseen pockets stratified by sequence similarity, structural similarity, and crypticity, and train `zPocket`, pocket-prediction heads on frozen co-folding features. The best model reaches **per-target AUPRC of 0.745 versus 0.598 for the strongest retrained baseline** `VN-EGNN` and 0.477 for the widely used `P2Rank`, the heads also improve centroid recall by clustering residue predictions or rescoring other models' proposals, and the method is demonstrated on crystallographic fragment screens and a proteome-scale scan for uncharacterized pockets on human proteins.

papers.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
papers.abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.
papers.summary: AI systems now generate long mathematical proofs, and checking them step by step is becoming a bottleneck, but training a learned verifier needs per-step correctness labels that are costly from humans and unavailable from final answers because proofs have none. `LeanPRM` has a model write a natural-language proof alongside a paired formal proof without feedback from `Lean`, lets the `Lean` proof assistant label every step, and uses a second model to discard failures caused only by formal syntax, yielding 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A `Qwen3-4B` verifier trained on this data **raises exact step-label accuracy on `LeanPRM-Bench` from 48.2 to 74.7**, compared to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on `PRM800K`, and it selects better proofs in best-of-N on IMO-level problems and beats the `PRM800K` verifier on three of four external benchmarks, with gains holding at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters.

papers.title: Understanding Gene Expression-to-Image Learning: Spatial Structure and Information Fidelity
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables cell-level analysis of biological heterogeneity, but learning effective representations from high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles remains challenging. Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) offers an effective learning strategy by arranging gene values on pixel grids for convolutional neural networks, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We study GE2I on full-transcriptome data while keeping the network and training procedure fixed. Our results reveal a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity. Structured mappings produce smooth, low-frequency patterns that support faster early optimization, whereas assigning multiple genes to the same pixel obscures expression differences and can reduce predictive performance. This trade-off explains why random mappings can compete with structured layouts when many genes are represented. One-to-one gene-to-pixel assignment improves prediction across the tested visual backbones even when image smoothness decreases. We further find that the benefits of pretraining and augmentation depend on the backbone and mapping. These findings provide practical guidance for pixel allocation and the transfer of vision priors to gene expression data.
papers.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) yields high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles that are hard to learn from, and Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) methods that arrange gene values on pixel grids for convolutional networks work without a clear account of why. Holding the network and training procedure fixed on full-transcriptome data, the study finds a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity: structured layouts produce smooth low-frequency images that speed early optimization, but stacking several genes on one pixel blurs expression differences and hurts prediction, which explains why random mappings can compete with structured ones. **One-to-one gene-to-pixel assignment improves prediction across all tested visual backbones** even when image smoothness drops, while the value of pretraining and augmentation depends on the backbone and the mapping.

papers.title: A Node Embedding Framework for Model-Centric Conformance Checking in Process Mining
papers.abstract: Evaluating the quality of process models discovered from event logs is a fundamental challenge in process mining. Traditional evaluation relies on conformance metrics such as fitness and precision, which are highly sensitive to noise and deviations in event logs and therefore often fail to give a consistent assessment of discovery algorithms. We introduce a model-centric evaluation framework that combines node embeddings with Procrustes alignment to enable cross-graph comparability, since embeddings derived from different graphs reside in distinct vector spaces. The proposed PetriNetGraph method transforms Petri net process models into graph representations compatible with embedding algorithms. Comparing the node embeddings of ground-truth and discovered models through a parameterized cosine distance yields a unified and bounded metric for evaluating process discovery across datasets and methods. We evaluate the framework under static and context-aware scenarios to examine how prior knowledge of activity existence influences the assessment of structural similarity. The framework also integrates a compliance checking mechanism that localizes deviations at the activity level and an entropy-regularized node distance aggregation function that quantifies global deviations across the model. Experiments on nine publicly available event logs show that the approach provides a reliable embedding-based conformance indicator that reflects the behavior of fitness and precision. Experiments on synthetic logs with controlled noise levels confirm that it is substantially more robust to log deviations than traditional conformance metrics, PetriNet2Vec, and its dynamic-window and Procrustes-aligned variants, while remaining sensitive to process model degradation. All implementation details and datasets are publicly available.
papers.summary: Judging the quality of process models discovered from event logs usually relies on fitness and precision, conformance metrics that react strongly to noise in the logs and therefore give inconsistent verdicts on discovery algorithms. The proposed framework converts Petri net process models into embedding-ready graphs with a `PetriNetGraph` transformation, computes node embeddings, aligns them across graphs with Procrustes analysis, and compares ground-truth and discovered models through a parameterized cosine distance, adding activity-level deviation localization and an entropy-regularized aggregation for global deviations. On nine public event logs the metric tracks fitness and precision, and on synthetic logs with controlled noise it is **substantially more robust to log deviations than traditional metrics and `PetriNet2Vec`** while still responding to model degradation.

papers.title: Pushback in a Haystack: Language Models Respond to Factual Errors Ambiguously and Ineffectively
papers.abstract: The sycophancy of language models, or their failure to push back against faulty user input, is now widely studied. However, if LMs do push back, is sycophancy solved? We show that LMs vary in how they present pushback, and thus vary in how effectively they correct user beliefs. We introduce a phrase-level, human-validated response labeling framework to uncover fine-grained insights into how LMs push against and/or affirm false inputs. We develop and apply our framework on model responses in five languages: English, German, Chinese, Hindi, and Yoruba. We find that when models do push back against users' false assertions, they tend to use indirect phrasing and mix in affirmation, with more indirectness in Hindi and Yoruba than in other languages considered. In a large-scale human study (n = 300), we find that the pushback ambiguity we identified may fail to correct and prevent users' factual misconceptions.
papers.summary: Sycophancy, a language model's failure to push back on faulty user input, is well studied, but even when models do push back they vary in how clearly they do it and therefore in how well they correct user beliefs. The authors build a human-validated, phrase-level labeling framework for how responses push against or affirm false assertions and apply it to model outputs in English, German, Chinese, Hindi, and Yoruba. Models that push back tend to use indirect phrasing mixed with affirmation, more so in Hindi and Yoruba, and **a 300-participant human study finds that this ambiguous pushback may fail to correct users' factual misconceptions**.

papers.title: A Differentiable 3D Scene Graph Metric via Contextual Hellinger Triplet Geometry
papers.abstract: 3D scene graph prediction is commonly supervised with local object and predicate classification losses. Although effective for slot-wise label prediction, this formulation does not provide a graph-level semantic distance between a predicted scene graph and its ground truth: semantically mild label errors and structurally disruptive relational errors can be treated similarly, and subject-predicate-object facts are not compared as scene-level units. We propose Contextual Hellinger Triplet Geometry, a graph-level supervision objective that measures the semantic and structural discrepancy between 3D scene graphs. Our key idea is to reinterpret the conventional classifier outputs of a 3D scene graph predictor as an aligned probabilistic scene graph field, where object and predicate predictions jointly define contextual subject-predicate-object facts. This formulation yields a differentiable metric-based training objective with an efficient factorized implementation and can be applied to existing 3D scene graph prediction architectures without modifying their network design. Experiments on 3DSSG demonstrate that our supervision improves downstream graph-conditioned 3D scene generation, while ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of the proposed graph-level terms and user studies show better graph descriptiveness, relation plausibility, and structural preservation.
papers.summary: 3D scene graph predictors are trained with per-slot object and predicate classification losses, which give no graph-level distance between a prediction and its ground truth, so a mild label mistake and a structurally disruptive relational error can be penalized alike. `Contextual Hellinger Triplet Geometry` reinterprets the classifier outputs as an aligned probabilistic scene graph field in which object and predicate predictions jointly define subject-predicate-object facts, yielding a differentiable metric-based objective with a factorized implementation that drops into existing architectures without changing their design. On `3DSSG`, **the supervision improves downstream graph-conditioned 3D scene generation**, ablations confirm the graph-level terms are complementary, and user studies report better descriptiveness, relation plausibility, and structural preservation.

papers.title: From Token Correction to Claim Admission: Training-Free Hallucination Mitigation for Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models often exhibit object hallucination, generating claims that are not supported by the input image. To mitigate this issue, we propose Evidence-Guided Visual Claim Admission (EGVCA), a training-free framework that admits a semantic claim only when it receives sufficient image-dependent support. EGVCA measures this support by comparing the claim likelihood under the observed image and a visual-null input. For captioning, it controls semantic expansion without altering token generation. For binary visual question answering, it combines atomic visual support with the image-induced change in the model's native Yes--No margin. Experiments on CHAIR, POPE, and MME across three LVLM backbones show that EGVCA substantially reduces object hallucination while preserving caption quality. It achieves the highest POPE F1 in eight of nine backbone--sampling settings and improves the native MME total score on all three backbones. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of claim-level admission as a simple alternative to token-level distribution correction.
papers.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate objects absent from the input image, and most mitigation methods try to correct the token-level output distribution. `Evidence-Guided Visual Claim Admission` (`EGVCA`) is training-free and instead admits a semantic claim only when it has enough image-dependent support, measured by comparing the claim's likelihood under the real image against a visual-null input; for captioning this controls semantic expansion without touching token generation, and for binary visual question answering it combines atomic visual support with the image-induced shift in the model's native Yes/No margin. Across `CHAIR`, `POPE`, and `MME` on three backbones it substantially reduces object hallucination while preserving caption quality, **achieving the highest `POPE` F1 in eight of nine backbone and sampling settings** and raising the native `MME` total on all three backbones.

papers.title: Focus on What You Need: Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
papers.abstract: Multimodal sarcasm detection has attracted increasing attention due to the widespread use of images and text on social media platforms. Existing studies generally treat the semantic or emotional inconsistency between images and text as a key cue for identifying sarcastic expressions. However, images in real-world scenarios often contain multiple visual objects, many of which are irrelevant to sarcasm-related semantics. Such redundant visual information may introduce noise during cross-modal interaction, distracting models from focusing on critical sarcasm cues and potentially leading to inaccurate predictions. To address this issue, we propose GLDA (Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention), a multimodal sarcasm detection framework that models cross-modal interactions from a global-to-local perspective. Specifically, GLDA first employs a global multimodal fusion module to capture high-level semantic interactions between visual and textual modalities, enabling the model to identify coarse-grained cross-modal inconsistencies. To further reduce the influence of irrelevant objects, GLDA introduces a local gated cross-modal attention mechanism that dynamically filters redundant visual and textual features and refines multimodal representations at a finer granularity. In addition, a multi-branch learning objective is designed to jointly optimize unimodal and multimodal representations. Experimental results demonstrate that GLDA effectively improves sarcasm detection performance and achieves competitive results compared with existing approaches. The code will be available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GLDA-DBE6.
papers.summary: Multimodal sarcasm detection on social media typically looks for semantic or emotional inconsistency between an image and its text, but real images contain many objects irrelevant to the sarcasm, and that visual clutter can distract cross-modal interaction. `GLDA` (Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention) first applies a global multimodal fusion module to capture coarse cross-modal inconsistency, then a local gated cross-modal attention mechanism that dynamically filters redundant visual and textual features, trained with a multi-branch objective over unimodal and multimodal representations. Experiments show it **improves sarcasm detection and is competitive with existing approaches**.

papers.title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/
papers.summary: Behavior cloning weights every demonstration state equally, yet in a few critical states a small deviation from the expert action causes failure while in most others the error is recoverable. The authors define state criticality as the worst-case drop in downstream value under a bounded perturbation of the expert action, and `SCRIM` (State CRIticality Measure) estimates it by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. Reweighting the behavior-cloning loss with these scores improves performance on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, and **selecting compact high-criticality subsets of demonstrations preserves performance while substantially cutting training data**, with the scores doubling as interpretable markers of which moments in a demonstration matter most.

papers.title: Adaptive-Group Process Rewards for GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Training graphical user interface (GUI) agents with reinforcement learning suffers from sparse outcome rewards, leading to inefficient learning. Process rewards offer a promising direction for credit assignment to intermediate actions; however, accurately evaluating an action requires identifying evidence across long-horizon GUI trajectories, as its value may depend on information beyond its immediate state and observation. In this paper, we propose an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically partitions a GUI trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups, enabling process reward estimation at both the action and group levels. At the action level, a critic evaluates each action based on the visual changes and subsequent actions within the group for action correctness and contribution to the subgoal. At the group level, the framework aggregates action-level evaluations to assess subgoal completion and contribution to the overall task, and further refines these assessments by leveraging the context of all groups in the trajectory. The process reward of each action is obtained by combining its action-level evaluation with the refined group-level evaluation. We further augment GRPO's outcome advantage with the proposed process rewards to provide finer-grained guidance for GUI agent training. Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for graphical user interface (GUI) agents suffers from sparse outcome rewards, and process rewards for intermediate actions are hard to compute because an action's value may depend on evidence far from its immediate observation in a long trajectory. The proposed framework adaptively partitions a trajectory into semantically coherent subgoal groups: a critic scores each action by the visual changes and later actions within its group, group-level scores aggregate these into subgoal completion and task contribution refined using the context of all groups, and the combined per-action reward augments the outcome advantage in `GRPO`. Experiments on process reward benchmarks and downstream RL training show the framework **improves GUI agent training**.

papers.title: Confine to the Task, Anchor the Rest: Concept-Guided Retention Regularizer for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been widely used, yet the adapted model suffers catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. While most existing work hardens the adapter by constraining where the weight update may lie, we note that constraining this weight channel does not constrain the activation channel. In this paper, we propose Concept-Guided Retention (CGR), a plug-and-play regularizer that constrains both for any PEFT base. CGR reads a frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) and treats two disjoint concept sets differently. It softly confines the update to the task-concept subspace (via weight channel), and anchors a selected set of general-purpose concepts to the frozen model (via activation channel). We also provide anchor value bounds based on weight updates to understand how they interact, and show that both terms are necessary. On a CLIP vision panel, CGR significantly improves retention at comparable accuracy for every base, and the same pattern holds for world-knowledge retention under Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning. Because the protected directions are named SAE concepts, CGR remains inspectable and controllable.
papers.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts models cheaply but still causes catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge, and existing defenses that constrain where the weight update may lie leave the activation channel unconstrained. `Concept-Guided Retention` (`CGR`) is a plug-and-play regularizer for any PEFT base that reads a frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) and treats two disjoint concept sets differently: it softly confines the update to the task-concept subspace through the weight channel and anchors a selected set of general-purpose concepts to the frozen model through the activation channel, with bounds on the anchor values showing both terms are needed. On a `CLIP` vision panel **`CGR` significantly improves retention at comparable accuracy for every PEFT base**, the same pattern holds for world-knowledge retention under `Llama-3.1-8B` instruction tuning, and the protected directions stay inspectable because they are named SAE concepts.

papers.title: MissPath-FM: Flow Matching with Structured Priors for Partially Observed Time Series
papers.abstract: Flow matching has emerged as a powerful alternative to diffusion models for generative modeling, but standard conditional flow matching is fundamentally misaligned with partially observed time series: starting from an uninformed Gaussian source forces the model to transport even already-observed entries from noise to the target, wasting capacity on trivially known regions. We propose MissPath-FM, a partial-observation-aware flow matching framework that redesigns the source prior and probability path for incomplete time series. MissPath-FM employs structured source priors (interpolation priors and Gaussian process posterior priors) to initialize the flow close to the observed signal, paired with a missingness-aware smooth path that allocates transport asymmetrically between observed and missing regions. We evaluate systematically across four datasets, four missingness mechanisms (MCAR, block, MNAR, irregular), two missing ratios, and three sequence lengths (T in {24, 48, 96}), totaling 48 settings against eight baselines. MissPath-FM wins 29 of 32 settings at T=48 and 45 of 48 overall (93.8%). Our ablations reveal a regime-dependent design hierarchy in which no single component suffices: under random missingness the source prior yields a large initial gain, but under structured block missingness it can fail entirely and the learned flow becomes indispensable; the missingness-aware path contributes a further 12%-26% across all regimes. Mechanistically, structured priors shorten observed-region transport by up to 15x, concentrating the velocity field on genuinely uncertain entries. Project page: https://zgp110.github.io/misspath-fm/
papers.summary: Standard conditional flow matching starts from an uninformed Gaussian source, so on partially observed time series it wastes capacity transporting already-known entries from noise to target. `MissPath-FM` replaces the source with structured priors, either interpolation or Gaussian process posteriors, that start the flow close to the observed signal, and pairs them with a missingness-aware path that allocates transport asymmetrically between observed and missing regions. Across four datasets, four missingness mechanisms, two missing ratios, and three sequence lengths against eight baselines it **wins 45 of 48 settings**, and ablations show a regime-dependent hierarchy in which the prior gives large gains under random missingness but can fail under block missingness, while the missingness-aware path adds 12% to 26% in every regime and structured priors shorten observed-region transport by up to 15x.

papers.title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.
papers.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets their evolving weaknesses while staying faithful to the waveform evidence. `ECG-RSI` is a recursive self-improvement loop that synthesizes waveform edits verified by signal remeasurement and searches over interventions guided by feedback: construction errors trigger generator repair, while learner errors motivate candidate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Over three rounds across seven benchmarks, **`Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` mean question-answering accuracy rises from 34.57% to 56.04%** and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03, with the preferred supervision shifting from direct reinforcement toward confusion-focused contrasts and external gains diminishing under continued feedback correction.

papers.title: Keep Your Receipts: Trustworthy Cleanup of Agent-Built Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Agents build knowledge graphs as memory, and building them has become easy. Maintaining them has not. When a source is retracted, overruled, or erased, everything built on top of it (entity merges, entailed edges, community summaries) must be re-examined, and the maintainer must choose between deleting too much and too little. Deployed pipelines delete only the directly extracted facts: on our corpus that reduces contaminated queries from 32.2% to 28.0% under a real retraction and changes nothing under predicate revocation. Rebuilding is no repair for a constructor that samples: two builds of the same 300-document corpus differ in 29,475 artifacts, five times the 6,248 that removing the 61 retracted documents changes. PolyGraph instead asks the constructor for receipts: for every artifact, alternative bundles of source evidence, each claimed sufficient on its own, emitted in the call that creates it. Cleanup is then set arithmetic over the receipts, with no model calls. Because receipts are the model's own self-report, a re-derivation audit checks them by deleting the cited evidence and testing whether the constructor still produces the artifact. The audit finds that a receipt is trustworthy when it is shaped like the claim it backs. Merge receipts, each backing one narrow claim, agree with re-derivation 68% and 85% of the time. Summary receipts, elicited per sentence but stored as one flat list for the whole text, are wrong about two thirds of the time, almost always by keeping dead content. One receipt per sentence instead is 100% and 88% faithful and lets cleanup keep 33 of 35 touched summaries. The result holds under a second oracle model, a claim-blind prompt, ten further deletions, a second domain and a second constructor. Distrusting the summary layer cuts contaminated queries to 0.4% and 0.8% at 99.8 to 100% of the recall a perfect maintainer would return.
papers.summary: Agents increasingly build knowledge graphs as memory, but when a source is retracted or overruled everything derived from it, including entity merges, entailed edges, and community summaries, must be re-examined; deployed pipelines that delete only directly extracted facts barely reduce contamination, and rebuilding is no fix because two runs of a sampling constructor on the same 300-document corpus differ in 29,475 artifacts, five times what removing the retracted documents changes. `PolyGraph` asks the constructor to emit receipts for every artifact at creation time, alternative bundles of source evidence each claimed sufficient on its own, so cleanup becomes set arithmetic with no model calls, and a re-derivation audit checks receipts by deleting the cited evidence and testing whether the constructor still produces the artifact. Receipts prove trustworthy when shaped like the claim they back: narrow merge receipts agree with re-derivation 68% to 85% of the time, flat per-text summary receipts are wrong about two thirds of the time, and per-sentence receipts reach 88% to 100% fidelity. **Distrusting the summary layer cuts contaminated queries to under 1% while retaining 99.8% to 100% of ideal recall**, and the result holds under a second oracle model, a claim-blind prompt, ten further deletions, a second domain, and a second constructor.

papers.title: Representation Geometry and Inductive Biases in Quantum Classifiers across Classical Visual Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has a theoretical advantage over classical algorithms for specific synthetic data that is computationally hard. However, it remains unclear whether such theoretical advantages play a meaningful role for realistic classical data, such as natural images. Quantum structural properties induced by unitary operations or entanglement introduce inductive biases that differ from those of classical models, potentially leading to distinct learning behavior on real-world data. In a fully quantum learning pipeline, classical real-world data are first encoded into quantum states via a quantum feature mapping, analogous to a classical feature extractor, and a quantum classifier then classifies the resulting states. Quantum feature mappings generate representations that are difficult to realize classically, while also inducing representation-level biases that do not necessarily match the structure of realistic data. To enable a fair comparison at the classifier level, we focus on the classifier and use classical feature extractors that already provide powerful representations for natural images. By controlling the data scale and supervision strength, we analyze how the unitary structure of quantum classifiers affects generalization, and show that their effectiveness depends strongly on the geometry of the input representations. These results indicate that quantum classifiers benefit from classical features that are aligned with quantum feature spaces. Our analysis shows that kernel alignment identifies representations compatible with quantum feature spaces, providing insights into translating classical models into quantum algorithms.
papers.summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) has provable advantages on certain synthetic data, but whether the distinctive inductive biases that unitary operations and entanglement impose help on realistic classical data such as natural images is unclear. To isolate the classifier, the study feeds quantum classifiers representations from strong classical feature extractors and varies data scale and supervision strength to see how unitary structure affects generalization. The results show that **quantum classifier effectiveness depends strongly on the geometry of the input representations**, that such classifiers benefit from classical features aligned with quantum feature spaces, and that kernel alignment can identify compatible representations.

papers.title: Upstream Influence, Downstream Re-Anchoring in LLM Agent Chains
papers.abstract: People act on evaluative judgments produced by LLM agents, and in multi-agent systems those judgments pass through several agents before reaching a person. We show that a workflow's information architecture---source access, handoff format, and which model reads the untrusted content---governs how much of a coordinated manipulation reaches the end. On 32 Taiwan~2025 recall cases, ten authentic Threads comments shown to one agent move its stance by $+0.171$ toward the injected position, and a mirrored set moves it the other way. Passing that judgment down a chain removes more than half of the shift by the third agent; keeping the comments in front of every agent sustains more of it. The reduction is not attrition in transit: each receiver discounts the inherited stance in proportion to how far it sits from its own reading of the evidence, returning to what that evidence implies for the case rather than to neutrality---consistent with partial re-anchoring. Handoff format is a second lever: a stance relayed without its reasoning is largely discounted. Susceptibility at the exposed seat varies fourfold across models, while the chain's arrangement does not matter at all. None of this is visible in the transcripts---the injected claims are almost never restated, so reasoning-trace audits miss the attack.
papers.summary: People act on evaluative judgments from LLM agents, and in multi-agent systems those judgments pass through several agents before reaching anyone, raising the question of how much a coordinated manipulation of one agent survives the chain. On 32 Taiwan 2025 recall cases, ten authentic Threads comments shown to one agent shift its stance by 0.171 toward the injected position, a mirrored set shifts it the other way, and **passing the judgment down a chain removes more than half of the shift by the third agent**, whereas keeping the comments in front of every agent sustains more of it. The loss is not attrition in transit: each receiver discounts the inherited stance in proportion to how far it sits from its own reading of the evidence, a stance relayed without its reasoning is largely discounted, susceptibility at the exposed seat varies fourfold across models while chain arrangement does not matter, and the injected claims are almost never restated, so reasoning-trace audits miss the attack.

papers.title: Evidence-First Agentic Verification
papers.abstract: Long-horizon, semi-verifiable agentic tasks often rely on rubric-based evaluation, but the evidence needed to assess these tasks can be spread across the environment state and the execution trace. A judge may overlook this evidence or accept unsupported claims, including an agent's own reports of success. When rubric verdicts serve as reinforcement-learning rewards, such errors can reinforce undesirable behavior. We introduce Sauron, an evidence-first agentic verifier that investigates both state and trace and relies on a claim only after independently validating it against its source. Bounded queries and joint investigation of related criteria reduce context use and redundant work, and each verdict carries an auditable receipt of its supporting evidence. Across 2,586 human-labeled criteria from 100 personal-assistant episodes, Sauron achieves the highest F1 of five verifiers on all eight backbones tested while costing less than Gandalf, the strongest baseline. With GPT-5.6 Sol, it reaches 0.96 F1 versus Gandalf's 0.92 at 23% lower cost, with a wider margin on process criteria. On a paired fault-injection suite covering 13 families, several of which simulate reward hacking, Sauron detects 97% of injected failures while flagging only 2% of clean controls, outperforming baselines even when they are given the full trace. On TRAIL, a benchmark for detecting and localizing real agent errors, Sauron leads both Gandalf and TRAIL's own judge on all three quality metrics.
papers.summary: Rubric-based judges for long-horizon agentic tasks can overlook evidence scattered across the environment state and execution trace, or accept an agent's own unsupported claims of success, and when those verdicts become reinforcement-learning rewards the mistakes get reinforced. `Sauron` is a verifier that actively investigates both state and trace, trusts a claim only after checking it against its source, bounds its queries, examines related rubric criteria jointly, and attaches an auditable evidence receipt to each verdict. On 2,586 human-labeled criteria from 100 personal-assistant episodes it achieves the highest F1 of five verifiers across all eight backbones tested while costing less than the strongest baseline `Gandalf`, reaching **0.96 F1 versus 0.92 at 23% lower cost** with `GPT-5.6 Sol`. On a fault-injection suite it detects 97% of injected failures while flagging only 2% of clean controls, and it leads `Gandalf` and the benchmark's own judge on all three quality metrics of `TRAIL`.

papers.title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. In continual learning scenarios, our method retains up to 9.6 points more capability on prior tasks than SFT->RL baselines, while matching or exceeding target-task performance.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents trained continually on new tasks tend to lose previously mastered skills, and the two standard post-training options trade off badly: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but forgets heavily, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves old capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. `TSRL` keeps RL as the optimization backbone and triggers SFT only on 'hard states' where the current policy fails, and the authors show that confining supervision to failure states bounds the cumulative parameter update, which limits forgetting relative to full SFT. Across `ALFWorld`, `WebShop`, and `Deep Search` at 7B and 32B scales the method improves consistently, and in continual-learning settings it **retains up to 9.6 points more prior-task capability than SFT-then-RL baselines** while matching or beating target-task performance.

papers.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
papers.abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL.md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/
papers.summary: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, and a malicious skill can look nearly identical to a legitimate automation, so a practical screen has to catch almost every attack without burying reviewers in false alarms. `SkillScreen` is a compact decision model trained to score a skill's maliciousness directly from its SKILL.md file in a single forward pass. On `MaliciousSkillBench` it **flags only 20-25% of benign skills while reaching 99% recall on unseen attack families**, far fewer than a word-level classifier or prompted LLM judges, and under the same training protocol it generalizes to unseen sources better than a fully fine-tuned encoder. The authors also find that unfamiliar benign skill collections sharply raise the false-positive rate, so recognizing new attacks does not by itself guarantee reliable screening of new sources.

papers.title: Safety for Whom? Benchmarking Understanding Beyond Refusal in Egocentric Multimodal Assistants
papers.abstract: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide what the user does next, so their outputs directly shape physical actions, including those that affect bystanders. Yet existing safety evaluations do not distinguish whom a response would harm, and score only whether a model refuses. Pooling all harms into one refusal rate hides two failures: a model may protect one target but not another, and it may refuse without understanding the risk, or understand it and comply anyway. We present STOU, a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries whose potential harm targets the user (Self), co-present individuals (The Others), or society at large (Others). Our evaluation decouples safety understanding from refusal behavior: beyond refusal, we score whether the model recognizes the user's intent, the presence and target of harm, and its downstream consequences. Across 10 open and closed source omnimodal and multimodal LLMs, we find that refusal varies systematically with the harm target, and that models often recognize a harm yet still assist with it. These results show that refusal rates alone cannot certify an assistant as safe, and that safety alignment must account for who would be harmed. Project page: https://onedayoneyeah.github.io/safety-for-whom
papers.summary: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide their next physical action, so unsafe outputs can hurt the user, people nearby, or society, yet existing safety evaluations collapse all of this into a single refusal rate. `STOU` is a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries whose potential harm targets the user, co-present individuals, or society at large, and its scoring separates safety understanding from refusal by checking whether a model recognizes the user's intent, the presence and target of harm, and the downstream consequences. Across 10 open and closed omnimodal and multimodal LLMs, **refusal rates vary systematically with who would be harmed, and models frequently recognize a harm yet still help carry it out**, so refusal alone cannot certify an assistant as safe.

papers.title: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA.
papers.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often trails full fine-tuning, and the authors trace the gap to geometry: a factorized update can only move within the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, and an analysis of ten LoRA variants shows that the gradient components left outside that space carry most of the gradient energy and are concentrated in a few spectral directions. Dynamic Tangent LoRA (`DT-LoRA`) splits a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch that tracks those principal residual directions, which the authors show are the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints, recovering them with matrix-free randomized SVD and a controlled write-back step that preserves accumulated updates. The method **adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA** yet improves consistently over LoRA and its variants across vision and language tasks, and it reaches state-of-the-art results on open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation despite being general-purpose.

papers.title: Understanding Machine Taste: Aesthetic Agreement Across Foundation Models in K-pop
papers.abstract: As foundation models enter creative industries, understanding their aesthetic preferences becomes an important step toward AI-assisted creative decision making. In this work, we investigate how foundation models evaluate creative content and characterize their ``machine taste'' using K-pop songs and music videos as a testbed. We formulate aesthetic evaluation as a pairwise ranking problem and systematically examine pairwise inter-model agreement, group-level consensus, and cross-modal preference alignment. Our results reveal stronger pairwise inter-model agreement and group-level consensus in visual evaluation than in audio evaluation, while preferences across the two modalities remain weakly aligned. We further examine how visual consensus rankings relate to real-world popularity using historical YouTube viewership data, finding positive but varying correlations across artist groups. These findings provide initial insights into machine aesthetic preferences and lay the groundwork for future AI-assisted creative decision making that considers creative content, artist identity, audience preferences, and market dynamics.
papers.summary: As foundation models move into creative industries, the authors ask what aesthetic preferences they actually hold, using K-pop songs and music videos as a testbed. They cast aesthetic judgment as pairwise ranking and measure pairwise inter-model agreement, group-level consensus, and how well preferences on audio line up with preferences on video. Models **agree with each other far more on visual evaluation than on audio evaluation**, while their audio and visual preferences are only weakly aligned, and visual consensus rankings correlate positively but inconsistently with historical YouTube viewership across artist groups.
