A random direction is just as detectable as a meaningful one and the signal is independent of the probed layer, indicating that steering produces a global, content-independent shift rather than a localized, recoverable semantic mark, and that shift is only strongly detectable when the text is degraded.

papers.title: Empowering Edge Agents: A Systematic Analysis of Edge-Cloud Collaboration in LLM Agent Execution
papers.abstract: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge-cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy-dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.
papers.summary: Edge-cloud collaboration lets an on-device model handle most of an LLM agent's work for lower inference cost and better data locality while invoking a stronger cloud model when needed, but in long-horizon tasks those cloud calls are interleaved throughout execution and their trajectory-level effects are poorly understood. `EC2-Bench` provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks with a unified evaluation of task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure, and is used to study diverse collaboration strategies. Collaboration strikes a better balance across the three axes than edge-only or cloud-only execution, and **as edge models grow stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance and differences between strategies shrink, while privacy exposure stays strongly strategy-dependent**. Stronger edge models also shift the preferred design from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward edge-controlled collaboration, with cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following identified as the key edge-side abilities.

papers.title: Follow the Perturbed Leader for Linear Bandits: $\sqrt{T}$ Regret over General Convex Sets
papers.abstract:
We give the first adversarial linear bandit algorithm based on Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) that achieves $\sqrt{T}$ regret over general convex action sets. Our algorithm attains $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{5/4}\sqrt{T})$ regret using only linear optimization oracles, and the near-optimal $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret when an optimal-design exploration distribution is further available. This improves on the $T^{2/3}$ regret of the FTPL algorithm of Dani and Hayes (2006) for general convex sets, and generalizes the $\sqrt{T}$ regret of L\'evy et al. (2026) over two special action sets (hypercube and Euclidean ball). Compared to previous oracle-efficient linear bandit algorithms based on continuous exponential weights, the FTPL approach generally has better computational efficiency, and is much simpler to implement.
  The key algorithmic element is a perturbation distribution that adapts to the estimated rewards. Its simplest form, an adaptive Gaussian perturbation, is straightforward to implement and already attains the regret bound above. We further extend it to two general constructions, random-weighting and elliptical perturbations, each covering distributions from light tails (Gaussian) to heavy tails (Student-$t_2$). On the technical side, we develop a systematic way to analyze the stability term in the FTPL regret through the Fisher information of the perturbation distribution. This builds a general framework for FTPL beyond existing ones such as the hazard rate and the FTRL-FTPL duality.
papers.summary: Adversarial linear bandits over general convex action sets previously had Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (`FTPL`) algorithms achieving only T^(2/3) regret, with √T rates known only for special sets such as the hypercube and the Euclidean ball. The new algorithm uses a perturbation distribution that adapts to the estimated rewards, in its simplest form an adaptive Gaussian perturbation, and **attains O~(d^(5/4)·√T) regret using only linear optimization oracles**, improving to the near-optimal O~(d·√T) when an optimal-design exploration distribution is also available. Two broader constructions, random-weighting and elliptical perturbations, cover distributions from light-tailed Gaussian to heavy-tailed Student-t, and the analysis bounds the stability term of the `FTPL` regret through the Fisher information of the perturbation distribution, giving a framework beyond existing hazard-rate and FTRL-FTPL duality arguments. Compared with oracle-efficient methods based on continuous exponential weights, the `FTPL` approach is generally more computationally efficient and simpler to implement.

papers.title: Same Attack, Different Judge: A First Controlled Adversarial Comparison of Jev, LLM Judges, and Purpose-Built Safety Classifiers
papers.abstract: TypeSafe AI's Jev is a new kind of safety judge. It generates no text and no label: it answers questions the developer defines in advance and returns a probability for each answer. The vendor admits that adversarial input can change these answers but gives no numbers. In this paper, we present the first controlled adversarial evaluation of Jev. We build a test harness that sends every system the same payload under the same policy, and run it on four public-data tasks, from rule-based ones (input moderation, injection detection, routing) to a judgment-based one (phishing detection), with fifty attack variants from thirteen families. The targets are Jev, five GPT and GLM judges, and two local classifiers (Llama Guard 3, Prompt Guard 2). We find that Jev is the most robust system on input moderation: eight forgeries of its structured input bypass none of its decisions, and a sentence asking only why someone might make a harmful request bypasses 9% of its blocks, against 56% for GPT-6 Astra. On phishing detection. However, the same forgeries bypass 19-29% of the emails it flags, and even without attack Jev detects only 62% of phishing emails, against 77-81% for the GLM judges. Jev is also the fastest judge, but it flags the most benign requests (27%). The local classifiers fail differently: a training-example statement makes Llama Guard 3 miss 62% of the phishing it had flagged. These results suggest that Jev resists attacks on tasks with a clear rule to check but is more exposed on tasks that call for an overall judgment.
papers.summary: `Jev`, a safety judge from TypeSafe AI, generates no text or label but returns a probability for each answer to questions the developer defines in advance, and its vendor acknowledges that adversarial input can change those answers without giving numbers. The authors build a harness that sends identical payloads under identical policies to `Jev`, five `GPT` and `GLM` judges, and two local classifiers (`Llama Guard 3` and `Prompt Guard 2`) across four public-data tasks, from rule-based input moderation, injection detection, and routing to judgment-based phishing detection, using fifty attack variants from thirteen families. **On input moderation, eight forgeries of `Jev`'s structured input bypass none of its decisions, and a sentence asking only why someone might make a harmful request bypasses 9% of its blocks against 56% for `GPT-6 Astra`**, but on phishing detection the same forgeries bypass 19 to 29% of the emails it flags and even unattacked it detects only 62% of phishing emails against 77 to 81% for the `GLM` judges. `Jev` is also the fastest judge yet flags the most benign requests at 27%, a training-example statement makes `Llama Guard 3` miss 62% of the phishing it had flagged, and the authors conclude that `Jev` resists attacks on tasks with a clear rule to check but is more exposed on tasks that call for overall judgment.

papers.title: Checking the Checkers: A Synthesis of Verifier Noise and Robustness in RLVR
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a principal recipe for improving the reasoning of large language models (LLMs). It rests on the assumption that the checker scoring each response is itself correct. In practice, rule-based checkers reject correct answers in unexpected formats, unit tests accept incorrect programs, and LLM judges can be led to approve empty or adversarial responses. This work surveys 58 studies that measure, analyze, or mitigate such verifier errors. We ask what errors verifiers make, how they affect training, which mitigations work against which errors, and how the findings extend to self-generated, rubric- and judge-based, and verifier-free rewards. The evidence suggests that the structure of an error matters more than its rate. Random errors mostly slow learning, though under a fixed budget or KL regularization they also lower final accuracy. False positives that the policy can learn to trigger can cause plateaus or collapse, sometimes even with a low initial error rate. Whether a verifier wrongly rejects or accepts depends on what it checks and who built it, not on its family. Its errors shift as the policy improves, and most mitigations have been tested against only one kind of error. We compile the findings into comparison tables, reconcile apparent conflicts in the literature, and propose a reporting protocol to make future results comparable.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) assumes the checker scoring each response is correct, yet rule-based checkers reject valid answers in unexpected formats, unit tests pass incorrect programs, and large language model (LLM) judges can be led to approve empty or adversarial responses. The survey synthesizes 58 studies that measure, analyze, or mitigate such verifier errors, asking what errors occur, how they affect training, which mitigations address which error types, and how the findings extend to self-generated, rubric-based, judge-based, and verifier-free rewards. **The structure of an error matters more than its rate**: random errors mostly slow learning, while false positives the policy can learn to trigger can cause plateaus or collapse even at a low initial error rate. Error patterns also shift as the policy improves, most mitigations have been tested against only one error type, and the authors compile comparison tables and propose a reporting protocol to make future results comparable.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Training Reward Models for Cross-Source Evidence Grounding in Search Agents
papers.abstract: Existing approaches to training and evaluating search agents focus heavily on final-answer quality, largely neglecting how generated answers map back to retrieved evidence. Recent methods track citations to enforce grounding, but citation support alone does not establish source independence or whether an answer appropriately handles conflicting evidence. We argue that credibility in open-web retrieval depends on principled cross-source evidence grounding that accounts for source independence and systematically attributes and adjudicates conflicting evidence, while hierarchical judgments of these grounding decisions provide a unified signal for training and evaluation. To this end, we propose an evaluation framework, Cross-Source Evidence Grounding (CSEG), that employs a fine-grained, six-layer decision tree over the complete search trajectory. We introduce CSEG-Bench and trainable reward models to provide targeted supervision following this framework. Our approach helps eliminating the severe data skew of natural trajectories by providing targeted coverage over complex, deep-layer decision paths, such as cross-source conflict resolution and nuanced attribution, that standard rollouts fail to capture. Specifically, (1) we define the hierarchy at label, node, and path levels; (2) we construct 1,160 verified trajectories over nine canonical paths by rewriting answers on real retrieved document pools, with independent frontier judges reproducing the entire gold path and human experts deciding inclusion; (3) we train CSEG-RM, which reaches 83.9% exact accuracy on our benchmark while lying on the performance-token efficiency Pareto frontier. Experiments that use this reward alone to supervise a frozen-retrieval answer policy raise the independently judged mean label from 2.83 to 4.19, and show that learning the hierarchy generalizes across layers at a fraction of frontier-judge cost.
papers.summary: Search agents are usually trained and evaluated on final-answer quality, which says little about whether an answer rests on independent sources or handles conflicting evidence appropriately. Cross-Source Evidence Grounding (`CSEG`) scores a complete search trajectory with a fine-grained six-layer decision tree covering source independence, attribution, and conflict adjudication, with judgments defined at label, node, and path levels. `CSEG-Bench` supplies 1,160 verified trajectories over nine canonical decision paths, built by rewriting answers on real retrieved document pools, reproduced by independent frontier judges, and screened by human experts to cover deep-layer decisions that natural rollouts rarely reach. The trained reward model `CSEG-RM` reaches **83.9% exact accuracy** on the benchmark while sitting on the accuracy-versus-token Pareto frontier, and using it as the sole reward for a frozen-retrieval answer policy raises the independently judged mean label from 2.83 to 4.19 at a fraction of frontier-judge cost.

papers.title: QK-Edit: Revisiting Attention-based Injection in MM-DiT for Image and Video Editing
papers.abstract: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction, where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention. However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation. Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference. QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.
papers.summary: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) concatenate image and text tokens and process them with a single Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) block, which makes the attention-manipulation editing techniques developed for U-Net diffusion models ineffective. `QK-Edit` is a training-free method that isolates and adjusts the query and key components of this attention to balance prompt fidelity against structural consistency, and it can be implemented as simple feature replacement at inference. It handles object addition, removal, and replacement, background, material, and color changes, and style transfer, and the authors report **superior editing results on `FLUX` and `HunyuanVideo`** for both image and video editing.

papers.title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing
papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are appealing for code generation because they can update many tokens in parallel, yet many are optimized for sequence synthesis rather than edit prediction. This setting is poorly matched to modern AI-assisted IDEs, where edit prediction must infer the next code change from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context. Such changes are usually sparse and preserve most source tokens, so regenerating a full code segment wastes computation. We propose Diff Diffusion, a diffusion-inspired LLM framework for code editing that predicts edit paths from an original snippet to its revised form. Diff Diffusion represents denoising as structured edit operations, and combines this formulation with multi-stage training and efficient parallel decoding. By focusing computation on changed regions, Diff Diffusion supports accurate low-latency edits and multi-position parallel modification. Across public edit-completion benchmarks, edit-prediction evaluations, and online validation, Diff Diffusion matches or leads autoregressive baselines while delivering 2.78 times faster inference on public edit-completion benchmarks and a 39.0% P50 model-latency reduction in production. This work provides a new modeling perspective for AI applications that require high accuracy and low latency.
papers.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can update many tokens in parallel, but most are optimized for generating whole sequences rather than predicting the sparse, token-preserving edits that AI-assisted IDEs need from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context. `Diff Diffusion` reframes denoising as a sequence of structured edit operations that transform an original snippet into its revised form, combined with multi-stage training and parallel decoding so computation concentrates on changed regions and supports multi-position edits. Across public edit-completion benchmarks, edit-prediction evaluations, and online validation, it matches or leads autoregressive baselines while running **2.78 times faster** on the public benchmarks and cutting P50 model latency by 39.0% in production.

papers.title: Agentic-MatriBO: Capability-Compiled Agentic Bayesian Optimization for Materials and Chemical Design
papers.abstract: Materials and chemical optimization must choose the next synthesis, characterization, or high-fidelity simulation from sequential observations under a limited budget. Large language models can use task knowledge to propose adjustments, but composing surrogates, acquisition functions, and search strategies is constrained by compatibility, parameter dependencies, and evidence requirements. We present Agentic-MatriBO, a capability-compiled agentic Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that represents BO components and selection conditions as composable capabilities. A language policy proposes BO recipes and candidate plans; a compiler checks proposals against the registered capability catalog; and a deterministic execution layer validates and commits candidates. Oracle observations are stored in research memory and inform later rounds. We compare Agentic-MatriBO with eight baselines on four offline finite candidate pools---COF, PCE10, Buchwald--Hartwig (BH), and Suzuki--Miyaura---using five seeds per condition; results are reported descriptively. Across the four tasks, Agentic-MatriBO has the best mean endpoint quality after orienting each objective so that higher is better. On COF, it reaches the tabulated optimum in all five seeds both in the end-to-end comparison and after shared initialization, where it also retains an advantage in cumulative quality. Its normalized area under the best-so-far quality curve during the BO stage (nAUC-BO) is substantially higher on COF, near parity with the best baseline on PCE10 and BH, and lower on Suzuki. COF ablations show that removing the capability compiler or evidence gate coincides with lower cumulative quality and fewer exact-optimum hits. The framework provides an inspectable interface for evidence-conditioned BO adaptation.
papers.summary: Materials and chemical optimization must choose the next synthesis, characterization, or simulation under a limited budget, and while large language models can propose adjustments, composing Bayesian optimization (BO) surrogates, acquisition functions, and search strategies is constrained by compatibility, parameter dependencies, and evidence requirements. `Agentic-MatriBO` represents BO components and their selection conditions as composable capabilities: a language policy proposes recipes and candidate plans, a compiler checks them against a registered catalog, a deterministic execution layer validates and commits candidates, and oracle observations feed a research memory for later rounds. Against eight baselines on the `COF`, `PCE10`, `Buchwald-Hartwig`, and `Suzuki-Miyaura` candidate pools with five seeds each, it has the best mean endpoint quality across tasks and **reaches the tabulated optimum on `COF` in all five seeds**. Its normalized area under the best-so-far curve is substantially higher on `COF`, near parity on `PCE10` and `Buchwald-Hartwig`, and lower on `Suzuki-Miyaura`, and ablations show that removing the capability compiler or evidence gate reduces cumulative quality.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Quantum Amplitude Embedding with Data Re-Uploading
papers.abstract: Amplitude embedding lets a variational quantum model read many classical features with few qubits, but the model output is then only a quadratic form in the normalized input. Data re-uploading, which encodes the input repeatedly between trainable blocks, can be used to enrich such a model. Because every additional upload of an amplitude embedding repeats a costly state preparation, the gain that an upload buys has to be known before the gates are spent. This tutorial thus addresses the problem of explaining what data re-uploading adds to an amplitude-embedded model and how large the gain is. We express sequential re-uploading and parallel re-uploading with two copies in one notation and show that each upload raises the reachable polynomial order by two. Under one trainable circuit family and one budget of trainable parameters, simulation results show that re-uploading raises the test coefficient of determination from 0.689 to between 0.883 and 0.975 on targets of order four and from 0.337 to between 0.642 and 0.783 on targets of order six, on all ten seeds. On a quadratic target and on handwritten digits, one upload remains the best choice, and every additional upload lowers the gate error that the classifier tolerates. These results help designers match the number of uploads to the polynomial order of the task at hand.
papers.summary: Amplitude embedding lets a variational quantum model read many classical features with few qubits, but the output is then only a quadratic form in the normalized input, and each additional data re-upload repeats a costly state preparation whose payoff should be known before the gates are spent. The tutorial expresses sequential re-uploading and two-copy parallel re-uploading in one notation and shows that **each upload raises the reachable polynomial order by two**. Under one trainable circuit family and a fixed parameter budget, simulations lift the test coefficient of determination from 0.689 to between 0.883 and 0.975 on fourth-order targets and from 0.337 to between 0.642 and 0.783 on sixth-order targets across all ten seeds. On a quadratic target and on handwritten digits a single upload remains best, and every additional upload lowers the gate error the classifier tolerates.

papers.title: ProtoArena: Can AI Agents Discover and Exploit Real-World Cross-Component Protocol Vulnerabilities?
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. We introduce ProtoArena, a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark with 80 cross-component vulnerability-exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories. Tasks are primarily informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms. Agents interact with running systems through scoped interfaces to achieve security-effect objectives without target source code. Three information levels assess guided reproduction, exploitation with mechanism and topology context, and effect-directed black-box exploration. A hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. We evaluate five LLMs. Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest observed success rates: 48.8% under L1 guidance and 12.5% under effect-directed black-box L3. In a separate DNSBomb optimization experiment, it achieves a peak downstream-response to average query-input byte-rate ratio exceeding 171,000 times. The results show that agents can achieve verifiable exploitation effects in some cross-component environments, but success with limited black-box information remains low and varies across domains and attack categories. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets; they do not test production systems or disclose previously unknown vulnerabilities.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, but existing benchmarks rarely cover exploits that depend on interactions among network protocol components, such as inconsistent message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. `ProtoArena` is a black-box, multi-component benchmark with 80 exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories, where agents act on running systems through scoped interfaces without source code at three information levels, and a hybrid verifier combines rule checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. Of five LLMs evaluated, `Claude Opus 4.8` scores highest with **48.8% success under guided reproduction but only 12.5% under effect-directed black-box exploration**, and in a separate `DNSBomb` optimization experiment it reaches a response-to-query byte-rate ratio above 171,000. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets and disclose no previously unknown vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Learning Adaptive Deliberation Control for Reliable Recognition with Multi-Agent Language Models
papers.abstract: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed controls cannot respond to changes in disagreement or reasoning quality. We present an adaptive multi-agent controller (ADMA) that learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination while keeping the task model frozen. Shared trace features describe quality, agreement, and progress, while role-specific features support decentralized control during inference. One controller trained on legal and financial reasoning is transferred without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two successive task-model versions. With Qwen3.5 held fixed, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2-14.2 percentage points over Direct and by 2.8-3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed. Paired bootstrap ranges for the Full-Fixed comparison are positive on three tasks. Outcome decompositions show that recoveries exceed introduced errors, while process assessment records fewer false-consensus events and more supported correct outcomes. Transfer to Qwen3.6 remains task dependent, which bounds the generality of the learned policy. Median token and latency ratios are 14.3-18.7 and 7.8-16.5 relative to Direct. These results show that adaptive deliberation can improve fixed-model recognition when its task-dependent gains justify the additional computation.
papers.summary: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed controls cannot respond to changes in disagreement or reasoning quality. The adaptive multi-agent controller (`ADMA`) learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination from shared trace features describing quality, agreement, and progress, while the task model stays frozen and role-specific features allow decentralized control at inference. A single controller trained on legal and financial reasoning transfers without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks, and with `Qwen3.5` fixed the full variant **improves accuracy by 6.2 to 14.2 percentage points over direct answering** and by 2.8 to 3.0 points over a fixed-policy variant, with recoveries exceeding introduced errors. Transfer to `Qwen3.6` is task dependent, and median token and latency costs are 14.3 to 18.7 and 7.8 to 16.5 times those of direct answering.

papers.title: FASHION-RQ: Mining Hierarchical Semantic Structure for Automated Evaluation of Fashion Retrieval
papers.abstract: Evaluating fashion retrieval systems remains challenging due to the limited availability of benchmarks that capture the fine-grained, open-ended queries encountered in real-world search and recommendation. Existing benchmarks often rely on manual curation, predefined taxonomies, or synthetic prompts, limiting scalability and semantic coverage. We introduce FASHION-RQ: Mining Hierarchical Semantic Structure for Automated Evaluation of Fashion Retrieval, an automated framework that derives user-type queries and relevance sets directly from catalog structure. Our key insight is that hierarchical discrete representations learned by Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoders (RQ-VAE) organize products into semantically coherent clusters at progressively finer granularities. We leverage this structure to construct FASHION-RQBENCH, a scalable benchmark without manual query annotation or predefined taxonomies. We propose four complementary tasks for evaluating ranking, relevance classification, fine-grained sibling discrimination, and paraphrase robustness, alongside query- and attribute-level relevance metrics. Experiments across recent retrieval models demonstrate that FASHION-RQBENCH differentiates model capabilities across query types and attributes. A human study further shows that benchmark queries achieve comparable naturalness and higher intent clarity than real user queries, supporting their validity for real-world evaluation. The code and FASHION-RQBENCH dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance.
papers.summary: Fashion retrieval benchmarks typically rely on manual curation, predefined taxonomies, or synthetic prompts, which limits their scale and semantic coverage. `FASHION-RQ` derives user-style queries and relevance sets automatically from catalog structure, exploiting the observation that Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoders (`RQ-VAE`) organize products into semantically coherent clusters at progressively finer granularities. The resulting `FASHION-RQBENCH` defines four tasks covering ranking, relevance classification, fine-grained sibling discrimination, and paraphrase robustness, plus query- and attribute-level relevance metrics, and differentiates recent retrieval models across query types and attributes. **A human study finds the benchmark queries match real user queries in naturalness and exceed them in intent clarity**, and the code and dataset are slated for release.

papers.title: GeoNIRS: Geometry-Aware Pretraining for Heterogeneous fNIRS Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides portable and spatially localized measurements of cortical hemodynamics, but differences in channel count, probe layout, signal distribution, and task type hinder joint pretraining across datasets. We introduce GeoNIRS, a geometry-aware framework that uses source-detector locations as a shared spatial reference across heterogeneous probe layouts. GeoNIRS compresses variable-size channel sets into a fixed-size latent representation and employs bidirectional HbO/HbR cross-reconstruction with contiguous temporal masking. GeoNIRS-base is pretrained on eight heterogeneous datasets, while GeoNIRS-large scales to 22 datasets. Neither downstream data nor labels are used during pretraining, enabling evaluation under a strict cross-task setting. To our knowledge, GeoNIRS is the first fNIRS framework to explicitly model physical channel geometry during joint pretraining across heterogeneous channel configurations, and the first to provide complete source code and downloadable pretrained checkpoints. We evaluate GeoNIRS on eight held-out tasks spanning clinical and auditory assessment, pain and affective processing, semantic decoding, and motor function. GeoNIRS achieves the highest task-averaged balanced accuracy among the evaluated conventional machine-learning, fNIRS-specific, general time-series, and fNIRS pretraining baselines. Compared with random initialization, pretraining improves average balanced accuracy by 4.12 percentage points under linear probing and 3.30 points under full fine-tuning, with larger benefits when labels are scarce. GeoNIRS also remains robust to missing input channels. Geometry perturbations and pretraining ablations further show that both channel geometry and cross-chromophore reconstruction contribute to the learned representations.
papers.summary: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides portable measurements of cortical hemodynamics, but differences in channel count, probe layout, signal distribution, and task type across datasets hinder joint pretraining. `GeoNIRS` uses source-detector locations as a shared spatial reference across probe layouts, compresses variable-size channel sets into a fixed-size latent, and pretrains with bidirectional oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbO/HbR) cross-reconstruction under contiguous temporal masking. A base model is pretrained on eight heterogeneous datasets and a large model on 22, with no downstream data or labels used, and the authors release full source code and checkpoints. On eight held-out clinical, affective, semantic, and motor tasks it achieves the highest task-averaged balanced accuracy among conventional, fNIRS-specific, time-series, and fNIRS-pretraining baselines, with pretraining adding **4.12 percentage points under linear probing** and 3.30 under full fine-tuning over random initialization, larger gains when labels are scarce, and robustness to missing channels.

papers.title: Persistence Positional Encoding: A Minimal Transformer Recipe for Persistence Diagrams
papers.abstract: Persistence diagrams (PDs) represent multiscale topological information as multisets of birth-death pairs $(b,d)$. How best to use them with Transformers, however, remains unclear. Connecting PDs to Transformers requires choosing how topological information is tokenized and exposed to self-attention. Prior methods use specialized designs for tokenization, aggregation, Transformer blocks, or attention, but are hard to compare since reported results rarely share PD inputs, splits, or model-selection rules. We instead confine the diagram-specific design to point representation, mapping each birth-death pair through fixed random Fourier features while leaving the Transformer backbone unchanged, and call this recipe Persistence Positional Encoding (PPE). In matched controls on eight TU graph benchmarks (TU8), changing only point representation shifts macro accuracy by 5.49 to 6.47 percentage points (pp), against 0.47 to 1.45 pp from changing the downstream module, identifying point representation as the dominant design variable tested. We further reevaluate vectorizations, kernels, learned representations, and Transformer-based models under one protocol with shared PD inputs, outer folds, and validation-only selection. Among all evaluated PD methods and downstream configurations, PPE achieves the highest mean on most benchmarks, including TU8, ORBIT5K, and MCB-C. Finally, we prove that grid averaging leaves a reconstruction error at any resolution, whereas a Transformer with fixed random Fourier frequencies is almost surely universal. PPE thus offers a minimal, Transformer-native baseline for persistence diagrams, and a common protocol for future comparison.
papers.summary: Persistence diagrams (PDs) represent multiscale topological information as multisets of birth-death pairs, but existing Transformer approaches use specialized tokenization, aggregation, or attention designs that are hard to compare because reported results rarely share inputs, splits, or model-selection rules. Persistence Positional Encoding (`PPE`) confines the diagram-specific design to point representation, mapping each birth-death pair through fixed random Fourier features and leaving the Transformer backbone unchanged. In matched controls on eight `TU` graph benchmarks, **changing only the point representation shifts macro accuracy by 5.49 to 6.47 percentage points**, versus 0.47 to 1.45 points from changing the downstream module, and under a unified protocol `PPE` achieves the highest mean on most benchmarks including `TU8`, `ORBIT5K`, and `MCB-C`. The authors also prove that grid averaging leaves a reconstruction error at any resolution, whereas a Transformer with fixed random Fourier frequencies is almost surely universal.

papers.title: MMTA: Benchmarking Multimodal Temporal Analysis with Time Series, Text, and Vision
papers.abstract: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- robotics, autonomous driving, human action, manufacturing, AR assistance, healthcare, recommendation, finance, and climate -- under video+TS and image+TS layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split covering classification and forecasting. The benchmark standardizes heterogeneous real-world sources into a shared schema with domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs reveals a shared bottleneck: representing time series as text creates very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence, especially in long-video settings. We then introduce TimeOmni-v, a multimodal LLM extension with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head. TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, showing that MMTA not only exposes representation and grounding failures but also motivates targeted model design.
papers.summary: Most multimodal time-series benchmarks pair signals with text or with plots derived from the same signal, leaving open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. `MMTA` provides tri-modal classification and forecasting tasks across nine domains including robotics, autonomous driving, healthcare, and finance, in video-plus-time-series and image-plus-time-series layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split, a shared schema with domain-specific prompts and provenance, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs exposes a shared bottleneck: **serializing time series as text produces very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence**, especially in long-video settings. The proposed `TimeOmni-v` extension adds a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head, improving long-video classification and inference efficiency.

papers.title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.
papers.summary: Agent Skills make task knowledge reusable across LLM agent sessions, but a single successful attempt often leaves a procedure and its conditions of use untested, limiting transfer. Socratic Skill Learning (`SSL`) interleaves guidance from an Educator with practice by a Student that remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, free to question, test, and adapt the advice, and `SkillTransferBench` measures reuse with 35 task families and 408 executable cases evaluated in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family cohort, Fixed-Window `SSL` reaches **0.801 utility versus 0.723 with no Skill**, 0.761 for adapted `Trace2Skill`, and 0.751 for adapted `SKILL-KD`, and interleaved guidance outperforms both expert authoring and post-hoc teaching across three model pairs. An Issue-Guided variant that tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions reaches 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens.

papers.title: TStruct: Learning Shared Temporal Structures for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Long-term time series forecasting requires temporal dependency modeling that remains stable and generalizable under temporal distribution shifts. However, real-world time series are often noisy and non-stationary, making deep learning models prone to fitting incidental temporal interactions in the training data. A key question is whether there exist temporal relationship structures that recur across different temporal positions and variables. We analyze temporal relationship matrices on commonly used time series datasets and find that samples from different temporal positions and different variables exhibit shared dominant temporal relationship structures. This indicates that temporal relationship structures contain patterns that recur stably across samples and variables. To learn such shared structures, we propose \textbf{T}emporal \textbf{Struct}ure Network (\textbf{TStruct}), a simple yet effective network for directly learning shared and generalizable temporal dependencies. Specifically, TStruct directly parameterizes a set of shared temporal dependency matrices and generates normalized combination weights using dynamic sample information and static variable priors. These weights represent a soft allocation of each sample-variable pair over shared temporal dependency structures, enabling the model to generate adaptive temporal dependency matrices under shared structural constraints, rather than fitting incidental interactions in a fully unconstrained manner. Notably, this simple structure-aware design consistently outperforms several strong baselines across all datasets, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining high computational efficiency.
papers.summary: Long-term time-series forecasting needs temporal dependency modeling that stays stable under distribution shift, yet noisy, non-stationary data lead deep models to fit incidental interactions in the training set. Analyzing temporal relationship matrices on common datasets, the authors find that samples from different positions and variables share dominant dependency structures, and propose Temporal Structure Network (`TStruct`), which directly parameterizes a set of shared temporal dependency matrices and softly allocates each sample-variable pair over them using dynamic sample information and static variable priors. This structure-constrained adaptive design **consistently outperforms several strong baselines across all evaluated datasets** while keeping computational cost low.

papers.title: RT-J: Large-Scale Pretraining of Relational Transformers for Context-Efficient Predictions
papers.abstract: Foundation models for tables and relational databases are increasingly used for predictive tasks across various scientific and industrial domains. However, adapting existing models to unseen datasets requires tens of thousands of examples. Here we introduce RT-J, an 85M-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) that makes accurate predictions even with hundreds of in-context examples or fewer. To achieve this, we first assemble the Join, a large collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks. We pretrain with long contexts of up to 8,192 database cells, using in-context examples from a novel lightweight random-walk retriever. Finally, we leverage context tuning and ensembling to scale up test-time compute. On in-context regression tasks from RelBench, RT-J requires 10x fewer examples on average to match strong feature engineering pipelines with LLM-agent or RDBLearn featurizers and TabICLv2 or LightGBM predictors. Overall, our work pushes the frontier for context-efficient predictions on relational data and highlights the importance of real-world semantics, context engineering and large-scale pretraining for RFMs.
papers.summary: Foundation models for tables and relational databases typically need tens of thousands of examples to adapt to an unseen dataset. `RT-J` is an 85M-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) pretrained on `Join`, a collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks, using contexts of up to 8,192 database cells assembled by a lightweight random-walk retriever, with context tuning and ensembling to scale test-time compute. On in-context regression tasks from `RelBench`, it **needs 10x fewer examples on average** to match strong feature-engineering pipelines that pair LLM-agent or `RDBLearn` featurizers with `TabICLv2` or `LightGBM` predictors.

papers.title: Prefilling-dLLM v2: Learned Chunk Routing for Long-Context Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models apply bidirectional attention over the whole context at every denoising step, so a longer context makes each step substantially more expensive. Sparsifying only at inference leaves the pretrained weights unchanged, so the model is never trained under the sparse pattern it runs with. We propose Prefilling-dLLM v2, which continues training a diffusion language model so that it routes with its native mask token. One mask is appended at the end of each chunk, and a learned role offset marks it as a routing slot. On every fourth layer, a query keeps a bidirectional local window and the top-K chunks scored from that mask; the other layers use a bidirectional sliding window. Starting from Dream-v0-Base-7B extended to 16K with YaRN, we compare Prefilling-dLLM v2 with bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA under the same layout, key budget, and dense initialization, using the same Fast-dLLM decoder. With the YaRN factor scaled to the evaluation length, Prefilling-dLLM v2 leads the other sparse methods on all three RULER tasks from 16K to 128K. Its mean accuracy at 128K is 7.4 points above NSA, the next sparse model, while DSA and SWA remain near zero. At the same length, decoding is 172x faster than with full dense attention.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models apply bidirectional attention over the entire context at every denoising step, so cost grows steeply with context length, and sparsifying only at inference leaves the model running under a pattern it was never trained for. `Prefilling-dLLM v2` continues training so the model routes with its native mask token: one mask appended to each chunk serves as a routing slot marked by a learned role offset, every fourth layer attends to a bidirectional local window plus the top-K chunks scored from those masks, and the other layers use a bidirectional sliding window. Starting from `Dream-v0-Base-7B` extended to 16K with `YaRN` and decoded with `Fast-dLLM`, it leads bidirectional `NSA`, `DSA`, and `SWA` on all three `RULER` tasks from 16K to 128K under the same layout, key budget, and initialization. **Mean accuracy at 128K is 7.4 points above `NSA`**, the next-best sparse method, while `DSA` and `SWA` fall near zero, and decoding at that length is 172x faster than full dense attention.

papers.title: ECMR: Evidence-Aware Deliberation Control for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. We introduce ECMR, an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs. At each step, ECMR summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then selects whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. We formulate this decision as finite-horizon budgeted control and derive sufficient conditions under which state conditioning, risk-triggered verification, and role correction improve cost-adjusted utility. Across a declared held-out evaluation of 9,000 records from MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, ECMR-Full increases pooled accuracy from 62.1% to 84.9%, reduces false-consensus rate from 40.7% to 17.0%, and raises evidence-support rate from 58.0% to 88.7%. State shuffling loses 11.7 accuracy points with only 0.7 fewer rounds, while harder traces shift from early stopping toward arbitration. ECMR-Full uses the largest token budget, yielding the strongest absolute reliability rather than uniformly superior token efficiency.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems usually commit to a deliberation protocol before inference, so they cannot spend more compute on unresolved instances and may mistake repeated, correlated rationales for independent confirmation, a failure the authors term semantic false consensus. `ECMR` is an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs that at each step summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then chooses to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. The decision is framed as finite-horizon budgeted control, with derived sufficient conditions under which state conditioning, risk-triggered verification, and role correction improve cost-adjusted utility. On a held-out evaluation of 9,000 records from `MedQA`, `CaseHOLD`, and `FinQA`, the full controller **raises pooled accuracy from 62.1% to 84.9%**, cuts the false-consensus rate from 40.7% to 17.0%, and lifts evidence-support rate from 58.0% to 88.7%, though it also uses the largest token budget of the compared configurations.

papers.title: Searching for What Matters: Open-Ended Discovery of Multiple Hypotheses with Agentic Data Exploration
papers.abstract: Discovering what drives an outcome from data is central to science and often requires deciding what is worth investigating before a specific hypothesis is known. Yet most existing hypothesis generation settings substantially narrow this search by providing a research question, target relationship, or curated context. We introduce open-ended multiple hypothesis discovery, where a system receives only a large tabular dataset and an outcome and must discover multiple data-supported hypotheses without knowing in advance the relevant variables, functional forms, conditions, or number of underlying mechanisms. To study this problem, we introduce a benchmark built from structural causal models grounded in real-world data schemas, containing 351 planted hypotheses across 15 tasks and five domains, with 53--65 variables and 1M--10M rows per task. The causal model is hidden from the discovery method and retained only by the evaluator, allowing proposed hypotheses to be tested through interventions and separating observational discovery from causal validation. We further propose HypAgent, which treats the dataset as an interactive environment and performs iterative search by proposing candidate directions, triaging and refining promising hypotheses, and removing explained signal so that each accepted discovery redirects subsequent search. HypAgent achieves 0.47 precision, 0.51 recall, and 0.49 F1, compared with 0.35 F1 for the strongest baseline. Our analysis shows that many failures occur after a relevant variable has already been surfaced, suggesting that correctly characterizing a mechanism's functional form and conditions, rather than merely identifying relevant variables, remains a key challenge in open-ended discovery.
papers.summary: Most hypothesis-generation settings supply a research question, target relationship, or curated context, whereas real discovery requires deciding what is worth investigating before any hypothesis is known. The authors define open-ended multiple hypothesis discovery, where a system receives only a large tabular dataset and an outcome, and build a benchmark from structural causal models grounded in real-world schemas with 351 planted hypotheses across 15 tasks, each with 53 to 65 variables and 1M to 10M rows, where the hidden causal model lets the evaluator test proposals through interventions. `HypAgent` treats the dataset as an interactive environment, iteratively proposing directions, triaging and refining candidates, and removing explained signal so each accepted discovery redirects the search, reaching **0.49 F1 against 0.35 for the strongest baseline** with 0.47 precision and 0.51 recall. Many failures occur after the relevant variable has already surfaced, suggesting that characterizing a mechanism's functional form and conditions is the harder problem.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Transfer of Evil Vectors Is Directionally Asymmetric
papers.abstract: Persona vectors are linear directions in the residual-stream activations of LLMs that encode behavioral traits and enable fine-grained control over model behavior. Among them, the evil persona vector is particularly relevant to understanding harmful behavior, jailbreak vulnerabilities, and the unlearning of harmful knowledge. Yet whether this vector reflects a genuinely cross-lingual concept, rather than an artifact of its extraction language, remains untested. We conduct a systematic evil-vector transfer study across two high-resource languages (English, Spanish) and two low-resource languages (Swahili, Telugu) on four open-source instruction-tuned LLMs, and find that transfer is directionally asymmetric. Evil vectors are harder to obtain reliably from low-resource languages, and the resulting vectors are largely ineffective at steering, even within their own language. In contrast, vectors extracted from high-resource languages transfer effectively to low-resource inputs while largely preserving general knowledge, as measured by MMLU. Geometric analysis further supports this pattern: evil vectors from the two high-resource languages are closely aligned, whereas low-resource vectors align only weakly with this shared direction. These results suggest that a shared cross-lingual evil direction exists and, once reliably extracted from a high-resource language, can be reused to steer behavior in low-resource languages without additional per-language data collection.
papers.summary: Persona vectors are linear directions in an LLM's residual-stream activations that encode behavioral traits, and the evil vector in particular bears on harmful behavior, jailbreak vulnerability, and unlearning, but whether it reflects a genuinely cross-lingual concept rather than an artifact of its extraction language has not been tested. Extracting and transferring evil vectors across English, Spanish, Swahili, and Telugu on four open-source instruction-tuned LLMs, the study finds the transfer is directionally asymmetric. **Vectors extracted from high-resource languages steer behavior effectively on low-resource inputs** while largely preserving general knowledge as measured by `MMLU`, whereas vectors from low-resource languages are hard to extract reliably and barely steer even their own language. Geometric analysis shows the English and Spanish vectors are closely aligned while the low-resource vectors align only weakly with that shared direction, suggesting a single cross-lingual evil direction that can be reused without per-language data collection.

papers.title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics
papers.abstract: Microscopic simulations resolve spatial patterns but are feasible only over small domains and short timescales, whereas bulk descriptions erase those patterns through spatial averaging. Mesoscopic fields preserve this spatial organisation, but their effective equations are known only for selected microscopic systems and scaling limits. We introduce Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics (DeepMesoD), which uses neural networks to learn an effective mesoscopic field equation from microscopic trajectories at a prescribed coarse-graining scale. For the nonconserved dissipative dynamics studied here, DeepMesoD learns the free-energy functional with a spatial interaction kernel and a state-dependent dissipation operator constrained by the fluctuation-dissipation relation. We first validate the construction in the Ising-Kac model, where the learned mesoscopic equation recovers the known hydrodynamic limit and rollouts remain stable far beyond the training horizon. We then treat two systems without closed-form mesoscopic descriptions. For a two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet governed by atomistic spin dynamics, DeepMesoD learns a mesoscopic model whose predictions match atomistic references up to 1 ns, and a rollout with an unseen initial condition remains bounded up to 25 ns. For layered CrBr$_3$, the learned kernel captures the suppression and sign reversal of interlayer coupling at a stacking fault whose location and strength are not supplied as inputs. Controlled changes to the learned interaction show how fault number and placement shape multistep magnetic responses, complementing our magneto-photoluminescence measurements. Across the two atomistic systems, DeepMesoD achieves a three-to-four-order-of-magnitude reduction in wall-clock time compared with atomistic spin dynamics.
papers.summary: Microscopic simulations resolve spatial patterns but only over small domains and short timescales, bulk descriptions average those patterns away, and mesoscopic field equations that preserve them are known only for selected systems and scaling limits. Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics (`DeepMesoD`) uses neural networks to learn an effective mesoscopic field equation from microscopic trajectories at a prescribed coarse-graining scale, learning a free-energy functional with a spatial interaction kernel and a state-dependent dissipation operator constrained by the fluctuation-dissipation relation. It recovers the known hydrodynamic limit of the `Ising-Kac` model with rollouts stable far beyond the training horizon, matches atomistic spin dynamics of a two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet up to 1 ns with an unseen-initial-condition rollout bounded to 25 ns, and for layered CrBr3 captures the suppression and sign reversal of interlayer coupling at a stacking fault whose location and strength were never supplied. Across the two atomistic systems it delivers a **three-to-four-order-of-magnitude reduction in wall-clock time** over atomistic spin dynamics.

papers.title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
papers.abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents working in teams need to share evidence, ask for missing information, and actually use what teammates provide, but final-task rewards say little about the value of any single message. `CoSIR` (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards) post-trains agents through self-play in a simple verifiable environment, using a Bayesian evaluator that rewards shared information by how much it reduces team surprisal, the summed negative log probability of the correct option given each agent's evidence, and rewards requests by the reduction they would achieve if answered truthfully. Applied to `Qwen3-4B`, `Qwen3-8B`, and `Gemma-3-4B-it`, the method **achieves the highest aggregate score across seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks** while staying competitive on general benchmarks, with agents disclosing more private evidence and ignoring teammate input less often.

papers.title: Swiss4Arg: A Parallel Dataset for Multilingual Argument Mining across Swiss National Languages
papers.abstract: We present Swiss4Arg, a multilingual dataset for argument mining based on official Swiss voting brochures, covering all four national languages: German, French, Italian, and Romansh (a Romance minority language exclusively spoken in Switzerland). The brochures contain explicitly formulated arguments systematically organized into pro and con sections, resulting in a cross-lingually aligned resource with balanced argumentative stance. We create a dataset that comprises 53 federal voting issues collected between 2019 and 2025, annotated for argument components (major claims, claims, premises, and non-argumentative units) and relations (support and attack) by three native speakers per language. Inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha) reaches 0.548 for component classification and 0.623 for relation and target classification, computed jointly across all annotators on the parallel data. We release both adjudicated labels and individual annotator annotations, enabling analyses of disagreement and cross-linguistic variation, and provide baseline results using GPT-5.4 and SwissBERT. Swiss4Arg establishes a novel benchmark for multilingual argument mining, with a particular focus on cross-lingual comparability and low-resource settings such as Romansh. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://anonymous-hf.up.railway.app/a/gozw0nion72y/ (HuggingFace) and https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MultiVote-03BD/ (GitHub).
papers.summary: Argument mining datasets rarely offer the same arguments across several languages, which limits cross-lingual comparison and leaves minority languages such as Romansh uncovered. `Swiss4Arg` draws on official Swiss federal voting brochures from 53 issues between 2019 and 2025, which present pro and con arguments in German, French, Italian, and Romansh in parallel, and has three native speakers per language annotate argument components (major claims, claims, premises, non-argumentative units) and support or attack relations. Inter-annotator agreement reaches **Krippendorff's alpha of 0.548 for component classification and 0.623 for relation and target classification**, and the release includes both adjudicated and individual annotations alongside baselines from `GPT-5.4` and `SwissBERT`.

papers.title: Interaction-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both \emph{evaluation} and \emph{generation} of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.
papers.summary: Coding agents increasingly build websites, desktop apps, and games, yet automated LLM judges typically evaluate them through code analysis and unit tests rather than by using them as a person would. Under the `Interaction-as-a-Judge` paradigm, computer-use agents (CUAs) directly operate the generated applications, and the authors release two datasets: 6,858 application pairs with human preferences and agent traces, and 222 applications with human-verified requirement labels. Interactive judging **raises human-preference prediction from 65.6% to 69.1% and requirement verification from 77.0% to 81.6%** over non-interactive baselines, with higher-quality interactions yielding further gains. Used as feedback at inference time, it repairs 75.5% of broken requirements within five attempts versus 55.4% for code-only self-feedback, and as a training reward it improves win rate over the base model by 6.7 points while cutting generated code length by 35.7% and build failures by 7.2 points relative to a code-only reward.

papers.title: Evaluating the Causal Faithfulness of SHAP as a Candidate Attribution Method for SAE Features
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders decompose language model representations into interpretable features, but feature interpretation in this literature remains predominantly correlational. Attribution methods offer more direct estimates of feature influence, yet their faithfulness to actual causal effects has not been systematically evaluated in the SAE setting. We apply SHAP-based attribution to SAE latent features and evaluate it against direct causal intervention, using sentiment classification on SST-2 with GPT-2 Small and a 32,768-feature layer-7 SAE as a testbed. We compare SHAP to Integrated Gradients, Gradient$\times$Input, and probe-weight baselines across linear and MLP probe arms, scoring each against feature ablation and activation steering measured through the language model's own logit difference. Most faithfulness associations we measure do not survive multiple-comparison correction, and attribution methods that agree strongly with one another ($\rho = 0.42$--$0.80$) agree poorly with measured causal effects, indicating that inter-method agreement is not evidence of causal faithfulness. Two effects hold under control. First, local per-example attribution retains a directional advantage over global averaged attribution, while its apparent importance advantage is explained by feature activity rather than superior causal ranking. Second, under known-ground-truth minimal pairs, attribution recovers inserted sentiment signal well above chance (AUROC $0.792$) but fails to localize deletions (AUROC $0.520$), suggesting that these methods detect the presence of a feature's influence more reliably than its absence. We argue that importance faithfulness and directional faithfulness are separable properties requiring separate evaluation, and that attribution agreement should not substitute for causal validation.
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are usually interpreted by correlation, and attribution methods that could estimate their influence have not been checked against actual causal effects in this setting. Using sentiment classification on `SST-2` with `GPT-2 Small` and a 32,768-feature layer-7 SAE, the study compares `SHAP` against `Integrated Gradients`, `Gradient×Input`, and probe-weight baselines, scoring each against feature ablation and activation steering measured by the model's own logit difference. Most faithfulness associations fail multiple-comparison correction, and **methods that agree strongly with each other (rank correlation 0.42 to 0.80) agree poorly with measured causal effects**, so inter-method agreement is not evidence of faithfulness. On minimal pairs with known ground truth, attribution detects inserted sentiment signal (AUROC 0.792) but not deletions (AUROC 0.520), leading the authors to argue that importance faithfulness and directional faithfulness must be evaluated separately.

papers.title: PaceReasoner: Label-Free Learning to Answer Briefly from Long Reasoning
papers.abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. Both modes share a trainable policy, creating a need for reliable supervision, sufficient SHORT training samples, and continued LONG responses to guide learning. PaceReasoner combines all-response and LONG-only answer consensus through progressive, confidence-weighted supervision. A behavior reward gradually shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration to rewarding agreement with LONG answers, while a ratio controller regulates the balance between modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, PaceReasoner improves average SHORT accuracy over the baselines by 7.4--13.5 percentage points, with fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response on average. Ablations support the key components, and cross-dataset results demonstrate transfer beyond the adaptation set.
papers.summary: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves accuracy but raises inference cost and latency, so the goal is to get correct answers from much shorter outputs. `PaceReasoner` is a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework in which a single policy operates in long and short modes, using consensus over the model's own long responses as progressive, confidence-weighted supervision for the short mode, with a behavior reward that shifts from encouraging short-mode exploration to rewarding agreement with long answers and a ratio controller balancing the two modes. Across three backbones and four benchmarks, it **improves average short-mode accuracy by 7.4 to 13.5 percentage points over baselines while using fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response**, and cross-dataset results show the gains transfer beyond the adaptation set.

papers.title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
papers.abstract: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication \emph{clip--shift--max} on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel. FlashMask-3 introduces a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization atop FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a mask-aware distributed extension: zero-communication mask localization, a sparsity-aware load balancer (HCC-IPO), and a mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing. On a single H100 across 12 masks at 4K--128K context, it improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45--141%, 34--71%, and 2--44%. At context-parallel degrees 4--32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31--75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP ring, Megatron-Core CP all-gather, and MagiAttention by $1.80\times$--$3.71\times$, $1.71\times$--$2.92\times$, and $1.09\times$--$1.46\times$. In end-to-end training of a 118B-A14B MoE at 128K on 128 H100 GPUs, it raises throughput by 7.3--11.0% over a Dual Chunk all-gather baseline, with attention forward+backward 24.5--44.9% faster.
papers.summary: Long-context training with structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, sliding-window, block-sparse) across many GPUs makes mask handling a major bottleneck, and the earlier `FlashMask` column-wise sparse mask was limited to Ampere GPUs and single-device use. `FlashMask-3` adds a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization on top of the `FlashAttention-3` TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a distributed extension that localizes masks per rank with zero communication via a clip-shift-max operation on the boundary vectors, a sparsity-aware load balancer, and mask-driven communication pruning. On a single H100 it improves achieved TFLOPs over `FlashMask`, `FlexAttention`, and `MagiAttention` by 45 to 141%, 34 to 71%, and 2 to 44% respectively, and at context-parallel degrees of 4 to 32 it delivers **1.80x to 3.71x higher throughput than Megatron-Core ring context parallelism**. End-to-end training of a 118B-A14B mixture-of-experts model at 128K context on 128 H100 GPUs runs 7.3 to 11.0% faster overall, with attention forward plus backward 24.5 to 44.9% faster.

papers.title: Visual Dependence Does Not Imply Answerability: A Systematic Analysis of Answerability Signals in Frozen InstructBLIP
papers.abstract: Visual question answering models often produce plausible responses even when the available visual evidence is insufficient to support a valid answer. Although prior work has introduced benchmarks and abstention mechanisms for unanswerable visual questions, it remains unclear which signals derived from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen image-question pairs. We systematically evaluate answerability signals on a stratified 10K subset of UNK-VQA using frozen InstructBLIP, covering predictive uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, visual grounding, visual dependence, internal representations, and learned probes. Answerability discrimination remains weak, with test AUROC largely confined to 0.50-0.54. CLIP alignment yields the highest point estimate but does not significantly outperform generation confidence under paired bootstrap analysis. Targeted removal of question-relevant visual evidence causes substantially larger changes in answer confidence than same-size random masking, yet intervention sensitivity provides essentially no answerability discrimination. Increasing probe capacity, combining multiple signals, and adding reason-aware supervision do not provide robust improvements, while post-freeze cross-validation yields similarly weak discrimination.
