This is followed by reinforcement-learning post-training that aligns the model with its inference-time use by rewarding held-out fit and penalizing expression size. On the black-box track of SRBench 2.0, RASR achieves the best mean test $R^2$ rank of all evaluated methods. Three RASR variants, trained with different size penalties, make up most of the accuracy-complexity Pareto front. On Strogatz, our method recovers more ground-truth expressions than any baseline, and on Feynman it is competitive with the best-performing methods.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression searches a combinatorial space of expressions to fit a dataset, and neural approaches amortize that search by pretraining on synthetic data, yet they still trail genetic programming on real, noisy data. `RASR` (Reinforced Amortized Symbolic Regression) argues the deficit lies in training rather than the paradigm and changes two things: a synthetic prior closer to real data, with inputs drawn from a tabular foundation model's prior, constants sampled bottom-up conditioned on the data, heteroscedastic and structured target noise, and standardization throughout; and a two-stage schedule in which supervised pretraining on reference expressions is followed by reinforcement-learning post-training that rewards held-out fit and penalizes expression size. On the black-box track of `SRBench 2.0`, **`RASR` achieves the best mean test R² rank of all evaluated methods**, and three variants trained with different size penalties make up most of the accuracy-complexity Pareto front. It recovers more ground-truth expressions than any baseline on `Strogatz` and is competitive with the best methods on `Feynman`.

papers.title: Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in Deep Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates the integration of Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) as a memory-efficient continual learning strategy for deep SNNs under low-latency constraints. The proposed framework combines Batch Normalization Through Time stabilized VGG9 SNNs with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), which provide forward-only explanations based on spike activity. These explanations are temporally aggregated into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches for replay, instead of storing full images. Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 show that SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets, and remains competitive while requiring substantially less storage.
papers.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient neuromorphic computing but, like conventional networks, forget earlier tasks catastrophically when trained sequentially. The work adapts Experience Packing and Replay (EPR), a memory-efficient continual learning strategy, to deep SNNs under low-latency constraints by pairing `VGG9` SNNs stabilized with Batch Normalization Through Time with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), forward-only explanations derived from spike activity that are aggregated over time into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches to store for replay instead of full images. On `Split CIFAR10` and `Split CIFAR100`, **SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets** and remains competitive while requiring substantially less storage.

papers.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate tokens in parallel in an order driven by the model's evolving predictability, but standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) decides which reference tokens are visible and how much generation space to allocate through random masking, independently of how inference proceeds. The authors show this training-inference mismatch can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, and that the attention-visible input length changes which response formulations the model favors even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (`PACS`) uses the model's own predictability to choose each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks it achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, **with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks**.

papers.title: SWEPatchTest: Evaluating Software Tests Beyond Reproduction
papers.abstract: Coding agents use generated tests to decide whether a proposed patch satisfies an issue's requirements. A suite that fails on the buggy program and passes after applying the reference patch can still accept an incorrect patch or reject a correct patch. We introduce SWEPATCHTEST, a test-generation benchmark with 619 tasks from SWE-bench Pro, SWE-bench Multilingual, and DeepSWE and 82,579 candidate patches collected from coding-agent trajectories. By replaying each suite on the buggy and patched codebases, \benchmark jointly measures issue reproduction, acceptance of correct patches, and rejection of incorrect patches. Joint Validation Rate (JVR), which requires all three criteria on the same task, exposes failures hidden by single-reference evaluation: the best-performing configuration achieves only 9.21% JVR despite reproducing the reference transition on 59.29% of tasks. We further use validation scores to select and scale demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The resulting training recipe approximately triples JVR and improves downstream repair across three SWE-bench benchmarks. Patch discrimination thus provides both a diagnostic measure of test quality and an execution-based signal for curating agent training data.
papers.summary: Coding agents rely on generated tests to judge whether a patch resolves an issue, but a suite that fails on the buggy program and passes after the reference patch can still accept incorrect patches or reject correct ones. `SWEPatchTest` is a test-generation benchmark of 619 tasks drawn from `SWE-bench Pro`, `SWE-bench Multilingual`, and `DeepSWE`, paired with 82,579 candidate patches collected from coding-agent trajectories; replaying each generated suite on buggy and patched codebases jointly measures issue reproduction, acceptance of correct patches, and rejection of incorrect ones. Under the Joint Validation Rate (JVR), which requires all three on the same task, **the best configuration reaches only 9.21% JVR despite reproducing the reference transition on 59.29% of tasks**. Using validation scores to select and scale demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) roughly triples JVR and improves downstream repair on three SWE-bench benchmarks.

papers.title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
papers.abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.
papers.summary: LLM agents that read private context and send emails on a user's behalf can leak sensitive details, and existing checker-repair defenses fix drafts by repeatedly calling a remote drafting model and a remote checker, which becomes expensive when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, or source evidence. The proposed local contract-conditioned rewriting intercepts an outgoing draft, builds an information-release contract stating what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local `Gemma` model, and only selectively invokes a final `PrivacyChecker`. On email tasks with normal prompts the `Gemma + Checker` configuration **cuts leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while raising the share of usable outputs from 85.2% to 92.6%**, and under strategic attack prompts it lowers leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablations show the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts.

papers.title: Fish Audio Drama 3 Technical Report
papers.abstract: We introduce Fish Audio Drama 3, an open-source speech generation model that turns text into directed performances, built on a 35B-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone that activates 3B parameters per token. It clones voices from multiple references, follows natural-language direction, revises a take when the next turn gives a note, voices multi-character scenes, edits existing speech by infilling, and synthesizes long-form and streaming audio. Multi-turn revision, scene dubbing, editing by infilling, and streaming text input are new in Drama 3, all in one model. Drama 3 pairs the hybrid linear-attention backbone with a new codebook multi-token-prediction audio decoder that predicts the acoustic codebooks of each frame in dedicated layers that attend over the entire sequence. The model is trained with a three-stage pre-training recipe, instruction fine-tuning, and large-batch reinforcement learning whose only reward is a single learned model of human preference. Its inference engine decodes a single stream at 271 frames per second on one H200, against 177 for Fish Audio S2, although Drama 3 has more than seven times as many parameters. The model weights are available on GitHub (https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3), and inference is available through SGLang-Omni (https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni). We highly encourage readers to visit https://fish.audio to direct their own performances.
papers.summary: `Fish Audio Drama 3` is an open-source speech generation model that produces directed performances rather than simply reading text aloud: it clones voices from multiple references, follows natural-language direction, revises a take when given a note, voices multi-character scenes, edits existing speech by infilling, and streams long-form audio. It combines a 35B-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone with hybrid linear attention, activating 3B parameters per token, with a codebook multi-token-prediction audio decoder that predicts each frame's acoustic codebooks in dedicated layers attending over the whole sequence; training proceeds through three pre-training stages, instruction fine-tuning, and large-batch reinforcement learning rewarded solely by a learned model of human preference. **Its inference engine decodes a single stream at 271 frames per second on one H200, versus 177 for `Fish Audio S2`, despite having more than seven times as many parameters.** Weights are released on GitHub and Hugging Face, with inference available through `SGLang-Omni`.

papers.title: Correcting or Continuing? What On-Policy Distillation Learns from Student Errors
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher, mitigating the distribution mismatch of off-policy supervision. While prior work has primarily trained on problems a student can largely solve, we ask whether OPD can improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails. We evaluate five representative OPD mechanisms with Qwen-3 and Phi-4 models under a unified competition-mathematics protocol. We find that OPD does not improve accuracy on this hard subset, with most mechanisms instead degrading performance despite continued decreases in training KL divergence. All eight configurations show a decline, and the two-sided sign test gives p=0.0078. In contrast, the same pipeline improves accuracy by 4.6 percentage points when training is not concentrated on failures, showing that the failure is conditional on the training regime rather than systematic. These findings suggest that OPD is effective when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, but can reinforce existing errors when training is concentrated on problems the student currently fails.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher, avoiding the distribution mismatch of off-policy supervision, but prior work has mostly trained on problems the student could already largely solve. Five representative OPD mechanisms are evaluated with `Qwen-3` and `Phi-4` models under a unified competition-mathematics protocol, with training restricted to problems the student currently fails. **OPD does not improve accuracy on this hard subset; all eight configurations decline (two-sided sign test p=0.0078) even as training KL divergence keeps falling**, whereas the same pipeline gains 4.6 percentage points when training is not concentrated on failures. The authors conclude that OPD works when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes but can reinforce existing errors when focused on problems the student gets wrong.

papers.title: LatentRemedy: Efficient Remedy For Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Non-prefix KV cache reuse is a promising approach for improving inference efficiency in multi-agent systems as agents share the same context blocks. However, when agents have conflicting tasks, directly reusing non-prefix KV caches across agents can severely degrade model performance, causing up to a 90% drop. Existing remedies, including selective recomputation and offset-based calibration, recover a limited fraction of this loss. We argue that the problem lies not only in contaminated KV representations but also in the agent's difficulty interpreting reused context under its own instructions. To this end, we introduce LatentRemedy, which uses a few task-conditioned latent tokens to help the target agent leverage reused context without recomputing the shared block. Specifically, we use an MLP to map the last hidden state of the target prefix into a small number of latent tokens, which are placed after the reused KV block to interact with the shared context. To guide subsequent predictions toward the target task, we train the MLP through full-prefill distillation. Experiments show that LatentRemedy consistently outperforms existing reuse baselines on conflicting tasks while maintaining TTFT close to direct reuse as cache size grows. Code and data are available at https://github.com/chenzhwsysu57/kvreuse.
papers.summary: Agents in a multi-agent system often share the same context blocks, which makes reusing non-prefix key-value (KV) caches attractive for inference efficiency, yet directly reusing them across agents with conflicting tasks can degrade performance by up to 90%, and existing remedies such as selective recomputation and offset-based calibration recover only a fraction of the loss. `LatentRemedy` argues the trouble is partly that the target agent cannot interpret reused context under its own instructions, and inserts a few task-conditioned latent tokens after the reused KV block: an MLP maps the last hidden state of the target prefix into these tokens, and the MLP is trained through full-prefill distillation so subsequent predictions follow the target task. **It consistently outperforms existing reuse baselines on conflicting tasks while keeping time-to-first-token close to direct reuse as cache size grows.** Code and data are released.

papers.title: Machine--human agreement in marking undergraduate assignments is specific to model, prompt and institution
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) promise to automate one of higher education's most resource-intensive activities: assessing student writing. Existing evaluations are typically limited to a single model, a single prompt and a single institution. Using 761 undergraduate psychology assignments from three UK universities, we evaluated three frontier LLMs, individually and in ensemble, on accuracy, prompt sensitivity, error independence, generalisability and evidential basis. Agreement between human and machine marks varied widely, with no model or prompt optimal across institutions. All models compressed marks towards a common central tendency, overvaluing the weakest assignments and undervaluing the strongest. Because this error was shared, ensembling failed to remove it. Machine marks also rewarded linguistic features more strongly than human marks. Since human-machine agreement was a joint product of model, prompt and institution, we conclude that current LLMs lack evaluative capacity transferable across contexts, and that single-context validation overstates readiness for deployment.
papers.summary: Studies of large language models (LLMs) as graders of student writing typically involve one model, one prompt, and one institution, leaving open whether results transfer. Using 761 undergraduate psychology assignments from three UK universities, three frontier LLMs were evaluated individually and in ensemble on accuracy, prompt sensitivity, error independence, generalisability, and evidential basis. **Agreement with human marks varied widely with no model or prompt optimal across institutions, and every model compressed marks toward a central tendency, overvaluing the weakest assignments and undervaluing the strongest**; because this error was shared, ensembling did not remove it, and machine marks rewarded linguistic features more strongly than human marks did. The authors conclude that current LLMs lack evaluative capacity that transfers across contexts and that single-context validation overstates readiness for deployment.

papers.title: FRACTION: Fraud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context Navigation
papers.abstract: Graph fraud explanation generation emerges as an important task, which requires jointly leveraging graph structure and content information to produce human-readable explanations for a given risk label. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs), which inject graph structure into LLMs via graph-conditioned instruction tuning or structure-aware embeddings. However, existing methods face two key challenges in graph fraud explanation generation: a lack of evaluation protocols tailored to explanation quality, and a mismatch between the granularity of graph information they provide and what explanation generation requires. In this paper, we propose FRaud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context NavigaTION (FRACTION), a framework for graph fraud explanation generation. To evaluate explanation quality, we introduce a task-specific rubric that assesses faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, and validate it against human judgments. To focus on fine-grained details of relevant neighbors without reading the entire neighborhood, we equip a language model with graph tools that progressively disclose neighbor records. To train our graph agent, we propose a rubric-guided trajectory distillation strategy through which the agent learns both tool-use behavior and structured explanation generation. Experimental results on three fraud datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under a human-aligned rubric.
papers.summary: Graph fraud explanation generation must combine graph structure and content information into a human-readable explanation for a given risk label, but adapting graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs) runs into two problems: no evaluation protocol for explanation quality, and a mismatch between the coarse graph information they inject and the fine-grained detail explanations need. `FRACTION` introduces a task-specific rubric covering faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, validated against human judgments, and equips a language model with graph tools that progressively disclose neighbor records so it can inspect relevant neighbors without reading the whole neighborhood. The agent is trained via rubric-guided trajectory distillation to learn both tool-use behavior and structured explanation writing. **On three fraud datasets it consistently improves over state-of-the-art baselines under the human-aligned rubric.**

papers.title: SHELDON: Reasoning through Dual Search over Hypothesis and Observation Spaces
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling has enabled LLMs to solve increasingly complex reasoning, discovery, and optimization tasks. However, existing approaches often gather observations while seeking evidence for current hypotheses, then generate new hypotheses conditioned on those hypotheses and their associated evidence. This couples observation discovery to existing hypotheses, favoring local refinements over exploration of unknown hypotheses regions. Inspired by the hypothetico-deductive method (Hempel, 1945) and dual-space models of scientific discovery (Klahr & Dunbar, 1988), we introduce SHELDON, a scientific reasoning harness that separately represents and jointly explores hypothesis and observation spaces. By actively seeking new observations along with new hypotheses, SHELDON can discover observations that its current hypotheses do not explain. These unexplained observations expose gaps in its understanding, motivate new investigations, and guide the generation of hypotheses beyond refinements of existing ones. Across diagnosis, abstract reasoning, and optimization benchmarks, SHELDON outperforms evaluated baselines by up to 26.7 points. Additional analysis shows that SHELDON generates up to 4.5x more novel solutions.
papers.summary: Test-time scaling approaches usually gather observations as evidence for current hypotheses and then propose new hypotheses conditioned on those, which couples observation discovery to existing hypotheses and favors local refinement over exploring unknown regions. Drawing on the hypothetico-deductive method and dual-space models of scientific discovery, `SHELDON` is a reasoning harness that separately represents and jointly explores hypothesis and observation spaces, deliberately seeking observations that current hypotheses cannot explain so the gaps motivate new investigations and hypotheses beyond refinements. **Across diagnosis, abstract reasoning, and optimization benchmarks it outperforms evaluated baselines by up to 26.7 points** and generates up to 4.5x more novel solutions.

papers.title: ChampionKV: Head-Wise Adaptive Budget Allocation for KV Cache Compression
papers.abstract: Some observation-window-based KV cache compressors use prompt attention to identify important tokens but allocate uniform or predefined budgets across heads, overlooking input-dependent differences in budget demand. We propose ChampionKV, an input-adaptive head-wise budget allocator for long-context KV cache compression. It uses the maximum aggregated observation-window attention score as a lightweight empirical proxy for attention concentration, assigning larger budgets to heads with dispersed attention and smaller budgets to concentrated heads. An abnormal-head mask and a floor-budget mechanism improve robustness under weak attention responses. ChampionKV plugs into compressors such as SnapKV and PyramidKV without changing their token-selection procedures. On LongBench and RULER, both Champion variants consistently improve over their SnapKV and PyramidKV base compressors; the improvements are largest and statistically significant on Llama3.1-70B-Instruct, especially under tight budgets, whereas results on the tested 7B/8B models remain competitive but mixed. ChampionKV does not uniformly outperform Ada-KV, whose global cross-head Top-K selection retains an advantage in several settings. Controlled analysis further shows improved retained attention mass over the corresponding base compressors at negligible overhead.
papers.summary: Observation-window KV cache compressors such as `SnapKV` and `PyramidKV` use prompt attention to pick important tokens but give every head a uniform or predefined budget, ignoring input-dependent differences in demand. `ChampionKV` is an input-adaptive head-wise budget allocator that uses the maximum aggregated observation-window attention score as a cheap proxy for attention concentration, granting larger budgets to heads with dispersed attention and smaller ones to concentrated heads, with an abnormal-head mask and a floor budget for robustness; it plugs into existing compressors without changing their token selection. On `LongBench` and `RULER` both variants consistently improve over their base compressors, **with the largest and statistically significant gains on `Llama3.1-70B-Instruct` under tight budgets**, while results on 7B/8B models are competitive but mixed and `Ada-KV` keeps an advantage in several settings. Controlled analysis shows more retained attention mass than the base compressors at negligible overhead.

papers.title: Can Machine Learning Potentials Be More Accurate Than the Methods They Are Trained On?
papers.abstract: Although machine learning potentials (MLPs) generalize across configurational and chemical compound spaces, their accuracy is commonly believed to be limited by their training methods, with improvements beyond this limit achieved so far only by refitting to experimental observables. In this Perspective, we argue that MLPs can also be made more accurate than their training methods non-empirically by generalizing across a third space, that of quantum-chemical methods. We propose routes to method-transferable MLPs that predict at unseen methods, with working implementations in both density-functional and wavefunction-based theories showing that they can be more accurate than any of their training methods. Aiming beyond the accuracy of the training methods could also make universal MLPs more accurate than single-method models, even when the method-transferable MLPs remain less accurate than those QM methods. Method-transferable MLPs will shape the construction of training datasets and the evaluation of models, pushing the accuracy limits of chemical simulations.
papers.summary: Machine learning potentials (MLPs) generalize across configurational and chemical compound spaces, but their accuracy is widely assumed to be capped by the quantum-chemical methods that generated their training data, with gains beyond that limit so far coming only from refitting to experimental observables. The authors argue MLPs can surpass their training methods non-empirically by generalizing across a third space, that of quantum-chemical methods themselves, and propose routes to method-transferable MLPs that predict at methods never seen in training. **Working implementations in both density-functional and wavefunction-based theories are shown to be more accurate than any of their training methods.** The authors suggest this could make universal MLPs more accurate than single-method models and will reshape how training datasets are built and how models are evaluated.

papers.title: Weighting-Based Strategies for Classification: Analysis and Local Peak Dynamics with CART Trees
papers.abstract: Tabular learning tasks often suffer from class imbalance, which is often addressed via weighting-based strategies. In this work, we compare the naive approach (unweighted) with the weighting-based rebalancing strategies. Somewhat surprisingly, we demonstrate that, asymptotically, as the predictor complexity increases with sample size, weighting strategies yield predictive performance identical to unweighted approaches across all evaluation metrics, up to a shift in the final threshold. To go beyond, we theoretically study the estimation of a linear regression function through weighted and unweighted CART trees with limited depths. In this setting, we prove that the points in the PR space for both strategies are distributed along the same curve, thus illustrating the similar nonasymptotic performance of the two strategies. Then, we numerically identify more complex synthetic settings where performance gaps, evaluated via fixed classifier complexity, favor weighting strategies. Thus, to guide practitioners, we introduce an indicator that aims at signaling whether a data set may benefit from weighting.
papers.summary: Class imbalance in tabular classification is commonly handled with weighting-based rebalancing, raising the question of whether weighting actually changes predictive performance relative to the unweighted approach. **Asymptotically, as predictor complexity grows with sample size, weighting strategies yield predictive performance identical to the unweighted approach on all evaluation metrics, up to a shift in the decision threshold.** A theoretical study of weighted versus unweighted depth-limited `CART` trees estimating a linear regression function shows the precision-recall points of both strategies lie along the same curve, while numerical experiments identify more complex synthetic settings where, at fixed classifier complexity, weighting does help. An indicator is proposed to signal whether a given dataset may benefit from weighting.

papers.title: Scaling Vision Transformers Without Training: Prune-and-Merge Token Compression
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.
papers.summary: Vision Transformers pay a quadratic cost in token interactions, and although training-free token reduction cuts that cost, its robustness has received little attention. `Prune-and-Merge ViT` is a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models that combines class-attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to remove redundant tokens while preserving semantic content, and two new metrics, Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR), quantify accuracy degradation and prediction consistency under image transformations. **On pretrained `ViT` and `DeiT` it reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods**, and the analysis suggests hybrid reduction introduces no hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability under common transformations.

papers.title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
papers.abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.
papers.summary: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are expensive to obtain through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurement, and super-resolution from coarse data is hard because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales and time. The proposed turbulence-aware framework couples a multiscale neural operator for recovering volumetric structure with a state space model for temporal consistency, adds Navier-Stokes residuals as soft physical constraints, and uses a mixture-of-experts mechanism for unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. **On canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data it reduces reconstruction error relative to learning-based and classical baselines** while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution.

papers.title: Beyond Black Boxes: Visual Grounding for Text Embeddings
papers.abstract:
In this paper, our goal is to represent text embeddings as sketches for three main reasons. First, to visualize text representation and to explore their potential their potential for AI explainability. Second, to investigate the potential benefits of the sketch-based representation for information retrieval. Third, to explore their potential for reasoning, drawing inspiration from the concept of mental imagery. We propose a sketch-based visual grounding framework that transforms text representations into visual topographic sketches. Our approach aims to emphasis the semantics content encoded in the text embeddings through the corresponding sketch.
  Evaluations are conducted on the MS-COCO dataset to examine the utility of these sketches for text retrieval. The comparative study of SBERT and Sketch-based method reveals that SBERT retains an advantage in strict top-1 retrieval accuracy while achieving comparable performance to the sketch-based method in top-5 retrieval. A cascaded approach combining SBERT and the sketch-based method outperforms SBERT alone, suggesting that the Sketch-based representation could offer significant potential for information retrieval if trained directly on text.
papers.summary: The aim is to represent text embeddings as sketches, motivated by visualizing representations for explainability, exploring benefits for information retrieval, and drawing on the idea of mental imagery for reasoning. A sketch-based visual grounding framework transforms text representations into visual topographic sketches meant to emphasize the semantic content encoded in the embedding. On `MS-COCO` text retrieval, `SBERT` retains the advantage in strict top-1 accuracy while the sketch-based method is comparable at top-5, and **a cascade combining `SBERT` with the sketch-based method outperforms `SBERT` alone**, which the authors take as a sign the representation could help retrieval if trained directly on text.

papers.title: inLoRA-MINT: Internal Representations for Auditing Training Data in Domain-adapted LLMs
papers.abstract:
This work investigates the application of the Membership Inference Test (MINT) to large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned with LoRA, aiming to determine whether specific samples were used during training and address concerns about data privacy, leakage, and transparency. Building on our previous LoRA-MINT framework, which relies exclusively on perplexity under a strict black-box setting, we propose an approach based on intermediate model representations, including activations and parameter-dependent signals. These representations enable a MINT classifier to distinguish training from non-training samples without requiring full access to model parameters.
  We evaluated the method on four LLMs (Qwen, Phi-4, DeepSeek-V3, and LLaMA 3.2-3B) fine-tuned on three datasets covering medical, mathematical, and academic reasoning tasks. Results show consistent performance across architectures and domains, achieving scores between 95% and 98%, with robustness to variations in model configurations and data distributions. The proposed approach enables efficient auditing of sensitive training data and supports data provenance and compliance with emerging privacy and AI governance regulations. Although our experiments focus on LoRA-based fine-tuning, the methodology can be extended to other LLM adaptation techniques and, more broadly, to other AI models.
papers.summary: Auditing whether specific samples were used to fine-tune a large language model (LLM) matters for privacy, leakage, and transparency. Extending the earlier `LoRA-MINT` framework, which applied the Membership Inference Test (MINT) using only perplexity in a strict black-box setting, this approach feeds intermediate representations such as activations and parameter-dependent signals to a MINT classifier that separates training from non-training samples without full access to model parameters. Evaluated on `Qwen`, `Phi-4`, `DeepSeek-V3`, and `LLaMA 3.2-3B` fine-tuned with LoRA on medical, mathematical, and academic reasoning datasets, **the method scores between 95% and 98% consistently across architectures and domains**, with robustness to variations in model configuration and data distribution. The authors position it as a tool for auditing sensitive training data and supporting provenance and compliance with emerging AI governance rules.

papers.title: Can Agents Forget When Asked? A Benchmark for Memory Unlearning in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-term memory has become a core component of large language model (LLM) agents. As agents accumulate personal information over long-term use, users increasingly ask them to delete sensitive or outdated facts. A memory system should honor such requests. It should remove exactly what was requested and keep the rest of its memory intact. However, existing memory benchmarks evaluate only memory writing, retrieval, and organization, so whether agents can forget at the user's explicit request remains under-evaluated. To address this gap, we propose Bemula, the first benchmark dedicated to memory unlearning. It comprises 50 multi-session dialogue instances, 135 forget requests of six types, and 1,742 test questions. Each dialogue has a control version without the requests, so that only systems that have stored the target can earn credit for forgetting. Across the paired versions, five test suites measure storage, removal of the requested information, preservation of unrelated memories, relearning of similar facts, and resistance to extraction attacks. On Bemula, we evaluate six mainstream memory systems under three backbone LLMs, together with the Full Context LLM on two of them. The results are negative. Across all evaluated systems and backbones, no system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end, and most pass none at all. These systems either leave the requested information extractable under simple attacks or delete far more than requested. Memory unlearning therefore remains an open challenge for agent memory design. We release our data and code at https://github.com/Nboxff/bemula-benchmark.
papers.summary: As large language model (LLM) agents accumulate personal information in long-term memory, users will ask them to delete sensitive or outdated facts, and a memory system should remove exactly what was requested and nothing more, yet existing memory benchmarks only test writing, retrieval, and organization. `Bemula` is a benchmark for memory unlearning with 50 multi-session dialogues, 135 forget requests of six types, and 1,742 test questions, where each dialogue has a control version without the requests so only systems that actually stored the target can earn credit for forgetting; five test suites measure storage, removal of the requested information, preservation of unrelated memories, relearning of similar facts, and resistance to extraction attacks. Evaluating six mainstream memory systems under three backbone LLMs plus a full-context baseline, **no system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end, and most pass none**, either leaving the information extractable under simple attacks or deleting far more than requested. Data and code are released.

papers.title: LADDER: A Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Benchmark
papers.abstract: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills effectively, but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks. Existing benchmarks cannot isolate failures because task horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variations. We propose LADDER, a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark scaling from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment over three suites (SimplerEnv-Long, RobotArena-$\infty$-Long, and RoboLab-Long), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodiments, and 2,024 simulated episodes per system. We evaluate two orchestration paradigms: text subgoals for learned low-level policies (VoLo) and tool selection orchestration (CaP-X, GPT-Policy, PSP-Agent, TiPToP). Given the full instruction directly, low-level policies achieve 85.4% on single-subgoal tasks, but drop to near zero on extended tasks. While orchestration remedies this, it remains bounded by physical execution errors of the low-level policy rather than high-level planning and achieves only ~25%. Tool selection orchestration with GPT-Policy on GPT-6 Astra significantly outperforms learned-policy methods, but incurs significant time and cost budget and succeeds only ~62%. Real-world experiments across two embodiments confirm the collapse of the low-level policy and the gain from orchestration. Project website: https://ladder.insait.ai
papers.summary: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills well but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks, and existing benchmarks cannot isolate the cause because horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variation. `LADDER` scales from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment across three suites (`SimplerEnv-Long`, `RobotArena-∞-Long`, and `RoboLab-Long`), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodiments, and 2,024 simulated episodes per system, and compares text-subgoal orchestration of learned low-level policies against tool-selection orchestration. **Low-level policies given the full instruction reach 85.4% on single-subgoal tasks but drop to near zero on extended tasks**; subgoal orchestration recovers only about 25%, bounded by physical execution errors rather than planning, while tool-selection orchestration with `GPT-Policy` on `GPT-6 Astra` reaches about 62% at substantial time and cost. Real-world experiments on two embodiments confirm both the collapse and the gain from orchestration.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving GNN Inference on Financial Transaction Graphs via Homomorphic Encryption
papers.abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) in financial networks requires modeling transaction patterns that span multiple institutions. In practice, however, banks cannot share account and transaction features due to strict privacy regulations. We propose a privacy-preserving graph neural network (GNN) inference framework tailored to this multi-bank setting. A central server holds the graph connectivity and pretrained model weights in plaintext, while each bank keeps its transaction features encrypted. Inference is then carried out entirely on encrypted features under the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, so that no plaintext transaction features or predictions are exposed to the server. The key to making this practical is an edge-centric GNN architecture, wherein message passing is expressed through operations on node--edge incidence matrices. This formulation not only preserves the edge-attributed multigraph structure of transaction networks but also reduces every aggregation step to plaintext--ciphertext matrix products. Since CKKS can evaluate only polynomial circuits, we also approximate each nonlinearity with a composite polynomial of the sign function, which we calibrate per activation site. On the IBM AML benchmark, our model achieves performance competitive with plaintext baselines, and with a consumer-grade GPU, classifies each queried transaction end-to-end in as little as \textbf{5.31} seconds, while per-transaction latency can be amortized to \textbf{1.65} seconds when optimized for throughput.
papers.summary: Anti-money laundering (AML) detection benefits from transaction patterns that span multiple banks, but privacy regulation prevents banks from sharing account and transaction features. The proposed framework runs graph neural network (GNN) inference under the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme: a central server holds graph connectivity and pretrained weights in plaintext while each bank keeps its transaction features encrypted, so no plaintext features or predictions are exposed to the server. An edge-centric GNN expresses message passing through node-edge incidence matrices, which preserves the edge-attributed multigraph and reduces every aggregation to plaintext-ciphertext matrix products, and each nonlinearity is replaced by a per-site calibrated composite polynomial approximation of the sign function. On the `IBM AML` benchmark the model is competitive with plaintext baselines, and **on a consumer-grade GPU it classifies a queried transaction end-to-end in as little as 5.31 seconds, amortizable to 1.65 seconds** when optimized for throughput.

papers.title: Reliable Scale-Free Bandits via Empirical Likelihood
papers.abstract: We study stochastic bandits without knowledge of reward scales or tail parameters. Almost-sure regret guarantees describe eventual learning but do not quantify expected performance or the risk of large regret in a finite run. We introduce $\texttt{EL-F}$, an anytime empirical-likelihood (EL) extension of the $g$-Forcing policy of Cowan and Katehakis (2020), and characterize its performance at three levels. First, for integrable rewards and non-decreasing, diverging exploration schedules $g$ with vanishing increments, $\texttt{EL-F}$ preserves the $g$-Forcing asymptotics for pseudo-regret $R(T)$: $R(T)/g(T)\to\sum_{i:\Delta_i>0}\Delta_i$ almost surely as $T\to\infty$, where $\Delta_i$ is the suboptimality gap of arm $i$. Second, on every sub-exponential instance, for non-decreasing $g(t)=\omega(\log t)$ satisfying a mild feasibility condition, expected pseudo-regret is at most $g(T)\sum_{i:\Delta_i>0}\Delta_i+C_{\underline{P}}$, where $C_{\underline{P}}$ is an instance-dependent constant independent of $T$. Moreover, we also establish finite-time tail bounds with super-polynomial decay in regret beyond the forced-exploration budget. For slowly varying $g$, we determine the exact exponent of linear regret deviations on two-armed Gaussian instances with common variance and establish a matching lower bound among policies satisfying the same expected-regret budget on every such Gaussian instance. These quantitative guarantees also cover the greedy variant obtained at zero EL radius. A fixed positive radius introduces local optimism while preserving the leading asymptotic regret. We establish coupled pathwise dominance over the greedy variant in two-armed bandits with a deterministic suboptimal arm. Experiments demonstrate reductions in prolonged suboptimal allocation compared with $g$-Forcing on challenging instances.
papers.summary: Stochastic bandits with unknown reward scales and tail parameters typically come only with almost-sure regret guarantees, which describe eventual learning but say nothing about expected performance or the risk of large regret in a finite run. `EL-F` is an anytime empirical-likelihood (EL) extension of the `g-Forcing` policy, analyzed at three levels: it preserves g-Forcing's almost-sure pseudo-regret asymptotics for integrable rewards; on every sub-exponential instance with exploration schedules growing faster than log t, **expected pseudo-regret is bounded by g(T) times the sum of suboptimality gaps plus an instance-dependent constant independent of T**, with finite-time tail bounds decaying super-polynomially; and for slowly varying schedules the exact exponent of linear-regret deviations on two-armed Gaussian instances is determined along with a matching lower bound. A fixed positive EL radius adds local optimism while preserving the leading asymptotics, and experiments show less prolonged suboptimal allocation than g-Forcing on hard instances.

papers.title: From Policy Evaluation to Off-Policy Control: Provable Emergence of In-Context Q-Learning
papers.abstract: Transformers can implement reinforcement-learning algorithms in context, yet how off-policy control emerges within Transformers remains poorly understood. We study Q-learning, a foundational model-free control algorithm that combines off-policy bootstrapping with greedy policy improvement. We prove that a two-layer attention-only Transformer can implement a finite-temperature form of Q-learning, where the temperature $\tau>0$ controls the approximation to greedy action selection, recovering window Q-learning as $\tau\to0$. We train the structured Transformer on randomly generated MDP tasks using output-only supervision. Experiments show that the theoretically predicted parameter structure emerges during training, including the internal greedy action-selection mechanism, and that the trained Transformer achieves performance comparable to Q-learning on unseen tasks. Our theoretical analysis further shows that the equivalent realizations form a solution manifold and that, under suitable task-diversity conditions, the training iterates converge locally to this manifold at an exponential rate. For the random-task model analyzed here, the local worst-case number of gradient steps needed to reduce the distance to the manifold by a factor $\epsilon$ is $\Theta\left(\tau^{-5}\log(1/\varepsilon)\right)$, quantifying the increasing optimization cost as the learned update approaches window Q-learning.
papers.summary: Transformers can run reinforcement-learning algorithms in context, but how off-policy control emerges inside them has been poorly understood. Focusing on Q-learning, which combines off-policy bootstrapping with greedy policy improvement, the authors prove that **a two-layer attention-only Transformer can implement a finite-temperature form of Q-learning**, with the temperature controlling how closely action selection approximates greedy choice and recovering window Q-learning as it goes to zero. Training this structured Transformer on randomly generated MDP tasks with output-only supervision, the predicted parameter structure, including the internal greedy action-selection mechanism, emerges, and the trained model performs comparably to Q-learning on unseen tasks. Further analysis shows the equivalent realizations form a solution manifold to which training converges locally at an exponential rate under task-diversity conditions, with the worst-case number of gradient steps scaling as τ^-5 log(1/ε), so optimization cost rises as the learned update approaches greedy Q-learning.

papers.title: A Benchmark for Bangla Task-Oriented Dialogue Understanding
papers.abstract: Task-oriented dialogue understanding remains underexplored for Bangla, particularly in multilingual settings involving English and romanized Bangla (Banglish). We introduce BanglaTOD, a parallel tri-lingual benchmark comprising 209 multi-turn dialogues across nine Bangladesh-specific service domains and 64 intents. Each conversational turn is aligned across Bangla, English, and Banglish, yielding 4,689 language-specific turn records annotated with intents, token-level slots, state updates, and accumulated dialogue states. We establish context-aware baselines for joint intent classification and slot filling using mBERT, BERT-base-uncased, and BanglaBERT. Cross-language analysis reveals substantial performance differences across models and linguistic representations, while removing dialogue history reduces intent accuracy by 19.0--25.7 percentage points. BanglaTOD provides a foundation for multilingual dialogue understanding and future dialogue state tracking research in Bangladesh-specific conversational applications. The dataset is publicly available at \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/afri7here/BanglaTOD}{Hugging Face}.
papers.summary: Task-oriented dialogue understanding is underexplored for Bangla, particularly in multilingual settings that mix Bangla, English, and romanized Bangla (Banglish). `BanglaTOD` is a parallel tri-lingual benchmark of 209 multi-turn dialogues spanning nine Bangladesh-specific service domains and 64 intents, with every turn aligned across the three representations and annotated with intents, token-level slots, state updates, and accumulated dialogue states, for 4,689 turn records in total. Context-aware baselines for joint intent classification and slot filling with `mBERT`, `BERT-base-uncased`, and `BanglaBERT` reveal large gaps across models and representations, and **removing dialogue history lowers intent accuracy by 19.0 to 25.7 percentage points**.

papers.title: Uncertainty Evaluation: Bridging Machine Learning and Measurement Science
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty evaluation is essential for assessing the trustworthiness of machine learning (ML) predictions, particularly in safety-critical applications. This paper explores conceptual analogies between uncertainty evaluation in ML and measurement science, drawing on the evolution of metrology from error-based approaches to the framework established by the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between process-level and result-level quality and to the limitations of the conventional classification of ML uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components. It is argued that this dichotomy, similarly to the traditional distinction between random and systematic measurement errors, is inherently model-dependent and provides an insufficient basis for a unified uncertainty evaluation framework. Further analogies between machine learning and measurement field of knowledge are identified concerning distribution shifts, anomalous operating conditions, and the validity of uncertainty evaluation. Building on the proposed considerations, the paper advocates a metrology-inspired approach based on the systematic identification, quantification, and propagation of uncertainty contributions. By extending the methodology already established in measurement science to ML, this approach could offer a potentially rigorous, consistent, and transferable framework for evaluating the trustworthiness of individual predictions.
papers.summary: Trustworthy machine learning (ML) predictions, especially in safety-critical settings, require reliable uncertainty evaluation, yet ML lacks the kind of unified framework that measurement science has developed. The authors draw analogies between ML uncertainty and metrology, tracing the field's shift from error-based thinking to the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM), and distinguish process-level from result-level quality. They argue that the aleatoric versus epistemic split, like the older random versus systematic error distinction, **is model-dependent and provides an insufficient basis for a unified uncertainty framework**, with further parallels drawn for distribution shift, anomalous operating conditions, and the validity of uncertainty estimates. In place of the dichotomy they advocate a metrology-style approach that systematically identifies, quantifies, and propagates individual uncertainty contributions to yield transferable trust assessments for single predictions.

papers.title: WorkRover: Scaling Long-Horizon Cowork Agent Training Via Recursive Environment Evolution
papers.abstract: Scaling interactive environments is important for training long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning. These environments often require further testing and refinement after initial generation, and correcting defects in a task may also require updating its work context and verifier. However, existing construction pipelines offer limited support for such iterative refinement while keeping these components aligned. We introduce WorkRover, a framework for training long-horizon cowork agents through recursive environment evolution. Its harness-driven synthesis enables construction agents to jointly build and validate semantically aligned work contexts, executable tasks, and evidence-grounded verifiers, adapting their actions to workspace state and execution feedback rather than following a fixed construction workflow. To support environment evolution, we introduce Factorial Compatibility Replay (FCR), which uses rollout feedback to evaluate combinations of component revisions through dependency-closed replay and selects the smallest validated repair among tested candidates while preserving task requirements and evaluation constraints. To provide finer-grained training signals, we propose Verifier-to-Turn Credit Assignment (VTCA), which augments trajectory-level GRPO advantages with signals from deterministic workspace-progress checks and assigns a bounded share of positive-progress credit to prerequisite turns using recorded tool-output and artifact dependencies. Using WorkRover, we post-train Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to obtain WorkRover-35B-A3B and evaluate it on several cowork-agent benchmarks. Its reported scores exceed those of Qwen3.5-35B-A3B by 26.27 percentage points on JobBench, 29.32 percentage points on OfficeQA Pro, and 413.25 Elo points on GDPval v2. These results suggest that WorkRover offers a promising foundation for scalable training of long-horizon cowork agents.
papers.summary: Training long-horizon agents with reinforcement learning needs many interactive environments, but generated environments require iterative testing and repair, and fixing a task often means updating its work context and verifier together, which existing construction pipelines support poorly. `WorkRover` addresses this with harness-driven synthesis, in which construction agents jointly build and validate semantically aligned work contexts, executable tasks, and evidence-grounded verifiers while adapting to workspace state and execution feedback, plus Factorial Compatibility Replay (FCR), which uses rollout feedback to test combinations of component revisions through dependency-closed replay and keeps the smallest validated repair. For finer training signals, Verifier-to-Turn Credit Assignment (VTCA) augments trajectory-level `GRPO` advantages with deterministic workspace-progress checks and assigns a bounded share of positive-progress credit to prerequisite turns based on recorded tool-output and artifact dependencies. Post-training `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` with the framework yields `WorkRover-35B-A3B`, whose reported scores **exceed the base model by 26.27 percentage points on `JobBench`, 29.32 points on `OfficeQA Pro`, and 413.25 Elo on `GDPval v2`**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Training long-horizon cowork agents with reinforcement learning needs many executable environments whose work context, task specification, and verifier stay mutually consistent, yet synthesized environments ship with defects whose repair must be coordinated across all three components. `WorkRover` answers with a dependency-tracking harness for environment synthesis, `Factorial Compatibility Replay` (FCR) for rollout-driven repair, and `Verifier-to-Turn Credit Assignment` (VTCA) for turn-level reinforcement learning credit.

- Harness-driven synthesis lets construction agents assemble files, skills, and mock applications into a workspace, has an independent demonstrator agent execute the task from a clean start to confirm feasibility and produce a reference state, and calibrates the verifier against an evaluation contract fixed before that reference state is inspected, so that it rejects starter and negative cases while accepting valid alternative solutions.
- When rollouts expose an environment defect rather than an agent mistake, `FCR` freezes one repair proposal each for the context, task, harness, and verifier, replays every combination of them, at most 16, with dependency-closed updates under matched seeds, and selects the smallest validated repair that preserves task intent, which raises the safe resolution rate on natural defects from **60.7%** with full regeneration to **70.3%**, cuts unintended task-intent changes from **14.3% to 1.3%**, and lifts the initial synthesis pass rate from 49.8% to **74.8%** against 68.8% for full regeneration.
- `VTCA` augments trajectory-level `GRPO` advantages with per-turn signals from frozen deterministic workspace-progress checks, keeping at least half of each positive increment with the turn that produced it, splitting the rest among earlier turns whose tool outputs or exact artifact versions were directly used, leaving negative increments local, and disabling all progress credit when integrity or safety checks fail, and under matched rollout budgets it beats episode-only `GRPO` on all five benchmarks with the largest gains of **+5.7 points** on `AutomationBench`, **+5.4 points** on `OfficeQA Pro`, and **+43 Elo** on `GDPval v2`.
- After SFT on 30,115 verified trajectories from `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B` and RL on 3,200 filtered task-verifier pairs, `WorkRover-35B-A3B` lifts its `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` backbone by **+26.27 percentage points** on `JobBench` to 36.89%, **+29.32 points** on `OfficeQA Pro` to 48.87%, **+413.25 Elo** on `GDPval v2` to 1218.00, +22.67 points on `AutomationBench`, and +13.63 points on `WorkBuddy Bench (Office)`, the best reported scores among 27–35B open-weight models on every benchmark.
- Caveats include that baseline comparisons rely on published scores under each source's own evaluator rather than re-runs, that the model still trails 400B+ open-weight models on `GDPval v2` and both `GPT-5.5` and `Claude Opus 4.7` on `JobBench` and `WorkBuddy Bench (Office)`, that the `VTCA` shaping signal is only as reliable as checker coverage and recorded dependencies, and that bounded enumeration in `FCR` returns the smallest tested repair rather than a global minimum.

papers.title: From Agents to Edges: Paired Optimization for Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.abstract: Strong individual agents do not guarantee effective collaboration. Communication must align what one agent conveys with how another interprets and uses it. This dependency makes the communication edge a natural unit of optimization. We introduce Paired Automated Communication Optimization (PACO), which jointly optimizes the instructions at both ends of each edge and their shared communication convention in systems built on black-box language models. PACO keeps model weights, agent roles, and workflow topology fixed. A state-aware discounted bandit selects edges for refinement, while execution feedback guides paired revisions evaluated through staged end-to-end execution. The optimized instructions integrate into existing agent prompts without additional model calls at deployment. On a four-agent workflow evaluated across diverse multi-agent benchmarks, PACO consistently outperforms leading prompt-optimization and communication baselines. Configurations learned on HotpotQA retain their advantage in cross-dataset transfer without target-specific optimization. These results demonstrate that optimizing how agents communicate can substantially improve collaboration within an otherwise fixed system.
papers.summary: Strong individual agents do not guarantee effective collaboration, because what one agent conveys must match how the receiving agent interprets and acts on it. Paired Automated Communication Optimization (PACO) treats each communication edge in a multi-agent workflow as the unit of optimization, jointly refining the instructions at both ends of the edge and their shared convention while leaving model weights, agent roles, and workflow topology untouched; a state-aware discounted bandit chooses which edge to refine, and execution feedback drives paired revisions scored through staged end-to-end runs. The optimized instructions fold into existing agent prompts, so deployment requires no extra model calls. On a four-agent workflow evaluated across diverse multi-agent benchmarks, **`PACO` consistently outperforms leading prompt-optimization and communication baselines**, and configurations learned on `HotpotQA` keep their advantage when transferred to other datasets without target-specific tuning.

papers.title: Causal Discovery Under Hard Selection Bias: A New Robust Score-Matching Approach
papers.abstract: Selection bias is a difficult yet widespread problem in causal discovery, occurring whenever non-random selection processes lead to data that is not representative of the underlying populations. Due to its practical importance, related works have been proposed to address the problem under local [Versteeg et al., 2022] or interventional settings [Dai et al., 2025a], but general algorithms for observational data remain elusive. In this paper, we focus on truncated data (hard selection), and provide a general result for Additive Noise Models (ANM). We show that score-based methods are a surprisingly suitable candidate due to a special property of the score function ($\nabla \log p(x)$): deterministic truncation preserves both the score of the joint distribution as well as the Jacobian of the score. While established score-matching algorithms still fail in most settings, we actively leverage this observation to propose a new method for causal discovery that is robust under truncated data with ANMs. Overall, our approach offers a general, robust solution that is agnostic to external information about the selection process and still achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art approaches when selection is not present.
papers.summary: Selection bias, in which non-random sampling produces data that misrepresents the underlying population, is a widespread obstacle to causal discovery, and general algorithms for purely observational data have remained out of reach. Focusing on truncated data (hard selection) under Additive Noise Models (ANM), the authors show that **deterministic truncation preserves both the score function of the joint distribution and the Jacobian of that score**, which makes score-based methods an unexpectedly natural fit. Because established score-matching algorithms still fail in most truncated settings, they build a new causal discovery method around this property that is robust to truncation, requires no external knowledge of the selection process, and matches state-of-the-art methods when no selection is present.

papers.title: Failure Recovery via Belief Updates and World Modeling for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BELIEFWEAVER, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these recurring IWM reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents often cannot recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can repair. `BELIEFWEAVER` maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints, so execution evidence updates frontier priorities across attempts and rollbacks while diagnostic evidence gates execution, and an implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. The recurring IWM reasoning components are then distilled into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks the framework raises aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native `Terminus-2` continuation, and **the distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while cutting estimated teacher API cost by 54.8%**.

papers.title: AReaL-RSI: Adaptive Scaling and Coordination of Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Scaling recursive self-improvement requires additional computation to produce useful research progress in reaching persistent objectives. Intuitively, more researcher agents can explore more hypotheses, but early evaluation scores might misrepresent their promise, shared findings could lose their applicability conditions, and useful procedures could remain confined to completed investigations. In this paper, we present AReaL-RSI, a framework for organizing a persistent research team of agents without updating backbone LLM weights. We formulate the scaling problem in terms of evaluated outcomes and whole-system resource expenditure. Concretely, a leader agent selects task-appropriate research orientations and guides ongoing investigations; conditional memory sharing distinguishes unresolved problems from supported findings and enables recipient adaptation. During recursive evolution, after each campaign, evidence-based review revises researcher orientation, knowledge, and skills for later campaigns. Experiments compare AReaL-RSI with Codex-Goal on downstream harness optimization, GPU kernel optimization, and AI research tasks using two backbones. Under the reported resource allocations, AReaL-RSI improves Terminal Bench performance by 2.2 percentage points for each backbone and increases mean KernelBench speedup by 32.2-36.8%; further scalability comparisons favor the design of AReaL-RSI over native scaling: combining experience sharing with specialized researcher roles yields 1.9-27.5% lower kernel latency than independent exploration and 1.3-33.9% lower latency than sharing alone across all seven comparable task-backbone pairs.
papers.summary: Adding more researcher agents to a recursive self-improvement loop does not automatically produce more progress, since early evaluation scores can misrepresent a hypothesis's promise, shared findings can lose their applicability conditions, and useful procedures can stay trapped inside completed investigations. `AReaL-RSI` organizes a persistent research team of agents without updating the backbone LLM's weights: a leader agent selects task-appropriate research orientations and guides ongoing investigations, conditional memory sharing separates unresolved problems from supported findings so recipients can adapt them, and after each campaign an evidence-based review revises researcher orientation, knowledge, and skills for later campaigns. Compared with `Codex-Goal` on harness optimization, GPU kernel optimization, and AI research tasks using two backbones, it **raises `Terminal Bench` by 2.2 percentage points for each backbone and increases mean `KernelBench` speedup by 32.2 to 36.8%**. Combining experience sharing with specialized researcher roles also yields 1.9 to 27.5% lower kernel latency than independent exploration and 1.3 to 33.9% lower than sharing alone across all seven comparable task-backbone pairs.

papers.title: Same Function, Different Trajectory: No Standard Optimizer Is Equivariant to Transformer Reparameterization
papers.abstract: We show that two Transformers representing the same function can follow different training trajectories. For example, doubling a query matrix and halving its key matrix preserves the model's function but changes the gradient scales seen by the optimizer. Our theoretical analysis establishes that standard block-local first-order optimizers fail to scale updates with parameters under a shared learning rate. For AdamW, transforming the first- and second-moment estimates alone does not correct the mismatch between parameter and update scales. To make runs restarted from equivalent checkpoints follow the same trajectory, we balance matrix pairs and transform their moment estimates together, bringing distinct but equivalent training states to the same starting point. To correct scale imbalance between paired Transformer matrices without changing predictions, we propose Symmetry-Aware Gradient Geometry Stabilization (SAGGS), which periodically equalizes the Frobenius norms of exact symmetry pairs, and its damped variant, Soft SAGGS. SAGGS reduces perplexity (PPL) by $0.374\pm0.026$ at 101M parameters on WikiText-103, and Soft SAGGS reduces PPL by $0.780\pm0.040$ in a 31M modern-architecture replication, both under scale imbalance. In a 123.8M checkpoint-resume experiment, reciprocally rescaling matrix pairs barely changes validation loss at restart but increases final PPL by $3.78\pm0.42$; hard and soft rebalancing recover to within $0.02$ PPL of the control.
papers.summary: Two Transformers that compute the same function can follow different training trajectories, because a reparameterization such as doubling a query matrix and halving its key matrix leaves predictions unchanged but alters the gradient scales the optimizer sees. The authors prove that standard block-local first-order optimizers fail to scale updates with parameters under a shared learning rate, and that for `AdamW` transforming the first- and second-moment estimates alone does not fix the mismatch; restarts from equivalent checkpoints only follow the same trajectory when matrix pairs are balanced and their moment estimates transformed together. Their Symmetry-Aware Gradient Geometry Stabilization (SAGGS) periodically equalizes the Frobenius norms of exact symmetry pairs, and a damped `Soft SAGGS` variant does so gradually; under scale imbalance these reduce perplexity (PPL) by 0.374 at 101M parameters on `WikiText-103` and by 0.780 in a 31M modern-architecture replication. In a 123.8M checkpoint-resume experiment, reciprocally rescaling matrix pairs barely changes validation loss at restart yet **raises final perplexity by 3.78**, and hard or soft rebalancing recovers to within 0.02 of the control.

papers.title: ResearchFlow-Eval: Tracing the Execution Gap in End-to-End Multi-Claim Autoresearch
papers.abstract: Autoresearch systems increasingly undertake entire research projects. In practice, scientific research requires systems to pursue multiple interdependent claims through a continuous, multi-stage workflow and revise experiments as evidence accumulates. Existing evaluations of autoresearch systems, however, typically score isolated tasks or final artifacts, leaving these process-level capabilities largely unmeasured. We therefore introduce ResearchFlow-Eval, a fine-grained framework for assessing continuous scientific execution and iteration at both the stage and claim levels. Each evaluation is grounded in a published anchor paper, from which we derive stage-specific rubrics that decompose each research stage into dimensions and separately scored rubric items.
