Using these rubrics, we score each research stage and examine experimental execution in detail, focusing on multi-claim completion and revisions across attempts. We apply the evaluation framework to general-purpose agent harnesses, skill-augmented harnesses, and systems with research-specific orchestration. Across all evaluated systems, experimental execution consistently lags behind design and planning. Within execution, systems struggle to produce high-quality results and meet claim requirements, and repeated attempts rarely yield measurable improvements. Moreover, neither skill augmentation nor research-specific orchestration reliably yields higher scores. ResearchFlow-Eval thus extends autoresearch evaluation beyond isolated, single-objective runs to continuous workflows in which systems pursue multiple claims and refine their work across iterations.
papers.summary: Autoresearch systems are taking on whole research projects, but real science means pursuing several interdependent claims through a continuous multi-stage workflow and revising experiments as evidence accumulates, while existing evaluations score isolated tasks or final artifacts. `ResearchFlow-Eval` grounds each evaluation in a published anchor paper, derives stage-specific rubrics that decompose every research stage into dimensions and separately scored items, and tracks multi-claim completion and revisions across attempts. Applied to general-purpose agent harnesses, skill-augmented harnesses, and systems with research-specific orchestration, it finds that **experimental execution consistently lags behind design and planning across every system evaluated**, that systems struggle to produce high-quality results and meet claim requirements, and that repeated attempts rarely yield measurable improvement. Neither skill augmentation nor research-specific orchestration reliably raised scores.

papers.title: One-Sided Verification Under Limited Expert Review
papers.abstract: AI has become increasingly helpful in scientific discovery, yet human expert review remains essential for those problems without reliable automated evaluation, posing a fundamental challenge as candidate generation scales beyond available review capacity. This paper studies verification under limited human effort, where rare valid solutions need to be prioritized while invalid candidates should be filtered out to reduce human workload. We adopt the one-sided verification objective that maximizes the rejection rate of invalid solutions (TNR) under a constraint on the false-rejection rate of valid ones (FNR), making human review cost an explicit term to minimize. Drawing on the intuition that verifying a specific error can be easier than discovering one, we introduce OSVerify, an algorithmic framework that decouples error proposal from error validation. The error proposer searches for errors in solutions across different granularities by hierarchical decomposition, while the validator distinguishes substantial errors from minor or hallucinated ones. Experiments on competition- and research-level benchmarks show that OSVerify reduces the number of human reviews of invalid solutions by 46% on average compared to voting baselines under the same empirical low FNR constraint. Our post-training of the validator further improves the reduction to 57%. As high-impact real-world use cases, we apply OSVerify to identify errors in published research papers that are subsequently confirmed by the original authors and help resolve three Langlands open conjectures that are confirmed by experts, demonstrating its utility to facilitate human-AI research collaboration.
papers.summary: As AI generates candidate solutions faster than experts can check them, human verification becomes the bottleneck for problems that lack reliable automated evaluation. The authors adopt a one-sided verification objective that maximizes the rejection rate of invalid solutions (TNR) under a constraint on the false-rejection rate of valid ones (FNR), making human review cost an explicit quantity to minimize, and introduce `OSVerify`, which decouples error proposal from error validation: a proposer searches for errors at multiple granularities via hierarchical decomposition, and a validator separates substantial errors from minor or hallucinated ones. On competition- and research-level benchmarks it **cuts human reviews of invalid solutions by 46% on average versus voting baselines at the same empirical FNR, rising to 57% after post-training the validator**. In deployment it identified errors in published papers that the original authors confirmed and helped resolve three open Langlands conjectures confirmed by experts.

papers.title: AM-Bench: Understanding Agents under Task Underspecification across Models and Harnesses
papers.abstract: Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clarification for language-model agents. Yet agents' responses to these information gaps remain poorly characterized across models and execution harnesses. We present AM-Bench, a benchmark built from 48 tasks adapted from Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench. Each task includes a fully specified reference and six variants spanning ambiguous or missing goals, context, and constraints. We evaluate every pairing of five models and four harnesses over 20,160 runs. Our results reveal distinct execution deficits: goal gaps hinder completion, context gaps increase token use, and constraint gaps weaken compliance without necessarily preventing completion. Missingness lowers success more than ambiguity in all three domains. These effects also reshape system comparisons: advantages under complete information need not persist, and rankings depend on model $\times$ harness pairings and the evaluation criterion -- completion, success, or repeat consistency. Estimates based on observed clarification requests and matched fully specified runs further suggest that clarification could recover unfinished work while leaving most constraint violations unresolved. Together, these findings motivate joint model-harness evaluation across information conditions and targeted clarification of unresolved requirements before dependent actions. To support future research on agents under task underspecification, we provide the AM-Bench project repository at https://github.com/s4-lab-cuhksz/AM-Bench.git.
papers.summary: Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clarification for language-model agents, yet agent behavior under such gaps has not been characterized across models and execution harnesses. `AM-Bench` adapts 48 tasks from `Terminal-Bench 2.0` and `Harness-Bench`, pairing each fully specified reference with six variants in which goals, context, or constraints are ambiguous or missing, and evaluates every pairing of five models and four harnesses over 20,160 runs. The gaps cause distinct deficits, with goal gaps hindering completion, context gaps raising token use, and constraint gaps weakening compliance without necessarily blocking completion, and **missing information lowers success more than ambiguity in all three domains**. Underspecification also reshuffles system rankings depending on the model-harness pairing and whether completion, success, or repeat consistency is measured, and estimates from observed clarification requests suggest that asking could recover unfinished work while leaving most constraint violations unresolved.

papers.title: LifeSearch: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents for Real-World Life and Productivity
papers.abstract: Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR agents' capabilities in real-world life and professional productivity settings insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LifeSearch, a challenging benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across 7 concrete life and productivity domains. With more than 4,500 hours of human annotation, we construct over 4,000 expert-written, fine-grained rubrics, covering both report-content criteria for coverage and accuracy and concrete criteria specifying values, units, dates, and URLs. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 advanced DR agents under a unified evaluation harness, systematically analyzing their performance patterns and failure modes. We find that even the best-performing frontier agent, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves a score of only 63.4%, leaving substantial room for improvement on realistic life and professional DR tasks. We select the grading configuration by comparing candidate LLM judges against human rubric labels, and a human ranking study shows strong alignment between aggregate benchmark scores and human judgments (Spearman's $\rho = 0.89$, Kendall's $\tau = 0.81$). LifeSearch provides a rigorous evaluation framework and foundation for advancing DR agents toward real-world life and productivity.
papers.summary: Deep research (DR) agents handle open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis, but existing benchmarks center on academic or synthetic tasks rather than everyday life and professional productivity. `LifeSearch` comprises 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across seven life and productivity domains, graded against more than 4,000 expert-written rubrics built with over 4,500 hours of annotation that cover report coverage and accuracy as well as concrete values, units, dates, and URLs. Evaluating 12 DR agents under a unified harness, **the best frontier agent, `GPT-5.6 Sol`, scores only 63.4%**. The grading configuration was chosen by comparing candidate LLM judges against human rubric labels, and a human ranking study shows aggregate benchmark scores align closely with human judgments, with a Spearman correlation of 0.89.

papers.title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
papers.abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.
papers.summary: AI companions provide emotional support and ongoing companionship, but sustained relational interaction introduces safety risks that prior work, which targets general harms or single platforms and relies on manually collected conversations, cannot evaluate or mitigate at scale. `CompanionSafe` pairs an evaluation component, `CompanionEval`, which constructs 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn-length tiers, with a mitigation component, `CompanionGuard`, that turns failures exposed by the benchmark into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, and **both closed- and open-source models grow less safe as interactions lengthen**.

papers.title: APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation
papers.abstract: Post-training is crucial for improving text-to-image models, yet existing pipelines typically rely on manually curated training data and fixed training distributions. We introduce APT (Agentic Post-Training), a fully automated framework that adaptively post-trains a base model according to its evolving capability profile. APT coordinates three agents to construct evaluation sets from user requirements, diagnose model-specific strengths and failure modes, and generate reinforcement learning data with an adaptive prompt distribution that emphasizes underperforming capabilities. By repeatedly evaluating, diagnosing, and updating the generator, APT lets the current model's behavior shape its next training tasks, forming a feedback loop inspired by recursive self-improvement. For general-purpose settings without user-specified evaluation scenarios, we further develop an evaluation harness that enables broad and diverse evaluation set generation. Experiments across multiple base models, benchmarks, and generation architectures demonstrate that APT is model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully automated.
papers.summary: Post-training text-to-image models typically depends on manually curated data and a fixed training distribution that ignores what the current model actually gets wrong. Agentic Post-Training (APT) automates the loop with three agents that build evaluation sets from user requirements, diagnose model-specific strengths and failure modes, and generate reinforcement learning data with an adaptive prompt distribution weighted toward underperforming capabilities, so each round of evaluation and diagnosis shapes the next round of training in a feedback loop modeled on recursive self-improvement. For general-purpose settings without user-specified scenarios, an evaluation harness generates broad and diverse evaluation sets. Across multiple base models, benchmarks, and generation architectures, the authors report that the method is **model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully automated**.

papers.title: From Spectral Saliency to Finite Deletion: Evaluating Selective Language Model Edits
papers.abstract: Deleting singular components offers a precise way to remove a capability from a language model, yet the first-order spectral saliency used to rank components predicts only a local loss change, whereas deletion is a finite intervention. In this paper, we study how prediction error affects selective editing, where selective editing requires degradation of a target task while preserving others. We decompose the error into derivative transfer across item splits and nonlinear response along the deletion path. We establish that outer interval screening retains every feasible candidate when every candidate's intervals contain its finite validation loss changes on every task. We evaluate these effects using one answer-only negative log-likelihood objective for search, validation, and test, with disjoint calibration and evaluation masks. The primary configuration targets arithmetic in Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 while preserving code and question answering; extensions cover Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and reversed target roles. In the primary study, which deletes 1024 coordinates from a support of 7168, calibrated intervals cover 968 of 1024 evaluation masks. Outer screening reaches the direct-selected edit after 25 verification checks, whereas direct verification abstains at a 32-check cap, but it rejects 4 of 74 feasible masks. All three selected edits pass validation, yet only one meets every test constraint. Interval coverage, feasible-candidate retention, and independent test preservation are therefore distinct properties and require separate assessment.
papers.summary: Deleting singular components from a language model's weights is a precise way to remove a capability, but the first-order spectral saliency used to rank components only predicts a local loss change, whereas deletion is a finite intervention. The authors study how this prediction error affects selective editing, which must degrade a target task while preserving others, decomposing the error into derivative transfer across item splits and nonlinear response along the deletion path, and showing that outer interval screening retains every feasible candidate when each candidate's intervals contain its finite validation loss changes on every task. The primary experiment deletes 1024 coordinates from a 7168-dimensional support to remove arithmetic from `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3` while preserving code and question answering, with extensions to `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` and reversed target roles: calibrated intervals cover 968 of 1024 evaluation masks, and outer screening reaches the direct-selected edit after 25 verification checks where direct verification abstains at a 32-check cap, though it rejects 4 of 74 feasible masks. **All three selected edits pass validation, yet only one meets every test constraint**, so interval coverage, feasible-candidate retention, and independent test preservation are distinct properties needing separate assessment.

papers.title: The Effect of Layer Ordering in Hybrid Architectures
papers.abstract: Hybrid attention is rapidly becoming the dominant architectural choice for frontier models. Despite their successes, such architectures complicate model design by introducing additional choices, including the types and locations of layers. This combinatorially large design space has been studied empirically, but given the vast expense of training and evaluating models with different configurations, a principled understanding of the effects of layer selection and ordering is needed. We provide the first such analysis, showing that the dominant hybrid architecture is highly task-specific. Concretely, for any layer configuration, we prove that there exists a task where we can construct a model with this configuration that provably outperforms any other model of any different configuration under fixed resource constraints. Empirically, we observe that for standard training, learned hybrid architectures exhibit separations between layer orderings that match our theoretical findings. For instance, under the same memory budget, the optimal architecture predicted by our theory for a segmented retrieval task consistently achieves perfect accuracy, whereas the next strongest plateaus below 0.5. These results extend to deeper models, where ``containing'' the dominant architecture for a task indicates whether the model attains high performance. In addition, we investigate the mechanisms learned by hybrids, observing that Transformer layers contribute the largest share of performance on associative recall across architectures. This work establishes insights into task-dependent hybrid architecture design relevant to the training and scaling of frontier-scale hybrids.
papers.summary: Hybrid architectures that mix attention with other layer types are becoming the default for frontier models, but choosing which layer types to use and where to put them is a combinatorially large design space that has been explored only empirically because training every configuration is prohibitively expensive. The authors provide a principled analysis showing the dominant hybrid is highly task-specific: **for any layer configuration, there exists a task on which a model with that configuration provably outperforms every model of any different configuration under fixed resource constraints**. Trained models reproduce these separations, for example on a segmented retrieval task under a fixed memory budget the theory-predicted architecture consistently reaches perfect accuracy while the next strongest plateaus below 0.5, and in deeper models whether the network contains the dominant architecture for a task predicts whether it performs well. A mechanistic analysis finds that Transformer layers contribute the largest share of associative-recall performance across hybrid designs.

papers.title: Chain of Thought Monitoring Can Fail Even When CoT Is Necessary
papers.abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) monitoring is used by frontier labs to detect misbehaviour of AI systems. Yet, its reliability remains poorly understood. We attribute this to the lack of a successful organizing principle that leads to generalizable conclusions about monitoring reliability in different regimes. Recent work attributes monitoring failures to the CoT not being necessary for the answer, and argues that CoT becomes monitorable when it is necessary. We show that this binary necessary/not-necessary organizing principle is too coarse by demonstrating that monitoring failures persist even if the CoT is necessary for the answer. In response, we introduce a more fine-grained organizing principle based on a hierarchy of four CoT necessity levels. Building on this hierarchy, we develop a framework for measuring CoT monitorability at the three lowest levels via intervention experiments. We demonstrate monitoring failures at all three of these levels on realistic, hard prediction tasks. On a difficult medical-diagnosis task, patient sex and a clinical attribute influence the answer in at least 19% and 24% of correct responses with a necessary CoT, respectively, yet their influence is almost never articulated. These results show that even when CoT is necessary, it is not guaranteed to be monitorable.
papers.summary: Frontier labs use chain of thought (CoT) monitoring to detect misbehavior in AI systems, and recent work has argued that monitoring becomes reliable whenever the CoT is necessary for producing the answer. The authors show that this binary necessary-or-not principle is too coarse, demonstrating that monitoring failures persist even when the CoT is necessary, and replace it with a hierarchy of four CoT necessity levels together with an intervention-based framework for measuring monitorability at the three lowest levels. On realistic, hard prediction tasks they observe failures at all three levels; **in a difficult medical-diagnosis task, patient sex and a clinical attribute influence the answer in at least 19% and 24% of correct responses with a necessary CoT, yet that influence is almost never articulated**. Necessity of the CoT therefore does not guarantee that it can be monitored.

papers.title: A CaLLM Judge is a Better Judge: Mitigating Bias in LLM-as-a-judge
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to predict which of two candidate answers a human evaluator would prefer, providing a scalable alternative when human evaluation is too costly. Unfortunately, LLM judgments can exhibit systematic biases. Prior work has documented position, verbosity or model family of the candidate answers influencing the judge decision rather than their quality, while additional biases may remain undocumented. $\textit{Multicalibration}$ provides a natural framework to address this problem: each bias corresponds to miscalibration on an identifiable group, $\textit{e.g.}$, family bias manifests as overconfidence in answers generated by models belonging to the same family of the judge. The challenge is to fix miscalibration simultaneously across many, potentially unknown groups. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{CaLLM}$, a post hoc framework that multicalibrates an LLM judge, thereby bounding all such biases simultaneously. We prove that $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ bounds the bias of every group whose error structure is captured by an available representation, and that augmenting it with explicit bias groups further reduces the residual bias. We then derive theoretical conditions under which $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ improves the judge's accuracy, rather than trading it for calibration. Finally, we evaluate $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ across pairwise preference benchmarks, showing that it reduces the multicalibration error on both specified and unspecified bias groups, while improving predictive performance of the judge.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as judges predicting which of two candidate answers a human would prefer, but their verdicts can be swayed by answer position, verbosity, or the model family that produced an answer, and other biases may remain undocumented. `CaLLM` is a post hoc framework that applies multicalibration to an LLM judge, treating each bias as miscalibration on an identifiable group, such as overconfidence in answers from the judge's own model family, and correcting many potentially unknown groups simultaneously. The authors **prove that `CaLLM` bounds the bias of every group whose error structure is captured by an available representation**, that adding explicit bias groups further reduces residual bias, and derive conditions under which it improves accuracy rather than trading accuracy for calibration. On pairwise preference benchmarks it lowers multicalibration error on both specified and unspecified bias groups while improving the judge's predictive performance.

papers.title: SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction
papers.abstract: Multimodal medical data captures complementary aspects of disease. It provides a comprehensive basis for diagnosis and the identification of biological associations linked to progression or treatment response. Established contrastive learning approaches exploit shared information across modalities, but fall short in exploiting complementary, modality-specific signals relevant for a task. Here, we propose a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE) framework that separates task-relevant unimodal and multimodal information from instance-specific variation task-irrelevant, allowing complementary signals across modalities to be leveraged for prediction. The method yields benefits even if modalities are missing at test time. We evaluate the method on a treatment response prediction task using medical imaging and RNA data. Empirical comparison with alignment-based and multimodal VAE state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates improved multimodal prediction performance, and consistent benefits for prediction from a single modality after multimodal training. The full code can be found here: https://github.com/cirmuw/SYNPRED.
papers.summary: Multimodal medical data captures complementary aspects of disease, but contrastive learning approaches exploit only the information shared across modalities and miss the modality-specific signals that matter for a given task. `SYNPRED` is a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE) that separates task-relevant unimodal and multimodal information from task-irrelevant instance-specific variation, so that complementary signals from each modality contribute to prediction and remain useful even when a modality is missing at test time. On a treatment response prediction task combining medical imaging with RNA data, it **outperforms alignment-based and multimodal VAE baselines on multimodal prediction** and consistently improves single-modality prediction after multimodal training.

papers.title: When Missingness Follows the Graph: Beyond Feature Propagation for Missing Features
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) commonly assume that node features are fully observed, despite missing features being pervasive in real-world applications. By leveraging the dependence between node features and graph structure, existing graph-specific methods handle missingness by propagating observed feature values along graph edges. However, these methods have mainly been evaluated in overly optimistic settings, where feature entries are removed independently and uniformly across the graph. This overlooks realistic scenarios in which missingness propagates among connected nodes, as can occur during localized sensing failures in sensor networks. We formalize this complementary notion as graph-structured mask dependence, where the joint distribution of missingness indicators is shaped by the graph, and introduce a controlled mechanism that instantiates this setting. We study propagation-based methods theoretically and empirically in this setting, showing that their effectiveness changes substantially compared with the uniformly random regime. Motivated by this limitation, we propose PEMix, designed to remain effective under challenging graph-structured missingness. Rather than propagating observed values, PEMix uses global structural representations to condition a probabilistic model of incomplete node features before message passing. Experiments under controlled graph-structured missingness and naturally occurring missingness show that PEMix remains robust across complex missingness regimes, with particularly strong performance as missingness becomes severe.
papers.summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) usually assume node features are fully observed, and existing graph-specific methods handle missing entries by propagating observed values along edges, but they have mostly been evaluated under optimistic masks in which entries vanish independently and uniformly across the graph. The authors formalize graph-structured mask dependence, in which the joint distribution of missingness indicators is shaped by the graph as happens during localized sensor failures, introduce a controlled mechanism to instantiate it, and show theoretically and empirically that **propagation-based methods lose much of their effectiveness once missingness follows the graph structure**. Their `PEMix` instead uses global structural representations to condition a probabilistic model of incomplete node features before message passing, and under both controlled graph-structured and naturally occurring missingness it stays robust, with the strongest performance as missingness becomes severe.

papers.title: Certifying Almost-Sure Reachability in Unknown MDPs
papers.abstract: {\em Specification-Guided Reinforcement Learning (RL)} has largely concerned itself with \emph{learning} an optimal policy against a formal specification in an unknown {\em Markov Decision Process (MDP)}. We take up the dual question. Given a policy already in hand, can one \emph{verify} that it is correct against a formal specification in an unknown MDP, using sampling access alone? Such a question arises naturally in safety-critical systems. We investigate it for the {\em almost-sure reachability property}, whose correctness is witnessed by a {\em ranking supermartingale (RSM)} certificate. Our first finding is negative. In the absence of any further information about the MDP, one can neither learn such a certificate nor verify a candidate one with probabilistic guarantees. On the positive side, we show that, under a mild restriction, a known lower bound $p_{\min}$ on nonzero transition probabilities, a correct certificate \emph{can} be learned with PAC-style guarantees. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of learning and verifying certificates for almost-sure reachability in unknown MDPs from sampling access alone. Finally, our experiments show that the $p_{\min}$-based sufficient condition, while sound, is conservative: the learned certificate often remains valid on the true MDP even when the condition fails.
papers.summary: Specification-guided reinforcement learning usually asks how to learn a policy that satisfies a formal specification in an unknown Markov Decision Process (MDP); the authors instead ask whether a policy already in hand can be verified against such a specification using sampling access alone. They focus on almost-sure reachability, whose correctness is witnessed by a ranking supermartingale (RSM) certificate, and show that without further information about the MDP one can neither learn such a certificate nor verify a candidate with probabilistic guarantees. **Given a known lower bound on nonzero transition probabilities, a correct certificate can be learned with PAC-style guarantees.** Experiments indicate this sufficient condition is conservative, since learned certificates often remain valid on the true MDP even when the condition fails.

papers.title: Narrative Lookahead in LLMs: Event-Level Decodability, Predictive Advantage, and Steering
papers.abstract: Do language models carry information about narrative events before writing them, and how far ahead? We examine narrative lookahead through salient, state-changing events rather than tokens or response-level attributes. We extract 23,355 LLM-annotated events from 2,000 stories generated by four open-weight LLMs, labeling them along three nonexclusive dimensions of change: within agents, between agents, and in the story world, with human validation on a subset. Event segmentation and plot-independent labels enable comparisons across stories at horizons measured in events rather than in tokens. At event ends, we probe hidden states for upcoming event types and compare predictions with text-only predictors using matched prefixes. Across four models, future event types are decodable above prevalence baselines for at least four subsequent events, but probes significantly outperform both primary text-only predictors only for the next event. In exploratory steering with OLMo-3.1-32B, a probe-derived direction shifts the proportion of the target event type in both intended directions at higher strengths. Our event-level approach links the prediction of future narrative developments to interventions that reshape subsequent event composition.
papers.summary: The question is whether language models encode information about upcoming narrative events before writing them, and how far ahead. The authors extract 23,355 LLM-annotated, state-changing events from 2,000 stories generated by four open-weight models, label each along three dimensions of change (within agents, between agents, and in the story world), and probe hidden states at event boundaries for the types of subsequent events, comparing against text-only predictors on matched prefixes. **Future event types are decodable above prevalence baselines for at least four events ahead, but probes beat text-only predictors only for the very next event.** In exploratory steering with `OLMo-3.1-32B`, a probe-derived direction shifts the proportion of a target event type in both intended directions at higher strengths.

papers.title: Cheap, Consistent, Calibrated, but Biased? Typed Decision Models as Judges
papers.abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability for each allowed answer instead of generating text, which makes them candidates for cheaply replacing LLM judges that compare two answers. Whether they share the biases of LLM judges is untested. We run the CALM benchmark's bias tests on eight TDMs and seven LLM judges of 2024 and 2026. Every TDM is biased, in three to eight of twelve tests. Emotional tone affects them most, and rewriting the better answer in such a tone lowers the accuracy of a typical TDM from 99% to 42%. TDMs are more biased than 2026 LLM judges. All eight change verdicts when the answers swap places, which the 2026 LLM judges hardly do, and several side with an answer that most people allegedly prefer or that a famous model allegedly wrote. Yet both kinds of judge are tripped up by the same prompts. The TDMs' probabilities show that most tests mainly flip verdicts the TDM was unsure of, and that good calibration does not protect against bias. As TDMs are more consistent and 37 times cheaper than 2026 LLM judges, our results suggest they can be attractive judges if their biases are tested for the task.
papers.summary: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability for each allowed answer rather than generating text, making them a cheap alternative to LLM judges for pairwise answer comparison, but whether they inherit the known biases of LLM judges had not been tested. The authors run the `CALM` benchmark's twelve bias tests on eight TDMs and seven LLM judges from 2024 and 2026. **Every TDM is biased on three to eight of the twelve tests, and rewriting the better answer in an emotional tone drops a typical TDM's accuracy from 99% to 42%.** TDMs are more biased than 2026 LLM judges, notably flipping verdicts when answers swap positions, yet both kinds of judge fail on the same prompts; since TDMs are more consistent and 37 times cheaper, the authors argue they remain attractive judges if their biases are tested for the task at hand.

papers.title: H-DDCM: Hadamard Codebooks for Fast Generative Image and Video Compression
papers.abstract: Training-free diffusion-based compression methods repurpose the generative priors of a diffusion or a flow model to compress data without retraining them as task-specific codecs. Recent codebook-based approaches such as Turbo-DDCM achieve strong perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates, but their reliance on dense Gaussian codebooks remains costly in both memory and computation, and scales poorly with the large latent dimensions of modern image and video generators. Their combinatorial bitstream encoding further becomes computationally heavy at this scale. We introduce H-DDCM, a scalable generative compression framework that replaces Gaussian codebooks with implicit randomized Hadamard dictionaries. The fast Walsh-Hadamard transform allows for implicitly synthesizing full-dimensional dictionaries with $O(d \log d)$ compute for projection and reconstruction and $O(d)$ memory, without materializing the full-dimensional dictionary. We further introduce an efficient table-free lexicographic coding scheme that makes combinatorial encoding practical at larger dimensions. Beyond images, we adapt the framework to an autoregressive video flow model and develop a streaming compression scheme that periodically re-encodes recently reconstructed frames into a fresh KV-cache prefix, preserving temporal context across segments at no additional transmitted bits. This enables long-form, close to real-time generative video compression on a single GPU. Across image and video benchmarks, H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance while substantially reducing the memory and computational overhead of codebook-based training-free generative compression.
papers.summary: Training-free diffusion-based compression reuses the generative prior of a diffusion or flow model as a codec, but codebook approaches such as `Turbo-DDCM` depend on dense Gaussian codebooks whose memory and compute scale poorly with the large latent dimensions of modern image and video generators. `H-DDCM` replaces these with implicit randomized Hadamard dictionaries synthesized through the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform, giving projection and reconstruction in O(d log d) compute and O(d) memory without materializing the dictionary, plus a table-free lexicographic coding scheme that keeps combinatorial bitstream encoding practical at scale. The framework is extended to an autoregressive video flow model with a streaming scheme that periodically re-encodes recently reconstructed frames into a fresh KV-cache prefix, preserving temporal context at no extra transmitted bits. **This enables long-form, close to real-time generative video compression on a single GPU**, with competitive rate-distortion-perception results on image and video benchmarks.

papers.title: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM Decisions Already Made
papers.abstract: Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the moment it is made; the action it commits to is latent, carried out later, in a changing world. We therefore introduce a timestamp theory of decision validity and a decision ledger that realises it. Six timestamps define a decision; a freshness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence guarantees at action time, placing the remaining risk in information published afterwards. Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities: routing, which delivers that information to affected decisions before their revision deadlines, and temporal judgment, which reads it for the time of action. The ledger is persistent state holding each decision's times, evidence and background knowledge, indexed by watch conditions written at decision time. Controlled decision streams with exact labels confirm four predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to frontier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on decisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows routing; the ledger's index sets what routing reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect dependencies at low exposure; and the remaining errors concern when a change takes effect. Freshness makes a decision right when it is made; routing and temporal judgment keep it right when it is carried out.
papers.summary: An LLM's decision is shaped by how fresh its information is at the moment of deciding, but the committed action is carried out later in a world that may have changed. The authors propose a timestamp theory of decision validity, in which six timestamps define a decision and a freshness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence can guarantee at action time, and realize it with a decision ledger that stores each decision's times, evidence, and background knowledge, indexed by watch conditions written when the decision is made. Accuracy then splits into routing, which delivers later-published information to affected decisions before their revision deadlines, and temporal judgment, which interprets that information for the time of action. **On controlled decision streams with exact labels across five LLMs from 8B to frontier scale, freshness alone yields exactly the accuracy the ceiling predicts, and accuracy thereafter tracks routing**, with remaining errors concentrated on when a change takes effect.

papers.title: Monitoring latent reasoning in looped language models
papers.abstract: Looped language models (LMs) reuse one block of layers several times per token generation, promising more latent computation at no additional storage cost. Despite their rising popularity, the analysis of looped LMs is still in its infancy: little is known about whether the iterative transformations actually improve their capabilities, or whether these models remain stable under prompt perturbation. We construct an inspection protocol rooted in Mechanistic Interpretability comprising five diverse lenses. We apply it to examine eight looped LMs from four families. Models differ in many aspects but the key one is whether the prompt is transmitted only within the looped state (carry loops: Ouro, LoopUS) or re-supplied at every iteration (re-read loops: Parcae, and Rec-OLMo & Huginn from the Raven family). The results of our study provide valuable insights concerning safety and efficient use of looped language models.
papers.summary: Looped language models reuse a single block of layers several times per generated token, promising more latent computation without additional parameter storage, yet it is largely unknown whether the repeated transformations actually improve capability or whether these models stay stable under prompt perturbation. The authors build an inspection protocol grounded in mechanistic interpretability, comprising five lenses, and apply it to eight looped models from four families. **The key architectural distinction is whether the prompt is carried only within the looped state (carry loops such as `Ouro` and `LoopUS`) or re-supplied at every iteration (re-read loops such as `Parcae`, `Rec-OLMo`, and `Huginn`).** The authors frame the resulting findings as bearing on the safety and efficient use of looped language models.

papers.title: Distance Prediction for Quantum Codes
papers.abstract: The distance of a quantum code is a fundamental metric that dictates its error-correction capability. While quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) families such as Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes offer a promising pathway to low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computing, computing their distance is challenging. Current exact solvers and even search heuristics that provide a distance upper bound suffer from severe computational bottlenecks, restricting the discovery of optimal codes. In this paper, we construct a dataset of BB codes with corresponding distance upper bounds obtained through high-budget heuristic searches. We introduce BB-Net, an attention-based neural network architecture for predicting the distance of BB codes. It achieves 96.39% accuracy on the reference distances in the test set, compared with 94.86% for state-of-the-art heuristics with a budget of up to $10^{4}$ times more computational runtime. On a subset with certified exact distances, BB-Net achieves 98.94%. By relieving the distance-calculation bottleneck, BB-Net enables faster screening of large code spaces, particularly in ML-driven search pipelines, and thereby can accelerate the discovery of novel quantum error-correcting codes, an important capability for advancing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/NadavSc/BBNet
papers.summary: The distance of a quantum error-correcting code determines how many errors it can correct, but for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) families such as Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes, exact solvers and even heuristic upper-bound searches are computationally expensive, limiting the search for good codes. The authors build a dataset of BB codes with distance upper bounds obtained from high-budget heuristic searches and train `BB-Net`, an attention-based network that predicts code distance directly. **The network reaches 96.39% accuracy against the reference distances on the test set, versus 94.86% for state-of-the-art heuristics given up to ten thousand times more runtime**, and 98.94% on a subset with certified exact distances. The authors position it as a fast screening tool for large code spaces in ML-driven code search pipelines, and the code is public.

papers.title: Revisiting Error Feedback for Model Quantization
papers.abstract: We study causal error-feedback coefficients as design variables for model quantization. Modeling instantaneous quantization errors as independent, zero-mean variables with a common fixed variance, we formulated a metric-dependent trace problem for designing feedback coefficients. The formulation resembles fixed-order GPTQ/LDLQ feedback and supports Jacobian-aware designs that account for downstream error propagation. For a positive-definite metric $\boldsymbol{H}$, we prove that the joint rotation-feedback trace minimum is $n\det(\boldsymbol{H})^{1/n}$ and present an attaining pair using the geometric mean decomposition. Experiments on synthetic networks, trained MLPs, and language models show benefits from downstream-sensitive feedback, but also reveal that trace optimality need not improve finite-level performance. Small QAT experiments further illustrate direct loss-driven feedback tuning with fixed or trainable network weights.
papers.summary: Error feedback in model quantization, as used by `GPTQ` and `LDLQ`, propagates each weight's rounding error into later weights, and the authors treat the causal feedback coefficients themselves as design variables. Modeling instantaneous quantization errors as independent zero-mean variables with common variance, they pose a metric-dependent trace minimization that resembles fixed-order feedback and admits Jacobian-aware designs accounting for downstream error propagation. **For a positive-definite metric H, the joint rotation-and-feedback trace minimum is proven to equal n times the n-th root of the determinant of H, attained via the geometric mean decomposition.** Experiments on synthetic networks, trained MLPs, and language models show gains from downstream-sensitive feedback but also that trace optimality does not necessarily translate into better performance at finite quantization levels, and small quantization-aware training experiments illustrate direct loss-driven tuning of the feedback.

papers.title: SparPR: Runtime KV-Cache Recovery for Resource-Constrained LLM Inference on Consumer Hardware
papers.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on consumer hardware is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with every decoded token and quickly exhausts the memory and bandwidth of a single consumer GPU. We present SparPR (Sparse Partial Recomputation), a runtime KV-cache recovery mechanism that does not modify model weights and requires no offline training. SparPR couples three online decisions: Query-Aware key-block selection scores historical blocks against the current query; dynamic budget control estimates per-block copy and recompute costs to decide how many blocks to retain; and on-demand local recomputation with cost-aware fallback merges retained blocks into continuous spans and switches between sparse recomputation and full recovery according to a runtime cost comparison. Implemented on FlexGen/FlexLLMGen, SparPR is evaluated on a single consumer laptop (RTX 3070 Ti 8GB, Ryzen 9 6900HX, 16GB RAM). It cuts end-to-end latency by 31%, 52%, and 63% at 1k, 2k, and 4k prompt tokens respectively, with 1.4x-2.7x higher throughput, and completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes where the FlexGen baseline times out. Under a fixed cache budget, SparPR retains a Needle Accuracy that stays well above StreamingLLM and H2O at every keep ratio, and ablation studies confirm that the three mechanisms act jointly.
papers.summary: Running large language models on consumer GPUs is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with every decoded token and quickly exhausts memory and bandwidth. `SparPR` (Sparse Partial Recomputation) is a runtime KV-cache recovery mechanism requiring no weight changes or offline training: it scores historical key blocks against the current query, uses a dynamic budget controller that estimates per-block copy and recompute costs to decide how many blocks to retain, and merges retained blocks into contiguous spans for on-demand local recomputation with a cost-aware fallback to full recovery. Implemented on `FlexGen`/`FlexLLMGen` and evaluated on a laptop with an 8GB RTX 3070 Ti and 16GB RAM, **it cuts end-to-end latency by 31%, 52%, and 63% at 1k, 2k, and 4k prompt tokens with 1.4x to 2.7x higher throughput**, and completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes where the baseline times out. Under a fixed cache budget it keeps needle-retrieval accuracy well above `StreamingLLM` and `H2O` at every keep ratio, and ablations show the three mechanisms work jointly.

papers.title: Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs
papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose CaRe (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time method for identifying and correcting modality misrouting. CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to identify a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, and flags potential misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the original joint prediction. For such cases, CaRe computes a residual direction from the discrepancy between the counterfactual and fused representations and uses it to steer the original multimodal state toward the relevant modality evidence, while retaining both modalities in the original audio-visual inference path. The intervention strength is adapted based on the confidence of the counterfactual branch. Experiments on CMM and AVHBench across two OLLMs show that CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.
papers.summary: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs), which jointly process audio and video, suffer cross-modal hallucinations when one modality interferes with another. The authors observe that for many incorrect joint predictions the question-relevant unimodal branch alone still recovers the right answer, a failure pattern they call modality misrouting, and propose `CaRe` (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time fix. A text-only modality probe picks a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, flags misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the joint one, and computes a residual direction from the gap between counterfactual and fused representations to steer the multimodal state toward the relevant modality's evidence, with intervention strength scaled by the counterfactual branch's confidence. **On `CMM` and `AVHBench` across two OLLMs, `CaRe` consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.**

papers.title: RadixFlow: Filling Execution Bubbles in Prefix-Cached Hybrid LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Prefix reuse improves LLM inference by sharing the KV cache of common prompt prefixes. This helps only if the scheduler can execute a matched branch in the current worker round. Schedulers assume that a matched prefix is ready, which holds for full attention but fails for hybrid LLMs. There, a branch (the consumer) may need recurrent state that another branch (the producer) is still computing in the same round. The native scheduler stops its waiting-queue scan at this blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking creates \emph{execution bubbles}: idle batch slots that independent work could fill. We introduce RadixFlow, which decouples prefix matching from state readiness. Its state-ready traversal turns a global scan barrier into a local wait: only the consumer is blocked until the next round, while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch under the native state check. On five hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers mean latency by 3\% to 24\% and worker rounds by 11\% to 44\% at almost unchanged reuse. On the larger Qwen3.5 models, ablations show that most of the gain comes from traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control. Heavier rounds limit how much of this saving reaches latency.
papers.summary: Prefix caching lets an LLM server share the KV cache of common prompt prefixes, but a matched branch can only run if its cached state is actually ready, which schedulers assume and which fails for hybrid models that mix attention with recurrent layers. There, a consumer branch may need recurrent state that a producer branch is still computing in the same round; the native scheduler halts its waiting-queue scan at the blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking leaves idle batch slots the authors call execution bubbles. `RadixFlow` decouples prefix matching from state readiness with a state-ready traversal that blocks only the consumer until the next round while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch. **Across five hybrid models it lowers mean latency by 3% to 24% and worker rounds by 11% to 44% at nearly unchanged reuse**, with ablations on the larger `Qwen3.5` models attributing most of the gain to the traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control.

papers.title: Attacking Only Half the Data: Two-Sided Evaluation of AI-Text Detector Robustness
papers.abstract: We investigate the robustness of widely used AI text detectors under attacks applied to both human and machine text. Prior evaluations typically attack only machine text, overlooking that human text is routinely modified through grammar correction, formatting, or invisible character insertion. We introduce a two-sided protocol that applies attacks to both classes. Across two corpora and nine detectors, reported AUROC gains vanish under two-sided evaluation, with attacked human text misclassified at rates up to 100%. While simple preprocessing reverses character-level attacks, word-level synonym substitution remains effective meaning-preserving, and irreversible.
papers.summary: Evaluations of AI-generated text detectors usually apply adversarial attacks only to machine text, ignoring that human text is also routinely altered by grammar correction, reformatting, or invisible character insertion. The authors introduce a two-sided protocol that applies the same attacks to both human and machine text and test it across two corpora and nine detectors. **Reported AUROC gains vanish under two-sided evaluation, with attacked human text misclassified at rates up to 100%.** Simple preprocessing reverses character-level attacks, but word-level synonym substitution remains effective, meaning-preserving, and irreversible.

papers.title: Learning a Group Element from Its Action: Galois Correspondences, Optimal ERM, and an Abel-Ruffini Threshold for the Natarajan Dimension
papers.abstract: We study learning an unknown element $g$ of a group acting with finite orbits on a countable set, from examples $(x,gx)$. After a sample on $A$, the consistent hypotheses are the restrictions of a coset of the pointwise stabilizer of $A$, and the sample forces exactly the labels of points this stabilizer fixes; for a Galois group, they form the field generated by the data. Through this correspondence, multiclass dimensions become group invariants: the DS and graph dimensions equal the height, the Littlestone dimension the longest irredundant sequence length, and the teaching dimension the minimal base size. Among deterministic learners, symmetry makes empirical risk minimization optimal: on nondegenerate classes every consistent learner, whatever its tie-breaking, attains the optimal realizable sample complexity up to constant factors, and every consistent online learner the optimal mistake bound. Agnostically, every ERM's sample complexity exceeds the known lower bound by at most the DS-to-Natarajan ratio, up to constants. For finite Galois extensions of countable fields, the Natarajan dimension equals a group invariant, the coset-cube number, which is at least the number of complemented factors of any chief series of any subgroup. Hence the dimensions coincide for every solvable Galois group, while for the groups $A_5$ and $S_5$ of the quintic they are $2<3$ and $3<4$, and $A_5$ is the smallest group with a gap. For the Galois group $S_n$ of the general equation of degree $n$, they coincide exactly when $n\le 4$, i.e., in characteristic zero, exactly when the equation is solvable by radicals; the implication is one-way, as the simple group $\mathrm{PSL}(2,8)$ has no gap. For linear, orthogonal and unitary maps of $\mathbb R^d$ or $\mathbb C^d$ both dimensions equal $d$, and a two-fibered pseudo-cube is a disjoint union of Natarajan cubes exactly when its monodromy group is abelian.
papers.summary: The setting is learning an unknown element of a group acting with finite orbits on a countable set, from example pairs of a point and its image. After observing a sample, the consistent hypotheses form a coset of the sample's pointwise stabilizer, and the sample determines exactly the labels of points that stabilizer fixes; for a Galois group these form the field generated by the data, and through this correspondence multiclass learning dimensions become group invariants (the DS and graph dimensions equal the height, the Littlestone dimension the longest irredundant sequence length, and the teaching dimension the minimal base size). Symmetry makes every consistent empirical risk minimizer optimal up to constants for realizable sample complexity and online mistake bounds, with the agnostic gap controlled by the DS-to-Natarajan ratio. **For finite Galois extensions the Natarajan and DS dimensions coincide for every solvable Galois group but differ for the quintic groups A5 and S5, so for the general degree-n equation they agree exactly when n is at most 4, that is, in characteristic zero, exactly when the equation is solvable by radicals**, though the implication is one-way since the simple group PSL(2,8) has no gap.

papers.title: When Do Learned Blocks Preserve Causal Meaning? Block Identifiability and Constructive Causal Abstractions
papers.abstract: Standard identifiability theory assumes one-dimensional latent factors, but learned representations can encode latent information across multidimensional blocks whose internal coordinates are not uniquely determined. When such blocks are used to represent and intervene on higher-level concepts, it is unclear whether their causal meaning survives the transformations left unresolved by block-identifiability. We connect block-identifiability to constructive causal abstraction. We show that block-diagonal invertible transformations followed by compatible coordinate permutations form the maximal class that preserves every constructive causal abstraction built on those blocks. This guarantee assumes that the correspondence between blocks and concepts is updated with the representation. A small synthetic experiment with additive autoencoders shows that high-level interventions can be transferred between independently learned representations while approximately preserving their intended effects.
papers.summary: Standard identifiability theory assumes one-dimensional latent factors, but learned representations often encode latent information in multidimensional blocks whose internal coordinates are not uniquely determined, raising the question of whether causal meaning survives when such blocks are used to represent and intervene on higher-level concepts. The authors connect block-identifiability to constructive causal abstraction. **Block-diagonal invertible transformations followed by compatible coordinate permutations form the maximal class of transformations that preserves every constructive causal abstraction built on those blocks**, provided the correspondence between blocks and concepts is updated along with the representation. A small synthetic experiment with additive autoencoders shows that high-level interventions can be transferred between independently learned representations while approximately preserving their intended effects.

papers.title: Fan Out or Relay? Ownership-Aware Routing for LLM Agents Querying Siloed Tables
papers.abstract: Inside organizations, a question's data often sit with several owners, who query their own tables but never hand them over. An LLM coordinator can fan out, sending the question to every owner at once, or relay, querying owners in turn and reusing earlier rows. We show that neither is safe in advance, because data ownership decides which one is right. Across thirteen settings on PeopleJoin and BIRD with three model families, fan-out is more accurate in twelve on questions one owner can answer, yet answers at most 4.3% of those joining two owners' tables. The flip follows ownership, not query shape: on BIRD two-table joins, fan-out answers 32-44% when one owner holds both and 1-4% otherwise. Relay wins by conditioning on returned rows, and hiding them from an otherwise identical planner cuts two-owner accuracy from 23.2% to 5.1%. Since ownership is public, we propose Ownership-Aware Routing (OAR), which drafts a schema-only SQL query, counts the owners whose tables it joins, and routes the question before any private row is read. In ten settings OAR is never significantly less accurate than the best fixed protocol, and beats every fixed protocol on PeopleJoin, by up to 9.3 points on held-out organizations.
papers.summary: Within organizations, answering a question often requires data held by several owners who will run queries on their own tables but never share the rows, so an LLM coordinator must either fan out the question to every owner at once or relay through owners in turn while reusing earlier results. Across thirteen settings on `PeopleJoin` and `BIRD` with three model families, fan-out is more accurate in twelve on questions a single owner can answer, **yet it answers at most 4.3% of questions requiring a join across two owners' tables**, and the flip is driven by ownership rather than query shape: on `BIRD` two-table joins, fan-out succeeds 32-44% of the time when one owner holds both tables and 1-4% otherwise. Relay wins by conditioning on returned rows, and hiding those rows from an otherwise identical planner drops two-owner accuracy from 23.2% to 5.1%. Since ownership is public, the proposed Ownership-Aware Routing (`OAR`) drafts a schema-only SQL query, counts the owners whose tables it joins, and routes accordingly before any private row is read; it is never significantly worse than the best fixed protocol in ten settings and beats every fixed protocol on `PeopleJoin` by up to 9.3 points on held-out organizations.

papers.title: When and How Order-Flow Interventions Work After Dealers Adapt
papers.abstract: Learning dealer agents can settle on persistently wide quotes, raising what customers pay to trade. A venue can route more orders to tighter quotes, but a wide quote may reflect real risk, and once dealers adapt, an end-to-end comparison cannot show why a rule works: because it intervenes more, picks better moments, is announced in advance, or rewards the right quote. We propose SOFA (State-aligned Order-Flow Allocation), a public order-flow contract with three parts: a State Scorer ranks market states from lagged public data, a Commitment Scheduler announces a budgeted intervention strength before dealers quote, and a Quote-to-Flow Allocator shifts a bounded share of fixed customer demand toward tighter quotes. Our paired re-adaptation protocol gives competing rules the same intervention strengths, only re-timed, lets dealers re-adapt to each rule from a shared checkpoint, and breaks one link at a time. Across 20 independently trained dealer populations in an ABIDES market, concentrating the intervention in states that the score ranks as low-risk lowers low-risk execution cost relative to random timing in every population, by 0.040 tick on average, while a stale announcement or a broken quote-to-flow link raises this cost. In the primary setting the gain comes at the expense of high-risk trades, whose costs rise, so state alignment pays off only for a venue that weighs low-risk costs more than 1.38 times as heavily as high-risk costs. Our code is available at https://github.com/moderncavemann/state-aligned-order-flow-contracts.
papers.summary: Learning dealer agents in a simulated market can settle on persistently wide quotes that raise customers' trading costs, and while a venue can route more order flow to tighter quotes, an end-to-end comparison cannot reveal why a routing rule works once dealers adapt to it. `SOFA` (State-aligned Order-Flow Allocation) is a public order-flow contract with three parts: a state scorer that ranks market states from lagged public data, a commitment scheduler that announces a budgeted intervention strength before dealers quote, and a quote-to-flow allocator that shifts a bounded share of fixed customer demand toward tighter quotes. A paired re-adaptation protocol gives competing rules identical intervention strengths that differ only in timing, lets dealers re-adapt from a shared checkpoint, and breaks one link at a time. **Across 20 independently trained dealer populations in an `ABIDES` market, concentrating intervention in states scored as low-risk lowers low-risk execution cost relative to random timing in every population, by 0.040 tick on average**, but high-risk trade costs rise, so state alignment only pays off for a venue that weighs low-risk costs more than 1.38 times as heavily as high-risk costs.

papers.title: Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy
papers.abstract: Sycophancy in Large Language Models, the tendency to align responses with user preferences over ground truth, has largely been studied using questions without a clear ground truth and with a single, plainly stated user opinion. We present a systematic study of which framings of a user's claim trigger sycophancy in factual question answering, where every answer is objectively verifiable without extra context. Evaluating 14 models on 42K questions, we express correct and incorrect user opinions through various claim framings over 8 dimensions and 21 types, and measure a broad set of opinion-driven behaviors. We find that all models are susceptible to user opinions regardless of size. Models are most influenced by how confidently an opinion is stated, whom it is attributed to, and whether it is presented as shared between the user and the model. In contrast to prior work, framings based on the user's expertise, authority over the model, or social pressure matter little in our factual setting. Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors. Our results call for sycophancy evaluations that probe how an opinion is framed, not merely whether one is present, and that measure multiple behaviors beyond a single flip rate.
papers.summary: Sycophancy, the tendency of large language models to align with user preferences over ground truth, has mostly been studied on questions without clear answers and with a single plainly stated user opinion. The authors evaluate 14 models on 42K objectively verifiable factual questions, expressing correct and incorrect user opinions through claim framings spanning 8 dimensions and 21 types, and measure a range of opinion-driven behaviors beyond a single flip rate. **All models are susceptible to user opinions regardless of size, and they are most swayed by how confidently an opinion is stated, whom it is attributed to, and whether it is framed as shared between user and model**, whereas framings based on user expertise, authority over the model, or social pressure matter little in this factual setting. Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors, which the authors take as a call for sycophancy evaluations that vary opinion framing and measure multiple behaviors.

papers.title: LoOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Looped Teachers
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation improves a model using guidance from the model itself, but it still requires a teacher that provides more useful predictions than the student. Existing approaches obtain such guidance by giving the teacher additional context or instructions. We ask whether it can instead come from changing how the same model uses its own layers. To address this, we introduce LoOPSD, which searches over a model's layer execution order to construct a stronger teacher and distills its advantage into the student. Specifically, we keep the model weights unchanged while searching for layers to repeat, and use the resulting teacher's predictions on student-generated prefixes to guide learning. We then alternate search and distillation, rebuilding the teacher from the updated student in each round so that the student progressively absorbs the gains from alternative layer execution. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show improvements across models. On GSM8K with a 400-token thinking budget, LoOPSD raises Qwen3-1.7B accuracy from 42.30% to 79.61%; subsequent distillation rounds yield further gains beyond the first round. Together, these findings show that by searching layer execution to construct teachers, we can turn a model's additional computation into improved student capabilities, opening a new avenue for self-distillation to derive supervision from the model's own computation.
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation improves a model using its own predictions as guidance, but it still needs a teacher that is more useful than the student, which prior work obtains by giving the teacher extra context or instructions. `LoOPSD` instead keeps the weights fixed and searches over the model's layer execution order, choosing layers to repeat, to construct a stronger teacher whose predictions on student-generated prefixes guide training; search and distillation then alternate, with the teacher rebuilt from the updated student each round. **On `GSM8K` with a 400-token thinking budget, `LoOPSD` raises `Qwen3-1.7B` accuracy from 42.30% to 79.61%**, with later rounds adding further gains, and improvements hold across models on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks. The authors frame this as deriving self-distillation supervision from the model's own additional computation.

papers.title: Random Probing for Structural Self-Interactions in Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) fundamentally lack the ability to capture structural properties defined by node self-interactions, such as cycle counts, subgraph centrality, and heat kernel signatures. Existing solutions often rely on computationally expensive higher-order architectures or hand-crafted features. In this work, we introduce DIAL, a message-passing layer that gives nodes access to graph structure through the diagonal of graph-derived operators. Our approach uses randomized probing to provide nodes with learnable, permutation equivariant access to diagonal entries. We prove that our approach can express important structural features, including cycle counts, subgraph centrality, and heat kernel signatures. The proposed method can be integrated directly into message passing layers. Experiments on molecular property prediction, cycle counting, and pattern detection demonstrate the effectiveness of DIAL across a range of graph learning tasks.
papers.summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) based on message passing cannot capture structural properties defined by node self-interactions, such as cycle counts, subgraph centrality, and heat kernel signatures, and existing remedies rely on expensive higher-order architectures or hand-crafted features. `DIAL` is a message-passing layer that gives nodes access to the diagonal of graph-derived operators through randomized probing, yielding learnable, permutation-equivariant access to those diagonal entries. **The authors prove the approach can express cycle counts, subgraph centrality, and heat kernel signatures**, and it can be dropped directly into existing message-passing layers. Experiments on molecular property prediction, cycle counting, and pattern detection support the approach across a range of graph learning tasks.

papers.title: Lifting Finite-Sample Gaussian Approximation of Wide Neural Networks to Functional Convergence
papers.abstract: Randomly initialised neural networks of width $m$ converge to Gaussian processes as $m \to \infty$, with two types of quantitative bounds characterising this convergence. Finite-sample bounds compare the network with its Gaussian limit at a fixed finite sample set, on an arbitrary domain, in the quadratic Wasserstein distance $\mathcal W_2$, achieving a convergence rate of $m^{-1/2}$ with explicit constants. However, these constants grow with the number of samples, so the bound becomes uninformative as the sample set is refined. Functional bounds remove that dependence by comparing the two as random functions, at the price of spherical input, metrics weaker than $\mathcal W_2$, or slower rates. In this paper, we therefore lift a finite-sample bound to a functional one. The lifting refines the sample set until it is dense in the domain, so the bound must first be made independent of the number of samples. We achieve this by measuring the error per sample, which makes the constant uniform. For a polynomial activation and any compact input set, this gives a rate of $m^{-1/2}$ in the supremum norm, with an explicit constant.
papers.summary: Randomly initialized neural networks converge to Gaussian processes as their width grows, and existing quantitative bounds come in two flavors: finite-sample bounds in the quadratic Wasserstein distance achieve a rate of one over the square root of the width with explicit constants, but those constants grow with the number of sample points, while functional bounds that compare the two as random functions avoid that dependence at the cost of spherical inputs, weaker metrics, or slower rates. The authors lift a finite-sample bound to a functional one by refining the sample set until it is dense in the domain, which first requires making the bound independent of the sample count; measuring the error per sample makes the constant uniform. **For polynomial activations on any compact input set, this yields convergence at rate one over the square root of the width in the supremum norm, with an explicit constant.**

papers.title: Back to the Future: Reverse-Consequence Modeling for Long-Horizon Particle Dynamics
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of object trajectories is fundamental to mechanical understanding and robotic control. However, autoregressive models inherently suffer from cumulative errors, leading to severe drift in long-horizon rollouts. Observing that in many physical systems with dissipative or convergence-to-rest behavior, the final states are often more predictable than transient dynamics (e.g., a sliding object resting under friction or a pendulum stabilizing at equilibrium), we propose ReStep, a cascaded approach that reverses the conventional forward-prediction paradigm. ReStep first employs a stochastic model to directly predict the final state, then leverages Anchored Diffusion to generate goal-conditioned intermediate trajectories. By conditioning on both ''boundary states'', it effectively constrains dynamics and reduces uncertainty, producing physically plausible and temporally coherent transitions. We further integrate ReStep dynamics as the physical engine within a 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, enabling a unified physical-visual framework for intuitive inference from images. Extensive experiments on diverse rigid and non-rigid collision datasets show that ReStep achieves superior long-term accuracy, substantially mitigating error accumulation via reverse-consequence modeling.
papers.summary: Autoregressive trajectory predictors accumulate error over long rollouts, but in dissipative physical systems the resting state is often easier to predict than the transient motion that leads to it. `ReStep` exploits this by first predicting the final state with a stochastic model and then using `Anchored Diffusion` to generate intermediate trajectories conditioned on both the start and end states. The resulting dynamics also serve as the physics engine inside a 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, so physical behavior can be inferred directly from images. **On rigid and non-rigid collision datasets, reverse-consequence modeling substantially reduces long-horizon error accumulation** compared with conventional forward prediction.

papers.title: TRACESTEER: Trace Driven Activation Steering for Hallucination Mitigation in Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, yet remain susceptible to hallucination. Activation steering offers a promising mitigation approach by guiding parallel token predictions through internal representations. However, existing steering methods largely overlook two characteristics of dLLMs: dynamic denoising states and temporal hallucination risks, which challenge predefined steering vectors and uniform intervention strengths.
