Beyond final-answer performance, our evaluation measures evidence recall from agent traces, agent behavior, and cost. Across nine proprietary and open-weight models in five coding-agent harnesses, even the strongest agents do not fully solve protocol digitization. Our analysis further shows that agents usually locate the required evidence but fail in the last mile of transcribing and structuring it. We further develop TrialScribe, a domain-specific harness that equips coding agents with task skills and a verification loop. TrialScribe improves a locally served open-weight model by 6.2-59.4 points across eight metrics, enabling it to match or surpass proprietary models such as GPT-5.6-Sol.
papers.summary: Clinical trial protocols are the source of truth for study design but live as unstructured PDFs, and it is unclear how reliably coding agents can turn such long documents into accurate structured data. `TrialPD-Bench` is an expert-annotated benchmark of 150 public protocol PDFs across four task categories, with evaluation that measures evidence recall from agent traces, agent behavior, and cost alongside final-answer accuracy. Across nine proprietary and open-weight models in five coding-agent harnesses none fully solves the task, and the failures concentrate in the last mile: agents usually locate the right evidence but go wrong when transcribing and structuring it. `TrialScribe`, a domain-specific harness that adds task skills and a verification loop, **improves a locally served open-weight model by 6.2 to 59.4 points across eight metrics**, letting it match or beat proprietary models such as `GPT-5.6-Sol`.

papers.title: Towards Safe Autonomy for Computer Use
papers.abstract: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.
papers.summary: Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act on raw screenshots, so there is no built-in boundary between trusted application interfaces and attacker-controlled content, which leaves them exposed to indirect prompt injection (IPI) that alignment training and safety classifiers cannot rule out. `SA-CUA` is a dual-LLM design that derives conservative deterministic rules from the operating system's accessibility tree to unmask only trusted screen regions for the privileged model, keeping untrusted content separated, while an endorsement channel lets values cross from the untrusted to the trusted domain after verification through trusted channels. The user is consulted only for the initial task specification rather than for each sensitive action, avoiding confirmation fatigue. In evaluation, **`SA-CUA` holds the attack success rate at zero while retaining much higher task utility than `CaMeL-CUA`**.

papers.title: The Smart Buildings Challenge: Learning Foundation Models for Real-World Optimization at Scale
papers.abstract: Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term. One of the biggest obstacles for building optimization is the lack of policy transfer. Most building control systems, whether simulation or learning based, don't generalize: they only work well for the building they were developed for, but not for other buildings. To solve this problem, we propose a challenge for the development of building foundation models that easily adapt to new buildings with minimal configuration and thereby enable building optimization to scale across the globe. Participants will build control policies on a set of simulated buildings, and have their policies evaluated on an unseen set of buildings. The buildings vary in size, layout, weather, material properties, and HVAC system. Successful outcomes from this initiative promise a massive leap forward in global sustainability efforts and demonstrate the great potential of ML to combat climate change.
papers.summary: Heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) accounts for roughly 40-60% of building emissions, yet learned and simulation-based building controllers rarely transfer beyond the building they were tuned for. The authors propose a public challenge to develop building foundation models: participants train control policies on a set of simulated buildings and are scored on a held-out set that differs in size, layout, weather, material properties, and HVAC system. **Success is defined as policies that adapt to unseen buildings with minimal configuration**, which the organizers argue is the main obstacle to scaling machine learning-driven building optimization globally.

papers.title: Approximating Optimal Policies in Heterogeneous Asynchronous Multi-player Bandits
papers.abstract: Motivated by applications to cognitive radio networks, multi-player multi-armed bandits (MMAB) have attracted considerable attention in recent years. The asynchronous variant, in which players are active only at a fraction of timesteps, better reflects real-world decentralized networks, where devices are not permanently active. Despite its practical relevance, this setting remains relatively understudied. Existing work on asynchronous MMAB has focused on homogeneous players, who share the same activation probability, a setting in which the optimal centralized allocation can be easily characterized. In contrast, efficiently computing the optimal allocation in the heterogeneous setting, where players have different activation probabilities, has remained an open problem. In this work, we investigate this problem and first establish its NP-hardness. We then turn to the greedy algorithm, which runs in polynomial time, and prove that it achieves a $\frac{1}{e}$-approximation of the optimal allocation. Furthermore, when players are processed in decreasing order of their activation probabilities, the approximation guarantee improves to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}$. Overall, our results establish the greedy algorithm as an efficient approximation to the optimal allocation, providing a practical oracle baseline for the design of online algorithms for heterogeneous asynchronous multi-player bandits.
papers.summary: In asynchronous multi-player multi-armed bandits (MMAB), motivated by cognitive radio networks, each player is active only at some fraction of timesteps, and the heterogeneous case where players have different activation probabilities lacked an efficient way to compute the optimal centralized allocation. The authors first prove that this allocation problem is NP-hard, then analyze the polynomial-time greedy algorithm. **Greedy achieves a 1/e approximation of the optimal allocation, improving to 1/sqrt(e) when players are processed in decreasing order of activation probability**, giving a practical oracle baseline for designing online algorithms in this setting.

papers.title: A Global View of How LLMs Value Human Time
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as personal assistants; however, little is known about how they capture national-level preferences on a global scale. Given that "time" is a universal and representative concept, we examine LLMs' time preferences by varying only users' country and measuring the compensation LLMs deem appropriate for a 60-minute appointment delay. We then compare LLMs' responses with GDP per capita on Purchasing Power Parity (GDP_PPP), Mean Income, and a literature-based index (Patience Score). Our results across 193 countries and 5 LLMs demonstrate that people's time across the world is evaluated in noticeably different ways among LLMs, as well as varying levels of robustness under prompt variations. LLMs consistently recommend the highest compensation for Europe, but mostly the lowest for Africa. Based on GDP_PPP, LLMs underestimate the value of time for users living in Asia and South America. These findings indicate that geographical patterns are embedded in LLMs and may translate in different treatment in agentic settings.
papers.summary: To probe whether large language models (LLMs) embed country-level biases, the authors vary only a user's stated country and ask five LLMs what compensation is appropriate for a 60-minute appointment delay, then compare the answers against GDP per capita on purchasing power parity, mean income, and a literature-based Patience Score. **Across 193 countries, the models consistently recommend the highest compensation for Europe and mostly the lowest for Africa**, with robustness to prompt variation differing between models. Relative to purchasing-power-adjusted GDP, the models undervalue the time of users in Asia and South America, which the authors argue could translate into unequal treatment when LLMs act as agents.

papers.title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
papers.abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup. At $50\%$ pruning of Qwen3-4B, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by $45\%$, improves compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on WikiText-2 from $0.670$ to $0.755$, and runs over $28\times$ faster than LLM-Surgeon on substantially weaker hardware. By preserving influence functions, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ supports effective data selection. On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the $5\%$ of data selected by $\texttt{CACTUS}$ achieves $49.44\%$ accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with $47.22\%$ using ALPS and $49.54\%$ using dense-model selection. Finally, integrating $\texttt{CACTUS}$ with LoGRA, a recent gradient-projection strategy, on Qwen3-4B with MLP layers pruned to 2:4 sparsity and a rank-64 correction retains a $0.711$ cosine alignment with dense LoGRA-projected C4 gradients.
papers.summary: Post-training pruning rarely preserves the alignment between a sparse model's gradients and those of the dense original, which matters for downstream uses such as influence-function-based data selection. `CACTUS` is an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) solver for a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients, supporting pruning as well as sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pretrained weights. **At 50% sparsity on `Qwen3-4B`, it cuts the `C4` perplexity gap to the dense model by 45% and runs over 28 times faster than `LLM-Surgeon` on weaker hardware**, while raising compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on `WikiText-2` from 0.670 to 0.755. Data selected by the pruned model for fine-tuning `Llama-3.2-3B` nearly matches dense-model selection on `BIG-Bench Hard` and beats `ALPS`.

papers.title: Imprinting: Knowledge Distillation Can Shift Student Behavior
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation trains student models on teacher-generated responses to transfer task capability, but those responses may also carry behavioral tendencies of their source. We investigate whether the source teacher can shape student behavior beyond the capability that distillation is intended to transfer. We construct harm-accepting and harm-avoiding variants of the same base teacher, use them to generate responses to ordinary reasoning and knowledge questions unrelated to safety, and distill those responses into students with different base models. Students generally acquire task capability while their downstream decisions shift toward the source teacher's safety-pragmatism disposition, a phenomenon we call imprinting. Distillation from the harm-accepting teacher reduces harm avoidance, whereas distillation from the harm-avoiding teacher increases it. Imprinting varies across teacher-student pairs and does not extend uniformly across different forms of safety behavior. Excluding a sparse set of divergence tokens reduces imprinting, whereas response rewriting preserves the source-dependent effect and can introduce additional rewriter-dependent shifts. Post-distillation preference optimization raises harm avoidance but does not eliminate the source-dependent difference. These results show that behavioral tendencies can be intentionally imprinted through the source teacher, even with ordinary task supervision.
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation trains a student on teacher outputs to transfer capability, but those outputs may also carry the teacher's behavioral dispositions. The authors build harm-accepting and harm-avoiding variants of the same base teacher, have each answer ordinary reasoning and knowledge questions unrelated to safety, and distill the responses into students built on different base models. **Students shift toward the source teacher's safety disposition even though the training data never touches safety**, with the harm-accepting teacher reducing harm avoidance and the harm-avoiding teacher increasing it. Removing a sparse set of divergence tokens weakens the effect, rewriting responses preserves it while adding rewriter-dependent shifts, and post-distillation preference optimization raises harm avoidance without erasing the source-dependent gap.

papers.title: The Geometry of Language Model Logits: Generic Structure and Learned Departures
papers.abstract:
Autoregressive language models produce, at every prediction step, a vocabulary-sized logit vector whose structure determines the conditional next-token distribution. We empirically identify that the ordered vocabulary-head logits follow a remarkably consistent log-linear relation
  \[ z_{(r)} \approx \mu - \alpha \log r. \] across prediction contexts, architectures, and scales, emerging progressively during pretraining. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic analysis of the logit geometry underlying the distributional assumptions used in the prior decoding work. While controlled order-statistic baselines spanning bounded, light-tailed, and heavier-tailed distributions can largely explain the observed log-linear geometry, they do not explain the systematic shift in the slope $\alpha$: trained language models exhibit $\alpha \approx 1.4$--$1.7$, sitting well above the initialization baseline ($\alpha \approx 0.2$) . Moreover, $\alpha$ correlates with predictive performance, suggesting that it captures learned structure beyond generic extreme-value effects.
papers.summary: Each next-token prediction in an autoregressive language model produces a vocabulary-sized logit vector, and the authors ask whether its sorted values follow a consistent shape. They find that **the r-th largest logit is approximately mu minus alpha times log r across contexts, architectures, and scales**, with this log-linear pattern emerging progressively during pretraining. Controlled order-statistic baselines from bounded, light-tailed, and heavier-tailed distributions reproduce the log-linear form but not the slope: trained models show alpha around 1.4 to 1.7 versus about 0.2 at initialization, and alpha correlates with predictive performance, suggesting it reflects learned structure rather than generic extreme-value effects.

papers.title: Lost in Implicit Routing: How LLM Agents Fail to Load Relevant Skills at Scale
papers.abstract: Reusable skills let LLM agents load task-specific instructions on demand, but they make execution depend on implicit routing over skill metadata. We test whether this design scales by holding SkillsBench tasks and their golden skills fixed while adding irrelevant skills. We find skill routing collapse: agents increasingly load fewer or no skills, even though the relevant skills remain available. With 1,000 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill recall falls from 73.6% to 27.4% and the zero-load rate rises from 9.3% to 51.6%, whereas explicit selection from the same library retains 73.9% recall. Loading other skills, including plausible alternatives to golden skills, is too rare to explain this decline. Masking only the descriptions of irrelevant skills largely restores skill loading, yet with the metadata intact, explicitly asking agents to plan skill use still yields lower recall than preselection. These findings point to semantic interference from descriptions and instruction interference when skill choice competes with task execution. We also evaluate explicit preselection as a practical mitigation, including its coverage and latency trade-offs. Our analysis informs skill protocols and evaluation for agents with growing skill libraries.
papers.summary: Reusable skills let an agent load task-specific instructions on demand, but the agent must implicitly route over skill metadata to decide which ones to load. Holding `SkillsBench` tasks and their golden skills fixed while adding irrelevant skills to the library, the authors observe a skill routing collapse in which agents load fewer or no skills at all. **With 1,000 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill recall drops from 73.6% to 27.4% and the zero-load rate climbs from 9.3% to 51.6%, while explicit preselection from the same library keeps recall at 73.9%.** Masking the descriptions of irrelevant skills largely restores loading, pointing to semantic interference from descriptions plus instruction interference when skill choice competes with task execution; explicit preselection is evaluated as a mitigation along with its coverage and latency costs.

papers.title: APTree: Extended Behavior Trees for Adaptive and Scalable Automated Robotic Task Planning in Construction
papers.abstract: Task planning for robots in off-site construction prefabrication is primarily manual, leading to planning inefficiencies and reluctance to adopt robotic solutions. Existing approaches provide limited support for scalable, modular automated task planning and localized runtime replanning. This paper proposes APTree, a model-driven framework that integrates automated task planning with modular task execution using behavior trees as the execution model. APTree repeatedly applies and coordinates heterogeneous symbolic planners to automatically generate and compose modular task plans at runtime. To support this approach, we develop a domain-specific language for the formal specification and validation of task plans, together with a compatible execution engine. We evaluate APTree on the real-world livMatS Biomimetic Shell pavilion, where it models the construction robotic fabrication domain, detects injected specification and planning errors at design time and runtime, and automatically generates large-scale task plans by coordinating three symbolic planners across numerous planning modules. A machine-checked formal analysis further shows that composed execution and local replanning are safe under explicitly stated assumptions, including planner soundness and non-interference of generated plans, providing practitioners with explicit conditions for dependable plan composition. APTree thus enables construction practitioners to leverage automated task planning without requiring detailed knowledge of symbolic planning techniques or APTree's internal implementation.
papers.summary: Task planning for robots in off-site construction prefabrication is still largely manual, and existing tools offer little support for scalable, modular automated planning with localized replanning at runtime. `APTree` is a model-driven framework that uses behavior trees as the execution model and repeatedly coordinates heterogeneous symbolic planners to generate and compose modular task plans on the fly, backed by a domain-specific language for specifying and validating plans and a matching execution engine. On the real-world `livMatS Biomimetic Shell` pavilion it detects injected specification and planning errors at design time and runtime and **generates large-scale plans by coordinating three symbolic planners across many planning modules**. A machine-checked formal analysis shows composed execution and local replanning are safe under stated assumptions such as planner soundness and non-interference of generated plans.

papers.title: Retrieval Disagreement as a Signal: Diagnosing and Steering Multilingual Dense Embedders
papers.abstract: Multilingual dense retrievers place all languages in one shared space so that a question finds relevant documents, regardless of which language they are written in. We show that the same question, asked in different languages, retrieves substantially different documents, and this disagreement is not because of weak language understanding. Each language performs well on its own and ranks candidates consistently with the other languages; divergence appears only when languages share an index. We trace the mechanism: each language keeps its own ranking, but in the shared index, its correct answers are pushed far down, buried under non-relevant documents that are either in the query's own language or in English, depending on the model. We introduce disagreement-guided steering: for each language, we contrast the documents that other languages agree on for a question against those that language retrieves idiosyncratically, and take the difference of their representations as a language-specific direction, added to that language's queries at inference. Against baselines of language-mean removal, subspace removal, and per-language rotation, it most strongly reduces same-language crowding while remaining competitive on recall, trading off against mean removal, which better preserves ranking quality.
papers.summary: Multilingual dense retrievers embed all languages in one shared space, yet the same question asked in different languages retrieves substantially different documents. The authors show this is not a language-understanding failure: each language performs well alone and ranks candidates consistently with the others, but in a shared index its correct answers get buried under non-relevant documents in either the query's own language or English, depending on the model. They propose disagreement-guided steering, which contrasts documents that other languages agree on against those a language retrieves idiosyncratically and adds the resulting difference vector to that language's queries at inference. **Against language-mean removal, subspace removal, and per-language rotation, it most strongly reduces same-language crowding** while staying competitive on recall, though mean removal better preserves ranking quality.

papers.title: How Reliable Are System-One Decisions in Medicine? A Comparative Study of Jev, Jev-like Models, and LLMs
papers.abstract: Jev has attracted considerable attention for its rapid, generalizable decision-making, yet its medical reliability remains under explored. To address this gap, our study compares various types of system-one decision models across 15 medical datasets comprising 8,742 instances under a unified protocol. Beyond accuracy, we assess decision stability and the ability to recognize unreliable decisions. Our results show that Jev rivals leading models on primarily text-driven tasks but is less effective on numerically driven tasks, revealing a distinct capability boundary. Under question-format variations, Jev demonstrates strong robustness, achieving the lowest decision reversal rate and relatively small accuracy fluctuations. Among evaluated open-source alternatives, only StartLux exhibits comparable robustness. But these strengths do not extend to reliable abstention awareness: most evaluated models show limitations in both recognizing missing correct answers and using optional abstention. Moreover, we find that Jev's probability-based answer selection can be improved by changing how decisions are scored: normalizing option-wise binary scores yields higher retained accuracy than choice scoring. Taken together, our findings provide early guidance for improving and applying decision models in medicine.
papers.summary: `Jev` has drawn attention for fast, generalizable system-one decision-making, but its reliability in medicine was untested. The authors compare `Jev`, `Jev`-like models, and large language models under a unified protocol on 15 medical datasets totaling 8,742 instances, measuring decision stability and recognition of unreliable decisions alongside accuracy. **`Jev` rivals leading models on primarily text-driven tasks but falls short on numerically driven ones**, shows the lowest decision reversal rate under question-format variation with only `StartLux` comparably robust among open-source alternatives, yet like most evaluated models it handles abstention poorly. Normalizing option-wise binary scores instead of choice scoring improves its retained accuracy.

papers.title: Euclidean Distance-Based Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Flow Matching has recently become popular as a technique for generative modeling with applications in many domains. In the standard Flow Matching formulation, we interpret the vector field as the solution of a least-squares regression problem, which is known to be sensitive to contamination. Therefore we leverage the viewpoint of robust statistics and replace the squared Euclidean distance with the Euclidean distance as a regression objective. This seemingly minor change strongly affects the properties of Flow Matching. We provide a probabilistic interpretation of the new regression target as a conditional geometric median and use this characterization to study distributional robustness of the Euclidean Distance-based Flow Matching. We analyze the mathematical properties of this changed objective and the effect of a contaminated target distribution on the involved conditional velocity distributions. We discuss the challenge of directly characterizing the distribution that our method induces. In specific contamination settings we show theoretically that our method yields an improvement for severe contamination. Finally, we present numerical experiments conducted on the CIFAR-10 image dataset where a proportion of the samples has been contaminated. Our Euclidean distance-based Flow Matching shows a clear advantage in scenarios of severe contamination of the target distribution.
papers.summary: Standard flow matching fits its vector field by least-squares regression, which is sensitive to contaminated training data. The authors replace the squared Euclidean distance with the plain Euclidean distance, reinterpreting the regression target as a conditional geometric median and using that robust-statistics view to analyze how a contaminated target distribution affects the conditional velocity distributions. They note that directly characterizing the induced distribution is hard, but prove an improvement in specific severe-contamination settings. **On `CIFAR-10` with a fraction of samples contaminated, the Euclidean-distance objective shows a clear advantage under severe contamination.**

papers.title: On Symmetry for Characterizing Agent Heterogeneity in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Understanding agent heterogeneity can inform the design of shared and agent-specific policy representations, however existing criteria provide no unified structural test. We study finite-horizon POSGs and define a type-compatible transformation as a policy-evaluation symmetry when complete policy evaluation commutes with it for every decentralized behavioral policy. Policy-evaluation symmetries form a group for which agent orbits define structural agent types. This classification does not depend on the particular policy chosen or the distribution of initial states. We prove that every componentwise environment automorphism is a policy-evaluation symmetry, but that the converse does not hold. Applying the framework to cooperative Dec-POMDPs shows that agents can belong to different structural types even when they share a common reward. For prescribed weighted reward aggregation, we derive an exact value identity and sufficient conditions for the resulting Dec-POMDP to inherit the policy-evaluation symmetries of the source POSG. Finally, we give sufficient conditions under which repeated model factorizations induce policy-evaluation symmetry, and show that preserving an optimal Boltzmann policy set neither implies nor follows from this symmetry in general.
papers.summary: Deciding which agents in a multi-agent system can share a policy representation requires a notion of agent heterogeneity, but existing criteria offer no unified structural test. For finite-horizon partially observable stochastic games (POSGs), the authors define a type-compatible transformation as a policy-evaluation symmetry when complete policy evaluation commutes with it for every decentralized behavioral policy; these symmetries form a group whose agent orbits define structural agent types independent of the chosen policy or initial-state distribution. **Every componentwise environment automorphism is a policy-evaluation symmetry, but the converse fails**, and in cooperative Dec-POMDPs agents sharing a common reward can still belong to different structural types. They also give sufficient conditions for weighted reward aggregation and repeated model factorizations to preserve these symmetries, and show that preserving an optimal Boltzmann policy set neither implies nor follows from the symmetry.

papers.title: Empathy Is Not the Scapegoat for Declines in Factuality and Reliability
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly expected to support users in stressful or uncertain situations, where warmth and empathy are desirable. While recent work associates warmer models with reduced reliability, we show that this conclusion is incomplete. Prior studies often train primarily on empathetic dialogue, making it difficult to separate tone effects from SFT-induced distribution shift. We revisit this issue at both the model and evaluation levels. We study prompting, SFT, and RL for inducing warm behavior, and comprehensively evaluate capability preservation using an 11-dataset benchmark suite and EMOFACT under emotional contexts. Across multiple model families, we find that warmth effects are task- and model-dependent, while task-aligned adaptive tone can improve empathy and targeted reliability, although some capability trade-offs remain. We further introduce human-validated empathy evaluators specifically developed to assess empathetic model responses. Our results suggest that models can be more supportive in social interactions while remaining reliable.
papers.summary: Recent work links warmer, more empathetic language models to lower reliability, but prior studies mostly fine-tune on empathetic dialogue, confounding tone with distribution shift from supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The authors induce warmth through prompting, SFT, and reinforcement learning (RL) across several model families and measure capability retention on an 11-dataset suite plus `EMOFACT` for factuality in emotional contexts, also introducing human-validated evaluators for empathetic responses. **Warmth effects turn out to be task- and model-dependent rather than uniformly harmful**, and task-aligned adaptive tone can raise both empathy and targeted reliability, though some capability trade-offs remain.

papers.title: Beyond the Encoder: Object-Centric Representations Emerging from Segmentation Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used as feature extractors for downstream tasks with limited data, typically through representations obtained from their encoders. However, foundation models trained for structured tasks such as segmentation also form object-specific representations during task execution, whose transferability remains largely unexplored. We investigate Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) object pointers, compact object-level representations produced through the segmentation pathway, as transferable representations for downstream tumour prediction. Through experiments on two PET/CT tumour prediction tasks, we find that object pointers learned using segmentation supervision alone already encode tumour-discriminative information, despite never being optimised for the downstream labels. We further introduce task-guided object pointers, where an auxiliary objective jointly shapes the object pointer space for the downstream prediction together with segmentation. Task-guided pointers improve cancer-type classification, outperforming conventional encoder-based transfer and radiomics, while segmentation-only pointers perform best on the more challenging recurrence prediction task. Representation analyses reveal associations between object pointers and interpretable radiomics features, class-dependent organisation of the learned representation space, and explicit spatial grounding around the segmented tumour. Together, these findings suggest that useful transferable representations can emerge through the execution of a foundation model's primary task, providing an alternative to conventional encoder-based transfer.
papers.summary: Foundation models are usually transferred via encoder features, but segmentation models also form object-specific representations while performing their task. The authors study Segment Anything Model 2 (`SAM2`) object pointers, compact object-level vectors produced in the segmentation pathway, as transferable features for tumour prediction on two PET/CT tasks. **Pointers trained with segmentation supervision alone already encode tumour-discriminative information**, and adding a task-guided auxiliary objective improves cancer-type classification beyond encoder-based transfer and radiomics, while segmentation-only pointers do best on the harder recurrence prediction task. Representation analyses tie the pointers to interpretable radiomics features and show explicit spatial grounding around the segmented tumour.

papers.title: Input-Conditioned Search for Efficient Test-Time Scaling of Recursive Reasoners
papers.abstract: People often tackle difficult problems by thinking more deeply or exploring more possibilities. Similarly, recursive reasoners, which reason by repeatedly applying a learned update rule to latent states, can also scale inference through more updates (depth) or additional trajectories generated by perturbing latent states (width). When people hit a dead end in their thinking, they may step back and approach the problem from a fresh angle. However, neither depth scaling nor perturbation-based width scaling of recursive reasoners can reliably achieve this: both may converge to incorrect attractors. To address this, we propose to explore diverse reasoning traces by applying different update maps to the same latent state, without any additional training. We realize this idea through \emph{Input-Conditioned Search (ICS)}, which searches over input conditions to induce alternative update maps from the pretrained reasoner. Across six reasoning tasks, ICS achieves the highest mean accuracy, while requiring up to two orders of magnitude fewer model FLOPs than the evaluated scaling baselines. Controlled experiments confirm that ICS can redirect trajectories from the same state. Our theoretical analysis and rigorous numerical verification also confirm that ICS can locally eliminate incorrect attracting fixed points. Together, these findings establish ICS as an effective axis for efficient test-time scaling and motivate further research on shaping recursive reasoning during training and at test time.
papers.summary: Recursive reasoners apply a learned update rule repeatedly to a latent state and can scale inference by more updates (depth) or by perturbing latent states to produce extra trajectories (width), but both can converge to the same incorrect attractor. Input-Conditioned Search (`ICS`) instead searches over input conditions to induce different update maps from the pretrained reasoner on the same latent state, requiring no additional training. **Across six reasoning tasks it achieves the highest mean accuracy while using up to two orders of magnitude fewer model FLOPs than the evaluated scaling baselines.** Controlled experiments show it can redirect trajectories from the same state, and theoretical analysis plus numerical verification confirm it can locally eliminate incorrect attracting fixed points.

papers.title: Understanding Circulant Permutation to Extend the CMinHash Estimator
papers.abstract: CMinHash promises a new direction for designing MinHash algorithms with reduced variance and storage space via circulant permutations. However, the original variance analysis is difficult to extend to other MinHash estimators. We present a new approach that gives explicit and easily comparable approximate variance expressions, and use it to analyze the Minner estimator. Numerical experiments show that our variance expression matches the empirical mean square error (MSE) of estimates. Our work thereby demonstrates how to apply circulant permutation to other MinHash estimators and compute their approximate variance.
papers.summary: `CMinHash` reduces variance and storage in MinHash sketching via circulant permutations, but its original variance analysis does not extend easily to other estimators. The authors develop a new approach that yields explicit, easily comparable approximate variance expressions and apply it to the `Minner` estimator. **Numerical experiments show the derived variance expression matches the empirical mean square error of the estimates**, demonstrating how circulant permutation can be carried over to other MinHash estimators.

papers.title: Unbalanced W-Flow: Unbalanced Wasserstein Drifting under Finite-Batch Marginal Fluctuations
papers.abstract: Teacher-free one-step generative models such as W-Flow learn directly from distributional objectives, with the Sinkhorn divergence providing the strongest empirical performance among the energies studied in W-Flow. However, Sinkhorn divergence is based on balanced optimal transport, whose exact marginal constraints can induce undesirable transport under finite minibatch fluctuations. We introduce UW-Flow, which replaces the balanced Sinkhorn energy with a debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence and derives the corresponding Wasserstein velocity. The resulting dynamics retain W-Flow's cross-minus-self structure, recover the balanced limit, and preserve target identifiability under suitable assumptions. We further characterize the finite-batch velocity error of balanced and unbalanced transport by comparing each minibatch field with its population counterpart. Our analysis identifies conditions under which marginal relaxation yields smaller minibatch-to-population velocity error, and shows that for separated matched modes, balanced sensitivity grows with inter-mode separation while the corresponding Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) sensitivity remains controlled by local transport geometry. Controlled experiments on fixed-support and continuous two-mode distributions support these predictions. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-100, UW-Flow improves generation under matched training budgets, with the largest gains in unconditional generation and consistent improvements in the class-conditional setting.
papers.summary: `W-Flow` trains teacher-free one-step generators directly from distributional objectives, with the Sinkhorn divergence performing best, but its balanced optimal transport enforces exact marginal constraints that can produce undesirable transport under finite minibatch fluctuations. `UW-Flow` swaps in a debiased unbalanced Sinkhorn divergence and derives the corresponding Wasserstein velocity, keeping the cross-minus-self structure, recovering the balanced limit, and preserving target identifiability under suitable assumptions. Analysis of minibatch-to-population velocity error shows that for separated matched modes, balanced sensitivity grows with inter-mode distance while the Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) version stays controlled by local transport geometry. **On `MNIST`, `CIFAR-10`, and `ImageNet-100`, it improves generation at matched training budgets, with the largest gains in unconditional generation.**

papers.title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Clipped SGD with Linear Decay
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the last-iterate convergence of clipped stochastic gradient descent under heavy-tailed noise. We assume that the stochastic gradients are unbiased and that the noise has a bounded central $p$-th moment, where $1<p\le2$. For smooth convex objectives, a linearly decreasing learning rate gives a high-probability error bound of order $O(LR^2\log(1/\delta)/T+\sigma R(\log(1/\delta)/T)^{(p-1)/p})$. We further establish last-iterate guarantees for nonsmooth composite objectives and smooth composite objectives with proximal updates. In addition, when a causal adversary replaces at most $q$ gradients, the same clipped update achieves a bound with $\log(1/\delta)$ replaced by $\log(1/\delta)+q$. The corresponding lower bounds for the clean and corrupted oracle models are also provided.
papers.summary: Clipped stochastic gradient descent is a standard remedy for heavy-tailed gradient noise, but last-iterate guarantees under such noise were incomplete. Assuming unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded central p-th moment for 1 < p <= 2, the authors show that a linearly decaying learning rate yields **a high-probability last-iterate error bound of order O(LR^2 log(1/delta)/T + sigma R (log(1/delta)/T)^((p-1)/p)) for smooth convex objectives**. They extend the guarantees to nonsmooth and smooth composite objectives with proximal updates, show that when a causal adversary replaces at most q gradients the same update pays only an additive q inside the logarithmic term, and supply lower bounds for both the clean and corrupted oracle models.

papers.title: Linear Last-Iterate Convergence Rates for Optimistic Learning in Harmonic Games
papers.abstract: We prove that the last iterate of Optimistic Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (OFTRL) converges at a linear rate to a Nash equilibrium in multiplayer harmonic games. Our result holds under a mild game-regularity condition and for a large family of regularizers, including entropy, Tsallis, and log-barrier. Our analysis is based on a dual perspective of OFTRL: we prove that the interaction between optimism and the global structure of harmonic games leads to the dissipation of an energy function along the dual iterates, for which we establish tight quantitative bounds. Our result also holds for the Extragradient FTRL variant.
papers.summary: In multiplayer harmonic games, the authors prove that **the last iterate of Optimistic Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (`OFTRL`) converges to a Nash equilibrium at a linear rate**, under a mild game-regularity condition and for a broad family of regularizers including entropy, Tsallis, and log-barrier. The proof takes a dual perspective, showing that the interaction between optimism and the global structure of harmonic games dissipates an energy function along the dual iterates, with tight quantitative bounds. The same result holds for the Extragradient FTRL variant.

papers.title: Rethinking Quality in Large Language Model Routing: Security-Conditioned Model-and-Budget Selection
papers.abstract:
Large language model (LLM) routers reduce serving cost by choosing which model to call and how many output tokens to grant it for each query. Existing routers rank model-budget actions using a single quality metric. This does not work for mixed workloads. For ordinary queries, a good answer is correct and useful (utility); for security-sensitive queries, a good answer refuses harmful requests or resists malicious instructions (security). These two objectives prefer different models and budgets.
  We propose SCRouter, a router that learns when to prioritize security and how to allocate the token budget. For each model-budget pair, it estimates the probability that the response finishes within budget. It uses this probability to predict utility and security separately. A small probe determines how to weight these two predictions for each query. SCRouter then selects the model and budget by balancing the weighted utility and security against cost. We also build SCRouterBench, a benchmark of 38,869 utility and security queries spanning nine security dimensions, each answered under all 144 combinations of 12 models and 12 budgets, plus 2,753 out-of-domain queries. SCRouter improves the baselines by 13-29 points in-domain and 19-23 points out-of-domain.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) routers pick which model to call and how many output tokens to allow per query, but ranking model-budget choices by a single quality score breaks down when a workload mixes ordinary requests, where correctness matters, with security-sensitive ones, where refusing harmful instructions matters, since the two goals favor different models and budgets. `SCRouter` estimates for each model-budget pair the probability that a response finishes within budget, uses that to predict utility and security separately, and trains a small probe to decide per query how to weight the two before trading them off against cost. The authors also release `SCRouterBench`, which covers 38,869 utility and security queries across nine security dimensions answered under all 144 combinations of 12 models and 12 budgets, plus 2,753 out-of-domain queries. **`SCRouter` beats baseline routers by 13 to 29 points in-domain and 19 to 23 points out-of-domain.**

papers.title: Configuring RAG Systems: What Breaks, Where Originates, and How to Fix
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a dominant paradigm for improving Large Language Model (LLM) by intertwining it with other components, such as a vector/graph database. Therefore, the resulting RAG systems are often highly configurable, under which a non-trivial amount of failures are related to the configurations. However, there remains a lack of systematic understanding regarding the configuration issues for RAG systems. To bridge this gap, in this paper, we conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 654 real-world configuration issues collected from 10 diverse RAG systems. Drawing on this, we provide a complete categorization of the symptoms, root causes, relevant stages, and fix patterns of configuration issues for RAG systems, as well as several new observations. Our findings not only reveal the characteristics of configuration issues, but also strongly link them to the unique pipeline stages of RAG, e.g., we found that most symptoms can be observed at the early or late stage, while the stage of the root cause might not be at the same stage as where the symptom is identified. We also provide nine actionable insights to the practitioners on testing, localizing, and fixing the configuration issues for RAG systems.
papers.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems wire a large language model to vector or graph databases and other components, which makes them highly configurable and prone to failures that stem from the configuration rather than the model. The authors collected and analyzed **654 real-world configuration issues from 10 open-source RAG systems**, producing a taxonomy of symptoms, root causes, pipeline stages, and fix patterns. A recurring observation is that symptoms surface mostly at the early or late stages of the pipeline while the root cause often sits in a different stage from where the symptom appears, and the study closes with nine practical recommendations for testing, localizing, and fixing such issues.

papers.title: CREATE: Creativity Evaluation of VLMs using the Visual Remote Associates Test
papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) are used in creative tasks such as visual storytelling, design ideation, art interpretation, and advertising. Yet we lack principled ways to measure the lateral reasoning of these models compared to human potential. We introduce CREATE, a semi-automatically constructed benchmark containing 155 visual Remote Associates Test problems. These problems require a solver to find an underlying connection among three seemingly dissimilar images. We conduct a human study (N=25) to validate and ground the quality of our benchmark, and evaluate 11 VLMs. Our findings show that most VLMs underperform humans on this task. Our experiments indicate that the associative ability of VLMs depends on the cue concepts provided in the text and does not universally extend to visual puzzles.
papers.summary: Vision language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for creative work like storytelling and design ideation, yet there has been no principled way to measure their lateral, associative reasoning against human ability. `CREATE` is a semi-automatically built benchmark of 155 visual Remote Associates Test problems, each asking the solver to find the hidden concept linking three seemingly unrelated images, validated through a study with 25 human participants. Evaluating 11 VLMs, the authors find that **most models fall short of human performance**, and that models' associative ability leans heavily on textual cue concepts rather than transferring to purely visual puzzles.

papers.title: Order-Consistent Latent Geometry for Reliable Short-Horizon Planning in World Models
papers.abstract: Latent planners often rank candidate action sequences by terminal Euclidean distance to a goal latent. Exact agreement with transition distance would make this score ideal, but is stronger than planning requires: along a transition-shortest rollout, the essential requirement is that latent distance does not reverse true transition progress. We show that this pathwise no-reversal requirement is precisely the classical self-approaching condition. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to identify self-approachingness as a planner-facing compatibility condition for terminal Euclidean latent planning and to connect its violation to an exact finite-horizon candidate-order reversal. Because visual world models predict discrete latent sequences, we analyze their polygonal interpolation. We prove that an acute bend creates a nonempty region in which terminal Euclidean distance ranks a transition-worse candidate ahead of one that makes genuine progress, even under exact rollouts. We further interpret latent dimension as angular capacity through a classical spherical-code bound. A controlled six-branch experiment, including a zero-padded three-dimensional baseline, validates the predicted ordering failure and separates angular arrangement from ambient dimensionality.
papers.summary: Latent-space planners commonly rank candidate action sequences by the Euclidean distance between their terminal latent and the goal latent, implicitly assuming that distance tracks true transition progress. The authors show that the weaker requirement planning actually needs, that latent distance never reverses progress along a shortest rollout, is exactly the classical geometric self-approaching condition, and they analyze the polygonal interpolations produced by visual world models that emit discrete latent sequences. **They prove that any acute bend in a latent trajectory creates a region where terminal Euclidean distance ranks a worse candidate ahead of one making genuine progress, even with exact rollouts**, interpret latent dimension as angular capacity via a spherical-code bound, and confirm the predicted ordering failure in a controlled six-branch experiment.

papers.title: LLM Agents for Automated Post-Training via Structured Recipe Optimization
papers.abstract: Automated post-training transforms pre-trained large language models (LLMs) into models capable of handling diverse domains by automatically constructing and optimizing a recipe of coupled decisions over data sources, data processing, cross-domain composition, and training configuration under a limited experimental budget. Existing automation either searches predefined recipe spaces that enable systematic optimization but remain fixed rather than adapting their available choices to the target tasks, or uses open-ended agents that discover task-specific choices but leave them implicit in trial-level edits, limiting their systematic reuse and recombination across trials. To fill this gap, we introduce optimization over a task-adapted recipe space, a novel paradigm that can adapt the recipe space itself to the target tasks while representing its choices explicitly for systematic reuse, recombination, and joint optimization. We instantiate this paradigm with Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO), comprising an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer that constructs the task-adapted recipe space and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer that uses structured trial evidence to guide LLM candidate construction and multi-objective Bayesian trial selection. Extensive experiments show that SRO achieves the highest average score in all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations. In joint post-training across three capability domains and six benchmarks, SRO reaches 41.1 versus 15.4 for the strongest baseline on Qwen3-1.7B with GPT-5.4, and 53.8 versus 40.8 on Qwen3-4B with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Our code is available at https://github.com/RuohLiuq/SRO.
papers.summary: Automated post-training must jointly decide data sources, processing, cross-domain mixing, and training configuration for a pre-trained large language model under a limited experiment budget, but existing approaches either search a fixed recipe space or rely on open-ended agents whose discoveries stay buried in ad hoc edits. `Structured Recipe Optimization` (SRO) pairs an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer, which builds a recipe space adapted to the target tasks, with a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer that uses structured trial evidence to drive LLM candidate construction and multi-objective Bayesian trial selection. **In joint post-training across three capability domains and six benchmarks, SRO scored 41.1 against 15.4 for the strongest baseline on `Qwen3-1.7B` with `GPT-5.4`**, and 53.8 against 40.8 on `Qwen3-4B` with `DeepSeek-V4-Flash`, with the highest average in every target-model and agent-LLM pairing tested.

papers.title: The Many Morals of AI: The cautionary bias of North American news narratives in global perspective
papers.abstract: The stories told about artificial intelligence (AI) play a central role in shaping public understanding, policy debates, and expectations about technological change. News media are especially influential in this process. Using a cross-regional corpus of 12,924 English-language news articles about AI published since 2022, we examine how storytelling about AI varies across media systems in four regions: North America, China, India, and the Middle East. Leveraging large language models, we extract the implicit narrative lessons conveyed by each article---commonly known as story morals---capturing value-laden interpretations that extend beyond thematic content or sentiment. We find that North American AI coverage is uniquely characterized by narratives of caution, while under-emphasizing narratives of innovation and collaboration that are more prevalent elsewhere. However, this pattern is largely explained by a broader regional negativity bias in North American news sentiment, rather than by heightened concern about AI itself. Our findings bring into view the culturally conditioned nature of AI news narratives.
papers.summary: News coverage shapes public expectations about artificial intelligence (AI), and the authors ask how the implicit lessons of that coverage differ across media systems. Using large language models to extract the story morals from 12,924 English-language AI articles published since 2022 in North America, China, India, and the Middle East, they compare the value-laden narratives each region favors. **North American coverage stands out for cautionary morals and under-emphasizes innovation and collaboration, but this is largely explained by a general negativity bias in North American news rather than AI-specific concern.**

papers.title: When More Objectives Make Identification Easier: The Role of Preferences and Feedback
papers.abstract: Best-arm identification (BAI) aims to identify the optimal arm using as few samples as possible. While most existing work focuses on a single objective, many real-world applications involve multiple criteria, which motivates the study of BAI in multi-objective bandits. Intuitively, multi-objective identification seems harder, since the learner must identify optimal arms in a higher-dimensional reward space; however, the additional objectives also provide richer feedback that can reduce the required exploration. In this paper, we characterize when and why multiple objectives can make BAI easier. For Gaussian bandits, we establish a characteristic-time lower bound for fixed-confidence identification that holds uniformly across preference orders. Through explicit comparisons under Pareto, linear, and lexicographic preferences, we reveal three phenomena: (i) identifying a larger optimal set can require fewer samples than identifying a unique optimum; (ii) the advantage of vector feedback over coordinate feedback depends fundamentally on the preference order; and (iii) multi-objective identification can require fewer samples than even the easiest corresponding single-objective problem. Finally, we propose Order-Aware Track-and-Stop (OATS), an algorithm that is correct at any prescribed confidence level and asymptotically matches the lower bound.
papers.summary: Best-arm identification (BAI) seeks the optimal arm of a bandit with as few samples as possible, and the multi-objective setting looks harder because the learner must resolve a higher-dimensional reward vector. For Gaussian bandits, the authors derive a characteristic-time lower bound for fixed-confidence identification that holds uniformly across preference orders and compare it under Pareto, linear, and lexicographic preferences. **They show that identifying a larger optimal set can need fewer samples than finding a unique optimum, that the value of vector feedback over coordinate feedback depends on the preference order, and that multi-objective identification can be easier than the easiest single-objective counterpart.** They also propose `Order-Aware Track-and-Stop` (OATS), which is correct at any confidence level and asymptotically matches the bound.

papers.title: Reading Right, Acting Wrong: Diagnosing Decision Failures of System One Models in Agent Loops
papers.abstract: System One models choose an agent's next action by scoring a supplied set of options in a single pass. This makes them fast and cheap, but when they choose wrongly there is nothing to inspect: did the model misread what the agent has seen, or read it correctly and still act wrongly? We answer behaviorally. On a frozen benchmark of agent decision states from simulated environments, customer-service policies, tool use, web navigation and coding, we pair every next-action question with factual probes about the same state, each answered independently. Across seventeen fast systems and a reasoning model, the answer is consistent: most wrong actions follow correct reading, and the more accurate a system, the more of its errors take this form. These errors are not noise; they gather on the same states across systems of every kind. Where the probed facts provably determine the action, models that read every fact still fail to combine them, and their own answers, composed by code, repair the failure. On real states, what is missing is often not a fact but the next sub-goal.
papers.summary: System One models select an agent's next action by scoring a provided set of options in a single forward pass, which is fast but leaves no trace of whether a wrong choice came from misreading the state or from reading it correctly and still deciding badly. On a frozen benchmark of decision states drawn from simulated environments, customer-service policies, tool use, web navigation, and coding, the authors pair each next-action question with independently answered factual probes about the same state and evaluate seventeen fast systems plus one reasoning model. **Most wrong actions follow correct reading of the state, and the more accurate a system is, the larger the share of its errors that take this form**, with failures clustering on the same states across systems; where the probed facts logically determine the action, composing the models' own factual answers in code repairs the mistake, while on real states the missing ingredient is often the next sub-goal rather than a fact.

papers.title: Compare to Correct: Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment for LLM Test-Time Scaling
papers.abstract: Sampling-based test-time scaling enhances LLM reasoning by aggregating multiple reasoning paths for the same query. Existing methods use answer frequencies or path confidence to compute candidate scores, which do not explicitly characterize comparisons between competing answers. Inspired by the Condorcet principle in social choice theory, we introduce pairwise confidence comparisons between paths supporting different answers to capture answer-level comparative advantage. We combine this comparative evidence with voting support through a KL-regularized objective. Theoretically, we show that this comparative-advantage is equivalent to the adjustment to the traditional voting logits. In this way, our proposed Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment (PGLA) framework allows comparative evidence to compensate for weaker voting support and correct voting-based ranking errors. Experiments on 10 challenging benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, knowledge reasoning, and code generation with 7 models ranging from 1.7B to 32B parameters speak to the effectiveness of this plug-and-play term. Additional evaluations with external reward scores and online sampling further demonstrate its applicability.
papers.summary: Sampling-based test-time scaling aggregates many reasoning paths for one query, but scoring candidates by answer frequency or path confidence ignores direct comparisons between competing answers. Drawing on the Condorcet principle from social choice theory, `Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment` (PGLA) computes pairwise confidence comparisons between paths that support different answers and merges this comparative evidence with voting support through a KL-regularized objective, which the authors show is equivalent to adjusting the voting logits. **Across 10 benchmarks spanning math, knowledge reasoning, and code generation with 7 models from 1.7B to 32B parameters, the plug-in term lets comparative evidence correct ranking errors made by voting alone**, and it also works with external reward scores and online sampling.

papers.title: GeoMER: A Joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic Geometry Framework for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) aims to understand human emotions by integrating information from multiple modalities such as speech and text. Psychological studies suggest that emotions exhibit latent hierarchical structured relationships in their semantic representations. However, most MER approaches rely on Euclidean representations, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but do not explicitly provide a geometric prior for organizing hierarchical emotional structures. To mitigate this gap, we propose GeoMER, a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic modeling framework that introduces hyperbolic emotion-core routing to capture higher-level, abstract emotional representations for MER. The proposed framework jointly models token-level cross-modal semantic interactions and latent emotion representations in two complementary geometric spaces. Specifically, GeoMER consists of a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (EuclFusion) for multimodal representation fusion and a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing (HypGeoRoute) module that performs geometry-aware core assignment and aggregation in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract feature representations. The HypGeoRoute module complements the Euclidean token-level modeling. We experiment on the IEMOCAP multimodal MER benchmark and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the best performance, with 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy, outperforming Euclidean baselines, including MemoCMT.
papers.summary: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) fuses signals such as speech and text, and most systems rely on Euclidean embeddings, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but offer no geometric prior for the hierarchical structure psychologists attribute to emotions. `GeoMER` combines a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (`EuclFusion`) for token-level fusion with a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing module (`HypGeoRoute`) that assigns and aggregates features around emotion cores in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract representations. **On `IEMOCAP` it reaches 83.54% weighted and 83.35% unweighted accuracy**, surpassing Euclidean baselines including `MemoCMT`.

papers.title: Decomposing and Predicting Annotation Disagreement in Harmful Content Across Languages
papers.abstract: Annotator disagreement is increasingly recognized as a meaningful property of subjective tasks, rather than merely noise to be removed. Predicting which items are likely to be contested could help allocate annotation effort and route difficult cases to human review. We propose predicting disagreement from interpretable semantic properties of the text. An LLM answers a set of binary questions covering harmful-content characteristics, disagreement-related cues such as borderline severity and missing context, and language-sensitive cues such as local slurs. A classifier predicts disagreement from these answers, and we analyze which questions contribute most to the predictions. Across four datasets in English, German, and Turkish and three open-weight LLMs, our structured question features outperform direct prompting by 10.5 ROC-AUC points and the strongest text-based baselines by 5.0 points. A compact subset of eight questions performs within 1.5 ROC-AUC points of the full twenty-question set. In leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, models retain roughly 90-95% of their in-domain ROC-AUC. Across models and datasets, questions about derogation, missing context, and decision boundaries serve as the strongest predictors, suggesting that what makes harmful content contested is partly observable in the text.
papers.summary: Annotator disagreement on harmful-content labels is increasingly treated as signal rather than noise, and predicting which items will be contested could help route hard cases to human review. The approach has a large language model answer a set of binary questions about a text covering harm characteristics, disagreement cues such as borderline severity or missing context, and language-specific cues like local slurs, then trains a classifier on those answers so the contributing questions can be inspected. **Across four datasets in English, German, and Turkish and three open-weight LLMs, the question features beat direct prompting by 10.5 ROC-AUC points and the best text-based baselines by 5.0 points**, a subset of eight questions comes within 1.5 points of the full twenty, and leave-one-dataset-out models keep roughly 90 to 95% of in-domain performance, with derogation, missing context, and decision-boundary questions the strongest predictors.

papers.title: Fairness under Prediction Error in Predict-then-Optimize Pipelines
papers.abstract: Fairness constraints in predict-then-optimize pipelines are necessarily enforced on predicted outcomes $\hat{y}$, since true outcomes $y$ are unobserved at decision time. We study whether a demographic parity constraint enforced this way continues to hold against $y$, and how the resulting violation scales with prediction error. Using a budget-constrained allocation problem solved as a linear program, we show empirically that the true-outcome fairness gap grows with prediction error $\sigma$ and saturates, well fit by $c(1 - e^{-\sigma/\tau})$ with $c = 0.1545 \pm 0.0103$ and $\tau = 3.9045 \pm 0.3745$; its mean is invariant to sample size while its variance decays at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ rate. We derive a two-part theoretical bound: a closed-form local sensitivity result showing the gap's first-order response to prediction error depends on only two individuals per group, validated against the solver to within three significant figures; and a universal, error-independent ceiling following from the boundedness of the decision variable, confirmed consistent with but looser than the empirical saturation level. On US Census income data, enforcing demographic parity on a trained predictor's output reduces an unconstrained disparity in true income to roughly one-third of its original size, leaving 34.4% $\pm$ 3.3% (California) and 35.7% $\pm$ 1.8% (Texas) of the disparity intact and undetectable from the predictions alone -- consistent not only in mechanism but in approximate magnitude across two states with different demographics and income distributions, and stable across ten independent train/test splits in each. A fairness constraint that appears fully satisfied at decision time can mask a substantial, systematic violation of the outcome it was meant to protect.
papers.summary: Fairness constraints in predict-then-optimize pipelines must be enforced on predicted outcomes because true outcomes are unknown at decision time, raising the question of whether demographic parity imposed on predictions still holds for the real outcomes. Using a budget-constrained allocation solved as a linear program, the authors show the true-outcome fairness gap grows with prediction error and saturates along a fitted exponential curve, and they derive both a closed-form local sensitivity bound, which depends on just two individuals per group, and a universal error-independent ceiling. **On US Census income data, enforcing demographic parity on a trained predictor leaves roughly 34 to 36% of the true-income disparity intact and invisible from the predictions**, consistently across California and Texas and across ten train/test splits.

papers.title: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.
papers.summary: Training and evaluating AI models for network defence requires realistic traffic, adversaries, and labelled data that are hard to obtain from production networks. The Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym combines high-fidelity network emulation, modelled benign user behaviour and adversarial profiles, and scenario generation from open toolkits, with live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels to produce labelled synthetic datasets for Deep Neural Network (DNN) based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) and to exercise modular components of autonomous defence agents. A DNN classifier trained in the gym achieves near-perfect recall on adversarial flows in-domain, but **even minor shifts in network composition, such as a changed protocol mix, cause a catastrophic collapse in detection performance**.

papers.title: ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but real-world deployment demands more: learning new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors. Existing continual RL methods on top of VLAs mitigate forgetting but rely on on-policy updates with limited forward transfer, whereas off-policy methods improve single-task sample efficiency without addressing learner persistence across tasks. We propose ACCRUE, a continual off-policy RL framework that carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks, allowing each stage to reuse behavioral and value knowledge acquired through prior RL. The inherited critic adapts only on current-task transitions and guides current-task actor learning, while prior behavior is preserved by distilling the actor toward cached targets on a small number of retained episodes. Fixed visual features keep the inherited learner and its replay compatible with base-policy updates. Across contact-rich assembly sequences in simulation and on real-robot hardware, ACCRUE accelerates subsequent-task learning with near-zero forgetting and significantly reduces real-robot training time by 31.0\% to 68.5\%.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training can push robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but deployment also demands learning new tasks efficiently without forgetting earlier ones, and existing continual methods on vision-language-action models rely on on-policy updates with weak forward transfer. `ACCRUE` is a continual off-policy RL framework that carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks: the inherited critic adapts only on current-task transitions and guides the actor, prior behaviour is preserved by distilling the actor toward cached targets on a few retained episodes, and frozen visual features keep the inherited learner and replay buffer compatible with base-policy updates. **On contact-rich assembly sequences in simulation and on real hardware, it accelerates later tasks with near-zero forgetting and cuts real-robot training time by 31.0% to 68.5%.**

papers.title: PhysicsSliders: Learning Physical Controls for Audio Foley Generation
papers.abstract: Physical properties provide intuitive controls for sounds made by interacting objects. The challenge is to make a generative model respond predictably to these controls, both individually and in combination. We present \method\ (PXS), trained on simulated contact sounds with 15 material, geometry and contact parameters. Two separately trained variants accept direct parameter inputs or numerical captions. PXS controls hardness, size, speed and damping, supports room descriptions and produces spectrally distinct outputs at fixed targets. When controlling damping and size together, specifying thickness improves frequency accuracy and joint target delivery. Measurements from real recordings define effective-damping targets, which simulator inversion maps to generation inputs without real-audio fine-tuning. Across 18 impact classes from five real-audio datasets, PXS-Physical follows these targets with mean grouped Spearman correlation $\rho=0.976$ and class-median error 0.094 dex (a factor of 1.24).
papers.summary: Physical properties like hardness, size, and damping are natural knobs for the sounds of colliding objects, but generative audio models rarely respond to such controls predictably, especially in combination. `PhysicsSliders` (PXS) is trained on simulated contact sounds annotated with 15 material, geometry, and contact parameters, in two variants that accept either direct parameter values or numerical captions, and it controls hardness, size, speed, and damping while supporting room descriptions. Effective-damping targets measured from real recordings are mapped to generation inputs by inverting the simulator without any fine-tuning on real audio, and **across 18 impact classes from five real-audio datasets, the physical-input variant tracks these targets with a mean grouped Spearman correlation of 0.976** and a class-median error of 0.094 dex.

papers.title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs
papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only $10$ to $20\%$ of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance. These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well. Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL, a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization, but only per-modality summary statistics.
