PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely. Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in $3$ of $7$ (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average $98\%$ of its score across the other four.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models are usually built by first training a projector to align a vision encoder with a language model on large image-caption sets, then jointly training the whole model, yet what the projector stage actually contributes has been unclear. The authors find that 10 to 20% of the alignment data already recovers most downstream gains and that projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated with little loss, suggesting the stage performs only a coarse alignment. Building on this, `PORTAL` initializes the projector with no paired data or gradient steps by computing an optimal-transport map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, and **without any image-caption pairs it matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks**, beating it in 3 of 7 encoder-LLM settings and averaging 98% of its score in the rest.

papers.title: Auditing Future-Memory Use in Point-in-Time Language Agents
papers.abstract: Point-in-time (PIT) agents can recall post-cutoff facts even when their external evidence respects a historical cutoff. We examine whether this access predicts evidence gathering in 48 historical company-comparison tasks. Independent closed-book revenue probes identify the better-remembered company for each model on tasks with unequal recall, fixing the predicted direction before agent runs. We then compare paired runs with real or anonymized company identities while keeping external evidence PIT-valid. Both Qwen and DeepSeek recalled future facts, but neither supported the prespecified shift toward the better-remembered company. Qwen's four allocation estimates on 28 unequal-recall tasks were negative, with descriptive intervals spanning zero. A prospective DeepSeek replication showed an inverse pattern across all four metrics on 20 such tasks, with intervals below zero. These estimates remained negative after each company, pair, and future-fact omission, and all four post-hoc max-T-adjusted sign-flip p-values were below .05. In a prospectively specified follow-up, explicit future facts produced small estimated shifts away from the supplied-fact company, with intervals spanning zero, while final choices shifted toward it. The mechanism behind the natural inverse pattern remains unresolved. These findings support separate assessments of memory accessibility, search allocation, and final outputs alongside cutoff checks on external evidence.
papers.summary: Point-in-time (PIT) agents are meant to reason only from evidence predating a historical cutoff, but their underlying models may still recall facts from after that date. The authors test whether such recall steers evidence gathering in 48 historical company-comparison tasks by first using closed-book revenue probes to identify which company each model remembers better, then comparing paired agent runs with real versus anonymized company names while keeping external evidence cutoff-valid. **Both `Qwen` and `DeepSeek` recalled post-cutoff facts, yet neither shifted search toward the better-remembered company, and `DeepSeek` showed a statistically significant inverse pattern across all four allocation metrics**; supplying explicit future facts nudged search slightly away from the named company while final choices moved toward it, leading the authors to recommend separately auditing memory accessibility, search allocation, and final outputs.

papers.title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents
papers.abstract: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.
papers.summary: Benchmarks say what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite but not whether a given release was engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe, and observable, or how strong the evidence for that is. `AgentStripes` defines maturity levels from 0 to 7 stripes, 12 process areas holding 40 capabilities, three gates (basic, safety, proof) that cap an agent's level regardless of score, and evidence grades E0 to E5, with each capability rated 0 to 3 and combined deterministically into a severity-weighted score while language-model judges interpret evidence gathered by instruments. **An exploratory run on 30 public Python agent repositories using static evidence alone capped every agent at 2 stripes, with 26 at one stripe and 4 at two, and re-judging changed the final stripe for 4 of 22 repositories**, so the authors frame the exercise as a demonstration rather than validation and note that the parameters are expert conventions not yet shown to predict reliability or safety.

papers.title: LLM2R: From Large Language Models to 3D Reassemblers
papers.abstract: 3D part assembly aims to reconstruct a complete shape from a set of unassembled parts by predicting a rigid SE(3) transformation for each part. Because the placement of a part is rarely determined by its own geometry, the task demands reasoning over the entire part set, and existing methods, which rely on pairwise relations or iterative generation and verification, scale poorly to objects with many parts. We present LLM2R, which casts part assembly as sequence modeling with a pretrained decoder-only large language model (LLM): a Point-BERT encoder and a Q-Former compress each part into a block of geometric tokens, the blocks of all parts are concatenated, and a causal LLM adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) processes the sequence in one forward pass. Causal attention, however, lets the hidden states of a part observe only the parts that precede it. LLM2R therefore appends a block of learnable summary tokens after the last part: these tokens follow every part, so their states aggregate the whole assembly at a constant token cost, and a part-aware pose head fuses each part's states with them before predicting its rotation and translation. One architecture thus handles semantic and geometric assembly and predicts all poses in a single non-autoregressive pass. LLM2R achieves the highest part accuracy and success rate on all three PartNet categories, the best rotation error, translation error, and part accuracy on PartNeXt, and the lowest translation error and fastest inference on Breaking Bad, where only a fracture-specialized method is more accurate. Its advantage grows with the number of parts: at 100 parts it exceeds GARF by 33.5 points in part accuracy on Breaking Bad and Assembler by 29.1 points on PartNet, and it transfers zero-shot to unseen categories with more than 16 points higher part accuracy than the strongest of three baselines.
papers.summary: 3D part assembly reconstructs a complete shape by predicting a rigid SE(3) pose for each of a set of loose parts, which requires reasoning over the whole part set, and existing pairwise or generate-and-verify methods scale poorly to objects with many parts. `LLM2R` recasts the problem as sequence modeling: a `Point-BERT` encoder and a Q-Former compress each part into geometric tokens, all parts are concatenated and processed in one pass by a causal large language model adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and learnable summary tokens appended after the last part aggregate the full assembly so a part-aware pose head can predict every rotation and translation non-autoregressively. It achieves the best part accuracy and success rate on all three `PartNet` categories, the best rotation, translation, and part accuracy on `PartNeXt`, and the lowest translation error and fastest inference on `Breaking Bad`, and **its lead widens with part count, exceeding `GARF` by 33.5 points in part accuracy at 100 parts on `Breaking Bad`** while transferring zero-shot to unseen categories.

papers.title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Dissecting Clinical Evidence Acquisition in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often diagnose full sight, static clinical cases well yet struggle in foresight, dynamic diagnosis. Prior work has improved this limitation by quantifying the information models acquire and by developing stronger follow-up strategies to improve diagnostic accuracy. In contrast, we introduce a distinctive hindsight to systematically dissect why LLMs fail to acquire diagnostically critical evidence, tracing the failure from evidence identification, utilization and downstream diagnostic updating through not only diagnostic accuracy, but also evidence coverage, trajectory dynamics, and elicited probability and information entropy. Starting experiments from the breakdown at the level of capabilities, to the diagnosis of the pre-event state before the evidence arrives, and to the post-event state transition after the evidence arrives, our research has revealed the profound limitations and internal causes existing in the dynamic diagnostic process. At the same time, we have also conducted sufficient verification and generalization experiments to prove that these limitations are widespread. Together, these findings shift the central challenge from whether LLMs possess relevant clinical knowledge to whether they can identify, acquire, and effectively use the right evidence under clinical diagnosis and conduct a more detailed mechanism analysis to identify the exact location of the capability gap.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) diagnose fully specified clinical cases well but struggle when they must actively gather evidence over a dynamic encounter, and prior work has addressed this mainly by quantifying acquired information or designing better follow-up strategies. The authors instead work backward from known diagnoses to trace where the process breaks, separating evidence identification, evidence utilization, and downstream diagnostic updating, and measuring not only accuracy but evidence coverage, trajectory dynamics, elicited probabilities, and information entropy before and after critical evidence arrives. Verification and generalization experiments indicate the limitations are widespread, and **the central challenge shifts from whether LLMs hold the relevant clinical knowledge to whether they can identify, acquire, and use the right evidence at the right time**.

papers.title: Beyond Answer Voting: Fine-Grained Correction of LLM Reasoning through Graph Alignment across Sampled Traces
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote. Experimental results across five benchmarks show that native zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 and 15.83 percentage points for Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. It also exceeds CoT, the evaluated GoT and GoV question-answering adaptations, and SC on this macro metric. DDRG links local verification to selective correction without enlarging the initial candidate bank.
papers.summary: Self-consistency (SC) improves multi-step reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but the vote never resolves disagreements between intermediate claims in the sampled traces. `DDRG` (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs) builds source-grounded claim graphs from a frozen bank of traces, aligns them to expose claim-level conflicts, and sends each localized conflict to an answer-blind verifier; only when a verifier-supported refutation reaches the majority answer's supporting path does it trigger one focused repair, otherwise it returns the plain SC vote. Across five benchmarks, zero-shot `DDRG` **raises macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 points on `Qwen2.5-7B` and 15.83 points on `Llama3.1-8B`**, and also beats chain-of-thought, graph-of-thought and graph-of-verification adaptations, and SC without enlarging the candidate bank.

papers.title: DPOison-VL: Clean Preference Poisoning in Vision-Language Direct Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a widely adopted approach for aligning vision-language models (VLMs), yet the security of multimodal preference data remains largely unexplored. Existing preference poisoning attacks either corrupt explicit supervision signals or require visible triggers, making them detectable under human inspection. We introduce DPOison-VL, the first clean preference poisoning attack against VLM-DPO, which manipulates model alignment solely through imperceptible perturbations on a small fraction of training images, while leaving all prompts, responses, and preference annotations semantically intact. We formulate poison construction as a bilevel optimization and derive a gradient alignment surrogate that efficiently steers image perturbations toward the attacker-specified preference. We further introduce a preference displacement score for principled poison selection with provable first-order optimality under a fixed poison budget, and derive a sufficient condition for preference inversion. Extensive experiments across diverse attack tasks, different VLM architectures and scales, and baseline comparisons demonstrate that DPOison-VL achieves up to 98\% ASR with only 2\% poisoned data and exhibits cross-model transferability, while largely preserving clean accuracy and general utility. Our findings reveal a critical vulnerability in VLM-DPO, where imperceptible image perturbations in preference training data can silently redirect alignment.
papers.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used to align vision-language models (VLMs), but existing preference poisoning attacks either corrupt the explicit labels or need visible triggers that humans can spot. `DPOison-VL` is a clean-label attack that steers alignment solely through imperceptible perturbations on a small fraction of training images, leaving prompts, responses, and preference annotations intact; poison construction is cast as a bilevel optimization solved with a gradient alignment surrogate, and a preference displacement score selects which images to poison under a fixed budget. Across attack tasks and VLM architectures, the attack reaches **up to 98% attack success rate with only 2% poisoned data**, transfers across models, and largely preserves clean accuracy and general utility.

papers.title: Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models
papers.abstract: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.
papers.summary: Dialogue and collaborative assistants must repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends, and typed decision models are proposed as an alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection tasks. `Jev-ToM` compares five typed decision models against seven generative baselines on 11,117 English questions drawn from nine ToM benchmarks spanning six capability groups. `TypeSafe Jev` **reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy and ranks first or second on all six capabilities**, leading on beliefs, goals and intentions, and emotions, while resource comparisons suggest lower cost and latency for repeated selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, supplied reasons can either repair or overturn answers, and most downstream gains trace to related-question cues.

papers.title: Legal-R1: Agentic Retrieval for Evidence-Based Legal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Legal question answering requires answers that are not only plausible, but also grounded in legally valid and citable evidence. Standard retrieval-augmented generation often relies on one-shot semantic matching, which is insufficient when legal evidence must be selected according to authority, applicability, and diversity across heterogeneous sources. We introduce Legal-R1, an agentic retrieval framework for evidence-based legal reasoning. Legal-R1 decomposes legal reasoning into a multi-agent workflow, where a Lawyer agent learns when to retrieve, which legal source to query, what evidence to seek, and when the collected evidence is sufficient. A Legal Assistant agent retrieves from normative legal sources and precedent cases with authority-aware and diversity-aware selection, while a Judge agent generates the final answer from the complete evidence trajectory. We post-train only the Lawyer agent with masked supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-aware reinforcement learning. Experiments on multiple Chinese legal benchmarks show that Legal-R1 improves over general-purpose, legal-specific, and retrieval-augmented baselines.
papers.summary: Legal question answering needs answers grounded in valid, citable evidence, and one-shot semantic retrieval struggles when evidence must be chosen by authority, applicability, and diversity across heterogeneous sources. `Legal-R1` splits the problem into a multi-agent workflow: a Lawyer agent decides when to retrieve, which source to query, what evidence to seek, and when enough has been gathered; a Legal Assistant agent retrieves from statutes and precedent cases with authority- and diversity-aware selection; and a Judge agent produces the final answer from the full evidence trajectory. Only the Lawyer agent is post-trained, using masked supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-aware reinforcement learning, and **the system outperforms general-purpose, legal-specific, and retrieval-augmented baselines on multiple Chinese legal benchmarks**.

papers.title: Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications
papers.abstract:
System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored.
  In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).
papers.summary: System One models such as `Jev` map open-ended semantic context into structured judgments that programs consume directly, which creates a risk the authors call Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled context can redirect program behavior through schema-valid judgments. `JevProbe` is an automated framework that traces adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces, through the decisions a program consumes, to downstream security consequences, using the observation that application logic maps model judgments to observable decisions. Across 228 popular real-world `Jev` applications and 2,273 test cases, **81.5% of applications exhibit decision flips, and 98.6% of those flips lead to potential downstream security impact**; the framework improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points over the strongest adapted baseline, existing defenses provide limited protection, and the accompanying `JevProbeBench` dataset and code are public.

papers.title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?
papers.abstract: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning
papers.summary: Self-distillation trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information such as correct answers or environment feedback, and recent methods report better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL). Two representative methods, `SDPO` (Self-Distillation Policy Optimization) and `OPSD` (On-Policy Self-Distillation), are re-examined across code, science, tool-use, and math tasks on `Qwen3` models from 1.7B to 14B and `OLMo-3-7B`. **The reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transfer of existing reasoning behavior rather than effective use of privileged information**, and self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward.

papers.title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.
papers.summary: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding at each step whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human, which requires a per-step confidence signal that predicts whether the whole rollout will eventually succeed; existing RL calibration methods instead score confidence against correctness of the current step. The proposed method calibrates verbalized confidence against episode outcome under `GRPO`, using the group of rollouts for a task as success labels and a proper scoring rule to score each step. In offline RL on recorded `Qwen2.5-7B` trajectories in `ALFWorld`, `TextWorld`, and `WebShop`, **AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68 to 0.85**, and the top 10% most confident steps succeed about 4.3 times more often than average; in online RL on `ALFWorld`, expected calibration error drops from 0.42 to below 0.12 without hurting task success. A new evaluation protocol shows the trained agent mostly learns to recognize from its first step which tasks it will fail, while distinguishing a succeeding from a failing attempt on the same task remains harder.

papers.title: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve
papers.abstract: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled ablations show the benefits of multi-turn programming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents revising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co-evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leopoldwhite/DKGI.
papers.summary: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while inspecting textual evidence, and predefined graph interfaces limit what evidence an agent can reach even when it composes tool calls in code. Direct knowledge graph interaction (`DKGI`) is a harness in which a language model agent writes Python directly over complete node and edge files to follow relations, combine node sets, and select text, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection, so that execution feedback drives tool revision and the evolving tools shape what evidence is gathered next. Without any training, `DKGI` **beats the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph across three domains**, and ablations show multi-turn programming outperforms both shell-only access and predefined graph tools.

papers.title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
papers.abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.
papers.summary: An embodied agent must prioritize among competing bodily needs, and in active inference it can respond to an urgent need either by raising the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. The two interventions are compared separately and together in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, measuring survival, perception, and the body model the agent learns. **Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival, while preference reweighting keeps bodily states farther from lethal boundaries but narrows the range of need levels the agent learns about**, lowering model quality overall; across 72 further layouts both interventions improve average survival and interact positively, though the predicted preference advantage on difficult layouts is not established.

papers.title: Deterministic Prediction as Global Velocity: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecast
papers.abstract: Accurate uncertainty quantification is critical for many time series forecasting applications, and recent studies have increasingly adopted generative models to capture predictive uncertainty. Existing approaches often combine deterministic forecasting with generative modeling to improve predictive performance. However, their joint training is typically unstable because the deterministic model is embedded within the generative process, resulting in deep computational graphs and changing the probability transport path. In this work, we propose DV-Flow, a unified flow-matching formulation that incorporates the deterministic predictor as a parallel velocity component rather than as the endpoint of the transport path. This design enables stable end-to-end optimization while subsuming several existing formulations as special cases, allowing direct comparisons among them. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that DV-Flow consistently improves probabilistic forecasting performance over strong baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/tufts-ml/dv-flow-time-series.
papers.summary: Generative models are increasingly used to quantify uncertainty in time series forecasting, often by combining a deterministic predictor with a generative process, but embedding the predictor inside the generative path makes joint training unstable through deep computational graphs and altered transport paths. `DV-Flow` is a flow-matching formulation that adds the deterministic predictor as a parallel velocity component rather than as the endpoint of the transport path, which permits stable end-to-end optimization and subsumes several existing formulations as special cases. **On six real-world datasets it consistently improves probabilistic forecasting over strong baselines**, and the shared framework enables direct comparison among the subsumed variants.

papers.title: Minimax rates for pointwise CATE estimation: the role of design smoothness
papers.abstract: We study the role of design smoothness in the minimax estimation of conditional average treatment effects at a fixed covariate point. For design densities bounded above and away from zero, without further regularity, we derive upper and lower risk bounds with an arbitrarily small gap in the convergence-rate exponent. Under uniform design, we obtain matching upper and lower bounds at interior points in the regime of low nuisance smoothness. These results show that rough covariate designs can lead to slower rates than uniform designs, even under the same smoothness assumptions on the treatment effect and nuisance functions, highlighting the role of the covariate distribution in pointwise causal estimation.
papers.summary: The question is how the smoothness of the covariate design affects minimax estimation of the conditional average treatment effect at a fixed covariate point. For design densities bounded above and away from zero with no further regularity, the analysis gives upper and lower risk bounds whose convergence-rate exponents differ by an arbitrarily small gap, and under uniform design it obtains matching bounds at interior points in the low nuisance smoothness regime. **Rough covariate designs can yield slower rates than uniform designs even under identical smoothness assumptions on the treatment effect and nuisance functions**, showing that the covariate distribution itself governs pointwise causal estimation rates.

papers.title: MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, A Multi-Sensor, Multi-Temporal Pretraining Dataset for Earth Observation
papers.abstract: Pretraining generalist Earth observation foundation models requires data that combine several sensors, varied temporal sampling and, increasingly, text, yet open datasets rarely provide all three in one consistent, easily accessible form. We introduce MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, a collection of 279,166 tiles of 10 km drawn from the Major-TOM grid by clustering AlphaEarth embeddings. Each tile stacks Sentinel-2 L1C, Landsat-8/9, Sentinel-1 RTC, Copernicus DEM and ESA WorldCover on a shared 1056x1056-pixel, 10 m grid, complemented by cloud masks, OpenStreetMap entities and ERA5 weather. The tiles are partitioned into three temporal regimes, Monotemporal (250,000 tiles, one acquisition), Monthly (12,500 tiles, twelve acquisitions spread over the annual cycle) and Burst (16,666 tiles, six acquisitions within 30 days), and are released as 6.3 TB of Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs indexed by TACO v3 Parquet metadata, a standard that allows cloud streaming, efficient data access, and filtering before any pixel is read. A companion library derives sensor-tagged fact sheets, captions and 16 families of vision-language tasks from these layers at load time. We test our design choices in short pretraining runs of OlmoEarth-Base. First, a 25% subset of Major-TOM Core-S2L2A curated with AlphaEarth embeddings matches or exceeds the full corpus on 8 of 9 benchmarks. Second, on Elliot-Pretrain, adding Landsat-8/9 improves or matches Sentinel-2 only pretraining on every benchmark. Third, using DEM and WorldCover as prediction targets during pretraining further improves 8 of 9 benchmarks, while giving the same maps to the encoder as inputs degrades 5 of 9. Fourth, Sentinel-1 helps on 7 of 9 benchmarks, particularly on benchmarks with radar inputs. Fifth, rule-based captions match a small language model at no cost. The dataset is openly available at https://source.coop/major-tom/elliot-pretrain.
papers.summary: Pretraining generalist Earth observation foundation models needs data that combine multiple sensors, varied temporal sampling, and text, which open datasets rarely offer in one consistent form. `MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain` provides 279,166 ten-kilometer tiles selected from the `Major-TOM` grid by clustering `AlphaEarth` embeddings, each stacking `Sentinel-2`, `Landsat-8/9`, `Sentinel-1`, Copernicus DEM, and ESA WorldCover on a shared 10 m grid with cloud masks, OpenStreetMap entities, and ERA5 weather, split into monotemporal, monthly, and burst regimes and released as 6.3 TB of cloud-streamable GeoTIFFs with a library that derives captions and 16 families of vision-language tasks at load time. Short pretraining runs of `OlmoEarth-Base` show that **a 25% embedding-curated subset of `Major-TOM Core-S2L2A` matches or exceeds the full corpus on 8 of 9 benchmarks**, adding Landsat and Sentinel-1 helps on most benchmarks, using DEM and WorldCover as prediction targets helps while feeding them as inputs hurts, and rule-based captions match a small language model.

papers.title: Falsification-proof non-market allocation mechanisms
papers.abstract: Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.
papers.summary: Allocating resources based on manipulable characteristics invites falsification: naively optimal rules induce it and lose allocative efficiency, while rules optimized with falsification in mind still induce it at heavy cost to agents and generate negative externalities. The work characterizes optimal falsification-proof allocation rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. It also gives **an honesty condition under which these rules solve the unconstrained problem of a planner maximizing a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agent welfare**.

papers.title: Breakdown of Conversational Involvement: A Joint Multi-Modal Analysis of Conversation Floors and F-formation Detection with Multiple Features
papers.abstract: Interactions happen universally and spontaneously in daily lives. Studying involvement in interactions helps us analyze who can influence who and has a wide potential in applications. Specifically, we consider conversational involvement in free-standing conversations. We study two operationalizations of an FCG: F-formations and conversation floors, and propose that current assumption that F-formations capture single conversations is insufficient. To illustrate how different implementations could impact the detected F-formations, we employ three analyses. First, we propose that speaking status can be used for estimating conversation floors, and leveraged it to analyze floors within F-formations. Second, we analyze spatial characteristics of the detection results by applying different feature sets on chosen baselines, and find that groups resulting from head features are more likely to be subsumed by groups detected using other features. Finally, we do a joint analysis which combines the spatial features and floor patterns in the conversation. We observe that certain pipelines can detect groups with single floors from upper body features, while retaining F-formations with lower body features. We conclude that a more detailed theory and framework is needed to holistically demonstrate conversational involvement within interactions.
papers.summary: Conversational involvement in free-standing group conversations can be operationalized either as F-formations, the spatial arrangements people form, or as conversation floors, and the common assumption that an F-formation captures a single conversation is argued to be insufficient. Three analyses probe the gap: speaking status is used to estimate conversation floors within detected F-formations, spatial characteristics of detection results are compared across feature sets on chosen baselines, and spatial features are jointly analyzed with floor patterns. **Groups detected from head features are more likely to be subsumed by groups detected using other features**, and certain pipelines detect single-floor groups from upper-body features while retaining F-formations from lower-body features, which the authors take as evidence that a more detailed theory and framework of conversational involvement is needed.

papers.title: Geometric Calibration of Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Recent studies investigate the weight geometry through its spectral structure, which characterizes how the weights transform different input directions. Within this view, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is shown to induce dense updates that perturb the spectral geometry of pre-SFT weights along their principal directions, potentially disrupting the model's prior knowledge. These observations motivate using the geometry of pre-SFT weights as a reference for refining learned SFT updates. We study this perspective as Geometric Calibration and develop SPACE Subspace Projection for Adapted Checkpoint Enhancement), a lightweight post-hoc method that selectively reverts SFT update components within the principal subspace of the pre-SFT weights while preserving those in its orthogonal complement. SPACE is a data-free, training-free method that requires only the pre- and post-SFT checkpoints. We evaluate SPACE on Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Llama-3.1, and Olmo-3 models ranging from 2B to 14B, across mathematical, coding, and medical SFT, as well as several SFT variants. Overall, SPACE mitigates out-of-domain (OOD) capability regression while further improving in-domain (ID) performance over the uncalibrated SFT checkpoints. For math SFT, SPACE yields average ID/OOD gains of 2.85/2.26 points on Qwen2.5-7B, and 2.41/1.52 points on Qwen3-14B-Base, respectively. These results highlight how the geometric relationship between SFT updates and pre-SFT weights shapes the adapted model's capabilities and, more broadly, motivate geometry-aware parameter updates for continual model improvement.
papers.summary: Viewing weights through their spectral structure, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has been shown to produce dense updates that perturb the principal directions of the pre-SFT weights and can disrupt prior knowledge. `SPACE` (Subspace Projection for Adapted Checkpoint Enhancement) is a data-free, training-free post-hoc method that needs only the pre- and post-SFT checkpoints and selectively reverts update components lying in the principal subspace of the pre-SFT weights while keeping those in the orthogonal complement. Evaluated on `Qwen2.5`, `Qwen3`, `Qwen3.5`, `Llama-3.1`, and `Olmo-3` models from 2B to 14B across math, coding, and medical SFT, `SPACE` mitigates out-of-domain (OOD) regression while also improving in-domain (ID) performance, with **math SFT gains of 2.85 ID and 2.26 OOD points on `Qwen2.5-7B`** and 2.41 and 1.52 points on `Qwen3-14B-Base`.

papers.title: DTScribe: Generating Models for Digital Twin Reporting using Local Large Language Models
papers.abstract:
The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming.
  In this article, we explore the automation of model generation using large language models, targeting the model required for digital twin reporting. Our approach is designed to ingest digital twin documents and output both the conceptual architecture visualization and a reporting page for that digital twin. We first extract from the input the key details aligning with our twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework described in previous work. Then, we generate a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language, representing the digital twin as a constellation of models, data, enablers, and services. We utilize refinement loops with large language models acting as judges and ontological reasoning to increase artifact quality as measured by our metrics.
  We investigate how architectural and parameter choices affect artifact quality, such as how refinement loops enable local large language models to produce sufficiently high-quality results comparable to larger models. We also detail insights and lessons learned useful for practitioners, such that they can integrate our techniques to accelerate their digital twin reporting or for other model generation tasks. These insights include the use of medium-sized local models (around 20 billion parameters), the avoidance of large language models as judges and clustering for characteristic extraction, and the recommendation of at least two reasoner loops for Ontological Modeling Language refinement.
papers.summary: Modeling a digital twin's conceptual architecture for reporting and consensus-building among stakeholders is tedious, so the work automates generating that model with large language models. `DTScribe` ingests digital twin documents, extracts details aligned with a twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework, generates a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language representing models, data, enablers, and services, and improves artifact quality through refinement loops that use LLM judges and ontological reasoning. Experiments on architectural and parameter choices show that **refinement loops let medium-sized local models of around 20 billion parameters produce results comparable to larger models**, and the practitioner lessons include avoiding LLM judges and clustering for characteristic extraction and running at least two reasoner loops for refinement.

papers.title: Grid or Nodes? Probing Object Memory in World Models Under Partial Observability
papers.abstract: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. A node memory instead keeps each object's position and velocity as numbers. We compare them in FloWM's own block world, with an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read changes its score: a single-cell probe finds 66% of out-of-view blocks, while FloWM's own probe 89%. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. Faster blocks defeat both until one more allowed speed takes the tracker to 94%, where FloWM's built-in shifts would need 25 copies of its grid. A learned node memory must still replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and the bounce.
papers.summary: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view, and `FloWM`, a learned world model, does so with a spatial grid of features shifted by five built-in velocities, whereas a node memory stores each object's position and velocity as numbers. The two are compared in `FloWM`'s own block world using an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read matters: a single-cell probe recovers 66% of out-of-view blocks versus 89% for `FloWM`'s own probe, and the tracker matches `FloWM`'s out-of-view range in 14 KB instead of 5.6 MB without any probe. **On diagonal motion outside its five velocities, `FloWM` finds only 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%**, and faster blocks defeat both until adding one allowed speed brings the tracker to 94%, where the grid approach would need 25 copies of its grid; a learned node memory would still need to replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and bounces.

papers.title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train
papers.abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the observation that representational convergence is most robust at the level of local neighborhoods, COMPASS decomposes model compatibility into two cheap-to-compute axes: a pair-specific ease, defined as the $k$-NN overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling, capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow. Together, these two axes provide a ranking of candidate model pairs and prescribe how to act on each pair: (i) prioritize pairs that already agree and whose paradigms are compatible, (ii) invest additional compute on pairs with compatible paradigms but low initial agreement, (iii) switch the pretraining paradigm when it cannot support sufficient agreement, or (iv) deprioritize pairs that score poorly on both axes. We apply COMPASS to $72$ cross-modal alignment experiments and $392$ task-arithmetic model merges and show that compatibility estimates by COMPASS strongly correlate with downstream success, achieving average Pearson correlation of $0.91$ on cross-modal alignment tasks and $0.70$ on model merging.
papers.summary: Combining pretrained models, whether aligning a vision encoder to a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints, usually requires expensive trial and error because compatibility is only known after the fact. `COMPASS` (COMPatibility ASsessment Score) estimates compatibility beforehand by decomposing it into two cheap axes: a pair-specific ease measured as k-nearest-neighbor overlap between the two encoders' representations, and a paradigm-level ceiling capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow, which together rank candidate pairs and prescribe whether to prioritize, invest more compute, switch paradigm, or deprioritize. Across 72 cross-modal alignment experiments and 392 task-arithmetic merges, `COMPASS` scores **correlate with downstream success at an average Pearson of 0.91 for cross-modal alignment and 0.70 for model merging**.

papers.title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization
papers.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.
papers.summary: The Key-Value (KV) cache dominates memory during large language model (LLM) inference on long-context and reasoning workloads, and prior quantization work has explored layer-wise precision and token-level preservation separately, leaving open how to split a fixed memory budget between these heterogeneous strategies. `MultiAlloc` runs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, then derives a precision allocation policy from the profiled memory-accuracy trade-off and applies it at inference without any online allocation search. **Under matched memory budgets it consistently outperforms layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods** on reasoning and long-context benchmarks across `Mistral`, `Llama`, `DeepSeek-Qwen`, and `QwQ` models.

papers.title: ST-GRU PredRNN-V2: A GRU-Based Reformulation of PredRNN-V2 for Video Prediction
papers.abstract: Video prediction requires models to capture complex spatiotemporal dependencies and to retain relevant information over long sequences. PredRNN and its successor PredRNN-V2 address this challenge with spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two separate memory states, at the cost of a relatively complex recurrent building block. In this work, we investigate whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) can be transferred to spatiotemporal predictive learning. To this end, we develop a spatiotemporal GRU (ST-GRU) unit as a GRU-based alternative to the ST-LSTM. The ST-GRU replaces the ST-LSTM's three gates per memory state with two GRU-style gates (update and reset), and merges the temporal memory state into the hidden state, which reduces the number of parameters by about 5%. We incorporate the ST-GRU into PredRNN-V2 and evaluate the resulting model on the Moving MNIST video prediction benchmark, following the original experimental protocol. Averaged over ten predicted frames, the ST-GRU-based PredRNN-V2 achieves an MSE of 55.1, an SSIM of 0.883, an LPIPS of 0.065 and a PSNR of 19.53dB. It does not surpass the original ST-LSTM-based PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM or PSNR, but it achieves a lower LPIPS and performs on par with the earlier ST-LSTM-based PredRNN, while using a simpler recurrent cell. These results suggest that ST-GRUs are a promising building block for spatiotemporal predictive learning and motivate further work on their design and integration.
papers.summary: Video prediction models must capture spatiotemporal dependencies over long sequences, and `PredRNN-V2` does this with spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two separate memory states at the cost of a complex recurrent cell. The work asks whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) transfers to this setting, proposing an `ST-GRU` unit that replaces the three gates per memory state with update and reset gates and merges the temporal memory into the hidden state, cutting parameters by about 5%. On `Moving MNIST`, the `ST-GRU`-based `PredRNN-V2` reaches an MSE of 55.1, SSIM of 0.883, LPIPS of 0.065, and PSNR of 19.53 dB; **it does not surpass the original ST-LSTM-based `PredRNN-V2` on MSE, SSIM, or PSNR**, but achieves lower LPIPS and performs on par with the earlier `PredRNN` using a simpler cell.

papers.title: Tiny Recursive Message Passing
papers.abstract: Message passing neural networks have shown remarkable performance in algorithmic and constraint reasoning, due to their ability to encode the structure of the task directly in the architecture. Recent work has shown that better results can be achieved using recursive transformers trained with deep supervision and truncated recursions, which make extremely deep loops stable to train, and equipped with test-time procedures such as discrete deduction lattices. In this work, we apply the same procedures to message passing networks, and show that the two ingredients are complementary, and lead to parameter efficient models: we obtain about $99\%$ test accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme with a model of $16$k parameters that trains in about $10$ minutes on an H100, or in $9$ hours on a CPU. We further show that the cost of truncating gradients grows with the number of rounds information needs to cross the graph, making the choice of wiring a trade-off between robustness to truncation and transfer across problem sizes. We conclude by showing that our models transfer zero-shot to larger instances than those seen during training, outperforming popular neural baselines on N-queens and Boolean satisfiability with a fraction of their parameters.
papers.summary: Message passing neural networks encode task structure directly for algorithmic and constraint reasoning, while recent recursive transformers gain from deep supervision, truncated recursions, and test-time discrete deduction lattices. Applying those same training and inference procedures to message passing networks turns out to be complementary and highly parameter efficient: **a 16k-parameter model reaches about 99% test accuracy on `Sudoku-Extreme`**, training in roughly 10 minutes on an H100 or 9 hours on a CPU. The cost of truncating gradients grows with the number of rounds information must travel across the graph, so graph wiring becomes a trade-off between robustness to truncation and transfer across problem sizes. The models transfer zero-shot to instances larger than those seen in training, beating popular neural baselines on `N-queens` and Boolean satisfiability with a fraction of their parameters.

papers.title: Does Pretraining Teach Chemical Language Models Chemistry?
papers.abstract: Chemical language models (CLMs) are pretrained on large corpora of molecules with the aim of learning representations that transfer to diverse downstream tasks. Here, we systematically study the effects of pretraining using a series of such CLMs across 64 molecular property prediction datasets. We find that the downstream gains of pretraining in CLMs do not scale and performance saturates below gradient-boosting baselines. Across the regimes evaluated, only supervised pretraining on traditional physico-chemical descriptors consistently improves downstream performance for the CLMs tested whereas some forms of pretraining result in models worse than a randomly initialized encoder. While models can resolve molecular structure well, they do so no better than a randomly initialized model, suggesting that, at best, CLMs learn descriptor-like properties in addition to low-level token statistics during pretraining, but surprisingly little chemistry beyond what classical molecular features already capture.
papers.summary: Chemical language models (CLMs) are pretrained on large molecular corpora in the hope of learning representations that transfer to downstream tasks, and this study systematically measures what that pretraining buys across 64 molecular property prediction datasets. **Downstream gains from pretraining do not scale, and performance saturates below gradient-boosting baselines.** Only supervised pretraining on traditional physico-chemical descriptors consistently helps the CLMs tested, while some pretraining schemes leave models worse than a randomly initialized encoder. The models resolve molecular structure well but no better than a randomly initialized model, suggesting they pick up descriptor-like properties and low-level token statistics rather than much chemistry beyond what classical molecular features already capture.

papers.title: AMemOps: Evaluating Memory Updates in Long Audio Streams
papers.abstract: Audio memory must recognise recurring sources across acoustic changes while keeping their attributes up to date. Overall accuracy does not reveal how these demands interact. We introduce Audio Memory Operations (AMemOps), a benchmark for latest-attribute retrieval, preservation of unchanged attributes and absent-source rejection in long audio streams. Paired controls vary recordings, training identities and earlier events to examine their effects on updating. Training on other recordings of the test instruments increases a reference delta-rule memory's update advantage over matched attention by 13.4 percentage points. At retrieval delays of 120\,s, matched histories separate benefits of consistent repetition from costs of conflicting earlier values, while additive-memory controls identify benefits of erasure.
papers.summary: Audio memory must recognise recurring sound sources across acoustic changes while keeping each source's attributes current, and overall accuracy hides how these demands interact. Audio Memory Operations (`AMemOps`) is a benchmark for latest-attribute retrieval, preservation of unchanged attributes, and rejection of absent sources in long audio streams, with paired controls that vary recordings, training identities, and earlier events. **Training on other recordings of the test instruments raises a reference delta-rule memory's update advantage over matched attention by 13.4 percentage points.** At 120-second retrieval delays, matched histories separate the benefits of consistent repetition from the costs of conflicting earlier values, and additive-memory controls isolate the benefits of erasure.

papers.title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
papers.abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.
papers.summary: Kwai Summary Attention (`KSA`) compresses distant context into a learnable summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to keep exact access to the original text. In that hybrid design the summary chunk size must be the same across layers, which prevents per-layer key-value (KV) cache compression, and the full-attention layers ignore the summary tokens yet still pay quadratic prefill cost. `KSA V2` addresses both bottlenecks by giving summary tokens two roles, as KV memory and as a sparse indexer for the full-attention layers. **The result is more flexible per-layer KV cache compression together with lower computation in the full-attention layers.**

papers.title: Texture Interpolation as Texton Matching
papers.abstract: Texture interpolation asks what should lie between two textures. Standard methods typically blend pixels or features at corresponding spatial locations, implicitly assuming that co-located elements should be mixed. For unrelated textures, however, this correspondence is arbitrary: a crack at one location has no particular relationship to a fiber at the same location in another image. We study whether this hidden pairing choice is itself a major determinant of interpolation quality. We represent textures as collections of local appearance vectors, or textons, and replace positional pairing with appearance-aware matching while keeping the encoder, representation, and decoder fixed. This isolates the effect of correspondence from changes in model capacity or training. Across texture pairs, appearance-aware matching consistently improves the distributional quality of interpolated midpoints over positional feature blending. Soft matching produces the strongest midpoint statistics, whereas one-to-one assignments yield more balanced transitions and closer agreement with the target endpoint. The same intervention also improves a second pretrained texture interpolator without retraining. These results identify correspondence as a first-class design choice in texture interpolation: meaningful transitions depend not only on how strongly two textures are mixed, but also on which local appearances are mixed with one another.
papers.summary: Texture interpolation asks what should lie between two textures, and standard methods blend pixels or features at matching spatial positions, implicitly assuming that co-located elements belong together even when the textures are unrelated. This work represents textures as collections of local appearance vectors, or textons, and swaps positional pairing for appearance-aware matching while holding the encoder, representation, and decoder fixed, which isolates the effect of correspondence from changes in capacity or training. **Appearance-aware matching consistently improves the distributional quality of interpolated midpoints over positional feature blending**, with soft matching giving the strongest midpoint statistics and one-to-one assignments giving more balanced transitions and closer agreement with the target endpoint. The same change also improves a second pretrained texture interpolator without retraining, identifying correspondence as a first-class design choice.

papers.title: Bayesian Test-Time Inference of Task-Aligned Similarity from Weak Interactive Feedback
papers.abstract: Language model systems repeatedly make test-time decisions by comparing similarity: they retrieve exemplars, rank candidates, and revise responses. Yet similarity is not unique: lexical, semantic, structural, and stylistic resemblance can point to different candidates, and the task-aligned notion can change across instances. We introduce BASIS (Bayesian Axis Selection via Interactive Signals), a training-free Bayesian method that uses weak test-time feedback to infer which criterion in a supplied, task-specific library governs the current decision. It maintains a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria, updates it from scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs, and selects probes by expected information gain. In a finite noisy model, we characterize when the target-criterion pair is recoverable and show why fixed-criterion and fixed-mixture rules can fail under criterion shift. Across concept recovery, reasoning exemplar selection, and response refinement, BASIS improves six-probe concept-recovery Success@1 from 56.0% to 68.1%, reasoning accuracy from 72.3% to 73.1%, and refinement win rate from 61.4% to 63.8% over tuned static mixtures. It also exceeds compute-matched best-of-N selection on reasoning (72.1%) and refinement (61.2%). Gains are largest under criterion mismatch and with larger candidate pools, and matched controls indicate that adaptive criterion weighting explains much of the benefit, with joint target-criterion inference adding further value. BASIS selects only among supplied criteria and does not discover new ones.
papers.summary: Language model systems repeatedly make similarity-based decisions when retrieving exemplars, ranking candidates, and revising responses, but lexical, semantic, structural, and stylistic resemblance can favor different candidates and the task-aligned criterion can change from instance to instance. `BASIS` (Bayesian Axis Selection via Interactive Signals) is a training-free method that keeps a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria from a supplied task-specific library, updates it from scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs, and chooses probes by expected information gain. **It lifts six-probe concept-recovery Success@1 from 56.0% to 68.1%** over tuned static mixtures, with smaller gains in reasoning accuracy (72.3% to 73.1%) and refinement win rate (61.4% to 63.8%), and it also beats compute-matched best-of-N selection. Gains are largest under criterion mismatch and with larger candidate pools, and the method only selects among supplied criteria rather than discovering new ones.

papers.title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schr\"odinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
papers.abstract: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schr\"odinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. Its twist is a closed-form plug-in surrogate, obtained by combining the velocity and score fields exposed by SB pretraining into an endpoint predictor and evaluating the likelihood there. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.
papers.summary: Training-free conditional samplers reuse a pretrained unconditional generative model as a prior and combine it with a task-specific likelihood, but such samplers exist for diffusion and flow models and not yet for Schrödinger bridge (SB) models. `BridgeTwist` fills this gap with a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme whose twist is a closed-form surrogate built by combining the velocity and score fields from SB pretraining into an endpoint predictor, with a time-varying exponent that downweights the surrogate at early steps where it is least reliable. A bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule concentrates proposal noise in the interior of the path, and telescoping importance weights cancel all intermediate twist factors, **yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior**. Empirically it outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation and is competitive with specialized inverse-problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.

papers.title: Known-Voice Cloning and the Limits of Personality Transfer for Character Design
papers.abstract: Recent advances in zero-shot voice cloning systems make it possible to reproduce a recognizable voice from a short recording and attach it to arbitrary virtual characters. Prior work suggests that familiar vocal identity can carry over associated personality impressions to new targets such as robots or virtual characters. However, these works have mainly examined familiarity and personalization effects rather than directly testing whether a cloned familiar voice systematically transfers personality impressions to an embodied virtual character. Such transference raises the concern that cloned voices could be used to manipulate people into engaging with virtual characters as capable social actors. Across two studies, we investigated whether personality impressions transfer when a virtual character speaks with the cloned voice of a familiar person. Study 1 examined this question in a real-world university setting using the cloned voice of a lecturer familiar to the participating students. Study 2 examined the same question online using voices of social media content creators and members of their communities. Drawing on the concepts of identity activation, trait transfer, and person reconstruction, we show that evidence of personality transfer was limited in both studies. Observed effects were selective and did not generalize across traits or study contexts. In the online study in particular, recognizable voice identity cues activated expectations about the speaker but did not reconstruct the broader person impression. Qualitative responses further indicated that judgments were frequently shaped by perceived artificiality and by whether voice and appearance fit together. Our findings moderate common concerns that cloned voices straightforwardly manipulate people into perceiving artificial characters as capable social actors.
papers.summary: Zero-shot voice cloning can attach a recognizable familiar voice to an arbitrary virtual character, raising the concern that the familiar person's personality impressions transfer to the character and make it seem a more capable social actor. Two studies test this directly, one in a university setting using the cloned voice of a lecturer known to the participating students, and one online using voices of social media creators judged by members of their communities. **Evidence of personality transfer was limited in both studies**, with effects that were selective and did not generalize across traits or contexts. Recognizable voice cues activated expectations about the speaker without reconstructing the broader person impression, and judgments were often shaped by perceived artificiality and by whether voice and appearance fit together.

papers.title: SMI: Ontology-Grounded Semantic IDs for Hierarchy-Aware Medical Concept Representation
papers.abstract: Biomedical language models (LMs) provide strong representations for clinical tasks, but they often fail to capture the hierarchical structure among medical concepts. This limitation is especially pronounced for rare and fine-grained clinical codes in long-tailed vocabularies, where hierarchy-agnostic LM representations become less informative as concept frequency decreases. We introduce Semantic Medical Identifier (SMI), a training-free framework for constructing ontology-grounded Semantic IDs and hierarchy-aware medical concept representations. For each diagnosis, procedure, or medication concept, SMI defines its Semantic ID as the coarse-to-fine path through an expert-defined medical ontology. SMI then aggregates frozen biomedical LM embeddings across the corresponding ontology levels to form hierarchy-aware medical concept representations that preserve coarse-to-fine clinical semantics. The base SMI uses uniform aggregation across ontology levels, while a level-weighted variant selects global level weights on validation data. Our theoretical analysis shows that SMI yields more informative medical concept representations than hierarchy-agnostic LM embeddings, particularly for rare and fine-grained clinical concepts. Experiments show that SMI captures meaningful hierarchical structure and improves clinical relation prediction. On MIMIC-IV, SMI improves mortality prediction, readmission prediction, drug recommendation, and rare drug prediction. On eICU, SMI yields more robust patient representations under cross-hospital distribution shift.
papers.summary: Biomedical language models (LMs) give strong clinical representations but miss the hierarchical structure among medical concepts, a gap that widens for rare, fine-grained codes in long-tailed vocabularies.
